p.seg: Huángdì was
the son of Shǎodiǎn,
surnamed Gōngsūn,
and named Xuānyuán.
He was spiritually endowed at birth,
able to speak in infancy,
quick and earnest in childhood,
diligent and perceptive in youth,
and wise and intelligent upon reaching maturity.
During Xuānyuán's time,
the Shénnóngshì lineage had declined.
The feudal lords invaded one another,
oppressing the common people,
and the Shénnóngshì were unable to subdue them.
Thereupon, Xuānyuán practiced the use of shield and spear,
to chastise those who did not pay tribute,
and all the feudal lords came to submit and follow him.
But Chīyóu was the most violent,
and none could attack him.
Yándì sought to encroach upon and bully the feudal lords,
and they all turned to Xuānyuán.
Xuānyuán then cultivated virtue and strengthened his army,
regulated the five energies,
planted the five grains,
pacified the myriad people,
measured the four directions,
and trained bears, brown bears, píxiū, chū, and tigers
to battle Yándì in the wilderness of Bǎnquán.
After three engagements,
he achieved his aim.
Chīyóu rebelled,
disobeying the emperor's commands.
Thereupon Huángdì summoned troops from the feudal lords,
and fought Chīyóu in the wilderness of Zhuōlù,
finally capturing and killing him.
And all the feudal lords honored Xuānyuán as the Son of Heaven,
succeeding the Shénnóngshì,
and he became known as Huángdì.
When there were those in the world who were disobedient,
Huángdì would go and chastise them,
pacifying them before departing,
clearing mountains and opening roads,
never resting in peace.
He went east to the sea,
ascending Wánshān,
and reaching Dàizōng.
Westward he went to Kōngtóng,
ascending Jītóu.
Southward he went to the river,
ascending Xióng and Xiāng.
Northward he drove away the Xūnyù,
united tallies at Fǔshān,
and established his capital in the vale of Zhuōlù.
He moved about without a fixed abode,
using his troops as camp guards.
Official titles were all named after clouds,
forming the Cloud Army.
He established left and right grand supervisors,
to oversee the myriad states.
The myriad states were harmonious,
and the sacrifices to ghosts, spirits, mountains, rivers, and the fēng and shàn ceremonies were numerous.
He obtained the precious tripod,
and welcomed the sun while推算 the stalks.
He elevated Fēnghòu, Lìmù, Chángxiān, and Dàhóng
to govern the people.
He followed the order of heaven and earth,
the divinations of dark and light,
the theories of life and death,
and the difficulties of survival and extinction.
He timely sowed the hundred grains, plants, and trees,
transformed birds, beasts, insects, and moths,
extensively arranged the sun, moon, stars, water waves,
earth, stones, metals, and jades,
exerting his heart, strength, ears, and eyes,
and frugally used water, fire, and materials.
There was an auspicious sign of earth's virtue,
hence he was called Huángdì.
Huángdì had twenty-five sons,
of whom fourteen received surnames.
Huángdì dwelled at Xuānyuán Hill,
and married a woman from Xīlíng,
who was Léizǔ.
Léizǔ was Huángdì's principal consort,
and bore two sons,
whose descendants later possessed the world:
the first was Xuánxiāo,
also known as Qīngyáng,
who descended to dwell by the Jiāng River;
the second was Chāngyì,
who descended to dwell by the Ruò River.
Chāngyì married a woman from the Shǔshānshì,
named Chāngpú,
and they bore Gāoyáng,
who possessed sagely virtue.
When Huángdì passed away,
he was buried at Qiáoshān.
His grandson, Gāoyáng, son of Chāngyì, ascended the throne,
and became known as Emperor Zhuānxū.
Emperor Zhuānxū Gāoyáng
was the grandson of Huángdì and son of Chāngyì.
Tranquil and profound, he was resourceful;
clear and understanding, he knew affairs;
he nurtured resources by utilizing the land,
and carried out the seasons
in accordance with heaven,
relying on ghosts and spirits to establish righteousness,
regulating the energies
to educate and transform,
and purifying sincerity in sacrifices.
Northward he reached Yōulíng,
southward to Jiāozhǐ,
westward to Liúshā,
and eastward to Pánmù.
All moving and still creatures,
great and small spirits,
wherever the sun and moon shone,
none failed to be subdued and attached.
Emperor Zhuānxū had a son named Qióngchán.
When Zhuānxū passed away,
Gāoxīn, the grandson of Xuánxiāo, ascended the throne,
and became known as Emperor Kù.
Emperor Kù Gāoxīn
was the great-grandson of Huángdì.
Gāoxīn's father was Jiǎojí,
Jiǎojí's father was Xuánxiāo,
and Xuánxiāo's father was Huángdì.
Neither Xuánxiāo nor Jiǎojí held the throne,
until Gāoxīn assumed the imperial position.
Gāoxīn was a clansman of Zhuānxū.
Gāoxīn was spiritually endowed at birth,
and spoke his own name.
He widely bestowed benefits on all things,
without seeking for himself.
His intelligence reached far,
and his clarity discerned the minute.
He followed heaven's righteousness,
and understood the people's needs.
Benevolent yet威严,
kind yet trustworthy,
he cultivated himself and the world submitted.
He took the wealth of the earth and used it frugally,
pacifying and educating the myriad people, benefiting and instructing them,
tracking the sun and moon to welcome and send them off,
clarifying ghosts and spirits and reverently serving them.
His countenance was dignified,
his virtue lofty.
His actions were timely,
and his attire was that of a scholar.
Emperor Kù irrigated, held to the mean, and reached throughout the world;
wherever the sun and moon shone,
wherever wind and rain reached,
none failed to follow and submit.
Emperor Kù married a woman from the Chénfēngshì,
and they bore Fàngxūn.
He married a woman from the Jūzīshì,
and they bore Zhì.
When Emperor Kù passed away,
Zhì succeeded him.
Emperor Zhì reigned,
but not well,
and his younger brother Fàngxūn took the throne,
becoming known as Emperor Yáo.
Emperor Yáo,
named Fàngxūn.
His benevolence was like heaven's,
his wisdom like a god's.
Approaching him was like the sun,
gazing at him was like clouds.
Wealthy yet not arrogant,
noble yet not lax.
He wore a yellow cap and plain clothes,
rode a red carriage drawn by white horses.
He was able to illuminate and tame virtue,
thereby drawing close the nine clans.
When the nine clans were harmonious,
he made clear the hundred surnames.
The hundred surnames were enlightened,
and the myriad states were united in harmony.
Then he appointed Xī and Hé,
reverently complying with the vast heaven,
calculating the laws of the sun, moon, and stars,
and reverently imparting the people's seasons.
He separately ordered Xīzhòng,
to dwell in Yùyí,
called Yánggǔ.
Reverently guiding the sunrise,
At the midday mark,
the constellation Star Bird,
was used to determine the middle of spring.
The people dispersed,
and birds and beasts mated and reproduced.
He then ordered Xī Shū,
to reside in the southern region.
He arranged the southern affairs,
with reverence.
As the days grew long,
the constellation Star Fire,
was used to determine the middle of summer.
The people rested,
and birds and beasts shed their fur.
He then ordered Hé Zhòng,
to reside in the western land,
called Mèi Gǔ.
He reverently observed the sunset,
and arranged the western harvest.
At the midnight mark,
the constellation Star Xū,
was used to determine the middle of autumn.
The people were at ease,
and birds and beasts grew new fur.
He then ordered Hé Shū,
to reside in the northern region,
called Yōu Dū.
He arranged for the storage of goods.
As the days grew short,
the constellation Star Mǎo,
was used to determine the middle of winter.
The people stayed warm,
and birds and beasts grew thick fur.
The year consisted of 366 days,
with intercalary months used to adjust the four seasons.
He earnestly instructed all officials,
and all tasks flourished.
Yáo said, "Who can undertake this duty?"
Fàng Qí said, "Your heir Dān Zhū is enlightened."
Yáo said, "Alas!
He is obstinate and unruly; he cannot be used."
Yáo then said, "Who else is suitable?"
Huān Dōu said, "Gòng Gōng has gathered achievements far and wide;
he can be used."
Yáo said, "Gòng Gōng speaks well,
but his actions are devious,
appearing respectful yet defying heaven;
he cannot be used."
Yáo then said, "Alas,
Four Peaks,
the vast floods reach the heavens,
overwhelming mountains and engulfing hills,
the common people are in distress;
is there anyone capable of controlling them?"
All said Gǔn could.
Yáo said, "Gǔn defies orders and ruins his clan;
he cannot be used."
The Peaks said, "It is different;
try him, and if he proves unusable, then stop."
Yáo then heeded the Peaks and employed Gǔn.
After nine years,
the task was not accomplished.
Yáo said,
"Alas! Four Peaks: I have been on the throne for seventy years;
can any of you carry out the mandate
and succeed me?"
The Peaks replied, "We are unworthy and would disgrace the throne."
Yáo said, "Recommend all, whether noble relatives or distant and obscure individuals."
All then said to Yáo,
"There is an unmarried man among the people,
named Yú Shùn."
Yáo said, "Yes,
I have heard of him.
What is he like?"
The Peaks said, "He is the son of a blind man.
His father is obstinate,
his mother is deceitful,
his brother is arrogant,
yet he harmonizes with them through filial piety,
managing smoothly
without falling into wrongdoing."
Yáo said, "I shall test him."
Thereupon, Yáo gave him his two daughters in marriage,
observing his virtue through them.
Shùn settled the two women at Guī Ruì,
according to the rites for wives.
Yáo approved of him,
then had Shùn carefully harmonize the five codes,
and the five codes were followed.
He then involved him in all official affairs,
and all officials were orderly.
He received guests at the four gates,
and the four gates were solemn,
with feudal lords and distant guests all showing respect.
Yáo sent Shùn into the mountains and forests,
rivers and marshes;
in violent winds and thunderstorms,
Shùn traveled without losing his way.
Yáo considered him sage,
summoned Shùn and said,
"You have planned affairs thoroughly and your words have borne fruit;
it has been three years.
You shall ascend the throne."
Shùn declined in favor of virtue, feeling unworthy.
On the first auspicious day of the first month,
Shùn received the final mandate at the Temple of the Cultural Ancestor.
The Cultural Ancestor
was Yáo's great ancestor.
Thereupon, Emperor Yáo grew old,
and ordered Shùn to act as regent in governing the kingdom,
to observe the mandate of heaven.
Shùn then observed the Jade Balance and the Jade Tube,
to align the seven administrations.
He then sacrificed to the Supreme Deity,
made offerings to the six honored ones,
paid homage to the mountains and rivers,
and distinguished among the various spirits.
He collected the five tokens of authority,
selected an auspicious month and day,
met with the Four Peaks and various governors,
and distributed the tokens.
In the second month of the year,
he toured east,
reaching Dài Zōng,
where he made burnt offerings,
and paid homage to the mountains and rivers in order.
He then met the chieftains of the east,
harmonized the seasons, months, and days,
unified pitch, measures, weights, and capacities,
revised the five rites,
the five jades,
the three silks,
the two live animals,
and the one dead animal
as gifts,
as with the five instruments,
and finally returned them.
In the fifth month,
he toured south;
in the eighth month,
he toured west;
in the eleventh month,
he toured north:
all as before.
Upon returning,
he reached the ancestral temple,
and performed the ritual with a special ox.
He toured once every five years,
and all lords came to court four times.
He widely instructed with words,
clearly tested with achievements,
and rewarded with chariots and robes according to merit.
He established twelve provinces,
and dredged rivers.
He set forth the canonical punishments,
with banishment as a leniency for the five punishments,
whipping as the official punishment,
caning as the educational punishment,
and fines as the redemption punishment.
For faults due to misfortune, pardon;
for persistent villainy,
punish.
Be reverent,
be reverent,
let punishments be tranquil!
Huān Dōu recommended Gòng Gōng,
Yáo said no but tested him as a foreman,
and Gòng Gōng indeed became corrupt and wayward.
The Four Peaks recommended Gǔn to control the great flood,
Yáo thought it unsuitable,
but the Peaks strongly requested to try him,
and when tried, he achieved nothing,
so the people were displeased.
The Sān Miáo
in the Jiāng Huái and Jīng Zhōu regions repeatedly caused chaos.
Thereupon, Shùn returned and reported to the Emperor,
requesting to banish Gòng Gōng to Yōu Líng,
to transform the Northern Dí;
exile Huān Dōu to Chóng Shān,
to transform the Southern Mán;
relocate the Sān Miáo to Sān Wēi,
to transform the Western Róng;
and execute Gǔn at Yǔ Shān,
to transform the Eastern Yí:
with these four punishments, all under heaven submitted.
Yáo, having reigned for seventy years, found Shùn,
and after twenty years grew old,
ordering Shùn to act as regent in governing the kingdom,
recommending him to heaven.
Yáo abdicated for twenty-eight years in total before passing away.
The people were grieving,
as if mourning their own parents.
For three years,
no music was played throughout the land,
as they remembered Yáo.
Yáo knew his son Dānzhū was unworthy
and unfit to inherit the realm,
so he provisionally handed it to Shùn instead.
By giving it to Shùn,
the realm would benefit while Dānzhū would suffer;
by giving it to Dānzhū,
the realm would suffer while Dānzhū would benefit.
Yáo declared, "I shall never cause the realm to suffer for the benefit of one man,"
and ultimately bequeathed the realm to Shùn.
After Yáo passed away,
when the three-year mourning period ended,
Shùn yielded and avoided Dānzhū south of the Nán Hé.
Yet the feudal lords paying homage did not go to Dānzhū but to Shùn,
those with legal disputes did not go to Dānzhū but to Shùn,
and those singing praises did not sing for Dānzhū but for Shùn.
Shùn said, "This is Heaven's will,"
and only then did he proceed to the central domain to ascend the Son of Heaven's throne,
becoming Emperor Shùn.
Yú Shùn,
named Chónghuá,
had a father named Gǔsǒu,
whose father was Qiáoniú,
whose father was Gōuwàng,
whose father was Jìngkāng,
whose father was Qióngchán,
whose father was Emperor Zhuānxū,
whose father was Chāngyì:
making seven generations down to Shùn.
From Qióngchán to Emperor Shùn,
all had declined to commoner status.
Shùn's father Gǔsǒu was blind,
and after Shùn's mother died,
Gǔsǒu remarried and had Xiàng,
who was arrogant.
Gǔsǒu favored his later wife's son,
often wanting to kill Shùn,
but Shùn would evade him;
when he had minor faults,
he accepted punishment.
He served his father, stepmother, and brother obediently,
daily becoming more devoted and cautious,
never slackening.
Shùn
was from Jìzhōu.
He farmed at Lìshān,
fished at Léizé,
made pottery by the river,
crafted utensils at Shòuqiū,
and traded at Fùxià.
His father Gǔsǒu was obstinate,
his mother deceitful,
and his brother Xiàng arrogant,
all wanting to kill Shùn.
Yet Shùn complied without failing in filial duties,
showing brotherly love and filial piety.
Though they wished to kill him,
they could not;
when they sought him,
he was always by their side.
At twenty, Shùn was known for his filial piety.
At thirty, Emperor Yáo inquired about capable candidates,
and the Four Peaks all recommended Yú Shùn,
saying he was suitable.
So Yáo gave his two daughters to Shùn as wives to observe his domestic conduct,
and sent nine sons to live with him to observe his external behavior.
Shùn dwelled at Guīruì,
and his conduct grew even more cautious.
Yáo's two daughters did not presume on their status in serving Shùn's relatives,
exemplifying wifely virtues.
Yáo's nine sons all became more sincere.
When Shùn farmed at Lìshān,
the people there yielded field boundaries;
when he fished at Léizé,
the fishermen yielded fishing spots;
when he made pottery by the river,
the wares were never crude.
In one year, his dwelling became a hamlet,
in two a town,
in three a city.
Yáo then bestowed upon Shùn fine garments,
a zither,
built him granaries,
and gave him oxen and sheep.
But Gǔsǒu still sought to kill him,
sending Shùn to plaster a granary roof,
then setting it ablaze from below.
Shùn used two bamboo hats to shield himself and leaped down,
escaping
unharmed.
Later, Gǔsǒu had Shùn dig a well,
and Shùn dug a hidden tunnel to the side.
Once Shùn was deep inside,
Gǔsǒu and Xiàng filled the well with earth,
but Shùn escaped through the tunnel,
and fled.
Gǔsǒu and Xiàng rejoiced,
thinking Shùn dead.
Xiàng said, "This was my plan."
He divided Shùn's possessions with his parents,
declaring:
"Shùn's wives, Yáo's two daughters,
and the zither,
I shall take.
The oxen, sheep, and granaries go to my parents."
Xiàng then moved into Shùn's house,
playing his zither.
But Shùn returned and appeared before him.
Xiàng was startled and dismayed,
saying:
"I was just missing you, feeling melancholy!"
Shùn replied, "Indeed,
you are nearly there!"
He continued serving Gǔsǒu and loving his brother with even greater care.
Then Yáo tested Shùn with the Five Canons and various offices,
all of which he governed well.
In the past, Gāoyángshì had eight talented sons,
benefiting their era,
called the "Eight Kǎi."
Gāoxīnshì had eight talented sons,
called the "Eight Yuán."
These sixteen clans
sustained their excellence through generations,
never tarnishing their names.
By Yáo's time,
he had not elevated them.
Shùn promoted the Eight Kǎi,
putting them in charge of the land,
to manage all affairs,
and everything was orderly.
He elevated the Eight Yuán,
tasking them to spread the five teachings throughout the land:
fathers being righteous,
mothers compassionate,
brothers friendly,
younger brothers respectful,
sons filial,
leading to peace within and harmony without.
In the past, Dìhóngshì had an unworthy son,
who suppressed righteousness and concealed wickedness,
fond of committing atrocities,
whom the world called Hùndùn.
Shǎohàoshì had an unworthy son,
who destroyed trust and hated loyalty,
glorifying evil speech,
whom the world called Qióngqí.
Zhuānxūshì had an unworthy son,
who was beyond instruction,
and incomprehensible in speech,
whom the world called Táowù.
These three clans were a perennial worry.
By Yáo's time,
he had not removed them.
Jìnyúnshì had an unworthy son,
gluttonous in food and drink,
greedy for wealth,
whom the world called Tāotiè.
The world despised him,
comparing him to the three villains.
Shùn hosted at the four gates,
then exiled these four villainous clans,
banishing them to the four frontiers,
to guard against chimei monsters,
thus opening the four gates,
signifying no more evil men.
Shùn entered the great wilderness,
where fierce winds and thunderstorms did not lead him astray,
so Yáo knew Shùn was fit to receive the realm.
As Yáo aged,
he had Shùn act in his stead governing as Son of Heaven,
and tour the domains.
Shùn had been recommended and active for twenty years
when Yáo had him act as regent.
After eight years as regent, Yáo passed away.
When the three-year mourning ended,
Shùn yielded to Dānzhū,
but the realm turned to Shùn.
As for Yǔ, Gāoyáo,
Xiè, Hòujì, Bóyí, Kuí, Lóng, Chuí, Yì, and Péngzǔ,
they had all been recommended since Yáo's time,
but without specific duties.
So Shùn went to the Ancestral Temple,
consulted the Four Peaks,
opened the four gates,
cleared communication in all directions,
instructed the twelve pastors to discuss imperial virtue,
practice profound virtue,
keep away flatterers,
and thus the barbarians submitted.
Shùn addressed the Four Peaks, saying:
"Is there anyone who can diligently
promote the achievements of Yáo,
to hold office and assist in governance?"
All replied:
"Bó Yǔ as Minister of Works
can glorify the imperial accomplishments."
Shùn said:
"Ah, indeed!
Yǔ,
you have regulated the waters and land,
strive to continue your efforts."
Yǔ bowed and touched his head to the ground,
yielding the position to Jì, Xiè, and Gāo Yáo.
Shùn said:
"Very well,
go and undertake your duties."
Shùn said:
"Jì,
the common people are beginning to suffer from hunger,
you as Minister of Agriculture shall sow the various grains in season."
Shùn said:
"Xiè,
the people are not harmonious,
the five relationships are not properly ordered,
you shall serve as Minister of Education,
and respectfully disseminate the five teachings,
with leniency."
Shùn said:
"Gāo Yáo,
the barbarians trouble our Xià realm,
with bandits, thieves, and treacherous schemes,
you shall serve as Minister of Justice,
the five punishments shall be appropriately applied,
with three locations for their execution;
the five exiles shall have their regulations,
with three degrees of distance for their settlement:
only clarity can ensure credibility."
Shùn said: "Who can manage our craftsmen?"
All said Chuí was suitable.
Thus Chuí was appointed as Minister of Works.
Shùn said:
"Who can manage our mountains, marshes, grasses, trees, birds, and beasts?"
All said Yì was suitable.
Thus Yì was appointed as my Minister of Natural Resources.
Yì bowed and touched his head to the ground,
yielding to the various officials Zhū Hǔ and Xióng Pí.
Shùn said:
"Go forth,
you shall cooperate."
Thus Zhū Hǔ and Xióng Pí were appointed as assistants.
Shùn said:
"Ah!
Four Peaks,
is there anyone who can oversee my three ceremonies?"
All said Bó Yí was suitable.
Shùn said:
"Ah!
Bó Yí,
I appoint you as Minister of Rites,
be reverent day and night,
upright, tranquil, and pure."
Bó Yí yielded to Kuí and Lóng.
Shùn said:
"Very well.
Let Kuí be Director of Music,
to teach the young,
straightforward yet gentle,
broad-minded yet respectful,
firm yet not cruel,
simple yet not arrogant;
poetry expresses intent,
song prolongs the words,
sound follows the chanting,
pitch harmonizes with sound,
the eight tones can be harmonized,
not interfering with each other's order,
so that spirits and humans are in harmony."
Kuí said:
"Oh!
I strike and tap the stones,
and all beasts follow dancing."
Shùn said:
"Lóng,
I fear slanderous talk and deceptive falsehoods,
that disturb my people,
I appoint you as Minister of Communications,
day and night convey my commands,
ensuring their credibility."
Shùn said:
"Ah!
You twenty-two men,
be reverent,
and thus assist in Heaven's affairs."
Every three years, achievements were assessed,
after three assessments, promotions and demotions were made,
and all accomplishments near and far flourished.
The Sān Miáo were divided and resettled.
These twenty-two men all accomplished their tasks:
Gāo Yáo as Chief Justice,
administered fairly,
and people acknowledged the truth of his judgments;
Bó Yí presided over rites,
and all, high and low, deferred to one another;
Chuí supervised the master craftsmen,
and all artisans achieved their work;
Yì managed the natural resources,
and mountains and marshes were opened up;
and all grains grew abundantly in season;
Xiè served as Minister of Education,
and the people lived in harmony and closeness;
Lóng hosted guests,
and people from distant lands came;
the twelve regional governors traveled, and none in the nine provinces dared to evade or disobey;
but Yǔ's achievements were the greatest,
he cleared nine mountains,
dredged nine marshes,
channeled nine rivers,
settled the nine provinces,
each according to their duties brought tribute,
without missing what was appropriate.
The territory extended five thousand li square, reaching the wild domains.
To the south, he pacified Jiāozhǐ and Běi Fā,
to the west, the Xī Róng, Xīzhī, Qú Sōu, Dī, and Qiāng,
to the north, the Shān Róng, Fā, and Xī Shèn,
to the east, the Cháng and Niǎo Yí,
within the Four Seas
all praised Emperor Shùn's achievements.
Thereupon Yǔ promoted the music of "Jiǔ Shāo",
attracting rare creatures,
and the phoenix came soaring.
The enlightened virtue of all under Heaven began with Emperor Yú.
Shùn was known for filial piety at age twenty,
at thirty Yáo recommended him,
at fifty he acted on behalf of the Son of Heaven,
at fifty-eight Yáo passed away,
at sixty-one he succeeded Yáo on the imperial throne.
He occupied the imperial throne for thirty-nine years,
toured southward,
and died in the wilds of Cāngwú.
He was buried south of the river at Jiǔyí,
which is Línglíng.
When Shùn ascended the throne,
he rode under the Son of Heaven's banner,
went to pay respects to his father Gǔsǒu,
trembling with reverence,
as befits a son's duty.
He enfeoffed his brother Xiàng as a feudal lord.
Shùn's son Shāng Jūn was also unworthy,
so Shùn beforehand recommended Yǔ to Heaven.
After seventeen years, he passed away.
When the three-year mourning period ended,
Yǔ also yielded to Shùn's son,
just as Shùn had yielded to Yáo's son.
The feudal lords turned to him,
and then Yǔ ascended the throne as Son of Heaven.
Yáo's son Dān Zhū,
and Shùn's son Shāng Jūn,
both had territories,
to maintain the sacrifices to their ancestors.
They wore their own robes,
and their rituals and music were as such.
They attended the Son of Heaven as guests,
the Son of Heaven did not treat them as subjects,
showing he did not dare to claim exclusive authority.
From Huángdì to Shùn and Yǔ,
all shared the same surname but had different state names,
to manifest their virtuous achievements.
Thus Huángdì was from Yǒuxióng,
Emperor Zhuānxū from Gāoyáng,
Emperor Kù from Gāoxīn,
Emperor Yáo from Táotáng,
Emperor Shùn from Yǒuyú.
Emperor Yǔ was from Xiàhòu with a separate clan name,
surname Sì.
Xiè was from Shāng,
surname Zǐ.
Jì was from Zhōu,
surname Jī.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Many scholars speak of the Five Emperors,
but this was long ago.
However, the "Shàng Shū" only records from Yáo onward;
while the various schools speak of Huángdì,
their writings are not elegant and reliable,
and gentlemen find them difficult to discuss.
The "Zǎi Yǔ Wèn Wǔdì Dé" and "Dì Xì Xìng" transmitted by Confucius,
some Confucians do not transmit.
I have traveled west to Kōngtóng,
north past Zhuōlù,
east to the sea,
south floating on the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
and the elders everywhere often mention places associated with Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn,
their customs and teachings certainly differ,
but overall, those not diverging from ancient texts are probably close to the truth.
In my study of the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Discourses of the States,
I find that they elucidate the chapters on "The Virtues of the Five Emperors" and "The Genealogy of the Emperors" in detail,
though they do not delve deeply into them.
What they present is all truthful.
The Book of Documents has gaps and omissions,
but its lost contents occasionally appear in other texts.
Without a love for learning and deep contemplation,
and understanding their meaning at heart,
it is indeed difficult to discuss this with those of shallow views and limited knowledge.
I have compiled and arranged these accounts,
selecting those words that are particularly elegant,
and thus present this as the first of the basic annals.
Xià Yǔ,
whose name was Wénmìng.
Yǔ's father was Gǔn,
Gǔn's father was Emperor Zhuānxū,
Zhuānxū's father was Chāngyì,
Chāngyì's father was Huángdì.
Thus, Yǔ
was the great-great-grandson of Huángdì and the grandson of Emperor Zhuānxū.
Both Yǔ's great-grandfather Chāngyì and his father Gǔn did not attain the imperial throne,
serving instead as subjects.
During the time of Emperor Yáo,
a great deluge flooded the heavens,
vastly engulfing the mountains and hills,
causing the common people to suffer.
Yáo sought someone capable of controlling the waters,
and all his ministers and the Four Peaks recommended Gǔn.
Yáo said:
"Gǔn is a man who defies orders and ruins his clan,
he is not suitable."
The Four Peaks said:
"Among equals, none is more capable than Gǔn,
we beg the Emperor to try him."
Thereupon, Yáo heeded the Four Peaks
and employed Gǔn to control the waters.
After nine years, the waters had not receded,
and the task was not accomplished.
Then Emperor Yáo sought another person
and found Shùn.
Shùn was elevated and employed,
acting in the administration of the Son of Heaven,
and he toured the realms.
Inspecting Gǔn's failure in water control,
he executed Gǔn at Yǔshān.
All under heaven considered Shùn's punishment just.
Thereupon, Shùn recommended Gǔn's son Yǔ
to continue Gǔn's work.
When Yáo passed away,
Emperor Shùn asked the Four Peaks:
"Is there anyone who can complete the splendid work of Yáo and be appointed to office?"
All replied:
"Bó Yǔ as Minister of Works
can accomplish Yáo's great task."
Shùn said:
"Ah, indeed!"
He commanded Yǔ:
"You shall pacify the waters and lands,
strive diligently in this."
Yǔ bowed and touched his head to the ground,
yielding to Xiè,
Hòujì, and Gāoyáo.
Shùn said:
"You shall go and attend to your duties."
Yǔ was quick and diligent by nature;
his virtue did not err,
his benevolence was approachable,
his words were trustworthy;
his voice set the standard for pitch,
his body for measurement,
balanced in all actions;
earnest and reverent,
he established order and discipline.
Yǔ then followed the emperor's command with Yì and Hòujì,
ordering the feudal lords and the people to mobilize laborers to work the land,
surveying the mountains and marking trees,
defining the high mountains and great rivers.
Yǔ grieved that his father Gǔn had failed in his task and been punished,
so he toiled his body and worried intensely,
staying away for thirteen years,
not daring to enter his own home when passing by.
He wore simple clothes and ate plain food,
showing reverence to the spirits.
He kept his dwellings humble,
devoting resources to ditches and canals.
On land he traveled by cart, on water by boat,
on mud by sled,
on mountains by spiked shoes.
With measuring tools in his left hand
and compasses and squares in his right,
he carried the four seasons with him,
opening up the nine provinces,
clearing the nine routes,
damming the nine marshes,
and surveying the nine mountains.
He ordered Yì to distribute rice to the masses,
suitable for planting in low, damp areas.
He commanded Hòujì to provide the people with hard-to-obtain food.
When food was scarce,
he regulated surplus to supply deficits,
equalizing among the feudal lords.
Yǔ then assessed the land's suitability for tribute,
considering the advantages of mountains and rivers.
Yǔ began his work from Jìzhōu.
Jìzhōu:
After dealing with Húkǒu,
he regulated Liáng and Qí.
After restoring Tàiyuán,
he reached Yuèyáng.
Tánhuái achieved results,
extending to Héngzhāng.
Its soil was white and loamy.
Tribute was top grade with variations,
field quality was medium-medium.
Cháng and Wèi were brought under control,
Dàlù was cultivated.
The Bird Tribes offered fur garments.
Passing by Jiéshí on the right,
they entered the sea.
Jì and Hé formed Yǎnzhōu:
The nine rivers were channeled,
Léixià became a marsh,
Yōng and Jǔ converged,
mulberry lands were sericultural,
so the people could descend from hills to live on plains.
Its soil was black and fertile,
with lush grass and tall trees.
Field quality was low-medium,
tribute was steady,
taking thirteen years to equalize.
Its tribute included lacquer and silk,
and baskets with woven patterns.
Transport was via Jì and Tà rivers,
connecting to the Hé.
From the sea to Dài was Qīngzhōu:
Yúyí was pacified,
Wéi and Zī were channeled.
Its soil was white and fertile,
with vast saline coasts,
and fields of alkaline soil.
Field quality was high-low,
tribute medium-high.
Its tribute included salt and fine linen,
various sea products,
silk, hemp, lead, pine, and strange stones from Dài's valleys,
Láiyí practiced herding,
with baskets of silkworm silk.
Transport was via Wèn river,
connecting to Jì.
From the sea and Dài to Huái was Xúzhōu:
Huái and Yí were regulated,
Méng and Yǔ were cultivated.
Dàyě became a lake,
Dōngyuán was leveled.
Its soil was red, clayey, and fertile,
with lush vegetation.
Field quality was high-medium,
tribute medium-medium.
Tribute included five-colored earth,
colorful pheasants from Yǔ valley,
solitary tong trees from Yìyáng,
floating stones from Sì banks,
pearls and fish from Huáiyí,
and baskets of black and white silk.
Transport was via Huái and Sì rivers,
connecting to Hé.
From Huái to the sea was Yángzhōu:
Pénglǐ became a lake,
where sunbirds dwelled.
The three rivers were channeled,
Zhènzé was stabilized.
Bamboo and arrow bamboo grew everywhere.
Its grasses were lush,
its trees tall,
its soil muddy.
Field quality was low-low,
tribute low-high with variations.
Tribute included three grades of metal,
jasper, kun gems, bamboo and arrow bamboo,
ivory, hides, feathers, and yak tails,
island tribes offered grass garments,
baskets contained patterned shells,
and packages of oranges and pomelos as special tribute.
Transport was balanced along rivers and sea,
connecting to Huái and Sì.
From Jīng Mountain to the southern side of Héng Mountain is the province of Jīngzhōu:
the Jiāng and Hàn rivers flow into the sea.
The nine branches of the Jiāng are well-regulated,
the Tuō and Cén rivers have been channeled,
and the Yún and Mèng marshes have been made arable.
Its soil is muddy.
Its fields are of the eighth grade,
its taxes of the third grade.
It presents feathers, yak tails, ivory, hides,
three kinds of metal,
chūn, gàn, guā, and bǎi trees,
grindstones, whetstones, arrow-stone, and cinnabar,
the jùn and lù bamboos, and hù wood,
three regions send their famous products as tribute,
bundles of green máo grass,
in their baskets, dark and red silks, pearls, and ribbons,
and from the nine branches of the Jiāng comes the great turtle.
They travel by the Jiāng, Tuō, Cén, and Hàn rivers,
cross over to the Luò,
and reach the southern Hé.
Between the Jīng and Hé rivers is the province of Yùzhōu:
the Yī, Luò, Chán, and Jiàn rivers have entered the Hé,
the Yíng marsh has become a lake,
the Hézé has been channeled,
and the Míngdū marsh has been drained.
Its soil is loamy,
the lower ground is rich and dark.
Its fields are of the fourth grade,
its taxes a mixture of the second and third grades.
It presents lacquer, silk, fine and coarse hempen cloth,
in their baskets, fine silk floss,
and on special order, stone for making chimes.
They travel by the Luò,
and reach the Hé.
From the southern side of Huà Mountain to the Hēi River is the province of Liángzhōu:
the Wèn and Bō mountains have been cultivated,
the Tuō and Cén rivers have been channeled,
the Cài and Méng mountains have been made passable,
and peace has been brought to the Héyí.
Its soil is greenish-black.
Its fields are of the seventh grade,
its taxes of the eighth grade with a mixture of others.
It presents fine jade, iron, silver, steel, arrow-stone, and chime-stones,
bears, brown bears, foxes, wildcats, and furs.
From Xīqīng, they come by the Huán River,
travel by the Qián,
cross over to the Miǎn,
enter the Wèi,
and cross the Hé.
From the Hēi River to the western Hé is the province of Yōngzhōu:
the Ruò River has been made to flow west,
the Jīng joins the Wèi at its bend.
The Qī and Jǔ rivers follow their courses,
and the Fēng River flows to the same place.
The Jīng and Qí mountains have been made passable,
from Zhōngnán and Dūnwù to Niǎoshǔ.
The plains and lowlands have been cultivated,
reaching to Dūyě.
The Sānwēi region has been settled,
and the Sānmiáo tribes greatly ordered.
Its soil is yellow loam.
Its fields are of the first grade,
its taxes of the sixth grade.
It presents fine jade, gemstones, and pearls.
They travel by the Jīshí Mountain,
reach the western Hé at Lóngmén,
and meet at the bend of the Wèi.
The furs from Kūnlún,
Xīzhī,
and Qúsōu,
the western Róng are thus arranged.
He regulated the nine mountains:
from Qiān and Qí to Jīng Mountain,
crossing the Hé;
from Húkǒu and Léishǒu
to Tàiyuè;
from Dǐzhǔ and Xīchéng to Wángwū;
from Tàiháng and Chángshān to Jiéshí,
entering the sea;
from Xīqīng, Zhūyǔ, Niǎoshǔ
to Tàihuà;
from Xióng'ěr, Wàifāng, Tóngbǎi to Fùwěi;
he regulated Bōzhǒng,
reaching to Jīng Mountain;
from Nèifāng to Dàbié;
from the southern side of Wèn Mountain to Héng Mountain,
passing the nine branches of the Jiāng,
to Fūqiǎnyuán.
He regulated the nine rivers:
the Ruò River to Hélí,
its remaining flow enters the Liúshā.
He regulated the Hēi River,
to Sānwēi,
entering the southern sea.
He regulated the Hé from Jīshí,
to Lóngmén,
south to Huáyīn,
east to Dǐzhǔ,
further east to Méngjīn,
east past Luòruì,
to Dàpī,
north past Jiàngshuǐ,
to Dàlù,
north dividing into nine branches of the Hé,
together forming the Nì Hé,
entering the sea.
From Bōzhǒng, he regulated the Yǎng,
east flowing as the Hàn,
further east as the Cānglàng waters,
passing Sānshì,
entering Dàbié,
south entering the Jiāng,
east collecting into the marsh of Pénglí,
east becoming the northern Jiāng,
entering the sea.
From Wèn Mountain, he regulated the Jiāng, east branching as the Tuō,
further east to Lǐ,
passing the nine branches of the Jiāng,
to Dōnglíng,
east turning north to meet at Huì,
east becoming the central Jiāng,
entering the sea.
He regulated the Yǎn River,
east becoming the Jǐ,
entering the Hé,
overflowing as the Yíng,
east emerging north of Táoqiū,
further east to Hé,
further northeast meeting the Wèn,
further northeast entering the sea.
He regulated the Huái from Tóngbǎi,
east meeting the Sì and Yí,
east entering the sea.
He regulated the Wèi from Niǎoshǔ Tóngxué,
east meeting the Fēng,
further northeast to the Jīng,
east past the Qī and Jǔ,
entering the Hé.
He regulated the Luò from Xióng'ěr,
northeast meeting the Jiàn and Chán,
further east meeting the Yī,
northeast entering the Hé.
Thus the nine provinces were made uniform,
the four domains were settled,
the nine mountains were cleared and made passable,
the nine rivers were cleansed to their sources,
the nine marshes were embanked,
and the four seas were united.
The six treasuries were well managed,
all lands were correctly assessed,
care was taken in the wealth and taxes,
all according to the three grades of soil to determine taxes.
The central kingdom bestowed lands and surnames:
"Revere virtue first,
do not oppose my actions."
He ordered that within five hundred lǐ from the Son of Heaven's capital was the Diànfú domain:
within one hundred lǐ, they bring the whole harvest,
within two hundred lǐ, the grain,
within three hundred lǐ, the straw,
within four hundred lǐ, millet,
within five hundred lǐ, polished rice.
Beyond the Diànfú domain five hundred lǐ was the Hóufú domain:
within one hundred lǐ, officials' lands,
within two hundred lǐ, states of responsibility,
within three hundred lǐ, the domains of the nobles.
Beyond the Hóufú domain five hundred lǐ was the Suífú domain:
within three hundred lǐ, promoting culture and education,
within two hundred lǐ, rousing military defense.
Beyond the Suífú domain five hundred lǐ was the Yāofú domain:
within three hundred lǐ, the Yí tribes,
within two hundred lǐ, the Cài tribes.
Beyond the Yāofú domain five hundred lǐ was the Huāngfú domain:
within three hundred lǐ, the Mán tribes,
within two hundred lǐ, the wandering tribes.
To the east, it extended to the sea,
to the west, it reached the Liúshā,
north and south it extended:
its influence and teachings reached to the four seas.
Then the Emperor bestowed upon Yǔ a dark jade tablet,
to announce his success to the world.
The world was thus peacefully governed.
Gāo Yáo became the minister of justice to govern the people.
Emperor Shùn held court,
Yǔ, Bó Yí, and Gāo Yáo spoke together before the Emperor.
Gāo Yáo related his plan, saying:
"Be sincere in your virtue and conduct,
make plans clear and assist harmoniously."
Yǔ said:
"Yes,
but how?"
Gāo Yáo said:
"Ah!
Be cautious in self-cultivation,
think long-term,
sincerely order the nine clans,
the multitude will be enlightened and highly supportive,
what is near can extend far through oneself."
Yǔ bowed in praise of these fine words,
saying:
"Indeed."
Gāo Yáo said:
"Ah!
It lies in understanding people,
in bringing peace to the populace."
Yǔ said: [19"Alas!
If all were thus,
even the Emperor would find it difficult.
Understanding people shows wisdom,
enabling the appointment of officials;
being able to bring peace to the populace shows benevolence,
and the common people will cherish them.
With the ability to understand and to be benevolent,
why worry about Huān Dōu,
why exile the Yǒu Miáo,
why fear glib-tongued, pleasant-faced flatterers?"
Gāo Yáo said:
"Yes, ah!
Moreover, conduct has nine virtues,
and speech too reflects one's virtue."
He then said:
"Begin with tasks,
broad yet stern,
gentle yet firm,
sincere yet respectful,
orderly yet reverent,
yielding yet resolute,
upright yet mild,
simple yet honest,
strong yet substantial,
vigorous yet righteous.
Display these consistently,
auspicious indeed!
Daily practicing three virtues,
early and late assisting the bright, one can have a family.
Daily strictly cultivating six virtues,
brilliant in service, one can have a state.
Embracing all and applying universally,
all nine virtues employed,
the talented in office,
all officials solemn and diligent.
Do not teach deceitful, excessive, or cunning schemes.
If the wrong person holds office,
this is called disrupting heaven's affairs.
Heaven punishes the guilty,
with five punishments for five offenses.
Can my words be put into practice?"
Yǔ said:
"Your words can indeed achieve results."
Gāo Yáo said:
"I know little,
but think to assist the Way."
Emperor Shùn said to Yǔ:
"You too speak well."
Yǔ bowed and said:
"Ah,
what have I to say!
I think only of toiling daily."
Gāo Yáo questioned Yǔ:
"What do you mean by toiling?"
Yǔ said:
"The floodwaters reached the heavens,
vastly surrounding mountains and engulfing hills,
the people below all subdued by water.
I traveled on land by cart,
on water by boat,
on mud by sled,
on mountains by spikes,
crossing hills and cutting trees.
With Yì, I gave the masses rice and fresh food.
By channeling the nine rivers to the four seas,
dredging field ditches
to lead them to the rivers.
With Jì, I gave the masses hard-to-obtain food.
When food was scarce,
I transferred surplus to supplement shortage,
and moved settlements.
Thus the people were settled,
and all states were governed."
Gāo Yáo said:
"Yes, this is praiseworthy."
Yǔ said:
"Ah, Emperor!
Be cautious in your position,
calm in your actions.
Assist virtue,
and the world will greatly respond.
Purify your intent to clearly await Heaven's mandate,
and Heaven will repeatedly bestow blessings."
The Emperor said:
"Alas,
ministers,
ministers!
Ministers are my limbs, ears, and eyes.
I wish to guide the people,
you assist me.
I wish to observe the symbols of the ancients,
the sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
creating embroidered robes and colors,
you clarify them.
I wish to hear the six pitches, five tones, and eight sounds,
to discern beginnings and subtleties,
to express through the five statements,
you listen.
If I err,
you correct and support me.
Do not flatter me to my face,
only to slander me behind my back.
Respect the four assisting ministers.
All slanderous and favored ministers,
if the ruler's virtue is sincerely applied, all will be pure."
Yǔ said:
"Yes.
If the Emperor is not timely,
mixing good and evil alike, there will be no achievement."
The Emperor said:
"Do not be like Dān Zhū, arrogant,
fond only of idle wandering,
boating where there is no water,
indulging with friends at home,
thus ending his lineage.
I cannot condone this."
Yǔ said:
"I married at Tú Shān,
on Xīn, Rén, Guǐ, Jiǎ days,
and when Qǐ was born, I did not care for him,
thus I could complete the water and earth works.
Assisting in establishing the five domains,
extending five thousand lǐ,
with twelve divisions in the provinces,
reaching to the four seas,
all establishing five chiefs,
each achieving merit.
The Miao stubbornly resist merit,
may the Emperor keep this in mind."
The Emperor said:
"Spreading my virtue,
it is your merit that orders it."
Gāo Yáo then respected Yǔ's virtue,
ordering the people to follow Yǔ.
Those who did not comply,
were punished accordingly.
Shùn's virtue greatly shone.
Then Kuí performed music,
ancestors arrived,
lords deferred to one another,
birds and beasts soared and danced,
the "Xiāo Sháo" completed nine movements,
phoenixes came to grace,
all beasts joined in dance,
all officials were sincere and harmonious.
The Emperor thus sang:
"Fulfilling Heaven's mandate,
timely and subtle."
He then sang:
"Limbs and joints rejoice,
the head rises,
all tasks flourish!"
Gāo Yáo bowed and proclaimed:
"Remember,
lead in initiating affairs,
be cautious with your laws,
revere them!"
He then sang in response:
"The head is bright,
limbs and joints are good,
all affairs are peaceful!"
He sang again:
"If the head is petty,
limbs and joints lazy,
all matters will fail!"
The Emperor bowed and said:
"Yes,
go forth and be reverent!"
Then all under heaven revered Yǔ's clear regulations and musical tones,
making him master of mountains and rivers' spirits.
Emperor Shùn recommended Yǔ to Heaven,
as successor.
After seventeen years, Emperor Shùn passed away.
After three years of mourning,
Yǔ declined to appoint Shùn's son Shāngjūn in Yángchéng.
The feudal lords of the world all left Shāngjūn and presented themselves to Yǔ.
Yǔ thus ascended to the position of Son of Heaven,
facing south to hold court over the world,
and named the state "Xiàhou,"
with the surname Sì.
Emperor Yǔ established Gāotāo, recommending him
and entrusted him with governance,
but Gāotāo passed away.
Gāotāo's descendants were enfeoffed in Yīng and Lù,
or perhaps in Xǔ.
Afterwards, Yǔ promoted Yì,
entrusting him with governance.
Ten years later,
Emperor Yǔ toured the east,
and passed away at Mount Huìjī.
He entrusted the world to Yì.
After three years of mourning,
Yì ceded the throne to Yǔ's son Qǐ,
and retired to the southern side of Mount Jī.
Yǔ's son Qǐ was wise,
and the world placed their hopes on him.
Upon Yǔ's death,
though Yì had been given the charge,
Yì's time assisting Yǔ was brief,
and the world was not unanimous.
Thus, the lords all left Yì and presented themselves to Qǐ,
saying "Our ruler is the son of Emperor Yǔ."
Consequently, Qǐ ascended to the position of Son of Heaven,
becoming Emperor Qǐ of the Xià Dynasty.
Emperor Qǐ of the Xià Dynasty,
son of Yǔ,
his mother was a woman of the Túshān clan.
The Yǒuhù clan did not submit,
so Qǐ attacked them,
engaging in a great battle at Gān.
Before the battle,
he composed the "Gān Oath,"
summoning his six ministers to declare it.
Qǐ said:
"Alas!
You men of six duties,
I swear to tell you:
The Yǒuhù clan has defied the Five Elements,
neglecting the Three Principles,
therefore Heaven has terminated their fate.
Now I shall carry out Heaven's punishment.
If those on the left do not strike on the left,
and those on the right do not strike on the right,
you are not committed to the cause.
If you do not control the politics of your horses,
you are not committed to the cause.
Those who fulfill their duty
will be rewarded at the temple;
those who do not
will be punished at the altar,
I will personally penalize you."
Thus, he annihilated the Yǒuhù clan.
All under Heaven came to court.
Emperor Qǐ of the Xià Dynasty passed away,
his son Emperor Tàikāng ascended.
Emperor Tàikāng lost the country,
and five brothers,
gathered at Luò Ruì,
composed the "Song of the Five Sons."
Tàikāng passed away,
and his brother Zhōngkāng ascended,
becoming Emperor Zhōngkāng.
During the time of Emperor Zhōngkāng,
Xī and Hé were indulging in luxury,
causing chaos in the calendar.
Yìn went to punish them,
composing the "Yìn's Campaign."
Zhōngkāng passed away,
his son Emperor Xiàng ascended.
Emperor Xiàng passed away,
his son Emperor Shàokāng ascended.
Emperor Shàokāng passed away,
his son Emperor Yǔ ascended.
Emperor Yǔ passed away,
his son Emperor Huái ascended.
Emperor Huái passed away,
his son Emperor Máng ascended.
Emperor Máng passed away,
his son Emperor Xiè ascended.
Emperor Xiè passed away,
his son Emperor Bùjiàng ascended.
Emperor Bùjiàng passed away,
and his brother Emperor Jiōng ascended.
Emperor Jiōng passed away,
his son Emperor Jǐn ascended.
Emperor Jǐn passed away,
Kǒng Jiǎ, the son of Emperor Bùjiàng, was enthroned,
becoming Emperor Kǒng Jiǎ.
Emperor Kǒng Jiǎ ascended,
greatly interested in ghosts and spirits,
engaging in corrupt practices.
The virtue of the Xià royal clan declined,
and the feudal lords rebelled against him.
Heaven sent down two dragons,
one male and one female,
but Kǒng Jiǎ could not feed them,
not having yet obtained the Dragon Caretaker clan.
After Táotáng declined,
his descendant Liú Lèi,
learned dragon care from the Dragon Caretaker clan,
to serve Kǒng Jiǎ.
Kǒng Jiǎ bestowed on him the surname Yùlóng,
recognizing him as a descendant of Shǐwéi.
One female dragon died,
and was served as food to the Xià ruler.
The Xià ruler sent for it,
but fearing reprisal,
Liú Lèi fled.
Kǒng Jiǎ passed away,
his son Emperor Gāo ascended.
Emperor Gāo passed away,
his son Emperor Fā ascended.
Emperor Fā passed away,
his son Emperor Lǚguǐ ascended,
known as Jié.
During Emperor Jié's time,
from Kǒng Jiǎ onwards, the lords frequently rebelled against Xià,
Jié did not practice virtue and acted violently, harming the people,
and the people could not endure it.
Consequently, he summoned Tāng and imprisoned him on Shataí,
but soon released him.
Tāng cultivated virtue,
and the feudal lords all supported Tāng,
so Tāng led troops to attack Xià's Jié.
Jié fled to Míngtiáo,
was then exiled and died.
Jié told others:
"I regret not having killed Tāng at Shataí,
which led to this."
Thus, Tāng ascended to the position of Son of Heaven,
replacing Xià to rule the world.
Tāng enfeoffed Xià's descendants,
until the Zhōu enfeoffed them at Yù.
Grand Historian Gōng said:
Yǔ bore the surname Sì,
his descendants were enfeoffed,
and took the state as their surname,
hence there were the Xiàhou, Yǒuhù, Nán, Zhēnxún,
Yù, Zēng, Xīn, Míng, Zhēn, Gē clans.
Confucius rectified the Xià calendar,
and many scholars passed down "Xià Xiǎozhèng."
From the time of Yú and Xià,
tributes and taxes were complete.
Some say Yǔ convened the lords south of the Yangtze,
evaluated their achievements and passed away,
hence was buried there,
naming it Huìjī,
signifying it was a convergence for accounting.
Yīnxiàn,
whose mother was Jiǎn-Dí,
a woman of the Yǒusōng clan,
was a secondary consort to the Emperor.
While three people were bathing,
they saw a dark bird drop an egg,
Jiǎn-Dí took and swallowed it,
and thus became pregnant and gave birth to Xiàn.
When Xiàn grew up, he assisted Yǔ in controlling the floods, earning merit.
Emperor Shùn then ordered Xiàn, saying:
"The people are not harmonious,
the Five Classes are not instructed,
you shall be the Minister of Instruction and respectfully promote the Five Teachings,
with leniency in the Five Teachings."
He was enfeoffed in Shāng,
and bestowed the surname Zǐ.
Xiàn thrived during the times of Táng, Yú, and Dà Yǔ,
his accomplishments evident among the people,
ensuring peace.
Xiàn passed away,
his son Zhāomíng ascended.
Zhāomíng passed away,
his son Xiàngtǔ ascended.
Xiàngtǔ passed away,
his son Chāngruò ascended.
Chāngruò passed away,
his son Cáoyǔ ascended.
Cáo Yù died,
and his son Míng succeeded him.
Míng died,
and his son Zhèn succeeded him.
Zhèn died,
and his son Wēi succeeded him.
Wēi died,
and his son Bào Dīng succeeded him.
Bào Dīng died,
and his son Bào Yǐ succeeded him.
Bào Yǐ died,
and his son Bào Bǐng succeeded him.
Bào Bǐng died,
and his son Zhǔ Rén succeeded him.
Zhǔ Rén died,
and his son Zhǔ Guǐ succeeded him.
Zhǔ Guǐ died,
and his son Tiān Yǐ succeeded him,
who became Chéng Tāng.
Chéng Tāng,
from Xiè to Tāng, moved the capital eight times.
Tāng first resided in Bó,
following the dwelling of the former kings,
and composed the "Dì Gào."
Tāng campaigned against the feudal lords.
The Earl of Gé did not offer sacrifices,
so Tāng began to attack him.
Tāng said:
"I have a saying:
One looks into water to see one's form,
and observes the people to know whether governance is achieved or not."
Yī Yǐn said:
"How illuminating!
If one can heed words,
the Way will advance.
Ruling the state and caring for the people,
all who do good shall hold positions in the king's court.
Strive hard,
strive hard!"
Tāng said:
"If you cannot respect the mandate,
I will severely punish and execute you,
with no pardon whatsoever."
He composed the "Tāng Zhēng."
Yī Yǐn was named Ā Héng.
Ā Héng wished to approach Tāng but had no means,
so he became a retainer of the Yǒu Shēn clan,
carrying cauldrons and stands,
using flavors to persuade Tāng,
leading him to the Way of the King.
Some say
Yī Yǐn was a recluse scholar,
and Tāng sent people to invite and welcome him,
and after five refusals, he finally agreed to follow Tāng,
speaking of the affairs of the Unrowned King and the Nine Sovereigns.
Tāng elevated and entrusted him with the state's governance.
Yī Yǐn left Tāng and went to Xià.
After becoming disgusted with the Xià,
he returned to Bó.
Entering through the north gate,
he encountered Nǚ Jiū and Nǚ Fáng,
and composed the "Nǚ Jiū Nǚ Fáng."
Tāng went out
and saw a net spread on all sides in the wild,
with a prayer saying:
"May all from under heaven and the four directions enter my net."
Tāng said:
"Alas,
that would exhaust them!"
So he removed three sides of the net,
and prayed:
"Those wishing to go left,
go left.
Those wishing to go right,
go right.
Those who do not heed the command,
then enter my net."
The feudal lords heard of this,
and said:
"Tāng's virtue is supreme,
extending even to birds and beasts."
At that time,
Xià Jié practiced cruel governance and licentious excess,
and the feudal lord Kūnwú氏 rebelled.
Tāng then raised an army and led the feudal lords,
with Yī Yǐn following Tāng,
Tāng personally wielding a battle-axe to attack Kūnwú,
and subsequently attacked Jié.
Tāng said:
"Come, you multitude,
approach,
and all listen to my words.
It is not I, the humble one,
who dare to initiate rebellion,
but the Xià have many crimes,
and I have heard your words,
that the Xià clan is guilty.
I fear the Supreme God,
and dare not not rectify this.
Now the Xià have many crimes,
and Heaven's mandate is to execute them.
Now you multitude,
you say, 'Our lord does not pity us,
abandoning our farming to impose harsh governance.'
You may ask, 'What of his crimes,
and what can be done?'
The Xià king exhausts the people's strength,
and plunders the Xià state.
The people are all weary and disunited,
saying,
'When will this sun perish? We would rather perish with you!'
Such is the virtue of Xià,
and now I must go.
If you assist me in carrying out Heaven's punishment,
I will greatly reward you.
Do not doubt me,
for I do not break my word.
If you do not follow this oath,
I will enslave and kill you,
with no pardon whatsoever."
He announced this to the army,
and composed the "Tāng Shì."
Thereupon, Tāng said, "I am very martial,"
and was titled the Martial King.
Jié was defeated at the ruins of Yǒu Sōng,
Jié fled to Míng Tiáo,
and the Xià army was utterly defeated.
Tāng then attacked Sān Zōng,
capturing their precious jades,
and Yì Bó and Zhòng Bó composed the "Diǎn Bǎo."
After Tāng had conquered Xià,
he wished to move their altar of the soil,
but could not,
so he composed the "Xià Shè."
Yī Yǐn reported.
Thereupon, all the feudal lords submitted,
and Tāng ascended the Son of Heaven's throne,
pacifying the land within the seas.
Tāng returned and reached Tài Juǎn Táo,
where Zhòng Huī made an announcement.
After abolishing the Xià mandate,
he returned to Bó,
and composed the "Tāng Gào":
"In the third month,
the king personally arrived at the eastern suburbs.
He announced to the feudal lords and all chiefs:
'Do not fail to achieve merit for the people,
diligently attend to your duties.
Otherwise, I will severely punish and execute you,
and you shall have no complaint.'
He said: 'In ancient times, Yǔ and Gāo Yáo toiled long abroad,
they achieved merit for the people,
and the people thus had peace.
To the east, the Jiāng,
to the north, the Jǐ,
to the west, the Hé,
to the south, the Huái,
the four rivers were regulated,
and the myriad people thus had dwellings.
Hòu Jì descended to sow,
and farming produced the hundred grains.
These three lords all had merit for the people,
hence their descendants were established.
In the past, Chī Yóu and his ministers brought chaos to the people,
and the Emperor did not grant them favor,
as there was evidence.
The words of the former kings must not be disregarded.'
He said: 'If you are unprincipled,
you shall not remain in your state,
and you shall not blame me.'"
He thus commanded the feudal lords.
Yī Yǐn composed the "Xián Yǒu Yī Dé,"
and Jiù Dān composed the "Míng Jū."
Tāng then changed the calendar and first month,
altered the color of garments,
adopting white as superior,
and held court audiences by day.
Tāng passed away,
and the crown prince Tài Dīng died before ascending,
so they established Tài Dīng's younger brother Wài Bǐng,
who became Emperor Wài Bǐng.
Emperor Wài Bǐng reigned for three years,
then passed away,
and they established Wài Bǐng's younger brother Zhōng Rén,
who became Emperor Zhōng Rén.
In the fourth year of Dì Zhōngrén's reign,
he passed away,
and Yī Yǐn then established Dàidīng's son Tài Jiǎ.
Tài Jiǎ,
the eldest grandson of Chéng Tāng,
became Emperor Tài Jiǎ.
In Emperor Tài Jiǎ's first year,
Yī Yǐn composed the "Yī Xùn",
"Sì Mìng", and
"Cú Hòu".
Three years after Emperor Tài Jiǎ took the throne,
he was dim-witted and tyrannical,
not adhering to Tāng's laws,
and his virtues were chaotic.
Therefore, Yī Yǐn exiled him to the Tóng Palace.
For three years,
Yī Yǐn managed state affairs,
holding court with the lords.
Emperor Tài Jiǎ resided in Tóng Palace for three years,
repented,
and turned towards goodness.
Consequently, Yī Yǐn escorted Emperor Tài Jiǎ back and returned governance to him.
Emperor Tài Jiǎ cultivated virtues,
the lords all returned to Yīn,
and the common people found peace.
Yī Yǐn praised him,
composing the "Tài Jiǎ Xùn" in three sections,
exalting Emperor Tài Jiǎ,
naming him Tài Zōng.
Tài Zōng passed away,
and his son Wòdīng ascended the throne.
During the reign of Emperor Wòdīng,
Yī Yǐn died.
After burying Yī Yǐn at Bó,
Jiù Shàn instructed on Yī Yǐn's affairs,
composing the "Wòdīng".
Wòdīng passed away,
and his younger brother Tài Gēng ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Tài Gēng.
Emperor Tài Gēng passed away,
and his son Emperor Xiǎo Jiǎ ascended the throne.
Emperor Xiǎo Jiǎ passed away,
and his younger brother Yōng Jǐ ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Yōng Jǐ.
The Yīn dynasty declined,
and some lords did not attend court.
Emperor Yōng Jǐ passed away,
and his younger brother Tài Wù ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Tài Wù.
Emperor Tài Wù appointed Yī Zhì as chancellor.
In Bó, there were auspicious omens with mulberry and grain growing together in the courtyard,
reaching great height overnight.
Emperor Tài Wù was afraid
and asked Yī Zhì.
Yī Zhì said:
"I have heard that omens do not surpass virtue;
is there perhaps a deficiency in the Emperor's governance? Let the Emperor cultivate virtue."
Tài Wù heeded this advice,
and the auspicious mulberry withered and disappeared.
Yī Zhì praised Wū Xián.
Wū Xián managed the royal household successfully,
composing the "Xián Ài",
and the "Tài Wù".
Emperor Tài Wù praised Yī Zhì at the ancestral temple,
declaring he was not like a minister,
Yī Zhì declined,
composing the "Yuán Mìng".
The Yīn dynasty revived,
with the lords returning,
hence he was called Zhōng Zōng.
Zhōng Zōng passed away,
and his son Emperor Zhōng Dīng ascended the throne.
Emperor Zhōng Dīng moved to Áo.
Héchéng Jiǎ resided in Xiāng.
Zǔ Yǐ moved to Xíng.
Emperor Zhōng Dīng passed away,
and his younger brother Wài Rén ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Wài Rén.
The records on "Zhòng Dīng" are incomplete.
Emperor Wài Rén passed away,
and his younger brother Héchéng Jiǎ ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Héchéng Jiǎ.
During Héchéng Jiǎ's time,
the Yīn dynasty declined again.
Héchéng Jiǎ passed away,
and his son Emperor Zǔ Yǐ ascended the throne.
Emperor Zǔ Yǐ ascended,
and the Yīn dynasty revived again.
Wū Xián held position.
Zǔ Yǐ passed away,
and his son Emperor Zǔ Xīn ascended the throne.
Emperor Zǔ Xīn passed away,
and his younger brother Wò Jiǎ ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Wò Jiǎ.
Emperor Wò Jiǎ passed away,
and established Wò Jiǎ's elder brother Zǔ Xīn's son Zǔ Dīng,
becoming Emperor Zǔ Dīng.
Emperor Zǔ Dīng passed away,
and established Wò Jiǎ's son Nán Gēng,
becoming Emperor Nán Gēng.
Emperor Nán Gēng passed away,
and established Emperor Zǔ Dīng's son Yáng Jiǎ,
becoming Emperor Yáng Jiǎ.
During Emperor Yáng Jiǎ's time,
the Yīn dynasty weakened.
From Zhōng Dīng onward,
the establishment of direct heirs was abolished, and instead younger siblings and sons were appointed,
with some competing to replace one another,
leading to nine generations of chaos,
thus the lords did not attend court.
Emperor Yáng Jiǎ passed away,
and his younger brother Pán Gēng ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Pán Gēng.
During Emperor Pán Gēng's time,
the Yīn capital was already north of the river,
and Pán Gēng crossed south of the river,
returning to the former residence of Chéng Tāng,
relocating five times,
with no permanent settlement.
The people of Yīn all complained,
unwilling to relocate.
Pán Gēng then instructed the lords and ministers, saying:
"In the past, the late Chéng Tāng settled the world with your ancestors,
and his laws are worthy of respect.
If neglected,
how can virtue be achieved?"
Thus he continued across the southern river,
governed Bó,
executing Tāng's principles,
leading to the people’s peace,
and the revival of the Yīn way.
The lords came to court,
because he adhered to the virtues of Chéng Tāng.
Emperor Pán Gēng passed away,
and his younger brother Xiǎo Xīn ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Xiǎo Xīn.
Emperor Xiǎo Xīn ascended,
and the Yīn dynasty declined again.
The people missed Pán Gēng,
composing the "Pán Gēng" in three sections.
Emperor Xiǎo Xīn passed away,
and his younger brother Xiǎo Yǐ ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Xiǎo Yǐ.
Emperor Xiǎo Yǐ passed away,
and his son Emperor Wǔ Dīng ascended the throne.
Emperor Wǔ Dīng ascended the throne,
wishing to revive the Yīn dynasty,
yet had not found a competent assistant.
For three years, he did not speak,
leaving decisions to the Chief Minister,
observing the ways of the state.
Wǔ Dīng dreamed one night of a sage,
named Yuè.
He checked all his ministers and officials,
but none matched the dream.
He then ordered craftsmen to search in the wilds,
finding Yuè among the rugged terrain.
At that time, Yuè was a laborer, constructing at the rugged terrain.
When presented to Wǔ Dīng,
Wǔ Dīng recognized him.
After conversing,
he indeed was a sage,
and was appointed as prime minister,
resulting in great governance for Yīn.
Thus, he adopted the surname Fùxiǎn,
and was named Fù Yuè.
Emperor Wǔ Dīng sacrificed to Chéng Tāng,
and the next day,
a flying pheasant perched on the cauldron's handle and cried out,
causing Wǔ Dīng to fear.
Zǔ Jǐ said:
"O King, do not worry,
first refine the governance."
Zǔ Jǐ instructed the King, saying:
"Only Heaven observes below and establishes its justice,
granting years long or short,
not by cutting the people short,
but ending their mandate.
The people cannot sustain virtue,
do not heed guilt,
Heaven affirms the mandate, correcting their virtue."
Then he said, "What can be done?"
Alas!
The king's heir should revere the people,
for none are not successors of Heaven,
and in regular sacrifices, do not perform rites that abandon the Way."
Wǔdīng improved governance and practiced virtue,
and all under heaven rejoiced,
leading to the revival of the Yīn dynasty.
Emperor Wǔdīng passed away,
and his son, Emperor Zǔgēng, ascended the throne.
Zǔjǐ praised Wǔdīng for regarding the auspicious pheasant as a virtue,
established a temple for him as Gāozōng,
and thus composed "Gāozōng Róng Rì" and "Xùn."
Emperor Zǔgēng passed away,
and his younger brother Zǔjiǎ ascended,
known as Emperor Jiǎ.
Emperor Jiǎ was decadent and chaotic,
and Yīn declined once more.
Emperor Jiǎ passed away,
and his son Emperor Lǐnxīn ascended.
Emperor Lǐnxīn passed away,
and his younger brother Gēngdīng ascended,
known as Emperor Gēngdīng.
Emperor Gēngdīng passed away,
and his son Emperor Wǔyǐ ascended.
Yīn again left Bó,
moving north of the river.
Emperor Wǔyǐ was unprincipled,
crafting figurines
and calling them heavenly gods.
He gambled with them,
having people move for them.
When the heavenly gods lost,
he would insult and humiliate them.
He made leather bags,
filled them with blood,
and shot arrows upward at them,
calling it "shooting at heaven."
While Wǔyǐ was hunting between the Hé and Wèi rivers,
a violent thunderstorm arose,
and Wǔyǐ was struck dead by lightning.
His son Emperor Tàidīng ascended.
Emperor Tàidīng passed away,
and his son Emperor Yǐ ascended.
With Emperor Yǐ's ascension,
Yīn declined further.
Emperor Yǐ's eldest son was Wēizǐ Qǐ,
but because Qǐ's mother was of low status,
he could not succeed to the throne.
The younger son was Xīn,
whose mother was the legitimate queen,
so Xīn became the heir.
Emperor Yǐ passed away,
and his son Xīn ascended,
known as Emperor Xīn,
whom all under heaven called Zhòu.
Emperor Zhòu was gifted, discerning, quick, and sharp;
his hearing and sight were exceptionally keen;
his physical strength surpassed others,
able to wrestle fierce beasts with his bare hands;
his wisdom was sufficient to reject advice,
and his words were enough to conceal wrongs;
he boasted of his abilities to his ministers,
elevated his reputation above all under heaven,
believing everyone was beneath him.
He indulged in heavy drinking and wanton pleasure,
and was infatuated with women.
He loved Dájǐ,
and followed whatever Dájǐ said.
Thus, he had the musician Juān create new, decadent music,
the Běilǐ dance,
and seductive melodies.
He heavily increased taxes to fill the Lùtái with money,
and overflowed the Jùqiáo with grain.
He collected more dogs, horses, and rare objects,
filling his palaces to capacity.
He further expanded the Shāqiū gardens and towers,
gathering many wild animals and birds to place within them.
He showed disrespect to the gods and spirits.
He held grand gatherings of music and entertainment at Shāqiū,
using wine to form a pool,
hanging meat to form a forest,
having men and women strip naked
and chase each other among them,
engaging in all-night drinking.
The common people resented this, and some feudal lords rebelled,
so Zhòu imposed severe punishments,
including the páogé method.
He appointed Xībó Chāng, Jiǔhóu, and Èhóu as the Three Dukes.
Jiǔhóu had a beautiful daughter,
whom he presented to Zhòu.
Jiǔhóu's daughter did not enjoy debauchery,
so Zhòu grew angry,
killed her,
and made Jiǔhóu into minced meat.
Èhóu strongly protested this,
arguing fervently,
and was also made into dried meat.
When Xībó Chāng heard of this,
he sighed in secret.
Chónghóu Hǔ learned of it,
reported it to Zhòu,
and Zhòu imprisoned Xībó in Yǒulǐ.
Xībó's ministers, such as Hóng Yāo and others,
sought beautiful women, rare objects, and fine horses to present to Zhòu,
and Zhòu then pardoned Xībó.
After his release, Xībó offered the land west of Luò
to request the abolition of the páogé punishment.
Zhòu agreed,
bestowed bows, arrows, axes, and battle-axes upon him,
enabling him to conduct campaigns,
and made him Xībó.
He appointed Fèi Zhòng to handle governance.
Fèi Zhòng was skilled at flattery,
loved profit,
and the Yīn people did not trust him.
Zhòu also employed È Lái.
È Lái was adept at slander and defamation,
causing the feudal lords to grow more distant.
Xībó returned to his domain,
secretly cultivating virtue and doing good,
and many feudal lords defected from Zhòu to join Xībó.
Xībó's influence grew,
and Zhòu gradually lost power and authority as a result.
Prince Bǐgān remonstrated with him,
but he would not listen.
Shāng Róng was a worthy man,
beloved by the people,
but Zhòu dismissed him.
When Xībó attacked the Jī state,
and destroyed it,
Zhòu's minister Zǔyī
heard of it and blamed Zhōu,
grew fearful,
and rushed to report to Zhòu, saying:
"Heaven has already ended our Yīn mandate,
and though we consult the great turtle,
none dare say it is auspicious.
It is not that the former kings do not aid us, their descendants,
but that the king, through debauchery and cruelty, has brought about his own ruin,
so Heaven has abandoned us,
leaving us without secure sustenance,
unable to understand Heaven's will,
and not following the statutes.
Now our people all wish for your demise,
saying, 'Why does Heaven not send down its wrath,
why does the great mandate not come?'
What will the king do now?"
Zhòu said, "Was I not born with a mandate from Heaven?"
Zǔyī returned,
and said:
"Zhòu cannot be remonstrated with anymore."
After Xībó passed away,
King Wǔ of Zhōu marched east to attack,
reaching Mèngjīn,
where eight hundred feudal lords, having defected from Yīn, joined Zhōu.
The feudal lords all said:
"Zhòu can be attacked."
King Wǔ said:
"You do not yet know Heaven's mandate."
So he returned.
Zhòu grew even more decadent and unrestrained.
Wēizǐ repeatedly remonstrated to no avail,
so he consulted with the Grand Tutor and Junior Tutor,
and then left.
Bǐgān said:
"As a minister,
one must strive even at the cost of death."
So he strongly remonstrated with Zhòu.
Zhòu angrily said:
"I have heard that a sage's heart has seven openings."
He cut open Bǐgān
to examine his heart.
Jīzǐ, in fear,
feigned madness and became a slave,
but Zhòu imprisoned him as well.
The Grand Tutor and Junior Tutor of Yīn then took their sacrificial instruments and fled to Zhōu.
King Wǔ of Zhōu then led the feudal lords to attack Zhòu.
Zhòu also mobilized his troops to resist them at Mùyě.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Zhòu's army was defeated.
Zhòu fled inside,
ascended the Lùtái,
put on his jade-adorned robes,
and threw himself into the fire to die.
King Wǔ of Zhōu then beheaded King Zhòu,
hanging his head on the great
white flag.
He executed Dájǐ.
He released Jīzǐ from imprisonment,
constructed a tomb for Bǐgān,
and erected a memorial gate for Shāng Róng.
He enfeoffed King Zhòu's son Wǔ Gēng Lùfù,
to continue the sacrifices of the Yīn dynasty,
ordering him to practice the governance of Pángēng.
The people of Yīn were greatly pleased.
Thereupon, King Wǔ of Zhōu became the Son of Heaven.
Later generations demoted the title of Emperor,
designating it as King.
And they enfeoffed the descendants of Yīn as feudal lords,
subordinate to Zhōu.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu died,
Wǔ Gēng, along with Guǎn Shū and Cài Shū, rebelled.
King Chéng ordered the Duke of Zhōu to execute them,
and established Wēizǐ in Sòng,
to continue the Yīn lineage.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I have compiled the affairs of Xié from the "Odes,"
from Chéng Tāng onward,
drawing from the "Book of Documents" and the "Book of Songs."
Xié's lineage bore the surname Zǐ,
and his descendants were enfeoffed,
taking their states as surnames,
including Yīnshì, Láishì, Sòngshì, Kōngtóngshì, Zhìshì,
Běiyīnshì, and Mùyíshì.
Confucius said,
the Yīn dynasty's chariots were excellent,
and they esteemed the color white.
Hòu Jì of Zhōu,
was named Qì.
His mother was a woman of the Táishì clan,
named Jiāng Yuán.
Jiāng Yuán was the principal consort of Emperor Kù.
Jiāng Yuán went into the wilderness,
saw a giant's footprint,
felt joyful in her heart,
and desired to step in it.
Upon stepping in it, her body moved as if she were pregnant.
After the due time, she gave birth to a child,
considering it inauspicious,
she abandoned it in a narrow alley,
but horses and oxen passing by all avoided stepping on it;
she moved it to a forest,
but it happened that many people were in the mountains and forests,
so she moved it again;
then she abandoned it on the ice in a ditch,
but birds covered and cushioned it with their wings.
Jiāng Yuán considered it divine,
and thus took it back to raise.
Initially intending to abandon it,
she named it Qì.
When Qì was a child,
he had the lofty ambitions of a great man.
In his play,
he enjoyed planting hemp and beans,
and his hemp and beans were excellent.
When he grew up,
he became fond of farming,
observing the suitability of the land,
and cultivating grains where appropriate,
and the people all followed his example.
Emperor Yáo heard of this,
appointed Qì as Minister of Agriculture,
and the world benefited from it,
achieving great merit.
Emperor Shùn said:
"Qì,
when the common people began to starve,
you, Hòu Jì, sowed the various grains in season."
He enfeoffed Qì in Tái,
bestowing the title Hòu Jì,
with the separate surname Jī.
The rise of Hòu Jì
occurred during the times of Táo Táng,
Yú, and Xià,
all known for their virtuous conduct.
When Hòu Jì died,
his son Bù Zhú succeeded him.
In the late years of Bù Zhú,
the governance of the Xià Hòu clan declined,
abandoning the office of Jì and neglecting its duties.
Bù Zhú, having lost his official position, fled among the Róng and Dí tribes.
When Bù Zhú died,
his son Jū succeeded him.
When Jū died,
his son Gōng Liú succeeded him.
Although Gōng Liú lived among the Róng and Dí tribes,
he restored the work of Hòu Jì,
focusing on farming,
and utilizing the land appropriately.
He crossed the Wèi River from Qī and Jǔ,
gathering materials for use,
so that travelers had resources,
and settlers had stored provisions.
The people relied on his blessings.
The common people cherished him,
and many moved to follow and rely on him.
The rise of the Zhōu way began from this,
hence poets sang joyfully of his virtue.
When Gōng Liú died,
his son Qìng Jié succeeded him,
establishing his state in Bīn.
When Qìng Jié died,
his son Huáng Pú succeeded him.
When Huáng Pú died,
his son Chāi Fú succeeded him.
When Chāi Fú died,
his son Huǐ Yú succeeded him.
When Huǐ Yú died,
his son Gōng Fēi succeeded him.
When Gōng Fēi died,
his son Gāo Yǔ succeeded him.
When Gāo Yǔ died,
his son Yà Yǔ succeeded him.
When Yà Yǔ died,
his son Gōng Shū Zǔ Lèi succeeded him.
When Gōng Shū Zǔ Lèi died,
his son Gǔ Gōng Dǎn Fù succeeded him.
Gǔ Gōng Dǎn Fù restored the work of Hòu Jì and Gōng Liú,
accumulating virtue and practicing righteousness,
and the people of the state all supported him.
The Xūnyù Róng and Dí tribes attacked him,
wanting to obtain wealth and goods,
and he gave it to them.
They attacked again,
wanting land and people.
The people were all angry,
and wanted to fight.
Gǔ Gōng said:
"The people establish a ruler
to benefit them.
Now the Róng and Dí attack and fight
for our land and people.
Whether the people are with me,
or with them,
what difference does it make?
If the people fight because of me,
killing fathers and sons to rule over them,
I cannot bear to do it."
So he left Bīn with his private followers,
crossed the Qī and Jǔ rivers,
crossed over Liáng Mountain,
and settled at the foot of Qí Mountain.
The people of Bīn, the entire state supporting the elderly and carrying the weak,
all returned to Gǔ Gōng at the foot of Qí Mountain.
When other neighboring states heard of Gǔ Gōng's benevolence,
many also came to join him.
Thereupon, Gǔ Gōng abandoned the customs of the Róng and Dí,
and built city walls, houses, and dwellings,
establishing separate settlements.
He established five officials with administrative duties.
The people all sang joyfully of him,
praising his virtue.
Gǔ Gōng had an eldest son named Tàibó,
and a second named Yú Zhòng.
Tài Jiāng gave birth to a youngest son, Jì Lì.
Jì Lì married Tài Rén,
both were virtuous women,
and she gave birth to Chāng,
who had auspicious signs of sagehood.
Gǔ Gōng said:
"Our lineage is destined to have one who will rise,
is it not Chāng?"
The eldest sons Tàibó and Yú Zhòng knew that Gǔ Gōng wished to establish Jì Lì to pass the throne to Chāng,
so the two fled to the land of the Jīng Mán,
tattooed their bodies and cut their hair,
to yield to Jì Lì.
When Gǔ Gōng died,
Jì Lì succeeded him,
known as Gōng Jì.
Gōng Jì continued the legacy of Gǔ Gōng,
devoted to practicing righteousness,
and the feudal lords submitted to him.
When Gōng Jì died,
his son Chāng succeeded him,
known as the Earl of the West.
The Earl of the West was called King Wén,
who followed the work of Hòu Jì and Gōng Liú,
emulated the laws of Gǔ Gōng and Gōng Jì,
was deeply benevolent,
respected the elderly,
and was kind to the young.
He treated the worthy with courtesy,
and was so busy receiving scholars that he had no time to eat at midday,
and thus many scholars came to join him.
Bóyí and Shūqí were in Gūzhú when
they heard that Xībó excelled at caring for the elderly,
so why not go and submit to him?
Tàidiān, Hóngyāo, Sǎnyíshēng, Yùzǐ, Xīnjiǎ dàfū, and their followers all went to submit to him.
Chónghóu Hǔ slandered Xībó to Yīn Zhòu, saying:
"Xībó accumulates good deeds and virtues,
and all the feudal lords are drawn to him,
which will be detrimental to the emperor."
Emperor Zhòu then imprisoned Xībó in Yǒulǐ.
Hóngyāo and his followers were troubled by this,
so they sought a beautiful woman from the Yǒushēn clan,
the patterned horses of Líróng,
nine teams of horses from Yǒuxióng,
and other rare and exotic items,
and through the favor of Yīn's corrupt official Fèi Zhòng, presented them to Zhòu.
Zhòu was greatly pleased,
saying:
"This one item alone is enough to release Xībó,
let alone so many!"
He then pardoned Xībó,
bestowed upon him bows, arrows, axes, and battle-axes,
and allowed Xībó to conduct military campaigns.
He said:
"The one who slandered Xībó
was Chónghóu Hǔ."
Xībó then offered the land west of Luò
to request that Zhòu abolish the punishment of the roasting grid.
Zhòu agreed.
Xībó secretly practiced good deeds,
and feudal lords all came to him to settle disputes.
At that time, the people of Yú and Ruì
had a legal dispute they could not resolve,
so they went to Zhōu.
Upon entering the territory,
they saw farmers yielding the boundaries of their fields,
and the custom among the people was to yield to elders.
The people of Yú and Ruì had not yet met Xībó,
but they were already ashamed,
saying to each other:
"What we contend over
is what the people of Zhōu consider shameful.
Why go further,
only to bring humiliation upon ourselves?"
They then turned back,
both yielding and departing.
The feudal lords heard of this,
saying, "Xībó is indeed the ruler who has received the Mandate."
The following year,
he attacked the Quǎnróng.
The next year,
he attacked Mìxū.
The next year,
he defeated the state of Qí.
Zǔ Yī of Yīn heard of this,
became fearful,
and reported it to Emperor Zhòu.
Zhòu said:
"Do I not have the Mandate of Heaven? What can he do!"
The next year,
he attacked Yú.
The next year,
he attacked Chónghóu Hǔ.
He then built the city of Fēng,
moving the capital from below Qí to Fēng.
The next year,
Xībó passed away,
and the crown prince Fā ascended,
becoming King Wǔ.
Xībó had reigned for fifty years.
During his imprisonment in Yǒulǐ,
he expanded the eight trigrams of the *Yì* to sixty-four hexagrams.
The poets spoke of Xībó,
saying that in the year he received the Mandate, he was called king and settled the dispute between Yú and Ruì.
He passed away ten years later,
and was posthumously honored as King Wén.
He reformed the laws and institutions,
and established the calendar.
He posthumously honored Gǔgōng as Tàiwáng,
and Gōngjì as Wángjì:
indeed, the royal auspices began with Tàiwáng.
When King Wǔ ascended the throne,
Tàigōng Wàng became his teacher,
Zhōugōng Dàn served as his assistant,
and Shàogōng, Bìgōng, and their followers supported the king,
all continuing the legacy of King Wén.
In the ninth year,
King Wǔ offered sacrifices at Bì.
He then reviewed his troops eastward,
reaching Méngjīn.
He made a wooden spirit tablet for King Wén,
carried it on a chariot,
and placed it in the central army.
King Wǔ referred to himself as Crown Prince Fā,
stating that he was following King Wén's will to attack,
not daring to act on his own authority.
He then addressed the Minister of War, Minister of Education, Minister of Works, and various officers:
"Be reverent and sincere! Truly,
I am without knowledge,
