but because my ancestors had virtuous ministers,
I, a humble descendant, inherit their achievements.
Establish rewards and punishments fully,
to secure their merits."
Thus, he raised an army.
Shīshàngfǔ commanded:
"Assemble your multitudes,
and bring your boats and oars;
those who arrive late will be executed."
As King Wǔ crossed the river,
in midstream,
a white fish leaped into the king's boat,
and King Wǔ bent down to retrieve it for sacrifice.
After crossing,
a fire descended from above to below,
reaching the king's roof,
and transformed into a crow,
its color red,
its cry resounding.
At that time,
eight hundred feudal lords gathered at Méngjīn without prior arrangement.
The feudal lords all said:
"Zhòu can be attacked."
But King Wǔ said:
"You do not yet know the Mandate of Heaven;
it is not yet time."
He then withdrew his army and returned.
After two years,
hearing that Zhòu had become even more chaotic and tyrannical,
killing Prince Bǐgān,
and imprisoning Jīzǐ.
Grand Master Cī and Junior Master Qiáng fled to Zhōu with their musical instruments.
Thereupon, King Wǔ announced to all the feudal lords:
"Yīn has committed grave crimes,
and we must fully attack them."
Following King Wén's will,
he led three hundred war chariots,
three thousand elite warriors,
and forty-five thousand armored soldiers,
marching east to attack Zhòu.
In the eleventh year, on the twelfth month, day Wǔwǔ,
the army fully crossed Méngjīn,
and all the feudal lords gathered.
They said: "Be diligent and do not slacken!"
King Wǔ then composed the "Great Declaration,"
addressing the multitudes:
"Now, King Zhòu of Yīn follows the words of his woman,
cutting himself off from Heaven,
destroying the three pillars of governance,
alienating his paternal uncles and brothers,
abandoning the music of his ancestors,
indulging in decadent tunes,
corrupting proper music,
to please his woman.
Therefore, I, Fā, now carry out Heaven's punishment.
Strive, my men!
Do not let it happen a second time,
nor a third!"
In the second month, at dawn on day Jiǎzǐ,
King Wǔ arrived in the morning at the outskirts of Shāng, at Mùyě,
and made his pledge.
King Wǔ held a yellow battle-axe in his left hand,
and a white banner in his right,
waving it to command.
He said: "Far have you come, people of the western lands!"
King Wǔ continued:
"Ah!
My great lords of the states,
Ministers of Education, War, and Works,
commanders and officers,
leaders of thousands and hundreds,
and men of Yōng, Shǔ, Qiāng, Máo, Wēi, Lú, Péng, and Pú,
raise your spears,
align your shields,
set up your spears,
and I will declare my pledge."
The king said: "The ancients had a saying, 'A hen does not announce the morning.
If a hen crows in the morning,
it brings ruin to the household.'
Now, King Zhòu of Yīn only follows the words of his woman,
abandoning the sacrifices to his ancestors without response,
recklessly forsaking his state and family,
casting aside his paternal uncles and brothers without employing them,
instead honoring and elevating fugitives from all corners who have committed many crimes,
trusting and employing them,
allowing them to oppress the common people,
and commit treachery in the land of Shāng.
Now, I, Fā, carry out Heaven's punishment.
In today's battle,
do not advance more than six or seven steps,
then halt and regroup."
Strive, my lord!
Do not exceed four, five, six, or seven strokes in battle,
then halt and array your forces.
Strive, my lord!
Be awe-inspiring,
like tigers and bears,
like jackals and dragons,
at the outskirts of Shāng.
Do not resist those who flee,
but employ them to serve the western lands.
Strive, my lord!
If you do not strive,
your body will face execution."
After the oath was sworn,
the assembled forces of the feudal lords numbered four thousand chariots,
arrayed at Mùyě.
When King Dì Zhòu heard of King Wǔ's arrival,
he also mobilized seven hundred thousand troops to confront King Wǔ.
King Wǔ sent Shī Shàngfù and a hundred warriors to challenge the enemy,
then charged King Dì Zhòu's army with his main force.
Though Zhòu's army was numerous,
none had the heart to fight,
their minds wishing for King Wǔ to swiftly enter.
Zhòu's soldiers turned their weapons to fight
and cleared the way for King Wǔ.
King Wǔ charged forward,
and Zhòu's troops crumbled and rebelled against him.
Zhòu fled,
returning to ascend the Lùtái platform,
draped in his rare jades,
and died by throwing himself into the fire.
King Wǔ, holding the great white banner, signaled the feudal lords,
who all bowed to King Wǔ.
King Wǔ then bowed in return to the feudal lords,
and they all followed him.
King Wǔ arrived at the Shāng capital,
where all the commoners awaited at the outskirts.
Thereupon, King Wǔ ordered his ministers to announce to the Shāng people:
"Heaven has bestowed blessings!"
The Shāng people all bowed twice and kowtowed,
and King Wǔ returned the bow.
He then entered
and reached the place where Zhòu had died.
King Wǔ shot arrows at him himself,
three times before dismounting,
struck him with a light sword,
and beheaded Zhòu with a yellow battle-axe,
hanging the head on the great white banner.
Then he came to Zhòu's two favored concubines,
who had both hanged themselves.
King Wǔ shot three more arrows,
struck them with his sword,
beheaded them with a black battle-axe,
and hung their heads on the small white banner.
King Wǔ then exited and returned to the army.
The next day,
he cleared the roads,
repaired the altars of the land and the palace of Shāng Zhòu.
At the appointed time,
a hundred men bearing rare banners led the way.
King Wǔ's younger brother Shū Zhènduó presented the ceremonial chariot,
Zhōu Gōngdàn held the great battle-axe,
Bì Gōng held the small battle-axe,
flanking King Wǔ.
Sǎn Yíshēng, Tàidiān, and Hóng Yāo all held swords to guard King Wǔ.
After entering,
they stood to the left of the main force south of the altar,
with all attendants following.
Máo Shūzhèng presented clear water,
Wèi Kāngshūfēng spread the mat,
Shào Gōngshì assisted with silks,
and Shī Shàngfù led the sacrificial animal.
Yǐn Yì read the prayer, saying:
"The last descendant of Yīn, Jí Zhòu,
abandoned and discarded the bright virtue of the former kings,
insulted and scorned the spirits, neglecting sacrifices,
tyrannized and oppressed the people of the Shāng city,
his crimes clearly known to the Heavenly Emperor."
Thereupon, King Wǔ bowed twice and kowtowed,
saying:
"I have received the great mandate,
overthrown Yīn,
and accepted Heaven's bright mandate."
King Wǔ again bowed twice and kowtowed,
then departed.
He enfeoffed Zhòu's son Lùfù with the remaining people of Yīn.
As Yīn was newly pacified and not yet settled,
King Wǔ sent his younger brothers Guǎn Shūxiān and Cài Shūdù to assist Lùfù in governing Yīn.
Then he ordered Shào Gōng to release Jīzǐ from imprisonment.
Ordered Bì Gōng to release the imprisoned commoners,
and erected a memorial at Shāng Róng's lane.
Ordered Nángōng Kuò to distribute the wealth from the Lùtái,
open the granaries at Jùqiáo,
to relieve the poor and weak, the commoners and slaves.
Ordered Nángōng Kuò and Shǐ Yì to display the Nine Cauldrons and precious jades.
Ordered Hóng Yāo to raise a mound over Bǐgān's tomb.
Ordered the ancestral priests to offer sacrifices in the army.
Then he withdrew the troops and returned west.
He conducted inspections,
recorded governmental affairs,
and composed the "Wǔchéng".
He enfeoffed feudal lords,
distributed ancestral vessels,
and composed the "Fēn Yīn zhī Qìwù".
King Wǔ, reflecting on the former sage kings,
honorably enfeoffed the descendants of Shénnóng at Jiāo,
the descendants of Huángdì at Zhù,
the descendants of Emperor Yáo at Jì,
the descendants of Emperor Shùn at Chén,
and the descendants of Great Yǔ at Qǐ.
Then he enfeoffed meritorious ministers and strategists,
with Shī Shàngfù as the first enfeoffed.
He enfeoffed Shàngfù at Yíngqiū,
called Qí.
Enfeoffed his younger brother Zhōu Gōngdàn at Qūfù,
called Lǔ.
Enfeoffed Shào Gōngshì at Yān.
Enfeoffed his younger brother Shūxiān at Guǎn,
and his younger brother Shūdù at Cài.
The rest were enfeoffed in order.
King Wǔ summoned the lords of the nine provinces,
ascended the heights of Bīn,
and gazed toward the Shāng capital.
When King Wǔ returned to Zhōu,
he did not sleep all night.
Zhōu Gōngdàn went to the king's place and said,
"Why do you not sleep?"
The king said:
"I tell you:
Heaven did not accept the sacrifices of Yīn,
from before my birth until now, sixty years,
when deer roamed the pastures,
and insects filled the fields.
Heaven did not favor Yīn,
and only now have we achieved success.
Heaven established Yīn,
appointing three hundred sixty worthy men,
yet they neither flourished nor perished,
until now.
I have not yet secured Heaven's protection,
how could I find time to sleep!"
The king said:
"To secure Heaven's protection,
rely on the Heavenly Temple,
seek out all the evil ones,
punish them as King Shòu of Yīn was.
Day and night, labor to pacify our western lands,
so that I may clearly serve,
and virtue will be fully manifest.
From Luòruì extending to Yīruì,
dwell in ease without fortifications,
for it was the dwelling of the Xià.
I look south to Sāntú,
north to Yuèbǐ,
gaze upon the Hé River,
observe Luò and Yī,
not far from the Heavenly Temple."
He established a Zhōu residence at Luòyì and then left.
He released the horses on the sunny side of Huà Shān,
set the cattle free in the wilderness of Táolín;
laid aside shields and spears,
disbanded the troops and released the armies:
showing the world they would not be used again.
After King Wǔ had conquered Yīn,
two years later,
he asked Jīzǐ why Yīn fell.
Jīzǐ could not bear to speak of Yīn's evils,
so he discussed the principles of preserving or losing a state.
King Wǔ felt ashamed, so he asked about the Way of Heaven.
King Wǔ fell ill.
The world was not yet settled, and the lords feared,
so they solemnly divined.
Zhōu Gōng then purified himself and fasted, offering himself as a substitute for King Wǔ,
and King Wǔ recovered.
Later, he passed away,
and the crown prince Sòng succeeded him,
becoming King Chéng.
King Chéng was young,
and Zhōu had newly stabilized the world,
so Zhōu Gōng feared the feudal lords would rebel against Zhōu.
He thus acted as regent, administering the government and ruling the state.
Guǎn Shū, Cài Shū, and the other brothers suspected Zhōu Gōng,
and together with Wǔ Gēng, they started a rebellion,
betraying Zhōu.
Zhōu Gōng, upholding King Chéng's order,
attacked and executed Wǔ Gēng and Guǎn Shū,
and exiled Cài Shū.
He appointed Wēizǐ Kāi to succeed the Yīn lineage,
establishing the state of Sòng.
He gathered the remaining people of Yīn,
and enfeoffed King Wǔ's younger brother Fēng as Wèi Kāngshū.
Jìn Tángshū obtained excellent grain,
and presented it to King Chéng,
who sent it to the Duke of Zhōu at his military camp.
The Duke of Zhōu received the grain in the eastern lands,
and proclaimed the Son of Heaven's mandate.
Earlier,
Guǎn and Cài had rebelled against Zhōu,
and the Duke of Zhōu campaigned against them,
completing the pacification after three years,
hence he first composed the "Great Announcement",
next the "Charge to Wēizǐ",
then "Returning the Grain",
then "Excellent Grain",
then "Announcement to Kāng", "Announcement about Drunkenness", and "Rǔn Wood",
the events of which are recorded in the chapter on the Duke of Zhōu.
The Duke of Zhōu administered the government for seven years,
until King Chéng came of age,
whereupon the Duke of Zhōu returned the government to King Chéng,
and took his place facing north among the ranks of ministers.
King Chéng was in Fēng,
and sent Shào Gōng to again build the city of Luòyì,
in accordance with King Wǔ's intention.
The Duke of Zhōu again divined and inspected it,
finally completing its construction,
and settled the nine tripods there.
He said:
"This is the center of the world,
equidistant for the tribute journeys from the four quarters."
He composed the "Announcement of Shào" and "Announcement concerning Luò".
After King Chéng had relocated the remaining people of Yīn,
the Duke of Zhōu proclaimed it with the king's mandate,
composing "The Numerous Officers" and "Against Luxurious Ease".
Shào Gōng served as Grand Guardian,
the Duke of Zhōu as Grand Tutor,
and they campaigned east against the Huáiyí,
destroyed Yǎn,
and moved its lord to Bógū.
King Chéng returned from Yǎn,
and while in Zōngzhōu,
composed "The Numerous Regions".
After having ended the Yīn mandate,
and attacked the Huáiyí,
he returned to Fēng,
and composed "The Officers of Zhōu".
He revived and rectified the rites and music,
whereupon regulations and institutions were reformed,
and the people lived in harmony,
with songs of praise arising.
After King Chéng had campaigned against the Eastern Yí,
Xīshèn came to congratulate him,
and the king bestowed gifts upon Róng Bó and composed "The Charge to the Xīshèn about the Gifts".
As King Chéng was about to die,
he feared that the crown prince Zhāo was not fit for the task,
so he ordered Shào Gōng and Bì Gōng to lead the feudal lords in assisting the crown prince and establishing him.
After King Chéng's death,
the two dukes led the feudal lords,
and presented crown prince Zhāo in the temple of the former kings,
earnestly instructing him on how King Wén and King Wǔ had established the royal enterprise with great difficulty,
emphasizing frugality,
and warning against excessive desires,
urging him to rule with sincerity and faithfulness,
composing "The Testamentary Charge".
Crown prince Zhāo was then established,
becoming King Kāng.
When King Kāng ascended the throne,
he announced it widely to the feudal lords,
proclaiming and reaffirming the enterprise of King Wén and King Wǔ,
composing "The Announcement to Kāng".
Thus, during the era of Kings Chéng and Kāng,
the world was peaceful and tranquil,
and punishments were set aside unused for over forty years.
King Kāng ordered the scribe Bì Gōng to divide the settlements and neighborhoods,
completing the suburbs of Chéngzhōu,
and composed "The Charge to Bì".
After King Kāng's death,
his son King Zhāo, Xiá, was established.
During King Zhāo's time,
the Kingly Way was slightly deficient.
King Zhāo went on an inspection tour south and did not return,
dying by the Jiāng River.
His death was not announced to the feudal lords,
to conceal the matter.
His son Mǎn was established,
becoming King Mù.
When King Mù ascended the throne,
he was already fifty years old.
The Kingly Way was in decline,
and King Mù, concerned about the deterioration of the ways of King Wén and King Wǔ,
ordered Bó Jiǒng to reiterate admonitions on the governance of the state to the Grand Servant,
composing "The Charge to Jiǒng".
Peace was restored.
When King Mù intended to campaign against the Quǎnróng,
Zhài Gōng Móufǔ admonished him, saying:
"It cannot be done.
The former kings displayed virtue, not military power.
Weapons are stored and only used at the proper time;
when used, they inspire awe;
displaying them leads to contempt;
contempt leads to loss of awe.
Therefore, the ode by Duke Zhōu of Wén says:
'Store up your shields and spears,
sheathe your bows and arrows;
I seek virtuous conduct,
to spread throughout this Xià,
truly the king preserves it.'
The former kings, in their treatment of the people,
cultivated their correct virtue and enriched their nature,
increased their wealth and improved their tools,
clarified the directions of benefit and harm,
and cultivated them with culture,
making them pursue benefits and avoid harms,
cherish virtue and fear authority,
thus they were able to preserve their lineage and make it flourish. In the past, our former kings, generations of Hòujì,
served Yú and Xià.
When Xià declined,
they abandoned agriculture,
and our former king Bù Zhú lost his office,
and fled among the Róng and Dí.
He did not dare neglect his work,
constantly cultivating his virtue,
following and cultivating his heritage,
cultivating his teachings and statutes,
diligent morning and night,
guarding it with earnest sincerity,
upholding it with loyalty and faithfulness.
Generation after generation carried on virtue,
not disgracing their predecessors.
Reaching King Wén and King Wǔ,
they illuminated the former brilliance and added kindness and harmony,
serving the spirits and protecting the people,
none were not pleased.
The Shāng king Dì Xīn was greatly hated by the people,
and the common people could not endure it,
gladly supporting King Wǔ,
leading to the campaign at Shāngmù.
Thus, the former kings were not intent on military force,
but diligently sympathized with the people's sufferings and removed their harms.
The system of the former kings was:
within the royal domain, Diàn service;
outside the royal domain, Hóu service;
beyond the Hóu domains, Bīn service;
for the Yí and Mán, Yāo service;
for the Róng and Dí, Huāng service.
Diàn service involves daily sacrifices,
Hóu service involves monthly sacrifices,
Bīn service involves seasonal offerings,
Yāo service involves annual tribute,
Huāng service involves acknowledging the king's suzerainty.
Daily sacrifices,
monthly sacrifices,
seasonal offerings,
annual tribute,
and once-in-a-lifetime acknowledgment.
The former kings, in following the sacrifices,
if there was failure in daily sacrifice, they cultivated their intent;
if failure in monthly sacrifice, they cultivated their speech;
if failure in seasonal offerings, they cultivated their culture;
if failure in annual tribute, they cultivated their reputation;
if failure in acknowledgment, they cultivated their virtue;
if after these steps in order there was still non-compliance, then they cultivated punishments.
Thus, there were punishments for failure in daily sacrifice,
attacks for failure in monthly sacrifice,
campaigns for failure in seasonal offerings,
reprimands for failure in annual tribute,
proclamations for failure in acknowledgment.
Thus, there were laws for punishments,
armies for attacks,
preparations for campaigns,
commands of威严 reprimands,
and proclamations in writing.
If after issuing orders and proclamations there was still non-compliance,
then they further cultivated their virtue,
and did not toil the people with distant campaigns.
Therefore, those nearby all obeyed,
and those far away all submitted.
Now, since the deaths of Dà Bì and Bó Shì,
the Quǎnróng have come to acknowledge the king according to their duty,
and the Son of Heaven says,
'I must campaign against them for failing in seasonal offerings,
and display my military power to them',
is this not abandoning the instructions of the former kings,
and jeopardizing the king's rule?
I have heard that the Quǎnróng have established steadfastness,
following their old virtue and steadfastly maintaining their constancy,
and they have means to resist us."
The king nevertheless campaigned against them,
and obtained four white wolves and four white deer before returning.
From then on, those in the Huāng service did not come.
When the feudal lords showed signs of discord,
Fǔ Hóu advised the king,
leading to the revision of penal laws.
The king said:
"Alas,
come!
You who possess states and lands,
I announce to you the principles of just punishment.
In pacifying the people today,
what should you choose if not the right persons?
What should you respect if not the penalties?
What should you establish if not what is appropriate?
When both parties are present,
the judges should hear the five types of testimony.
If the testimonies are clear and credible,
they are verified against the five punishments.
If they do not align with the five punishments,
they are verified against the five fines.
If the five fines are not accepted,
they are verified against the five oversights.
The flaws in the five oversights,
whether in official or internal cases,
must be examined to ascertain the crime,
only then balancing the fault.
If there is doubt in the five punishments, grant pardon;
if there is doubt in the five fines, grant pardon;
scrutinize them thoroughly.
Gather the masses for clarity and credibility,
and ensure that interrogations are meticulous.
Without clarity, there is no doubt;
together, revere the majesty of Heaven.
For tattooing punishment with doubt, grant pardon,
the fine is one hundred units,
examine to ascertain the crime.
For nose-cutting punishment with doubt, grant pardon,
the fine is double that,
examine to ascertain the crime.
For knee-cutting punishment with doubt, grant pardon,
the fine is double with a reduction,
examine to ascertain the crime.
For castration punishment with doubt, grant pardon,
the fine is five hundred units,
examine to ascertain the crime.
For capital punishment with doubt, grant pardon,
the fine is one thousand units,
examine to ascertain the crime.
The categories of tattooing fines number a thousand,
the categories of nose-cutting fines number a thousand,
the categories of knee-cutting fines number five hundred,
the categories of castration fines number three hundred,
the categories of capital fines number two hundred:
thus, the categories of the five punishments total three thousand."
It was named "The Punishments of Fǔ."
King Mù reigned for fifty-five years,
then passed away,
and his son King Gōng, Yīhù, ascended the throne.
King Gōng was traveling along the Jīng River,
with Mì Kānggōng in his retinue,
when three women fled to him.
His mother said:
"You must present them to the king.
For beasts, three form a herd;
for people, three form a crowd;
for women, three form a splendor.
The king does not take a herd while hunting,
a lord does not dismount for a crowd,
and the king does not keep three women from the same clan.
Splendor is a thing of beauty.
If the crowd brings beautiful things to you,
what virtue do you have to bear it?
Even the king could not endure it,
how much less you, a minor figure!
A minor figure amassing such things
will surely perish in the end."
Kānggōng did not offer them,
and within a year,
King Gōng destroyed Mì.
King Gōng passed away,
and his son King Yì, Jiān, ascended the throne.
During King Yì's time,
the royal house declined,
and poets wrote satires.
King Yì passed away,
and King Gōng's younger brother, Bìfāng, ascended the throne,
becoming King Xiào.
King Xiào passed away,
and the feudal lords reinstated King Yì's crown prince, Xiè,
who became King Yí.
King Yí passed away,
and his son King Lì, Hú, ascended the throne.
In the thirtieth year of King Lì's reign,
he was fond of profit,
and drew close to Róng Yìgōng.
The minister Ruì Liángfū admonished King Lì, saying:
"Is the royal house about to decline? This Rónggōng loves monopolizing profits and does not foresee great calamity.
Profit
is produced from all things,
borne by heaven and earth,
yet to monopolize it
brings much harm.
Heaven, earth, and all things will demand it;
how can it be monopolized? It provokes much anger,
without preparing for great calamity.
To teach the king thus,
can his reign last long? A true king
should guide profits to distribute them above and below.
Ensuring that spirits, people, and all things receive their due,
he still fears the arrival of resentment daily.
Thus, the 'Odes' say:
'Think of the cultured Hòujì,
who could match heaven,
establishing our multitude of people,
none failing to reach your standard.'
The 'Great Odes' say:
'He spread blessings and founded Zhōu.'
Was this not distributing profits while fearing calamity,
thus enabling Zhōu to endure until now?
Now the king learns to monopolize profits;
is that permissible? If a commoner monopolizes profits,
he is called a robber;
if the king practices it,
few will support him.
If Rónggōng is employed,
Zhōu will surely fall."
King Lì did not listen,
and eventually appointed Rónggōng as minister,
entrusting him with affairs.
The king acted tyrannically, extravagant, and arrogant,
and the people of the state criticized him.
Shào Gōng admonished him, saying:
"The people can no longer bear your decrees."
The king grew angry,
obtained a Wèi shaman,
and set him to monitor critics,
killing those reported.
Criticism dwindled,
and the feudal lords ceased attending court.
In the thirty-fourth year,
the king intensified his severity,
and the people dared not speak,
communicating with their eyes on the roads.
King Lì was pleased,
and told Shào Gōng:
"I can silence criticism;
they dare not speak."
Shào Gōng said:
"This is blocking them.
Stopping the mouths of the people
is worse than damming water.
Water, when blocked, will burst forth,
injuring many;
so it is with the people.
Therefore, to manage water, channel it to guide it;
to manage the people, encourage them to speak.
Thus, when the son of heaven hears governance,
he has dukes, ministers, down to ranked scholars present poems,
blind musicians present songs,
historians present documents,
masters offer admonitions,
blind reciters chant,
sightless ones recite,
artisans advise,
commoners convey messages,
close attendants exhaust remonstrance,
relatives supplement and scrutinize,
blind musicians and historians teach,
elders refine it,
and only then does the king deliberate,
so affairs proceed without conflict.
The people having mouths
is like the land having mountains and rivers—
resources and goods emerge from them;
like having plains, marshes, and fertile fields—
food and clothing are born from them.
When mouths speak out,
good and bad governance arise.
Practicing good and preparing against bad
is how resources, food, and clothing are produced.
The people ponder in their hearts and speak with their mouths,
acting once formed.
If you block their mouths,
how long can you last?" The king did not listen.
Thus, none in the state dared speak out,
and after three years,
they rebelled together,
attacking King Lì.
King Lì fled to Zhì.
King Lì's heir, Jìng, hid in the household of Duke Zhào.
When the people of the state heard about it,
they surrounded the residence.
Duke Zhào said:
"In the past, I repeatedly admonished the king,
but the king did not listen,
leading to this calamity.
Now if we kill the king's heir,
would the king consider me an enemy and hold a grudge? Those who serve their ruler
face danger without harboring enmity,
bear grievances without showing anger—
how much more so when serving a king!"
So he used his own son as a substitute for the king's heir,
and the heir ultimately escaped.
Dukes Zhào and Zhōu, the two ministers, jointly administered the government,
an era called the "Gònghé Regency."
In the fourteenth year of Gònghé,
King Lì died in Zhì.
Heir Jìng, having grown up in Duke Zhào's household,
was jointly enthroned by the two ministers as king,
known as King Xuān.
Upon King Xuān's accession,
the two ministers assisted him,
repairing governance,
emulating the legacy of Kings Wén, Wǔ, Chéng, and Kāng,
and the feudal lords once again revered Zhōu.
In his twelfth year,
Duke Wǔ of Lǔ came to court.
King Xuān neglected the ceremonial plowing at Qiānmǔ,
and Duke Wén of Guó advised against it,
but the king did not listen.
In his thirty-ninth year,
a battle was fought at Qiānmǔ,
where the royal forces were defeated by the Jiāngshì Róng.
After King Xuān lost the army of the southern states,
he conducted a census of the people in Tàiyuán.
Zhòngshān Fǔ admonished him:
"The people should not be subjected to a census."
King Xuān did not heed him,
and ultimately carried out the census.
In his forty-sixth year,
King Xuān passed away,
and his son, King Yōu, Gōngshēng, succeeded him.
In the second year of King Yōu,
an earthquake struck the three rivers of Western Zhōu.
Bóyáng Fǔ said:
"Zhōu is about to perish.
For the qì of heaven and earth
must not lose their order;
if they exceed their order,
it is due to the chaos among the people.
When yáng is suppressed and cannot emerge,
and yīn is constrained and cannot ascend,
then earthquakes occur.
Now that the three rivers have indeed quaked,
it is because yáng has lost its place and is blocked by yīn.
When yáng is displaced and resides in yīn,
the river sources must be blocked;
if the sources are blocked,
the state must perish.
For it is through the flow of water and soil that the people have sustenance.
If the land has nothing to flow,
the people will lack resources,
and what awaits but destruction!
In the past, the Yi and Luò rivers dried up, and Xià perished;
the Yellow River dried up, and Shāng perished.
Now the virtue of Zhōu resembles that of the two dynasties in their decline;
its rivers and sources are again blocked,
and blockage must lead to drying up.
A state must rely on its mountains and rivers;
if mountains collapse and rivers dry up,
it is an omen of a perishing state.
When rivers dry up, mountains must collapse.
If the state perishes, it will not exceed ten years,
for that is the end of a cycle.
Those abandoned by heaven
will not outlast their cycle."
That very year,
the three rivers dried up,
and Mount Qí collapsed.
In the third year,
King Yōu became infatuated with Bāo Sì.
Bāo Sì bore a son named Bófú,
and King Yōu wished to depose the crown prince.
The crown prince's mother was the daughter of the Marquis of Shēn,
and she was the queen.
Later, King Yōu obtained Bāo Sì,
loved her,
and wanted to depose Queen Shēn,
along with removing Crown Prince Yíjiù,
making Bāo Sì queen,
and Bófú crown prince.
The Grand Historian of Zhōu, Bóyáng, reading the historical records, said:
"Zhōu is doomed."
Long ago, during the decline of the Xià clan,
two divine dragons descended into the court of the Xià emperor and said:
"We
are the two lords of Bāo."
The Xià emperor divined about killing them, driving them away, or keeping them,
but none was auspicious.
Divining about requesting their saliva and storing it
proved auspicious.
So he set out offerings and prayed to them,
the dragons left, and their saliva remained,
which was stored in a chest and removed.
When Xià perished,
this vessel was passed to Shāng.
When Shāng perished,
it was again passed to Zhōu.
Through these three dynasties,
none dared open it.
At the end of King Lì's reign,
it was opened and examined.
The saliva flowed into the court,
and could not be removed.
King Lì had women strip naked and shout at it.
The saliva transformed into a black turtle,
which entered the king's rear palace.
A young maiden in the rear palace, who had just lost her baby teeth, encountered it,
and upon reaching adulthood, became pregnant,
giving birth without a husband,
and in fear, abandoned the child.
During King Xuān's time, a girl's ballad said:
"Mulberry bow and quiver of arrowweed
will truly destroy the state of Zhōu."
Hearing this, King Xuān
ordered a couple selling these items
to be arrested and executed.
They fled on the road,
and encountered the abandoned demon child from the rear palace maiden on the path,
hearing her cry at night,
took pity and adopted her,
and the couple then fled,
running to Bāo.
When a man of Bāo committed a crime,
he requested to present the abandoned girl from the rear palace to the king
to atone for his crime.
The abandoned girl came from Bāo,
and she was Bāo Sì.
In the third year of King Yōu,
he saw her in the rear palace and loved her,
she bore a son named Bófú,
and ultimately he deposed Queen Shēn and the crown prince,
making Bāo Sì queen,
and Bófú crown prince.
Grand Historian Bóyáng said:
"The disaster is complete;
there is nothing to be done!"
Bāo Sì did not like to laugh,
and King Yōu tried every method to make her laugh,
but still she did not laugh.
King Yōu set up beacon fires and large drums,
so that when invaders came, the beacon fires would be lit.
The feudal lords all came,
but there were no invaders,
and Bāo Sì then laughed heartily.
King Yōu was pleased,
and repeatedly lit the beacon fires.
After that, he was not trusted,
and the feudal lords came less and less.
King Yōu appointed Guó Shífù as minister,
entrusting him with affairs,
and the people of the state all resented it.
Shífù was cunning and flattering,
skilled in sycophancy and fond of profit,
yet the king employed him.
He also deposed Queen Shēn
and removed the crown prince.
The Marquis of Shēn was enraged,
and allied with Zēng
and the western barbarians, the Quǎnróng, to attack King Yōu.
King Yōu lit the beacon fires to summon troops,
but no troops came.
Thus, they killed King Yōu at the foot of Mount Lí,
captured Bāo Sì,
and took all of Zhōu's treasures before leaving.
Then the feudal lords joined the Marquis of Shēn and together installed the former crown prince of King Yōu, Yíjiù,
as King Píng,
to continue the sacrifices of Zhōu.
Upon King Píng's accession,
he moved east to Luòyì,
to avoid the barbarian invaders.
During King Píng's time,
the Zhōu court declined,
the feudal states grew strong and annexed the weak,
Qí, Chǔ, Qín, and Jìn began to rise,
and governance fell to the regional lords.
In the forty-ninth year,
Duke Yǐn of Lǔ ascended the throne.
In the fifty-first year,
King Píng passed away.
The crown prince, Xièfù, had died early,
so his son Lín was established,
and he became King Huán.
King Huán
was the grandson of King Píng.
In the third year of King Huán,
Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng paid a court visit,
but King Huán did not treat him with due courtesy.
In the fifth year,
Zhèng, bearing a grudge,
exchanged the field of Xǔ with Lǔ.
The field of Xǔ
was the land used by the Son of Heaven for sacrifices at Mount Tài.
In the eighth year,
Lǔ killed Duke Yǐn
and established Duke Huán.
In the thirteenth year,
they attacked Zhèng,
and Zhèng shot and wounded King Huán.
King Huán withdrew and returned.
In the twenty-third year,
King Huán passed away,
and his son, King Zhuāng Tuó, ascended the throne.
In the fourth year of King Zhuāng,
Zhōu Gōng Hēijiān wanted to kill King Zhuāng and establish Prince Kè.
Xīn Bó informed the king,
and the king killed Zhōu Gōng.
Prince Kè fled to Yān.
In the fifteenth year,
King Zhuāng passed away,
and his son, King Xí Húqí, ascended the throne.
In the third year of King Xí,
Duke Huán of Qí began his hegemony.
In the fifth year, King Xí passed away,
and his son, King Huì Làng, ascended the throne.
In the second year of King Huì. Earlier,
King Zhuāng had a favored concubine, Yáo,
who gave birth to a son, Tuí.
Tuí enjoyed favor.
When King Huì ascended the throne,
he seized the gardens of his high officials to make a royal park.
Therefore, five senior officials, including Biān Bó, rebelled,
planning to summon the armies of Yān and Wèi to attack King Huì.
King Huì fled to Wēn and later resided in Lì of Zhèng.
They established Tuí, the younger brother of King Xí, as king.
Music and dances were performed extensively.
The rulers of Zhèng and Guó were angered.
In the fourth year, Zhèng and the ruler of Guó attacked and killed King Tuí,
and restored King Huì.
In the tenth year of King Huì,
he granted Duke Huán of Qí the title of Bó.
In the twenty-fifth year,
King Huì passed away,
and his son, King Xiāng Zhèng, ascended the throne.
King Xiāng’s mother had died early,
and his stepmother was called Queen Huì.
Queen Huì gave birth to Shūdài,
who enjoyed the favor of King Huì,
and King Xiāng feared him.
In the third year,
Shūdài conspired with the Róng and Dí tribes to attack King Xiāng.
King Xiāng wanted to execute Shūdài,
so Shūdài fled to Qí.
Duke Huán of Qí sent Guǎn Zhòng to pacify the Róng for Zhōu,
and sent Xí Péng to pacify the Róng for Jìn.
The king offered Guǎn Zhòng the rites due to a high minister.
Guǎn Zhòng declined, saying:
"I am a lowly official.
There are the two guardians of the Son of Heaven, Guó and Gāo, present.
If they come in spring and autumn to receive the king’s commands,
how could I be treated with such rites?
I, your servant, dare to decline."
The king said:
"Uncle,
I commend your merits.
Do not disobey my command."
Guǎn Zhòng ultimately accepted the rites due to a lower minister and returned.
In the ninth year,
Duke Huán of Qí passed away.
In the twelfth year,
Shūdài returned to Zhōu.
In the thirteenth year,
Zhèng attacked Huá.
The king sent Yóusūn and Bófú to plead for Huá,
but the people of Zhèng imprisoned them.
Duke Wén of Zhèng bore a grudge because King Huì had not granted him a ceremonial cup like the one given to Duke Lì,
and also resented King Xiāng for siding with Wèi and Huá.
Therefore, he imprisoned Bófú.
The king was angry
and planned to use the Dí to attack Zhèng.
Fù Chén remonstrated, saying:
"When our Zhōu moved east,
we relied on Jìn and Zhèng.
During the rebellion of Zǐ Tuí,
it was also Zhèng that settled it.
Now, over a minor grievance, you would abandon them!"
The king did not listen.
In the fifteenth year,
the king sent down the Dí army to attack Zhèng.
The king was grateful to the Dí people
and planned to take one of their women as his queen.
Fù Chén remonstrated, saying:
"Kings Píng,
Huán, Zhuāng, and Huì all received assistance from Zhèng.
Now you abandon your kin and favor the Dí.
This should not be followed."
The king did not listen.
In the sixteenth year,
the king dismissed the Dí queen.
The Dí people came to demand justice,
and killed Tán Bó.
Fù Chén said:
"I have repeatedly remonstrated without being heeded.
If I do not go out now,
will the king think I bear resentment?"
So he and his followers died in battle.
Earlier,
Queen Huì had wanted to establish Prince Dài,
so she had opened the way for the Dí with her faction.
The Dí people then entered Zhōu.
King Xiāng fled to Zhèng,
and Zhèng settled the king at Fàn.
Zǐ Dài was established as king,
and took the dismissed Dí queen of King Xiāng to live with him in Wēn.
In the seventeenth year,
King Xiāng urgently appealed to Jìn for help.
Duke Wén of Jìn restored the king and executed Shūdài.
King Xiāng then granted Duke Wén of Jìn a jade scepter, fragrant wine, bows, and arrows,
making him Bó,
and gave him lands within Hénèi.
In the twentieth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn summoned King Xiāng.
King Xiāng met him at Héyáng and Jiàntǔ.
All the feudal lords came to pay homage.
The records euphemistically wrote, "The Heavenly King hunted at Héyáng."
In the twenty-fourth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn passed away.
In the thirty-first year,
Duke Mù of Qín passed away.
In the thirty-second year,
King Xiāng passed away,
and his son, King Qǐng Rénchén, ascended the throne.
In the sixth year of King Qǐng,
he passed away,
and his son, King Kuāng Bān, ascended the throne.
In the sixth year of King Kuāng,
he passed away,
and his younger brother Yú ascended the throne,
becoming King Dìng.
In the first year of King Dìng,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked the Lùhún Róng,
stationed his troops at Luò,
and sent someone to inquire about the Nine Tripods.
The king sent Wángsūn Mǎn to respond with appropriate words,
and the Chǔ army then withdrew.
In the tenth year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng surrendered,
but was later restored.
In the sixteenth year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ passed away.
In the twenty-first year,
King Dìng passed away,
and his son, King Jiǎn Yí, ascended the throne.
In the thirteenth year of King Jiǎn,
Jìn killed its ruler, Duke Lì,
and welcomed Zǐ Zhōu from Zhōu,
establishing him as Duke Dào.
In the fourteenth year,
King Jiǎn passed away,
and his son, King Líng Xièxīn, ascended the throne.
In the twenty-fourth year of King Líng,
Cuī Zhù of Qí assassinated his ruler, Duke Zhuāng.
In the twenty-seventh year,
King Líng passed away,
and his son, King Jǐng Guì, ascended the throne.
In the eighteenth year of King Jǐng,
the queen’s crown prince, Shèng, died early.
In the twentieth year,
King Jǐng favored Zǐ Cháo.
Intending to establish him,
the king passed away,
and the faction of Zǐ Gài contended for the throne.
The people of the state installed the eldest son Měng as king,
but Zǐ Cháo attacked and killed Měng.
Měng was known as King Dào.
The people of Jìn attacked Zǐ Cháo and installed Gài,
who became King Jìng.
In the first year of King Jìng,
the Jìn forces entered to support King Jìng,
while Zǐ Cháo proclaimed himself king.
King Jìng could not enter the capital,
so he resided in Zé.
In the fourth year,
Jìn led the feudal lords to escort King Jìng into Zhōu,
Zǐ Cháo became a subject,
and the feudal lords fortified the capital.
In the sixteenth year,
the followers of Zǐ Cháo rebelled again,
and King Jìng fled to Jìn.
In the seventeenth year,
Duke Dìng of Jìn then escorted King Jìng into Zhōu.
In the thirty-ninth year,
Tián Cháng of Qí killed his lord, Duke Jiǎn.
In the forty-first year,
Chǔ destroyed Chén.
Confucius passed away.
In the forty-second year,
King Jìng passed away,
and his son King Yuán, Rén, ascended the throne.
In the eighth year of King Yuán,
he passed away,
and his son King Dìng, Jiè, ascended.
In the sixteenth year of King Dìng,
the three Jìn states destroyed Zhì Bó,
and divided his territory among themselves.
In the twenty-eighth year,
King Dìng passed away,
his eldest son Qùjí ascended,
becoming King Āi.
King Āi had reigned for three months
when his younger brother Shū assassinated him and seized the throne,
becoming King Sī.
King Sī had reigned for five months
when his youngest brother Wéi attacked and killed him, taking the throne,
becoming King Kǎo.
These three kings were all sons of King Dìng.
In the fifteenth year of King Kǎo,
he passed away,
and his son King Wēiliè, Wǔ, ascended.
King Kǎo enfeoffed his younger brother in Hénán,
who became Duke Huán,
to continue the official duties of the Duke of Zhōu.
Duke Huán passed away,
and his son Duke Wēi succeeded him.
Duke Wēi passed away,
and his son Duke Huì succeeded him,
who then enfeoffed his youngest son in Gǒng to serve the king,
titled Duke Huì of Eastern Zhōu.
In the twenty-third year of King Wēiliè,
the Nine Cauldrons trembled.
He appointed Hán, Wèi, and Zhào as feudal lords.
In the twenty-fourth year,
he passed away,
and his son King Ān, Jiāo, ascended.
That year, bandits killed King Shēng of Chǔ.
King Ān reigned for twenty-six years,
passed away,
and his son King Liè, Xǐ, ascended.
In the second year of King Liè,
the Grand Historian Dān of Zhōu met with Duke Xiàn of Qín and said:
"Initially, Zhōu and the state of Qín were united and then separated;
after five hundred years of separation, they will reunite,
and seventeen years after reuniting, a hegemon king will emerge."
In the tenth year,
King Liè passed away,
his younger brother Biǎn ascended,
becoming King Xiǎn.
In the fifth year of King Xiǎn,
he congratulated Duke Xiàn of Qín,
and Duke Xiàn was titled Bó.
In the ninth year,
he presented the sacrificial meat of King Wén and King Wǔ to Duke Xiào of Qín.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Qín met with the feudal lords in Zhōu.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Zhōu conferred the title of Bó upon Duke Xiào of Qín.
In the thirty-third year,
he congratulated King Huì of Qín.
In the thirty-fifth year,
he presented the sacrificial meat of King Wén and King Wǔ to King Huì of Qín.
In the forty-fourth year,
King Huì of Qín proclaimed himself king.
After that, all the feudal lords became kings.
In the forty-eighth year,
King Xiǎn passed away,
and his son King Shènjìng, Dìng, ascended.
King Shènjìng reigned for six years,
passed away,
and his son King Nǎn, Yán, ascended.
During King Nǎn's time, Eastern and Western Zhōu were divided and ruled separately.
King Nǎn moved the capital to Western Zhōu.
The crown prince of Duke Wǔ of Western Zhōu died,
leaving five sons by concubines,
with no clear heir.
Sīmǎ Jiǎn said to the King of Chǔ:
"It would be better to grant land to support Prince Jiù,
and request that he be made crown prince."
Zuǒ Chéng said:
"That cannot be done.
If Zhōu does not agree,
your wisdom will be thwarted and your relations with Zhōu will become strained.
It is better to ask the ruler of Zhōu whom he wishes to appoint,
and secretly inform Jiǎn,
then Jiǎn can request that Chǔ support him with land."
In the end, Prince Jiù was installed as crown prince.
In the eighth year,
Qín attacked Yíyáng,
and Chǔ came to its rescue.
But Chǔ, because Zhōu was seen as aligned with Qín,
planned to attack Zhōu.
Sū Dài spoke to the King of Chǔ on behalf of Zhōu, saying:
"Why say that Zhōu is a trouble for Qín?
To claim that Zhōu serves Qín more than Chǔ does
is to want Zhōu to join Qín,
hence the term 'Zhōu-Qín'.
If Zhōu knows it cannot resolve this,
it will surely join Qín,
which is the essence of Qín's strategy to take over Zhōu.
For Your Majesty's plan,
whether Zhōu aligns with Qín or not, speak well of it,
to create distance between Zhōu and Qín.
If Zhōu is cut off from Qín,
it will surely come to Yǐng."
Qín sought to pass through the territory between the two Zhōu states,
intending to attack Hán.
Zhōu feared that granting passage would anger Hán,
and not granting it would anger Qín.
Shǐ Yàn said to the ruler of Zhōu:
"Why not send someone to tell Lord Gōngshū of Hán,
'The reason Qín dares to cut through Zhōu to attack Hán
is that it trusts Eastern Zhōu.
Why not give land to Zhōu
and send a hostage envoy to Chǔ'?
Then Qín will suspect Chǔ and distrust Zhōu,
and Hán will not be attacked.
Also, tell Qín:
'Hán is forcibly giving land to Zhōu
to make Qín suspicious of Zhōu,
and Zhōu dares not refuse.'
Then Qín will have no pretext to stop Zhōu from accepting,
and Zhōu will receive land from Hán while obeying Qín."
Qín summoned the ruler of Western Zhōu,
who was reluctant to go,
so he sent someone to tell the King of Hán:
"Qín has summoned the ruler of Western Zhōu
to use him to attack Your Majesty's Nányáng.
Why not send troops to Nányáng? The ruler of Zhōu will use this as an excuse with Qín.
If the ruler of Zhōu does not go to Qín,
Qín will not dare cross the river to attack Nányáng."
Eastern Zhōu and Western Zhōu went to war,
and Hán came to the aid of Western Zhōu.
Someone spoke to the King of Hán on behalf of Eastern Zhōu, saying:
"Western Zhōu is the former state of the Son of Heaven,
with many precious vessels and treasures.
If Your Majesty holds back troops and does not send them out,
you can win the favor of Eastern Zhōu,
and the treasures of Western Zhōu will surely be exhausted."
King Nǎn was called Chéng Jūn.
Chǔ besieged Yōngshì,
and Hán demanded troops and grain from Eastern Zhōu.
The ruler of Eastern Zhōu was afraid,
so he summoned Sū Dài and told him.
Dài said:
"Why worry about this, my lord?
I can make Hán cease demanding troops and grain from Zhōu,
and even get Gāodū for you."
The ruler of Zhōu said:
"If you can do this,
I will entrust the state to you."
Dài went to see the Chancellor of Hán and said:
"Chǔ has besieged Yōngshì,
with a deadline of three months,
but now it's five months and they haven't captured it—
this shows Chǔ is weakened."
Now the chancellor is demanding armor and grain from Zhōu,
which is to announce Hán's weakness to Chǔ."
The Hán chancellor said:
"Well said.
The envoy has already departed."
Dài replied:
"Why not give Gāodū to Zhōu?"
The Hán chancellor became furious and said:
"I've already refrained from demanding armor and grain from Zhōu enough times,
why should I give them Gāodū?"
Dài said:
"By giving Gāodū to Zhōu,
you make Zhōu turn and submit to Hán.
When Qín hears of this, they will surely be enraged at Zhōu,
and will immediately cut off diplomatic relations with Zhōu.
Thus, by sacrificing Gāodū you preserve Zhōu intact.
Why not give it?"
The chancellor said:
"Well said."
He indeed gave Gāodū to Zhōu.
In the thirty-fourth year,
Sū Lì said to the Zhōu ruler:
"Qín has defeated Hán and Wèi,
crushed general Wǔ's army,
and captured Zhào's Lín and Líshí to the north -
all these were achieved by Bái Qǐ.
He is skilled in using troops,
and also enjoys heaven's mandate.
Now he is again leading troops beyond the passes to attack Liáng.
If Liáng falls, Zhōu will be in danger.
I say,
why doesn't Your Majesty send someone to persuade Bái Qǐ? Say: 'In Chǔ there was one Yǎng Yóujī,
an expert archer.
He could shoot at willow leaves from a hundred paces away,
hitting them a hundred times out of a hundred shots.
Several thousand spectators stood watching,
all praising his archery skills.
There was one man standing beside him
who said, "Excellent,
now you can be taught archery."
Yǎng Yóujī became angry,
put down his bow and gripped his sword,
saying,
"How can you, sir, teach me archery?"
The man replied,
"It's not that I can teach you how to draw the bow.
But shooting at willow leaves from a hundred paces away,
hitting them a hundred times out of a hundred shots -
if you don't rest when at your peak,
soon your energy will decline and your strength tire,
your bow will twist and arrows curve,
and with one missed shot,
all your hundred hits will be forgotten."
Now you have defeated Hán and Wèi,
crushed general Wǔ's army,
and captured Zhào's Lín and Líshí to the north -
your achievements are already numerous.
Now you are again leading troops beyond the passes,
passing through the two Zhōu states,
turning your back on Hán,
to attack Liáng.
If this single campaign fails,
all your previous achievements will be wasted.
You'd better claim illness and not go out.'"
In the forty-second year,
Qín broke the Huáyáng agreement.
Mǎ Fàn said to the Zhōu ruler:
"Please let me have Liáng build walls for Zhōu."
He then went to the Liáng king and said:
"If the Zhōu king dies of illness,
then I will certainly be executed.
I beg to bring the nine tripods and present them to Your Majesty,
and Your Majesty, upon receiving the tripods, can protect me."
The Liáng king said:
"Well said."
He then gave him troops,
claiming they were to garrison Zhōu.
Mǎ Fàn then went to the Qín king and said:
"Liáng is not garrisoning Zhōu,
but plans to attack Zhōu.
Your Majesty might try sending troops to the border to observe this."
Qín indeed sent out troops.
He then returned to the Liáng king and said:
"The Zhōu king is gravely ill,
I beg for a postponement until later to fulfill my promise.
Now that Your Majesty has sent troops to Zhōu,
the other states have become suspicious,
and future actions will not be trusted.
It would be better to have the troops build walls for Zhōu,
thus concealing the true purpose."
The Liáng king said:
"Well said."
He then had them build walls for Zhōu.
In the forty-fifth year,
a retainer of the Zhōu ruler who had gone to Qín said to Zhōu Zuì:
"You should praise the Qín king's filial piety,
and accordingly offer Yìng as maintenance land for the queen dowager.
The Qín king will certainly be pleased,
and this will give you connections with Qín.
If relations are good,
the Zhōu ruler will certainly credit you.
If relations turn bad,
those who urged the Zhōu ruler to go to Qín will certainly be blamed."
When Qín attacked Zhōu,
Zhōu Jù said to the Qín king:
"For Your Majesty's strategy, attacking Zhōu is unwise.
To attack Zhōu
brings little substantial benefit,
yet the reputation frightens the world.
When the world fears Qín because of this reputation,
they will certainly ally east with Qí.
If troops are exhausted at Zhōu,
and the world unites with Qí,
then Qín cannot achieve kingship.
Those who wish to exhaust Qín
urge Your Majesty to attack Zhōu.
If Qín is exhausted by the world,
then your commands will not be obeyed."
In the fifty-eighth year,
the Three Jìn resisted Qín.
Zhōu sent its chancellor to Qín,
but because Qín treated them lightly,
he turned back mid-journey.
A visitor said to the chancellor:
"Whether Qín values us or not is unknown.
Qín wants to know the situation of the three states.
You should urgently see the Qín king and say,
'Let me observe changes in the east for Your Majesty.'
The Qín king will certainly value you.
If he values you,
that means Qín values Zhōu,
and Zhōu thereby gains Qín's favor.
If Qí values us,
we already have Zhōu Jù to maintain relations with Qí:
thus Zhōu never fails to maintain relations with valued states."
Qín trusted Zhōu,
and sent troops to attack the Three Jìn.
In the fifty-ninth year,
Qín took Hán's Yángchéng and Fùshǔ.
Western Zhōu grew fearful,
betrayed Qín,
and allied with the other states,
leading elite troops from all under heaven through Yīquē to attack Qín,
preventing Qín from reaching Yángchéng.
King Zhāo of Qín was enraged,
and sent general Jiū to attack Western Zhōu.
The ruler of Western Zhōu fled to Qín,
kowtowed to accept blame,
and offered all his thirty-six cities,
with thirty thousand people.
Qín accepted his offering,
and returned the ruler to Zhōu.
The Zhōu ruler, King Nǎn, died,
and the Zhōu people fled eastward.
Qín took the nine tripods and precious vessels, and moved the Duke of Western Zhōu to Dànhú.
Seven years later,
King Zhuāngxiāng of Qín destroyed Eastern Zhōu.
Both Eastern and Western Zhōu were incorporated into Qín,
and the Zhōu sacrifices came to an end.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Scholars all say that when Zhōu defeated Zhòu,
they established their capital at Luòyì,
but examining the facts, this is not so.
King Wǔ planned it,
King Chéng had Shào Gōng divine the location,
placed the nine tripods there,
yet Zhōu again made Fēng and Hào their capital.
Not until the Quǎnróng defeated King Yōu
did Zhōu move east to Luòyì.
The saying "Duke of Zhōu was buried at Bì" -
Bì was located in Dù, southeast of Hào.
Qín destroyed Zhōu.
More than ninety years after Hàn's rise,
the Son of Heaven was about to sacrifice at Tàishān,
and while touring east reached Hénán,
sought descendants of Zhōu,
enfeoffed one later descendant named Jiā with thirty lǐ of land,
titled him Lord Zhōu Zǐnán,
equivalent to a ranked marquis,
to maintain sacrifices to his ancestors.
Qín's ancestors
were descendants of Emperor Zhuānxū.
A granddaughter named Nǚ Xiū.
While Nǚ Xiū was weaving,
a dark bird dropped an egg,
Nǚ Xiū swallowed it,
and gave birth to Dà Yè.
Dà Yè took as wife a daughter of Shǎodiǎn,
named Nǚ Huá.
Nǚ Huá gave birth to Dà Fèi,
who assisted Yǔ in controlling the floods.
After the work was completed,
Emperor Shùn bestowed a dark jade tablet.
Yǔ received it and said:
"It was not I alone who accomplished this;
Dà Fèi also assisted."
Emperor Shùn said:
"Ah, you, Fèi,
who aided Yǔ's achievement,
I bestow upon you a black banner.
Your descendants shall greatly flourish."
He then gave him a maiden of the Yáo clan as a wife.
Dà Fèi bowed and accepted,
and assisted Shùn in taming birds and beasts.
Many birds and beasts became tame,
and he was called Bó Yì.
Shùn bestowed upon him the surname Yíng.
Dà Fèi had two sons:
one named Dà Lián,
who became the ancestor of the Niǎosú clan;
the second named Ruò Mù,
who became the ancestor of the Fèi clan.
His great-great-grandson was named Fèi Chāng.
Some of his descendants remained in the Central States,
while others went to the barbarian regions.
Fèi Chāng lived during the time of Xià Jié.
He left Xià and joined Shāng,
serving as Tāng's charioteer,
and helped defeat Jié at Míngtiáo.
Dà Lián's great-great-grandson
was named Mèng Xì and Zhōng Yǎn,
who had bird bodies and human speech.
Emperor Tài Wù heard of them
and divined about employing them as charioteers.
The divination was auspicious,
so he employed them as charioteers and gave them wives.
From Tài Wù onward,
the descendants of Zhōng Yǎn
achieved merit generation after generation,
assisting the Yīn state.
Therefore, the Yíng surname became prominent,
and they became feudal lords.
His great-great-grandson was named Zhōng Jué,
who lived among the Western Róng,
guarding the western frontier.
He fathered Fěi Lián.
Fěi Lián fathered È Lái.
È Lái was strong,
and Fěi Lián was swift-footed.
Father and son both served
King Zhòu of Yīn with their abilities.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu attacked Zhòu,
he also killed È Lái.
At that time, Fěi Lián
was gathering stones for Zhòu in the north.
Returning,
he had no one to report to,
so he built an altar at Mount Huòtài to report,
where he found a stone coffin
inscribed with the words:
"The Emperor commands Chǔ Fù
not to participate in the chaos of Yīn,
and bestows upon you a stone coffin to glorify your clan."
He died
and was buried at Mount Huòtài.
Fěi Lián also had a son named Jì Shèng.
Jì Shèng fathered Mèng Zēng.
Mèng Zēng was favored by King Chéng of Zhōu,
and was called Zhái Gāoláng.
Gāoláng fathered Héng Fù,
and Héng Fù fathered Zào Fù.
Zào Fù, skilled in charioteering, was favored
by King Mù of Zhōu.
He obtained the steeds Jì,
Wēnlí,
Huáliú,
and Lù'ěr,
and with these four horses, the king toured the west,
enjoying himself so much that he forgot to return.
When Xú Yǎnwáng rebelled,
Zào Fù drove for King Mù,
racing back to Zhōu,
covering a thousand miles in a single day
to quell the rebellion.
King Mù enfeoffed Zào Fù with Zhàochéng,
and from then on, Zào Fù's clan took the surname Zhào.
From Fěi Lián fathering Jì Shèng, five generations later
came Zào Fù,
who settled separately in Zhào.
Zhào Cuī was his descendant.
È Lái Gé was the son of Fěi Lián,
but died early.
He had a son named Nǚ Fáng.
Nǚ Fáng fathered Páng Gāo,
Páng Gāo fathered Tài Jī,
Tài Jī fathered Dà Luò,
and Dà Luò fathered Fēi Zǐ.
Due to Zào Fù's favor,
they all enjoyed the protection of Zhàochéng,
and took the surname Zhào.
Fēi Zǐ lived in Quǎnqiū,
and was fond of horses and livestock,
skilled in breeding and raising them.
The people of Quǎnqiū reported this to King Xiào of Zhōu,
and King Xiào summoned him to oversee
the horses between the Qiān and Wèi rivers.
The horses multiplied greatly.
King Xiào wished to make him the rightful heir of Dà Luò.
The daughter of the Marquis of Shēn was Dà Luò's wife,
and had given birth to a son named Chéng,
who was the rightful heir.
The Marquis of Shēn then said to King Xiào:
"In the past, my ancestor's daughter from Lìshān
married Róng Xūxuān,
and gave birth to Zhōng Jué.
Due to kinship, he submitted to Zhōu,
guarding the western frontier,
and the western frontier was peaceful because of this.
Now I have again married my daughter to Dà Luò,
and she bore the rightful heir Chéng.
The marriage alliance between Shēn and Luò
ensures the submission of the Western Róng,
which is beneficial for the king.
May the king consider this."
Thereupon, King Xiào said:
"In the past, Bó Yì managed livestock for Shùn,
and the livestock multiplied,
so he was granted land
and bestowed the surname Yíng.
Now his descendant has also multiplied horses for me.
I shall grant him land
as a vassal."
He enfeoffed him at Qín,
allowing him to continue the sacrifices of the Yíng clan,
and he was called Qín Yíng.
He also did not abolish the status of the Marquis of Shēn's daughter's son
as the rightful heir of Luò,
to maintain peace with the Western Róng.
Qín Yíng fathered Qín Hóu.
Qín Hóu reigned for ten years and died.
He fathered Gōng Bó.
Gōng Bó reigned for three years and died.
He fathered Qín Zhòng.
Qín Zhòng had reigned for three years
when King Lì of Zhōu acted tyrannically,
and some feudal lords rebelled against him.
The Western Róng turned against the royal house,
and annihilated the clan of Dà Luò of Quǎnqiū.
When King Xuān of Zhōu ascended the throne,
he appointed Qín Zhòng as a senior official
to attack the Western Róng.
The Western Róng killed Qín Zhòng.
Qín Zhòng had reigned for twenty-three years
when he died among the Róng.
He had five sons,
the eldest named Zhuāng Gōng.
King Xuān of Zhōu summoned Zhuāng Gōng and his four brothers,
gave them seven thousand soldiers,
and sent them to attack the Western Róng,
defeating them.
Thereupon, he restored
to Qín Zhòng's descendants
their ancestral land of Quǎnqiū, which had belonged to Dà Luò,
granting them both territories,
and appointed Zhuāng Gōng as the senior official of the western frontier.
Zhuāng Gōng resided in the old western Quǎnqiū,
and had three sons,
the eldest named Shì Fù.
Shì Fù said:
"The Róng killed my grandfather Zhòng;
unless I kill the Róng king,
I dare not enter the city."
He then led an attack against the Róng,
yielding his position to his younger brother Xiāng Gōng.
Xiāng Gōng became the heir apparent.
Zhuāng Gōng reigned for forty-four years,
died,
and the heir apparent Xiāng Gōng succeeded him.
In the first year of Xiāng Gōng's reign,
he gave his younger sister Mù Yíng in marriage to the King of Fēng.
In the second year of Xiāng Gōng's reign,
the Róng besieged Quǎnqiū.
Shì Fù attacked them,
but was captured by the Róng.
Over a year later,
Shì Fù was returned.
In the spring of the seventh year,
King Yōu of Zhōu, influenced by
Bāo Sì, deposed the crown prince,
and made Bāo Sì's son the rightful heir.
He repeatedly deceived the feudal lords,
and they rebelled against him.
The Western Róng, the Quǎn Róng,
and the Marquis of Shēn attacked Zhōu,
killing King Yōu at the foot of Mount Lì.
Duke Xiāng of Qín led troops to rescue Zhōu,
fought with great effort,
and achieved merit.
Zhōu, avoiding the threat of the Quǎnróng,
moved east to Luòyì,
and Duke Xiāng escorted King Píng of Zhōu with his troops.
King Píng enfeoffed Duke Xiāng as a feudal lord,
granting him the lands west of Qí.
He said:
"The Róng are without virtue,
invading and seizing our lands of Qí and Fēng;
if Qín can attack and drive out the Róng,
it shall possess these lands."
He made an oath with him,
bestowing the title and rank.
Duke Xiāng then began his state,
exchanging envoys with the feudal lords
and performing the rituals of visits and offerings.
He used
three red-maned colts, three yellow oxen, and three rams,
to sacrifice to the Supreme Deity at the Western Altar.
In the twelfth year,
he attacked the Róng and reached Qí,
where he died.
He was succeeded by Duke Wén.
In the first year of Duke Wén,
he resided in the Western Border Palace.
In the third year,
Duke Wén went east hunting with seven hundred soldiers.
In the fourth year,
he reached the confluence of the Qiān and Wèi rivers.
He said:
"In the past, Zhōu settled our ancestor Qín Yíng here,
and later we finally became feudal lords."
He then divined
about residing there,
and the omen indicated auspiciousness,
so he built a settlement there.
In the tenth year,
he first established the Fū Altar,
using three sets of sacrificial animals.
In the thirteenth year,
he first had historians to record events,
and many of the people were transformed.
In the sixteenth year,
Duke Wén attacked the Róng with his troops,
and the Róng were defeated and fled.
Thereupon, Duke Wén gathered the remaining people of Zhōu and possessed them,
his territory reaching Qí,
and he presented the lands east of Qí to Zhōu.
In the nineteenth year,
he obtained the Chén Treasure.
In the twentieth year,
for the first time, the law included
the punishment of exterminating three clans.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he cut down the large catalpa tree of the Southern Mountain and the large bull of Fēng.
In the forty-eighth year,
Duke Wén's crown prince died,
and was posthumously honored as Duke Jìng.
Duke Jìng's eldest son became the crown prince,
who was Duke Wén's grandson.
In the fiftieth year,
Duke Wén died,
and was buried at Western Mountain.
Duke Jìng's son ascended the throne,
known as Duke Níng.
In the second year of Duke Níng,
the duke moved to reside in Píngyáng.
He sent troops to attack Dàngshè.
In the third year,
he battled with Bó,
and the King of Bó fled to the Róng,
whereupon Dàngshè was destroyed.
In the fourth year,
the Lǔ prince Huī
assassinated his ruler, Duke Yǐn.
In the twelfth year,
he attacked the Dàng clan,
and captured it.
Duke Níng ascended the throne at the age of ten,
reigned for twelve years, and died,
buried at Western Mountain.
He fathered three sons:
the eldest, Duke Wǔ,
was the crown prince.
Duke Wǔ's younger brother was Duke Dé,
born of the same mother, a daughter of Lǔ.
She also gave birth to Chūzǐ.
After Duke Níng's death,
the high officials Fújì, Wēilěi, and Sānfù deposed
the crown prince and set up Chūzǐ as ruler.
In the sixth year of Chūzǐ,
Sānfù and others again conspired
to have Chūzǐ assassinated.
Chūzǐ had ascended the throne at the age of five,
reigned for six years, and died.
Sānfù and others then reinstated
the former crown prince, Duke Wǔ.
In the first year of Duke Wǔ,
he attacked the Péngxì clan,
reaching below Huà Mountain,
and resided in the Fēng Palace of Píngyáng.
In the third year,
he executed Sānfù and others
and exterminated their three clans,
for having killed Chūzǐ.
In Zhèng, Gāo Qúmǐ killed his ruler, Duke Zhāo.
In the tenth year,
he attacked the Guī and Jì Róng,
and for the first time established counties there.
In the eleventh year,
he first established counties in Dù and Zhèng.
He destroyed Xiǎoguó.
In the thirteenth year,
men of Qí, Guǎn Zhìfù and Lián Chēng, among others, killed
their ruler Duke Xiāng and set up Gōngsūn Wúzhī.
Jìn destroyed Huò, Wèi, and Gěng.
Qí's Yōng Lǐn killed Wúzhī, Guǎn Zhìfù, and others
and set up Duke Huán of Qí.
Qí and Jìn became powerful states.
In the nineteenth year,
Qūwò of Jìn first became the Marquis of Jìn.
Duke Huán of Qí became hegemon at Juàn.
In the twentieth year, Duke Wǔ died,
and was buried at Yōng Píngyáng.
For the first time, people were buried with the dead,
sixty-six individuals followed in death.
He had one son,
named Bái.
Bái did not ascend the throne,
but was enfeoffed at Píngyáng.
His younger brother Duke Dé was set up.
In the first year of Duke Dé,
he first resided in the Dàzhèng Palace of Yōng City.
He used three hundred sets of sacrificial animals at the Fū Altar.
He divined about residing in Yōng.
It was prophesied that later descendants
would water their horses at the Yellow River.
Earl Liáng and Earl Ruì came to court.
In the second year,
the first "Fu" ceremony was held,
using dogs to ward off poison.
Duke Dé ascended the throne at thirty-three,
reigned for two years, and died.
He fathered three sons:
the eldest, Duke Xuān,
the middle, Duke Chéng,
and the youngest, Duke Mù.
The eldest, Duke Xuān, ascended the throne.
In the first year of Duke Xuān,
Wèi and Yān attacked Zhōu,
expelled King Huì,
and set up Prince Tuí.
In the third year,
Earl of Zhèng and Shū of Guó killed Tuí
and restored King Huì.
In the fourth year,
he built the Mì Altar.
He battled with Jìn at Héyáng,
and was victorious.
In the twelfth year, Duke Xuān died.
He fathered nine sons,
none were set up,
and his younger brother Duke Chéng was established.
In the first year of Duke Chéng,
Earl Liáng and Earl Ruì came to court.
Duke Huán of Qí attacked the Shānróng,
and stationed at Gūzhú.
Duke Chéng reigned for four years and died.
He had seven sons,
none were set up,
and his younger brother Duke Mù was established.
In the first year of Duke Mù, Rènhǎo,
he personally led troops to Máojīn,
and was victorious.
In the fourth year,
he welcomed a bride from Jìn,
who was the elder sister of Crown Prince Shēnshēng of Jìn.
That year,
Duke Huán of Qí attacked Chǔ,
reaching Shàolíng.
In the fifth year,
Duke Xiàn of Jìn exterminated Yú and Guó,
capturing the ruler of Yú and his minister Bǎi Lǐ Xī,
because Yú had accepted bribes of jade and horses.
After capturing Bǎi Lǐ Xī,
he was sent as part of the dowry entourage to the wife of Duke Mù of Qín.
Bǎi Lǐ Xī fled from Qín to Wǎn,
where he was seized by local people of Chǔ.
Duke Mù, hearing of Bǎi Lǐ Xī's worthiness,
wished to ransom him heavily,
but fearing the people of Chǔ would not agree,
sent a messenger to say to Chǔ:
"My dowry servant Bǎi Lǐ Xī is there,
I request to ransom him with five black rams' skins."
The people of Chǔ then agreed to give him up.
At this time,
Bǎi Lǐ Xī was already over seventy years old.
Duke Mù freed him from captivity,
and discussed state affairs with him.
Bǎi Lǐ Xī declined, saying:
"I am a minister of a lost state,
hardly worth consulting!"
Duke Mù said:
"The ruler of Yú did not employ you,
hence his downfall,
not your fault."
He insisted on consulting him,
and after three days of conversation,
Duke Mù was greatly pleased,
entrusted him with state governance,
and titled him the Minister of Five Rams.
Bǎi Lǐ Xī deferred, saying:
"I am not equal to my friend Jiǎn Shū,
who is worthy but unknown to the world.
I often wandered in distress
in Qí and begged for food in Zhì,
Jiǎn Shū took me in.
I then wished
to serve the ruler of Qí, Wúzhī,
but Jiǎn Shū stopped me,
and I escaped the troubles in Qí,
then went to Zhōu.
Prince Tuí of Zhōu was fond of oxen,
I sought his favor by tending oxen.
When Tuí was about to employ me,
Jiǎn Shū stopped me,
I left,
and avoided execution.
When serving the ruler of Yú,
Jiǎn Shū stopped me.
I knew the ruler of Yú would not employ me,
but I truly coveted the salary and rank,
and stayed.
Twice I followed his advice,
and escaped;
once I did not,
and encountered the disaster with the ruler of Yú:
thus I know his worthiness."
Thereupon, Duke Mù sent an envoy with generous gifts to invite Jiǎn Shū,
and appointed him as Senior Minister.
In autumn,
Duke Mù personally led an army to attack Jìn,
battling at Héqū.
Lí Jī of Jìn caused turmoil,
the crown prince Shēnshēng died in Xīnchéng,
while Chóng'ěr and Yí Wú fled.
In the ninth year,
Duke Huán of Qí met with the feudal lords
at Kuíqiū.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn passed away.
Lí Jī's son Xī Qí was installed,
but his minister Lǐ Kè killed Xī Qí.
Xún Xī installed Zhuó Zǐ,
and Lǐ Kè again killed Zhuó Zǐ and Xún Xī.
Yí Wú sent a messenger to request Qín's help,
seeking to enter Jìn.
Duke Mù then agreed,
sending Bǎi Lǐ Xī with troops to escort Yí Wú.
Yí Wú said to him:
"If I am truly established,
I will cede the eight cities west of the river in Jìn
to Qín."
But when he arrived,
and was installed,
he sent Pī Zhèng to apologize to Qín,
breached the agreement by not giving the cities west of the river,
and killed Lǐ Kè.
Pī Zhèng heard of this,
feared,
and thus plotted with Duke Mù, saying:
"The people of Jìn do not want Yí Wú,
but truly desire Chóng'ěr.
Now he has breached the agreement with Qín and killed Lǐ Kè,
all are schemes of Lǚ Shēng and Xì Ruì.
I wish you would urgently lure
Lǚ and Xì with benefits,
once Lǚ and Xì arrive,
it would be convenient to reinstate Chóng'ěr."
Duke Mù agreed,
sent a messenger with Pī Zhèng back,
to summon Lǚ and Xì.
Lǚ, Xì, and others suspected Pī Zhèng had deceit,
thus advised Yí Wú to kill Pī Zhèng.
Pī Zhèng's son Pī Bào fled to Qín,
and advised Duke Mù, saying:
"The ruler of Jìn is unprincipled,
the common people are not close to him,
he can be attacked."
Duke Mù said:
"If the common people are truly discontent,
why could he execute his ministers?
Being able to execute his ministers,
shows his harmony."
He did not listen,
but secretly employed Bào.
In the twelfth year,
Guǎn Zhòng and Xí Péng of Qí died.
Jìn suffered drought,
and came to request grain.
Pī Bào advised Duke Mù not to give,
but to attack them during the famine.
Duke Mù asked Gōngsūn Zhī,
Zhī said:
"Famine and plenty alternate,
we cannot not give."
He asked Bǎi Lǐ Xī,
Xī said:
"Yí Wú has offended you,
but what crime have his people committed?"
Thereupon, following the words of Bǎi Lǐ Xī and Gōngsūn Zhī,
he eventually gave them grain.
Using boats and carts for transport,
from Yōng, a continuous line
reached Jiàng.
In the fourteenth year,
Qín suffered famine,
and requested grain from Jìn.
The ruler of Jìn consulted his ministers.
Guó Shè said:
"Attack them during their famine,
we can achieve great success."
The ruler of Jìn followed this.
In the fifteenth year,
he raised troops to attack Qín.
Duke Mù dispatched troops,
appointed Pī Bào as general,
and personally went to attack.
On the renxū day of the ninth month,
he engaged in battle with Duke Huì of Jìn, Yí Wú, at Hán.
The ruler of Jìn abandoned his army,
competed for advantage with Qín,
and upon turning back, his horse foundered.
Duke Mù and his followers galloped in pursuit,
but failed to capture the ruler of Jìn,
and were instead surrounded by the Jìn army.
Jìn attacked Duke Mù,
and Duke Mù was wounded.
Then, three hundred men from Qíxià who had eaten the fine horses
charged recklessly into the Jìn army,
the Jìn army lifted the siege,
thus freeing Duke Mù and in turn
capturing the ruler of Jìn alive.
Earlier,
Duke Mù had lost fine horses,
which over three hundred rustics from Qíxià
had caught and eaten;
officials pursued and caught them,
intending to punish them by law.
Duke Mù said:
"A gentleman does not harm people for the sake of livestock.
I have heard that eating fine horse meat without drinking wine
harms people."
Then he bestowed wine upon them all
and pardoned them.
These three hundred men, hearing that Qín was attacking Jìn,
all sought to follow,
and following,
seeing Duke Mù in distress,
all pushed forward to fight to the death,
to repay the kindness of the horse meat.
Thus Duke Mù captured the ruler of Jìn
and returned,
issuing an order in the state,
"Fast and purify,
I will sacrifice the ruler of Jìn to the Supreme Deity."
The Son of Heaven of Zhōu heard of it, saying
"Jìn is of the same surname as I,"
and pleaded for the ruler of Jìn.
Yí Wú's sister was also Duke Mù's wife,
the wife heard of it,
then donned mourning dress and went barefoot,
saying:
"I, your handmaid, could not save my own brother, thus shaming your command."
Duke Mù said:
"I captured the ruler of Jìn as an achievement,
but now the Son of Heaven intercedes for him,
and my wife worries about this."
So he made a covenant with the ruler of Jìn,
promising to send him back,
moved him to superior quarters,
and presented him with seven sets of sacrificial animals.
In the eleventh month,
he returned the Jìn ruler Yíwú,
who offered the land west of the Yellow River,
and sent his heir Yǔ as a hostage to Qín.
Qín gave a royal daughter to Yǔ in marriage.
At this time, Qín's territory extended east
to the Yellow River.
In the eighteenth year,
Duke Huán of Qí died.
In the twentieth year,
Qín destroyed Liáng and Ruì.
In the twenty-second year,
Prince Yǔ of Jìn heard that the Jìn ruler was ill,
and said:
"Liáng,
my mother's homeland,
was destroyed by Qín.
I have many brothers,
so when the ruler passes away,
Qín will surely detain me,
while Jìn, considering me insignificant,
will install another son."
Yǔ then fled back to Jìn.
In the twenty-third year,
Duke Huì of Jìn died,
and Yǔ ascended as ruler.
Qín resented Yǔ's escape,
so they welcomed Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn
from Chǔ,
and gave him Yǔ's former wife in marriage.
Chóng'ěr initially declined,
but later accepted.
Duke Mù treated him with increasing courtesy and generosity.
In the spring of the twenty-fourth year,
Qín sent a messenger to inform Jìn's high officials,
intending to install Chóng'ěr.
Jìn agreed,
and thus sent Chóng'ěr back.
In the second month,
Chóng'ěr became the ruler of Jìn,
known as Duke Wén.
Duke Wén sent someone to kill Yǔ.
Yǔ was known as Duke Huái.
That autumn,
Dài, brother of King Xiāng of Zhōu,
attacked the king with the Dí tribe,
forcing the king to flee and reside in Zhèng.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the Zhōu king sent messengers to report the crisis to Jìn and Qín.
Duke Mù of Qín led troops to assist Duke Wén of Jìn
in restoring King Xiāng,
and killed the king's brother Dài.
That autumn,
Dài, brother of King Xiāng of Zhōu,
attacked the king with the Dí tribe,
forcing the king to flee and reside in Zhèng.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the Zhōu king sent messengers to report the crisis to Jìn and Qín.
Duke Mù of Qín led troops to assist Duke Wén of Jìn
in restoring King Xiāng,
and killed the king's brother Dài.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn defeated Chǔ at Chéngpú.
In the thirtieth year,
Duke Mù helped Duke Wén of Jìn besiege Zhèng.
A messenger from Zhèng said to Duke Mù:
"The fall of Zhèng would strengthen Jìn,
which benefits Jìn,
but offers no advantage to Qín.
A stronger Jìn
is a concern for Qín."
Duke Mù then withdrew his troops and returned.
Jìn also withdrew.
In the winter of the thirty-second year,
Duke Wén of Jìn died.
A man from Zhèng offered to betray Zhèng to Qín, saying:
"I control the city gate,
so Zhèng can be surprised."
Duke Mù consulted Jiǎn Shū and Bǎilǐ Xī,
who replied:
"To traverse several states over a thousand lǐ
and surprise an enemy,
rarely brings gain.
Moreover, if someone betrays Zhèng,
how do we know our own people haven't informed Zhèng
of our plans?
It cannot be done."
Duke Mù said:
"You do not understand;
I have already decided."
He then dispatched troops,
commanding Bǎilǐ Xī's son Mèngmíng Shì,
Jiǎn Shū's son Xīqǐ Shù,
and Báiyǐ Bǐng to lead the army.
On the day of departure,
Bǎilǐ Xī and Jiǎn Shū wept for them.
Duke Mù heard of this and angrily said:
"I dispatch troops, yet you weep to demoralize my army;
why?"
The two elders said:
"We dare not demoralize your army.
As the army marches,
our sons are with it;
we are old,
and fear we may not see them return in time,
so we weep."
After the two elders withdrew,
they told their sons:
"Your army will be defeated,
certainly at the narrow pass of Xiáo."
In the spring of the thirty-third year,
the Qín army marched east,
crossed Jìn territory, and passed the northern gate of Zhōu.
Wángsūn Mǎn of Zhōu said:
"The Qín army shows no respect;
how can they not be defeated!"
The troops reached Huá,
where a Zhèng merchant named Xián Gāo,
driving twelve oxen to sell in Zhōu,
encountered the Qín army.
Fearing death or capture,
he presented his oxen, saying:
"Hearing the great state intends to punish Zhèng,
the ruler of Zhèng has carefully prepared defenses,
and sent me with twelve oxen to provision your troops."
The three Qín generals said to each other:
"We planned to surprise Zhèng,
but now Zhèng is aware;
proceeding would be futile."
They destroyed Huá instead.
Huá was a border town of Jìn.
At that time,
Duke Wén of Jìn had died but was not yet buried.
His heir, Duke Xiāng, angrily said:
"Qín insults us in our mourning,
destroying our Huá during the funeral."
He then donned black mourning garments,
deployed troops to block the Qín army at Xiáo,
attacked, and heavily defeated them,
with not a single man escaping.
They captured the three Qín generals and returned.
The wife of Duke Wén,
a woman from Qín,
pleaded for the three captured generals:
"Duke Mù's hatred for these three
runs to the marrow;
I wish to send them back,
so my lord can personally enjoy boiling them alive."
The Jìn ruler agreed,
and returned the three generals to Qín.
When the three generals arrived,
Duke Mù, in plain clothes,
met them outside the city,
faced them and wept, saying:
"I failed to heed the advice of Bǎilǐ Xī and Jiǎn Shū,
bringing shame upon you three;
what crime have you committed?
Devote yourselves to avenging this disgrace,
and do not slacken."
He then restored their official ranks as before,
and treated them even more generously.
In the thirty-fourth year,
Shāngchén, heir of Chǔ,
murdered his father King Chéng and succeeded him.
Duke Mù then again sent Mèngmíng Shì
and others to lead troops against Jìn,
fighting at Péngyá.
Qín fared poorly,
and withdrew its forces.
The Róng king sent Yóu Yú to Qín.
Yóu Yú,
whose ancestors were from Jìn,
had fled to the Róng,
and could speak the Jìn language.
Hearing of Duke Mù's virtue,
he sent Yóu Yú to observe Qín.
Duke Mù of Qín showed him the palaces and stores.
Yóu Yú said:
"If ghosts were made to do it,
it would exhaust the spirits.
If men were made to do it,
it would torment the people."
Duke Mù found this strange and asked:
"The Central States govern through the Odes, Documents, rites, music,
laws, and measures,
yet there are still periodic disorders.
Now the Róng and Yí peoples lack these,
by what means do they govern?
Is it not difficult?"
Yóu Yú laughed and said:
"This is precisely why the Central States are in disorder.
Since the supreme sage Huángdì
created the rites, music, laws, and measures,
personally practicing them first,
it only led to minor order.
By later generations,
they became increasingly arrogant and decadent daily.
Relying on the authority of laws and measures to supervise and demand from those below,
when the subordinates are exhausted to the extreme,
they resent their superiors over benevolence and righteousness,
superiors and subordinates contend in mutual resentment
and usurp and assassinate each other,
to the extent of exterminating clans,
all due to such reasons.
The Róng and Yí are not like this.
Superiors embody pure virtue in treating their subordinates,
subordinates harbor loyalty and trust in serving their superiors,
the governance of the whole state is like managing one body,
without knowing the means of governance,
this is truly the governance of a sage."
Thereupon Duke Mù withdrew
and asked Nèishǐ Liào:
"I have heard that when a neighboring state has a sage,
it is a worry for the rival state.
Now Yóu Yú is worthy,
a threat to me,
