what should be done about it?"
Nèishǐ Liào said:
"The king of the Róng resides in remote obscurity,
and has not heard the sounds of the Central States.
My lord, try sending him female musicians,
to divert his will;
make a request for Yóu Yú,
to create distance between them;
detain him and do not send him back,
so he misses his deadline.
The Róng king will find it strange,
and will surely suspect Yóu Yú.
When there is distance between ruler and minister,
then he can be captured.
Moreover, if the Róng king delights in music,
he will neglect governance."
Duke Mù said: "Good."
Then he sat with Yóu Yú on connected mats,
passed vessels while eating,
asked about the terrain
and fully understood their military situation,
and afterwards ordered Nèishǐ Liào to send sixteen female musicians to the Róng king.
The Róng king accepted them and was pleased,
for a whole year he did not return.
Thereupon Qín returned Yóu Yú.
Yóu Yú repeatedly remonstrated
but was not heeded,
Duke Mù also repeatedly sent
people to secretly invite Yóu Yú,
and Yóu Yú then left and surrendered to Qín.
Duke Mù treated him with the礼节 of a guest,
and asked about the situation for attacking the Róng.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Duke Mù again treated Mèng Míng and others more generously,
had them lead troops to attack Jìn,
crossed the river and burned the boats,
greatly defeated the Jìn people,
took Wángguān and Hào,
to avenge the battle of Xiáo.
The Jìn people all guarded their walls and did not dare come out.
Thereupon Duke Mù then crossed the river from Máojīn,
interred the corpses at Xiáo,
held a funeral,
and mourned them for three days.
Then he made a pledge to the army:
"Alas, officers and soldiers!
Listen without clamor,
I pledge to tell you.
The ancients consulted the yellow-haired and white-haired,
then had no faults."
To express regret for not using
Jiǎn Shū and Bǎilǐ Xī's counsel,
therefore he made this pledge,
to let later generations remember my fault.
Gentlemen heard of it,
all shed tears, saying:
"Alas!
Duke Mù of Qín's thoroughness with people,
finally obtained the good fortune of Mèng Míng."
In the thirty-seventh year,
Qín used Yóu Yú's plan to attack the king of the Róng,
added twelve states,
opened up a thousand lǐ of territory,
and thus became hegemon over the Western Róng.
The Son of Heaven sent Shào Gōng Guò
to congratulate Duke Mù with metal drums.
In the thirty-ninth year,
Duke Mù died,
and was buried at Yōng.
Those following in death numbered one hundred seventy-seven,
among them three good ministers of Qín of the Zǐyú clan,
named Yǎnxī,
Zhòngháng, and Qiánhǔ,
were also among those following in death.
The people of Qín mourned them,
and composed the poem "Yellow Bird."
Gentlemen said:
"Duke Mù of Qín expanded territory and added states,
subdued powerful Jìn in the east,
became hegemon over the Róng and Yí in the west,
yet he did not become leader of the feudal lords' alliances,
and rightly so.
In death he abandoned the people,
gathered his good ministers to follow him in death.
Moreover, when the former kings passed away,
they still left behind virtue and established models,
how much more should one not take away the good men and fine
ministers whom the common people mourn?
Therefore we know that Qín could not again
campaign eastward."
Duke Mù had forty sons,
his crown prince Yīng succeeded him,
who was Duke Kāng.
In the first year of Duke Kāng.
In the previous year when Duke Mù died,
Duke Xiāng of Jìn also died;
Duke Xiāng's younger brother was named Yōng,
born of a Qín woman,
and was in Qín.
Zhào Dùn of Jìn wanted to establish him,
sent Suí Huì to come and escort Yōng,
Qín sent troops to escort him to Línghú.
Jìn established Duke Xiāng's son
and instead attacked the Qín army,
the Qín army was defeated,
Suí Huì came fleeing.
In the second year,
Qín attacked Jìn,
took Wǔchéng,
in retaliation for the battle of Línghú.
In the fourth year,
Jìn attacked Qín,
took Shǎoliáng.
In the sixth year,
Qín attacked Jìn,
took Jìmǎ.
Fought at Héqū,
greatly defeated the Jìn army.
The people of Jìn worried that Suí Huì in Qín
would cause trouble,
then sent Wèi Chóuyú
to pretend to rebel,
to conspire with Huì,
deceived and obtained Huì,
and Huì then returned to Jìn.
Duke Kāng reigned for twelve years and died,
his son Duke Gōng succeeded.
In the second year of Duke Gōng,
Zhào Chuān of Jìn assassinated his ruler Duke Líng.
In the third year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ was strong,
his northern troops reached Luò,
inquired about the Zhōu ding vessels.
Duke Gōng reigned five years and died,
his son Duke Huán succeeded.
In the third year of Duke Huán,
Jìn defeated one of our generals.
In the tenth year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ subdued Zhèng,
defeated the Jìn army north by the river.
At this time,
Chǔ was hegemon,
convened meetings and alliances to assemble the feudal lords.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Duke Lì of Jìn had just ascended,
and with Duke Huán of Qín swore an alliance across the river.
After returning, Qín betrayed the alliance,
and conspired with the Dí to attack Jìn.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Jìn led the feudal lords to attack Qín,
the Qín army was defeated and fled,
pursued to the Jīng River and then returned.
Duke Huán reigned twenty-seven years and died,
his son Duke Jǐng succeeded.
In the fourth year of Duke Jǐng's reign,
Luán Shū of Jìn assassinated his ruler, Duke Lì.
In the fifteenth year,
(Qín) rescued Zhèng,
defeating the Jìn army at Lì.
At this time, Duke Dào of Jìn was the hegemon.
In the eighteenth year,
as Duke Dào of Jìn grew powerful,
he frequently assembled the feudal lords,
leading them to attack Qín,
and defeated the Qín army.
The Qín forces fled,
while the Jìn troops pursued them,
crossing the Jīng River,
and turned back only upon reaching Yùlín.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Duke Jǐng went to Jìn,
forming an alliance with Duke Píng,
but later betrayed it.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Prince Wéi of Chǔ assassinated his ruler and usurped the throne,
becoming King Líng.
Duke Jǐng's younger brother by the same mother, Hòuzǐ Zhēn, was favored,
and being wealthy,
someone slandered him;
fearing execution,
he fled to Jìn,
with a baggage train of a thousand chariots.
Duke Píng of Jìn asked:
"If Hòuzǐ is so wealthy,
why would he exile himself?"
He replied:
"The Duke of Qín is unprincipled;
I fear execution,
and wish to wait until a later reign to return."
In the thirty-ninth year,
as King Líng of Chǔ grew powerful,
he assembled the feudal lords at Shēn,
assuming hegemony,
and executed Qìng Fēng of Qí.
Duke Jǐng died after reigning for forty years,
and his son, Duke Āi, ascended the throne.
Hòuzǐ then returned to Qín.
In the eighth year of Duke Āi's reign,
Prince Qì Jí of Chǔ assassinated King Líng and usurped the throne,
becoming King Píng.
In the eleventh year,
King Píng of Chǔ came seeking a daughter of Qín to marry his heir apparent, Jiàn.
But when she arrived in the state,
he found her beautiful and married her himself.
In the fifteenth year,
King Píng of Chǔ intended to execute Jiàn,
who fled into exile;
Wǔ Zǐxū then fled to Wú.
The Jìn ducal house was weak while the six ministers were strong,
and they were inclined to fight among themselves,
so for a long time, Qín and Jìn did not attack each other.
In the thirty-first year,
King Hé Lǘ of Wú and Wǔ Zǐxū attacked Chǔ,
causing the King of Chǔ to flee to Suí,
and Wú subsequently entered Yǐng.
The Chǔ senior official Shēn Bāoxū came to report the emergency,
fasting for seven days,
weeping day and night.
Thereupon, Qín dispatched five hundred chariots to rescue Chǔ,
defeating the Wú army.
The Wú forces withdrew,
and King Zhāo of Chǔ was able to re-enter Yǐng.
Duke Āi died in his thirty-sixth year.
The heir apparent, Yí Gōng,
died early,
and did not ascend the throne;
instead, Yí Gōng's son was enthroned,
becoming Duke Huì.
In the first year of Duke Huì's reign,
Confucius served as acting minister of Lǔ.
In the fifth year,
the Jìn ministers Zhōngháng and
Fàn turned against Jìn,
and Jìn sent the Zhì
and Zhào Jiǎnzǐ to attack them,
so the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans fled to Qí.
Duke Huì died after a ten-year reign,
and his son, Duke Dào, ascended the throne.
In the second year of Duke Dào's reign,
Tián Qǐ of Qí assassinated his ruler, Rúzǐ,
and enthroned his elder brother Yángshēng,
who became Duke Dào.
In the sixth year,
Wú defeated the Qí army.
The people of Qí assassinated Duke Dào,
and enthroned his son, Duke Jiǎn.
In the ninth year,
Duke Dìng of Jìn and King Fū Chāi of Wú formed an alliance,
vying for precedence at Huángchí,
and ultimately Wú took the lead.
Wú grew powerful, dominating the central states.
In the twelfth year,
Tián Cháng of Qí assassinated Duke Jiǎn,
enthroning his younger brother, Duke Píng,
with Cháng serving as his chancellor.
In the thirteenth year,
Chǔ annihilated Chén.
Duke Dào of Qín died after a fourteen-year reign,
and his son, Duke Lì Gòng, ascended the throne.
Confucius died in the twelfth year of Duke Dào's reign.
In the second year of Duke Lì Gòng's reign,
envoys from Shǔ came with tribute.
In the sixteenth year,
they dug trenches along the river.
With twenty thousand troops, they attacked Dàlì,
capturing its royal city.
In the twenty-first year,
they first established Pínyáng as a county.
Jìn captured Wǔchéng.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Jìn was in turmoil,
and Zhì Bó was killed,
his territory divided among Zhào, Hán, and Wèi.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Zhì Kāi and his townspeople came to surrender.
In the thirty-third year,
they attacked Yìqú,
capturing its king.
In the thirty-fourth year,
a solar eclipse occurred.
Duke Lì Gòng died,
and his son, Duke Zào, ascended the throne.
In the second year of Duke Zào's reign,
Nánzhèng rebelled.
In the thirteenth year,
Yìqú came to attack,
reaching south of the Wèi River.
In the fourteenth year,
Duke Zào died,
and his younger brother, Duke Huái, was enthroned.
In the fourth year of Duke Huái's reign,
the senior official Cháo and other ministers
besieged Duke Huái,
who committed suicide.
Duke Huái's heir apparent was named Zhāozǐ,
but he died early,
so the ministers enthroned Zhāozǐ's son,
who became Duke Líng.
Duke Líng was Duke Huái's grandson.
In the sixth year of Duke Líng's reign,
Jìn fortified Shǎoliáng,
and Qín attacked them.
In the thirteenth year,
they fortified Jígū.
Duke Líng died,
and his son, Duke Xiàn, did not ascend the throne;
instead, Duke Líng's youngest uncle, Dàozǐ, was enthroned,
becoming Duke Jiǎn.
Duke Jiǎn
was Zhāozǐ's younger brother and Duke Huái's son.
In the sixth year of Duke Jiǎn's reign,
officials were first ordered to wear swords.
They dug trenches along the Luò River.
They fortified Chóngquán.
He died in the sixteenth year,
and his son, Duke Huì, ascended the throne.
In the twelfth year of Duke Huì's reign,
his son, Chūzǐ, was born.
In the thirteenth year,
they attacked Shǔ,
capturing Nánzhèng.
Duke Huì died,
and Chūzǐ ascended the throne.
In the second year of Chūzǐ's reign,
the senior official Gǎi welcomed Duke Líng's son, Duke Xiàn,
from west of the Yellow River and enthroned him.
They killed Chūzǐ and his mother,
drowning them by a deep pool.
Due to Qín's frequent changes of rulers in the past,
causing turmoil between ruler and ministers,
Jìn regained strength,
seizing Qín's territory west of the Yellow River.
In the first year of Duke Xiàn's reign,
he abolished the practice of following in death.
In the second year,
they fortified Yuèyáng.
In the fourth year, on the first month, day Gēngyín,
Duke Xiào was born.
In the eleventh year,
the Zhōu court's Grand Historian Dān
visited Duke Xiàn and said:
"Zhou was once united with the state of Qín,
then separated,
after five hundred years they reunited,
and seventeen years after the reunion,
a hegemon king would emerge."
In the sixteenth year,
peach trees bloomed in winter.
In the eighteenth year,
metal rained down in Yuèyáng.
In the twenty-first year,
they fought with Jìn at Shímén,
beheaded sixty thousand,
and the Son of Heaven congratulated them
with ceremonial robes.
In the twenty-third year,
they battled Wèi and Jìn at Shǎoliáng,
capturing their general Gōngsūn Cuó.
In the twenty-fourth year, Duke Xiàn died,
and his son Duke Xiào ascended the throne,
already twenty-one years old.
In the first year of Duke Xiào's reign,
east of the Yellow River and mountains,
there were six powerful states,
including Qí under King Wēi, Chǔ under King Xuān, Wèi under King Huì,
Yān under Duke Dào, Hán under Duke Āi,
and Zhào under Marquis Chéng.
Between the Huái and Sì rivers were over ten smaller states.
Chǔ and Wèi shared borders with Qín.
Wèi built a long wall,
from Zhèng along the Luò River northward,
possessing the Shàngjùn region.
Chǔ, from Hànzhōng, held Bā and Qiánzhōng to the south.
The Zhōu court was weak,
the feudal lords exerted force in governance,
competing to annex each other.
Qín was secluded in Yōngzhōu,
not participating in the meetings and alliances of the central states' feudal lords,
treated as barbarians.
Duke Xiào thus extended favors,
relieved the orphans and widows,
recruited warriors,
and clarified rewards for achievements.
He issued an order throughout the state:
"In the past, our Duke Mù from between Qí and Yōng,
cultivated virtue and practiced military arts,
pacified the turmoil in Jìn to the east,
taking the river as the boundary,
dominated the Róng and Dí to the west,
expanded the territory by a thousand li,
the Son of Heaven granted him the title of Bà,
the feudal lords all congratulated him,
laying the foundation for future generations,
truly glorious and admirable.
However, in the times of Lì, Zào, Jiǎn, and the exiled
sons, there was unrest,
the state faced internal troubles,
with no leisure for external affairs,
the three Jìn states attacked and seized
the land west of the river from our former rulers,
the feudal lords looked down upon Qín,
a shame beyond compare.
When Duke Xiàn ascended the throne,
he pacified the borders,
moved the capital to Yuèyáng,
and intended to campaign eastward,
to recover the former territories of Duke Mù,
and restore Duke Mù's governance.
I, the unworthy one, ponder the intentions of our former rulers,
often feeling pain in my heart.
If any guest or minister
can devise extraordinary strategies to strengthen Qín,
I will honor them with high office,
and share the land with them."
Thereupon, he sent troops east
to besiege Shǎnchéng,
and west to behead the Huán king of the Róng.
Wèi Yāng heard of this order,
entered Qín from the west,
and through Jǐng Jiàn sought an audience with Duke Xiào.
In the second year,
the Son of Heaven sent sacrificial meat.
In the third year, Wèi Yāng advised Duke Xiào
to reform laws and amend punishments,
focusing internally on farming,
and externally encouraging rewards and penalties for dying in battle,
which Duke Xiào approved.
Gān Lóng, Dù Zhí, and others disagreed,
and debated with him.
Ultimately, Yāng's laws were adopted,
and the common people suffered from them;
after three years,
the people found them beneficial.
Then Yāng was appointed as Zuǒ Shùzhǎng.
These events are recorded in the accounts of Lord Shāng.
In the seventh year,
he met with King Huì of Wèi at Dùpíng.
In the eighth year,
they fought Wèi at Yuánlǐ,
achieving success.
In the tenth year,
Wèi Yāng became Dà Liáng Zào,
leading troops to besiege Wèi's Ānyì and forcing its surrender.
In the twelfth year,
they built Xiányáng, erecting palace towers,
and Qín moved its capital there.
They merged small villages and settlements,
consolidating them into large counties,
each county with one magistrate,
totaling forty-one counties.
They opened up field boundaries for farmland.
Eastern territories extended across the Luò River.
In the fourteenth year,
they first implemented a tax system.
In the nineteenth year,
the Son of Heaven granted the title of Bà.
In the twentieth year,
the feudal lords all congratulated.
Qín sent Gōngzǐ Shǎoguān to lead troops
to meet the feudal lords at Féngzé,
and pay respects to the Son of Heaven.
In the twenty-first year,
Qí defeated Wèi at Mǎlíng.
In the twenty-second year,
Wèi Yāng attacked Wèi,
capturing Wèi's Gōngzǐ Áng.
Yāng was enfeoffed as a marquis,
titled Lord Shāng.
In the twenty-fourth year,
they fought Jìn at Yànmén,
capturing their general Wèi Cuò.
Duke Xiào died,
and his son Lord Huìwén succeeded him.
That year,
Wèi Yāng was executed.
When Yāng first implemented laws in Qín,
the laws were not followed,
as the crown prince violated the禁令.
Yāng said:
"The laws are not upheld
because of the nobility.
If you wish to enforce the laws,
start with the crown prince.
The crown prince cannot be tattooed,
so tattoo his tutors."
Thereupon, the laws were greatly enforced,
and Qín was well-governed.
When Duke Xiào died,
the crown prince ascended,
and the royal clan harbored much resentment towards Yāng,
so Yāng fled,
was accused of rebellion,
and was ultimately torn apart by chariots as a warning to Qín.
In the first year of Lord Huìwén,
people from Chǔ, Hán, Zhào, and Shǔ
came to court.
In the second year,
the Son of Heaven congratulated.
In the third year,
the king was crowned.
In the fourth year,
the Son of Heaven sent sacrificial meat for civil and military rites.
Qí and Wèi declared themselves kings.
In the fifth year,
Xī Shǒu from Yīnjìn became Dà Liáng Zào.
In the sixth year,
Wèi ceded Yīnjìn,
and Yīnjìn was renamed Níngqín.
In the seventh year,
Gōngzǐ Áng battled Wèi,
capturing their general Lóng Jiǎ,
and beheading eighty thousand.
In the eighth year,
Wèi ceded the land west of the river.
In the ninth year,
they crossed the river,
capturing Fényīn and Píshì.
They met with the king of Wèi at Yìng.
They besieged Jiāo,
and it surrendered.
In the tenth year,
Zhāng Yí became chancellor of Qín.
Wèi ceded fifteen counties of Shàngjùn.
In the 11th year,
Yìqú was made a county.
Jiāo and Qūwò were returned to Wèi.
The lord of Yìqú acknowledged himself as a vassal.
Shǎoliáng was renamed Xiàyáng.
In the 12th year,
the Là sacrifice was first instituted.
In the 13th year, on the Wǔwǔ day of the fourth month,
the lord of Wèi declared himself king,
and Hán also declared itself a kingdom.
Zhāng Yí was sent to attack and capture Shǎn,
expelling its inhabitants and giving it to Wèi.
In the 14th year,
the calendar was reset to the first year.
In the 2nd year,
Zhāng Yí met with ministers of Qí and Chǔ at Nièsāng.
In the 3rd year,
the crown princes of Hán and Wèi came to court.
Zhāng Yí became chancellor of Wèi.
In the 5th year,
the king toured as far as the Northern River.
In the 7th year,
Yuè Chí became chancellor of Qín.
Hán, Zhào, Wèi, Yān, and Qí
led the Xiōngnú in a joint attack on Qín.
Qín sent Shùzhǎng Jí to battle them at Xiūyú,
capturing their general Shēn Chā,
defeating Zhào's prince Kě and Hán's crown prince Huàn,
and decapitating 82,000.
In the 8th year,
Zhāng Yí again became chancellor of Qín.
In the 9th year,
Sīmǎ Cuò attacked Shǔ,
and annihilated it.
He attacked and captured Zhào's Zhōngdū and Xīyáng.
In the 10th year,
Hán's crown prince Cāng came as a hostage.
They attacked and captured Hán's Shízhāng.
They attacked and defeated Zhào's general Ní.
They attacked and captured twenty-five cities of Yìqú.
In the 11th year,
Chùlǐ Jí attacked Wèi's Jiāo,
and forced its surrender.
He defeated Hán at Ànmén,
decapitating ten thousand,
and their general Xī Shǒu fled.
Prince Tōng was enfeoffed in Shǔ.
The lord of Yān yielded his throne to his minister Zǐ Zhī.
In the 12th year,
the king met with the king of Liáng at Línjìn.
Shùzhǎng Jí attacked Zhào,
and captured Zhào's general Zhuāng.
Zhāng Yí became chancellor of Chǔ.
In the 13th year,
Shùzhǎng Zhāng attacked Chǔ at Dānyáng,
capturing their general Qū Gài,
and decapitating 80,000;
he also attacked Chǔ's Hànzhōng,
seizing 600 lǐ of territory,
and established the Hànzhōng Commandery.
Chǔ besieged Yōngshì,
so Qín sent Shùzhǎng Jí to aid Hán
and then attack Qí to the east,
while Dào Mǎn aided Wèi in attacking Yān.
In the 14th year,
they attacked Chǔ,
and captured Zhàolíng.
Dān and Lí submitted as vassals,
and Shǔ's chancellor Zhuàng killed the marquis of Shǔ
and came to surrender.
King Huì died,
and his son King Wǔ ascended the throne.
Hán, Wèi, Qí, Chǔ, and Yuè
all submitted and followed.
In the 1st year of King Wǔ,
he met with King Huì of Wèi at Línjìn.
He executed Shǔ's chancellor Zhuàng.
Zhāng Yí and Wèi Zhāng both went east to Wèi.
They attacked Yìqú, Dān, and Lí.
In the 2nd year,
the positions of chancellor were first established,
with Chùlǐ Jí and Gān Mào
appointed as left and right chancellors.
Zhāng Yí died in Wèi.
In the 3rd year,
he met with King Xiāng of Hán outside Línjìn.
Nángōng Jiē died,
and Chùlǐ Jí became chancellor of Hán.
King Wǔ said to Gān Mào:
"I wish to have a carriage pass through Sānchuān,
to look upon the Zhōu court,
and then I would die without regret."
That autumn,
he sent Gān Mào and Shùzhǎng Fēng to attack Yíyáng.
In the 4th year,
they captured Yíyáng,
decapitating 60,000.
They crossed the Yellow River,
and fortified Wǔsuì.
The crown prince of Wèi came to court.
King Wǔ was strong and enjoyed feats of strength,
and strongmen Rén Bǐ,
Wū Huò, and Mèng Yuè all attained high office.
The king competed with Mèng Yuè in lifting a ding,
and broke his knee.
In the eighth month,
King Wǔ died.
Mèng Yuè's clan was exterminated.
King Wǔ had taken a daughter of Wèi as his queen,
but she had no son.
A half-brother was set up,
who became King Zhāoxiāng.
King Zhāoxiāng's mother was from Chǔ,
of the Mǐ clan,
and was titled Queen Dowager Xuān.
When King Wǔ died,
King Zhāoxiāng was a hostage in Yān,
and the people of Yān sent him back,
so he could ascend the throne.
In the 1st year of King Zhāoxiāng,
Yán Jūn Jí became chancellor.
Gān Mào left for Wèi.
In the 2nd year,
a comet appeared.
Shùzhǎng Zhuàng conspired with senior ministers,
nobles, and princes
to rebel, and all were executed,
including Queen Huìwén, who did not die a natural death.
Queen Dào Wǔ left and returned to Wèi.
In the 3rd year,
the king was capped.
He met with the king of Chǔ at Huángjí,
and gave Shàngyōng to Chǔ.
In the 4th year,
they captured Púbǎn.
A comet appeared.
In the 5th year,
the king of Wèi came to court at Yìngtíng,
and Púbǎn was returned to Wèi.
In the 6th year,
the marquis of Shǔ, Huī, rebelled,
and Sīmǎ Cuò pacified Shǔ.
Shùzhǎng Huàn attacked Chǔ,
decapitating 20,000.
Lord Jīngyáng went as a hostage to Qí.
There was a solar eclipse,
and it was dark during the day.
In the 7th year,
they captured Xīnchéng.
Chùlǐzǐ died.
In the 8th year,
General Mǐ Róng was sent to attack Chǔ,
and captured Xīnshì.
Qí sent Zhāngzǐ,
Wèi sent Gōngsūn Xǐ,
Hán sent Bào Yuān
to jointly attack Chǔ's Fāngchéng,
capturing Táng Miè.
Zhào destroyed Zhōngshān,
its ruler fled,
and eventually died in Qí.
Wèi's prince Jìn
and Hán's prince Cháng became nobles.
In the 9th year,
Mèngcháng Jūn Xuē Wén came to be chancellor of Qín.
Huàn attacked Chǔ,
capturing eight cities,
and killed their general Jǐng Kuài.
In the 10th year,
King Huái of Chǔ came to court in Qín,
and Qín detained him.
Xuē Wén was dismissed due to Jīn Shòu.
Lóu Huǎn became chancellor.
In the 11th year,
Qí, Hán, Wèi, Zhào, Sòng,
and Zhōngshān—five states in total—jointly attacked Qín,
reaching Yánshì before withdrawing.
Qín made peace with Hán and Wèi by ceding territory north of the Yellow River and Fēnglíng.
A comet appeared.
King Huái of Chǔ fled to Zhào,
but Zhào did not accept him,
so he returned to Qín,
where he died shortly after,
and his body was sent back for burial.
In the 12th year,
Lóu Huǎn was dismissed,
and Ráng Hóu Wèi Rǎn became chancellor.
Fifty thousand shí of grain were given to Chǔ.
In the 13th year,
Xiàng Shòu attacked Hán,
and captured Wǔshǐ.
Zuǒgēng Bái Qǐ attacked Xīnchéng.
Wǔdàfū Lǐ fled and defected to Wèi.
Rén Bǐ became governor of Hànzhōng.
In the fourteenth year,
Zuǒ Gēng Bái Qǐ attacked Hán and Wèi at Yīquē,
beheading 240,000 men,
capturing Gōngsūn Xǐ,
and capturing five cities.
In the fifteenth year,
Dàliángzào Bái Qǐ attacked Wèi,
captured Yuán,
but later returned it.
He attacked Chǔ,
capturing Wǎn.
In the sixteenth year,
Zuǒ Gēng Cuò captured Zhǐ and Dèng.
Rǎn was dismissed.
Fēng the young master Shì at Wǎn,
young master Kuī at Dèng,
and Wèi Rǎn at Táo,
making them feudal lords.
In the seventeenth year,
Chéngyáng Jūn came to court,
and the ruler of Dōng Zhōu also came to court.
Qín changed Yuán to Púbàn and Píshì.
The king went to Yíyáng.
In the eighteenth year,
Cuò attacked Yuán and Héyōng,
destroying a bridge to capture them.
In the nineteenth year,
the king claimed the title of Western Emperor,
while Qí claimed Eastern Emperor,
but both later renounced the titles.
Lǚ Lǐ came and submitted.
Qí destroyed Sòng,
the king of Sòng was in Wèi,
and died in Wēn.
Rèn Bǐ passed away.
In the twentieth year,
the king went to Hànzhōng,
then to Shàngjùn
and Běi Hé.
In the twenty-first year,
Cuò attacked Wèi's Hénèi. Wèi offered Ānyì,
Qín expelled its people,
recruited settlers for Hédōng,
bestowed ranks,
and pardoned convicts to relocate them.
Jīngyáng Jūn was enfeoffed at Wǎn.
In the twenty-second year,
Méng Wǔ attacked Qí.
Hédōng was divided into nine counties.
The king met with the king of Chǔ at Wǎn.
He met with the king of Zhào at Zhōngyáng.
In the twenty-third year,
Wèi Sīlí along with Sān Jìn and Yān
attacked Qí,
defeating them west of Jì.
The king met with the king of Wèi at Yíyáng,
and with the king of Hán at Xīnchéng.
In the twenty-fourth year,
he met with the king of Chǔ at Yān,
and again at Rǎng.
Qín took Wèi's Ānchéng,
reaching Dàliáng,
Yān and Zhào came to rescue,
and the Qín army withdrew.
Wèi Rǎn was dismissed as chancellor.
In the twenty-fifth year,
two cities of Zhào were captured.
The king met with the king of Hán at Xīnchéng,
and with the king of Wèi at Xīnmíngyì.
In the twenty-sixth year,
convicts were pardoned and relocated to Rǎng.
Hóu Rǎn resumed as chancellor.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Cuò attacked Chǔ.
Convicts were pardoned and relocated to Nányáng.
Bái Qǐ attacked Zhào,
capturing the city of Dàiguāngláng.
Sīmǎ Cuò was sent from Lǒngxī,
and via Shǔ attacked Chǔ's Qiánzhōng,
capturing it.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Dàliángzào Bái Qǐ attacked Chǔ,
capturing Yān and Dèng,
and pardoned convicts to relocate there.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Dàliángzào Bái Qǐ attacked Chǔ,
capturing Yǐng and establishing Nánjùn,
the king of Chǔ fled.
The ruler of Zhōu came.
The king met with the king of Chǔ at Xiānglíng.
Bái Qǐ was made Wǔ'ān Jūn.
In the thirtieth year,
Shǔ governor Ruò attacked Chǔ,
capturing Wūjùn,
and the region south of the river, establishing Qiánzhōngjùn.
In the thirty-first year,
Bái Qǐ attacked Wèi,
capturing two cities.
Chǔ people rebelled and took back our territory south of the river.
In the thirty-second year,
Chancellor Rǎnghóu attacked Wèi,
reaching Dàliáng,
defeated Bào Yuān,
beheading 40,000 men,
Yuān fled,
and Wèi offered three counties to seek peace.
In the thirty-third year,
Kèqīng Hú Yáng
attacked Wèi's Juǎn, Càiyáng, and Chángshè,
capturing them.
He attacked Máng Mǎo at Huáyáng,
defeated him,
beheading 150,000 men.
Wèi offered Nányáng to seek peace.
In the thirty-fourth year,
Qín combined the territories of Wèi and Hán in Shàngyōng
into one commandery,
and pardoned subjects of Nányáng
to relocate there.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Qín assisted Hán, Wèi, and Chǔ in attacking Yān.
Nányángjùn was initially established.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Kèqīng Zào attacked Qí,
capturing Gāng and Shòu,
and gave them to Rǎnghóu.
In the thirty-eighth year,
Zhōng Gēng Hú Yáng
attacked Zhào's Yānyǔ,
but failed to capture it.
In the fortieth year,
the crown prince Dào died in Wèi,
and was buried in Zhǐyáng.
In the forty-first year, summer,
Qín attacked Wèi,
capturing Xīngqiū and Huái.
In the forty-second year,
Ānguó Jūn was made crown prince.
In the tenth month,
Xuān Tàihòu passed away,
and was buried at Lìshān in Zhǐyáng.
In the ninth month,
Rǎnghóu left for Táo.
In the forty-third year,
Wǔ'ān Jūn Bái Qǐ attacked Hán,
capturing nine cities,
and beheading 50,000 men.
In the forty-fourth year,
Qín attacked Hán's Nánjùn,
and openly captured it.
In the forty-fifth year,
Wǔdàfū Bēn attacked Hán,
capturing ten cities.
Yèyáng Jūn Kuī left for his fief,
but died before arriving.
In the forty-seventh year,
Qín attacked Hán's Shàngdǎng,
Shàngdǎng surrendered to Zhào,
so Qín attacked Zhào instead,
Zhào sent troops to attack Qín,
and they confronted each other.
Qín sent Wǔ'ān Jūn Bái Qǐ to attack,
who heavily defeated Zhào at Chángpíng,
and killed over 400,000 men.
In the forty-eighth year, tenth month,
Hán offered Yuányōng.
The Qín army was divided into three forces.
Wǔ'ān Jūn returned.
Wáng Hé led an attack on Zhào
at Wǔ'ān Píláo,
and captured it.
Sīmǎ Gěng pacified Tàiyuán in the north,
and took all of Hán's Shàngdǎng.
In the first month,
the troops were withdrawn,
and they resumed guarding Shàngdǎng.
In the tenth month of that year,
Wǔdàfū Líng attacked Zhào's Hándān.
In the forty-ninth year, first month,
more troops were sent to assist Líng.
Líng did not fight well,
was dismissed,
and Wáng Hé replaced him as commander.
In the tenth month of that year,
General Zhāng Táng attacked Wèi,
but because the defender of Cài abandoned his post,
he was executed upon return.
In the fiftieth year, tenth month,
Wǔ'ān Jūn Bái Qǐ was found guilty,
reduced to common soldier status,
and exiled to Yīnmì.
Zhāng Táng attacked Zhèng,
and captured it.
In the twelfth month,
more troops were deployed to station near Fénchéng.
Lord Wǔ'ān, Bái Qǐ, having committed a crime,
was executed.
O4 Hé attacked Hándān,
but failed to capture it,
withdrew,
and returned to join the Fén army
for over two months. They attacked the Jìn army,
decapitating six thousand,
and twenty thousand from Jìn and Chǔ drowned in the river.
They attacked Fénchéng,
then followed by capturing Níngxīnzhōng from Táng,
and Níngxīnzhōng was renamed Ānyáng.
The first bridge over the Yellow River was constructed.
In the fifty-first year,
General Jiū attacked Hán,
seizing Yángchéng and Fùshǔ,
and decapitating forty thousand.
They attacked Zhào,
capturing over twenty counties,
with ninety thousand heads and prisoners.
The ruler of Western Zhōu betrayed Qín,
forming an alliance with the other states,
and led the finest troops from across the land
out of Yīquē to attack Qín,
aiming to cut off Qín's access to Yángchéng.
Thereupon, Qín sent General Jiū to attack Western Zhōu.
The ruler of Western Zhōu fled and came to surrender,
bowing in submission to accept punishment,
offering all his thirty-six cities,
and a population of thirty thousand.
The King of Qín accepted the offering,
and returned the ruler to Zhōu.
In the fifty-second year,
the people of Zhōu fled eastward,
and their nine ceremonial tripods were brought into Qín.
Thus, Zhōu began its decline.
In the fifty-third year,
all under heaven came to pay homage.
Wèi was late,
so Qín sent Jiū to attack Wèi,
seizing Wúchéng.
The King of Hán came to court,
and Wèi submitted the state and obeyed orders.
In the fifty-fourth year,
the king performed suburban rites to meet the Supreme God at Yōng.
In the autumn of the fifty-sixth year,
King Xiāng of Qín died,
and his son, King Xiàowén, ascended the throne.
He honored Táng Bāzǐ
as Queen Dowager Táng,
and had her buried together with the previous king.
The King of Hán, wearing mourning attire,
came to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and the other states all sent their generals and ministers
to offer condolences and sacrifices,
overseeing the funeral affairs.
In the first year of King Xiàowén,
he pardoned criminals,
honored the meritorious officials of previous kings,
rewarded and treated relatives generously,
and opened up imperial parks and hunting grounds.
After King Xiàowén completed the mourning period,
he ascended the throne on the tenth month, Jǐhài day,
and died three days later on Xīnchǒu day,
whereupon his son, King Zhuāngxiāng, ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Zhuāngxiāng,
he granted a general amnesty to criminals,
honored the meritorious officials of previous kings,
bestowed virtue and generosity upon kin
and spread benevolence among the people.
The ruler of Eastern Zhōu conspired with other states against Qín,
so Qín sent Chancellor Lǚ Bùwéi to execute him,
and annexed his entire state.
Qín did not extinguish their sacrifices,
granting the land of Yángrén to the Zhōu ruler,
to continue their ancestral worship.
They sent Méng Ào to attack Hán,
and Hán offered Chénggāo and Gǒng.
Qín's border reached Dàliáng,
and the Sānchuān Commandery was first established.
In the second year,
they sent Méng Ào to attack Zhào,
pacifying Tàiyuán.
In the third year,
Méng Ào attacked Gāodū and Jí in Wèi,
capturing them.
He attacked Yúcì, Xīnchéng, and Lángmèng in Zhào,
seizing thirty-seven cities.
In April, there was a solar eclipse.
In the fourth year,
Wáng Hé attacked Shàngdǎng.
The Tàiyuán Commandery was first established.
The Wèi general Wújì led the armies of five states
to attack Qín,
and Qín retreated beyond the river.
Méng Ào was defeated,
and withdrew to depart.
On the fifth month, Bǐngwǔ day,
King Zhuāngxiāng died,
and his son Zhèng ascended the throne,
who became the First Emperor of Qín.
In the twenty-sixth year of King Zhèng of Qín's reign,
he first unified the world into thirty-six commanderies,
and was titled the First Emperor.
The First Emperor died after fifty-one years,
and his son Húhài ascended the throne,
becoming the Second Generation Emperor.
In the third year,
the states rose together in rebellion against Qín,
Zhào Gāo killed the Second Generation Emperor,
and set up Zǐyīng.
Zǐyīng reigned for over a month,
when the states executed him,
thus destroying Qín.
The details are recorded in "The Basic Annals of the First Emperor."
The Grand Historian remarks:
The ancestors of Qín bore the surname Yíng.
Later, they were enfeoffed,
taking their states as surnames,
hence there were the Xú, Tán, and Jǔ clans,
the Zhōnglí, Yùnyǎn, and Túqiú clans,
the Jiāngliáng, Huáng, and Jiāng clans,
the Xiūyú and Báimíng clans,
the Fěilián and Qín clans.
However, because their ancestor Zàofù
was enfeoffed at Zhàochéng,
they became the Zhào clan.
The First Emperor of Qín
was the son of King Zhuāngxiāng of Qín.
While King Zhuāngxiāng was a hostage in Zhào for Qín,
he saw Lǚ Bùwéi's concubine,
was pleased and took her,
and she gave birth to the First Emperor.
He was born in Hándān
in the first month of the forty-eighth year of King Zhāo of Qín.
At birth,
he was named Zhèng,
with the surname Zhào.
At thirteen years old,
King Zhuāngxiāng died,
and Zhèng succeeded him as King of Qín.
At that time,
Qín's territory had already annexed Bā, Shǔ, and Hànzhōng,
crossed Yuān and possessed Yǐng,
establishing the Nán Commandery;
to the north, they had taken Shàngjùn and eastward,
possessing Hédōng,
Tàiyuán, and Shàngdǎng Commanderies;
east to Xíngyáng,
they destroyed the two Zhōu states,
and established the Sānchuān Commandery.
Lǚ Bùwéi served as chancellor,
enfeoffed with a hundred thousand households,
and titled Marquis Wénxìn.
He attracted guests and wandering scholars,
intending to unify the world.
Lǐ Sī served as a retainer.
Méng Ào, Wáng Yǐ, and Biāo Gōng, among others, served as generals.
The king was young,
having just ascended the throne,
and entrusted state affairs to his ministers.
Jìnyáng rebelled,
in the first year,
General Méng Ào attacked and pacified it.
In the second year,
Biāo Gōng led troops to attack Juǎn,
decapitating thirty thousand.
In the third year,
Méng Ào attacked Hán,
seizing thirteen cities.
Wáng Yǐ died.
In October,
General Méng Ào attacked Chàng and Yǒuguǐ of Wèi.
There was a great famine that year.
In the fourth year,
they captured Chàng and Yǒuguǐ.
In March,
the army was disbanded.
The Qín hostage returned from Zhào,
and the Zhào crown prince left to return to his state.
On October Gēngyín day,
locusts came from the east,
darkening the sky.
A plague spread across the land.
Commoners who contributed a thousand dàn of grain internally
were granted one rank of nobility.
In the fifth year,
General Áo attacked Wèi,
pacifying Suānzǎo, Yān, Xū,
Chángpíng, Yōngqiū, and Shānyáng city,
capturing them all and taking twenty cities.
The Dōngjùn commandery was first established.
There was thunder in winter.
In the sixth year,
Hán, Wèi, Zhào, Wèi, and Chǔ jointly attacked Qín,
capturing Shòulíng.
Qín dispatched troops,
and the five states' armies withdrew.
Wèi was captured,
pressing on Dōngjùn,
its ruler Jiǎo led his clan
to move to Yěwáng,
using the mountains as a defense to protect Wèi's Hénèi.
In the seventh year,
a comet first appeared in the east,
was seen in the north,
and in May appeared in the west.
General Áo died.
He attacked Lóng, Gū, and Qìngdū,
then turned troops to attack Jí.
The comet reappeared in the west for sixteen days.
Queen Dowager Xià died.
In the eighth year,
the king's younger brother Cháng'ān Jūn Chéngjiǎo, as general, attacked Zhào,
rebelled,
died at Túnliú,
his officers were all executed,
and the people were relocated to Líntáo.
The general died in his fortifications,
soldiers at Túnliú and Púzhè rebelled,
and their corpses were mutilated.
River fish swam upstream in great numbers,
light carriages and heavy horses went east for food.
Lào Ǎi was enfeoffed as Chángxìn Hóu.
He was given the Shānyáng territory,
and ordered to reside there.
Palaces, carriages, gardens, and hunts were at Ǎi's disposal.
All matters, great and small, were decided by Ǎi.
Furthermore, the Héxī Tàiyuán commandery was made Ǎi's domain.
In the ninth year,
a comet appeared,
sometimes spanning the sky.
They attacked Wèi's Yuán and Púyáng.
In April,
the king stayed at Yōng.
On Jǐyǒu day,
the king was capped,
and girded with a sword.
Chángxìn Hóu Ǎi started a rebellion but was discovered,
forging the king's and queen dowager's seals
to mobilize county soldiers, guards, official cavalry, Róngdí leaders, and retainers,
intending to attack Qínián Palace to rebel.
The king learned of it,
ordered Chancellors Chāngpíng Jūn and Chāngwén Jūn to send troops against Ǎi.
They battled in Xiányáng,
beheaded several hundred,
all were granted ranks,
and even eunuchs in the battle
were also granted one rank each.
Ǎi and others fled in defeat.
An order was issued throughout the state:
whoever captures Ǎi alive will be rewarded one million coins;
whoever kills him, five hundred thousand.
Ǎi and others were all captured.
Commandant of the Guards Jié, Interior Official Sì, Assistant Archer Jié, Chief of the Palace Gentlemen Qí, and twenty others were all beheaded and displayed.
They were torn apart by chariots as a warning,
and their clans exterminated.
As for their retainers,
the lesser ones were sentenced to "ghost fuel" labor.
Over four thousand families were stripped of ranks and exiled to Shǔ,
residing in Fánglíng.
In this month, there was severe cold,
and some died.
Yáng Duānhé attacked Yǎnshì.
A comet appeared in the west,
then in the north,
stretching from the Dipper southward for eighty days.
In the tenth year,
Chancellor Lǚ Bùwéi was implicated in Lào Ǎi's case
and dismissed.
Huán Yǐ was made general.
Qí and Zhào came to set up a banquet.
A man from Qí, Máo Jiāo, advised the King of Qín:
"Qín is now engaged in the affairs of the world,
yet Your Majesty has the reputation of banishing the queen mother,
I fear the feudal lords will hear of it,
and because of this, turn against Qín."
The King of Qín then welcomed the queen mother from Yōng
back to Xiányáng,
and she resided again in Gānquán Palace.
A great search was conducted,
and guests were expelled.
Lǐ Sī submitted a memorial to persuade the king,
and the order to expel guests was stopped.
Lǐ Sī then advised the King of Qín,
requesting to first take Hán to intimidate other states,
so Shī was sent to subdue Hán.
The King of Hán was troubled by this,
and plotted with Hán Fēi to weaken Qín.
A man from Dàliáng, Wèi Liáo, came
and advised the King of Qín:
"With Qín's strength,
the feudal lords are like commandery and county rulers,
I only fear they will form a vertical alliance,
and unite to strike unexpectedly,
this is how Zhì Bó, Fūchāi, and Mǐn Wáng perished.
I hope Your Majesty will not begrudge wealth,
but bribe their powerful ministers,
to disrupt their plans.
At most, spend three hundred thousand jin of gold,
and the feudal lords can all be vanquished."
The King of Qín followed his plan,
treated Wèi Liáo with equal courtesy,
and shared the same clothing, food, and drink as Liáo.
Liáo said:
"The King of Qín's character,
has a prominent nose like a wasp,
long eyes,
a chest like a hawk,
a voice like a jackal,
little kindness and a heart of a tiger or wolf.
In hardship, he easily humbles himself,
in success, he readily devours others.
I am a commoner,
yet when he sees me, he often humbles himself before me.
If the King of Qín truly achieves his ambition over the world,
all under heaven will become his captives.
One cannot associate with him for long."
So he fled.
The King of Qín realized,
firmly stopped him,
appointed him as Commandant of Qín,
and ultimately used his strategies.
And Lǐ Sī held power.
In the eleventh year,
Wáng Jiǎn, Huán Yǐ, and Yáng Duānhé attacked Yè,
capturing nine cities.
Wáng Jiǎn attacked Èyǔ and Liáoyáng,
all combined into one army.
Jiǎn commanded for eighteen days,
the army returned
those below a dǒu of food ration, two out of ten
were conscripted. They captured Yè's Ānyáng,
with Huán Yǐ commanding.
In the twelfth year,
Wénxìn Hóu Bùwéi died,
and was buried secretly.
Those of his retainers who attended the funeral,
if from Jìn, were expelled;
Qín people of six hundred dàn rank or above were stripped of their titles,
and exiled;
those below five hundred dàn who did not attend,
were exiled,
but not stripped of titles.
From now on,
those who handle state affairs improperly like Lào Ǎi and Bùwéi
shall have their families registered,
take this as example.
In autumn,
the exiled retainers of Lào Ǎi in Shǔ were allowed to return.
At that time,
there was a great drought under heaven,
rain did not come until June to August.
In the thirteenth year,
Huán Yǐ attacked Zhào's Píngyáng,
killed Zhào's general Hùzhé,
and beheaded a hundred thousand.
The king went to Hénán.
In the first month,
a comet appeared in the east.
In the tenth month,
Huán Yǐ attacked Zhào.
In the fourteenth year,
they attacked the Zhào army at Píngyáng,
captured Yì'ān,
defeated them,
and killed their general.
Huán Yǐ secured Píngyáng and Wǔchéng.
Hán Fēi was sent to Qín,
Qín used Lǐ Sī's scheme,
detained Fēi,
and Fēi died in Yúnyáng.
The King of Hán requested to become a subject.
In the fifteenth year,
a great army was raised,
one force reached Yè,
one force reached Tàiyuán,
capturing Lángmèng.
There was an earthquake.
In the sixteenth year, in the ninth month,
troops were dispatched to take over the land of Nányáng from Hán,
with Acting Governor Téng in charge.
For the first time, men were ordered to record their ages.
Wèi offered territory to Qín.
Qín established the town of Lìyì.
In the seventeenth year,
the Interior Secretary Téng attacked Hán,
captured King Ān of Hán,
incorporated all of its territory,
made the land into a commandery,
and named it Yǐngchuān.
An earthquake occurred.
Dowager Huáyáng passed away.
The people suffered a great famine.
In the eighteenth year,
a massive army was raised to attack Zhào.
Wáng Jiǎn commanded from the upper lands,
descended through Jǐngxíng,
Duānhé commanded from Hénèi,
Qiāng Huì attacked Zhào,
and Duānhé besieged the city of Hándān.
In the nineteenth year,
Wáng Jiǎn and Qiāng Huì completely secured and took the eastern lands of Zhào, capturing the King of Zhào.
They led troops intending to attack Yān,
stationing at Zhōngshān.
The King of Qín went to Hándān,
and all those who had grudges against his mother's family from when he was born in Zhào were buried alive.
The King of Qín returned,
passing through Tàiyuán and Shàngjùn.
The mother of the First Emperor, the Queen Dowager, passed away.
Prince Jiā of Zhào
led several hundred of his clan to Dài,
proclaimed himself King of Dài,
joined forces with Yān to the east,
and stationed troops at Shànggǔ.
A great famine occurred.
In the twentieth year,
Prince Dān of Yān feared Qín troops would reach his state,
was terrified,
and sent Jīng Kē to assassinate the King of Qín.
The King of Qín detected it,
dismembered Kē as a warning,
and sent Wáng Jiǎn and Xīn Shèng to attack Yān.
Yān and Dài dispatched troops to attack the Qín army,
but the Qín army defeated Yān west of the Yì River.
In the twenty-first year,
Wáng Bēn attacked Jīng.
More troops were sent to Wáng Jiǎn's army,
which then defeated Prince Dān's forces,
captured the Yān capital city of Jì,
and obtained the head of Prince Dān.
The King of Yān gathered forces in Liáodōng to the east
and ruled there.
Wáng Jiǎn pleaded illness due to old age and returned home.
Xīnzhèng rebelled.
Lord Chāngpíng was relocated to Yǐng.
Heavy snow fell,
reaching a depth of two feet five inches.
In the twenty-second year,
Wáng Bēn attacked Wèi,
diverted the river to flood Dàliáng,
the walls of Dàliáng crumbled,
its king requested surrender,
and all its territory was taken.
In the twenty-third year,
the King of Qín recalled Wáng Jiǎn again,
insisting he take command,
and sent him to attack Jīng.
They captured from Chén south to Píngyú,
and captured the King of Jīng.
The King of Qín toured to Yǐngchén.
The Jīng general Xiàng Yàn installed Lord Chāngpíng as King of Jīng,
and rebelled against Qín south of the Huái River.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Wáng Jiǎn and Méng Wǔ attacked Jīng,
defeated the Jīng army,
Lord Chāngpíng died,
and Xiàng Yàn then committed suicide.
In the twenty-fifth year,
a massive army was raised,
with Wáng Bēn in command,
attacking Yān's Liáodōng,
capturing King Xǐ of Yān.
Returning, they attacked Dài,
capturing King Jiā of Dài.
Wáng Jiǎn then secured the Jīng
lands south of the Yangtze;
accepted the surrender of the Yuè lord,
and established the Kuàijī Commandery.
In the fifth month,
a great celebration was held throughout the land.
In the twenty-sixth year,
King Jiàn of Qí and his chancellor Hòu Shèng dispatched troops to guard their western border,
cutting off communication with Qín.
Qín sent General Wáng Bēn to attack Qí from the south via Yān,
capturing King Jiàn of Qí.
Qín for the first time unified all under heaven,
and ordered the chancellor and imperial secretaries, saying:
"Previously, the King of Hán presented land and offered his seal,
requesting to be a vassal,
but then broke the treaty,
allying with Zhào and Wèi against Qín,
so troops were raised to punish him,
and his king was captured.
I thought this would be good,
hoping to end warfare.
The King of Zhào sent his chancellor Lǐ Mù to form an alliance,
so his hostage was returned.
But then he broke the alliance,
attacked our Tàiyuán,
so troops were raised to punish him,
and his king was captured.
Prince Jiā of Zhào then proclaimed himself King of Dài,
so troops were dispatched to attack and destroy him.
The King of Wèi initially agreed to submit and enter Qín,
but then conspired with Hán and Zhào to attack Qín,
Qín officers and troops punished him,
and thus defeated him.
The King of Jīng offered territory west of Qīngyáng,
but then violated the treaty,
attacked our Nánjùn,
so troops were raised to punish him,
his king was captured,
and thus his Jīng lands were secured.
The King of Yān was deluded and chaotic,
his prince Dān secretly ordered Jīng Kē to commit assassination,
officers and troops punished him, destroying his state.
The King of Qí followed Hòu Shèng's plan,
cut off Qín envoys,
intending to rebel,
officers and troops punished him,
his king was captured,
and the Qí lands were pacified.
I, with my insignificant person,
raised troops to punish violence and chaos,
relying on the spirits of the ancestral temple,
the six kings all acknowledged their guilt,
and all under heaven was greatly settled.
Now, if the title and name are not changed,
there is no way to proclaim the achievements,
and transmit to later generations.
Deliberate on the imperial title."
Chancellor Wǎn, Imperial Secretary Jié,
Commandant of Justice Sī, and others all said:
"In the past, the Five Emperors had territories of a thousand li square,
beyond which were the marquis and barbarian domains
where the lords might pay homage or not,
and the Son of Heaven could not control them.
Now Your Majesty has raised righteous troops,
punished the cruel and treacherous,
pacified all under heaven,
making the lands within the seas into commanderies and counties,
with laws and decrees unified,
unprecedented since high antiquity,
surpassing the Five Emperors.
We have carefully deliberated with the academicians and say:
'In ancient times there was the Heavenly Sovereign,
the Earthly Sovereign,
and the Great Sovereign,
and the Great Sovereign is the most noble.'
We risk death to present the honorable title,
that the king become 'Qín Sovereign'.
Decrees be called 'edicts',
orders be called 'rescripts',
and the Son of Heaven refer to himself as 'zhèn'."
The king said:
"Remove 'Great',
retain
'Sovereign',
adopt the ancient
title 'Emperor',
and be called 'Huángdì' (Emperor).
The rest as proposed."
The edict said: "Approved."
Posthumously honored King Zhuāngxiāng
as Tàishàng Huáng (Grand Emperor).
The edict said:
"I have heard that in high antiquity there were titles
but no posthumous names,
in middle antiquity there were titles,
and after death, posthumous names were given based on conduct.
Thus,
sons would discuss their fathers,
ministers would discuss their rulers,
which is most improper,
and I do not adopt it.
From now on,
the practice of posthumous names is abolished.
I am the First Emperor.
Later generations shall count numerically,
second generation, third generation, continuing for ten thousand generations,
passing on endlessly."
The First Emperor applied the cyclical theory of the Five Virtues,
believing that the Zhou dynasty had possessed the Virtue of Fire,
and since Qin was replacing Zhou's virtue,
it must adopt what Zhou could not overcome.
Thus began the current era of the Water Virtue.
He changed the beginning of the year,
making court congratulations start from the first day of the tenth month.
Clothing, banners, and flags were all to be predominantly black.
The number six was established as the standard:
tallies and official hats were six inches,
carriages were six feet wide,
six feet made a pace,
and six horses drew a carriage.
He renamed the Yellow River the "Virtuous Water,"
considering it the inception of the Water Virtue.
With firmness and severity,
all matters were decided by law,
carving away without benevolence, kindness, or harmony,
thereby aligning with the tally of the Five Virtues.
Hence, laws were enforced harshly,
and those long guilty were not pardoned.
Chancellor Wǎn and others said:
"The feudal lords have just been defeated,
and the lands of Yān, Qí, and Jīng are distant.
If we do not establish kings there,
we have no means to pacify them.
We request to install your sons,
hoping Your Majesty will grant this."
The First Emperor referred their proposal to his ministers,
who all considered it expedient.
The Commandant of Justice, Lǐ Sī, argued:
"King Wén and King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed many sons and brothers of the same surname,
yet as generations passed, they grew distant,
attacking each other like enemies,
with the feudal lords warring incessantly,
and the Zhōu Son of Heaven unable to stop it.
Now, thanks to Your Majesty's divine might, the empire is unified,
all divided into commanderies and counties.
Your sons and meritorious officials can be richly rewarded from public taxes,
making them easily controlled.
With no dissent in the empire,
this is the way to ensure peace.
Establishing feudal lords is not expedient."
The First Emperor said:
"The world has long suffered from endless warfare,
all because of feudal lords and kings.
Relying on the ancestral temples,
the empire is newly stabilized,
and to re-establish states
is to sow the seeds of war.
To seek peace and rest thereafter
would indeed be difficult!
The Commandant of Justice is correct."
He divided the empire into thirty-six commanderies,
each with a governor, commandant, and inspector.
He renamed the common people "Qiánshǒu" (Black Heads).
A great feast was held.
Weapons from across the empire were collected,
gathered in Xiányáng,
melted down to cast bells and bell stands,
and twelve metal statues,
each weighing a thousand shi,
were placed in the palace courtyards.
Standards for weights and measures were unified.
Carriages had uniform axle widths.
Writing used the same characters.
The territory extended east to the sea and Cháoxiǎn,
west to Líntáo and Qiāngzhōng,
south to Běixiàng Hù,
north to the river as a barrier,
and along the Yīn Mountains to Liáodōng.
One hundred twenty thousand wealthy and powerful families were relocated to Xiányáng.
The various temples, along with Zhāngtái and Shànglín, were all south of the Wèi River.
Whenever Qin defeated a feudal state,
it would copy its palaces,
building them on the northern slopes of Xiányáng,
facing south toward the Wèi,
from Yōng Gate east to the Jīng and Wèi Rivers,
with interconnected halls, covered walkways, and encircling pavilions.
The beautiful women, bells, and drums obtained from the feudal lords
were moved in to fill them.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the First Emperor toured Lǒngxī and Běidì,
exited at Jītóu Mountain,
and passed through Huízhōng.
He built the Trust Palace south of the Wèi,
later renaming it the Polar Temple,
symbolizing the celestial pole.
A road connected the Polar Temple to Líshān,
and the Front Hall of Gānquán was constructed.
A covered passageway was built,
linking it to Xiányáng.
That year,
one rank of nobility was granted.
Imperial highways were constructed.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the First Emperor traveled east through the commanderies and counties,
ascending Zōu Yì Mountain.
He erected a stone,
consulted with the scholars of Lǔ,
and inscribed it to eulogize Qin's virtue,
discussing the fēng and shàn sacrifices and the worship of mountains and rivers.
Then he ascended Tài Mountain,
set up a stone,
performed the fēng sacrifice, and offered rituals.
Upon descending,
a sudden storm arose,
and he rested under a tree,
subsequently enfeoffing the tree as "Fifth Rank Grandee."
He performed the shàn sacrifice at Liángfù.
The erected stone was inscribed,
with the text reading:
The Emperor ascends the throne,
establishing institutions and clarifying laws,
and his ministers cultivate and rectify themselves.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he first unified the world,
and none failed to submit.
Personally touring distant lands and the common people,
he ascends this Tài Mountain,
surveying the eastern extremes.
His attendants reflect on his traces,
tracing the origins of his enterprise,
reverently reciting his virtues and achievements.
The way of governance operates,
all productions are appropriate,
and all have their models.
Great righteousness is splendid and bright,
passed down to later generations,
to be followed without change.
The Emperor in person is sagely,
having pacified the world,
and is untiring in governance.
Rising early and retiring late,
he builds lasting benefits,
focusing on exalting instruction.
Teaching the classics and spreading understanding,
far and near are all orderly,
all receiving his sage will.
Noble and base are distinct,
men and women observe propriety,
carefully adhering to their duties.
Clearly separating inner and outer,
all is pure and unsullied,
extending to posterity.
His influence reaches endlessly,
honoring and upholding his behest,
eternally bearing his weighty admonitions.
Then he traveled along the Bó Sea eastward,
passing Huáng and Chuí,
reaching the end of Chéng Mountain,
ascending Zhīfú,
where he set up a stone praising Qin's virtue before departing.
He went south to Lángyá,
greatly delighted by it,
and stayed for three months.
He relocated thirty thousand Qiánshǒu households below the Lángyá Terrace,
exempting them from taxes for twelve years.
He built the Lángyá Terrace,
erected a stone inscription,
eulogizing Qin's virtue,
and proclaiming his satisfaction.
It said:
In the twenty-eighth year,
the Emperor initiates.
He rectifies and standardizes the laws and measures,
the guiding principles for all things.
To clarify human affairs,
he harmonizes father and son.
With sage wisdom, benevolence, and righteousness,
he makes the principles clear and evident.
He pacifies the eastern lands in the east,
inspecting the soldiers.
With great tasks completed,
he approaches the sea.
The Emperor's achievements,
diligently labor at fundamental affairs.
Promoting agriculture and eliminating non-essentials,
the Qiánshǒu are enriched.
Across the wide heavens below,
hearts are focused and wills united.
Implements and tools have one measure,
writing uses the same script.
Wherever the sun and moon shine,
wherever boats and carriages reach,
all fulfill their destinies,
and none are unsatisfied.
Acting in accordance with the times,
this is the Emperor.
Rectifying and correcting divergent customs,
he traversed lands and crossed waters.
Caring for and comforting the common people,
he never slackened day or night.
Removing doubts and establishing laws,
all knew what to avoid.
Regional lords divided their duties,
all governance was straightforward and easy.
Every action taken was appropriate,
none were not as clear as a drawing.
The Emperor's brilliance
oversaw and inspected the four directions.
Noble and humble, high and low,
none overstepped their ranks.
Villainy and evil were not tolerated,
all strived for integrity and goodness.
Small and great exerted their efforts,
none dared to be idle or negligent.
Far and near, in remote and hidden places,
all focused on solemnity and dignity.
Upright, honest, sincere, and loyal,
affairs and tasks followed constant principles.
The Emperor's virtue
preserved and stabilized the four extremes.
Punishing chaos and eliminating harm,
he promoted benefits and brought fortune.
Regulating affairs according to the seasons,
all productions multiplied.
The common people were peaceful and tranquil,
with no need for weapons or armor.
The six relations protected each other,
ultimately free from bandits and thieves.
Joyfully following the teachings,
all knew the laws and regulations.
Within the six directions,
all is the Emperor's land.
To the west, crossing the flowing sands,
to the south, reaching the northern households.
To the east, there is the Eastern Sea,
to the north, beyond Dàxià.
Wherever human footprints reach,
there are none who do not submit.
His achievements surpass those of the Five Emperors,
his grace extends even to oxen and horses.
None do not receive his virtue,
each secure in their abode.
The King of Qín, having united all under heaven,
established the title of Emperor,
then pacified the eastern lands,
reaching Lángyá.
Marquis Wǔchéng, a ranked noble, Wáng Lí;
Marquis Tōngwǔ, a ranked noble, Wáng Bēn;
Marquis Jiànchéng, a secondary noble, Zhào Hài;
Marquis Chāngwǔ, a secondary noble, Chéng;
Marquis Wǔxìn, a secondary noble, Féng Wúzé;
Chancellor Wěi Lín, Chancellor Wáng Wǎn;
Minister Lǐ Sī, Minister Wáng Wù;
Grand Masters of the Fifth Rank Zhào Yīng and Yáng Jiū accompanied,
and deliberated with him upon the sea.
They said:
"The ancient emperors
held lands no more than a thousand lǐ,
with feudal lords each guarding their domains,
some paying homage, some not,
invading and violently clashing with each other,
slaughtering and attacking without cease,
yet they still inscribed metal and stone,
to make records for themselves.
The ancient Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns,
their knowledge and teachings differed,
their laws and measures unclear,
borrowed authority from ghosts and spirits,
to deceive distant regions,
their reality not matching their names,
thus they did not last long.
Before their bodies perished,
the feudal lords rebelled and betrayed,
and their decrees were not implemented.
Now the Emperor has unified the entire realm,
establishing commanderies and counties,
bringing peace and harmony to all under heaven.
He has glorified the ancestral temple,
embodied the Way and practiced virtue,
achieving a great and honored title.
We, the assembled ministers, together
recite the Emperor's merits and virtues,
to be carved on metal and stone,
as a model and standard."
After this,
a man from Qí, Xú Fú, and others submitted a memorial,
saying there were three spirit mountains in the sea,
named Pénglái,
Fāngzhàng, and Yíngzhōu,
where immortals dwell.
They requested to fast and purify,
and with boys and girls, seek them.
Thereupon, he sent Xú Fú
to dispatch several thousand boys and girls,
to enter the sea in search of immortals.
The First Emperor returned,
passed by Péngchéng,
fasted, prayed, and sacrificed,
wishing to retrieve the Zhōu ding from the Sì River.
He sent a thousand men to dive into the water to seek it,
but it was not found.
Then he traveled southwest across the Huái River,
to Héngshān and Nánjùn.
Sailing on the river,
he reached the Xiāngshān Shrine.
Encountering a great wind,
he nearly could not cross.
The Emperor asked the court scholars:
"What deity is Xiāng Jūn?"
The scholars replied:
"We have heard,
she is the daughter of Yáo,
wife of Shùn,
and buried here."
Thereupon, the First Emperor was greatly angered,
sent three thousand convicts to cut down the trees of Xiāngshān,
and turned the mountain bare.
The Emperor then returned from Nánjùn via Wǔguān.
In the twenty-ninth year,
the First Emperor traveled east.
Reaching Bólángshā in Yángwǔ,
he was startled by bandits.
The search for them was unsuccessful,
so he ordered a great ten-day search throughout the land.
He ascended Zhīfú,
and carved a stone inscription.
The inscription read:
In the twenty-ninth year,
at the mid-spring season,
the warm harmony was just arising.
The Emperor traveled east,
toured and ascended Zhīfú,
overlooking the sea.
The attending ministers admired the view,
reflecting on the splendid achievements,
recalling and reciting the origins.
The great sage established governance,
set up and fixed laws and measures,
making the guiding principles clear and prominent.
Externally instructing the feudal lords,
gloriously bestowing civil kindness,
illuminating with righteousness and reason.
The six states were perverse and wicked,
greedy and cruel without satisfaction,
slaughtering and oppressing without end.
The Emperor pitied the masses,
thus dispatched punitive armies,
vigorously displaying martial virtue.
Righteous in punishment, faithful in action,
his might blazed far and wide,
and none did not submit.
Exterminating the strong and violent,
rescuing and relieving the common people,
he comprehensively stabilized the four extremes.
Universally applying enlightened laws,
he organized and governed all under heaven,
eternally setting a model and standard.
How great it is!
Within the cosmos and the realm,
all follow the sage's will.
The ministers recite his merits,
requesting to carve them in stone,
to display and perpetuate a constant model.
The eastern inscription said:
In the twenty-ninth year,
the Emperor traveled in spring,
inspecting and observing distant regions.
Reaching the seashore,
he then ascended Zhīfú,
facing the morning sun.
Gazing upon the vast and beautiful scenery,
the attending ministers all reflected,
on the Way's utmost clarity.
The sage's laws first arose,
cleansing and ordering within the borders,
externally punishing the violent and strong.
Martial might spread everywhere,
shaking the four extremes,
capturing and destroying the six kings.
Opening and unifying all under heaven,
disasters and harms ceased and ended,
forever laying down arms.
The emperor, with brilliant virtue,
governed the realm,
never neglecting his observations and hearings.
He established great righteousness,
displayed and set up instruments,
all with insignias and banners.
Officials adhered to their duties,
each knowing their responsibilities,
so affairs were free from suspicion.
The common people transformed,
near and far shared the same standards,
surpassing the ancients without fault.
Regular duties being settled,
descendants followed the legacy,
long upholding the sage rule.
Ministers praised the virtue,
reverently recited the holy achievements,
requesting to carve at Zhīfú.
Then,
proceeded to Lángyé,
entering via Shàngdǎng.
In the thirtieth year,
nothing occurred.
In the twelfth month of the thirty-first year,
renamed the winter sacrifice as "Jiāpíng".
Bestowed upon each village six dan of rice,
and two sheep.
The First Emperor traveled incognito in Xiányáng,
accompanied by four warriors,
went out at night and encountered robbers at Lánchí,
was cornered,
the warriors struck and killed the robbers,
a twenty-day search was conducted within the passes.
Rice cost sixteen hundred per dan.
In the thirty-second year,
the First Emperor went to Jiéshí,
sent the Yan native Lú Shēng
to seek Xiànmén and Gāoshì.
Carved at the gate of Jiéshí.
Demolished city walls,
breached and connected dikes.
The inscription read:
Thus raised armies,
executed the unprincipled,
suppressed rebellions.
By force eliminated violent rebels,
by culture restored the innocent,
all hearts submitted.
Kindly discussed merits,
rewards extended to oxen and horses,
grace enriched the land.
The emperor exerted might,
virtue united the feudal lords,
first unified in great peace.
Razed city walls,
breached river dikes,
leveled obstacles.
With terrain settled,
the people free from corvée,
all under heaven pacified.
Men delight in their fields,
women pursue their tasks,
all affairs in order.
Grace covers all produce,
long-term and new farmers,
none not settled.
Ministers recite achievements,
request to carve this stone,
to eternalize the model.
Thereupon sent Hán Zhōng, Hóu Gōng,
and Shí Shēng to seek the elixir of immortality.
The First Emperor inspected the northern border,
entering from Shàngjùn.
The Yan native Lú Shēng, returning from a sea mission,
through matters of ghosts and spirits,
presented a prophetic text,
saying, "The one who will destroy Qin is Hú."
The First Emperor then sent General Méng Tián to dispatch
three hundred thousand troops north to attack the Hú,
capturing the land south of the river.
In the thirty-third year,
conscripted those who had been fugitives,
live-in sons-in-law, and merchants to
seize the Lùliáng land,
establishing Guìlín, Xiàngjùn, and Nánhǎi commanderies,
using exiles for garrison duty.
Expelled the Xiōngnú in the northwest.
From Yúzhōng along the river eastward,
connecting to Yīnshān,
made into forty-four counties,
fortified the river with defenses.
Also sent Méng Tián across the river to take Gāoquē,
Táoyáng Shān, and Běijià Zhōng,
building outposts to drive out the Róng people.
Relocated exiles,
to populate the new counties.
Banned unauthorized sacrifices.
A bright star appeared in the west.
In the thirty-fourth year,
punished unjust law officials,
sent them to build the Great Wall
and the Nányuè lands.
The First Emperor hosted a banquet at Xiányáng Palace,
seventy academicians came forward to toast.
Commandant Zhōu Qīngchén presented
praise, saying:
"In the past, the Qin territory was no more than a thousand li,
relying on Your Majesty's divine brilliance and sage wisdom,
pacified the realm,
expelled the barbarians,
wherever the sun and moon shine,
none do not submit.
Turning feudal states into commanderies and counties,
everyone lives in peace and happiness,
free from the scourge of war,
to be passed down for ten thousand generations.
Since high antiquity, none have matched
Your Majesty's might and virtue."
The First Emperor was pleased.
Academician Chúnyú Yuè from Qí
stepped forward and said:
"I heard that the kings of Yīn and Zhōu
reigned for over a thousand years,
enfeoffing sons, brothers, and meritorious officials,
as supporting branches.
Now Your Majesty possesses the realm,
yet your sons and brothers are commoners,
if suddenly there are ministers like Tián Cháng or the Six High Ministers,
without support,
how can you be saved?
Affairs not modeled on antiquity
yet able to last long, I have not heard of.
Now Zhōu Qīngchén flatters to your face
to magnify Your Majesty's errors,
he is no loyal minister."
The First Emperor referred his proposal for discussion.
Chancellor Lǐ Sī said:
"The Five Emperors did not repeat each other,
the Three Dynasties did not imitate one another,
each ruled in their own way,
not because they opposed each other,
but because times changed.
Now Your Majesty initiates great enterprises,
establishes merits for ten thousand generations,
certainly beyond the understanding of foolish scholars.
Moreover, Yuè's words are about the Three Dynasties' affairs,
what worth is there to emulate?
In the past, feudal lords competed,
generously attracting itinerant scholars.
Now the realm is settled,
laws and decrees come from one source,
the common people at home should focus on farming and crafts,
scholars should study laws and decrees
to avoid prohibitions.
Now these scholars do not learn from the present but study antiquity,
to criticize the current age,
confusing and misleading the common people.
Chancellor, your subject Sī, dares to speak at the risk of death:
In ancient times, the realm was fragmented and chaotic,
none could unify it,
hence feudal lords arose together,
discourses all praised antiquity to harm the present,
embellished empty words to confuse reality,
people cherished their private studies,
to criticize what the ruler established.
Now the emperor possesses the entire realm,
distinguishes black from white and establishes one authority.
Private studies
that mutually oppose laws and teachings,
when people hear decrees issued,
each criticizes them based on their own learning,
inwardly disapproving in heart,
outwardly discussing in alleys,
boasting to the ruler for fame,
adopting heterodoxy to appear superior,
leading the masses to create slander.
If this is not prohibited,
then the ruler's authority declines above,
and factions form below.
It is expedient to prohibit it.
I request that the court historian
burn all records not of Qin.
Except for what the academicians are tasked with,
anyone in the realm daring to possess the "Book of Songs",
"Book of Documents", or the writings of the hundred schools,
must deliver them to the governor or commandant for mixed
burning.
Those daring to discuss the "Book of Songs" and "Book of Documents" in pairs
shall be executed in the market.
Those using antiquity to criticize the present
shall be exterminated along with their clans.
Officials who know of such but do not report it
shall share the same crime.
If the decree is not complied with within thirty days,
they shall be tattooed and made to build walls.
What are not to be eliminated
are books on medicine, divination, and agriculture.
If one wishes to study laws and decrees,
take officials as teachers."
The emperor approved:
"It is permitted."
In the thirty-fifth year,
roads were constructed from Jiǔyuán to Yúnyáng,
cutting through mountains and filling valleys,
to create a direct route.
Thereupon, Shǐ Huáng believed that Xiányáng had too many people,
and the former kings' palaces were too small.
"I have heard that King Wén of Zhōu
had his capital at Fēng,
and King Wǔ at Hào;
between Fēng and Hào,
is the capital of emperors and kings."
So he began constructing a court palace
in the Shànglín Garden south of the Wèi River.
First, the front hall, Ēpáng, was built,
measuring five hundred paces from east to west,
and fifty zhàng from north to south.
Above, it could seat ten thousand people;
below, it could hoist flags of five zhàng.
Covered passageways circled around,
stretching directly from the hall to the Southern Mountains.
The peak of the Southern Mountains was marked
to serve as a gate tower.
Elevated pathways were built,
crossing the Wèi River from Ēpáng,
connecting to Xiányáng,
to symbolize
the celestial pole's passage crossing the Milky Way to reach the constellation Yíngshì.
The Ēpáng Palace was not completed;
upon completion,
it was intended to choose a more fitting name for it.
As the palace was built at Ēpáng,
it came to be called the Ēpáng Palace by all under heaven.
Over seven hundred thousand convicts and laborers
were divided to work on the Ēpáng Palace,
or on Lìshān.
Stone from the Northern Mountains was quarried for coffins,
and timber from Shǔ and Jīng regions
was all transported there.
Within the Guānzhōng area, there were three hundred palaces in total,
and over four hundred outside.
Then a stone was erected at the border of Qú by the Eastern Sea,
to serve as the eastern gate of Qín.
Consequently, thirty thousand households were relocated to Lìyì,
and fifty thousand to Yúnyáng,
all exempted from corvée for ten years.
Lú Shēng advised Shǐ Huáng, saying:
"We, your subjects, seeking miraculous herbs, elixirs, and immortals,
often fail to encounter them,
as if something is hindering us.
In esoteric practices,
the ruler should sometimes move incognito
to avoid evil spirits.
When evil spirits are avoided,
the true immortals will arrive.
If the places where the ruler resides are known to his subjects,
it harms the spiritual connection.
The true immortals
enter water without getting wet,
enter fire without being burned,
ride the clouds,
and endure as long as heaven and earth.
Now, Your Majesty governs all under heaven,
yet cannot attain tranquility.
I wish that the places where you reside would not be known to others,
then the elixir of immortality might
be obtainable."
Thereupon, Shǐ Huáng said:
"I admire the true immortals,
and will call myself 'True Immortal,'
not using 'Zhèn'."
He then ordered that within two hundred lǐ around Xiányáng, two hundred seventy palaces and towers be connected by elevated pathways and covered corridors,
filled with curtains, bells, drums,
and beautiful women,
each stationed according to register without moving.
Wherever he traveled, if anyone revealed his location,
the crime was punishable by death.
Once, Shǐ Huáng visited Liángshān Palace,
and from the mountain
saw the numerous carriages and horsemen of the chancellor,
which displeased him.
A palace attendant informed the chancellor,
who later reduced his retinue.
Shǐ Huáng angrily said:
"This attendant leaked my words."
Upon investigation, no one confessed.
At that time,
he ordered the arrest of all who were present then,
and had them all executed.
From then on, no one knew
his whereabouts.
When holding court,
officials received decisions on affairs
entirely at the Xiányáng Palace.
Hóu Shēng and Lú Shēng conspired together, saying:
"Shǐ Huáng's nature
is inherently stubborn and self-willed.
Having risen from among the feudal lords,
and unified the world,
he achieves his wishes and follows his desires,
believing that none since ancient times can match him.
He exclusively employs prison officials,
who gain his favor.
Though there are seventy erudites,
they are merely for show and not utilized.
The chancellor and other high officials
all receive settled matters,
relying on the emperor for decisions.
He delights in using punishments and executions to assert authority,
causing all under heaven to fear punishment
and cling to their salaries,
none daring to be fully loyal.
The emperor hears no criticism of his faults
and grows more arrogant daily,
while those below tremble and deceive
to gain favor.
Under Qín law,
if one's methods
prove ineffective,
they are put to death.
Yet, there are up to three hundred astrologers,
all capable men,
who fear taboos and flatter,
not daring to speak frankly of his errors.
Matters under heaven, great or small,
are all decided by the emperor,
who even weighs documents by the dàn,
requiring a daily quota,
and cannot rest unless the quota is met.
So greedy for power and influence,
he is not fit for seeking the elixir of immortality."
Thereupon, they fled.
Shǐ Huáng heard of their flight,
and flew into a rage, saying:
"I previously collected all books of the world
and eliminated those deemed useless.
I summoned numerous scholars and masters of esoteric arts,
hoping to bring about great peace,
and the alchemists sought to refine extraordinary elixirs.
Now I hear that Hán Zhòng left without reporting,
Xú Fú and others spent countless millions,
yet ultimately obtained no elixir,
and only reports of deceit and profit abound daily.
I honored and rewarded Lú Shēng and others richly,
yet now they slander me,
thereby加重 my lack of virtue.
As for the scholars in Xiányáng,
I have had them investigated,
and some spread absurd rumors
to confuse the common people."
Thereupon, he ordered the imperial censors
to interrogate all the scholars thoroughly.
The scholars implicated each other under questioning,
leading to over four hundred sixty who confessed to violating the禁令,
all of whom were buried alive in Xiányáng,
to make it known to all under heaven,
as a warning to posterity.
More exiles were sent to the borders.
Shǐ Huáng's eldest son, Fú Sū, remonstrated, saying:
"The world is newly stabilized,
and the common people in distant regions are not yet settled.
The scholars all study and emulate Confucius;
now if Your Majesty severely punishes them with laws,
I fear it will unsettle the world.
I implore you to consider this."
Shǐ Huáng was angered,
and sent Fú Sū north to supervise Méng Tián
in Shàngjùn.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Mars remained in the Heart constellation.
A falling star descended in Dōngjùn,
landing as a stone,
on which some common people carved the words
"The First Emperor will die, and the land will be divided."
Shǐ Huáng heard of this,
dispatched censors to investigate thoroughly,
but no one confessed.
He then had all the people living near the stone
executed,
and the stone was burned and destroyed.
Shǐ Huáng was unhappy,
and ordered the erudites to compose "The Poem of the Immortal True One,"
which was performed wherever he traveled across the world,
with musicians commanded to sing and play it.
In autumn, an envoy traveling from Guandong passed by night through the Pingshu Road at Huáyīn,
when someone holding a jade disc stopped the envoy and said:
"Please deliver this for me to the Lord of Hàochí."
He then added:
"This year, the Ancestral Dragon will die."
The envoy asked for an explanation,
but the man suddenly vanished,
leaving the jade disc behind.
The envoy presented the disc and reported the incident in full.
The First Emperor remained silent for a long time,
then said:
"Mountain spirits, after all, can only foresee
events of a single year."
Later, in private, he remarked:
"The Ancestral Dragon
refers to the forebear of men."
He ordered the imperial treasury to examine the jade disc,
and it turned out to be the very disc he had cast into the river
while crossing the Yangtze in his twenty-eighth year of reign.
Thereupon, the First Emperor consulted the oracle,
and the divination indicated that travel and relocation would bring good fortune.
He relocated thirty thousand households to Yúzhōng north of the Yellow River.
He granted them one rank of nobility.
In the tenth month, on the Guichou day, of the thirty-seventh year,
the First Emperor embarked on a tour.
The Left Chancellor Lǐ Sī accompanied him,
while the Right Chancellor Féng Qùjí remained to guard the capital.
His youngest son Hú Hài, out of affection and admiration,
requested to join the tour,
and the emperor permitted it.
In the eleventh month,
they reached Yúnmèng,
where he performed a distant sacrifice to Emperor Shùn at the Jiǔyí Mountains.
They then sailed down the river,
viewed Jí Kē,
and crossed Hǎi Zhǔ.
Passing through Dānyáng,
they arrived at Qiántáng.
Facing the Zhèjiāng River,
the waves were fierce,
so they traveled west 120 li to cross at a narrow point.
Ascending Kuàijī Mountain,
he sacrificed to Great Yǔ,
gazed towards the Southern Sea,
and erected a stone inscription praising the virtues of Qín.
The text read:
The Emperor's splendid achievements,
unifying all within the seas,
his virtue and beneficence enduring and long.
In the thirty-seventh year,
he personally tours the world,
viewing distant regions far and wide.
