Thus he ascends Kuàijī,
inspecting and proclaiming customs,
the common people reverent and solemn.
Ministers recite his merits,
tracing the origins of deeds,
recalling his lofty wisdom.
The sage of Qín rules the state,
first establishing laws and names,
displaying the ancient statutes clearly.
Initially setting legal standards,
discerning duties and responsibilities,
to establish constant norms.
The six kings were arrogant and rebellious,
greedy, cruel, and violently proud,
leading their masses in self-aggrandizement.
Acting violently and arbitrarily,
relying on strength with arrogance,
repeatedly mobilizing armies.
Secretly communicating through spies,
forming vertical alliances,
their actions devious and unrighteous.
Internally devising deceitful plots,
externally invading the borders,
thus bringing forth calamity.
With righteous might, he punished them,
extinguishing their violent rebellion,
the rebels and traitors perishing.
His sage virtue vast and profound,
throughout the six directions,
bathed in his boundless grace.
The Emperor unifies the cosmos,
hearing all matters,
near and far entirely purified.
Managing all affairs,
examining facts and realities,
each recorded by its name.
Noble and humble alike communicate,
good and bad laid out openly,
with no hidden truths.
Adorning and proclaiming righteousness,
remarrying while having sons,
betrays the dead and lacks chastity.
Separating inner and outer spheres,
forbidding licentiousness,
men and women pure and sincere.
If a husband acts like a stray boar,
killing him is no crime,
men uphold righteous codes.
If a wife flees to remarry,
her children disown her as mother,
all transformed to integrity and purity.
Greatly cleansing customs,
the world follows this influence,
covered in excellent teachings.
All adhere to measures and tracks,
harmonious, peaceful, earnest, and diligent,
none disobeying commands.
The common people cultivated and pure,
joyfully sharing the same rules,
happily preserving great peace.
Hereafter reverently upholding laws,
eternal rule without end,
carriage and boat unshaken.
Attending ministers recite his exploits,
requesting this stone be carved,
shining with glorious inscriptions.
Returning, they passed through Wú,
crossing from Jiāngchéng.
Along the coast, north to Lángyá.
The alchemist Xú Fú and others, having gone to sea
to seek the elixir of immortality,
for years had not obtained it,
spending much funds,
feared reprimand,
so they deceitfully said:
"The Pénglái elixir can be obtained,
but we are often troubled by giant sharks,
thus unable to reach it.
We wish to have skilled archers accompany us,
to shoot them with repeating crossbows upon sight."
The First Emperor dreamed of battling the sea god,
who appeared in human form.
Consulting a dream interpreter, a court academician said:
"The water god is invisible,
manifesting through giant fish and dragons as omens.
Now, Your Majesty's prayers and sacrifices are thorough and reverent,
yet such an evil spirit appears;
it should be eliminated,
so that the good spirit may be attracted."
So he ordered those going to sea
to equip themselves with tools to catch huge fish,
and he personally waited with a repeating crossbow
to shoot any giant fish that emerged.
From Lángyá north to Róngchéng Mountain,
none were seen.
Upon reaching Zhīfú,
they spotted a giant fish,
and shot one dead.
Then they proceeded west along the coast.
Reaching the ferry at Píngyuán, he fell ill.
The First Emperor detested speaking of death,
so none of his ministers dared mention matters of dying.
As his illness worsened,
he prepared a sealed decree
bestowing upon Prince Fú Sū, saying:
"Join the funeral at Xiányáng
for burial."
The letter was sealed,
and kept in the office of Zhào Gāo, the Prefect of the Central Chariots,
who handled tallies and seals,
but it was not yet given to a messenger.
On the seventh month, Bǐngyín day,
the First Emperor passed away at Shāqiū's Píngtái.
Chancellor Lǐ Sī, because the emperor died outside the capital,
feared unrest among the princes and across the land,
so he kept it secret,
not announcing the death.
The coffin was placed in a warm chariot,
with favored eunuchs attending as companions,
and food was presented as usual at stops.
Officials submitted reports as before,
and the eunuchs would approve them from within the warm chariot.
Only the son Hú Hài, Zhào Gāo,
and five or six favored eunuchs knew of the emperor's death.
Zhào Gāo had previously taught Hú Hài calligraphy
and legal statutes and affairs,
so Hú Hài privately favored him.
Gāo then conspired with Prince Hú Hài
and Chancellor Lǐ Sī in secret,
destroying the sealed letter the First Emperor had for Prince Fú Sū,
and forged a decree claiming that Chancellor Lǐ Sī received
the First Emperor's posthumous edict at Shāqiū,
establishing Hú Hài as crown prince.
They also wrote another letter to Princes Fú Sū and Méng Tián,
listing their crimes,
and ordering them to commit suicide.
The details are recorded in "The Biography of Lǐ Sī."
They traveled on, via Jǐngxíng to Jiǔyuán.
It happened to be summer,
and the emperor's warm chariot began to smell,
so they ordered the accompanying officials
to load a cart with a shi of salted fish,
to mask the odor.
The procession followed the straight road to Xiányáng,
where the funeral was held.
Crown Prince Húhài succeeded to the throne,
becoming the Second Emperor.
In the ninth month,
the First Emperor was buried at Lìshān.
When the First Emperor first ascended the throne,
he began excavating and constructing at Lìshān.
By the time he unified the world,
over 700,000 conscripted laborers from across the empire were sent there,
digging through three layers of springs,
pouring bronze to secure the outer coffin,
and filling it with palaces, towers, officials,
rare artifacts and treasures,
all moved and stored to capacity.
Artisans were ordered to create crossbow mechanisms that would
automatically shoot at anyone attempting to tunnel near.
Mercury was used to simulate hundreds of rivers,
the Yangtze, Yellow River, and great seas,
with mechanical systems circulating it;
the ceiling depicted the celestial phenomena,
and the floor represented the geography.
Lamp oil made from human-fish blubber
was estimated to burn undiminished for a long time.
The Second Emperor said:
"For the childless women of the late emperor's harem,
it is improper to let them out."
He ordered them all to accompany in death,
resulting in numerous deaths.
After the burial was completed,
someone mentioned that the artisans who built the mechanisms
knew all the secrets of the treasures,
and if the treasures were heavy, it would leak out.
Once the great affair was finished,
and the treasures were stored,
the central passage was closed,
the outer gate was lowered,
trapping all the artisans and treasure keepers inside,
with none ever coming out again.
Trees and plants were planted to resemble a mountain.
In the first year of the Second Emperor,
he was twenty-one years old.
Zhào Gāo became the Prefect of the Gentlemen of the Palace,
wielding power and managing affairs.
The Second Emperor issued an edict
to increase the sacrificial offerings at the First Emperor's temple
and the rituals for mountains, rivers, and various sacrifices.
He ordered the ministers to deliberate
on honoring the First Emperor's temple.
The ministers all bowed their heads and said:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven had seven temples,
feudal lords had five,
and high officials had three,
and they were never destroyed even after ten thousand generations.
Let the First Emperor's temple be the ultimate temple,
to which all within the four seas present tribute and duties,
with increased sacrifices,
and rituals all complete,
leaving nothing to add.
The temples of previous kings
were either in Western Yōng
or in Xiányáng.
The Son of Heaven's ceremony should uniquely offer libations and sacrifices at the First Emperor's temple.
Those from Duke Xiāng downwards should be destroyed.
In total, seven temples are established.
Ministers shall perform sacrifices according to ritual,
honoring the First Emperor's temple as the ancestral temple
of the emperors.
The emperor again
refers to himself as 'Zhèn'."
The Second Emperor plotted with Zhào Gāo, saying:
"I am young,
newly ascended to the throne,
and the common people have not yet gathered and submitted.
The late emperor toured the commanderies and counties,
to demonstrate strength,
awing the empire into submission.
If now we remain peaceful and do not tour,
it will show weakness,
and we cannot rule the world as subjects."
In spring,
the Second Emperor traveled east through the commanderies and counties,
with Lǐ Sī accompanying.
They reached Jiéshí,
followed the coast south to Kuàijī,
and inscribed all the steles erected by the First Emperor,
adding beside the stones
the names of the accompanying ministers,
to manifest the late emperor's achievements and great virtue:
The
Emperor said:
"The metal and stone inscriptions were all made by the First Emperor.
Now that I have inherited the title, if the inscriptions do not refer to the First Emperor,
in the distant future it will seem as if later descendants made them,
failing to match his achievements and great virtue."
The Chancellor, your subject Lǐ Sī, your subject Qùjí,
and the Imperial Secretary, your subject Dé, risk death to say:
"We request to fully inscribe the edict on the stone,
making it clear.
We risk death to ask."
The decree said: "Approved."
They then proceeded to Liáodōng and returned.
Thereupon, the Second Emperor followed Zhào Gāo's advice,
and enforced the laws and decrees.
He then secretly plotted with Zhào Gāo, saying:
"The great ministers are disobedient,
the officials are still powerful,
and the various princes will surely contend with me;
what should be done about it?"
Gāo said:
"I have long wished to speak but did not dare.
The late emperor's great ministers
are all renowned nobles from generations in the empire,
accumulating merits and labors
passed down through ages for a long time.
Now I, Gāo, was originally lowly and insignificant,
yet Your Majesty graciously promoted me,
placing me in a high position,
in charge of palace affairs.
The great ministers are discontent,
only outwardly following me,
but in their hearts, they are truly不服.
Now that you are touring,
if you do not take this opportunity to investigate
and execute the guilty commandery governors and commandants,
punishing them,
it will enhance your awe over the empire above,
and eliminate those whom you have always disliked below.
Now is not the time to learn from civility
but to decide through military force.
I urge Your Majesty to follow the times without doubt,
so that the ministers cannot plan in time.
A wise ruler gathers and promotes the remaining people,
ennobling the humble,
enriching the poor,
drawing close the distant,
then high and low will unite, and the state will be secure."
The Second Emperor said: "Good."
Thereupon, he executed great ministers
and the various princes,
implicating and arresting minor officials and imperial guards for crimes,
leaving none to stand,
and six princes were executed in Dù.
Prince Jiānglǘ and his two brothers
were imprisoned in the inner palace,
their crimes deliberated last.
The Second Emperor sent an envoy to order Jiānglǘ:
"You, Prince, have been disloyal,
a crime deserving death,
the officials will enforce the law."
Jiānglǘ said:
"In court rituals,
I have never dared not to follow the ushers;
in temple positions,
I have never dared to lose propriety;
in receiving orders and responding,
I have never dared to misspeak.
How can I be disloyal?
I wish to hear my crime before dying."
The envoy said:
"I cannot participate in the deliberation,
I only carry out the edict."
Jiānglǘ then looked up to heaven and cried out to heaven three times,
saying:
"Heaven!
I am innocent!"
The three brothers all shed tears
and drew their swords to commit suicide.
The imperial clan trembled with fear.
Ministers who remonstrated were accused of slander,
high officials clung to their salaries to please the emperor,
and the common people were terrified.
In the fourth month,
the Second Emperor returned to Xiányáng,
and said:
"The late emperor found the Xiányáng court small,
hence he built the Ēpáng Palace. The halls
were not completed,
when he passed away,
so the construction was halted,
and labor was redirected to Lìshān.
Now that Lìshān's affairs are largely finished,
if we abandon the Ēpáng Palace unfinished,
it would reveal the late emperor's errors in undertakings."
He resumed construction on the Ēpáng Palace.
He pacified the four barbarians externally,
following the First Emperor's plan.
He conscripted all its elite troops, fifty thousand men,
to garrison and guard Xiányáng,
ordering them to practice archery
and hunt dogs, horses, and wild animals.
With many to feed,
and supplies estimated insufficient,
he ordered the commanderies and counties
to transport beans, grains, and fodder.
All were ordered to bring their own provisions,
and within three hundred lǐ of Xiányáng,
they were not allowed to eat its grain.
The enforcement of laws became increasingly severe.
In the seventh month,
garrison soldier Chén Shèng and others
rebelled in the former land of Jīng,
establishing
"Zhāng Chǔ."
Shèng proclaimed himself King of Chǔ,
residing in Chén,
and sent various generals to seize territories.
The youths from the commanderies and counties east of the mountains,
suffering under Qín officials,
all killed their governors, commandants,
magistrates, and assistants in revolt,
responding to Chén Shè,
supporting each other as marquises and kings,
forming alliances heading west,
under the banner of attacking Qín,
too numerous to count.
A court reporter returning from the east
reported the rebels to Èrshì.
Èrshì was enraged,
and had him handed over to the officials.
When later envoys arrived,
the emperor inquired,
and they replied:
"They are mere bandits;
the commandery governors and commandants are pursuing and capturing them,
and now they are nearly all caught,
not worth worrying about."
The emperor was pleased.
Wǔ Chén proclaimed himself King of Zhào,
Wèi Jiū as King of Wèi,
Tián Dān as King of Qí.
The Lord of Pèi rose in Pèi.
Xiàng Liáng raised troops in the Kuàijī Commandery.
In the winter of the second year,
the forces sent by Chén Shè, led by Zhōu Zhāng and others,
advanced west to Xì,
with troops numbering hundreds of thousands.
Èrshì was greatly alarmed,
and consulted with his ministers, saying:
"What should we do?"
The minor treasurer Zhāng Hán said:
"The bandits have arrived,
their forces are strong,
and mobilizing nearby counties now would be too late.
There are many convicts at Líshān;
I request to pardon them,
and arm them to attack the rebels."
Èrshì then issued a great pardon throughout the land,
appointed Zhāng Hán as general,
who defeated Zhōu Zhāng's army and forced them to flee,
subsequently killing Zhāng at Cáoyáng.
Èrshì further dispatched the senior scribes Sīmǎ Xīn and Dǒng Yì
to assist Zhāng Hán in attacking the bandits,
killing Chén Shèng at Fùfù,
defeating Xiàng Liáng at Dìngtáo,
and destroying Wèi Jiū at Línjì.
With the renowned rebel leaders in Chǔ land dead,
Zhāng Hán then crossed the river north,
attacking King Xiē of Zhào and others at Jùlù.
Zhào Gāo advised Èrshì, saying:
"The late emperor ruled the world for a long time,
so the ministers did not dare to do wrong
or present deceitful proposals.
Now, Your Majesty is young,
newly ascended to the throne,
why decide matters in court with the high officials?
If a matter turns out wrong,
it would expose Your Majesty's shortcomings to the ministers.
The Son of Heaven is called 'Zhèn,'
and indeed should not be heard directly."
Thereupon, Èrshì often stayed in the inner palace,
deciding all matters with Gāo.
Thereafter, the high officials rarely had audience with him,
bandits and rebels increased,
and troops from Guānzhōng
were continuously dispatched east to attack the rebels.
The Right Chancellor Qùjí, Left Chancellor Lǐ Sī,
and General Féng Jié presented a remonstrance, saying:
"Bandits east of the pass have risen together;
Qín has dispatched troops to suppress them,
killing vast numbers,
yet they still do not cease.
The bandits are numerous
largely due to the hardships of garrison duty, water transport,
labor services,
and heavy taxes.
We request to halt the construction of the Ēpáng Palace,
and reduce garrison duties and transport on the four borders."
Èrshì said:
"I have heard from Hán Fēizǐ:
'Yáo and Shǔn used rough-hewn rafters without planing,
thatched roofs untrimmed,
ate from earthen bowls,
drank from earthen vessels;
even a gatekeeper's sustenance
is not more meager than this.
Yǔ dredged the Lóngmén,
connected to the great plains,
channeled stagnant river waters,
releasing them to the sea,
personally carrying the spade and basket,
his shins without hair,
the toil of a slave or captive
is not more arduous than this.'
In general, the reason for valuing possession of the world
is to indulge desires to the utmost,
with the ruler emphasizing clear laws,
so that those below dare not do wrong,
thereby controlling the realm.
The rulers of Yú and Xià,
honored as Sons of Heaven,
personally endured the reality of poverty and hardship,
to serve the common people;
what use had they for laws?
I, honored as the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
lack the substance thereof;
I wish to assemble a procession of a thousand chariots,
a following of ten thousand chariots,
to fulfill my title and name.
Moreover, the late emperor rose from among the feudal lords,
unified the world,
and after stabilizing the realm,
expelled the barbarians to secure the borders,
built palaces to manifest his achievements,
and you, sir, see that the late emperor's accomplishments have their legacy.
Now, within two years of my accession,
bandits have risen together,
and you, sir, cannot stop them,
yet wish to abandon what the late emperor did;
this shows you have not repaid the late emperor above,
and have not served me with loyalty and effort below;
why remain in your positions?"
He handed Qùjí, Lǐ Sī, and Jié over to the officials,
investigating and charging them with other crimes.
Qùjí and Jié said:
"Generals and chancellors cannot be humiliated."
They committed suicide.
Lǐ Sī was imprisoned,
and subjected to the five punishments.
In the third year,
Zhāng Hán and others led their troops
to besiege Jùlù,
while the Chǔ supreme general Xiàng Yǔ led Chǔ troops
to rescue Jùlù.
In winter,
Zhào Gāo became chancellor,
and finally tried Lǐ Sī and had him killed.
In summer,
Zhāng Hán and others fought but repeatedly retreated,
Èrshì sent someone to reprimand Hán,
who grew fearful,
and sent the senior scribe Xīn to report.
Zhào Gāo refused to see him,
and also distrusted him.
Xīn, afraid,
fled,
and Gāo sent men to pursue but could not catch him.
Xīn met Hán and said:
"Zhào Gāo holds power at court;
whether you, General, achieve merit or not, you will be executed."
Xiàng Yǔ pressed the attack on the Qín army,
captured Wáng Lí,
and Hán and others then
surrendered with their troops to the feudal lords.
On the eighth month, Jǐhài day,
Zhào Gāo intended to rebel,
but feared the ministers would not obey,
so he first set a test,
presenting a deer to Èrshì,
saying:
"It is a horse."
Èrshì laughed and said:
"Is the chancellor mistaken?
Calling a deer a horse."
He asked those around him,
some remained silent,
some called it a horse to flatter and comply with Zhào Gāo.
Those who called it a deer,
Gāo secretly framed
under the law.
Thereafter, all ministers feared Gāo.
Gāo had previously repeatedly said
"The bandits east of the pass are incapable,"
but when Xiàng Yǔ captured the Qín general
Wáng Lí and others at Jùlù and advanced,
and Zhāng Hán's army repeatedly retreated,
they submitted a request for reinforcements.
Yān, Zhào, Qí, Chǔ, Hán, Wèi
had all declared themselves kings,
and east of the Hángu Pass,
most areas rebelled against Qín officials
in response to the feudal lords,
who all led their forces westward.
The Pei Gōng, leading tens of thousands of troops,
had already sacked Wǔguān,
and sent a secret envoy to Zhào Gāo.
Fearing the Second Emperor's anger,
which might lead to his own execution,
Zhào Gāo excused himself from court due to illness.
The Second Emperor dreamed of a white tiger biting
the left-side horse of his chariot,
killing it,
and felt unhappy,
so he consulted a dream interpreter.
The diviner said:
"The Jīng River is causing this trouble."
The Second Emperor then fasted at the Wàngyí Palace,
intending to sacrifice to the Jīng River,
and sank four white horses.
He sent an envoy to reprimand Zhào Gāo
about the bandit uprising.
Zhào Gāo, afraid,
secretly plotted with his son-in-law Yán Lè, the magistrate of Xiányáng,
and his younger brother Zhào Chéng, saying:
"The emperor does not heed advice,
and now, in this crisis,
he wants to shift the blame to our clan.
I plan to replace the emperor,
and install Prince Yīng instead.
Prince Yīng is benevolent and frugal,
and the people all trust his words."
They had the chief of the palace guards
act as an insider,
falsely reported a major bandit attack,
and ordered Yán Lè to summon officials and mobilize troops,
then seized Yán Lè's mother
and placed her in Zhào Gāo's residence.
They sent Yán Lè with over a thousand officers and soldiers
to the gate of Wàngyí Palace,
where they bound the captain of the guard and his lieutenants,
saying:
"Bandits have entered here;
why didn't you stop them?"
The captain replied:
"The guard posts are set up with great care;
how could bandits dare enter the palace?"
Yán Lè then beheaded the captain,
led his men straight in,
and they advanced, shooting arrows.
The palace attendants and eunuchs were terrified,
some fleeing, some resisting,
and those who resisted were killed,
with dozens dead.
The chief of the palace guards entered with Yán Lè,
and shot arrows into the emperor's tent and curtains.
The Second Emperor, enraged,
called for his attendants,
but they were all panicked and did not fight.
Only one eunuch remained nearby,
staying to serve, not daring to leave.
The emperor went inside
and said to him:
"Why didn't you warn me earlier?
That it has come to this!"
The eunuch replied:
"I dared not speak,
so I survived.
Had I spoken earlier,
I would have been executed,
and how could I be here now?"
Yán Lè approached the Second Emperor and enumerated his faults:
"You are arrogant and arbitrary,
killing unjustly;
the whole world has turned against you.
You must decide your own fate."
The Second Emperor said:
"May I see the chancellor?"
Yán Lè said: "No."
The emperor said:
"I wish to be king of a commandery."
It was denied.
He then said: "I wish to be a marquis with ten thousand households."
It was denied.
He said:
"I wish to live as a commoner with my wife and children,
like the other princes."
Yán Lè said:
"I act on the chancellor's orders,
to execute you for the world's sake.
Though you plead much,
I dare not report it."
He signaled his troops to advance.
The Second Emperor committed suicide.
Yán Lè returned to report to Zhào Gāo,
who then summoned all the senior ministers
and princes,
and informed them of the execution of the Second Emperor.
He said:
"Qín was originally a kingdom;
only after the First Emperor ruled the world
was he called emperor.
Now the six states have restored themselves,
and Qín's territory has shrunk;
to use the empty title of emperor is improper.
It is fitting to revert to being king, as before."
They installed Prince Yīng, the nephew of the Second Emperor,
as King of Qín.
The Second Emperor was buried as a commoner
in the Yìchūn Garden south of Dù.
Prince Yīng was ordered to fast,
to meet at the ancestral temple,
and receive the king's seal.
After five days of fasting,
Prince Yīng plotted with his two sons, saying:
"Chancellor Zhào Gāo killed the Second Emperor at Wàngyí Palace,
and fearing the ministers would execute him,
he pretended it was righteous to install me.
I heard Zhào Gāo made a pact with Chǔ,
to exterminate the Qín royal house
and rule Guānzhōng himself.
Now he has me fast and meet at the temple,
intending to kill me there.
If I claim illness and do not go,
the chancellor will surely come himself,
and then we can kill him."
Zhào Gāo sent messengers
several times to urge Prince Yīng,
but he did not go.
Zhào Gāo indeed went in person,
saying:
"The ancestral temple is a grave matter;
why does the king not go?"
Prince Yīng then stabbed Zhào Gāo to death in the fasting palace,
exterminated his three clans,
and displayed them in Xiányáng as a warning.
Prince Yīng was King of Qín for forty-six days
when the Chǔ general Pei Gōng defeated the Qín army
and entered Wǔguān,
advancing to Bàshàng,
and sent envoys to demand Prince Yīng's surrender.
Prince Yīng tied a silk ribbon around his neck,
with a white horse and plain carriage,
holding the imperial seal and credentials,
surrendered by the side of Zhǐdào.
Pei Gōng then entered Xiányáng,
sealed the palaces and treasuries,
and withdrew his army to Bàshàng.
After over a month,
the feudal lords' troops arrived,
and Xiàng Jí, as chief commander,
killed Prince Yīng and all the Qín princes and clans.
They then sacked Xiányáng,
burned its palaces,
took its women and children captive,
seized its treasures and wealth,
and divided them among the feudal lords.
After destroying Qín,
they divided its land into three parts,
named Yōng King,
Sāi King, and Dí King,
collectively called the Three Qín.
Xiàng Yǔ became the Overlord of Western Chǔ,
presiding over the division of the world
and enfeoffing the feudal lords as kings,
and thus Qín was utterly destroyed.
Five years later,
the world was stabilized under Hàn.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Qín's ancestor Bó Yì
once rendered service during the times of Táng and Yú,
receiving land and a surname.
During the periods of Yīn and Xià,
they declined and scattered.
By the decline of Zhōu,
Qín rose,
establishing a city in the western frontier.
From Duke Mù onward,
they gradually encroached upon the feudal lords,
culminating in the First Emperor.
The First Emperor considered his merits surpassing the Five Emperors,
his territory broader than the Three Dynasties' kings,
and felt ashamed to be compared with them.
How well did Jiǎ Shēng analyze this in his discourse!
He said:
Qín annexed the feudal lords and established over thirty commanderies east of the mountains,
fortified the passes and ferries,
occupied strategic strongholds,
and maintained armor and weapons to guard them.
Yet Chén Shè, with a few hundred ragged conscripts,
raised his arms and shouted,
without using bows or halberds,
but with hoes, clubs, and plain staves,
feeding off the land as they marched,
rampaged across the world.
The Qín people abandoned their strategic defenses without guarding them,
left their passes and bridges unsecured,
did not wield their long halberds to stab,
nor drew their strong crossbows to shoot.
When the Chǔ army advanced deep into their territory,
fighting at Hóngmén,
they encountered no more difficulty than leaping over a low fence.
Then the lands east of the mountains fell into great turmoil,
the feudal lords rose up together,
and heroic men established themselves one after another.
Qín sent Zhāng Hán to lead troops east on an expedition,
yet Zhāng Hán used the masses of the three armies
to strike a bargain abroad,
plotting against his sovereign.
The faithlessness of the ministers
can be seen from this.
When Zǐ Yīng was enthroned,
he still did not awaken to reality.
Had Zǐ Yīng possessed even mediocre ability as a ruler,
with merely average assistance,
even if the lands east of the mountains were in chaos,
the territory of Qín could have been preserved and held,
and the sacrifices at the ancestral temple need not have been cut off.
The land of Qín, guarded by mountains and girded by rivers, was considered secure,
a state fortified on all sides.
From Duke Mù onward,
down to the King of Qín,
more than twenty rulers
consistently stood as the strongest among the feudal lords.
Was it because they were all worthy generation after generation?
It was due to the advantage of their geographical position.
Moreover, the world once united in heart and joined forces
to attack Qín.
In that era,
wise and intelligent men stood side by side,
excellent generals led their troops,
and capable ministers devised strategies,
yet they were hindered by the treacherous terrain
and could not advance.
Qín then lured them into battle
by opening its passes for them,
causing a million troops to flee in defeat and collapse.
Was it due to a lack of courage, strength, or wisdom?
No, it was because the terrain was unfavorable,
and the circumstances were disadvantageous.
Qín consolidated small towns into large cities,
garrisoned troops at strategic points,
built high ramparts and avoided battle,
closed its passes and held the narrow defiles,
guarding them with halberds at the ready.
The feudal lords rose from commoners,
united by profit,
lacking the virtue of an uncrowned king.
Their alliances were not close,
their followers were not loyal,
and though they claimed to destroy Qín,
their true motive was self-interest.
When they saw how difficult it was to breach Qín's defenses,
they would surely withdraw their armies.
Qín could have pacified its land and rested its people,
awaiting their exhaustion,
gathered the weak and supported the weary,
to command the rulers of the great states,
and would have had no trouble achieving its ambitions across the land.
Though honored as the Son of Heaven,
and possessing the wealth of the world,
to be captured oneself
was due to misguided efforts to avert defeat.
The King of Qín, self-satisfied, sought no advice,
persisting in error without change.
Èr Shì inherited this,
followed without alteration,
and added cruelty and oppression, deepening the calamity.
Zǐ Yīng stood isolated without kin,
endangered and weak without support.
These three rulers were deluded and never awakened in their lifetimes;
was their downfall not fitting?
At that time,
it was not that the world lacked men of deep thought who understood transformation,
but the reason they did not dare to give their full loyalty
and rectify errors
was that Qín's customs were full of prohibitions and taboos.
Before loyal words could fully leave their mouths,
they themselves were executed and obliterated.
Thus, the scholars of the world
listened with strained ears,
stood with feet rooted in fear,
and sealed their mouths in silence.
Therefore, the three rulers lost the Way,
loyal ministers dared not remonstrate,
wise men dared not plan,
and by the time the world was in chaos,
the misdeeds did not reach the ruler's ears.
Is this not lamentable!
The former kings understood
that obstruction harms the state,
so they established dukes, ministers, officials, and scholars
to elaborate laws and institute punishments,
and the world was well-governed.
When it was strong,
it suppressed violence and punished rebellion,
and the world submitted.
When it was weak,
the Five Hegemons campaigned
and the feudal lords followed.
When it declined,
it maintained internal order and external alliances,
and the state survived.
Thus, when Qín was prosperous,
its complex laws and harsh punishments made the world tremble;
but when it declined,
the common people resented and complained,
and the land rebelled.
Therefore, the Zhōu dynasty, with its proper five orders, followed the Way,
and lasted over a thousand years without interruption.
Qín failed in both fundamentals and details,
so it did not endure long.
From this perspective,
the principles of safety and danger are vastly different.
A rustic saying goes,
"Do not forget the affairs of the past,
for they are teachers for the future."
Thus, when a noble person governs a state,
he observes antiquity,
tests it in the present,
considers human affairs,
examines the principles of prosperity and decline,
judges the appropriateness of power and circumstances,
makes choices in an orderly manner,
and adapts to changes in due time.
Therefore, over long days and years,
the state remains secure.
Duke Xiào of Qín, relying on the strength of Xiáo and Hán,
and holding the territory of Yōngzhōu,
firmly guarded it with his ministers while eyeing the Zhōu court,
with the intent to roll up the world like a mat,
encompass the universe,
and gather the four seas into a bag,
aspiring to swallow all within the eight directions.
At that time,
Shāng Jūn assisted him,
establishing laws and regulations internally,
promoting farming and weaving,
and preparing defenses for both protection and attack.
Externally, he practiced horizontal alliances
to set the feudal lords against each other,
so the Qín people effortlessly took the lands west of the Yellow River.
After Duke Xiào passed away,
King Huì and King Wǔ inherited the enterprise,
following the legacy plans,
annexing Hànzhōng to the south,
seizing Bā and Shǔ to the west,
cut off fertile lands to the east,
and acquiring strategic commanderies.
The feudal lords grew fearful,
forming alliances and plotting to weaken Qín,
sparing no precious vessels, treasures, or rich lands
to attract the talents of the world,
forging vertical alliances,
and uniting as one.
At that time,
Qí had Mèngcháng,
Zhào had Píngyuán,
Chǔ had Chūnshēn,
and Wèi had Xìnlíng.
These four lords
were all wise, discerning, loyal, and trustworthy,
broad-minded, generous, and caring toward the people,
honoring the worthy and esteeming scholars,
forming vertical alliances to break up the horizontal ones,
and uniting the masses of Hán, Wèi, Yān, Chǔ,
Qí, Zhào, Sòng, Wèi, and Zhōngshān.
Thus, the scholars of the six states
included such men as Nìng Yuè, Xú Shàng, Sū Qín,
and Dù Hè, who devised strategies for them;
Qí Míng, Zhōu Zuì, Chén Zhěn, Zhāo Gǔ,
Lóu Huǎn, Zhái Jǐng, Sū Lì,
and Yuè Yì, who communicated their ideas;
Wú Qǐ, Sūn Bìn, Dài Tuó, Ní Liáng,
Wáng Liào, Tián Jì, Lián Pō,
and Zhào Shē, who commanded their troops.
Often with ten times the territory
and a million troops,
they struck at the passes and attacked Qín.
The Qín people opened their passes to admit the enemy,
and the armies of the nine states hesitated, fled,
and dared not advance.
Qín did not spend a single arrow or lost a single arrowhead,
yet the feudal lords of the world were already exhausted.
Thereupon, the vertical alliance dissolved and the covenants broke,
as they vied to cede territory and offer it to Qín.
Qín had strength to spare to exploit their weakness,
pursuing the fleeing and defeating the routed,
leaving a million corpses strewn about,
with blood flowing enough to float shields.
Seizing opportunities and advantages,
they carved up the empire,
divided the mountains and rivers,
with powerful states submitting in deference,
and weaker ones paying homage at court.
Extending to King Xiàowén and King Zhuāngxiāng,
their reigns were brief and the state saw no major events.
When it came to the King of Qín,
he carried forward the accumulated achievements of six generations,
brandishing his long whip to rule the world,
annexing the two Zhōu and eliminating the feudal lords,
ascending to the supreme position to control the six directions,
wielding the whip to chastise all under heaven,
his might shaking the four seas.
To the south, he seized the land of Bǎiyuè,
establishing Guìlín and Xiàng commanderies,
the chieftains of Bǎiyuè bowed their heads
and placed ropes around their necks,
entrusting their fates to low-ranking officials.
He then sent Méng Tián north to build the Great Wall
and guard the frontiers,
repelling the Xiōngnú over seven hundred lǐ away,
so the northern tribes dared not come south
to pasture their horses,
and warriors dared not string their bows to seek revenge.
Thereupon, he abolished the ways of the former kings,
burned the writings of the hundred schools,
to stupefy the common people.
He demolished famous cities,
executed outstanding heroes,
collected all the weapons of the empire
and gathered them in Xiányáng,
melting down the blades to cast bells
and twelve metal statues,
to weaken the common people.
Then he cut through Mount Huà to form walls,
utilized the Yellow River as a moat,
relying on towering fortifications,
facing unfathomable gorges
for defense.
Skilled generals with powerful crossbows guarded strategic points,
trusted ministers and elite troops displayed sharp weapons to challenge passersby,
and the empire was thus settled.
In the heart of the King of Qín,
he believed the defenses of Guānzhōng were impregnable,
a golden city stretching a thousand lǐ,
an imperial enterprise for ten thousand generations of his descendants.
After the King of Qín passed away,
his lingering might still resonated in distant lands.
Chén Shè,
a son of humble means with a broken window and rope-hinged door,
a menial laborer,
a conscripted drifter,
whose talent fell short of average,
possessing neither the virtue of Zhòngní or Mò Dí,
nor the wealth of Táo Zhū or Yī Dùn,
yet stepping into the ranks of soldiers,
rose defiantly from among the troops,
leading weary and scattered soldiers,
commanding a few hundred men,
turned to attack Qín.
They cut trees to make weapons,
raised poles as banners,
the world gathered like clouds and responded like echoes,
carrying provisions and following like shadows,
the heroes east of the mountains rose together
and destroyed the Qín dynasty.
Moreover, the empire was not small or weak;
the land of Yōngzhōu,
the natural defenses of Yáohán remained as they were.
Chén Shè's status
was not nobler than the rulers of Qí, Chǔ, Yān,
Zhào, Hán, Wèi, Sòng,
Wèi, or Zhōngshān;
his farm tools and thorn sticks
were not sharper than hooked halberds and long spears;
his conscripted masses
were no match for the armies of the nine states;
in deep strategies and long-term planning,
the art of maneuvering troops and employing soldiers,
he did not compare to the talents of former times.
Yet success and failure reversed,
their achievements turned opposite.
If we were to measure the states east of the mountains against Chén Shè in length and size,
comparing their authority and strength,
they could not be mentioned in the same breath.
Yet Qín, with its modest territory,
the power of a thousand chariots,
summoned the eight provinces and made its peers pay homage,
for over a hundred years.
Then it made the six directions its home,
Yáohán its palace,
but one man's uprising
caused the ancestral temples to collapse,
his body died at the hands of others,
and he became the laughingstock of the world.
Why?
Because he failed to practice benevolence and righteousness,
and the circumstances of offense and defense had changed.
Qín unified the lands and annexed the feudal lords,
facing south to proclaim himself emperor,
to nourish the four seas,
and the scholars of the world turned admiringly toward his influence.
Why was this so?
It is said:
"For a long time in recent antiquity, there had been no true king.
The Zhōu house was humble and weak,
the five hegemons had perished,
and orders were not carried out across the empire.
Thus, the feudal lords governed by force,
the strong invading the weak,
the many oppressing the few,
with weapons and armor never resting,
and the scholars and people exhausted.
Now that Qín faced south and ruled the world,
there was an emperor above.
Since the common people hoped
to secure their lives,
none failed to open their hearts
and look up to their ruler.
At this time,
maintaining authority and securing achievements,
the foundation of safety and danger lay herein.
The King of Qín harbored a greedy and despicable heart,
exercising his self-aggrandizing wisdom,
distrusting his meritorious officials,
not befriending the scholars and people,
abolishing the kingly way,
establishing private authority,
banning writings and enforcing harsh laws,
prioritizing deceit and force over benevolence and righteousness,
making tyranny the beginning for the world.
For unification, deceit and force are exalted;
for stability,
obedience and adaptability are valued.
This means that seizing and keeping
require different methods.
Qín emerged from the Warring States
to rule the world,
yet its ways did not change,
its governance unaltered,
which is why its methods of gaining
and keeping power were no different.
Isolated and possessive,
its downfall was imminent.
Had the King of Qín considered the affairs of past ages,
and emulated the paths of Yīn and Zhōu,
to regulate his governance,
even if later there were wanton and arrogant rulers,
there would have been no risk of collapse.
Thus, the three kings who founded the empire,
their names and titles illustrious and admirable,
their achievements long-enduring.
Now that the Second Emperor of Qín ascended,
all under heaven looked up
to observe his governance.
Those who are cold find short coarse garments beneficial,
and the hungry savor chaff and husks;
the cries of the people
are the resources for a new ruler.
This means that it is easy to practice benevolence toward a weary people.
If the Second Emperor had the conduct of an ordinary ruler,
and employed the loyal and worthy,
with ruler and ministers united in heart
and concerned for the troubles of the land,
dressed in plain white to rectify the former emperor's errors,
dividing land and people
to enfeoff the descendants of meritorious officials,
establishing states and appointing rulers to show courtesy to the world,
emptying the prisons and abolishing corporal punishments,
removing the crimes of confiscating families and defilement,
allowing everyone to return to their hometowns,
opening the granaries,
distributing wealth and coins,
to relieve the lonely and impoverished,
lightening taxes and reducing labor,
to aid the urgent needs of the common people,
simplifying laws and reducing penalties thereafter,
enabling all under heaven to start anew,
changing their conduct and cultivating virtue,
each cautious of their own actions,
fulfilling the hopes of the myriad people,
and uniting the world with authority and virtue,
the empire would have been united.
Then within the four seas,
all would be joyful
and content in their places,
fearing only any disruption.
Although there were cunning people,
they had no intention of betraying their ruler,
so treacherous ministers had no way to display their cleverness,
and violent disturbances would cease.
The Second Emperor did not follow this method,
but compounded it with unprincipled rule,
damaging the ancestral temples and oppressing the people,
starting construction of the Epáng Palace anew,
imposing numerous punishments and severe executions,
governing with harshness and depth,
rewarding and punishing inappropriately,
levying taxes without limit,
the empire was full of troubles,
officials could not maintain order,
the common people were impoverished
and the ruler did not relieve or pity them.
Then treachery and deceit arose together,
and superiors and subordinates deceived each other,
those who incurred punishments were numerous,
executions could be seen one after another on the roads,
and the whole empire suffered from it.
From high officials down to the masses,
everyone harbored a sense of personal danger,
personally experiencing the reality of hardship and poverty,
all were不安于 their positions,
hence easily stirred to action.
Therefore, although Chén Shè
did not possess the virtue of Tāng and Wǔ,
nor rely on the dignity of dukes and marquises,
raised his arms in the great marsh
and the whole empire responded,
it was because the people were in peril.
Thus the former kings observed the changes from beginning to end,
understood the pivotal points of survival and perish,
so the way of governing the people,
lies solely in making them secure.
Even if there are rebellious ministers in the empire,
they will certainly lack the support of responsive aid.
Hence the saying
"Secure people can be led to righteousness,
while those in peril are easily led into wrongdoing,"
this is what it means.
Though honored as the Son of Heaven,
and possessing the wealth of the entire empire,
one cannot avoid being killed,
because correcting instability was not done properly.
This was the fault of the Second Emperor.

After a moment,
Liáng glanced at Jí and said:
"It is time to act!"
Thereupon Jí drew his sword and cut off the Governor's head.
Xiàng Liáng took the Governor's head,
and fastened the official seal and ribbon to his own belt.
The Governor's retinue was thrown into great alarm,
and chaos erupted.
Jí struck down several tens to a hundred men.
The entire office was cowed into submission,
none dared to rise.
Liáng then summoned the powerful officials he previously knew,
explaining to them his reason for starting this great undertaking,
and thus raised troops in Wúzhōng.
He sent men to take control of the subordinate counties,
acquiring eight thousand elite soldiers.
Liáng appointed the local heroes of Wúzhōng as Colonels, Majors, and Captains.
One man was not given a post,
and complained to Liáng.
Liáng said:
"Some time ago, at a certain funeral, I put you in charge of a certain matter,
and you failed to manage it.
That is why I am not employing you, Sir."
The crowd then all conceded.
Thereupon, Liáng became Governor of Kuàijī,
with Jí as his Lieutenant General,
pacifying the subordinate counties.
Meanwhile, Zhào Píng of Guǎnglíng was acting for King Chén to pacify Guǎnglíng,
but had not yet succeeded.
Hearing that King Chén had been defeated and fled,
and Qín troops were about to arrive,
he crossed the river and, falsely using King Chén's command,
appointed Liáng as the King of Chǔ's Supreme Pillar of State.
Saying:
"The region east of the river is already pacified,
quickly lead your troops west to attack Qín."
Xiàng Liáng then led his eight thousand men across the river westward.
Hearing that Chén Yīng had already taken Dōngyáng,
he sent an envoy seeking to ally and march west together.
This Chén Yīng
was a former Clerk to the Magistrate of Dōngyáng,
residing in the county,
known for his trustworthiness and caution,
and regarded as a respectable elder.
The young men of Dōngyáng had killed their Magistrate,
gathered several thousand men,
and wanted to set up a leader.
Finding no suitable candidate,
they invited Chén Yīng.
Yīng declined, pleading inability,
but they forcibly installed Yīng as their leader,
and the county followers numbered twenty thousand.
The young men wanted to make Yīng king immediately,
a unique army with distinctive blue-turbaned troops.
Chén Yīng's mother said to Yīng:
"Since I became a wife in your family,
I have never heard that your ancestors included any noble figures.
Now suddenly gaining great fame,
is inauspicious.
It would be better to subordinate yourself to another.
If the endeavor succeeds, you may still be enfeoffed as a Marquis.
If it fails, it is easier to escape notice,
and you won't be specifically targeted by the world."
Yīng then did not dare to become king.
He told his army officers:
"The Xiàng family has been a lineage of generals for generations,
renowned in Chǔ.
Now, to undertake a great endeavor,
if the commander is not the right person,
it will not do.
If we rely on a famous clan,
we will surely topple Qín."
Thereupon, the multitude followed his words,
and placed their troops under Xiàng Liáng's command.
When Xiàng Liáng crossed the Huái River,
Qíng Bù and General Pú also brought their troops to join him.
In total, they numbered sixty to seventy thousand men,
and encamped at Xiàpī.
At that time,
Qín Jiā had already installed Jǐng Jū as King of Chǔ,
encamping east of Péngchéng,
intending to resist Xiàng Liáng.
Xiàng Liáng said to his army officers:
"King Chén was the first to initiate the uprising,
but his campaign fared poorly,
and his whereabouts are unknown.
Now Qín Jiā has betrayed King Chén by installing Jǐng Jū,
an act of treason and immorality."
He then advanced his troops to attack Qín Jiā.
Qín Jiā's army was defeated and fled,
pursued to Húlíng.
Jiā turned to fight for one day,
Jiā died,
and his army surrendered.
Jǐng Jū fled and died in Liáng territory.
Xiàng Liáng, having absorbed Qín Jiā's army,
encamped at Húlíng,
and prepared to lead his troops westward.
When Zhāng Hán's army reached Lì,
Xiàng Liáng sent his separate commander Zhū Jīshí
and Yú Fán Jūn to engage him.
Yú Fán Jūn died.
Zhū Jīshí's army was defeated,
and he fled to Húlíng.
Xiàng Liáng then led his troops into Xuē,
and executed Jīshí. Previously, Xiàng Liáng had sent Xiàng Yǔ on a separate campaign to attack Xiāngchéng,
which held out firmly and would not surrender.
After it was finally captured,
all its defenders were buried alive.
Yǔ returned and reported to Xiàng Liáng.
When Xiàng Liáng heard that King Chén was definitely dead,
he summoned all his separate commanders to meet at Xuē to discuss plans.
At this time, the Pèi Gōng had also risen up in Pèi,
and went to join them.
Fàn Zēng of Jūcháo,
aged seventy,
who had hitherto lived at home,
and was fond of remarkable stratagems,
went to persuade Xiàng Liáng, saying:
"Chén Shèng's defeat was inevitable.
When Qín annihilated the six states,
Chǔ was the most blameless.
Since King Huái entered Qín and never returned,
the people of Chǔ have pitied him to this day.
Therefore, the southern sage of Chǔ said, 'Even if Chǔ has but three households,
it will be Chǔ that destroys Qín.'
Now Chén Shèng initiated the uprising,
but instead of establishing a descendant of Chǔ, he set himself up,
so his influence could not last.
Now you, Sir, have risen east of the river,
and the swarming generals of Chǔ all vie to join you,
precisely because your family has been generals of Chǔ for generations,
and they believe you can re-establish the descendants of Chǔ."
Thereupon, Xiàng Liáng agreed with his words,
and sought out a grandson of King Huái of Chǔ, named Xīn, who was among the common people,
herding sheep for a living.
He was established as King Huái of Chǔ,
to comply with the people's hopes.
Chén Yīng was made Supreme Pillar of State of Chǔ,
enfeoffed with five counties,
and resided with King Huái at Xūyí.
Xiàng Liáng styled himself Lord Wǔxìn.
After several months had passed,
he led his troops to attack Kàngfù,
and together with Qí's Tián Róng and Sīmǎ Lóngjū's army, they rescued Dōng'ē,
where they heavily defeated the Qín army.
Tián Róng then led his troops back,
expelling his king Jiǎ.
Jiǎ fled to Chǔ.
Jiǎ's chancellor Tián Jiǎo fled to Zhào.
Jiǎo's younger brother Tián Jiàn, a former Qí general,
remained in Zhào and dared not return.
Tián Róng established Tián Dān's son Fú as the king of Qí.
After Xiàng Liáng had defeated the army at Dōng'ē,
he pursued the Qín forces.
He repeatedly sent envoys to urge Qí's troops,
wishing to advance west together.
Tián Róng said:
"If Chǔ kills Tián Jiǎ,
and Zhào kills Tián Jiǎo and Tián Jiàn,
then I will send troops."
Xiàng Liáng said:
"Tián Jiǎ is the king of an allied state,
who came to me in desperation;
I cannot bear to kill him."
Zhào also refused to kill Tián Jiǎo and Tián Jiàn to curry favor with Qí.
Thus, Qí would not send troops to aid Chǔ.
Xiàng Liáng sent Péi Gōng and Xiàng Yǔ to separately attack Chéngyáng,
where they massacred the city.
They defeated the Qín army east of Púyáng to the west,
and the Qín forces withdrew into Púyáng.
Péi Gōng and Xiàng Yǔ then attacked Dìngtáo.
Dìngtáo had not yet fallen
when they left,
advancing westward to Yōngqiū,
where they heavily defeated the Qín army,
killing Lǐ Yóu.
They turned back to attack Wàihuáng,
but Wàihuáng did not fall.
Xiàng Liáng set out from Dōng'ē,
heading west,
and by the time he reached Dìngtáo,
he had defeated the Qín army again,
while Xiàng Yǔ and others also killed Lǐ Yóu,
growing more contemptuous of Qín,
and displaying arrogance.
Sòng Yì then advised Xiàng Liáng, saying:
"Victory in battle followed by a general's arrogance and soldiers' laziness leads to defeat.
Now the troops are somewhat lax,
while Qín's forces grow daily;
I fear for you, my lord."
Xiàng Liáng did not listen.
Instead, he sent Sòng Yì on a mission to Qí.
On the way, Sòng Yì met Qí's envoy Gāolíng Jūn Xiǎn,
and said:
"Are you going to see Wǔxìn Jūn?"
The envoy replied:
"Yes."
Sòng Yì said:
"I predict that Wǔxìn Jūn's army will surely be defeated.
If you travel slowly, you will avoid death;
if you hurry, you will meet disaster."
Qín indeed mobilized all its troops to reinforce Zhāng Hán,
who attacked the Chǔ army,
heavily defeating them at Dìngtáo,
and Xiàng Liáng died.
Péi Gōng and Xiàng Yǔ left Wàihuáng to attack Chénliú,
but Chénliú held firm and could not be taken.
Péi Gōng and Xiàng Yǔ consulted each other, saying:
"Now that Xiàng Liáng's army is defeated,
the soldiers are afraid."
So they, along with Lǚ Chén's army, led their troops eastward.
Lǚ Chén's army was stationed east of Péngchéng,
Xiàng Yǔ's west of Péngchéng,
and Péi Gōng's in Dàng.
After Zhāng Hán had defeated Xiàng Liáng's army,
he considered the troops in Chǔ's territory no longer a concern,
so he crossed the river to attack Zhào,
heavily defeating them.
At this time,
Zhào Xiē was king,
Chén Yú was general,
and Zhāng Ěr was chancellor,
all of whom fled into the city of Jùlù.
Zhāng Hán ordered Wáng Lí and Shè Jiān to besiege Jùlù,
with Zhāng Hán's army to the south,
building a walled road to transport grain.
Chén Yú, as general,
led tens of thousands of troops and stationed north of Jùlù,
which was called the army north of the river.
After the Chǔ army was defeated at Dìngtáo,
King Huái grew fearful,
moving from Xūyí to Péngchéng,
merging the armies of Xiàng Yǔ
and Lǚ Chén under his personal command.
He appointed Lǚ Chén as Minister over the Masses,
and his father Lǚ Qīng as Prime Minister.
Péi Gōng was made governor of Dàng Commandery,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔ'ān,
and commanded the troops of Dàng Commandery.
Earlier, Gāolíng Jūn Xiǎn, the Qí envoy whom Sòng Yì had met, was in the Chǔ army
and said to the King of Chǔ:
"Sòng Yì predicted that Wǔxìn Jūn's army would surely be defeated;
a few days later,
the army was indeed defeated.
To foresee signs of defeat before a battle is fought—
this can be called knowing warfare."
The king summoned Sòng Yì to discuss matters and was greatly pleased with him,
thus appointing him as supreme general;
Xiàng Yǔ, as Duke of Lǔ,
was made second general,
Fàn Zēng was made junior general,
and they were to rescue Zhào.
All other generals were placed under Sòng Yì's command,
and he was titled the 'Noble Son's Crown General.'
They marched to Ānyáng,
where they remained for forty-six days without advancing.
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"I have heard that the Qín army has besieged the King of Zhào at Jùlù;
we should quickly lead our troops across the river,
with Chǔ attacking from without,
and Zhào responding from within,
and we will surely defeat the Qín army."
Sòng Yì said:
"Not so.
A gadfly that bites a cow cannot break its lice.
Now Qín attacks Zhào;
if they win, their troops will be exhausted,
and we can take advantage of their weakness;
if they do not win,
then we lead our troops westward with drums beating,
and will surely conquer Qín.
So it is better to let Qín and Zhào fight first.
In wearing strong armor and wielding sharp weapons,
I am not your equal;
but in sitting and devising strategies,
you are not my equal."
Thereupon, he issued an order to the army:
"Those as fierce as tigers,
as stubborn as sheep,
as greedy as wolves,
and too strong-willed to obey orders,
shall all be executed."
He then sent his son Sòng Xiāng to Qí as chancellor,
personally escorting him to Wúyán,
where they held a grand drinking feast.
The weather was cold with heavy rain,
and the soldiers suffered from cold and hunger.
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"We are supposed to join forces and attack Qín,
yet we linger here without moving.
This year, there is famine and the people are poor;
the soldiers eat taro and beans,
and the army has no stored grain,
yet he holds grand drinking feasts.
Instead of leading the troops across the river to use Zhào's provisions,
and joining forces with Zhào to attack Qín,
he says 'wait for their weakness.'
With Qín's strength,
attacking the newly established Zhào,
they are bound to conquer it.
If Zhào falls, Qín will grow stronger;
what weakness will there be to exploit!
Moreover, our army has recently been defeated,
and the king cannot rest easy on his mat,
having gathered all forces within the borders and entrusted them to the general—
the safety of the state
hinges on this one move.
Now he shows no concern for the soldiers but pursues his private interests;
he is no minister of the state."
Xiàng Yǔ paid a morning visit to Supreme General Sòng Yì,
and in his tent, beheaded him,
then issued an order to the army:
"Sòng Yì plotted with Qí to rebel against Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ secretly ordered me to execute him."
At that time,
all the generals were cowed and submitted,
none daring to resist.
They all said:
"The one who first established Chǔ
was your family, General.
Now you have put down a rebellion."
So together they established Yǔ as acting supreme general.
He sent men to pursue Sòng Yì's son,
catching up with him in Qí,
and killed him.
He sent Huán Chǔ to report to King Huái.
King Huái then appointed Xiàng Yǔ as supreme general,
with Dāngyáng Jūn and the Pú General under his command.
After Xiàng Yǔ had killed the 'Noble Son's Crown General,'
his might shook the state of Chǔ,
and his fame spread among the feudal lords.
He then sent Dāngyáng Jūn and the Pú General with twenty thousand troops to cross the river,
to rescue Jùlù.
The battle brought little advantage,
and Chén Yú again requested reinforcements.
Xiàng Yǔ then led all his troops across the river,
sank all the boats,
smashed the cooking pots and cauldrons,
burned the huts,
and took only three days' rations,
to show the soldiers his determination to fight to the death,
with no thought of return.
Upon arrival, they surrounded Wáng Lí,
encountered the Qín army,
fought nine battles,
cut off their supply route,
and inflicted a major defeat,
killing Sū Jiǎo
and capturing Wáng Lí.
Shè Jiān refused to surrender to Chǔ
and burned himself to death.
At that time,
the Chǔ army outshone all other feudal lords.
The armies of the feudal lords who came to rescue Jùlù had over ten camps,
but none dared to deploy their troops.
When Chǔ attacked Qín,
all the generals watched from their ramparts.
Every Chǔ warrior fought like ten men,
their battle cries shaking the heavens,
and the feudal lords' armies were filled with fear.
After defeating the Qín army,
Xiàng Yǔ summoned the feudal lords' generals;
as they entered the camp gate,
they all advanced on their knees,
not daring to look up.
From then on, Xiàng Yǔ became the supreme general of the feudal lords,
and they all submitted to him.
Zhāng Hán's army was at Jíyuán,
Xiàng Yǔ's at the south of the Zhāng River,
locked in a stalemate without battle.
The Qín army repeatedly retreated,
and Èr Shì sent someone to reprimand Zhāng Hán.
Zhāng Hán grew fearful,
and sent Chief Clerk Xīn to report and seek instructions.
Arriving in Xiányáng,
he was detained at the Sima Gate for three days,
but Zhào Gāo refused to see him,
showing signs of distrust.
Chief Clerk Xīn, afraid,
fled back to his army,
not daring to take the usual route.
Zhào Gāo indeed sent men to pursue him,
but failed to catch up.
When Xīn returned to the army,
he reported:
"Zhào Gāo holds power at court,
and those below can do nothing.
If we win the battle now,
Gāo will surely envy our achievements;
if we lose,
we cannot escape death.
I urge you, General, to consider this carefully."
Chén Yú also sent a letter to Zhāng Hán, saying:
"Bái Qǐ, as a Qín general,
campaigned south to conquer Yānyǐng,
north to bury alive the forces of Mǎfú,
capturing cities and seizing lands
beyond count,
yet in the end was ordered to die.
Méng Tián, as a Qín general,
drove out the northern barbarians,
opening up thousands of miles in Yúzhōng,
yet was executed in Yángzhōu.
Why?
Because their merits were too great,
and Qín could not reward them all,
so they were executed under the law.
Now you, General, have served Qín for three years,
with losses numbering in the hundreds of thousands,
while the feudal lords rise together and grow ever more numerous.
That Zhào Gāo has long been given to flattery;
now in this crisis,
he fears Èr Shì will execute him,
so he plans to kill you, General, by law to shift blame,
and send someone to replace you to escape his own misfortune.
You, General, have long been abroad,
with many internal conflicts;
whether you achieve merit or not,
you will be executed either way.
Moreover, Heaven's will to destroy Qín
is known to all, wise and foolish alike.
Now you, General, cannot remonstrate directly at court,
and abroad you are a general of a doomed state,
standing alone yet hoping to survive long—
is that not lamentable!
Why not turn your troops around and ally with the feudal lords,
agree to attack Qín together,
divide its land and rule,
facing south as a king?
How does that compare to laying your neck on the block,
with wife and children executed?"
Zhāng Hán hesitated,
but secretly sent Hòu Shǐchéng as an envoy to Xiàng Yǔ,
seeking an agreement.
Before the pact was made,
Xiàng Yǔ sent General Pú to lead troops day and night across Sānhù,
stationing south of the Zhāng River,
engaging the Qín army
and defeating them again.
Xiàng Yǔ then led all his forces to attack the Qín army at the Wū River,
crushing them utterly.
Zhāng Hán sent someone to see Xiàng Yǔ,
wishing to make a pact.
Xiàng Yǔ summoned his officers to discuss:
"Our provisions are low;
I intend to accept their offer."
The officers all said:
"Agreed."
Xiàng Yǔ then set a meeting south of the Huán River at the ruins of Yīn.
After the alliance was sworn,
Zhāng Hán met Xiàng Yǔ and wept,
speaking of Zhào Gāo.
Xiàng Yǔ then appointed Zhāng Hán as King of Yōng,
keeping him in the Chǔ army.
He made Chief Clerk Xīn the supreme general,
leading the Qín troops as the vanguard.
They reached Xīn'ān.
The officers and soldiers of the feudal lords had previously been conscripted or stationed in Qín territory,
where Qín officials often mistreated them.
Now that the Qín army had surrendered to the feudal lords,
their officers and soldiers, riding on victory, often enslaved and used them,
humiliating and abusing the Qín soldiers.
The Qín soldiers whispered among themselves:
"General Zhāng and others deceived us into surrendering to the feudal lords.
If we can enter the passes and defeat Qín,
that would be best;
but if not,
the feudal lords will take us east as captives,
and Qín will surely execute all our parents, wives, and children."
The generals got wind of this talk
and reported it to Xiàng Yǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ then called Qíng Bù and General Pú to plan:
"The Qín soldiers are still numerous,
and their hearts are not subdued.
If they rebel once we reach Guānzhōng,
it will be dangerous.
Better to attack and kill them now,
and only take Zhāng Hán,
Chief Clerk Xīn, and Commandant Yì into Qín."
So the Chǔ army attacked by night and buried alive over 200,000 Qín soldiers south of Xīn'ān.
They then advanced to pacify the Qín lands.
At Hángǔ Pass, there were troops guarding it,
and they could not enter.
Hearing that Pèi Gōng had already taken Xiányáng,
Xiàng Yǔ was enraged,
and sent Dāngyáng Jūn and others to attack the pass.
Xiàng Yǔ then entered,
reaching west of Xì.
Pèi Gōng's army was at Bàshàng,
and he had not yet met Xiàng Yǔ.
Pèi Gōng's Left Sima Cáo Wúshāng sent someone to tell Xiàng Yǔ:
"Pèi Gōng intends to become king of Guānzhōng,
make Zǐ Yīng his chancellor,
and keep all the treasures for himself."
Xiàng Yǔ was furious,
saying:
"Tomorrow, feast the soldiers,
and we will crush Pèi Gōng's army!"
At that time,
Xiàng Yǔ had 400,000 troops,
at Hóngmén in Xīnfēng,
while Pèi Gōng had 100,000,
at Bàshàng.
Fàn Zēng advised Xiàng Yǔ:
"When Pèi Gōng was east of the mountains,
he was greedy for wealth and goods,
and fond of beautiful women.
Now, having entered the passes,
he takes no goods,
and favors no women—
this shows his ambitions are not small.
I had someone observe his aura,
and it appeared as dragons and tigers,
in five colors—
this is the aura of a Son of Heaven.
Attack quickly; do not miss this chance."
Xiàng Bó, the Left Yin of Chǔ,
was Xiàng Yǔ's uncle,
and had long been friendly with Liú Hóu Zhāng Liáng.
Zhāng Liáng was then following Pèi Gōng,
so Xiàng Bó rode by night to Pèi Gōng's camp,
privately met Zhāng Liáng,
told him everything,
and wanted to call Zhāng Liáng to leave with him,
saying:
"Do not follow him to your death."
Zhāng Liáng said:
"I was sent by the King of Hán to accompany you, Lord of Pèi.
Now that you, Lord of Pèi, are facing an emergency,
it would be unrighteous for me to flee without informing you,
so I must tell you."
Liáng then entered
and reported everything to the Lord of Pèi.
The Lord of Pèi was greatly alarmed
and said:
"What should I do about this?"
Zhāng Liáng asked:
"Who advised Your Majesty to adopt this plan?"
The Lord of Pèi replied:
"A petty scholar urged me, saying, 'Secure the passes,
do not let the other lords enter,
and you can rule all of Qín.'
So I followed his advice."
Liáng said:
"Do you estimate your troops are sufficient to withstand King Xiàng?"
The Lord of Pèi fell silent,
then said:
"Certainly not.
But what can I do about it?"
Zhāng Liáng said:
"Allow me to go speak to Xiàng Bó,
and tell him that you, Lord of Pèi, dare not betray King Xiàng."
The Lord of Pèi asked:
"How are you acquainted with Xiàng Bó?"
Zhāng Liáng replied:
"During the Qín dynasty, he and I traveled together.
When Xiàng Bó killed a man,
I saved his life.
Now that there is an emergency,
he has fortunately come to inform me."
The Lord of Pèi asked: "Who is older, you or he?"
Liáng said:
"He is older than I."
The Lord of Pèi said: "Please summon him in for me,
I will treat him as an elder brother."
Zhāng Liáng went out
and invited Xiàng Bó.
Xiàng Bó immediately entered to see the Lord of Pèi.
The Lord of Pèi offered him a cup of wine and proposed a toast,
pledging to form a marriage alliance,
saying:
"Since I entered the passes,
I have not dared to take even the slightest thing,
but have registered the officials and people,
sealed the treasuries and storehouses,
and awaited the general's arrival.
The reason I sent generals to guard the passes
was to prevent bandits from entering and other emergencies.
Day and night I have hoped for the general's arrival—
how would I dare to rebel!
I hope you will fully explain that I would not dare to betray his virtue."
Xiàng Bó agreed.
He said to the Lord of Pèi:
"You must come early tomorrow morning to apologize to King Xiàng in person."
The Lord of Pèi said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon, Xiàng Bó returned that night,
reached the camp,
and fully reported the Lord of Pèi's words to King Xiàng.
He added:
"If the Lord of Pèi had not first broken through into Guānzhōng,
would you have dared to enter?
Now that a man has achieved great merit, to attack him
is unrighteous.
It would be better to treat him kindly instead."
King Xiàng agreed.
The next morning, the Lord of Pèi came with over a hundred riders to see King Xiàng.
Arriving at Hóngmén,
he apologized:
"You and I joined forces to attack Qín,
you fought north of the Yellow River,
I fought south of it.
Yet I did not expect to be the first to enter the passes and defeat Qín,
and to meet you again here.
Now there are words from a petty man
that have caused a rift between you and me."
King Xiàng said:
"This was said by your left minister, Cáo Wúshāng of Pèi.
Otherwise,
why would I have come to this?"
That day, King Xiàng kept the Lord of Pèi to drink with him.
King Xiàng and Xiàng Bó sat facing east,
Yàfù sat facing south.
Yàfù
was Fàn Zēng.
The Lord of Pèi sat facing north,
and Zhāng Liáng attended facing west.
Fàn Zēng repeatedly glanced at King Xiàng,
and three times raised the jade pendant he wore to signal him,
but King Xiàng remained silent and unresponsive.
Fàn Zēng rose,
went out, and summoned Xiàng Zhuāng,
saying to him:
"Our king is too soft-hearted.
You go in and propose a toast,
after the toast,
request to perform a sword dance,
and then strike the Lord of Pèi where he sits,
killing him.
Otherwise,
you and your kind will all be captured by him."
Xiàng Zhuāng then entered and proposed a toast.
After the toast,
he said:
"Our king is drinking with the Lord of Pèi,
but there is no entertainment in the army.
May I perform a sword dance?"
King Xiàng said:
"Agreed."
Xiàng Zhuāng drew his sword and began to dance,
Xiàng Bó also drew his sword and danced,
constantly using his body to shield the Lord of Pèi like wings,
so Xiàng Zhuāng could not strike.
Thereupon, Zhāng Liáng went to the camp gate
and saw Fán Kuài.
Fán Kuài asked:
"How are things today?"
Liáng said:
"Very critical.
Now Xiàng Zhuāng has drawn his sword to dance,
but his true intention is always against the Lord of Pèi."
Kuài said:
"This is urgent!
I request to enter
and share his fate."
Kuài immediately took his sword and shield and entered the camp gate.
The guards crossed their halberds to stop him from entering,
but Fán Kuài tilted his shield and charged,
knocking the guards to the ground.
Kuài then entered,
parted the curtain, and stood facing west,
glaring at King Xiàng with wide eyes,
his hair standing on end,
and the corners of his eyes nearly splitting.
King Xiàng pressed his hand on his sword and rose on his knees, saying:
"Who is this visitor?"
Zhāng Liáng said:
"He is Fán Kuài, the Lord of Pèi's personal guard."
King Xiàng said:
"A brave warrior!
Give him a cup of wine."
So he was given a large cup of wine.
Kuài bowed in thanks,
rose,
and drank it standing.
King Xiàng said:
"Give him a pig's leg."
So he was given a raw pig's leg.
Fán Kuài placed his shield upside down on the ground,
put the pig's leg on it,
drew his sword, cut the meat, and ate it.
King Xiàng said:
"Brave warrior,
can you drink more?"
Fán Kuài replied:
"I do not even shun death,
why would I decline a cup of wine!
The King of Qín had the heart of a tiger or wolf,
killing people as if he could not finish,
punishing them as if afraid it was not enough,
so the whole world rebelled against him.
King Huái made a pact with the generals, saying, 'The first to defeat Qín and enter Xiányáng shall be its king.'
Now the Lord of Pèi has first defeated Qín and entered Xiányáng,
yet he did not dare to take even a hair,
sealed the palaces,
withdrew his troops to Bàshàng,
to await your arrival.
The reason he sent generals to guard the passes
was to prevent bandits from entering and other emergencies.
For such toil and high merit,
he has received no enfeoffment or reward,
yet you listen to petty talk
and intend to kill a meritorious man.
This is merely continuing the perished Qín's ways.
I privately believe this is not what you should do."
King Xiàng had no reply,
but said:
"Sit."
Fán Kuài sat beside Liáng.
After sitting a short while,
the Lord of Pèi rose to go to the toilet,
and signaled for Fán Kuài to come out.
After the Lord of Pèi had gone out,
King Xiàng sent commandant Chén Píng to summon the Lord of Pèi.
The Lord of Pèi said:
"Now that I have come out,
I have not taken my leave.
What should I do about this?"
Fán Kuài said:
"In great undertakings one does not dwell on trivial details;
in grand ceremonies one does not stand on petty courtesies.
Now they are the chopping board and knife,
while we are the fish and meat.
Why take leave?"
Thereupon they departed.
He ordered Zhāng Liáng to stay behind and offer apologies.
Liáng asked:
"What gifts did Your Majesty bring?"
He replied:
"I have a pair of white jade discs
intended for King Xiàng,
and a pair of jade wine vessels
meant for Yàfù.
But encountering their anger,
I dared not present them.
Please offer these for me."
Zhāng Liáng said:
"As you wish."
At that time,
King Xiàng's army was at Hóngmén,
while the Pèi Duke's forces were at Bàshàng,
forty lǐ apart.
The Pèi Duke abandoned his chariots and cavalry,
slipped away riding alone,
and with Fán Kuài, Xiàhóu Yīng, Jìn Jiāng, and Jì Xìn - four men carrying swords and shields running on foot
- descended from Lìshān,
taking the path through Zhǐyáng secretly.
The Pèi Duke told Zhāng Liáng:
"From this path to our camp,
it's no more than twenty lǐ.
Estimate when I've reached the army,
then you may enter."
After the Pèi Duke had left,
and secretly reached his camp,
Zhāng Liáng entered to apologize,
saying:
"The Pèi Duke cannot handle much wine,
and thus could not take proper leave.
He respectfully sends me, Liáng, to present a pair of white jade discs,
with repeated bows to Your Majesty;
and a pair of jade wine vessels,
with repeated bows to the Great General."
King Xiàng asked:
"Where is the Pèi Duke now?"
Liáng replied:
"Hearing that Your Majesty intended to reprimand him,
he slipped away alone,
and has already reached his army."
King Xiàng then accepted the discs,
placing them on his seat.
Yàfù received the jade vessels,
set them on the ground,
drew his sword and smashed them,
saying:
"Alas!
This fool is not worth scheming with!
The one who will seize King Xiàng's empire
must be the Pèi Duke.
We shall all be his captives now!"
When the Pèi Duke reached his camp,
he immediately executed Cáo Wúshāng.
After several days,
Xiàng Yǔ led his troops west to slaughter at Xiányáng,
killed Zǐyīng, the surrendered Qín prince,
burned the Qín palaces,
the fires raging for three months without extinguishing;
then gathered treasures and women and headed east.
Someone advised King Xiàng:
"Guānzhōng is protected by mountains and rivers on all sides,
the land is fertile,
it would make a capital for hegemony."
But King Xiàng saw the Qín palaces all burned and ruined,
and his heart yearned to return east,
saying:
"To gain wealth and honor without returning home
is like wearing embroidered robes at night -
who would know of it!"
The adviser said:
"They say the Chǔ people are like monkeys with hats on -
indeed so!"
King Xiàng heard this,
and had the adviser boiled alive.
King Xiàng sent to report to King Huái.
King Huái said:
"As agreed."
So they honored King Huái as Yìdì.
King Xiàng wanted to make himself king,
first enfeoffing his generals and ministers.
He declared:
"When the empire first rose in rebellion,
we temporarily established descendants of nobles to attack Qín.
But those who donned armor and took up arms to initiate the cause,
exposed in the wilds for three years,
and destroyed Qín to stabilize the empire -
that was due to the efforts of you generals, ministers, and me, Jí.
Though Yìdī has no merit,
he should still have land divided for his rule."
The generals all said:
"Good."
So they divided the empire,
establishing the generals as kings and marquises.
King Xiàng and Fàn Zēng, suspicious of the Pèi Duke's ambitions,
though having reached reconciliation,
disliked breaking the agreement,
yet feared the nobles would rebel,
plotted secretly:
"Bā and Shǔ have treacherous paths,
where Qín's exiles all dwell."
So they declared:
"Bā and Shǔ are also Guānzhōng territory."
Thus they made the Pèi Duke King of Hàn,
ruling Bā, Shǔ, and Hànzhōng,
with capital at Nánzhèng.
Then they divided Guānzhōng into three,
setting up surrendered Qín generals as kings to block the Hàn King.
King Xiàng made Zhāng Hán King of Yōng,
ruling west of Xiányáng,
capital at Fèiqiū.
Chief Clerk Xīn,
formerly prison officer at Yuèyáng,
had once shown kindness to Xiàng Liáng;
Commandant Dǒng Yì
had originally persuaded Zhāng Hán to surrender to Chǔ.
So they made Sīmǎ Xīn King of Sài,
ruling from Xiányáng east to the river,
capital at Yuèyáng;
made Dǒng Yì King of Dí,
ruling Shàngjùn,
capital at Gāonú.
They moved King Bào of Wèi to be King of Western Wèi,
ruling Hédōng,
capital at Píngyáng.
Xiàqiū Shēn Yáng,
favorite of Zhāng Ěr,
first captured Hénán,
welcoming Chǔ at the river,
so was made King of Hénán,
capital at Luòyáng.
King Chéng of Hán remained in his original capital,
at Yángzhái.
Zhào general Sīmǎ Áng secured Hénèi,
with numerous achievements,
so was made King of Yīn,
ruling Hénèi,
capital at Zhāogē.
King Xiē of Zhào was moved to be King of Dài.
Zhào chancellor Zhāng Ěr, always worthy,
also followed into the pass,
so was made King of Chángshān,
ruling Zhào territory,
capital at Xiāngguó.
Dāngyáng Jūn Qíng Bù, as Chǔ general,
often led the army,
so was made King of Jiǔjiāng,
capital at Lù.
Pó Jūn Wú Ruì, leading Bǎiyuè allies,
also followed into the pass,
so was made King of Héngshān,
capital at Zhū.
Yìdì's pillar-of-state Gòng Áo led troops against Nánjùn,
with many merits,
so was made King of Línjiāng,
capital at Jiānglíng.
King Hánguǎng of Yān was moved to be King of Liáodōng.
Yān general Zāng Tú followed Chǔ to rescue Zhào,
then followed into the pass,
so was made King of Yān,
capital at Jì.
King Tián Fú of Qí was moved to be King of Jiāodōng.
Qí general Tián Dū followed the rescue of Zhào,
then followed into the pass,
so was made King of Qí,
capital at Línzī.
Tián Ān, grandson of King Jiàn of Qí destroyed by Qín,
while Xiàng Yǔ was crossing the river to rescue Zhào,
captured several cities in Jìběi,
leading his troops to surrender to Xiàng Yǔ,
so was made King of Jìběi,
capital at Bóyáng.
Tián Róng,
having repeatedly betrayed Xiàng Liáng,
and refusing to lead troops with Chǔ against Qín,
was thus not enfeoffed.
Lord Chéng'ān Chén Yú abandoned his general's seal and left,
not following into the pass,
but being known for worthiness,
and having merit for Zhào,
and heard to be at Nánpí,
was enfeoffed with three surrounding counties.
Fān Jūn's general Méi Xuān had many merits,
so was made a marquis of 100,000 households.
King Xiàng made himself Hegemon King of Western Chǔ,
ruling nine commanaderies,
with capital at Péngchéng.
In the first year of the Hàn dynasty, in the fourth month,
the feudal lords withdrew from under the command
and each went to their own states.
King Xiàng went out to his state,
and sent men to move the Righteous Emperor,
saying:
"The emperors of antiquity ruled over a thousand lǐ of territory,
and always resided upstream."
He then sent an envoy to move the Righteous Emperor to Chēn County in Chángshā.
Urging the Righteous Emperor to depart,
his ministers gradually betrayed him,
so he secretly ordered the kings of Héngshān and Línjiāng to attack and kill him in the river.
Hán King Chéng had no military achievements,
so King Xiàng did not let him go to his state,
but took him along to Péngchéng,
demoted him to a marquis,
and later killed him.
Zāng Tú went to his state,
and then drove Hán Guǎng to Liáodōng.
Guǎng was not grateful,
so Tú attacked and killed Guǎng at Wúzhōng,
and became king over his territory.
Tián Róng heard that Xiàng Yǔ had moved Qí King Shì to Jiāodōng,
and set up the Qí general Tián Dū as King of Qí,
so he became very angry,
refused to send the Qí king to Jiāodōng,
and consequently rebelled with Qí,
meeting and attacking Tián Dū.
Tián Dū fled to Chǔ.
Qí King Shì feared King Xiàng,
so he fled to Jiāodōng to take up his state.
Tián Róng was angry,
pursued and killed him at Jímò.
Róng then made himself King of Qí,
and westward attacked and killed Jìběi King Tián Ān,
becoming king over the three Qí.
Róng gave Péng Yuè a general's seal,
ordering him to rebel in Liáng territory.
Chén Yú secretly sent Zhāng Tóng and Xià Yuì to persuade Qí King Tián Róng, saying:
"Xiàng Yǔ, as the arbiter of the empire,
is unjust.
Now he has made all the former kings rulers of wretched lands,
while making his ministers and generals rulers of good lands,
and drove away his former lord, Zhào King,
who then went north to reside in Dài.
I consider this unacceptable.
Hearing that Your Majesty has raised troops,
and does not listen to what is unrighteous,
I hope Your Majesty will supply me with troops,
to request to attack Chángshān,
to restore the Zhào king,
and request to use my state as a protective screen."
The Qí king agreed,
and consequently sent troops to Zhào.
Chén Yú mobilized all the troops from three counties,
and together with Qí, attacked Chángshān with combined force,
greatly defeating it.
Zhāng Ěr fled and returned to Hàn.
Chén Yú welcomed the former Zhào King Xiē from Dài,
