and returned him to Zhào.
The Zhào king then established Chén Yú as King of Dài.
At this time,
Hàn returned and secured the three Qín.
Xiàng Yǔ heard that the Hàn king had already annexed Guānzhōng,
and was about to go east,
while Qí and Zhào had rebelled against him:
he was greatly angered.
He then made the former Wú magistrate Zhèng Chāng King of Hán,
to resist Hàn.
He ordered Xiāo Duke Jiǎo and others to attack Péng Yuè.
Péng Yuè defeated Xiāo Duke Jiǎo and others.
Hàn sent Zhāng Liáng to pacify Hán,
and then sent a letter to King Xiàng, saying:
"The Hàn king has been deprived of his position,
and wishes to obtain Guānzhōng.
If the agreement is fulfilled, he will stop,
and dare not go east."
He also sent a letter of rebellion from Qí and Liáng to King Xiàng, saying:
"Qí wishes to join with Zhào to destroy Chǔ together."
Chǔ, for this reason, had no intention to go west,
and instead attacked Qí to the north.
He levied troops from Jiǔjiāng King Bù.
Bù claimed illness and did not go,
sending a general with several thousand men.
King Xiàng hence bore a grudge against Bù.
In the second year of Hàn, in winter,
Xiàng Yǔ then went north to Chéngyáng,
and Tián Róng also led his troops to join battle.
Tián Róng was defeated,
fled to Píngyuán,
where the people of Píngyuán killed him.
He then went north, burning and leveling the city walls and houses of Qí,
buried alive all of Tián Róng's surrendered soldiers,
and captured their old, weak, women, and children.
Pacifying Qí as far as Běihǎi,
he caused much destruction and slaughter.
The people of Qí gathered together and rebelled against him.
Thereupon, Tián Róng's younger brother Tián Héng gathered Qí's scattered soldiers, obtaining several tens of thousands of men,
and rebelled at Chéngyáng.
King Xiàng consequently remained,
but after repeated battles, could not capture it.
In spring,
the Hàn king assembled the troops of five feudal lords,
totaling five hundred and sixty thousand men,
and went east to attack Chǔ.
King Xiàng heard of this,
immediately ordered his generals to attack Qí,
and personally led thirty thousand elite troops south from Lǔ to Hǔlíng.
In the fourth month,
Hàn had already entered Péngchéng,
seized its treasures and beautiful women,
and daily held grand banquets.
King Xiàng then went west from Xiāo,
attacked the Hàn army at dawn and moved east,
reaching Péngchéng by
noon,
and greatly defeated the Hàn army.
The Hàn army all fled,
following each other into the Gǔ and Sì rivers,
and over a hundred thousand Hàn soldiers were killed.
The Hàn soldiers all fled south to the mountains,
and Chǔ pursued and attacked them to the east of Língbì on the Suī River.
The Hàn army retreated,
was pressed by Chǔ,
many were killed,
over a hundred thousand Hàn soldiers fell into the Suī River,
and the Suī River ceased to flow because of them.
They surrounded the Hàn king three times.
Then a great wind arose from the northwest,
breaking trees and tearing off roofs,
lifting sand and stones,
darkening the day into obscurity,
and blowing against the Chǔ army.
The Chǔ army was thrown into great confusion,
broken and scattered,
and thus the Hàn king was able to escape with several tens of cavalry.
He wished to pass by Pèi,
gather his family and go west;
Chǔ also sent men to pursue him to Pèi,
to capture the Hàn king's family;
the family had all fled,
and did not meet with the Hàn king.
On the road, the Hàn king encountered and found Xiàohuì and Lǔyuán,
and carried them along.
Chǔ cavalry pursued the Hàn king,
the Hàn king was in haste,
pushed Xiàohuì and Lǔyuán out of the carriage,
but Lord Téng often got down, picked them up, and carried them.
This happened three times.
He said:
"Although the situation is urgent, we cannot drive faster,
how can we abandon them?"
Thus they managed to escape.
He searched for Tàigōng and Empress Lǚ but did not meet them.
Shěnyìjī followed Tàigōng and Empress Lǚ, traveling discreetly,
seeking the Hàn king,
but instead encountered the Chǔ army.
The Chǔ army then took them back,
reported to King Xiàng,
and King Xiàng often kept them in the army.
At this time, Empress Lǚ's elder brother, Zhōulǚ Marquis, was a Hàn general leading troops stationed at Xiàyì,
the Hàn king went discreetly to join him,
and gradually gathered his soldiers.
Reaching Yíngyáng,
all the defeated troops assembled,
and Xiāo Hé also sent all the old, weak, and unregistered from Guānzhōng to Yíngyáng,
so they were greatly revived.
Chǔ, starting from Péngchéng,
often pursued the defeated northward,
and fought with Hàn between Jīng and Suǒ, south of Yíngyáng,
Hàn defeated Chǔ,
so Chǔ for this reason could not pass Yíngyáng to go west.
When King Xiàng went to rescue Péngchéng,
and pursued the Hàn king to Yíngyáng,
Tián Héng also managed to recover Qí,
and established Tián Róng's son Guǎng as King of Qí.
After the Hàn king's defeat at Péngchéng,
the feudal lords all again sided with Chǔ and turned against Hàn.
The Hàn army was at Yíngyáng,
built a corridor connecting to the river,
to obtain grain from the Áo Granary.
In the third year of Hàn,
King Xiàng repeatedly invaded and seized the Hàn corridor,
the Hàn king lacked food,
was afraid,
requested peace,
and offered to cede the area west of Yíngyáng to Hàn.
King Xiàng intended to agree.
Lìyáng Marquis Fàn Zēng said:
"Hàn is easy to deal with,
if we let them go now and do not take them,
we will surely regret it later."
King Xiàng then, together with Fàn Zēng, urgently besieged Yíngyáng.
The King of Hàn grew troubled by this,
and thus employed Chén Píng's stratagem to sow discord with King Xiàng.
When King Xiàng's envoy arrived,
they prepared a grand sacrificial feast
and were about to present it.
But upon seeing the envoy,
they feigned shock and exclaimed:
"We thought you were Fàn Zēng's envoy,
but you turn out to be King Xiàng's messenger!"
They then took the feast away
and served King Xiàng's envoy meager food.
When the envoy returned and reported to King Xiàng,
the king became suspicious that Fàn Zēng had secret dealings with Hàn,
and gradually stripped him of his authority.
Fàn Zēng, in great anger,
said:
"The empire's affairs are largely settled;
Your Majesty may handle them yourself.
I wish to be granted my bones to return to the ranks."
King Xiàng permitted this.
Before reaching Péngchéng,
Fàn Zēng developed a boil on his back and died.
The Hàn general Jì Xìn advised the King of Hàn, saying:
"The situation has become critical;
I beg to deceive Chǔ by posing as the king,
so that you may escape unnoticed."
Thereupon, the King of Hàn sent two thousand women in armor out the eastern gate of Xíngyáng at night,
and Chǔ troops attacked them from all sides.
Jì Xìn rode in a yellow-canopied carriage,
with a left-side banner,
declaring:
"The city's food is exhausted;
the King of Hàn surrenders."
The Chǔ army all cheered "Wànsuì!"
Meanwhile, the King of Hàn escaped through the western gate with several dozen cavalry,
fleeing to Chénggāo.
When King Xiàng saw Jì Xìn,
he asked:
"Where is the King of Hàn?"
Jì Xìn replied:
"The King of Hàn has already left."
King Xiàng burned Jì Xìn to death.
The King of Hàn ordered the Censor-in-Chief Zhōu Kē, Cōng Gōng, and Wèi Bào to guard Xíngyáng.
Zhōu Kē and Cōng Gōng plotted, saying:
"A king who has rebelled
is difficult to trust with defending the city."
So they jointly killed Wèi Bào.
When Chǔ captured Xíngyáng city,
they took Zhōu Kē alive.
King Xiàng said to Zhōu Kē:
"Become my general,
and I shall appoint you as Grand General,
enfeoffing you with thirty thousand households."
Zhōu Kē retorted angrily:
"If you do not swiftly surrender to Hàn,
Hàn will capture you now,
for you are no match for Hàn."
King Xiàng, enraged,
boiled Zhōu Kē to death
and also killed Cōng Gōng.
After the King of Hàn left Xíngyáng,
he fled south to Wǎn and Yè,
joined by the King of Jiǔjiāng, Yīng Bù,
gathered troops along the way,
and reentered to defend Chénggāo.
In the fourth year of Hàn,
King Xiàng advanced and besieged Chénggāo.
The King of Hàn escaped,
solely with Lord Téng out the northern gate of Chénggāo,
crossed the river to Xiūwǔ,
and joined the armies of Zhāng Ěr and Hán Xìn.
The other generals gradually managed to leave Chénggāo
and follow the King of Hàn.
Chǔ then captured Chénggāo
and intended to head west.
Hàn sent troops to block them at Gǒng,
preventing their westward advance.
At this time,
Péng Yuè crossed the river and attacked Chǔ at Dōng'ē,
killing the Chǔ general Lord Xuē.
King Xiàng then personally went east to attack Péng Yuè.
The King of Hàn obtained the troops of Huáiyīn Hóu
and planned to cross the river south.
Zhèng Zhōng advised the King of Hàn,
who then halted and fortified at Hénèi.
He sent Liú Jiǎ to lead troops assisting Péng Yuè,
burning Chǔ's stockpiles.
King Xiàng went east and defeated them,
driving Péng Yuè to flee.
The King of Hàn then led his troops across the river,
retook Chénggāo,
stationed at Guǎngwǔ,
and utilized the food supplies from Áo Granary.
King Xiàng, having pacified the eastern regions, returned,
headed west,
and faced Hàn at Guǎngwǔ, both armies encamped,
maintaining a standoff for several months.
At this juncture,
Péng Yuè repeatedly rebelled in Liáng territory,
cutting off Chǔ's food supplies,
which troubled King Xiàng.
He set up a high chopping block,
placed Liú Bāng's father on it,
and warned the King of Hàn:
"If you do not surrender immediately,
I will boil your father."
The King of Hàn replied:
"I and Xiàng Yǔ both received orders from King Huái facing north,
saying 'we swore to be brothers',
so my father is your father;
if you insist on boiling your father,
then I hope you'll share a cup of the broth with me."
King Xiàng was furious
and wanted to kill him.
But Xiàng Bó said:
"The outcome of the empire is uncertain;
moreover, those who contend for the empire do not care for their families.
Killing him would be of no benefit,
only adding to the calamity."
King Xiàng heeded his advice.
The stalemate between Chǔ and Hàn dragged on unresolved,
with the able-bodied suffering from warfare
and the old and weak exhausted from supply transport.
King Xiàng said to the King of Hàn:
"The empire has been in turmoil for years
merely because of the two of us.
I wish to challenge you to a duel to decide supremacy,
and not needlessly torment the people of the world."
The King of Hàn laughed and declined:
"I would rather fight with wisdom
than with brute force."
King Xiàng then ordered a warrior to issue a challenge.
Hàn had an expert archer named Lóu Fán,
and whenever a Chǔ challenger appeared,
Lóu Fán would shoot and kill him.
King Xiàng, in a rage,
personally donned armor and wielded a halberd to challenge.
When Lóu Fán aimed to shoot him,
King Xiàng glared and shouted at him,
causing Lóu Fán to dare not look,
dare not release the arrow,
so he fled back into the fortress
and dared not come out again.
The King of Hàn sent someone to inquire discreetly
and learned it was King Xiàng himself.
The King of Hàn was greatly alarmed.
Thereupon, King Xiàng approached and conversed with the King of Hàn across the ravine at Guǎngwǔ.
The King of Hàn enumerated his faults,
angering King Xiàng,
who desired a decisive battle.
The King of Hàn refused,
and King Xiàng had a crossbow shot that wounded the King of Hàn.
Injured, the King of Hàn
fled into Chénggāo.
King Xiàng heard that Huáiyīn Hóu had taken Héběi,
defeated Qí and Zhào,
and was about to attack Chǔ,
so he sent Lóng Jū to attack him.
Huáiyīn Hóu engaged in battle,
with cavalry general Guàn Yīng attacking,
routing the Chǔ army decisively
and killing Lóng Jū.
Hán Xìn thereupon proclaimed himself King of Qí.
King Xiàng, upon learning of Lóng Jū's defeat,
became fearful
and sent Wǔ Shè from Xūyí to persuade Huáiyīn Hóu.
But Huáiyīn Hóu did not listen.
At this time,
Péng Yuè rebelled again,
capturing Liáng territory
and cutting off Chǔ's food supply.
King Xiàng then said to Hǎichūn Hóu, the Grand Marshal Cáo Jiù, and others:
"Guard Chénggāo carefully.
If Hàn challenges to battle,
be cautious not to engage,
just prevent them from advancing east.
Within fifteen days, I will surely defeat Péng Yuè,
stabilize Liáng,
and rejoin you, generals."
He then headed east,
attacking Chénliú
and Wàihuáng along the way.
Wàihuáng did not surrender.
After several days,
it had already surrendered,
but King Xiàng was enraged,
ordering all males aged fifteen and above to gather east of the city,
intending to bury them alive.
The thirteen-year-old son of a retainer to the magistrate of Wàihuáng
went to persuade King Xiàng, saying:
"Péng Yuè forcibly seized Wàihuáng,
and the people of Wàihuáng, in fear,
temporarily surrendered,
awaiting Your Majesty.
Now that Your Majesty has arrived,
if you bury them all alive,
how could the people have any inclination to submit?
From here eastward,
the more than ten cities of Liáng territory would all be terrified,
and none would be willing to surrender." King Xiàng found his words reasonable,
and thus pardoned those in Wàihuáng slated for execution.
As he moved east to Suīyáng,
upon hearing this, all rushed to surrender to King Xiàng.
The Hàn forces repeatedly challenged the Chǔ army to battle,
but the Chǔ army did not engage.
They sent men to insult them,
and after five or six days,
the Grand Marshal grew angry,
leading troops across the Sì River.
When half the soldiers had crossed,
the Hàn forces attacked,
crushing the Chǔ army,
and seizing all of Chǔ's wealth and supplies.
Grand Marshal Jiù, Chief Historian Yì, and King of Sài Xīn all cut their own throats by the Sì River.
Grand Marshal Jiù
was formerly a prison officer in Qí,
and Chief Historian Xīn was also a former prison official in Yuèyáng;
both had once shown kindness to Xiàng Liáng,
hence King Xiàng trusted them.
At that time,
King Xiàng was in Suīyáng,
and upon hearing of the defeat of Hǎichūn Hóu's army,
he led his troops back.
The Hàn army was besieging Zhōnglí Mò east of Xíngyáng,
but when King Xiàng arrived,
the Hàn forces, fearing Chǔ,
all fled to difficult terrain.
At this time,
the Hàn troops were numerous and well-supplied,
while King Xiàng's army was exhausted and out of provisions.
Hàn sent Lù Jiǎ to persuade King Xiàng,
requesting the return of Tàigōng,
but King Xiàng refused.
King of Hàn then sent Hóu Gōng to persuade King Xiàng,
and King Xiàng agreed to a treaty with Hàn,
dividing the empire in half,
with the land west of the Hóng Gōu going to Hàn,
and that east of it to Chǔ.
King Xiàng consented,
and immediately returned King of Hàn's parents, wife, and children.
The army all cheered "Wànsuì!"
King of Hàn then enfeoffed Hóu Gōng as Lord Píngguó.
He hid and refused to see him again,
saying:
"This man is a persuader of the empire,
wherever he resides, he can overturn states,
hence he is titled Lord Píngguó."
With the treaty settled,
King Xiàng led his troops to disband and return east.
Hàn intended to return west,
but Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng advised:
"Hàn holds the greater part of the empire,
and all the nobles have submitted.
The Chǔ army is exhausted and out of supplies;
this is Heaven's time to destroy Chǔ.
It would be best to seize this opportunity and take it.
To let it go now without attack
is what is called
'raising a tiger only to bring trouble upon oneself'."
King of Hàn heeded them.
In the fifth year of Hàn,
King of Hàn pursued King Xiàng to south of Yángxià,
halted his army,
and arranged to join forces with Hánxīn, Marquis of Huáiyīn, and Péng Yuè, Marquis of Jiànchéng, to attack the Chǔ army.
Upon reaching Gùlíng,
however, the troops of Hánxīn and Péng Yuè did not arrive.
Chǔ attacked the Hàn army,
crushing it.
King of Hàn retreated into his fortifications,
digging deep trenches to defend himself.
He said to Zhāng Zǐfáng:
"The nobles are not honoring the agreement;
what can be done?"
The reply was:
"The Chǔ army is about to be defeated,
yet Hánxīn and Péng Yuè have no allocated territories;
it is only natural they did not come.
If Your Majesty can share the empire with them,
they can be summoned immediately.
If not,
the outcome is uncertain.
If you can grant the land from Chén eastward to the sea
entirely to Hánxīn;
and from Suīyáng north to Gǔchéng
to Péng Yuè,
making them fight for themselves,
then Chǔ can be easily defeated."
King of Hàn said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he sent messengers to inform Hánxīn and Péng Yuè:
"Join forces to attack Chǔ.
Once Chǔ is defeated,
the land from Chén east to the sea will go to the King of Qí,
and from Suīyáng north to Gǔchéng to Chancellor Péng."
When the messengers arrived,
Hánxīn and Péng Yuè both replied:
"We request to advance our troops now."
Hánxīn then marched from Qí,
while Liú Jiǎ's army advanced concurrently from Shòuchūn,
sacking Chéngfù,
and reaching Gāixià.
Grand Marshal Zhōu Yīn defected from Chǔ,
using Shū to massacre Liù,
raised the Jiǔjiāng troops,
and together with Liú Jiǎ and Péng Yuè, all converged at Gāixià,
advancing toward King Xiàng.
King Xiàng's army was encamped at Gāixià,
with few troops and exhausted supplies,
surrounded by multiple layers of Hàn and allied forces.
At night, hearing the Hàn army singing Chǔ songs on all sides,
King Xiàng was greatly startled, saying:
"Has Hàn already taken all of Chǔ?
Why are there so many people of Chǔ!"
King Xiàng rose that night,
and drank in his tent.
He had a beloved concubine named Yú,
who often accompanied him;
a fine horse named Zhuī,
which he often rode.
Thereupon, King Xiàng sang a sorrowful and passionate song,
composing a poem himself:
"My strength plucked mountains, my spirit overshadowed the world;
But the times are against me, and Zhuī will not advance.
Zhuī not advancing, what can I do?
Yú, oh Yú, what will become of you!"
After singing several verses,
his concubine joined in.
King Xiàng shed tears in streams,
and all his attendants wept,
unable to look up.
Thereupon, King Xiàng mounted his horse,
with over eight hundred brave horsemen following him,
broke through the encirclement southward that very night,
and galloped away.
At dawn,
the Hàn army realized it,
ordering the cavalry general Guàn Yīng to pursue with five thousand cavalry.
King Xiàng crossed the Huái River,
with only over a hundred horsemen able to keep up.
Reaching Yīnlíng,
he lost his way,
and asked an old farmer,
who deceived him, saying "Left."
Going left,
he became mired in a great marsh.
Thus, the Hàn pursuers caught up.
King Xiàng led his troops east again,
reaching Dōngchéng,
with only twenty-eight horsemen left.
The pursuing Hàn cavalry numbered several thousand.
King Xiàng reckoned he could not escape.
He said to his horsemen:
"I have risen in arms for eight years now,
fought over seventy battles,
those I faced were defeated,
those I attacked submitted,
never defeated,
until I dominated the empire.
Yet now I am trapped here,
this is Heaven's destruction of me,
not any fault in my fighting."
Today I am resolved to die,
but I wish to fight a swift battle for you all,
vowing to triumph three times over the enemy,
to break through the encirclement for you,
behead their general,
and cut down their flag,
so that you may know it is Heaven that destroys me,
and no fault of my warfare."
He then divided his cavalry into four squadrons,
facing outward in all directions. The Hàn army surrounded them in multiple layers.
King Xiàng addressed his riders, saying:
"I will fetch one of their generals for you."
He ordered the cavalry to charge down from all sides,
with a plan to regroup at three locations east of the hill.
Thereupon, King Xiàng gave a great shout and charged down,
and the Hàn army scattered in disarray,
whereupon he beheaded a Hàn general.
At that time,
the Marquis of Chìquán was a cavalry commander
pursuing King Xiàng.
King Xiàng glared at him and shouted,
causing both the Marquis of Chìquán and his horse to panic,
retreating several lǐ in fear.
He regrouped with his cavalry at the three locations.
The Hàn army, not knowing where King Xiàng was,
divided their forces into three
and surrounded him again.
King Xiàng then charged,
beheading another Hàn commandant,
and killing several dozen to a hundred men.
He gathered his riders once more,
having lost only two of them.
He then said to his cavalry:
"How was that?"
The riders all bowed and replied:
"It was just as Your Majesty said."
Thereupon, King Xiàng intended to cross the Wū River to the east.
The Wū River station master had moored a boat and awaited him,
saying to King Xiàng:
"Though Jiāngdōng is small,
its territory spans a thousand lǐ,
and its people number hundreds of thousands,
sufficient for you to be king.
I urge Your Majesty to cross quickly.
Now only I have a boat;
when the Hàn army arrives,
there will be no means to cross."
King Xiàng laughed and said:
"Heaven is destroying me;
what use is crossing for me!
Moreover, I, Jí, crossed the river westward with eight thousand sons of Jiāngdōng,
and not one has returned;
even if the elders of Jiāngdōng pity me and make me king,
what face have I to see them?
Even if they say nothing,
would I not feel shame in my heart?"
He then said to the station master:
"I know you are a worthy man.
I have ridden this horse for five years,
and it has never met its match,
once covering a thousand lǐ in a day.
I cannot bear to kill it,
so I give it to you."
He then ordered his riders to dismount and proceed on foot,
engaging in close combat with short weapons.
Jí alone killed several hundred Hàn soldiers.
King Xiàng himself also suffered more than ten wounds.
Catching sight of the Hàn cavalry marshal Lǚ Mǎtóng,
he said:
"Are you not my old acquaintance?"
Mǎtóng faced him
and pointed him out to Wáng Yì, saying:
"This is King Xiàng."
King Xiàng then said:
"I have heard the Hàn has offered a thousand in gold for my head,
with a fief of ten thousand households.
Let me do you this favor."
Thereupon, he cut his own throat and died.
Wáng Yì took his head,
and the remaining cavalry trampled over each other contending for King Xiàng's body,
resulting in several dozen deaths among themselves.
In the end,
the court gentleman cavalryman Yáng Jiā,
cavalry marshal Lǚ Mǎtóng,
and court gentlemen Lǚ Shèng and Yáng Wǔ each obtained one part of his body.
The five men assembled the parts together,
and they matched.
Therefore, the land was divided into five parts:
Lǚ Mǎtóng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhōngshuǐ,
Wáng Yì as Marquis of Dùyǎn,
Yáng Xǐ as Marquis of Chìquán,
Yáng Wǔ as Marquis of Wúfáng,
and Lǚ Shèng as Marquis of Nièyáng.
After King Xiàng's death,
all of Chǔ territory surrendered to Hàn,
except for Lǔ, which held out.
Hàn then led the forces of the realm intending to massacre it,
but because its people upheld ritual and righteousness,
and died faithfully for their lord,
they brought King Xiàng's head to show Lǔ,
and only then did the elders of Lǔ surrender.
Initially, King Huái of Chǔ
had first enfeoffed Xiàng Jí as the Duke of Lǔ,
and upon his death,
Lǔ was the last to surrender,
so he buried King Xiàng at Gǔchéng with the rites due to the Duke of Lǔ.
The King of Hàn mourned for him,
wept, and then departed.
All the collateral branches of the Xiàng clan
were spared execution by the King of Hàn.
Instead, he enfeoffed Xiàng Bó as Marquis of Shèyáng.
The Marquis of Táo, Marquis of Pínggāo, and Marquis of Xuánwǔ were all of the Xiàng clan,
and were granted the surname Liú.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I have heard from Mr. Zhōu that
"Shùn's eyes were double-pupiled,"
and I have also heard that Xiàng Yǔ was double-pupiled.
Could Yǔ have been his descendant?
How sudden was his rise!
When Qín lost its proper governance,
Chén Shè first raised the difficulty,
and heroes swarmed forth,
contending with one another,
too many to be counted.
Yet Yǔ, without an inch of territory to start with,
arose from the fields,
and in three years,
led the five feudal lords to destroy Qín,
divided the empire,
enfeoffed kings and marquises,
issued all government decrees,
and was titled the "Hegemon King."
Though his position did not last,
such a thing has not been seen since ancient times.
But when he turned his back on Guānzhōng and longed for Chǔ,
exiled the Righteous Emperor and set himself up,
and resented the kings and marquises for betraying him,
it became difficult.
Proud of his own achievements,
he exerted his personal wit without learning from the past,
claiming the enterprise of a hegemon king,
and sought to manage the empire through military campaigns,
yet within five years, his state perished,
and he died at Dōngchéng,
still unaware and without self-reproach,
which was a fault.
And to claim, "Heaven destroys me,
it is no fault of my strategy,"
is it not absurd!
Gāozǔ
was a man of Zhōngyáng Village in Fèng County of Pèi,
of the surname Liú,
and his courtesy name was Jì.
His father was called Tàigōng,
and his mother, Liú Ǎo.
Previously, Liú Ǎo had once rested by the banks of a great marsh,
and dreamed of encountering a spirit.
At that time, there was thunder, lightning, and darkness,
and when Tàigōng went to look,
he saw a dragon atop her.
Thereafter, she was with child,
and gave birth to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ's appearance
featured a prominent nose and a dragon-like countenance,
with beautiful beard and whiskers,
and seventy-two black moles on his left thigh.
He was benevolent and loved others,
fond of giving,
and his disposition was open and generous.
He always had great magnanimity,
and did not engage in the livelihood or tasks of his family.
When he came of age,
he tried being a minor official,
serving as the station master of Sìshuǐ,
and he familiarized and mocked all the officials in the court.
He was fond of wine and women.
He often bought wine on credit from Old Woman Wáng and Wǔ Fù,
and when he lay drunk,
Wǔ Fù and Old Woman Wáng would see a dragon above him,
and found it strange.
Whenever Gāozǔ bought wine and stayed to drink,
they sold several times the usual amount.
Because of these strange occurrences,
at the year's end,
these two families often broke the tallies and canceled his debts.
Gāozǔ once went to Xiányáng for labor service,
and gazing freely about,
he saw the Qín emperor,
sighed deeply, and said:
"Ah,
a true man should be like this!"
Lǚ Gōng from Dān Fù was well-regarded by the Pei magistrate.
To avoid enmity, he became a guest,
and thus settled in Pei.
The local elites and officials in Pei heard that the magistrate had important guests,
and all went to offer congratulations.
Xiāo Hé was the chief official,
in charge of reception,
and said to the assembled gentlemen:
"Those who bring gifts worth less than a thousand coins
should be seated below the hall."
Gāo Zǔ, who was a village head,
often dismissed the officials,
so he deceitfully said he brought "ten thousand coins in congratulations,"
though he hadn't carried a single coin.
When presented,
Lǚ Gōng was greatly surprised,
rose,
and greeted him at the door.
Lǚ Gōng, who
was skilled at judging people,
saw Gāo Zǔ's appearance,
and thus respected him highly,
inviting him in to sit.
Xiāo Hé remarked:
"Liú Jì often boasts without achieving much."
Gāo Zǔ then jested with the other guests,
taking the seat of honor,
without any humility.
When the drinking was at its height,
Lǚ Gōng insisted on keeping Gāo Zǔ.
Gāo Zǔ continued drinking
until late.
Lǚ Gōng said:
"I have long been good at judging people,
and have judged many,
yet none compare to Jì.
I hope Jì will take care of himself.
I have a young daughter,
and wish her to be Jì's servant and wife."
When the drinking ended,
Lady Lǚ was angry with Lǚ Gōng, saying:
"You always wanted to marry this daughter to someone noble.
Yet when Pei's magistrate, who appreciates you,
asked, you did not agree,
so why offer her to Liú Jì so presumptuously?"
Lǚ Gōng said:
"This is not something women can understand."
In the end, he gave her to Liú Jì.
Lǚ Gōng's daughter became Empress Lǚ,
mother to Xiàohuì Emperor and Princess Lǔ Yuán.
When Gāo Zǔ was a village head,
he often claimed the fields
to the official.
Empress Lǚ and their two children were weeding in the fields,
when an elderly man stopped by to ask for a drink.
Empress Lǚ then offered him food.
The old man judged Empress Lǚ, saying:
"Madam, you are a person of high status under the heavens."
He then judged the two children.
Seeing Xiàohuì,
he said:
"The reason for Madam's honor is this boy."
Judging Lǔ Yuán,
he also said she would be honored.
After the old man left,
Gāo Zǔ came from another house,
and Empress Lǚ recounted the guest's visit,
saying he judged mother and sons all to be highly esteemed.
Gāo Zǔ asked,
"Not far?"
And pursued him,
asking the old man.
The old man said:
"Madam and the child both resemble you.
Your honor is beyond words."
Gāo Zǔ thanked him,
saying:
"If it's as you say,
I will not forget this kindness."
Later, when Gāo Zǔ was honored,
he could no longer find the old man.
When Gāo Zǔ was a village head,
he made a hat from bamboo strips,
to catch thieves at Xiè and handle matters there.
He sometimes wore it,
and continued to wear it when honored,
becoming known as the "Liú family hat."
Gāo Zǔ, as a village head, escorted prisoners to Lì Mountain.
Many escaped along the way.
He thought if this continued, all would escape,
so when they reached Fēng's western marsh,
he stopped to drink.
At night, he released the prisoners,
saying:
"You can all go,
I will also leave from here!"
About ten strong men wished to follow him.
Gāo Zǔ was drunk,
walking through the marsh at night,
ordering one man to walk ahead.
The man returned, reporting:
"There is a large snake blocking the path ahead;
we wish to turn back."
Gāo Zǔ, drunk, said:
"Brave men go, why fear!"
He went forward,
drew his sword, and struck, cutting the snake.
The snake split in two,
opening the path.
A few miles further,
he was drunk and lay down.
Later people arrived where the snake had been,
and saw an old woman weeping at night.
They asked why she was crying.
The woman said:
"Someone killed my son,
so I am crying for him."
People said:
"Why was your son killed?"
The woman said:
"My son
was the son of the White Emperor,
transformed into a snake,
blocking the path.
He was killed by the son of the Red Emperor,
that's why I'm crying."
People thought she was insincere,
wanting to accuse her,
when the woman suddenly disappeared.
When others arrived,
Gāo Zǔ awoke.
They told Gāo Zǔ,
and he was secretly delighted,
feeling proud.
His followers increasingly respected him.
The First Emperor of Qin often said:
"There is an aura of an emperor in the southeast,"
so he traveled east to suppress it.
Gāo Zǔ often doubted himself,
hiding in the marsh rocks of Máng and Dàng mountains.
Empress Lǚ, with others, searched for him,
and often found him.
Gāo Zǔ was curious and asked her.
Empress Lǚ said:
"There is always a cloud above Jì's location,
so I come and always find Jì."
Gāo Zǔ was pleased.
Many young men in Pei heard this,
and wished to join him.
In the first year of the Second Emperor of Qin, in autumn,
Chén Shèng rose in Qí,
reached Chén and became a king,
calling himself "Zhāng Chǔ."
Many counties and prefectures killed their chief officials to support Chén Shèng.
The magistrate of Pei was afraid,
wanting Pei to support Shèng.
Liason and chief official Xiāo Hé and Cáo Cān said:
"You are a Qin official.
Now wanting to rebel
and lead Pei's youth,
we fear they will not listen.
It is best to summon the exiles from outside,
who can gather hundreds,
then they can force the order,
and the crowd will not dare to disobey."
Thus Fán Kuài was sent to summon Liú Jì.
Liú Jì had already gathered dozens of men.
Then Fán Kuài joined Liú Jì.
The Pei magistrate regretted,
fearing changes,
so he closed the city for defense,
planning to execute Xiāo and Cáo.
Xiāo and Cáo feared,
climbing over the city to join Liú Jì.
Liú Jì then wrote on silk, shooting it onto the city,
addressing Pei's elders:
"The people have suffered Qin for too long.
Though elders guard the magistrate,
lords have risen together;
now we slaughter Pei."
Now if we together kill the magistrate,
select a suitable youth from among our sons and younger brothers to establish as leader,
and respond to the other lords,
then our families will be preserved.
Otherwise,
fathers and sons will all be slaughtered,
and it will be futile."
The elders then led the sons and younger brothers to jointly kill the magistrate of Pèi,
opened the city gates to welcome Liú Jì,
and wanted to make him the magistrate of Pèi.
Liú Jì said:
"The world is in turmoil,
with various lords rising up together.
If we now appoint a commander improperly,
we will be utterly defeated.
I dare not consider myself overly important,
but I fear my abilities are meager,
and I cannot fully protect the fathers, brothers, sons, and younger brothers.
This is a great matter;
I hope you will mutually recommend and select a suitable person."
Xiāo Hé, Cáo Shēn, and others were all civil officials,
cautious about their own safety,
and feared that if the endeavor failed,
the Qin would later exterminate their families.
So they all yielded to Liú Jì.
The elders all said:
"We have always heard of the various rare and extraordinary signs about Liú Jì,
indicating he is destined for nobility.
Moreover, we have divined it,
and none is more auspicious than Liú Jì."
Thereupon, Liú Jì repeatedly declined.
As no one else dared to take the position,
they established Jì as the Lord of Pèi.
They sacrificed to the Yellow Emperor,
offered sacrifices to Chīyóu in the court of Pèi,
and anointed the drums and flags with blood,
with all banners being red.
This was because the serpent killed was the son of the White Emperor,
and the killer was the son of the Red Emperor,
hence they exalted the color red.
Thereupon, young brave officials like Xiāo Hé, Cáo Shēn, and Fán Kuài gathered two to three thousand men from the sons and younger brothers of Pèi,
attacked Húlíng and Fāngyǔ,
then returned to defend Fēng.
In the second year of the Second Emperor of Qin,
Zhōu Zhāng, a general under Chén Shè, led his army west to Xì and then turned back.
Yān, Zhào, Qí, and Wèi all declared themselves kings.
The Xiàng clan rose in Wú.
Píng, the inspector of Qin's Sìchuān, led troops to besiege Fēng.
After two days,
they came out to battle,
and defeated him.
Liú Jì ordered Yǒng Chǐ to guard Fēng,
and led his troops to Xuē.
Zhuàng, the governor of Sìchuān, was defeated at Xuē,
fled to Qī,
where the Left Marshal of the Lord of Pèi captured Zhuàng, the governor of Sìchuān,
and killed him.
The Lord of Pèi returned his army to Gāngfǔ,
and reached Fāngyǔ,
when Zhōu Fú came to attack Fāngyǔ, but they did not engage in battle.
King Chén sent Zhōu Fú, a man of Wèi, to seize territory.
Zhōu Fú sent someone to tell Yǒng Chǐ:
"Fēng
was formerly a relocated capital of Liáng.
Now several dozen cities in Wèi territory have been pacified.
If Chǐ now surrenders to Wèi,
Wèi will appoint Chǐ as a marquis to guard Fēng.
If you do not surrender,
we will slaughter Fēng."
Yǒng Chǐ had never wished to be subordinate to the Lord of Pèi,
and when Wèi summoned him,
he immediately turned to guard Fēng for Wèi.
The Lord of Pèi led his troops to attack Fēng,
but could not capture it.
The Lord of Pèi fell ill,
and returned to Pèi.
The Lord of Pèi resented Yǒng Chǐ and the sons and younger brothers of Fēng for betraying him.
Hearing that Dōngyáng Nìng Jūn and Qín Jiā had established Jǐng Jū as acting king,
in Liú,
he went to join them,
hoping to request troops to attack Fēng.
At that time, the Qin general Zhāng Hán was pursuing from Chén,
and his deputy general Sìmǎ was leading troops north to pacify Chǔ territory,
slaughtering Xiàng,
and reaching Dàng.
Dōngyáng Nìng Jūn and the Lord of Pèi led their troops west,
and fought west of Xiāo,
but were unsuccessful.
They regrouped their forces at Liú,
led their troops to attack Dàng,
and took Dàng after three days.
Thereby, they gathered the troops of Dàng,
obtaining five to six thousand men.
They attacked Xiàyì,
and captured it.
Then they returned their army to Fēng.
Hearing that Xiàng Liáng was at Xuē,
he went with over a hundred cavalry to see him.
Xiàng Liáng reinforced the Lord of Pèi with five thousand soldiers,
and ten commanders of the fifth rank.
The Lord of Pèi returned,
and led his troops to attack Fēng.
After following Xiàng Liáng for over a month,
Xiàng Yǔ had already captured Xiāngchéng and returned.
Xiàng Liáng summoned all his deputy generals to gather at Xuē.
Hearing that King Chén was definitely dead,
they established the later King Huái of Chǔ's grandson, Xīn, as King of Chǔ,
ruling from Xūyí.
Xiàng Liáng was titled Lord Wǔxìn.
After several months,
they attacked Gāngfǔ to the north,
rescued Dōng'ē,
and defeated the Qin army.
The Qí army returned home,
while Chǔ alone pursued the defeated,
sending the Lord of Pèi and Xiàng Yǔ to separately attack Chéngyáng,
slaughtering it.
They stationed east of Púyáng,
engaged the Qin army in battle,
and defeated them.
The Qin army revived,
defended Púyáng,
surrounded by water.
The Chǔ army left and attacked Dìngtáo,
but did not capture it.
The Lord of Pèi and Xiàng Yǔ campaigned west to the area of Yōngqiū,
engaged the Qin army in battle,
greatly defeated them,
and beheaded Lǐ Yóu.
They returned to attack Wàihuáng,
but did not capture it.
Xiàng Liáng defeated the Qin army again,
and became arrogant.
Sòng Yì advised him,
but he did not listen.
Qin reinforced Zhāng Hán with troops,
who attacked Xiàng Liáng at night with silent advance,
greatly defeating him at Dìngtáo,
and Xiàng Liáng died.
The Lord of Pèi and Xiàng Yǔ were just attacking Chénliú
when they heard of Xiàng Liáng's death,
and led their troops east together with General Lǚ.
Lǚ Chén's army was east of Péngchéng,
Xiàng Yǔ's army was west of Péngchéng,
and the Lord of Pèi's army was at Dàng.
After Zhāng Hán had defeated Xiàng Liáng's army,
he considered the troops in Chǔ territory insufficient to worry about,
so he crossed the river,
attacked Zhào to the north,
and greatly defeated them.
At that time,
Zhào Xiē was king,
and the Qin general Wáng Lí besieged him in the city of Jùlù,
which was what was called the army north of the river.
In the third year of the Second Emperor of Qin,
King Huái of Chǔ, seeing that Xiàng Liáng's army was defeated,
grew fearful,
moved the capital from Xūyí to Péngchéng,
and merged the armies of Lǚ Chén and Xiàng Yǔ, taking personal command.
He appointed the Lord of Pèi as the chief of Dàng Commandery,
enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Wǔ'ān,
and put him in command of the troops of Dàng Commandery.
He enfeoffed Xiàng Yǔ as the Marquis of Cháng'ān,
with the title Lord of Lǔ.
Lǚ Chén was made Minister over the Masses,
and his father Lǚ Qīng was made Prime Minister.
Zhào repeatedly requested rescue,
so King Huái appointed Sòng Yì as Grand General,
Xiàng Yǔ as Second General,
Fàn Zēng as Junior General,
to go north and rescue Zhào.
He ordered the Lord of Pèi to campaign west into the Pass.
He made a pact with the various generals,
that whoever first pacified Guānzhōng would be made its king.
At that time,
the Qin army was strong,
often pursuing the defeated in victory,
and none of the generals saw advantage in being the first to enter the Pass.
Only Xiàng Yǔ, resentful that Qin had destroyed Xiàng Liáng's army,
was fervent,
and wished to go west into the Pass with the Lord of Pèi.
The veteran generals of King Huái all said:
"Xiàng Yǔ is by nature fierce, cunning, and cruel.
Xiàng Yǔ once attacked Xiāngchéng,
and left no one alive in Xiāngchéng,
burying them all in pits.
Everywhere he passed, he left nothing but destruction.
Moreover, Chǔ has repeatedly taken the offensive,
but former King Chén and Xiàng Liáng both were defeated.
It would be better to send a virtuous elder to proceed west upholding righteousness,
and proclaim to the fathers and brothers of Qin."
The fathers and brothers of Qín have long suffered under their ruler,
and if now a truly virtuous elder were to go,
without committing violence or oppression,
it should be possible to subdue them.
But Xiàng Yǔ is fierce and reckless,
so he cannot be sent now.
Only Lord Pei has always been magnanimous and is a virtuous elder,
so he can be sent."
In the end, they did not permit Xiàng Yǔ to go,
but sent Lord Pei westward to seize territory,
gathering the scattered soldiers of King Chén and Xiàng Liáng.
Then he traveled via Dàng to Chéngyáng,
and faced the Qín army at Gānglǐ with their fortifications opposite,
defeating the two armies of Wèi and Qín.
The Chǔ army sent troops to attack Wáng Lí,
and thoroughly defeated him.
Lord Pei led his troops westward,
encountered Péng Yuè at Chāngyì,
and together they attacked the Qín army,
but the battle was unfavorable.
Returning to Lì,
he met Gāngwǔ Hóu,
took command of his army,
about four thousand men,
and merged them with his own.
Together with the armies of Wèi generals Huáng Xīn and Wèi Shēntú Wǔ Pú, they attacked Chāngyì,
but Chāngyì was not captured.
Going west past Gāoyáng,
Lì Yìjī, who was a gatekeeper,
said:
"Many generals have passed by here,
but I see Lord Pei as a great and virtuous elder."
Then he sought an audience to persuade Lord Pei.
Lord Pei was sitting with his legs apart on a couch,
having two women wash his feet.
Lì Shēng did not bow,
but made a long salute with clasped hands,
saying:
"If you truly wish to punish the unprincipled Qín,
you should not receive an elder with your legs apart."
Thereupon, Lord Pei stood up,
straightened his clothes and apologized,
inviting him to take the seat of honor.
Lì Yìjī advised Lord Pei to attack Chénliú by surprise,
where they obtained Qín's stored grain.
Then he appointed Lì Yìjī as Lord Guǎngyě,
and Lì Shāng as a general,
leading the troops of Chénliú,
together they attacked Kāifēng,
but Kāifēng was not captured.
Westward, they fought the Qín general Yáng Xióng at Báimǎ,
and again east of Qūyù,
thoroughly defeating him.
Yáng Xióng fled to Xíngyáng,
where the Second Emperor sent an envoy to behead him as a warning.
They attacked Yǐngyáng to the south,
and massacred it.
Through Zhāng Liáng, they then seized the Hán territory of Huányuán.
At that time,
the separate general of Zhào, Sīmǎ Áng, was about to cross the river and enter the pass,
so Lord Pei attacked Píngyīn to the north,
cutting off the river crossing.
To the south,
they fought east of Luòyáng,
but the army fared poorly,
so they returned to Yángchéng,
gathered the army's horses and cavalry,
and fought the governor of Nányáng, Yǐ, east of Chōu,
defeating him.
They overran the Nányáng commandery,
and the governor of Nányáng, Yǐ, fled,
fortifying the city and defending Wǎn.
Lord Pei led his troops past it westward.
Zhāng Liáng advised:
"Although you wish to enter the pass quickly,
the Qín forces are still numerous,
and hold strategic positions.
If you do not take Wǎn now,
and Wǎn attacks from behind,
with strong Qín forces ahead,
this would be a dangerous path."
Thereupon, Lord Pei led his troops back by another route at night,
changed the flags and banners,
and at dawn,
surrounded the city of Wǎn three layers deep.
The governor of Nányáng wanted to cut his own throat.
His retainer Chén Huī said:
"It's not too late to die."
Then he climbed over the city wall to see Lord Pei,
saying:
"I have heard of your agreement,
that whoever enters Xiányáng first will be king there.
Now you are detained here at Wǎn.
Wǎn
is the capital of a large commandery,
with dozens of connected cities,
a large population,
and abundant supplies.
The officials believe that surrendering would mean certain death,
so they all firmly defend the city walls.
If you persist in attacking all day,
many soldiers will die or be wounded;
if you lead your troops away from Wǎn,
Wǎn will surely follow behind you:
ahead, you would lose the chance to fulfill the agreement on Xiányáng,
and behind, you would face the threat of a strong Wǎn.
For your sake,
it would be best to accept their surrender,
enfeoff its governor,
and have him remain in defense,
then lead his armored troops west with you.
Other cities not yet taken,
upon hearing this, will compete to open their gates and await you,
allowing you to pass through unhindered."
Lord Pei said:
"Good."
Then he made the governor of Wǎn the Marquis of Yīn,
and enfeoffed Chén Huī with a thousand households.
Leading his troops west,
there was none who did not submit.
Reaching Dànshuǐ,
Marquis Gāowǔ, Sāi, and Marquis Xiāng, Wáng Líng, surrendered at Xīlíng.
Returning to attack Húyáng,
he met Méi Xuān, a subordinate general of Fān Jūn,
and together with him,
accepted the surrender of Xī and Lì.
He sent Níng Chāng, a man of Wèi, as an envoy to Qín,
but the envoy had not yet returned.
At that time, Zhāng Hán had already surrendered with his army to Xiàng Yǔ in Zhào.
Earlier,
Xiàng Yǔ and Sòng Yì went north to rescue Zhào,
and after Xiàng Yǔ killed Sòng Yì,
he took over as supreme general,
with all generals like Qíng Bù under his command,
defeated the Qín general Wáng Lí's army,
accepted Zhāng Hán's surrender,
and all the nobles submitted to him.
After Zhào Gāo had killed the Second Emperor,
he sent someone to come,
wishing to make an agreement to divide and rule within the pass.
Lord Pei considered it a trick,
so he used Zhāng Liáng's plan,
sending Lì Shēng and Lù Jiǎ to persuade the Qín generals,
tempting them with profit,
then launching a surprise attack on Wǔguān,
and captured it.
They also fought the Qín army south of Lántián,
displaying more deceptive troops and banners,
and ordered no plundering wherever they passed,
which pleased the Qín people,
and the Qín army disintegrated,
leading to a great defeat.
They fought again north of there,
and thoroughly defeated them.
Riding on the victory,
they finally crushed them.
In the tenth month of the first year of Hàn,
Lord Pei's troops thus reached Bàshàng ahead of the other nobles.
The Qín prince, Zǐ Yīng, with a plain carriage and white horse,
a silk ribbon around his neck,
sealed the imperial seal, tally, and credentials,
and surrendered by the side of the road at Zhǐdào.
Some generals suggested executing the Qín king.
Lord Pei said:
"Initially, King Huái sent me,
precisely because I could be tolerant;
moreover, the person has already submitted and surrendered,
and to kill him now,
would be inauspicious."
So he handed the Qín king over to the officials,
and then entered Xiányáng to the west.
He wished to stay in the palace and rest,
but Fán Kuài and Zhāng Liáng advised against it,
so he sealed up the treasuries with Qín's valuable goods and财物,
and returned the army to Bàshàng.
He summoned the elders and prominent men of the various counties, saying:
"Elders, you have long suffered under the harsh laws of Qín,
where those who criticized were exterminated with their clans,
and those who talked in pairs were executed in the market.
I made an agreement with the nobles,
that whoever entered the pass first would be king there,
so I should be king within the pass.
I make a pact with you elders,
with just three laws:
murderers shall die,
those who injure others or steal shall be punished accordingly.
All other Qín laws are abolished.
All officials shall remain at their posts as before.
The reason I have come here,
is to rid you elders of harm,
not to commit violence or oppression,
so do not fear!
Moreover, the reason I have returned the army to Bàshàng,
is to wait for the other nobles to arrive and establish the regulations together."
He then sent men to accompany Qin officials on tours through the counties, towns, and villages,
to announce and instruct the people.
The Qin people were greatly pleased,
vying to bring cattle, sheep, wine, and food to offer and feast the soldiers.
Pei Gōng again declined to accept,
saying:
"The granaries have plenty of grain,
there is no shortage,
I do not wish to burden the people."
The people grew even more delighted,
fearing only that Pei Gōng would not become the King of Qin.
Someone advised Pei Gōng, saying:
"Qin is ten times wealthier than the rest of the empire,
and its terrain is strong.
Now I have heard that Zhāng Hán has surrendered to Xiàng Yǔ,
and Xiàng Yǔ has titled him the Yōng King,
to rule within the Pass.
If he comes now,
I fear you, Pei Gōng, will not be able to hold this land.
You should quickly send troops to guard Hángǔ Pass,
not allowing the armies of the other lords to enter,
and gradually recruit soldiers from within the Pass to strengthen yourself,
to resist him."
Pei Gōng approved of this plan,
and followed it.
In mid-November,
Xiàng Yǔ indeed led the armies of the lords westward,
intending to enter the Pass,
but the pass gates were closed.
Hearing that Pei Gōng had already secured the area within the Pass,
he was greatly angered,
and sent Qíng Bù and others to attack and break through Hángǔ Pass.
In mid-December,
they then reached Xì.
Pei Gōng's Left Marshal Cáo Wúshāng heard that King Xiàng was angry,
and intended to attack Pei Gōng,
so he sent someone to say to Xiàng Yǔ:
"Pei Gōng wishes to be king within the Pass,
to make Zǐ Yīng his chancellor,
and to possess all the treasures."
He hoped by this to gain a fief.
Yàfù urged Xiàng Yǔ to attack Pei Gōng.
They were feasting the soldiers,
and planned to join battle the next day.
At this time, Xiàng Yǔ had four hundred thousand troops,
claimed to be a million.
Pei Gōng had a hundred thousand troops,
claimed to be two hundred thousand,
and was no match in strength.
It happened that Xiàng Bó wished to save Zhāng Liáng's life,
and went by night to see Liáng,
who then used reason to persuade Xiàng Yǔ,
and Xiàng Yǔ desisted.
Pei Gōng, accompanied by over a hundred cavalry,
rode to Hóngmén,
to see and apologize to Xiàng Yǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"This was said by your Left Marshal Cáo Wúshāng.
Otherwise,
how would I, Jí, have come to this!"
Thanks to Fán Kuài and Zhāng Liáng,
Pei Gōng was able to extricate himself and return.
Upon returning,
he immediately executed Cáo Wúshāng.
Xiàng Yǔ then went west,
plundered and burned the Qin palaces in Xiányáng,
and wherever he passed, nothing was left undestroyed.
The Qin people were greatly disappointed,
but were fearful,
and dared not disobey.
Xiàng Yǔ sent someone to report back to King Huái.
King Huái said:
"Abide by the covenant."
Xiàng Yǔ resented that King Huái had not allowed him to go west into the Pass together with Pei Gōng,
but sent him north to rescue Zhào,
thus falling behind in the race to fulfill the covenant.
So he said:
"As for King Huái,
he was set up by my uncle Xiàng Liáng,
and has no merit or achievements;
how can he preside over the covenant!
The true pacifiers of the empire
are the various generals and I, Jí."
So he pretended to honor King Huái as the Yì Emperor,
but in reality did not follow his commands.
In the first month,
Xiàng Yǔ proclaimed himself the Overlord of Western Chǔ,
ruling over the nine commanaderies of Liáng and Chǔ,
with his capital at Péngchéng.
Breaking the covenant,
he instead established Pei Gōng as the King of Hàn,
ruling over Bā, Shǔ, and Hànzhōng,
with his capital at Nánzhèng.
He divided the area within the Pass into three parts,
establishing three Qin generals as kings:
Zhāng Hán as the Yōng King,
with his capital at Fèiqiū;
Sīmǎ Xīn as the Sài King,
with his capital at Yuèyáng;
Dǒng Yì as the Dí King,
with his capital at Gāonú.
The Chǔ general Xiáqiū Shēnyáng was made the King of Hénán,
with his capital at Luòyáng.
The Zhào general Sīmǎ Áng was made the Yīn King,
with his capital at Zhāogē.
The King of Zhào, Xiē, was moved to become King of Dài.
The Zhào chancellor Zhāng Ěr was made the Chángshān King,
with his capital at Xiāngguó.
The Dāngyáng Lord Qíng Bù was made the Jiǔjiāng King,
with his capital at Lù.
King Huái's Pillar of State Gòng Áo was made the Línjiāng King,
with his capital at Jiānglíng.
the Fān Lord Wú Ruì was made the Héngshān King,
with his capital at Zhū.
The Yān general Zāng Tú was made the Yān King,
with his capital at Jì.
The former Yān King Hán Guǎng was moved to become King of Liáodōng.
Guǎng refused,
and Zāng Tú attacked and killed him at Wúzhōng.
He enfeoffed Chéng'ān Lord Chén Yú with three counties in Héjiān,
and he resided at Nánpí.
He enfeoffed Méi Xuān with a hundred thousand households.
In the fourth month,
the armies were disbanded at the foot of the commander's standard,
and the various lords each went to their own states.
When the King of Hàn went to his state,
King Xiàng sent thirty thousand soldiers to accompany him,
and from Chǔ and among the lords, those who admired and followed him numbered tens of thousands;
they entered through Dù south into Shízhōng.
As they left, they burned and destroyed the plank roads,
to guard against the other lords sending troops to raid him,
and also to show Xiàng Yǔ that he had no intention of going east.
When they reached Nánzhèng,
many of the generals and soldiers deserted along the way and returned home,
and the soldiers all sang songs, longing to return east.
Hán Xìn advised the King of Hàn, saying:
"Xiàng Yǔ made kings of those generals who had merit,
yet you, King, alone reside in Nánzhèng,
which is like an exile.
Your officers and soldiers are all men from Shāndōng,
who day and night stand on tiptoe hoping to return;
if you use them while their edge is sharp,
you can achieve great merit.
Once the empire is settled,
everyone will seek their own peace,
and they can no longer be used.
It would be better to decide on a strategy to head east,
and contend for power over the empire."
Xiàng Yǔ,
upon leaving the Pass,
said:
"He sent someone to move the Yì Emperor. 'The emperors of ancient times
held lands
a thousand li square, and must reside upstream.'"
So he sent an envoy to move the Yì Emperor to Chēn County in Chángshā,
urging
the Yì Emperor to depart; his ministers
gradually betrayed him,
and he secretly ordered the Héngshān King
and the Línjiāng King to attack him,
and they killed the Yì Emperor south of the river.
Xiàng Yǔ bore a grudge against Tián Róng,
and set up the Qí general Tián Dū as the King of Qí.
Tián Róng was angry,
and thereupon proclaimed himself King of Qí,
killed Tián Dū, and rebelled against Chǔ;
he gave Péng Yuè a general's seal,
and ordered him to rebel in Liáng territory.
Chǔ ordered Lord Xiāo Jiǎo to attack Péng Yuè,
and Péng Yuè defeated him soundly.
Chén Yù resented that Xiàng Yǔ had not made him a king,
and ordered Xià Yuè to persuade Tián Róng,
requesting troops to attack Zhāng Ěr.
Qí gave troops to Chén Yù,
who attacked and defeated the Chángshān King Zhāng Ěr,
and Zhāng Ěr fled and returned to Hàn.
He welcomed the King of Zhào, Xiē, from Dài,
and restored him as King of Zhào.
The King of Zhào then set up Chén Yù as King of Dài.
Xiàng Yǔ was greatly angered,
and attacked Qí to the north.
In the eighth month,
the King of Hàn, adopting Hán Xìn's strategy,
returned via the old road,
and launched a surprise attack on the Yōng King, Zhāng Hán.
Hán met and attacked the Hàn forces at Chéncāng,
the Yōng troops were defeated,
and retreated;
they made a stand and fought at Hǎozhì,
were again defeated,
and fled to Fèiqiū.
The King of Hàn thus secured the territory of Yōng.
He advanced east to Xiányáng,
led his troops to besiege the King of Yōng at Fèiqiū,
and dispatched his generals to conquer and pacify Lǒngxī, Běidì, and Shàngjùn.
He ordered generals Xuē Ōu and Wáng Xī to exit Wǔguān,
and, joining with Wáng Líng's troops in Nányáng,
went to welcome the Grand Patriarch and Empress Lǚ from Pèi.
Chǔ, hearing of this,
sent troops to block them at Yángxià,
preventing their advance.
They appointed the former magistrate of Wú, Zhèng Chāng, as King of Hán,
to resist the Hàn army.
In the second year,
the King of Hàn campaigned eastward to seize territory,
and the King of Sài, Sīmǎ Xīn, the King of Dí, Dǒng Yì, and the King of Hénán, Shēn Yáng, all surrendered.
The King of Hán, Zhèng Chāng, did not submit,
so Hán Xìn was sent to attack and defeat him.
Thereupon, the commanaderies of Lǒngxī, Běidì, Shàngjùn, Wèinán, Héshàng, and Zhōngdì were established;
and outside the passes, the Hénán commandery was set up.
The Grand Commandant of Hán, Xìn, was made King of Hán.
Generals who surrendered with ten thousand men or with a commandery
were enfeoffed with ten thousand households.
The defenses along the river were repaired and maintained.
All the former parks, gardens, and ponds of Qín
were opened for people to cultivate.
In the first month,
the younger brother of the King of Yōng, Zhāng Píng, was captured.
A general amnesty for criminals was declared.
When the King of Hán exited the pass and reached Shǎn,
he comforted the elders outside the pass,
then returned.
Zhāng Ěr came for an audience,
and the King of Hán treated him generously.
In the second month,
he ordered the abolition of the Qín altars of soil and grain,
and established the Hàn altars in their place.
In the third month,
the King of Hán crossed from Línjìn,
with the King of Wèi, Bào, leading troops to follow.
They captured Hénèi,
captured the King of Yīn,
and established the Hénèi commandery.
Crossing south at Píngyīnjīn,
they reached Luòyáng.
An elder of Xīnchéng, Dǒng Gōng, intercepted and advised the King of Hán about the death of the Righteous Emperor.
The King of Hán, upon hearing this,
bared his shoulder and wept loudly.
He then held a funeral for the Righteous Emperor,
mourning for three days.
He sent messengers to announce to the various lords:
"All under heaven jointly established the Righteous Emperor,
and pledged allegiance to him.
Now Xiàng Yǔ has exiled and murdered the Righteous Emperor south of the river,
an act of great treason and immorality.
I personally have held the funeral,
and all the lords are in mourning attire.
I am mobilizing all troops within the passes,
gathering men from the three river regions,
and floating south on the Jiāng and Hàn rivers to descend,
wishing to join the kings and lords in attacking Chǔ, the killer of the Righteous Emperor."
At that time, King Xiàng was attacking Qí in the north,
and Tián Róng engaged him in battle at Chéngyáng.
Tián Róng was defeated,
fled to Píngyuán,
where the people killed him.
All of Qí surrendered to Chǔ.
Chǔ then burned their cities and walls,
and enslaved their women and children.
The people of Qí rebelled.
Tián Róng's younger brother, Tián Héng, set up Róng's son, Tián Guǎng, as King of Qí,
and the King of Qí rebelled against Chǔ at Chéngyáng.
Although Xiàng Yǔ heard that Hàn was moving east,
he was already engaged with Qí's forces,
and intended to defeat them first before attacking Hàn.
The King of Hàn, taking advantage of this, was able to compel the troops of five lords,
and thus entered Péngchéng.
Xiàng Yǔ, hearing of this,
led his troops away from Qí,
passed through Lǔ from Hǔlíng,
reached Xiāo,
and engaged Hàn in a great battle east of Péngchéng, between Língbì and the Suī River,
where he severely defeated the Hàn army,
killing many soldiers,
so that the Suī River was blocked with bodies and ceased to flow.
He then captured the King of Hàn's parents, wife, and children from Pèi,
and held them in his army as hostages.
At this time,
the various lords, seeing Chǔ's strength and Hàn's defeat,
all turned away from Hàn and returned to Chǔ.
The King of Sài, Sīmǎ Xīn, fled and joined Chǔ.
Empress Lǚ's brother, the Marquis of Zhōulǚ, commanded troops for Hàn,
stationed at Xiàyì.
The King of Hàn joined him,
gradually regrouping his soldiers,
and encamped at Dàng.
The King of Hàn then went west through Liáng territory,
reaching Yú.
He sent the receptionist Suí Hé to the place of the King of Jiǔjiāng, Yīng Bù,
saying:
"If you can make Bù raise troops in rebellion against Chǔ,
Xiàng Yǔ will surely stay to attack him.
If he is detained for several months,
my capture of all under heaven is assured."
Suí Hé went to persuade the King of Jiǔjiāng, Yīng Bù,
and Bù indeed turned against Chǔ.
Chǔ sent Lóng Qiě to attack him.
After the King of Hàn was defeated at Péngchéng and fled west,
he sent someone to find his family,
but they had also fled,
and could not be found.
After the defeat, he only managed to find Xiàohuì later,
and in the sixth month,
he was established as Crown Prince,
with a general amnesty for criminals.
The Crown Prince was ordered to guard Yuèyáng,
and the sons of the various lords who were in Guānzhōng all gathered at Yuèyáng for defense.
They diverted water to flood Fèiqiū,
Fèiqiū surrendered,
and Zhāng Hán committed suicide.
Fèiqiū was renamed Huáilǐ.
Thereupon, the officials in charge of sacrifices were ordered to offer sacrifices to heaven, earth, the four directions, the supreme deities, mountains, and rivers,
according to the seasons.
They raised troops within the passes to man the defenses.
At this time, the King of Jiǔjiāng, Yīng Bù, fought with Lóng Qiě,
but was unsuccessful,
and fled with Suí Hé to join Hàn.
The King of Hàn gradually regrouped his soldiers,
and with his generals and additional troops from Guānzhōng,
thus greatly bolstered his forces at Xíngyáng,
defeating Chǔ between Jīng and Suǒ.
In the third year,
the King of Wèi, Bào, requested leave to visit his family,
but upon arrival, he cut off the river crossings,
and rebelled in favor of Chǔ.
The King of Hàn sent Lì Shēng to persuade Bào,
but Bào would not listen.
The King of Hàn dispatched General Hán Xìn to attack,
who defeated him soundly,
and captured Bào.
Thus, the territory of Wèi was pacified,
and three commanderies were established,
named Hédōng, Tàiyuán, and Shàngdǎng.
The King of Hàn then ordered Zhāng Ěr and Hán Xìn to advance east and attack Zhào at Jǐngxíng,
where they beheaded Chén Yú and the King of Zhào, Xiē.
The following year,
Zhāng Ěr was made King of Zhào.
The King of Hàn encamped south of Xíngyáng,
building a walled roadway connecting to the river,
to transport supplies from Áocāng.
They faced off against Xiàng Yǔ for over a year.
Xiàng Yǔ repeatedly attacked and cut off the Hàn supply route,
causing the Hàn army to run short of food,
and then besieged the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn sued for peace,
offering to cede the territory west of Xíngyáng to Hàn.
King Xiàng refused.
The King of Hàn, troubled by this,
employed Chén Píng's stratagem,
giving Chén Píng forty thousand catties of gold,
to sow discord among the Chǔ ruler and his ministers.
Thereupon, Xiàng Yǔ became suspicious of Yàfù.
Yàfù at that time urged Xiàng Yǔ to press the attack on Xíngyáng,
but when he found himself under suspicion,
he grew angry,
pleaded old age,
and asked to be allowed to retire to the ranks,
but died before reaching Péngchéng.
The Hàn army, cut off from supplies,
then sent out more than two thousand women through the eastern gate at night,
clad in armor,
and Chǔ attacked from all sides.
General Jì Xìn then took the king's carriage,
pretending to be the King of Hàn,
to deceive Chǔ,
and the Chǔ soldiers all shouted "Long live,"
gathering east of the city to watch,
thus allowing the King of Hàn to escape through the western gate with several dozen cavalry.
He ordered the Imperial Secretary Zhōu Kē, Wèi Bào, and Cōng Gōng to guard Xíngyáng.
Those officers and soldiers who could not follow
all remained in the city.
Zhōu Kē and Cōng Gōng said to each other:
"A king who has rebelled
is hard to trust with defending the city."
Thereupon, they killed Wèi Bào.
When the King of Hàn left Xíngyáng and entered the pass,
he gathered troops intending to head east again.
Yuán Shēng advised the King of Hàn, saying:
"Hàn and Chǔ have been facing off at Xíngyáng for several years,
and Hàn has often been hard-pressed."
I hope Your Majesty will march out of the Wǔguān Pass,
so Xiàng Yǔ will surely lead his troops southward,
while Your Majesty fortifies the defenses,
allowing the area between Xíngyáng and Chénggāo to rest.
Send Hán Xìn and others to pacify the Zhào territory north of the Yellow River,
connecting Yān and Qí,
after which Your Majesty may return to Xíngyáng,
and it will not be too late.
In this way,
Chǔ will have to defend against many fronts,
their forces divided,
while Hàn gets to rest,
and then engaging them in battle again,
defeating Chǔ is certain."
The King of Hàn followed this plan,
leading his army between Wǎn and Yè,
and together with Qíng Bù, they recruited soldiers along the way.
When Xiàng Yǔ heard that the King of Hàn was in Wǎn,
he indeed led his troops south.
The King of Hàn fortified his positions and did not engage in battle.
At that time, Péng Yuè crossed the Suī River,
battled Xiàng Shēng and Xuē Gōng at Xiàpī,
and Péng Yuè severely defeated the Chǔ army.
Xiàng Yǔ then led his troops east to attack Péng Yuè.
The King of Hàn also led his troops north and stationed them at Chénggāo.
After Xiàng Yǔ had defeated and driven away Péng Yuè,
he heard that the King of Hàn had again stationed his army at Chénggāo,
so he led his troops back west,
captured Xíngyáng,
executed Zhōu Kē and Cōng Gōng,
and captured the King of Hán, Hán Xìn,
then besieged Chénggāo.
The King of Hàn fled,
alone with Lord Téng in a carriage, exiting Chénggāo through the Yùmén Gate,
crossed the Yellow River northward,
and galloped to stay overnight at Xiūwǔ.
Claiming to be an envoy,
he rode at dawn into the camp of Zhāng Ěr and Hán Xìn,
and seized command of their army.
He then sent Zhāng Ěr north to recruit more troops in Zhào territory,
and dispatched Hán Xìn east to attack Qí.
With Hán Xìn's army under his command,
the King of Hàn regained strength.
He led his troops to the river,
feasted the army south of Xiǎo Xiūwǔ,
intending to fight again.
The court gentleman Zhèng Zhōng then advised the King of Hàn to stop,
suggesting to build high ramparts and deep moats,
and not engage in battle.
The King of Hàn heeded his advice,
sending Lú Wǎn and Liú Jiǎ to lead twenty thousand infantry,
and several hundred cavalry,
crossing at the Báimǎ Crossing,
entering Chǔ territory,
and together with Péng Yuè, they again defeated the Chǔ army west of Yān's outer city,
thus recapturing more than ten cities in Liáng territory.
Huáiyīn (Hán Xìn) had already received orders to go east,
but had not yet crossed at Píngyuán.
The King of Hàn sent Lì Shēng to persuade the King of Qí, Tián Guǎng,
who rebelled against Chǔ,
made peace with Hàn,
and jointly attacked Xiàng Yǔ.
Hán Xìn, following Kuǎi Tōng's strategy,
launched a surprise attack and defeated Qí.
The King of Qí boiled Lì Shēng alive,
and fled east to Gāomì.
When Xiàng Yǔ heard that Hán Xìn had raised the northern army, defeated Qí and Zhào,
and was about to attack Chǔ,
he sent Lóng Jū and Zhōu Lán to attack him.
Hán Xìn engaged them in battle,
with cavalry general Guàn Yīng attacking,
severely defeating the Chǔ army,
and killing Lóng Jū.
The King of Qí, Guǎng, fled to Péng Yuè.
At this time,
Péng Yuè stationed his troops in Liáng territory,
repeatedly harassing the Chǔ army,
cutting off their food supplies.
In the fourth year,
Xiàng Yǔ said to Hǎichūn Hóu, the Grand Marshal Cáo Jiù:
"Guard Chénggāo carefully.
If Hàn challenges to battle,
be cautious and do not engage,
just prevent them from advancing eastward.
I will surely pacify Liáng territory within fifteen days,
and then rejoin you, General."
He then went to attack Chénliú, Wàihuáng, and Suīyáng,
and captured them.
Hàn indeed repeatedly challenged the Chǔ army,
but the Chǔ army did not come out,
so they sent men to insult them for five or six days,
until the Grand Marshal grew angry,
and led his troops across the Sì River.
When the soldiers were halfway across,
Hàn attacked them,
severely defeating the Chǔ army,
and seizing all of Chǔ's gold, jade, and valuables.
Grand Marshal Jiù and Chief Clerk Xīn both cut their own throats by the Sì River.
When Xiàng Yǔ reached Suīyáng,
he heard that Hǎichūn Hóu had been defeated,
so he led his troops back.
The Hàn army was just then besieging Zhōnglí Mò east of Xíngyáng,
and when Xiàng Yǔ arrived,
they all fled to fortified positions.
After Hán Xìn had defeated Qí,
he sent a messenger to say:
"Qí borders Chǔ,
my authority is light,
if I am not made acting king,
I fear I cannot pacify Qí."
The King of Hàn wanted to attack him.
Liú Hóu said:
"It would be better to enfeoff him as such,
and let him guard it himself."
So he sent Zhāng Liáng to bring the seal and appoint Hán Xìn as King of Qí.
When Xiàng Yǔ heard that Lóng Jū's army had been defeated,
he became fearful,
and sent Wǔ Shè from Xūyí to persuade Hán Xìn.
Hán Xìn did not listen.
The conflict between Chǔ and Hàn dragged on without resolution,
the able-bodied suffered from the campaigns,
and the old and weak were exhausted from transporting supplies.
The King of Hàn and Xiàng Yǔ faced each other across the Guǎngwǔ ravine and spoke.
Xiàng Yǔ wanted to challenge the King of Hàn to single combat.
The King of Hàn enumerated Xiàng Yǔ's crimes, saying:
"Initially, we both received orders from King Huái,
stating that whoever first pacified Guānzhōng would be its king,
but Xiàng Yǔ broke this promise,
and made me king in Shǔ and Hàn,
this is crime one.
Xiàng Yǔ falsely killed the Qīngzǐ champion and exalted himself,
crime two.
After Xiàng Yǔ had rescued Zhào,
he should have returned to report,
but instead he arbitrarily coerced the feudal lords' troops to enter the pass,
crime three.
King Huái agreed that upon entering Qín, there would be no violence or plunder,
but Xiàng Yǔ burned the Qín palaces,
excavated the First Emperor's tomb,
and privately seized its treasures,
crime four.
Moreover, he forcibly killed the surrendered king of Qín, Zǐyīng,
crime five.
He deceitfully buried alive two hundred thousand Qín soldiers at Xīn'ān,
while making their generals kings,
crime six.
Xiàng Yǔ enfeoffed all his generals in good lands,
but exiled the former rulers,
causing their ministers to contend and rebel,
crime seven.
Xiàng Yǔ expelled the Righteous Emperor from Péngchéng,
made it his own capital,
seized the land of the King of Hán,
and made himself king of both Liáng and Chǔ,
taking much for himself,
crime eight.
Xiàng Yǔ sent someone to secretly assassinate the Righteous Emperor south of the Yangtze,
crime nine.
To be a subject and assassinate one's sovereign,
kill those who have surrendered,
govern unjustly,
break promises made to one's lord,
is intolerable to the world,
the greatest treason and immorality,
crime ten.
I lead a righteous army with the feudal lords to punish this brutal villain,
and would have criminals and sinners strike down Xiàng Yǔ,
why should I trouble myself to engage in single combat with you!"
Xiàng Yǔ was greatly enraged,
and a hidden crossbow shot and hit the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn was wounded in the chest,
but he clutched his foot and said:
"The rogue hit my toe!"
The King of Hàn lay ill from the wound,
but Zhāng Liáng insisted that he rise and inspect the troops,
to reassure the soldiers,
and not let Chǔ take advantage over Hàn.
The King of Hàn went out to review the army,
but his illness was severe,
so he galloped into Chénggāo.
After he recovered,
he went west into the pass,
reached Yuèyáng,
comforted the elders,
held a feast,
and displayed the head of the former King of Sài, Sīmǎ Xīn, in the Yuèyáng market.
After staying four days,
he returned to the army,
stationed at Guǎngwǔ.
More troops came out from Guānzhōng.
At this time,
Péng Yuè commanded troops stationed in the land of Liáng,
harassing the Chǔ forces back and forth,
cutting off their food supplies.
Tián Héng went to join him.
Xiàng Yǔ repeatedly attacked Péng Yuè and others,
while the King of Qí, Hán Xìn, also advanced to strike Chǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ grew fearful,
so he made a pact with the King of Hàn,
dividing the empire in half,
with the land west of the Hóng Gōu belonging to Hàn,
and that to the east to Chǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ returned the King of Hàn's parents, wife, and children,
and the entire army hailed with cheers of "Long live!",
before they parted ways and departed.
Xiàng Yǔ disbanded his forces and headed east to return.
The King of Hàn intended to lead his troops west back home,
but upon the advice of Liú Hóu and Chén Píng,
he instead advanced his army to pursue Xiàng Yǔ,
halting at the south of Yáng Xià,
and arranged to meet with the King of Qí Hán Xìn and the Marquis of Jiànchéng Péng Yuè to attack the Chǔ army together.
When they reached Gù Líng,
the others did not show up.
Chǔ attacked the Hàn army,
crushing it decisively.
The King of Hàn retreated into his fortifications,
digging deep trenches to defend.
Following Zhāng Liáng's strategy,
Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè then came.
When Liú Jiǎ entered Chǔ territory,
besieging Shòu Chūn,
and the King of Hàn was defeated at Gù Líng,
he sent envoys to summon Grand Marshal Zhōu Yīn to raise the troops of Jiǔjiāng and welcome
King Wǔ,
who marched through and slaughtered Chéngfù,
joining Liú Jiǎ and the various lords of Qí and Liáng for a grand assembly at Gāi Xià.
King Wǔ Bù was established as the King of Huáinán.
In the fifth year,
Gāozǔ together with the forces of the feudal lords jointly attacked the Chǔ army,
engaging Xiàng Yǔ in a decisive battle at Gāi Xià.
The Marquis of Huáiyīn commanded three hundred thousand troops facing them head-on,
General Kǒng on the left,
General Fèi on the right,
the Emperor in the rear,
with the Marquis of Jiàng and General Chái behind the Emperor.
Xiàng Yǔ's troops numbered about a hundred thousand.
The Marquis of Huáiyīn engaged first,
but it went unfavorably,
and he retreated.
Generals Kǒng and Fèi then launched an attack,
putting the Chǔ forces at a disadvantage,
and the Marquis of Huáiyīn took advantage to strike again,
inflicting a major defeat at Gāi Xià.
Xiàng Yǔ's soldiers heard the Hàn army singing Chǔ songs,
thinking that Hàn had taken all of Chǔ's land,
so Xiàng Yǔ was defeated and fled,
leading to a great rout of his army.
He sent cavalry general Guàn Yīng to pursue and kill Xiàng Yǔ at Dōng Chéng,
beheading eighty thousand,
and thus pacified the land of Chǔ.
Lǔ held out firmly for Chǔ and would not surrender.
The King of Hàn led the feudal lords' troops north,
showed the elders of Lǔ the head of Xiàng Yǔ,
and only then did Lǔ surrender.
Then, under the title of the Duke of Lǔ, Xiàng Yǔ was buried at Gǔ Chéng.
Returning to Dìng Táo,
he rode swiftly into the camp of the King of Qí,
and seized his army.
In the first month,
the feudal lords, generals, and ministers together requested that the King of Hàn be honored as Emperor.
The King of Hàn said:
"I have heard that the title of Emperor is for the worthy;
empty words and vain talk
are not what I uphold,
I dare not assume the imperial throne."
The officials all said:
"Your Majesty rose from humble origins,
punished the violent and rebellious,
pacified the four seas,
and those with merit were enfeoffed with land as kings and marquises.
If Your Majesty does not assume the honorable title,
all will be doubtful and distrustful.
We insist on this with our lives."
The King of Hàn declined three times,
but having no alternative,
said:
"If you gentlemen all deem it appropriate,
then let it benefit the state."
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
he ascended the imperial throne north of the Fàn Shuǐ.
The Emperor said that Emperor Yì had no heir.
The King of Qí, Hán Xìn, being familiar with Chǔ customs,
was transferred to be King of Chǔ,
with his capital at Xià Pī.
The Marquis of Jiànchéng, Péng Yuè, was established as King of Liáng,
with his capital at Dìng Táo.
The former King of Hán, Xìn, remained King of Hán, with his capital at Yáng Zhái.
The King of Héngshān, Wú Ruì, was transferred to be King of Chángshā,
with his capital at Lín Xiāng.
Méi Xuān, a general under the Lord of Pó, had rendered service,
having followed into Wǔ Guān,
so the Emperor showed favor to the Lord of Pó.
The King of Huáinán, Bù,
the King of Yān, Zāng Tú, and the King of Zhào, Áo, all remained as before.
The empire was greatly settled.
Gāozǔ made Luòyáng his capital,
and all the feudal lords submitted as subjects.
The former King of Línjiāng, Huān, had rebelled against Hàn for Xiàng Yǔ,
so he ordered Lú Wǎn and Liú Jiǎ to besiege him,
but they could not take it.
After several months, he surrendered,
and was executed at Luòyáng.
In the fifth month,
the troops were all disbanded and returned home.
The sons of feudal lords in Guānzhōng were exempted from taxes and corvée for twelve years,
those who returned home for six years,
and were provided with food for one year.
Gāozǔ held a banquet at the Southern Palace in Luòyáng.
Gāozǔ said:
"Marquises and generals, do not dare hide from me,
speak all the truth.
How did I gain the empire?
How did the Xiàng clan lose the empire?"
Gāo Qǐ and Wáng Líng replied:
"Your Majesty is arrogant and insults others,
while Xiàng Yǔ is benevolent and loves people.
However, when Your Majesty sends men to attack cities and seize lands,
you award them what they capture,
sharing benefits with all under heaven.
Xiàng Yǔ was jealous of the worthy and envious of the capable,
harming those with achievements,
suspecting the virtuous,
winning battles but not rewarding merits,
gaining lands but not sharing the profits,
this is why he lost the empire."
Gāozǔ said:
"You know one aspect,
but not the other.
In devising strategies within the tent,
and securing victory a thousand miles away,
I am not as good as Zǐfáng.
In governing the state,
comforting the people,
ensuring supply provisions,
and keeping the grain routes open,
I am not as good as Xiāo Hé.
In leading a million-strong army,
fighting to win every battle,
attacking to take every objective,
I am not as good as Hán Xìn.
These three men
are all outstanding talents,
and I was able to employ them,
this is how I gained the empire.
Xiàng Yǔ had one Fàn Zēng but could not use him,
that is why he was captured by me."
Gāozǔ initially wanted to make Luòyáng his permanent capital,
but the man from Qí, Liú Jìng, advised him,
and Liú Hóu urged the Emperor to move the capital to Guānzhōng,
so Gāozǔ set out that very day,
and established the capital in Guānzhōng.
In the sixth month,
a great amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
In the tenth month,
the King of Yān, Zāng Tú, rebelled,
capturing the land of Dài.
Gāozǔ personally led troops to attack him,
and captured the King of Yān, Zāng Tú.
He then appointed Grand Marshal Lú Wǎn as King of Yān.
He sent Chancellor Kuài to lead troops to attack Dài.
That autumn,
Lì Jī rebelled,
Gāozǔ personally led troops to attack him,
and Lì Jī fled.
Lì Jī
was a general under the Xiàng clan.
When the Xiàng clan was defeated,
Lì Jī became the Magistrate of Chén,
did not follow Xiàng Yǔ,
but fled and surrendered to Gāozǔ,
who enfeoffed him as a marquis in Yǐng Chuān.
When Gāozǔ arrived in Luòyáng,
he summoned all those on the register of full marquises,
and Lì Jī, fearing,
rebelled.
In the sixth year,
Gāozǔ paid respects to Tàigōng every five days,
observing the rituals of family members, father and son.
The steward of Tàigōng advised Tàigōng, saying:
"There are not two suns in the sky,
nor two kings over the land.
Now Gāozǔ, though your son,
is the ruler of men;
Tàigōng, though his father,
is a subject.
How can we let the ruler bow to a subject!
If this continues,
then his authority and dignity will not be upheld."
Later, when Gāozǔ came to pay his respects,
Tàigōng, holding a broom,
welcomed him at the gate, walking backward.
Gāozǔ was greatly startled,
dismounted and supported Tàigōng.
Tàigōng said:
"The Emperor,
is the ruler of men,
how can you, because of me, disrupt the laws of the realm!"
Thereupon, Gāozǔ honored Tàigōng as Tàishàng Huáng.
He thought well of the steward's words,
and bestowed five hundred catties of gold.
In the twelfth month,
someone reported a suspicious matter, accusing the King of Chǔ, Xìn, of plotting rebellion.
The Emperor asked his attendants,
and they all vied to attack him.
Adopting Chén Píng's strategy,
he pretended to tour Yúnmèng,
gathering the feudal lords at Chén.
When the King of Chǔ, Xìn, came to welcome him,
he seized him on the spot.
That day,
a great amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
Tián Kěn came to congratulate him,
and took the opportunity to advise Gāozǔ, saying:
"Your Majesty has captured Hán Xìn,
and also governs Qínzhōng.
Qín,
is a country of strategic advantage,
girded by the perils of rivers and mountains,
separated by a thousand lǐ,
with a million halberd-bearing troops,
Qín gains a hundredfold strength from two.
