I sustain the palace of the first emperor,
always fearing its disgrace,
why need a terrace!"
The emperor often wore coarse clothes,
even for the beloved Shèn Fūrén,
he ordered that clothes should not trail on the ground,
curtains and canopies should not be embroidered,
to display simplicity,
setting an example for the world.
The provisions for Bàlíng were all pottery,
prohibited the use of gold, silver, copper, and tin as decorations,
no tomb building,
aimed for frugality,
not to burden the people.
The King of Nányuè, Wèi Tuó, proclaimed himself Emperor of Wu,
yet the emperor summoned and honored Wèi Tuó’s brothers,
repaying them with virtue,
Tuó then renounced the title of Emperor and submitted.
Made peace with the Xiongnu,
when the Xiongnu broke the treaty to raid,
he ordered border defenses,
refrained from deploying troops deep,
to avoid troubling the people.
The King of Wú feigned illness to avoid the court,
bestowed him with a staff.
Other ministers like Yuán Àng spoke candidly in praise,
but still supported him.
Ministers like Zhāng Wǔ accepted bribes of gold and money,
when discovered, the emperor then bestowed gold and money from the imperial treasury,
to shame them,
without sending them to the judiciary.
Focused on governing through virtue,
thus the entire realm flourished and prospered,
with advancements in propriety.
Seven years later, in the sixth lunar month on the day jǐhài,
the Emperor passed away at Weiyang Palace.
His final edict stated:
"I have heard that all things in the world that are born,
none escape death.
Death is the principle of Heaven and Earth,
the natural way of things,
so why should there be excessive mourning?
In these times,
the world generally celebrates life and fears death,
extravagant burials ruin families,
long mourning harms the living,
I do not approve.
Since I am without virtue,
unable to assist the people;
now that I die,
yet you allow prolonged mourning,
disrupting the cycle of seasons,
grieving the fathers and sons of men,
hurting the ambitions of the young and old,
diminishing their sustenance,
and severing the sacrifices to spirits,
thus increasing my lack of virtue,
what will the world think!
I have maintained the ancestral temple,
entrusted with the position of sovereign over all under Heaven for over twenty years.
Relying on the spirits of Heaven and Earth,
and the blessings of the state,
within the borders there is peace,
there is no warfare or strife.
As I am not astute,
I constantly fear transgressions,

I am not insightful,

Shàojūn, formerly the Marquis of Shēnzé, was entrusted with methods.

People heard of his ability to control objects and not die,

People believed he accumulated wealth without running businesses,

The unknown origin of his abilities fueled greater belief,

Shàojūn capitalized on the affinity for these methods,

Once he drank with Wǔ’ān Marquis,

Recognizing the place,
the gathering was completely astonished.
When Shàojūn met the emperor,

"This vessel dates from the tenth year of Duke Huán of Qí,

The entire palace was amazed,

Shàojūn advised the emperor:

Huángdì did this.
I once traveled to the sea,

Ān Qīshēng is an immortal,

Consequently, the emperor began to personally sacrifice to the hearth,

After some time,
Lǐ Shàojūn fell ill and died.

The next year,

After this, structures like the Bóliáng Terrace, bronze pillars, and immortal palms for receiving dew were built.
The year after Wénchéng's death,

"The Son of Heaven need not worry about his illness.

A great amnesty was declared,

The most revered among the divine lords was Tàiyī,

They were not visible,

They came and went intermittently,

They resided within curtained chambers.
Sometimes they spoke by day,

The emperor performed purification rites,

A shaman acted as host,

Their desires were conveyed and acted upon.
Additionally, the Shòugōng and Běigōng were set up,

What the divine lord said,

Their utterances
were common knowledge in the world,
nothing extraordinary,
yet the Son of Heaven alone delighted in them.
The affairs were secret,
unknown to the world.

The following winter,
the Son of Heaven performed suburban sacrifices at Yōng,
and deliberated:
"Now I personally sacrifice to the Supreme Deity in the suburbs,
but the Earth Deity has no sacrifice,
which is ritually incomplete."
The officials, along with Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān and ritual official Kuān Shū, discussed:
"For heaven and earth, sacrificial animals should have small, firm horns.
Now that Your Majesty personally sacrifices to the Earth Deity,
it should be at a circular mound in a marsh, with five altars,
each with a yellow calf and full sacrificial offerings,
buried after the ceremony,
with attendants wearing yellow robes."
The Son of Heaven then went east,
and first established the Earth Deity shrine on the heights of Fényīn,
as Kuān Shū and others advised.
He personally gazed and bowed,
as in the rites to the Supreme Deity.
After the ceremony,
he proceeded to Xíngyáng and then returned.
Passing through Luòyáng,
he issued an edict:
"The Three Dynasties are remote and severed,
too distant to preserve.
Let thirty lǐ of land be granted to a descendant of the Zhōu as the Lord of Zhōu Zǐnán,
to continue the sacrifices to the former kings."
That year,
the Son of Heaven began touring the commanderies and counties,
gradually approaching Tàishān.
That spring,
Marquis Lèchéng submitted a memorial about Luán Dà.
Luán Dà,
a retainer in Jiāodōng,
had once studied under the same master as General Wénchéng,
and later became a court official for the King of Jiāodōng.
The elder sister of Marquis Lèchéng was the queen of King Kāng,
but had no son.
When King Kāng died,
a son by another consort ascended the throne.
The former queen, involved in immoral conduct,
was at odds with the new king,
and they endangered each other through legal means.
Hearing of Wénchéng's death,
she sought to ingratiate herself with the emperor,
so she sent Luán Dà through Marquis Lèchéng to seek an audience and present his methods.
The Son of Heaven, having executed Wénchéng,
later regretted his early death,
lamenting that his methods were not fully obtained.
Upon meeting Luán Dà,
he was greatly pleased.
Luán Dà was tall and handsome,
eloquent in strategies,
bold in making grand claims,
and unwavering in his demeanor.
He declared:
"I have traveled across the seas,
and seen Ānqī, Xiànmén, and others.
But they considered me lowly,
and did not trust me.
They also regarded King Kāng as merely a feudal lord,
unworthy of receiving their methods.
I repeatedly advised King Kāng,
but he did not heed my words."
My teacher said:
'Gold can be produced,
the river's breach can be stopped,
the elixir of immortality can be obtained,
and immortals can be summoned.'
I fear that if I end up like Wénchéng,
then all alchemists will cover their mouths,
how would they dare speak of formulas!"
The Emperor said:
"Wénchéng died from eating horse liver.
If you can truly cultivate his methods,
why would I be sparing!"
Luàn Dà said:
"My teacher does not seek people,
rather people seek him.
If Your Majesty truly wishes to summon him,
then honor his messenger,
ensure he has family connections,
treat him with guest rituals,
do not demean him,
have him wear his credential seals,
only then can he communicate with the divine beings.
The divine beings may still be willing or unwilling.
Honor his messenger to the utmost,
then he can be summoned."
Thereupon the Emperor had him first demonstrate minor formulas,
battling flags,
where the flags spontaneously struck each other.
At that time the Emperor was worried about the river's breach,
and the gold production was unsuccessful,
so he appointed Luàn Dà as General of the Five Benefits.
After over a month,
he obtained four gold seals,
wearing the seals of General of Celestial Scholars, General of Terrestrial Scholars, General of Great Penetration, and General of Heavenly Way.
An imperial decree to the Censor stated:
"In ancient times Yǔ dredged the Nine Rivers,
and opened the Four Waterways.
Recently the river overflowed the highlands,
and dyke corvée never ceased.
I have overseen the empire for twenty-eight years,
as if Heaven sent me a scholar who greatly penetrates it.
The Qián hexagram refers to the 'flying dragon',
'the wild goose gradually reaches the riverbank',
meaning I nearly match this.
Let two thousand households be enfeoffed to General of Terrestrial Scholars Luàn Dà as Marquis of Lètōng."
He was granted a marquis's first-class residence,
and a thousand servants.
Carriages, horses, canopies, tents and utensils from the imperial equipage were used to fill his household.
Moreover, he was given the Eldest Princess of Wèi as wife,
with ten thousand jin of gold as dowry,
and her city was renamed Dānglì Princess.
The Son of Heaven personally visited the residence of the Five Benefits General.
Envoys delivering provisions and inquiries
formed an unbroken line on the road.
From the Grand Princess down to generals and ministers,
all set up banquets at his home,
presenting gifts to him.
Thereupon the Son of Heaven also carved a jade seal reading "General of Heavenly Way",
and had an envoy wear feathered robes,
stand on white reeds at night,
while General of the Five Benefits also wore feathered robes,
standing on white reeds to receive the seal,
to show he was not treated as a subject.
For one wearing "Heavenly Way"
would guide the Son of Heaven to the heavenly gods.
Thereupon the Five Benefits General often performed nocturnal rituals at home,
wishing to summon deities.
Before the deities arrived, hundreds of spirits gathered,
yet he could somewhat command them.
Later he packed his belongings and traveled,
eastward entering the sea,
seeking his teacher, it is said.
Within months of Luàn Dà's appearance,
wearing six seals,
his prestige shook the empire,
and along the coasts between Yān and Qí,
none failed to clutch their wrists claiming to possess secret recipes,
able to perform divine immortality.
That summer in the sixth month,
the shaman Jǐn of Fényīn, while conducting a folk sacrifice near the shrine of Hòutǔ at Wèi Shuí,
saw the ground shaped like a hook,
and upon digging discovered a ding.
This ding was remarkably different from ordinary dings,
with patterned engravings but no inscription,
finding it strange,
he reported it to officials.
The officials informed Governor Shèng of Hédōng,
and Shèng reported it upward.
The Son of Heaven sent envoys to verify that Shaman Jǐn's discovery involved no fraud,
then performed a ritual sacrifice,
welcoming the ding to Gānquán,
accompanying it on the journey,
and presenting it above.
Reaching Zhōngshān,
the weather was warm and calm,
with a yellow cloud canopy above.
A roe deer passed by,
the Emperor shot it himself,
and used it for sacrifice.
Arriving at Cháng'ān,
all dukes, ministers and senior officials proposed honoring the precious ding.
The Son of Heaven said:
"Lately the river overflowed,
harvests failed for several years,
so I toured and sacrificed to Hòutǔ,
praying to grow grain for the common people.
This year's abundant harvest has not yet been repaid.
Why then has this ding appeared?"
The officials all replied:
"We hear that in ancient times the Great Emperor created one divine ding,
representing unity,
where all things between heaven and earth converge.
Huángdì made three precious dings,
symbolizing heaven, earth and man.
Yǔ collected metal from the nine provinces,
casting nine dings,
all used to cook offerings for the Supreme Deity and spirits.
They emerge when encountering sages,
passing to Xià and Shāng.
When Zhōu's virtue declined,
the altar of Sòng perished,
the dings sank hidden and disappeared.
The Ode says: 'From the hall to the foundation,
from the sheep to the oxen;
the great ding and the small ding,
without error without pride,
blessing for long life.'
Now the ding has come to Gānquán,
shining bright, transforming like a dragon,
receiving endless blessings.
Combined with this, at Zhōngshān,
yellow and white clouds descended as canopies,
the beast served as an omen,
with road bows and carriage arrows,
gathered and captured below the altar,
repaid in grand sacrificial feast.
Only one who receives the mandate and becomes emperor understands its meaning and matches its virtue.
The ding should be presented at the ancestral temple,
stored in the imperial court,
to correspond with the clear response."
The decree said:
"Approved."
Those who entered the sea seeking Pénglái
said Pénglái was not far,
but they couldn't reach it,
likely because they didn't see its aura.
The Emperor then sent aura-observing assistants to watch for its aura.
That autumn,
the Emperor visited Yōng,
and was to perform the suburban sacrifice.
Someone said, "The Five Emperors
are assistants of Tàiyī,
we should establish Tàiyī and have the Emperor personally perform the suburban sacrifice to him."
The Emperor hesitated, undecided.
Gōngsūn Qīng of Qí said:
"This year we obtained the precious ding,
and this winter, on the xīn-sì day, the new moon morning is the winter solstice,
the same as in Huángdì's time."
Qīng had a bamboo text saying:
"Huángdì obtained the precious ding at Wǎnqú,
and asked Guǐ Yúqū.
Qū replied:
'You obtained the precious ding and divine tallies,
this year jǐ-yǒu, new moon morning winter solstice,
obtained heaven's cycle,
ending and beginning again.'
Thereupon Huángdì welcomed the sun and推算 tallies,
afterwards every twenty years obtaining new moon morning winter solstice,
twenty推 total,
three hundred eighty years,
Huángdì ascended to heaven as an immortal."
Qīng sought to present this through Suǒ Zhōng.
Suǒ Zhōng considered the text unorthodox,
suspected it was fabricated,
and declined, saying:
"The matter of the precious ding is already settled,
what use is this!"
Qīng then presented it through a favorite.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
summoned and questioned Qīng.
He replied:
"I received this book from Shēn Gōng,
Shēn Gōng has died."
The Emperor said:
"Who is Shēn Gōng?"
Qīng said:
"Shēn Gōng
was a man of Qí.
He associated with Ānqī Shēng,
received Huángdì's teachings,
no books,
only this ding book."
It was said: 'The rise of the Hàn dynasty coincides with the era of the Yellow Emperor.
The sage of Hàn shall emerge among the grandsons and great-grandsons of Emperor Gāozǔ.
When the precious tripod appears, it shall connect with divine forces,
leading to the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
Seventy-two kings have performed the Fēng and Shàn rituals,
but only the Yellow Emperor succeeded in ascending Mount Tài to conduct the Fēng sacrifice.'
Shēngōng stated:
'The Hàn sovereign should also perform the Fēng sacrifice,
for by doing so, he can achieve immortality and ascend to heaven.
During the Yellow Emperor's time, there were ten thousand feudal lords,
with seven thousand territories dedicated to spiritual deities.
Of the eight famous mountains under heaven,
three lie in barbarian lands,
and five are in the Central Plains.
These five—Huà Shān, Shǒu Shān, Tài Shì, Tài Shān, and Dōng Lái—
were places the Yellow Emperor frequently roamed,
communing with deities.
The Yellow Emperor waged wars while learning the arts of immortality.
Fearing that the people might oppose his path,
he executed those who denied the spirits.
After over a century, he finally achieved communion with the divine.
The Yellow Emperor performed the suburban sacrifice to the Supreme Deity at Yōng,
residing there for three months.
Guǐ Yúqū, also known as Dà Hóng,
was buried at Yōng after his death,
hence the name Hóng Zhǒng (Great Mound).
Thereafter, the Yellow Emperor received myriad spirits at the Míng Tíng.
The Míng Tíng
refers to Gān Quán.
The so-called Hán Mén
is the entrance to the valley.
The Yellow Emperor mined copper from Shǒu Shān,
casting a tripod at the foot of Jīng Shān.
Once the tripod was completed,
a dragon descended with its beard hanging down to welcome the Yellow Emperor.
The Yellow Emperor mounted it,
followed by over seventy of his ministers and consorts who climbed onto the dragon,
which then ascended skyward.
Minor officials who could not board
grabbed the dragon's beard,
but it tore off,
causing them to fall with the Yellow Emperor's bow.
The people, gazing up as the Yellow Emperor rose to heaven,
clung to his bow and the dragon's beard, wailing.
Thus, later generations named the place Dǐng Hú (Tripod Lake),
and the bow was called Wū Háo.'
Upon hearing this, the Son of Heaven exclaimed:
'Alas!
If I could truly become like the Yellow Emperor,
I would regard leaving my wife and children as shedding worn sandals.'
He then appointed the scholar as a court gentleman,
sending him east to await divine signs at Tài Shì.
The emperor subsequently performed the suburban sacrifice at Yōng,
journeyed to Lǒng Xī,
ascended Kōng Tóng in the west,
and visited Gān Quán.
He ordered ritual officials like Kuān Shū to prepare the altar for the Tài Yī sacrifice,
modeled after Bó Jì's Tài Yī altar,
with three tiers.
The altars for the Five Emperors encircled it below,
each aligned with its respective direction,
the Yellow Emperor's to the southwest,
with eight paths cleared for spirits.
The offerings for Tài Yī
mirrored those at Yōng's altars,
supplemented with sweet wine, dates, dried meat, and the like,
and a yak was slaughtered for the sacrificial vessels.
The Five Emperors received only vessels and sweet wine.
The surrounding areas
served for offerings to the retinue of deities and the Northern Dipper.
After the sacrifices,
the leftover offerings were burned.
The oxen were white,
with deer placed inside them,
and pigs inside the deer,
all soaked in water.
A ox was used for sun sacrifices,
and a sheep or pig for moon sacrifices.
The priests of Tài Yī wore purple and embroidered robes.
The Five Emperors' robes matched their colors,
red for the sun,
white for the moon.
On the first day of the eleventh month, at dawn on the winter solstice,
in the dim light,
the Son of Heaven began the suburban worship of Tài Yī.
He bowed to the rising sun in the morning,
and to the moon in the evening,
then saluted;
his audience with Tài Yī followed the rites of Yōng.
The prayer recited:
'Heaven has bestowed the precious tripod and divine counsel upon the emperor,
with cycles upon cycles,
endings and new beginnings,
and the emperor reverently pays homage.'
He wore yellow robes above.
Fires lined the altar during the sacrifice,
with cooking utensils alongside.
Officials reported, 'There was light above the altar.'
Ministers stated, 'When the emperor first suburbanly worshipped Tài Yī at Yún Yáng,
officials presented jade discs and fine offerings.
That night, a beautiful glow appeared,
and by day,
a yellow aura rose to touch the sky.'
The Grand Historian and ritual officials like Kuān Shū said:
'Such divine blessings,
bringing fortune and omens,
warrant the establishment of a Tài Zhì altar here to manifest the response.
Let the Grand Invocator oversee it,
with sacrifices in autumn and at year's end.
The Son of Heaven shall perform the suburban worship every three years.'
That autumn,
to campaign against Nán Yuè,
prayers were offered to Tài Yī,
using a male vitex branch to paint banners with the sun, moon, Northern Dipper, and ascending dragon,
symbolizing the three stars of Tiān Yī,
as Tài Yī's vanguard,
named the 'Numinous Banner.'
For military prayers,
the Grand Historian would hold it toward the target kingdom.
Meanwhile, General Wǔ Lì dared not venture to sea,
instead going to sacrifice at Tài Shān.
The emperor sent spies to follow and verify,
finding nothing.
Wǔ Lì falsely claimed to have seen his master,
and when his methods were exhausted,
most proved untrue.
The emperor then executed Wǔ Lì.
That winter,
Gōngsūn Qīng awaited spirits in Hé Nán,
sighting immortal footprints on the walls of Gōu Shì City,
and an object like a pheasant,
moving back and forth atop the walls.
The Son of Heaven personally visited Gōu Shì City to inspect the traces.
He asked Qīng:
'Are you not imitating Wén Chéng and Wǔ Lì?'
Qīng replied:
'Immortals do not seek out rulers;
rulers seek them.
Unless the path is given some leeway,
the spirits will not come.
Matters of the divine
may seem absurd and far-fetched,
yet perseverance over years can summon them.'
Thereupon, commanderies and states cleared roads,
repairing palaces, towers, and shrines at famous mountains,
in anticipation of the imperial visit.
That year,
after the conquest of Nán Yuè,
the emperor's favorite courtier Lǐ Yánnián gained audience for his musical talents.
Pleased,
the emperor consulted his ministers, saying:
'Even folk sacrifices have drumming and dance music;
should our suburban rites lack it,
is that fitting?'
The ministers replied:
'In ancient times, sacrifices to heaven and earth included music,
allowing reverence to the deities.'
Some said:
'The Tài Dì had Sù Nǚ play a fifty-string zither,
but its melancholy
moved him to ban it, unsuccessfully,
so he split it into a twenty-five-string zither.'
Thus, after pacifying Nán Yuè,
during sacrifices to Tài Yī and Hòu Tǔ,
music and dance were introduced,
with more singers recruited,
and the twenty-five-string zither and konghou began from this.
The following winter,
the emperor proposed:
'In antiquity, troops were first mustered and disbanded,
before the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.'
He then toured north to Shuò Fāng,
marshaling over a hundred thousand troops,
and on return, sacrificed at the Yellow Emperor's tomb at Qiáo Shān,
disbanding the army at Xū Rú.
The emperor said:
'I heard the Yellow Emperor never died;
why is there a tomb?'
Someone answered:
'The Yellow Emperor achieved immortality and ascended to heaven;
his ministers buried his clothes and cap.'
Upon reaching Gān Quán,
in preparation for the rites at Tài Shān,
he first performed a lei sacrifice to Tài Yī.
Since obtaining the precious tripod,
the emperor had deliberated with ministers and scholars on the Fēng and Shàn.
These rituals were rare and long discontinued,
with their exact ceremonies unknown,
so the Confucians compiled elements from the Fēng and Shàn sections of the Shàng Shū,
Zhōu Guān, and Wáng Zhì regarding the wàng sacrifice and ox slaughter.
Dīng Gōng of Qí, over ninety years old, said:
"Fēng sacrifice
is about attaining the name of immortality.
The Qín emperor failed to perform the Fēng sacrifice.
If Your Majesty insists on ascending,
once you ascend slightly without encountering wind or rain,
you may then proceed to perform the Fēng sacrifice."
The emperor then ordered the Confucian scholars to practice shooting oxen
and draft the ceremonial procedures for the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
After several years,
the time for execution approached.
Having heard the words of Gōngsūn Qīng and the fāngshì,
that Huángdì and earlier rulers performed Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
all encountering strange phenomena and communicating with spirits,
the emperor wished to emulate Huángdì by attempting to connect with immortals and Pénglái scholars,
to surpass worldly virtue and compare to the Nine Sovereigns,
while somewhat adopting Confucian methods to embellish it.
The Confucian scholars were unable to clarify the matters of Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
and were further constrained by the ancient texts of the Shī and Shū, not daring to improvise.
When the emperor showed them the sacrificial vessels for the Fēng ceremony,
some scholars said they "did not match antiquity,"
Xú Yǎn also said "the ceremonial performances of the Tàicháng scholars are not as good as those of Lǔ,"
and Zhōu Bà was assigned to plan the Fēng sacrifice matters.
Thus, the emperor dismissed Yǎn and Bà,
discharging all the Confucian scholars from service.
In the third month,
he traveled east to Gōushì,
paying ceremonial respects at the Tài Shì peak of Mount Zhōngyuè.
Attendants below the mountain heard what seemed like cries
of "wànsuì" (long live).
When asked above,
those above did not speak;
when asked below,
those below did not speak.
Thus, he enfeoffed three hundred households to maintain sacrifices at Tài Shì,
naming it the district of Chónggāo.
Ascending east to Mount Tàishān,
where the grass and trees had not yet sprouted leaves,
he ordered stones to be carried up and erected at the summit of Mount Tàishān.
The emperor then toured eastward along the coast,
performing ceremonies to worship the Eight Deities.
People from Qí submitted tens of thousands of memorials about spirits, strange phenomena, and miraculous recipes,
but none proved effective.
He then increased the number of ships,
sending several thousand people who spoke of divine mountains in the sea to seek immortals from Pénglái.
Gōngsūn Qīng, holding the ceremonial staff, often went ahead to scout famous mountains,
reaching Dōnglái,
where he claimed to have seen a man at night,
several zhàng tall,
who disappeared when approached,
leaving very large footprints,
resembling those of birds or beasts.
Some ministers reported seeing an old man leading a dog,
saying "I wish to see the great lord,"
then suddenly vanishing.
Having seen the large footprints,
the emperor was initially skeptical,
but when ministers mentioned the old man,
he became convinced it was an immortal.
He lingered by the sea,
sending thousands of fāngshì in relay carriages and special envoys to seek immortals.
In the fourth month,
he returned to Fènggāo.
The emperor considered that the Confucian scholars and fāngshì all had different views on the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
which were unorthodox,
and difficult to implement.
The Son of Heaven went to Liángfù,
to ceremonially worship the Earth Deity.
On the yǐmǎo day,
he ordered Confucian court attendants dressed in ceremonial caps and sashes
to perform the ox-shooting ritual.
The Fēng sacrifice was performed east of Mount Tàishān,
following the ceremony for Tàiyī.
The Fēng altar was twelve chǐ wide,
nine chǐ high,
beneath which was a jade tablet with inscriptions,
the contents secret.
After the ceremony,
the Son of Heaven alone with the court attendant Fèngchē Zǐhóu ascended Mount Tàishān,
performing another Fēng sacrifice.
These matters were kept confidential.
The next day,
they descended via the northern path.
On the bǐngchén day,
the Shàn sacrifice was performed at Sùrán Mountain northeast of Mount Tàishān's base,
following the ceremony for Hòutǔ.
The Son of Heaven personally paid respects,
wearing yellow robes and with full musical accompaniment.
A three-ribbed grass from the Jiāng-Huái region was used as the divine mat.
The five-colored earth was added to the Fēng sacrifice.
Rare animals, flying birds, white pheasants, and other creatures from distant lands
were added to the sacrifices.
Rhinoceroses, yaks, elephants, and such were not used.
All proceeded to Mount Tàishān before departing.
During the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
there seemed to be light at night,
and white clouds rose from the Fēng altar by day.
The Son of Heaven returned from the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
sat in the Míngtáng hall,
and the ministers took turns offering congratulations.
He then issued an edict to the Yùshǐ:
"I, with my insignificant person, have received the supreme honor,
and am cautious, fearing I am not worthy.
My virtue is meager,
and I am not well-versed in rites and music."
Cultivating sacrifices to Tàiyī,
there seemed to be auspicious light,
vaguely visible,
and I was awed by strange phenomena,
wishing to stop but not daring,
so I ascended to perform the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tàishān,
proceeded to Liángfù,
and then performed the Shàn sacrifice at Sùrán.
Renewing myself,
I joyfully begin anew with the officials,
granting one ox and ten dàn of wine per hundred households,
and two bolts of cloth each to those over eighty, orphans, and widows.
Exempting Bó, Fènggāo, Shéqiū, and Lìchéng
from this year's taxes.
Pardoning the empire,
as in the yǐmǎo pardon edict.
No forced labor in the areas I passed through.
Matters occurring over two years ago
shall not be prosecuted."
He also issued an edict:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven toured every five years,
performing ceremonies at Mount Tàishān,
and the feudal lords had lodging grounds.
Let the feudal lords each build residences at the foot of Mount Tàishān."
Having performed the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices at Mount Tàishān
without encountering wind, rain, or disasters,
and the fāngshì further claiming that the divine mountains like Pénglái might be attainable,
the emperor became hopeful of encountering them,
so he went east again to gaze over the sea,
hoping to find Pénglái.
Fèngchē Zǐhóu suddenly fell ill
and died in one day.
The emperor then departed,
traveling along the coast,
north to Jiéshí,
touring from Liáoxī,
along the northern border to Jiǔyuán.
In the fifth month,
he returned to Gānquán.
The officials stated that since the precious dǐng appeared during the Yuándǐng era,
this year should be the first year of Yuánfēng.
That autumn,
a comet appeared in Dōngjǐng.
Over ten days later,
a comet appeared in Sāntái.
The cloud observer Wáng Shuò said:
"I alone saw a star emerge like a gourd,
remaining for about a meal's time before disappearing."
The officials said:
"Your Majesty established the Hàn dynasty's Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
and Heaven rewards with this virtuous star."
The following winter,
he performed the suburban sacrifice to the Five Deities at Yōng,
and upon returning,
offered prayers and sacrifices to Tàiyī.
The prayer of offering said:
"The virtuous star shines expansively,
a sign of great auspiciousness.
The star of longevity appears again,
radiant and bright.
The faithful star clearly manifests,
the emperor reverently offers this sacrifice to Tàiyī."
That spring,
Gōngsūn Qīng claimed to have seen a divine man at Dōnglái Mountain,
who seemed to say 'I wish to see the Son of Heaven.'
The Son of Heaven then went to Gōushì City,
appointing Qīng as Zhōngdàfū.
He proceeded to Dōnglái,
staying for several days,
but saw nothing,
except large footprints.
He again sent thousands of fāngshì to seek spirits, strange phenomena, and gather magical mushrooms and herbs.
That year, there was a drought.
Since the emperor had traveled without clear purpose,
he prayed at Wànlǐshā,
and passed by to sacrifice at Mount Tàishān.
Returning to Hùzǐ,
he personally supervised the blocking of the breached Yellow River,
stayed for two days,
offered submerged sacrifices, and left.
He sent two high officials with soldiers to block the breach,
diverting the river into two channels,
restoring the ancient course from Yǔ's time.
At that time, after the conquest of Nányuè,
a Yuè man named Yǒng Zhī remarked, "The Yuè people customarily believe in ghosts,
and in their shrines, ghosts are often seen,
frequently with tangible effects.
In the past, the King of Dōng'ōu revered ghosts,
and lived to be one hundred and sixty years old.
Later generations became negligent and disrespectful,
hence the decline."
He then ordered Yuè shamans to establish Yuè sacrificial shrines,
with platforms but no altars,
also worshiping heavenly deities, the Supreme God, and hundreds of ghosts,
using chicken divination.
The Emperor believed in it,
and thus Yuè shrines and chicken divination began to be employed.
Gōngsūn Qīng said:
"Immortals can be seen,
but when Your Majesty goes to visit, it is often too hasty,
hence they are not seen.
Now, if Your Majesty could build observation towers,
like in Gōushì City,
and set out dried meat and dates,
divine beings should be able to be summoned.
Moreover, immortals prefer residing in multi-storied buildings."
Thereupon, the Emperor ordered Cháng'ān to construct the Fēilián and Guì observation towers,
and Gānquán to build the Yì Yánshòu observation tower,
sending Gōngsūn Qīng with credentials to prepare and await the divine beings.
He then erected the Tōngtiān Terrace,
placing sacrificial utensils beneath it,
intending to attract the likes of immortals and spirits.
Subsequently, Gānquán was further enhanced with a front hall,
beginning the expansion of various palaces.
In summer,
a mushroom grew inside the hall's foundation.
The Son of Heaven, for stemming the river and
erecting the Tōngtiān Terrace,
as if there were a glow,
issued an edict stating:
"A nine-stemmed mushroom has grown at the Gānquán foundation;
pardon the empire,
and cease further constructions."
The following year,
they attacked Cháoxiǎn.
Summer,
there was a drought.
Gōngsūn Qīng said:
"In Huángdì's time, during the fēng sacrifice, it turned dry,
parching the sacrifice for three years."
The Emperor then issued an edict:
"The drought,
does it mean the sacrifice is parched?
Let the empire honor and sacrifice to the Língxīng star."
The next year,
the Emperor performed suburban rites at Yōng,
opened the Huízhōng road,
and toured it.
In spring,
he reached Míngzé,
returning via the Xīhé.
The following winter,
the Emperor toured Nánjùn,
reaching Jiānglíng and then heading east.
He ascended and performed rites at Qián's Tiānzhù Mountain,
naming it Nányuè.
Sailing the river,
from Xúnyáng to Zōngyáng,
passing Pénglí,
he sacrificed to its famous mountains and rivers.
North to Lángyá,
along the coast.
In mid-April,
he arrived at Fènggāo to perform the fēng sacrifice.
Initially,
when the Son of Heaven performed the fēng sacrifice on Tàishān,
the northeastern foothills had an ancient site for a Bright Hall,
but it was precarious and not spacious.
The Emperor wished to build a Bright Hall near Fènggāo,
but did not know its design.
Gōng Wángdài from Jǐnán presented a diagram of Huángdì's Bright Hall.
The diagram showed a hall
without walls on all four sides,
roofed with thatch,
with water channels,
a circular palace wall with a double pathway,
and a tower above,
entered from the southwest,
named Kūnlún,
through which the Son of Heaven would enter
to worship the Supreme God.
So, the Emperor ordered Fènggāo to construct the Bright Hall on the Wèn River,
following Gōng's diagram.
During the quinquennial fēng sacrifice,
he sacrificed to Tàiyī and the Five Emperors in the Bright Hall's upper seats,
with Emperor Gāozǔ's seat facing them.
In the lower chamber, he sacrificed to the Earth Goddess,
with twenty sets of sacrificial animals.
The Son of Heaven entered via the Kūnlún path,
beginning the Bright Hall worship with suburban rites.
After the rites,
offerings were burned below the hall.
Then, ascending Tàishān again,
he performed a secret sacrifice at its peak.
At the foot of Tàishān, sacrifices to the Five Emperors
were made according to their directions,
with Huángdì alongside Chìdì,
and officials attending the sacrifices.
When fire was lit on Tàishān,
below all responded in kind.
Two years later,
on the first day of the eleventh month, the winter solstice,
calendar experts used it as the base for calculations.
The Son of Heaven personally went to Tàishān,
sacrificing to the Supreme God in the Bright Hall on that day,
each time performing the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
The prayer read:
"Heaven grants the Emperor the Tàiyuán divine tally,
cycling anew.
The Emperor reverently worships Tàiyī."
East to the sea,
examining those who entered the sea and magicians seeking spirits,
none proved effective,
yet he sent more,
hoping to encounter them.
On the yǐyǒu day of the eleventh month,
the Bǎiliáng Terrace burned down.
On the first day of the twelfth month,
the Emperor personally performed the shàn sacrifice at Gāolǐ,
worshiping the Earth Goddess.
Approaching the Bó Sea,
he intended to gaze and sacrifice to the likes of Pénglái,
hoping to reach a divine realm.
Upon returning,
due to the Bǎiliáng fire,
he held court and received reports at Gānquán.
Gōngsūn Qīng said:
"Huángdì had the Qīnglíng Terrace,
which burned after twelve days,
so Huángdì built the Bright Court.
The Bright Court
is Gānquán."
Many magicians claimed ancient emperors had capitals at Gānquán.
Later, the Son of Heaven again held court for nobles at Gānquán,
where residences for nobles were built.
Yǒng Zhī then said:
"In Yuè custom, after a fire,
rebuilding must be on a grand scale,
to overcome it."
Thus, the Jiànzhāng Palace was constructed,
designed with thousands of gates and rooms.
Its front hall surpassed Wèiyāng in height.
To the east stood the Phoenix Tower,
over twenty zhàng high.
To the west was Tángzhōng,
with a tiger enclosure spanning tens of lǐ.
To the north, a large pond was dug,
with a Jiàn Terrace over twenty zhàng high,
named the Tàiyè Pond,
containing Pénglái, Fāngzhàng, Yíngzhōu, and Húliáng,
resembling divine mountains, turtles, and fish in the sea.
To the south were the Jade Hall,
the Jade Gate, giant birds, and the like.
Then, the Shénmíng Terrace and Jǐnghàn Tower were erected,
over fifty zhàng high,
connected by imperial pathways.
In summer,
the Hàn dynasty reformed the calendar,
making the first month the start of the year,
with yellow as the esteemed color,
and official titles and seals changed to five characters,
marking the Tàichū era's first year.
That year,
they campaigned against Dàyuān in the west.
Locusts swarmed greatly.
Dīng Fūrén,
Luòyáng's Yú Chū, and others used magical sacrifices to curse the Xiōngnú and Dàyuān.
The following year,
officials reported that the five altars at Yōng lacked prepared sacrificial animals,
and fragrances were incomplete.
So, the sacrificial officers were ordered to provide calves and prepared animals for the altars,
with five-colored foods according to the conquering element,
and wooden horse figures replaced colts.
Only for the Five Emperors were colts used,
and for personal suburban sacrifices, colts were employed.
For famous mountains and rivers where colts were used,
all were replaced by wooden figures.
When passing through,
colts were used.
Other rituals remained as before.
In the following year,
he traveled east to inspect the coastal regions,
investigating matters related to immortals and spirits,
but found no verifiable evidence.
A fangshi claimed,
"During Huángdì's time, the Five Cities and Twelve Towers were built
to await divine beings at Zhíqī,
and it was named the Welcoming of the Year."
The emperor approved its construction according to the method,
naming it the Next Year.
He personally worshipped the Supreme Deity in ceremony,
dressed in yellow robes.
Gōng Yù Dài said:
"Although Huángdì sealed Tàishān,
Fēng Hòu, Fēng Jù, and Qí Bó advised Huángdì to also seal the Eastern Tàishān
and perform the feng and shan rituals at Fán Shān to match the tallies,
after which he attained immortality."
The Son of Heaven then ordered the preparation of sacrificial items,
and upon reaching the Eastern Tàishān,
found it too small and low,
unworthy of its reputation,
so he directed the ritual officers to conduct ceremonies there
without performing the feng and shan.
Afterward, he ordered Dài to maintain the shrine and await divine manifestations.
In summer,
he returned to Tàishān,
repeating the five-year ceremony as before,
and added the shan sacrifice at Shílǘ.
Shílǘ,
located south at the foot of Tàishān,
was said by many fangshi to be the gateway for immortals,
so the emperor personally performed the shan there.
Five years later,
he returned to Tàishān to renew the feng sacrifice,
and on his way back, sacrificed at Chángshān.
The current Son of Heaven's established sacrifices,
such as Tàiyī and Hòutǔ,
involved personal suburban ceremonies every three years,
establishing the Hàn dynasty's feng and shan rituals,
with a renewal every five years.
The sacrifices to Bó Jì's Tàiyī, Sānyī, Míngyáng, Mǎ Xíng, and Chìxīng—
five in total—
were conducted annually by the ritual officers under Kuān Shū.
All six shrines
were overseen by the Grand Invocator.
As for the Eight Deities and other spirits,
like Next Year and Fán Shān's other names,
they were worshipped when passed by,
and ceased once left.
Shrines established by fangshi
were managed independently by them,
ending with their deaths,
and not maintained by ritual officers.
Other sacrifices continued as before.
The current emperor's feng and shan
occurred every twelve years,
covering all Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers.
Yet the fangshi's attempts to await divine beings
and seek Pénglái by sea
ultimately yielded no proof.
Even Gōngsūn Qīng, who awaited spirits,
still explained things through giant footprints,
without effect.
The Son of Heaven grew increasingly weary of the fangshi's bizarre and far-fetched tales,
yet he continued to indulge them without cutting ties,
hoping to encounter the genuine article.
From then on,
fangshi speaking of spirit worship multiplied,
but the results were evident.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I accompanied the inspections and sacrifices to heaven, earth, various spirits, famous mountains, and rivers, including the feng and shan.
Entering the Shòu Palace to serve during spirit communications,
I thoroughly observed the words of the fangshi and ritual officers,
then stepped back to compile and discuss those who have dealt with ghosts and spirits since ancient times,
fully revealing their inner and outer aspects.
May later gentlemen
have the opportunity to review this.
As for the details of sacrificial vessels, jades, and silks,
and the rituals of offerings and toasts,
these are recorded by the relevant officials.
The Grand Historian remarks:
The records of the Five Emperors
and the Three Dynasties
are ancient.
Before the Yīn, the feudal lords cannot be reliably chronicled,
but from the Zhōu onward, they can be somewhat documented.
Kǒngzǐ, based on historical texts, compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals,
recording the regnal years,
correcting the times, days, and months,
providing great detail.
However, in editing the Shàngshū, it is brief,
lacking years and months;
though some exist,
many are missing,
making them unrecordable.
Thus, where in doubt, he passed on the doubt,
showing his caution.
I have read genealogical records,
which list year counts from Huángdì onward.
Examining the calendar, genealogies, and the transmissions of the Five Virtues' cycles,
the ancient texts all differ,
conflicting and divergent.
Was the Master's refusal to compile their years and months
without reason!
Therefore, I have used the Five Emperors' genealogies
and the Shàngshū to assemble a chronological table from Huángdì to the Gònghé period. |

Master Zhāng Fūzǐ asked Master Chǔ, saying:
"The Book of Songs states that both Xiè
and Hòujì were born without fathers.
Yet examining various historical records, all say they had fathers,
and their fathers were all sons of Huángdì.
Does this not contradict the Book of Songs?"
Master Chǔ replied:
"Not so.
The Book of Songs says Xiè was born from an egg,
and Hòujì from a human footprint,
to show they had the Mandate of Heaven and were conceived with spiritual sincerity.
Spirits and ghosts cannot create themselves,
they must be born through humans -
how could anyone be born without a father!
Some accounts say they had fathers,
others say they had none;
what is credible is transmitted as credible,
what is doubtful is transmitted as doubtful,
hence both versions are recorded.
Yáo knew that both Xiè
and Jì were worthy men,
born of Heaven,
so he enfeoffed Xiè with seventy li of land.
After more than ten generations, this reached Tāng,
who ruled the world.
Yáo knew that Hòujì's descendants would later become kings,
so he additionally enfeoffed him with a hundred li.
His descendants continued for nearly a thousand years,
until King Wén possessed the world.
The commentary to the Book of Songs states:
'Tāng's ancestor was Xiè,
born without a father.
Xiè's mother was bathing with her sisters in Xuánqiū River
when a swallow carrying an egg dropped it.
Xiè's mother retrieved it
and put it in her mouth,
accidentally swallowing it,
whereupon she gave birth to Xiè.
Xiè was born worthy,
so Yáo appointed him as Minister of Education
and gave him the surname Zǐ.
Zǐ means 'this';
'this' means to grow greater.
The poets praised and eulogized him, saying:
'The Shāng altar vast and wide,
the Mandate came through the dark bird,
which descended and gave birth to Shāng.'
Shāng means substance,
which was the name of the Yīn dynasty.
King Wén's ancestor was Hòujì,
who was also born without a father.
Hòujì's mother was Jiāngyuán.
Going out, she saw a giant's footprint and stepped in it.
Becoming aware in her body,
she then gave birth to Hòujì.
Jiāngyuán thought he had no father,
so considering him base, abandoned him in the road,
but oxen and sheep avoided trampling him.
She carried him into the mountains,
where the mountain people raised him.
She then abandoned him in the great marsh,
where birds covered and fed him.
Jiāngyuán found this strange,
then realized he was a Son of Heaven,
so she retrieved and raised him.
Yáo knew he had worthy talent,
so appointed him as Minister of Agriculture
and gave him the surname Jī.
Jī means
'origin.'
The poets praised and eulogized him, saying:
'The first birth of our people'
means deeply cultivating until achievement was complete,
referring to Hòujì's beginnings.'
Confucius said:
'In ancient times, Yáo commanded Xiè to take the surname Zǐ
because there would be Tāng.
He commanded Hòujì to take the surname Jī
because there would be King Wén.
The Great King appointed Jìlì
to manifest Heaven's auspicious signs.
Tàibó went to Wú,
thus establishing its origin.'
The Mandate of Heaven is difficult to explain;
none but sages can perceive it.
Shùn, Yǔ,
Xiè, and Hòujì were all descendants of Huángdì.
Huángdì received the Mandate of Heaven and governed the world;
his virtue and beneficence deeply affected later generations.
Thus his descendants all again became Sons of Heaven -
this is Heaven's reward for virtue.
People who don't know this
think they casually rose from common cloth-wearing men.
How could common cloth-wearing men rise without cause to rule the world?
It was because they had the Mandate of Heaven."
"Why did Huángdì's descendants rule the world for so long?"
He replied:
"Tradition says that when the world's ruler petitions for the lives of the black-haired masses of ten thousand families, he becomes Emperor,
bringing blessings for ten thousand generations.
Huángdì was such.
When the five governmental affairs are clear, he cultivates ritual righteousness,
and raising armies to attack according to Heaven's timing brings benefit - such a one becomes King,
bringing blessings for a thousand generations.
The King of Shǔ
was a descendant of Huángdì.
To this day, five thousand li southwest of Hàn,
he regularly comes to pay homage,
offering tribute to Hàn.
Is this not because his ancestors had virtue,
with beneficence flowing to later generations?
How can practicing moral virtue be neglected!
Rulers and kings should consider this.
The great Hàn general Huò Zǐmèng, named Guāng,
is also a descendant of Huángdì.
This can be discussed with the widely learned and far-seeing,
but is difficult to explain to the shallowly informed.
Why do I say this?
In ancient times, feudal lords took their state as surname.
Huò
was a state's name.
King Wǔ enfeoffed his younger brother Shūchǔ at Huò.
Later, Duke Xiàn of Jìn destroyed the Duke of Huò,
whose descendants became commoners,
traveling to live in Píngyáng.
Píngyáng is in Hédōng,
Hédōng being Jìn territory,
divided into the state of Wèi.
According to the Book of Songs,
this could also be considered the Zhōu era.
Zhōu arose from Hòujì,
who was born without a father.
According to the genealogical records of the Three Dynasties,
Hòujì had a father named Gāoxīn;
Gāoxīn
was Huángdì's great-grandson.
The Huángdì Beginning and End Tradition states:
'A hundred-some years after Hàn's rise,
there will be a man neither short nor tall,
from the land of white swallows,
who will hold the world's government
while an infant is sovereign,
pushing the carriage backward.'
General Huò
originally lived in Píngyáng's White Swallow village.
When I was a court gentleman,
I met with the fāngshì at the examination hall beneath the flag tower,
and he told me this.
Is this not magnificent!"
The Grand Historian Simǎ Qiān, reading the chronicles and genealogies of the Spring and Autumn period,
upon reaching the reign of King Lì of Zhōu,
would always put down the scroll and sigh.
He said: Alas,
Master Zhì foresaw it!
When King Zhòu used ivory chopsticks, Jīzǐ lamented.
As the way of Zhōu decayed,
poets rooted it in domestic life,
hence the "Guān Jū" was composed.
When benevolence and righteousness declined,
the "Lù Míng" served as criticism.
By the time of King Lì,
who loathed hearing of his faults,
the ministers feared execution and turmoil arose,
so King Lì fled to Zhì,
chaos beginning from the capital,
and the Hé'ěr Regency governed.
Thereafter, some relied on forceful governance,
the strong overpowering the weak,
raising armies without consulting the Son of Heaven.
Yet, under the pretext of supporting the royal house,
they used punitive expeditions to become alliance leaders,
governance fell to the Five Hegemons,
the feudal lords acted wantonly,
indulging in extravagance and lawlessness,
and treacherous ministers and usurping sons increasingly arose.
States like Qí, Jìn,
Qín, and Chǔ were insignificant in Chéngzhōu's time,
with fiefs of maybe a hundred or fifty lǐ.
Jìn was shielded by the three rivers,
Qí backed by the Eastern Sea,
Chǔ nestled between the Jiāng and Huái,
Qín secured by the strongholds of Yōngzhōu,
each rose in turn across the realm,
succeeding as hegemonic lords,
and the great fiefdoms honored by King Wén and King Wǔ
all submitted to their might.
Thus, Confucius elucidated the kingly way,
approached over seventy rulers,
yet none could employ him,
so he journeyed west to observe the Zhōu court,
discussed historical records and old accounts,
drew from Lǔ's traditions to compile the Spring and Autumn Annals,
beginning with Duke Yǐn
and ending with Duke Āi's capture of the qílín,
condensing its language,
removing redundancies,
to establish principles and models,
thus perfecting the kingly way,
and thoroughly covering human affairs.
His seventy disciples orally received its transmitted intent,
as the texts containing criticism, praise, taboos, and omissions could not be fully written down.
The Lǔ scholar Zuǒ Qiū Míng, fearing disciples would each follow different interpretations,
adhering to their own views,
and lose the true meaning,
thus based on Confucius's historical records fully elaborated the accounts,
completing the Zuǒ Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Duó Jiāo, tutor to King Wēi of Chǔ,
because the king could not read the entire Spring and Autumn Annals,
selected accounts of successes and failures,
culminating in forty chapters,
titled Duó's Subtleties.
During the reign of King Xiàochéng of Zhào,
his minister Yú Qīng, drawing from the Spring and Autumn Annals above
and observing recent trends below,
also composed eight essays,
titled Yú's Spring and Autumn Annals.
Lǚ Bùwéi,
chancellor to King Zhuāngxiāng of Qín,
likewise examined antiquity,
edited the Spring and Autumn Annals,
compiled events from the six states' era,
creating the Eight Observations,
Six Discourses,
and Twelve Chronicles,
titled Lǚ's Spring and Autumn Annals.
As for figures like Xúnzǐ,
Mencius,
Gōngsūn Gù,
Hán Fēi, and others,
each often gathered passages from the Spring and Autumn Annals to write books,
too numerous to record fully.
Hàn's chancellor Zhāng Cāng calendared the Five Virtues,
Grandee Dǒng Zhòngshū expounded the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
producing substantial writings.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Confucians determined their principles,
rhetoricians displayed their eloquence,
without striving to synthesize the whole story;
calendar specialists took the years and months,
numerologists emphasized mystical cycles,
genealogies solely recorded lineages and posthumous titles,
their accounts brief,
making it hard to grasp the essentials at a glance.
Therefore, I tabulate the twelve feudal lords,
from the Hé'ěr Regency to Confucius,
presenting in this work the main points of prosperity and decline as criticized by scholars of the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Guóyǔ,
offering a concise version for those mastering ancient texts.

Grand Historian reading the Qín records,
reached when the Quǎnróng defeated King Yōu,
Zhōu moved east to Luòyì,
Qín Duke Xiāng was first enfeoffed as a feudal lord,
established the Xīzhì to serve the Supreme God,
signs of usurpation appeared.
The Rites say:
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
feudal lords sacrifice to the famous mountains and great rivers within their domains."
Now Qín mixed with the customs of the Róng and Dí,
prioritized violence,
only later benevolence and righteousness,
being a vassal yet conducting suburban sacrifices,
gentlemen feared this.
When Duke Wén crossed Lǒng,
repelled the Yí and Dí,
honored Chénbǎo,
operated between Qí and Yōng,
and Duke Mù improved governance,
eastern border reached the river,
then matched the central states' lords like Qí Huán and Jìn Wén.
Afterwards, ministers held power,
great officers inherited fiefs,
the six ministers monopolized Jìn's authority,
waged wars and held alliances,
their prestige surpassed the feudal lords.
When Tián Cháng killed Duke Jiǎn and became Qí's chancellor,
the feudal lords remained calm and did not punish,
the world contended for military achievements.
Eventually the three states divided Jìn,
Tián Hé also destroyed Qí and possessed it,
the prosperity of the six states began here.
Focused on strengthening armies and annexing enemies,
schemes and deceptions were used, and vertical-horizontal strategies arose.
False claims swarmed out,
oaths and alliances were not trusted,
even with hostages and split tallies, they could not be restrained.
Qín initially was a small remote state,
the central states ostracized it,
comparing it to the Róng and Dí,
but after Duke Xiàn, it often dominated the feudal lords.
Judging Qín's virtue and righteousness, it was inferior to even the violent states of Lǔ and Wèi,
measuring Qín's military, it was not stronger than the three Jìn,
yet it eventually unified the world,
not necessarily due to strategic advantages,
as if aided by Heaven.
Some say "The east is where things begin to grow,
the west is where things mature."
Those who initiate affairs are often in the southeast,
but those who reap success are usually in the northwest.
Thus Yǔ rose from the Xīqiāng,
Tāng started from Bó,
Zhōu's kingship used Fēnghào to attack Yīn,
Qín's emperorship rose from Yōngzhōu,
Hàn's rise came from Shǔhàn.
After Qín achieved its ambition,
it burned the world's Shī and Shū,
especially the historical records of the feudal lords,
because they contained criticism.
The reason Shī and Shū reappeared,
is that many were hidden in homes,
but the historical records were solely kept in the Zhōu court,
hence they were destroyed.
A pity,
a pity!
Only the Qín records remained,
yet they did not record dates,
their texts were brief and incomplete.
However, the stratagems of the Warring States also have much to be adopted,
why must it be ancient times?
Qín's way of taking the world was violent,
but times changed,
and its achievements were great.
The tradition says "Emulate the later kings",
why?
Because they are closer to us and their changing customs are similar,
their discussions are humble and easy to implement.
Scholars are constrained by what they have heard,
seeing Qín's reign was brief,
without examining its beginning and end,
thus they ridicule it,
dare not speak of it,
this is no different from eating with ears.
How sad!
Therefore, I based on the Qín records,
following the Spring and Autumn period,
starting from King Yuán of Zhōu,
tabulating the events of the six states' times,
ending with the Second Emperor,
totaling 270 years,
recording the origins of rise and fall as I have learned.
May later gentlemen
observe and reflect upon it.||

Grand Historian Sima Qian, reading about the period between Qín and Chǔ,
said: Initially, the uprising
was started by Chén Shè;
the cruel destruction of Qín
came from the Xiàng clan;
the restoration of order and elimination of tyranny,
pacifying the realm,
and finally ascending the imperial throne
was achieved by the Hàn house.
Within five years,
authority changed hands three times.
Since the beginning of humanity,
never had the Mandate of Heaven been received so rapidly.
In ancient times, the rise of Yú
and Xià
accumulated virtue and merit over decades,
their virtue reached the common people,
they temporarily administered governance,
tested by Heaven,
and only then assumed the throne.
As for the kingship of Tāng
and Wǔ,
it originated from Xiè and Hòujì practicing benevolence and righteousness for over ten generations,
when eight hundred lords gathered at Mèngjīn without prior arrangement,
they still considered it premature,
and only later did they depose and execute the tyrants.
Qín rose from Duke Xiāng,
flourished under Duke Wén,
Mù,
and after Duke Xiàn and Duke Xiào,
gradually encroached upon the Six States,
over more than a hundred years,
until the First Emperor could unite all civilized states.
With such virtue in ancient times,
and such effort here,
unification was indeed this difficult.
After Qín became emperor,
troubled by incessant warfare,
attributed to the existence of feudal lords,
thus abolished all land grants,
destroyed famous cities,
melted down weapons,
eliminated powerful leaders,
aiming for eternal peace.
Yet the rise of royal traces
began in alleyways,
with alliances for campaigns,
surpassing the Three Dynasties,
while Qín's prohibitions
only aided the worthy in overcoming difficulties.
Thus, through determined actions, they became heroes of the realm;
how can it be said that without land, one cannot be king?
Is this not what the traditions call the Great Sage?
Is it not Heaven's will,
is it not Heaven's will!
If not a Great Sage, who could receive this Mandate and become emperor?===>

The Grand Historian says:
The Shàng and before are remote.
Zhōu enfiefed five ranks:
Duke, Marquis,
Earl, Viscount, Baron.
Yet enfiefed Bóqín,
Kāngshū at Lǔ, Wèi,
lands each four hundred lǐ,
cherishing kinship
principle,
honoring the virtuous;
Tàigōng at Qí,
combined lands of five marquises,
honoring toil and merit.
King Wǔ, Chéng, Kāng enfiefed hundreds,
among them fifty-five same surname,
lands largest not exceeding hundred lǐ,
smallest thirty lǐ,
to protect the royal house.
Guǎn, Cài,
Kāngshū, Cáo, Zhèng,
some exceeded or fell short.
After Lì, Yōu,
royal house declined,
marquis-earls' strong states arose,
Son of Heaven weakened,
unable to rectify.
Not virtue impure,
but situation weak.
Hàn rose,
ordered two ranks.
Gāozǔ's late years,
non-Liú clan
made kings,
or without merit the sovereign did not establish
as marquises,
all under heaven would punish them.
Gāozǔ's sons, brothers, same surname as kings: nine states,
only Chángshā different surname,
and meritorious marquises over a hundred.
From Yànmén, Tàiyuán east to Liáoyáng,
were Yān, Dài states;
south of Chángshān,
left of Tàiháng turning,
crossing Huáng Hé, Jǐ Shuǐ,
Ē,
Zhèn east to near sea,
were Qí, Zhào states;
from Chén west,
south to Jiǔyí,
east girded by Cháng Jiāng,
Huái, Gǔ, Sì rivers,
near Kuàijī,
were Liáng, Chǔ,
Huáinán, Chángshā states:
all externally
connected to Hú, Yuè.
And inland
north reaching mountains eastward
all feudal lords' lands,
largest maybe five-six commanderies,
linked cities tens,
established hundred officials
palaces,
usurping Son of Heaven's.
Hàn only had Sānhé,
Dōngjùn,
Yǐngchuān, Nányáng,
from Jiānglíng west to Shǔ,
north from Yúnzhōng to Lǒngxī,
with Nèishǐ total fifteen commanderies,
and princesses, marquises
mostly had estates therein.
Why?
All under heaven newly settled,
flesh-and-bone same surname few,
so broadened strengthened cadet lines,
to pacify four seas,
using them to protect Son of Heaven.
Hàn settled, within a century,
relatives
grew distant,
feudal lords some arrogant extravagant,
habituated evil ministers' plots
to debauchery,
major ones rebelled,
minor ones transgressed laws,
endangering their lives,
perishing losing states.
Son of Heaven observed antiquity,
then bestowed grace,
let feudal lords extend favor dividing lands among sons, brothers,
so Qí divided seven,
Zhào divided six,
Liáng divided five,
Huáinán divided three,
and Son of Heaven's cadet sons as kings,
kings' cadet sons as marquises,
over a hundred.
Wú-Chǔ times,
before-after feudal lords
some by offense lost land,
thus Yān, Dài no northern border commanderies,

up sufficient for tribute duty,

dog-teeth mutually adjacent,
holding their strategic terrain advantages,
strengthening trunk,

The Grand Historian remarks:
In ancient times, the merits of ministers were of five grades:
Establishing ancestral temples through virtue
and securing the altars of land and grain
is called "xūn";
through speech
is called "láo";
through exertion of strength
is called "gōng";
clarifying their rank
is called "fá";
accumulating seniority
is called "yuè".
The oath of enfeoffment said:
"Should the Yellow River become a narrow belt,
and Mount Tài a whetstone.
May the state enjoy eternal peace,
extending to your descendants."
Initially, it was not that they did not wish
to strengthen its root and foundation,
yet the branches and leaves
gradually declined and weakened.
I have read about Gaozu enfeoffing his meritorious ministers,
examined their initial enfeeoffments,
and the reasons for their losses,
and say:
How different from what I have heard!
The Documents say
"Harmonizing the myriad states",
passing to
the Xià and Shāng,
some lasted several thousand years.
Indeed, the Zhōu enfeeoffed eight hundred,
after Yōu and Lì,
they are seen in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
The Shàngshū records the marquises and earls of Táng and Yú,
passing through the three dynasties
for over a thousand years,
preserving themselves fully while protecting the Son of Heaven as vassals,
was this not due to their deep commitment to benevolence and righteousness,
and adherence to the laws of their superiors?
With the rise of Hàn,
over one hundred meritorious ministers received enfeeoffments.
The empire was newly stabilized,
thus large cities and famous capitals were scattered and depopulated,
the registered households that could be
counted were only two or three out of ten,
therefore the largest marquises had no more than ten thousand households,
the smallest five or six hundred.
After several generations,
the people all returned to their villages,
households increasingly multiplied,
those like Xiāo, Cáo, Jiàng, Guàn and their kind
some reached forty thousand,
smaller marquises doubled,
their wealth and prosperity likewise.
Their descendants grew arrogant and excessive,
forgetting their ancestors,
indulging in debauchery.
By the Tàichū era, within a span of a hundred years,
only five marquises remained,
the rest all faced legal punishment
losing their lives and states,
they were wiped out.
The laws were also somewhat stringent,
yet all failed to be cautious
regarding the prohibitions of their time.
Living in the present age,
remembering the ways of antiquity,
serves as a mirror for oneself,
though not entirely identical.
Emperors and kings each had different rituals and duties, but all took achievement as their guiding principle,
how can they be bound by one pattern?
Observing how they gained honor and favor
and how they faced dismissal and disgrace,
is also a forest of successes and failures of the time,
why must it be old tales?
Therefore, I carefully record their beginnings and ends,
and tabulate the text,
There are some details that do not fully capture the beginning and end;
I have recorded what is clear,
and left out what is doubtful.
If future gentlemen
wish to extend and compile them,
they may refer to this. ==>

Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān, reading the enfeoffment records
up to Marquis Biàn,
said:
There is reason for this!
The King of Chángshā,
recorded in Ordinance A,
is praised for his loyalty.
In the past, Gāozǔ pacified the realm,
among the meritorious ministers, eight states were enfeoffed as kings despite not being of the same surname with territorial power.
By the time of Xiàohuì,
only Chángshā remained intact,
passed down for five generations,
extinguished due to lack of an heir,
ultimately without fault,
guarding the border and fulfilling duties,
truly trustworthy.
Thus, his favor extended to collateral branches,
several persons were enfeoffed as marquises without merit.
And from Xiàohuì
to the interval ending with Xiàojǐng, fifty years,
pursuing and restoring Gāozǔ's era's remaining meritorious ministers,
and those who came from Dài,
the labors of Wú and Chǔ,
feudal lords' sons and brothers like close kin,
foreign states returning to righteousness,
those enfeoffed numbered over ninety.
All recorded from start to finish,
these are the prominent examples of benevolence, righteousness, and successful achievements of that time. |

Right, thirty from the era of Xiào Jǐng
The Grand Historian remarks:
The Xiongnu severed peaceful relations,
attacked the frontier passes;
Mínyuè arbitrarily launched campaigns,
Dōng'ōu sought to surrender.
With these two barbarians encroaching alternately,
at the peak of the mighty Hàn,
this shows how the meritorious officials received enfeoffments matching those of their ancestors.
Why is that?
Since the Odes and Documents praise the Three Dynasties for
"repelling the Róng and Dí,
subduing Jīng and Shǔ,"
Duke Huán of Qí crossed Yān to attack the Shānróng,
King Wǔlíng with the small state of Zhào subdued the Chányú,
Duke Mù of Qín used Bǎilǐ to dominate the Western Róng,
the rulers of Wú and Chǔ as feudal lords subdued the Bǎiyuè.
How much more so when the Central Land is unified,
with an enlightened Son of Heaven above,
combining civil and martial virtues,
sweeping across the four seas,
harmonizing millions within,
could it be that they remained peaceful without conducting campaigns on the borders!
From then on,
they dispatched armies north to punish the strong Hú,
south to exterminate the powerful Yuè,
and the generals and officers were enfeoffed in due order.
The country's name; Hóu Gōng; Yuán Guāng; Yuán Shuò; Yuán Shòu; Yuán Dǐng; Yuán Fēng; Tàichū thereafter…
