The main table of the right Grand Historian |
Dāngtū, Wèi Bùhài,
as the prison guard, arrested the rebels Gōngsūn Yǒng and others in Huáiyáng, was made a marquis.
Pú, Sūchāng,
as the prison official historian, arrested the rebels Gōngsūn Yǒng and others in Huáiyáng, was made a marquis.
Lǎoyáng, Jiāngdé,
as the gardener and granary manager, arrested the rebels Gōngsūn Yǒng and others in Huáiyáng, was made a marquis.
Fùmín, Tián Qiānqiū,
lived in Chánglíng.
As the former caretaker of Gaomiao, he wrote to remonstrate against Emperor Xiàowǔ saying:
"A son wielding his father’s soldiers,
is a crime deserving of a beating.
The anger between father and son,
is an ancient occurrence.
Chíyóu rebelled against his father,
the Yellow Emperor crossed the river" .
When the letter was received,
he was appointed as the Grand Herald.
In the fourth year of Zhenghe he became Chancellor,
was given three thousand households.
He died of illness during the time of Emperor Zhāo,
his son Shùn took over,
as General of the Tiger’s Teeth,
fought against the Xiongnu,
but did not report,
was executed and the state was abolished.
The right records of Emperor Xiàowǔ's titles
Later, the scholar Chǔ Xiān said:
The works of the Grand Historian end with Emperor Xiàowǔ's affairs,
so he compiled the records of Emperor Zhāo’s ministers and marquises,
placing them to the left,
allowing later scholars to observe the successes and failures across ages,
to use as a warning for themselves.
For contemporary gentlemen,
practice power skilfully,
measure the times appropriately,
apply accordingly,
build achievements and receive lands to be marquises,
establish their names in the present,
is this not grand!
Observing their way of maintaining accomplishments,
all lack humility,
arrogant and competitive,
delighting in spreading their reputation,
knowing advancement and not retreat,
ultimately leading to self-destruction and the loss of their states.
With their fortune,
in their era, losing it,
unable to pass achievements to future generations,
ensuring their kindness flows to descendants,
is this not sorrowful!
The Dragon Luò Marquis once served as forward general,
benevolent and kind to common people,
generous, respectful, and trustworthy,
avoiding politics,
retiring and loving others.
His ancestors began from the era of the Six Ministers of Jin.
Since holding land and ruling nations,
becoming kings and marquises,
successive generations without interruption,
enduring through ages,
reaching this day,
lasting over a hundred years,
how can they be compared to those marquises who lost everything in their lifetime?
Oh, how tragic,
future generations must take heed!
Bólù, Huò Guāng,
lived in Píngyáng.
Became powerful due to his elder brother, General of Agile Cavalry.
Served Emperor Wǔ before,
captured and executed the traitorous attendant Ma Héluo and others, made a marquis,
of three thousand households.
Acted as regent for the young Emperor Zhāo,
served as Grand General.
Faithful and trustworthy,
exercised power and governance,
honored as Grand Marshal,
increased fiefs to ten thousand households.
Afterwards served Emperor Xuān.
Served three emperors,
trusted by the people of the empire,
increased fiefs to twenty thousand households.
His son Yǔ succeeded him,
plotted rebellion,
family exterminated,
state abolished. |
Dù: Jīn Wēngshū, named Mìdī,
as the crown prince of the Xiūtú King of the Xiōngnú, followed the Húnxié King leading fifty thousand troops,
surrendered to the Hàn and pledged allegiance,
served as Palace Attendant,
served Emperor Wǔ,
detected and captured the rebellious Palace Attendants Mǎ Héluó and others, earning him the rank of Marquis,
with a fief of three thousand households.
Later served Emperor Zhāo,
was cautious and honest,
and was granted an additional three thousand households.
His son Hóng succeeded him,
became Commander of the Imperial Chariots,
and served Emperor Xuān.||
Ānyáng: Shàngguān Jié,
his family was from Lǒngxī.
He joined the army skilled in horsemanship and archery.
Gradually rose to prominence,
served Emperor Wǔ,
became Left General.
Detected, captured, and executed the rebellious Palace Attendant Mǎ Héluó's younger brother, Marquis of Chónghé, Tōng, earning him the rank of Marquis,
with a fief of three thousand households.
Later served Emperor Zhāo,
contended for power with the Grand General Huò Guāng,
and as a result plotted rebellion,
leading to the extermination of his clan,
and the abolition of his fief.||
Sānglè: Shàngguān Ān.
Because his father Jié was a general, he was initially honored,
served as Palace Attendant,
and served Emperor Zhāo.
Ān's daughter became Emperor Zhāo's consort,
and was established as Empress, thus he was made Marquis,
with a fief of three thousand households.
He became arrogant and unruly,
contended for power with the Grand General Huò Guāng,
and as a result, he and his father plotted rebellion,
leading to the extermination of their clan,
and the abolition of the fief.||
Fùpíng: Zhāng Ānshì,
his family was in Dùlíng.
As the son of the former Imperial Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Tāng, he served in the Imperial Secretariat during Emperor Wǔ's time,
became Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Served Emperor Zhāo,
was cautious, honest, and experienced in affairs,
became Commandant of the Palace Guard and Right General.
Assisted in governance for thirteen years,
without major faults,
made Marquis with three thousand households.
Later served Emperor Xuān,
succeeded Huò Guāng as Grand Marshal,
wielded power,
and was granted an additional sixteen thousand households.
His son Yánshòu succeeded him,
became Grand Coachman,
and Palace Attendant.||
Yìyáng: Fù Jièzǐ,
his family was from Běidì.
He joined the army and became a Gentleman,
became Supervisor of Pínglè.
During Emperor Zhāo's time,
he assassinated a foreign king,
and the Emperor issued an edict stating:
"Pínglè Supervisor Fù Jièzǐ, on a mission to a foreign state,
killed the King of Lóulán,
avenged grievances with righteousness,
without burdening the army,
performed a meritorious deed,
he shall be enfeoffed as Marquis of Yìyáng with a fief of one thousand three hundred households."
His son Lì succeeded him,
engaged in disputes over wealth and filed lawsuits,
committed crimes,
leading to the abolition of the fief.||
Shānglì: Wáng Shān,
a man from Qí.
Formerly a Clerk to the Chancellor,
when the Cavalry General Shàngguān Ān plotted rebellion,
Shān persuaded Ān to enter the Chancellor's office with him,
and beheaded Ān.
Shān was made Marquis for his military merit,
with a fief of three thousand households.
He submitted a request to govern the people,
became Governor of Dài.
Someone submitted a memorial accusing him,
he was imprisoned and sentenced to death,
but was pardoned,
released as a commoner,
and the fief was abolished.||
Jiànpíng: Dù Yánnián.
As the son of the former Imperial Censor-in-Chief Dù Zhōu, he served in the Grand General's headquarters,
uncovered the crimes of the rebellious Cavalry General Shàngguān Ān and others,
was enfeoffed as Marquis,
with a fief of two thousand seven hundred households,
appointed as Grand Coachman.
In the first year (of a reign),
he became Governor of Xīhé.
In the third year of Wǔfèng,
he entered court as Imperial Censor-in-Chief.||
Yìyáng: Rèn Gōng.
As the former Chief of the Shanglin Park, he captured and killed the rebellious Left General Shàngguān Jié,
killing him at the Biànmén gate,
was enfeoffed as Marquis,
with two thousand households.
Later became Minister of Ceremonies,
and acted as Commandant of the Guards.
He was frugal, cautious, and trustworthy,
died of old age,
and his title passed to his descendants.||
Yíchéng: Yàn Cāng.
As a former military officer in the Grand General's headquarters, he uncovered the crimes of the rebellious Cavalry General Shàngguān Ān, performing a meritorious deed,
was enfeoffed as Marquis,
with a fief of two thousand households.
Became Governor of Rǔnán,
known for his capability.||
Yíchūn: Wáng Xīn,
his family was in Qí.
Originally a minor clerk,
gradually promoted to Commandant of the Right Auxiliary.
Emperor Wǔ frequently visited Fúfēng Commandery,
Xīn assisted in preparations,
was appointed as Governor of the Right Fúfēng.
By Emperor Zhāo's time,
he succeeded Sāng Hóngyáng as Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
In the third year of Yuánfèng,
he succeeded Tián Qiānqiū as Chancellor,
enfeoffed with two thousand households.
After two years in office,
someone submitted a memorial accusing him of tyranny,
he committed suicide,
but did not die.
His son succeeded him,
became Commandant of Dependent States.||
Ānpíng: Yáng Chǎng,
his family was in Huáyīn.
Formerly served in the Grand General's headquarters,
gradually promoted to Minister of Agriculture,
became Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
In the sixth year of Yuánfèng,
he succeeded Wáng Xīn as Chancellor,
enfeoffed with two thousand households.
After two years in office,
he died of illness.
His son Bēn succeeded him,
died of illness after thirteen years.
His son Wēngjūn succeeded him,
became Superintendent of Dependent States.
After three years,
due to his uncle Yùn's offensive remarks,
he was imprisoned and sentenced to death,
but was spared,
became a commoner,
and the fief was abolished.|
The above are the names of the fiefs enfeoffed during Emperor Zhāo's time|
Yángpíng: Cài Yì,
his family was in Wēn.
Formerly studied the Hán School of the Classic of Poetry,
became Erudite,
served in the Grand General's headquarters,
became Guardian of the Dùchéng Gate.
Entered court as Palace Attendant,
taught Emperor Zhāo the Hán School of the Classic of Poetry,
became Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
At that time, he was eighty years old,
frail with age,
often needed support from two people to walk.
However, the senior ministers deliberated,
considering him the Emperor's teacher,
he should be made Chancellor.
In the first year of Yuánpíng, he succeeded Yáng Chǎng as Chancellor,
enfeoffed with two thousand households.
Died of illness,
left no heirs,
and the fief was abolished.||
Fúyáng: Wéi Xián,
his family was in Lǔ.
Well-versed in the Classic of Poetry,
Classic of Rites, and Classic of Documents,
became Erudite,
taught as a great Confucian scholar of Lǔ,
entered court as Palace Attendant,
became Emperor Zhāo's teacher,
promoted to Grandee of the Palace Guard,
Chief Minister of the Dependencies,
and Lesser of the Chángxìn Palace.
As the Emperor's teacher,
in the third year of Běnshǐ, he succeeded Cài Yì as Chancellor,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Fúyáng,
with one thousand eight hundred households.
Served as Chancellor for five years,
was lenient,
but inexperienced in administrative affairs,
was dismissed and returned to his residence,
died of illness.
His son Xuánchéng succeeded him,
became Minister of Ceremonies.
Due to riding a horse in the ancestral temple,
he was stripped of his title,
and became a Marquis of the Imperial Domain.||
Pínglíng: Fàn Míngyǒu,
whose home was in Lǒngxī.
Due to his family's generations of familiarity with foreign affairs,
he was sent to oversee the Western Qiāng.
He served Emperor Zhāo,
was appointed as General Who Crosses Liáo,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis for his merit in attacking the Wūhuán,
with a fief of two thousand households.
He took Huò Guāng's daughter as his wife.
In the fourth year of the Dìjié era,
he conspired with the various members of the Huò family, such as Zǐyǔ, to rebel,
resulting in the extermination of his clan,
and the abolition of his fiefdom.||
Yíngpíng: Zhào Chōngguó.
He attained office by joining the army as a Lǒngxī cavalryman,
served as a Palace Attendant,
and served Emperor Wǔ.
He repeatedly led troops to attack the Xiōngnú with merit,
became a Protector of the Army Commandant,
served as a Palace Attendant,
and served Emperor Zhāo.
When Emperor Zhāo passed away,
he participated in the deliberation to establish Emperor Xuān,
resolving doubts and setting the strategy,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis for his merit in stabilizing the imperial ancestral temple,
with a fief of two thousand five hundred households.||
Yángchéng: Tián Yánnián.
He served Emperor Zhāo as a military officer;
he uncovered the plot of Shàngguān Jié to rebel,
but later was delayed and not enfeoffed,
becoming the Grand Minister of Agriculture.
He originally proposed the plan to depose the Prince of Chāngyì and establish Emperor Xuān,
resolving doubts and setting the strategy,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis for his merit in stabilizing the imperial ancestral temple,
with a fief of two thousand seven hundred households.
At the time of Emperor Zhāo's passing,
when state affairs were urgent,
he consequently embezzled thirty million cash from the capital treasury.
When this was discovered,
he committed suicide,
and his fiefdom was abolished.||
Píngqiū: Wáng Qiān,
whose home was in Wèi.
He was a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat,
skilled in the writing of official documents.
He served as a Palace Attendant,
and served Emperor Zhāo.
When the Emperor passed away,
and Emperor Xuān was established,
he resolved doubts and set the strategy,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis for his merit in stabilizing the imperial ancestral temple,
with a fief of two thousand households.
He became a Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments,
with a salary of fully two thousand dàn.
He was implicated in accepting money and valuables from the feudal princes.
He leaked confidential matters,
was executed,
and his fiefdom was abolished.||
Lèchéng: Huò Shān.
Shān was
the son of the elder brother of the Grand General Huò Guāng.
Before Guāng died, he submitted a memorial saying:
"My elder brother, the Swift Cavalry General Qùbìng, served in the army with merit,
but fell ill and died,
and was posthumously honored as Marquis Jǐnghuán,
but his line ended without an heir.
I, Guāng, wish to divide the three thousand five hundred households of my fief in Dōngwǔyáng and give them to Shān."
The Son of Heaven approved this,
and appointed Shān as a marquis.
Later, he was implicated in a plot to rebel,
resulting in the extermination of his clan,
and the abolition of his fiefdom.||
Guànjūn: Huò Yún.
He was enfeoffed as a marquis as the legitimate grandson of the elder brother of the Grand General, the Swift Cavalry General.
In the third year of the Dìjié era,
the Son of Heaven issued an edict saying:
"The Swift Cavalry General Qùbìng attacked the Xiōngnú with merit,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guànjūn.
He passed away,
and his son succeeded as marquis,
but fell ill and died without an heir.
According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
good deeds extend to descendants,
so let three thousand households of the fief be used to enfeoff Yún as Marquis of Guànjūn."
Later, he was implicated in a plot to rebel,
resulting in the extermination of his clan,
and the abolition of his fiefdom.||
Píng'ēn: Xǔ Guǎnghàn,
whose home was in Chāngyì.
He was implicated in an affair and sent to the silkworm chamber,
and had only one daughter,
whom he married off.
Before Emperor Xuān was established,
he had always been close to Guǎnghàn,
and a fortune-teller said he would achieve great nobility,
so for this reason, Guǎnghàn showed him great kindness.
In the third year of the Dìjié era,
he was enfeoffed as a marquis,
with a fief of three thousand households.
He fell ill and died without an heir,
and his fiefdom was abolished.||
Chāngshuǐ: Tián Guǎngmíng.
He was formerly a Gentleman,
served as a Marshal,
and gradually rose to the rank of Commandant of Nánjùn,
Governor of Huáiyáng,
Minister of Ceremonies,
and Left Administrator of Féngyì.
When Emperor Zhāo passed away,
he participated in the deliberation to depose the Prince of Chāngyì,
and establish Emperor Xuān,
resolving doubts and setting the strategy,
to stabilize the imperial ancestral temple.
In the third year of the Běnshǐ era,
he was enfeoffed as a marquis,
with a fief of two thousand three hundred households.
He became Imperial Secretary.
Later, he served as General of Qílián,
attacking the Xiōngnú,
but his army did not reach the designated place,
for which he deserved death,
so he committed suicide,
and his fiefdom was abolished.||
Gāopíng: Wèi Xiàng,
whose home was in Jìyīn.
In his youth, he studied the Yìjīng,
served as a Clerk in a commandery office,
was recommended as a Worthy and Excellent candidate and became Magistrate of Mùlíng,
and was promoted to Governor of Hénán.
He was implicated in wrongfully killing an innocent person,
imprisoned,
and sentenced to death,
but encountered an amnesty,
and was reduced to commoner status.
By edict, he was appointed as Acting Magistrate of Mùlíng,
became Inspector of Yángzhōu,
entered the court as a Grand Master of Remonstrance,
again became Governor of Hénán,
was promoted to Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and Imperial Secretary.
In the third year of the Dìjié era,
he slandered and undermined Wéi Xián,
and replaced him as Chancellor,
enfeoffed with one thousand five hundred households.
He fell ill and died,
and his eldest son Bīn succeeded him,
but was implicated in an offense during ancestral temple ceremonies and lost his marquis title.||
Bówàng: Xǔ Zhōngwēng.
He was enfeoffed as a marquis as the younger brother of Marquis Píng'ēn Xǔ Guǎnghàn,
with a fief of two thousand households.
He also had previous personal connections,
and served as Commandant of the Chánglè Palace Guard.
Upon his death, his son Yánnián succeeded him.||
Lèpíng: Xǔ Wēngsūn.
He was enfeoffed as a marquis as the youngest brother of Marquis Píng'ēn Xǔ Guǎnghàn,
with a fief of two thousand households.
He was appointed as General of Strong Crossbowmen,
defeated the Western Qiāng,
returned, and was further appointed as Grand Marshal,
and Superintendent of the Imperial Household.
He also had previous personal connections,
hence he was able to be enfeoffed.
He was fond of drink and women,
and died early from illness.
His son Tāng succeeded him.||
Jiānglíng: Shǐ Zǐhuí.
He was enfeoffed as a marquis due to his relation to Emperor Xuān's grandmother's family,
with a fief of two thousand six hundred households,
and was a cousin of Marquis Píngtái.
Zǐhuí's wife Yìjūn,
formerly a granddaughter of a prince,
was jealous,
and strangled over forty servant girls to death,
and secretly cut off the arms and knees of women who had just given birth for use in witchcraft to gain favor.
This was reported to the throne by someone,
and she was sentenced to public execution.
Zǐhuí, because of his relation to the imperial family,
did not lose his marquis title.||
Píngtái: Shǐ Zǐshū.
He was enfeoffed as a marquis due to his relation to Emperor Xuān's grandmother's family,
with a fief of two thousand five hundred households.
During the time of Crown Prince Wèi,
the Shǐ family had one daughter enter the palace for the Crown Prince,
and married another daughter to the Prince of Lǔ,
so now the Prince of Lǔ is also a grandson of the Shǐ family.
Having kinship with the imperial family,
they were therefore noble,
and repeatedly received rewards.||
Lèlíng: Shǐ Zǐcháng.
He was noble due to his relation to Emperor Xuān's grandmother's family,
served as a Palace Attendant,
and was dignified, sincere, and loyal.
For uncovering the plot of the Huò family to rebel,
he was enfeoffed with three thousand five hundred households.
Bóchéng | Zhāng Zhāng,
whose father was originally from Yǐngchuān,
served as a village head in Cháng'ān.
After losing his position,
he went to the northern gate to submit a memorial,
staying at the residence of the Huò family,
sleeping by the horse's stables.
At night, he overheard the stable servants talking,
discussing the conspiracy of rebellion by the descendants of the Huò family.
He then submitted a memorial to report the rebellion,
and became a marquis,
with a fief of three thousand households. ||
Dūchéng | Jīn Ānshàng,
originally from the Xiōngnú.
Because he exposed the plot of rebellion by Huò Guāng's son, Yǔ, and others,
he was made a marquis,
with a fief of two thousand eight hundred households.
Ānshàng, being
the noble carriage captain and Dù Hou's descendant,
behaved cautiously and virtuously,
maintaining oneself with humility,
hoping to pass down his accomplishments and virtues to his descendants. ||
Píngtōng | Yáng Yùn,
whose family was in Huáyīn,
was the youngest son of former Chancellor Yáng Chǎng,
and served as a gentleman.
He appreciated scholars,
and prided himself on understanding people,
always expressing goodwill among the people.
Because of this, Dǒng Zhōng, the Marquis of Gāochāng, privately confided in him,
reporting the conspiracy of the Huò family,
and jointly disclosed the rebellion to gain the marquis title,
with two thousand households,
and served as Guanglu official.
In the fourth year of Wǔfèng,
due to making heretical statements,
he was executed for treason,
and his state was abolished. ||
Gāochāng | Dǒng Zhōng,
whose father was originally from Yangzhai in Yǐngchuān,
studied literary arts and went to Cháng'ān.
Zhōng possessed talent and strength,
was skilled in horse riding and archery,
and used short weapons,
serving in the imperial gates.
Knowing Zhāng Zhāng,
Zhāng informed Zhōng of Huò Yǔ's rebellion,
and Zhōng informed the regular attendant Yáng Yùn,
exposing the plot to become marquis,
with two thousand households.
Currently serving as an eagle rider captain,
and attending to the emperor.
He was punished for using a small carriage to perform sacrifices at the ancestral temple,
losing one hundred households. ||
Yuánqī | Zhào Chéng.
By discovering a matter in the state of Chǔ, he became a marquis,
with two thousand three hundred households.
In the first year of Dìjié,
the King of Chǔ conspired with the King of Guǎnglíng,
and Chéng uncovered the rebellion,
the emperor commended his virtue and loyalty,
issuing an edict stating
"Do not prosecute the King of Guǎnglíng,"
and Guǎnglíng remained unchanged.
Later accused of wicked incantations and having his state abolished,
he committed suicide,
and his state was annulled.
The current emperor reestablished his son as the King of Guǎnglíng. ||
Cuān | In the third year of Dìjié,
the emperor issued an edict stating:
"I have heard that at the rise of the Hàn,
the Chancellor Xiāo Hé had the greatest achievements,
but now his lineage has ended,
which I deeply pity,
thus we will grant a fief of three thousand households to Xiāo Hé's great-grandson Jiànshì as the Marquis of Cuān." ||
Píngchāng | Wáng Zhǎngjūn,
whose family resided in the State of Zhào,
from Chángshān Guǎngwàng.
In the time of the Crown Prince,
she is married into the Crown Prince's household,
serving as the Crown Prince's female historian consort,
giving birth to a son,
without further communication.
After more than forty years,
until the first year of Yuánkāng,
she was summoned by edict,
established as a marquis,
with five thousand households.
She is the uncle of Emperor Xuān. ||
Lèchāng | Wáng Zhìjūn,
whose home was in the State of Zhào,
from Chángshān Guǎngwàng.
As the external family of the emperor's maternal uncle,
granted a fief of five thousand households.
He is the brother of the Marquis of Píngchāng, Wáng Zhǎngjūn. ||
Qióngchéng | Wáng Fèngguāng,
whose family was in Fánglíng.
With his daughter established as the empress,
received a fief of fifteen hundred households.
It is said that at Fèngguāng's birth,
celestial light was seen above,
leading some to believe he was destined to nobility.
Ultimately, he became marquis because of his daughter. ||
Ānyuǎn | Zhèng Jí,
whose family was in Kuàijī.
Rising from a common soldier to serve in the army as a gentleman,
tasked with escorting and overseeing prisoners to Tiánqúlí.
During the death of the Xiōngnú chanyu,
the state was in turmoil,
with internal conflicts,
the Sunzhú King leading the people surrendered to the Hàn,
seeking Jí’s assistance first,
Jí led several hundred officers and soldiers to welcome them.
Some had thoughts of returning,
but those leaders were executed,
ultimately bringing them into Hàn.
With military achievements became marquis,
with two thousand households. ||
Bóyáng | Bǐng Jí,
whose home was in Lǔ.
Initially working on litigations as an associate censor,
serving in the Grand General's office.
Always extending past favors to Emperor Xuān,
he was promoted to Imperial Censor,
and became marquis,
with two thousand households.
In the second year of Shénjué,
he replaced Wèi Xiāng as Chancellor.
Served for five years,
then died of illness.
His son, Wēngmèng, succeeded him,
becoming a general,
and attendant to the emperor.
In the first year of Sweet Dew,
he was punished for riding to the temple gate instead of using a large carriage during temple sacrifices,
receiving punishment,
losing his title,
and was demoted to an internal marquis. ||
Jiànchéng | Huáng Bà,
whose family resided in Yángxià,
and relocated to Yúnyáng due to labor duties.
As an honest official became the county defender of Hénèi,
later promoted to chief judge,
and acting position as long history of the Chancellor.
Accused of disrespectful misconduct due to knowing Xiàhóu Shèng,
and endured a long imprisonment of three years,
learning the Book of Documents from Shèng.
Pardoned,
he was recognized for virtue and appointed governor of Yángzhōu,
and Prefect of Yǐngchuān.
Promoted good governance,
separated men and women's pathways,
farmers respectfully shared field borders,
awarded one hundred jin of gold,
with an official rank of two thousand dàn.
Lived in Yǐngchuān,
served as the grand tutor of the crown prince,
and became Imperial Censor.
In the third year of Wǔfèng,
replaced Bǐng Jí as Chancellor,
with one thousand eight hundred households. ||
Xīpíng | Yú Dìngguó,
whose home was in Dōnghǎi.
Initially working on legal cases as a court historian,
gradually promoted to associate imperial censor.
Submitted a memorial to admonish the King of Chāngyì,
promoted to Guanglu noble,
and became Chief Judge.
Learned from masters of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
transformed the path and promoted virtue,
meticulously caring for people.
Promoted to Imperial Censor,
replacing Huáng Bà as Chancellor. |
Documenting the appointees during the reign of Emperor Xiāoxuān |
Yángpíng | Wáng Zhìjūn,
whose family was in Wèijùn.
Former chancellor historian.
His daughter became the Crown Prince’s consort.
The Crown Prince ascended as emperor,
and his daughter became empress,
thus marquis,
with one thousand two hundred households.
Since Yuánchuān,
he was influential during flourishing times,
many seeking official posts in the capital city relied on his influence,
though his wise strategies and achievements were rarely mentioned beyond state affairs. |
Imperial edict to the Censorate:
"If any vassal princes wish to confer personal favors by dividing their fiefs among their kin,
they must submit each case,
and I will personally determine their titles."
The Grand Historian remarks:
How magnificent is
the virtue of the Son of Heaven!
When one man has cause for celebration,
the whole realm relies on it.|

The Grand Historian said:
"Ah, the splendid virtue!
Governing all things,
employing the masses,
how could it be merely human effort?
When I reached the grand official of rites,
I observed the gains and losses of the Three Dynasties,
and then I understood that ritual was formed according to human sentiment,
and according to human nature, rituals were devised,
its origin is ancient indeed.
The human way is vast,
rules and standards apply uniformly,
guiding with benevolence and righteousness,
restraining with punishment and laws,
therefore, those with great virtue have high positions,
and those with rich remuneration have honor and glory,
this is how the unified realm is governed and the people harmonized.
Human bodies enjoy comfort in rides,
thus they create golden carriages to enhance the embellishments;
eyes delight in colors,
thus they create embroidered patterns to show talent;
ears find music in bells and chimes pleasant,
thus they harmonize the eight tones to soothe the heart;
tongues savor the five flavors,
thus they prepare sour and salty dishes to attain beauty;
emotions like precious and good things,
thus they carve jade disks to convey meaning.
Therefore, the main path crosses the seat mats,
leather caps and cloth skirts,
red strings delve and penetrate,
great broth and black wine,
thus preventing excess,
saving it from decay and decline.
Therefore, the order of ruler and subject at court, high and low,
extends to the people's carriages, garments, houses, food, marriage, and funerary and sacrificial rites,
things are fitting in their occasions,
and objects follow regulation.
Confucius said,
'From the completion of the libation ceremony onwards,
I did not wish to view it anymore.' "
As the Zhōu dynasty declined,
rites and music fell into disuse and ruin,
with the great and small overstepping their bounds.
In the household of Guǎn Zhòng,
he possessed the three returns concurrently.
Those who followed the laws and upheld righteousness were insulted by the world,
while the extravagant and presumptuous were called illustrious and honored.
Even Zǐxià,
the most highly accomplished among the disciples,
still said,
"When I go out and see the splendor and magnificence, I am pleased;
when I come in and hear the Master's Way, I am joyful.
These two contend in my heart,
and I have not been able to decide for myself."
How much more so for those below the mediocre,
gradually steeped in lack of instruction,
and clad in established customs?
Confucius said,
"What is necessary is to rectify names,"
but in Wèi, he found no agreement.
After Confucius passed away,
his disciples who had received his teachings sank into obscurity and were not promoted.
Some went to Qí or Chǔ,
others entered the rivers and seas.
Is this not grievous!
When Qín possessed the empire,
it incorporated all the rites and ceremonies of the six states,
selecting the good among them.
Although they did not match the sage's institutions,
their emphasis on honoring the ruler and restraining the ministers,
and the dignified atmosphere of the court,
followed ancient traditions.
By the time of Gāozǔ,
who brilliantly held the four seas,
Shūsūn Tōng made some additions and subtractions,
but largely followed Qín's old practices.
From the designations of the Son of Heaven down to the assistants and officials, and the names of palaces and offices,
there were few changes.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
the officials proposed to establish ceremonial rites,
but Emperor Wén favored the teachings of the Daoists,
believing that elaborate rites and adorned appearances
were of no benefit to governance.
He thought personal transformation was what mattered,
so he dismissed the proposals.
During Emperor Jǐng's time,
the Imperial Censor Cháo Cuò, well-versed in administrative affairs and legalist doctrines,
repeatedly remonstrated with Emperor Jǐng, saying:
"The feudal lords are protective barriers,
and ministers and sons are of one kind—
this is the system of past and present.
Now the great states exclusively govern with different policies,
not reporting to the capital.
I fear this cannot be passed on to posterity."
Emperor Jǐng employed his strategy,
and the six states rebelled,
naming Cuò as the primary culprit.
The Son of Heaven executed Cuò to resolve the crisis.
The events are recorded in the account of Yuán Àng.
After this, officials merely cultivated connections and secured their emoluments,
with none daring to propose further discussions.
When the current emperor ascended the throne,
he summoned scholars of Confucian learning,
ordering them to jointly establish ceremonies,
but over ten years passed without completion.
Some said that in ancient times of great peace,
when the myriad people were harmonious and joyful,
and auspicious responses clearly arrived,
then customs were gathered,
and institutions were established.
The emperor heard this
and issued an edict to the Imperial Censor, saying:
"Those who receive the mandate and become kings
each have their own ways of rise,
different paths but the same destination,
meaning they act according to the people,
and create institutions following customs.
The discussers all praise high antiquity,
but what do the common people hope for?
Hàn is also one family's affair;
if the statutes and laws are not transmitted,
what will be said to our descendants?
Those with profound transformation are broad and extensive;
those with shallow governance are narrow and limited.
Should we not strive!"
Thus, in the first year of Tàichū, the calendar was reformed,
the color of garments changed,
Tàishān was fēnged,
and the ceremonies for the ancestral temple and all officials were established,
to serve as constant standards,
handed down to posterity.
Rites arise from human nature.
Humans are born with desires;
if desires are not fulfilled, there cannot be no resentment;
if resentment has no measure, there is conflict;
conflict leads to chaos.
The former kings detested such chaos,
so they established ritual principles to nurture human desires,
and supply human needs,
ensuring that desires are not exhausted by things,
and things are not depleted by desires.
The two support each other and grow;
this is the origin of rites.
Thus, rites are for nurturing.
Grains and the five flavors
are to nourish the mouth;
pepper, orchids, and fragrant herbs
are to nourish the nose;
bells, drums, pipes, and strings
are to nourish the ears;
carvings and patterns
are to nourish the eyes;
spacious rooms, beds, mats, and tables
are to nourish the body:
thus, rites are for nurturing.
The gentleman, having obtained this nurturing,
also values its distinctions.
The so-called distinctions mean
the noble and humble have their ranks,
the old and young have their differences,
and the rich and poor, light and heavy, all have their correspondences.
Thus, the Son of Heaven's great carriage with rush mats
is to nourish the body;
the fragrant herbs placed beside
are to nourish the nose;
the adorned crossbar in front
is to nourish the eyes;
the harmonious bells,
with steps matching "Wǔ Xiàng,"
and gallops matching "Sháo Huò,"
are to nourish the ears;
the dragon banner with nine tassels
is to nourish trust;
the recumbent rhinoceros and gripping tiger,
with shark-skin bridles and dragon-adorned yokes,
are to nourish authority.
Thus, the horses for the great carriage
must be truly well-trained and obedient,
only then are they mounted,
to ensure safety.
Who knows that risking death for essential integrity is to nurture life?
Who knows that light spending is to nurture wealth?
Who knows that reverence, respect, deference, and yielding are to nurture safety?
Who knows that ritual principles and refined patterns are to nurture emotions?
If a person only sees life,
such a one will surely die;
if only seeing profit,
such a one will surely be harmed;
if taking laziness as peace,
such a one will surely face danger;
if letting emotions prevail as peace,
such a one will surely be destroyed.
Therefore, the sage unifies them with ritual principles,
and both are attained;
if unified with emotions and nature,
then both are lost.
Thus, the Confucians aim to enable people to attain both,
while the Mohists lead people to lose both.
This is the distinction between Confucians and Mohists.
It is the ultimate means of governance,
the foundation of strength and stability,
the way to assert authority,
and the summation of achievements and fame.
When kings and lords follow it,
they unify the world,
subjugating the feudal lords;
if they do not follow it,
they bring ruin to the state.
Thus, sturdy armor and sharp weapons are not enough to ensure victory,
high walls and deep moats are not enough to guarantee security,
harsh commands and numerous punishments are not enough to establish authority.
Following the right path leads to success,
while straying from it results in failure.
The people of Chǔ used shark skin, rhinoceros, and wild ox hides
to make armor,
as hard as metal or stone;
with the great iron of Wǎn,
their weapons were as piercing as bee or scorpion stings,
light and swift,
their troops moving like a whirlwind.
Yet their army was defeated at Chuíshè,
where Táng Mèi died;
when Zhuāng Qiāo rose up,
Chǔ was divided into three or four parts.
Was this due to a lack of sturdy armor or sharp weapons?
It was because they did not govern by the right path.
They relied on the Rǔ and Yǐng rivers as natural barriers,
the Jiāng and Hàn rivers as moats,
blocked by the Dèng Forest,
and bordered by the Fángchéng walls.
Yet when the Qín army reached Yānyǐng,
they captured it as easily as shaking dry leaves.
Was this due to a lack of strong defenses or natural obstacles?
It was because they did not govern by the right path.
King Zhòu cut out Bǐ Gān's heart,
imprisoned Jīzǐ,
created the roasting pillar punishment,
and executed the innocent,
so that his ministers trembled with fear,
uncertain of their lives.
Yet when the Zhōu army arrived,
his orders were not obeyed below,
and he could not command his people.
Was this due to lenient commands
or light punishments?
It was because he did not govern by the right path.
In ancient times,
weapons were merely spears, halberds, bows, and arrows,
yet enemy states submitted without a trial of strength.
City walls were not built,
moats were not dug,
fortresses were not erected,
and traps were not set,
yet the state remained secure and unafraid of external threats,
for no other reason
than that the Way was clear and benefits were shared fairly,
with timely labor and genuine care for the people,
so that the lower ranks responded like shadows and echoes.
If anyone disobeyed orders,
only then were punishments applied,
and the people understood their guilt.
Thus, punishing one person made the whole world submit.
The guilty did not blame their superiors,
knowing the fault lay with themselves.
Therefore, punishments were minimal yet authority flowed like a stream,
for no other reason
than following the right path.
So, following the Way leads to success,
while straying from it leads to failure.
In ancient times, when Emperor Yáo governed the world,
he executed one person and punished two, and the world was well-ordered.
The texts say:
"Authority is stern yet untested,
punishments are in place but unused."
Heaven and Earth are
the root of life;
ancestors are
the root of kinship;
rulers and teachers are
the root of governance.
Without Heaven and Earth, how could life exist?
Without ancestors, how could we emerge?
Without rulers and teachers, how could there be order?
If any of these three is neglected,
there will be no peace for humanity.
Thus, in rites,
we serve Heaven above,
Earth below,
honor ancestors, and revere rulers and teachers—
these are the three roots of ritual.
Hence, the king honors Heaven and the founding ancestor,
feudal lords do not presume,
officials and scholars have their constant lineages,
thereby distinguishing noble from base.
When nobility and baseness are properly ordered,
the foundation is secured.
The suburban sacrifice is reserved for the Son of Heaven,
the earth altar extends to feudal lords,
and includes officials and scholars,
distinguishing how the honored serve the honored,
the humble serve the humble,
with grandness where it is fitting,
and modesty where it is appropriate.
Thus, those who rule all under Heaven sacrifice to seven generations,
those with a state sacrifice to five,
those with land for five chariots sacrifice to three,
those with land for three chariots sacrifice to two,
and those who eat only simple offerings may not establish ancestral temples,
thereby showing that deep accumulation leads to widespread blessings,
while shallow accumulation leads to narrow blessings.
In the great feast, the dark vessel is elevated,
the sacrificial stand offers raw fish,
beginning with the grand broth,
honoring the origins of food and drink.
The great feast elevates the dark vessel yet uses light wine,
serves millet and sorghum before rice and fine grains,
offers a taste of the grand broth before enjoying various delicacies,
valuing the roots while embracing practical use.
Valuing the roots is called refinement,
embracing practical use is called principle,
the two combine to form culture,
returning to the Great One,
which is called the great exaltation.
Thus, elevating the dark vessel,
the stand with raw fish,
and the bowl with the grand broth first
are one in essence.
The ritual cup is not sipped,
the completed sacrifice is not tasted from the stand,
the three exhortations are not eaten,
the great marriage has not abandoned fasting,
the great temple has not received the effigy,
at death, the initial cessation has not undergone the minor dressing—
these are one in principle.
The plain canopy of the great carriage,
the hemp crown of the suburban sacrifice,
the mourning clothes starting with loose hemp—
these are one in spirit.
The three-year mourning without restraint in weeping,
the "Qīng Miào" song sung once with three responses,
a single bell hung, still struck on the frame,
red strings with open holes—
these are one in essence.
All rites begin with simplicity,
develop into refinement,
and end with ease.
Thus, at their most complete,
both emotion and form are fully expressed;
next,
emotion and form alternate in dominance;
at the lowest,
emotion is restored to return to the Great One.
Heaven and Earth are harmonized,
sun and moon are brightened,
the four seasons follow in order,
stars and planets move in course,
rivers flow,
all things flourish,
likes and dislikes are moderated,
joy and anger are appropriate.
Applied below, it brings obedience;
applied above, it brings clarity.
The Grand Historian says:
How perfect it is!
Establishing the exalted as the ultimate standard,
so that nothing in the world can add or subtract from it.
Root and branch follow in sequence,
end and beginning respond to each other,
the most refined has means to distinguish,
the most discerning has means to persuade.
Those in the world who follow it achieve order,
those who do not fall into chaos;
followers find peace,
non-followers face danger.
Petty men cannot emulate it.
The appearance of ritual is indeed profound;
the subtleties of hardness and whiteness, sameness and difference,
enter into it and are weakened.
Its appearance is indeed grand;
the doctrines of those who presumptuously create canons and institutions, narrow and shallow,
enter into it and are diminished.
Its appearance is indeed lofty;
the violent, arrogant, unrestrained, and reckless,
those who despise custom and consider themselves lofty,
enter into it and fall.
Thus, if the marking line is truly laid out,
one cannot be deceived about straightness and crookedness;
if the balance is truly suspended,
one cannot be deceived about lightness and heaviness;
if the compass and square are truly set,
one cannot be deceived about squareness and roundness;
if the gentleman examines ritual,
he cannot be deceived by fraud and deceit.
Therefore, the marking line
is the ultimate in straightness;
the balance
is the ultimate in fairness;
the compass and square
are the ultimate in squareness and roundness;
ritual
is the ultimate of the human way.
However, those who do not model themselves on ritual are insufficient in ritual,
and are called people without a proper path;
those who model themselves on ritual and are sufficient in ritual
are called scholars with a proper path.
Within ritual,
being able to think and reflect
is called being able to deliberate;
being able to deliberate without changing
is called being able to be firm.
Being able to deliberate and be firm,
and adding a love for it,
is sagehood.
Heaven
is the ultimate in height;
earth
is the ultimate in depth;
the sun and moon
are the ultimate in brightness;
the boundless
is the ultimate in vastness;
the sage
is the ultimate of the Way.
Using material goods for practical purposes,
using nobility and baseness for ornamentation,
using abundance and scarcity for differentiation,
using richness and reduction as the essential.
When ornamentation and appearance are elaborate,
and desires and emotions are restrained,
that is the richness of ritual;
when ornamentation and appearance are restrained,
and desires and emotions are elaborate,
that is the reduction of ritual;
when ornamentation, appearance, desires, and emotions serve as inner and outer, surface and core,
proceeding together and intermingling,
that is the middle course of ritual.
The gentleman, in its highest form, attains its richness,
in its lowest form, exhausts its reduction,
and in the middle, dwells in its mean.
Whether walking slowly, galloping, or roaming widely, he does not go beyond it;
thus, the nature of the gentleman is guarded within the palace courtyard.
One whose domain is this domain
is a scholar-gentleman.
Outside of this,
is a common person.
Within this,
roaming and circulating comprehensively,
perfectly attaining its sequence and order,
is a sage.
Therefore, thickness
is the accumulation of ritual;
greatness
is the breadth of ritual;
height
is the richness of ritual;
brightness
is the completeness of ritual.
The Grand Historian says:
Whenever I read the *Yú Shū*,
and come to where ruler and ministers admonished each other,
striving for stability and security,
yet the assistants were not good,
and all affairs crumbled and were ruined,
I have never failed to shed tears.
King Chéng composed odes,
reflecting on himself to correct his faults,
lamenting the troubles of that family—
can it not be said that he was trembling with fear,
good at preserving and good at ending well?
The gentleman, when not constrained, cultivates virtue;
when full, he abandons ritual.
In ease, he can think of the beginning;
in comfort, he can remember the start.
Bathing in rich blessings yet singing of toil and hardship—
who but one of great virtue could be like this!
The *Zhuàn* says:
"When governance is settled and achievements are complete,
ritual and music then flourish."
Within the seas, the human way grows deeper,
its virtue becomes more ultimate,
and what brings joy becomes more diverse.
Fullness without reduction leads to overflow;
fullness without restraint leads to collapse.
Generally, those who create music
do so to regulate joy.
The gentleman takes humility and yielding as ritual,
and takes reduction and decrease as music,
finding joy in being so.
Considering that regions differ and states vary,
and emotions and customs are not the same,
therefore they broadly collected customs,
harmonized and compared tones and pitches,
to remedy shortcomings and transform,
aiding the dissemination of governance and teaching.
The Son of Heaven personally attended the Bright Hall to observe,
and all the people were cleansed of depravity and filth,
moderated and filled,
to adorn their nature.
Thus it is said that when the tones of the *Yǎ* and *Sòng* are ordered, the people are rectified;
when the sounds of shouts and cries arise, the officers are roused;
when the tunes of Zhèng and Wèi move, hearts become licentious.
And when they are harmonized and attuned,
even birds and beasts are fully affected—
how much more those who embrace the five constants,
harbor likes and dislikes—
is this not the natural tendency?
When the way of governance was deficient and defective, the music of Zhèng arose.
Feudal lords and hereditary rulers,
famous and prominent in neighboring regions,
competed to surpass each other.
Since even Zhòngní could not allow the entertainers of Qí to be accommodated in Lǔ,
and though he withdrew to rectify music to guide the age,
composing five stanzas to criticize the times,
still he could not transform them.
Decline continued until the Six States,
indulging in dissipation and drowning in excess,
they proceeded onward without return,
ending in the loss of life and destruction of clans,
and the states were annexed by Qín.
The Second Emperor of Qín especially considered this entertaining.
Chéngxiàng Lǐ Sī offered admonition, saying:
"Abandoning the *Shī* and *Shū*,
indulging to the utmost in music and beauty—
this is what Zǔ Yǐ feared;
neglecting the accumulation of minor faults,
indulging the heart through long nights—
this is why Zhòu perished."
Zhào Gāo said:
"The music of the Five Emperors
and Three Kings each had different names,
showing they did not follow one another.
From the court above
to the people below,
they were able to connect in joy,
unite in earnestness.
Without this, harmony and delight would not circulate,
favor and grace would not flow.
Each also had the transformation of its own age,
the music fitting its time.
Why must one have the Lù'ěr steed of Huà Shān to travel far?"
The Second Emperor agreed with him.
Gāozǔ, passing through Pèi, composed the poem "The Chapter of the Three Marquises,"
and had children sing it.
When Gāozǔ passed away,
he ordered that Pèi could sing and dance it in the ancestral temple throughout the four seasons.
Xiàohuì,
Xiàowén,
and Xiàojǐng made no additions or changes,
only practicing the usual and rehearsing the old in the Music Bureau.
Up to the present emperor's accession,
he composed nineteen stanzas,
ordering the Attendant-in-Ordinary Lǐ Yánnián to arrange their tones in order,
and appointing him as Commandant of Harmonious Pitch.
Scholars versed in a single classic could not alone understand the words;
they all gathered the experts of the *Five Classics*,
together discussing, studying, and reading them,
only then could they fully comprehend the meaning,
which contained much elegant language.
The Hàn court often offered sacrifices to the Great One at Gānquán on the first xīn day of the first month,
beginning the ceremony at dusk
and continuing until dawn.
Frequently, meteors would pass over the sacrificial altar.
Seventy boys and girls were employed to sing in unison.
In spring, they sang "Qīngyáng";
in summer, "Zhūmíng";
in autumn, "Xīhào";
in winter, "Xuánmíng."
These songs are widely known,
so they need not be discussed here.
Moreover, when a divine horse was obtained from the waters of Wòwā,
it was commemorated in the "Song of the Great One."
The lyrics said:
"The Great One presents us, a heavenly steed descends,
Drenched in crimson sweat, frothing a ruddy flow.
Galloping with ease, it strides ten thousand miles;
Now what can match it? Only the dragon as its friend."
Later, when the expedition against Dàyuān brought back a thousand-mile horse,
named Púshāo,
another song was composed.
The verse read:
"The heavenly horse comes from the western extreme,
Traversing ten thousand miles to a virtuous ruler.
Bearing divine might, it subdues foreign lands,
Crossing flowing sands, all tribes submit."
Commandant of the Palace Guard Jí Àn remonstrated:
"When a king creates music,
it should honor the ancestors above
and educate the masses below.
Now that Your Majesty has acquired horses,
you compose verses about them
and perform them in the ancestral temple.
How could the former emperors and the common people understand such music?"
The emperor fell silent and displeased.
Chancellor Gōngsūn Hóng said:
"Jí Àn slanders the imperial creation
and deserves execution with his clan."
All music arises
from the human mind.
The stirrings of the mind
are caused by external things.
Moved by things, it stirs,
thus manifesting in sound;
sounds respond to each other,
producing variations;
when variations form patterns,
it is called music;
setting music to notes,
along with shields, axes, feathers, and plumes,
is called performance.
Performance is
what gives rise to music,
its root lying in the mind being moved by things.
Thus, when moved by sorrow,
the sound is anxious and cut short;
when moved by joy,
the sound is expansive and relaxed;
when moved by delight,
the sound is exuberant and free;
when moved by anger,
the sound is harsh and fierce;
when moved by reverence,
the sound is straightforward and pure;
when moved by love,
the sound is harmonious and gentle.
These six are not innate
but arise from being moved by things;
thus, the ancient kings were cautious about what influenced them.
Hence, rites guided their will,
music harmonized their sounds,
governance unified their conduct,
and punishments prevented their crimes.
Rites, music, punishments, and governance
share the same ultimate goal:
to unite the people's hearts and achieve order.
All music
is born of the human mind.
When emotions stir within,
they take form in sound;
when sounds are patterned, it is called music.
Thus, the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
reflecting harmony;
the music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
reflecting discord;
the music of a fallen state is sorrowful and pensive,
reflecting the people's hardship.
The way of sound and music
is interconnected with governance.
The gōng note represents the ruler,
the shāng note the ministers,
the jué note the people,
the zhǐ note affairs,
and the yǔ note things.
If these five are not disordered,
there will be no discordant music.
If gōng is disordered, it becomes wild,
indicating the ruler's arrogance;
if shāng is disordered, it becomes erratic,
indicating the ministers' corruption;
if jué is disordered, it becomes mournful,
indicating the people's resentment;
if zhǐ is disordered, it becomes sorrowful,
indicating excessive toil in affairs;
if yǔ is disordered, it becomes perilous,
indicating scarcity of resources.
If all five are disordered,
overwhelming each other,
it is called decadence.
Then the state's destruction is imminent.
The music of Zhèng and Wèi
is that of a chaotic age,
akin to decadence.
The music of Sāngjiān and Púshàng
is that of a fallen state,
where governance is lax,
the people are adrift,
and deceit against superiors and selfishness run rampant unchecked.
All music
is born of the human mind;
performance
connects with ethical principles.
Thus, those who know sound but not music
are like beasts;
those who know music but not performance
are the common folk.
Only the noble person can understand performance.
Hence, by examining sound, one knows music;
by examining music, one knows performance;
by examining performance, one knows governance,
and the way to order is complete.
Thus, one who does not understand sound cannot discuss music;
one who does not understand music cannot discuss performance.
Understanding performance brings one close to rites.
Mastery of both rites and music
is called virtue.
Virtue means attainment.
Therefore, the grandeur of performance
does not lie in extreme sounds;
the rites of feasting
do not seek the utmost flavors.
The zither in the Qīngmiào temple,
with vermilion strings and wide sound holes,
one lead singer and three responders,
leaves a lingering resonance.
In the grand feast rites,
plain water is honored and raw fish offered,
the great broth unseasoned,
leaving a lingering taste.
Thus, when the ancient kings instituted rites and music,
it was not to indulge the desires of mouth, belly, ears, and eyes,
but to teach the people to balance likes and dislikes and return to the proper way of humanity.
Humans are born tranquil,
which is their heavenly nature;
moved by things, they act,
which is the expression of their nature.
When things arrive, knowledge perceives them,
and then likes and dislikes take form.
If likes and dislikes are unregulated within,
and knowledge is lured from without,
unable to return to oneself,
the heavenly principle is extinguished.
Since things endlessly stimulate humans,
and human likes and dislikes are unregulated,
then when things come, humans become transformed by them.
To be transformed by things
is to destroy the heavenly principle and indulge human desires.
Then arise rebellious, deceitful, and hypocritical hearts,
and licentious, disorderly deeds.
Thus, the strong oppress the weak,
the many brutalize the few,
the cunning deceive the simple,
the brave torment the timid,
the sick go uncared for,
the old, young, orphaned, and widowed find no place,
this is the path to great chaos.
Therefore, the ancient kings instituted rites and music
to provide human regulation:
mourning garments and weeping
regulate funeral observances;
bells, drums, shields, and axes
harmonize joy and peace;
marriage and coming-of-age ceremonies
distinguish male and female;
archery, village banquets, and feasts
rectify social interactions.
Rites regulate the people's hearts,
music harmonizes the people's voices,
governance puts them into practice,
punishments prevent their abuse.
When rites, music, punishments, and governance permeate all without conflict,
then the kingly way is complete.
Music unifies,
while rites differentiate.
Unity fosters affection,
differentiation cultivates respect.
Excessive music leads to dissipation,
excessive rites create alienation.
Harmonizing emotions and refining appearances
are the functions of rites and music.
When ritual principles are established,
noble and humble are distinguished;
when musical patterns are unified,
superior and inferior harmonize;
when preferences and aversions are clear,
the worthy and unworthy are distinguished;
punishments restrain violence,
titles promote the worthy,
then governance becomes balanced.
Benevolence to love them,
righteousness to correct them,
thus the people's governance is implemented.
Music emerges from within,
rites operate from without.
Music emerging from within
brings tranquility;
rites operating from without
create refinement.
Great music must be simple,
great rites must be concise.
Perfect music eliminates resentment,
perfect rites prevent conflict.
Governing the world through courtesy and deference
refers to rites and music.
When violent people do not arise,
feudal lords submit,
weapons remain unused,
five punishments need not be applied,
the common people have no troubles,
the Son of Heaven shows no anger,
thus music achieves its purpose.
Uniting the affection between father and son,
clarifying the order between elder and younger,
to show respect throughout the world.
When the Son of Heaven acts thus,
rites are implemented.
Great music harmonizes with heaven and earth,
great rites follow the rhythms of heaven and earth.
Harmony ensures nothing is lost;
rhythm enables worship of heaven and earth.
In the visible realm there are rites and music,
in the invisible realm there are spirits and deities,
thus the world shares respect and love.
Rites
distinguish affairs to unite respect;
music
varies patterns to unite love.
The essence of rites and music being the same,
enlightened kings therefore continue their tradition.
Thus affairs align with the times,
names correspond to achievements.
Therefore bells, drums, pipes, chimes, feather ornaments, shields, and axes
are instruments of music;
bending, stretching, bowing, rising, formations, and tempos
are patterns of music.
Food vessels, sacrificial utensils, regulations, and decorations
are instruments of rites;
ascending, descending, circling, and changing ceremonial robes
are patterns of rites.
Thus those who understand the essence of rites and music can create them,
those who recognize the patterns of rites and music can transmit them.
Creators are called sagely,
transmitters are called enlightened.
Enlightened and sagely
refer to transmission and creation.
Music
represents the harmony of heaven and earth;
rites
represent the order of heaven and earth.
Harmony makes all things transform;
order makes all things distinct.
Music originates from heaven,
rites are modeled on earth.
Excessive regulation causes chaos,
excessive creation leads to violence.
Understanding heaven and earth,
one can then promote rites and music.
Perfect harmony without harm
is the essence of music;
joyful delight and loving affection
are the function of music.
Uprightness without deviation
is the substance of rites;
dignity, reverence, respect, and compliance
are the regulation of rites.
As for applying rites and music through metal and stone instruments,
expressing them through sounds,
using them in ancestral temples and state altars,
serving mountain, river, and ancestral spirits,
this is how they are shared with the people.
When kings achieve merit, they create music;
when governance is stabilized, they establish rites.
Greater merit yields more complete music;
more orderly governance yields more完备 rites.
Dances with shields and axes
do not constitute complete music;
offering cooked sacrifices
does not constitute perfect rites.
The Five Emperors had different eras,
and did not continue each other's music;
the Three Kings had different ages,
and did not copy each other's rites.
Extreme music leads to worry,
crude rites lead to bias.
As for achieving rich music without worry,
complete rites without bias,
is this not only for the great sages?
Heaven above, earth below,
all things scattered and distinct,
thus rites are implemented;
flowing unceasingly,
uniting and transforming,
thus music arises.
Spring sowing and summer growth
represent benevolence;
autumn harvest and winter storage
represent righteousness.
Benevolence approximates music,
righteousness approximates rites.
Music promotes harmony,
following the divine nature of heaven;
rites distinguish appropriateness,
following the spiritual nature of earth.
Therefore sages create music to correspond with heaven,
establish rites to match earth.
When rites and music are clear and complete,
heaven and earth fulfill their functions.
Heaven honored, earth humble,
so ruler and minister are fixed.
High and low being displayed,
noble and humble are positioned.
Movement and stillness having constancy,
great and small are distinguished.
Things gather by category,
beings divide by group,
thus their natures differ.
In heaven forming images,
on earth forming shapes,
thus rites represent the distinctions of heaven and earth.
Earth's energy rising,
heaven's energy descending,
yin and yang rubbing together,
heaven and earth interacting,
stirred by thunder,
aroused by wind and rain,
moved by the four seasons,
warmed by sun and moon,
thus all transformations arise,
and music represents the harmony of heaven and earth.
Untimely transformation yields no growth,
indistinct genders lead to disorder,
this is the nature of heaven and earth.
When rites and music reach to heaven and spread through earth,
operate through yin and yang and communicate with spirits,
penetrating the highest and deepest, measuring the profound,
music manifests the primal beginning while rites reside in completed things.
Manifesting ceaseless movement is heaven,
manifesting stillness is earth.
One moving, one still
—this is the space between heaven and earth.
Therefore the sage says
"such are rites, such is music."
In ancient times, Shùn created the five-stringed qín,
to sing the "Southern Wind";
Kuí began to compose music,
to reward the feudal lords.
Thus, when the Son of Heaven creates music,
it is to reward those feudal lords who possess virtue.
When virtue flourishes and teachings are revered,
and the five grains ripen in season,
only then are they rewarded with music.
Therefore, those who govern with toil for the people,
their dance formations have long rows;
those who govern with ease for the people,
their dance formations have short rows.
Thus, by observing their dance, one knows their virtue;
by hearing their posthumous title, one knows their conduct.
"Dà Zhāng"
is to manifest it;
"Xián Chí"
is to be complete;
"Sháo"
is to continue;
"Xià"
is to be great;
the music of Yīn and Zhōu is exhaustive.
The way of heaven and earth:
if cold and heat are untimely, illness arises;
if wind and rain are unregulated, famine occurs.
Teachings
are the cold and heat for the people;
if teachings are untimely, they harm the world.
Affairs
are the wind and rain for the people;
if affairs are unregulated, they achieve no success.
Thus, when the ancient kings created music,
it was to govern by law;
if good, then actions emulate virtue.
Raising pigs to make wine
is not intended to create calamity;
yet lawsuits increase,
then the flow of wine gives rise to disaster.
Therefore, the ancient kings established the rites of wine:
in the ceremony of one offering,
host and guest bow a hundred times,
drinking all day without becoming intoxicated—
this is how the ancient kings prepared against the calamity of wine.
Thus, wine and food
are means to foster joy.
Music
is to symbolize virtue;
rites
are to curb excess.
Therefore, when the ancient kings had great sorrows,
they necessarily used rites to express grief;
when they had great blessings,
they necessarily used rites to express joy:
the distinction between grief and joy
is always defined by rites.
Music
is giving;
rites
are repaying.
Music delights in its origin;
while rites
return to their beginning.
Music manifests virtue;
rites repay feelings and return to the origin.
What is called the great carriage
is the chariot of the Son of Heaven;
the dragon banner with nine tassels
is the pennant of the Son of Heaven;
the green and black edged
is the precious turtle of the Son of Heaven;
followed by herds of cattle and sheep,
these are what are bestowed upon feudal lords.
Music
is that which cannot be altered in emotion;
rites
are that which cannot be changed in principle.
Music unifies the same;
rites distinguish differences;
the theory of rites and music penetrates human feelings.
To explore the root and understand change
is the essence of music;
to manifest sincerity and eliminate falsehood
is the constant principle of rites.
Rites and music follow the sincerity of heaven and earth,
reach the virtue of the divine and bright,
raise and lower the spirits above and below,
and solidify the substances of the refined and coarse,
governing the rules between father and son, ruler and minister.
Therefore, when the great man promotes rites and music,
heaven and earth will become illuminated.
Heaven and earth joyfully unite,
yīn and yáng harmonize,
nurturing and covering all things;
then grasses and trees flourish,
buds break through,
feathers and wings stir,
horns and antlers grow,
hibernating insects awaken,
the feathered brood and hatch,
the furry conceive and nourish,
the viviparous do not abort and the oviparous do not break their eggs—
then the way of music returns herein.
Music
does not merely mean Huáng Zhōng and Dà Lǚ, strings, songs, shields, and dances;
these are the minor aspects of music,
hence performed by youths;
spreading mats and seats,
setting out wine vessels and stands,
arranging bamboo and wooden dishes,
using rising and descending as rites—
these are the minor aspects of rites,
hence managed by officials.
Music masters understand sounds and poetry,
thus they face north and play strings;
ancestral priests understand the rites of the ancestral temple,
thus they follow the impersonator of the dead;
shāng priests understand funeral rites,
thus they follow the host.
Therefore, virtue achieved is superior,
skill achieved is inferior;
conduct achieved comes first,
tasks achieved come after.
Thus, the ancient kings had superior and inferior,
first and last,
only then could they establish regulations for the world.
Music
is what the sages delighted in,
and it can improve the people's hearts.
It moves people deeply,
transforms customs easily;
therefore, the ancient kings established its teachings.
Humans have the nature of blood, breath, heart, and knowledge,
but without constant sorrow, joy, anger, or pleasure;
they respond to stimuli and are moved by things,
then the inclinations of the heart take form.
Thus, when subtle, anxious, and decaying music arises,
the people brood with worry;
when gentle, slow, easy, elaborate, and simple-rhythmed music arises,
the people are healthy and joyful;
when harsh, fierce, rising, energetic, and expansive music arises,
the people are firm and resolute;
when upright, direct, correct, dignified, and sincere music arises,
the people are solemn and respectful;
when generous, smooth, harmonious, and moving music arises,
the people are kind and loving;
when decadent, depraved, dissolute, excessive, and corrupt music arises,
the people become licentious and disorderly.
Therefore, the ancient kings based them on the nature of emotions,
examined them by measures and numbers,
regulated them with ritual principles,
harmonized them with the balance of vital energies,
guided them with the conduct of the five constants,
making the yáng not scattered,
the yīn not dense,
the rigid energy not angry,
the soft energy not timid,
the four [qualities] flowing freely within and manifesting without,
all resting in their places without usurping each other.
Then they established levels of learning,
broadened the rhythms,
refined the patterns,
to measure moral depth.
They classified the proportions of small and large,
compared the sequences of beginning and end,
to symbolize affairs and conduct,
making the principles of closeness and distance, nobility and baseness, elder and younger, male and female all visible in music:
Hence it is said
"Observing music, one sees its depth."
If the land is exhausted, grasses and trees do not grow;
if the waters are troubled, fish and turtles do not grow large;
if the energy declines, living things do not reproduce;
if the age is chaotic, rites are abandoned and music becomes decadent.
Thus, its sound is sorrowful but not dignified,
joyful but not tranquil,
frivolous and violating measure,
dissolute and forgetting the root.
Broad, it tolerates wickedness;
narrow, it stirs desires;
arousing turbulent energies and extinguishing the virtue of peace and harmony—
therefore, the gentleman despises it.
When depraved sounds affect people, a perverse energy responds to them;
when this perverse energy takes form, lewd music arises.
When upright sounds affect people, a harmonious energy responds to them;
when this harmonious energy takes form, harmonious music arises.
Call and response echo each other,
with deviations and rectitude each returning to their proper place,
and the principles of all things move according to their categories.
Therefore, the noble person returns to innate feelings to harmonize their will,
and compares categories to perfect their conduct.
Depraved sounds and chaotic sights do not linger in their ears and eyes,
lewd music and abandoned rituals do not connect with their heart-mind,
and the energies of indolence, arrogance, and wickedness are not established in their body,
causing the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, heart-mind, and all parts of the body to follow harmony and uprightness,
thereby practicing righteousness.
Only then do they express through sounds,
adorn with qín and sè,
move with shields and battle-axes,
decorate with feathers and ox-tails,
follow with pipes and flutes,
arouse the light of ultimate virtue,
stir the harmony of the four energies,
to manifest the principles of all things.
Thus, its clarity and brightness resemble heaven,
its vastness and breadth resemble earth,
its beginning and end resemble the four seasons,
its revolutions resemble wind and rain;
the five colors form patterns without chaos,
the eight winds follow pitch-pipes without deviation,
all measures attain their numbers with constancy;
small and great complete each other,
end and beginning generate each other,
call and response, clear and turbid,
alternate to form the warp.
Thus, when music is practiced, human relations are clear,
ears and eyes are acute,
blood and vital energy are peaceful,
customs are transformed,
and all under heaven are tranquil.
Hence it is said
"Music (yuè) is joy (lè)."
The noble person finds joy in attaining the Way,
the petty person finds joy in satisfying desires.
Using the Way to control desires,
then there is joy without chaos;
forgetting the Way for desires,
then there is confusion without joy.
Therefore, the noble person returns to innate feelings to harmonize their will,
expands music to complete their teaching,
and when music is practiced, the people turn toward direction,
whereby virtue can be observed.
Virtue
is the pinnacle of nature;
music
is the flowering of virtue;
metal, stone, silk, and bamboo
are the instruments of music.
Poetry speaks its will;
song prolongs its sounds;
dance moves its appearance:
these three originate from the heart,
and only then does the energy of music follow them.
Therefore, when feelings are deep, culture is bright;
when energy is abundant, transformation is spiritual;
harmony and obedience accumulate within, and elegance flowers without—
only music cannot be falsified.
Music
is the movement of the heart;
sound
is the image of music;
ornamentation and rhythm
are the adornment of sound.
The noble person moves its root,
delights in its image,
and only then orders its adornment.
Therefore, first drumming to warn and alert,
three steps to show the direction,
repeating the beginning to emphasize the past,
returning to disorder to prepare the return,
vigorous and swift yet not excessive,
extremely subtle yet not hidden.
Alone delighting in their will,
not weary of their Way;
fully practicing their Way,
not indulging their desires.
Thus feelings are revealed and righteousness established,
music ends and virtue is honored;
the noble person thereby loves goodness,
the petty person thereby ceases faults:
hence it is said
"In the way of nurturing the people,
music is of great importance."
The noble person says:
Ritual and music cannot be separated from the person for even a moment.
Applying music to govern the heart,
then a heart of ease, uprightness, kindness, and sincerity spontaneously arises.
When this heart arises, there is joy;
with joy comes peace;
with peace comes endurance;
with endurance comes heavenliness;
with heavenliness comes spirituality.
Heaven does not speak yet is trusted,
spirit is not angry yet is awe-inspiring.
Applying music
is to govern the heart;
applying ritual
is to govern the body.
Governing the body brings dignity and reverence,
dignity and reverence bring solemn authority.
If the heart-mind for a moment lacks harmony and joy,
then base and deceitful thoughts enter it;
if the outer appearance for a moment lacks dignity and reverence,
then negligent and disrespectful thoughts enter it.
Therefore, music
moves within;
ritual
moves without.
Music reaches ultimate harmony,
ritual reaches ultimate obedience.
Harmonious within and obedient without,
then people observe their countenance and do not contend with them,
gaze upon their demeanor and do not generate negligence or disrespect.
When virtue shines within, the people all accept and listen;
when principle manifests without, the people all accept and obey.
Hence it is said
"Knowing the way of ritual and music,
applying it to all under heaven presents no difficulty."
Music
moves within;
ritual
moves without.
Therefore, ritual emphasizes humility,
music emphasizes fullness.
Ritual is humble yet advancing,
taking advancement as its pattern;
music is full yet returning,
taking return as its pattern.
If ritual is humble but does not advance,
it decays;
if music is full but does not return,
it becomes dissipated.
Therefore, ritual has reciprocity and music has return.
When ritual attains its reciprocity, there is joy;
when music attains its return, there is peace.
The reciprocity of ritual,
the return of music—
their meaning is one.
Music is joy,
an unavoidable aspect of human emotion.
Joy must manifest in sounds and tones,
take form in movements and stillness,
which is the way of human conduct.
Sounds, tones, movements, and stillness—
the changes in one's nature and methods—
are fully expressed herein.
Thus, humans cannot be without joy,
and joy cannot be without form.
When form is not guided by the Way,
it cannot avoid chaos.
The ancient kings detested such chaos,
so they created the sounds of the "Yǎ" and "Sòng" to guide it,
making the sounds sufficient for joy without excess,
making the lyrics sufficient to inspire without ceasing,
making the melodies, whether straight or curved, complex or simple, refined or robust, in rhythm,
sufficient to move people's good hearts and nothing more,
not allowing reckless minds and evil influences to connect with it.
This was the method by which the ancient kings established music.
Therefore, when music is played in the ancestral temple,
and rulers and ministers, high and low, listen together,
none fail to be harmonious and respectful;
in clans, villages, and communities,
when elders and youth listen together,
none fail to be harmonious and obedient;
within the household,
when fathers, sons, and brothers listen together,
none fail to be harmonious and affectionate.
Thus, music
examines the fundamental to establish harmony,
compares things to adorn the rhythm,
and combines rhythms to form patterns,
thereby harmonizing fathers and sons, rulers and ministers,
and uniting the myriad people in closeness.
This was the method by which the ancient kings established music.
So, listening to the sounds of the "Yǎ" and "Sòng,"
one's will and mind are broadened;
holding the shield and axe,
practicing the bowing and stretching,
one's demeanor becomes dignified;
following the formations and markers,
aligning with the rhythm,
the ranks become orderly,
and advances and retreats become uniform.
Thus, music is the harmony of heaven and earth,
the guiding principle of balance and harmony,
an unavoidable aspect of human emotion.
Music is
what the ancient kings used to adorn joy;
armies and battle-axes
are what they used to adorn anger.
Thus, the joys and angers of the ancient kings all achieved their proper balance.
When joyful, all under heaven harmonized with them;
when angry, those who were violent and chaotic feared them.
The Way of the ancient kings, with rites and music, can be called magnificent.
Wèi Wén Hóu asked Zǐ Xià:
"When I dress formally and listen to ancient music, I only fear falling asleep;
but when I listen to the music of Zhèng and Wèi, I do not feel tired.
May I ask why ancient music is like that,
and why?
Why is new music like this,
and why?"
Zǐ Xià replied:
"As for ancient music,
it advances and retreats in unison,
harmonious, correct, and broad;
strings, gourds, sheng, and reeds all follow the drum's lead,
beginning with civil tunes,
ending with martial ones,
managing chaos with coordination,
and speeding up with elegance.
The nobleman then speaks of it,
then recounts the past,
cultivating self and family,
and bringing balance to all under heaven:
this is the expression of ancient music.
As for new music,
it advances and retreats haphazardly,
with corrupt sounds leading to excess,
indulgent and unstoppable,
involving actors and dwarfs,
mixing men and women chaotically,
oblivious to father-son relationships.
When the music ends, one cannot speak of it,
nor recount the past:
this is the expression of new music.
Now, what you ask about is music,
but what you enjoy is mere sound.
Music and sound
are similar but not the same."
Wén Hóu said:
"May I ask how they differ?"
Zǐ Xià replied:
"In ancient times, heaven and earth were harmonious, the four seasons timely,
the people virtuous, and the five grains abundant,
diseases did not arise, and there were no omens,
this was called great harmony.
Then the sages established the relationships between father and son, ruler and minister as the guiding principles,
and once the principles were correct,
all under heaven was greatly settled,
all under heaven greatly settled,
then they standardized the six pitch-standards,
harmonized the five tones,
and sang the "Shī" and "Sòng" with strings,
this is called virtuous sound,
and virtuous sound is called music.
The "Shī" says:
'His virtuous sound is profound,
his virtue can shine,
shining and classifying,
leading and ruling.
Ruling this great state,
he can comply and assist.
Assisting King Wén,
his virtue knows no regret.
Having received divine blessings,
he extends them to his descendants.'
This is what it means.
Now, what you enjoy,
is it not the drowning sounds?"
Wén Hóu said:
"May I ask where these drowning sounds come from?"
Zǐ Xià replied:
"The music of Zhèng is overly indulgent and corrupts the will,
the music of Sòng pleases women and drowns the will,
the music of Wèi is hurried and troubles the will,
the music of Qí is arrogant and makes one proud,
all four are excessive in sensuality and harmful to virtue,
