thus they are not used in sacrifices.
The "Shī" says:
'Solemn and harmonious, the sounds mingle,
the ancestors listen to them.'
Solemn
means respect;
harmonious
means accord.
With respect and accord,
what cannot be accomplished?
As a ruler,
one must be cautious in one's likes and dislikes.
If the ruler likes it, the ministers will do it;
if those above practice it, the people will follow.
The "Shī" says
'Guiding the people is very easy,'
this is what it means.
Then the sages made the táo drum, qiāng qiā, xūn, and chí,
these six instruments
are the sounds of virtuous sound.
Then bells, chimes, yú, and sè were used to harmonize them,
and shields, axes, plumes, and di were used to dance to them.
This is for sacrificing in the temples of the ancient kings,
for offering toasts and libations,
for ordering the noble and humble each appropriately,
and for showing later generations the sequence of respect and humility, elder and younger.
The sound of bells is clanging,
clanging to establish commands,
commands to establish momentum,
momentum to establish martial spirit.
The nobleman, hearing the bells, thinks of martial ministers.
The sound of stone is firm,
firm to establish distinction,
distinction to dedicate to death.
The nobleman, hearing the chimes, thinks of ministers who die defending the borders.
The sound of strings is sorrowful,
sorrowful to establish integrity,
integrity to establish resolve.
The nobleman, hearing the qín and sè, thinks of ministers with righteous resolve.
The sound of bamboo is expansive,
expansive to assemble,
assembling to gather the masses.
The nobleman, hearing the yú, shēng, xiāo, and guǎn, thinks of ministers who gather and store.
The sound of war drums is clamorous,
clamorous to incite action,
action to advance the masses.
The nobleman, hearing the war drums, thinks of commander ministers.
When the nobleman listens to sounds,
it is not just to hear their clanging and clashing,
but to find something that resonates with him."
Bīn Móu Jiǎ sat in attendance with Confucius,
and Confucius spoke with him,
touching on music,
saying:
"Why does the 'Wǔ' music have such prolonged preparations?"
Why is that?"
He replied:
"For fear of not gaining the support of the masses."
"Why the prolonged sighs,
the lingering melodies?"
The reply was:
"Fear of not accomplishing the task in time."
"Why the early display of vigorous movements and stomping?"
The answer:
"To act timely on the matters."
"In the 'Wǔ' dance, why kneel with the right knee up and left knee down?"
The response:
"That is not a posture of the 'Wǔ' dance."
"Why do the sounds overflow into the 'Shāng' mode?"
The answer:
"That is not the music of 'Wǔ'."
The Master said:
"If it's not the music of 'Wǔ',
then what music is it?"
The reply:
"The officials have lost the tradition.
If it were not for that,
then King Wǔ's intent would be considered neglected."
The Master said:
"What I, Qiū, heard from Cháng Hóng
aligns with what you, sir, have said."
Bīn Móu Jiǎ stood up,
left his mat, and asked:
"That the 'Wǔ' dance's preparatory warnings are long,
I have already understood.
May I ask why the delays are so prolonged?"
The Master said:
"Sit,
and I will tell you.
Music
symbolizes accomplishment.
Holding shields and standing firm like mountains
represents King Wǔ's task;
the vigorous movements and stomping
express Tài Gōng's resolve;
the martial disorder all kneeling
signifies the governance of Zhōu and Shào.
Moreover, the 'Wǔ' dance
begins with marching north,
in the second part, it destroys Shāng,
in the third, it turns south,
in the fourth, it establishes the southern states as borders,
in the fifth, it divides Shǎn,
with Zhōu Gōng on the left,
Shào Gōng on the right,
and in the sixth, it returns to formation,
to honor the Son of Heaven,
with flanking vibrations and four strikes,
displaying might throughout the central states.
Advancing in divided flanks
ensures early success.
Long standing in formation
awaits the arrival of the feudal lords.
And have you not heard the tale of Mùyě?
King Wǔ, having overcome Yīn and returned to Shāng,
before even dismounting his chariot,
enfeoffed the descendants of Huángdì at Jì,
those of Emperor Yáo at Zhù,
and those of Emperor Shùn at Chén;
after dismounting, he enfeoffed the descendants of the Xiàhòu clan at Qǐ,
those of Yīn at Sòng,
built a tomb for Prince Bǐgān,
released Jīzǐ from imprisonment,
and had Shāng Róng reinstated to his position.
The common people were relieved from harsh policies,
and officials had their salaries doubled.
Crossing the river westward,
he released horses on the sunny side of Huà Shān, never to ride them again;
cattle were set free in the fields of Táolín, never to be used again;
chariots and armor were stored away in arsenals, never to be reused;
weapons were inverted,
wrapped in tiger skins;
the generals and soldiers
were made feudal lords,
and this was called
'Jiàngāo':
then all under heaven knew King Wǔ would no longer use arms.
Disbanding the army for archery in the suburbs,
shooting left to 'Lí Shǒu',
right to 'Zōu Yú',
ceased the piercing of leather targets;
wearing ceremonial robes and inserting tablets,
the tiger-warriors sheathed their swords;
sacrificing in the Míngtáng,
the people learned filial piety;
at court audiences,
feudal lords understood their duties as subjects;
plowing the imperial field,
they learned respect:
these five were the great teachings for all under heaven.
Feeding the Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng in the Tàixué,
the Son of Heaven bared his arm to cut the sacrificial animal,
served sauce with his own hands,
and offered wine with a cup,
wearing the crown and holding a shield,
to teach the feudal lords brotherly respect.
Thus,
the way of Zhōu reached everywhere,
rituals and music intermingled,
so the prolonged nature of the 'Wǔ' dance
is indeed appropriate, is it not?"
Zǐgòng met Shī Yǐ and asked him,
saying:
"I, Cì, have heard that songs suit different people;
what song is suitable for one like me?"
Shī Yǐ said:
"I, Yǐ,
am a lowly musician,
hardly fit to advise on suitability.
Let me recite what I've heard,
and you, sir, can decide for yourself.
Those broad and calm,
gentle and upright, should sing the 'Sòng';
those vast and serene,
open and trustworthy, the 'Dà Yǎ';
those respectful, frugal, and fond of rituals, the 'Xiǎo Yǎ';
those upright, pure, and humble, the 'Fēng';
those straightforward and compassionate, the 'Shāng';
those gentle, kind, and decisive, the 'Qí'.
Singing
is to express one's virtue directly;
stirring oneself, heaven and earth respond,
the four seasons harmonize,
stars align,
and all things flourish.
Thus, the 'Shāng'
is the legacy of the Five Emperors,
remembered by the Shāng people,
hence called 'Shāng';
the 'Qí'
is the heritage of the Three Dynasties,
recalled by the Qí people,
so named 'Qí'.
Understanding the poems of 'Shāng'
enables one to decide promptly in affairs;
grasping those of 'Qí'
leads to yielding in the face of profit.
Deciding promptly in affairs
is courage;
yielding at profit
is righteousness.
Having both courage and righteousness,
who but through song can preserve this?
Therefore, in singing,
the high notes seem lifted,
the low ones falling,
turns sharp as breaks,
stops still as dry wood,
centered like a square,
curved like a hook,
continuous as a string of pearls.
Thus, singing as speech
is elongated speech.
Delighted,
one speaks;
if speech is insufficient,
one elongates it;
if that is not enough,
one sighs over it;
if sighing falls short,
unconsciously, hands dance and feet stomp."
"Zǐgòng Asks about Music."
All sounds stem from the human heart,
and heaven and humans connect,
like shadows following forms,
echoes responding to sounds.
Thus, for the good, heaven rewards with blessings,
for the evil, it brings calamities,
as is natural.
Thus, when Shùn strummed the five-stringed qín,
singing the poem of the "Southern Wind," the world was well-governed;
while Zhòu indulged in the music of Zhāogē and the northern vulgar tunes,
leading to his death and the fall of his state.
How broad was the Way of Shùn!
How narrow was the Way of Zhòu!
The poem of the "Southern Wind" is the sound of growth and life,
which Shùn delighted in,
finding joy in harmony with heaven and earth,
winning the hearts of all states,
hence the world was well-governed.
As for Zhāogē, it was untimely,
the north signifies defeat,
and vulgar means base,
yet Zhòu delighted in it,
diverging in heart from all states,
so the feudal lords did not support him,
the common people did not cherish him,
the world turned against him,
thus he died and his state perished.
During the time of Duke Líng of Wèi,
as he was about to go to Jìn,
he stopped by the banks of the Pú River.
At midnight, he heard the sound of a qín being played,
and asked his attendants,
who all replied,
"We did not hear it."
So he summoned Shī Juān and said:
"I heard the sound of a qín,
but when I asked my attendants,
none of them heard it.
It seemed like it was from ghosts or spirits;
listen for me and transcribe it."
Shī Juān said:
"Yes."
Thereupon, he sat upright, took up a qín,
listened and transcribed it.
The next day,
he said:
"I have grasped it,
but I am not yet practiced;
please allow me to stay overnight to practice it."
Duke Líng said:
"You may."
So he stayed another night.
The next day,
he reported:
"I am practiced."
They then left for Jìn,
and met with Duke Píng of Jìn.
Duke Píng hosted a banquet at the Shīhuì Tower.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Duke Líng said:
"On this journey here,
I heard a new melody;
I request to have it performed."
Duke Píng said:
"You may."
He then had Shī Juān sit beside Shī Kuàng,
who took up the qín and played it.
Before it ended,
Shī Kuàng pressed his hand to stop him, saying:
"This is the music of a fallen state;
it should not be completed."
Duke Píng asked:
"From where does this tune originate?"
Shī Kuàng replied:
"It was composed by Shī Yán.
He created decadent music for Zhòu,
and when King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
Shī Yán fled east,
throwing himself into the Pú River.
Thus, this sound must be heard by the Pú River,
and whoever hears it first will see their state diminished."
Duke Píng said:
"What I love is music;
I wish to hear it to the end."
So Shī Juān played it through.
Duke Píng asked:
"Is there no music sadder than this?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"There is."
Duke Píng said:
"May I hear it?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"Your virtue and righteousness are shallow;
you should not listen to it."
Duke Píng said:
"What I love is music;
I wish to hear it."
Shī Kuàng had no choice,
so he took up the qín and played it.
At the first playing,
sixteen black cranes gathered at the corridor gate;
at the second playing,
they stretched their necks and sang,
spread their wings and danced.
Duke Píng was greatly pleased,
stood up, and toasted Shī Kuàng.
Returning to his seat,
he asked:
"Is there no music sadder than this?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"There is.
In the past, Huángdì used it to grandly assemble ghosts and spirits,
but now your virtue and righteousness are shallow;
you are not fit to hear it,
for hearing it will bring ruin."
Duke Píng said:
"I am old;
what I love is music;
I wish to hear it to the end."
Shī Kuàng had no choice,
so he took up the qín and played it.
At the first playing,
white clouds arose from the northwest;
at the second playing,
a great wind came, followed by rain,
blowing off the roof tiles of the corridor,
and all the attendants fled.
Duke Píng was terrified,
and crouched among the corridor rooms.
Jìn then suffered a great drought,
with barren land for three years.
Thus, listeners may encounter fortune or misfortune.
Music should not be recklessly performed.
The Grand Historian remarks:
When the enlightened kings of antiquity promoted music,
it was not to amuse themselves or indulge in pleasure,
nor to gratify desires and whims,
but to aim for good governance.
Proper education all begins with music,
for when music is correct, conduct is correct.
Therefore, music serves
to stir the blood and pulses,
to circulate the spirit and harmonize the upright heart.
Thus, the gōng note stirs the spleen and harmonizes with sageliness;
the shāng note stirs the lungs and harmonizes with righteousness;
the jué note stirs the liver and harmonizes with benevolence;
the zhǐ note stirs the heart and harmonizes with propriety;
the yǔ note stirs the kidneys and harmonizes with wisdom.
Hence, music internally aids in rectifying the heart and externally distinguishes the noble from the humble;
above, it serves the ancestral temples,
below, it transforms the common people.
The qín is eight feet one inch long,
a standard measurement.
The largest string is the gōng,
positioned in the center,
representing the ruler.
The shāng is strung to the right,
with the others arranged in order of size,
not losing their sequence,
so the positions of ruler and ministers are correct.
Therefore, hearing the gōng note
makes one warm, relaxed, and broad-minded;
hearing the shāng note
makes one upright and fond of righteousness;
hearing the jué note
makes one compassionate and loving toward others;
hearing the zhǐ note
makes one joyful in goodness and generous in giving;
hearing the yǔ note
makes one orderly and fond of propriety.
Propriety enters from without,
while music emerges from within.
Thus, a noble person cannot be separated from propriety for a moment,
for being apart from it even briefly leads to violent and arrogant behavior externally;
nor can they be separated from music for a moment,
for being apart from it even briefly leads to treacherous and evil behavior internally.
Therefore, musical sounds are
what the noble person cultivates for righteousness.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven and feudal lords never left the court without listening to bells and chimes,
and ministers and officials never left their presence without hearing the sounds of qín and sè,
all to cultivate righteous conduct and prevent licentiousness.
Licentiousness arises from the absence of propriety,
so the sage kings had people's ears hear the music of the "Yǎ" and "Sòng,"
their eyes behold the dignified rites,
their feet practice respectful demeanor,
and their mouths speak the way of benevolence and righteousness.
Thus, the noble person, speaking all day, has no way for depravity to enter.
The kings established affairs and enacted laws,
regulating things and setting norms,
all based on the six pitch-standards,
which are the foundation of all matters.
This is especially important in military affairs,
hence it is said
"Observing the enemy, one knows fortune or misfortune;
hearing the sounds, one discerns victory or defeat,"
a principle unchanged through a hundred reigns.
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
sounding the pipes and listening to the music,
from early spring to late winter,
the forces of death converged,
and the sound lingered in the palace.
Similar voices follow each other,
it is the nature of things,
what is there to marvel at?
Warfare,
was used by the sages to suppress the strong and fierce,
to pacify chaotic times,
to level the perilous obstacles,
and to rescue those in danger.
When even beasts with fangs and horns attack when provoked,
how much more so will humans harbor preferences and emotions like joy and anger?
When there is joy, affection arises,
when there is anger, venom stings,
this is the rationale of natural disposition.
In the past, Emperor Huáng had the Battle of Zhuó Lù,
to settle the fire calamity;
Zhuān Xū had the punishment of Gòng Gōng,
to pacify the water disaster;
Chéng Tāng had the campaign against Náncháo,
to eradicate the chaos of Xià.
They rose and fell in succession,
the victorious take control,
receiving it from Heaven.
Afterward,
famous people rose and fell,
Jìn used Jiùfàn,
while Qí used Wángzǐ,
Wú used Sūn Wǔ,
explaining military regulations,
ensuring rewards and punishments were trustworthy,
surpassing the dukes and marquises,
annexing the lands of numerous states,
though not reaching the oaths of the Three Dynasties,
yet their person received favor and the ruler was honored,
renowned in their time,
can this not be called glory?
How can they be like the scholars of the time who are ignorant of the great principles,
not weighing the light and heavy,
rashly speaking of virtue and transformation,
saying that war should not be used,
leading to great disgrace for the ruler in failing to defend,
or lesser offenses causing encroachment and weakening,
stubbornly holding to positions that do not change?
Therefore, teaching and punishment cannot be abandoned in families,
penalties and fines cannot be discarded in the state,
punishment and conquest cannot be stopped in the world,
it is a matter of skill or ineptitude in its use,
and of being against or compliant in its execution.
Xià Jié and
Yīn Zhòu fought tigers and wolves with their hands,
pursued four horses with their feet,
their courage was not slight;
they achieved victory in every battle,
and the dukes and marquises feared and submitted,
their power was not insignificant.
Under the Second Emperor of Qín, the army camped in places of no use,
and troops were stationed at the borders,
their strength was not weak;
grievances were formed with the Xiongnu,
disaster was entailed by Yuè,
their position was not lacking.
When their authority and power reached their limits,
even the common people of the alleys became their enemies.
The fault lay in not knowing to stop in their extreme military pursuits,
and in the insatiable desire for gain.
And then, Gāozǔ ruled the world,
with the frontiers turned outward;
though the kings of the great states declared themselves as helping tributaries,
their loyalty was incomplete.
When Gāozǔ grew weary of military affairs,
also with the schemes of Xiāo and
Zhāng,
thus he ceased warfare for a respite,
with restraining ties left unprepared.
During the reign of Emperor Xiàowén,
General Chén Wǔ and others discussed, saying:
"Nányuè and
Chosŏn, since the time of Qín's unification, were subjects,
later they amassed troops and blocked the passes,
selecting and observing.
In Gāozǔ's time, the world had just been settled,
the people had finally found some peace,
and it was not yet appropriate to raise troops again.
Now, Your Majesty shows kindness and benevolence to the people,
with grace bestowed throughout the land,
it is suitable to take advantage of the people's desire for peace,
to punish the rebellious factions,
and thereby unify the borders."
Emperor Xiàowén replied:
"I can handle the affairs of state,
but have not thought of this.
With the Lü clan's chaos,
the ministers and royal family felt no shame,
wrongfully holding the rightful positions,
always in a state of anxiety and fear,
worried that tasks would not be completed.
Besides, weapons are instruments of evil,
even if one achieves what one desires,
any movement causes damage and harm,
what is to be said to the people of distant lands?
The late Emperor knew that wearying the people was undesirable,
and thus disregarded such concerns.
How can I claim to be capable?
Now the Xiongnu invade,
military officials achieve no merit,
frontier dwellers father and son have borne arms for long,
I am always troubled and pained,
never a day forgetting it.
Now unable to undo this hostility,
my hope is to strengthen the border and set scouts,
to establish peace and communication,
to let the northern frontier rest in peace,
and that is already a great achievement.
Also, do not discuss military campaigns."
Therefore, the people were free from internal and external demands,
able to rest in the fields,
the world became prosperous and wealthy,
grain cost only a few coins,
chickens crowed and dogs barked,
smoke rose thousands of miles,
can this not be called harmony and joy?
Chancellor Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"During Emperor Wéndì's time,
the world was recently freed from calamity,
the people enjoyed their work,
following their desires,
being able not to disturb them,
so the people were at ease.
Even elder people aged sixty or seventy never went to the marketplace,
wandering and playing like children.
Is this not what Confucius called a virtuous gentleman?
The 'Shū Jīng' says 'Seven virtues,'
twenty-eight constellations.
The law of harmonics and calendar,
Heaven's way to communicate the five phases and eight harmonious energies,
Heaven's way to complete all things.
Constellations,
are where the sun and moon lodge.
Constellations,
unfold the energy.
Bùzhōu wind occupies the northwest,
governs the passage of life and death.
Dōngbì occupies the Bùzhōu wind east,
governs the avoidance of life energy flowing east.
As far as Yíng Shì.
Yíng Shì,
governs the nurturing of embryonic yang energy and its birth.
Eastwards to Wēi.
Wēi, means broken.
It speaks of the breaking of yang energy,
hence it is called Wēi.
The tenth month,
the law corresponds to Yīngzhōng.
Yīngzhōng,
corresponds to yang energy,
without application in practice.
Among the twelve Earthly Branches, it is Hai.
Hai,
means encompassing.
It implies the yin energy stored below,
therefore it encompasses."
The Vast Emptiness Wind dwells in the north.
"Vast Emptiness"
means that the yang qi is below,
and the yin is so empty that the yang is vast and great,
hence called Vast Emptiness.
Eastward it reaches Xū.
"Xū"
signifies the ability to be full or empty,
meaning yang qi in winter lies hidden within emptiness;
on the winter solstice, one yin descends to hide,
while one yang ascends and expands,
hence called Xū.
Eastward it reaches Xūnǚ.
This refers to the place where all things change and move,
with yin and yang qi not yet separated,
still awaiting each other,
hence called Xūnǚ.
It corresponds to the eleventh month,
and the pitch-pipe is Huángzhōng.
"Huángzhōng"
means yang qi treads forth from the Yellow Springs.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it is Zǐ.
"Zǐ"
means to nourish;
"nourish"
refers to all things being nourished below.
Among the ten heavenly stems, it is Rén and Guǐ.
"Rén" expresses the idea of bearing,
meaning yang qi bears and nurtures all things below.
"Guǐ" conveys the sense of measuring,
indicating that all things can be assessed,
hence called Guǐ.
Eastward it reaches Qiānniú.
"Qiānniú"
means yang qi pulls and leads all things forth.
"Niú" (ox)
means to brave,
signifying that even though the earth is frozen,
it can brave it and grow.
"Ox"
also refers to plowing and planting all things.
Eastward it reaches Jiànxīng.
"Jiànxīng"
means to establish all living things.
It corresponds to the twelfth month,
and the pitch-pipe is Dàlǚ.
"Dàlǚ."
Among the twelve earthly branches, it is Chǒu.
The Regulating Wind dwells in the northeast,
governing the emergence of all things.
"Tiáo" implies putting all things in order and bringing them forth,
hence called the Regulating Wind.
Southward it reaches Jī.
"Jī"
means the roots of all things are set like a base,
hence called Jī.
It corresponds to the first month,
and the pitch-pipe is Tàicù.
"Tàicù"
means all things cluster and grow,
hence called Tàicù.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it is Yín.
"Yín" indicates all things begin to grow vigorously,
hence called Yín.
Southward it reaches Wěi,
meaning all things start to grow like a tail.
Southward it reaches Xīn,
meaning all things begin to grow with a flourishing heart.
Southward it reaches Fáng.
"Fáng"
signifies the gateway of all things,
reaching the gate means emerging.
The Bright Multitude Wind dwells in the east.
"Bright Multitude"
means all things are fully revealed.
It corresponds to the second month,
and the pitch-pipe is Jiázhōng.
"Jiázhōng"
means yin and yang press against each other.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it is Mǎo.
"Mǎo" conveys lushness,
indicating all things are lush.
Among the ten heavenly stems, it is Jiǎ and Yǐ.
"Jiǎ"
means all things break through their shells and emerge;
"Yǐ"
signifies the vigorous growth of all things.
Southward it reaches Dī.
"Dī"
means all things have arrived.
Southward it reaches Kàng.
"Kàng"
means all things rise and appear.
Southward it reaches Jiǎo.
"Jiǎo"
indicates all things have branches and stems like horns.
It corresponds to the third month,
and the pitch-pipe is Gūxiǎn.
"Gūxiǎn"
means all things are washed and grow.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it is Chén.
"Chén"
refers to the stirring of all things.
The Pure Bright Wind dwells in the southeast corner,
governing the blowing of all things westward.
It reaches Zhěn.
"Zhěn."
means all things grow larger and more abundant.
Westward it reaches Yì.
"Yì"
signifies all things have wings.
It corresponds to the fourth month,
and the pitch-pipe is Zhōnglǚ.
"Zhōnglǚ"
means all things complete their journey and move westward.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it is Sì.
"Sì"
indicates yang qi is exhausted.
Westward it reaches Qīxīng.
"Qīxīng"
refers to the yang number completing at seven,
hence called Seven Stars.
Westward it reaches Zhāng.
"Zhāng"
means all things are expanded.
Westward it reaches Zhù.
"Zhù"
signifies the beginning of decline for all things,
with yang qi descending,
hence called Zhù.
It corresponds to the fifth month,
and the pitch-pipe is Ruíbīn.
"Ruíbīn"
means yin qi is still young and scant,
hence called Ruí;
and withered yang does not govern,
hence called Bīn.
The Scenic Wind dwells in the south.
"Jǐng" (scenic)
means the path of yang qi is complete,
hence called Scenic Wind.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it is Wǔ.
"Wǔ"
signifies the intersection of yin and yang,
hence called Wǔ.
Among the ten heavenly stems, it is Bǐng and Dīng.
"Bǐng"
means the yang path is evident and bright,
hence called Bǐng;
"Dīng"
refers to the robustness of all things,
hence called Dīng.
Westward it reaches Hú.
"Hú"
means all things are withered and nearing death.
Westward it reaches Láng.
"Láng" (wolf)
signifies that all things can be measured,
and decisively cut off,
hence called Láng.
The Cool Wind resides in the southwest quarter,
governing the Earth.
The Earth
sinks and seizes the vital energy of all things.
In the sixth month,
the pitch pipe corresponds to Línzhōng.
Línzhōng
signifies that all things approach death in a dense, forest-like manner.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it corresponds to Wèi.
Wèi
means that all things have matured,
possessing flavor and substance.
To the north, it reaches Fá.
Fá
indicates that the energy of all things is seized and they can be cut down.
To the north, it reaches Shēn.
Shēn means that all things can be assessed or compared,
hence it is called Shēn.
In the seventh month,
the pitch pipe corresponds to Yízé.
Yízé
signifies the harmful effect of yin energy on all things.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it corresponds to Shēn.
Shēn
means that yin energy is in charge,
extending harm to all things,
hence it is called Shēn.
To the north, it reaches Zhuó.
Zhuó
means to touch or collide,
indicating that all things encounter death,
hence it is called Zhuó.
To the north, it reaches Liú.
Liú
means the lingering of yang energy,
hence it is called Liú.
In the eighth month,
the pitch pipe corresponds to Nánlǚ.
Nánlǚ
signifies the journey of yang energy into hiding.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it corresponds to Yǒu.
Yǒu
represents the aging of all things,
hence it is called Yǒu.
The Changhe Wind resides in the west.
Chāng
means to initiate;
Hé
means to store.
It signifies that yang energy guides all things,
storing them in the Yellow Springs.
Among the ten heavenly stems, it corresponds to Gēng and Xīn.
Gēng
means that yin energy changes all things,
hence it is called Gēng;
Xīn
refers to the bitter birth of all things,
hence it is called Xīn.
To the north, it reaches Wèi.
Wèi
means that yang energy is about to be stored,
all gathered together.
To the north, it reaches Lóu.
Lóu
means calling all things inward to contain them.
To the north, it reaches Kuí.
Kuí
governs the poisoning and killing of all things,
then storing them away.
In the ninth month,
the pitch pipe corresponds to Wúyì.
Wúyì
indicates that yin energy is strong and in charge,
with no yang energy remaining,
hence it is called Wúyì.
Among the twelve earthly branches, it corresponds to Xū.
Xū
means that all things are completely extinguished,
hence it is called Xū.

The method for generating Huángzhōng:
For descending generation,
double the numerator,
triple the denominator.
For ascending generation,
quadruple the numerator,
triple the denominator.
Upper nine,
Shāng eight,
Yǔ seven,
Jué six,
Gōng five,
Zhǐ nine.
Set one and multiply by three nine times to get the denominator.
The numerator equals the denominator,
yielding one inch in length.
In total, it gives nine inches,
named
"the Gōng of Huángzhōng".
Thus, sound begins with Gōng,
and ends with Jué;
numbers start from one,
end at ten,
and are completed by three;
energy begins at the winter solstice,
cycles and regenerates.
Spirit arises from non-being,
form takes shape in being,
form then gives rise to number,
form produces sound,
hence it is said that spirit commands energy,
energy coalesces into form.
The principles of form can be categorized accordingly.
Some are not yet formed and not categorized,
some share the same form and category,
categories can be ordered,
categories can be recognized.
The sage knows the distinctions of heaven and earth,
thus proceeding from being to non-being,
to grasp what is as fine as energy,
as subtle as sound.
However, the sage relies on spirit to preserve it,
no matter how profound, it must manifest its essence,
examining its flowering path makes it clear.
Without a sagely mind and keen intelligence,
who can preserve the spirit of heaven and earth and understand the nature of form?
Spirit
is received by things, yet they cannot know its coming and going,
thus the sage reveres it and seeks to preserve it.
Only by desiring to preserve it,
spirit too is preserved.
Those who wish to preserve it,
therefore nothing is more valuable.
The Grand Historian says:
In using the rotating jade sighting-tube to harmonize the seven administrations,
it aligns with the heavens, earth, and twenty-eight constellations.
The ten heavenly stems,
twelve earthly branches,
and pitch pipes have been regulated since ancient times.
Establishing pitch pipes, calculating calendars, and creating daily measures,
can be relied upon for measurement.
Matching tallies and tokens,
penetrating the Way and its virtue,
this is what is meant by following these principles.
In ancient times,
the calendar was established in early spring.
At that time, the ice melted and hibernating insects emerged,
all kinds of plants flourished,
and the zǐfú bird started chirping.
Things are prepared for the year,
giving birth in the east,
following the order of the four seasons,
and ending at the winter solstice.
At that time, the rooster crowed thrice,
signaling the dawn.
Observing the twelve months,
ending at chǒu.
Sun and moon complete their cycles,
thus there is clarity.
Clarity is the beginning,
obscurity is the infancy,
and the cycle of light and dark is like male and female.
Male and female alternate in cycles,
following the order of correct and just.
The sun returns to the west,
rises with clarity in the east;
the moon returns to the east,
rises with clarity in the west.
Lacking accord with the heavens,
and not following proper human methods,
all things will easily fall into disorder and be difficult to accomplish.
When a king changes dynasties and receives the mandate,
he must be cautious from the beginning,
alter the calendar,
change the color of clothing,
trace back to the origin of the heavens,
and follow its meaning.
Historian Tàishǐ Gōng said:
Before Shénnóng, it was already esteemed.
It was Huángdì who evaluated and fixed the celestial calendar,
established the five elements,
initiated the understanding of the waxing and waning,
corrected the intercalation,
thus there were officials for heaven, earth, spirits, and all things,
known as the five officials.
Each managed their sequence,
without disorder.
Hence, the people could be trusted,
the spirits had clear virtues.
The people and spirits had distinct works,
respected without defilement,
thus the spirits bestowed good growth,
the people offered things,
disasters and calamities did not arise,
what was sought was not lacking.
When the Shàohào clan declined,
the Jiǔlí caused disorder,
the people and spirits were mixed and disturbed,
unable to manage all things,
calamities frequently occurred,
no one could fully express their spirit.
Zhuān Xǔ inherited it,
ordered Nánzhèng Chóng to oversee the heavens and relate to the spirits,
and ordered Huǒzhèng Lí to oversee the earth and relate to the people,
restoring the old norms,
without mutual interference.
Afterwards, the Sānmiao admired the Jiǔlí's virtues,
so both officials were dismissed from their duties,
intercalations went astray,
Mèngzōu was annihilated,
the celestial pole had no order,
the calendar counts lost sequence.
Yáo reinstated the successors of Chóng and Lí,
not forgetting the old ways,
appointed them again,
and established the office of Xī and Hé.
When the times were clarified and measures corrected,
yin and yang were balanced,
wind and rain were moderate,
lush energy arrived,
and the people were free from early death and epidemics.
In old age, Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
reiterating the admonishments of Wénzǔ,
saying
"Heaven's calendar is upon you."
Shùn also instructed Yǔ similarly.
From this we can see,
the importance placed by kings.
The Xia set the first month as the start,
the Yin led with the twelfth month,
and the Zhou used the eleventh month.
The correct time-keeping of the three kings was like a cycle,
going to its limit and returning to the origin.
When heaven was in order in the world,
it did not lose its sequence;
without order,
the calendar was not enforced among the feudal lords.
After Yōu
and Lì,
the Zhou court weakened,
power fell into the hands of ministers,
records ceased to be kept accurately,
the rulers did not proclaim the beginnings of months,
thus officials and their children scattered,
some among the Central Plains,
others among the barbarians,
hence their prophecies were abolished and not unified.
In the twenty-sixth year of King Xiāng of Zhou, there was an intercalary third month,
which the "Spring and Autumn Annals" criticized.
The ancients' setting of correct time,
laid the foundation in the beginning,
held the standard in the middle,
returned to the proper end.
Starting correctly,
with a sequence that does not err;
holding the standard in the middle,
the people are not confused;
returning to the proper end,
affairs do not contradict.
Later, the Warring States engaged in mutual strife,
focusing on subduing enemies of strong states,
merely seeking emergency relief and resolving disputes,
who then could ponder these matters?
At this time, only Zhōu Yǎn,
was knowledgeable about the transmission of the five virtues,
distributing the understanding of waxing and waning,
thus enlightening the feudal lords.
Yet it coincided with Qín extinguishing the six states,
wars greatly troubled,
and ascending to supreme status was recent,
there was no leisure.
Yet he somewhat promoted the concept of the five successes,
believing he had obtained the auspices of water virtue,
renaming the Yellow River as
"Virtuous Water,"
and set the calendar with the tenth month,
with black as the superior color.
However, in terms of calendrical calculations and intercalations,
it was not yet able to reveal the truth.
When the Han arose,
Gaozu said
"The northern sacrifice awaits my ascension,"
also believing to have obtained the auspices of the water virtue.
Though understanding the calendar and ZHāng Cāng and others,
all considered it so.
At this time, the world was newly stabilized,
beginnings of rule and great foundations,
under Empress Lü's female leadership,
all were not leisurely,
thus followed Qin's calendar and clothing color.
By the time of Filial Wen,
Lǔ’s Gōngsūn Chén submitted a proposal on the cycle of the five virtues,
stating
"The Han has received the Earth virtue,
should change its origin,
alter the calendar,
and change the clothing color.
Auspices should be seen,
as a Yellow Dragon appeared."
This matter was referred to Chancellor ZHāng Cāng,
who also studied laws and calendrical calculations,
deemed it incorrect,
and dismissed it.
Later, when a Yellow Dragon appeared in Chéngjì,
ZHāng Cāng resigned himself,
unable to make his recommendations.
But with Xīnyuánpíng observing qi,
he somewhat spoke of the correct calendar and clothing colors,
gaining favor,
yet later created chaos,
thus Emperor Wén abolished but did not revisit the issue.
Up to the time when the present Emperor ascended the throne,
he summoned the fangshì Táng Dū,
who divided the celestial regions;
and Bā Luòxià Hóng calculated and reformed the calendar,
after which the degrees of the sun and stars aligned with the Xià calendar.
Then the era name was changed,
official titles were altered,
and Mount Tài was fēng-sacrificed.
Thereupon, an edict was issued to the Yùshǐ, saying:
"Previously,
the officials stated that the stellar degrees were not yet fixed,
so extensive consultations were held,
to rectify the stellar degrees,
but they could not be fully verified.
It is heard that in ancient times, Huángdì harmonized them and achieved immortality,
examining names and verifying degrees,
determining the clear and turbid,
establishing the five divisions,
and setting the fractions for qì and phenomena.
However, that was long ago.
Texts are incomplete and music has deteriorated,
which greatly distresses us.
We have not been able to follow and illuminate it clearly,
but by continuing the daily fractions,
it corresponds to the triumph of the Water Virtue.
Now, the sun accords with the summer solstice,
with Huángzhōng as the gōng,
Línzhōng as the zhǐ,
Tàicù as the shāng,
Nánlǚ as the yǔ,
and Gūxiǎn as the jué.
From this time onward,
the qì returns to correctness,
the yǔ tone becomes clear again,
names resume their proper transformations,
until the zǐ day coincides with the winter solstice,
then the way of yīn and yáng separating and uniting operates.
The winter solstice at the dawn of the first day of the month, on the jiǎzǐ day in the eleventh month, has been verified,
so let the seventh year be changed to the first year of Tàichū.
The year name
is 'Yānféng Shètítgé',
the month name
is 'Bìjù',
the day is jiǎzǐ,
with the winter solstice at midnight and dawn."

Above is the "Calendrical Treatise":
The major remainder refers to
days.
The minor remainder refers to
months.
Duānméng is
the year name.
Branches: Chǒu is named Chìfènruò,
Yín is named Shètítígé.
Stems: Bǐng is named Yóuzhào.
Due north,
winter solstice falls at the zǐ hour;
due west,
at the yǒu hour;
due south,
at the wǔ hour;
due east,
at the mǎo hour.
In the central palace, the Polar Star,
the brightest one among them,
is where Tàiyī constantly resides;
the three stars beside it are the Three Dukes,
or said to be the sons' domain.
Behind, four stars in a curve,
the large star at the end is the principal consort,
the remaining three stars belong to the rear palace.
Encircling them are twelve stars forming a defense,
the feudal ministers.
All are called the Purple Palace.
In front, aligned with the Dipper's mouth, three stars,
following the northern end sharp,
appearing as if visible or not,
are called Yīndé,
or some say Tiānyī.
Three stars to the left of the Purple Palace are called Tiānqiāng,
five stars to the right are called Tiānbàng,
behind, six stars cross the Milky Way reaching Yíngshì,
called Gédào.
The Big Dipper's seven stars,
are what is called
"the revolving jade sighting-tube and jade balance to harmonize the seven administrations."
The handle points to the Dragon's horn,
the bowl aligns with the Southern Dipper,
the ladle rests on Shēn's head.
Using dusk to establish directions is the handle;
the handle, from Huà and southwestward.
Using midnight to establish directions is the bowl;
the bowl, aligns with the central region between the Hé and Jǐ rivers.
Using dawn to establish directions is the ladle;
the ladle, from the sea and Dài northeastward.
The Dipper is the Emperor's chariot,
moving in the center,
overseeing the four directions.
Dividing yin and yang,
establishing the four seasons,
balancing the five phases,
shifting the nodal divisions,
fixing the various cycles,
all are connected to the Dipper.
On the Dipper's ladle, six stars wearing a basket are called the Wénchāng Palace:
first is the Supreme General,
second is the Secondary General,
third is the Noble Minister,
fourth is the Director of Destinies,
fifth is the Director of Center,
sixth is the Director of Emoluments.
In the middle of the Dipper's ladle,
is the prison of nobles.
Below the ladle, six stars,
paired closely together,
are named Sāntái.
If the Sāntái's colors are uniform,
ruler and minister are harmonious;
if not uniform,
there is discord.
If the auxiliary star is bright and close,
supporting ministers are intimate and strong;
if faint and small,
they are distant and weak.
At the end of the handle are two stars:
one inner is the spear,
Zhāoyáo;
one outer is the shield,
Tiānfēng.
There are fifteen stars in a curved circle,
attached to the handle,
called the prison of commoners.
If the stars in this prison are full, then prisoners are many;
if empty, then they are released.
If Tiānyī,
Qiāng, Bàng,
spear, shield shake,
and their angles are large,
troops will rise.
The eastern palace is the Azure Dragon,
Fáng, Xīn.
Xīn is the bright hall,
its large star is the Heavenly King,
the front and rear stars are the sons' domain.
They should not be aligned straight;
if straight, the Heavenly King makes errors in strategy.
Fáng is the mansion,
called Tiānsì.
To its north,
is the right side horse.
Beside it are two stars called the collar;
one star to the north is called the linchpin.
To the northeast, twelve stars in a curve are called the banner.
In the banner, four stars are called Tiānshì;
within them, six stars are called the market tower.
If the stars in the market are numerous, it signifies abundance;
if sparse, it signifies waste.
South of Fáng, many stars are called the cavalry officials.
Left horn,
is the judge; right horn,
is the general. The great horn,
is the Heavenly King's imperial court.
On its two sides, each has three stars,
forming a tripod curve,
called Shètí.
Shètí,
aligns with where the Dipper's handle points,
used to establish the seasons,
hence it is called
"Shètítígé."
Kàng is the sparse temple,
governing illnesses.
Its two large stars north and south,
are called the Southern Gate.
Dĭ is the heavenly root,
governing epidemics.
Wěi is the nine sons,
said to be ruler and ministers;
if repelled and cut off,
there is disharmony.
Jī is the wandering guest,
said to be gossip.
If Mars offends or guards the horn,
then there will be war.
If it involves Fáng, Xīn,
the king dislikes it.
The southern palace is the Vermilion Bird,
comprising Quán and Héng.
Héng represents Tàiwēi,
the court of the three luminaries.
Twelve stars form its protective enclosure,
symbolizing feudal lords:
to the west, the general;
to the east, the chancellor;
four stars to the south,
the law executors;
in the center, the main gate;
to the left and right of the gate,
the side gates.
Inside the gates are six stars,
representing the nobles.
Within them, five stars
form the seats of the Five Emperors.
Behind, a cluster of fifteen stars,
densely packed,
is called the positions of court gentlemen;
beside them, one large star
marks the general's position.
When the moon and five planets enter smoothly,
following the path,
their exit is monitored,
and what they guard
indicates whom the Son of Heaven will punish.
If they enter against the order,
or do not follow the path,
their offense is named accordingly;
if they traverse the central seat,
manifesting forms,
it signifies conspiracies among subordinates.
Venus and Mars are particularly significant.
West of the court's enclosure, five descending stars
are called Shǎowēi,
representing scholars and officials.
Quán is Xuānyuán.
Xuānyuán
has the form of a yellow dragon.
The large star in front
symbolizes the queen;
the small stars beside it
represent the attendants and imperial concubines.
When the moon or five planets guard or offend these,
interpret as with Héng.
Dōngjǐng governs water affairs.
The curved star to its west is called Yuè.
North of Yuè
is Běihé;
south, Nánhé;
between the two rivers
and Tiānquè lies the pass and bridge.
Yúguǐ
concerns sacrificial matters;
the white one in the center is the essence.
If Mars guards Běihé or Nánhé,
armies will rise,
and grains will not ripen.
Thus, virtue is completed in Héng,
observations in Huáng,
harm in Yuè,
calamity in Jǐng,
and punishment in the essence.
Liǔ is the bird's beak,
governing trees and plants.
Qīxīng,
the neck, is the round office,
overseeing urgent matters.
Zhāng, plain,
is the kitchen,
hosting guests with wine.
Yì forms the wings,
governing distant visitors.
Zhěn is the chariot,
governing wind.
Beside it, a small star
is called Chángshā,
which should not shine brightly;
if it shines as brightly as the four stars,
or if the five planets enter Zhěn,
great armies will rise.
South of Zhěn, numerous stars are called Tiānkùlóu;
the treasury has five chariots.
If the chariot stars have horns or multiply,
or are incomplete,
there will be no place for chariots and horses.
The western palace is Xiánchí,
called Tiānwǔhuáng.
Wǔhuáng
is the carriage house of the Five Emperors.
If Mars enters,
drought ensues; Venus,
war; Water Star,
floods. Inside are three pillars;
if the pillars are incomplete,
armies rise.
Kuí is called the sealed swine,
governing ditches and drains.
Lóu gathers crowds.
Wèi is the celestial granary.
The numerous stars to its south are called Kuàijī.
Mǎo is called the shaggy head,
the star of the barbarians,
signaling gatherings in white garments.
Bì is called the rare chariot,
representing border troops,
governing hunting.
The small star beside its large star is the attached ear.
If the attached ear shakes,
slanderous and rebellious ministers are at the side.
Between Mǎo and Bì lies the celestial street.
Its shady side
belongs to dark kingdoms;
the sunny side, to bright kingdoms.
Shēn is the white tiger.
The three stars in a straight line
are the weighing stone.
Below them, three stars,
sharp, are called Fá,
governing execution and cutting.
Outside, four stars
form the left and right shoulders and thighs.
Three small stars set at a corner
are called Zīxī,
the tiger's head,
overseeing provisions and travel.
To the south, four stars
are called Tiāncè.
Below Tiāncè, one star
is called Tiānshǐ.
If the arrow is yellow, it is auspicious;
blue, white,
or black, inauspicious.
To the west, nine curved stars
arrange in three groups:
one is Tiānqí,
two Tiānyuàn,
three Jiǔyóu.
To the east, a large star is called Láng.
If Láng's horn changes color,
there will be many robbers and thieves.
Below, four stars are called Hú,
pointing straight at Láng.
Near the earth, opposite Láng, a large star
is called the Southern Pole Old Man.
If the Old Man appears,
governance is peaceful;
if not,
armies rise.
Often observed south of the suburb during the autumn equinox.
If the attached ear enters Bì,
armies rise.
The northern palace is the Dark Warrior,
comprising Xū and Wēi.
Wēi represents building houses;
Xū governs mourning and weeping.
To the south, numerous stars
are called the Feathery Forest Celestial Army.
West of the army is the fortress,
or called Yuè.
Beside it, a large star is Běiluò.
If Běiluò appears faint or vanishes,
and the army stars move with fewer angles,
or if the five planets offend Běiluò,
entering the army,
armies will rise.
Mars, Venus,
and Mercury are especially significant:
Mars brings army worries;
Mercury, flood disasters;
Jupiter and Saturn,
army auspiciousness.
East of Wēi, six stars,
paired in twos,
are called Sīkōng.
The Encampment constitutes the Pure Temple,
called the Detached Palace,
and the Covered Passageway.
The four stars within the Han River,
are named the Celestial Team.
Beside them is one star,
called Wáng Liáng.
When Wáng Liáng whips his horse,
chariots and cavalry fill the wilds.
Nearby are eight stars,
crossing the Han River,
named the Celestial Pond.
Beside the Celestial Pond,
is the River Star.
When the River Star moves,
people wade through water.
The Pestle
and Mortar, four stars,
are south of Rooftop.
The Gourd,
if guarded by a blue-black star,
indicates fish and salt become expensive.
The Southern Dipper serves as the temple,
with the Establishment stars to its north.
The Establishment stars
represent a banner.
The Oxherd serves as sacrificial animals.
To its north is the Drum at the River.
The great star of the Drum at the River
is the supreme general;
those to its left and right,
are the left and right generals.
The Maiden,
has the Weaving Maid to her north.
The Weaving Maid
is the celestial granddaughter.
Observing the paths of the sun
and moon to gauge the progress or regression of Jupiter.
It is said to belong to the east, element wood,
governing spring,
and the days Jiǎ and Yǐ.
When righteousness is lost,
punishment comes from Jupiter.
Jupiter's advance and retreat,
determine the fate of the state corresponding to its lodge.
The state where it resides cannot be attacked,
but it can punish others.
If it hastens ahead of its lodge, it is called advancing;
falling behind its lodge is called retreating.
Advancing means the state will have troops but not return;
retreating means the state will have worries,
its generals will perish,
and the state will collapse.
Where it resides,
if all five stars follow and gather in one lodge,
the state below can attain the world through righteousness.
In the Shètítígé year:
the year's shadow moves left to Yín,
Jupiter moves right and resides at Chǒu.
In the first month,
it appears in the east at dawn with the Dipper
and Oxherd,
named Jiāndé.
Its color is azure and luminous.
If it misses its order,
a response will be seen in the Willow.
If the year is early,
there will be flood; if late,
drought.
Jupiter appears,
moves east twelve degrees,
stops after a hundred days,
then reverses and moves retrograde;
retrogrades eight degrees,
over a hundred days,
then resumes eastward movement.
It travels thirty and seven-sixteenths degrees per year,
averaging one-twelfth of a degree daily,
completing a circuit in twelve years.
It always appears in the east,
at dawn;
and sets in the west,
at dusk.
In the Chányān year:
the year's shadow is at Mǎo,
the star resides at Zǐ.
In the second month, it appears at dawn with the Maiden,
Emptiness, and Rooftop,
named Jiàngrù.
It is very luminous.
If it misses its order,
a response will be seen in the Spread.
That year will have great floods.
In the Zhíxú year:
the year's shadow is at Chén,
the star resides at Hài.
In the third month, it appears at dawn with the Encampment
and Eastern Wall,
named Qīngzhāng.
Its azure color is very prominent.
If it misses its order,
a response will be seen in the Chariot Platform.
If the year is early,
drought; if late,
flood.
In the Dàhuāngluò year:
the year's shadow is at Sì,
the star resides at Xū.
In the fourth month, it appears at dawn with the Legs
and Bond,
named Piánzhǒng.
It is blazing red in color,
and luminous.
If it misses its order,
a response will be seen in the Neck.
In the Dūnzāng year:
the year's shadow is at Wǔ,
the star resides at Yǒu.
In the fifth month, it appears at dawn with the Stomach,
Hairy Head, and Net,
named Kāimíng.
It is flaming and luminous.
Lay down arms;
only beneficial for the duke and king,
not favorable for military affairs.
If it misses its order,
a response will be seen in the Room.
If the year is early,
drought; if late,
flood.
In the Yèqià year:
the year's shadow is at Wèi,
the star resides at Shēn.
In the sixth month, it appears at dawn with the Turtle
and Triaster,
named Chángliè.
It is bright and luminous.
Favorable for military campaigns.
If it misses its order,
a response will be seen in the Winnowing Basket.
In the Tūntān year:
the year's shadow is at Shēn,
the star resides at Wèi.
In the seventh month, it appears at dawn with the Eastern Well
and Ghosts,
named Dàyīn.
It is brilliantly white.
If it misses its order,
a response will be seen in the Oxherd.
In the Zuò'è year:
the year's shadow is at Yǒu,
the star resides at Wǔ.
In the eighth month, it appears at dawn with the Willow,
Seven Stars,
and Spread,
named Chángwáng.
It is radiant with sharp light.
The state will prosper,
and grains ripen.
If it misses its order,
a response will be seen in Rooftop.
There will be drought yet prosperity,
but also loss of women,
and people's suffering.
In the Yānmào year:
the year's shadow is at Xū,
the star resides at Sì.
In the ninth month, it appears at dawn with the Wings
and Chariot Platform,
named Tiānsuī.
It is white and very bright.
If it misses its order,
a response will be seen in the Eastern Wall.
That year will have floods,
and loss of women.
In the year of Dàyuānxiàn:
The Year Yin is in Hài,
and the star resides in Chén.
It appears in the morning with Jiǎo and
Kàng in the tenth month,
called Dàzhāng.
It is azure in color,
and the star seems to leap while emerging darkly at dawn,
this is termed
"Zhèngpíng".
When armies are raised,
their leaders must be martial;
if the state possesses virtue,
it will rule all within the seas.
If it misses its station,
there will be a corresponding appearance in Lóu.
In the year of Kùndūn:
The Year Yin is in Zǐ,
and the star resides in Mǎo.
It appears in the morning with Dī,
Fáng, and Xīn in the eleventh month,
called Tiānquán.
Its dark color is very bright.
Rivers and ponds will flourish,
but it is unfavorable to raise troops.
If it misses its station,
there will be a corresponding appearance in Mǎo.
In the year of Chìfènruò:
The Year Yin is in Chǒu,
and the star resides in Yín.
It appears in the morning with Wěi and
Jī in the twelfth month,
called Tiānhào.
Its deep black color is very bright.
If it misses its station,
there will be a corresponding appearance in Shēn.
If it should reside but does not,
or resides and sways left and right,
or leaves when it should not,
and meets with other stars,
then the state will face misfortune.
If it resides long,
the state will have abundant virtue.
If its horns move,
now small now large,
and its color changes frequently,
the ruler will have worries.
If it misses its station and lodge below,
moving northeast,
in three months Tiānbàng will appear,
four zhǎng long,
with a pointed end.
Moving southeast,
in three months a comet will appear,
two zhǎng long,
resembling a broom.
Retreating northwest,
in three months Tiānchán will appear,
four zhǎng long,
with a pointed end.
Retreating southwest,
in three months Tiānqiāng will appear,
several zhǎng long,
pointed at both ends.
Carefully observe the state where these are seen,
and do not undertake affairs or use troops.
If it appears as if floating or sinking,
the state will have earthworks;
if as sinking or floating,
its fields will be lost.
If it is red and has horns,
the state where it resides will prosper.
Those who fight facing its horns
will not win.
If the star is red-yellow and sinks,
the fields where it resides will have great harvests.
If it is blue-white and red-gray,
the fields where it resides will have worries.
If the Year Star enters the moon,
its fields will have expelled ministers;
if it fights with Tàibái,
its fields will have defeated armies.
The Year Star is also called Shètí,
Chónghuá,
Yìngxīng,
and Jìxīng.
Yíngshì is the clear temple,
the temple of the Year Star.
Observe the strong qi to locate Yínghuò.
It is said to belong to the south, fire,
governing summer,
and the days Bǐng and
Dīng. When rites are lost,
punishment comes from Yínghuò,
that is when Yínghuò errs in its path.
When it appears, there is war;
when it enters, war disperses.
It determines the fate of the state by its lodge.
Yínghuò signifies rebellion,
atrocities,
disease, mourning,
famine, and war.
If it retrogrades two lodges or more,
and resides there,
in three months there will be calamity,
in five months it will suffer war,
in seven months half its land is lost,
in nine months most of its land is lost.
If it enters and exits together with others,
the state's sacrifices will be cut off.
If it resides,
calamity will return,
great events may turn small;
if it comes late,
small events may turn great.
To its south, men will be lost;
to its north, women will be lost.
If its horns move and circle around,
and it moves forward and back suddenly,
left and right,
the calamity increases.
If it fights with another star,
and their lights reach each other,
it causes harm;
if not,
no harm.
If all five stars follow and gather in one lodge,
the state below can attract the world with rites.
By its rule,
it emerges and moves east sixteen lodges then stops;
retrogrades two lodges;
in sixty days,
it resumes eastward movement,
counting tens of lodges from where it stopped,
and in ten months enters the west;
it moves hidden for five months,
then emerges in the east.
If it emerges in the west, it is called
"Fǎnmíng",
which those in command dislike.
It moves east rapidly,
covering one and a half degrees per day.
Whether it moves east,
west, south,
or north swiftly,
troops gather below it;
in battle,
following it brings victory,
opposing it brings defeat.
If Yínghuò follows Tàibái,
the army will have worries;
if it separates,
the army will retreat.
If it emerges on the dark side of Tàibái,
there will be divided forces;
if on the bright side,
there will be battles with deputy generals.
When it is moving,
if Tàibái catches up,
armies are broken and generals killed.
If it intrudes upon or assaults Tàiwēi,
Xuānyuán,
or Yíngshì,
those in command dislike it.
Xīn is the bright hall,
the temple of Yínghuò.
Observe this carefully.
Calculate the meeting with the Dipper to fix the position of Zhènxīng.
It is said to belong to the center, earth,
governing late summer,
and the days Wù and
Jǐ, representing Huángdì,
virtue,
and the image of the queen.
It fills one lodge each year,
and the state where it resides is auspicious.
If it resides where it should not,
or leaves and returns,
and resides again,
the state gains land,
or else gains women.
If it should reside but does not,
or having resided,
moves east or west away,
the state loses land,
or else loses women,
and should not undertake affairs or use troops.
If it resides long,
the state's blessings are thick;
if it moves, blessings are thin.
One is named Dìhóu,
presiding over the year.
It traverses thirteen and five over one hundred twelve degrees annually,
moving one over twenty-eight degrees daily,
completing a celestial cycle in twenty-eight years.
Where it resides,
the five stars follow and gather in one constellation,
and the state below it
can heavily influence the world.
If rites, virtue,
righteousness, execution,
and punishments are all lost,
then the Tǔxīng (Saturn) will shake accordingly.
If it advances,
the king will be unsettled;
if it retreats,
armies will not return.
Tǔxīng,
its color is yellow,
with nine rays,
and its musical note is Huángzhōng Gōng.
If it deviates upward by two or three constellations, it is called advancement,
leading to unfulfilled sovereign decrees,
or else great floods.
If it deviates downward by two or three constellations, it is called retreat,
causing royal sorrow,
and the year will not recover,
or else the sky may split or the earth quake.
The Dipper is the Grand Chamber of culture,
the temple of Tǔxīng,
the star of the Son of Heaven.
When Mùxīng (Jupiter) aligns with Tǔxīng,
it signifies internal strife,
famine, and the ruler should not engage in battle,
or face defeat; with Shuǐxīng (Mercury), plans change and affairs alter;
with Huǒxīng (Mars), drought ensues;
with Jīnxīng (Venus), it brings gatherings in white garments or floods.
If Jīnxīng is to the south, it is called male and female union,
and the grain harvest is abundant.
If Jīnxīng is to the north,
the year's harvest is partial or none.
Huǒxīng aligning with Shuǐxīng signifies tempering,
with Jīnxīng, melting,
and mourning,
all indicating that no actions should be taken,
and military campaigns will be greatly defeated.
With Tǔxīng, it brings worry,
and trouble among high ministers;
great famine,
defeat in battle,
formation of the northern army,
military distress,
and major failures in undertakings.
Tǔxīng aligning with Shuǐxīng,
brings abundance yet obstruction,
with armies overturned,
and the state should not initiate actions.
If it emerges, land is lost;
if it enters, land is gained.
With Jīnxīng, it brings illness,
internal conflict,
and loss of land.
If three stars align,
the state in that constellation will face internal and external strife and mourning,
with changes in rulers or dukes.
If four stars align,
warfare and mourning arise together,
the noble worry,
and the common people flee.
If five stars align,
this signifies a change in rule,
where virtue
brings celebration,
and a new great leader is established,
encompassing the four directions,
with descendants flourishing;
without virtue,
it brings calamity or ruin.
If all five stars are large,
the events are also major;
if all are small,
the events are minor as well.
Early emergence is called advancement,
and the advancer is the guest.
Late emergence is called retreat,
and the retreater is the host.
There must be a celestial response seen in the pointer stars.
Sharing a constellation is called alignment.
Encroaching upon each other is called conflict,
and within seven degrees, it is inevitable.
If the five stars appear white and circular,
it signifies mourning and drought;
if red and circular,
then there is internal unrest,
and warfare;
if blue and circular,
it brings worry of floods;
if black and circular,
it means disease,
and many deaths;
if yellow and circular,
then it is auspicious.
Red horns侵犯 my city,
yellow horns indicate disputes over land,
white horns bring sounds of weeping,
blue horns signal military worries,
black horns mean floods.
Intentions lead to the end of relentless warfare.
If the five stars share the same color,
the world lays down arms,
and the people thrive in peace.
Spring winds and autumn rains,
winter cold and summer heat,
their fluctuations often relate to this.
Tǔxīng appears for one hundred twenty days and then retrogresses westward,
moving west for one hundred twenty days before turning eastward.
It is visible for three hundred thirty days and then disappears,
vanishing for thirty days before reappearing in the east.
When the Grand Year is in Jiǎ Yín,
Zhènxīng is in Dōngbì,
thus it resides in Yíngshì.
Observe the sun's motion to determine Tàibái's position.
It is associated with the west,
autumn, days Gēng and
Xīn, presiding over execution.
If execution is erred,
punishment comes from Tàibái.
If Tàibái errs in its path,
the state corresponding to its constellation is affected.
It emerges for eighteen constellations over two hundred forty days and then disappears.
Disappearing in the east,
it moves hidden for eleven constellations over one hundred thirty days;
disappearing in the west,
it moves hidden for three constellations over sixteen days before emerging.
If it should emerge but does not,
or should disappear but does not,
this is called losing its place,
and if not the army is shattered,
then the ruler of the state will be usurped.
Its record begins from the Upper Epoch,
in the year of Shètítígé,
it appears in the east with Yíngshì at dawn,
and sets when reaching Jiǎo;
it appears in the west with Yíngshì at dusk,
and sets when reaching Jiǎo;
it appears at dawn with Jiǎo,
and sets in Bì, ;
it appears at dusk with Jiǎo,
and sets in Bì;
it appears at dawn with Bì,
and sets in Jī;
it appears at dusk with Bì,
and sets in Jī;
it appears at dawn with Jī,
and sets in Liǔ;
it appears at dusk with Jī,
and sets in Liǔ;
it appears at dawn with Liǔ,
and sets in Yíngshì;
it appears at dusk with Liǔ,
and sets in Yíngshì.
In total, it rises and sets five times each in the east and west,
taking eight years,
and two hundred twenty days,
then reappears in the east with Yíngshì at dawn.
Generally,
it completes one circuit of the heavens in a year.
When it first appears in the east,
it moves slowly,
at a rate of half a degree per day,
for one hundred twenty days;
it must retrograde one or two lunar lodges;
reaching its highest point and then turning back,
it moves eastward,
traveling one and a half degrees per day,
for one hundred twenty days before setting.
When it is low,
close to the sun,
it is called Míngxīng,
and is gentle; when high,
far from the sun,
it is called Dàxiāo,
and is firm. When it first appears in the west,
it moves swiftly,
at a rate of one and a half degrees per day,
for one hundred twenty days;
reaching its highest point and then moving slowly,
at half a degree per day,
for one hundred twenty days,
it sets at dawn,
and must retrograde one or two lunar lodges before setting.
When it is low,
close to the sun,
it is called Tàibái,
and is gentle; when high,
far from the sun,
it is called Dàxiāng,
and is firm. It rises at Chén and
Xū, and sets at Chǒu and
Wèi.
If it fails to appear when it should,
or sets when it should not,
arms are laid down worldwide,
and if troops are abroad,
they return. If it appears when it should not,
or fails to set when it should,
war breaks out worldwide,
and states are destroyed.
If it appears at the expected time,
the state prospers.
If it rises in the east, it governs the east;
if it sets in the east, it governs the north;
if it rises in the west, it governs the west;
if it sets in the west, it governs the south.
Where it lingers long,
that direction benefits;
if it moves quickly, that direction suffers misfortune.
From west to east,
the due west states are auspicious.
From east to west,
the due east states are auspicious.
It does not traverse the heavens;
if it traverses the heavens,
governments change worldwide.
If it stirs with small angles,
military action arises.
If it appears large at first,
then small later,
the military is weak;
if it appears small at first,
then large later,
the military is strong.
If it appears high,
deep military engagements are auspicious,
shallow ones inauspicious;
if low, shallow engagements are auspicious,
deep ones inauspicious.
When the sun is south and the metal star is to its south,
or when the sun is north and the metal star is to its north,
it is called excess,
and feudal kings are unsettled,
with military advances auspicious and retreats inauspicious.
When the sun is south and the metal star is to its north,
or when the sun is north and the metal star is to its south,
it is called contraction,
and feudal kings have worries,
with military retreats auspicious and advances inauspicious.
In employing the military, emulate Tàibái:
if Tàibái moves swiftly,
advance swiftly;
if slow, advance slowly.
If it has angles, be bold in battle.
If it shakes and is restless,
be restless. If it is round and calm,
be calm. Follow the direction of its angles,
for auspiciousness; oppose it,
and all is inauspicious.
When it rises, send out troops;
when it sets, withdraw troops.
Red angles,
mean there will be battle;
white angles,
mean there will be mourning;
black round angles,
mean worries and water-related affairs;
green round small angles,
mean worries and wood-related affairs;
yellow round harmonious angles,
mean earth-related affairs,
and a fruitful year.
If it has been out for three days and then retreats,
fading as it sets,
and after three days emerges strongly again,
this is called weakness,
and the states below will suffer military defeat and generals fleeing.
If it has set for three days and then emerges faintly again,
and after three days sets strongly once more,
the states below will have worries;
though the army has provisions and weapons,
they will be left for others to use;
though the soldiers are numerous,
the general will be captured.
If it appears in the west and deviates from its path,
foreign states are defeated;
if it appears in the east and deviates from its path,
the central states are defeated.
If its color is greatly round and yellowish glossy,
favorable events can be undertaken;
if it is round and greatly red,
the military is strong but does not engage in battle.
When Venus appears white,
it is likened to the Wolf Star;
when red, to the Heart Star;
when yellow, to the left shoulder of the Three Stars;
when bluish, to the right shoulder of the Three Stars;
when black, to the great star of the Dipper.
If all five planets follow Venus and gather in one lunar lodge,
the state below can raise armies to conquer the world.
If it occupies a full position,
there will be gains;
if it occupies an empty position,
there will be no gains.
Movement overcomes color,
color overcomes position,
having a position overcomes having none,
having color overcomes having none,
and full movement overcomes all.
If it emerges and lingers among the Mulberry and Elm trees,
it harms the state below.
If it rises swiftly,
not completing its days,
and passes mid-heaven,
it harms the opposing state.
Rising then descending,
descending then rising,
indicates a rebellious general.
If it enters the moon,
the general will be executed.
When Metal and Wood stars conjunct,
if bright, battles below will not engage,
armies may rise but not fight;
if the conjunction destroys each other,
there will be defeated armies in the fields.
Appearing in the west,
if at dusk it emerges in the yin,
yin armies are strong;
if at evening meal time, somewhat weak;
if at midnight, moderately weak;
if at cockcrow, very weak:
this is called yin sinking into yang.
In the east,
riding the dawn and emerging in the yang,
yang armies are strong;
if at cockcrow, somewhat weak;
if at midnight, moderately weak;
if at dusk, very weak:
this is called yang sinking into yin.
If Venus is hidden,
and one sends out armies,
the armies will suffer calamity.
If it emerges south of Mǎo,
the south defeats the north;
if north of Mǎo,
the north defeats the south;
if directly at Mǎo,
eastern states benefit.
If emerging north of Yǒu,
the north defeats the south;
if south of Yǒu,
the south defeats the north;
if directly at Yǒu,
western states prevail.
If it offends against the fixed stars,
there will be minor battles;
if against the five planets,
major battles.
In such offenses,
if Venus appears south of them,
southern states are defeated;
if north of them,
northern states are defeated.
Moving swiftly indicates military affairs; not moving,
civil affairs.
If white with five rays,
emerging early causes lunar eclipses,
late causes celestial omens and comets,
and will affect that state.
Emerging in the east signifies virtue,
undertake affairs facing it with left side, auspicious.
Emerging in the west signifies punishment,
undertake affairs turning right side away from it, auspicious.
Opposite actions bring misfortune.
If Venus's light casts shadows,
victory in battle.
If visible by day and crossing the sky,
this is called contending for brightness,
strong states weaken,
small states strengthen,
and the queen prospers.
Kàng is the sparse temple,
the temple of Venus.
Venus
represents high ministers,
its title is Senior Duke.
Its other names are Yīn Star,
Tàizhèng,
Yíng Star,
Guān Star,
Gōng Star,
Míng Star,
Great Decline,
Great Marsh,
Final Star,
Great Minister,
Tiānhào,
Xù Star,
and Yuèwěi.
The Grand Minister of War should carefully observe these.
Observe the conjunctions of the sun and celestial markers,
to determine the position of Mercury.
It is said to belong to the north, water,
the essence of the Great Yin,
governing winter,
and the days Rén
and Guǐ. For failures in punishment,
the penalty comes from Mercury,
determining the state by its lodge.
It rectifies the four seasons:
in mid-spring at the spring equinox,
it appears in the evening beyond Kuí,
Lóu, and Wèi, east five lodges,
for Qí;
in mid-summer at the summer solstice,
it appears in the evening beyond Dōngjǐng,
Yǔguǐ,
and Liǔ, east seven lodges,
for Chǔ;
in mid-autumn at the autumn equinox,
it appears in the evening beyond Jiǎo,
Kàng, Dī,
and Fáng, east four lodges,
for Hàn;
in mid-winter at the winter solstice,
it appears in the morning beyond the east,
with Wěi,
Jī, Dǒu,
and Qiānniú all to the west,
for the Central States.
Its appearances and disappearances usually occur at Chén,
Xū, Chǒu,
and Wèi.
If it appears early,
it indicates a lunar eclipse;
if late, a comet and celestial calamities.
When it should manifest but fails to, this is an aberration,
signifying armies abroad will not engage in battle.
If it fails to appear in one season,
there will be disharmony in that season;
if in all four seasons,
great famine will strike the land.
When it appears as expected,
a white color signifies drought,
yellow indicates abundant harvests of the five grains,
red foretells warfare,
and black predicts floods.
If it emerges in the east,
large and white,
there are troops abroad,
but they will disband.
Normally in the east,
if it appears red,
the central states will be victorious;
if red in the west,
foreign nations will benefit.
If it turns red without troops abroad,
war will arise.
When it appears in the east together with Tàibái (Venus),
both red and horned,
foreign nations will be greatly defeated,
and the central states will prevail;
when both appear in the west,
red and horned,
foreign nations will benefit.
When the five planets divide the sky's center,
gathering in the east,
the central states benefit;
gathering in the west,
foreign nations using arms will benefit.
If all five stars follow Chénxīng (Mercury) and converge in one lunar lodge,
the state corresponding to that lodge can rule the world through laws.
When Chénxīng does not appear,
Tàibái acts as the guest;
when it appears,
Tàibái acts as the host.
If they appear but do not follow each other,
though there are armies in the field,
they will not fight.
If one emerges in the east
and Tàibái in the west;
or if one emerges in the west,
and Tàibái in the east,
this is called "confrontation"—even with troops in the field, there will be no battle.
Appearing at the wrong time
brings cold when it should be warm,
and warmth when it should be cold.
When it should appear but does not,
this is called "striking the ranks,"
and major military uprisings will occur.
If it enters Tàibái and emerges above,
armies will be broken and generals killed,
with the guest army victorious;
if it emerges below,
the guest will lose territory.
When Chénxīng approaches Tàibái,
and Tàibái does not move away,
the general will die.
If it emerges straight upward like a banner,
armies will be broken and generals killed,
with the guest victorious;
if it emerges downward,
the guest will lose territory.
Observe the direction the banner points
to determine which army will be defeated.
If it circles around Tàibái,
as if fighting with it,
a great battle will ensue,
and the guest will win.
If the rabbit (Mercury) passes Tàibái,
with space enough to sheathe a sword between them,
a minor battle will occur,
and the guest will prevail.
If the rabbit stays ahead of Tàibái,
the army will withdraw;
if it emerges to Tàibái's left,
a small battle will happen;
if it brushes against Tàibái,
tens of thousands will fight,
and the host's officers will die;
if it emerges to Tàibái's right,
three feet away,
the army will urgently seek battle.
Blue horns indicate military worries;
black horns,
floods.
Red movement signifies the end of exhaustive warfare.
The rabbit has seven names:
Xiǎo Zhèng,
Chénxīng,
Tiān Chán,
Ānzhōu Xīng,
Xì Shuǎng,
Néng Xīng,
Gōu Xīng.
If its color is yellow and small,
and it appears in changing positions,
the world's patterns will change for the worse.
The rabbit's five colors:
blue and round signifies sorrow,
white and round means mourning,
red and round indicates internal strife,
black and round brings good fortune.
Red horns invading our city,
yellow horns disputes over land,
white horns the sound of wailing.
When it emerges in the east,
traveling four lunar lodges over forty-eight days,
with a count of twenty days,
it then returns to the east;
when it emerges in the west,
traveling four lodges over forty-eight days,
with a count of twenty days,
it returns to the west.
One can observe it in the lodges Yíngshì,
Jiǎo, Bì,
Jī, Liǔ.
If it appears between Fáng
and Xīn,
an earthquake will occur.
Chénxīng's colors:
In spring, blue-yellow;
in summer, red-white;
in autumn, blue-white,
and the year's harvest will be ripe;
in winter, yellow but not bright.
If it changes from these colors,
the season will not prosper.
If not seen in spring,
great winds will come,
and autumn will bear no fruit.
If not seen in summer,
there will be sixty days of drought,
and a lunar eclipse.
If not seen in autumn,
war will arise,
and spring will not bring growth.
If not seen in winter,
sixty days of rain will fall,
with flooded cities,
and summer will not see growth.
Jiǎo,
Kàng, Dī
correspond to Yǎnzhōu.
Fáng, Xīn
to Yùzhōu.
Wěi, Jī
to Yōuzhōu.
Dǒu corresponds to the rivers
and lakes. Qiānniú
and Wùnǚ
to Yángzhōu.
Xū, Wēi
to Qīngzhōu.
Yíngshì to Dōngbì
to Bīngzhōu.
Kuí, Lóu,
Wèi to Xúzhōu.
Mǎo, Bì
to Jìzhōu.
Zīxī,
Shēn to Yìzhōu.
Dōngjǐng,
Yúguǐ
to Yōngzhōu.
Liǔ, Qīxīng,
Zhāng to Sānhé.
Yì, Zhěn
to Jīngzhōu.
The seven stars form the circular office,
the temple of Chénxīng,
the star of the barbarian tribes.
When two armies confront each other,
and a solar halo appears;
if the halos are equal,
their strengths are balanced;
if thick, long, and large,
there will be victory;
if thin, short, and small,
there will be no victory.
Heavy overlapping leads to great defeat or none at all.
Overlapping signifies harmony,
while backing away indicates discord,
representing separation and distance.
A straight halo signifies self-reliance,
establishing feudal kings;
it breaks armies and kills generals.
Bearing and supporting,
brings joy.
If encircled within,
the inner side wins;
if outside,
the outer side wins.
Blue outside and red inside,
signifies harmony and departure;
red outside and blue inside,
signifies conflict and departure.
If the halo arrives first and departs later,
the stationed army will be victorious.
Arriving first and leaving first,
benefits the front but harms the rear;
arriving later and leaving later,
harms the front but benefits the rear;
arriving late and leaving early,
both front and rear suffer,
and the stationed army will not prevail.
If it appears and then leaves,
its occurrence is swift,
and even if victorious, there is no merit.
If visible for more than half a day,
the merit is great.
A white rainbow, curved and short,
pointed at both ends,
if present, indicates great bloodshed below.
A solar halo determines victory,
with near terms of thirty days,
and far terms of sixty days.
In an eclipse,
the eclipsed part signifies不利;
if it regenerates,
the regenerated part signifies利;
and if the eclipse worsens to completion,
it pertains to the ruler's position.
Based on its alignment and the constellation where the sun lodges,
combined with the day and time,
it dictates the fate of that state.
When the moon follows the middle path,
there is peace and harmony.
In the yīn interval,
there is much water,
and yīn affairs.
Three chǐ north of the outer path,
is the Yīn Star.
Three chǐ further north,
is the Tàiyīn,
indicating great floods,
and military affairs. In the yáng interval,
there is arrogance and willfulness.
The Yáng Star,
brings many violent legal cases.
The Tàiyáng,
signifies great drought and mourning.
At the Horn and Tiānmén,
the tenth month corresponds to the fourth month,
the eleventh to the fifth,
the twelfth to the sixth,
when floods occur,
near ones three chǐ deep,
far ones five chǐ.
If it侵犯 the Four Supports,
the supporting ministers will be executed.
Passing through the Northern and Southern Rivers,
interpreted by yīn-yáng principles,
indicates drought, floods, war, and mourning.
When the moon eclipses Jupiter,
the region of its lodge
suffers famine or loss.
With Mars, there is chaos;
with Saturn, subordinates rebel against superiors;
with Venus, a strong state is defeated in war;
with Mercury, there is disorder among women.
Eclipsing Dàjiǎo,
