is dreaded by those in command;
if the Heart, it signifies internal treachery and disorder;
with other stars,
the region of their lodge faces worry.
Starting from the day of a lunar eclipse,
five-month intervals occur six times,
six-month intervals five times,
five-month intervals again six times,
six-month intervals once,
and five-month intervals five times,
totaling one hundred thirteen months before repeating.
Thus, lunar eclipses
are common;
solar eclipses,
are inauspicious.
For days Jiǎ and Yǐ,
beyond the Four Seas,
sun and moon omens are not interpreted.
For Bǐng and Dīng,
it concerns Jiāng, Huái,
and Hǎi-Dài.
For Wù and Jǐ,
it is Zhōngzhōu,
the Hé and Jǐ rivers.
For Gēng and Xīn,
west of Huà Shān.
For Rén and Guǐ,
north of Héng Shān.
A solar eclipse
concerns the state ruler;
a lunar eclipse,
corresponds to generals and ministers.
The Guóhuáng Star,
large and red,
resembles the South Pole.
Where it appears,
armies rise below it,
and the military is strong;
the opposing side faces不利.
The Zhāomíng Star,
large and white,
without horns,
moves up and down abruptly.
The state where it appears
sees armies rise,
with many changes.
The Wǔcán Star,
appears in the wilds due east.
This star resembles Chénxīng,
about six zhàng above the ground.
The Dàzéi Star,
appears in the wilds due south.
The star is about six zhàng above the ground,
large and red,
frequently moving,
with a glow.
The Sīwēi Star,
appears in the wilds due west.
The star is about six zhàng above the ground,
large and white,
similar to Tàibái.
The Yùhàn Star,
appears in the wilds due north.
The star is about six zhàng above the ground,
large and red,
frequently moving,
and upon close inspection, blue at the center.
These four wild stars,
if appearing out of their proper direction,
indicate armies below,
and the opposing side faces不利.
The Sìtián Stars,
appear from the four corners,
about four zhàng above the ground.
Dìwéi Xián Guāng,
also emerges from the four corners,
about three zhàng above the ground,
like the moon just risen.
Where seen,
there is disorder below;
the disorderly will perish,
the virtuous will prosper.
The Zhú Star,
shaped like Tàibái,
does not move when it appears.
It vanishes upon sight.
Where it illuminates,
cities and towns face disorder.
Like a star but not a star,
like a cloud but not a cloud,
it is named Guīxié.
When Guīxié appears,
there must be someone returning to their state.
Stars are
the dispersed qi of metal,
their essence being fire.
When stars are numerous,
the state is auspicious;
when few, inauspicious.
The Milky Way is
also the dispersed qi of metal,
its essence being water.
When the Milky Way has many stars,
there is much water;
when few, drought—
this is the general principle.
The Heavenly Drum
has a sound like thunder yet is not thunder,
its sound originates from the sky and reaches down to the earth.
Where it goes,
troops will be mobilized below.
The Heavenly Dog
resembles a great shooting star,
makes a sound,
and where it lands on the earth,
it is dog-like.
Where it falls,
it appears like blazing flames rushing skyward.
The area below is circular, covering several qǐng of land;
if it is pointed above, it appears yellow,
and within a thousand lǐ, armies will be shattered and generals killed.
The Gé zé star
looks like flaming fire.
Yellow-white in color,
it rises from the ground upward.
Wide at the bottom,
pointed at the top.
When it appears,
there is harvest without planting;
if there are no construction projects,
there will surely be great harm.
The banner of Chīyóu
resembles a broomstar but curves at the back,
shaped like a banner.
When it appears, the king will campaign against the four directions.
Xún shǐ
emerges beside the Big Dipper,
shaped like a rooster.
When agitated,
it turns blue-black,
resembling a crouching turtle.
Wǎng shǐ
is like a large meteor,
moving serpentine and dark blue,
appearing as if covered in feathers.
Cháng gēng
is like a bolt of cloth spread across the sky.
When this star appears,
military conflicts arise.
When a star falls to the ground,
it becomes a stone.
Between the Hé and Jì rivers,
falling stars are occasionally seen.
When the sky is clear, the Jǐng star appears.
The Jǐng star
is a star of virtue.
Its form is not constant,
often appearing in states governed by the Way.
In observing cloud qi,
looking upward,
it can be seen for three to four hundred lǐ;
looking horizontally,
above the mulberry and elm trees,
for over a thousand to two thousand lǐ;
climbing high to look,
extending down to the earth for three thousand lǐ.
If clouds have animal-like forms above,
it signifies victory.
South of Huà,
the qi is black below and red above.
In the suburbs of Sōnggāo
and the three Hé regions,
the qi is pure red.
North of Héngshān,
the qi is black below and blue above.
Between Bó, Jié,
the sea, and Dài,
the qi is all black.
Between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
the qi is all white.
Qi of laborers is white.
Qi of earthworks is yellow.
Chariot qi rises and falls abruptly,
often gathering.
Cavalry qi is low and spread out.
Infantry qi is concentrated.
If low in front and high in back,
it indicates speed; if square in front and high in back,
it is sharp; if sharp in back and low,
it signifies retreat. Qi that is level indicates slow movement.
If high in front and low in back,
it stops and turns back.
When qi confronts each other,
the low overcomes the high,
the sharp overcomes the square.
If qi comes low and follows the chariot path,
within three to four days,
it can be seen five to six lǐ away.
If qi comes seven to eight chǐ high,
within five to six days,
it can be seen over ten lǐ away.
If qi comes over one zhàng to two zhàng high,
within thirty to forty days,
it can be seen fifty to sixty lǐ away.
If wispy clouds are pure white,
the general is fierce,
but the soldiers are timid.
If the base is large and extends far forward,
battle is imminent.
Blue-white clouds
with the front low
indicate victory in battle;
if the front is red and raised,
defeat in battle.
Battle array clouds stand like walls.
Shuttle clouds resemble a weaver's shuttle.
Axle clouds are concentrated with both ends pointed.
Rope-like dipper clouds
stretch across the sky in front,
half covering the sky.
Curling clouds resemble flags, hence the name.
Hook clouds are curved.
When such clouds appear,
they are interpreted with the five colors.
If glossy, concentrated, and dense,
their appearance is striking,
then there is an omen;
military conflict will surely arise,
and combat will occur where they point.
What Wáng Shuò observed
was determined by the sun's side.
Cloud qi beside the sun
represents the sovereign's image.
All are interpreted according to their shapes.
Thus, the qi of the northern barbarians is like herds of livestock and felt tents,
the qi of the southern barbarians resembles boats and banners.
In places of great floods,
defeated armies' grounds,
ruins of destroyed states,
where money is buried,
above gold and treasures,
there is always qi,
which must be observed.
Sea mirage qi looks like towers and pavilions;
wilderness qi forms like palaces and gate towers.
Cloud qi each reflects the mountains, rivers, and people gathered there.
Thus, to assess prosperity or decline,
enter a state or city,
observe the order of borders and fields,
the upkeep of city walls, houses, and gates,
then the refinement of vehicles, clothing, and livestock.
If substantial and thriving,
it is auspicious; if empty and declining,
inauspicious.
What looks like smoke but is not smoke,
like clouds but not clouds,
luxuriant and chaotic,
twisting and coiling,
is called qīng yún.
Qīng yún
is an auspicious qi.
What looks like fog but is not fog,
where clothes and hats do not get wet,
appears when that area is arming and rushing to war.
As for thunder and lightning,
rainbows,
thunderclaps,
and night glow,
these are movements of yang qi,
emerging in spring and summer,
hiding in autumn and winter,
so observers always monitor them.
The heavens unfold the county's phenomena,
the earth quakes and splits apart.
Mountains collapse and shift,
rivers block and streams stagnate;
waters ripple and land rises,
marshes dry up revealing their patterns.
City walls and village gates,
inner doors and standards wither;
palaces, temples, and residences,
are where the people dwell.
Observe their customs, carriages, and attire,
watch what the people eat and drink.
For the five grains, trees, and plants,
observe where they belong.
Granaries, treasuries, stables, and storehouses,
are the four accessible roads.
The six domestic animals and wild beasts,
their production and movements;
fish, turtles, birds, and rodents,
observe their habitats.
Ghosts wail as if calling,
encountering them brings misfortune.
Transformed words,
truly so.
In general, to predict whether the year will be good or bad,
carefully observe the beginning of the year.
The year's start may be the winter solstice,
when life's energy begins to sprout.
The day after the La festival,
the masses celebrate the end of the year,
gathering for a feast,
to emit yang energy,
hence called the initial year.
The first dawn of the first month,
is the king's start of the year;
the day of the beginning of spring,
marks the start of the four seasons.
These four beginnings,
are the days for observation.
And Hàn Wèi Xiān compiled methods to determine the eight winds from the day after the La festival and the first dawn of the first month.
If the wind comes from the south,
there will be a great drought;
from the southwest,
a minor drought;
from the west,
there will be warfare;
from the northwest,
soybeans will thrive,
with light rain,
hastening troops;
from the north,
it signifies an average year;
from the northeast,
a bountiful year;
from the east,
great floods;
from the southeast,
the people will suffer from epidemics,
and a bad year.
Thus, the eight winds each oppose their counterparts,
and the one that prevails in assessment is the victor.
More prevails over less,
long-lasting over brief,
swift over slow.
From dawn to breakfast time,
pertains to wheat;
from breakfast to midday,
to millet;
from midday to late afternoon,
to broomcorn millet;
from late afternoon to dusk,
to beans;
from dusk to sunset,
to hemp.
It is desired that throughout the day there be clouds,
wind,
and sun.
If the sun appears at its proper time,
the crops will be deep-rooted and fruitful;
if there are no clouds but wind and sun,
at the right time,
they will be shallow-rooted but still fruitful;
if there are clouds and wind,
but no sun,
at the proper time,
they will be deep-rooted but yield little;
if there is sun,
no clouds,
and no wind,
crops at that time will fail.
If this lasts for a meal's duration,
the failure is minor;
if for the time to cook five dou of rice,
the failure is major.
But if the wind rises again,
with clouds,
the crops will recover.
Each uses the cloud color at its time to divinate the suitable crops.
If it rains, snows, or is cold,
the year will be bad.
On this day, if it is bright,
listen to the sounds of the people in the capital and cities.
If the sound is gōng,
the year will be good,
auspicious; if shāng,
there will be warfare;
if zhǐ, drought;
if yǔ, flood;
if jué, a bad year.
Some count the rains consecutively from the first dawn of the first month.
Typically, one shēng per day for food,
up to seven shēng as the limit;
beyond that,
it is not used for divination.
Count up to twelve days,
each day corresponding to a month,
to predict floods and droughts.
For an area within a thousand lǐ,
it serves as a prediction for the whole realm,
throughout the first month.
Based on the moon's position among the constellations,
the sun, wind,
and clouds, predict the state's fortune.
Yet one must examine where the Tàisuì is located.
In metal,
abundance; in water,
ruin; in wood,
famine; in fire,
drought. This is the general principle.
On the first jiǎ day of the first month,
if the wind comes from the east,
it is good for silkworms;
if from the west,
or if there are yellow clouds at dawn,
it is bad.
At the winter solstice, when the day is shortest,
hang an earthenware and charcoal,
if the charcoal moves,
deer shed their antlers,
orchid roots emerge,
springs water leaps,
roughly knowing the solstice arrival,
but key is to determine by gnomon's shadow.
Where the year star resides,
the five grains will flourish.
Its opposite is the clash,
bringing calamity to the year.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Since the beginning of human life,
have not the world's rulers always calendared the sun, moon, and stars?
Through the time of the Five Families and
the Three Dynasties,
they inherited and elucidated it,
internally governing the civilized,
externally dealing with the barbarians,
dividing the central land into twelve provinces,
looking up to observe celestial phenomena,
looking down to emulate earthly categories.
Heaven has the sun and moon,
earth has yin and yang.
Heaven has the five stars,
earth has the five phases.
Heaven has the constellations,
earth has the provincial regions.
The three luminaries,
are the essence of yin and yang,
their energy rooted in the earth,
and the sages systematically manage them.
Before Yōu and Lì,
it is remote.
The celestial changes observed,
all varied by state's cave,
each family divining anomalies,
to match timely responses,
their texts, charts, and records of omens were not standard.
Thus, Confucius, discussing the Six Classics,
recorded anomalies but did not write about their explanations.
As for the way of heaven and fate,
it is not transmitted;
if passed to the right person,
no need for instruction;
if told to the wrong person,
even spoken, it does not become evident.
In ancient times, those who transmitted celestial calculations were:
before Gāoxīn,
Zhòng and Lí;
in the times of Táng [Yáo] and
Yú [Shùn], Xī and
Hé;
in Xià, Kūnwú;
in Yīn-Shāng,
Wū Xián;
in the Zhōu court,
Shǐ Yì and
Cháng Hóng;
in Sòng,
Zǐ Wéi;
in Zhèng, then Pí Zào;
in Qí,
Gān Gōng;
in Chǔ, Táng Mò;
in Zhào, Yǐn Gāo;
in Wèi, Shí Shēn.
Now, the movement of heaven
undergoes a minor change every thirty years,
a medium change in a century,
and a major change every five hundred years;
three major changes form one cycle,
and after three cycles, it is fully established:
this is the grand numeration.
Those who govern states must value the cycles of three and five.
Above and below, each spanning a thousand years,
and then the connection between heaven and humanity is fully prepared.
The Grand Historian [Sīmǎ Qiān] examined ancient celestial changes,
but found none that could be verified in the present.
He roughly used the 242 years of the Spring and Autumn period,
during which there were thirty-six lunar eclipses,
three appearances of comets,
and in the time of Duke Xiāng of Sòng, stars fell like rain.
The Son of Heaven was weak,
the feudal lords governed by force,
the Five Hegemons arose in succession,
and took turns as masters of the mandate.
After this,
the many oppressed the few,
the large annexed the small.
Qín, Chǔ,
Wú, and Yuè,
though considered barbarians,
became powerful hegemons.
The Tián clan usurped Qí,
the three families partitioned Jìn,
and together they became the Warring States.
They contended in attack and conquest,
warfare repeatedly erupted,
cities were frequently slaughtered,
and thus there were famines, epidemics, and sufferings,
ministers and rulers shared worries and hardships,
and their observation of omens and celestial phenomena became especially urgent.
In recent times, the twelve feudal lords and seven states proclaimed themselves kings,
advocates of vertical and horizontal alliances followed one after another,
and Yǐn Gāo,
Táng Mò, Gān Gōng,
and Shí Shēn, according to the affairs of their time, discussed their texts and traditions,
so their prognostications became mixed and trivial.
The twenty-eight lunar mansions govern the twelve provinces,
with the Dipper simultaneously overseeing them,
a practice of long standing.
When Qín was strong,
its omen was Tàibái [Venus],
and its divination lay in Láng [Wolf] and
Hú [Bow]. For Wú and
Chǔ's strength,
the omen was Yínghuò [Mars],
divined by Niǎo Héng [Bird Balance].
For Yān and Qí's strength,
the omen was Chénxīng [Mercury],
divined by Xū and
Wēi.
For Sòng and Zhèng's strength,
the omen was Suìxīng [Jupiter],
divined by Fáng and
Xīn.
For Jìn's strength,
the omen was also Chénxīng [Mercury],
divined by Shēn and Fá.
When Qín annexed the three Jìn states,
Yān, and Dài,
the area south of the Hé River and mountains became the Central States.
Within the Four Seas, the Central States are in the southeast,
which is yang;
yang corresponds to the Sun,
Suìxīng [Jupiter],
Yínghuò [Mars],
and Tiánxīng [Saturn];
divination is south of the celestial street,
governed by Bì.
To the northwest are the Hú, Mò, Yuèzhī, and other peoples who wear felt and fur and draw bows,
which is yīn;
yīn corresponds to the Moon,
Tàibái [Venus],
and Chénxīng [Mercury];
divination is north of the celestial street,
governed by Mǎo.
Thus, the mountains and rivers of the Central States flow northeast,
their axis,
beginning in Lǒng and
Shǔ, and ending in Bó [Sea] and
Jié. Therefore, Qín and
Jìn frequently engaged in warfare,
and again divined by Tàibái [Venus],
for Tàibái governs the Central States;
while the Hú and
Mò repeatedly invaded and plundered,
solely divined by Chénxīng [Mercury],
as Chénxīng moves in and out swiftly and urgently,
often governing the barbarians;
this is the general principle.
This alternates as guest and host.
Yínghuò [Mars] signifies disorder,
externally it governs military affairs,
internally it governs administration.
Hence it is said,
"Even if there is an enlightened Son of Heaven,
he must observe where Yínghuò is located."
The feudal lords alternated in strength,
and calamities and anomalies were recorded from time to time,
but none are worth recording.
During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng,
comets appeared four times in fifteen years,
the longest lasting eighty days,
and some stretching across the sky.
Afterwards, Qín used military force to destroy the six kings,
unified the Central States,
repelled the four barbarians abroad,
and the dead were like tangled hemp,
leading to the simultaneous rise of Zhàng Chǔ,
and within thirty years, troops trampled each other,
beyond counting.
Since Chīyóu,
it had never been like this.
When Xiàng Yǔ rescued Jùlù,
a crooked arrow flowed westward,
and the states east of the mountains then formed a vertical alliance,
marched west to trap the Qín people,
and slaughtered them in Xiányáng.
At the rise of Hàn,
the five planets gathered in Dōngjǐng.
During the siege of Píngchéng,
the moon was haloed around Shēn and
Bì sevenfold.
When the various Lǚ clans rebelled,
there was a solar eclipse,
and daylight turned dark.
When the seven states of Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
a comet stretched several zhàng,
and the celestial dog passed over the fields of Liáng;
when the uprising began,
corpses fell and blood flowed beneath it.
During Yuánguāng and
Yuánshòu,
the banner of Chīyóu reappeared,
stretching half the sky.
Afterwards, imperial armies marched out in all four directions,
subduing the barbarians for decades,
and the campaigns against the Hú were especially severe.
At the fall of Yuè,
Yínghuò guarded the Dipper;
when Cháoxiān was captured,
a comet swept the Hé garrison;
when troops campaigned against Dàyuān,
a comet swept Zhāoyáo:
these are the most prominent examples.
As for minor and intricate changes,
they are too numerous to recount.
From this perspective,
there has never been a sign that appeared without a corresponding response.
Now, among those who practiced celestial calculations in Hàn times,
for stars, it was Táng Dū,
for atmospheric phenomena, Wáng Shuò,
for divining the year, Wèi Xiān.
Thus, the methods of Gān Gōng and
Shí Shēn for calculating the five planets,
only Yínghuò had retrograde motion;
when it retrograded and stationed,
and when other stars retrograde,
or when the sun and moon are eclipsed,
all were used for divination.
I have studied the Records of the Grand Historian,
examining past events,
and found that within a century,
none of the five planets appeared without eventually turning retrograde;
when they turned retrograde,
they often grew prominent and changed color;
solar and lunar eclipses occurred,
and their paths north and south followed their times:
these are their grand patterns.
Thus, the Purple Palace,
Fáng and Xīn,
Quánhéng,
Xiánchí,
Xū and Wēi, and the constellations and stellar divisions,
these are the five celestial officials in their seats,
serving as the warp,
unmoving and unshifting,
varying in size,
constant in breadth and narrowness.
Mercury,
Venus,
Jupiter,
Mars,
and Saturn—these five planets
are the five assistants of heaven,
serving as the weft,
appearing and hiding at their times,
with their transits, advances, and retreats having their measures.
When the sun changes, cultivate virtue;
when the moon changes, reduce punishments;
when the stars change, promote harmony.
For all celestial changes,
only when they exceed the norm should divination be made.
If the ruler is strong and great,
the virtuous will prosper;
if weak and small,
those who practice deceit will perish.
The highest practice is to cultivate virtue,
next to improve governance,
next to implement remedies,
next to perform rituals of aversion,
the lowest being to do nothing.
Changes in the fixed stars are rare,
but divinations based on the three luminaries are frequently used.
Solar and lunar halos and eclipses,
clouds and winds,
these are the transient influences of heaven,
and their manifestations also follow great cycles.
Yet their correspondence with political affairs
is closest to the signs of heaven and humanity.
These five
are heaven's responses.
Those who study the ways of heaven
must comprehend the three luminaries and five planets.
From ancient to modern times, from beginning to end,
deeply observing the changes of the era,
examining their subtleties and coarseness,
then the office of astronomy is complete.
When the Green Emperor practices virtue,
the Gate of Heaven opens for him.
When the Red Emperor practices virtue,
the Celestial Prison empties for him.
When the Yellow Emperor practices virtue,
celestial harmony arises for him.
When the wind comes from the northwest,
it must be on Gēng
or Xīn days. In one autumn,
if it comes five times,
a great amnesty is granted;
if three times,
a minor amnesty.
When the White Emperor practices virtue,
on the twentieth
and twenty-first day of the first month,
if the moon is haloed,
it often carries a great amnesty,
said to be due to the Great Sun.
One saying:
When the White Emperor practices virtue,
Bì and Mǎo form a halo for him.
If the halo lasts three nights,
virtue is achieved;
if not three nights,
or the halo is incomplete,
virtue is not achieved.
Another saying:
if haloed at dawn,
it will occur within ten days.
When the Black Emperor practices virtue,
the Celestial Pass moves for him.
If heaven practices virtue,
the Son of Heaven changes the reign title;
if not virtuous,
wind and rain shatter stones.
The Three Platforms
and Three Balances
are the Celestial Court.
If a guest star appears in the Celestial Court,
there will be extraordinary decrees.
Since ancient times, which emperor receiving the mandate
has not performed the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices?
There may be those who performed the rites without the corresponding signs,
but none witnessed auspicious omens and did not proceed to Mount Tài. Even if receiving the mandate but achievements are insufficient,
or reaching Liángfù
but virtue is not pervasive,
or if pervasive
yet time is insufficient,
thus actual performances are rare.
The tradition says:
"If rites are not performed for three years,
they will be abandoned;
if music is not played for three years,
it will be ruined."
In every era of prosperity,
the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices respond to it,
ceasing when it declines.
The intervals have been long,
over a thousand years,
or short, several hundred years,
so their ceremonies have been lost and obliterated,
and their details cannot be recorded or heard.
The Shàngshū says:
Shun observed the jade sighting-tube and jade balance,
to harmonize the seven governments.
Then he sacrificed to the Supreme Deity,
offered to the six honored ones,
paid homage to the mountains and rivers,
and universally honored all spirits.
He collected the five tokens of jade,
selected an auspicious month and day,
met the four peaks and various governors,
and returned the tokens.
In the second month of the year,
he toured east,
reaching Dàizōng.
Dàizōng
is Mount Tài.
He offered burnt sacrifices,
and paid homage in order to the mountains and rivers.
Then he received the eastern lords.
The eastern lords
were the feudal lords.
He harmonized the seasons, months, and days,
unified pitch, measures, and weights,
cultivated the five rites,
with five jades, three silks,
two live and one dead animals as offerings.
In the fifth month,
he toured to the southern peak.
The southern peak
is Mount Héng.
In the eighth month,
he toured to the western peak.
The western peak
is Mount Huà.
In the eleventh month,
he toured to the northern peak.
The northern peak
is Mount Héng.
All followed the rites of Dàizōng.
The central peak
is Sōnggāo.
He toured once every five years.
Yǔ followed this.
After fourteen generations,
to Emperor Kǒng Jiǎ,
who was licentious in virtue and fond of spirits,
the spirits were profaned,
and two dragons departed.
After three more generations,
Tāng attacked Jié,
wishing to move the Shè altar of Xià,
but could not, and composed the "Xià Shè".
After eight generations,
to Emperor Tài Wù,
a mulberry and paper-mulberry tree grew in the court,
reaching full size in one night,
causing fear.
Yì Zhì said:
"The monstrous cannot overcome virtue."
Tài Wù cultivated virtue,
and the mulberry and paper-mulberry tree died.
Yì Zhì praised Wū Xián,
and the rise of Wū Xián began from this.
After fourteen generations,
Emperor Wǔdīng obtained Fù Yuè as his chancellor,
and Yīn was restored to prosperity,
earning him the title Gāozōng.
A pheasant alighted
on the tripod's ear and crowed,
frightening Wǔdīng.
Zǔ Jǐ said:
"Cultivate virtue."
Wǔdīng followed his advice,
and his reign was long and peaceful.
After five generations,
Emperor Wǔyǐ offended the gods and was struck dead.
After three more generations,
Emperor Zhòu indulged in debauchery,
and King Wǔ attacked him.
From this we observe,
they began with reverence,
but later grew negligent.
The "Zhōu Guān" states,
on the winter solstice,
heaven is worshipped in the southern suburb,
welcoming the arrival of longer days;
on the summer solstice,
the earth deity is sacrificed to.
Both use music and dance,
so the deities may be ritually honored.
The Son of Heaven sacrifices to the famous mountains and great rivers under heaven,
treating the Five Peaks as the Three Dukes,
the Four Waterways as feudal lords,
while feudal lords sacrifice to
the famous mountains and great rivers within their domains.
The Four Waterways are:
the Jiāng, Hé, Huái, and Jǐ.
The Son of Heaven has the Míngtáng
and Bìyōng,
feudal lords have the Pàngōng.
After the Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng,
he performed suburban sacrifices to Hòujì
to pair with heaven,
and ancestral sacrifices to King Wén in the Míngtáng
to pair with the Supreme Deity.
Since Yǔ's rise, soil altars were maintained,
and Hòujì cultivated crops,
hence the Jì shrine existed;
the suburban and soil sacrifices have a long history.
After Zhōu overcame Yīn
for fourteen generations,
each generation declined further,
rites and music were abandoned,
feudal lords acted arbitrarily,
and King Yōu was defeated by the Quǎnróng,
so Zhōu moved east to Luòyì.
Duke Xiāng of Qín attacked the Rong to rescue Zhōu,
and was first ranked among the feudal lords.
Once Duke Xiāng of Qín became a feudal lord,
he resided in the western frontier,
believing himself to host Shǎohào's deity,
built the Xīzhì altar,
sacrificed to the White Emperor,
using one red colt, one yellow ox, and one ram as offerings, it is said.
Sixteen years later,
Duke Wén of Qín hunted east between the Qiān and Wèi rivers,
divined to settle there
and found it auspicious.
Duke Wén dreamed of a yellow snake
descending from heaven to the earth,
its mouth resting at Fūyǎn.
Duke Wén asked the scribe Dūn,
and Dūn said:
"This is a sign of the Supreme Deity,
you should sacrifice to it."
Thus, he built the Fūzhì altar,
and used three animals in a suburban sacrifice to the White Emperor.
Before the Fūzhì was built,
there were the old Wúyáng Wǔzhì near Yōng,
and the Hǎozhì east of Yōng,
all abandoned with no sacrifices.
Some said:
"Since ancient times, Yōngzhōu, being elevated,
is a deep abode of spirits,
so altars were established
for suburban sacrifices to the Supreme Deity,
and various spirit shrines gathered there.
It is said that in Huángdì's time, sacrifices were held,
and even in late Zhōu
suburban sacrifices were performed there."
Such accounts are rarely seen in classics,
and officials do not speak of them.
Nine years after building Fūzhì,
Duke Wén obtained something like a stone, it is said,
and enshrined it in a city on the northern slope of Chéncāng.
The deity might not come some years,
or come several times a year,
often arriving at night,
shining like a meteor,
coming from the southeast to gather at the shrine city,
then resembling a rooster,
its voice rumbling, it is said,
with pheasants crowing at night.
A single set of animal offerings was sacrificed,
named Chén Bǎo.
Seventy-eight years after building Fūzhì,
Duke Dé of Qín was established,
divined to reside in Yōng,
"so that later descendants could water horses at the Hé River,"
and thus made Yōng the capital.
The various sacrifices in Yōng flourished from then on.
Three hundred sets of offerings were used at Fūzhì.
A shrine for the hidden was built.
Dogs were dismembered at the four city gates,
to ward off pestilence and disasters.
Duke Dé died after two years of reign.
Sixty-four years later,
Duke Xuān of Qín built the Mìzhì south of the Wèi River,
sacrificing to the Green Emperor.
Fourteen years later,
Duke Mù of Qín was established,
fell ill and lay unconscious for five days;
upon waking,
he spoke of dreaming of the Supreme Deity,
who commanded Duke Mù to quell the Jìn rebellion.
The scribe recorded this and stored it in the archives.
Later generations all said Duke Mù of Qín ascended to heaven.
In the ninth year of Duke Mù of Qín's reign,
Duke Huán of Qí had already become hegemon,
met with feudal lords at Kuíqiū,
and wished to perform the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"In ancient times, seventy-two families
performed Fēng on Tàishān and Shàn on Liángfù,
and of those, I remember twelve.
In the past, Wúhuáishì performed Fēng on Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Fúxī performed Fēng on Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Shénnóng
performed Fēng on Tàishān, and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Yándì
performed Fēng on Tàishān, and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Huángdì performed Fēng on Tàishān,
and Shàn at Tíngtíng;
Zhuānxū
performed Fēng on Tàishān, and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Emperor Kù
performed Fēng on Tàishān, and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Yáo
performed Fēng on Tàishān, and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Shùn performed Fēng on Tàishān, and Shàn at Yúnyún;
Yǔ performed Fēng on Tàishān,
and Shàn at Kuàijī;
Tāng performed Fēng on Tàishān,
and Shàn at Yúnyún;
King Chéng of Zhōu performed Fēng on Tàishān,
and Shàn at Shèshǒu:
all received the mandate
before they could perform Fēng and Shàn."
Duke Huán said:
"I campaigned north against the Shānróng,
passing through Gūzhú;
campaigned west against Dàxià,
crossing the Liúshā desert,
binding horses and suspending chariots,
ascended Bēi'ěr Mountain;
campaigned south to Zhàolíng,
climbed Xióng'ěr Mountain
to gaze upon the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
I held three military assemblies,
and six carriage assemblies,
united the feudal lords nine times,
rectified the world once,
and no feudal lord defied me.
How does this differ
from the ancient three dynasties receiving the mandate?"
Seeing that Duke Huán could not be swayed by words,
Guǎn Zhòng then set forth matters, saying:
"In ancient times for the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
the millet from Hàoshàng,
the grain from Běilǐ
were used for the offerings;
from between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
the three-ribbed thatch grass
was used for the mats.
The Eastern Sea presented the flatfish,
the Western Sea presented the birds that share wings,
and then there were fifteen kinds of creatures that came of their own accord without being summoned.
Now, the phoenix and qílín do not come,
the auspicious grains do not grow,
while weeds and tares flourish,
and owls frequently arrive.
Yet you wish to perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices—
is this not inappropriate?"
Thereupon, Duke Huán gave up the idea.
That year,
Duke Mù of Qín reinstated Prince Yíwú of Jìn.
Afterwards, he three times installed rulers of the Jìn state,
quelling its turmoil.
Duke Mù reigned for thirty-nine years and then died.
More than a hundred years later,
Confucius discussed the six arts,
and his transmitted summaries mention
that over seventy kings had changed their surnames and ruled,
performing the fēng sacrifice on Tàishān and the shàn at Liángfù.
The rituals of the sacrificial vessels were not clearly recorded,
making it difficult to speak of them in detail.
Someone asked about the meaning of the dì sacrifice,
and Confucius said:
"I do not know.
If one knew the meaning of the dì sacrifice,
managing the world would be as easy as looking at one's palm."
The Book of Songs says that while King Zhòu was on the throne,
King Wén received the Mandate,
but his governance did not extend to Tàishān.
King Wǔ overthrew the Yīn in his second year,
but the world was not yet at peace when he died.
It was with King Chéng that the virtue of Zhōu became pervasive,
and King Chéng's performance of the fēng and shàn sacrifices came close to the ideal.
Later, when vassal ministers held power,
the Jì family made offerings at Tàishān,
and Zhòngní criticized them.
At that time, Cháng Hóng
used occult arts to serve King Líng of Zhōu.
The feudal lords did not pay court to Zhōu,
and Zhōu's power was weak.
Cháng Hóng then elucidated affairs of ghosts and spirits,
setting up the shooting of the "Lí Shǒu."
The "Lí Shǒu"
targeted the feudal lords who did not come.
Relying on strange phenomena, he sought to attract the feudal lords.
The feudal lords did not comply,
and the people of Jìn captured and killed Cháng Hóng.
The people of Zhōu who spoke of occult and strange matters started with Cháng Hóng.
More than a hundred years later,
Duke Líng of Qín built the Wúyáng Upper Shrine,
to sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor;
he built the Lower Shrine,
to sacrifice to the Flame Emperor.
Forty-eight years later,
Dān, the Grand Historian of Zhōu, met Duke Xiàn of Qín and said:
"Qín originally united with Zhōu,
then separated,
and after five hundred years they will reunite,
and seventeen years after the reunion, a hegemon king will arise."
In Lìyáng, metal fell like rain,
and Duke Xiàn of Qín believed he had received an auspicious sign of metal.
Therefore, he built the Qí Shrine in Lìyáng
and sacrificed to the White Emperor.
A hundred and twenty years later, Qín destroyed Zhōu,
and the Nine Tripods of Zhōu went to Qín.
Some say the altar of the Shè at Tàiqiū in Sòng was lost,
and the tripods sank in the Sì River under Péngchéng.
A hundred and fifteen years later, Qín unified the world.
Qín Shǐ Huáng, having unified the world
and become emperor,
had some say:
"The Yellow Emperor attained the virtue of earth,
and a yellow dragon and earthworms appeared.
The Xià attained the virtue of wood,
a green dragon stopped in the suburbs,
and plants grew lushly.
The Yīn attained the virtue of metal,
and silver overflowed from the mountains.
The Zhōu attained the virtue of fire,
and there was the omen of the red crow.
Now Qín has replaced Zhōu,
which is the time for the virtue of water.
Formerly, when Duke Wén of Qín went hunting,
he captured a black dragon,
which is the auspicious sign for the virtue of water."
Thereupon, Qín renamed
the river as "Virtue Water,"
made the tenth month of winter the start of the year,
exalted the color black,
used six as the standard in measurements,
exalted the Dàlǚ musical note,
and governed with an emphasis on law.
In the third year of his reign as emperor,
he toured east through the commanderies and counties,
sacrificed at Zōu Yì Mountain,
and extolled Qín's achievements.
Then he summoned seventy scholars and erudites from Qí and Lǔ,
bringing them to the foot of Tàishān.
Some of the scholars debated, saying:
"In ancient times, for the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
they used wheeled vehicles,
to avoid damaging the mountain's soil, stones, plants, and trees;
they swept the ground to sacrifice,
used straw mats for seating,
indicating it was easy to follow."
The First Emperor heard that
these opinions were conflicting,
difficult to implement,
and thus dismissed the scholars.
He then cleared a road for carriages,
ascended from the southern side of Tàishān to the summit,
erected a stone to praise the virtue of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
and proclaimed his right to perform the fēng sacrifice.
He descended via the northern route,
and performed the shàn sacrifice at Liángfù.
The rituals somewhat adopted
those used by the Grand Invocator in sacrificing to the Supreme God in Yōng,
but the contents of the sealed repositories were kept secret,
so the world could not record them.
When the First Emperor ascended Tàishān,
he encountered a violent storm halfway up the slope,
and rested under a large tree.
The scholars, having been dismissed,
could not participate in the fēng sacrifice rituals,
and upon hearing that the First Emperor had encountered wind and rain,
ridiculed him.
Thereupon, the First Emperor traveled east to the sea,
performing rituals and sacrifices
to the famous mountains, great rivers, and the eight spirits,
seeking immortals like Xiànmén and his kind.
The eight spirits have existed since ancient times,
some say they were established since the time of Tàigōng.
The reason Qí is called Qí is because of the Tiānqí.
When its sacrifices ceased is unknown.
The eight spirits are:
first, the Lord of Heaven,
sacrificed to at Tiānqí.
Tiānqí is a deep spring,
located at the foot of the southern suburban mountain in Línzī.
Second, the Lord of Earth,
sacrificed to at Tàishān and Liángfù.
It is said that Heaven favors yin,
so its sacrifice must be below a high mountain,
on a small hill,
named a "shrine";
Earth values yang,
so its sacrifice must be on a round mound in a marsh.
Third, the Lord of War,
sacrificed to at Chīyóu.
Chīyóu is in Dōngpíng Lù Jiànxiāng,
in the western territory of Qí.
Fourth, the Lord of Yin,
sacrificed to at Sānshān.
Fifth, the Lord of Yang,
sacrificed to at Zhīfú.
Sixth, the Lord of the Moon,
sacrificed to at Láishān.
all are located north of Qí,
bordering the Bohai Sea.
The seventh is the Lord of the Sun,
worshiped at Chéngshān.
Chéngshān projects into the sea,
situated at the northeasternmost corner of Qí,
to greet the sunrise, it is said.
The eighth is the Lord of the Four Seasons,
worshiped at Lángyé.
Lángyé lies to the east of Qí,
marking the beginning of the year.
Each was sacrificed with a set of one sacrificial animal,
but the invocations by shamans and priests varied,
with differences in jade tablets and silk offerings.
Since the time of King Wēi and King Xuān of Qí,
scholars like Zōu Zǐ
theorized about the cycles of the Five Virtues,
and when the Qín emperor
ascended, men of Qí presented these theories,
so the First Emperor adopted them.
Moreover, Sòng Wújì, Zhèng Bóqiáo, Chōng Shàng,
and Xiànméngāo were all from Yān,
practicing the ways of immortality,
claiming liberation from the body through dissolution,
relying on matters of ghosts and spirits.
Zōu Yǎn gained fame among the feudal lords
with his theories of Yīn-Yáng
and the dominance of cycles,
but the magicians of Yān and Qí along the coast
could not fully grasp his techniques,
leading to the rise of those who were bizarre, flattering, and opportunistic,
too numerous to count.
From the times of King Wēi, King Xuān, and King Zhāo of Yān,
they sent people to sea
to seek Pénglái, Fāngzhàng, and Yíngzhōu.
These three divine mountains,
according to legend, are in the Bohai Sea,
not far from humans;
but when trouble approaches,
the ships are blown away by the wind.
It is said that some have reached them,
where immortals and the elixir of immortality reside.
All creatures and animals there are pure white,
and palaces are made of gold and silver.
Before arriving,
they appear like clouds from a distance;
upon approach,
the three divine mountains sink beneath the water.
When nearing them,
the wind always drives one away,
and ultimately, none can reach them, it is said.
No ruler of the time failed to yearn for them.
When the First Emperor of Qín unified the empire,
and went to the coast,
the tales from magicians were countless.
The First Emperor himself thought that by reaching the coast
he might miss the opportunity,
so he sent people with young boys and girls
to sea to seek them.
Ships crisscrossed the sea,
all blaming the wind for their failure,
saying they could not reach the mountains,
but had glimpsed them.
The following year,
the First Emperor traveled to the coast again,
reached Lángyé,
passed by Héng Shān,
and returned via Shàngdǎng.
Three years later,
he toured Jiéshí,
investigated the sea-bound magicians,
and returned via Shàngjùn.
Five years later,
the First Emperor went south to Xiāng Shān,
then ascended Kuàijī,
traveling along the coast,
hoping to encounter the miraculous drugs of the three divine mountains in the sea.
Failing to obtain them,
he returned and died at Shāqiū.
In the first year of the Second Emperor,
he toured east to Jiéshí,
traveled south along the sea,
passed Tài Shān,
and reached Kuàijī,
performing rituals and sacrifices at all these places,
and had inscriptions carved beside the steles erected by the First Emperor,
to glorify his virtues and achievements.
That autumn,
the feudal lords rebelled against Qín.
Three years later, the Second Emperor was assassinated.
Twelve years after the First Emperor's Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
Qín fell.
The Confucian scholars resented Qín
for burning the "Book of Songs" and "Book of Documents",
and executing literati,
the common people hated its laws,
and the empire rebelled against it,
all falsely claiming:
"The First Emperor ascended Tài Shān,
was struck by a violent storm,
and could not perform the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices."
Is this not a case of lacking the virtue
yet undertaking such affairs?
In ancient times, the rulers of the Three Dynasties
all resided between the Yellow River and Luò River,
so Sōnggāo was considered the Central Peak,
and the Four Peaks corresponded to their directions,
with the Four Rivers all east of the mountains.
When Qín declared empire,
with its capital at Xiányáng,
then the Five Peaks and Four Rivers were all to the east.
From the Five Emperors to Qín,
dynasties rose and fell,
and the famous mountains and great rivers
were sometimes under feudal lords,
sometimes under the Son of Heaven,
with rituals increasing or decreasing
as generations differed,
too numerous to record.
When Qín unified the empire,
it ordered the sacrificial officials
to regularly worship the famous mountains
and great rivers, ghosts and spirits, establishing a proper order.
Thus, east of Yáo,
there were five famous mountains,
and two great rivers for sacrifice.
Namely, Tàishì.
Tàishì is Sōnggāo.
Héng Shān,
Tài Shān,
Kuàijī,
Xiāng Shān.
The waters: Jǐ,
and Huái.
In spring, dried meat and wine were used for the annual sacrifice,
when the ice melted;
in autumn, when water dried or froze;
in winter, prayers and sacrifices were held.
The sacrificial animals included one calf each,
with varying sets of offerings, jade tablets, and silks.
West of Huà,
there were seven famous mountains,
and four famous rivers.
Namely, Huà Shān,
Bó Shān.
Bó Shān is also called Shuāi Shān.
Yuè Shān,
Qí Shān,
Wú Yuè,
Hóng Zhǒng,
Dú Shān.
Dú Shān is the Wén Shān in Shǔ.
The waters: Hé,
sacrificed at Línjìn;
Miǎn,
sacrificed at Hànzhōng;
Qiū Yuān,
sacrificed at Cháonǎ;
Jiāng Shuǐ,
sacrificed in Shǔ.
Also in spring and autumn,
sacrifices were held at ice-melt, drought, freeze, and for prayers,
like those for the famous mountains and rivers in the east;
with sacrificial calves and sets
of jade tablets and silks varying.
And for the four great tombs, Hóng, Qí, Wú, and Yuè,
there were offerings of grain.
Chénbǎo would appear for sacrifices at its season.
For the Hé River, there were additional offerings of wine.
All these were within the territory of Yōngzhōu,
close to the Son of Heaven's capital,
so an extra chariot was added,
and four red-maned colts.
The Bà, Chǎn, Chángshuǐ, Fēng, Láo,
Jīng, and Wèi rivers are not major rivers,
but because they are near Xiányáng,
they all received sacrifices comparable to mountains and rivers,
without any additional honors.
The two deep pools of Qiān and Luò,
Míngzé, Púshān, Yuèxū
Mountain, and similar places are considered minor mountains and rivers,
and also receive annual prayers, ice-breaking, and dry-season sacrifices,
though the rituals are not necessarily the same.
In Yōng, there are temples for the Sun,
Moon, Orion, Planets, Big Dipper and Southern Dipper,
Mars, Venus, Jupiter, Saturn,
Mercury,
the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions, the Wind Master,
the Rain Master, the Four Seas, the Nine Ministers, the Fourteen Ministers,
various Bù, various Yán, various Qiú, and the like,
totaling over a hundred temples.
In the west, there are also several dozen shrines.
At Hú, there is a shrine to the Zhou Son of Heaven.
At Xiàguī, there is a Celestial Deity.
At Fēng and Hào, there are Zhāomíng
and the Son of Heaven's Bìchí.
At Shèdù and Bó, there are shrines to the Three Shè
Lords and the Longevity Star;
and in Yōng's Jiān Temple, there is also the Dù Lord.
The Dù Lord,
originally the Right General of Zhōu,
is considered the deity of the smallest ghost in Qínzhōng.
Each is worshipped at the appropriate season.
Only the Four Altars of Yōng to the Supreme Deity
are held in the highest esteem,
and the one whose apparitions stir the people
is only Chénbǎo.
Thus, at the Four Altars of Yōng,
spring is for annual prayers,
coinciding with the thawing of ice,
autumn for the dry season and freezing,
winter for the closing sacrifices,
in the fifth month, offerings of colts are made,
and during the four mid-months
sacrifices are performed, as well as monthly sacrifices,
and when the Chénbǎo festival comes, one sacrifice is held.
In spring and summer, red horses are used,
in autumn and winter, black-maned horses.
Four colts are offered at each altar,
one carriage with wooden dragon ornaments and luán,
one carriage with wooden horses,
each matching the color of its respective deity.
Four yellow calves and four lambs,
with jade tablets and silk offerings in set numbers,
are all buried alive,
without the use of sacrificial vessels.
A suburban sacrifice is held every three years.
Qín considered the tenth month of winter as the start of the year,
so they often performed the suburban appearance in the first part of the tenth month,
lighting beacon fires,
and paying respects near Xiányáng,
wearing white on top,
with rituals as in regular sacrifices.
The Xīzhì and Qízhì altars
were sacrificed to as before,
but the emperor did not attend in person.
All these sacrifices were regularly overseen by the Grand Invocator,
who performed them according to the seasons.
As for other famous mountains, rivers, various ghosts,
and the eight deities,
if the emperor passed by, they were sacrificed to;
once he left, it ceased.
For distant shrines in commanderies and counties,
the people performed their own sacrifices,
not under the jurisdiction of the emperor's invocators.
The invocators included secret invocators;
if there were disasters or omens,
they would perform invocations
to transfer the blame to the subordinates.
When Hàn rose,
Emperor Gāozǔ in his humble days
once killed a great serpent.
Something said:
"The serpent
is the son of the White Emperor,
and the killer is the son of the Red Emperor."
When Gāozǔ first raised his rebellion,
he prayed at the Fēng Fényú Shè.
Marching through Pèi,
he became the Lord of Pèi,
then sacrificed to Chīyóu,
and smeared blood on drums and banners.
Subsequently, in the tenth month, he reached Bàshàng,
pacified Xiányáng with the other lords,
and was established as King of Hàn.
Thus, he took the tenth month as the start of the year,
and the color red was elevated.
In the second year,
he campaigned east against Xiàng Jí
and returned through the pass,
asking:
"Which deities were sacrificed to as the Supreme Deity in the former Qín times?"
The reply was:
"Four deities,
with sacrifices to the White, Green, Yellow, and Red Emperors."
Gāozǔ said: "I have heard Heaven has five emperors,
yet here there are only four; why is that?"
No one knew the explanation.
Thereupon, Gāozǔ said:
"I understand now;
it awaits me to complete the five."
So he established a shrine to the Black Emperor,
naming it the Northern Altar.
Officials performed the sacrifices,
and the emperor did not attend in person.
He summoned all the former Qín invocators,
reinstated the Grand Invocator and Grand Butcher,
following the old rituals and ceremonies.
He also ordered each county to establish a public shè.
He issued an edict saying:
"I greatly value sacrifices and revere worship.
Now, sacrifices to the Supreme Deity
and to the mountains, rivers, and various deities that should be worshipped
shall each be performed at their proper times as before."
Four years later,
when the empire was settled,
he ordered the Censor,
commanding Fēng to carefully maintain the Fényú Shè,
and regularly in the four seasons,
especially in spring, to sacrifice with sheep and pigs.
He ordered the invocators
to establish a shrine to Chīyóu in Cháng'ān.
Cháng'ān was to have invocators and priestesses.
Among them, the Liáng priestesses
sacrificed to Heaven, Earth, Tiānshè,
Tiānshuǐ, Fángzhōng, Tángshàng, and the like;
the Jìn priestesses,
sacrificed to the Five Emperors, Dōngjūn,
Yúnzhōngjūn, Sīmìng, Wūshè,
Wūcí, Zúrén, Xiānchuī, and the like;
the Qín priestesses,
sacrificed to Shèzhǔ, Wūbǎo,
Zúléi, and the like;
the Jīng priestesses,
sacrificed to Tángxià, Wūxiān,
Sīmìng, Shīmí, and the like;
the Nine Heavens priestesses,
sacrificed to the Nine Heavens:
all performed seasonal sacrifices in the palace.
The Hé priestesses sacrificed to the Hé River at Línjìn,
while the Nánshān priestesses sacrificed
to Nánshān and Qínzhōng.
Qínzhōng refers to
the Second Emperor.
Each had specific times, months, and days.
Two years later,
someone said that when Zhōu rose, it established a city at Tái,
and set up a shrine to Hòujì,
which to this day
receives blood sacrifices throughout the land.
Thereupon, Gāozǔ decreed to the Censor:
"Let the commanderies, states, and counties
establish Shining Star shrines,
and regularly sacrifice with cattle each year."
In the spring of the tenth year of Gāozǔ's reign,
officials requested that counties
regularly in the second and third months of spring and at the seasonal là festival
sacrifice to the Shè and Jì with sheep and pigs,
and that village shè in communities provide their own resources for sacrifices.
The decree was: "Approved."
Eighteen years later,
Emperor Xiàowén ascended the throne.
Thirteen years into his reign,
he issued an edict saying:
"Now, the secret sacrifices
are misplaced below,
I deeply disapprove.
From now on, abolish them."
Originally, the famous mountains and great rivers
were under the control of vassal lords,
and the sacrifices were performed by the lords themselves,
without the emperor's officials overseeing them.
When the states of Qí and Huáinán were abolished,
it was ordered that the Grand Minister of Sacrifices
conduct annual rites
as before.
That year,
a proclamation declared:
"I have now reigned for thirteen years,
relying on the spirits of the ancestors,
and the blessings of the land,
the realm is peaceful,
and the people are free from illness.
Recently, the harvests have been bountiful for consecutive years,
I, lacking virtue,
how can I enjoy this?
It is all granted by the spirits and gods.
I have heard that the ancients
repaid the gods' virtues
by recognizing their achievements,
wishing to increase offerings to the gods.
Officials propose increasing the offerings at the five altars in Yong
by one chariot for each road,
fully equipped;
one chariot each for Xizhi and Qizhi altars,
with four horses,
fully equipped;
at the rivers, pools, and the Hàn River,
add two jades each;
at all the sacrifices,
expand the platforms and grounds,
increase the jade and ceremonial vessels
as appropriate.
But those who bless the sacrifices
bestow blessings upon me,
excluding the common people.
Command the officials to pay respects,
without any supplications."
A man from Lǔ, Gōngsūn Chén, submitted a memorial saying:
"Initially, Qín followed the Water Virtue,
now Hàn inherits it,
considering the end and beginning,
Hàn should follow the Earth Virtue,
and a yellow dragon is the omen of Earth Virtue.
It is appropriate to change the calendar,
alter the color of attire to
emphasize yellow."
At this time Chancellor Zhāng Cāng,
who loved laws and calendars,
believed that Hàn
was the beginning of Water Virtue,
hence the river breaking
the gold embankment,
was a sign.
The year began in the tenth month of winter,
colors outside were black, inside red,
conforming to the virtues.
Like Gōngsūn Chén's words,
it was not.
It was dismissed.
Three years later,
a yellow dragon appeared in Chéngjì.
Emperor Wéndì then summoned Gōngsūn Chén,
appointed him as an academician,
to draft changes to the calendar and attire with scholars.
That summer,
issued an edict saying:
"The manifestation of divine creatures in Chéngjì,
causes no harm to the people,
and the year has been favorable.
I have prayed at the suburban altar to the supreme deity
and the gods,
the Ritual Officers suggested,
not to overburden me with taboos."
The officials all said:
"In ancient times the Son of Heaven personally offered sacrifices in summer,
worshipped the supreme deity in the suburbs,
hence it is called suburban."
So in the fourth month of summer,
Emperor Wéndì began the suburban sacrifices
and visited the Yong five altar sacrifices,
wearing attire with red upper garments.
The following year,
Xīnyuán Píng from Zhào
made a celestial observation and noticed,
"There is a divine aura northeast of Cháng'ān,
forming five colors,
like a person crowned and veiled.
Some say it is the dwelling of a northeast deity,
and the grave of a western deity."
Heaven's auspicious sign is revealed,
it is proper to establish a shrine to the supreme deity,
to match the sign."
So a temple to the Five Emperors was constructed at Weiyang,
under one roof,
with one hall for each emperor,
each facing five doors,
each matching the color of the emperor.
The offerings and ceremonies used
were like those of the Yong five altars.
In the fourth month of summer,
Emperor Wéndì personally
offered a sacrifice at the Bàwèi Assembly,
to worship and see the Five Emperors at Weiyang.
The temple for the Five Emperors faced the Wei River to the south,
with a pond crossing in the north,
and when they burned the offering fire,
it seemed to connect with the heavens.
Thus, bestowing honor upon Minister Píng,
granting him thousands of gold.
He then ordered the scholars to annotate the Six Classics
to draft the "Rules of the King",
and plan the touring hunts
and sealing and sacrificing affairs.
Emperor Wéndì left the Chángmén Gate,
and seeing five people north of the road,
he erected five altars directly north,
and offered five sacrifices.
The following year,
Xīnyuán Píng sent someone with a jade cup,
offering it in a memorial below the palace tower.
Píng told the emperor:
"From beneath the tower, a treasure with a jade aura has arrived."
Upon inspection,
indeed a jade cup was offered,
inscribed with
"Ruler of Men, Extend Your Life".
Píng further added,
"Your servant observed the sun crossing through twice".
Shortly after,
the sun again crossed through.
Hence began again
with the seventeenth year as the first year,
declaring a grand feast for the realm.
Píng declared:
"The lost Zhōu tripod is in the Sìshǔi,
and now the river overflows and connects to the Sì River,
I foresee treasure in the northeast,
directly in Fényīn,
perhaps the Zhōu tripod might emerge?
If the omen is not greeted,
it will not appear."
So the emperor sent an emissary to prepare the temple to the south of Fényīn,
by the river,
hoping to invoke the Zhōu tripod.
Someone submitted a memorial accusing
Xīnyuán Píng of fabricating stories of auras and spirits.
Píng was tried and executed,
and after this event,
Emperor Wéndì lost interest in changing
the calendar, colors, and matters of the gods.
As for the Five Emperors of Weiyang and Chángmén,
temple officials were assigned to oversee,
offering rites in due time,
but he no longer personally attended.
The following year,
the Xiongnu frequently invaded the borders,
and troops were raised for defense.
In subsequent years, there were poor harvests.
After several years, Emperor Xiàojǐng ascended the throne.
In the sixteenth year,
the officials in charge of sacrifices
performed the seasonal sacrifices as before,
with no new actions initiated,
up to the present emperor.
When the present emperor first ascended the throne,
he was especially reverent toward the sacrifices to spirits and gods.
In the first year of his reign,
the Han dynasty had been established for over sixty years,
the realm was peaceful,
and all officials and intellectuals hoped that the emperor
would perform the Feng and Shan sacrifices and amend the calendar,
so the emperor inclined towards Confucian practices,
invited worthy and talented men,
appointing Zhào Wǎn, Wáng Zāng, and others
to high ministerial positions for their learning,
planning to discuss the establishment of the Mingtang south of the city,
to receive the feudal lords.
The revision of the calendar and adjustments in clothing colors
had not yet been completed.
However, Empress Dowager Dòu practiced Huáng-Lǎo thought,
disliking Confucian practices,
and secretly ordered spies to discover evidence of Zhào Wǎn and others
engaging in corrupt activities,
summoned both Wǎn and Zāng for interrogation,
leading them to commit suicide,
and all new initiatives were abandoned.
Six years later,
Empress Dowager Dòu passed away.
The next year,
scholars like Gōngsūn Hóng were summoned.
The following year,
the current emperor first arrived at Yōng,
officiated a ceremony at the five shrines.
Subsequently, the ceremony was held once every three years.
At the time, the emperor sought a divine figure,
and housed it in the Tiǎn Family's observation tower in the imperial forest.
This divine figure
was a woman from Chánglíng,
who appeared as a spirit after her son died,
resembling her former self.
She sacrificed to it in her home,
and many people came to offer sacrifices.
The Lord of Píngyuán
went to offer sacrifices,
and afterwards, his descendants became prominent.
When the present emperor ascended the throne,
he gave generous honors
and established sacrifices within Gong.
It was said that one could hear her words,
but could not see her person.
At this time, Li Shàojūn
also used sacrificial methods for the kitchen deity,
the grain path, and methods to counter aging to meet the emperor,
who held him in high esteem.
Shàojūn
had been a retainer of the Marquis of Shēnzé,
dedicated to special techniques.
He concealed his age and background,
claiming to be seventy years old,
and was said to manipulate objects
to thwart aging.
He traveled to various states with his methods,
having no wife or children.
People heard of his abilities to manipulate objects and avoid death,
and lavished him with gifts,
ensuring he never lacked gold, money, or provisions.
Everyone believed he did not engage in regular occupations yet was abundantly supplied,
and not knowing his origins,
they deepened their belief,
and vied to serve him.
Shàojūn loved these arts,
excelling in clever demonstrations that amazed and astonished.
Once, while drinking with Marshal of Wǔ'ān,
there was an old man in the gathering over ninety years old,
Shàojūn mentioned
roaming with this man’s grandfather
at a hunting ground,
the old man recalled accompanying his grandfather there as a child,
recognizing the place,
and the entire gathering was amazed.
When Shàojūn presented to the emperor,
there was an ancient bronze vessel,
the emperor asked Shàojūn about it.
Shàojūn said, "This vessel
was presented in Qí Huán Gōng's tenth year at Bóu and Willows"
and on inspection, it was indeed an artifact of Qí Huán Gōng.
The whole palace was shocked,
believing Shàojūn to be a spirit,
a being several hundred years old.
Shàojūn told the emperor,
"Offering sacrifices to the kitchen deity can invoke things,
and cinnabar can be turned into gold,
the resulting gold used to make vessels for food and drink
can extend life,
and with longevity,
one can behold immortals like those in Pénglái overseas,
and by performing the Feng and Shan sacrifices in their way,
one can achieve immortality,
as did the Yellow Emperor."
I once traveled
to the sea, seeing An Qí Shēng,
who ate enormous dates,
as big as melons.
An Qí Shēng, an immortal,
connected within Pénglái,
appearing when fate allows,
and concealing himself when not."
Thus the emperor began personally venerating the kitchen deity,
sending practitioners into the sea
to seek Pénglái and figures like An Qí Shēng,
and engaged in refining cinnabar
and other medicines into gold.
Eventually,
Li Shàojūn fell ill and died.
The emperor believed he had transformed and not died,
and directed Scribe Huang Chuíshǐ Kuānshū
to inherit his arts.
Efforts to find Pénglái and An Qí Shēng
yielded no results,
but many practitioners from the coastal states of Yān and Qí
descended with tale upon tale of divine phenomena.
A man from Bó named Mòu Jì
submitted a method for worshiping Tài Yī,
saying,
"The esteemed deity of Heaven is Tài Yī,
and his assistants are the Five Emperors.
In ancient times, the emperor
sacrificed to Tài Yī in the southeast suburbs in spring and autumn,
using the Grand Sacrifice,
for seven days,
building an altar
to open the ghostly paths."
Thus the emperor commanded the Chief of Rituals
to establish the worship site in the southeast suburbs of Cháng'ān,
continuously offering sacrifices as per Jì's methods.
Later, someone presented a memorial,
stating
"In ancient times, the emperor
offered a Grand Sacrifice every three years
to worship the three central deities:
Tiān Yī, Dì Yī, and Tài Yī."
The emperor agreed,
directed the Chief of Rituals to oversee the sacrifices
at the Tài Yī altar established by Jì,
as per the method.
Subsequently another memorial was submitted,
suggesting,
"In ancient times, the emperor in spring
performed a resolution sacrifice,
sacrificing a hawk and broken mirror to the Yellow Emperor;
a goat for Yum Yáng;
a blue stallion for running horses;
an ox for Tài Yī, Zé Shān Jūn, and Earth Lord;
dried fish for Wǔyí Jūn;
an ox for the messengers of yīn and yáng forces".
The ritual officers were commanded
to conduct these offerings
at a spot beside the Tài Yī altar of Jì.
Subsequently,
a white deer was found in the emperor's garden,
its hide was made into a currency,
used to manifest auspicious responses,
and white gold was fashioned.
In the following year,
during the suburban sacrifice at Yōng,
a single-horned beast was captured,
resembling a páo deer.
The officials said:
"Your Majesty has devoutly performed the suburban sacrifices,
and the Supreme Deity has responded to the offering,
bestowing this single-horned beast,
which appears to be a qílín."
Thereupon it was presented at the Five Altars,
with an additional ox burned at each altar.
The feudal lords were granted white gold,
signs that heavenly responses aligned with omens.
Thereupon, the King of Jìběi believed the Son of Heaven
was about to perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
so he submitted a memorial
offering Tài Shān and its surrounding territories,
and the Son of Heaven compensated him
with other counties.
The King of Chángshān committed a crime,
was banished,
and the Son of Heaven enfeoffed his younger brother at Zhēndìng,
to continue their ancestors' sacrifices,
while making Chángshān a commandery,
so that thereafter the Five Sacred Mountains
all belonged to the Son of Heaven's domain.
The next year,
a man from Qí named Shàowēng appeared before the emperor with methods for communicating with spirits.
The emperor had a favored Lady Wáng,
who passed away,
and Shàowēng used his arts
to manifest Lady Wáng's likeness
along with the kitchen god's appearance at night,
which the emperor saw from behind a curtain.
Thereupon he appointed Shàowēng
as General Wénchéng,
bestowing abundant rewards,
treating him with guest rites.
General Wénchéng said:
"If Your Majesty wishes to communicate with spirits,
your palaces and garments must resemble those of spirits,
or divine beings will not come."
So they painted cloud-patterned carriages,
and on propitious days
drove them to ward off evil spirits.
They also built Gānquán Palace,
with a central tower chamber
depicting Heaven, Earth, Tàiyī, and various spirits,
and placed sacrificial vessels
to summon celestial deities.
After over a year,
his methods waned,
and no spirits came.
He then wrote on silk to feed an ox,
pretending ignorance,
saying
this ox had something extraordinary in its belly.
When slaughtered, they found the writing,
containing strange words.
The emperor recognized his handwriting,
questioned the man,
confirming it was forged,
so he executed General Wénchéng
and concealed the matter.
Afterward, they constructed Bǎiliáng Terrace, bronze pillars,
and Immortal's Palm dew-collectors.
The year after Wénchéng's death,
the emperor fell gravely ill at Dǐnghú,
with all shamans and doctors summoned,
yet unrecovered.
Yóushuǐ Fàgēn said
a shaman in Shàngjùn Commandery,
when ill, had spirits descend upon him.
The emperor summoned him
to make offerings at Gānquán.
When ill,
he sent men to consult the Divine Lord.
The Divine Lord said:
"The Son of Heaven need not worry about his illness.
When slightly better,
force yourself to meet me at Gānquán."
Thereupon he recovered,
rose,
went to Gānquán,
and his illness truly ended.
A great amnesty was declared,
establishing the Divine Lord at Shòu Palace.
The highest noble at Shòu Palace was Tàiyī,
assisted by Dàjìn,
Sīmìng, and others,
all following him.
Unseen,
his words were heard,
sounding like human speech.
He came and went,
arriving with a rustling wind.
He dwelled within curtained chambers.
Sometimes speaking by day,
but mostly at night.
The emperor performed purification rites,
then entered.
Using shamans as hosts,
they managed food and drink.
What was spoken,
was implemented below.
They also established Shòu Palace and Běi Palace,
displaying feathered banners,
setting out sacrificial vessels,
to honor the Divine Lord.
The Divine Lord's words
were recorded by the emperor's men,
named "Methods of Painting."
His utterances were common knowledge,
nothing extraordinary,
yet the emperor alone delighted in them.
The matter was secret,
unknown to the world.
Three years later,
officials proposed
era names should use heavenly omens,
not sequential numbers.
The first era was "Inauguration,"
the second for a long star
called "Radiance,"
the third for the suburban single-horned beast
called "Hunt."
The next winter,
the emperor performed suburban rites at Yōng,
and deliberated:
"Now I personally sacrifice to Heaven,
but Earth has no sacrifice,
so rites are unanswered."
Officials with Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān
and ritualist Kuān Shū proposed:
"For Heaven and Earth,
sacrificial animals should have small horns.
Now Your Majesty personally sacrifices to Earth,
which should be at a round mound in marshland with five altars,
each with a yellow calf as grand sacrifice,
buried after offering,
with attendants wearing yellow."
Thereupon the emperor went east,
first establishing Earth sacrifice at Fényīn Shuī Hill,
as Kuān Shū advised.
The emperor personally gazed and bowed,
as to Heaven.
After rites,
he reached Xíngyáng and returned.
Passing Luòyáng,
he decreed:
"The Three Dynasties are remote,
distant and hard to preserve.
Let thirty lǐ of land
be granted to Zhōu's descendant
as Lord Zhōu Zǐnán,
to continue their ancestral sacrifices."
That year,
the emperor began touring commanderies,
gradually approaching Tài Shān.
That spring,
Marquis Lèchéng memorialized
about Luán Dà.
Luán Dà,
a servant of Jiāodōng Palace,
formerly studied with General Wénchéng,
later becoming Jiāodōng King's provisioner.
Marquis Lèchéng's sister was King Kāng's queen,
childless.
When King Kāng died,
another consort's son became king.
Queen Kāng had illicit affairs,
clashing with the king,
endangering each other through legal means.
Empress Wáng heard that Wénchéng had died,
and wishing to curry favor with the Emperor,
she sent Luán Dà
through the Marquis of Yuèchéng
to request an audience and present his methods.
The Son of Heaven, having executed Wénchéng,
later regretted his early death,
lamenting that his techniques were not fully transmitted,
so when he saw Luán Dà, he was greatly pleased.
Dà was tall and handsome,
versed in many strategies,
and bold in making grand claims,
which he maintained without doubt.
He declared:
"I have often traveled across the seas,
and seen Ānqī and Xiànmén and their like.
But they regarded me as lowly,
and did not trust me.
They also considered the King of Kāng merely a feudal lord,
unworthy of sharing their methods.
I repeatedly advised the King of Kāng,
but he did not employ me.
My master said:
'Gold can be produced,
the breach of the Yellow River can be sealed,
the elixir of immortality can be obtained,
and immortals can be summoned.'
Yet I fear to suffer Wénchéng's fate,
which would make all alchemists fall silent—
how would they dare speak of their methods then!"
The Emperor replied:
"Wénchéng died from eating horse liver.
If you can truly cultivate his arts,
why would I begrudge you anything!"
Dà said:
"My master does not seek people;
it is people who seek him.
If Your Majesty truly wishes to summon him,
you must honor his envoy,
grant him kin,
treat him with the rites due a guest,
not demean him,
and let each bear their credential seals—
only then can they communicate with the divine beings.
Whether the immortals will consent or not
depends on honoring their envoy;
only then can they be summoned."
Thereupon, the Emperor tested his minor arts:
chess pieces
moved and struck each other on their own.
At that time, the Emperor was troubled by the Yellow River's breach
and the failure to produce gold,
so he appointed Dà as General of the Five Powers.
After over a month,
he obtained four seals,
bearing the titles General of Celestial Forces, General of Terrestrial Forces,
and General of Great Penetration.
An imperial edict to the Censor stated:
"In the past, Yǔ dredged the Nine Rivers
and opened the Four Waterways.
Lately, the Yellow River has flooded the lowlands,
and dike corvée never ceases.
I have ruled the realm for twenty-eight years,
and Heaven has sent me a man to achieve great penetration.
The Qián hexagram speaks of the 'soaring dragon,'
and the 'wild goose gradually advances to the bank'—
I believe this aligns with my aspirations.
Let the General of Terrestrial Forces, Dà,
be enfeoffed as Marquis of Lètōng with two thousand households."
He was granted a mansion fit for a marquis,
a thousand servants,
and carriages, horses, canopies, and utensils to fill his household.
Moreover, the Emperor gave him the Eldest Princess of Wèi
in marriage,
with ten thousand catties of gold as dowry,
renaming her city Dānglì Princess.
The Son of Heaven personally visited the residence of the General of the Five Powers.
Envoys delivering provisions and inquiries lined the roads.
From the Grand Princess down to generals and ministers,
all hosted banquets at his home,
presenting him with gifts.
Then the Son of Heaven had a jade seal carved
reading 'General of the Heavenly Way,'
and sent an envoy clad in feathered robes
to stand
on white reeds at night,
while the General of the Five Powers also donned feathered robes
and stood on white reeds to receive the seal,
symbolizing he was not a subject.
For one bearing the title 'Heavenly Way'
was to guide the Son of Heaven to the celestial gods.
Thereafter, the General of the Five Powers often held nocturnal rituals at home,
seeking to summon deities.
Before any god arrived, hundreds of spirits gathered,
and he could somewhat command them.
Later, he prepared for a journey,
heading east to the sea
to seek his master, it was said.
Within months of his appearance,
Dà wore six seals,
his prestige shaking the empire,
and along the coasts between Yān and Qí,
countless people clenched their wrists
claiming to possess secret formulas
and the power to become immortals.
In midsummer of that year,
a shaman named Jǐn from Fényīn, while conducting a folk sacrifice
near the shrine of the Earth Queen at Wèi Shuí,
saw a hook-shaped mark on the ground,
dug, and uncovered a ding cauldron.
The cauldron was remarkably different from others,
decorated with patterns but no inscriptions,
which puzzled him,
so he reported it to the officials.
The officials informed the Governor of Hédōng, Shèng,
who relayed it to the Emperor.
The Son of Heaven sent envoys to investigate the shaman
and the recovered cauldron,
finding no deceit,
so he performed a ritual sacrifice,
escorted the cauldron to Gānquán,
accompanying it personally,
and offered it up.
Upon reaching Zhōngshān,
the weather cleared,
and a yellow cloud canopy appeared above.
A roe deer passed by,
and the Emperor shot it himself,
using it in the sacrifice.
When they arrived in Cháng'ān,
the dukes, ministers, and officials all debated
and requested the honoring of the precious cauldron.
The Son of Heaven said:
"Lately, the Yellow River has flooded,
and harvests have failed for years,
so I toured to sacrifice to the Earth Queen,
praying to nurture grain for the people.
Now the year is abundant,
yet I have not repaid the favor—
why has this cauldron appeared?"
The officials replied:
"We have heard that in ancient times, the Tài Emperor created one divine cauldron,
symbolizing unity,
the bond of all things in heaven and earth.
Huángdì made three precious cauldrons,
representing heaven, earth, and man.
Yǔ collected metal from the nine provinces,
casting nine cauldrons.
All were used to cook offerings
for the Supreme Deity and spirits.
They emerge in the age of sages,
and the cauldrons passed to Xià and Shāng.
When the virtue of Zhōu declined,
the altars of Sòng perished,
and the cauldrons sank into obscurity,
hidden from sight.
The Odes say:
'From hall to foundation,
from sheep to oxen;
the great cauldrons and the small,
not noisy, not proud—
such is the blessing of long life.'
Now the cauldron has come to Gānquán,
glossy and transforming like a dragon,
bearing endless blessings.
Coupled with the events at Zhōngshān,
where yellow and white clouds descended like a canopy,
and the beast served as an omen,
The emperor's carriage bows and arrows,
gathered at the altar below,
reported sacrifices with grand offerings.
Only those who receive the mandate and become emperors
understand the intent in their hearts
and align with virtue.
The tripod should be presented to the ancestral temples,
stored in the imperial court,
to correspond with the clear omens."
The decree stated: "Approved."
Those who went to sea seeking Pénglái
said Pénglái was not far,
yet they could not reach it,
likely because they did not see its aura.
The emperor then sent an assistant in observing auras
to watch for its aura.
That autumn,
the emperor visited Yōng,
and was to perform the suburban sacrifice.
Someone said,
"The Five Emperors
are assistants of Tàiyī,
so Tàiyī should be established
and the emperor should personally perform the suburban sacrifice to him."
The emperor was undecided.
A man from Qí named Gōngsūn Qīng said:
"This year, the precious tripod was obtained,
and in winter, on the xīnsì day, the new moon and the morning of the winter solstice coincide,
just as in Huángdì's time."
Qīng had a written record saying:
"Huángdì obtained the precious tripod in Wǎnqú,
and asked Guǐ Yúqū about it.
Guǐ Yúqū replied:
'Huángdì obtained the precious tripod and divine tallies,
and in that year, the jǐyǒu day marked the new moon and morning of the winter solstice,
grasping the celestial cycle,
which ends and begins anew.'
Thereupon, Huángdì welcomed the sun and calculated with tallies,
after which approximately every twenty years
the new moon and morning of the winter solstice would coincide again,
making twenty calculations in total,
over three hundred and eighty years,
and Huángdì ascended to heaven as an immortal."
Qīng sought to present this through Suǒ Zhōng.
Suǒ Zhōng found the text unorthodox,
suspecting it to be fabricated,
and declined, saying:
"The matter of the precious tripod is already decided,
what more is there to do!"
Qīng then presented it through a favored courtier.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and summoned Qīng for questioning.
He replied:
"I received this text from Shēn Gōng,
and Shēn Gōng has already died."
The emperor asked: "Who is Shēn Gōng?"
Qīng said:
"Shēn Gōng was a man of Qí.
He associated with Ānqī Shēng,
received Huángdì's teachings,
with no written records,
only this text about the tripod.
It said
'The Hàn dynasty's rise
coincides again with Huángdì's time.'
It said
'The sage of Hàn will be among Gāozǔ's grandsons or great-grandsons.
When the precious tripod appears, it connects with the divine,
leading to the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
Seventy-two kings performed fēng and shàn,
but only Huángdì was able to perform fēng on Tài Shān.'
Shēn Gōng said:
'The Hàn ruler should also perform the fēng sacrifice,
and doing so will enable him to ascend to heaven as an immortal.
In Huángdì's time, there were ten thousand feudal lords,
with seven thousand enfeoffed as divine spirits.
There are eight famous mountains under heaven,
three in the barbarian lands,
and five in the Central Kingdom.
In the Central Kingdom: Huà Shān, Shǒu Shān,
Tài Shì, Tài Shān, and Dōng Lái—
these five mountains were where Huángdì often traveled,
meeting with the spirits.
Huángdì waged war
while learning immortality.
Worried that the people might oppose his way,
he executed those who denied the spirits.
After over a hundred years, he finally connected with the divine.
Huángdì performed the suburban sacrifice to Shàngdì at Yōng,
staying for three months.
Guǐ Yúqū, also known as Dà Hóng,
was buried at Yōng upon his death,
hence the Hóng Zhǒng tomb there.
Afterward, Huángdì received all spirits
at the Míng Tíng.
The Míng Tíng
is Gānquán.
The so-called Hán Mén
is Gǔkǒu.
Huángdì mined copper from Shǒu Shān,
and cast a tripod at the foot of Jīng Shān.
Once the tripod was completed,
a dragon descended with its beard hanging down to welcome Huángdì.
Huángdì mounted it,
with over seventy ministers and consorts following him
upward,
and the dragon ascended.
The minor officials who could not ascend
grabbed the dragon's beard,
which broke off,
causing them to fall,
and Huángdì's bow dropped too.
The people, looking up and seeing Huángdì had ascended to heaven,
clung to his bow and the dragon's beard, wailing,
so later generations named the place
Dǐnghú,
and the bow Wūhào.' "
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven said:
"Alas!
If I could truly be like Huángdì,
I would regard leaving my wives and children as shedding worn sandals."
He then appointed Qīng as a court gentleman,
sending him east to await spirits at Tài Shì.
The emperor subsequently performed the suburban sacrifice at Yōng,
went to Lǒngxī,
ascended Kōngtóng in the west,
and visited Gānquán.
He ordered the ritual officials Kuān Shū and others
