to prepare the altar for the Tàiyī sacrifice,
modeled after the Bó Jì Tàiyī altar,
with three tiers.
The altars for the Five Emperors surrounded it below,
each according to their direction,
with Huángdì to the southwest,
and eight paths cleared for spirits.
For Tàiyī,
the offerings were like those at the Yōng altar,
with added sweet wine, dates, dried meat, and such,
and a single dappled ox
served as the sacrificial animal.
For the Five Emperors, only sweet wine was offered in addition.
In the four directions below,
food was set out for the retinue of spirits and the Northern Dipper.
After the sacrifice,
the leftover meat was all burned.
The ox was white,
with a deer inside it,
and a pig inside the deer,
soaked in water.
A ox was used to sacrifice to the sun,
and a sheep or pig alone for the moon.
The officiant for Tàiyī
wore purple and embroidered robes.
The Five Emperors each had their corresponding colors,
red for the sun,
white for the moon.
On the xīnsì day of the eleventh month, at the new moon and morning
of the winter solstice,
at dawn,
the Son of Heaven began the suburban sacrifice to Tàiyī.
He bowed to the rising sun in the morning,
and to the moon in the evening, with a salute;
and when paying respects to Tàiyī, he followed the ritual of the Yōng suburban sacrifice.
The prayer of offering said:
"Heaven first
bestowed the precious tripod and divine tallies upon the emperor,
with new moons upon new moons,
ending and beginning anew,
and the emperor reverently pays homage."
He wore yellow robes above.
The sacrifice had fires arrayed all over the altar,
with cooking utensils beside it.
The officials reported that "above the sacrifice
there was a glow."
The dukes and ministers said
"The emperor first performed the suburban sacrifice at Yúnyáng to the Great One,
where officials presented the jade disc
and fine sacrificial animals as offerings.
That night, there was a beautiful light,
and by daytime,
a yellow vapor rose up to connect with the heavens."
The Grand Historian and ritual officials such as Kuān Shū
said:
"The blessings of the spirits,
bringing good fortune and auspicious signs,
should be honored by establishing an altar for the Great One at this illuminated place
to manifest the response.
Order the Grand Invocator to oversee it,
with sacrifices performed in autumn and during the La festival period.
The Son of Heaven should perform the suburban sacrifice once every three years."
That autumn,
to campaign against Nányuè,
they prayed to the Great One.
Using male chaste tree branches, they painted banners with the sun, moon, Big Dipper, and ascending dragon,
symbolizing the three stars of the Great One,
creating a vanguard for the Great One,
named the "Numinous Banner."
When praying for military success,
the Grand Historian would hold it pointing toward the country to be attacked.
Meanwhile, General Wǔlì
dared not go to sea,
going instead to offer sacrifices at Tàishān.
The emperor sent people
to follow and verify,
but they actually saw nothing.
Wǔlì falsely claimed to have seen his master,
and when his methods were exhausted,
most proved untrue.
The emperor then executed Wǔlì.
That winter,
Gōngsūn Qīng awaited spirits in Hénán,
reporting sighting immortal footprints
on the walls of Gōushì city,
and something like a pheasant
moving back and forth atop the walls.
The Son of Heaven personally visited Gōushì city to inspect the footprints.
He asked Qīng:
"Are you not imitating Wénchéng and Wǔlì?"
Qīng replied:
"Immortals do not seek out rulers;
it is rulers who seek them.
If the way is not given some leeway,
the spirits will not come.
Speaking of spiritual matters,
they may seem far-fetched and fantastic,
requiring years of accumulation
before they can be attained."
Thereupon, the commanderies and kingdoms each cleared roads,
repaired palaces and observatories
at places named for spiritual shrines,
hoping for the imperial visit.
That spring,
after the destruction of Nányuè,
the emperor had a favorite courtier Lǐ Yánnián
who presented himself through his love of music.
The emperor approved of him,
and consulted the ministers,
saying:
"Even common people's sacrifices
include drumming and dance music,
yet now our suburban sacrifices lack music;
is this appropriate?"
The ministers said: "In ancient times,
sacrifices to heaven and earth all included music,
allowing the deities to be properly honored."
Some said:
"The Great Emperor had Sùnǚ
play the fifty-string zither,
but it was so mournful,
the emperor could not stop it,
so he broke the zither
into twenty-five strings."
Thus, after pacifying Nányuè,
while sacrificing to the Great One and Hòutǔ,
they began using music and dance,
summoned more singers,
and created the twenty-five-string zither and konghou zithers
from this time onward.
The following winter,
the emperor proposed:
"In ancient times, they first mobilized troops
and toured the marshes,
then performed the feng and shan sacrifices."
So he toured north to Shuòfāng,
marshaling over a hundred thousand troops,
then returned to sacrifice at Huángdì's tomb at Qiáoshān,
dismissing the troops at Xūrú.
The emperor said: "I heard Huángdì did not die,
yet there is a tomb; why is that?"
Someone replied:
"Huángdì had already ascended to heaven as an immortal,
and his ministers buried his clothes and cap."
After arriving at Gānquán,
and preparing for the ceremonies at Tàishān,
they first performed the léi sacrifice to the Great One.
Since obtaining the precious ding,
the emperor had been discussing the feng and shan sacrifices
with his ministers and scholars.
The feng and shan sacrifices were rare
and long discontinued,
with no one knowing their rituals,
so the Confucians compiled matters from the feng and shan sections of the Shàngshū,
Zhōuguān, and Wángzhì
concerning the wàng sacrifice and ox shooting.
A man from Qí named Dīng Gōng, over ninety years old,
said:
"The feng and shan sacrifices
are associated with the name of immortality.
The Qín emperor failed to perform the feng sacrifice.
If Your Majesty is determined to ascend,
if you ascend gradually, there will be no wind or rain,
and you will succeed in performing the feng sacrifice."
The emperor then ordered the scholars
to practice shooting oxen
and draft the feng and shan rituals.
After several years,
they were about to proceed.
The Son of Heaven, having heard the words of Gōngsūn Qīng and the magicians
that Huángdì and those before him performed the feng and shan sacrifices,
all encountered strange phenomena and communicated with spirits,
wished to emulate Huángdì and earlier rulers
to connect with immortals and gentlemen of Pénglái,
surpassing the world
and comparing his virtue to the Nine Sovereigns,
while somewhat adopting Confucian methods
to embellish it.
The Confucians were already unable
to clarify the matters of the feng and shan sacrifices,
and were further constrained by the ancient texts of the Shī and Shū, unable to be flexible.
When the emperor showed the ritual vessels for the feng and shan sacrifices
to the Confucians,
some said
"they do not match antiquity,"
and Xú Yǎn added:
"The行礼 of the Tàicháng's scholars
is not as good as that of Lǔ,"
while Zhōu Bà was entrusted with planning the feng and shan matters.
Thereupon, the emperor dismissed Yǎn and Bà,
and completely dismissed the scholars,
not employing them.
In the third month,
he then traveled east to Gōushì,
ceremoniously ascending the central peak Tàishì.
Attending officials below the mountain
heard what seemed like cries
of "ten thousand years!"
When asked above,
those above did not speak;
when asked below,
those below did not speak.
So he enfeoffed three hundred households
to maintain the sacrifices at Tàishì,
naming it the District of Chónggāo.
Proceeding east to Tàishān,
where the grass and trees had not yet sprouted leaves,
he ordered people to carry stones up
and erect them on the summit of Tàishān.
The emperor then toured eastward along the coast,
performing rituals and sacrificing to the Eight Deities.
Men from Qí
who submitted memorials about spirits, strange phenomena, and miraculous methods
numbered in the tens of thousands,
yet none proved valid.
So he increased the number of ships sent out,
ordering several thousand who spoke of divine mountains in the sea
to seek the divine beings of Pénglái.
Gōngsūn Qīng, holding the ceremonial staff,
often went ahead to await at famous mountains.
Arriving at Dōnglái,
it was said that at night a giant figure was seen,
several zhàng tall,
but upon approaching, it vanished,
leaving behind enormous footprints,
resembling those of a bird or beast, it was reported.
Some ministers claimed to have seen an old man
leading a dog,
who said, "I wish to see the great lord,"
and then suddenly disappeared.
The Emperor, having seen the large footprints,
was initially skeptical,
but when the ministers spoke of the old man,
he became convinced he was an immortal.
He lingered by the sea,
granting relay carriages to magicians
and sending numerous envoys to seek immortals by the thousands.
In the fourth month,
he returned to Fènggāo.
The Emperor considered the various scholars'
and magicians' differing opinions on the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
finding them inconsistent,
lacking in classical basis,
and difficult to implement.
The Son of Heaven went to Liángfù,
where he ceremoniously sacrificed to the Earth Deity.
On the yǐmǎo day,
he ordered the scholarly attendants in ceremonial caps and sashes
to perform the ritual of shooting an ox.
He conducted the fēng sacrifice east of Mount Tài,
following the rites used for the suburban sacrifice to Tàiyī.
The fēng altar was twelve chǐ wide,
nine chǐ high,
beneath which lay a jade tablet with inscriptions,
the contents kept secret.
After the ceremony,
the Son of Heaven, accompanied only by the attendant Fèngchē Zǐhóu,
ascended Mount Tài,
where another fēng sacrifice was made.
These events were kept confidential.
The next day,
they descended by the northern path.
On the bǐngchén day,
the shàn sacrifice was performed at Sùrán Mountain northeast of Mount Tài's base,
following the rites for the Earth Goddess.
The Son of Heaven personally paid homage,
dressed in yellow robes
and with full musical accompaniment.
Three-ridged grass from the Jiāng-Huái region
served as sacred mats.
The five-colored earth was used to enrich the fēng altar.
Rare animals and birds from distant lands,
such as white pheasants,
were incorporated with enhanced rituals.
Creatures like rhinoceroses, elephants, and others were not used.
All proceeded to Mount Tài to sacrifice to the Earth Goddess.
At the fēng and shàn sacrifices;
that night, there seemed to be a glow,
and by day, white clouds rose from the fēng altar.
The Son of Heaven returned from the shàn sacrifice,
sat in the Bright Hall,
and the ministers took turns offering congratulations.
Thereupon, an edict was issued to the Imperial Secretary:
"I, with my insignificant person,
have received the supreme honor,
trembling with fear that I am not equal to the task.
My virtue is meager,
and I am not well-versed in rites and music.
In sacrificing to Tàiyī,
there were apparitions and radiant lights,
as if something was glimpsed from afar,
startled by strange phenomena,
I wished to stop but dared not,
so I ascended to perform the fēng on Mount Tài,
proceeded to Liángfù,
and then conducted the shàn at Sùrán.
Renewing myself,
I joyfully begin anew with the officials,
granting one ox per hundred households,
ten dàn of wine,
and an additional two bolts of cloth and silk for those aged eighty, orphans, and widows.
Exempt Bó, Fènggāo, Shéqiū, and Lìchéng
from this year's taxes.
Let a great amnesty be proclaimed throughout the land,
as per the yǐmǎo amnesty decree.
No forced labor shall be imposed along the route traveled.
Matters from over two years ago
shall not be prosecuted."
Another decree was issued:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven
toured the realm every five years,
performing rites at Mount Tài,
and the feudal lords had lodging grounds for audiences.
Let it be ordered that the feudal lords
each maintain a residence at the foot of Mount Tài."
The Son of Heaven, having completed the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài
without encountering wind or rain disasters,
and with the magicians further claiming
that the deities of Pénglái might be attainable,
was thus delighted
and hopeful of encountering them,
so he went east again to gaze out over the sea,
hoping to find Pénglái.
Fèngchē Zǐhóu
suddenly fell ill
and died within a day.
The Emperor then departed,
traveling along the coast,
north to Jiéshí,
touring from Liáoxī,
passing through the northern border to Jiǔyuán.
In the fifth month,
he returned to Gānquán.
The officials reported that the precious tripod's appearance
marked the Yuándǐng era,
and this year
was designated the first year of Yuánfēng.
That autumn,
a comet appeared in Dōngjǐng.
Over ten days later,
another comet appeared in Sāntái.
The astrologer Wáng Shuò reported:
"I alone observed the planet Zhènxīng appear as large as a melon,
and after a meal's duration, it vanished again."
The officials all said:
"Your Majesty has established the Hàn dynasty's fēng and shàn sacrifices,
and Heaven responds with this virtuous star."
The following winter,
he performed the suburban sacrifice to the Five Deities at Yōng.
Upon returning,
he offered prayers and sacrifices to Tàiyī.
The eulogy proclaimed:
"The virtuous star shines expansively,
a sign of great auspiciousness.
The star of longevity reappears,
radiating brilliant light.
The faithful star is clearly visible,
the Emperor reverently bows to the Grand Invocator's offering."
That spring,
Gōngsūn Qīng reported
seeing a divine figure at Dōnglái Mountain,
who supposedly said
"I wish to see the Son of Heaven."
The Emperor then visited Gōushī City,
appointing Qīng as a Grand Master of the Palace.
He proceeded to Dōnglái,
staying for several days,
but saw nothing,
except for giant footprints, it was said.
He again dispatched magicians
by the thousands to seek spirits and gather magical herbs and mushrooms.
That year, there was a drought.
As the Emperor had set out without a clear reason,
he prayed at Wànlǐshā,
and passed by to sacrifice at Mount Tài.
Returning to Hùzǐ,
he personally supervised the blocking of the breached river,
stayed for two days,
sank offerings in the river, and departed.
He sent two ministers with troops
to seal the breach,
diverting two channels,
restoring the ancient course as in Yǔ's time.
At that time, having conquered both Yuè states,
a Yuè man named Yǒngzhī stated
"The Yuè people customarily worship ghosts,
and in their sacrifices, they often see apparitions,
with frequent efficacy.
In the past, the King of Dōng'ōu revered ghosts,
and lived to one hundred sixty years.
Later generations grew negligent,
hence their decline and demise."
于是命令越地巫师
建立越式祝祷祠庙，
设高台而无祭坛，
同时祭祀天神
上帝及众鬼神，
并用鸡骨进行占卜。
皇上深信不疑，
越式祠庙与鸡骨占卜自此开始采用。
公孙卿进言：
"仙人本可得见，
然陛下往昔行程仓促，
故而未能相遇。
今若陛下建造观台，
如缑氏城规制，
陈列干肉枣果，
神明应当会降临。
况且仙人偏爱楼居"。
于是皇上诏令长安
建造飞廉观与桂观，
甘泉宫则建造益延寿观，
派遣公孙卿持符节
备置法器
恭候神明降临。
又修筑通天茎台，
台下陈列祭祀器具，
用以招引仙神之属。
继而扩建甘泉宫前殿，
开始增筑诸多宫室。
夏季，
殿房内生长灵芝。
天子因堵塞黄河决口，
兴建通天台时，
仿佛见到祥光显现，
遂颁布诏书：
"甘泉宫房内
生出九茎灵芝，
特赦天下囚徒，
免除劳役赋税。"
次年，
征伐朝鲜。
夏季，
大旱。
公孙卿称：
"黄帝封禅时
天降旱情，
持续三年干封。"
皇上遂下诏曰：
"天现旱象，
莫非暗示干封？
着令天下尊祀灵星。"
又次年，
皇上雍地郊祀，
开通回中道，
亲往巡行。
春日至鸣泽，
取道西河返回。
翌年冬季，
皇上巡视南郡，
至江陵折向东行。
登临礼祭潜县天柱山，
封为南岳。
泛舟长江，
从寻阳抵达枞阳，
途经彭蠡泽，
祭祀沿途名山大川。
北行至琅邪，
沿海岸巡游。
四月中旬，
抵达奉高举行封禅。
当初天子泰山封禅时，
泰山东北麓
存有古明堂遗址，
地势险峻不够开阔。
皇上欲在奉高附近修建明堂，
却不谙其规制。
济南人公玉带呈献
黄帝时期明堂图样。
图中明堂设有一座殿宇，
四面无墙，
茅草覆顶，
引水环绕，
圆形宫墙筑复道，
上设楼阁，
自西南方入，
命名为昆仑，天子由此进入，
礼拜祭祀上帝。
于是皇上诏令
在汶水畔奉高修建明堂，
依公玉带图样施工。
至五年后封禅时，
在明堂上座祭祀太一神与五方天帝，
令汉高皇帝神位与之相对。
在下房祭祀后土神，
用二十太牢之礼。
天子从昆仑道进入，
始行明堂拜祭
如郊祀大礼。
典礼完毕，
在堂下焚祭品。
而后皇上再登泰山，
秘密举行山顶祭祀。
泰山脚下祭祀五方天帝，
各按方位排列，
黄帝
与赤帝并列，
由官员陪祭。
山顶举火为号，
山下皆举火响应。
两年之后，
十一月甲子
朔日冬至，
历法家以此为新纪元起点。
天子亲至泰山，
于十一月甲子朔冬至日在明堂祭祀上帝，
未行封禅大典。
祝祷辞曰：
"上天赐授皇帝
太元神策，
周而复始循环不息。
皇帝敬拜太一神。"
东行至海滨，
查考方士
入海求仙者，
均无应验，
却增派更多人员，
期望得遇真仙。
十一月乙酉，
柏梁台遭火灾。
十二月甲午朔，
皇上亲至高里山禅祭，
祭祀后土神。
亲临渤海，
遥望祭祀蓬莱仙岛诸神，
期盼抵达殊异仙境。
皇上返朝后，
因柏梁台火灾之故，
在甘泉宫接受郡国计簿。
公孙卿称：
"黄帝筑青灵台，
十二日后遭焚，
黄帝遂改建明廷。
明廷即
甘泉宫。"
方士多称
古代帝王有建都甘泉者。
其后天子
在甘泉宫接见诸侯，
甘泉宫兴建诸侯府邸。
勇之遂进言：
"越地风俗遇火灾后，
重建屋舍必更加宏伟，
以此压制火患。"
于是建造建章宫，
规划千门万户之制。
前殿高度超过未央宫。
东侧立凤阙，
高二十余丈。
西设唐中苑，
周边数十里设虎圈。
北面修筑大池，
渐台高二十余丈，
命名为太液池，
池中设蓬莱、方丈、
瀛洲、壶梁诸岛，
象征海中仙山龟鱼等神物。
南面建有玉堂、璧门、
巨型铜凤等建筑。
又立神明台、井干楼，
高达五十丈，
以辇道相互连接。
In summer,
the Hàn dynasty reformed the calendar,
taking the first month as the start of the year,
and elevating the color yellow,
with official titles and seals changed to use five characters,
marking the first year of the Tàichū era.
That year,
they campaigned westward against Dàyuān.
Locusts swarmed massively.
Dīng Fūrén, Luòyáng's Yú Chū, and others
used rituals to curse the Xiōngnú and
Dàyuān.
The following year,
officials reported
that the five altars at Yōng lacked complete sacrificial animals,
and the aromatic offerings were insufficient.
So they ordered the ritual officers
to present young cattle as sacrifices at the altars,
with colors and foods corresponding to the conquering elements,
and used wooden horse figures
to replace live foals.
Only in the fifth month were foals offered,
and when the emperor personally performed suburban sacrifices, foals were used.
For all famous mountains and rivers where foals were required,
they were entirely replaced by wooden horse figures.
Only when the emperor passed by were foals used.
Other rituals remained as before.
The next year,
he toured east to the seashore;
investigating matters of immortals and spirits,
but none were verified.
A methodist said
"During Huángdì's time,
he built five cities and twelve towers,
to await divine beings at Zhíqī,
naming it 'Welcoming the Year'."
The emperor approved its construction
according to the method,
and named it 'Next Year'.
The emperor personally performed rituals to worship Heaven there.
Gōngyù Dài said:
"During Huángdì's time,
though he fēnged Tài Shān,
Fēnghòu, Fēng Jù, and Qí Bó
had Huángdì fēng Dōng Tài Shān,
and shàn Fán Shān,
matching tallies,
after which he attained immortality."
The Son of Heaven then ordered sacrificial preparations,
but upon reaching Dōng Tài Shān,
[Dōng Tài Shān was low and small,
not matching its reputation,
so he ordered ritual officers to perform ceremonies there,
but did not perform fēng and shàn.
Afterward, he ordered Dài to maintain sacrifices and await divine manifestations.
In summer,
he returned to Tài Shān,
performing the five-year ceremony
as before,
and added the shàn sacrifice at Shí Lǘ.
Shí Lǘ
is south at the foot of Tài Shān,
where methodists often said
this was the gateway of immortals,
so the emperor personally performed shàn there.
Five years later,
he again went to Tài Shān to perform fēng.
On return, he sacrificed at Héng Shān.
Now, the sacrifices established by the Son of Heaven,
Tàiyī and Hòutǔ,
involved personal suburban sacrifices every three years,
establishing the Hàn dynasty's fēng and shàn,
with fēng performed every five years.
Bó Jì's Tàiyī
and Sānyī, Míngyáng, Mǎxíng, Chìxīng,
five in total,
were managed by ritual officers like Kuān Shū
who conducted ceremonies seasonally.
In all, six sacrifices,
all overseen by the Grand Invocator.
As for the Eight Spirits and other deities,
Míngnián, Fán Shān, and other named sacrifices,
they were performed when passing by,
and ceased after departure.
Sacrifices initiated by methodists
were each managed independently,
ending when the person died,
with ritual officers not in charge.
Other sacrifices all remained as before.
The current emperor's fēng and shàn,
twelve years later upon return,
had covered all five sacred mountains and four great rivers.
Yet the methodists' waiting for divine beings,
and seeking Pénglái in the sea,
ultimately had no verification.
And Gōngsūn Qīng, who awaited spirits,
still explained it through giant footprints,
with no results.
The Son of Heaven grew increasingly weary
of the methodists' strange and far-fetched talk,
yet he restrained them without cutting off,
hoping to encounter the genuine.
After this,
those speaking of spirit sacrifices among methodists
grew even more numerous,
but their effectiveness was evident.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I followed the inspections and sacrifices to heaven and earth
and all spirits of famous mountains and rivers
and the fēng and shàn.
Entering the Shòu Palace to serve during spirit utterances,
I thoroughly observed
the intentions of methodists and ritual officers,
then stepped back to compile and order
those who dealt with ghosts and spirits since ancient times,
fully revealing their outward and inward aspects.
May later gentlemen
have this to examine.
As for details like sacrificial vessels, jades, and silks,
and the rituals of offerings and toasts,
these are preserved by the officials.
The Xià Shū says:
Yǔ controlled the floods for thirteen years,
passing his home without entering.
On land, he traveled by cart,
on water, by boat,
through mud, on sledges,
in mountains, on spiked shoes.
He demarcated the nine provinces,
following the mountains to dredge rivers,
assigning tributes according to the land.
He opened nine routes,
banked nine marshes,
and measured nine mountains.
Yet the Hé River's overflow
harmed the central states most severely.
This was his primary task.
So he channeled the Hé from Jīshí past Lóngmén,
south to Huáyīn,
east down Dǐzhù,
to Méngjīn and Luòruì,
reaching Dàpī.
Then Yǔ, considering the Hé's source high,
its waters swift and fierce,
difficult to traverse flat land,
and frequently causing disasters,
split it into two channels to divert the river.
He carried it north to high ground,
past Jiāngshuǐ,
reaching Dàlù,
spreading into nine rivers,
converging as the Nì Hé,
entering the Bó Sea.
Once the nine rivers were dredged,
and the nine marshes cleared,
all of Xià was pacified,
his achievements benefiting the three dynasties.
After this,
from Xíngyáng, the Hé was channeled southeast as the Hóng Gōu,
connecting Sòng, Zhèng, Chén, Cài, Cáo, and Wèi,
meeting Jì, Rǔ, Huái, and Sì.
In Chǔ,
westward, canals connected the Hàn River and Yúnmèng marshes,
eastward, the Hóng Gōu linked the Huái and Jiāng.
In Wú,
canals joined the three Jiāngs and five Hús.
In Qí,
they connected Zī and Jì.
In Shǔ,
Governor Bīng excavated Lí Duì,
averting the Mò Shuǐ's harm,
and channeled two Jiāngs through Chéngdū.
These canals can all accommodate boats,
and any excess is used for irrigation,
benefiting the common people.
As for the places it passes through,
the water is often drawn to further irrigate fields and canals,
measured in the countless billions,
but none can sufficiently count it all.
Xīmén Bào diverted the Zhang River to irrigate Yè,
enriching the Hénèi of Wèi.
Meanwhile, Hán heard of Qín's interest in projects,
and sought to stop it,
preventing an eastern expedition.
Thus, they sent the hydraulic engineer Zhèng Guó to secretly persuade Qín,
to excavate the Jīng River from Zhōngshān's Xīdi Hùkǒu to create a canal,
running east alongside the northern mountains for over three hundred lǐ,
intending to irrigate fields.
Midway through construction, they discovered the plan,
and Qín wanted to execute Zhèng Guó.
Zhèng Guó said,
"At first, I was indeed a spy,
but now that the canal is halfway complete, it also greatly benefits Qín."
Qín agreed with this,
and ultimately allowed the canal to be completed.
Once finished,
it directed Qín's water to irrigate saline lands of over forty thousand qǐng,
yielding over a zhōng per mǔ.
Thus Guānzhōng became fertile,
experiencing no famines,
and Qín was rich and powerful,
ultimately annexing all the feudal lords.
Hence, it was named the Zhèngguó Canal.
In the thirty-ninth year since the founding of Hàn,
during the reign of Xiàowén, the river breached at Suānzǎo,
flooding eastward, breaking through Jīntí.
Consequently, the Eastern Commandery dispatched a large military force to repair it.
After more than forty years,
during the reign of the current emperor Yuánguāng,
the river breached again at Hùzi,
flowing southeast into the Jùyè,
connecting with the Huái and Sì Rivers.
In response, the emperor dispatched Jí Àn and Zhèng Dāngshí to mobilize workers to block them.
However, it repeatedly failed.
At that time, Marquess Wǔān, Tián Fén, was the Chancellor,
and his fiefdom was Shù.
Shù was located north of the river,
and if the river breached southwards, Shù would be without flood,
yielding plentiful harvests.
Fén said to the emperor,
"The breaches of rivers and lakes are acts of Heaven,
not easily countered by human effort with strong dikes,
for such repairs may not align with Heaven's will."
The diviners and numerists concurred.
Hence, the emperor delayed further efforts at repair.
At the time, Zhèng Dāngshí was the Grand Herald.
He proposed,
"In the past, grain was ferried east from Guānzhōng via the Wèi River,
taking six months for completion,
over a distance of over nine hundred lǐ,
with frequent obstacles.
Excavating a canal from Cháng'ān
alongside the southern mountains
would bring it to the river within over three hundred lǐ,
reducing the ferry distance,
and shortening the journey to three months;
and it would also irrigate over ten thousand qǐng of farmland below the canal,
benefiting the lands,
making the grain transport easier, reducing labor,
and enriching Guānzhōng with grain."
The emperor agreed,
and ordered the hydraulic engineer Xú Bóbiǎo of Qí,
to mobilize tens of thousands of workers to excavate the transport canal,
which took three years to complete.
Upon completion,
the convenience for grain transport was immense.
Later, grain transport increased,
and the lower canal settlers significantly benefitted from irrigation.
Later, the governor of Hédōng, Fān Xì, reported,
"Transport from the east of the mountains has declined,
with the current flow causing much loss,
and being expensive.
Digging a canal to divert the Fén River, irrigating Píshì and the lower Fényīn,
and the Yellow River to irrigate the lower Fényīn and Púbàn,
could reclaim five thousand qǐng.
These five thousand qǐng were unused wastelands along the riverbank,
which the people grazed
with livestock.
Now irrigating them can yield over two million shǐ of grain.
Grain from the upper Wèi,
is as good as that from Guānzhōng,
and to the east of the Jǐor does not require further grain transport."
The emperor agreed,
and mobilized tens of thousands to create a canal farm.
After several years,
the river shifted,
rendering the canal ineffective,
making farmers unable to repay their seeds.
After a long time,
the Hédōng canal farm was abandoned,
given to Yuè people,
with the Lesser Treasury considering it slight income.
Subsequently, someone suggested opening the Bāo-Xié road and improving grain transport,
under the supervision of the Chief Prosecutor Zhāng Tāng.
Tāng investigated the matter,
stating,
"Traveling to Shǔ via the old road,
full of slopes,
is far and circuitous.
Now excavating the Bāo-Xié road,
with fewer slopes,
is four hundred lǐ closer;
and with the Bāo River connecting to the Miǎn,
and the Xié River to the Wèi,
boats can be used for grain transport.
Transport from the south via Nányáng into the Miǎn, entering Bāo,
is only intermittently interrupted for over one hundred lǐ without water,
using carts for transport,
from Xié down to the Wèi.
In this way,
grain from Hànzhōng can be delivered,
with no limits on transport from Shāndōng via the Miǎn,
improving the grain transport at Jǐor.
Moreover, Bāo-Xié is rich in timber, bamboo, and arrows,
comparable to Bāshǔ."
The emperor agreed,
appointed Tāng's son, Áng, as the governor of Hànzhōng,
mobilized tens of thousands to construct the winding Xié road over five hundred lǐ.
Though the road proved convenient and closer,
the water's rapids and rocks made transport impractical.
Later, Zhuāng Xióngbī proposed,
"The people of Línjìn wish to dig the Luò River to irrigate the wasteland east of Zhòngquán.
If water is obtained,
each mŭ could yield ten shǐ."
Thus, they mobilized over ten thousand workers to dig a canal,
channeling Luò water from Zhèng over to the foot of Shānyán Mountain.
The banks tended to collapse,
leading to the excavation of wells,
some over forty zhàng deep.
Wells were dug everywhere,
connecting underground to channel water.
Water transported over mountain crests for over ten lǐ.
Hence, the first well canal system began.
Discovering dragon bones,
it was named ‘Dragon Head Canal.’
After constructing for over ten years,
the canal was partially operational,
yet its full benefits were not realized.
Over twenty years have passed since the Hùzǐ river breach.
Due to poor harvests,
territories of Liáng and Chǔ were especially harshly affected.
After the emperor performed the Feng and Shàn rituals to the mountains and rivers,
the next year,
drought caused little rain in Qiánfēng.
The emperor then ordered Jí Rén and Guō Chāng to rally tens of thousands to block the Hùzǐ breach.
Meanwhile, the emperor engaged with Wànlǐshā activities,
then personally inspected the river breach,
sacrificing a white horse and jade bi to the river,
and commanded courtiers and officers, from generals on down, to carry wood to fill the river breach.
At that time, Eastern Commandery was burning grass,
resulting in a shortage of firewood,
leading to the cutting of bamboo from Qíyuán for dam material.
The Son of Heaven, having personally witnessed the breach at the Hùzǐ River,
lamented the failure to complete the flood control works;
thus he composed a song saying:
"When the Hùzǐ breaches, what can be done?
Vast and expansive, the villages are exhausted to become rivers!
Exhausted to become rivers, the land finds no peace,
The works never cease until Wú Mountain is leveled.
When Wú Mountain is leveled, Jùyě overflows,
Fish teem densely even as winter approaches.
The extended channels slacken, departing from their constant flow,
While flood dragons gallop, roaming far and wide.
Return to your old course, O spirits, be generous!
Had I not feng and shan sacrifices, how would I know what lies beyond?
For my sake, tell the River Earl: Why so unkind,
Ceaselessly overflowing, bringing sorrow to our people?
Nièsāng floats, Huái and Sì rivers full,
Long not returning, the water's restraint slackens."
Another version says:
"The river, vast and mighty, rushes and gurgles,
Northward crossing the marsh, dredging the flow is hard.
Pulling long reeds, sinking beautiful jades,
The River Earl consents, but firewood is insufficient.
Firewood insufficient, the people of Wèi are to blame,
Burning desolately, alas, how to ward off the waters!
Lay bamboo from the sparse woods, set stone pillars as dikes,
When Xuānfáng is blocked, ten thousand blessings will come."
Thereupon, they finally blocked the Hùzǐ breach,
built a palace upon it,
named Xuānfáng Palace.
And they channeled the river northward into two canals,
restoring Yǔ's ancient traces,
so the lands of Liáng and Chǔ were again peaceful,
free from flood disasters.
From this time onward,
those in power competed to speak of water conservancy.
Shuòfāng, Xīhé, Héxī, and Jiǔquán all diverted the Yellow River and stream valleys to irrigate fields;
while in Guānzhōng, Fǔ Canal and Língzhǐ diverted stagnant waters;
Rǔnán and Jiǔjiāng diverted the Huái River;
Dōnghǎi diverted Jùdìng;
below Tàishān, they diverted the Wèn River:
all dug canals for field irrigation,
each over ten thousand qǐng.
Other small canals cutting through mountains and opening paths
were too numerous to mention.
Yet the most notable was at Xuānfáng.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I journeyed south, ascended Lúshān,
observed how Yǔ channeled the Nine Rivers,
then proceeded to Kuàijī's Tàihuáng,
ascended Gūsū,
gazed upon the Five Lakes;
eastward, I peered at Luòruì and Dàpī,
faced the Yellow River,
traveled along the Huái, Sì, Jǐ, Tà, and Luò canals;
westward, I viewed Shǔ's Mínshān and Líduī;
northward, from Lóngmén to Shuòfāng.
I say:
How profound
are the benefits and harms of water!
Having joined in carrying firewood to block Xuānfáng,
I was moved by the "Hùzǐ" poem and thus wrote the "Treatise on Rivers and Canals."
With the rise of the Hàn,
inheriting Qín's abuses,
men followed the army campaigns,
the old and weak transported grain supplies,
tasks were arduous and resources scarce,
even the Son of Heaven could not procure a team of four horses of the same color,
while generals and ministers sometimes rode ox carts,
and the common people had nothing stored or covered.
Thus, because Qín's currency was heavy and difficult to use,
they ordered the people to mint coins anew,
one catty of gold,
simplifying laws and reducing restrictions.
Yet unscrupulous profit-seekers
hoarded surplus goods to corner the market,
prices soared,
rice reached ten thousand coins per shí,
a horse cost a hundred gold.
Once the empire was pacified,
Emperor Gāozǔ decreed that merchants could not wear silk or ride carriages,
imposing heavy taxes to oppress and humiliate them.
During the reigns of Emperor Huì and Empress Dowager Gāo,
due to the recent stabilization of the empire,
they relaxed the laws on merchants,
yet the descendants of market folk were still barred from official posts.
They measured officials' salaries,
estimated government expenses,
to levy taxes on the people.
And the revenues from mountains, rivers, gardens, ponds, and market taxes,
from the Son of Heaven down to the enfeoffed lords'汤沐邑,
were each used for private maintenance,
not included in the state's regular finances.
They transported grain from Shāndōng by water and land,
to supply the capital officials,
annually no more than several hundred thousand shí.
By Emperor Wén's time,
jiǎ coins became more numerous,
lighter in value,
so they minted new four-zhu coins,
inscribed "bàn liǎng,"
allowing people to mint coins freely.
Thus Wú, a feudal state,
minted coins from its mountains,
wealth rivaling the Son of Heaven's,
later ending in rebellion.
Dèng Tōng,
a high official,
amassed wealth from minting coins surpassing the king's.
Hence, Wú and Dèng's coins spread throughout the empire,
and the prohibition on minting coins arose.
The Xiōngnú repeatedly invaded and plundered the northern borders,
garrison troops were numerous,
border grain insufficient to feed those stationed there.
Thus, they recruited people who could deliver or transport grain to the border, granting them ranks,
ranks attainable up to dà shù zhǎng.
During Emperor Jǐng's reign,
a drought struck west of Shàngjùn,
they again enforced the sale of ranks,
lowering prices to attract people;
and convicts serving sentences
could deliver grain to the government to atone for crimes.
They increased the breeding of horses in parks to broaden their use,
and palaces, towers, carriages, and horses were increasingly built and repaired.
By the time the current emperor ascended the throne a few years later,
over seventy years since Hàn's rise,
the state was free of troubles,
barring floods or droughts,
the people were well-fed and self-sufficient,
granaries in cities and countryside were full,
and government storehouses overflowed with goods and wealth.
Coins in the capital accumulated by the millions,
strings rotting, uncountable.
Grain in the Tàicāng piled up layer upon layer,
spilling over to accumulate outdoors,
until it rotted and became inedible.
Commoners had horses in the streets and alleys,
herds gathered between fields,
and those riding mares were shunned and excluded from gatherings.
Gatekeepers ate fine grains and meat,
officials saw their children and grandchildren grow up in post,
some took their official titles as surnames.
Thus, everyone valued self-respect and feared breaking the law,
prioritizing righteousness over avoiding shame.
At this time,
laws were lax and the people wealthy,
arrogant with their riches,
some even forming powerful cliques for兼并,
dominating villages by force.
From the imperial clan and landed nobility down to ministers and high officials,
they vied in extravagance,
their houses, carriages, and attire exceeding regulations without limit.
When things peak, they decline—
such is the inevitable change.
From then on,
Yán Zhù and Zhū Mǎichén attracted the Eastern Ōu,
engaged with the two Yuè states,
the Jiāng-Huái region was drained and burdened with expenses.
Táng Méng and Sīmǎ Xiàngrú opened roads to the Southwestern Yí,
cutting through mountains for over a thousand lǐ,
expanding Bā-Shǔ,
yet the people of Bā-Shǔ were exhausted by it.
Péng Wú traded and subdued Cháoxiān,
established the Cānghǎi Commandery,
then Yān and Qí regions were stirred into action.
When Wáng Huī set the trap at Mǎyì,
the Xiōngnú severed the peace marriage,
harassing the northern borders,
war persisted without resolution,
the empire suffered from the toil,
and conflicts grew daily.
Those on the march carried supplies,
those at home saw them off,
Disturbances both domestically and abroad were mutually supported,
while the people resorted to crafty methods for their own gain,
and revenues dwindled and were insufficient to cover expenses.
Those who offered goods received official positions,
and those who delivered goods were pardoned from offenses.
The selection of officials declined,
and integrity and shame were mutually compromised,
with military force gaining preference,
and laws were stringently enforced.
This marked the beginning of ministers seeking profits.
Subsequently, the Han dispatched tens of thousands of cavalry annually to attack the Xiongnu,
and General Wèi Qīng captured Xiongnu territory south of the Yellow River,
constructing Shuòfāng.
At that time,
the Han opened the roads to the southwestern barbarians,
involving tens of thousands of people,
carrying supplies over a thousand leagues,
where more than ten measures were needed to transport just one.
Distributing currency to the Qióng and Bó people to gather them.
For several years the roads were impassable,
causing repeated attacks by the barbarians,
and officials dispatched troops to punish them.
The taxes and levies of Bā Shǔ were insufficient to maintain this,
so they recruited affluent citizens to cultivate Nán Yí land,
sending grain to the county officials,
while receiving money in the capital.
From the eastern sea counties,
the costs of moving people were comparable to those of Nán Yí.
They also raised over a hundred thousand people to build Wèi Shuòfāng,
with grain transport over long distances,
extending labor to all areas east of the mountains,
costing tens of millions,
depleting governmental stores.
Hence, they recruited civilians who could supply slaves and maids to receive lifelong exemption,
promoting people to lords by increasing ranks
resulting in sacrifices like sheep for lords
starting from this point.
Four years later,
the Han dispatched generals with six commanders,
totaling over a hundred thousand troops,
to attack Yòu Xián Wáng,
capturing ten thousand
and five hundred prisoners.
The next year,
the grand general with six commanders again attacked the Xiongnu,
taking nineteen thousand prisoners.
Those soldiers who captured and executed prisoners received rewards totaling more than two hundred thousand jins of gold,
with tens of thousands of those captured receiving generous rewards,
their clothing and sustenance supplied by county officials;
however, over a hundred thousand Han soldiers and horses died,
and the costs of armaments and transport were not included therein.
Thereupon, the Grand Minister of Agriculture reported the depletion of stored funds,
and despite taxes being exhausted,
it was still not enough to support the soldiers.
The ministers declared:
"The Emperor said, 'I have heard the teachings of the Five Emperors did not overlap but maintained order,
the methods of Yǔ and Tāng differed yet they ruled,
though their approaches varied,
yet they all aimed to establish virtue.
The northern frontier is not stable,
I am deeply troubled by this.
Recently,
the grand general attacked the Xiongnu,
capturing nineteen thousand prisoners,
leaving those captured with no food.
It is proposed that the people be allowed to buy titles and redeem imprisonment to reduce penalties.'
Arrange for a rewards office,
name it the Marquis of Martial Success.
With ranks totaling one hundred seventy thousand,
valued at more than three million gold.
Those purchasing martial titles will first be appointed as officials,
beginning with personal ranks;
the rank of Qianfu equates to that of Wu Dafu;
with offenses reduced by two ranks;
the title can reach the rank of Le Qing:
to showcase military merit."
Military achievements often superseded ranks,
with the greatest achieving marquis status, ministers, and grand officers,
while the lesser became junior officials.
The administrative path became convoluted and multi-faceted,
consequently, official duties were neglected and discarded.
Since Gōngsūn Hóng used the principles of the "Spring and Autumn Annals" to regulate subordinates as Han chancellor,
Zhāng Tāng used strict written judgments to administer justice as the court's official judge,
thus the methodology of inspection emerged,
and the dismissal, obstruction, defamation, and investigation of cases were employed.
The following year,
rebellions by the kings of Huáinán, Héngshān, and Jiāngdū were discovered,
and the court pursued the matter thoroughly,
tracking down their associates,
resulting in the executions of tens of thousands,
with magistrates becoming more strict and laws more perspicacious.
At the time,
there was an invitation for upstanding, virtuous, and scholarly individuals,
some reaching high-ranking minister positions.
Gōngsūn Hóng as Han chancellor
wore humble clothing,
did not consume lavish food,
setting an example for the world.
Yet this did not benefit customs,
gradually pursuing achievement and profit.
The following year,
the Cavalry General again set out to attack the Xiongnu,
seizing forty thousand heads.
In the autumn,
the King of Húnxié led tens of thousands to surrender,
prompting the Han to send twenty thousand carriages to welcome them.
Upon arrival,
they received rewards,
rewarding those with merit.
That year the costs exceeded hundreds of millions.
Initially,
more than ten years prior, the Yellow River burst its banks,
flooding the regions of Liang and Chu, causing multiple disasters,
and counties bordering the river constructed and blocked the river,
which repeatedly breached and collapsed,
resulting in incalculable costs.
Later, the Bānxi desired to decrease grain transport,
digging Fen and river channels for irrigation,
employing tens of thousands;
Zhèng Dāngshí proposed an alternate route for the Wei Canal,
digging a direct canal from Chang’an to Huáyīn,
involving tens of thousands of workers;
channels were also dug in Shuòfāng,
employing tens of thousands;
each undertaking lasted two to three periods,
results were incomplete,
and costs reached tens of millions in each case.
The Emperor, to combat the Xiongnu,
extensively reared horses,
with tens of thousands driven to Chang’an for feeding,
but caretakers were insufficient in Guanzhong,
prompting a requisition from nearby counties.
The Xiongnu captives were all provided by county officials,
who could not sustain them,
prompting the Emperor to reduce his meals,
release his chariot horses,
and take from the imperial reserves to support them.
The following year,
Shandong suffered flooding,
leaving many people hungry and destitute,
prompting the Emperor to dispatch envoys to open the state granaries to relieve the impoverished citizens.
Still insufficient,
they then recruited affluent individuals to provide loans.
Still unable to adequately assist,
they subsequently relocated the impoverished west beyond the pass,
settling them in Nán and Xīn Qín in Shuòfāng,
totaling over seventy thousand households,
all supported by the county officials.
Over several years,
assets were supplemented by loans,
with envoys overseeing different regions,
the roads lined with carriages and covers.
These expenses reached billions,
beyond calculation.
Thus, the state treasury was greatly depleted.
Meanwhile, wealthy merchants and large traders amassed wealth,
oppressing the poor,
with hundreds of transport wheels,
residing idly in the towns,
receiving support from lords.
Smelting and salt boiling,
earning wealth in the millions,
while not assisting the state's urgent needs,
and the common people remained deeply afflicted.
Thereupon, the Emperor and ministers deliberated,
to remake currency to supply needs,
and crush the extravagant and monopolistic.
At this time, the imperial park had a white deer, and the lesser treasury had abundant silver and tin.
Ever since Emperor Xiàowén remade the four-zhu coin, about forty years prior,
since the beginning of Jiànyuán,
use was limited,
but frequently county officials found copper mountains and minted money,
the people also secretly counterfeited money,
beyond count.
As money increased, its weight lessened,
The officials reported:
"In ancient times, leather currency
was used by feudal lords for diplomatic gifts and tributes.
There were three grades of metal,
with gold being the highest,
white silver the middle,
and red copper the lowest.
Now the Bànliǎng coins are supposed to weigh four zhū,
but unscrupulous people secretly file the coin backs to collect the copper dust,
making coins increasingly lightweight while goods become more expensive,
causing distant regions trouble with cumbersome currency expenses."
Thus, they made one-foot-square white deer leather
edged with colored designs
into leather currency,
valued at 400,000.
For royal relatives and nobles attending court or presenting tributes,
they must present jade discs accompanied by this leather currency
before being allowed to proceed.
They also created white metal from silver and tin alloy.
Believing nothing surpasses the dragon for heaven,
the horse for earth,
and the tortoise for humankind,
they made three grades of white metal:
The first weighing eight liǎng,
circular in shape,
with dragon pattern,
named 'Báixuǎn',
valued at 3,000;
the second slightly lighter in weight,
square in shape,
with horse pattern,
valued at 500;
the third even smaller,
oval in shape,
with tortoise pattern,
valued at 300.
They ordered government mints to melt down Bànliǎng coins
and recast Sānzhū coins instead,
with inscriptions matching their weight.
The penalty for illicit minting of any metal currency was death,
yet officials and commoners illicitly minting white metal became countless.
Thereupon, Dōngguō Xiányáng and Kǒng Jǐn were appointed as Grand Minister of Agriculture deputies,
overseeing salt and iron affairs;
Sāng Hóngyáng rose to power through computational skills,
serving as Palace Attendant.
Xiányáng
was a major salt boiler from Qí,
Kǒng Jǐn,
a great smelter from Nányáng,
both having amassed fortunes of thousands of gold,
hence recommended by Zhèng Dāngshí.
Hóngyáng,
son of a Luòyáng merchant,
through mental calculation,
became Palace Attendant at age thirteen.
Thus these three men could dissect profit matters down to the finest hair.
As laws grew stricter,
many officials were dismissed.
With frequent military campaigns,
many commoners purchased exemptions or fifth-rank nobility,
making conscripted soldiers increasingly scarce.
Thus those with thousand-man or fifth-rank titles were made officials,
or provided horses if unwilling;
former officials were generally assigned to clear thorns in the Shanglin Park,
constructing Kūnmíng Lake.
The following year,
the Great General and Swift Cavalry General launched major attacks against the Hú,
capturing 80-90,000 enemy heads,
rewarding 500,000 gold,
while over 100,000 Han army horses died,
not counting transport and equipment costs.
At this time finances were depleted,
and many soldiers went unpaid.
Officials reported Sānzhū coins were too light,
easily counterfeited,
so requested commanderies and principalities mint Wǔzhū coins instead,
with raised rims underneath,
preventing filing of metal dust.
Grand Minister of Agriculture deputies Kǒng Jǐn and Xiányáng memorialized:
"Mountains and seas,
treasuries of heaven and earth,
should belong to the Privy Treasury,
yet Your Majesty selflessly
assigns them to the Grand Minister to supplement revenues.
We wish to recruit people bearing their own costs,
using government equipment to boil salt,
with officials providing cauldrons.
Drifters and speculators seeking to monopolize mountain and sea goods,
amassing great wealth,
exploit the common people.
Obstructive proposals
are too numerous to hear.
Those daring to privately smelt iron or boil salt
shall have left feet shackled,
with implements confiscated.
Commanderies without iron deposits
shall establish minor iron offices,
subordinate to local counties."
They dispatched Kǒng Jǐn and Dōngguō Xiányáng by carriage to implement salt-iron policy nationwide,
establishing government offices,
appointing wealthy former salt-iron families as officials.
The official recruitment path grew increasingly mixed,
unselective,
with many merchants included.
Merchants exploited currency changes,
hoarding goods for profit.
Thus ministers proposed:
"Since commanderies suffer disasters frequently,
landless poor people
should be recruited to relocate to fertile lands.
Though Your Majesty reduces meals and expenses,
releasing imperial funds to relieve the masses,
reducing taxes,
yet people don't uniformly return to farming,
while merchants multiply.
The poor lack accumulated stores,
all relying on government support.
Previously we taxed carts and merchants' cash differentially,
we request reinstating such taxes.
All merchants, peddlers, lenders, traders,
urban hoarders of goods,
and profit-seeking dealers,
even without market registration,
must self-declare their goods,
at rate of one suàn per 2,000 strings of cash.
All artisans with rents or smelting,
at rate of one suàn per 4,000 strings.
Non-officials except village elders and northern frontier cavalry
pay one suàn per cart;
merchants' carts pay two suàn;
boats over five zhàng pay one suàn.
Concealing without declaration,
or incomplete declaration,
receives one-year frontier garrison duty,
with cash confiscated.
Informers
receive half the confiscated amount.
Registered merchants
and their families
are forbidden to register farmland,
to benefit agriculture.
Violators
have fields and servants confiscated."
The Emperor then remembered Bǔ Shì's words,
summoning and appointing him as Palace Attendant,
with nobility rank of Left庶长,
granting 100 qǐng of land,
and announcing nationwide,
making it widely known.
Originally,
Bǔ Shì
was from Hénán,
engaged in farming and herding.
After his parents died,
Shì had a younger brother who, upon reaching adulthood,
Shì left the household taking only over 100 sheep, giving all land, property and assets to his brother.
Shì herded in mountains for over ten years,
breeding sheep to over 1,000 head,
purchasing land and property.
When his brother repeatedly lost his assets,
Shì redistributed shares to him several times.
While Hàn was frequently sending generals against the Xiōngnú,
Bǔ Shì petitioned,
wishing to donate half his family wealth to assist the frontier.
The Emperor sent an envoy asking Shì:
"Do you want an official post?"
Shì replied: "I've herded since youth,
unfamiliar with officialdom,
and don't desire it."
The envoy asked: "Does your family have grievances
you wish to petition about?"
Shì said:
"In my life, I have never contended with others.
In my district, I lent to the poor,
and guided those who were unvirtuous toward goodness.
Wherever I lived, people all followed me.
Why then would I be wronged by anyone?
I have nothing more to say."
The envoy asked:
"If so, what is your purpose in acting this way?"
Shì replied:
"The Son of Heaven is attacking the Xiōngnú.
I believe that the worthy should die with integrity at the frontier,
and the wealthy should contribute their resources.
Only thus can the Xiōngnú be vanquished."
The envoy reported his words in full to the emperor.
The Son of Heaven relayed this to Chancellor Hóng.
Hóng said:
"This goes against human nature.
A minister who acts improperly
should not be made an example, lest it disrupt the law.
I beg Your Majesty not to grant his request."
Thereupon, the emperor delayed responding to Shì for a long time.
After several years,
he finally dismissed Shì.
Shì returned home
and resumed farming and herding.
A little over a year later,
as the armies were frequently deployed,
with Húnxié Wáng and others surrendering,
the government expenses grew heavy,
and the granaries and treasuries were depleted.
The following year,
a great migration of poor people occurred,
all relying on government support,
which could not fully sustain them.
Bǔ Shì contributed two hundred thousand coins to the Governor of Hénán,
to aid the migrating people.
When Hénán submitted a register of wealthy individuals assisting the poor,
the Son of Heaven saw Bǔ Shì's name,
recognized him,
and said,
"This is the one who previously wished to donate half his family's wealth to support the frontier."
He then granted Shì exemptions from corvée labor for four hundred men.
Shì again donated it all to the government.
At that time, the rich and powerful vied to hide their wealth,
while only Shì was especially eager to contribute to the expenses.
The Son of Heaven thus regarded Shì as a truly virtuous elder,
and honored him to set an example for the common people.
Initially,
Shì was unwilling to serve as a court gentleman.
The emperor said:
"I have sheep in the Shànglín Park;
I wish you to tend them."
Shì then accepted the post of gentleman,
wearing common clothes and straw sandals to herd the sheep.
Over a year later,
the sheep grew fat and multiplied.
The emperor passed by, saw the sheep,
and praised them.
Shì said:
"It is not only with sheep;
governing the people is also like this.
Let them follow the seasons in their routines;
remove the bad ones promptly,
lest they ruin the flock."
The emperor found Shì remarkable,
appointed him as magistrate of Gōushì to test him,
and Gōushì benefited from his governance.
He was promoted to magistrate of Chénggāo,
where he excelled in water transport.
The emperor, considering Shì honest and loyal,
appointed him as Grand Tutor to the King of Qí.
Meanwhile, Kǒng Jǐn, tasked with overseeing the casting of utensils nationwide,
was appointed as Grand Minister of Agriculture within three years,
ranking among the Nine Ministers.
Sāng Hóngyáng served as Deputy Grand Minister of Agriculture,
managing financial accounts,
and gradually established the equal transportation system to facilitate the flow of goods.
It was then decreed that officials could contribute grain for appointments,
with gentleman posts costing up to six hundred dàn.
Five years after the creation of the white gold and wǔzhū coins,
tens of thousands of officials and commoners sentenced to death for counterfeiting were pardoned.
Those undetected or killed in the process
were too numerous to count.
Over a million turned themselves in under the pardon.
Yet less than half surrendered,
and nearly everyone in the land was minting coins.
With offenders so numerous,
officials could not arrest and punish all,
so Erudites Chǔ Dà, Xú Yǎn, and others were dispatched in groups to tour the commanderies and kingdoms,
to report on local officials and powerful figures profiteering from monopolies.
Meanwhile, Imperial Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Tāng was highly influential and in power,
with Jiǎn Xuān, Dù Zhōu, and others as his deputies,
while Yì Zòng, Yǐn Qí, Wáng Wēnshū, and others, known for their harshness, rose to the Nine Ministers,
and direct investigators like Xià Lán began to emerge.
Then Grand Minister of Agriculture Yán Yì was executed.
Initially,
Yì was a local chief in Jǐnán,
and through integrity and honesty, gradually rose to the Nine Ministers.
When the emperor and Zhāng Tāng created the white deer hide currency,
they consulted Yì.
Yì said:
"Now the kings and marquises present dark jade discs for court congratulations,
worth only a few thousand,
yet the hide mats are valued at four hundred thousand,
making the primary and secondary values disproportionate."
The Son of Heaven was displeased.
Zhāng Tāng also had a grudge against Yì,
and when someone accused Yì of other criticisms,
the case was handed to Zhāng Tāng to investigate Yì.
Yì was speaking with a guest,
who mentioned that the new decree had its drawbacks,
Yì did not respond,
but slightly curled his lips.
Zhāng Tāng reported that Yì, as a Nine Minister, saw the decree as flawed,
did not speak out but harbored silent dissent,
and should be sentenced to death.
From then on,
the law of "silent dissent" was established as a precedent,
and many high officials resorted to flattery and sycophancy.
After the Son of Heaven issued the property tax decree and honored Bǔ Shì,
the common people still did not contribute wealth to support the government,
so Yáng Kě's enforcement of the property tax accusations began in earnest.
Many commanderies and kingdoms illicitly minted coins,
leading to lightweight currency,
so the high officials requested that the capital mint red-rimmed coins by the Zhōng official,
each equivalent to five,
and for official taxes, only red-rimmed coins were acceptable.
White gold gradually depreciated,
and the people did not value it,
so the government banned it by decree,
but to no avail.
Over a year later,
white gold was finally abolished and ceased circulation.
That year,
Zhāng Tāng died, and the people did not mourn him.
Two years later,
red-rimmed coins depreciated,
the people cunningly used them by law,
finding it inconvenient,
and they too were abolished.
Thereupon, all commanderies and kingdoms were prohibited from minting coins,
and only the Three Officials of Shànglín were authorized to mint.
With coins abundant,
it was decreed that only Three Officials coins could circulate nationwide,
and all coins previously minted by commanderies and kingdoms were melted down,
with the copper delivered to the Three Officials.
Thus, private minting decreased significantly,
as the cost outweighed the profit,
and only skilled, large-scale counterfeiters dared to engage in it.
Bǔ Shì served as Chancellor of Qí,
while Yáng Kě's property tax accusations swept the land,
with most middle-class households and above facing accusations.
Dù Zhōu handled the cases,
and few were exonerated.
Then censors and court justices were dispatched in groups
to investigate property taxes in the commanderies and kingdoms,
confiscating people's wealth amounting to hundreds of millions,
slaves and maidservants by the tens of millions,
land in large counties measuring several hundred qǐng,
and in small counties over a hundred qǐng,
with residences similarly seized.
Consequently, merchant households of the middle class and above were largely ruined,
and the people indulged in fine food and clothing,
no longer engaging in productive savings or industries,
while the government, due to the salt, iron, and property taxes,
grew increasingly wealthy.
The passes were expanded,
and left and right auxiliary regions were established.
Initially,
the Minister of Agriculture managed salt and iron monopolies with numerous official cloth currencies,
so the Office of the Imperial Parks was established,
intending to oversee salt and iron;
but after Yáng Kě's reporting on hidden wealth,
the Shanglin Park became filled with abundant goods,
thus the Office of the Imperial Parks was ordered to manage Shanglin instead.
Once Shanglin was fully stocked,
it expanded further.
At that time, the Yuè sought to engage the Hàn in naval battles,
so the Kūnmíng Pond was extensively renovated,
with pavilions arranged around it.
Tower ships were built,
over ten zhàng high,
with flags mounted atop,
appearing very majestic.
Moved by this,
the Son of Heaven then constructed the Bóliáng Tower,
dozens of zhàng high.
The construction of palaces
grew increasingly splendid from then on.
He then distributed the confiscated wealth among various offices,
and the Office of the Imperial Parks, the Privy Treasury, the Minister of Agriculture, and the Master of Horses each established agricultural officials,
often farming on confiscated lands in the commanderies and counties.
The confiscated slaves
were distributed to various parks to raise dogs, horses, and wild animals,
and also given to various offices.
As more miscellaneous offices were set up,
and the number of slaves increased,
the grain transported via the Yellow River reached four million dàn,
and even with official purchases, it was just sufficient.
Suǒ Zhōng reported:
"Young men from prominent families or wealthy individuals engage in cockfighting, dog and horse racing,
archery, hunting, and gambling,
disrupting the common people."
Thus, those who violated the laws were summoned,
leading to several thousand people implicated,
named 'entangled convicts'.
Those who contributed wealth could become court gentlemen,
and the selection of gentlemen declined.
At that time, the region east of the mountains suffered from Yellow River disasters,
and for several years the harvests failed,
with some people resorting to cannibalism,
across an area of one to two thousand lǐ.
The Son of Heaven took pity on them,
issuing an edict:
"In Jiāngnán, where fire farming and water weeding are practiced,
let the famine-stricken people migrate to the areas between the Jiāng and Huái rivers for food;
those who wish to stay
may settle there."
Envoys were sent in continuous processions along the roads,
to protect them,
and grain from Bā and Shǔ was dispatched to relieve them.
The following year,
the Son of Heaven began touring the commanderies and kingdoms.
Crossing the Yellow River eastward,
the governor of Hédōng, unprepared for the imperial arrival,
and unable to provide adequately,
committed suicide.
Traveling west over Lǒng,
the governor of Lǒngxī, due to the suddenness of the visit,
left the imperial attendants without food,
and he too committed suicide.
Thereupon, the emperor went north through Xiāo Pass,
with tens of thousands of cavalry,
hunted in Xīn Qínzhōng,
and returned after inspecting the border troops.
In Xīn Qínzhōng, some areas lacked watchtowers for a thousand lǐ,
so officials from the governor of Běidì down were executed,
and the people were allowed to herd livestock in border counties,
with the government lending them broodmares,
to be returned after three years,
along with a ten percent interest,
in lieu of wealth reporting,
to populate Xīn Qínzhōng.
After obtaining the precious tripods,
altars for Hòutǔ and Tàiyī were established,
and the dukes and ministers discussed the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
while all commanderies and kingdoms prepared roads and bridges,
repaired old palaces,
and counties along the imperial routes
stocked official supplies,
set up provisions,
and awaited the imperial visit.
The next year,
Nányuè rebelled,
and the Western Qiāng invaded the borders aggressively.
Thus, due to shortages east of the mountains,
the Son of Heaven pardoned all prisoners,
and sent over 200,000 tower ship soldiers from the south to attack Nányuè,
tens of thousands of cavalry from west of Sānhé to strike the Western Qiāng,
and another tens of thousands to cross the river and build Língjū.
Initially, Zhāngyì and Jiǔquán commanderies were established,
and agricultural offices were set up in Shàngjùn, Shuòfāng, Xīhé, and Héxī,
with 600,000 border soldiers stationed to farm and guard.
The central provinces repaired roads and supplied grain,
some from as far as 3,000 lǐ,
others over a thousand lǐ away,
all relying on the Minister of Agriculture.
When border troops were insufficiently equipped,
weapons from the armory workshops were issued to supply them.
With chariot and cavalry horses in short supply,
and the court's funds low,
buying horses was difficult,
so a decree was issued,
ordering nobles and officials of 300 dàn rank and above
to contribute mares to stations across the empire,
so each station kept breeding horses,
with annual foal quotas.
The chancellor of Qí, Bǔ Shì, submitted a memorial:
"I have heard that when the ruler worries, his ministers feel disgraced.
Since Nányuè has rebelled,
I wish to go with my son and Qí's skilled sailors to fight to the death."
The Son of Heaven issued an edict:
"Although Bǔ Shì personally farms and herds,
he does not seek profit,
and often aids the court with his surplus.
Now that the empire faces an emergency,
he eagerly offers to die with his son,
and though not yet in battle,
his righteousness shines from within.
He is bestowed the title of Marquis within the Pass,
60 catties of gold,
and 100 qǐng of land."
This was proclaimed throughout the empire,
yet none responded.
Hundreds of marquises
none sought to join the army against the Qiāng or Yuè.
At the ancestral liquor offering,
the Privy Treasury inspected the gold,
and over a hundred marquises lost their titles for deficient gold.
Bǔ Shì was then appointed Grandee Secretary.
Once in office,
he observed that many commanderies found the state's salt and iron monopolies inconvenient,
with iron tools of poor quality,
prices high,
and some forced sales on the people.
Moreover, ships were taxed,
reducing trade,
and goods became expensive,
so he spoke to Kǒng Jǐn about the ship tax.
This displeased the emperor with Bǔ Shì.
After three years of continuous warfare,
the Qiāng were suppressed,
Nányuè destroyed,
and seventeen new commanderies established from Pānyú west to southern Shǔ,
governed according to their customs,
with no taxes imposed.
Commanderies from Nányáng and Hànzhōng onward
supplied the new commanderies' officials and soldiers with food, currency, and goods according to proximity,
along with carriages, horses, and equipment.
Yet the new commanderies occasionally rebelled on a small scale,
killing officials,
so Hàn sent southern troops to suppress them,
with over ten thousand men annually,
all expenses covered by the Minister of Agriculture.
The Minister used equal transportation and salt and iron monopolies to supplement taxes,
thus managing to support them.
However, in counties the troops passed through,
only essential supplies were provided to avoid shortages,
not daring to impose unauthorized levies.
The following year,
the first year of Yuánfēng,
Bǔ Shì was demoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
Meanwhile, Sāng Hóngyáng became the Commandant of Grain,
overseeing the Minister of Agriculture,
and fully replaced Jǐn in managing the empire's salt and iron.
Hóngyáng observed that various offices each made their own purchases,
competing with each other,
causing prices to soar,
and some tax shipments didn't cover transport costs,
so he requested dozens of Assistant Ministers of Agriculture,
each assigned to commanderies and kingdoms,
and established equal transportation and salt and iron offices in various counties,
ordering distant regions to pay taxes with goods that merchants would buy at high prices, facilitating interchange.
A price stabilization office was established in the capital,
which received tribute and taxes from across the land.
Artisans and officials were summoned to manufacture carts and various implements,
all funded by the Minister of Agriculture.
The various offices under the Minister of Agriculture monopolized all commodities in the empire,
selling them when prices were high,
and buying them when prices were low.
In this way,
wealthy merchants and great traders could no longer reap excessive profits,
thus returning to fundamental pursuits,
and preventing prices of all goods from soaring.
Hence, by suppressing prices throughout the empire,
it was named "Píngzhǔn" (Price Stabilization).
The Son of Heaven deemed this appropriate,
and approved it.
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven traveled north to Shuòfāng,
east to Tàishān,
toured along the coast,
and returned along the northern border.
The rewards bestowed along the way
used over a million bolts of silk
and countless coins and gold,
all supplied sufficiently by the Minister of Agriculture.
Sāng Hóngyáng further requested that officials be permitted to contribute grain for official appointments,
and for criminals to redeem their offenses.
He ordered that commoners who could deliver grain to Gānquán would receive varying exemptions,
including lifelong exemption from labor service,
and immunity from property confiscation.
Other commanaderies each transported supplies to critical locations,
while various agricultural offices delivered grain,
increasing the annual grain shipment from Shāndōng to six million shí.
Within a year,
the Tàicāng and Gānquán granaries were full.
Surplus grain and other goods from the borders, along with equalized tribute, amounted to five million bolts of silk.
The people's taxes were not increased, yet the empire enjoyed abundant resources.
Thereupon, Sāng Hóngyáng was bestowed the title of Left庶长 (Shùzhǎng)
and two hundred jīn of gold.
That year, there was a minor drought,
and the emperor ordered officials to pray for rain.
Bǔ Shì remarked:
"Officials should merely consume rents and wear taxes,
yet now Sāng Hóngyáng has officials sitting in market stalls,
peddling goods to seek profit.
If you boil Hóngyáng,
then Heaven will send rain."
The Grand Historian remarks:
When the ways of exchange among farmers, artisans, and merchants are open,
then currencies of tortoise shells, cowries, gold, coins, knives, and cloth arise.
This has existed since ancient times,
dating back even before Gāoxīn Shì,
too remote to be recorded.
Thus, the Shū documents the era of Táng and Yú,
the Shī recounts the ages of Yīn and Zhōu,
where in times of peace, schools were promoted,
fundamentals were prioritized over peripherals,
and ritual and righteousness were used to guard against profit-seeking;
but when affairs changed and troubles arose, the opposite occurred.
Hence, when things flourish, they then decline,
when times reach an extreme, they turn,
alternating between substance and refinement,
such is the transformation from beginning to end.
In the Yǔ Gòng's nine provinces,
each according to its land's suitability
and the people's numbers, paid tribute.
Tāng and Wǔ inherited flaws and implemented changes,
keeping the people from weariness,
each diligently striving for order,
yet gradually declining and weakening.
Duke Huán of Qí employed Guǎn Zhòng's strategies,
mastered the balance of monetary轻重 (qīngzhòng),
monopolized the resources of mountains and seas,
to make the feudal lords pay homage,
using tiny Qí to achieve renown as a hegemon.
Wèi employed Lǐ Kè,
maximized land productivity,
becoming a powerful ruler.
From then on,
the empire contended in the Warring States period,
valuing deceit and force while despising benevolence and righteousness,
prioritizing wealth over deference.
Thus, some commoners amassed immense fortunes,
while the poor could not even fill themselves with chaff;
some powerful states annexed smaller ones and subjugated feudal lords,
while weak states saw their sacrifices cut off and lineages extinguished.
Until Qín,
finally unified the realm.
The currencies of Yú and Xià
had three grades of metal,
some yellow,
some white,
some red;
some were coins,
some cloth,
some knives,
some tortoise shells and cowries.
By the time of Qín,
the currency of the unified empire was divided into two grades:
gold, measured by the yì,
was the higher currency;
copper coins inscribed "bàn liǎng",
weighing as marked,
were the lower currency.
While pearls, jade, tortoise shells, silver, tin, and such were used for ornaments and treasures,
not as currency.
Yet each varied with the times, their values inconstant.
Then, externally repelling the barbarians,
internally undertaking great projects,
the men of the realm toiled at farming yet had insufficient grain for provisions,
women wove yet had insufficient clothing.
In ancient times, they exhausted the empire's resources to serve their superiors,
yet still felt it was not enough.
There is no other reason to say,
but that the flow of events,
mutually inciting, made it so—
why find it strange?
Wú Tàibó,
and his younger brother Zhòngyōng,
were both sons of King Tàiwáng of Zhōu,
and older brothers of Jì Lì.
Jì Lì was worthy,
and had a sagely son named Chāng.
King Tàiwáng wished to establish Jì Lì so that Chāng would succeed,
so Tàibó
and Zhòngyōng fled to Jīngmán,
tattooed their bodies and cut their hair,
to show they were unfit for use,
thus yielding to Jì Lì.
Jì Lì indeed succeeded,
becoming King Jì,
and Chāng became King Wén.
Tàibó, fleeing to Jīngmán,
named himself Gōuwú.
The Jīngmán people admired his righteousness,
and over a thousand households followed and submitted to him,
establishing him as Wú Tàibó.
Tàibó died,
without a son,
so his younger brother Zhòngyōng succeeded him,
becoming Wú Zhòngyōng.
Zhòngyōng died,
and his son Jì Jiǎn succeeded.
Jì Jiǎn died,
and his son Shū Dá succeeded.
Shū Dá died,
and his son Zhōu Zhāng succeeded.
At that time, King Wǔ of Zhōu conquered Yīn,
and sought the descendants of Tàibó
and Zhòngyōng,
finding Zhōu Zhāng.
Zhōu Zhāng was already ruler of Wú,
so he was enfeoffed accordingly.
He then enfeoffed Zhōu Zhāng's younger brother Yú Zhòng at the former site of Xià in the north of Zhōu,
who became Yú Zhòng,
listed among the feudal lords.
Zhōu Zhāng died,
and his son Xióng Suí succeeded him.
Xióng Suí died,
and his son Kē Xiāng succeeded him.
Kē Xiāng died,
and his son Qiáng Jiūyí succeeded him.
Qiáng Jiūyí died,
and his son Yúqiáo Yíwú succeeded him.
Yúqiáo Yíwú died,
and his son Kē Lú succeeded him.
Kē Lú died,
and his son Zhōu Yáo succeeded him.
Zhōu Yáo died,
and his son Qū Yǔ succeeded him.
Qū Yǔ died,
and his son Yí Wú succeeded him.
Yí Wú died,
and his son Qín Chǔ succeeded him.
Qín Chǔ died,
and his son Zhuǎn succeeded him.
Zhuǎn died,
and his son Pō Gāo succeeded him.
Pō Gāo died,
and his son Gōu Bēi succeeded him.
At this time, Duke Xiàn of Jìn exterminated Duke Yú of the northern Zhōu,
thereby initiating Jìn's campaign against Guó.
Gōu Bēi died,
and his son Qù Qí succeeded him.
Qù Qí died,
and his son Shòu Mèng succeeded him.
With Shòu Mèng's accession, Wú began to grow significantly stronger,
and he assumed the title of King.
Since Tài Bó founded Wú,
five generations passed until King Wǔ of Zhōu conquered Yīn,
who enfeoffed his descendants in two branches:
one was Yú,
located in the Central States;
the other was Wú,
situated among the barbarian tribes.
Twelve generations later, Jìn exterminated the Yú of the Central States.
Two generations after the Yú of the Central States were destroyed,
the Wú of the barbarian tribes rose to prominence.
In total, from Tài Bó to Shòu Mèng, there were nineteen generations.
In the second year of King Shòu Mèng,
Shēn Gōng Wū Chén, an exiled senior official of Chǔ, resentful of Chǔ general Zǐ Fǎn, fled to Jìn,
and from Jìn was sent to Wú,
where he taught the Wú people military tactics and chariot warfare,
appointing his son as Wú's diplomatic envoy,
thus initiating Wú's relations with the Central States.
Wú attacked Chǔ.
In the sixteenth year,
King Gòng of Chǔ attacked Wú,
reaching Héngshān.
In the twenty-fifth year,
King Shòu Mèng died.
Shòu Mèng had four sons,
the eldest named Zhū Fán,
the second named Yú Zhài,
the third named Yú Mò,
and the youngest named Jì Zhá.
Jì Zhá was virtuous,
and Shòu Mèng wished to establish him as successor,
but Jì Zhá declined and refused,
so the eldest son Zhū Fán was established instead,
acting as regent and governing the state.
In the first year of King Zhū Fán,
after Zhū Fán had completed the mourning period,
he yielded the throne to Jì Zhá.
Jì Zhá declined, saying:
"At the death of Duke Xuān of Cáo,
the feudal lords and the people of Cáo considered the Cáo ruler unrighteous,
and intended to establish Zǐ Zāng,
but Zǐ Zāng departed from them,
thus enabling the Cáo ruler to remain,
and the gentleman said
'He was able to maintain his integrity.'
You, my lord, are the rightful heir;
who would dare to oppose you!
To possess the state
is not in accordance with my principles.
Though I, Zhá, lack talent,
I wish to follow the righteousness of Zǐ Zāng."
The people of Wú insisted on establishing Jì Zhá,
but Jì Zhá abandoned his home and took up farming,
so they relented.
In autumn, Wú attacked Chǔ,
and Chǔ defeated our army.
In the fourth year,
Duke Píng of Jìn first ascended the throne.
In the thirteenth year,
King Zhū Fán died.
He had decreed that his younger brother Yú Zhài should succeed him,
intending the succession to pass in order,
until it inevitably reached Jì Zhá and ended with him,
thus fulfilling the intention of the late King Shòu Mèng,
and also honoring Jì Zhá's righteousness,
so that all brothers desired to pass the state to him,
arranging for it to reach him gradually.
Jì Zhá was enfeoffed at Yánlíng,
hence he was called Yánlíng Jìzǐ.
In the third year of King Yú Zhài,
Qìng Fēng, the chancellor of Qí, having committed crimes,
fled from Qí to Wú.
Wú granted Qìng Fēng the county of Zhūfāng,
as his fief,
gave him a daughter in marriage,
and he became wealthier than he had been in Qí.
In the fourth year,
Wú sent Jì Zhá on a diplomatic mission to Lǔ,
where he requested to observe the music of Zhōu.
They performed the songs of "Zhōu Nán"
and "Shào Nán".
He said:
"How beautiful!
These lay the foundation,
yet they are not complete.
Nevertheless, they reflect diligence without resentment."
They performed the songs of "Bèi",
"Yōng",
and "Wèi".
He said:
"How beautiful!
How profound!
They convey worry without distress.
I have heard that Wèi Kāngshū
and Duke Wǔ possessed such virtue—
is this not the 'Airs of Wèi'?"
They performed the songs of "Wáng".
He said:
"How beautiful!
They express longing without fear—
is this from the time when Zhōu moved east?"
They performed the songs of "Zhèng".
He said:
"They are overly intricate,
the people cannot endure it—
will this state be the first to perish?"
They performed the songs of "Qí".
He said:
"How beautiful!
How vast, like a great wind!
The one who represents the Eastern Sea—
must it be Tàigōng?
The state's potential cannot be measured."
They performed the songs of "Bīn".
He said:
"Excellent!
How expansive!
Joyful yet not excessive—
is this from when the Duke of Zhōu went east?"
They performed the songs of "Qín".
He said:
"This is what is called the music of Xià.
For what can embody Xià becomes great,
the pinnacle of greatness—
is this not Zhōu's legacy?"
They performed the songs of "Wèi".
He said:
"How beautiful!
How harmonious!
Grand and broad,
frugal yet easy,
guided by virtue—
this signifies a leader of alliances."
They performed the songs of "Táng".
He said:
"How profound the thoughts!
Do they carry the legacy of Táotángshì?
If not,
why such deep concern?
If not descendants of illustrious virtue,
who could achieve this!"
They performed the songs of "Chén".
He said:
"The state lacks a true ruler—
can it last long?"
From "Kuài" onward,
he offered no criticism.
They performed the "Minor Odes".
He said:
"How beautiful!
Reflective yet not divided,
resentful yet not outspoken—
does this reflect the decline of Zhōu's virtue?
Still, there remain the people who remember the former kings."
They performed the "Major Odes".
He said:
"How vast!
How splendid!
Graceful yet with upright substance—
is this the virtue of King Wén?"
They performed the "Odes".
He said:
"Perfect indeed!
Upright but not arrogant,
bent but not broken,
close but not oppressive,
distant but not alienated,
changing but not excessive,
repeating but not tiresome,
sorrowful but not distressed,
joyful but not unrestrained,
used but not exhausted,
broad but not showy,
bestowed but not wasteful,
taken but not greedy,
stationary but not stagnant,
moving but not drifting.
The five tones are harmonious,
the eight winds balanced,
rhythms measured,
order maintained—
this is the commonality of supreme virtue."
Seeing the dance "Xiáng Shuò"
and "Nán Yuè",
he said:
"How beautiful!
Yet there is still regret."
Seeing the dance "Great Wǔ",
he said:
"How beautiful!
Is this the prosperity of Zhōu?"
Seeing the dance "Sháo Hù",
he said:
"Great as the sage is,
he still feels shame in virtue—
how difficult it is to be a sage!"
Seeing the dance "Great Xià",
he said:
"How beautiful!
