Diligent yet not claiming virtue—
who but Yǔ could achieve this?"
Seeing the dance "Zhāo Xiāo",
he said:
"Virtue has reached its peak!
How immense,
like the heavens covering all,
like the earth bearing all.
Even the greatest virtue
can add no more.
This is the ultimate spectacle;
if there were other music,
I would not dare to watch."
He left Lǔ
and proceeded to Qí.
He advised Yàn Píngzhòng:
"Quickly surrender your fief and authority.
Without fief or authority,
you can avoid disaster.
The governance of Qí will find its place;
until it does,
calamity will not cease."
Thus, Yànzǐ, through Chén Huánzǐ, surrendered his authority and fief,
thereby escaping the disaster of Luán and Gāo.
He left Qí
and went to Zhèng.
He met Zǐchǎn,
as if old friends.
He told Zǐchǎn:
"Zhèng's rulers are extravagant;
disaster approaches,
and governance will fall to you.
When you govern,
be cautious and uphold ritual.
Otherwise,
Zhèng will decline."
He left Zhèng
and went to Wèi.
He praised Qú Yuàn,
Shǐ Gǒu,
Shǐ Qiū,
Gōngzǐ Jīng,
Gōngshū Fā,
and Gōngzǐ Cháo, saying:
"Wèi has many noble men;
it will have no troubles."
From Wèi, he went to Jìn,
intending to stay in Sù.
Hearing bell sounds,
he said:
"How strange!
I have heard that
cleverness without virtue
leads to punishment.
This master has offended his lord and is here;
fear is not enough,
how can he indulge in pleasure?
For him to be here
is like a swallow nesting on a tent.
With the lord's coffin still present, how can there be music?"
So he left.
Wénzǐ heard of this
and never listened to string music again.
He went to Jìn,
and said to Minister Wén of Zhào,
Minister Xuān of Hán,
and Minister Xiàn of Wèi:
"The state of Jìn will likely be gathered into the hands of these three families!"
As he was about to leave,
he said to Shūxiàng:
"You must strive diligently!
The ruler is extravagant and has many capable men,
the senior officials are all wealthy,
and governance will soon fall to the three families.
You are upright,
and must think of how to avoid calamity yourself."
When Jì Zhá first went on his mission,
he passed northward by the lord of Xú.
The lord of Xú admired Jì Zhá's sword,
but did not dare speak of it.
Jì Zhá knew it in his heart,
but as he was on a mission to the superior states,
he did not present it.
Upon returning to Xú,
the lord of Xú had already died,
whereupon he untied his precious sword,
hung it on a tree at the lord of Xú's grave mound, and left.
His attendants said:
"The lord of Xú is already dead,
to whom are you giving this?"
Master Jì said:
"Not so.
From the beginning, my heart had already promised it to him;
how could I betray my heart because of his death!"
In the seventh year,
Prince Wéi of Chǔ assassinated his king Jiá Áo and replaced him,
becoming King Líng.
In the tenth year,
King Líng of Chǔ assembled the feudal lords to attack Wú's Zhūfāng,
in order to punish Qí's Qìng Fēng.
Wú also attacked Chǔ,
capturing three towns before leaving.
In the eleventh year,
Chǔ attacked Wú,
reaching Yúlóu.
In the twelfth year,
Chǔ came again to attack,
encamping at Gānxī,
but the Chǔ army was defeated and fled.
In the seventeenth year,
King Yújì died,
and his younger brother Yúmò succeeded him.
In the second year of King Yúmò,
Prince Qìjí of Chǔ assassinated his ruler King Líng and replaced him.
In the fourth year,
King Yúmò died,
and wished to pass the throne to his younger brother Jì Zhá.
Jì Zhá declined,
and fled.
Thereupon the people of Wú said:
"The former king had a command:
when an elder brother dies, the younger brother succeeds,
but it must reach Jìzǐ.
Now Jìzǐ has fled the position,
so King Yúmò was the one who succeeded.
Now that he has died,
his son should succeed."
So they set up King Yúmò's son Liáo as king.
In the second year of King Liáo,
Prince Guāng attacked Chǔ,
was defeated, and lost the king's boat.
Guāng, in fear,
launched a surprise attack on Chǔ,
and recovered the king's boat before returning.
In the fifth year,
Wǔ Zǐxū, a fugitive official from Chǔ, came fleeing,
and Prince Guāng treated him as a guest.
Prince Guāng was
the son of King Zhūfán.
He always thought that since his father and his three brothers,
the succession should have reached Jìzǐ.
If Jìzǐ would not accept the state,
then his own father, being the eldest, should have been established.
If it was not passed to Jìzǐ,
then he, Guāng, should be the one to succeed.
Secretly, he gathered worthy men,
intending to launch a surprise attack on King Liáo.
In the eighth year,
Wú sent Prince Guāng to attack Chǔ,
defeated the Chǔ army,
and brought back the mother of the former Chǔ crown prince Jiàn from Jūcháo.
Then, advancing north,
he defeated the armies of Chén
and Cài.
In the ninth year,
Prince Guāng attacked Chǔ,
capturing Jūcháo
and Zhōnglí.
Earlier, a girl from the border town of Bēiliáng in Chǔ and a girl from a Wú border town quarreled over mulberry trees;
the two families, angered, destroyed each other,
and when the chiefs of the two border towns heard of it,
they angrily attacked each other,
and destroyed Wú's border town.
The king of Wú was enraged,
and therefore attacked Chǔ,
taking two cities before leaving.
When Wǔ Zǐxū first fled to Wú,
he urged the advantages of attacking Chǔ to King Liáo.
Prince Guāng said:
"Zǐxū's father and elder brothers were executed by Chǔ;
he merely wishes to avenge his own grievance.
The benefit to us is not evident."
Thereupon, Wǔ Yuán realized that Guāng had other ambitions,
so he sought out the brave warrior Zhuān Zhū,
and introduced him to Guāng.
Guāng was pleased,
and then treated Wǔ Zǐxū as a guest.
Zǐxū withdrew and farmed in the countryside,
awaiting Zhuān Zhū's undertaking.
In the winter of the twelfth year,
King Píng of Chǔ died.
In the spring of the thirteenth year,
Wú wanted to take advantage of Chǔ's mourning to attack it,
and sent Prince Gàiyú
and Zhúyōng with troops to besiege Chǔ's Lù
and Qián. They sent Jì Zhá to Jìn,
to observe the changes among the feudal lords.
Chǔ dispatched troops to cut off the Wú army's retreat,
and the Wú troops could not return.
Thereupon, Prince Guāng of Wú said:
"This opportunity must not be lost."
He told Zhuān Zhū:
"If we do not seek, how shall we gain!
I am the true royal heir,
I should be the one established;
I wish to seek it.
Even if Jìzǐ returns,
he will not depose me."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"King Liáo can be killed.
His mother is old and his sons young,
and the two princes are leading troops to attack Chǔ,
with Chǔ blocking their route.
Now Wú is externally beset by Chǔ,
and internally empty of resolute ministers;
they can do nothing to us."
Guāng said:
"My person
is your person."
On the day Bǐngzǐ of the fourth month,
Guāng hid armored warriors in a cellar room,
and invited King Liáo to drink.
King Liáo had soldiers line the road,
from the royal palace to Guāng's home;
at the gates, steps, doors, and mats,
all were King Liáo's close attendants,
each holding a pī-sword at his side.
Prince Guāng feigned a foot ailment,
entered the cellar room,
and had Zhuān Zhū place a dagger in a roasted fish to present the food.
With his hand, he stabbed King Liáo with the dagger;
the pī-swords crossed in his chest,
and thus he assassinated King Liáo.
Prince Guāng ultimately succeeded to the throne as king,
becoming King Hélú of Wú.
Hélú then made Zhuān Zhū's son a minister.
When Jìzǐ arrived,
he said:
"If the former rulers' sacrifices are not abandoned,
if the people are not without a lord,
if the altars of soil and grain receive offerings,
then he is my ruler.
How dare I resent anyone?
I mourn the dead and serve the living,
awaiting Heaven's mandate.
It was not I who started the disorder;
I follow the one established,
as is the way of our ancestors."
He reported on his mission,
mourned at Liáo's tomb,
and returned to his post to await orders.
The two Wú princes, Zhúyōng
and Gàiyú, who were leading troops and besieged by Chǔ,
heard that Prince Guāng had assassinated King Liáo and set himself up,
so they surrendered with their troops to Chǔ,
and Chǔ enfeoffed them at Shū.
In the first year of King Hélú,
he raised Wǔ Zǐxū to the position of foreign minister and consulted with him on state affairs.
Chǔ executed Bózhōulí,
and his grandson Bó Pǐ fled to Wú,
where Wú made him a senior official.
In the third year,
King Hélú of Wú, along with Zǐxū and
Bó Pǐ, led an army to attack Chǔ.
They captured Shū,
and killed two exiled princes of Wú.
Guang planned to enter Yǐng,
but General Sūn Wǔ said,
"The people are weary,
it is not yet feasible,
let us wait."
In the fourth year,
they attacked Chǔ again,
capturing Liù and Qián.
In the fifth year,
they attacked Yuè,
and defeated it.
In the sixth year,
Chǔ sent Zǐcháng Nāngwǎ to attack Wú.
They intercepted and defeated him,
achieving a great victory over the Chǔ army at Yùzhāng,
capturing the Chǔ's Jūchāo before returning.
In the ninth year,
King Hélú of Wú consulted with Wǔ Zǐxū and
Sūn Wǔ, saying,
"You previously said entering Yǐng was not feasible,
how do you think it is now?"
The two men replied,
"The Chǔ general Zǐcháng is greedy,
and both Táng and
Cài are resentful of him.
If the King desires a larger campaign,
it must involve Táng and
Cài to succeed."
Hélú agreed,
mustered the entire army,
and with Táng and
Cài, advanced westward to attack Chǔ,
reaching the Hàn River.
Chǔ also dispatched troops to resist Wú,
setting up camps on both sides of the river.
Hélú's younger brother Fūgài wanted to engage in battle,
but Hélú did not permit it.
Fūgài said,
"The King has entrusted the troops to me,
and in military matters, advantage is paramount,
what else should we wait for?"
He proceeded to lead 5,000 troops to launch a surprise attack on Chǔ,
and the Chǔ forces were greatly defeated,
fleeing. Thereupon, the King of Wú released his forces to pursue them.
By the time they reached Yǐng,
they had fought five battles,
and Chǔ was defeated in all five.
King Zhāo of Chǔ fled Yǐng,
taking refuge in Yún.
Yún Gōng's younger brother sought to assassinate King Zhāo,
so King Zhāo and Yún Gōng fled to Suí.
Meanwhile, Wú forces entered Yǐng.
Zǐxū and
Bó Pǐ whipped the corpse of King Píng to avenge their fathers.
In the spring of the tenth year,
upon hearing that the King of Wú was in Yǐng,
and the country was empty,
Yuè attacked Wú.
Wú dispatched separate troops to fight Yuè.
Chǔ urgently sought help from Qín,
and Qín sent troops to aid Chǔ against Wú,
defeating the Wú army.
Hélú's younger brother Fūgài saw that Qín and Yuè had jointly defeated Wú,
and as the King of Wú stayed in Chǔ and did not leave,
Fūgài fled back to Wú and established himself as King.
Hearing this,
Hélú led his troops back,
and attacked Fūgài.
Fūgài was defeated and fled to Chǔ.
Thus, in September, King Zhāo of Chǔ re-entered Yǐng,
appointing Fūgài as head of the Tāngxī,
establishing him as the Tāngxī clan.
In the eleventh year,
the King of Wú sent Crown Prince Fūchāi to attack Chǔ,
capturing Fān.
Terrified, Chǔ abandoned Yǐng and moved to Ruò.
In the fifteenth year,
Kǒngzǐ became the chancellor of Lǔ.
In the summer of the nineteenth year,
Wú attacked Yuè,
and Yuè King Gōujiàn met and combated them at Zuìlǐ.
Yuè dispatched warriors to challenge,
marching three times to Wú's army,
shouting, and then committing suicide.
The Wú forces watched,
and Yuè then attacked Wú,
defeating them at Gūsū,
injuring King Hélú of Wú's finger,
and forcing the army back seven li.
The King of Wú succumbed to his wound and died.
Hélú ordered the establishment of Crown Prince Fūchāi,
saying,
"Will you forget that Gōujiàn killed your father?"
He replied,
"I dare not!"
In the third year,
he avenged Yuè.
In the first year of King Fūchāi's reign,
he appointed Bó Pǐ as Grand Chancellor.
He practiced warfare and archery,
always aspiring to avenge Yuè.
In the second year,
King Wú led elite troops to attack Yuè,
defeating them at Fūzhāo,
avenging the earlier loss at Gūsū.
King Gōujiàn of Yuè then stationed 5,000 soldiers at Kuàijī,
and sent Minister Zhòng to negotiate peace with Wú's Grand Chancellor Pǐ,
offering the nation to become their servants.
The King of Wú was about to agree,
but Wǔ Zǐxū advised,
"In the past, the state of Youguò killed Zhēnguàn and attacked Zhēnxún,
destroying the Xia dynasty's Emperor Xiang.
Emperor Xiang's consort, Queen Min, was pregnant,
fleeing to Yǒuréng and giving birth to Shàokāng.
Shàokāng became a shepherd for Yǒuréng.
Youguò again sought to kill Shàokāng,
who fled to Yǒuyú.
Yǒuyú cherished the virtues of Xia,
and so married him to their two daughters and settled him in Lún,
with land and people sufficient to form a pact.
Later, he gathered the Xia people,
restored their official positions.
He sent someone to lure him,
and eventually destroyed Youguò,
restoring the achievements of Yǔ,
worshipping Xia as veneration to heaven,
without losing the old ways.
Now Wú is not as strong as Youguò,
and Gōujiàn is greater than Shàokāng.
If we do not take this opportunity to destroy him,
and instead spare him,
is it not difficult!
Moreover, Gōujiàn is capable of enduring hardship,
if not destroyed now,
it will be regretted later."
The King of Wú did not listen,
following Grand Chancellor Pǐ's advice,
ultimately agreeing to peace with Yuè,
forming an alliance and withdrawing troops.
In the seventh year,
King Fūchāi of Wú heard that Duke Jǐng of Qí had died, and that prominent ministers were vying for favor,
the new ruler was weak,
so he launched a northern campaign against Qí.
Zǐxū advised,
"King Gōujiàn of Yuè eats simply,
dresses plainly,
mourns the dead and cares for the sick,
clearly intending to use his resources.
If this man remains alive,
he will surely become a threat to Wú.
Now with the enemy in our heartland, while the King does nothing about it,
and instead focuses on Qí,
is this not absurd!"
The King of Wú did not heed his advice,
proceeded with the northern campaign against Qí,
and defeated the Qí army at Àilíng.
Upon reaching Céng,
he summoned Duke Aīgōng of Lǔ, demanding a hundred livestock.
Jì Kàngzǐ sent Zǐgòng to speak with Grand Chancellor Pǐ using the Zhou rituals,
thus managing to stop him.
Consequently, they stayed to annex territories south of Qí and Lǔ.
In the ninth year,
he campaigned against Lǔ on behalf of Zou,
arriving to form an alliance with Lǔ before withdrawing.
In the tenth year,
they attacked and returned from Qí.
In the eleventh year,
they once again launched a northern campaign against Qí.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè led his people to pay homage to Wú,
presenting generous tributes,
which pleased the King of Wú.
Only Wǔ Zǐxū was alarmed,
saying:
"This means the abandonment of Wú."
He admonished:
"Yuè lies at our heartland,
and now achieving our ambition in Qí
is like a rocky field,
of no use.
Moreover, the 'Announcement of Pán Gēng' says to cut off and eliminate without leaving any,
through which Shāng rose."
The King of Wú did not listen,
but sent Zǐxū to Qí.
Zǐxū entrusted his son to the Bào family of Qí,
then returned to report to the King of Wú.
When the King of Wú heard of this,
he was greatly enraged,
and bestowed upon Zǐxū the sword Yǐlòu to die by.
As he was about to die,
he said:
"Plant catalpa trees on my grave,
so they may be made into vessels.
Gouge out my eyes and place them at the eastern gate of Wú,
to watch Yuè destroy Wú."
The Bào family of Qí assassinated Duke Dào of Qí.
When the King of Wú heard this,
he wept outside the army's gate for three days,
then attacked Qí by sea.
The people of Qí defeated Wú,
and the King of Wú led his troops back.
In the thirteenth year,
Wú summoned the rulers of Lǔ
and Wèi to meet at Tuó Gāo.
In the spring of the fourteenth year,
the King of Wú met with the feudal lords north at Huáng Chí,
intending to dominate the Central States and preserve the Zhōu court.
On the bǐngzǐ day of the sixth month,
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè attacked Wú.
On the yǐyǒu day,
five thousand Yuè troops engaged Wú in battle.
On the bǐngxū day,
they captured Wú's crown prince Yǒu.
On the dīnghài day,
they entered Wú.
The people of Wú reported the defeat to King Fū Chāi,
who loathed the news being heard.
When someone leaked the words,
the King of Wú was furious,
and executed seven men under the tent.
On the xīnchǒu day of the seventh month,
the King of Wú contended for precedence with Duke Dìng of Jìn.
The King of Wú said:
"In the Zhōu lineage, I am the eldest."
Duke Dìng of Jìn said:
"Among the Jī surname, I am the senior."
Zhào Yǎng was angered,
and prepared to attack Wú,
so precedence was given to Duke Dìng of Jìn.
After the King of Wú had sworn the covenant,
and parted with Jìn,
he intended to attack Sòng.
Grand Steward Pǐ said:
"We could win but cannot hold it."
So he led the troops back to the state.
The state had lost its crown prince,
and was empty inside,
while the king had long been abroad,
and the soldiers were all exhausted.
Thereupon, he sent rich gifts to make peace with Yuè.
In the fifteenth year,
Tián Cháng of Qí killed Duke Jiǎn.
In the eighteenth year,
Yuè grew stronger.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè led troops again to attack and defeat the Wú army at Lì Zé.
Chǔ destroyed Chén.
In the twentieth year,
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè attacked Wú again.
In the twenty-first year,
he besieged Wú.
On the dīngmǎo day of the eleventh month in the twenty-third year,
Yuè defeated Wú.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè wanted to move King Fū Chāi of Wú to Yǒng Dōng,
granting him a hundred households to dwell.
The King of Wú said:
"I am old,
and cannot serve you, my king.
I regret not following Zǐxū's advice,
bringing myself to this plight."
Thereupon, he cut his own throat and died.
The King of Yuè destroyed Wú,
executed Grand Steward Pǐ,
deeming him disloyal,
and then returned.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Confucius said
"Tài Bó may be said to have possessed the highest virtue,
thrice declining the empire,
so that the people could not praise him enough."
I have read the ancient texts of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and thus know that Yú of the Central States and Gōu Wú of the Jīng Mán were brothers.
The benevolent heart of Jì Zǐ of Yánlíng,
his endless admiration for righteousness,
seeing the subtle to know purity and turbidity.
Alas,
how broad his sight and learned he was, a true gentleman!
Tài Gōng Wàng, Lǚ Shàng,
was a man from the eastern sea region.
His ancestor once served as one of the Four Peaks,
assisting Yǔ in regulating the waters and land with great merit.
Between the times of Yú and Xià, he was enfeoffed at Lǚ,
or at Shēn,
with the surname Jiāng.
During the Xià and Shāng periods,
Shēn and Lǚ were sometimes enfeoffed to branch descendants,
sometimes becoming commoners,
and Shàng was their later descendant.
Originally surnamed Jiāng,
he took his fief's name as surname,
hence called Lǚ Shàng.
Lǚ Shàng had experienced poverty and hardship,
and was advanced in age,
when he fished to attract the attention of Xī Bó of Zhōu.
Xī Bó was about to go hunting,
and divined,
saying, "What I will catch is neither dragon nor serpent,
neither tiger nor bear,
but the assistant of a hegemon king."
Thereupon, Xī Bó of Zhōu went hunting,
and indeed met Tài Gōng on the north bank of the Wèi River,
and conversing with him, was greatly pleased,
saying:
"My late father Tài Gōng said,
'There will be a sage coming to Zhōu,
and Zhōu will thereby rise.'
Are you truly he?
My Tài Gōng has long awaited you."
Hence, he was called
"Tài Gōng Wàng,"
taken back together in the carriage,
and appointed as master.
Some say
Tài Gōng was widely learned,
and had once served Zhòu.
Zhòu being unprincipled,
he left him.
Traveling to persuade the feudal lords,
he met with no success,
and eventually went west to join Xī Bó of Zhōu.
Others say
Lǚ Shàng was a retired scholar,
living in seclusion by the sea.
When Xī Bó of Zhōu was imprisoned in Yǒu Lǐ,
Sǎn Yí Shēng
and Hóng Yāo, who had long known of him, summoned Lǚ Shàng.
Lǚ Shàng also said,
"I have heard that Xī Bó is virtuous,
and also good at caring for the elderly,
why not go to him?"
The three men sought beautiful women and rare treasures for Xī Bó,
presenting them to Zhòu,
to ransom Xī Bó.
Xī Bó was thus able to get out,
and return to his state.
Though accounts of how Lǚ Shàng came to serve Zhōu differ,
in essence, he became the master of Wén and Wǔ.
When Xī Bó Chāng of Zhōu was released from Yǒu Lǐ and returned,
he and Lǚ Shàng secretly plotted to cultivate virtue to overthrow the Shāng government,
their affairs involving much military strategy and ingenious plans,
so later generations discussing military matters and Zhōu's covert strategies all regard Tài Gōng as the originator.
Xī Bó of Zhōu governed peacefully,
and when he settled the dispute between Yú and Ruì,
the poets acclaimed Xī Bó as having received the mandate, calling him King Wén.
He attacked Chóng,
Mì Xū,
and the Quǎn Yí,
and greatly built the city of Fēng.
Of the three parts under heaven,
two turned to Zhōu,
largely due to Tài Gōng's strategies and plans.
King Wén passed away,
and King Wǔ ascended the throne.
In the ninth year,
he wished to continue King Wén's enterprise,
and launched an eastern campaign to observe whether the feudal lords would rally.
As the army set out,
Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ, holding a yellow battle-axe in his left hand
and a white yak-tail banner in his right, made an oath:
"Cāngsì, Cāngsì,
assemble your multitudes,
and man your boats!
Whoever arrives late shall be beheaded!"
Thereupon they reached Mèngjīn.
Eight hundred feudal lords gathered without prior arrangement.
The feudal lords all said:
"Zhòu can be attacked."
But King Wǔ said:
"Not yet."
He withdrew the army
and composed this "Great Oath" with Tàigōng.
After two years,
Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān
and imprisoned Jīzǐ.
When King Wǔ was about to attack Zhòu,
he consulted the tortoise shell for an omen,
which was inauspicious,
and a violent storm arose.
All the dukes were terrified,
but only Tàigōng strongly urged King Wǔ on,
so King Wǔ proceeded.
On the jiǎzǐ day of the first month in the eleventh year,
he made an oath at Mùyě
and attacked King Zhòu of Shāng.
Zhòu's army was defeated.
Zhòu fled back,
ascended the Lùtái Tower,
and was pursued and beheaded.
The next day,
King Wǔ stood at the altar of the land,
the dukes presented clear water,
Wèi Kāngshū Fēng spread a colored mat,
Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ led the sacrificial animal,
and the court scribe Yì recited the prayer,
announcing to the gods Zhòu's crimes.
They distributed the money from the Lùtái Tower
and disbursed the grain from the Jùqiáo Granary
to relieve the poor.
They built a tomb for Bǐgān
and released Jīzǐ from imprisonment.
They moved the Nine Tripods,
reformed the Zhōu government,
and made a new beginning with all under heaven.
Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ's strategies contributed greatly to this.
Thus, having pacified Shāng and become king over all under heaven,
King Wǔ enfeoffed Grand Tutor Shàngfǔ at Yíngqiū in Qí.
As he journeyed east to his state,
he traveled slowly, lodging along the way.
An innkeeper said:
"I have heard that opportunity is hard to gain but easy to lose.
You, guest, rest very comfortably;
you are probably not one going to take possession of a state."
Hearing this, Tàigōng
set out dressed by night
and reached his state at daybreak.
The Marquis of Lái came to attack,
contending with him for Yíngqiū.
Yíngqiū bordered on Lái.
The Lái people were barbarians
who, taking advantage of the turmoil under Zhòu and the recent establishment of Zhōu,
before distant regions could be pacified,
thus contended with Tàigōng for the state.
Upon arriving in his state, Tàigōng
improved the administration,
adapted to local customs,
simplified the rituals,
promoted commerce and industry,
and facilitated the benefits of fish and salt,
so many people turned to Qí,
and Qí became a great state.
When King Chéng of Zhōu was young,
Guǎn and Cài rebelled,
and the Huáiyí turned against Zhōu,
so he sent Duke Shào Kāng to command Tàigōng:
"From east to the sea,
west to the Hé River,
south to Mùlíng,
north to Wūdì,
the five ranks of nobles and nine regions' chiefs,
you may indeed campaign against them."
Thus Qí gained the right to wage campaigns
and became a great state,
with its capital at Yíngqiū.
Tàigōng lived to be over a hundred years old,
and his son, Duke Dīng Lǚ Jí, succeeded him.
When Duke Dīng died,
his son, Duke Yǐ Dé, succeeded.
When Duke Yǐ died,
his son, Duke Guǐ Címǔ, succeeded.
When Duke Guǐ died,
his son, Duke Āi Bùchén, succeeded.
During Duke Āi's time,
Marquis Jǐ slandered him to Zhōu,
and Zhōu boiled Duke Āi to death, setting up his brother Jìng instead,
who was Duke Hú.
Duke Hú moved the capital to Bógū,
during the time of King Yí of Zhōu.
Duke Āi's younger maternal brother Shān resented Duke Hú,
so he, along with his followers, led the people of Yíngqiū in a surprise attack, killing Duke Hú and making himself ruler,
who was Duke Xiàn.
In the first year of Duke Xiàn's reign,
he expelled all of Duke Hú's sons
and moved the capital from Bógū,
governing from Línzī.
In the ninth year,
Duke Xiàn died,
and his son, Duke Wǔ Shòu, succeeded.
In the ninth year of Duke Wǔ,
King Lì of Zhōu fled
and resided in Zhì.
In the tenth year,
the royal house was in turmoil,
and the great ministers administered the government,
which was called
"the Hé'éng Regency."
In the twenty-fourth year,
King Xuān of Zhōu first ascended the throne.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Duke Wǔ died,
and his son, Duke Lì Wújì, succeeded.
Duke Lì was tyrannical and cruel,
so Duke Hú's sons returned to Qí,
and the people of Qí wanted to enthrone one of them,
thus joining in the attack that killed Duke Lì.
Duke Hú's son also died in the battle.
The people of Qí then set up Duke Lì's son Chì as ruler,
who was Duke Wén,
and executed seventy of those who had killed Duke Lì.
Duke Wén died in the twelfth year of his reign,
and his son, Duke Chéng Tuō, succeeded.
Duke Chéng died in the ninth year of his reign,
and his son, Duke Zhuāng Gòu, succeeded.
In the twenty-fourth year of Duke Zhuāng,
the Quǎnróng killed King Yōu,
and Zhōu moved east to Luò.
Qín began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the fifty-sixth year,
Jìn assassinated its ruler, Marquis Zhāo.
In the sixty-fourth year,
Duke Zhuāng died,
and his son, Duke Xí Lùfǔ, succeeded.
In the ninth year of Duke Xí,
Duke Yǐn of Lǔ first ascended the throne.
In the nineteenth year,
Duke Huán of Lǔ killed his elder brother Duke Yǐn and made himself ruler.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the Běiróng attacked Qí.
Zhèng sent its crown prince Hū to rescue Qí,
and Qí wanted to marry a daughter to him.
Hū said:
"Zhèng is small, Qí is large;
I am no match for her."
Thus he declined.
In the thirty-second year,
Duke Xí's maternal brother Yí Zhòngnián died.
His son was called Gōngsūn Wúzhī,
and Duke Xí doted on him,
ordering that his rank, attire, and support be equal to the crown prince's.
In the thirty-third year,
Duke Xí died,
and the crown prince Zhū'ér succeeded,
who was Duke Xiāng.
In the first year of Duke Xiāng,
back when he was crown prince,
he had once fought with Wúzhī,
and upon his accession,
he reduced Wúzhī's rank and attire,
so Wúzhī resented him.
In the fourth year,
Duke Huán of Lǔ went to Qí with his wife.
Duke Xiāng of Qí had previously had a secret affair with the wife of the Duke of Lǔ.
This wife of the Duke of Lǔ
was Duke Xiāng's younger sister,
who had been married to Duke Huán of Lǔ since the time of Duke Xī,
and when Duke Huán came, Duke Xiāng resumed the affair with her.
Duke Huán of Lǔ found out about it,
was angry with his wife,
and she informed Duke Xiāng of Qí.
Duke Xiāng of Qí drank with the Lord of Lǔ,
got him drunk,
and had a strong man named Péng Shēng carry him up into the Lord of Lǔ's carriage,
then used the opportunity to break Duke Huán of Lǔ's ribs and kill him;
by the time Duke Huán got down from the carriage, he was already dead.
The people of Lǔ protested this,
and Duke Xiāng of Qí killed Péng Shēng to appease Lǔ.
In the eighth year,
he attacked Jì,
and Jì relocated away from its city.
In the twelfth year,
initially, Duke Xiāng had sent Lián Chēng
and Guǎn Zhìfù to garrison Kuíqiū,
they went at the time of the melons,
and were to be replaced when the melons came again.
They went to garrison for one year,
and when the melon season ended, the Duke had not sent replacements.
Someone requested replacements for them,
but the Duke did not consent.
Therefore, these two men were angry,
and conspired with Gōngsūn Wúzhī to plot a rebellion.
Lián Chēng had a female cousin in the Duke's palace,
who was not favored,
so they had her spy on Duke Xiāng,
saying,
"If the affair succeeds, we will make you Wúzhī's wife."
In the twelfth month of winter,
Duke Xiāng traveled to Gūfén,
and then hunted at Pèiqiū.
He saw a boar,
and his attendants said,
"It's Péng Shēng."
The Duke was enraged,
shot at it,
and the boar stood up like a man and cried out.
The Duke was terrified,
fell from his carriage and injured his foot,
losing his shoe.
Upon returning, he whipped the keeper of his shoes, Fú, three hundred times.
Fú left the palace.
And Wúzhī,
Lián Chēng,
Guǎn Zhìfù, and others, hearing that the Duke was injured,
then led their followers to attack the palace.
They encountered the shoe keeper Fú,
and Fú said:
"Wait, do not enter and alarm the palace,
an alarmed palace is not easily entered."
Wúzhī did not believe him,
so Fú showed him his wounds,
and then he believed.
They waited outside the palace,
and ordered Fú to enter first.
Fú entered first,
then hid Duke Xiāng among the doors.
After a long time,
Wúzhī and others grew fearful,
so they entered the palace.
Fú, in turn, along with those in the palace and the Duke's favored ministers, attacked Wúzhī and others,
but did not prevail,
and all died.
Wúzhī entered the palace,
and could not find the Duke.
Someone saw a person's feet among the doors,
uncovered and looked,
and it was Duke Xiāng,
so they assassinated him,
and Wúzhī set himself up as the Lord of Qí.
In the spring of the first year of Duke Huán,
the Lord of Qí, Wúzhī, was traveling in Yōnglín.
The people of Yōnglín had previously held a grudge against Wúzhī,
and when he went to travel there,
the people of Yōnglín attacked and killed Wúzhī,
announcing to the high officials of Qí:
"Wúzhī assassinated Duke Xiāng and set himself up,
we have carefully carried out his execution.
We ask the high officials to establish another prince who ought to be set up,
and we will obey your command."
Initially,
when Duke Xiāng drunkenly killed Duke Huán of Lǔ,
had an affair with his wife,
executed and punished many inappropriately,
was licentious with women,
and repeatedly deceived his high officials,
his younger brothers feared disaster would reach them,
so the next younger brother, Jiū, fled to Lǔ.
His mother was a woman from Lǔ.
Guǎn Zhòng
and Zhào Hū tutored him.
The next younger brother, Xiǎobái, fled to Jǔ,
and Bào Shū tutored him.
Xiǎobái's mother
was a woman from Wèi,
and was favored by Duke Xī.
Xiǎobái had been fond of the high official Gāo Xī since his youth.
When the people of Yōnglín killed Wúzhī,
and they discussed establishing a lord,
Gāo and Guó first secretly summoned Xiǎobái from Jǔ.
Lǔ heard of Wúzhī's death,
also sent troops to escort Prince Jiū,
and had Guǎn Zhòng lead a separate force to block the road from Jǔ,
shooting and hitting Xiǎobái's belt hook.
Xiǎobái feigned death,
and Guǎn Zhòng sent someone swiftly to report to Lǔ.
The escorts for Jiū from Lǔ then traveled even more slowly,
taking six days to reach Qí,
by which time Xiǎobái had already entered,
and Gāo Xī had established him,
who became Duke Huán.
When Duke Huán was hit by the hook,
he feigned death to mislead Guǎn Zhòng,
then later was carried in a covered carriage traveling swiftly,
and also had Gāo
and Guó responding from within,
thus he was able to enter first and be established,
and sent troops to block Lǔ.
In autumn, they fought with Lǔ at Gānshí,
the troops of Lǔ were defeated and fled,
and the troops of Qí cut off Lǔ's retreat route.
Qí sent a letter to Lǔ saying:
"Prince Jiū is our brother,
we cannot bear to execute him,
we ask Lǔ to kill him themselves.
Zhào Hū
and Guǎn Zhòng are our enemies,
we ask to capture them and be satisfied to mince them.
Otherwise,
we will besiege Lǔ."
The people of Lǔ were troubled by this,
so they killed Zǐ Jiū at Shēngdú.
Zhào Hū committed suicide,
and Guǎn Zhòng requested imprisonment.
When Duke Huán was established,
he sent troops to attack Lǔ,
intending to kill Guǎn Zhòng.
Bào Shūyá said:
"I am fortunate to have followed you, my lord,
and you ultimately achieved establishment.
As for your lordship's dignity,
I have no means to enhance it.
If you, my lord, wish to govern Qí,
then Gāo Xī and I are sufficient.
But if you, my lord, desire to become hegemon and king,
then without Guǎn Yíwú it is impossible.
Wherever Yíwú resides, that state becomes important,
he must not be lost."
Thereupon, Duke Huán followed his advice.
So he pretended to summon Guǎn Zhòng wishing to vent his hatred,
but actually intended to employ him.
Guǎn Zhòng knew this,
so he requested to go.
Bào Shūyá went to meet and receive Guǎn Zhòng,
and at Tángfù removed his shackles,
purified him with a ritual, and presented him to Duke Huán.
Duke Huán treated him with great courtesy, making him a high official,
and entrusted him with governance.
After Duke Huán obtained Guǎn Zhòng,
along with Bào Shū,
Xí Péng,
and Gāo Xī, he reformed the governance of Qí,
organized the armies of the five families,
established the benefits of light and heavy taxes and the profits from fish and salt,
to relieve the poor,
rewarded the worthy and capable,
and the people of Qí were all pleased.
In the second year,
he attacked and destroyed Tán,
and the Viscount of Tán fled to Jǔ.
Initially, when Duke Huán was in exile,
he passed through Tán,
and Tán treated him discourteously,
hence he attacked it.
In the fifth year,
he attacked Lǔ,
and the Lǔ generals were defeated.
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ requested to surrender the city of Suì to make peace,
to which Duke Huán agreed,
and met with Lǔ at Kē to form an alliance.
As Lǔ was about to swear the oath,
Cáo Mèi threatened Duke Huán on the altar with a dagger,
saying:
"Return the invaded land of Lǔ!"
Duke Huán agreed.
Afterward, Cáo Mèi put away the dagger
and took his place among the ministers facing north.
Duke Huán later regretted it
and wanted to neither give Lǔ the land nor kill Cáo Mèi.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"To go back on your promise after being forced and betray trust by killing him
might bring a moment of satisfaction,
but to break faith with the feudal lords,
losing the support of the world,
is not permissible."
Thus, he returned to Lǔ the land lost in three defeats by Cáo Mèi.
When the feudal lords heard of this,
they all trusted Qí and wished to align with it.
In the seventh year,
the feudal lords met with Duke Huán at Zhēn,
and from then on, Duke Huán began his hegemony.
In the fourteenth year,
Wán, son of Duke Lì of Chén,
also known as Jìng Zhòng,
fled to Qí.
Duke Huán of Qí wanted to make him a minister,
but he declined; thus, he was appointed as the director of works.
He was the ancestor of Tián Chéngzǐ Cháng.
In the twenty-third year,
the Shān Róng attacked Yān.
Yān appealed to Qí for help.
Duke Huán of Qí rescued Yān,
then attacked the Shān Róng,
reaching Gūzhú before returning.
Duke Zhuāng of Yān then escorted Duke Huán into Qí territory.
Duke Huán said:
"Except for the Son of Heaven,
feudal lords should not escort each other beyond their borders;
I must not be discourteous to Yān."
So he divided the land and gave the area where the Yān ruler had reached to Yān,
ordering the Yān ruler to restore the governance of Shào Gōng,
paying tribute to Zhōu,
as in the times of Chéng and Kāng.
When the feudal lords heard of this,
they all followed Qí.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the mother of Duke Mǐn of Lǔ, named Āi Jiāng,
was the younger sister of Duke Huán.
Āi Jiāng had an affair with Qìng Fǔ, a prince of Lǔ,
and Qìng Fǔ assassinated Duke Mǐn,
with Āi Jiāng wanting to install Qìng Fǔ,
but the people of Lǔ instead installed Duke Xī.
Duke Huán summoned Āi Jiāng
and killed her.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Duke Wén of Wèi faced trouble from the Dí,
and appealed to Qí for help.
Qí led the feudal lords to fortify Chǔqiū and establish the ruler of Wèi.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Duke Huán was frolicking in a boat with his wife, Cài Jī.
Cài Jī, being skilled in water,
rocked the boat,
frightening the Duke,
who told her to stop,
but she did not,
so he left the boat,
angry, and sent Cài Jī back to Cài,
though not divorcing her.
Cài was also angered
and married her off to someone else.
Duke Huán heard of this and was enraged,
raising an army to attack.
In the spring of the thirtieth year,
Duke Huán of Qí led the feudal lords to attack Cài,
and Cài collapsed.
Then they attacked Chǔ.
King Chéng of Chǔ raised an army and asked:
"Why have you entered my land?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Previously, Shào Kāng Gōng commanded our former lord Tài Gōng, saying:
'The five ranks of nobles and nine regions,
you may truly campaign against them,
to assist the Zhōu court.'
He granted our former lord jurisdiction east to the sea,
west to the river,
south to Mùlíng,
and north to Wúdì.
Chǔ has not presented the bundled thatch for tribute,
causing the royal sacrifices to be incomplete,
hence we have come to demand.
Also, King Zhāo's southern campaign did not return,
so we have come to inquire."
The King of Chǔ said:
"The tribute not being sent,
that is true,
and it is my fault,
how dare I not supply it!
As for King Zhāo not returning from his expedition,
you should ask the riverbanks."
The Qí army advanced and encamped at Xíng.
In summer, the King of Chǔ sent Qū Wán to lead troops to resist Qí,
and the Qí army retreated to encamp at Shàolíng.
Duke Huán boasted to Qū Wán of his multitude of troops.
Qū Wán said:
"If you act with righteousness, it is acceptable;
if not,
then Chǔ will use the Fángchéng Mountains as its walls,
and the Jiāng and Hàn rivers as its moats,
how could you advance?"
So they made a covenant with Qū Wán and left.
Passing through Chén,
Yuán Táotú of Chén deceived Qí,
directing them to exit eastward,
but they realized it. In autumn,
Qí attacked Chén.
That year,
Jìn killed the crown prince Shēnshēng.
In the summer of the thirty-fifth year,
he met with the feudal lords at Kuíqiū.
King Xiāng of Zhōu sent Zǎi Kǒng to bestow upon Duke Huán the sacrificial meat of King Wén and King Wǔ,
red bows and arrows,
and a grand carriage,
commanding him not to bow.
Duke Huán was about to agree,
but Guǎn Zhòng said
"It is not permissible,"
so he descended and bowed to receive the gifts.
In autumn, he again met with the feudal lords at Kuíqiū,
showing even more arrogance.
Zhōu sent Zǎi Kǒng to the meeting.
Many feudal lords began to rebel.
The Marquis of Jìn was ill,
arrived late, and met Zǎi Kǒng.
Zǎi Kǒng said:
"The Marquis of Qí is arrogant;
you should not go."
He heeded the advice.
That year,
Duke Xiàn of Jìn died,
Lǐ Kè killed Xī Qí
and Zhuó Zǐ,
and Duke Mù of Qín sent his wife's brother, Prince Yí Wú, to become the ruler of Jìn.
Duke Huán then intervened in the disorder of Jìn,
reaching Gāoliáng,
sent Xí Péng to establish the ruler of Jìn,
and returned.
At that time, the Zhōu court was weak,
with only Qí,
Chǔ, Qín,
and Jìn being strong.
Jìn had just joined the meetings,
but after Duke Xiàn's death,
the state fell into internal chaos.
Duke Mù of Qín was remote
and did not participate in the central states' meetings and alliances.
King Chéng of Chǔ was initially pacifying the Jīng Mán and ruling them,
setting himself up as a barbarian.
Only Qí convened the central states for meetings and alliances,
and Duke Huán was able to promote his virtue,
so the feudal lords gathered as guests.
Then Duke Huán declared:
"I campaigned south to Shàolíng,
gazing upon Xióng Mountain;
north against the Shān Róng,
Lízhī,
and Gūzhú;
west to Dàxià,
crossing the Liúshā;
bound the horses and hung the chariots to ascend Tàiháng,
reaching Bēi'ěr Mountain before returning.
No feudal lord dares to oppose me.
I have held three military assemblies,
and six carriage meetings,
uniting the feudal lords nine times,
once rectifying the world.
In the past, the three dynasties received the mandate;
how is this any different?
I wish to perform the Fēng sacrifice on Tài Mountain,
and the Shàn sacrifice on Liángfù."
Guǎn Zhòng firmly advised against it,
but he would not listen;
so he persuaded Duke Huán that only when rare treasures from distant lands arrived could he perform the Fēng sacrifice,
and Duke Huán then desisted.
In the thirty-eighth year,
King Xiāng of Zhōu's younger brother Dài conspired with the Róng
and Dí tribes to attack Zhōu.
Qí sent Guǎn Zhòng to pacify the Róng in Zhōu.
Zhōu wished to treat Guǎn Zhòng with the rites due to a high minister,
but Guǎn Zhòng bowed his head to the ground and said:
"I am but a minister's minister,
how dare I accept!"
After three refusals,
he finally accepted the reception for a lower minister and appeared.
In the thirty-ninth year,
King Xiāng of Zhōu's younger brother Dài came fleeing to Qí.
Qí sent Zhòngsūn to petition the king,
to apologize for Dài.
King Xiāng was angry
and would not listen.
In the forty-first year,
Duke Mù of Qín captured Duke Huì of Jìn,
but later returned him.
That year,
Guǎn Zhòng
and Xí Péng both died.
When Guǎn Zhòng was ill,
Duke Huán asked him:
"Which of my ministers is fit to be chancellor?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"No one knows your ministers better than you, my lord."
The Duke asked:
"What about Yì Yá?"
He answered:
"He killed his own son to please his lord,
this goes against human nature,
he cannot be used."
The Duke asked:
"What about Kāi Fāng?"
He answered:
"He abandoned his parents to please his lord,
this goes against human nature,
he is difficult to be close to."
The Duke asked:
"What about Shù Diāo?"
He answered:
"He castrated himself to please his lord,
this goes against human nature,
he is difficult to be intimate with."
After Guǎn Zhòng died,
Duke Huán did not follow Guǎn Zhòng's advice,
and eventually drew close to and employed these three men,
who monopolized power.
In the forty-second year,
the Róng attacked Zhōu,
Zhōu appealed urgently to Qí for help,
and Qí ordered the various states to send troops to garrison Zhōu.
That year,
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn came,
and Duke Huán gave him a wife.
In the forty-third year.
Originally, Duke Huán of Qí had three principal wives:
named Wáng Jī,
Xú Jī,
and Cài Jī,
all of whom had no sons.
Duke Huán was fond of women,
and had many favored concubines,
six of whom were treated as wives:
the elder Wèi Jī,
bore Wú Guǐ;
the younger Wèi Jī,
bore Duke Huì's Yuán;
Zhèng Jī,
bore Duke Xiào's Zhāo;
Gě Yíng,
bore Duke Zhāo's Pān;
Mì Jī,
bore Duke Yì's Shāngrén;
Sòng Huázi,
bore Prince Yōng.
Duke Huán and Guǎn Zhòng entrusted Duke Xiào to Duke Xiāng of Sòng,
intending him to be crown prince.
Yōng Wú was favored by Wèi Gòng Jī,
and through the eunuch Shù Diāo presented generous gifts to Duke Huán,
gaining favor as well,
and Duke Huán promised to establish Wú Guǐ as heir.
After Guǎn Zhòng died,
the five princes all sought to be established.
On the day Yǐhài in the tenth month,
Duke Huán of Qí died.
Yì Yá entered the palace,
and together with Shù Diāo used the favored concubines to kill many officials,
and established Prince Wú Guǐ as ruler.
Crown Prince Zhāo fled to Sòng.
When Duke Huán was ill,
the five princes each formed factions contending for succession.
After Duke Huán died,
they attacked each other,
so the palace was empty,
and no one dared to coffin the body.
Duke Huán's corpse lay on the bed for sixty-seven days,
and maggots crawled out the door.
On the day Yǐhài in the twelfth month,
Wú Guǐ was established,
and only then was the coffin announced.
On the night of Xīnsì,
the burial was conducted.
Duke Huán had more than ten sons,
but ultimately five succeeded to the throne:
Wú Guǐ reigned for three months and died,
with no posthumous title;
next was Duke Xiào;
next Duke Zhāo;
next Duke Yì;
next Duke Huì.
In the first year of Duke Xiào, in the third month,
Duke Xiāng of Sòng led the troops of various states to escort Crown Prince Zhāo of Qí and attack Qí.
The people of Qí were frightened,
and killed their ruler Wú Guǐ.
The people of Qí were about to establish Crown Prince Zhāo,
but the followers of the four princes attacked the crown prince,
so the crown prince fled to Sòng,
and Sòng then fought against the four princes of Qí.
In the fifth month,
Sòng defeated the armies of Qí's four princes and established Crown Prince Zhāo,
who became Duke Xiào of Qí.
Sòng came to campaign
because Duke Huán and Guǎn Zhòng had entrusted the crown prince to them.
Due to the turmoil,
Duke Huán of Qí was not buried until the eighth month.
In the sixth year, in spring,
Qí attacked Sòng,
because Sòng had not allied with Qí.
In summer, Duke Xiāng of Sòng died.
In the seventh year,
Duke Wén of Jìn was established.
In the tenth year,
Duke Xiào died,
and Duke Xiào's younger brother Pān, with the help of Prince Kāi Fāng of Wèi, killed Duke Xiào's son and established Pān,
who became Duke Zhāo.
Duke Zhāo
was a son of Duke Huán,
his mother was named Gě Yíng.
In the first year of Duke Zhāo,
Duke Wén of Jìn defeated Chǔ at Chéngpú,
and then met with the various states at Jiàntǔ,
paid homage to Zhōu,
and the Son of Heaven made Jìn hegemon.
In the sixth year,
the Dí tribes invaded Qí.
Duke Wén of Jìn died.
The Qín army was defeated at Xiáo.
In the twelfth year,
Duke Mù of Qín died.
In the nineteenth year, in the fifth month,
Duke Zhāo died,
and his son Shè was established as ruler of Qí.
Shè's mother was not favored by Duke Zhāo,
and the people of the state did not fear him.
Duke Zhāo's younger brother Shāngrén had failed in his bid for succession after Duke Huán's death,
so he secretly associated with worthy scholars,
attached himself to and loved the common people,
and the common people were pleased.
After Duke Zhāo died,
and his son Shè was established,
who was isolated and weak,
Shāngrén then in the tenth month with his followers killed the Qí ruler Shè at the tomb,
and Shāngrén established himself,
becoming Duke Yì.
Duke Yì
was a son of Duke Huán,
his mother was named Mì Jī.
In the fourth year of spring under Duke Yì's reign,
previously, when Duke Yì was still a prince,
he went hunting with Bǐng Róng's father,
and they contended over the prey, but he did not win.
Upon ascending the throne,
he had Bǐng Róng's father's feet amputated,
yet made Bǐng Róng his attendant.
Yōng Zhí's wife was beautiful,
so the duke took her into his palace,
and made Yōng Zhí his carriage attendant.
In the fifth month,
Duke Yì was touring at Shēnchí,
the two men were bathing
and jesting. Zhí said:
"Son of the amputated!"
Róng retorted:
"Wife-stealer!"
Both were pained by these words,
and grew resentful.
They plotted to accompany the duke into a bamboo grove,
where the two assassinated Duke Yì in his carriage;
they abandoned him in the bamboo grove and fled.
When Duke Yì was established,
he was arrogant, and the people did not support him.
The people of Qí deposed his son and welcomed Prince Yuán from Wèi,
establishing him,
who became Duke Huì.
Duke Huì
was a son of Duke Huán.
His mother was a woman from Wèi,
named Shǎo Wèijī,
who had fled the turmoil in Qí,
hence was in Wèi.
In the second year of Duke Huì,
the Cháng Dí came,
Wángzǐ Chéngfù attacked and killed them,
burying them at the north gate.
In Jìn, Zhào Chuān assassinated his ruler, Duke Líng.
In the tenth year,
Duke Huì died,
and his son Duke Qǐng, Wú Yě, succeeded him.
Earlier, Cuī Zhù had been favored by Duke Huì,
but after Duke Huì's death,
the Gāo and Guó families feared his influence,
so they expelled him,
and Cuī Zhù fled to Wèi.
In the first year of Duke Qǐng,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ was powerful,
and attacked Chén;
in the second year,
he besieged Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng surrendered,
but later restored the state to the Earl of Zhèng.
In the sixth year, spring,
Jìn sent Xì Kè to Qí,
and Qí had the lady observe him from behind a curtain.
As Xì Kè ascended,
the lady laughed at him.
Xì Kè said:
"If I do not avenge this,
I will not cross the river again!"
Returning, he requested to attack Qí,
but the Marquis of Jìn did not permit it.
When Qí's envoys arrived in Jìn,
Xì Kè captured four Qí envoys at Hénèi,
and killed them.
In the eighth year,
Jìn attacked Qí,
and Qí sent Prince Qiáng as a hostage to Jìn,
whereupon the Jìn troops withdrew.
In the tenth year, spring,
Qí attacked Lǔ
and Wèi. The ministers of Lǔ
and Wèi went to Jìn to request troops,
all relying on Xì Kè.
Jìn sent Xì Kè with 800 chariots as commander of the central army,
Shì Xiè leading the upper army,
Luán Shū leading the lower army,
to rescue Lǔ
and Wèi, and attack Qí.
On the rénshēn day of the sixth month,
they joined battle with the Qí troops below Míjī.
On the guǐyǒu day,
they deployed at Ān.
Páng Chǒufǔ was the right-hand attendant for Duke Qǐng of Qí.
Duke Qǐng said:
"Charge them,
we'll defeat the Jìn army and feast together."
They shot and wounded Xì Kè,
blood flowing down to his shoes.
Kè wanted to retreat into the fortifications,
but his driver said:
"Since we entered the battle,
you've been wounded twice,
yet dare not speak of the pain,
fearing to dishearten the soldiers.
I beg you to endure it."
So they fought again.
In the battle, Qí was hard-pressed,
and Chǒufǔ feared the Qí duke would be captured,
so he exchanged places with him,
making Duke Qǐng the right-hand attendant,
but the chariot got caught on a tree and stopped.
The Jìn junior officer Hán Jué knelt before the Qí duke's chariot and said,
"My humble ruler has sent me to rescue Lǔ
and Wèi,"
mocking him.
Chǒufǔ sent Duke Qǐng down to fetch water,
thus enabling him to escape,
get away,
and rejoin his army.
Xì Kè of Jìn wanted to kill Chǒufǔ.
Chǒufǔ said:
"If one who dies in place of his ruler is executed,
no minister will be loyal to his ruler hereafter."
Kè spared him,
and Chǒufǔ thus managed to escape back to Qí.
Thereupon, the Jìn army pursued Qí to Mǎlíng.
The Qí duke offered precious vessels in apology,
but they refused;
they insisted on getting Xiāo Tóng Shūzǐ, who had laughed at Kè,
and demanded that Qí reorient its fields eastward.
The reply was:
"Shūzǐ
is the mother of the Qí ruler.
The mother of the Qí ruler is like the mother of the Jìn ruler;
how would you deal with her?
Moreover, you launched a righteous campaign but follow it with violence,
is that acceptable?"
Thereupon, they agreed,
ordering the return of the invaded lands of Lǔ
and Wèi.
In the eleventh year,
Jìn first established the six ministers,
rewarding the achievements at the Battle of Ān.
Duke Qǐng of Qí paid homage to Jìn,
intending to honor King Jìng of Jìn as hegemon,
but Duke Jìng of Jìn dared not accept,
so he returned.
Upon returning, Duke Qǐng opened up the parks and gardens,
reduced taxes,
relieved the orphans and visited the sick,
emptied the granaries to save the people,
and the people were greatly pleased.
He treated the feudal lords with generous courtesy.
By the end of Duke Qǐng's reign,
the people were devoted,
and the feudal lords did not invade.
In the seventeenth year,
Duke Qǐng died,
and his son Duke Líng, Huán, succeeded him.
In the ninth year of Duke Líng,
Luán Shū of Jìn assassinated his ruler, Duke Lì.
In the tenth year,
Duke Dào of Jìn attacked Qí,
and Qí sent Prince Guāng as a hostage to Jìn.
In the nineteenth year,
they established his son Guāng as crown prince,
with Gāo Hòu as his tutor,
and ordered him to meet with the feudal lords to form an alliance at Zhōnglí.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Jìn sent Zhōngxíng Xiànzǐ to attack Qí.
The Qí army was defeated,
and Duke Líng fled into Línzī.
Yàn Yīng tried to stop Duke Líng,
but Duke Líng did not listen.
He said:
"My lord, you lack courage too!"
The Jìn troops then besieged Línzī,
and the defenders of Línzī dared not come out,
so Jìn burned the outer city and left.
In the twenty-eighth year,
initially, Duke Líng married a woman from Lǔ,
who bore him a son named Guāng,
and he was designated as the crown prince.
There were also Zhòng Jī
and Róng Jī.
Róng Jī was favored,
while Zhòng Jī bore a son named Yá,
and entrusted him to Róng Jī.
Róng Jī requested that Yá be made crown prince,
and the duke agreed.
Zhòng Jī said:
"This cannot be.
Guāng's establishment
has been recognized by the various states,
and to depose him without cause now
will surely bring you regret."
The duke replied:
"It is within my power."
Thereupon, he exiled Crown Prince Guāng to the east
and appointed Gāo Hòu as tutor to Yá, making him crown prince.
When Duke Líng fell ill,
Cuī Zhù welcomed the former crown prince Guāng and installed him,
who became Duke Zhuāng.
Duke Zhuāng killed Róng Jī.
On the renchén day of the fifth month,
Duke Líng passed away,
and Duke Zhuāng ascended the throne.
He captured Crown Prince Yá at the hill of Gōudòu
and executed him.
In the eighth month,
Cuī Zhù killed Gāo Hòu.
Jìn, hearing of Qí's turmoil,
invaded Qí
and advanced as far as Gāotáng.
In the third year of Duke Zhuāng,
the Jìn senior official Luán Yíng fled to Qí,
and Duke Zhuāng treated him as a distinguished guest.
Yàn Yīng
and Tián Wénzǐ admonished against it,
but the duke did not listen.
In the fourth year,
Duke Zhuāng of Qí sent Luán Yíng to sneak into Qūwò in Jìn as an insider,
and followed with troops,
ascending Tàiháng,
and entering Méngmén.
Luán Yíng was defeated,
and the Qí army withdrew,
capturing Zhāogē on their return.
In the sixth year,
initially, the wife of Táng Gōng was beautiful;
after Táng Gōng died,
Cuī Zhù married her.
Duke Zhuāng had an affair with her,
frequently visiting the Cuī residence,
and even gave away Cuī Zhù's cap as a gift.
An attendant said:
"This should not be done."
Cuī Zhù grew angry,
and taking advantage of the campaign against Jìn,
he wished to collude with Jìn to launch a surprise attack on Qí but found no opportunity.
Duke Zhuāng had once flogged the eunuch Jiǎ Jǔ,
who later resumed his service
and acted as Cuī Zhù's informant against the duke to seek revenge.
In the fifth month,
the ruler of Jǔ paid a court visit to Qí,
and Qí held a feast for him on the jiǎxū day.
Cuī Zhù claimed illness and did not attend to affairs.
On the yǐhài day,
the duke inquired about Cuī Zhù's illness
and then went after Cuī Zhù's wife.
Cuī Zhù's wife entered a chamber,
and she and Cuī Zhù shut the door and did not come out,
while the duke leaned against a pillar and sang.
The eunuch Jiǎ Jǔ blocked the duke's attendants from entering,
closed the gates,
and Cuī Zhù's followers emerged with weapons.
The duke climbed a platform and pleaded for a pardon,
but it was denied;
he asked to form a covenant,
but it was denied;
he requested to commit suicide in the temple,
but it was denied.
They all said:
"Your servant Zhù is gravely ill
and cannot obey orders.
We are close to the duke's palace.
We, the accompanying servants, are hastening to deal with an adulterer
and know no other commands."
The duke climbed over a wall,
was shot in the thigh,
fell back down,
and was thus assassinated.
Yàn Yīng stood outside Cuī Zhù's gate
and said:
"If the ruler dies for the state, then I will die with him;
if he flees for the state, I will flee with him.
But if he dies or flees for his own sake,
unless one is his personal favorite,
who would dare to share the responsibility!"
He then entered as the gate opened,
laid his head on the duke's corpse and wept,
leaped three times in mourning, and left.
Someone told Cuī Zhù:
"You must kill him."
Cuī Zhù said:
"He is the people's hope;
sparing him will win the people's hearts."
On the dīngchǒu day,
Cuī Zhù installed Duke Zhuāng's half-brother Chǔjiù,
who became Duke Jǐng.
Duke Jǐng's mother
was the daughter of Shūsūn Xuānbó of Lǔ.
Upon Duke Jǐng's accession,
he appointed Cuī Zhù as right minister
and Qìng Fēng as left minister.
The two ministers, fearing unrest,
made a covenant with the people of the state, declaring:
"Those who do not align with Cuī and Qìng shall die!"
Yànzǐ looked up to the sky and said:
"I, Yīng, will only follow those who are loyal to the ruler and benefit the state!"
He refused to join the covenant.
Qìng Fēng wanted to kill Yànzǐ,
but Cuī Zhù said:
"He is a loyal minister;
spare him."
The Grand Historian of Qí recorded
"Cuī Zhù assassinated Duke Zhuāng,"
and Cuī Zhù killed him.
His younger brother rewrote the record,
and Cuī Zhù killed him too.
When the youngest brother again wrote the same,
Cuī Zhù then spared him.
In the first year of Duke Jǐng,
initially, Cuī Zhù had sons named Chéng and Qiáng,
and after their mother died,
he married a woman from the Eastern Guō clan,
who bore Míng.
The Eastern Guō woman had her former husband's son Wújiù and her brother Yǎn oversee the Cuī household.
Chéng committed an offense,
and the two overseers pressed for his punishment,
establishing Míng as heir.
Chéng requested to retire to Cuī,
and Cuī Zhù agreed,
but the two overseers refused,
saying:
"Cuī
is the ancestral fief,
it cannot be."
Chéng and Qiáng were enraged,
and reported to Qìng Fēng.
Qìng Fēng had a grudge against Cuī Zhù
and wished for his downfall.
Chéng and Qiáng killed Wújiù
and Yǎn at the Cuī residence,
and the household all fled.
Cuī Zhù, furious,
found no one around,
had a eunuch drive him
to see Qìng Fēng.
Qìng Fēng said:
"Allow me to eliminate them for you."
He sent Cuī Zhù's enemy Lúpú Piè to attack the Cuī family,
killing Chéng
and Qiáng, and exterminating the entire Cuī clan.
Cuī Zhù's wife committed suicide.
Cuī Zhù, with nowhere to return,
also took his own life.
Qìng Fēng became chancellor,
wielding absolute power.
In the tenth month of the third year,
Qìng Fēng went out hunting.
Previously, after Qìng Fēng had killed Cuī Zhù,
he became increasingly arrogant,
indulging in heavy drinking and hunting,
neglecting governmental affairs.
Qìng Shè handled the administration,
but internal rifts had already developed.
Tián Wénzǐ said to Huánzǐ:
"Chaos is about to erupt."
The Tián, Bào,
Gāo, and Luán clans conspired together against the Qìng clan.
Qìng Shè dispatched troops to surround Qìng Fēng's palace,
but the four families' followers jointly attacked and defeated them.
Qìng Fēng returned,
but could not enter,
and fled to Lǔ.
The people of Qí protested to Lǔ,
so Fēng fled to Wú.
Wú granted him Zhūfāng,
where he gathered his clan to reside,
becoming wealthier than he had been in Qí.
That autumn,
the people of Qí moved to rebury Duke Zhuāng,
and exposed Cuī Zhù's corpse in the marketplace to appease the masses.
In the ninth year,
Duke Jǐng sent Yàn Yīng to Jìn,
who privately told Shūxiàng:
"The governance of Qí will ultimately fall to the Tián clan.
Although the Tián clan lacks great virtue,
they use public authority for private gain,
yet they have shown kindness to the people,
and the people love them."
In the twelfth year,
Duke Jǐng went to Jìn,
met with Duke Píng,
and wished to join him in attacking Yān.
In the eighteenth year,
the duke again went to Jìn,
and met with Duke Zhāo.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he hunted in the suburbs of Lǔ,
then entered Lǔ,
and together with Yàn Yīng inquired about the rituals of Lǔ.
In the thirty-first year,
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ, fleeing the troubles caused by the Jì clan,
fled to Qí.
Qí intended to enfeoff him with a thousand shè,
but Zǐjiā劝阻 Duke Zhāo,
so Duke Zhāo instead requested Qí to attack Lǔ,
and they took Yùn to settle Duke Zhāo.
In the thirty-second year,
a comet appeared.
Duke Jǐng was sitting in the Bǎi Qǐn hall,
and sighed, saying:
"How magnificent!
Who will possess this?"
All the ministers wept,
but Yànzǐ laughed,
angering the duke.
Yànzǐ said:
"I laugh at the ministers for their excessive flattery."
Duke Jǐng said:
"The comet has appeared in the northeast,
corresponding to Qí's celestial division,
and I am troubled by it."
Yànzǐ said:
"You have high towers and deep pools,
collect taxes as if fearing insufficiency,
and impose punishments fearing they are not severe enough.
A baleful star is about to appear,
why fear a comet?"
The duke said:
"Can it be averted through sacrifices?"
Yànzǐ said:
"If spirits could be summoned by prayers,
they could also be driven away by sacrifices.
But the people's sufferings and grievances number in the tens of thousands,
and you order one person to perform sacrifices to avert it,
how can that overcome the voices of the multitude?"
At that time, Duke Jǐng was fond of building palaces,
collecting dogs and horses,
living luxuriously,
imposing heavy taxes and severe punishments,
hence Yànzǐ admonished him with these words.
In the forty-second year,
King HéLǘ of Wú attacked Chǔ,
and entered Yǐng.
In the forty-seventh year,
Yáng Hǔ of Lǔ attacked his lord,
but was unsuccessful,
fled to Qí,
and requested Qí to attack Lǔ.
Bàozǐ advised Duke Jǐng,
so they imprisoned Yáng Hǔ.
Yáng Hǔ managed to escape,
and fled to Jìn.
In the forty-eighth year,
he held a friendly meeting with Duke Dìng of Lǔ at Jiāgǔ.
Lí Chú said:
"Kǒng Qiū understands rituals but is timid;
request the Lái people to perform music,
then seize the lord of Lǔ,
and we can achieve our aim."
Duke Jǐng was wary of Kǒng Qiū serving as minister of Lǔ,
fearing Lǔ's hegemony,
so he followed Lí Chú's plan.
During the meeting,
when Lái music was presented,
Kǒngzǐ ascended the steps rapidly,
ordered the officials to seize the Lái people and execute them,
then reproached Duke Jǐng with ritual propriety.
Duke Jǐng felt ashamed,
returned the invaded territory to Lǔ as apology,
and withdrew.
That year,
Yàn Yīng died.
In the fifty-fifth year,
Fàn and Zhōngháng turned against their lord in Jìn,
and when Jìn attacked them fiercely,
they came to request grain.
Tián Qǐ, wishing to stir rebellion,
sought to form an alliance with these rebellious ministers,
persuaded Duke Jǐng, saying:
"Fàn
and Zhōngháng have repeatedly shown kindness to Qí,
we must rescue them."
So he sent Qǐ to rescue them and supplied them with grain.
In the summer of the fifty-eighth year,
the son of Duke Jǐng's primary wife, Yān Jī, died.
Duke Jǐng's favored concubine, Ruì Jī, had borne a son named Tú,
Tú was young,
his mother was of low status,
and he lacked virtue.
The various great ministers feared he would become heir,
so they expressed their wish to choose the eldest and most virtuous among the sons as crown prince.
Duke Jǐng was old,
detested discussing succession matters,
and loved Tú's mother,
wishing to establish Tú,
but hesitated to voice it.
He thus said to the great ministers:
"Let us enjoy ourselves;
why worry that the state will have no lord?"
In autumn, Duke Jǐng fell ill,
ordered Guó Huìzǐ
and Gāo Zhāozǐ to establish his youngest son Tú as crown prince,
expelled the other sons,
and relocated them to Lái.
Duke Jǐng died,
Crown Prince Tú ascended,
known as Yàn Rúzǐ.
In winter, before the burial,
the other sons, fearing execution,
all fled into exile.
Tú's half-brothers, Gōngzǐ Shòu,
Jū, and Qián fled to Wèi,
while Gōngzǐ Zǎng
and Yángshēng fled to Lǔ.
The people of Lái sang about them:
"When Duke Jǐng died, we were not involved in his burial;
when the three armies' affairs arose, we were not consulted.
Oh, ministers, oh ministers,
to whom do you pledge allegiance?"
In the first year of Yàn Rúzǐ's reign, during the spring,
Tián Qǐ pretended to serve the high ministers Gāo
and Guó,
attending court daily.
Qǐ would ride as their carriage attendant,
saying:
"Since you have gained the ruler's favor,
the other ministers all feel endangered
and are plotting rebellion."
He then told the various ministers:
"Gāo Zhāozǐ is fearsome -
before he makes his move,
we should strike first."
The ministers followed his advice.
In the sixth month,
Tián Qǐ
and Bào Mù led the ministers with troops into the ducal palace,
attacking Gāo Zhāozǐ.
When Zhāozǐ heard of this,
he joined Guó Huìzǐ to rescue the duke.
The duke's forces were defeated,
and Tián Qǐ's followers pursued them.
Guó Huìzǐ fled to Jǔ,
while they turned back and killed Gāo Zhāozǐ.
Yàn Yǔ fled to Lǔ.
In the eighth month,
Qí Bǐng Yìzī.
After Tián Qǐ defeated the two ministers,
he sent someone to Lǔ to summon Prince Yángshēng.
When Yángshēng arrived in Qí,
he secretly hid in Tián Qǐ's home.
On the wùzǐ day of the tenth month,
Tián Qǐ invited the various ministers, saying:
"My wife is making fish and bean offerings for sacrifice,
I would be honored if you could come to drink together."
During the drinking gathering,
Tián Qǐ had concealed Yángshēng in a sack,
placing it in the center of the seating area.
He opened the sack to reveal Yángshēng,
declaring:
"This is the new ruler of Qí!"
The ministers all prostrated themselves in reverence.
As they were about to swear an oath with the ministers to establish him,
Bào Mù was drunk,
and Qǐ falsely told the ministers:
"Bào Mù and I conspired together to establish Yángshēng."
Bào Mù angrily said:
"Have you forgotten Duke Jǐng's command?"
The various ministers looked at each other and wanted to reconsider,
but Yángshēng came forward,
kowtowing and saying:
"If it's acceptable, then establish me;
if not, then forget it."
Bào Mù, fearing disaster would arise,
then said again:
"We are all sons of Duke Jǐng,
why would it be unacceptable!"
So they swore the oath,
establishing Yángshēng,
who became known as Duke Dào.
When Duke Dào entered the palace,
he sent people to move Yàn Rúzǐ to Tái,
killing him under a tent,
and expelling Rúzǐ's mother Ruìzǐ.
Ruìzǐ was originally of low status and Rúzǐ was young,
so they had no power,
and the people of the state looked down upon them.
In the first year of Duke Dào's reign,
Qí attacked Lǔ,
capturing Huān
and Chǎn. Previously,
when Yángshēng was exiled in Lǔ,
Jì Kāngzǐ had given him his younger sister as wife.
When he returned and took the throne,
he sent for her.
But Jì Jī had been having an affair with Jì Fánghóu,
and when she confessed the situation,
Lǔ didn't dare send her,
so Qí attacked Lǔ,
and eventually brought Jì Jī back.
Jì Jī became favored,
and Qí returned the invaded territory to Lǔ.
Bàozǐ had a rift with Duke Dào,
and their relationship was poor.
In the fourth year,
Wú and Lǔ attacked the southern borders of Qí.
Bàozǐ assassinated Duke Dào,
and reported it to Wú.
King Fūchāi of Wú wept outside the army gates for three days,
preparing to sail by sea to attack Qí.
The people of Qí defeated them,
and the Wú army withdrew.
Zhào Yāng of Jìn attacked Qí,
reaching Lài before withdrawing.
The people of Qí jointly established Duke Dào's son Rén,
who became known as Duke Jiǎn.
In the fourth year of Duke Jiǎn's reign, during spring,
previously, when Duke Jiǎn and his father Yángshēng were both in Lǔ,
Jiān Zhǐ had been favored by them.
When he ascended the throne,
he appointed him to office.
Tián Chéngzǐ feared him,
and frequently glanced back at court.
Yù Yāng advised Duke Jiǎn, saying:
"Tián
and Jiān cannot coexist,
you must choose between them."
He didn't listen.
When Zǐwǒ was on night duty,
Tián Nì killed someone,
and encountering him,
Zǐwǒ arrested him and brought him in.
The Tián clan was then in harmony,
so they made the prisoner feign illness and sent wine to the guards,
who got drunk and were killed by the prisoner,
allowing him to escape.
Zǐwǒ made the Tián clan swear an oath at the Chén ancestral temple.
Previously, Tián Bào wanted to become Zǐwǒ's subordinate,
and had Gōngsūn speak for Bào,
but Bào had a mourning period and stopped.
Later he finally became his subordinate,
and was favored by Zǐwǒ.
Zǐwǒ said to him:
"I will expel all the Tián clan and establish you,
is that acceptable?"
He replied:
"I am distantly related to the Tián clan.
Moreover, those who oppose you are only a few individuals,
why expel them all!"
He then reported this to the Tián clan.
Zǐháng said:
"Since he has gained the ruler's favor,
if we don't act first,
he will certainly bring disaster upon you."
Zǐháng took up residence in the ducal palace.
In summer, on the rénshēn day of the fifth month,
Chéngzǐ and his brothers rode in four carriages to see the duke.
Zǐwǒ was in his tent,
came out to greet them,
then they entered
and closed the gates.
A eunuch resisted them,
and Zǐháng killed the eunuch.
The duke was drinking with women in the Tántái,
and Chéngzǐ moved them to the bedchamber.
The duke seized a spear and was about to strike him,
but Grand Historian Zǐyú said:
"This is not for ill intent,
but to eliminate harm."
Chéngzǐ went out and stayed at the armory,
hearing the duke was still angry,
and was about to leave,
saying:
"Where is there no ruler!"
Zǐháng drew his sword and said:
"Hesitation
is the ruin of affairs.
Who here is not of the Tián clan?
If I don't kill you, may the Tián ancestors bear witness!"
So he stopped.
Zǐwǒ returned,
gathered his followers and attacked the side gate and main gate,
but couldn't overcome either,
so he fled.
The Tián clan pursued him.
The people of Fēngqiū captured Zǐwǒ and reported it,
killing him at the outer gate.
Chéngzǐ was about to kill Dàlù Zǐfāng,
but Tián Nì pleaded for him and he was spared.
Using the duke's order, he took a carriage on the road,
and exited through the Yōng Gate.
Tián Bào offered him a carriage,
but he refused it,
saying:
"Nì pleaded for me,
and Bào gives me a carriage -
this shows I have private connections.
Having served Zǐwǒ yet having private dealings with his enemies,
how could I face the gentlemen of Lǔ
and Wèi?"
On the gēngchén day,
Tián Cháng captured Duke Jiǎn at Xúzhōu.
The duke said:
"If only I had followed Yù Yāng's advice earlier,
I wouldn't have come to this."
On the jiǎwǔ day,
Tián Cháng assassinated Duke Jiǎn at Xúzhōu.
Tián Cháng then established Duke Jiǎn's younger brother Áo,
who became known as Duke Píng.
When Duke Píng ascended the throne,
Tián Cháng served as his minister,
monopolizing Qí's government,
and appropriating the territory east of Ānpíng in Qí as the Tián clan's fiefdom.
In the eighth year of Duke Píng,
Yuè destroyed Wú.
He died in the twenty-fifth year,
and his son, Duke Xuān Jī, succeeded him.
Duke Xuān died in the fifty-first year,
and his son, Duke Kāng Dài, succeeded him.
Tián Huì rebelled in Lǐnqiū.
In the second year of Duke Kāng,
Hán,
Wèi, and Zhào began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the nineteenth year,
Tián Cháng's great-grandson Tián Hé became a feudal lord,
and Duke Kāng was moved to the seashore.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Duke Kāng died,
and the Lǚ clan's sacrifices were thus cut off.
The Tián clan eventually took possession of the state of Qí,
becoming King Wēi of Qí,
and grew powerful in the world.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I traveled to Qí,
from Tàishān to Lángyá,
bounded by the sea to the north,
with two thousand lǐ of fertile land,
and its people are broad-minded and adept at concealing their wisdom,
which is their innate nature.
With the sagacity of Tàigōng,
who laid the foundation of the state,
and the prosperity of Duke Huán,
who cultivated good governance,
it was fitting for them to assemble the feudal lords for alliances,
and be called a hegemon,
was it not appropriate?
How magnificent indeed,
truly the demeanor of a great state!
Zhōu Gōng Dàn
was the younger brother of King Wǔ of Zhōu.
Even during King Wén's time,
Dàn was filial as a son,
sincere and benevolent,
different from the other sons.
When King Wǔ ascended the throne,
Dàn often assisted and supported King Wǔ,
handling many affairs.
In the ninth year of King Wǔ,
he marched east to Měngjīn,
with Zhōu Gōng accompanying him.
In the eleventh year,
they attacked Zhòu,
reaching Mùyě,
where Zhōu Gōng aided King Wǔ
in composing the "Mù Shì."
After defeating Yīn,
they entered the Shāng palace.
Once Zhòu was killed,
Zhōu Gōng held the great battle-axe,
while Shào Gōng held the small battle-axe,
flanking King Wǔ,
and performed the blood sacrifice at the altar,
announcing Zhòu's crimes to heaven
and the people of Yīn.
They released Jīzǐ from imprisonment.
They enfeoffed Zhòu's son Wǔ Gēng Lùfǔ,
appointing Guǎn Shū
and Cài Shū as his tutors,
to continue the sacrifices of Yīn.
They widely enfeoffed meritorious officials and relatives of the same surname.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn was enfeoffed at Qūfù, the ruins of Shàohào,
and became the Duke of Lǔ.
Zhōu Gōng did not go to his fief,
but remained to assist King Wǔ.
Two years after King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
before the world was fully settled,
King Wǔ fell ill,
and was uneasy,
frightening his ministers.
Tàigōng
and Shào Gōng then performed divination.
Zhōu Gōng said:
"We must not distress our former kings."
Zhōu Gōng then offered himself as a hostage,
set up three altars,
stood facing north,
wearing a jade disc and holding a jade tablet,
and prayed to Tàiwáng,
Wáng Jì,
and King Wén.
The scribe recorded the prayer:
"Your eldest grandson, King Fā,
is toiling and afflicted with illness.
If you three kings bear the responsibility in heaven for a son's debt,
let Dàn take the place of King Fā.
Dàn is clever and capable,
talented and skilled,
and can serve the ghosts and spirits.
King Fā is not as talented or skilled as Dàn,
and cannot serve the ghosts and spirits.
He received the mandate in the court of the Lord on High,
to spread protection over the four quarters,
thus able to secure your descendants below,
so that the people of the four quarters all revere and fear him.
Do not let fall the precious mandate bestowed by heaven,
so that our former kings may also have an eternal reliance.
Now I will receive the command through the great tortoise shell.
If you grant my request,
I will return with my disc and tablet,
awaiting your command.
If you do not grant it,
I will set aside the disc and tablet."
After Zhōu Gōng had the scribe pray to Tàiwáng,
Wáng Jì,
and King Wén,
wishing to substitute for King Wǔ Fā,
he then divined before the three kings.
The diviners all said it was auspicious,
and when they opened the reading,
it was indeed auspicious.
Zhōu Gōng was pleased,
unlocked the case,
and saw the reading was auspicious.
Zhōu Gōng entered to congratulate King Wǔ, saying:
"Your Majesty will come to no harm.
Dàn has just received a mandate from the three kings,
planning for a long and enduring rule.
This way, they can heed my plea."
Zhōu Gōng stored the prayer in a metal-bound casket,
instructing the guards not to dare speak of it.
The next day,
King Wǔ recovered.
Later, after King Wǔ passed away,
King Chéng was young,
still in swaddling clothes.
Fearing the world would hear of King Wǔ's death and rebel,
Zhōu Gōng ascended the throne to act as regent for King Chéng, administering the state.
Guǎn Shū and his brothers spread rumors in the state, saying:
"Zhōu Gōng will act against King Chéng."
Zhōu Gōng then told Tàigōng Wàng
and Shào Gōng Shì:
"The reason I did not avoid suspicion and acted as regent
is that I feared the world would rebel against Zhōu,
and I would have nothing to report to our former kings Tàiwáng,
Wáng Jì,
and King Wén.
The three kings long toiled anxiously for the world,
and only now has it been accomplished.
King Wǔ died early,
King Chéng is young,
and to complete the work of Zhōu,
this is why I have acted thus."
He then became King Chéng's prime minister,
and sent his son Bó Qín to take his place in the fief of Lǔ.
Zhōu Gōng admonished Bó Qín, saying:
"I am the son of King Wén,
the younger brother of King Wǔ,
and the uncle of King Chéng;
my status in the world is not lowly.
Yet, I often interrupt my bath to clasp my hair,
and my meal to spit out the food,
rising to receive scholars,
fearing I might miss the worthy men of the world.
When you go to Lǔ,
be careful not to let your state make you arrogant toward others."
Guǎn Shū,
Cài Shū, Wǔ Gēng, and others indeed led the Huáiyí in rebellion.
Zhōu Gōng, under King Chéng's order,
raised an army and marched east to attack them,
composing the "Great Announcement."
He then executed Guǎn Shū,
killed Wǔ Gēng,
and exiled Cài Shū.
He gathered the remaining people of Yīn,
enfeoffing Kāng Shū in Wèi,
and Wēizǐ in Sòng,
to continue the sacrifices of Yīn.
He pacified the Huáiyí in the eastern lands,
and in two years, all was settled.
The feudal lords all submitted and honored Zhōu.
Heaven bestowed blessings,
and Táng Shū obtained grains,
which grew from different stalks but shared the same ear.
He presented them to King Chéng,
who ordered Táng Shū to deliver them to the Duke of Zhōu in the eastern territories,
composing the "Presentation of Grains."
After the Duke of Zhōu received the mandated grains,
he praised the Son of Heaven's decree,
composing the "Excellent Grains."
With the eastern lands pacified,
the Duke of Zhōu returned to report to King Chéng,
and composed a poem for the king,
naming it "The Owl."
The king, however, did not dare to reprimand the Duke of Zhōu.
In the second month of the seventh year of King Chéng's reign, on the day Yǐwèi,
the king set out from Zhōu,
arriving at Fēng,
and sent the Grand Guardian Shào Gōng ahead to Luò to survey the land.
In the third month,
the Duke of Zhōu went to oversee the construction of Chéngzhōu Luòyì,
divining for a place to settle,
and it was deemed auspicious,
so he established the capital there.
When King Chéng came of age,
he was able to handle governance.
Thereupon, the Duke of Zhōu returned the reins of government to King Chéng,
who began to hold court.
When the Duke of Zhōu acted on behalf of King Chéng in governance,
he faced south with his back to a screen to receive the feudal lords.
After seven years,
he returned the government to King Chéng,
taking his place facing north as a subject,
humble and reverent as if in awe.
Earlier,
when King Chéng was young,
he fell ill, and the Duke of Zhōu cut his own nails and sank them into the river,
praying to the spirits:
"The king is young and unaware;
it is I, Dàn, who have offended the divine decree."
He also stored the prayer text in the archives.
King Chéng recovered from his illness.
When King Chéng assumed power,
someone slandered the Duke of Zhōu,
and he fled to Chǔ.
King Chéng opened the archives,
saw the Duke of Zhōu's prayer document,
and wept,
then recalled the Duke of Zhōu.
Upon his return,
the Duke of Zhōu feared that as King Chéng grew older,
he might become indulgent and lax in governance,
so he composed "The Numerous Officers,"
and "Against Luxurious Ease."
"Against Luxurious Ease" states:
"As parents,
they toil to build an enduring legacy,
yet their descendants, arrogant and wasteful, forget it,
leading to the loss of their family.
How can one not be cautious as a child!"
Thus, in the past, King Zhōngzōng of the Yīn,
reverent and awed by the Mandate of Heaven,
governed the people with self-restraint,
trembling with fear and not daring to be indolent or complacent,
so Zhōngzōng enjoyed a reign of seventy-five years.
As for Gāozōng,
he long labored abroad,
living among the common people.
When he ascended the throne,
he observed the mourning hut,
remaining silent for three years,
and when he spoke, his words were joyful.
He dared not be indolent or complacent,
bringing tranquility to the Yīn state,
so that none, great or small, held grievances,
thus Gāozōng enjoyed a reign of fifty-five years.
As for Zǔ Jiǎ,
he deemed it unrighteous to be king,
and long lived abroad among the common people,
understanding their reliance.
He was able to protect and benefit the common people,
not oppressing the widowed or orphaned,
so Zǔ Jiǎ enjoyed a reign of thirty-three years."
"The Numerous Officers" states:
"From Tāng to Dì Yǐ,
none failed to uphold sacrifices and manifest virtue,
and none failed to be worthy of Heaven.
But now the successor king, Zhòu,
indulged in excess and luxury,
disregarding Heaven and the people's welfare.
His people all deserved punishment."
"King Wén toiled from noon till evening without time to eat,
yet enjoyed a reign of fifty years."
These were composed to admonish King Chéng.
While in Fēng,
with the realm already pacified,
but the official administration of Zhōu not yet fully ordered,
the Duke of Zhōu composed "The Offices of Zhōu,"
to distinguish the appropriate duties of officials.
He also composed "The Establishment of Government,"
to benefit the common people.
The people were pleased.
While in Fēng,
the Duke of Zhōu fell ill and was near death.
He said:
"Bury me in Chéngzhōu,
to show that I dare not leave King Chéng."
After the Duke of Zhōu's death,
