King Chéng, in deference,
buried him in Bì,
near King Wén,
to show that he, the young king, dared not treat the Duke of Zhōu as a subject.
After the Duke of Zhōu's death,
before the autumn harvest,
a violent storm with thunder struck,
laying all the grain flat,
and uprooting great trees.
The state of Zhōu was thrown into great fear.
King Chéng and his ministers, in court attire, opened the metal-bound casket documents,
and the king then learned of the Duke of Zhōu's offer to substitute himself for King Wǔ.
The two dukes and the king questioned the historians and various officials,
who said:
"It is true;
the Duke of Zhōu commanded us not to speak of it."
King Chéng held the documents and wept,
saying:
"From now on, let there be no careless divination!
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu toiled diligently for the royal house,
but I, in my youth, did not know.
Now Heaven has stirred its might to illuminate the Duke of Zhōu's virtue.
I, the young one, shall welcome it,
and the rites of our state should reflect this."
The king went to the suburbs,
and Heaven sent rain,
the wind reversed,
and the grain all stood upright again.
The two dukes ordered the people
to prop up all the flattened great trees.
The year then yielded a great harvest.
Thereupon, King Chéng granted Lǔ the privilege of offering suburban sacrifices to King Wén.
The fact that Lǔ possessed the rites and music of the Son of Heaven
was to honor the virtue of the Duke of Zhōu.
After the Duke of Zhōu's death,
his son Bó Qín, who had already been enfeoffed earlier,
became the Duke of Lǔ.
When Bó Qín, the Duke of Lǔ, first received the fief of Lǔ,
he reported on his administration only after three years.
The Duke of Zhōu asked:
"Why so late?"
Bó Qín replied:
"I changed their customs,
reformed their rites,
and mandated three years of mourning before its conclusion,
hence the delay."
Tài Gōng was also enfeoffed in Qí,
and reported on his administration after just five months.
The Duke of Zhōu asked:
"Why so swift?"
He said:
"I simplified the rites between ruler and subject,
and followed their customs."
Later, when he heard of Bó Qín's delayed report,
he sighed and said:
"Alas,
in later generations, Lǔ will serve Qí facing north!
If governance is not simple and easy,
the people will not be close;
if it is plain and easy, close to the people,
the people will surely turn to it."
After Bóqín ascended the throne,
Guǎn Shū and
Cài Shū, among others, rebelled,
and the Huáiyí and
Xúróng also rose up in revolt simultaneously.
Thereupon, Bóqín led his army to attack them at Bì,
and composed the "Bì Shì,"
saying:
"Prepare your armor and helmets,
dare not do so improperly.
Do not dare to harm the livestock pens.
If horses or cattle stray,
or if male and female servants flee,
do not dare to pursue them beyond bounds;
respectfully return them.
Do not dare to plunder or steal,
or climb over walls.
People of Lǔ from the three suburbs and three tunnels,
prepare your fodder,
provisions,
and construction materials;
dare not fail to meet the requirements.
On the jiǎxū day, I will build fortifications and campaign against the Xúróng;
do not dare to be late,
or you will face severe punishment."
After composing this "Bì Shì,"
he then pacified the Xúróng,
and stabilized Lǔ.
Duke Lǔ Bóqín died,
and his son, Duke Kǎo Qiú, succeeded him.
Duke Kǎo died after four years,
and his younger brother Xī was established,
who was called Duke Yáng.
Duke Yáng built the Máoquè Gate.
He died after six years,
and his son, Duke Yōu Zǎi, succeeded him.
In the fourteenth year of Duke Yōu,
his younger brother Fèi killed Duke Yōu and established himself,
who was known as Duke Wèi.
Duke Wèi died after fifty years,
and his son, Duke Lì Zhuó, succeeded him.
Duke Lì died after thirty-seven years,
and the people of Lǔ established his younger brother Jù,
who was known as Duke Xiàn.
Duke Xiàn died after thirty-two years,
and his son, Duke Zhēn Bì, succeeded him.
In the fourteenth year of Duke Zhēn,
King Lì of Zhōu acted tyrannically,
fled to Zhì,
and the Hé'éng Regency administered the government.
In the twenty-ninth year,
King Xuān of Zhōu ascended the throne.
In the thirtieth year,
Duke Zhēn died,
and his younger brother Áo succeeded him,
who was known as Duke Wǔ.
In the spring of the ninth year of Duke Wǔ,
Duke Wǔ, along with his eldest son Guà
and younger son Xì,
went west to pay homage to King Xuān of Zhōu.
King Xuān favored Xì,
and wanted to establish Xì as the crown prince of Lǔ.
Fán Zhòngshānfǔ of Zhōu advised King Xuān, saying:
"To depose the elder and establish the younger
is improper;
if it is improper,
it will inevitably violate the king's command;
violating the king's command,
must be punished:
therefore, issuing commands cannot be improper.
If commands are not carried out,
government cannot be established;
if carried out improperly,
the people will abandon their superiors.
For inferiors to serve superiors,
and the young to serve the elder,
is the way to maintain propriety.
Now if the Son of Heaven establishes feudal lords,
and sets up the younger,
it teaches the people to rebel.
If Lǔ follows this,
and other feudal lords imitate it,
the king's commands will be obstructed;
if they do not follow and are punished,
it is the king's own command that is being punished.
To punish is a mistake,
not to punish is also a mistake;
may the king consider this."
King Xuān did not listen,
and ultimately established Xì as the crown prince of Lǔ.
In the summer, Duke Wǔ returned and died,
Xì succeeded him,
who was known as Duke Yì.
In the ninth year of Duke Yì,
Bóyù, the son of Duke Yì's elder brother Guà, along with the people of Lǔ, attacked and assassinated Duke Yì,
and established Bóyù as the ruler.
After Bóyù had been on the throne for eleven years,
King Xuān of Zhōu attacked Lǔ,
killed its ruler Bóyù,
and inquired among the princes of Lǔ for one who could guide and comply with the feudal lords,
to be made the successor of Lǔ.
Fán Mùzhōng said:
"Chēng, the younger brother of Duke Yì of Lǔ,
is reverent and respectful to the bright spirits,
and honors the elderly;
in administering affairs and carrying out punishments,
he always consults the inherited teachings and seeks advice from solid facts;
he does not interfere with what is inquired,
nor violate what is advised."
King Xuān said:
"Indeed,
he can educate and govern his people."
Then he established Chēng at the Yí Palace,
who was known as Duke Xiào.
From then on,
many feudal lords rebelled against the king's commands.
In the twenty-fifth year of Duke Xiào,
the feudal lords rebelled against Zhōu,
and the Quǎnróng killed King Yōu.
Qín began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Duke Xiào died,
and his son Fúhuáng succeeded him,
who was known as Duke Huì.
In the thirtieth year of Duke Huì,
the people of Jìn assassinated their ruler Marquis Zhāo.
In the forty-fifth year,
the people of Jìn again assassinated their ruler Marquis Xiào.
In the forty-sixth year,
Duke Huì died,
and his eldest son by a concubine, Xī, acted as regent in charge of the state,
performing the duties of the ruler,
who was known as Duke Yǐn.
Initially, Duke Huì's legitimate wife had no son,
and his low-ranking concubine Shēngzǐ gave birth to a son, Xī.
When Xī grew up,
a marriage was arranged for him with a woman from Sòng.
The Sòng woman arrived and was beautiful,
so Duke Huì took her for himself and made her his wife.
She gave birth to a son, Yǔn.
He elevated the Sòng woman to be his principal wife,
and made Yǔn the crown prince.
When Duke Huì died,
because Yǔn was young,
the people of Lǔ collectively ordered Xī to act as regent,
not declaring his accession to the throne.
In the fifth year of Duke Yǐn,
he went to Táng to observe fishing.
In the eighth year,
he exchanged with Zhèng the king's city of Bēng at Tàishān and the field of Xǔ,
which the gentlemen criticized.
In the winter of the eleventh year,
Prince Huì flatteringly said to Duke Yǐn:
"The common people find it convenient for you to be ruler,
you should formally take the throne.
I ask to kill Zǐ Yǔn for you,
and you appoint me as chancellor."
Duke Yǐn said:
"There is the former ruler's command.
Because Yǔn was young,
I am acting as regent.
Now Yǔn has grown up,
I am planning to build a retirement place at Tùqiú and grow old there,
handing over the government to Zǐ Yǔn."
Huì feared that Zǐ Yǔn would hear of this and instead have him killed,
so he went and slandered Duke Yǐn to Zǐ Yǔn, saying:
"Duke Yǐn wants to formally take the throne,
and remove you;
you should consider this.
I ask to kill Duke Yǐn for you."
Zǐ Yǔn agreed.
In the eleventh month,
when Duke Yǐn was sacrificing to Zhōng Wū,
fasting at Shèpǔ,
and staying at the Wěi family's residence,
Huì sent someone to assassinate Duke Yǐn at the Wěi family's,
and established Zǐ Yǔn as ruler,
who was known as Duke Huán.
In the first year of Duke Huán,
Zhèng exchanged a jade disk for the king's field of Xǔ.
In the second year,
he brought the bribed tripod from Sòng into the ancestral temple,
which the gentlemen criticized.
In the third year,
he sent Huī to welcome a bride from Qí to be his wife.
In the sixth year,
the wife gave birth to a son,
on the same day as Duke Huán of Qí,
so he was named Tóng.
When Tóng grew up,
he was made crown prince.
In the sixteenth year,
a meeting was held in Cáo,
to attack Zhèng,
and restore Duke Lì.
In the spring of the eighteenth year,
the duke was about to travel,
and thus went to Qí with his wife.
Shēn Xū advised against it,
but the duke did not listen,
and proceeded to Qí.
Duke Xiāng of Qí had an affair with Duke Huán's wife.
The duke was angry with his wife,
and she informed the Marquis of Qí.
In the summer, on the bǐngzǐ day of the fourth month,
Duke Xiāng of Qí feasted the duke,
the duke became drunk,
and had the nobleman Péng Shēng carry Duke Huán of Lǔ,
then ordered Péng Shēng to break his ribs,
and the duke died in the carriage.
The people of Lǔ reported to Qí, saying:
"Our humble ruler, fearing your majesty's authority,
dared not remain idle at home,
and came to renew friendly relations.
The rites were completed, yet he did not return,
with no one to blame,
we request to have Péng Shēng to remove this disgrace among the feudal lords."
The people of Qí killed Péng Shēng to appease Lǔ.
Crown Prince Tóng was established,
this was Duke Zhuāng.
Duke Zhuāng's mother, the wife, remained in Qí,
not daring to return to Lǔ.
In the winter of Duke Zhuāng's fifth year,
they attacked Wèi,
and restored Duke Huì of Wèi.
In the eighth year,
the nobleman Jiǔ of Qí came fleeing.
In the ninth year,
Lǔ wanted to install Jiǔ in Qí,
but after Duke Huán,
Duke Huán raised troops to attack Lǔ,
Lǔ was in a crisis,
and killed Jiǔ.
Zhào Hū died.
Qí demanded Lǔ to deliver Guǎn Zhòng alive.
Shī Bó of Lǔ said:
"Qí wants Guǎn Zhòng,
not to kill him,
but to use him,
and if they use him, he will become a threat to Lǔ.
It would be better to kill him,
and give them his corpse."
Duke Zhuāng did not listen,
and instead imprisoned Guǎn Zhòng and sent him to Qí.
The people of Qí made Guǎn Zhòng chancellor.
In the thirteenth year,
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ met with Duke Huán of Qí at Kē, along with Cáo Mò,
Cáo Mò seized Duke Huán of Qí,
demanding the return of Lǔ's invaded territory,
and after the covenant was made, released Duke Huán.
Duke Huán wanted to break the covenant,
but Guǎn Zhòng advised against it,
and ultimately returned the invaded territory to Lǔ.
In the fifteenth year,
Duke Huán of Qí began his hegemony.
In the twenty-third year,
Duke Zhuāng went to Qí to observe the shè sacrifice.
In the thirty-second year,
earlier, Duke Zhuāng had built a terrace overlooking the Dǎng family,
where he saw the daughter of the Mèng family,
was pleased and loved her,
promising to make her his wife,
and cut his arm to swear an oath.
The daughter of the Mèng family gave birth to a son, Bān.
When Bān grew up,
he fancied a daughter of the Liáng family,
and went to see her.
The stableman Luò was flirting with the Liáng family daughter from outside the wall.
Bān was angry,
and whipped Luò.
Duke Zhuāng heard of this,
and said:
"Luò is a man of strength,
if you kill him, that's one thing,
but you cannot just whip him and let it be."
Bān had not yet managed to kill him.
Then Duke Zhuāng fell ill.
Duke Zhuāng had three younger brothers,
the eldest was Qìngfù,
the next was Shū Yá,
and the next was Jì Yǒu.
Duke Zhuāng took a woman from Qí as his wife, named Āi Jiāng.
Āi Jiāng had no sons.
Āi Jiāng's younger sister was Shū Jiāng,
who gave birth to a son, Kāi.
Duke Zhuāng had no legitimate heir,
and loved the daughter of the Mèng family,
wishing to establish her son Bān.
Duke Zhuāng was ill,
and asked about the succession from his younger brother Shū Yá.
Shū Yá said:
"Eldest son succeeds or younger brother succeeds,
is the common practice in Lǔ.
Qìngfù is here,
he can be the successor,
why should my lord worry?"
Duke Zhuāng was troubled that Shū Yá wanted to establish Qìngfù,
and after dismissing him, asked Jì Yǒu.
Jì Yǒu said:
"I beg to stake my life on establishing Bān."
Duke Zhuāng said:
"Earlier, Shū Yá wanted to establish Qìngfù,
what can be done?"
Jì Yǒu, using Duke Zhuāng's order, commanded Yá to wait at the Qián Wū family's residence,
and had Qián Jì force Shū Yá to drink poison,
saying:
"Drink this, and you will have descendants to continue your sacrifices;
if not,
you will die without descendants."
Yá then drank the poison and died,
and Lǔ established his son as the Shūsūn family.
On the guǐhài day of the eighth month,
Duke Zhuāng died,
and Jì Yǒu finally established Zǐ Bān as ruler,
according to Duke Zhuāng's command.
While attending the funeral,
he stayed at the Dǎng family's residence.
Previously, Qìngfù had been in an illicit relationship with Āi Jiāng,
and wanted to establish Āi Jiāng's sister's son Kāi.
When Duke Zhuāng died and Jì Yǒu established Bān,
on the jǐwèi day of the tenth month,
Qìngfù had the stableman Luò kill the Lǔ nobleman Bān at the Dǎng family's.
Jì Yǒu fled to Chén.
Qìngfù finally established Duke Zhuāng's son Kāi,
this was Duke Mǐn.
In the second year of Duke Mǐn,
Qìngfù's relationship with Āi Jiāng became even more intense.
Āi Jiāng conspired with Qìngfù to kill Duke Mǐn and establish Qìngfù.
Qìngfù had Bǔ Yǐ ambush and kill Duke Mǐn at the Wǔwéi gate.
Jì Yǒu heard of this,
and from Chén, went to Zhū with Duke Mǐn's younger brother Shēn,
requesting Lǔ to allow them to enter.
The people of Lǔ wanted to execute Qìngfù.
Qìngfù was afraid,
and fled to Jǔ.
Thereupon, Jì Yǒu escorted Zǐ Shēn into the state,
and established him,
this was Duke Xī.
Duke Xī was also a younger son of Duke Zhuāng.
Āi Jiāng was afraid,
and fled to Zhū.
Jì Yǒu went with bribes to Jǔ to seek Qìngfù,
Qìngfù returned,
and they sent someone to kill Qìngfù,
Qìngfù begged to be allowed to flee,
but they did not listen,
and instead sent the great officer Xī Sī to go weeping.
When Qìngfù heard Xī Sī's voice,
he then committed suicide.
Duke Huán of Qí heard that Āi Jiāng and Qìngfù's disorder had endangered Lǔ,
so summoned her from Zhū and killed her,
returning with her corpse,
and exposed it in Lǔ.
Duke Xī of Lǔ requested and buried her.
Jì Yǒu's mother was a woman from Chén,
so he had taken refuge in Chén,
and Chén consequently assisted in escorting Jì Yǒu and his son Shēn back.
Before Jì Yǒu was born,
his father, Duke Huán of Lǔ, had someone perform divination,
which said:
"It is a boy,
and his name shall be
'Yǒu',
he will stand between the two shrines,
and serve as a pillar to the ducal house.
If Jì Yǒu perishes,
then Lǔ will not prosper."
When he was born,
there was a mark on his palm resembling the character
"Yǒu",
so he was named accordingly,
and styled Chéng Jì.
His descendants became the Jì clan,
while Qìng Fǔ's line later became the Mèng clan.
In the first year of Duke Xī,
he enfeoffed Jì Yǒu with Wènyáng Bì.
Jì Yǒu served as chancellor.
In the ninth year,
Lǐ Kè of Jìn killed his rulers Xī Qí and
Zhuō Zǐ.
Duke Huán of Qí led Duke Xī to quell the turmoil in Jìn,
reaching Gāoliáng before returning,
and established Duke Huì of Jìn.
In the seventeenth year,
Duke Huán of Qí died.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn ascended the throne.
In the thirty-third year,
Duke Xī passed away,
and his son Xīng succeeded him,
known as Duke Wén.
In the first year of Duke Wén,
the Chǔ crown prince Shāng Chén assassinated his father King Chéng and
took the throne.
In the third year,
Duke Wén paid homage to Duke Xiāng of Jìn.
On the jiǎwǔ day of the tenth month in the eleventh year,
Lǔ defeated the Dí at Xián,
capturing the tall Dí leader Qiáo Rú,
Fùfǔ Zhōngshēng thrust at his throat,
and killed him with a dagger-axe,
burying his head at the Zǐjū Gate,
naming Xuān Bó after this event.
Earlier,
during the time of Duke Wǔ of Sòng,
Sōumán attacked Sòng,
Minister of War Huángfǔ led troops to resist them,
defeating the Dí at Chángqiū,
and captured the tall Dí leader Yuán Sī.
When Jìn destroyed Lù,
they captured Qiáo Rú's brother Fén Rú.
In the second year of Duke Huì of Qí,
Sōumán attacked Qí,
and Qí's Wángzǐ Chéngfù captured his brother Róng Rú,
burying his head at the North Gate.
The people of Wèi captured their youngest brother Jiǎn Rú.
Sōumán thus perished.
In the fifteenth year,
Jì Wénzǐ was sent on a mission to Jìn.
In the second month of the eighteenth year,
Duke Wén died.
Duke Wén had two consorts:
the elder, a woman from Qí named Āi Jiāng,
bore sons È and Shì;
the younger, Jìng Yíng,
was favored and beloved,
bearing a son Tuī.
Tuī privately served Xiāng Zhòng,
and Xiāng Zhòng wanted to install him,
but Shū Zhòng objected.
Xiāng Zhòng sought approval from Duke Huì of Qí,
who, newly enthroned,
wished to ally with Lǔ,
granted it.
In the tenth month of winter,
Xiāng Zhòng killed È and Shì and established Tuī,
who became Duke Xuān.
Āi Jiāng returned to Qí,
weeping as she passed through the market,
saying:
"Heavens!
Xiāng Zhòng has acted unjustly,
killing the rightful heir to establish a concubine's son!"
The market crowd all wept,
and the people of Lǔ called her
"Āi Jiāng".
From this, the ducal house of Lǔ declined,
and the Three Huáns grew powerful.
In the twelfth year of Duke Xuān Tuī,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ was strong,
and besieged Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng surrendered,
but was restored to his state.
In the eighteenth year,
Duke Xuān died,
and his son Duke Chéng Hēigōng succeeded him,
known as Duke Chéng.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
"It was Xiāng Zhòng who caused me to kill the rightful heir and establish a concubine's son, losing great support."
After Xiāng Zhòng established Duke Xuān,
Gōngsūn Guīfǔ enjoyed favor.
Duke Xuān wanted to eliminate the Three Huáns,
and plotted with Jìn to attack them.
But Duke Xuān died,
and Jì Wénzǐ resented this,
so Guīfǔ fled to Qí.
In the spring of the second year of Duke Chéng,
Qí attacked and captured our Lóng.
In summer, the duke together with Xì Kè of Jìn defeated Duke Qǐng of Qí at Ān,
and Qí returned our invaded territory.
In the fourth year,
Duke Chéng went to Jìn,
but Duke Jǐng of Jìn showed disrespect to Lǔ.
Lǔ considered betraying Jìn to ally with Chǔ,
but was advised against it,
and did not proceed.
In the tenth year,
Duke Chéng visited Jìn.
Duke Jǐng of Jìn died,
and Duke Chéng was detained to attend the funeral,
which Lǔ considered an embarrassment.
In the fifteenth year,
they first met with King Shòumèng of Wú at Zhōnglí.
In the sixteenth year,
Xuān Bó reported to Jìn,
seeking to have Jì Wénzǐ executed.
But Wénzǐ was righteous,
and the people of Jìn refused.
In the eighteenth year,
Duke Chéng died,
and his son Wǔ succeeded him,
known as Duke Xiāng.
At that time, Duke Xiāng was three years old.
In the first year of Duke Xiāng,
Jìn established Duke Dào.
The previous winter,
Luán Shū of Jìn had assassinated his ruler Duke Lì.
In the fourth year,
Duke Xiāng paid homage to Jìn.
In the fifth year,
Jì Wénzǐ died.
His household had no concubines clothed in silk,
his stables no horses fed on grain,
his treasury no gold or jade,
yet he served as chancellor to three rulers.
The gentleman said:
"Jì Wénzǐ was incorruptible and loyal."
In the ninth year,
they joined Jìn in attacking Zhèng.
Duke Dào of Jìn performed the capping ceremony for Duke Xiāng in Wèi,
with Jì Wǔzǐ accompanying,
assisting in the rites.
In the eleventh year,
the Three Huáns divided into three armies.
In the twelfth year,
they paid homage to Jìn.
In the sixteenth year,
Duke Píng of Jìn ascended the throne.
In the twenty-first year,
they paid homage to Duke Píng of Jìn.
In the twenty-second year,
Kǒng Qiū was born.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Cuī Zhù of Qí assassinated his ruler Duke Zhuāng,
and established his younger brother as Duke Jǐng.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Yánlíng Jìzǐ of Wú visited Lǔ,
inquired about the Zhōu music,
understood its meaning thoroughly,
and was respected by the people of Lǔ.
In the sixth month of the thirty-first year,
Duke Xiāng passed away.
In the ninth month of that year,
the crown prince died.
The people of Lǔ installed Chóu, son of Qí Guī, as ruler,
who became Duke Zhāo.
Duke Zhāo was nineteen years old,
yet still had a childlike heart.
Mù Shū did not wish to install him,
saying:
"When the crown prince dies,
if there is a full brother he can be installed;
otherwise, install the eldest.
If ages are equal, choose the worthy;
if virtue is equal, then divine it.
Now Chóu is not the rightful heir,
and moreover, during mourning his mind is not on grief but he has a joyful expression.
If he is indeed installed,
he will surely bring trouble to the Jì family."
Jì Wǔzǐ did not listen,
and finally installed him.
By the time of the burial,
he had changed mourning garments three times.
A nobleman remarked:
"This means he will not end well."
In the third year of Duke Zhāo,
he went to pay homage to Jìn but reached the river,
where Duke Píng of Jìn declined and sent him back,
which shamed Lǔ.
In the fourth year,
King Líng of Chǔ assembled the feudal lords at Shēn,
but Duke Zhāo claimed illness and did not go.
In the seventh year,
Jì Wǔzǐ died.
In the eighth year,
King Líng of Chǔ completed the Zhānghuá Terrace,
and summoned Duke Zhāo.
Duke Zhāo went to offer congratulations,
and was bestowed precious vessels;
but later the king regretted it,
and deceitfully took them back.
In the twelfth year,
he went to pay homage to Jìn and reached the river,
where Duke Píng of Jìn declined and sent him back.
In the thirteenth year,
the Chǔ prince Qìjí assassinated his ruler King Líng,
and took the throne.
In the fifteenth year,
he went to pay homage to Jìn,
and Jìn detained him to attend the burial of Duke Zhāo of Jìn,
which shamed Lǔ.
In the twentieth year,
Duke Jǐng of Qí and Yànzǐ hunted at the border,
and then entered Lǔ to inquire about rituals.
In the twenty-first year,
he went to pay homage to Jìn and reached the river,
where Jìn declined and sent him back.
In the spring of the twenty-fifth year,
magpies came to nest.
Shī Jǐ said:
"In the era of Duke Wén and Duke Chéng, a children's rhyme said:
'When magpies come to nest,
the duke is at Gānhóu.
When magpies enter to dwell,
the duke is in the wilds.'"
The Jì family and the Hòu family had a cockfight,
with the Jì family using mustard on their cock's feathers,
and the Hòu family using metal spurs.
Jì Píngzǐ was angry and encroached upon the Hòu family,
and Hòu Zhāobó was also angry with Píngzǐ.
Zāng Zhāobó's younger brother Huì falsely slandered the Zāng family,
and hid with the Jì family,
so Zāng Zhāobó imprisoned a man from the Jì family.
Jì Píngzǐ was angry,
and imprisoned an elder of the Zāng family.
The Zāng and Hòu families reported the trouble to Duke Zhāo.
Duke Zhāo attacked the Jì family on the wùxū day of the ninth month,
and entered their residence.
Píngzǐ ascended a platform and pleaded:
"My lord, due to slander, has not investigated my crime;
if you wish to execute me,
I beg to be exiled to the Yí River."
It was not allowed.
He begged to be imprisoned in Bì,
but it was not allowed.
He begged to leave with five chariots,
but it was not allowed.
Zǐjiā Jū said:
"My lord, you should allow it.
Governance has long been in the hands of the Jì family,
and their followers are many;
the multitude will unite in conspiracy."
He did not listen.
The Hòu family said:
"He must be killed."
Lì, a retainer of the Shūsūn family, said to his followers:
"Is it more beneficial with or without the Jì family?"
All said:
"Without the Jì family, there is no Shūsūn family."
Lì said:
"Indeed,
rescue the Jì family!"
Thus they defeated the duke's army.
Mèng Yìzǐ, hearing that the Shūsūn family had won,
also killed Hòu Zhāobó.
Hòu Zhāobó was on a mission for the duke,
so the Mèng family captured him.
The three families jointly attacked the duke,
and the duke fled.
On the jǐhài day,
the duke reached Qí.
Duke Jǐng of Qí said:
"I offer a thousand communities to host you."
Zǐjiā said:
"Abandoning the legacy of the Duke of Zhōu to become a subject of Qí—
is that acceptable?"
So he stopped.
Zǐjiā said:
"Duke Jǐng of Qí is untrustworthy;
it would be better to go to Jìn early."
He did not follow.
Shūsūn saw the duke and returned,
met Píngzǐ,
and Píngzǐ kowtowed.
Initially, they intended to welcome Duke Zhāo back,
but Mèngsūn
and Jìsūn later regretted it,
and stopped.
In the spring of the twenty-sixth year,
Qí attacked Lǔ,
captured Yùn, and settled Duke Zhāo there.
In summer, Duke Jǐng of Qí planned to restore the duke,
ordering that no bribes from Lǔ be accepted.
Shēn Fēng
and Rǔ Jiǎ promised the Qí officials Gāo Hé
and Zǐjiāng five thousand yǔ of grain.
Zǐjiāng said to the Marquis of Qí:
"Your ministers cannot serve the ruler of Lǔ,
as there are anomalies.
Duke Yuán of Sòng went to Jìn for Lǔ's sake,
seeking his restoration,
but died on the way.
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ sought to restore his ruler,
and died without illness.
Is it that Heaven has abandoned Lǔ,
or that the ruler of Lǔ has offended the spirits?
I hope you will wait."
Duke Jǐng of Qí followed this advice.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Duke Zhāo went to Jìn,
seeking restoration.
Jì Píngzǐ privately contacted the six ministers of Jìn,
who accepted bribes from the Jì family,
and advised the Jìn ruler,
so the Jìn ruler stopped,
and settled Duke Zhāo at Gānhóu.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Duke Zhāo went to Yùn.
Duke Jǐng of Qí sent someone with a letter for Duke Zhāo,
referring to himself
as "sovereign."
Duke Zhāo felt shamed,
angrily left for Gānhóu.
In the thirty-first year,
Jìn intended to restore Duke Zhāo,
and summoned Jì Píngzǐ.
Píngzǐ went in plain clothes and barefoot,
apologizing through the six ministers.
The six ministers spoke on his behalf:
"Jìn wishes to restore Duke Zhāo,
but the multitude does not comply."
The people of Jìn stopped.
In the thirty-second year,
Duke Zhāo died at Gānhóu.
The people of Lǔ jointly installed Duke Zhāo's younger brother Sòng as ruler,
who became Duke Dìng.
Duke Dìng was established,
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ asked Shǐ Mò:
"Will the Jì clan perish?"
Shǐ Mò replied:
"They will not perish.
Jì Yǒu had great achievements in Lǔ,
received Fèi as high minister,
reaching to Wénzǐ,
Wǔzǐ,
each generation expanded their enterprise.
When Duke Wén of Lǔ died,
Dōngmén Suì killed the legitimate heir and established a concubine's son,
whereupon the ruler of Lǔ lost the state's governance.
Governance lay with the Jì clan,
to this day through four rulers.
The people do not recognize the ruler,
how can one obtain the state!
Therefore a ruler must be cautious with vessels and titles,
and cannot lend them to others."
In the fifth year of Duke Dìng,
Jì Píngzǐ died.
Yáng Hǔ, bearing a private grudge,
imprisoned Jì Huánzǐ,
made a covenant with him,
and then released him.
In the seventh year,
Qí attacked us,
capturing Yùn,
making it Yáng Hǔ's town to conduct governance.
In the eighth year,
Yáng Hǔ wanted to completely kill the legitimate heirs of the Three Huán,
and instead establish their favored concubine sons to attack them;
he carried Jì Huánzǐ intending to kill him,
but Huánzǐ deceived him and managed to escape.
The Three Huán jointly attacked Yáng Hǔ,
Yáng Hǔ resided at Yángguān.
In the ninth year,
Lǔ attacked Yáng Hǔ,
Yáng Hǔ fled to Qí,
and later fled to the Zhào clan of Jìn.
In the tenth year,
Duke Dìng met with Duke Jǐng of Qí at Jiāgǔ,
Confucius served as master of ceremonies.
Qí wanted to ambush the ruler of Lǔ,
Confucius ascended the steps according to ritual,
condemned Qí's lewd music,
the Marquis of Qí feared,
and then stopped,
returning Lǔ's invaded territory and apologizing for the offense.
In the twelfth year,
Zhòng Yóu was sent to dismantle the Three Huán's city walls,
and collect their armor and weapons.
The Mèng clan refused to demolish their walls,
they were attacked,
but the attack was unsuccessful and stopped.
Jì Huánzǐ accepted Qí's female musicians,
Confucius departed.
In the fifteenth year,
Duke Dìng died,
his son Jiāng was established,
this was Duke Āi.
In the fifth year of Duke Āi,
Duke Jǐng of Qí died.
In the sixth year,
Tián Qǐ of Qí assassinated his ruler Rúzǐ.
In the seventh year,
King Fūchāi of Wú was powerful,
attacked Qí,
reached Zēng,
and demanded one hundred sets of sacrificial animals from Lǔ.
Jì Kāngzǐ sent Zǐgòng to persuade the King of Wú and Grand Steward Pǐ,
using ritual to refute them.
The King of Wú said:
"I am tattooed,
not worthy of being reproached about ritual."
Then he stopped.
In the eighth year,
Wú attacked Lǔ for Zōu,
reached the city walls,
made a covenant and left.
Qí attacked us,
capturing three towns.
In the tenth year,
we attacked Qí's southern border.
In the eleventh year,
Qí attacked Lǔ.
The Jì clan employed Rǎn Yǒu with success,
longed for Confucius,
Confucius returned to Lǔ from Wèi.
In the fourteenth year,
Tián Cháng of Qí assassinated his ruler Duke Jiǎn at Xúzhōu.
Confucius requested to attack him,
but Duke Āi would not listen.
In the fifteenth year,
Zǐfú Jǐngbó was sent,
with Zǐgòng as deputy,
to Qí,
Qí returned our invaded territory.
Tián Cháng had just become minister,
and wanted to befriend the feudal lords.
In the sixteenth year,
Confucius died.
In the twenty-second year,
King Gōujiàn of Yuè destroyed King Fūchāi of Wú.
In the twenty-seventh year spring,
Jì Kāngzǐ died.
In summer, Duke Āi worried about the Three Huán,
intending to use the feudal lords to coerce them,
the Three Huán also worried about the duke causing trouble,
so there was much estrangement between ruler and ministers.
The duke was traveling at Língbǎn,
met Mèng Wǔbó on the street,
and said:
"May I ask, will I die a good death?"
He replied:
"I do not know."
The duke wanted to use Yuè to attack the Three Huán.
In August,
Duke Āi went to the Xíng clan.
The Three Huán attacked the duke,
the duke fled to Wèi,
left for Zōu,
and then went to Yuè.
The people of the state welcomed Duke Āi back,
and he died at the Yǒushān clan.
His son Níng was established,
this was Duke Dào.
During Duke Dào's time,
the Three Huán prevailed,
Lǔ was like a small marquisate,
inferior to the Three Huán families.
In the thirteenth year,
the Three Jìn destroyed Zhì Bó,
and divided his territory among themselves.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Duke Dào died,
his son Jiā was established,
this was Duke Yuán.
Duke Yuán died in the twenty-first year,
his son Xiǎn was established,
this was Duke Mù.
Duke Mù died in the thirty-third year,
his son Fèn was established,
this was Duke Gòng.
Duke Gòng died in the twenty-second year,
his son Tún was established,
this was Duke Kāng.
Duke Kāng died in the ninth year,
his son Yǎn was established,
this was Duke Jǐng.
Duke Jǐng died in the twenty-ninth year,
his son Shū was established,
this was Duke Píng.
At this time, the six states all claimed kingship.
In the twelfth year of Duke Píng,
King Huì of Qín died.
In the twentieth year,
Duke Píng died,
his son Jiǎ was established,
this was Duke Wén.
In the first year of Duke Wén,
King Huái of Chǔ died in Qín.
In the twenty-third year,
Duke Wén died,
his son Chóu was established,
this was Duke Qǐng.
In the second year of Duke Qǐng,
Qín captured Chǔ's Yǐng,
King Qǐng of Chǔ moved east to Chén.
In the nineteenth year,
Chǔ attacked us,
capturing Xúzhōu.
In the twenty-fourth year,
King Kǎoliè of Chǔ attacked and destroyed Lǔ.
Duke Qǐng fled,
was moved to a minor town,
became a commoner,
Lǔ's sacrifices were cut off.
Duke Qǐng died at Kē.
Lǔ from the Duke of Zhōu to Duke Qǐng,
altogether thirty-four generations.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I have heard Confucius exclaim,
"How extreme was the decline of the ways of Lǔ!
Between the Zhū and Sì rivers, there was constant bickering."
Observing the circumstances of Qìngfù, Shūyá, and Mǐn Gōng,
how chaotic they were!
The affairs of Yǐn and Huán;
Xiāng Zhòng killing the legitimate heir and establishing a concubine's son;
the three families serving as ministers facing north,
personally attacking Zhāo Gōng,
causing Zhāo Gōng to flee.
As for their ceremonial etiquette of bowing and yielding, they followed it,
yet in their actions, how contrary they were!
Shào Gōng Shì was of the same surname as the Zhōu,
bearing the surname Jī.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu destroyed Zhòu,
he enfeoffed Shào Gōng in Northern Yān.
During the time of King Chéng,
Shào Gōng was one of the Three Dukes:
west of Shǎn,
Shào Gōng presided;
east of Shǎn,
Zhōu Gōng presided.
King Chéng being young,
Zhōu Gōng acted as regent,
governing the state and ascending the throne,
Shào Gōng doubted him,
and composed the "Jūn Shì."
The "Jūn Shì" expressed displeasure with Zhōu Gōng.
Zhōu Gōng then declared,
"In the time of Tāng, there was Yī Yǐn,
who communed with the August Heaven;
in the time of Tài Wù,
there were the likes of Yī Zhì,
Chén Hù,
who communed with the Supreme Deity,
and Wū Xián, who governed the royal house;
in the time of Zǔ Yǐ,
there was the like of Wū Xián;
in the time of Wǔ Dīng,
there was the like of Gān Pán:
all these had their ministers in array,
protecting and governing Yīn."
Thereupon, Shào Gōng was pleased.
Shào Gōng's governance of the western regions
greatly won the harmony of the myriad people.
When Shào Gōng toured the villages and towns,
there was a pear tree,
under which he adjudicated legal cases and conducted government affairs,
from nobles to commoners, each found their proper place,
with none neglecting their duties.
After Shào Gōng's death,
the people remembered Shào Gōng's governance,
cherished the pear tree and dared not cut it down,
sang of it,
and composed the poem "Gāntáng."
From Shào Gōng down, nine generations passed to Huì Hóu.
Yān Huì Hóu's time coincided with King Lì of Zhōu fleeing to Zhì,
during the period of the Republic.
Huì Hóu died,
and his son Xī Hóu succeeded.
That year,
King Xuān of Zhōu first ascended the throne.
In the twenty-first year of Xī Hóu,
Zhèng Huán Gōng was first enfeoffed in Zhèng.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Xī Hóu died,
and his son Qǐng Hóu succeeded.
In the twentieth year of Qǐng Hóu,
King Yōu of Zhōu was licentious and disorderly,
and was killed by the Quǎn Róng.
Qín began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Qǐng Hóu died,
and his son Āi Hóu succeeded.
Āi Hóu died in his second year,
and his son Zhèng Hóu succeeded.
Zhèng Hóu died in his thirty-sixth year,
and his son Mù Hóu succeeded.
In the seventh year of Mù Hóu,
it was the first year of Lord Yǐn of Lǔ.
He died in the eighteenth year,
and his son Xuān Hóu succeeded.
Xuān Hóu died in the thirteenth year,
and his son Huán Hóu succeeded.
Huán Hóu died in the seventh year,
and his son Zhuāng Gōng succeeded.
In the twelfth year of Zhuāng Gōng,
Qí Huán Gōng began his hegemony.
In the sixteenth year,
together with Sòng
and Wèi, they attacked King Huì of Zhōu,
King Huì fled to Wēn,
and they established King Huì's brother Tuí as King of Zhōu.
In the seventeenth year,
Zhèng captured Yān Zhòngfù and restored King Huì to Zhōu.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the Shān Róng came to invade us,
Qí Huán Gōng rescued Yān,
then marched north to attack the Shān Róng and returned.
The Lord of Yān escorted Qí Huán Gōng out of the border,
Huán Gōng thus ceded the territory he had reached to Yān,
ordering Yān to jointly pay tribute to the Son of Heaven,
as in the duties of the Chéng Zhōu era;
and had Yān restore the laws of Shào Gōng.
He died in the thirty-third year,
and his son Xiāng Gōng succeeded.
In the twenty-sixth year of Xiāng Gōng,
Jìn Wén Gōng held the meeting at Jiàntǔ,
proclaiming himself Hegemon.
In the thirty-first year,
the Qín army was defeated at Xiáo.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Qín Mù Gōng died.
In the fortieth year,
Xiāng Gōng died,
and Huán Gōng succeeded.
Huán Gōng died in the sixteenth year,
and Xuān Gōng succeeded.
Xuān Gōng died in the fifteenth year,
and Zhāo Gōng succeeded.
Zhāo Gōng died in the thirteenth year,
and Wǔ Gōng succeeded.
That year, Jìn exterminated the three Xì great officers.
Wǔ Gōng died in the nineteenth year,
and Wén Gōng succeeded.
Wén Gōng died in the sixth year,
and Yì Gōng succeeded.
In the first year of Yì Gōng,
Qí Cuī Zhù assassinated his lord Zhuāng Gōng.
He died in the fourth year,
and his son Huì Gōng succeeded.
In the first year of Huì Gōng,
Qí Gāo Zhǐ came fleeing.
In the sixth year,
Huì Gōng had many favored concubines,
he wanted to remove the various great officers and establish his favored concubine Sòng,
the great officers jointly executed Concubine Sòng,
Huì Gōng feared,
and fled to Qí.
In the fourth year,
Qí Gāo Yǎn went to Jìn,
requesting to jointly attack Yān,
and restore their lord.
Jìn Píng Gōng agreed,
and together with Qí attacked Yān,
restoring Huì Gōng.
Huì Gōng reached Yān and died.
Yān established Dào Gōng.
Dào Gōng died in the seventh year,
and Gòng Gōng succeeded.
Gòng Gōng died in the fifth year,
and Píng Gōng succeeded.
The Jìn ducal house was humbled,
and the Six Ministers began to grow powerful.
In the eighteenth year of Píng Gōng,
the King of Wú Hé Lǘ broke Chǔ and entered Yǐng.
He died in the nineteenth year,
and Jiǎn Gōng succeeded.
Jiǎn Gōng died in the twelfth year,
and Xiàn Gōng succeeded.
Jìn Zhào Yǎng besieged Fàn
and Zhōngháng at Zhāogē.
In the twelfth year of Xiàn Gōng,
Qí Tián Cháng assassinated his lord Jiǎn Gōng.
In the fourteenth year,
Confucius died.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Xiàn Gōng died,
and Xiào Gōng succeeded.
In the twelfth year of Xiào Gōng,
Hán, Wèi,
and Zhào destroyed Zhì Bó,
divided his territory,
and the Three Jìn became powerful.
In the fifteenth year,
Duke Xiào died,
and Duke Chéng took the throne.
Duke Chéng died in the sixteenth year of his reign,
and Duke Mǐn took the throne.
Duke Mǐn died in the thirty-first year of his reign,
and Duke Xī took the throne.
That year,
the three states of Jìn were ranked among the feudal lords.
In the thirtieth year of Duke Xī's reign,
Yān attacked and defeated Qí at Línyíng.
Duke Xī died,
and Duke Huán took the throne.
Duke Huán died in the eleventh year of his reign,
and Duke Wén took the throne.
That year,
Duke Xiàn of Qín died.
Qín grew stronger.
In the nineteenth year of Duke Wén's reign,
King Wēi of Qí died.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Sū Qín first came for an audience,
and persuaded Duke Wén.
Duke Wén gave him carriages, horses, gold, and silk to go to Zhào,
where King Sù of Zhào employed him.
Thereupon, he formed an alliance of the six states,
serving as the leader of the vertical coalition.
King Huì of Qín gave his daughter in marriage to the crown prince of Yān.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Duke Wén died,
and the crown prince ascended the throne,
known as King Yì.
Soon after King Yì took the throne,
King Xuān of Qí took advantage of Yān's mourning period to attack us,
capturing ten cities;
Sū Qín persuaded Qí,
causing them to return the ten cities to Yān.
In the tenth year,
the ruler of Yān became king.
Sū Qín had a secret affair with the wife of Duke Wén of Yān,
and fearing execution,
he persuaded the king to send him to Qí as a double agent,
intending to sow chaos in Qí.
King Yì died after twelve years on the throne,
and his son Yān Kuài succeeded him.
After Yān Kuài ascended the throne,
the people of Qí killed Sū Qín.
While Sū Qín was in Yān,
he formed a marriage alliance with the chancellor Zǐzhī,
and Sū Dài was friends with Zǐzhī.
After Sū Qín's death,
King Xuān of Qí again employed Sū Dài.
In the third year of Yān Kuài's reign,
Yān allied with Chǔ
and the three states of Jìn to attack Qín,
but returned without victory.
Zǐzhī served as chancellor of Yān,
holding high status and authority,
and making decisive judgments.
When Sū Dài was sent as an envoy from Qí to Yān,
the King of Yān asked him:
"What is the King of Qí like?"
He replied:
"He will certainly not achieve hegemony."
The King of Yān asked:
"Why?"
He replied:
"He does not trust his ministers."
Sū Dài intended to stimulate the King of Yān to honor Zǐzhī.
Thereupon, the King of Yān greatly trusted Zǐzhī.
Zǐzhī then gave Sū Dài a hundred pieces of gold,
and allowed him to do as he pleased.
Lù Máo Shòu said to the King of Yān:
"It would be better to yield the state to Chancellor Zǐzhī.
People say Yáo was worthy
because he yielded the empire to Xǔ Yóu,
and Xǔ Yóu did not accept it,
so Yáo gained the reputation of yielding the empire without actually losing it.
Now if Your Majesty yields the state to Zǐzhī,
Zǐzhī certainly would not dare accept it,
and thus Your Majesty would be acting like Yáo."
The King of Yān then entrusted the state to Zǐzhī,
and Zǐzhī became extremely powerful.
Someone said:
"Yǔ recommended Yì,
but then appointed Qǐ's men as officials.
When he grew old,
he considered Qǐ's men insufficient to govern the empire,
so he passed the throne to Yì.
Later, Qǐ and his faction attacked Yì,
and seized the throne from him.
The world says Yǔ nominally passed the empire to Yì,
but in reality allowed Qǐ to take it himself.
Now when Your Majesty says you are entrusting the state to Zǐzhī,
yet all the officials are the crown prince's men,
this is nominally entrusting it to Zǐzhī while in reality the crown prince holds power."
The king then collected the seals of all officials of three hundred dàn rank and above and presented them to Zǐzhī.
Zǐzhī faced south and acted as king,
while Kuài, grown old, no longer attended to governance,
but became a subject,
and all state affairs were decided by Zǐzhī.
After three years,
the state fell into great chaos,
and the common people were terrified.
General Shì Bèi conspired with Crown Prince Píng,
planning to attack Zǐzhī.
The generals said to King Mǐn of Qí:
"If we take advantage of this opportunity to intervene,
we will certainly crush Yān."
The King of Qí then sent someone to tell Crown Prince Píng of Yān:
"I have heard of your righteousness, Crown Prince,
that you will abolish private interests and establish public good,
rectify the principles of ruler and minister,
and clarify the positions of father and son.
My state is small,
and insufficient to serve as your vanguard or rearguard.
Nevertheless,
I will follow whatever orders you give."
The crown prince then gathered partisans and masses,
and General Shì Bèi besieged the ducal palace,
attacking Zǐzhī,
but did not prevail.
General Shì Bèi and the common people turned to attack Crown Prince Píng,
General Shì Bèi died,
and his body was displayed as a warning.
Thus, strife continued for several months,
tens of thousands died,
the masses were terrified,
and the common people became disheartened.
Mèng Kē said to the King of Qí:
"To attack Yān now
is an opportunity like that of King Wén
and King Wǔ;
it must not be lost."
The king then ordered Zhāngzǐ to lead the troops of the five capitals,
and, with the forces of the northern territories, to attack Yān.
The soldiers did not fight,
the city gates were not closed,
the ruler of Yān, Kuài, died,
and Qí won a great victory.
Two years after the death of Zǐzhī of Yān,
the people of Yān together established Crown Prince Píng,
who became King Zhāo of Yān.
King Zhāo of Yān ascended the throne after Yān's defeat,
humbling himself and offering generous rewards to attract worthy men.
He said to Guō Wěi:
"Qí took advantage of our state's turmoil to attack and crush Yān;
I am well aware that Yān is small and weak,
and insufficient for revenge.
But if I can truly obtain worthy scholars to share the governance of the state,
and to wipe away the shame of the former king,
that is my wish.
Sir, if you see anyone suitable,
I will personally serve him."
Guō Wěi said:
"If Your Majesty truly wishes to attract scholars,
start with Wěi.
How much more would those worthier than Wěi
regard a thousand lǐ as too far!"
Thereupon, King Zhāo built a new palace for Wěi and served him as a teacher.
Yuè Yì came from Wèi,
Zōu Yǎn came from Qí,
Jù Xīn came from Zhào,
and scholars competed to go to Yān.
The King of Yān mourned the dead and cared for the orphaned,
sharing weal and woe with the common people.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Yān became prosperous and wealthy,
and the soldiers were eager and lighthearted about battle.
Thereupon, Yuè Yì was appointed supreme general,
and together with Qín,
Chǔ, and the three states of Jìn, plotted to attack Qí.
The Qí army was defeated,
and King Mǐn fled into exile.
The Yān army alone pursued the defeated forces northward,
entering as far as Línzī,
taking all of Qí's treasures,
and burning its palaces and ancestral temples.
Of the cities of Qí that did not fall,
only Liáo,
Jǔ, and Jímò remained,
all the others belonged to Yān,
for six years.
King Zhāo died in the thirty-third year of his reign,
and his son King Huì took the throne.
When King Huì was crown prince,
he had a grudge against Yuè Yì;
upon ascending the throne,
he grew suspicious of Yì,
appointing Qí Jié to replace him as commander.
Yuè Yì fled to Zhào.
Tián Dān of Qí, from Jímò, defeated the Yān army,
Qí Jié perished,
the Yān troops withdrew and returned,
and Qí fully recovered its former cities.
King Mǐn died in Jǔ,
so his son was established as King Xiāng.
In the seventh year of King Huì, he passed away.
Hán, Wèi,
and Chǔ jointly attacked Yān.
King Wǔchéng of Yān was enthroned.
In the seventh year of King Wǔchéng,
Qí's Tián Dān attacked us,
capturing Zhōngyáng.
In the thirteenth year,
Qín defeated Zhào at Chángpíng, with over 400,000 casualties.
In the fourteenth year,
King Wǔchéng died,
and his son King Xiào succeeded him.
In the first year of King Xiào,
the Qín siege of Hándān was lifted and they withdrew.
In the third year, he died,
and his son, the current king Xǐ, was enthroned.
In the fourth year of the current king Xǐ,
King Zhāo of Qín died.
The king of Yān ordered his chancellor Lì Fù to make a friendly pact with Zhào,
presenting 500 jin of gold for the king of Zhào's banquet.
Upon returning, he reported to the king of Yān:
"The strong men of Zhào all died at Chángpíng,
their orphans are not yet grown,
so we can attack them."
The king summoned Lè Xián, lord of Chāngguó, to inquire.
He replied:
"Zhào is a state accustomed to war on all fronts,
its people are trained in arms,
we cannot attack them."
The king said:
"I would use five to attack one."
He replied:
"It cannot be done."
The king of Yān was angered,
and all his ministers believed it feasible.
Eventually, two armies were raised,
with 2,000 chariots,
Lì Fù leading to attack Hào,
and Qīng Qín attacking Dài.
Only senior official Jiàng Qú said to the king of Yān:
"Having opened borders and made a pact with others,
presenting 500 jin for their king's drink,
then upon the envoy's return attacking them—
it is inauspicious,
the army will not succeed."
The king of Yān did not listen,
personally leading a flank army to follow.
Jiàng Qú grabbed the king's sash to stop him, saying:
"Your Majesty must not go personally,
if you go, you will not succeed."
The king kicked him with his foot.
Jiàng Qú wept, saying:
"It is not for my own sake,
but for Your Majesty!"
The Yān army reached Sòngzǐ,
Zhào sent Lián Pō to command,
who defeated Lì Fù at Hào.
Yuè Chéng defeated Qīng Qín at Dài.
Lè Xián fled to Zhào.
Lián Pō pursued them over 500 li,
besieging their capital.
The people of Yān sought peace,
but those of Zhào would not allow it,
insisting that Jiàng Qú handle the peace.
The Yān chancellor Jiàng Qú thus managed the peace.
Zhào heeded Jiàng Qú,
and lifted the siege of Yān.
In the sixth year,
Qín extinguished Eastern Zhōu,
establishing the Sānchuān Commandery.
In the seventh year,
Qín captured Yúcì and 37 cities from Zhào,
and Qín established the Tàiyuán Commandery.
In the ninth year,
King Zhèng of Qín first ascended the throne.
In the tenth year,
Zhào sent Lián Pō to attack Fányáng,
and he captured it.
King Xiàochéng of Zhào died,
and King Dàoxiāng was enthroned.
He sent Yuè Chéng to replace Lián Pō,
but Lián Pō refused to obey,
attacked Yuè Chéng,
Yuè Chéng fled,
and Lián Pō fled to Dàliáng.
In the twelfth year,
Zhào sent Lǐ Mù to attack Yān,
capturing Wǔsuì
and Fāngchéng.
Jù Xīn had formerly lived in Zhào,
and was friendly with Páng Xuān,
but later fled to Yān.
Yān, seeing Zhào repeatedly hard-pressed by Qín,
and Lián Pō gone,
with Páng Xuān now commanding,
wished to take advantage of Zhào's exhaustion to attack.
They consulted Jù Xīn,
who said:
"Páng Xuān is easy to deal with."
Yān sent Jù Xīn to command an attack on Zhào,
Zhào sent Páng Xuān to counterattack,
capturing 10,000 Yān troops,
and killing Jù Xīn.
Qín captured 20 cities from Wèi,
establishing the Dōng Commandery.
In the nineteenth year,
Qín captured Yè and nine cities from Zhào.
King Dàoxiāng of Zhào died.
In the twenty-third year,
Crown Prince Dān was a hostage in Qín,
but fled back to Yān.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Qín captured and extinguished Hán's King Ān,
establishing the Yǐngchuān Commandery.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Qín captured King Qiān of Zhào,
extinguishing Zhào.
Prince Jiā of Zhào proclaimed himself king of Dài.
Yān saw that Qín was about to extinguish the six states,
with Qín troops reaching the Yì River,
and disaster impending for Yān.
Crown Prince Dān secretly nurtured 20 stalwart men,
sending Jīng Kē to present the Dūkāng map to Qín,
intending to assassinate the king of Qín.
The king of Qín detected it,
killed Kē,
and sent General Wáng Jiǎn to attack Yān.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Qín attacked and captured our Jì,
the king of Yān fled,
moving to Liáodōng,
and executed Dān to offer to Qín.
In the thirtieth year,
Qín extinguished Wèi.
In the thirty-third year,
Qín captured Liáodōng,
took King Xǐ of Yān captive,
and finally extinguished Yān.
That year,
the Qín general Wáng Bēn also captured King Jiā of Dài.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Shào Gōng Shì can be called benevolent indeed!
The sweet pear tree is still remembered,
how much more so the man himself?
Yān was externally pressed by the barbarians,
internally situated with Qí
and Jìn, navigating perilously among powerful states,
being the smallest and weakest,
and nearly extinguished several times.
Yet the state endured for eight or nine hundred years,
among the Jī surname states it was the last to perish,
was this not the achievement of Shào Gōng?
Guǎn Shū Xiān
and Cài Shū Dù
were sons of King Wén of Zhōu and younger brothers of King Wǔ.
King Wǔ had ten brothers of the same mother.
Their mother was Tài Sì,
the principal consort of King Wén.
The eldest was Bó Yì Kǎo,
next was King Wǔ Fā,
next was Guǎn Shū Xiān,
next was Zhōu Gōng Dàn,
next was Cài Shū Dù,
next was Cáo Shū Zhènduó,
next was Chéng Shū Wǔ,
next was Huò Shū Chǔ,
next was Kāng Shū Fēng,
next was Rǎn Jì Zǎi.
Rǎn Jì Zǎi was the youngest.
These ten were brothers of the same mother,
only Fā
and Dàn were worthy,
assisting King Wén on his left and right,
so King Wén passed over Bó Yì Kǎo and made Fā the crown prince.
When King Wén died and Fā succeeded,
he became King Wǔ.
Bó Yì Kǎo had already died earlier.
King Wǔ, having overthrown King Zhòu of Yīn,
pacified the realm,
and enfeoffed his meritorious ministers and brothers.
Thus, he enfeoffed Shū Xiǎn in Guǎn,
and Shū Dù in Cài:
these two oversaw Wǔ Gēng Lù Fù, the son of Zhòu,
governing the remaining people of Yīn.
He enfeoffed Shū Dàn in Lǔ and made him regent of Zhōu,
known as the Duke of Zhōu.
He enfeoffed Shū Zhènduó in Cáo,
Shū Wǔ in Chéng,
and Shū Chǔ in Huò.
Kāng Shū Fēng and
Rǎn Jì Zǎi were both young,
and had not yet received fiefs.
After King Wǔ passed away,
King Chéng was young,
so the Duke of Zhōu, Dàn, took charge of the royal house.
Guǎn Shū and
Cài Shū suspected the Duke of Zhōu of acting against King Chéng's interests,
so they joined forces with Wǔ Gēng to rebel.
The Duke of Zhōu, Dàn, under King Chéng's orders, attacked and executed Wǔ Gēng,
killed Guǎn Shū,
and exiled Cài Shū,
relocating him
with ten chariots
and seventy followers.
He divided the remaining people of Yīn into two parts:
one part enfeoffed Wēizǐ Qǐ in Sòng,
to continue the sacrifices of Yīn;
the other part enfeoffed Kāng Shū as the ruler of Wèi,
known as Wèi Kāng Shū.
He enfeoffed Jì Zǎi in Rǎn.
Rǎn Jì and
Kāng Shū both had virtuous conduct,
so the Duke of Zhōu appointed Kāng Shū as Minister of Justice of Zhōu,
and Rǎn Jì as Minister of Works of Zhōu,
to assist King Chéng in governance,
and both gained good reputations throughout the realm.
Cài Shū Dù died after his relocation.
His son was named Hú,
and Hú reformed his behavior,
practicing virtue and goodness.
The Duke of Zhōu heard of this,
and promoted Hú to be a high minister in Lǔ,
where the state was well-governed.
Then the Duke of Zhōu spoke to King Chéng,
and re-enfeoffed Hú in Cài,
to continue the sacrifices of Cài Shū,
known as Cài Zhòng.
The other five uncles all went to their states,
with none serving as officials of the Son of Heaven.
Cài Zhòng passed away,
and his son Cài Bó Huāng succeeded him.
Cài Bó Huāng passed away,
and his son Gōng Hóu succeeded him.
Gōng Hóu passed away,
and his son Lì Hóu succeeded him.
Lì Hóu passed away,
and his son Wǔ Hóu succeeded him.
During Wǔ Hóu's time,
King Lì of Zhōu lost his state,
fled to Zhì,
and the Regency was established,
with many feudal lords rebelling against Zhōu.
Wǔ Hóu passed away,
and his son Yí Hóu succeeded him.
In the eleventh year of Yí Hóu,
King Xuān of Zhōu ascended the throne.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Yí Hóu passed away,
and his son Xī Hóu Suǒshì succeeded him.
In the thirty-ninth year of Xī Hóu,
King Yōu of Zhōu was killed by the Quǎnróng,
and the Zhōu house declined and moved east.
Qín began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the forty-eighth year,
Xī Hóu passed away,
and his son Gòng Hóu Xīng succeeded him.
Gòng Hóu passed away after two years,
and his son Dài Hóu succeeded him.
Dài Hóu passed away in the tenth year,
and his son Xuān Hóu Cuòfù succeeded him.
In the twenty-eighth year of Xuān Hóu,
Duke Yǐn of Lǔ first ascended the throne.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Xuān Hóu passed away,
and his son Huán Hóu Fēngrén succeeded him.
In the third year of Huán Hóu,
Lǔ assassinated its ruler Duke Yǐn.
In the twentieth year,
Huán Hóu passed away,
and his younger brother Āi Hóu Xiànwǔ succeeded him.
In the eleventh year of Āi Hóu,
initially, Āi Hóu married a woman from Chén,
and Xī Hóu also married a woman from Chén.
When the wife of Xī Hóu was returning,
she passed through Cài,
and the Marquis of Cài was disrespectful.
Xī Hóu was angered,
and requested of King Wén of Chǔ:
"Come and attack me,
I will seek help from Cài,
Cài will surely come,
and Chǔ can then attack them,
which may lead to success."
King Wén of Chǔ agreed,
captured Āi Hóu of Cài, and took him back.
Āi Hóu remained for nine years,
and died in Chǔ.
In total, he reigned for twenty years before his death.
The people of Cài established his son Xī as ruler,
known as Mù Hóu.
Mù Hóu gave his younger sister as a wife to Duke Huán of Qí.
In the eighteenth year,
Duke Huán of Qí was frolicking on a boat with the woman from Cài,
the lady rocked the boat,
Duke Huán stopped her,
but she did not cease,
so the duke grew angry,
and sent the Cài woman back but did not sever relations.
The Marquis of Cài was angered,
and married his sister to another.
Duke Huán of Qí was enraged,
attacked Cài;
Cài collapsed,
and he captured Mù Hóu,
going south to Shàolíng in Chǔ.
Later, the feudal lords interceded for Cài with Qí,
and the Marquis of Qí returned the Marquis of Cài.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Mù Hóu passed away,
and his son Zhuāng Hóu Jiǎwǔ succeeded him.
In the third year of Zhuāng Hóu,
Duke Huán of Qí passed away.
In the fourteenth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn defeated Chǔ at Chéngpú.
In the twentieth year,
the crown prince of Chǔ, Shāngchén, assassinated his father King Chéng and succeeded him.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Duke Mù of Qín passed away.
In the thirty-third year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ ascended the throne.
In the thirty-fourth year,
Zhuāng Hóu passed away,
and his son Wén Hóu Shēn succeeded him.
In the fourteenth year of Wén Hóu,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Chén,
and killed Xià Zhēngshū.
In the fifteenth year,
Chǔ besieged Zhèng,
Zhèng surrendered to Chǔ,
and Chǔ released them.
In the twentieth year,
Wén Hóu passed away,
and his son Jǐng Hóu Gù succeeded him.
In the first year of Jǐng Hóu,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ passed away.
In the forty-ninth year,
Jǐng Hóu arranged a marriage for his crown prince Bān with a woman from Chǔ,
but Jǐng Hóu had an affair with her.
The crown prince assassinated Jǐng Hóu and proclaimed himself,
known as Líng Hóu.
In the second year of Líng Hóu,
the noble Wéi of Chǔ assassinated his king Jiá Áo and proclaimed himself,
becoming King Líng.
In the ninth year,
the Minister of War Zhāo of Chén assassinated his ruler Duke Āi.
Chǔ sent the noble Qìjí to destroy Chén and take possession of it.
In the twelfth year,
King Líng of Chǔ, on the grounds that Líng Hóu had killed his father,
lured Líng Hóu of Cài to Shēn,
set up ambushed soldiers and feasted him,
got him drunk and killed him,
and executed seventy of his soldiers.
He ordered the noble Qìjí to besiege Cài.
In the eleventh month,
Cài was destroyed,
and Qìjí was made Duke of Cài.
Three years after Chǔ destroyed Cài,
Prince Qìjí of Chǔ assassinated his sovereign King Líng and took the throne,
becoming King Píng.
King Píng then sought out Lú, the youngest son of Marquis Jǐng of Cài,
and established him,
who became Marquis Píng.
That same year,
Chǔ also restored Chén.
King Píng of Chǔ, newly enthroned,
wished to build goodwill with the feudal lords,
hence he restored the successors of Chén
and Cài.
Marquis Píng died after nine years,
and Dōngguó, grandson of Marquis Bān of Líng, attacked Marquis Píng's son and seized the throne himself,
becoming Marquis Dào.
Marquis Dào's father was called Crown Prince Yǒu, the hidden heir.
Crown Prince Yǒu, the hidden heir,
was the crown son of Marquis Líng.
When Marquis Píng was established, he killed the hidden crown prince,
so after Marquis Píng's death, Dōngguó, son of the hidden crown prince, attacked Marquis Píng's son and replaced him,
becoming Marquis Dào.
Marquis Dào died after three years,
and his younger brother Shēn, Marquis Zhāo, succeeded him.
In the tenth year of Marquis Zhāo,
he paid homage to King Zhāo of Chǔ,
bringing two fine fur robes,
presenting one to King Zhāo and wearing the other himself.
The Chǔ chancellor Zǐchǎng desired it,
but was not given it.
Zǐchǎng slandered the Marquis of Cài,
detaining him in Chǔ for three years.
The Marquis of Cài, realizing this,
then presented his robe to Zǐchǎng;
Zǐchǎng accepted it,
and then spoke for the Marquis of Cài's return.
The Marquis of Cài returned and went to Jìn,
requesting to join Jìn in attacking Chǔ.
In the spring of the thirteenth year,
he met with Duke Líng of Wèi at Shàolíng.
The Marquis of Cài privately sought to outrank Wèi through Zhǎohóng of Zhōu;
Wèi sent Shǐqiū to speak of the merits and virtues of Kāngshū,
and thus Wèi was given precedence.
In summer, Cài destroyed Shěn for Jìn,
angering Chǔ,
which attacked Cài.
Marquis Zhāo of Cài sent his son as a hostage to Wú,
to jointly attack Chǔ.
In winter, together with King Hélǘ of Wú, they defeated Chǔ and entered Yǐng.
Cài harbored resentment against Zǐchǎng,
who, in fear,
fled to Zhèng.
In the fourteenth year,
Wú withdrew and King Zhāo of Chǔ restored his state.
In the sixteenth year,
the Chǔ prime minister wept for his people while plotting against Cài,
and Marquis Zhāo of Cài grew fearful.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Confucius went to Cài.
King Zhāo of Chǔ attacked Cài,
which, in fear,
appealed urgently to Wú for help.
Wú found Cài too distant,
so proposed relocating it closer,
to facilitate mutual aid;
Marquis Zhāo agreed privately,
without consulting his ministers.
When Wú troops came to rescue Cài,
they moved Cài to Zhōulái.
In the twenty-eighth year,
as Marquis Zhāo was about to pay homage to Wú,
his ministers, fearing further relocation,
ordered the assassin Lì to kill Marquis Zhāo;
afterward, they executed Lì to atone for the crime,
and established Shuò, son of Marquis Zhāo,
who became Marquis Chéng.
In the fourth year of Marquis Chéng,
Sòng destroyed Cáo.
In the tenth year,
Tiáncháng of Qí assassinated his sovereign Duke Jiǎn.
In the thirteenth year,
Chǔ destroyed Chén.
In the nineteenth year,
Marquis Chéng died,
and his son Chǎn, Marquis Shēng, succeeded him.
Marquis Shēng died after fifteen years,
and his son Marquis Yuán succeeded.
Marquis Yuán died after six years,
and his son Qí, the Hóu, succeeded.
In the fourth year of Hóu Qí,
King Huì of Chǔ destroyed Cài,
Hóu Qí of Cài fled,
and thus Cài's ancestral sacrifices were cut off.
This was thirty-three years after Chén's destruction.
Bó Yìkǎo,
his descendants' fief is unknown.
Wǔwáng Fā,
his descendants became Zhōu,
as recorded in the Basic Annals.
Guǎnshū Xiān rebelled, was executed, and died,
leaving no heir.
Zhōugōng Dàn,
his descendants became Lǔ,
as recorded in the Hereditary Houses.
Càishū Dù,
his descendants became Cài,
as recorded in the Hereditary Houses.
Cáoshū Zhènduó,
his descendants became Cáo,
as recorded in the Hereditary Houses.
Chéngshū Wǔ,
his descendants are not seen in records.
Huòshū Chǔ,
his descendants were destroyed by Duke Xiàn of Jìn.
Kāngshū Fēng,
his descendants became Wèi,
as recorded in the Hereditary Houses.
Rǎn Jìzǎi,
his descendants are not seen in records.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Guǎn and Cài's rebellion,
is not worth recording.
However, when King Wǔ of Zhōu passed away,
and King Chéng was young,
the world was filled with doubt,
relying on his younger brothers by the same mother, Chéngshū,
Rǎn Jì, and about ten others as assistants,
thus the feudal lords ultimately honored Zhōu,
hence they are attached to the Hereditary Houses.
Cáoshū Zhènduó
was the younger brother of King Wǔ of Zhōu.
After King Wǔ had conquered King Zhòu of Yīn,
he enfeoffed Shū Zhènduó with Cáo.
Shū Zhènduó died,
and his son Tài Bó Pí succeeded.
Tài Bó died,
and his son Zhòng Jūn Píng succeeded.
Zhòng Jūn Píng died,
and his son Gōng Bó Hóu succeeded.
Gōng Bó Hóu died,
and his son Xiào Bó Yún succeeded.
Xiào Bó Yún died,
and his son Yí Bó Xǐ succeeded.
In the twenty-third year of Yí Bó,
King Lì of Zhōu fled to Zhì.
He died in the thirtieth year,
and his younger brother Yōu Bó Qiáng succeeded.
In the ninth year of Yōu Bó,
his younger brother Sū killed Yōu Bó and took the throne,
becoming Dài Bó.
In the first year of Dài Bó,
King Xuān of Zhōu had been enthroned for three years.
In the thirtieth year,
Dài Bó died,
and his son Huì Bó Sì succeeded.
In the twenty-fifth year of Huì Bó,
King Yōu of Zhōu was killed by the Quǎnróng,
leading to the eastward move,
further diminishing his stature,
and the feudal lords rebelled against him.
Qín began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Huì Bó died,
and his son Shífǔ succeeded,
but his younger brother Wǔ killed him and took the throne,
becoming Duke Mù.
Duke Mù died after three years,
and his son Zhōngshēng, Duke Huán, succeeded.
In the thirty-fifth year of Duke Huán,
Duke Yǐn of Lǔ was established.
In the forty-fifth year,
Lǔ assassinated its sovereign Duke Yǐn.
In the forty-sixth year,
Huáfǔ Dū of Sòng assassinated his sovereign Duke Shāng,
and also Kǒngfǔ.
In the fifty-fifth year,
Duke Huán died,
and his son Xīgū, Duke Zhuāng, succeeded.
In the twenty-third year of Duke Zhuāng,
Duke Huán of Qí began his hegemony.
In the thirty-first year,
Duke Zhuāng died,
and his son Duke Xí Yí ascended.
Duke Xí died in his ninth year,
and his son Duke Zhāo Bān ascended.
In the sixth year of Duke Zhāo,
Duke Huán of Qí defeated Cài,
then proceeded to Shàolíng in Chǔ.
In the ninth year,
Duke Zhāo died,
and his son Duke Gōng Xiāng ascended.
In the sixteenth year of Duke Gōng,
earlier, when Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn was in exile and passed through Cáo,
the ruler of Cáo was disrespectful,
wanting to see his fused ribs.
Xí Fùjī remonstrated,
but was not heeded,
so he privately befriended Chóng'ěr.
In the twenty-first year,
Duke Wén of Jìn, Chóng'ěr, attacked Cáo,
captured Duke Gōng and took him back,
ordering the army not to enter the clan neighborhood of Xí Fùjī.
Someone advised Duke Wén of Jìn, saying:
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí assembled the feudal lords,
restoring those of different surnames;
now you imprison the ruler of Cáo,
destroying one of the same surname,
how can you command the feudal lords?"
Jìn then returned Duke Gōng.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn died.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Duke Gōng died,
and his son Duke Wén Shòu ascended.
Duke Wén died in his twenty-third year,
and his son Duke Xuān Qiáng ascended.
Duke Xuān died in his seventeenth year,
and his younger brother Duke Chéng Fùchú ascended.
In the third year of Duke Chéng,
Duke Lì of Jìn attacked Cáo,
captured Duke Chéng and took him back,
but later released him.
In the fifth year,
Luán Shū and
Zhōngháng Yǎn of Jìn sent Chéng Huá to assassinate their ruler Duke Lì.
In the twenty-third year,
Duke Chéng died,
and his son Duke Wǔ Shèng ascended.
In the twenty-sixth year of Duke Wǔ,
Prince Qìjí of Chǔ assassinated his ruler King Líng and took the throne.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Duke Wǔ died,
and his son Duke Píng Xū ascended.
Duke Píng died in his fourth year,
and his son Duke Dào Wǔ ascended.
That year,
Sòng, Wèi,
Chén, and Zhèng all suffered fires.
In the eighth year of Duke Dào,
Duke Jǐng of Sòng ascended.
In the ninth year,
Duke Dào paid a court visit to Sòng,
but Sòng imprisoned him;
Cáo installed his younger brother Yě,
who was Duke Shēng.
Duke Dào died in Sòng,
and his body was returned for burial.
In the fifth year of Duke Shēng,
Duke Píng's younger brother Tōng assassinated Duke Shēng and took the throne,
becoming Duke Yǐn.
In the fourth year of Duke Yǐn,
Duke Shēng's younger brother Lù assassinated Duke Yǐn and took the throne,
becoming Duke Jìng.
Duke Jìng died in his fourth year,
and his son Bó Yáng ascended.
In the third year of Bó Yáng,
a person in the state dreamed of many noblemen standing at the shrine of the land god,
plotting to destroy Cáo;
Cáo Shū Zhènduó stopped them,
asking to wait for Gōngsūn Qiáng,
and they agreed.
At dawn, they searched throughout Cáo,
but found no such person.
The dreamer warned his son, saying:
"After my death,
if you hear that Gōngsūn Qiáng is in power,
you must leave Cáo,
to avoid the calamity of Cáo."
When Bó Yáng ascended the throne,
he enjoyed hunting and archery.
In the sixth year,
a commoner from Cáo, Gōngsūn Qiáng, also enjoyed hunting and archery,
captured a white wild goose and presented it,
and discussed the methods of hunting and archery,
then moved on to discuss governance.
Bó Yáng was greatly pleased with him,
favored him,
and appointed him as Minister of Works to handle state affairs.
The dreamer's son then fled.
Gōngsūn Qiáng spoke to the Earl of Cáo about the way of hegemony.
In the fourteenth year,
the Earl of Cáo followed his advice,
and turned against Jìn in favor of Sòng.
Duke Jǐng of Sòng attacked them,
and the people of Jìn did not come to their rescue.
In the fifteenth year,
Sòng destroyed Cáo,
captured the Earl of Cáo, Bó Yáng, and Gōngsūn Qiáng, took them back, and killed them.
Thus, Cáo's lineage was cut off.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I consider that Duke Gōng of Cáo did not employ Xí Fùjī,
yet had three hundred carriage-riding officials,
showing he knew not to establish virtue.
As for Zhènduó's dream,
was it not meant to prolong Cáo's sacrifices?
But because Gōngsūn Qiáng did not attend to governance properly,
the sacrifices to Shū Duó suddenly ended.
As for Chén's Duke Hú Mǎn,
he was a descendant of Emperor Shùn of Yú.
In the past, when Shùn was a commoner,
Yáo gave him his two daughters in marriage,
and they lived at Guīruì,
hence their descendants took this as their clan name,
the Guī clan.
After Shùn passed away,
he passed the empire to Yǔ,
while Shùn's son Shāngjūn was enfeoffed.
During the time of the Xià rulers,
the line was sometimes lost, sometimes continued.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu defeated King Zhòu of Yīn,
he sought out Shùn's descendants again,
found Guī Mǎn,
enfeoffed him at Chén,
to continue the sacrifices to Emperor Shùn,
and he became Duke Hú.
Duke Hú died,
and his son Duke Shēn Xīhóu ascended.
Duke Shēn died,
and his younger brother Duke Xiàng Gāoyáng ascended.
Duke Xiàng died,
and Duke Shēn's son Tū was installed,
becoming Duke Xiào.
Duke Xiào died,
and his son Duke Shèn Yǔróng ascended.
Duke Shèn's time corresponded to that of King Lì of Zhōu.
Duke Shèn died,
and his son Duke Yōu Níng ascended.
In the twelfth year of Duke Yōu,
King Lì of Zhōu fled to Zhì.
In the twenty-third year,
Duke Yōu died,
and his son Duke Xī Xiào ascended.
In the sixth year of Duke Xī,
King Xuān of Zhōu ascended the throne.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Duke Xī died,
and his son Duke Wǔ Líng ascended.
Duke Wǔ died in his fifteenth year,
and his son Duke Yí Yuè ascended.
That year,
King Yōu of Zhōu ascended the throne.
Duke Yí died in his third year,
and his younger brother Duke Píng Xiè ascended.
In the seventh year of Duke Píng,
King Yōu of Zhōu was killed by the Quǎnróng,
and Zhōu moved east.
Qín began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the twenty-third year,
Duke Píng died,
and his son Duke Wén Yǔ ascended.
In the first year of Duke Wén,
he married a woman from Cài,
who gave birth to a son, Tuó.
In the tenth year,
Duke Wén died,
and his eldest son Duke Huán Bào ascended.
In the twenty-third year of Duke Huán,
Duke Yǐn of Lǔ first ascended.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Wèi killed its ruler Zhōuxū.
In the thirty-third year,
Lǔ assassinated its ruler Duke Yǐn.
In the thirty-eighth year, on the day Jǐchǒu of the first month,
Duke Huán Bào passed away.
Tuó, the younger brother of Duke Huán,
whose mother was a woman from Cài,
thus the people of Cài killed Wǔfù and Duke Huán's crown prince Miǎn, establishing Tuó in their place,
who became known as Duke Lì.
As Duke Huán fell ill, chaos erupted,
and the people of the state scattered,
hence the double obituary notices were sent.
In the second year of Duke Lì's reign,
he had a son named Wán, also known as Jìngzhòng.
When a Grand Historian of Zhōu passed through Chén,
Duke Lì of Chén had him perform a divination using the "Zhōu Yì,"
and the hexagram obtained was "Guān" changing to "Pǐ":
"This signifies observing the glory of the state,
beneficial for being a guest of the king.
Does this mean he will replace Chén and possess a state?
Not in this land,
but perhaps in another state?
Not in his own person,
but in his descendants.
If in another state,
it must be of the Jiāng surname.
The Jiāng surname
are descendants of Tàiyuè.
Nothing can have two greats simultaneously;
when Chén declines,
will this one flourish?"
Duke Lì married a woman from Cài,
who had illicit relations with men of Cài,
and Duke Lì frequently went to Cài for debauchery.
In the seventh year,
the three younger brothers of Crown Prince Miǎn of Duke Huán, whom Duke Lì had killed—
the eldest named Yuè,
the middle named Lín,
and the youngest named Chǔjiù—
together had men from Cài lure Duke Lì with beautiful women,
and they joined forces with the men of Cài to kill Duke Lì and establish Yuè,
who became known as Duke Lì.
This Duke Lì
was a son of Duke Huán.
Duke Lì reigned for five months and died,
after which the middle brother Lín was established,
known as Duke Zhuāng.
Duke Zhuāng died in the seventh year of his reign,
and the youngest brother Chǔjiù was established,
known as Duke Xuān.
In the third year of Duke Xuān,
King Wǔ of Chǔ died,
and Chǔ began to grow strong.
In the seventeenth year,
King Huì of Zhōu married a woman from Chén as his queen.
In the twenty-first year,
Duke Xuān had a favored concubine who bore a son named Kuǎn,
and wishing to establish him,
he killed his crown prince Yùkòu.
Yùkòu had always been fond of Wán, the son of Duke Lì,
and Wán, fearing the disaster would reach him,
fled to Qí.
Duke Huán of Qí wanted to make Chén Wán a minister,
but Wán said:
"I am a traveling minister,
fortunate to be spared burdens;
this is your grace,
but I dare not assume high office."
Duke Huán then made him a master of crafts.
Yì Zhòng of Qí wanted to marry his daughter to Chén Jìngzhòng,
and upon divining,
the oracle said:
"This is called 'the phoenixes flying together,
their harmonious cries clanging.'
A descendant of Guī,
will be nurtured among Jiāng.
In five generations, they will flourish,
and rank with chief ministers.
After eight generations,
none will rival their greatness."
In the thirty-seventh year,
Duke Huán of Qí attacked Cài,
and Cài was defeated;
he then advanced south to invade Chǔ,
reaching Zhàolíng,
and on his return passed through Chén.
Yuán Táotú, a senior official of Chén, disliked their passing through Chén,
and deceitfully directed the Qí army to take the eastern route.
The eastern route was treacherous,
and Duke Huán, enraged,
seized Chén's Yuán Táotú.
That year,
Duke Xiàn of Jìn killed his crown prince Shēnshēng.
In the forty-fifth year,
Duke Xuān died,
and his son Kuǎn was established,
known as Duke Mù.
In the fifth year of Duke Mù,
Duke Huán of Qí died.
In the sixteenth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn defeated the Chǔ army at Chéngpú.
That year,
Duke Mù died,
and his son Duke Gòng Shuò was established.
In the sixth year of Duke Gòng,
the crown prince of Chǔ, Shāngchén, murdered his father King Chéng and took the throne,
becoming known as King Mù.
In the eleventh year,
Duke Mù of Qín died.
In the eighteenth year,
Duke Gòng died,
and his son Duke Líng Píngguó was established.
In the first year of Duke Líng,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ ascended the throne.
In the sixth year,
Chǔ attacked Chén.
In the tenth year,
Chén made peace with Chǔ.
In the fourteenth year,
Duke Líng, along with his senior officials Kǒng Níng
and Yí Xíngfù, all had affairs with Xià Jī,
and they wore her intimate garments to jest in court.
Xiè Yě admonished, saying:
"When ruler and ministers indulge in debauchery,
what example does it set for the people?"
Duke Líng informed the two men,
who requested to kill Xiè Yě;
the duke did not forbid it,
so they killed Xiè Yě.
In the fifteenth year,
Duke Líng drank with the two men at the Xià household.
The duke jested with the two, saying:
"Zhēngshū resembles you."
The two replied:
"He also resembles you, my lord."
Zhēngshū grew angry.
When Duke Líng finished drinking and left,
Zhēngshū ambushed him at the stable gate with a crossbow and shot him dead.
Kǒng Níng
and Yí Xíngfù both fled to Chǔ,
while Duke Líng's crown prince Wǔ fled to Jìn.
Zhēngshū declared himself the Marquis of Chén.
Zhēngshū
was originally a senior official of Chén.
Xià Jī
was the wife of Yù Shū
and the mother of Zhēngshū.
In the winter of the first year of Duke Chéng,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ, on account of Xià Zhēngshū killing Duke Líng,
led the feudal lords to attack Chén.
He declared to Chén:
"Do not fear,
I am only here to punish Zhēngshū."
After executing Zhēngshū,
he annexed Chén as a county of Chǔ,
and all his ministers came to congratulate him.
Shěn Shūshí, who had been on a mission to Qí and had just returned,
alone did not offer congratulations.
King Zhuāng asked the reason,
and he replied:
"There is a saying among the common folk:
'If a man leads his ox through another's field,
the field's owner seizes the ox.'
The trespass is indeed wrong,
but to seize the ox—
is that not excessive?
Now, Your Majesty, considering Zhēngshū a traitor who murdered his ruler,
raised troops among the feudal lords,
and righteously attacked him;
yet after the deed, you took possession of Chén,
profiting from its land.
How then will you command the world hereafter?
That is why I do not congratulate you."
King Zhuāng said:
"Well said."
He then welcomed Duke Líng's crown prince Wǔ from Jìn and established him,
restoring Chén's rule as before,
and he became known as Duke Chéng.
When Confucius read the historical records up to Chǔ's restoration of Chén,
he said:
"How worthy was King Zhuāng of Chǔ!
He valued a single word more than a state of a thousand chariots."
In the eighth year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ died.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Chén betrayed its covenant with Chǔ.
In the thirtieth year,
King Gòng of Chǔ attacked Chén.
That year,
Duke Chéng died,
and his son Duke Āi, named Ruò, ascended the throne.
Chǔ, because of Chén's mourning,
withdrew its troops and left.
In the third year of Duke Āi,
Chǔ besieged Chén,
but later released it.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Prince Wéi of Chǔ assassinated his ruler Jiá Áo and installed himself,
becoming King Líng.
In the thirty-fourth year,
earlier, Duke Āi had married a woman from Zhèng,
and the elder consort gave birth to Crown Prince Shī,
while the younger consort gave birth to Yǎn.
Two favored concubines,
the elder concubine gave birth to Liú,
and the younger concubine gave birth to Shèng.
Liú was favored by Duke Āi,
and Duke Āi entrusted him to his younger brother, the Minister of Education, Zhāo.
When Duke Āi fell ill,
in the third month,
Zhāo killed Crown Prince Shī,
and installed Liú as crown prince.
Duke Āi was enraged,
and wanted to execute Zhāo,
but Zhāo mobilized troops to besiege and guard Duke Āi,
and Duke Āi hanged himself.
Zhāo eventually installed Liú as the ruler of Chén.
In the fourth month,
Chén sent an envoy to Chǔ.
When King Líng of Chǔ heard of the turmoil in Chén,
he killed Chén's envoy,
and sent Prince Qìjí to dispatch troops to attack Chén,
and the ruler of Chén, Liú, fled to Zhèng.
In the ninth month,
Chǔ besieged Chén.
In the eleventh month,
Chǔ annihilated Chén.
It appointed Qìjí as the Duke of Chén.
When Zhāo killed Crown Prince Shī,
the crown prince's son, named Wú,
fled to Jìn.
Duke Píng of Jìn asked the Grand Historian Zhào:
"Is Chén then doomed to perish?"
He replied:
"Chén
is of the lineage of Zhuānxū.
When the Chén clan gains power in Qí,
it will eventually perish.
From Mù to Gǔsǒu,
none violated the mandate.
Shùn further enhanced it with his brilliant virtue.
Down to Suì,
it was preserved generation after generation.
When it reached Duke Hú,
Zhōu bestowed the surname upon him,
and had him sacrifice to Emperor Yú.
Moreover, a lineage of great virtue will endure,
and its sacrifices will surely last for a hundred generations.
The lineage of Yú has not ended yet;
will it not be in Qí?"
Five years after King Líng of Chǔ annihilated Chén,
Prince Qìjí of Chǔ assassinated King Líng and took his place,
becoming King Píng.
When King Píng first ascended the throne,
wishing to achieve harmony among the feudal lords,
he sought out Wú, the son of the former Crown Prince Shī of Chén,
and installed him as the Marquis of Chén,
who became Duke Huì.
When Duke Huì was installed,
he traced back to the year of Duke Āi's death and made that his first year,
thus accounting for the five-year gap.
In the tenth year,
a fire broke out in Chén.
In the fifteenth year,
King Liáo of Wú sent Prince Guāng to attack Chén,
capturing Hú
and Shěn before withdrawing.
In the twenty-eighth year,
King HéLǘ of Wú, along with Wǔ Zǐxū, defeated Chǔ and entered Yǐng.
That year,
Duke Huì died,
and his son Duke Huái, named Liǔ, ascended the throne.
In the first year of Duke Huái,
Wú defeated Chǔ,
and while in Yǐng,
summoned the Marquis of Chén.
The Marquis of Chén intended to go,
but a senior official said:
"Wú is newly triumphant;
although the King of Chǔ has fled,
he has old ties with Chén,
and we must not betray him."
Duke Huái then declined Wú's summons on grounds of illness.
In the fourth year,
Wú again summoned Duke Huái.
Duke Huái, afraid,
went to Wú.
