Wú, angered by his previous refusal to come,
detained him,
and he consequently died in Wú.
Chén then installed Duke Huái's son Yuè,
who became Duke Mǐn.
In the sixth year of Duke Mǐn,
Confucius went to Chén.
King Fūchāi of Wú attacked Chén,
capturing three towns before withdrawing.
In the thirteenth year,
Wú again came to attack Chén,
and Chén appealed for help to Chǔ.
King Zhāo of Chǔ came to the rescue,
stationing his army at Chéngfù,
and the Wú army withdrew.
That year,
King Zhāo of Chǔ died at Chéngfù.
At that time, Confucius was in Chén.
In the fifteenth year,
Sòng annihilated Cáo.
In the sixteenth year,
King Fūchāi of Wú attacked Qí,
defeating them at Àilíng,
and sent a messenger to summon the Marquis of Chén.
The Marquis of Chén, afraid,
went to Wú.
Chǔ then attacked Chén.
In the twenty-first year,
Tián Cháng of Qí assassinated his ruler Duke Jiǎn.
In the twenty-third year,
Báigōng Shèng of Chǔ killed the Prime Minister Zǐxī
and Zǐqí,
and attacked King Huì.
Duke Shè attacked and defeated Báigōng,
and Báigōng committed suicide.
In the twenty-fourth year,
King Huì of Chǔ restored the state,
and leading his troops north on a campaign,
killed Duke Mǐn of Chén,
thus annihilating Chén and taking possession of it.
That year,
Confucius died. Qǐ
As for Dōnglóu Gōng,
he was a descendant of Hòu Yǔ of the Xià.
During the Yīn dynasty, the line was sometimes enfeoffed and sometimes broken.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu defeated Yīn Zhòu,
he sought the descendants of Yǔ,
and found Dōnglóu Gōng,
enfeoffing him at Qǐ,
to continue the sacrifices of the Xià Hòu clan.
Dōnglóu Gōng begat Xīlóu Gōng,
Xīlóu Gōng begat Tí Gōng,
Tí Gōng begat Móuqǔ Gōng.
Móuqǔ Gōng lived during the reign of King Lì of Zhōu.
Móuqǔ Gōng begat Wǔ Gōng.
Wǔ Gōng reigned for forty-seven years and died,
whereupon his son Jìng Gōng succeeded him.
Jìng Gōng died after twenty-three years,
and his son Gòng Gōng succeeded.
Gòng Gōng died after eight years,
and his son Dé Gōng succeeded.
Dé Gōng died after eighteen years,
and his younger brother Huán Gōng Gūróng succeeded.
Huán Gōng died after seventeen years,
and his son Xiào Gōng Gài succeeded.
Xiào Gōng died after seventeen years,
and his younger brother Wén Gōng Yìgū succeeded.
Wén Gōng died after fourteen years,
and his younger brother Píng Gōng Yù succeeded.
Píng Gōng died after eighteen years,
and his son Dào Gōng Chéng succeeded.
Dào Gōng died after twelve years,
and his son Yǐn Gōng Qǐ succeeded.
In the seventh month,
Yǐn Gōng's younger brother Suì assassinated Yǐn Gōng and installed himself,
becoming known as Xī Gōng.
Xī Gōng died after nineteen years,
and his son Mǐn Gōng Wéi succeeded.
In the fifteenth year of Mǐn Gōng,
King Huì of Chǔ destroyed Chén.
In the sixteenth year,
Mǐn Gōng's younger brother Èlù assassinated Mǐn Gōng and took his place,
becoming known as Āi Gōng.
Āi Gōng reigned for ten years and died,
whereupon Mǐn Gōng's son Chù succeeded,
becoming known as Chū Gōng.
Chū Gōng died after twelve years,
and his son Jiǎn Gōng Chūn succeeded.
He had been on the throne for one year,
when in the forty-fourth year of King Huì of Chǔ,
Qǐ was destroyed. Qǐ
lasted thirty-four years after Chén's demise. Qǐ
was small and insignificant,
its affairs not worth recounting.
The descendants of Shùn,
whom King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed in Chén,
until King Huì of Chǔ destroyed it,
are recorded in a Hereditary House.
The descendants of Yǔ,
whom King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed in Qǐ,
and King Huì of Chǔ destroyed,
are recorded in a Hereditary House.
The descendants of Xiè became the Yīn,
and Yīn is recorded in a Basic Annals.
After Yīn was defeated,
Zhōu enfeoffed its descendants in Sòng,
which King Mǐn of Qí destroyed,
and it is recorded in a Hereditary House.
The descendants of Hòujì became the Zhōu,
which King Zhāo of Qín destroyed,
and it is recorded in a Basic Annals.
The descendants of Gāoyáo
were enfeoffed in Yīng and
Lù, which King Mù of Chǔ destroyed,
but there is no genealogy.
The descendants of Bóyí,
until King Wǔ of Zhōu re-enfeoffed them in Qí,
known as Tàigōng Wàng,
and the Chén clan destroyed it,
are recorded in a Hereditary House.
The descendants of Bóyì,
until King Píng of Zhōu enfeoffed them as Qín,
which Xiàng Yǔ destroyed,
are recorded in a Basic Annals.
Chuí, Yì,
Kuí, and Lóng—
their descendants' enfeeoffments are unknown,
and they are not seen.
These eleven men
were all ministers of merit and virtue from the time of Táng and Yú;
the descendants of five of them rose to be emperors or kings,
while the rest became prominent feudal lords.
Téng, Xuē,
Zōu were enfeeffments from the Xià,
Yīn, and Zhōu periods,
but they were small and not worth enumerating,
so they are not discussed.
During the time of King Wǔ of Zhōu,
there were still over a thousand marquises and earls.
But after the times of Yōu and
Lì,
the feudal lords attacked and annexed each other by force.
Jiāng, Huáng,
Hú, Shěn, and the like
were too numerous to count,
so they were not selected for inclusion in the records.
The Grand Historian remarks:
The virtue of Shùn can be called supreme!
He abdicated in favor of the Xià,
and his descendants enjoyed sacrificial offerings through three dynasties.
Even after Chǔ destroyed Chén,
Tián Cháng gained power in Qí,
eventually establishing a state,
which lasted for a hundred generations without interruption,
his progeny flourishing,
so that those with land were not lacking.
As for Yǔ,
in the Zhōu period, his line was Qǐ,
which was very insignificant,
not worth counting.
King Huì of Chǔ destroyed Qǐ,
and later, King Gōujiàn of Yuè rose.
Wèi Kāngshū, named Fēng,
was the younger full brother of King Wǔ of Zhōu.
After him, there was also Rǎn Jì,
and Rǎn Jì was the youngest.
After King Wǔ had defeated Yīn Zhòu,
he again enfeoffed Zhòu's son Wǔ Gēng Lùfù with the remaining people of Yīn,
ranking him among the feudal lords,
to continue the sacrifices to his ancestors without interruption.
Because Wǔ Gēng was not yet settled,
and fearing he might have treacherous intentions,
King Wǔ ordered his brothers Guǎn Shū and
Cài Shū to serve as tutors and ministers to Wǔ Gēng Lùfù,
to pacify his people.
After King Wǔ passed away,
King Chéng was young.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn governed on behalf of King Chéng,
ruling the state.
Guǎn Shū and
Cài Shū suspected Zhōu Gōng,
and together with Wǔ Gēng Lùfù, they started a rebellion,
intending to attack Chéngzhōu.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn, under the order of King Chéng, raised an army to attack Yīn,
killing Wǔ Gēng Lùfù and
Guǎn Shū,
and exiled Cài Shū,
then enfeoffed Kāngshū as the lord of Wèi with the remaining people of Wǔ Gēng's Yīn,
settling him between the Hé and
Qí rivers in the old Shāng ruins.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn, fearing that Kāngshū was too young,
exhorted him, saying:
"You must seek out the worthy, noble, and elder men of Yīn,
and ask them why Yīn rose
and why it fell,
and strive to love the people."
He told him that Zhòu's fall was due to his indulgence in wine,
the errors of drunkenness,
and his obsession with women,
so Zhòu's chaos began from this.
He composed the "Zǐcái,"
to show the nobleman what could be emulated.
Thus, he issued the "Kāng Gào,"
"Jiǔ Gào,"
and "Zǐcái" to command him.
When Kāngshū went to his state,
having received these commands,
he was able to harmonize and gather his people,
and the people were greatly pleased.
When King Chéng grew up
and took charge of governance,
he appointed Kāngshū as the Minister of Justice of Zhōu,
bestowing upon Wèi precious sacrificial vessels,
to honor his virtue.
Kāngshū died,
and his son Kāng Bó succeeded him.
Kāng Bó died,
and his son Kǎo Bó succeeded.
Kǎo Bó died,
and his son Sì Bó succeeded.
Sì Bó died,
and his son Jié Bó succeeded. Jié
Bó died,
and his son Jìng Bó succeeded.
Jìng Bó died,
and his son Zhēn Bó succeeded.
Zhēn Bó died,
and his son Qǐng Hóu succeeded.
Qǐng Hóu generously bribed King Yí of Zhōu,
and King Yí appointed Wèi as a marquisate.
Qǐng Hóu died after twelve years,
and his son Xī Hóu succeeded.
In the thirteenth year of Xī Hóu,
King Lì of Zhōu fled to Zhì,
and the Héguǎn Regency began.
In the twenty-eighth year,
King Xuān of Zhōu ascended the throne.
In the forty-second year,
Marquis Lí died,
and Crown Prince Gòngbó Yú ascended as ruler.
Gòngbó's younger brother Hé was favored by Marquis Lí,
who gave him many gifts;
Hé used these gifts to bribe warriors,
launching a surprise attack on Gòngbó at the tomb,
where Gòngbó entered Marquis Lí's burial passage and committed suicide.
The people of Wèi buried him beside Marquis Lí,
posthumously naming him Gòngbó,
and established Hé as the Marquis of Wèi,
known as Duke Wǔ.
When Duke Wǔ took the throne,
he continued the governance of Kāngshū,
bringing harmony and stability to the people.
In the forty-second year,
the Quǎnróng killed King Yōu of Zhōu,
and Duke Wǔ led troops to aid Zhōu against them,
achieving great merit,
so King Píng of Zhōu appointed Duke Wǔ as a Duke.
In the fifty-fifth year,
he died, and his son Duke Zhuāng Yáng succeeded him.
In the fifth year of Duke Zhuāng,
he took a woman from Qí as his primary wife,
who was beloved but bore no son.
He also took a woman from Chén as a wife,
who bore a son,
but he died young.
The younger sister of the Chén woman also gained Duke Zhuāng's favor,
and bore a son named Wán.
After Wán's mother died,
Duke Zhuāng ordered his primary wife, the woman from Qí, to raise him,
and established him as crown prince.
Duke Zhuāng had a favored concubine,
who bore a son named Zhōuyù.
In the eighteenth year,
Zhōuyù grew up,
fond of warfare,
and Duke Zhuāng put him in command of troops.
Shí Què advised Duke Zhuāng, saying:
"A son by a concubine fond of warfare,
given command,
will bring disorder from this."
Duke Zhuāng did not listen.
In the twenty-third year,
Duke Zhuāng died,
and Crown Prince Wán succeeded him,
known as Duke Huán.
In the second year of Duke Huán,
his younger brother Zhōuyù became arrogant and extravagant,
so Duke Huán demoted him,
and Zhōuyù fled into exile.
In the twelfth year,
the younger brother Duàn of the Earl of Zhèng attacked his elder brother,
but did not succeed,
fleeing, and Zhōuyù sought to befriend him.
In the sixteenth year,
Zhōuyù gathered exiled men of Wèi to launch a surprise attack and kill Duke Huán,
then established himself as ruler of Wèi.
To aid Duàn of Zhèng in attacking Zhèng, he sought assistance from Sòng,
Chén, and Cài to join him,
and all three states agreed with Zhōuyù.
Zhōuyù, newly in power,
fond of warfare,
and having assassinated Duke Huán,
was disliked by the people of Wèi.
Shí Què then, through Duke Huán's maternal family in Chén,
pretended to be friendly with Zhōuyù.
When they reached the outskirts of Zhèng,
Shí Què conspired with the Marquis of Chén,
sending Yòuzǎi Chǒu to present food,
and killed Zhōuyù at Pú,
then welcomed Duke Huán's younger brother Jìn from Xíng and established him,
known as Duke Xuān.
In the seventh year of Duke Xuān,
Lǔ assassinated its ruler Duke Yǐn.
In the ninth year,
Sòng's Dū assassinated its ruler Duke Shāng,
and also Kǒngfǔ.
In the tenth year,
Jìn's Qūwò Zhuāngbó assassinated its ruler Duke Āi.
In the eighteenth year,
earlier, Duke Xuān loved his wife Yí Jiāng,
who bore a son named Jí,
made crown prince,
and had Yòu Gōngzǐ tutor him.
Yòu Gōngzǐ found a woman from Qí for the crown prince,
but before she entered the household,
Duke Xuān saw the intended bride and found her beautiful,
so he took her for himself,
and found another woman for the crown prince.
Duke Xuān, with the woman from Qí,
had sons named Shòu
and Shuò,
and had Zuǒ Gōngzǐ tutor them.
After Crown Prince Jí's mother died,
Duke Xuān's primary wife and Shuò together slandered Crown Prince Jí.
Duke Xuān, already guilty over taking the crown prince's wife,
disliked the crown prince,
and wanted to depose him.
Hearing the slanders,
he grew furious,
and sent Crown Prince Jí to Qí, ordering bandits to ambush and kill him at the border,
giving the crown prince a white yak-tail banner,
and instructing the border bandits to kill whoever carried the white banner.
As he was about to depart,
Shuò's elder brother Shòu,
the crown prince's half-brother,
knowing Shuò's malice and the ruler's intent to kill him,
said to the crown prince:
"The border bandits will see the white banner and
kill you;
you should not go."
The crown prince said:
"To disobey my father's command for survival
is not permissible."
So he proceeded.
Seeing the crown prince would not stop,
Shòu stole the white banner and raced ahead to the border.
The border bandits, seeing the proof,
killed him.
After Shòu died,
Crown Prince Jí arrived,
and told the bandits:
"The one to be killed is me."
The bandits killed Crown Prince Jí as well,
reporting to Duke Xuān.
Duke Xuān then made his son Shuò crown prince.
In the nineteenth year,
Duke Xuān died,
and Crown Prince Shuò succeeded him,
known as Duke Huì.
Zuǒ and Yòu Gōngzǐ were discontent with Shuò's succession.
In the fourth year of Duke Huì,
they resented his slander and the killing of former Crown Prince Jí to take the throne,
so they rebelled,
attacked Duke Huì,
and established Crown Prince Jí's younger brother Qiánmóu as ruler,
while Duke Huì fled to Qí.
Lord Wèi Qiánmóu reigned for eight years,
then Duke Xiāng of Qí led feudal lords under the king's command to attack Wèi,
restoring Duke Huì,
and executing Zuǒ and Yòu Gōngzǐ.
Lord Wèi Qiánmóu fled to Zhōu,
and Duke Huì was restored.
Duke Huì had been in exile for three years before his restoration,
and after eight years in exile, he returned,
making a total of thirteen years including his previous reign.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Duke Huì resented Zhōu for harboring Qiánmóu,
and joined Yān in attacking Zhōu.
King Huì of Zhōu fled to Wēn,
and Wèi and Yān established the king's younger brother Tuí as king.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Zhèng restored King Huì.
In the thirty-first year,
Duke Huì died,
and his son Duke Yì Chì succeeded him.
When Duke Yì took the throne,
he was fond of cranes,
indulging in excess and luxury.
In the ninth year,
the Dí attacked Wèi,
and Duke Yì wanted to mobilize troops,
but some soldiers mutinied.
A minister said:
"Since you love cranes,
let the cranes fight the Dí."
The Dí then entered,
killing Duke Yì.
When Duke Yì was established,
the people and ministers were discontent.
From Duke Yì's father Duke Huì Shuò slandering and killing Crown Prince Jí to seize the throne until Duke Yì's reign,
they often sought to undermine him,
finally destroying Duke Huì's line and establishing Shēn, son of Qiánmóu's younger brother Zhāobó Wán, as ruler,
known as Duke Dài.
Duke Dài Shēn died in his first year.
Duke Huán of Qí, due to Wèi's repeated turmoil,
led feudal lords to attack the Dí,
built Chǔqiū for Wèi,
and established Duke Dài's younger brother Huǐ as ruler of Wèi,
known as Duke Wén.
Duke Wén had fled to Qí due to the turmoil,
and the people of Qí supported his return.
Initially,
when Dí people killed Duke Yì,
the people of Wèi pitied him,
and considered re-establishing the descendants of Crown Prince Jí, who had died before Duke Xuān.
But Jí's son had also died,
and Zǐ Shòu, who died in Jí's place, had no sons either.
Crown Prince Jí had two younger brothers from the same mother:
one was called Qiánmóu,
who had once replaced Duke Huì as ruler
for eight years before leaving again;
the other was called Zhāobó.
Since both Zhāobó
and Qiánmóu had died earlier,
they established Zhāobó's son Shēn as Duke Dài.
When Duke Dài passed away,
they established his younger brother Huǐ as Duke Wén.
Upon his accession, Duke Wén
lightened taxes and fairly judged crimes,
labored personally,
and shared hardships with the common people,
thereby winning over the people of Wèi.
In the sixteenth year,
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn passed through,
but was treated discourteously.
In the seventeenth year,
Duke Huán of Qí died.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Duke Wén died,
and his son Zhèng became Duke Chéng.
In the third year of Duke Chéng's reign,
Jìn sought to pass through Wèi to aid Sòng,
but Duke Chéng refused.
Jìn then crossed from the southern river,
and rescued Sòng.
They requested troops from Wèi,
and the senior officials of Wèi wished to consent,
but Duke Chéng would not agree.
The senior official Yuán Xuǎn attacked Duke Chéng,
who fled the state.
Duke Wén of Jìn, Chóng'ěr, attacked Wèi,
dividing its land and giving it to Sòng,
in retaliation for the previous discourtesy and refusal to aid Sòng in its distress.
Duke Chéng of Wèi then fled to Chén.
After two years,
he went to Zhōu to seek restoration,
and met with Duke Wén of Jìn.
Jìn sent someone to poison Duke Chéng of Wèi,
but Duke Chéng privately bribed the Zhōu official in charge of the poison,
ordering it to be diluted,
so he did not die.
Later, Zhōu interceded with Duke Wén of Jìn,
and eventually he was restored to Wèi,
whereupon Yuán Xuǎn was executed,
and the ruler of Wèi, Xiá, fled.
In the seventh year,
Duke Wén of Jìn died.
In the twelfth year,
Duke Chéng paid court to Duke Xiāng of Jìn.
In the fourteenth year,
Duke Mù of Qín died.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Bǐng Chù of Qí assassinated his ruler, Duke Yì.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Duke Chéng died,
and his son Sù became Duke Mù.
In the second year of Duke Mù,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Chén,
killing Xià Zhēngshū.
In the third year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Zhèng,
which surrendered,
but was then released.
In the eleventh year,
Sūn Liángfū rescued Lǔ and attacked Qí,
recovering the invaded territory.
Duke Mù died,
and his son Zāng became Duke Dìng.
Duke Dìng died in the twelfth year,
and his son Kàn became Duke Xiàn.
In the thirteenth year of Duke Xiàn,
he ordered instructor Cáo to teach the palace concubines to play the qin,
but a concubine was not skilled,
so Cáo caned her.
The concubine, favored by the duke, slandered Cáo to him,
and the duke also caned Cáo three hundred times.
In the eighteenth year,
Duke Xiàn invited Sūn Wénzǐ
and Nìng Huìzǐ to dine,
and both went.
As it grew late without being summoned,
he went instead to shoot geese in the park.
The two followed him there,
but the duke did not remove his archery attire to speak with them.
Angered,
the two went to Sù.
Sūn Wénzǐ's son often attended the duke at drink,
and the duke had instructor Cáo sing the final stanza of "Qiǎo Yán."
Instructor Cáo, still resentful for having been caned three hundred times,
sang it,
intending to anger Sūn Wénzǐ,
and take revenge on Duke Xiàn of Wèi.
Wénzǐ discussed it with Qú Bóyù,
who said:
"I know nothing of this."
Thereupon, he attacked and expelled Duke Xiàn.
Duke Xiàn fled to Qí,
where he was placed in Jùyì by Qí.
Sūn Wénzǐ
and Nìng Huìzǐ together established Duke Dìng's younger brother Qiū as ruler of Wèi,
known as Duke Shāng.
Upon Duke Shāng Qiū's accession,
he enfeoffed Sūn Wénzǐ Línfǔ at Sù.
In the twelfth year,
Nìng Xǐ and Sūn Línfǔ vied for favor and grew to hate each other,
so Duke Shāng sent Nìng Xǐ to attack Sūn Línfǔ.
Línfǔ fled to Jìn,
and sought to restore the former Duke Xiàn of Wèi.
Duke Xiàn was in Qí,
and Duke Jǐng of Qí, hearing of this,
went with Duke Xiàn of Wèi to Jìn to seek restoration.
Jìn thereupon attacked Wèi,
luring them into an alliance.
Duke Shāng of Wèi met with Duke Píng of Jìn,
who detained Duke Shāng and Nìng Xǐ, and restored Duke Xiàn of Wèi.
Duke Xiàn had been in exile for twelve years before returning.
In the first year after Duke Xiàn's restoration,
he executed Nìng Xǐ.
In the third year,
Jìzǐ of Yánlíng from Wú passed through Wèi on a mission,
and upon seeing Qú Bóyù
and Shǐ Qiū,
said:
"Wèi has many noble men;
thus, the state is without troubles."
Passing through Sù,
he heard Sūn Línfǔ striking the qìng,
and said:
"There is no joy in it;
the sound is too sorrowful,
it was this that caused the turmoil in Wèi."
That year,
Duke Xiàn died,
and his son È became Duke Xiāng.
In the sixth year of Duke Xiāng,
King Líng of Chǔ met with the feudal lords,
but Duke Xiāng pleaded illness and did not attend.
In the ninth year,
Duke Xiāng died.
Earlier, Duke Xiāng had a low-ranking concubine,
whom he favored,
and she became pregnant.
She dreamed someone told her:
"I am Kāngshū,
and I decree that your son will surely possess Wèi;
name your son
'Yuán'."
The concubine found it strange,
and asked Kǒng Chéngzǐ.
Chéngzǐ said:
"Kāngshū
is the ancestor of Wèi."
When the child was born,
it was a boy,
and she reported it to Duke Xiāng.
Duke Xiāng said:
"It is heaven's will."
He named him Yuán.
The primary wife of Duke Xiāng had no sons,
so they established Yuán as heir,
who became Duke Líng.
In the fifth year of Duke Líng,
he paid court to Duke Zhāo of Jìn.
In the sixth year,
Prince Qìjí of Chǔ assassinated King Líng and made himself ruler,
becoming King Píng.
In the eleventh year,
a fire occurred.
In the thirty-eighth year,
Confucius came,
and was provided a stipend as in Lǔ.
Later, there was a rift,
and Confucius left.
He later returned.
In the thirty-ninth year,
Crown Prince Kuǎikuì had animosity with Duke Líng's wife Nánzǐ,
and wanted to kill her.
Kuǎikuì plotted with his follower Xìyáng Sù,
planning to have him kill the lady during court audience.
But Xìyáng regretted,
and did not carry it out.
Kuǎikuì repeatedly signaled him with his eyes,
which the lady noticed,
and in fear, she cried out:
"The crown prince wants to kill me!"
Duke Líng was enraged,
so Crown Prince Kuǎikuì fled to Sòng,
and later went to the Zhào clan in Jìn.
In the spring of the forty-second year,
Duke Líng was touring the suburbs,
and ordered Yǐng to drive his carriage.
Yǐng was Duke Líng's youngest son,
courtesy name Zǐnán.
Duke Líng resented the crown prince's flight,
and said to Yǐng:
"I intend to establish you as my successor."
Yǐng replied:
"Yǐng is not worthy to disgrace the state,
please consider another plan."
In summer, Duke Líng died,
and the lady ordered Yǐng to be crown prince,
saying:
"This was Duke Líng's command."
Yǐng said:
"The son of the exiled crown prince Kuǎikuì, Zhé, is still here,
I dare not assume this position."
Thereupon, Wèi made Zhé the ruler,
who was Duke Chū.
On the yǒu day of the sixth month,
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ wanted to install Kuǎikuì,
so he ordered Yáng Hǔ to disguise more than ten men from Wèi in mourning clothes to return,
and Jiǎnzǐ escorted Kuǎikuì.
The people of Wèi heard of this,
and sent troops to attack Kuǎikuì.
Kuǎikuì could not enter,
so he entered Sù and fortified there,
and the Wèi troops also withdrew.
In the fourth year of Duke Chū Zhé,
Tián Qǐ of Qí assassinated his ruler Rúzǐ.
In the eighth year,
Bào Zǐ of Qí assassinated his ruler Duke Dào.
Confucius entered Wèi from Chén.
In the ninth year,
Kǒng Wénzǐ asked Zhòngní about military affairs,
but Zhòngní did not respond.
Later, Lǔ welcomed Zhòngní,
and Zhòngní returned to Lǔ.
In the twelfth year,
previously, Kǒng Yǔ Wénzǐ had married the elder sister of Crown Prince Kuǎikuì,
and they gave birth to Kuī.
The servant of the Kǒng family, Hún Liángfū, was handsome,
and after Kǒng Wénzǐ died,
Liángfū had an affair with Kuī's mother.
The crown prince was in Sù,
and Kuī's mother sent Liángfū to the crown prince.
The crown prince said to Liángfū:
"If you can help me enter my state,
I will reward you with a carriage,
exempt you from three death penalties,
and you will be free from any obligations."
He made an alliance with him,
and promised to make Kuī's mother his wife.
In the intercalary month,
Liángfū and the crown prince entered,
and stayed at the outer garden of the Kǒng family.
At dusk, the two covered themselves with clothes and rode,
with a eunuch Luó driving,
to the Kǒng residence.
The steward of the Kǒng family, Luán Níng, questioned them,
and they claimed to be relatives' concubines.
They then entered,
and went to Bó Jī's quarters.
After eating,
Kuī's mother took a spear and led the way,
the crown prince and five others donned armor,
and followed with a sacrificial pig.
Bó Jī forced Kuī in the side room,
compelled him to swear an alliance,
and then forced him to ascend the tower.
Luán Níng was about to drink,
with roast meat not yet cooked,
when he heard of the disturbance,
and sent word to Zhòng Yóu.
He summoned Hù to prepare the carriage,
drank and ate roast meat while traveling,
and escorted Duke Chū Zhé to flee to Lǔ.
As Zhòng Yóu was about to enter,
he met Zǐgāo who was leaving,
who said:
"The gate is already closed."
Zǐlù said:
"I shall go there anyway."
Zǐgāo said:
"It's too late,
do not tread into this disaster."
Zǐlù said:
"Having eaten their salary, I cannot avoid their difficulties."
Zǐgāo then left.
Zǐlù entered,
and when he reached the gate,
Gōngsūn Gǎn closed the gate,
saying:
"Do not enter!"
Zǐlù said:
"Is that Gōngsūn?
You seek profit but flee from hardship.
I, Yóu, am not like that;
having benefited from their emolument,
I must rescue them from calamity."
When a messenger came out,
Zǐlù managed to enter.
He said:
"Why does the crown prince need Kǒng Kuī?
Even if you kill him,
someone will surely succeed him."
And he added:
"The crown prince lacks courage.
If you set fire to the tower,
he will surely release Kǒng Shū."
The crown prince heard this,
feared, and sent down Shí Qǐ
and Yú Yǎn to confront Zǐlù.
They struck him with spears,
cutting his cap strings.
Zǐlù said:
"A gentleman may die,
but his cap must not be removed."
He tied his cap strings and died.
When Confucius heard of the turmoil in Wèi,
he said:
"Alas!
Chái will probably come back,
but Yóu will die."
Kǒng Kuī eventually installed Crown Prince Kuǎikuì,
who became Duke Zhuāng.
Duke Zhuāng Kuǎikuì
was the father of Duke Chū,
and having lived abroad,
he resented the senior officials for not welcoming and installing him.
In the first year of his reign,
he wanted to execute all the senior ministers,
saying:
"I have lived abroad for a long time,
have you heard about it?"
The ministers planned to revolt,
so he stopped.
In the second year,
Kǒng Qiū of Lǔ died.
In the third year,
Duke Zhuāng went up the city wall,
and saw Róngzhōu.
He said:
"Why are these Róng barbarians here?"
Róngzhōu took offense.
In October,
Róngzhōu informed Zhào Jiǎnzǐ,
and Jiǎnzǐ besieged Wèi.
In November,
Duke Zhuāng fled,
and the people of Wèi installed Prince Bānshī as the ruler of Wèi.
Qí attacked Wèi,
captured Bānshī,
and installed Prince Qǐ as the ruler of Wèi instead.
In the first year of Wèi's ruler Qǐ,
Shí Mànfū of Wèi expelled his ruler Qǐ,
and Qǐ fled to Qí.
Duke Chū Zhé of Wèi returned from Qí and was reinstated.
Previously, Duke Chū had reigned for twelve years before fleeing,
and after four years in exile, he returned.
In the first year after Duke Chū's return,
he rewarded those who had followed him in exile.
He reigned for twenty-one years and died,
and Duke Chū's younger uncle Qián attacked Duke Chū's son and installed himself,
becoming Duke Dào.
Duke Dào died after five years,
and his son Duke Jìng Fú succeeded him.
Duke Jìng died after nineteen years,
and his son Duke Zhāo Jiū succeeded him.
At that time, the three Jìn families were strong,
and Wèi was like a small marquisate,
subordinate to them.
In the sixth year of Duke Zhāo,
Prince Wěi assassinated him and took the throne,
becoming known as Duke Huái.
In the eleventh year of Duke Huái,
Prince Tuí assassinated Duke Huái and succeeded him,
known as
Duke Shèn.
Duke Shèn's father
was Prince Shì;
Shì's father
was Duke Jìng.
Duke Shèn died in his forty-second year,
and his son Duke Shēng Xùn ascended.
Duke Shēng died in his eleventh year,
and his son Marquis Chéng Sù succeeded him.
In the eleventh year of Marquis Chéng,
Gōngsūn Yāng entered Qín.
In the sixteenth year,
Wèi further demoted its title to Hóu.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Marquis Chéng died,
and his son Marquis Píng ascended.
Marquis Píng died in his eighth year,
and his son Lord Sìjūn succeeded him.
In the fifth year of Lord Sìjūn,
the title was further reduced to Jūn,
retaining only Púyáng.
He died in his forty-second year,
and his son Lord Huáijūn ascended.
In the thirty-first year of Lord Huáijūn,
he paid homage to Wèi,
but Wèi imprisoned and killed him.
Wèi then installed Lord Sìjūn's younger brother,
known as Lord Yuán.
Lord Yuán was Wèi's son-in-law,
hence Wèi established him.
In the fourteenth year of Lord Yuán,
Qín captured Wèi's eastern territories,
initially establishing the Dōngjùn commandery,
and moved Wèi to Yěwáng County,
merging Púyáng into Dōngjùn.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Lord Yuán died,
and his son Lord Jiǎo succeeded him.
In the ninth year of Lord Jiǎo,
Qín unified the empire,
and established the First Emperor.
In the twenty-first year,
the Second Emperor demoted Lord Jiǎo to a commoner,
and Wèi's lineage was severed.
Grand Historian comments:
Reading the hereditary houses' records,
regarding Duke Xuān's heir apparent being executed due to a woman,
and his younger brother Shòu vying to die in mutual deference,
this parallels how Jìn's heir apparent Shēnshēng dared not expose Lí Jī's faults,
both fearing to hurt their fathers' intentions.
Yet they ultimately met death—
how sorrowful it is!
Some fathers and sons kill each other,
brothers destroy one another;
why is this so?
Wēizǐ Kāi
was the eldest son of Emperor Yǐ of Yīn and the half-brother of Emperor Zhòu.
After Zhòu ascended,
he lacked clarity,
indulging in chaotic governance,
so Wēizǐ repeatedly admonished him,
but Zhòu would not listen.
When Zǔ Yī, seeing Zhōu's Xībó Chāng cultivating virtue,
eliminating the Yǎn state,
feared disaster was imminent,
he reported it to Zhòu.
Zhòu said:
"Was I not born with a mandate from heaven?
What can they do!"
Thus, Wēizǐ judged that Zhòu would never heed advice,
considered dying for it,
or leaving,
but could not decide,
so he consulted the Grand Tutor
and Junior Tutor, saying:
"Yīn lacks orderly governance,
failing to rule the four quarters.
Our ancestors achieved much above,
yet Zhòu drowns in wine below,
favors women,
corrupting Tāng's virtue.
All in Yīn, great and small, engage in thievery and villainy;
ministers and officials act unlawfully,
all guilty,
yet none are apprehended;
the common people rise up,
becoming mutual enemies.
Now Yīn is sure to fall!
Like wading water with no shore in sight.
Yīn's downfall
has reached this day."
He added:
"Grand Tutor,
Junior Tutor,
should I depart?
Or safeguard our house in ruin?
Now you have inexplicably told me
of collapse;
what should I do?"
The Grand Tutor replied:
"Prince,
heaven has heavily sent disasters to destroy Yīn,
yet he fears nothing,
disregarding the elders.
Now the Yīn people neglect the rites to gods and spirits.
If one could truly govern the state,
dying without regret would be fine.
But if dying
still fails to bring order,
it's better to leave."
So he fled.
Jīzǐ
was a relative of Zhòu.
When Zhòu first used ivory chopsticks,
Jīzǐ sighed:
"With ivory chopsticks,
he'll surely have jade cups;
with such cups,
he'll crave rare delicacies from afar.
Luxury in carriages, horses, and palaces will start from this,
irrecoverable."
As Zhòu grew decadent,
Jīzǐ admonished him,
but he didn't listen.
Someone said:
"You can leave now."
Jīzǐ replied:
"A minister who leaves after his advice is ignored
exposes his ruler's faults to win popular favor,
which I cannot bear to do."
So he disheveled his hair and feigned madness, becoming a slave.
He then concealed himself, playing the qin to express his sorrow,
hence the composition known as "Jīzǐ's Melody."
Prince Bǐgān
was also Zhòu's relative.
Seeing Jīzǐ's advice ignored and his enslavement,
he said:
"If a ruler errs and one doesn't risk death to remonstrate,
what hope have the people!"
So he directly admonished Zhòu.
Zhòu angrily said:
"I hear a sage's heart has seven apertures;
is this true?"
He then killed Prince Bǐgān,
cutting out his heart to examine it.
Wēizǐ said:
"Father and son share a blood bond,
while ruler and minister are bound by duty.
So if a father errs,
and the son advises thrice unheeded,
he may follow with lamentation;
if a minister advises thrice unheeded,
by duty he may leave."
Thus, the Grand Tutor
and Junior Tutor urged Wēizǐ to depart,
and he left.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu overthrew Zhòu and conquered Yīn,
Wēizǐ took the sacrificial vessels to the army gate,
bared his upper body, bound his hands behind,
led a sheep with his left,
held grass with his right,
and knelt walking forward to surrender.
King Wǔ then released Wēizǐ,
restoring his position as before.
King Wǔ enfeoffed Zhòu's son Wǔgēng Lùfù to continue Yīn's sacrifices,
appointing Guǎn Shū
and Cài Shū as his mentors.
After conquering Yīn,
King Wǔ visited Jīzǐ.
King Wǔ said:
"Alas!
Heaven silently stabilizes the people below,
harmonizing their dwellings,
yet I don't understand the principles of the ancient emperors' order."
Jīzǐ replied:
"In the past, Gǔn blocked the Flood,
disrupting the arrangement of the Five Elements,
so the Emperor became enraged,
not following the nine categories of the Great Plan,
causing the constant principles to be neglected.
Gǔn was then executed,
and Yǔ succeeded to continue the work.
Heaven then bestowed upon Yǔ the nine categories of the Great Plan,
thereby ordering the constant principles."
"First is the Five Elements;
second is the Five Matters;
third is the Eight Governmental Offices;
fourth is the Five Regulations;
fifth is the Royal Ultimate;
sixth is the Three Virtues;
seventh is the Examination of Doubts;
eighth is the Various Verifications;
ninth is the Encouragement through Five Blessings,
and Awe through Six Extremities."
"Five Elements:
first is water,
second is fire,
third is wood,
fourth is metal,
fifth is earth.
Water is called moistening downward,
fire is called flaming upward,
wood is called bending and straightening,
metal is called following and changing,
earth is called sowing and reaping.
Moistening downward produces saltiness,
flaming upward produces bitterness,
bending and straightening produces sourness,
following and changing produces acridity,
sowing and reaping produces sweetness."
"Five Matters:
first is appearance,
second is speech,
third is vision,
fourth is hearing,
fifth is thinking.
Appearance should be respectful,
speech should be accordant,
vision should be clear,
hearing should be distinct,
thinking should be profound.
Respectfulness leads to solemnity,
accordance leads to orderliness,
clearness leads to wisdom,
distinctness leads to deliberation,
profundity leads to sageliness."
"Eight Governmental Offices:
first is food,
second is goods,
third is sacrifices,
fourth is Minister of Works,
fifth is Minister of Education,
sixth is Minister of Justice,
seventh is reception of guests,
eighth is military affairs."
"Five Regulations:
first is year,
second is month,
third is day,
fourth is stars and planets,
fifth is calendrical calculations."
"Royal Ultimate:
the sovereign establishes the ultimate standard,
gathering these five blessings,
to bestow upon the common people.
Only then do the common people support your standard,
and you are granted the preservation of the standard.
All the common people,
should not form illicit cliques,
and people should not have collusive conduct,
only the sovereign establishes the ultimate standard.
All the common people,
who have plans, actions, and principles,
you should consider them.
Those who do not conform to the standard,
but do not fall into crime,
the sovereign should accept them.
And with calm and pleasant countenance,
saying 'I love virtue',
you should then bestow blessings upon them.
Such people will then support the sovereign's ultimate standard.
Do not oppress the widowed and orphaned, nor fear the lofty and brilliant.
Those who have abilities and achievements,
encourage them to improve their conduct,
and the state will prosper.
All your officials,
already wealthy, should be guided to goodness.
If you cannot make them contribute to your household,
such people will be at fault.
As for those without merit,
even if you bestow blessings upon them,
they will bring you harm.
Do not be partial, do not be biased,
follow the king's righteousness.
Do not have personal preferences,
follow the king's way.
Do not have personal aversions,
follow the king's path.
Do not be partial, do not form factions,
the king's way is broad and level.
Do not form factions, do not be partial,
the king's way is peaceful and even.
Do not deviate, do not incline,
the king's way is straight and upright.
Gather at the ultimate standard,
return to the ultimate standard.
The dissemination of the king's ultimate standard,
is to be practiced and followed,
and is in accord with the Emperor's will.
All the common people,
the dissemination of the ultimate standard,
should be followed and practiced,
to approach the Son of Heaven's brilliance.
The Son of Heaven serves as parent to the people,
to be king over all under heaven."
"Three Virtues:
first is uprightness and correctness,
second is firmness and overcoming,
third is gentleness and overcoming.
In peace and tranquility, be upright and correct;
against the unyielding and hostile, use firmness to overcome;
toward the yielding and friendly, use gentleness to overcome;
for the deeply reserved, use firmness to overcome;
for the lofty and brilliant, use gentleness to overcome.
Only the sovereign may confer blessings,
only the sovereign may display authority,
only the sovereign may enjoy precious food.
Ministers should not confer blessings, display authority, or enjoy precious food.
If ministers confer blessings, display authority, and enjoy precious food,
it will harm your household,
and bring disaster to your state.
Officials will become partial and corrupt,
the people will transgress and err."
"Consulting Doubts:
Select and appoint diviners.
Then command the divination,
called rain,
called clearing,
called cloudiness,
called mist,
called victory,
called the inner hexagram,
called the outer hexagram,
totaling seven.
Five from turtle shells,
two used for prognostication,
with variations and interpretations.
Appoint timely persons for divination,
if three persons divine, follow the words of two.
If you have great doubts,
consult your own heart,
consult the high officials,
consult the common people,
consult the turtle shells and stalks.
If you consent,
the turtle consents,
the stalks consent,
the high officials consent,
the common people consent,
this is called great harmony,
then your person will be healthy and strong,
and your descendants will be prosperous and auspicious.
If you consent,
the turtle consents,
the stalks consent,
the high officials oppose,
the common people oppose,
it is auspicious. If the high officials consent,
the turtle consents,
the stalks consent,
you oppose,
the common people oppose,
it is auspicious. If the common people consent,
the turtle consents,
the stalks consent,
you oppose,
the high officials oppose,
it is auspicious. If you consent,
the turtle consents,
the stalks oppose,
the high officials oppose,
the common people oppose,
for internal affairs it is auspicious,
for external affairs it is inauspicious.
If both turtle and stalks together go against the people,
remaining still is auspicious,
taking action is inauspicious.
"Various Signs:
called rain,
called sunshine,
called warmth,
called cold,
called wind,
called timeliness.
If these five come fully,
each in its proper order,
the myriad grasses will flourish luxuriantly.
If one is extremely excessive,
it is inauspicious. If one is extremely lacking,
it is inauspicious. Auspicious Signs:
called reverence,
timely rain follows;
called orderliness,
timely sunshine follows;
called wisdom,
timely warmth follows;
called deliberation,
timely cold follows;
called sageliness,
timely wind follows.
Ominous Signs:
called arrogance,
constant rain follows;
called excess,
constant sunshine follows;
called indolence,
constant warmth follows;
called haste,
constant cold follows;
called dimness,
constant wind follows.
The king's governance is like the year,
the high officials like the month,
the officers like the day.
If the year, month, day, and season do not change,
the hundred grains will ripen,
governance will be clear,
the talented people will be illustrious,
the state will be peaceful and prosperous.
If the sun, moon, year, and season change,
the hundred grains will not ripen,
governance will be dark and unclear,
the talented people will be obscure,
the state will not be tranquil.
The common people are like the stars,
some stars favor wind,
some stars favor rain.
The movements of the sun and moon,
have winter and summer.
When the moon follows the stars,
it brings wind and rain.
"Five Blessings:
first is longevity,
second is wealth,
third is health and peace,
fourth is love of virtue,
fifth is a natural death.
Six Extremities:
first is untimely death,
second is sickness,
third is sorrow,
fourth is poverty,
fifth is wickedness,
sixth is weakness."
Thereupon King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed Jīzǐ in Cháoxiān but did not treat him as a subject.
Later, Jīzǐ came to court to Zhōu,
passing by the old ruins of Yīn,
feeling sorrowful over the destroyed palaces,
where millet grew,
Jīzǐ grieved over it,
wanting to wail but could not,
wanting to weep but feared it would seem womanly,
so he composed the "Poem of Wheat Tassels" to sing of it.
The poem said:
"Wheat tassels wave gently,
millet grows lush and green.
That cunning boy,
is not good to me!"
The so-called cunning boy
was Zhòu.
The people of Yīn heard it,
and all shed tears.
King Wǔ passed away,
King Chéng was young,
Zhōu Gōng Dàn acted as regent governing the state.
Guǎn and Cài suspected him,
and together with Wǔ Gēng started a rebellion,
intending to attack King Chéng
and Zhōu Gōng.
After Zhōu Gōng, under King Chéng's order, executed Wǔ Gēng,
killed Guǎn Shū,
and exiled Cài Shū,
he commanded Wēizǐ Kāi to succeed the Yīn lineage,
to continue their ancestral sacrifices,
composing "The Mandate of Wēizǐ" to declare it,
and established the state in Sòng.
Wēizǐ was originally capable, benevolent, and worthy,
thus succeeding Wǔ Gēng,
so the remaining people of Yīn greatly respected and loved him.
Wēizǐ Kāi died,
and his brother Yǎn was established,
known as Wēi Zhòng.
Wēi Zhòng died,
his son Duke Jī of Sòng was established.
Duke Jī of Sòng died,
his son Duke Dīng Shēn was established.
Duke Dīng Shēn died,
his son Duke Mǐn Gòng was established.
Duke Mǐn Gòng died,
his younger brother Duke Yáng Xī was established.
When Duke Yáng ascended the throne,
Duke Mǐn's son Fùsì assassinated Duke Yáng and established himself,
saying
"I should be established,"
known as Duke Lì.
Duke Lì died,
his son Duke Xī Jǔ was established.
In the seventeenth year of Duke Xī,
King Lì of Zhōu fled to Zhì.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Duke Xī died,
his son Duke Huì Jiàn was established.
In the fourth year of Duke Huì,
King Xuān of Zhōu ascended the throne.
In the thirtieth year,
Duke Huì died,
his son Duke Āi was established.
Duke Āi died in the first year of his reign,
his son Duke Dài was established.
In the twenty-ninth year of Duke Dài,
King Yōu of Zhōu was killed by the Quǎnróng,
and Qín began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the thirty-fourth year,
Duke Dài passed away,
and his son, Duke Wǔ, also known as Sīkōng, succeeded him.
Duke Wǔ had a daughter who became the wife of Duke Huì of Lǔ,
and she gave birth to Duke Huán of Lǔ.
In the eighteenth year,
Duke Wǔ died,
and his son, Duke Xuān, named Lì, ascended the throne.
Duke Xuān had a crown prince named Yǔyí.
In the nineteenth year,
Duke Xuān fell ill,
and he yielded the throne to his younger brother Hé,
saying:
"When a father dies, the son succeeds;
when an elder brother dies, the younger brother follows.
This is the universal principle of the world.
I shall establish Hé."
Hé also declined three times before accepting it.
After Duke Xuān's death,
his younger brother Hé took the throne,
becoming known as Duke Mù.
In the ninth year of Duke Mù's reign,
he fell ill and summoned the Grand Marshal Kǒngfù, telling him:
"The late Duke Xuān passed over the crown prince Yǔyí to establish me,
and I dare not forget.
When I die,
you must enthrone Yǔyí."
Kǒngfù said:
"All the ministers wish to establish the noble Féng."
Duke Mù replied:
"Do not enthrone Féng;
I cannot betray Duke Xuān."
Thereupon, Duke Mù sent Féng to reside in Zhèng.
On the Gēngchén day of the eighth month,
Duke Mù died,
and his elder brother Duke Xuān's son Yǔyí was enthroned,
becoming Duke Shāng.
The noblemen heard of this,
and said:
"Duke Xuān of Sòng can be said to have known men well;
he established his younger brother to fulfill righteousness,
and yet his son ultimately enjoyed the throne again."
In the first year of Duke Shāng's reign,
the noble Zhōuyù of Wèi assassinated his ruler Wán and seized the throne,
desiring to win over the feudal lords.
He sent a message to Sòng, saying:
"Féng is in Zhèng,
and will surely cause turmoil;
you can join me in attacking him."
Sòng agreed,
and joined in attacking Zhèng,
but turned back upon reaching the east gate.
In the second year,
Zhèng attacked Sòng
in retaliation for the battle at the east gate.
Thereafter, the feudal lords repeatedly came to invade and attack.
In the ninth year,
the wife of Grand Marshal Kǒngfù Jiā was beautiful;
when she went out,
she met Grand Steward Huá Dū on the road,
and Dū was captivated,
staring at her intently.
Dū coveted Kǒngfù's wife,
so he sent people to spread a declaration in the state:
"Duke Shāng has been on the throne for only ten years,
yet we have fought eleven battles,
and the people suffer unbearably,
all because of Kǒngfù;
I will kill Kǒngfù to bring peace to the people."
That year,
Lǔ assassinated its ruler Duke Yǐn.
In the tenth year,
Huá Dū attacked and killed Kǒngfù,
taking his wife.
Duke Shāng was enraged,
so Dū then assassinated Duke Shāng,
and welcomed Duke Mù's son Féng from Zhèng to enthrone him,
who became Duke Zhuāng.
In the first year of Duke Zhuāng's reign,
Huá Dū served as chancellor.
In the ninth year,
they captured Zhèng's Jì Zhòng,
compelling him to establish Tū as the ruler of Zhèng.
Jì Zhòng agreed,
and eventually enthroned Tū.
In the nineteenth year,
Duke Zhuāng died,
and his son Duke Mǐn, named Jié, succeeded him.
In the seventh year of Duke Mǐn's reign,
Duke Huán of Qí ascended the throne.
In the ninth year,
Sòng suffered a flood,
and Lǔ sent Zāng Wénzhòng to offer condolences for the flood.
Duke Mǐn blamed himself, saying:
"I, the unworthy one, have failed to serve the spirits and gods,
and my governance is not well-ordered,
hence the flood."
Zāng Wénzhòng praised these words.
These words were actually taught to Duke Mǐn by the noble Zǐyú.
In the summer of the tenth year,
Sòng attacked Lǔ,
battling at Shèngqiū,
where Lǔ captured Nángōng Wàn of Sòng alive.
The people of Sòng requested Wàn's return,
and Wàn went back to Sòng.
In the autumn of the eleventh year,
Duke Mǐn went hunting with Nángōng Wàn,
and during a game, they argued over precedence.
Duke Mǐn became angry,
insulting him,
saying:
"At first, I respected you;
now, you are
a captive of Lǔ."
Wàn was strong,
and resented these words,
so he killed Duke Mǐn at Méngzé with a game board.
The minister Qiú Mù heard of this,
and went armed to the duke's gate.
Wàn fought Mù,
and Mù died with his teeth embedded in the door leaf.
Then Wàn killed Grand Steward Huá Dū,
and established the noble Yóu as the new ruler.
The other nobles fled to Xiāo,
and the noble Yùyuè fled to Bó.
Wàn's younger brother Nángōng Niú led troops to besiege Bó.
In winter, Xiāo and the nobles of Sòng jointly attacked and killed Nángōng Niú,
assassinated Sòng's new ruler Yóu, and established Duke Mǐn's younger brother Yùyuè,
who became Duke Huán.
Wàn of Sòng fled to Chén.
The people of Sòng requested his extradition with bribes to Chén.
The people of Chén had a woman give him strong wine to drink,
then wrapped him in leather,
and returned him to Sòng.
The people of Sòng minced Wàn.
In the second year of Duke Huán's reign,
the feudal lords attacked Sòng,
but withdrew upon reaching the outskirts.
In the third year,
Duke Huán of Qí began his hegemony.
In the twenty-third year,
they welcomed the noble Huǐ of Wèi from Qí,
and established him,
who became Duke Wén of Wèi.
Duke Wén's younger sister became the wife of Duke Huán.
Duke Mù of Qín ascended the throne.
In the thirtieth year,
Duke Huán fell ill,
and the crown prince Zīfǔ yielded the succession to his elder half-brother Mùyí.
Duke Huán appreciated the crown prince's intent,
but ultimately did not consent.
In the spring of the thirty-first year,
Duke Huán died,
and the crown prince Zīfǔ succeeded him,
becoming Duke Xiāng.
He appointed his elder half-brother Mùyí as chancellor.
Before the burial was completed,
Duke Huán of Qí met with the feudal lords at Kuíqiū,
and Duke Xiāng went to attend.
In the seventh year of Duke Xiāng's reign,
meteorites fell like rain in Sòng,
descending together with the rain;
six fish hawks flew backward,
due to the strong wind.
In the eighth year,
Duke Huán of Qí died,
and Sòng sought to form a league.
In the spring of the twelfth year,
Duke Xiāng of Sòng held the alliance at Lùshàng,
seeking the support of the feudal lords from Chǔ,
and the people of Chǔ agreed.
Prince Mùyí remonstrated, saying:
"For a small state to contend for hegemony,
is a calamity."
But the duke did not listen.
In autumn, the feudal lords met with the Duke of Sòng to form an alliance at Yú.
Mùyí said:
"Is the calamity not here?
My lord's desires are too extreme;
how can this be endured!"
Thereupon, Chǔ seized Duke Xiāng of Sòng to attack Sòng.
In winter, they met at Bó,
and released the Duke of Sòng.
Zǐyú said:
"The calamity is not yet over."
In summer of the thirteenth year,
Sòng attacked Zhèng.
Zǐyú said:
"The calamity lies here."
In autumn, Chǔ attacked Sòng to rescue Zhèng.
Duke Xiāng was about to engage in battle,
Zǐyú remonstrated:
"Heaven has abandoned Shāng for a long time;
it cannot be done."
In winter,
in the eleventh month,
Duke Xiāng battled with King Chéng of Chǔ at Hóng.
Before the Chǔ army had crossed the river,
Mùyí said:
"They are many, we are few;
strike them before they have crossed."
The duke did not listen.
After they had crossed but before they had formed ranks,
he said again:
"They can be attacked."
The duke said:
"Wait until they have formed ranks."
When the ranks were formed,
the men of Sòng attacked them.
The Sòng army was greatly defeated,
and Duke Xiāng was wounded in the thigh.
The people of the state all blamed the duke.
The duke said:
"A gentleman does not inflict distress upon others,
nor does he drum an attack on those not in formation."
Zǐyú said:
"In war, victory is the goal;
what use are conventional sayings!
If we must act as you say,
we might as well serve them as slaves;
why even engage in battle?"
After King Chéng of Chǔ had rescued Zhèng,
Zhèng feasted him;
he then left, taking two princesses of Zhèng with him.
Shū Zhān said:
"King Chéng is without propriety;
will he not die an unnatural death?
In propriety, ending without distinction,
this shows he will not achieve hegemony."
That year,
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn passed through Sòng,
and Duke Xiāng, wounded by Chǔ,
desiring Jìn's support,
treated Chóng'ěr lavishly with twenty teams of horses.
In summer of the fourteenth year,
Duke Xiāng died from the wound sustained at Hóng,
and his son, Duke Chéng Wángchén, ascended.
In the first year of Duke Chéng,
Duke Wén of Jìn came to the throne.
In the third year,
Sòng turned away from Chǔ, allied with and drew close to Jìn,
because of the kindness shown to Duke Wén.
In the fourth year,
King Chéng of Chǔ attacked Sòng,
and Sòng appealed urgently to Jìn.
In the fifth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn rescued Sòng,
and the Chǔ army withdrew.
In the ninth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn died.
In the eleventh year,
the Crown Prince Shāngchén of Chǔ murdered his father King Chéng and replaced him.
In the sixteenth year,
Duke Mù of Qín died.
In the seventeenth year,
Duke Chéng died.
Duke Chéng's younger brother Yù killed the Crown Prince and the Grand Minister of War Gōngsūn Gù, then made himself ruler.
The people of Sòng together killed the ruler Yù and established Duke Chéng's youngest son Chǔjiù,
who became Duke Zhāo.
In the fourth year of Duke Zhāo,
Sòng defeated the Tall Dí Yuánsī at Chángqiū.
In the seventh year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ ascended the throne.
In the ninth year,
Duke Zhāo was unprincipled,
and the people did not support him.
Duke Zhāo's younger brother Bàogé was virtuous and treated scholars with respect.
Previously, Duke Xiāng's wife had wished to have an affair with Prince Bào,
but was refused,
so she then assisted him in distributing alms in the state,
and through the minister Huá Yuán, he became the Right Marshal.
When Duke Zhāo went out hunting,
the wife, Wáng Jī, sent Wèi Bó to attack and kill Duke Zhāo Chǔjiù.
His younger brother Bàogé was established,
becoming Duke Wén.
In the first year of Duke Wén,
Jìn led the feudal lords to attack Sòng,
condemning the regicide.
Hearing that Duke Wén had been firmly established,
they withdrew.
In the second year,
Duke Zhāo's son, along with Duke Wén's maternal brother Xū and the clans of Wǔ,
Mù, Dài,
Zhuāng, and Huán, started a rebellion,
Duke Wén executed them all,
and expelled the Wǔ
and Mù clans.
In spring of the fourth year,
Chǔ ordered Zhèng to attack Sòng.
Sòng sent Huá Yuán to command,
Zhèng defeated Sòng,
and captured Huá Yuán.
Before Huá Yuán went into battle,
he killed sheep to feed his soldiers,
but his chariot driver did not get any mutton soup,
so he bore a grudge,
drove into the Zhèng army,
thus the Sòng army was defeated,
and Huá Yuán was captured.
Sòng ransomed Huá Yuán with a hundred war chariots and four hundred fine horses.
Before the full ransom was delivered,
Huá Yuán escaped back to Sòng.
In the fourteenth year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng surrendered to Chǔ,
and Chǔ released him.
In the sixteenth year,
Chǔ sent an envoy passing through Sòng,
Sòng, bearing a past grudge,
seized the Chǔ envoy.
In the ninth month,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Sòng.
In the seventeenth year,
Chǔ had besieged Sòng for five months without relief,
the city of Sòng was in dire straits,
with no food,
Huá Yuán then went secretly at night to see the Chǔ general Zǐ Fǎn.
Zǐ Fǎn reported to King Zhuāng.
The king asked:
"How are things in the city?"
He replied:
"They are splitting bones for fuel,
and exchanging children to eat."
King Zhuāng said:
"Truly so your words!
My army also has only two days' rations."
Because of their honesty,
he then withdrew his troops and left.
In the twenty-second year,
Duke Wén died,
and his son Duke Gòng Xiá ascended.
He began the practice of lavish burials.
The gentleman criticized Huá Yuán for not fulfilling his ministerial duties.
In the tenth year of Duke Gòng,
Huá Yuán was on good terms with the Chǔ general Zǐ Zhòng,
and also with the Jìn general Luán Shū,
and brokered alliances between Jìn and Chǔ.
In the thirteenth year,
Duke Gòng died.
Huá Yuán was the Right Marshal,
Yú Shí was the Left Marshal.
The Minister of War Tángshān attacked and killed the Crown Prince Féi,
and wanted to kill Huá Yuán,
Huá Yuán fled to Jìn,
but Yú Shí stopped him,
and when he reached the river, he returned,
and executed Tángshān.
They then established Duke Gòng's youngest son Chéng,
who became Duke Píng.
In the third year of Duke Píng,
King Gòng of Chǔ captured Péngchéng of Sòng,
and enfeoffed it to Sòng's Left Minister Yú Shí.
In the fourth year,
the feudal lords jointly executed Yú Shí,
and returned Péngchéng to Sòng.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Prince Wéi of Chǔ assassinated his sovereign and established himself,
becoming King Líng.
In the forty-fourth year,
Duke Píng passed away,
and his son Duke Yuán, Zuǒ, succeeded him.
In the third year of Duke Yuán,
Prince Qì Jí of Chǔ assassinated King Líng,
and established himself as King Píng.
In the eighth year,
a fire broke out in Sòng.
In the tenth year,
Duke Yuán was untrustworthy,
deceitfully killing the various princes,
leading to the great officers Huá
and the Xiàng clan to rebel.
Prince Jiàn of King Píng of Chǔ came fleeing,
witnessed the conflict and chaos among the Huá clan,
and Jiàn left for Zhèng.
In the fifteenth year,
Duke Yuán, because Duke Zhāo of Lǔ was avoiding the Jì clan and living abroad,
sought to help him return to Lǔ,
but died on the journey,
and his son Duke Jǐng, Tóu Màn, succeeded him.
In the sixteenth year of Duke Jǐng,
Yáng Hǔ of Lǔ came fleeing,
but soon left again.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Confucius passed through Sòng,
and Sòng's Marshal Huán Tuí disliked him,
wanting to kill Confucius,
so Confucius left in disguise.
In the thirtieth year,
Cáo betrayed Sòng,
and also betrayed Jìn,
so Sòng attacked Cáo,
and Jìn did not rescue,
thus Cáo was destroyed and annexed.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Tián Cháng of Qí assassinated Duke Jiǎn.
In the thirty-seventh year,
King Huì of Chǔ destroyed Chén.
Marshal (the planet Mars) guarded the Heart constellation.
The Heart constellation corresponds to the domain of Sòng.
Duke Jǐng was troubled by this.
The astrologer Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be shifted to the chancellor."
Duke Jǐng said:
"The chancellor
is my limbs and arms."
He said:
"It can be shifted to the people."
Duke Jǐng said:
"A ruler relies on the people."
He said:
"It can be shifted to the harvest."
Duke Jǐng said:
"If the harvest fails and the people suffer,
for whom would I be ruler!"
Zǐ Wéi said:
"Heaven is high but hears the lowly.
You, as ruler, have spoken three worthy statements,
Marshal should indeed move."
Thereupon they watched for it,
and it indeed shifted three degrees.
In the sixty-fourth year,
Duke Jǐng passed away.
The Sòng prince Tè attacked and killed the crown prince, establishing himself,
known as Duke Zhāo.
Duke Zhāo
was the great-grandson of Duke Yuán by a concubine.
Duke Zhāo's father was Gōngsūn Jiū,
Jiū's father was Prince Duī Qín,
and Duī Qín was the younger son of Duke Yuán.
Duke Jǐng had killed Duke Zhāo's father Jiū,
hence Duke Zhāo resented this and killed the crown prince to establish himself.
Duke Zhāo died in his forty-seventh year,
and his son Duke Dào, Gòu Yóu, succeeded him.
Duke Dào died in his eighth year,
and his son Duke Xiū, Tián, succeeded him.
Duke Xiū Tián died in his twenty-third year,
and his son Duke Pì, Pì Bīng, succeeded him.
Duke Pì died in his third year,
and his son Tī Chéng succeeded him.
In the forty-first year of Tī Chéng,
his younger brother Yǎn attacked Tī Chéng,
Tī Chéng was defeated and fled to Qí,
and Yǎn established himself as the lord of Sòng.
In the eleventh year of Lord Yǎn,
he declared himself king.
He defeated Qí in the east,
capturing five cities;
defeated Chǔ in the south,
taking three hundred lǐ of land;
defeated the Wèi army in the west,
thus making Qí
and Wèi his enemy states.
He filled a leather bag with blood,
hung it up and shot it,
naming it
"Shooting Heaven."
He indulged in wine and women.
Ministers who remonstrated were immediately shot.
Thereupon the feudal lords all said
"the Jié of Sòng."
"Sòng is repeating the deeds of Zhòu,
and must be punished."
They requested Qí to attack Sòng.
In the forty-seventh year of King Yǎn's reign,
King Mǐn of Qí, along with Wèi
and Chǔ, attacked Sòng,
killed King Yǎn,
then destroyed Sòng and divided its territory three ways.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Confucius said
"Wēizǐ left him,
Jīzǐ became his slave,
Bǐgān remonstrated and died,
Yīn had three benevolent men."
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticize the chaos of Sòng starting from Duke Xuān deposing the crown prince and establishing his brother,
causing the state to be unsettled for ten generations.
In the time of Duke Xiāng,
he cultivated benevolence and righteousness,
desiring to be the hegemon.
His great officer Zhèng Kǎofǔ praised him,
thus traced back the way of Qì,
Tāng, and Gāozōng,
how Yīn rose,
and composed the "Eulogies of Shāng."
After Duke Xiāng was defeated at Hóng,
yet gentlemen sometimes considered him praiseworthy,
grieving that the Central States lacked ritual and righteousness,
thus extolling him,
for Duke Xiāng of Sòng had ritual and deference.
Shū Yú of Táng in Jìn
was the son of King Wǔ of Zhōu and younger brother of King Chéng.
Initially, when King Wǔ was with Shū Yú's mother,
he dreamed Heaven said to King Wǔ:
"I command you to bear a son,
named Yú,
and I give him Táng."
When the child was born,
the character on his hand read
"Yú,"
so he was thus named Yú.
After King Wǔ passed away,
King Chéng succeeded,
Táng was in chaos,
and the Duke of Zhōu destroyed Táng.
King Chéng was playing with Shū Yú,
cut a tung leaf into a guī scepter and gave it to Shū Yú,
saying:
"With this I enfeoff you."
The historian Yì thereupon requested to choose a day to establish Shū Yú.
King Chéng said:
"I was only joking with him."
Yì said:
"The Son of Heaven does not speak in jest.
Words are recorded by historians,
fulfilled with rituals,
and sung with music."
Thereupon Shū Yú was enfeoffed in Táng.
Táng was east of the Hé
and Fén rivers,
a hundred lǐ square,
hence called Shū Yú of Táng.
His surname was Jī,
courtesy name Zǐyú.
Shū Yú of Táng's son Xiè
became the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn's son Níng Zú
became Marquis Wǔ.
Marquis Wǔ's son Fú Rén
became Marquis Chéng.
Marquis Chéng's son Fú
became Marquis Lì.
Marquis Lì's son Yí Jiù
became Marquis Jìng.
From Marquis Jìng onward,
the chronology can be traced.
From Shū Yú to Marquis Jìng were five generations,
but their years are not recorded.
In the seventeenth year of Marquis Jìng,
King Lì of Zhōu, deluded and tyrannical,
caused the people to revolt.
King Lì fled to Zhì,
and the great ministers administered the government,
hence it was called:
"the Joint Harmony."
In the eighteenth year,
Marquis Jìng died,
and his son, Marquis Lí, named Sītú, ascended.
In the fourteenth year of Marquis Lí,
King Xuān of Zhōu first ascended the throne.
In the eighteenth year,
Marquis Lí died,
and his son, Marquis Xiàn, named Jí, ascended.
Marquis Xiàn died in the eleventh year of his reign,
and his son, Marquis Mù, named Fèiwáng, ascended.
In the fourth year of Marquis Mù,
he took a woman of the Qí state, of the Jiāng clan, as his wife.
In the seventh year,
he attacked Tiáo.
There, his heir, named Chóu, was born.
In the tenth year,
he attacked Qiānmǔ,
achieving merit.
There, his younger son was born,
named Chéngshī.
Shīfú of Jìn said:
"How strange,
the names the lord has given his sons!
The heir is named Chóu,
meaning 'enemy.'
The younger son is named Chéngshī,
'Great Leader,'
signifying success.
Names are self-proclaimed;
things define themselves.
Now, the names of the legitimate and the branch are inverted;
can Jìn thereafter avoid chaos?"
In the twenty-seventh year,
Marquis Mù died,
and his younger brother, Shāng Shū, usurped the throne,
forcing the heir Chóu to flee.
In the third year of Shāng Shū,
King Xuān of Zhōu passed away.
In the fourth year,
the heir Chóu of Marquis Mù led his followers to attack and overthrow Shāng Shū, establishing himself,
known as Marquis Wén.
In the tenth year of Marquis Wén,
King Yōu of Zhōu ruled without virtue,
and the Quǎnróng killed King Yōu,
causing Zhōu to move east.
Meanwhile, Duke Xiāng of Qín began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Marquis Wén Chóu died,
and his son, Marquis Zhāo, named Bó, ascended.
In the first year of Marquis Zhāo,
he enfeoffed his father's younger brother, Chéngshī, at Qūwò.
Qūwò was larger than Yì.
Yì was the capital of the Jìn ruler.
Chéngshī, enfeoffed at Qūwò,
was titled Huán Shū.
Luán Bīn, a grandson of Marquis Jìng by a concubine, served as Huán Shū's minister.
Huán Shū was fifty-eight at the time,
virtuous and kind,
and the people of Jìn all supported him.
A nobleman remarked:
"The chaos in Jìn will surely arise from Qūwò.
When the branch is greater than the trunk and wins the people's hearts,
how can chaos not follow!"
In the seventh year,
the Jìn minister Pān Fǔ assassinated his lord Marquis Zhāo and invited Huán Shū of Qūwò.
Huán Shū sought to enter Jìn,
but the people of Jìn raised troops to attack him.
Huán Shū was defeated,
and returned to Qūwò.
The people of Jìn collectively established Marquis Zhāo's son, Píng, as lord,
known as Marquis Xiào.
They executed Pān Fǔ.
In the eighth year of Marquis Xiào,
Huán Shū of Qūwò died,
and his son, Shàn, succeeded him,
known as Zhuāng Bó of Qūwò.
In the fifteenth year of Marquis Xiào,
Zhuāng Bó of Qūwò assassinated the Jìn lord Marquis Xiào at Yì.
The people of Jìn attacked Zhuāng Bó of Qūwò,
and Zhuāng Bó retreated back to Qūwò.
The people of Jìn reestablished Marquis Xiào's son, Xì, as lord,
known as Marquis È.
In the second year of Marquis È,
Duke Yǐn of Lǔ first ascended the throne.
Marquis È died in the sixth year.
When Zhuāng Bó of Qūwò heard of Marquis È's death,
he raised troops to attack Jìn.
King Píng of Zhōu sent the Duke of Guó to lead troops against Zhuāng Bó of Qūwò,
and Zhuāng Bó fled back to Qūwò.
The people of Jìn collectively established Marquis È's son, Guāng, as lord,
known as Marquis Āi.
In the second year of Marquis Āi,
Zhuāng Bó of Qūwò died,
and his son, Chēng, succeeded him,
known as Wǔ Gōng of Qūwò.
In the sixth year of Marquis Āi,
Lǔ assassinated its lord Duke Yǐn.
In the eighth year of Marquis Āi,
Jìn invaded Xíngtíng.
Xíngtíng conspired with Wǔ Gōng of Qūwò,
and in the ninth year,
they attacked Jìn by the Fén River,
capturing Marquis Āi.
The people of Jìn then established Marquis Āi's son, Xiǎozi, as lord,
known as Lord Xiǎozi.
In the first year of Lord Xiǎozi,
Wǔ Gōng of Qūwò sent Hán Wàn to kill the captured Marquis Āi.
Qūwò grew stronger,
and Jìn could do nothing about it.
In the fourth year of Lord Xiǎozi of Jìn,
Wǔ Gōng of Qūwò lured and summoned Lord Xiǎozi, killing him.
King Huán of Zhōu sent Guó Zhòng to attack Wǔ Gōng of Qūwò,
and Wǔ Gōng retreated into Qūwò,
leading to the establishment of Marquis Āi's younger brother, Mín, as the Marquis of Jìn.
In the fourth year of Marquis Mín of Jìn,
Sòng captured Jì Zhòng of Zhèng and established Tū as the lord of Zhèng.
In the nineteenth year of Marquis Mín,
Guǎn Zhìfǔ of Qí assassinated his lord Duke Xiāng.
In the twenty-eighth year of Marquis Mín,
Duke Huán of Qí began his hegemony.
Wǔ Gōng of Qūwò attacked Marquis Mín of Jìn,
annihilating him,
and used all his treasures to bribe and present to King Xī of Zhōu.
King Xī appointed Wǔ Gōng of Qūwò as the Marquis of Jìn,
ranking him among the feudal lords,
thus he merged all of Jìn's territory under his rule.
Wǔ Gōng of Qūwò had already been on the throne for thirty-seven years,
and he changed his title to Wǔ Gōng of Jìn.
Wǔ Gōng of Jìn first made Jìn his capital,
having previously ruled from Qūwò,
totaling thirty-eight years in power.
Wǔ Gōng, named Chēng,
was a great-grandson of the former Marquis Mù of Jìn,
and a grandson of Huán Shū of Qūwò.
Huán Shū
was first enfeoffed at Qūwò.
Wǔ Gōng
was the son of Zhuāng Bó.
From the initial enfeoffment of Huán Shū at Qūwò until Wǔ Gōng's destruction of Jìn,
sixty-seven years passed in total,
and he finally replaced Jìn as a feudal lord.
Wǔ Gōng ruled Jìn for two years
and died. Including his time in Qūwò,
he reigned for a total of thirty-nine years before his death.
His son, Duke Xiàn, named Guǐzhū, ascended.
In the first year of Duke Xiàn,
Tuí, the younger brother of King Huì of Zhōu, attacked King Huì,
forcing him to flee,
and he resided in the city of Lì in Zhèng.
In the fifth year,
he attacked the Lìróng,
capturing Lì Jī
and her younger brother,
both of whom he favored and doted on.
In the eighth year,
Shì Wěi advised the duke:
"The many scions of the former Jìn house are numerous;
if not eliminated,
chaos will arise."
So, he had all the scions killed,
and built a capital at Jù,
naming it Jiàng,
and began to rule from Jiàng.
In the ninth year,
the surviving Jìn scions fled to Guó,
and Guó, for this reason, attacked Jìn twice,
but failed to conquer it.
In the tenth year,
Jìn intended to attack Guó,
but Shì Wěi said:
"Wait for their internal chaos first."
In the twelfth year,
Lí Jī gave birth to Xī Qí.
Duke Xiǎn intended to depose the crown prince,
so he said:
"Qūwò is where the ancestral temple of our forebears is located,
while Pú borders Qín,
and Qū borders Dí.
If I do not have my sons reside in these places,
I fear [the consequences]."
Thereupon, he sent Crown Prince Shēnshēng to reside in Qūwò,
Prince Chóng'ěr to reside in Pú,
and Prince Yíwú to reside in Qū.
Duke Xiǎn and Lí Jī's son Xī Qí remained in Jiàng.
From this, the state of Jìn knew that the crown prince would not be established.
Crown Prince Shēnshēng's
mother was a daughter of Duke Huán of Qí,
named Qí Jiāng,
who died early.
Shēnshēng's full younger sister became the wife of Duke Mù of Qín.
Chóng'ěr's mother
was a woman from the Hú clan of Dí.
Yíwú's mother
was Chóng'ěr's mother's younger sister.
Duke Xiǎn had eight sons,
and Crown Prince Shēnshēng,
Chóng'ěr,
and Yíwú all had worthy conduct.
After obtaining Lí Jī,
he distanced himself from these three sons.
In the sixteenth year,
Duke Xiǎn of Jìn established two armies.
The duke commanded the upper army,
Crown Prince Shēnshēng commanded the lower army,
with Zhào Sù as charioteer,
and Bì Wàn as the right guard,
attacking and destroying Huò,
destroying Wèi,
and destroying Gěng.
Upon returning, he built a city at Qūwò for the crown prince,
bestowed Gěng upon Zhào Sù,
and bestowed Wèi upon Bì Wàn,
appointing them as senior officials.
Shì Wěi said:
"The crown prince will not be established.
He is given a capital city,
and positioned as a minister,
first brought to the extreme,
how could he still be established!
It would be better to flee,
and not let the crime come upon him.
To become a Tàibó of Wú,
would that not be acceptable?
He would still have a good name."
The crown prince did not follow this advice.
Bǔ Yǎn said:
"Bì Wàn's descendants will surely become great.
Wàn means a full number;
Wèi means a great name.
To begin rewards with this,
Heaven has opened the way.
The Son of Heaven speaks of 'millions of people',
feudal lords speak of 'ten-thousands of people',
now he is given a great name,
following a full number,
he is sure to have multitudes."
Earlier, Bì Wàn had divined about serving in the state of Jìn,
and encountered Zhūn changing to Bǐ.
Xīn Liào interpreted it, saying:
"Auspicious.
Zhūn signifies firmness, Bǐ signifies entry,
what could be more auspicious than this?
His descendants will surely flourish."
In the seventeenth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Crown Prince Shēnshēng to attack Dōngshān.
Lǐ Kè advised Duke Xiǎn, saying:
"The crown prince is responsible for the sacrificial offerings to the state altars,
and for overseeing the ruler's meals morning and evening,
hence he is called the heir.
When the ruler travels, he guards [the state];
if there is someone guarding, then he follows;
following is called overseeing the army,
guarding is called supervising the state -
this is the ancient system.
Leading troops
involves exclusive execution of plans;
addressing the army
is what the ruler and state ministers deliberate on -
these are not the crown prince's affairs.
The army's role lies in controlling orders;
receiving commands lacks authority,
while acting independently shows lack of filial piety,
therefore the ruler's designated heir should not command troops.
You are failing in your official duty,
and the army leadership will lack authority -
what use is there in this?"
The duke said:
"I have sons,
but do not know who will be established as crown prince."
Lǐ Kè did not reply and withdrew,
then went to see the crown prince.
The crown prince said:
"Am I to be deposed?"
Lǐ Kè said:
"Crown Prince, exert yourself!
You are being instructed in military affairs -
you should fear not fulfilling your duties,
why would you be deposed?
Moreover, you should fear being unfilial,
not fear not being established.
Cultivate yourself without blaming others,
and you will avoid disaster."
When the crown prince led the army,
the duke dressed him in parti-colored garments,
and adorned him with a golden jué.
Lǐ Kè pleaded illness,
and did not follow the crown prince.
The crown prince then attacked Dōngshān.
In the nineteenth year,
Duke Xiǎn said:
"When our former rulers Zhuāngbó
and Duke Wǔ suppressed the rebellions in Jìn,
Guó often assisted Jìn in attacking us,
and also harbored Jìn's fugitive princes,
indeed causing trouble.
If we do not eliminate them,
they will leave worries for our descendants."
He then sent Xún Xī with horses from Qūchǎn to borrow a path through Yú.
Yú granted passage,
so they attacked Guó,
capturing Xià Yáng and returning.
Duke Xiǎn privately told Lí Jī:
"I wish to depose the crown prince
and replace him with Xī Qí."
Lí Jī wept and said:
"The establishment of the crown prince
is already known by all the feudal lords,
and he has repeatedly commanded troops,
with the common people supporting him.
How can you depose the legitimate heir and establish a lesser son because of a lowly concubine?
If you insist on doing this,
I will commit suicide."
Lí Jī outwardly praised the crown prince,
while secretly having people slander and malign him,
wanting to establish her own son.
In the twenty-first year,
Lí Jī said to the crown prince:
"The lord dreamed of Qí Jiāng;
you should quickly offer sacrifices in Qǔwò,
and present the blessings to the lord."
The crown prince then sacrificed to his mother Qí Jiāng in Qǔwò,
and presented the sacrificial meat to Duke Xiàn.
Duke Xiàn was away hunting at the time,
so the meat was left in the palace.
Lí Jī had someone place poison in the meat.
After two days,
when Duke Xiàn returned from the hunt,
the cook presented the meat to Duke Xiàn,
who was about to eat it.
Lí Jī stopped him from the side,
saying:
"This meat has come from afar;
it should be tested."
They offered it to the earth,
and the earth swelled;
they gave it to a dog,
and the dog died;
they gave it to a servant,
and the servant died.
Lí Jī wept and said:
"How cruel the crown prince is!
He would kill his own father to take his place,
let alone others?
Moreover, you are old,
a man of twilight years,
and he could not even wait but sought to kill you!"
She said to Duke Xiàn:
"The reason the crown prince did this
is none other than because of me and Xī Qí.
I wish for my son and me to flee to another state,
or to take my own life early,
so as not to let us be slaughtered by the crown prince.
When you first wanted to depose him,
I still resented it;
but now,
I deeply regret my mistake in this matter."
When the crown prince heard this,
he fled to Xīnchéng.
Duke Xiàn was enraged,
and executed his tutor Dù Yuánkuǎn.
Someone said to the crown prince:
"It was Lí Jī who prepared this poison;
why don't you explain yourself and clarify the truth?"
The crown prince said:
"Our lord is old;
without Lí Jī,
he cannot sleep peacefully,
nor eat with enjoyment.
If I explain,
the lord will be angry with her.
It cannot be done."
Someone said to the crown prince:
"You could flee to another state."
The crown prince said:
"If I leave bearing this evil name,
who would take me in?
I will take my own life."
On the wùshēn day of the twelfth month,
Shēnshēng committed suicide in Xīnchéng.
At this time, Chóng'ěr and
Yí Wú came to court.
Someone informed Lí Jī:
"The two princes resent Lí Jī for slandering and causing the crown prince's death."
Lí Jī was afraid,
so she slandered the two princes:
"They knew about the poison in Shēnshēng's sacrificial meat."
When the two heard this,
they were afraid. Chóng'ěr fled to Pú,
and Yí Wú fled to Qū,
securing their cities
and preparing their defenses.
Earlier, Duke Xiàn had sent Shì Wěi to build walls for the two princes at Pú and
Qū,
but they were not completed.
Yí Wú reported this to the duke,
who was angry with Shì Wěi.
Shì Wěi apologized, saying:
"Border cities face few bandits;
what use are they?"
Withdrawing, he sang:
"The fox fur is disheveled;
one state has three lords—
whom should I follow?"
Eventually, the walls were completed.
After Shēnshēng's death,
the two also returned to secure their cities.
In the twenty-second year,
Duke Xiàn was angry that the two had left without taking leave,
suspecting they had plots indeed,
so he sent troops to attack Pú.
The eunuch Bó Dī of Pú ordered Chóng'ěr to quickly commit suicide.
Chóng'ěr leaped over the wall,
and the eunuch pursued and cut off his sleeve.
Chóng'ěr then fled to Dí.
He sent men to attack Qū,
but Qū was well defended
and could not be taken.
That year,
Jìn again borrowed a path through Yú to attack Guó.
The Yú official Gōng Zhīqí advised the lord of Yú:
"Do not grant Jìn passage,
for they will destroy Yú."
The lord of Yú said:
"Jìn shares our surname;
they would not attack us."
Gōng Zhīqí said:
"Tàibó and
Yúzhòng
were sons of King Tài;
Tàibó fled,
so he did not succeed.
Guó Zhòng and
Guó Shū
were sons of King Jì,
serving as ministers to King Wén;
their merits are recorded in the royal court,
stored in the covenant archives.
If they will destroy Guó,
why would they spare Yú?
Moreover, is Yú's kinship closer than that of the Huán and
Zhuāng clans?
What crime did the Huán and Zhuāng clans commit,
that they were utterly exterminated?
Yú and Guó
are like lips and teeth;
if the lips are gone, the teeth will be cold."
The Duke of Yú did not listen
and granted Jìn passage.
Gōng Zhīqí left Yú with his clan.
That winter,
Jìn destroyed Guó,
and Duke Chǒu of Guó fled to Zhōu.
On the return, they attacked and destroyed Yú,
capturing the Duke of Yú and his official Jǐng Bó Bǎilǐ Xī, who were given as dowry attendants to Qín Mù Jī,
while continuing the sacrifices of Yú.
Xún Xí led the previously gifted Qūchǎn horses of Yú and presented them to Duke Xiàn,
who laughed and said:
"The horses are indeed my horses,
but their teeth have grown old!"
In the twenty-third year,
Duke Xiàn sent Jiǎ Huá and others to attack Qū,
and Qū fell.
Yí Wú was about to flee to Dí.
Jì Ruì said:
"Do not;
Chóng'ěr is already there.
If we go now,
Jìn will surely shift troops to attack Dí;
Dí fears Jìn,
and disaster will befall us.
Better to flee to Liáng,
which is near Qín;
Qín is strong,
and after our lord's passing, we can seek help there."
So he fled to Liáng.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Jìn attacked Dí;
because of Chóng'ěr, Dí
also attacked Jìn at Nièsāng,
and the Jìn troops withdrew and left.
At this time,
Jìn was strong,
with Héxī to the west,
bordering Qín,
Dí to the north,
and reaching Hénèi to the east.
Lí Jī's younger sister gave birth to Dào Zǐ.
In the summer of the twenty-sixth year,
Duke Huán of Qí convened a grand assembly of feudal lords at Kuíqiū.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn was ill,
and set out afterward,
but before arriving,
he encountered Zhǎi Kǒng of Zhōu.
Zhǎi Kǒng said:
"Duke Huán of Qí grows increasingly arrogant,
neglecting virtue and pursuing distant campaigns;
the feudal lords are discontent.
You, my lord, should not attend the meeting—
what can Jìn do about it anyway?"
Duke Xiàn, also ill,
turned back and returned.
As his illness worsened,
he said to Xún Xī:
"I have appointed Xī Qí as my successor,
but he is young,
and the senior ministers will not submit to him.
I fear turmoil will arise—
can you establish him?"
Xún Xī replied:
"I can."
Duke Xiàn asked:
"How will you prove it?"
He answered:
"Even if the dead were to revive,
the living would feel no shame—
this shall be my proof."
Thereupon, he entrusted Xī Qí to Xún Xī.
Xún Xī served as chancellor,
overseeing state affairs.
In the autumn, the ninth month,
Duke Xiàn passed away.
Lǐ Kè
and Pī Zhèng wished to bring back Chóng Ĕr,
and with the followers of the three princes, they started a rebellion.
They said to Xún Xī:
"The resentment of the three princes is about to erupt,
supported by Qín and Jìn—
what will you do?"
Xún Xī said:
"I cannot betray the late ruler's words."
In the tenth month,
Lǐ Kè killed Xī Qí during the mourning period,
before Duke Xiàn was buried.
Xún Xī was about to die for this,
but someone suggested it would be better to establish Xī Qí's younger brother, Dào Zǐ, and serve as his tutor.
Xún Xī established Dào Zǐ and buried Duke Xiàn.
In the eleventh month,
Lǐ Kè assassinated Dào Zǐ in the court,
and Xún Xī died for it.
The gentleman remarked:
"As the *Book of Songs* says,
'A flaw in a white jade scepter
can still be ground away;
but a flaw in these words
cannot be undone.'
This surely refers to Xún Xī!
