He did not betray his word."
Earlier, when Duke Xiàn was about to attack the Lí Róng,
a divination stated:
'Teeth and jaws will bring disaster.'
After defeating the Lí Róng,
he captured Lí Jī,
doted on her,
and ultimately brought chaos to Jìn.
After Lǐ Kè and others had killed Xī Qí
and Dào Zǐ,
they sent someone to welcome Prince Chóng Ĕr from Dí,
intending to install him.
Chóng Ĕr declined, saying:
"I fled against my father's command;
upon his death, I could not perform the duties of a son in mourning.
How dare I enter now!
Let the ministers install another son."
When this was reported back to Lǐ Kè,
he sent someone to welcome Yí Wú from Liáng.
Yí Wú intended to go,
but Lǚ Shěng
and Xì Ruì said:
"There are still princes inside the state who could be installed, yet we seek one from outside—
this is hard to trust.
If we do not seek Qín's help,
and enter with the support of a powerful state's might,
I fear it will be perilous."
So they sent Xì Ruì to richly bribe Qín,
pledging:
"If I am able to enter,
I will grant Qín the land west of the Yellow River in Jìn."
And they sent a letter to Lǐ Kè, saying:
"If I am truly installed,
I will enfeoff you with the city of Fényáng."
Duke Mù of Qín then dispatched troops to escort Yí Wú into Jìn.
Duke Huán of Qí, hearing of Jìn's internal strife,
also led the feudal lords to Jìn.
When Qín's troops and Yí Wú arrived in Jìn,
Qí sent Xí Péng to join Qín in escorting Yí Wú inside,
and he was installed as the ruler of Jìn,
known as Duke Huì.
Duke Huán of Qí reached Gāoliáng in Jìn and then returned.
In the first year of Duke Huì Yí Wú,
he sent Pī Zhèng to apologize to Qín, saying:
"Initially, Yí Wú promised you the land west of the river,
but now that I have fortunately been installed,
the ministers say:
'The land belonged to the former ruler;
how could you, while in exile abroad,
presume to promise it to Qín?'
I argued but could not prevail,
hence I apologize to Qín."
He also did not grant Lǐ Kè the city of Fényáng,
instead stripping him of his power.
In the fourth month,
King Xiāng of Zhōu sent Zhōu Gōng Jì Fù to join with ministers from Qí
and Qín in ceremonially acknowledging Duke Huì of Jìn.
Duke Huì, concerned that Chóng Ĕr was abroad,
feared Lǐ Kè might instigate a revolt,
and ordered Lǐ Kè to commit suicide.
He said to him:
"Without you, sir, I could not have been installed.
Nevertheless,
you have killed two rulers and one high official—
is it not difficult to be your ruler?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"If there had been no removals,
how could you, my lord, have risen?
If you wish to execute me,
is there any lack of pretext?
So you speak thus!
I have heard your command."
Thereupon, he fell on his sword and died.
At that time, Pī Zhèng was on a mission to apologize to Qín and had not returned,
so he avoided the calamity.
The Jìn ruler reburied the revered heir, Shēn Shēng.
In autumn, Hú Tū went to Xiàguó,
where he encountered Shēn Shēng.
Shēn Shēng took him into his carriage and told him:
"Yí Wú has been disrespectful;
I have obtained permission from the Emperor,
and will give Jìn to Qín,
and Qín will sacrifice to me."
Hú Tū replied:
"I have heard that spirits do not accept sacrifices from those not of their lineage;
would your sacrifices not then cease?
Please consider this."
Shēn Shēng said:
"Very well,
I will request the Emperor again.
Ten days from now,
a shaman will see me in the western outskirts of Xīnchéng."
He agreed,
and then disappeared.
When Hú Tū went at the appointed time,
he saw him again,
and Shēn Shēng informed him:
"The Emperor has agreed to punish the guilty,
and they will fall at Hán."
Children then sang:
"The revered heir has been reburied;
after fourteen years,
Jìn will not prosper,
and prosperity will rest with the elder brother."
When Pī Zhèng was on his mission to Qín,
he heard of Lǐ Kè's execution,
and advised Duke Mù of Qín:
"Lǚ Shěng,
Xì Chēng,
and Jì Ruì are truly disloyal.
If you bribe them heavily and conspire with them,
to expel the Jìn ruler
and bring in Chóng Ĕr,
the plan will surely succeed."
Duke Mù of Qín agreed,
and sent someone to return with him to report to Jìn,
offering rich bribes to the three men.
The three said:
"Such generous gifts and sweet words—
this must be Pī Zhèng betraying us to Qín."
They then killed Pī Zhèng, along with Lǐ Kè
and Pī Zhèng's faction, the seven carriage ministers.
Pī Zhèng's son, Bào, fled to Qín,
and urged an attack on Jìn,
but Duke Mù did not listen.
Upon Duke Huì's installation,
he reneged on the land to Qín and to Lǐ Kè,
executed the seven carriage ministers,
and the people of the state did not support him.
In the second year,
Zhōu sent Shào Gōng Guò to ceremonially acknowledge Duke Huì of Jìn,
but Duke Huì behaved arrogantly during the ceremony,
and Shào Gōng criticized him.
In the fourth year,
Jìn suffered a famine,
and begged for grain from Qín.
Duke Mù of Qín consulted Bǎilǐ Xī,
who said:
"Natural disasters are rampant,
and every state is bound to experience them in turn.
To relieve disasters and show compassion to neighbors
is the way of a state.
Give it to them."
Pī Zhèng's son Bào said:
"Attack them."
Duke Mù said:
"We detest their ruler,
but what crime have their people committed!"
He finally provided grain,
extending from Yōng to Jiàng."
In the fifth year,
Qín suffered a famine,
and requested grain from Jìn.
The ruler of Jìn consulted about it.
Qìng Zhèng said:
"Thanks to Qín you gained the throne,
yet you later broke the territorial agreement.
When Jìn had a famine, Qín lent us grain;
now Qín is in famine and requests grain—
why hesitate to give it?
And yet you consult about it!"
Guó Shè said:
"In previous years, Heaven granted Jìn to Qín,
but Qín did not know to take it and instead lent us grain.
Now Heaven grants Qín to Jìn;
how can Jìn go against Heaven?"
They then attacked Qín."
Duke Huì of Jìn followed Guó Shè's plan,
did not give Qín grain,
and instead raised troops to attack Qín.
Qín was greatly angered,
and also raised troops to attack Jìn.
In the spring of the sixth year,
Duke Mù of Qín led troops to attack Jìn.
Duke Huì of Jìn said to Qìng Zhèng:
"The Qín army has penetrated deep;
what should we do?"
Zhèng said:
"Qín helped you gain the throne internally,
yet you broke your promise of territory;
when Jìn had a famine, Qín transported grain,
but when Qín had a famine, Jìn turned against them,
and even sought to attack them in their distress—
isn't their deep penetration quite appropriate!"
Jìn divined for charioteer and right-hand guard,
and both positions were auspicious for Qìng Zhèng.
The duke said:
"Zhèng is disrespectful."
So he changed the order, having Bù Yáng drive the war chariot,
and Jiāpú Tú as the right-hand guard,
then advanced the troops.
In the ninth month, on the Rénxū day,
Duke Mù of Qín
and Duke Huì of Jìn joined battle at Hányuán.
Duke Huì's horse sank and would not move;
the Qín troops arrived,
and the duke was in distress,
so he summoned Qìng Zhèng to drive.
Zhèng said:
"You did not follow the divination;
isn't defeat only fitting!"
He then left.
They changed to Liáng Yǎomí driving
and Guó Shè as the right-hand guard,
and intercepted Duke Mù of Qín.
Duke Mù's brave warriors broke through the Jìn army;
the Jìn army was defeated,
and they lost Duke Mù of Qín,
but instead captured the Duke of Jìn and returned.
Qín intended to sacrifice him to the Supreme Deity.
The elder sister of the Duke of Jìn was Duke Mù's wife,
and she wept in mourning dress.
The duke said:
"Capturing the Marquis of Jìn was meant to be a joy,
but now it has come to this.
Moreover, I heard that Jīzǐ, upon seeing Táng Shū's initial enfeeffment,
said
'His descendants are bound to be great';
how could Jìn be extinguished!"
So he made a covenant with the Marquis of Jìn at Wángchéng and allowed him to return.
The Marquis of Jìn also sent Lǚ Shěng and others to report to the people of the state:
"Though I have been allowed to return,
I have no face to see the altars of soil and grain.
Divine for a day to enthrone my son Yǔ."
When the people of Jìn heard this,
they all wept.
Duke Mù of Qín asked Lǚ Shěng:
"Is the state of Jìn harmonious?"
He replied:
"It is not harmonious.
The petty men fear losing their ruler and their kin,
and do not hesitate to enthrone Zǐ Yǔ,
saying
'We must take revenge,
even if it means serving the Róng
and Dí.'
The noble men, however, love their ruler and acknowledge their guilt,
awaiting Qín's command,
saying
'We must repay the virtue.'
For these two reasons,
it is not harmonious."
Thereupon, Duke Mù of Qín changed the residence of Duke Huì of Jìn,
and presented him with seven sets of sacrificial animals.
In the eleventh month,
he returned the Marquis of Jìn.
When the Marquis of Jìn reached his state,
he executed Qìng Zhèng,
and improved governance and education.
He plotted, saying:
"Chóng'ěr is abroad,
and many feudal lords would benefit from installing him."
He wanted to send someone to kill Chóng'ěr in Dí.
Chóng'ěr heard of this,
and went to Qí.
In the eighth year,
he sent his heir Yǔ to be a hostage in Qín.
Earlier, when Duke Huì was in exile in Liáng,
the Earl of Liáng gave him his daughter as a wife,
and they bore a son and a daughter.
The Earl of Liáng divined about them,
and the boy would be a subject,
the girl a concubine,
so they named the boy Yǔ (prisoner),
and the girl Qiè (concubine).
In the tenth year,
Qín extinguished Liáng.
The Earl of Liáng was fond of construction works,
building walls and moats,
and the people were exhausted and resentful.
The populace repeatedly alarmed each other,
saying
"The Qín invaders are coming",
and the people were terrified and confused.
Qín eventually extinguished it.
In the thirteenth year,
Duke Huì of Jìn fell ill,
and there were several sons within.
Heir Yǔ said:
"My mother's family is in Liáng,
and Liáng has now been extinguished by Qín,
so I am lightly regarded abroad by Qín and have no support at home.
If the ruler does not recover,
the senior officials will look down on me,
and enthrone another prince."
So he plotted to flee back with his wife.
The Qín woman said:
"You are the heir of a state,
demeaned here.
Qín made me, a humble servant, attend you,
to secure your heart.
If you flee,
I will not follow you,
nor dare I speak of it."
Zǐ Yǔ then fled back to Jìn.
In the ninth month of the fourteenth year,
Duke Huì died,
and Heir Yǔ ascended,
becoming Duke Huái.
Because of Zǐ Yǔ's flight,
Qín resented him,
and sought out Prince Chóng'ěr,
intending to install him.
Upon Zǐ Yǔ's accession,
fearing an attack by Qín,
he ordered all in the state who had followed Chóng'ěr in exile to return by a set date,
and those who did not come by the deadline would have their families exterminated.
Hú Tū's sons Máo and Yǎn were with Chóng'ěr in Qín,
and he refused to summon them.
Duke Huái was angry,
and imprisoned Hú Tū.
Tū said:
"My sons have served Chóng'ěr for years;
to summon them now
is to teach them to betray their ruler.
How can I instruct them thus?"
Duke Huái eventually killed Hú Tū.
Duke Mù of Qín then sent troops to escort and install Chóng'ěr,
and had someone inform the partisans of Luán
and Xì to act as internal allies,
killed Duke Huái at Gāoliáng,
and brought in Chóng'ěr.
Chóng'ěr ascended,
becoming Duke Wén.
Jìn Wéngōng Chóng'ěr,
was the son of Jìn Xiàngōng.
From a young age, he was fond of scholars,
and at the age of seventeen,
he had five virtuous scholars:
named Zhào Cuī;
Hú Yǎn Jiùfàn,
who was Wéngōng's maternal uncle;
Jiǎ Tuó;
Xiān Zhěn;
and Wèi Wǔzǐ.
Ever since Xiàngōng was the crown prince,
Chóng'ěr had already grown to adulthood.
When Xiàngōng ascended the throne,
Chóng'ěr was twenty-one years old.
In the thirteenth year of Xiàngōng's reign,
because of Lí Jī,
Chóng'ěr was sent to guard Púchéng against Qín.
In the twenty-first year of Xiàngōng's reign,
Xiàngōng killed the crown prince Shēnshēng,
and Lí Jī slandered him,
so Chóng'ěr, in fear, did not bid farewell to Xiàngōng and went to guard Púchéng.
In the twenty-second year of Xiàngōng's reign,
Xiàngōng sent the eunuch Lǚ Dī to hasten and kill Chóng'ěr.
Chóng'ěr leaped over the wall,
and the eunuch chased him, cutting off his sleeve.
Chóng'ěr then fled to Dí.
Dí was his mother's homeland.
At this time, Chóng'ěr was forty-three years old.
He was accompanied by these five scholars,
along with several dozen others whose names are not recorded,
and they reached Dí.
Dí attacked Jiùrú,
and captured two women:
they gave the elder daughter to Chóng'ěr as a wife,
who gave birth to Bó Tiáo,
and Shū Liú;
and the younger daughter to Zhào Cuī as a wife,
who gave birth to Dùn.
After living in Dí for five years, Jìn Xiàngōng died,
and Lǐ Kè had already killed Xī Qí
and Dào Zǐ,
so he sent someone to welcome Chóng'ěr,
intending to establish him as ruler.
Chóng'ěr feared being killed,
and thus firmly declined,
not daring to return.
Soon after, Jìn instead welcomed his younger brother Yí Wú and established him,
who became Huìgōng.
In the seventh year of Huìgōng's reign,
fearing Chóng'ěr,
he sent the eunuch Lǚ Dī with strong men to kill Chóng'ěr.
Chóng'ěr heard of this,
and discussed with Zhào Cuī and others, saying:
"When I first fled to Dí,
it was not because I thought it could be of use,
but because it was close and easy to reach,
so I rested my feet there for a while.
I have rested long enough,
and I truly wish to move to a larger state.
Now, Qí Huángōng is fond of goodness,
with ambitions to be a hegemon and king,
and he gathers and comforts the various lords.
Now I hear that Guǎn Zhòng
and Xí Péng have died,
so he must also wish to obtain worthy assistants;
why not go there?"
So they set off.
Chóng'ěr said to his wife:
"Wait for me twenty-five years; if I do not return,
then marry."
His wife laughed and said:
"In twenty-five years,
the cypress on my grave will be large.
Even so,
I will wait for you."
Chóng'ěr stayed in Dí for a total of twelve years before leaving.
Passing through Wèi,
Wèi Wéngōng did not treat him with courtesy.
Leaving, they passed Wǔlù,
and being hungry, they begged for food from the villagers,
who offered them earth in a vessel.
Chóng'ěr was angry.
Zhào Cuī said:
"Earth
symbolizes having land;
my lord, you should bow and accept it."
Arriving in Qí,
Qí Huángōng treated him with great courtesy,
and gave him a daughter of the royal clan as a wife,
along with twenty teams of horses,
and Chóng'ěr felt content there.
Chóng'ěr had been in Qí for two years when Huángōng died,
and it happened that Shù Diāo and others caused internal strife,
with Qí Xiàogōng's establishment,
troops from various lords arrived several times.
He stayed in Qí for a total of five years.
Chóng'ěr loved the woman from Qí,
and had no intention of leaving.
Zhào Cuī
and Jiùfàn then plotted under a mulberry tree to depart.
A maid of the Qí woman, who was in the mulberry tree overhead, heard them,
and reported it to her mistress.
Her mistress then killed the maid,
and urged Chóng'ěr to hasten his departure.
Chóng'ěr said:
"In life, one seeks peace and happiness;
who cares about anything else!
I will surely die here,
and cannot leave."
The Qí woman said:
"You are a prince of a state,
who came here in distress,
and several scholars stake their lives on you.
If you do not quickly return to your state,
to repay your toiling ministers,
but cling to a woman's virtue,
I secretly feel ashamed for you.
Moreover, if you do not seek it,
when will you achieve merit?"
So she plotted with Zhào Cuī and others,
got Chóng'ěr drunk,
and carried him away in a carriage.
When they had gone far and he woke,
Chóng'ěr was greatly angered,
and took a spear intending to kill Jiùfàn.
Jiùfàn said:
"If killing me completes your mission,
it is Yuǎn's wish."
Chóng'ěr said:
"If the matter does not succeed,
I will eat my uncle's flesh."
Jiùfàn said:
"If the matter does not succeed,
my flesh is rank and foul,
hardly worth eating!"
So he stopped,
and they proceeded.
Passing through Cáo,
Cáo Gōnggōng did not treat them with courtesy,
and wanted to see Chóng'ěr's fused ribs.
The Cáo senior official Lí Fùjī said:
"The Jìn prince is worthy,
and moreover of the same clan;
he comes to us in distress,
how can we not treat him with courtesy!"
Gōnggōng did not follow his advice.
Fùjī then privately sent food to Chóng'ěr,
placing a jade disc beneath it.
Chóng'ěr accepted the food,
but returned the jade disc.
Leaving,
they passed through Sòng.
Sòng Xiānggōng had recently been defeated by Chǔ troops,
wounded at Hóng,
and hearing of Chóng'ěr's worthiness,
treated him with the rites due a ruler.
The Sòng minister of war Gōngsūn Gù was friendly with Jiùfàn,
and said:
"Sòng is a small state and newly defeated,
not sufficient to help you enter your state;
go on to a larger state."
So they left.
Passing through Zhèng,
Zhèng Wéngōng did not treat them with courtesy.
Zhèng's Shū Zhàn advised his lord, saying:
"The Jìn prince is worthy,
and his followers are all capable of being chief ministers of states,
and moreover, they are of the same clan.
Zhèng descends from King Lì,
and Jìn from King Wǔ."
The Zhèng lord said:
"Many exiled princes of states pass through here;
how can I treat them all with full courtesy!"
Shū Zhàn said:
"If my lord does not treat him with courtesy,
it would be better to kill him,
lest he later become a calamity for our state."
The Zhèng lord did not listen.
Chóng'ěr left for Chǔ,
where King Chéng of Chǔ received him with the rites due to a feudal lord,
but Chóng'ěr declined, not daring to accept.
Zhào Cuī said:
"You have been in exile for over a decade;
even small states have treated you lightly,
let alone a great state?
Now Chǔ, a great state, insists on treating you thus,
you should not decline,
for this is Heaven opening the way for you."
So he met the king with the rites for a guest.
King Chéng treated Chóng'ěr generously,
and Chóng'ěr was very humble.
King Chéng said:
"If you return to your state,
how will you repay me?"
Chóng'ěr replied:
"Feathers, furs, ivory, horns, jade, and silk—
these are things you have in abundance,
and I do not know how to repay you."
The king said:
"Even so,
how will you repay me?"
Chóng'ěr said:
"If forced to,
and I meet Your Majesty with war chariots on the plains or marshes,
I would retreat three encampments for you."
The Chǔ general Zǐ Yù angrily said:
"The king has treated the Jìn prince most generously,
yet now Chóng'ěr speaks disrespectfully;
I request to kill him."
King Chéng said:
"The Jìn prince is worthy but long distressed abroad;
his followers are all talents of the state.
This is Heaven's arrangement—
how can he be killed?
Moreover, what else could he have said!"
After staying in Chǔ for several months,
the Jìn crown prince Yǔ fled from Qín,
and Qín resented him;
hearing Chóng'ěr was in Chǔ,
they summoned him.
King Chéng said:
"Chǔ is distant,
passing through several states to reach Jìn.
Qín and Jìn share a border;
the ruler of Qín is worthy,
you should strive to go!"
He sent Chóng'ěr off lavishly.
Chóng'ěr arrived in Qín,
where Duke Mù married five royal daughters to him,
including the former wife of his nephew Yǔ.
Chóng'ěr did not wish to accept,
but Minister of Works Jìzǐ said:
"His state you will attack,
let alone his former wife!
Accept to forge ties with Qín and seek entry to your state;
would you cling to minor etiquette,
forgetting great disgrace?"
So he accepted.
Duke Mù drank joyfully with Chóng'ěr.
Zhào Cuī sang the poem "Shǔ Miáo."
Duke Mù said:
"I know you wish to return to your state urgently."
Zhào Cuī and Chóng'ěr descended,
bowing twice and saying:
"We look up to you,
as all grains await the timely rain."
It was autumn in the fourteenth year of Duke Huì of Jìn.
Duke Huì died in September,
and his son Yǔ succeeded him.
In November,
Duke Huì was buried.
By December,
Jìn ministers such as Luán
and Xì, hearing Chóng'ěr was in Qín,
secretly urged Chóng'ěr
and Zhào Cuī to return,
with many as internal supporters.
Thereupon, Duke Mù of Qín sent troops to escort Chóng'ěr back to Jìn.
Jìn, hearing of Qín's troops,
also dispatched forces to resist.
Yet they secretly knew Prince Chóng'ěr was entering.
Only former high officials of Duke Huì like Lǚ
and Xì's faction opposed installing Chóng'ěr.
Chóng'ěr had been in exile for nineteen years before returning,
aged sixty-two then,
and many in Jìn supported him.
In spring, the first year of Duke Wén,
Qín escorted Chóng'ěr to the river.
Jiù Fàn said:
"I have followed you roaming the world,
and my faults are many.
I still remember them,
how much more you?
I ask to leave from here."
Chóng'ěr said:
"If I return to the state,
and do not share it with you, Zǐ Fàn,
may the River God witness it!"
He then threw a jade into the river,
swearing an oath with Zǐ Fàn.
At that time, Jiè Zǐ Tuī was following,
in the boat,
and laughed, saying:
"Heaven truly opened the way for the prince,
yet Zǐ Fàn claims it as his own merit and bargains with the lord—
truly shameful.
I cannot bear to share rank with him."
He then hid himself and crossed the river.
Qín troops surrounded Línghú,
while Jìn forces were at Lúliǔ.
On February Xīnchǒu,
Jiù Fàn made a pact with Qín and Jìn ministers at Xún.
On Rényín,
Chóng'ěr entered the Jìn army.
On Bǐngwǔ,
he entered Qūwò.
On Dīngwèi,
he paid respects at the Wǔ Palace,
ascended as the ruler of Jìn,
becoming Duke Wén.
All ministers attended.
Duke Huái Yǔ fled to Gāoliáng.
On Wùshēn,
he sent someone to kill Duke Huái.
Former ministers of Duke Huái, Lǚ Shěng
and Xì Ruì, had not supported Duke Wén initially;
after Duke Wén's accession,
fearing execution,
they plotted with followers to burn the duke's palace
and kill Duke Wén.
Duke Wén was unaware.
The eunuch Lǚ Dī, who had once tried to kill Duke Wén, learned of the plot
and sought to inform Duke Wén,
to atone for past crimes,
requesting an audience.
Duke Wén refused,
sending a reproach:
"At Púchéng,
you cut my sleeve.
Later, when I hunted with the Dí lord,
you came for Duke Huì to kill me.
Duke Huì gave you three days,
yet you arrived in one—
why so hasty?
Think on that."
The eunuch said:
"I am one maimed by punishment,
but dared not serve two masters disloyally,
thus offending you.
Now you have returned to your state;
are there no more Pú or Dí affairs?
Moreover, Guǎn Zhǒng shot the hook,
yet Duke Huán achieved hegemony.
Now a penal survivor brings warning, yet you refuse audience—
disaster will strike again."
Thereupon, Duke Wén met him,
and he informed Duke Wén of Lǚ
and Xì's plot.
Duke Wén wished to summon Lǚ
and Xì, but their faction was large;
fearing betrayal by his people upon his recent return,
he traveled incognito,
meeting Duke Mù of Qín at Wángchéng,
unknown to his countrymen.
On March Jǐchǒu,
Lǚ and Xì indeed rebelled,
burning the duke's palace
but failing to capture Duke Wén.
Duke Wén's guards fought them,
and as Lǚ and Xì led troops to flee,
Duke Mù of Qín lured Lǚ
and Xì's group,
killing them by the river.
Jìn was pacified, and Duke Wén returned.
In summer, he welcomed his wife from Qín,
and she whom Qín had married to Duke Wén became his duchess.
Qín sent three thousand men as guards
to safeguard against turmoil in Jìn.
Duke Wén undertook governmental reforms,
bestowing benefits upon the common people.
He rewarded those who followed him in exile and his meritorious officials,
granting the most prominent fiefs and
honoring the lesser with noble titles.
Before the rewards were fully distributed,
King Xiāng of Zhōu, forced to flee due to the troubles caused by his brother Dài, took refuge in Zhèng territory,
and sent an urgent appeal to Jìn for help.
Jìn, having just stabilized,
intended to dispatch troops,
but feared other disturbances might arise;
thus, the reward for following in exile had not yet reached the recluse Jiè Zǐtuī.
Tuī did not speak of emoluments,
and emoluments did not come to him.
Tuī said:
"Of the nine sons of Duke Xiàn,
only you, my lord, remain.
Neither Duke Huì nor Duke Huái had close kin,
and both were abandoned by those within and without;
Heaven has not severed Jìn,
so there must be a ruler,
and who but you, my lord,
is to preside over the sacrifices of Jìn?
It was truly Heaven that opened the way,
yet a few men claim it as their own achievement—
is that not deceitful?
To steal another's wealth
is still called theft;
how much more so to greedily take Heaven's merit as one's own?
Those below conceal their crimes,
while those above reward their deceit;
with superiors and subordinates deceiving each other,
it is difficult to dwell among them!"
His mother said:
"Why not also seek reward?
To die with resentment—whom would you blame?"
Tuī replied:
"To condemn and then imitate them
would be an even greater offense.
Moreover, having voiced grievances,
I will not partake of their emoluments."
His mother said:
"Then let them know of this—
what do you think?"
He answered:
"Words are the adornment of the person;
if one intends to live in seclusion,
what need is there for adornment?
To adorn oneself
is to seek prominence."
His mother said:
"Can you truly do this?
I will join you in seclusion."
They remained unseen until their deaths.
A follower of Jiè Zǐtuī, pitying him,
hung a message on the palace gate saying:
"A dragon sought to ascend the heavens,
with five serpents as its aides.
The dragon has risen on the clouds,
four serpents each found their abodes,
but one serpent alone harbored resentment,
never finding its place."
Duke Wén, upon exiting,
saw the message and said:
"This refers to Jiè Zǐtuī.
I have been concerned with the royal house's troubles
and have not yet considered his merits."
He sent someone to summon him,
but Tuī had fled.
They then searched for his whereabouts,
hearing he had entered Miánshàng Mountain.
Thereupon, Duke Wén encircled Miánshàng Mountain and enfeoffed it,
designating it as Jiè Tuī's field,
naming it Jiè Mountain,
"to record my fault
and to honor a virtuous man."
Hú Shū, a humble official who had followed in exile, said:
"You have thrice distributed rewards,
yet none have reached me.
I dare ask what my offense is."
Duke Wén replied:
"Those who guided me with benevolence and righteousness,
and restrained me with virtue and kindness—
these receive the highest rewards.
Those who assisted me in action,
leading to the establishment of our state—
these receive the next level of reward.
Those who faced the perils of arrows and stones,
and exerted themselves in the toil of battle—
these receive the subsequent reward.
As for those who served me with mere strength but did not remedy my shortcomings,
they also receive a further level of reward.
After these three rounds of rewards,
it will then be your turn."
The people of Jìn heard this,
and all were pleased.
In the spring of the second year,
the Qín army stationed at the Hé River,
intending to escort the king back.
Zhào Cuī said:
"To seek hegemony, nothing is better than restoring the king and honoring Zhōu.
Zhōu and Jìn share the same surname;
if Jìn does not restore the king first,
and later Qín does so,
we will have no authority to command the world.
Honoring the king now
is Jìn's advantage."
In the third month on Jiǎchén,
Jìn dispatched troops to Yángfán,
besieged Wēn,
and restored King Xiāng to Zhōu.
In the fourth month,
they killed the king's brother Dài.
King Xiāng of Zhōu granted Jìn the territory of Yángfán in Hénèi.
In the fourth year,
King Chéng of Chǔ and the feudal lords besieged Sòng,
and Gōngsūn Gù of Sòng went to Jìn to report the emergency.
Xiān Zhěn said:
"To repay kindness and secure hegemony—
the time is now."
Hú Yǎn said:
"Chǔ has recently acquired Cáo and newly formed a marriage alliance with Wèi;
if we attack Cáo
and Wèi, Chǔ is sure to rescue them,
and then Sòng will be spared."
Thereupon, Jìn formed three armies.
Zhào Cuī recommended Xì Hú to command the central army,
with Xì Zhēn as his deputy;
he appointed Hú Yǎn to command the upper army,
with Hú Máo as his deputy,
and named Zhào Cuī as a minister;
Luán Zhī commanded the lower army,
with Xiān Zhěn as his deputy;
Xún Línfǔ drove the chariot,
and Wèi Chōu served as the guard on the right:
they set out to attack.
In the twelfth month of winter,
the Jìn troops first descended east of the mountains,
and Yuán was enfeoffed to Zhào Cuī.
In the spring of the fifth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn wished to attack Cáo,
and sought passage through Wèi,
but the people of Wèi refused.
Returning, they crossed from the south of the river,
invaded Cáo,
and attacked Wèi.
In the first month,
they captured Wǔlù.
In the second month,
the Marquis of Jìn
and the Marquis of Qí formed an alliance at Liǎnyú.
The Marquis of Wèi requested an alliance with Jìn,
but the people of Jìn refused.
The Marquis of Wèi wished to align with Chǔ,
but the people of the state did not want this,
so they expelled their ruler to please Jìn.
The Marquis of Wèi resided in Xiāngniú,
while Gōngzǐ Mǎi guarded Wèi.
Chǔ came to rescue Wèi,
but did not succeed.
The Marquis of Jìn besieged Cáo.
In the third month on Bǐngwǔ,
the Jìn army entered Cáo,
reprimanding them for not heeding Lí Fùjī's advice
and employing three hundred beauties in carriages.
They ordered the army not to enter the ancestral home of Xī Fùjī to repay his virtue.
Chǔ besieged Sòng,
and Sòng again urgently appealed to Jìn.
Duke Wén wished to rescue Sòng but that meant attacking Chǔ,
for Chǔ had once shown him kindness,
and he was reluctant to attack;
yet to abandon Sòng,
which had also shown kindness to Jìn,
troubled him.
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Capture the Earl of Cáo,
and divide the lands of Cáo
and Wèi to give to Sòng;
Chǔ, concerned for Cáo
and Wèi, will likely release Sòng."
Thereupon, Duke Wén followed this plan,
and King Chéng of Chǔ then led his troops back.
Chǔ general Zǐ Yù said:
"The king treated Jìn with utmost generosity,
yet now knowing Chǔ's urgency regarding Cáo and
Wèi, they deliberately attack them—
this shows contempt for the king."
The king replied:
"The Marquis of Jìn wandered in exile for nineteen years,
enduring prolonged hardship,
but ultimately returned to his state.
He knows all perils and difficulties thoroughly,
can employ his people effectively,
and is opened by Heaven's will—
none can withstand him."
Zǐ Yù requested:
"I dare not claim certain merit,
but wish to seize this opportunity to silence slanderous mouths."
The King of Chǔ grew angry
and gave him few troops.
Thereupon Zǐ Yù sent Wǎn Chūn to inform Jìn:
"Please restore the Marquis of Wèi and reestablish Cáo,
and I shall likewise release Sòng."
Jiù Fàn said:
"Zǐ Yù acts without propriety—
the ruler gains one,
the minister gains two;
do not consent."
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Stabilizing others is called propriety.
Chǔ's single statement stabilizes three states,
while your single statement would destroy them—
then we would lack propriety.
Not agreeing with Chǔ
means abandoning Sòng.
Better to secretly promise Cáo and
Wèi to lure them,
detain Wǎn Chūn to anger Chǔ,
and plan further after battle."
The Marquis of Jìn then imprisoned Wǎn Chūn in Wèi
and secretly promised to restore Cáo
and Wèi. Cáo
and Wèi declared severance from Chǔ.
Chǔ's Dé Chén grew furious,
attacked the Jìn army,
and the Jìn army retreated.
The officers asked:
"Why retreat?"
Duke Wén replied:
"Formerly in Chǔ,
I pledged to retreat three stages;
how can I break that promise!"
The Chǔ army wished to withdraw,
but Dé Chén refused.
On the fourth month, Wù Chén,
the Duke of Sòng,
the general of Qí,
and the general of Qín with the Marquis of Jìn encamped at Chéng Pú.
On Jǐ Sì,
they engaged the Chǔ forces in battle,
the Chǔ troops were defeated,
and Dé Chén gathered his remaining soldiers and left.
On Jiǎ Wǔ,
the Jìn army returned to Héng Yōng,
and built a royal palace at Jiàn Tǔ.
Earlier,
Zhèng had aided Chǔ,
and after Chǔ's defeat,
feared, sending someone to request alliance with the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn allied with the Earl of Zhèng.
On the fifth month, Dīng Wèi,
they presented Chǔ captives to Zhōu:
a hundred chariots with armored teams,
a thousand foot soldiers.
The Son of Heaven sent Wáng Zǐ Hǔ to appoint the Marquis of Jìn as Hegemon,
bestowing a grand carriage,
a hundred red bows and arrows,
a thousand black bows and arrows,
a yǒu of jù chàng aromatic wine,
a jade libation ladle,
and three hundred tiger warriors.
The Marquis of Jìn declined thrice,
then bowed and accepted.
Zhōu composed the "Appointment of the Marquis of Jìn Wén":
"The King speaks thus:
Father Yì Hé,
greatly illustrious Wén
and Wǔ, who could carefully manifest virtue,
shining above,
renowned below,
thus did God confer their mandate upon Wén
and Wǔ. Have compassion on my person,
that I may long remain in position as the One Man."
Thereupon Duke Wén of Jìn became Hegemon.
On Guǐ Hài,
Wáng Zǐ Hǔ convened the feudal lords for a covenant at the royal court.
Jìn set fire to the Chǔ army,
the flames burning for days unceasing,
and Duke Wén sighed.
His attendants asked:
"Having defeated Chǔ, my lord still worries—
why?"
Duke Wén said:
"I have heard only sages can win battles and remain secure,
hence I fear.
Moreover, Zǐ Yù still lives—
how can I rejoice!"
When Zǐ Yù returned defeated,
King Chéng of Chǔ was angry that he had not heeded his words
and greedily engaged Jìn in battle,
reproaching and blaming Zǐ Yù,
and Zǐ Yù committed suicide.
Duke Wén of Jìn said:
"I attacked from without,
Chǔ punished from within—
inside and outside corresponded."
Thereupon he rejoiced.
In the sixth month,
the people of Jìn restored the Marquis of Wèi.
On Rén Wǔ,
the Marquis of Jìn crossed the river north and returned to his state.
Distributing rewards,
Hú Yǎn was placed first.
Someone said:
"Regarding the affair at Chéng Pú,
it was Xiān Zhěn's strategy."
Duke Wén replied:
"At Chéng Pú,
Yǎn urged me not to break faith.
Xiān Zhěn said,
'In military affairs, victory is paramount,'
and I used this to win.
But this was advice for the moment,
while Yǎn's words served for ten thousand generations' merit.
How can I prioritize temporary advantage over eternal achievement?
Therefore I place him first."
In winter,
the Marquis of Jìn met the feudal lords at Wēn,
wishing to lead them to court Zhōu,
but his power was insufficient,
fearing some might rebel,
so he sent word that King Xiāng of Zhōu was hunting at Hé Yáng.
On Rén Shēn,
he then led the feudal lords to court the king at Jiàn Tǔ.
When Confucius read the historical records up to Duke Wén,
he said
"Feudal lords do not summon the king"
and "The king hunted at Hé Yáng"
were cases where the Spring and Autumn Annals used concealed language.
On Dīng Chǒu,
the feudal lords besieged Xǔ.
A minister of the Earl of Cáo persuaded the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"Duke Huán of Qí assembled the feudal lords to establish states of different surnames,
yet now you, my lord, convene a meeting and extinguish a state of the same surname.
Cáo descends from Shū Zhèn Duó;
Jìn descends from Táng Shū.
To assemble the feudal lords and destroy a brother state
is contrary to propriety."
The Marquis of Jìn was pleased,
and restored the Earl of Cáo.
Thereupon Jìn first established three army divisions.
Xún Lín Fǔ commanded the central division,
Xiān Gǔ commanded the right division,
and Xiān Miè commanded the left division.
In the seventh year,
Duke Wén of Jìn
and Duke Mù of Qín jointly besieged Zhèng,
because it had shown disrespect when Duke Wén passed through in exile,
and at Chéng Pú, Zhèng had aided Chǔ.
Besieging Zhèng,
they wished to capture Shū Zhān.
Shū Zhān heard of this
and killed himself.
Zhèng presented Shū Zhān's head to Jìn.
Jìn said:
"We must capture the ruler of Zhèng to be satisfied."
Zhèng, terrified,
secretly sent an envoy to tell Duke Mù of Qín:
"Destroying Zhèng strengthens Jìn—
this benefits Jìn,
but does nothing for Qín.
Why does my lord not release Zhèng,
gaining an eastern ally?"
The Earl of Qín was pleased
and withdrew his troops.
Jìn also withdrew.
In the winter of the ninth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn died,
and his son Duke Xiāng, Huān, succeeded him.
That year the Earl of Zhèng also died.
Some people of Zhèng sold their state to Qín,
and Duke Mù of Qín dispatched troops to launch a surprise attack on Zhèng.
In the twelfth month,
the Qín army passed by our suburbs.
In the spring of the first year of Duke Xiāng,
the Qín army passed through Zhōu,
behaving without propriety,
so Wángsūn Mǎn ridiculed them.
When the troops reached Huá,
a Zhèng merchant Xián Gāo, who was about to trade in Zhōu,
encountered them,
and presented twelve oxen to feast the Qín army.
The Qín army, startled, turned back,
destroyed Huá and left.
Xiān Zhěn of Jìn said:
"The Earl of Qín did not heed Jiǎn Shū,
and has turned his people's hearts against him;
this is an opportunity to attack."
Luán Zhī said:
"We have not yet repaid the kindness our former lord received from Qín;
to attack them
is not permissible."
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Qín has insulted our orphaned state,
and attacked our kinsmen;
what virtue is there to repay?"
So they attacked them.
Duke Xiāng dyed his mourning garments black.
In the fourth month,
they defeated the Qín army at Xiáo,
capturing the three Qín generals Mèngmíng Shì,
Xīqǐ Shú,
and Báiyǐ Bǐng, and brought them back.
Then, in black mourning dress, they buried Duke Wén.
Duke Wén's wife was a woman from Qín,
and she said to Duke Xiāng:
"Qín wishes to retrieve its three generals to execute them."
The duke agreed,
and sent them back.
Xiān Zhěn heard of this,
and said to Duke Xiāng:
"Trouble will arise from this."
Zhěn then pursued the Qín generals.
The Qín generals were crossing the river,
and were already in the boat;
they kowtowed in apology,
but ultimately did not return.
Three years later,
Qín indeed sent Mèngmíng to attack Jìn,
to avenge the defeat at Xiáo,
and captured Jìn's Wāng before returning.
In the fourth year,
Duke Mù of Qín raised a great army to attack us,
crossed the river,
took Wángguān,
buried the dead at Xiáo, and then left.
Jìn was terrified,
dared not venture out,
and thus fortified the city for defense.
In the fifth year,
Jìn attacked Qín,
captured Xīnchéng,
in retaliation for the battle at Wángguān.
In the sixth year,
Zhào Cuī, Chéngzǐ,
Luán Zhēnzǐ,
Jiù Jì Zǐfàn,
and Huò Bó all died.
Zhào Dùn succeeded Zhào Cuī in governance.
In the eighth month of the seventh year,
Duke Xiāng died.
The crown prince Yí Gāo was young.
The people of Jìn, due to the difficulties,
wished to install an elder as lord.
Zhào Dùn said:
"Install Yōng, the brother of Duke Xiāng.
He is virtuous and elder,
and was loved by the former lord;
moreover, he is close to Qín,
an old ally.
Installing a good man ensures stability,
serving an elder ensures order,
Qín's affection ensures filiality,
and maintaining old alliances ensures peace."
Jiǎ Jì said:
"Not as good as his brother Lè.
Chén Yíng was favored by two lords,
installing her son,
the people are sure to be at peace with it."
Zhào Dùn said:
"Chén Yíng was lowly,
ranked below nine others;
how could her son command any awe!
Moreover, being favored by two lords
is licentious.
As for the former lord's son,
unable to seek greatness and living in a small state,
is obscurity.
The mother licentious, the son obscure,
they have no authority;
Chén is small and distant,
with no support:
how could it be acceptable!"
He sent Shì Huì to go to Qín to welcome Prince Yōng.
Jiǎ Jì also sent someone to summon Prince Lè from Chén.
Zhào Dùn dismissed Jiǎ Jì,
because he had killed Yáng Chǔfǔ.
In the tenth month,
they buried Duke Xiāng.
In the eleventh month,
Jiǎ Jì fled to Dí.
That year,
Duke Mù of Qín also died.
In the first year of Duke Líng, in the fourth month,
Duke Kāng of Qín said:
"In the past, when Duke Wén entered, he had no guard,
hence there were the troubles of Lǚ and Xì."
So he provided Prince Yōng with many guards.
The crown prince's mother Mióu Yíng day and night held the crown prince and wailed in court,
saying:
"What crime did the former lord commit?
What crime has his heir committed?
To abandon the rightful heir and seek a lord from outside,
where will you place this child?"
Leaving the court,
she then went holding him to Zhào Dùn's residence,
kowtowed and said:
"The former lord presented this child to you and entrusted him to you,
saying
'If this child is capable,
I shall receive your reward;
if incapable,
I shall resent you.'
Now the lord has died,
his words still ring in our ears,
yet you abandon him;
how can this be?"
Zhào Dùn and the various great officers were all troubled by Mióu Yíng,
and fearing execution,
they betrayed the one they had welcomed and installed the crown prince Yí Gāo,
who became Duke Líng.
They dispatched troops to resist those of Qín who were escorting Prince Yōng.
Zhào Dùn served as general,
went to attack Qín,
and defeated them at Línghú.
Xiān Miè
and Suí Huì fled to Qín.
In autumn, the rulers of Qí,
Sòng, Wèi,
Zhèng, Cáo,
and Xǔ all met with Zhào Dùn,
forming an alliance at Hù,
due to Duke Líng's recent accession.
In the fourth year,
they attacked Qín,
capturing Shǎoliáng.
Qín also took Jìn's Xiáo.
In the sixth year,
Duke Kāng of Qín attacked Jìn,
taking Jīmǎ.
The Marquis of Jìn was angered,
and sent Zhào Dùn,
Zhào Chuān,
and Xì Quē to attack Qín,
engaging in a great battle at Héqū,
where Zhào Chuān achieved the greatest merit.
In the seventh year,
the six ministers of Jìn, troubled by Suí Huì's presence in Qín,
where he often caused trouble for Jìn,
feigned ordering Wèi Shòu Yú to rebel against Jìn and surrender to Qín.
Qín sent Suí Huì to Wèi,
whereupon they captured Huì and brought him back to Jìn.
In the eighth year,
King Qǐng of Zhōu passed away,
the dukes and ministers contended for power,
so the funeral was not announced.
Jìn sent Zhào Dùn with eight hundred chariots to pacify the turmoil in Zhōu and install King Kuāng.
That year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ first ascended the throne.
In the twelfth year,
the people of Qí assassinated their ruler, Duke Yì.
In the fourteenth year,
Duke Líng reached adulthood,
and became extravagant, imposing heavy taxes to decorate his palace walls.
He would shoot pellets at people from a tower,
watching them dodge the projectiles.
When a cook prepared bear's paw undercooked,
Duke Líng grew angry,
killed the cook,
and had women carry his corpse out to discard it,
passing through the court.
Zhào Dùn and
Suí Huì had repeatedly remonstrated before,
but he wouldn't listen;
later, when they saw the dead man's hand,
both came to admonish again.
Suí Huì advised first,
but was ignored.
Duke Líng grew troubled by this
and sent Chú Ní to assassinate Zhào Dùn.
Finding Dùn's bedroom door open
and his living quarters modest,
Chú Ní withdrew,
sighing:
"To kill a loyal minister
or to disobey my lord's command
are equally criminal."
He then crashed into a tree and died.
Earlier,
Dùn often hunted at Shǒu Shān,
where he saw a starving man under a mulberry tree.
The starving man
was Shìmī Míng.
Dùn gave him food,
but he ate only half.
Asked why,
he said:
"Having served as an official for three years,
I don't know if my mother survives,
so I wish to save this for her."
Dùn, moved by his righteousness,
gave him more rice and meat.
Later, he became a cook in Jìn,
though Zhào Dùn didn't recognize him.
In the ninth month,
Duke Líng of Jìn hosted a banquet for Zhào Dùn,
planning to ambush him with hidden soldiers.
The duke's cook Shìmī Míng learned of this,
feared Dùn might be too drunk to escape,
and advised:
"When the ruler bestows wine upon a subject,
three rounds of toasts suffice to conclude."
He sought to help Zhào Dùn leave early,
urging him to depart first
and avoid the danger.
After Dùn left,
before Duke Líng's soldiers could assemble,
he first unleashed a fierce dog named Áo.
Míng fought and killed the dog for Dùn.
Dùn remarked:
"Abandoning people to use dogs,
however fierce, what good are they?"
Yet he didn't know Míng was repaying a hidden kindness.
Soon Duke Líng sent his hidden soldiers to pursue Zhào Dùn,
but Shìmī Míng counterattacked the duke's troops,
preventing their advance,
and ultimately helped Dùn escape.
When Dùn asked his reason,
he said:
"I am the starving man under the mulberry tree."
Dùn asked his name,
but he declined to give it.
Míng then also fled into exile.
Dùn thus fled,
but hadn't yet left Jìn's borders.
On the yǐchǒu day,
Dùn's cousin General Zhào Chuān ambushed and killed Duke Líng in the Peach Garden and welcomed Zhào Dùn back.
Zhào Dùn, long esteemed,
enjoyed popular support;
Duke Líng, being young
and extravagant, lacked people's allegiance,
making the regicide easy.
Dùn resumed his position.
The Grand Historian of Jìn, Dǒng Hú, recorded
"Zhào Dùn assassinated his ruler",
and displayed it at court.
Dùn protested:
"The assassin was Zhào Chuān,
I am innocent."
The Grand Historian replied:
"You were the chief minister,
yet fled without leaving the state's borders,
and returned without punishing the state's disruptors;
if not you, then who?"
Confucius, hearing of this,
said:
"Dǒng Hú
was a fine historian of antiquity,
recording truthfully without concealment.
Xuānzǐ (Zhào Dùn)
was a good minister,
yet bore the blame for the principle's sake.
A pity,
had he crossed the border, he would have been exempt."
Zhào Dùn sent Zhào Chuān to welcome Duke Xiāng's younger brother Hēitún from Zhōu and established him,
who became Duke Chéng.
Duke Chéng
was the youngest son of Duke Wén,
his mother a woman from Zhōu.
On the rénshēn day,
he held court at the Wǔ Palace.
In the first year of Duke Chéng's reign,
he granted the Zhào family the status of ducal clan.
They attacked Zhèng,
because Zhèng had betrayed Jìn.
In the third year,
the Earl of Zhèng newly established,
aligned with Jìn and abandoned Chǔ.
Chǔ, angered,
attacked Zhèng,
and Jìn went to its rescue.
In the sixth year,
they attacked Qín,
capturing the Qín general Chì.
In the seventh year,
Duke Chéng contended for supremacy with King Zhuāng of Chǔ,
and met with feudal lords at Hù.
Chén, fearing Chǔ,
did not attend.
Jìn sent Zhōngháng Huánzǐ to attack Chén,
thereby rescuing Zhèng,
and battled Chǔ,
defeating the Chǔ army.
That year,
Duke Chéng died,
and his son Duke Jǐng Jù succeeded him.
In the spring of Duke Jǐng's first year,
the Chén minister Xià Zhēngshū assassinated his ruler, Duke Líng.
In the second year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Chén,
executing Zhēngshū.
In the third year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Zhèng,
and Zhèng appealed urgently to Jìn for help.
Jìn sent Xún Línfǔ to command the central army,
Suí Huì the upper army,
Zhào Shuò the lower army,
with Xì Kè,
Luán Shū,
Xiān Gǔ,
Hán Jué,
and Gǒng Shuò assisting.
In the sixth month,
they reached the Yellow River.
Hearing that Chǔ had already subdued Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng had bared his shoulder to swear allegiance and departed,
Xún Línfǔ wished to turn back.
Xiān Gǔ said:
"We came to rescue Zhèng;
not reaching it is unacceptable,
and would dishearten the commanders."
They finally crossed the river.
Chǔ, having subdued Zhèng,
wished to water their horses at the river as a pretext to leave.
Chǔ and the Jìn army engaged in a major battle.
Zhèng, newly allied with Chǔ,
feared them,
and instead aided Chǔ in attacking Jìn.
The Jìn army was defeated,
fled to the river,
scrambled to cross,
with many fingers cut off from those clinging to boats.
Chǔ captured our general Zhì Yīng.
Returning, Línfǔ said:
"As the commanding general,
I deserve death for the army's defeat;
I request execution."
Duke Jǐng was inclined to agree.
But Suí Huì said:
"When Duke Wén battled Chǔ at Chéngpú,
King Chéng returned and killed Zǐ Yù,
which pleased Duke Wén.
Now Chǔ has defeated our army,
and if we also execute our general,
it would be aiding Chǔ in killing their rival."
Thus, he refrained.
In the fourth year,
Xiān Hú, having caused the defeat of the Jin army at the river through his own planning,
feared execution,
so he fled to the Dí,
and plotted with the Dí to attack Jin.
Jin discovered this,
and exterminated Hú's clan.
Hú was
the son of Xiān Zhěn.
In the fifth year,
they attacked Zhèng,
because it had aided Chǔ.
At this time, King Zhuāng of Chǔ was strong,
having defeated the Jin army at the river.
In the sixth year,
Chǔ attacked Sòng,
and Sòng came to report the emergency to Jin.
Jin wanted to rescue them,
but Bó Zōng advised:
"Chǔ,
Heaven is now opening the way for them,
they cannot be opposed."
So they sent Xiè Yáng to pretend to be rescuing Sòng.
The people of Zhèng captured him and handed him over to Chǔ.
Chǔ richly rewarded him,
and made him reverse his words,
ordering Sòng to quickly surrender.
Xiè Yáng pretended to agree,
but ultimately delivered the words of the Jin ruler.
Chǔ wanted to kill him,
but someone remonstrated,
so they returned Xiè Yáng.
In the seventh year,
Jin sent Suí Huì to destroy the Red Dí.
In the eighth year,
they sent Xì Kè to Qí.
The mother of Duke Qìng of Qí watched from a tower and laughed at him.
The reason for this was that
Xì Kè was hunchbacked,
the Lǔ envoy was lame,
and the Wèi envoy was blind in one eye,
so Qí had also arranged for people with similar disabilities to guide the guests.
Xì Kè was angered,
and upon returning to the river,
said:
"If I do not take revenge on Qí,
may the River God witness it!"
Upon returning to the state,
he requested an audience with the ruler,
wishing to attack Qí.
Duke Jǐng inquired and learned the reason,
saying:
"Your personal grievance,
how can it be sufficient to trouble the state!"
He did not listen.
Wèi Wénzǐ requested to retire due to age,
yielding his position to Xì Kè,
and Kè took over governance.
In the ninth year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ died.
Jin attacked Qí,
and Qí sent its crown prince, Qiáng, as a hostage to Jin,
and the Jin army withdrew.
In the spring of the eleventh year,
Qí attacked Lǔ,
capturing Lóng.
Lǔ reported the emergency to Wèi,
and both Wèi and Lǔ appealed to Jin for help through Xì Kè.
Jin then sent Xì Kè,
Luán Shū,
and Hán Jué with 800 war chariots to join Lǔ and
Wèi in attacking Qí.
In summer, they battled Duke Qìng at Ān,
wounding and trapping Duke Qìng.
Duke Qìng then exchanged positions with his right-hand attendant,
descended to fetch a drink,
and thus managed to escape.
The Qí army was defeated and fled,
with Jin pursuing them north to Qí.
Duke Qìng offered precious vessels to seek peace,
but it was not accepted.
Xì Kè said:
"We must obtain Xiāo Tóng Zhízǐ as a hostage."
The Qí envoy said:
"Xiāo Tóng Zhízǐ
is Duke Qìng's mother;
Duke Qìng's mother is like the mother of the Jin ruler.
Why must you obtain her?
It is unjust,
we request to fight again."
Jin then agreed to make peace and left.
Chǔ's Shēngōng Wū Chén stole Xià Jī and fled to Jin,
and Jin appointed Wū Chén as senior official of Xíng.
In the winter of the twelfth year,
Duke Qìng of Qí went to Jin,
wishing to honor Duke Jǐng of Jin as king,
but Duke Jǐng declined, not daring to accept.
Jin first established six armies,
with Hán Jué,
Gǒng Shuò,
Zhào Chuān,
Xún Zhuī,
Zhào Kuò,
and Zhào Zhān all becoming ministers.
Zhì Yīng returned from Chǔ.
In the thirteenth year,
Duke Chéng of Lǔ paid court to Jin,
but Jin did not treat him with respect,
so Lǔ left in anger,
and turned against Jin.
Jin attacked Zhèng,
capturing Fán.
In the fourteenth year,
Mount Liáng collapsed.
They consulted Bó Zōng,
who considered it not worthy of astonishment.
In the sixteenth year,
the Chǔ general Zǐ Fǎn, bearing a grudge against Wū Chén,
exterminated his clan.
Wū Chén was enraged,
and sent a letter to Zǐ Fǎn saying:
"I will surely make you exhausted from constant rushing!"
He then requested to be sent to Wú,
had his son serve as Wú's diplomat,
and taught Wú to use chariots and practice warfare.
Wú and Jin began relations,
agreeing to attack Chǔ together.
In the seventeenth year,
they executed Zhào Tóng
and Zhào Kuò,
exterminating their clan.
Hán Jué said:
"How can the merits of Zhào Cuī
and Zhào Dùn be forgotten?
How can we let their line be cut off!"
So they reinstated Zhào's collateral descendant Wǔ as Zhào's heir,
and restored his city.
In the summer of the nineteenth year,
Duke Jǐng fell ill,
and established his crown prince, Shòu Màn, as ruler,
who was Duke Lì.
More than a month later,
Duke Jǐng died.
In the first year of Duke Lì,
newly enthroned,
he wished to harmonize with the various lords,
and formed a pact with Duke Huán of Qín across the river.
But upon returning, Qín broke the pact,
and plotted with the Dí to attack Jin.
In the third year,
he sent Lǚ Xiàng to reprimand Qín,
and then joined with the various lords to attack Qín.
They reached Jīng,
defeated Qín at Másuì,
and captured their general Chéng Chā.
In the fifth year,
the three Xì clans slandered Bó Zōng,
and had him killed.
Bó Zōng incurred this disaster because of his fondness for straightforward remonstrance,
and because of this, the people of the state did not support Duke Lì.
In the spring of the sixth year,
Zhèng betrayed Jìn and formed an alliance with Chǔ,
enraging Jìn.
Luǎn Shū said:
"We cannot lose the feudal lords during our time."
Thus, troops were dispatched.
Duke Lì personally led the army,
crossing the river in May.
Hearing that Chǔ troops were coming to rescue,
Fàn Wénzǐ requested the duke to consider retreat.
Xì Zhì said:
"We raised an army to punish rebels;
if we retreat upon seeing strength,
we will have no means to command the feudal lords."
So they engaged in battle.
On Guǐsì day,
an arrow hit King Gòng of Chǔ in the eye,
and the Chǔ army was defeated at Yānlíng.
Zǐ Fǎn gathered the remaining troops,
consoling and preparing to fight again,
which worried Jìn.
King Gòng summoned Zǐ Fǎn,
but his attendant Shù Yánggǔ offered him wine,
and Zǐ Fǎn got drunk,
unable to appear.
The king was furious,
reprimanded Zǐ Fǎn,
and Zǐ Fǎn died.
The king then led his troops back.
From then on, Jìn intimidated the feudal lords,
seeking to command the world and strive for hegemony.
Duke Lì had many favored concubines from outside,
and upon returning, he wanted to remove all senior officials and install the brothers of his concubines.
The brother of a favored concubine was named Xū Tóng,
who had a grudge against Xì Zhì.
Luǎn Shū also resented Xì Zhì for not following his plan yet still defeating Chǔ,
so he sent someone to secretly thank Chǔ.
Chǔ deceitfully told Duke Lì:
"The Battle of Yānlíng
was actually summoned by Xì Zhì,
who intended to rebel,
installing your son Zhōu internally.
But the allied states were not fully prepared,
so the plan failed."
Duke Lì informed Luǎn Shū.
Luǎn Shū said:
"It might be true!
I hope you can send someone to Zhōu to investigate discreetly."
Indeed, Xì Zhì was sent to Zhōu.
Luǎn Shū also had Prince Zhōu meet Xì Zhì,
unaware that he was being betrayed.
Duke Lì verified it,
found it credible,
thus bore a grudge against Xì Zhì,
and wanted to kill him.
In the eighth year,
during a hunt,
Duke Lì drank with his concubines,
Xì Zhì killed a boar and presented it,
but a eunuch snatched it.
Xì Zhì shot and killed the eunuch.
The duke was angry,
saying:
"Jìzǐ deceives me!"
He planned to execute the three Xìs,
but had not yet acted.
Xì Qí wanted to attack the duke,
saying:
"Even if I die,
the duke will also suffer."
Xì Zhì said:
"Loyalty does not betray the ruler,
wisdom does not harm the people,
courage does not incite rebellion.
Without these three virtues,
who would follow me?
I would rather die!"
On the Rénwǔ day of the twelfth month,
the duke ordered Xū Tóng to lead 800 soldiers in a surprise attack, killing the three Xìs.
Xū Tóng then took the opportunity to seize Luǎn Shū and
Zhōngháng Yǎn at court,
saying:
"If we do not kill these two,
trouble will surely reach you."
The duke said:
"Having killed three ministers in one day,
I cannot bear to add more."
In reply:
"Others will bear to harm you."
The duke did not listen,
apologized to Luǎn Shū and others for the crime of executing the Xì clan:
"Ministers, return to your posts."
The two bowed and said:
"How fortunate, how fortunate!"
The duke appointed Xū Tóng as a minister.
On the Yǐmǎo day of the intercalary month,
Duke Lì was visiting Jiànglíshì,
when Luǎn Shū
and Zhōngháng Yǎn with their faction launched a surprise arrest of Duke Lì,
imprisoned him,
killed Xū Tóng,
and sent someone to welcome Prince Zhōu from Zhōu to establish him,
who became Duke Dào.
In the first year of Duke Dào, on the Gēngshēn day of the first month,
Luǎn Shū
and Zhōngháng Yǎn assassinated Duke Lì,
burying him with only one carriage.
Duke Lì died after six days in captivity,
and ten days after his death, on Gēngwǔ day,
Zhì Yīng welcomed Prince Zhōu,
who arrived at Jiàng,
where a chicken was sacrificed, and an alliance was made with the ministers to establish him,
becoming Duke Dào.
On Xīnsì day,
he paid respects at Wǔ Palace.
On the Yǐyǒu day of February,
he ascended the throne.
Duke Dào Zhōu's grandfather,
named Jié,
was the youngest son of Duke Xiāng of Jìn,
but did not succeed to the throne,
and was titled Huán Shū,
who was most beloved.
Huán Shū fathered Huì Bó Tán,
and Tán fathered Duke Dào Zhōu.
When Zhōu was established,
he was fourteen years old.
Duke Dào said:
"My grandfather
and father both failed to succeed and took refuge in Zhōu,
dying there as guests.
I considered myself distant and unrelated,
with little hope of becoming ruler.
Now, the ministers have not forgotten the intentions of Dukes Wén
and Xiāng and kindly established a descendant of Huán Shū,
relying on the spirits of the ancestral temple and the ministers' support,
I am able to continue Jìn's sacrifices—
how could I not tread cautiously?
May the ministers also assist me!"
Thereupon, he expelled seven disloyal officials,
restored past merits,
bestowed virtue and kindness,
and gathered the descendants of those who contributed when Duke Wén entered the state.
In autumn, they attacked Zhèng.
The Zhèng army was defeated,
and they advanced to Chén.
In the third year,
Jìn met with the feudal lords.
Duke Dào asked his ministers who could be employed,
and Qí Xī recommended Xiè Hú.
Xiè Hú
was Qí Xī's enemy.
Asked again,
he recommended his own son, Qí Wǔ.
A nobleman remarked:
"Qí Xī can be said to be impartial!
Recommending externally without concealing enemies,
recommending internally without concealing his son."
While meeting with the feudal lords,
Duke Dào's brother Yáng Gān disrupted the ranks,
and Wěi Jiàng executed his attendant.
Duke Dào was angry,
but after being advised,
he ultimately esteemed Jiàng,
entrusted him with governance,
sent him to make peace with the Róng,
and the Róng became very friendly and attached.
In the eleventh year,
Duke Dào said:
"Since I employed Wěi Jiàng,
we have united the feudal lords nine times,
and made peace with the Róng
and Dí—all thanks to Wěi's efforts."
He awarded him musical instruments,
which after three declines, he accepted.
In winter, Qín captured our Lì.
In the fourteenth year,
Jìn sent the six ministers to lead the feudal lords in attacking Qín,
crossed the Jīng River,
greatly defeated the Qín army,
and reached Yùlín before withdrawing.
In the fifteenth year,
Duke Dào asked Shī Kuàng about governing the state.
Shī Kuàng said:
"Only benevolence and righteousness are fundamental."
In winter, Duke Dào passed away,
and his son, Duke Píng Biāo, succeeded him.
In the first year of Lord Píng,
he attacked Qí.
Lord Líng of Qí battled him at Míxià,
but the Qí army was defeated and fled.
Yàn Yīng said:
"My lord, you lack courage too;
why not stop the fighting?"
Thereupon he left.
Jìn pursued them,
then besieged Línzī,
burning and slaughtering throughout its outer city.
East to Jiāo,
south to Yí,
Qí fortified all its cities for defense,
so Jìn led its troops back.
In the sixth year,
Lord Xiāng of Lǔ paid court to Jìn.
Luán Chěng of Jìn, having committed crimes,
fled to Qí.
In the eighth year,
Lord Zhuāng of Qí secretly sent Luán Chěng to Qūwò,
with troops following him.
The Qí army ascended Tàiháng,
while Luán Chěng turned back from within Qūwò,
sneaking into Jiàng.
Jiàng was unprepared,
and Lord Píng wanted to commit suicide,
but Fàn Xiànzǐ stopped the lord,
and with his followers attacked Chěng,
who was defeated and fled to Qūwò.
Qūwò attacked Chěng,
Chěng died,
and thus the Luán clan was exterminated.
Chěng was
the grandson of Luán Shū.
His entry into Jiàng
was plotted with the Wèi clan.
When Lord Zhuāng of Qí heard of Chěng's defeat,
he then returned,
taking Jìn's Zhāogē before leaving,
in retaliation for the battle of Línzī.
In the tenth year,
Cuī Zhù of Qí assassinated his lord Zhuāng.
Jìn, taking advantage of Qí's turmoil,
attacked and defeated Qí at Gāotáng before leaving,
in retaliation for the Tàiháng campaign.
In the fourteenth year,
Jìzǐ of Yánlíng from Wú came as an envoy,
and spoke with Zhào Wénzǐ,
Hán Xuānzǐ,
and Wèi Xiànzǐ,
saying:
"The governance of the Jìn state
will eventually fall to these three families."
In the nineteenth year,
Qí sent Yàn Yīng to Jìn,
where he conversed with Shū Xiàng.
Shū Xiàng said:
"Jìn
is in its last days.
The lord heavily taxes for building towers and ponds without caring for governance;
power lies with private families—
how can it last long!"
Yànzǐ agreed with him.
In the twenty-second year,
they attacked Yān.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Lord Píng died,
and his son Lord Zhāo, Yí, succeeded him.
Lord Zhāo died in the sixth year of his reign.
The six ministers were strong,
and the ducal house was weak.
His son Lord Qǐng, Qùjí, succeeded him.
In the sixth year of Lord Qǐng,
King Jǐng of Zhōu passed away,
and the princes contended for the throne.
The six ministers of Jìn quelled the disorder in the royal house,
establishing King Jìng.
In the ninth year,
the Jì clan of Lǔ expelled their lord Zhāo,
who resided at Gānhóu.
In the eleventh year,
Wèi and Sòng sent envoys to request Jìn to restore the Lǔ lord.
Jì Píngzǐ privately bribed Fàn Xiànzǐ,
who accepted it,
then said to the Jìn lord:
"The Jì clan is without fault."
Thus, the Lǔ lord was not restored.
In the twelfth year,
the grandson of Qí Xī from Jìn's ancestral family,
and the son of Shū Xiàng,
were at odds with the lord.
The six ministers, wishing to weaken the ducal house,
then used the law to exterminate their entire clans,
dividing their towns into ten counties,
each appointing their sons as grand officers.
Jìn grew weaker,
and the six ministers all became powerful.
In the fourteenth year,
Lord Qǐng died,
and his son Lord Dìng, Wǔ, succeeded him.
In the eleventh year of Lord Dìng,
Yáng Hǔ of Lǔ fled to Jìn,
and Zhào Yāng, Jiǎnzǐ, hosted him.
In the twelfth year,
Confucius served as minister in Lǔ.
In the fifteenth year,
Zhào Yāng sent the grand officer of Hándān, Wǔ,
but distrusting him,
wanted to kill Wǔ.
Wǔ, along with Zhōngháng Yín
and Fàn Jíshè, personally attacked Zhào Yāng,
who fled to secure Jìnyáng.
Lord Dìng besieged Jìnyáng.
Xún Lì,
Hán Bùxìn,
and Wèi Chǐ, being enemies of Fàn
and Zhōngháng,
shifted their troops to attack Fàn
and Zhōngháng.
Fàn and Zhōngháng rebelled,
the Jìn lord attacked them,
defeating Fàn
and Zhōngháng.
Fàn and Zhōngháng fled to Zhāogē,
and fortified it.
Hán and Wèi apologized to the Jìn lord on behalf of Zhào Yāng,
who then pardoned Zhào Yāng,
restoring his position.
In the twenty-second year,
Jìn defeated the Fàn
and Zhōngháng clans,
and the two fled to Qí.
In the thirtieth year,
Lord Dìng met with King Fūchāi of Wú at Huángchí,
vying for precedence.
Zhào Yāng was in attendance at the time,
and ultimately Wú took the lead.
In the thirty-first year,
Tián Cháng of Qí assassinated his lord Jiǎn,
and set up Jiǎn's brother Áo as Lord Píng.
In the thirty-third year,
Confucius died.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Lord Dìng died,
and his son Lord Chū, Zào, succeeded him.
In the seventeenth year of Lord Chū,
Zhì Bó, along with Zhào,
Hán, and Wèi, divided the lands of Fàn
and Zhōngháng as their towns.
Lord Chū was angered,
and informed Qí
and Lǔ, intending to attack the four ministers.
The four ministers, fearing this,
turned to attack Lord Chū.
Lord Chū fled to Qí,
but died on the way.
Thus, Zhì Bó set up Jiāo, the great-grandson of Lord Zhāo, as the Jìn lord,
known as Lord Āi.
Lord Āi's grandfather Yōng
was the youngest son of Lord Zhāo of Jìn,
styled as Lord Dài.
Lord Dài sired Jì.
Jì was on good terms with Zhì Bó,
but died early,
so Zhì Bó wanted to annex Jìn entirely,
yet did not dare,
and thus set up Jì's son Jiāo as lord.
At that time,
all Jìn's governance was decided by Zhì Bó,
and Lord Āi of Jìn had no control.
Zhì Bó then possessed the lands of Fàn
and Zhōngháng,
and was the strongest.
In the fourth year of Lord Āi,
Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
Hán Kāngzǐ,
and Wèi Huánzǐ together killed Zhì Bó,
annexing all his lands.
In the 18th year,
Duke Āi died,
and his son Duke Yōu Liǔ succeeded him.
During Duke Yōu's time,
Jìn was weakened,
and instead paid homage to the rulers of Hán,
Zhào,
and Wèi.
It only retained Jiàng
and Qūwò,
while the rest fell to the three states of Jìn.
In the 15th year,
Wèi Wénhóu first ascended.
In the 18th year,
Duke Yōu engaged in debauchery with women,
sneaking out of the city at night,
where he was killed by bandits.
Wèi Wénhóu used troops to quell the disorder in Jìn,
establishing Duke Yōu's son Zhǐ,
who became Duke Liè.
In the 19th year of Duke Liè,
King Wēiliè of Zhōu bestowed upon Zhào,
Hán,
and Wèi the title of feudal lords.
In the 27th year,
Duke Liè died,
and his son Duke Xiào Qí succeeded him.
In the 9th year of Duke Xiào,
Wèi Wǔhóu first ascended,
attacked Hándān,
but withdrew without success.
In the 17th year,
Duke Xiào died,
and his son Duke Jìng Jùjiǔ succeeded him.
That year,
marked the first year of King Wēi of Qí.
In the second year of Duke Jìng,
Wèi Wǔhóu,
Hán Āihóu,
and Zhào Jìnghóu extinguished the state of Jìn and divided its territory among themselves.
Duke Jìng was demoted to a commoner,
and the Jìn lineage ceased its sacrifices.
Grand Historian comments:
Duke Wén of Jìn,
known in antiquity as an enlightened ruler,
spent nineteen years in exile abroad,
enduring extreme hardship and poverty.
Yet upon ascending the throne and distributing rewards,
he still forgot Jiè Zǐtuī—
how much more so for arrogant rulers?
After Duke Líng was assassinated,
his successors, Duke Chéng
and Duke Jǐng, enforced strictness,
culminating in Duke Lì's severe harshness.
High officials feared execution,
leading to calamity.
After Duke Dào, the state declined daily,
with the six ministers monopolizing power.
Thus, the way a ruler governs his ministers
is indeed no easy task!
The ancestors of Chǔ descended from Emperor Zhuānxū Gāoyáng.
Gāoyáng
was the grandson of Huángdì
and the son of Chāngyì.
Gāoyáng begot Chēng,
Chēng begot Juànzhāng,
Juànzhāng begot Zhònglí.
Zhònglí served as the Fire Official under Emperor Kù Gāoxīn,
achieving great merit
and illuminating the world with his brilliance.
Emperor Kù named him Zhùróng.
When the Gònggōng clan rebelled,
Emperor Kù sent Zhònglí to suppress them, but he did not complete the task.
So the emperor executed Zhònglí on the gēngyín day,
and appointed his younger brother Wú Huí as Zhònglí's successor,
reinstating him as Fire Official,
and naming him Zhùróng.
Wú Huí begot Lù Zhōng.
Lù Zhōng had six sons,
all born by cesarean section.
The eldest was Kūnwú;
the second was Cānhú;
the third was Péngzǔ;
the fourth was Huìrén;
the fifth was of the Cáo surname;
the sixth was Jìlián,
of the Mǐ surname,
from whom Chǔ descended.
The Kūnwú clan
served as a feudal lord during the Xià dynasty,
but was destroyed by Tāng during Jié's reign.
The Péngzǔ clan
served as a feudal lord during the Yīn dynasty,
but was extinguished in the late Yīn period.
Jìlián begot Fùjū,
Fùjū begot Xuéxióng.
Thereafter, the lineage declined,
some remaining in the central states,
others among the barbarian tribes,
making it impossible to record their generations.
During the time of King Wén of Zhōu,
a descendant of Jìlián named Yùxióng emerged.
Yùxióng served King Wén like a son,
but died early.
His son was Xióng Lì.
Xióng Lì begot Xióng Kuáng,
Xióng Kuáng begot Xióng Yì.
During the reign of King Chéng of Zhōu,
in recognition of the diligent service of King Wén
and King Wǔ's descendants,
Xióng Yì was enfeoffed in the Chǔ barbarian lands,
granted a domain of the zǐ and nán ranks,
with the surname Mǐ,
and residing in Dānyáng.
Chǔ's lord Xióng Yì, along with Lǔ's Duke Bóqín,
Wèi's Kāngshū's son Móu,
Jìn's Marquis Xiè,
and Qí's Tàigōng's son Lǚ Jí, all served King Chéng.
Xióng Yì begot Xióng Ài,
Xióng Ài begot Xióng Dá,
Xióng Dá begot Xióng Shèng.
Xióng Shèng was succeeded by his younger brother Xióng Yáng.
Xióng Yáng begot Xióng Qú.
Xióng Qú had three sons.
During the time of King Yí of Zhōu,
the royal house declined,
some feudal lords ceased paying homage,
and they attacked each other.
Xióng Qú greatly won the support of the people between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
so he raised troops to attack Yōng
and Yángyuè,
reaching È.
Xióng Qú declared:
"We are barbarians,
and do not adopt the titles and posthumous names of the central states."
He then established his eldest son Kāng as the King of Gōudǎn,
his middle son Hóng as the King of È,
and his youngest son Zhícī as the King of Yuèzhāng,
all in the Chǔ barbarian lands along the river.
But when King Lì of Zhōu came to power,
known for his tyranny,
Xióng Qú, fearing an attack on Chǔ,
also abandoned his kingly titles.
Later, his successor was Xióng Wúkāng,
but Wúkāng died early.
After Xióng Qú's death,
his son Xióng Zhìhóng succeeded him.
When Zhìhóng died,
his younger brother assassinated him and took the throne,
becoming Xióng Yán.
Xióng Yán begot Xióng Yǒng.
In the sixth year of Xióng Yǒng,
the Zhōu people rebelled,
attacking King Lì,
who fled to Zhì.
In the tenth year of Xióng Yǒng,
he died, and his younger brother Xióng Yán succeeded him.
In the tenth year of Xióng Yán,
he died, leaving four sons:
the eldest Bó Shuāng,
the middle one Zhòng Xuě,
the next Shū Kān,
and the youngest Jì Xún.
After Xióng Yán's death,
the eldest son Bó Shuāng succeeded him,
becoming Xióng Shuāng.
In the first year of Xióng Shuāng,
King Xuān of Zhōu first ascended.
In the sixth year of Xióng Shuāng,
he died, and his three younger brothers contended for the throne.
Zhòng Xuě died;
Shū Kān fled,
seeking refuge in Pú;
and the youngest brother Jì Xún took the throne,
becoming Xióng Xún.
In the 16th year of Xióng Xún,
Duke Huán of Zhèng was first enfeoffed in Zhèng.
In the 22nd year,
Xióng Xún died,
and his son Xióng È succeeded him.
In the ninth year of Xióng È,
he died, and his son Xióng Yí succeeded him,
becoming Ruò Áo.
In the twentieth year of Ruò'áo's reign,
King Yōu of Zhōu was killed by the Quǎnróng,
the Zhōu court moved east,
and Duke Xiāng of Qín began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Ruò'áo died,
and his son Xióng Kǎn succeeded him,
known as Xiāo'áo.
In the sixth year of Xiāo'áo,
he died, and his son Xióng Xùn succeeded him,
known as Fénmào.
In the thirteenth year of Fénmào,
Jìn began to fall into turmoil,
due to the affair of Qūwò.
In the seventeenth year of Fénmào,
he died. Fénmào's younger brother Xióng Tōng killed Fénmào's son and took the throne,
becoming King Wǔ of Chǔ.
In the seventeenth year of King Wǔ,
Zhuāng Bó of Qūwò in Jìn killed Marquis Xiào of Jìn, the ruler of the state.
In the nineteenth year,
Duàn, the younger brother of the Earl of Zhèng, started a rebellion.
In the twenty-first year,
Zhèng invaded the Son of Heaven's fields.
In the twenty-third year,
Wèi assassinated its ruler Duke Huán.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Lǔ assassinated its ruler Duke Yǐn.
In the thirty-first year,
Huá Dū, the Grand Steward of Sòng, killed its ruler Duke Shāng.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Chǔ attacked Suí.
Suí said:
"We are innocent."
Chǔ replied:
"We are barbarians.
Now all the feudal lords are rebelling and invading each other,
or killing one another.
We have worn-out armor,
and wish to observe the politics of the Central States,
requesting the royal court to honor our title."
The people of Suí went to Zhōu,
to request honoring Chǔ,
but the royal court did not consent,
and they returned to report to Chǔ.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Xióng Tōng of Chǔ angrily said:
"Our ancestor Yù Xióng,
was a teacher of King Wén,
but died early.
King Chéng elevated our former lord,
granting him the fields of a viscount or baron and ordering him to reside in Chǔ,
and the barbarians all submitted,
yet the king did not increase our rank,
so we will honor ourselves."
He then proclaimed himself King Wǔ,
made a covenant with the people of Suí, and left.
Thus, he began to open up the Pú territory and possess it.
In the fifty-first year,
Zhōu summoned the Marquis of Suí,
reproaching him for establishing Chǔ as king.
Chǔ was angered,
believing Suí had betrayed them,
and attacked Suí.
King Wǔ died in the army, and the troops withdrew.
His son King Wén, Xióng Zī, succeeded him,
and first established the capital at Yǐng.
In the second year of King Wén,
while attacking Shēn, he passed through Dèng,
and the people of Dèng said
"The King of Chǔ can be easily captured,"
but the Marquis of Dèng did not agree.
In the sixth year,
he attacked Cài,
captured Marquis Āi of Cài and brought him back,
but later released him.
Chǔ grew strong,
oppressing the small states between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
and the small states all feared it.
In the eleventh year,
Duke Huán of Qí began his hegemony,
and Chǔ also began to expand.
In the twelfth year,
he attacked Dèng,
and destroyed it.
In the thirteenth year,
he died, and his son Xióng Jiān succeeded him,
known as Zhuāng Áo.
In the fifth year of Zhuāng Áo,
he wanted to kill his younger brother Xióng Yùn,
so Yùn fled to Suí,
and together with Suí, he attacked and killed Zhuāng Áo, taking the throne,
becoming King Chéng.
In the first year of King Chéng, Yùn,
just having ascended the throne,
he spread virtue and bestowed favors,
renewing old friendships with the feudal lords.
He sent people to offer tribute to the Son of Heaven,
who bestowed sacrificial meat upon him,
saying:
"Pacify the rebellions of the southern barbarians Yuè,
and do not invade the Central States."
Thus, the territory of Chǔ extended a thousand lǐ.
In the sixteenth year,
Duke Huán of Qí led troops to invade Chǔ,
reaching Xíng Mountain.
King Chéng of Chǔ sent General Qū Wán with troops to resist him,
and made a covenant with Duke Huán.
Duke Huán reproached him for not paying tribute to the Zhōu royal court,
Chǔ agreed,
and he then left.
In the eighteenth year,
King Chéng led troops north to attack Xǔ,
the Lord of Xǔ bared his upper body in apology,
and he was then released.
In the twenty-second year,
he attacked Huáng.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he destroyed Yīng.
In the thirty-third year,
Duke Xiāng of Sòng wanted to hold a league meeting,
and summoned Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ angrily said:
"He summons me,
I will go pretending to be friendly and then surprise and humiliate him."
He then set out,
reached Yú,
captured and humiliated the Duke of Sòng,
and later released him.
In the thirty-fourth year,
Duke Wén of Zhèng came south to court Chǔ.
King Chéng of Chǔ went north to attack Sòng,
defeated them at Hóng,
shot and wounded Duke Xiāng of Sòng,
and Duke Xiāng subsequently died of his wounds.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn passed through Chǔ,
King Chéng entertained him with the rites due to a feudal lord's guest,
and generously sent him on to Qín.
In the thirty-ninth year,
Duke Xī of Lǔ came to request troops to attack Qí,
Chǔ sent Shēn Hóu to lead troops against Qí,
captured Gǔ,
and established Duke Huán of Qí's son Yōng there.
The seven sons of Duke Huán of Qí all fled to Chǔ,
and Chǔ appointed them all as senior ministers.
They destroyed Kuí,
because Kuí did not offer sacrifices to Zhùróng
and Yù Xióng.
In summer,
they attacked Sòng,
Sòng appealed urgently to Jìn for help,
Jìn rescued Sòng,
and King Chéng withdrew and returned.
General Zǐ Yù requested to fight,
but King Chéng said:
"Chóng'ěr lived in exile abroad for a long time,
and finally managed to return to his state,
he is favored by Heaven,
and cannot be opposed."
Zǐ Yù insisted on his request,
so he gave him a small force and sent him off.
Jìn indeed defeated Zǐ Yù at Chéngpú.
King Chéng was enraged,
and executed Zǐ Yù.
In the forty-sixth year,
initially, King Chéng intended to make Shāng Chén his crown prince,
and informed Lìngyǐn Zǐ Shàng.
Zǐ Shàng said:
"Your age is not yet advanced,
and you have many favored concubines;
to depose one would cause disorder.
In the state of Chǔ, succession often falls to the youngest.
Moreover, Shāng Chén has the eyes of a wasp and the voice of a jackal—
he is a cruel man,
and should not be established."
The king did not listen,
and established him.
Later, he wished to appoint his son Zhí and depose Crown Prince Shāng Chén.
Shāng Chén heard of this but was unsure,
so he told his tutor Pān Chóng:
"How can I learn the truth?"
Chóng said:
"Host a feast for the king's favored concubine Jiāng Mǐ but show her disrespect."
Shāng Chén followed his advice.
Jiāng Mǐ angrily said:
"No wonder the king wants to kill you and establish Zhí!"
Shāng Chén reported to Pān Chóng:
"It is true."
Chóng asked:
"Can you serve him?"
He replied:
"I cannot."
"Can you flee into exile?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"Can you undertake a great deed?"
He said:
"I can."
In the tenth month of winter,
Shāng Chén surrounded King Chéng with palace guards.
King Chéng requested to eat bear's paw before dying,
but they did not comply.
On the day Dīngwèi,
King Chéng hanged himself.
Shāng Chén succeeded to the throne,
becoming King Mù.
Upon his accession,
King Mù gave his former crown prince's palace to Pān Chóng,
appointing him as Grand Tutor,
to oversee state affairs.
In the third year of King Mù's reign,
he extinguished the state of Jiāng.
In the fourth year,
he extinguished Liù
and Liǎo. Liù
and Liǎo were descendants of Gāo Yáo.
In the eighth year,
he attacked Chén.
In the twelfth year,
he died, and his son King Zhuāng, Lǚ, succeeded him.
After King Zhuāng ascended the throne for three years,
he issued no decrees,
indulging in pleasure day and night,
and proclaimed to the state:
"Anyone who dares to remonstrate will be put to death without pardon!"
Wǔ Jǔ entered to advise him.
King Zhuāng held a woman from Zhèng on his left and a maiden from Yuè on his right,
seated among bells and drums.
Wǔ Jǔ said:
"I wish to present a riddle."
He said:
"There is a bird perched on a hill,
for three years it has neither flown nor sung—
what kind of bird is this?"
King Zhuāng replied:
"If it does not fly for three years,
it will soar to the heavens;
if it does not sing for three years,
its song will astonish all.
You may withdraw,
I understand."
After several months,
his indulgence worsened.
The minister Sū Cóng then entered to remonstrate.
The king said:
"Have you not heard my decree?"
He responded:
"To die enlightening my lord
is my wish."
Thereupon, the king ceased his wanton pleasures,
began to govern,
executed several hundred people,
and promoted several hundred others,
entrusting Wǔ Jǔ
and Sū Cóng with administration,
to the great delight of the people.
That year, they extinguished Yōng.
In the sixth year,
they attacked Sòng,
capturing five hundred chariots.
In the eighth year,
they attacked the Lùhún Róng,
reaching as far as Luò,
and displayed their troops in the outskirts of Zhōu.
King Dìng of Zhōu sent Wángsūn Mǎn to greet the king of Chǔ.
The king of Chǔ inquired about the size and weight of the Nine Tripod Cauldrons,
to which he replied:
"It depends on virtue, not on the cauldrons."
King Zhuāng said:
"Do not withhold the Nine Cauldrons from me!
The broken tips of Chǔ's hooks alone
are enough to cast the Nine Cauldrons."
Wángsūn Mǎn said:
"Alas!
Has the king forgotten?
In the heyday of Yú and Xià,
distant lands all came,
presenting metal from the nine provinces,
casting cauldrons with images of creatures,
preparing all things
so the people could distinguish divine and evil.
When Jié had corrupt virtue,
the cauldrons moved to Yīn,
lasting six hundred years.
When King Zhòu of Yīn was tyrannical,
the cauldrons moved to Zhōu.
If virtue is splendid,
even small things are weighty;
if it is corrupt and chaotic,
even large things are light.
Formerly, King Chéng placed the cauldrons at Jiárǔ,
divining thirty generations,
and seven hundred years—
this is the mandate of Heaven.
Though Zhōu's virtue has declined,
Heaven's mandate has not changed.
The weight of the cauldrons
is not to be inquired about."
