The king of Chǔ then returned.
In the ninth year,
the prime minister was of the Ruò Áo clan.
Someone slandered him to the king,
and fearing execution,
he rebelled against the king.
The king attacked and exterminated the Ruò Áo clan.
In the thirteenth year,
he extinguished Shū.
In the sixteenth year,
he attacked Chén,
killing Xià Zhēng Shū.
Zhēng Shū had assassinated his ruler,
hence he was executed.
After conquering Chén,
he made it a county.
All ministers congratulated him,
but Shěn Shū Shí, returning from Qí,
did not offer congratulations.
The king asked why,
and he replied:
"A common saying goes:
'If a man leads his ox through another's field,
the field owner takes his ox.'
The trespasser is in the wrong,
but is taking his ox not excessive?
Moreover, the king attacked Chén with the feudal lords due to its disorder,
acting righteously, yet coveting its land as a county—
how then can you command the world again?"
King Zhuāng then restored the state to Chén's descendants.
In the spring of the seventeenth year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Zhèng,
and captured it in three months.
Entering through the Huáng Gate,
the Earl of Zhèng, baring his upper body and leading a sheep, came to meet him,
saying:
"I, not favored by Heaven,
have failed to serve Your Majesty,
causing you to harbor anger,
and bring it upon my humble city—
this is my crime.
How dare I not obey your command?
If you banish me to the southern sea,
or grant me as a servant to the feudal lords,
I will also obey your command.
But if you do not forget Lì,
Xuān, and Huán,
and do not cut off our altars of land and grain,
allowing us to reform and serve you,
that is my wish,
though I dare not hope for it.
I venture to bare my innermost thoughts."
The ministers of Chǔ said:
"Your Majesty should not grant this."
King Zhuāng said:
"Their ruler can humble himself before others;
he will surely be able to earn the trust and service of his people.
How can we annihilate them?"
King Zhuāng personally took the flag,
waved it left and right to command the army,
withdrew his troops thirty lǐ and encamped,
then granted them peace.
Pān Wāng entered to swear a covenant,
and Zǐ Liáng went out as a hostage.
In the summer, the sixth month,
Jìn came to rescue Zhèng,
clashed with Chǔ in battle,
and was greatly defeated by the Chǔ army at the river,
which then proceeded to Héngyōng before returning.
In the twentieth year,
Chǔ besieged Sòng,
because it had killed a Chǔ envoy.
After besieging Sòng for five months,
when the city's food was exhausted,
people exchanged children to eat,
and split bones for firewood.
Huà Yuán of Sòng came out and reported the situation.
King Zhuāng said:
"What a noble man!"
Thereupon, he withdrew his troops and left.
In the twenty-third year,
King Zhuāng passed away,
and his son, King Gòng, Shěn, ascended the throne.
In the sixteenth year of King Gòng,
Jìn attacked Zhèng.
Zhèng appealed for help,
and King Gòng went to rescue Zhèng.
Battling the Jìn army at Yānlíng,
Jìn defeated Chǔ,
and an arrow hit King Gòng's eye.
King Gòng summoned General Zǐ Fǎn.
Zǐ Fǎn was fond of drink,
and his attendant, Shù Yánggǔ, offered him wine, getting him drunk.
The king was enraged,
had Zǐ Fǎn executed by shooting,
then withdrew the army and returned.
In the thirty-first year,
King Gòng passed away,
and his son, King Kāng, Zhāo, ascended the throne.
King Kāng reigned for fifteen years and died,
his son Yuán ascended,
known as Jiá Áo.
King Kāng favored his younger brothers, the princes Wéi,
Zǐ Bǐ,
Zǐ Xī,
and Qìjí.
In the third year of Jiá Áo,
he appointed his uncle, Prince Wéi (younger brother of King Kāng), as Lìng Yǐn,
in charge of military affairs.
In the fourth year,
Wéi was sent to Zhèng,
but on the way, hearing of the king's illness, he returned.
On the twelfth month, day Jǐyǒu,
Wéi entered to inquire about the king's illness,
strangled and murdered him,
then killed his sons Mò and Píngxià.
He sent an envoy to announce the news in Zhèng.
Wǔ Jǔ asked:
"Who is the successor?"
The reply was:
"Our great officer Wéi."
Wǔ Jǔ then rephrased it:
"Wéi, the eldest son of King Gòng."
Zǐ Bǐ fled to Jìn,
and Wéi ascended the throne,
becoming King Líng.
In the sixth month of the third year of King Líng,
Chǔ sent an envoy to inform Jìn,
wishing to meet with the feudal lords.
The feudal lords all gathered with Chǔ at Shēn.
Wǔ Jǔ said:
"In the past, Xià Qǐ had a feast at Jūntái,
Shāng Tāng had a mandate at Jǐngbó,
King Wǔ of Zhōu had an oath at Méngjīn,
King Chéng had a hunt at Qíyáng,
King Kāng held a court at Fēng Palace,
King Mù convened a meeting at Túshān,
Qí Huán had an army at Zhàolíng,
Jìn Wén had a covenant at Jiàntǔ.
Which will Your Majesty adopt?"
King Líng said:
"I will adopt Lord Huán's."
At that time, Zǐchǎn of Zhèng was present.
Thereupon, Jìn,
Sòng, Lǔ, and Wèi did not attend.
After King Líng had sworn the covenant,
he wore a proud expression.
Wǔ Jǔ said:
"When Jié held a meeting at Yǒuréng,
Yǒumín rebelled.
When Zhòu convened at Líshān,
the Eastern Yí rebelled.
When King Yōu made a covenant at Tàishì,
the Róng and Dí rebelled.
May Your Majesty be cautious of the outcome!"
In the seventh month,
Chǔ led the feudal lords' troops to attack Wú,
besieging Zhūfāng.
In the eighth month,
they captured it,
imprisoned Qìng Fēng,
and exterminated his clan.
They paraded Fēng,
saying:
"Let no one imitate Qí's Qìng Fēng, who murdered his ruler and weakened his orphan,
then forced a covenant upon the great officers!"
Fēng retorted:
"None match the son of a concubine of King Gòng of Chǔ, Wéi, who murdered his elder brother's son Yuán and replaced him on the throne!"
Thereupon, King Líng had him quickly killed.
In the seventh year,
the Zhànghuá Tower was completed,
and he ordered it to be populated with fugitives from within.
In the eighth year,
he sent Prince Qìjí to lead troops and destroy Chén.
In the tenth year,
he summoned the Marquis of Cài,
got him drunk, and killed him.
He appointed Qìjí to pacify Cài,
and thus made him the Duke of Chén and Cài.
In the eleventh year,
he attacked Xú to intimidate Wú.
King Líng stationed at Qiánxī to await them.
The king said:
"Qí,
Jìn, Lǔ,
and Wèi—all received precious vessels upon their enfeeffment,
yet I alone did not.
Now I am sending an envoy to Zhōu to request the cauldron as my share;
will they grant it to me?"
Xīfù replied:
"They will surely give it to Your Majesty!
In the past, our former king Xióng Yì dwelt secluded in the Jīng Mountains,
enduring hardships amidst the wilds,
trekking through forests and hills to serve the Son of Heaven,
offering only peach-wood bows and thornwood arrows for the royal affairs.
Qí was the king's maternal uncle;
Jìn, along with Lǔ
and Wèi, were the king's brothers by the same mother:
thus Chǔ had no share while they all did.
Now Zhōu and the four states serve Your Majesty,
and will follow your commands obediently;
how would they dare begrudge the cauldron?"
King Líng said:
"Long ago, my royal ancestor's elder brother Kūnwú resided in the old Xǔ territory,
but now the people of Zhèng covet its fields,
and do not yield them to me;
if I demand them now,
will they grant them to me?"
The reply was:
"If Zhōu does not begrudge the cauldron,
how would Zhèng dare begrudge the fields?"
King Líng said:
"Formerly, the feudal lords distanced themselves from me and feared Jìn,
but now I have fortified the great cities of Chén,
Cài, and Bùgēng,
each with a levy of a thousand chariots;
do the feudal lords fear me now?"
The reply was:
"They do indeed fear you!"
King Líng rejoiced and said:
"Xīfù speaks well of ancient matters."
In the spring of the twelfth year,
King Líng of Chǔ delighted in Qiánxī,
and could not bring himself to leave.
The people suffered under the corvée labor.
Earlier, King Líng had assembled troops at Shēn,
where he humiliated the Yuè official Cháng Shòuguò,
and killed the Cài official Guān Qǐ.
Qǐ's son, Cóng, fled into exile in Wú,
and there urged the King of Wú to attack Chǔ,
instigating a rebellion by the Yuè official Cháng Shòuguò,
acting as a spy for Wú.
He had someone forge an order from Prince Qìjí to summon Prince Bǐ from Jìn;
upon reaching Cài,
he joined with Wú
and Yuè troops intending to raid Cài.
He instructed Prince Bǐ to meet with Qìjí,
and they made a covenant at Dèng.
Thereupon, they entered and killed King Líng's crown prince Lù,
set up Zǐ Bǐ as king,
made Prince Zǐxī the Lìngyǐn,
and Qìjí the Sīmǎ.
After first cleansing the royal palace,
Guān Cóng followed the army to Qiánxī,
and declared to the Chǔ masses:
"The state now has a king.
Those who return first
will have their ranks, fiefs, lands, and homes restored.
Those who come later will be exiled."
The Chǔ masses all disbanded,
abandoning King Líng and returning home.
When King Líng heard of the death of Crown Prince Lù,
he threw himself from his chariot,
and said:
"Do people love their sons like this as well?"
An attendant said:
"Even more so."
The king said:
"I have killed many men's sons;
can I escape such a fate?"
The Yòuyǐn said:
"I beg to wait in the suburbs and heed the people's will."
The king said:
"The rage of the masses cannot be provoked."
The Yòuyǐn said:
"Then enter a major district and seek troops from the feudal lords."
The king said:
"They have all rebelled."
He said further:
"Or flee to a feudal lord and await the consideration of a major state."
The king said:
"Great fortune does not come twice;
it would only bring disgrace."
Thereupon, the king boarded a boat intending to enter Yān.
The Yòuyǐn, realizing the king would not follow his advice,
feared they would die together,
and also left the king to flee.
King Líng then wandered alone in the mountains,
with no villager daring to take him in.
While traveling, the king met a former groom,
and said to him:
"Find me some food,
for I have not eaten for three days."
The groom said:
"The new king has decreed
that anyone daring to supply the king or follow him
will be punished with the extinction of three clans,
and moreover, I have no food to give."
The king then laid his head on the man's lap and slept.
The groom replaced himself with a lump of earth,
and fled.
The king awoke to find him gone,
and, weakened by hunger, could not rise.
Shēn Hài, son of the Yùyǐn Shēn Wúyǔ, said:
"My father twice violated the king's command,
yet the king did not execute him;
what grace could be greater than this!"
He then searched for the king,
and found him starving in the Lí marshes,
whereupon he escorted him back.
On the summer month, fifth, day guǐchǒu,
the king died in Shēn Hài's home,
and Shēn Hài had his two daughters follow in death,
burying them together.
At this time, although Chǔ had already set up Bǐ as king,
they feared King Líng might return,
and had not yet heard of his death;
thus Guān Cóng said to the newly enthroned Bǐ:
"If you do not kill Qìjí,
even if you gain the state, you will still suffer calamity."
The king said:
"I cannot bear to."
Cóng said:
"Others will bear to do it to you, my king."
The king did not listen,
and Cóng left.
Qìjí returned.
The people were startled every night,
crying:
"King Líng has entered!"
On the night of yǐmǎo,
Qìjí had boatmen run along the river shouting:
"King Líng has arrived!"
The people grew even more alarmed.
He also sent Màn Chéngrán to inform the newly enthroned King Bǐ and Lìngyǐn Zǐxī:
"The king has arrived!
The people are about to kill you,
and the Sīmǎ is arriving soon!
You had better plan early,
and avoid disgrace.
The fury of the masses is like flood and fire,
impossible to save."
Thereupon, the newly enthroned king and Zǐxī committed suicide.
On bǐngchén,
Qìjí ascended the throne as king,
changing his name to Xióng Jū,
becoming King Píng.
King Píng, having deceitfully murdered two kings to seize the throne himself,
feared rebellion from the people and feudal lords,
and thus bestowed favors upon the common folk.
He restored the lands of Chén and Cài and reestablished their heirs as before,
and returned the encroached territories to Zhèng.
He comforted and cared for the state internally,
and cultivated governance and education.
Wú, taking advantage of Chǔ's turmoil,
captured five commanders and returned.
King Píng said to Guān Cóng:
"Choose whatever you desire."
He wished to become the Bǔyǐn,
and the king granted it.
Initially,
King Gòng had five favored sons,
with no designated heir,
so he conducted a ritual to all the deities,
asking the gods to decide
who should rule the state.
Secretly, he and Consort Bā buried a jade disc in the chamber,
then summoned the five princes to enter after fasting.
King Kāng stepped over it,
King Líng's elbow touched it,
Zǐ Bǐ and
Zǐ Xī both stayed far from it.
King Píng was young
and was carried over it to bow,
pressing the cord.
Thus, King Kāng was established as the eldest,
but his son lost the throne;
Wéi became King Líng,
and was assassinated during his reign;
Zǐ Bǐ was king for over ten days,
Zǐ Xī never attained the throne,
and both were executed.
All four sons died without heirs.
Only Qì Jí was later established,
becoming King Píng,
and ultimately continued the Chǔ sacrifices,
as the divine sign had indicated.
Earlier,
when Zǐ Bǐ returned from Jìn,
Hán Xuānzǐ asked Shū Xiàng:
"Will Zǐ Bǐ succeed?"
He replied:
"He will not."
Xuānzǐ said:
"Those with shared grievances seek each other out,
like merchants in a market;
why would he not succeed?"
He replied:
"Without allies in his favor,
who will share his grievances?
To seize a state, there are five difficulties:
having favor but no supporters,
is the first;
having supporters but no leadership,
is the second;
having leadership but no strategy,
is the third;
having strategy but no people,
is the fourth;
having people but no virtue,
is the fifth.
Zǐ Bǐ has been in Jìn for thirteen years,
with no known followers from Jìn or Chǔ,
so he can be said to have no supporters;
his clan is estranged and relatives have turned against him,
so he can be said to have no leadership;
acting without an opportune moment,
so he can be said to have no strategy;
living as an exile all his life,
so he can be said to have no people;
in exile, he shows no signs of being loved,
so he can be said to have no virtue.
The king is cruel but unrestrained,
and Zǐ Bǐ faces these five difficulties in assassinating the ruler—
who could help him succeed!
The one to possess Chǔ,
will it not be Qì Jí?
He governs Chén and Cài,
with territories beyond Fāngchéng under his control.
No harshness or evil occurs,
thieves and bandits remain hidden,
private desires do not override public good,
and the people hold no resentment.
The spirits first commanded it,
and the people trust him.
When the Mǐ surname faces turmoil,
it is always the youngest who is established—
this is Chǔ's tradition.
As for Zǐ Bǐ's rank,
he is only a Right Yǐn;
in terms of noble favor,
he is a concubine's son;
by the divine command,
he is distant from it;
the people do not cherish him—
how can he be established?"
Xuānzǐ said:
"Weren't Duke Huán of Qí
and Duke Wén of Jìn the same?"
He replied:
"Duke Huán of Qí
was the son of Consort Wèi,
favored by Duke Xī.
He had Bào Shūyá,
Bīn Xūwú,
and Xí Péng as assistants,
with Jǔ and
Wèi as external supporters,
and Gāo and
Guó as internal supporters.
He followed good advice like flowing water,
and tirelessly bestowed benefits.
Was it not fitting for him to possess the state?
Our former Duke Wén
was the son of Hú Jì Jī,
favored by Duke Xiàn.
He was diligent in learning without weariness.
At seventeen,
he had five scholars,
with former senior officials Zǐyú
and Zǐfàn as his confidants,
and Wéi Chōu
and Jiǎ Tuó as his aides,
with Qí,
Sòng, Qín,
and Chǔ as external supporters,
and Luán,
Xì, Hú,
and Xiān as internal supporters.
In exile for nineteen years,
he held firm to his resolve.
Dukes Huì and Huái abandoned the people,
and the people followed and supported him.
Thus, was it not fitting for Duke Wén to possess the state?
Zǐ Bǐ has given nothing to the people,
has no external aid;
leaving Jìn,
Jìn did not see him off;
returning to Chǔ,
Chǔ did not welcome him.
How can he possess the state!"
Zǐ Bǐ indeed did not last,
and the one finally established was Qì Jí,
just as Shū Xiàng had said.
In the second year of King Píng's reign,
he sent Fèi Wújì to Qín to fetch a bride for Crown Prince Jiàn.
The bride was beautiful;
on her way, before she arrived,
Wújì returned first
and advised King Píng:
"The Qín woman is beautiful;
you should marry her yourself,
and find another for the crown prince."
King Píng listened to him,
and eventually married the Qín woman himself,
bearing Xióng Zhēn.
He found another bride for the crown prince.
At that time, Wǔ Shē was the crown prince's senior tutor,
and Wújì was the junior tutor.
Wújì was not favored by the crown prince
and often slandered Crown Prince Jiàn.
Jiàn was fifteen at the time,
his mother being a woman from Cài,
who was not favored by the king,
so the king gradually distanced and alienated Jiàn.
In the sixth year,
he sent Crown Prince Jiàn to reside in Chéngfù,
to guard the border.
Wújì again slandered the crown prince day and night to the king:
"Since I brought the Qín woman,
the crown prince resents it,
and cannot but hold a grudge against you;
you should be on guard.
Moreover, the crown prince resides in Chéngfù,
commands troops,
and allies with external lords—
he is planning to enter the capital."
King Píng summoned his tutor Wǔ Shē and reprimanded him.
Wǔ Shē, knowing Wújì had slandered him,
said:
"How can you, king, alienate your own flesh and blood over a minor official?"
Wújì said:
"If we do not act now,
we will regret it later."
Thereupon, the king imprisoned Wǔ Shē.
He then ordered Marshal Fèn Yáng to summon Crown Prince Jiàn,
intending to execute him.
The crown prince heard of this
and fled to Sòng.
Wújì said:
"Wǔ Shē has two sons;
if not killed, they will become a calamity for the state of Chǔ.
Why not summon them by promising to spare their father?
They will surely come."
Thereupon, the king sent an envoy to tell Shē:
"If you can make your two sons come, you will live;
if not, you will die."
Shē said:
"Shàng will come,
Xū will not."
The king asked:
"Why is that?"
Shē replied:
"Shàng's character
is upright and willing to die for principles,
kind, filial, and benevolent.
Hearing that his father will be spared if he comes,
he will surely arrive,
regardless of his own death.
Xū's character
is wise and fond of strategy,
brave and proud of his achievements.
Knowing that coming would mean certain death,
he will definitely not come.
Yet, the one who will bring worry to Chǔ is surely this son."
Thereupon, the king sent men to summon them,
saying:
"Come,
and I will spare your father."
Wǔ Shàng said to Wǔ Xū:
"To hear that our father is to be spared yet not rush to him
is unfilial;
if our father is killed and not avenged,
shows lack of planning;
to assess one's ability to undertake a task
is wisdom.
You should go,
and I will return to die."
Wǔ Shàng then returned.
Wǔ Xū bent his bow and fitted an arrow,
went out to meet the envoy,
and said:
"If our father is guilty,
why summon his sons?"
As he was about to shoot,
the envoy turned and fled,
and so he fled to Wú.
Wǔ Shē heard of this,
and said:
"With Xū gone,
the state of Chǔ is in danger."
The people of Chǔ then killed Wǔ Shē and Shàng.
In the tenth year,
the mother of Chǔ's crown prince Jiàn was in Jūcháo,
and opened contact with Wú.
Wú sent prince Guāng to attack Chǔ,
defeated Chén
and Cài, and took prince Jiàn's mother away.
Chǔ grew fearful,
and fortified Yǐng.
Earlier, a child from Wú's border town Bēiliáng and one from Chǔ's border town Zhōnglí quarreled over mulberry trees,
leading the two families to angrily attack each other,
and the Bēiliáng people were wiped out.
The magistrate of Bēiliáng was enraged,
mobilized the town's militia, and attacked Zhōnglí.
The king of Chǔ heard this and was angry,
dispatched the state's army, and annihilated Bēiliáng.
The king of Wú heard this and was greatly angered,
also sent troops,
ordering prince Guāng to attack Chǔ via prince Jiàn's mother's family,
and thus destroyed Zhōnglí
and Jūcháo.
Chǔ then, in fear, fortified Yǐng.
In the thirteenth year,
King Píng died.
General Zǐcháng said:
"Crown prince Zhēn is young,
and his mother was originally betrothed to the former crown prince Jiàn."
He wanted to install Lìngyǐn Zǐxī.
Zǐxī
was King Píng's half-brother,
and was righteous.
Zǐxī said:
"The state has established laws;
changing the succession causes chaos,
and speaking of it invites punishment."
So they installed crown prince Zhēn,
who became King Zhāo.
In the first year of King Zhāo,
the people of Chǔ were displeased with Fèi Wújì,
because his slanders had caused crown prince Jiàn's exile,
and the deaths of Wǔ Shē, his son, and Xì Wǎn.
Wǎn's clansman Bó's son Pǐ and Zǐxū both fled to Wú,
and Wú troops repeatedly invaded Chǔ,
making the people deeply resent Wújì.
Chǔ's Lìngyǐn Zǐcháng executed Wújì to appease the masses,
and the people were pleased.
In the fourth year,
three princes of Wú fled to Chǔ,
and Chǔ enfeoffed them to resist Wú.
In the fifth year,
Wú attacked and took Chǔ's Lù
and Qián. In the seventh year,
Chǔ sent Zǐcháng to attack Wú,
but Wú defeated Chǔ at Yùzhāng.
In the tenth year, winter,
the king of Wú Hélǘ,
Wǔ Zǐxū,
Bó Pǐ, along with Táng
and Cài, jointly attacked Chǔ.
Chǔ was heavily defeated,
Wú troops entered Yǐng,
desecrated King Píng's tomb,
all because of Wǔ Zǐxū.
When Wú troops approached,
Chǔ sent Zǐcháng with troops to meet them,
forming battle lines on both sides of the Hàn River.
Wú attacked and defeated Zǐcháng,
who fled to Zhèng.
Chǔ troops retreated,
Wú pursued victoriously,
and after five battles reached Yǐng.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
King Zhāo fled.
On Gēngchén,
the men of Wú entered Yǐng.
King Zhāo in his flight reached Yúnmèng.
The people of Yúnmèng did not recognize him as king,
and shot and wounded him.
The king fled to Yún.
Yún's lord's brother Huái said:
"King Píng killed my father;
now if I kill his son,
would that not be fitting?"
The lord of Yún stopped him,
but fearing he might assassinate King Zhāo,
fled with the king to Suí.
The king of Wú heard King Zhāo had gone there,
advanced to attack Suí,
and told the people of Suí:
"The descendants of Zhōu enfeoffed between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers
have all been exterminated by Chǔ."
He wanted to kill King Zhāo.
The king's attendant Zǐqí then hid the king deeply,
presenting himself as the king,
and said to the people of Suí:
"Hand me over to Wú."
The people of Suí divined about handing him to Wú,
and it was inauspicious,
so they declined to the king of Wú:
"King Zhāo has fled,
he is not in Suí."
Wú requested to enter and search themselves,
Suí did not permit,
and Wú withdrew.
When King Zhāo fled Yǐng,
he sent Shēn Bàoxū to seek help from Qín.
Qín sent five hundred chariots to rescue Chǔ,
and Chǔ also gathered its remaining scattered troops,
joining Qín to attack Wú.
In the eleventh year, sixth month,
they defeated Wú at Jì.
Meanwhile, the king of Wú's brother Fūgài, seeing the king's troops wounded and defeated,
fled back,
and proclaimed himself king.
Hélǘ heard this,
led his troops away from Chǔ,
and returned to attack Fūgài.
Fūgài was defeated,
fled to Chǔ,
where Chǔ enfeoffed him at Tángxī,
and he was known as the Tángxī clan.
King Zhāo of Chǔ exterminated Táng.
In the ninth month,
he returned to Yǐng.
In the twelfth year,
Wú again attacked Chǔ,
and took Pó.
Chǔ, in fear,
left Yǐng,
and moved the capital north to Ruò.
In the sixteenth year,
Confucius served as prime minister of Lǔ.
In the twentieth year,
Chǔ destroyed Dùn,
and wiped out Hú.
In the twenty-first year,
King Hé lǘ of Wú attacked Yuè.
King Gōu jiàn of Yuè shot and wounded the King of Wú,
who subsequently died.
From then on, Wú harbored resentment against Yuè and did not campaign westward against Chǔ.
In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
Wú attacked Chén,
King Zhāo of Chǔ came to its rescue,
stationing his army at Chéngfù.
In the tenth month,
King Zhāo fell ill in the army camp,
and there appeared crimson clouds resembling birds,
flanking the sun as they flew.
King Zhāo inquired of the Grand Historian of Zhōu,
who said:
"This portent harms the King of Chǔ,
but it can be transferred to the generals and ministers."
Upon hearing these words, the generals and ministers
requested to offer themselves in prayer to the spirits.
King Zhāo said:
"The generals and ministers
are my own limbs and backbone;
to shift the misfortune onto them now—
how could that remove it from my person!"
He did not consent.
Divination indicated the Hé River was the cause of the trouble,
and the senior officials requested to pray to the Hé River.
King Zhāo said:
"Since our former kings received their fief,
our sacrifices have not extended beyond the Jiāng
and Hàn Rivers, so the Hé River is not one for which we could have incurred offense."
He stopped them and did not permit it.
Confucius, while in Chén,
heard of these words,
and said:
"King Zhāo of Chǔ understands the great way.
That he did not lose his state
is fitting indeed!"
As King Zhāo's illness worsened,
he summoned the various princes and senior officials, saying:
"I, lacking in virtue,
have twice brought disgrace upon Chǔ's armies;
now that I am able to end my days with a natural lifespan,
it is my good fortune."
He yielded the throne to his younger brother, Prince Shēn,
who declined.
He then yielded to the next younger brother, Prince Jié,
who also declined.
Then he yielded to the next younger brother, Prince Lǘ;
after five offers,
the latter finally agreed to become king.
As they were about to engage in battle,
on the gēngyín day,
King Zhāo died in the army camp.
Zǐ Lǘ said:
"The king was gravely ill,
and set aside his own sons to yield to his ministers;
the reason I agreed to the king
was to broaden his intentions.
Now that the king has passed away,
how dare I forget the king's will!"
Thereupon, together with Zǐ Xī
and Zǐ Qí, they devised a plan,
deploying troops to block the roads,
and welcomed Zhāng, the son of the Yuè woman, establishing him as king,
who became King Huì.
Only then did they withdraw the troops and return,
burying King Zhāo.
In the second year of King Huì,
Zǐ Xī summoned Shèng, the son of the former Crown Prince Jiàn of King Píng, from Wú,
appointing him as the magistrate of Cháo,
with the title Lord Bái.
Lord Bái was fond of military affairs and treated his subordinates with respect,
desiring to seek revenge.
In the sixth year,
Lord Bái requested troops from Prime Minister Zǐ Xī to attack Zhèng.
Originally, Lord Bái's father, Jiàn, had fled to Zhèng,
where he was killed by Zhèng;
Lord Bái then fled to Wú,
and Zǐ Xī later recalled him,
hence he bore a grudge against Zhèng
and wished to attack it.
Zǐ Xī agreed but did not dispatch troops.
In the eighth year,
Jìn attacked Zhèng,
Zhèng sought urgent help from Chǔ,
Chǔ sent Zǐ Xī to rescue Zhèng,
who accepted bribes and then withdrew.
Lord Bái Shèng was enraged,
and thereupon, along with brave stalwarts like Shí Qǐ and others, ambushed and killed Prime Minister Zǐ Xī
and Zǐ Qí at court,
then took King Huì hostage,
placing him in the Gāo Mansion,
intending to assassinate him.
King Huì's attendant, Qū Gù, carried the king on his back and fled to the palace of King Zhāo's wife.
Lord Bái proclaimed himself king.
Over a month later,
when the Lord of Yè came to rescue Chǔ,
the followers of King Huì of Chǔ joined forces to attack Lord Bái,
and killed him.
King Huì then resumed the throne.
That same year,
Chǔ destroyed Chén and made it a county.
In the thirteenth year,
King Fū chāi of Wú grew powerful,
pressuring Qí
and Jìn, and came to attack Chǔ.
In the sixteenth year,
Yuè destroyed Wú.
In the forty-second year,
Chǔ destroyed Cài.
In the forty-fourth year,
Chǔ destroyed Qǐ.
They made peace with Qín.
At that time, Yuè had already destroyed Wú but could not control the area north of the Jiāng
and Huái Rivers;
Chǔ expanded eastward,
extending its territory to the area of Sìshàng.
In the fifty-seventh year,
King Huì died,
and his son, King Jiǎn, Zhōng, ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Jiǎn,
he campaigned north and destroyed Jǔ.
In the eighth year,
Marquess Wén of Wèi,
Lord Wǔ of Hán,
and Lord Huán of Zhào began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
In the twenty-fourth year,
King Jiǎn died,
and his son, King Shēng, Dāng, ascended the throne.
In the sixth year of King Shēng,
bandits assassinated King Shēng,
and his son, King Dào, Xióng Yí, ascended the throne.
In the second year of King Dào,
the Three Jìn came to attack Chǔ,
reaching Shèngqiū before turning back.
In the fourth year,
Chǔ attacked Zhōu.
Zhèng killed Zǐ Yáng.
In the ninth year,
Chǔ attacked Hán,
capturing Fùshǔ.
In the eleventh year,
the Three Jìn attacked Chǔ,
defeating us at Dàliáng
and Yúguān.
Chǔ heavily bribed Qín,
and made peace with them.
In the twenty-first year,
King Dào died,
and his son, King Sù, Zāng, ascended the throne.
In the fourth year of King Sù,
Shǔ attacked Chǔ,
capturing Zīfāng.
Thereupon, Chǔ built the Hànguān Pass to defend against them.
In the tenth year,
Wèi captured our Lǔyáng.
In the eleventh year,
King Sù died,
leaving no son,
so his younger brother, Xióng Liángfū, was established,
who became King Xuān.
In the sixth year of King Xuān,
the Son of Heaven of Zhōu congratulated Duke Xiàn of Qín.
Qín began to grow strong again,
while the Three Jìn became even more powerful,
with King Huì of Wèi
and King Wēi of Qí being especially strong.
In the thirtieth year,
Qín enfeoffed Wèi Yāng in Shāng,
and he encroached southward upon Chǔ.
That year,
King Xuān died,
and his son, King Wēi, Xióng Shāng, ascended the throne.
In the sixth year of King Wēi,
King Xiǎn of Zhōu presented the sacrificial meat of King Wén and King Wǔ to King Huì of Qín.
In the seventh year,
Tián Yīng, father of Lord Mèngcháng of Qí, deceived Chǔ,
so King Wēi of Chǔ attacked Qí,
defeating them at Xúzhōu,
and demanded that Qí must expel Tián Yīng.
Tián Yīng was terrified,
and Zhāng Chǒu deceitfully said to the King of Chǔ:
"The reason Your Majesty triumphed at Xúzhōu
is because Tián Pànzǐ was not employed.
Pànzǐ
had rendered meritorious service to the state,
and the common people were willing to serve under him.
Lord Yīng did not favor him and instead used Shēn Jì.
Shēn Jì,
however, was not supported by the high officials,
and the common people were unwilling to serve under him,
hence Your Majesty defeated them.
Now if Your Majesty expels Lord Yīng,
and Lord Yīng is expelled,
Pànzǐ will surely be employed.
He will then rally his troops to confront Your Majesty,
which would certainly not be to Your Majesty's advantage."
The King of Chǔ consequently did not expel him.
In the eleventh year,
King Wēi passed away,
and his son King Huái, Xióng Huái, ascended the throne.
Wèi, hearing of Chǔ's mourning,
attacked Chǔ,
capturing our Jīngshān.
In the first year of King Huái,
Zhāng Yí began serving as chancellor to King Huì of Qín.
In the fourth year,
King Huì of Qín first declared himself king.
In the sixth year,
Chǔ dispatched its Pillar of State, Zhāo Yáng, to lead troops and attack Wèi,
defeating them at Xiānglíng,
and capturing eight cities.
He then shifted his troops to attack Qí,
and the King of Qí grew concerned.
Chén Zhěn happened to be on a mission from Qín to Qí,
and the King of Qí said:
"What should we do about this?"
Chén Zhěn replied:
"Your Majesty need not worry,
allow me to persuade him to withdraw."
He then went to see Zhāo Yáng in his army camp,
saying:
"I wish to inquire about the laws of Chǔ:
how is one honored for destroying armies and killing generals?"
Zhāo Yáng said:
"The office would be that of Supreme Pillar of State,
with the highest noble rank of Zhíguī."
Chén Zhěn asked:
"Is there any honor higher than this?"
Zhāo Yáng replied:
"The Lìngyǐn."
Chén Zhěn said:
"Now you are already the Lìngyǐn,
the pinnacle of the state's honors.
Allow me to offer an analogy.
There was a man who gave his retainer a goblet of wine,
and the retainers said to each other:
'Several of us drinking this
would not be enough for all,
so let us draw snakes on the ground,
and the one who finishes his snake first shall drink it alone.'
One man said:
'My snake is done first.'
He picked up the wine and stood up,
saying:
'I can add feet to it.'
As he was adding the feet,
another man snatched the wine and drank it,
saying:
'A snake originally has no feet,
now that you've added feet,
it is not a snake.'
Now you serve as chancellor of Chǔ and attacked Wèi,
destroying armies and killing generals,
with achievements unsurpassed,
and honors that cannot be increased.
Now if you shift troops to attack Qí,
even if you defeat Qí,
your office and rank will not rise beyond this;
if you attack and do not win,
you may die and lose your rank,
damaging Chǔ:
this is like adding feet to the snake.
It would be better to withdraw your troops and show virtue to Qí,
this is the way to maintain fullness."
Zhāo Yáng said:
"Well said."
He then led his troops away.
Yān and
Hán's rulers first declared themselves kings.
Qín sent Zhāng Yí to meet with Chǔ,
Qí, and Wèi,
forming an alliance at Nièshāng.
In the eleventh year,
Sū Qín formed a vertical alliance of the six states east of the mountains to attack Qín together,
with King Huái of Chǔ as the leader of the alliance.
When they reached Hángǔ Pass,
Qín sent troops to attack the six states,
and the armies of the six states all withdrew and returned,
with only Qí lagging behind.
In the twelfth year,
King Mǐn of Qí attacked and defeated the armies of Zhào
and Wèi,
while Qín also attacked and defeated Hán,
competing with Qí for supremacy.
In the sixteenth year,
Qín desired to attack Qí,
but Chǔ was allied with Qí in close friendship,
so King Huì of Qín grew concerned,
and thus announced that Zhāng Yí was dismissed from his chancellorship,
sending Zhāng Yí south to see the King of Chǔ,
who said to the King of Chǔ:
"The one my king admires most is none other than Your Majesty,
and even I, Yí, wish for no one more than Your Majesty to serve as a gatekeeper.
The one my king detests most is none other than the King of Qí,
and even I, Yí, detest no one more than the King of Qí.
Yet Your Majesty maintains harmony with him,
which is why my king cannot serve Your Majesty,
and why I, Yí, cannot become your gatekeeper either.
If Your Majesty would close the passes and sever relations with Qí for my sake,
and send an envoy to follow me west to receive the six hundred lǐ of territory in Chǔ's former Shāngwū land that Qín had partitioned,
thus Qí would be weakened.
This would weaken Qí in the north,
earn Qín's gratitude in the west,
and privately enrich you with Shāngwū,
achieving three benefits with one strategy."
King Huái was greatly pleased,
and bestowed the chancellor's seal upon Zhāng Yí,
feasting with him daily,
proclaiming
"I have regained my land of Shāngwū."
All the ministers congratulated him,
but only Chén Zhěn mourned.
King Huái asked:
"Why?"
Chén Zhěn replied:
"The reason Qín values Your Majesty
is because you have Qí's alliance.
Now, before obtaining the land, you first sever ties with Qí,
which would isolate Chǔ.
Why would Qín then value an isolated state?
They would surely look down on Chǔ.
Moreover, if Qín were to give the land first and then you break with Qí,
that would not serve Qín's strategy.
If you break with Qí first and then demand the land,
you will surely be deceived by Zhāng Yí.
If deceived by Zhāng Yí,
Your Majesty would resent him.
Resenting him,
would stir up trouble with Qín in the west,
and sever ties with Qí in the north.
With trouble from Qín in the west,
and severed ties with Qí in the north,
then the armies of both states would surely come.
Hence I mourn."
The King of Chǔ did not listen,
and sent a general west to receive the granted land.
Zhāng Yí arrived in Qín,
feigned drunkenness and fell from his carriage,
claiming illness and refusing to appear for three months,
so the land was not handed over.
The King of Chǔ said:
"Does Yí think my severance of relations with Qí is not thorough enough?"
Then he sent the warrior Sòng Yì north to insult the King of Qí.
The King of Qí was greatly angered,
broke the treaty tally with Chǔ and allied with Qín.
When Qín and Qí formed an alliance,
Zhāng Yí then rose and attended court,
saying to the Chǔ general:
"Why do you not accept the land?
From such-and-such a place to such-and-such a place,
it measures six lǐ in area."
The Chǔ general said:
"What I was commanded to receive was six hundred lǐ,
I have not heard of six lǐ."
He immediately returned and reported to King Huái.
King Huái was furious,
raised an army and prepared to attack Qín.
Chén Zhěn again said:
"Attacking Qín is not a sound strategy.
It would be better to bribe them with a major city,
and join them in attacking Qí.
This way, our loss to Qín
can be compensated from Qí,
and our state can still be preserved.
Now Your Majesty has already broken with Qí and yet demands redress from Qín for deception,
this will cause us to unite Qín and Qí's alliance and attract the forces of the world against us,
and our state will surely suffer great harm."
The King of Chǔ did not listen,
then broke the peace with Qín,
and sent troops west to attack Qín.
Qín also dispatched troops to strike back.
In the spring of the seventeenth year,
they battled Qín at Dānyáng,
where Qín severely defeated our army,
decapitated eighty thousand armored soldiers,
captured our senior general Qū Gài,
lieutenant general Féng Hóu Chǒu, and over seventy others,
and subsequently took the commandery of Hànzhōng.
King Huái of Chǔ was enraged,
then mobilized the entire state's forces to again attack Qín,
fought at Lántián,
and was badly defeated.
Hán and Wèi, hearing of Chǔ's plight,
then attacked Chǔ from the south,
reaching as far as Dèng.
Chǔ, upon hearing this,
withdrew its troops and returned.
In the eighteenth year,
Qín sent an envoy to propose reestablishing friendly relations with Chǔ,
offering half of Hànzhōng to make peace with Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ said:
"I wish to obtain Zhāng Yí,
and do not desire the land."
Zhāng Yí heard this,
and requested to go to Chǔ.
The King of Qín said:
"Chǔ seeks vengeance against you,
what is to be done?"
Zhāng Yí said:
"I am on good terms with his courtier Jìn Shàng,
and Jìn Shàng has influence with the king's favored consort Zhèng Xiù,
whose words are always heeded.
Moreover, I previously caused Chǔ to be wronged over the Shāngyú agreement,
and now that Qín and Chǔ have fought a great war,
there is enmity;
unless I personally apologize to Chǔ, it will not be resolved.
Besides, with Your Majesty in power,
Chǔ should not dare to harm me.
If my death indeed benefits the state,
it is my wish."
Yí then went as an envoy to Chǔ.
Upon arrival,
King Huái refused to see him,
and instead imprisoned Zhāng Yí,
intending to kill him.
Yí privately contacted Jìn Shàng,
and Jìn Shàng pleaded with King Huái, saying:
"If you detain Zhāng Yí,
the King of Qín will surely be angered.
When the world sees Chǔ without Qín's support,
they will despise Your Majesty."
He also said to the lady Zhèng Xiù:
"The King of Qín greatly cherishes Zhāng Yí,
and now our king wishes to kill him,
so Qín is about to bribe Chǔ with the six counties of Shàngyōng,
send beauties to wed the King of Chǔ,
and include skilled singers from the palace as maids.
The King of Chǔ values land,
and the Qín women will surely be honored,
while you, madam, will be sidelined.
It would be better for you to speak up and have him released."
Zhèng Xiù eventually spoke to the king about Zhāng Yí and secured his release.
After Yí was freed,
King Huái treated him well,
and Yí persuaded the King of Chǔ to break the vertical alliance and form a friendly union with Qín,
arranging a marriage alliance.
After Zhāng Yí had left,
Qū Yuán returned from his mission to Qí,
and admonished the king, saying:
"Why not execute Zhāng Yí?"
King Huái regretted it,
sent men to pursue Yí,
but failed to catch him.
That year,
King Huì of Qín died.
In the twentieth year,
King Mǐn of Qí wished to become the leader of the vertical alliance,
and resented Chǔ's alliance with Qín,
so he sent a messenger with a letter to the King of Chǔ, saying:
"I am concerned that Chǔ does not recognize the importance of honor and reputation.
Now that King Huì of Qín is dead,
King Wǔ has ascended,
Zhāng Yí has fled to Wèi,
Chūlǐ Jí
and Gōngsūn Yǎn are in power,
yet Chǔ serves Qín.
Now Chūlǐ Jí is friendly with Hán,
and Gōngsūn Yǎn with Wèi;
if Chǔ must serve Qín,
Hán and Wèi, in fear,
will surely seek alliance with Qín through these two men,
then Yān
and Zhào should also serve Qín.
If four states compete to serve Qín,
then Chǔ will be reduced to a commandery or county.
Why does Your Majesty not join forces with me to win over Hán,
Wèi, Yān,
and Zhào, form a vertical alliance to honor the Zhōu court,
and thereby halt arms and give the people rest,
issuing commands to the world?
None would dare not gladly obey,
and then Your Majesty's fame will be achieved.
If you lead the allied states in a joint attack,
you will surely defeat Qín.
Your Majesty can take Wǔguān,
Shǔ, and the Hàn region,
monopolize the wealth of Wú
and Yuè and control the profits of the rivers and seas,
while Hán and Wèi cede Shàngdǎng,
pressing west to Hángǔ,
then Chǔ's strength will be multiplied a hundredfold.
Moreover, Your Majesty was deceived by Zhāng Yí,
lost the land of Hànzhōng,
suffered military defeat at Lántián,
and none in the world do not share Your Majesty's anger.
Yet now you wish to be the first to serve Qín!
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this."
The King of Chǔ, already inclined to make peace with Qín,
upon reading the King of Qí's letter,
hesitated and could not decide,
so he submitted the matter for discussion among his ministers.
Some ministers advised making peace with Qín,
while others said to heed Qí.
Zhāo Jū said:
"Although Your Majesty has taken territory from Yuè in the east,
it is not enough to wipe away the shame;
you must take land from Qín
before you can sufficiently erase the shame in the eyes of the feudal lords.
Your Majesty would do better to deeply befriend Qí
and Hán to bolster Chǔlǐ Jí's importance;
thus, Your Majesty will gain the support of Hán
and Qí to demand territory.
Qín destroyed Hán's Yíyáng,
yet Hán still serves Qín
because their former king's tomb is in Píngyáng,
and Qín's Wǔsuì is only seventy lǐ away,
hence they particularly fear Qín.
Otherwise,
if Qín attacks Sānchuān,
Zhào attacks Shàngdǎng,
and Chǔ attacks Héwài,
Hán would surely perish.
Chǔ's rescue of Hán
cannot prevent Hán from falling,
yet it is Chǔ that preserves Hán.
Since Hán has obtained Wǔsuì from Qín,
using the rivers and mountains as fortifications,
no one repays virtue as generously as Chǔ,
so I believe they will swiftly serve Your Majesty.
The reason Qí trusts Hán
is because Hán's Prince Mò is the chancellor of Qí.
Now that Hán has gained Wǔsuì from Qín,
if Your Majesty treats them well,
and has them use Qí
and Hán's influence to bolster Chǔlǐ Jí,
then Jí, with the support of Qí
and Hán,
their ruler will not dare to abandon Jí.
Now, if we add Chǔ's weight to it,
Chǔlǐzǐ is sure to persuade Qín
to return the invaded land to Chǔ."
Thereupon, King Huái agreed,
ultimately not aligning with Qín,
but with Qí to befriend Hán.
In the twenty-fourth year,
he turned against Qí and allied with Qín.
King Zhāo of Qín had just ascended the throne,
and sent generous bribes to Chǔ.
Chǔ went to fetch a bride.
In the twenty-fifth year,
King Huái entered and made a covenant with King Zhāo of Qín,
meeting at Huángjí.
Qín returned Shàngyōng to Chǔ.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Qí, Hán,
and Wèi, because Chǔ had betrayed their alliance and joined Qín,
jointly attacked Chǔ.
Chǔ sent the crown prince to Qín as a hostage and requested rescue.
Qín then sent the guest minister Tōng to lead troops to save Chǔ,
and the three states withdrew their armies.
In the twenty-seventh year,
a Qín official had a private fight with the Chǔ crown prince,
and the Chǔ crown prince killed him and fled back.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Qín then joined with Qí,
Hán, and Wèi to attack Chǔ,
killed Chǔ general Táng Mò,
and took our Zhòngqiū before leaving.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Qín attacked Chǔ again,
greatly defeating Chǔ,
with twenty thousand Chǔ soldiers dead,
and our general Jǐng Quē killed.
King Huái, frightened,
sent the crown prince as a hostage to Qí to seek peace.
In the thirtieth year,
Qín again attacked Chǔ,
taking eight cities.
King Zhāo of Qín sent a letter to the King of Chǔ, saying:
"Initially, I and the King swore to be brothers,
made a covenant at Huángjí,
with the crown prince as hostage,
and it was most harmonious.
The crown prince insulted and killed my important minister,
and fled without apology,
I truly could not contain my anger,
and sent troops to invade Your Majesty's borders.
Now I hear that Your Majesty has sent the crown prince as a hostage to Qí to seek peace.
I and Chǔ share borders,
and thus have intermarried,
and have long been close.
But now if Qín and Chǔ are not harmonious,
we cannot command the feudal lords.
I wish to meet with Your Majesty at Wǔguān,
face to face to make an agreement,
form an alliance, and then part,
that is my desire.
I dare to inform Your Majesty's subordinate."
King Huái of Chǔ saw the Qín king's letter,
and was troubled by it.
He wanted to go,
but feared being deceived;
not to go,
he feared Qín's anger.
Zhāo Jū said:
"Your Majesty should not go,
but instead raise troops to defend yourself.
Qín is a tiger and wolf,
not to be trusted,
and has the intention to annex the feudal lords."
King Huái's son Zǐlán urged the king to go,
saying:
"How can we sever Qín's friendly intentions!"
Thereupon, he went to meet King Zhāo of Qín.
King Zhāo deceitfully ordered a general to ambush troops at Wǔguān,
pretending to be the Qín king.
When the King of Chǔ arrived,
they closed Wǔguān,
and then took him west to Xiányáng,
where he paid homage at Zhāngtái,
treated as a vassal,
not given equal courtesy.
King Huái of Chǔ was greatly angered,
regretting not heeding Zhāo Jū's words.
Qín then detained the King of Chǔ,
demanding the cession of the prefectures of Wū
and Qiánzhōng.
The King of Chǔ wanted to make a covenant,
but Qín wanted to obtain the land first.
The King of Chǔ angrily said:
"Qín deceived me and now forcibly demands land from me!"
He refused to agree to Qín's terms.
Qín thus detained him.
The great ministers of Chǔ were worried,
and so plotted together, saying:
"Our king is in Qín and cannot return,
held to cede land,
while the crown prince is a hostage in Qí.
If Qí and Qín conspire together,
then Chǔ will be lost."
They then wanted to enthrone one of King Huái's sons who was in the state.
Zhāo Jū said:
"The king and the crown prince are both trapped among the feudal lords,
and now to go against the king's command and enthrone his庶子[commoner son],
is not proper."
So they deceitfully sent a message to Qí,
and King Mǐn of Qí said to his chancellor:
"It would be better to detain the crown prince to demand Huáiběi from Chǔ."
The chancellor said:
"No,
if Yǐng establishes a king,
then we would be holding an empty hostage and acting unjustly under heaven."
Someone said:
"Not so.
If Yǐng establishes a king,
we can then bargain with the new king, saying,
'Give me your eastern territories,
and I will kill the crown prince for you;
otherwise,
I will join the three states to enthrone him,'
and then the eastern territories can certainly be obtained."
The King of Qí ultimately used his chancellor's plan and returned the Chǔ crown prince.
The crown prince Héng arrived,
was enthroned as king,
known as King Qǐngxiāng.
He then announced to Qín:
"Thanks to the spirits of the land and grain,
the state has a king."
In the first year of King Qǐngxiāng Héng's reign,
Qín detained King Huái and failed to obtain territory,
so Chǔ established a new king to counter Qín.
King Zhāo of Qín was enraged,
sent troops through Wǔguān to attack Chǔ,
decisively defeated the Chǔ army,
beheaded fifty thousand,
and captured fifteen cities including Xī before withdrawing.
In the second year,
King Huái of Chǔ escaped and tried to return,
but Qín detected this,
blocked the main routes to Chǔ,
and King Huái,
fearing for his safety, took backroads to Zhào seeking repatriation.
Lord Fù of Zhào was in Dài,
while his son King Huì, newly enthroned,
was governing the kingdom,
and feared to admit the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ then sought to go to Wèi,
but Qín pursuers arrived,
so he went back to Qín with Qín envoys.
King Huái subsequently fell ill.
In the third year of King Qǐngxiāng,
King Huái died in Qín,
and Qín returned his coffin to Chǔ.
The people of Chǔ all pitied him,
grieving as for a close relative.
The feudal lords henceforth did not regard Qín as righteous.
Chǔ and Qín severed relations.
In the sixth year,
Qín sent Bái Qǐ to attack Hán at Yīquē,
achieving a great victory,
beheading two hundred forty thousand.
Qín then sent a letter to the King of Chǔ saying:
"Chǔ has betrayed Qín,
and Qín will lead the feudal lords to attack Chǔ,
contending for survival in a single day.
We hope Your Majesty will ready your troops
for an enjoyable battle."
King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ grew concerned,
and planned to reestablish peace with Qín.
In the seventh year,
Chǔ welcomed a bride from Qín,
and Chǔ and Qín restored peaceful relations.
In the eleventh year,
Qí and Qín each declared themselves emperor;
over a month later,
they reverted from emperor to king.
In the fourteenth year,
King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ and King Zhāo of Qín held a friendly meeting at Yuān,
concluding a peace and marriage alliance.
In the fifteenth year,
the King of Chǔ joined Qín,
the Three Jìn,
and Yān in attacking Qí,
capturing Huáiběi.
In the sixteenth year,
he held a friendly meeting with King Zhāo of Qín at Yān.
That autumn,
he met again with the King of Qín at Rǎng.
In the eighteenth year,
a man of Chǔ who enjoyed using a weak bow and fine silk cord to shoot returning wild geese
came to King Qǐngxiāng's attention,
who summoned and questioned him.
He replied:
"Your servant's pleasure in shooting wild geese and
small birds with
tiny arrows
is hardly worth mentioning to Your Majesty.
Considering the greatness of Chǔ
and Your Majesty's wisdom,
the targets are not merely these.
In ancient times, the Three Sovereigns aimed at morality,
the Five Hegemons at the Warring States.
Thus Qín,
Wèi, Yān,
and Zhào
are the wild geese;
Qí, Lǔ,
Hán, and Wèi
are the green-headed birds;
Zōu, Fèi,
Tán, and Pī
are the small birds.
Beyond these, the rest are not worth shooting.
Seeing twelve birds,
what would Your Majesty take?
Why not use the sage as your bow,
the brave as your cord,
and shoot at the opportune moment?
These twelve birds
can be captured and bagged.
The pleasure is not just momentary,
the gain not merely wildfowl.
If Your Majesty aims south of Wèi's Dàliáng,
extending the right arm to connect directly to Hán,
then the central routes are cut and Shàngcài Commandery falls.
Turning to shoot east of Yǔ,
disabling Wèi's left flank and striking Dìngtáo beyond,
then Wèi's eastern territories are abandoned and Dà Sòng
with Fāngyǔ Commandery are taken.
With Wèi's two arms severed,
it topples;
striking Tán state squarely,
Dàliáng can be captured.
Your Majesty winding the cord at Lántái,
watering horses at Xīhé,
securing Wèi's Dàliáng,
this is the pleasure of one shot.
If Your Majesty truly enjoys archery without tiring,
then bring out the precious bow,
string a new cord,
shoot at the birds of the Eastern Sea,
return to fortify the Great Wall as defense,
shoot Dōng Jǔ at dawn,
release at Pèiqiū by dusk,
press Jímò by night,
secure Wǔdào with a glance,
then the east of the Great Wall is gathered and north of Tàishān is taken.
Bordering Zhào to the west and reaching Yān to the north,
three states spreading wings,
an alliance can form without a pact.
Gazing north to Liáodōng of Yān and looking south to Kuàijī of Yuè,
this is the pleasure of a second shot.
As for the twelve feudal lords of Sìshàng,
entangling left and brushing right,
they can be finished in a day.
Now Qín, having broken Hán, bears lasting worry,
gaining cities but not daring to hold them;
attacking Wèi without success,
striking Zhào only to be weakened,
so Qín and Wèi's strength is exhausted,
and Chǔ's former lands Hànzhōng,
Xī, Lì can be recovered.
Your Majesty, bring out the precious bow,
string a new cord,
cross Méngsài,
and wait for Qín's exhaustion;
Shāndōng
and Hénèi can be unified.
Resting the people and troops,
you can face south and claim kingship.
Thus it is said Qín is a great bird,
bearing the seas within its grasp,
facing east,
its left arm holding southwestern Zhào,
its right arm touching Chǔ's Yānyǐng,
striking Hán and Wèi at the breast,
lowering its head over the central states,
positioned with advantageous form,
situated with strategic terrain,
flapping wings and beating feathers,
spanning three thousand lǐ,
so Qín cannot be singled out for a night shot."
Intending to provoke King Xiāng,
he thus replied with these words.
King Xiāng then summoned him for discussion,
and he further stated:
"The former king was deceived by Qín and died abroad,
there is no greater resentment.
Even a commoner with a grievance
can seek revenge against a mighty state,
as with Bái Gōng
and Wǔ Zǐxū.
Now Chǔ's territory spans five thousand lǐ,
with a million armored troops,
sufficient to leap across the central plains,
yet we sit and accept hardship—
your servant privately believes this is not for Your Majesty."
Thereupon King Qǐngxiāng sent envoys to the feudal lords,
renewing the vertical alliance,
intending to attack Qín.
Qín, hearing of this,
dispatched troops to attack Chǔ.
Chǔ intended to ally with Qí and Hán to attack Qín,
and thereby sought to plot against Zhōu.
King Nǎn of Zhōu sent Duke Wǔ to say to Chǔ’s minister Zhāozǐ:
“The three states plan to use troops to carve up the outskirts of Zhōu’s territory to facilitate transport,
and then move the ritual vessels southward to honor Chǔ.
I consider this unwise.
To assassinate the common sovereign,
and subjugate the ruler of a generation,
will cause the great states not to befriend you;
to use the many to coerce the few,
will cause the small states not to submit.
If the great states are not friendly,
and the small states do not submit,
you cannot achieve both reputation and substance.
Without gaining reputation and substance,
you will not be able to harm the people.
To have the reputation of plotting against Zhōu
is not a means to issue commands.”
Zhāozǐ said:
“As for plotting against Zhōu, there is no such thing.
Nevertheless,
why should Zhōu not be plotted against?”
He replied:
“An army not five times larger should not attack,
a city not ten times larger should not be besieged.
One Zhōu is equivalent to twenty Jìn,
as you well know.
Hán once attacked a city of Jìn with two hundred thousand troops,
its elite soldiers died,
its regular soldiers were wounded,
yet Jìn was not captured.
You do not have a force a hundred times Hán’s to plot against Zhōu,
this is known throughout the world.
To incur the hatred of the two Zhōu and block the hearts of Zōu and Lǔ,
to sever relations with Qí,
to lose reputation in the world,
this would make the endeavor perilous.
To endanger the two Zhōu and enrich Sānchuān,
the lands beyond Fāngchéng will surely be weakened by Hán.
How do we know this is so?
The territory of Western Zhōu,
even if its length is cut and its shortness supplemented,
does not exceed a hundred lǐ.
Though it is named the common sovereign of the world,
dividing its land would not suffice to enrich a state,
gaining its people would not suffice to strengthen an army.
Even if you do not attack it,
you would bear the name of regicide.
Yet rulers fond of meddling,
and ministers eager for attack,
when issuing commands and employing troops,
have never failed to begin and end with Zhōu.
Why is this?
They see the sacrificial vessels there,
and desire the arrival of the vessels, forgetting the chaos of regicide.
Now that Hán believes the vessels are in Chǔ,
I fear the world will hate Chǔ because of the vessels.
Allow me to offer an analogy.
Tiger meat is rank,
and its claws and teeth are sharp,
yet people still attack it.
If a marsh deer were covered with a tiger’s skin,
people would attack it ten thousand times more than the tiger.
Dividing Chǔ’s territory
would suffice to enrich a state;
humiliating Chǔ’s name
would suffice to honor a sovereign.
Now you intend to kill and destroy the world’s common sovereign,
possess the transmitted vessels of the Three Dynasties,
swallow the three-legged and six-winged tripods,
to elevate yourself above the world’s rulers—
if this is not greed, what is it?
The Zhōushū says:
‘To rise, do not be first.’
Therefore, if the vessels move south, troops will arrive.”
Thereupon, Chǔ abandoned its plan and did not proceed.
In the nineteenth year,
Qín attacked Chǔ,
the Chǔ army was defeated,
and they ceded Shàngyōng
and the land north of the Hàn River to Qín.
In the twentieth year,
the Qín general Bái Qǐ captured our Xīlíng.
In the twenty-first year,
the Qín general Bái Qǐ then captured our Yǐng,
burned the tombs of the former kings at Yílíng.
King Xiāng of Chǔ’s troops scattered,
and he did not engage in battle again,
retreating northeast to defend the city of Chén.
In the twenty-second year,
Qín again captured our Wū
and Qiánzhōng commanderies.
In the twenty-third year,
King Xiāng gathered troops from the eastern territories,
obtaining over a hundred thousand men,
and again marched west to recapture the fifteen districts along the river that Qín had taken from us, making them a commandery,
to resist Qín.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he sent thirty thousand men to assist the Three Jìn in attacking Yān.
He again made peace with Qín,
and sent the crown prince as a hostage to Qín.
Chǔ sent a Zuǒtú to attend the crown prince in Qín.
In the thirty-sixth year,
King Qǐngxiāng fell ill,
and the crown prince fled back home.
In autumn, King Qǐngxiāng died,
and the crown prince, Xióng Yuán, succeeded him,
becoming King Kǎoliè.
King Kǎoliè appointed the Zuǒtú as Lìngyǐn,
enfeoffed him with Wú,
and titled him Lord Chūnshēn.
In the first year of King Kǎoliè,
he ceded Zhōu to Qín to make peace.
At this time, Chǔ grew even weaker.
In the sixth year,
Qín besieged Hándān,
Zhào urgently sought aid from Chǔ,
and Chǔ sent General Jǐng Yáng to rescue Zhào.
In the seventh year,
they reached Xīnzhōng.
The Qín troops withdrew.
In the twelfth year,
King Zhāo of Qín died,
and the King of Chǔ sent Lord Chūnshēn to offer condolences and sacrifices in Qín.
In the sixteenth year,
King Zhuāngxiāng of Qín died,
and the King of Qín, Zhào Zhèng, ascended the throne.
In the twenty-second year,
Chǔ joined the other states in attacking Qín,
but, finding it unfavorable, withdrew.
Chǔ moved its capital east to Shòuchūn,
calling it Yǐng.
In the twenty-fifth year,
King Kǎoliè died,
and his son, King Yōu, Hàn, succeeded him.
Lǐ Yuán killed Lord Chūnshēn.
In the third year of King Yōu,
Qín and Wèi attacked Chǔ.
The Qín chancellor Lǚ Bùwéi died.
In the ninth year,
Qín destroyed Hán.
In the tenth year,
King Yōu died,
and his younger brother by the same mother, Yóu, succeeded him,
becoming King Āi.
King Āi had been on the throne for a little over two months
when his elder half-brother Fùchú’s followers attacked and killed King Āi, establishing Fùchú as king.
That year,
Qín captured the King of Zhào, Qiān.
In the first year of King Fùchú,
the Crown Prince of Yān, Dān, sent Jīng Kē to assassinate the King of Qín.
In the second year,
Qín sent a general to attack Chǔ,
routed the Chǔ army,
and captured over ten cities.
In the third year,
Qín destroyed Wèi.
In the fourth year,
the Qín general Wáng Jiǎn defeated our army at Qí,
and killed General Xiàng Yàn.
In the fifth year,
the Qín generals Wáng Jiǎn
and Méng Wǔ then destroyed the state of Chǔ,
captured the King of Chǔ, Fùchú,
and extinguished Chǔ, making it a commandery.
The Grand Historian remarks:
When King Líng of Chǔ was meeting the feudal lords at Shēn,
executing Qìng Fēng of Qí,
building the Zhānghuá Terrace,
and seeking the Nine Tripods of Zhōu,
he regarded the world as small;
yet when he starved to death in the house of Shēn Hài,
he became the laughingstock of the world.
How lamentable that he failed to uphold proper conduct!
Alas!
As for the influence of circumstances on a person,
can one not be cautious?
Qìjí seized the throne through turmoil,
indulged in debauchery with Qín women—
how extreme!
He nearly caused the state to perish a second time!
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè,
whose ancestor was a descendant of Yǔ,
and the son of Shǎo Kāng, the emperor of the Xià dynasty.
He was enfeoffed in Kuàijī,
to uphold the sacrifices to Yǔ.
Tattooed and with cropped hair,
he cleared the wilderness and established a city there.
After more than twenty generations,
it came to Yǔn Cháng.
During Yǔn Cháng's time,
he fought with King Hé Lǘ of Wú and they held grudges against each other.
When Yǔn Cháng died,
his son Gōu Jiàn succeeded him,
becoming the King of Yuè.
In the first year of his reign,
King Hé Lǘ of Wú heard of Yǔn Cháng's death,
and raised an army to attack Yuè.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè sent death-defying warriors to provoke a fight,
in three rows,
they advanced to the Wú battle formation,
shouted and slit their own throats.
While the Wú army watched them,
Yuè took the opportunity to assault the Wú forces,
defeating them at Zuìlǐ,
and shooting and wounding King Hé Lǘ of Wú.
As Hé Lǘ was dying,
he told his son Fū Chāi:
"Never forget Yuè."
In the third year,
Gōu Jiàn heard that King Fū Chāi of Wú was drilling his troops day and night,
preparing to take revenge on Yuè,
so Yuè wanted to strike first before Wú could launch its attack.
Fàn Lǐ advised against it, saying:
"It is not advisable.
I have heard that weapons are instruments of ill omen,
warfare is contrary to virtue,
and contention is the lowest of affairs.
Scheming against virtue,
fondness for using instruments of ill omen,
and testing oneself in the lowest pursuits—
Heaven forbids it,
and those who engage in it will not benefit."
The King of Yuè said:
"I have already made up my mind."
So he raised an army.
When the King of Wú heard this,
he dispatched all his elite troops to attack Yuè,
defeating them at Fūjiāo.
The King of Yuè then retreated with his remaining five thousand troops to hold out at Kuàijī.
The King of Wú pursued and besieged him there.
The King of Yuè said to Fàn Lǐ:
"Because I did not listen to you, I have come to this.
What should I do now?"
Lǐ replied:
"To maintain fullness, one must accord with Heaven;
to stabilize peril, one must accord with humanity;
to regulate affairs, one must accord with Earth.
Use humble words and generous gifts to appease them;
if they do not agree,
then offer yourself in person to make a deal."
Gōu Jiàn said:
"Agreed."
He then sent Minister Wén Zhǒng to seek peace with Wú,
who crawled on his knees and kowtowed, saying:
"Your subject Gōu Jiàn, through his minister Zhǒng, dares to inform your attendants:
Gōu Jiàn begs to be your servant,
and his wife to be your handmaid."
The King of Wú was about to agree.
Zǐ Xū said to the King of Wú:
"Heaven has given Yuè to Wú;
do not agree."
Zhǒng returned,
and reported to Gōu Jiàn.
Gōu Jiàn intended to kill his wife and children,
burn his precious vessels,
and fight to the death.
Zhǒng stopped Gōu Jiàn, saying:
"The Grand Steward Pǐ of Wú is greedy;
we can tempt him with profit.
Allow me to go secretly and speak with him."
So Gōu Jiàn gave beautiful women and precious vessels to Zhǒng to secretly present to Grand Steward Pǐ of Wú.
Pǐ accepted them,
and then arranged for Minister Zhǒng to see the King of Wú.
Zhǒng kowtowed and said:
"I beg Your Majesty to pardon Gōu Jiàn's crimes,
and he will surrender all his precious vessels.
If unfortunately he is not pardoned,
Gōu Jiàn will kill all his wife and children,
burn his precious vessels,
and lead all five thousand men in a desperate fight,
which will surely take a toll."
Pǐ then persuaded the King of Wú, saying:
"Since Yuè has submitted as your vassal,
if you pardon them,
it will be to the state's advantage."
The King of Wú was about to agree.
Zǐ Xū advised him:
"If we do not destroy Yuè now,
we will surely regret it later.
Gōu Jiàn is a worthy ruler,
and Zhǒng and Lǐ are capable ministers.
If they return to their state,
they will cause trouble."
The King of Wú did not listen,
and finally pardoned Yuè,
withdrawing his troops and returning home.
When Gōu Jiàn was trapped at Kuàijī,
he sighed deeply and said:
"Am I to end here?"
Zhǒng said:
"Tāng was imprisoned at Xiàtái,
King Wén was confined in Yǒulǐ,
Chóng'ěr of Jìn fled to Dí,
and Xiǎo Bái of Qí fled to Jǔ,
yet they eventually became kings or hegemons.
From this perspective,
how can we know this will not turn out to be a blessing?"
After Wú pardoned Yuè,
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè returned to his state,
where he subjected himself to hardships and anxious thoughts,
placing a gallbladder in his chamber.
Whenever he sat or lay down, he would look up at the gallbladder,
and when he ate or drank, he would taste the gallbladder,
saying:
"Have you forgotten the shame of Kuàijī?"
He personally worked the fields,
and his wife wove cloth;
they ate without meat,
wore no colorful garments,
humbled themselves to treat worthies with respect,
generously received guests,
relieved the poor and mourned the dead,
sharing the toils with the common people.
He wanted to put Fàn Lǐ in charge of state affairs,
but Lǐ replied:
"In matters of military and arms,
Zhǒng is not as good as Lǐ;
but in stabilizing the state,
and winning the people's allegiance,
Lǐ is not as good as Zhǒng."
So he entrusted the governance of the state to Minister Zhǒng,
and sent Fàn Lǐ with Minister Zhè Jī to negotiate peace,
serving as a hostage in Wú.
After two years, Wú returned Lǐ.
Seven years after Gōu Jiàn returned from Kuàijī,
he comforted and nurtured his officials and people,
intending to use them to take revenge on Wú.
Minister Féng Tóng advised him:
"Our state has only recently recovered from exile,
and now that it is becoming prosperous again,
if we repair and prepare our weapons,
Wú will surely become fearful,
and fear will inevitably lead to disaster.
Moreover, when a bird of prey strikes,
it must conceal its form.
Now Wú's armies press upon Qí and
Jìn, its grudges run deep with Chǔ and
Yuè, its fame overshadows the world,
but in reality, it harms the Zhōu court.
With little virtue but many achievements,
it is bound to become arrogant and self-important.
For Yuè's strategy,
it would be best to ally with Qí,
befriend Chǔ,
attach to Jìn,
and thereby indulge Wú.
Wú's ambitions will expand,
and it will inevitably take warfare lightly.
Thus, we can manipulate the balance of power,
and when the three states attack it,
Yuè can exploit its weakness,
and overcome it."
Gōu Jiàn said:
"Excellent."
Two years later,
the King of Wú intended to attack Qí.
Wǔ Zǐxū admonished him, saying:
"It is not advisable.
I have heard that Gōu Jiàn eats without multiple dishes,
sharing hardships and joys with the common people.
If this man does not die,
he will surely become a calamity for the state.
Having Yuè in Wú
is like a disease in the heart and abdomen,
while Qí to Wú
is merely a skin rash.
I hope Your Majesty will abandon Qí and deal with Yuè first."
The King of Wú did not listen,
and proceeded to attack Qí,
defeating them at Àilíng,
capturing Qí's generals Gāo and
Guó, and bringing them back.
He then reproached Zǐxū.
Zǐxū said:
"Your Majesty, do not rejoice!"
The king was angered,
and Zǐxū wanted to commit suicide,
but the king heard of it and stopped him.
Yuè's minister Wén Zhǒng said:
"I observe that the King of Wú's governance has become arrogant;
please allow me to test him by borrowing grain,
to divine the situation."
He requested to borrow grain,
and the King of Wú wanted to grant it,
but Zǐxū advised against giving it.
The king then gave it to them,
and Yuè secretly rejoiced.
Zǐxū declared:
"The king does not heed advice;
in three years, Wú will be in ruins!"
Grand Steward Pǐ heard this,
and repeatedly argued with Zǐxū over the Yuè matter,
then slandered Zǐxū, saying:
"Wǔ Yún appears loyal but is actually a cruel man;
he did not care for his own father and brothers,
how could he care for the king?
When the king earlier wanted to attack Qí,
Yún strongly admonished against it,
yet after there was success,
he resented the king for it.
If the king does not guard against Wǔ Yún,
Yún will surely cause rebellion."
He conspired with Féng Tóng,
and slandered him to the king.
The king initially did not comply,
but then sent Zǐxū to Qí,
and upon hearing that he had entrusted his son to the Bào family,
the king became greatly enraged,
saying:
"Wǔ Yún has indeed deceived me!"
When the mission returned,
he sent a man to give Zǐxū the Dúlòu sword to commit suicide.
Zǐxū laughed heartily and said:
"I made your father a hegemon,
and I established you;
you initially wanted to give me half of Wú,
which I did not accept.
Now,
alas,
alas,
a man truly cannot stand alone!"
He told the messenger:
"Be sure to take my eyes and place them at the east gate of Wú,
to watch the Yuè troops enter!"
Thereupon, Wú entrusted governance to Pǐ.
Three years later,
Gōu Jiàn summoned Fàn Lǐ, saying:
"Wú has already killed Zǐxū,
and there are many flatterers;
is it time?"
Fàn Lǐ replied:
"Not yet."
By the next spring,
the King of Wú went north to meet with the feudal lords at Huángchí,
taking Wú's elite troops with him,
leaving only the old, weak, and the crown prince to guard the state.
Gōu Jiàn asked Fàn Lǐ again,
and Lǐ said,
"It is time."
They then dispatched two thousand trained marines,
forty thousand drilled soldiers,
six thousand gentlemen warriors,
and a thousand various officers
to attack Wú.
The Wú army was defeated,
and they killed the Wú crown prince.
Wú urgently reported to the king,
who was meeting with the feudal lords at Huángchí;
fearing that the world would hear of it,
he kept it secret.
After the King of Wú had made the covenant at Huángchí,
he sent someone with generous gifts to seek peace with Yuè.
Yuè, considering itself unable to destroy Wú yet,
made peace with Wú.
Four years later,
Yuè again attacked Wú.
Wú's soldiers and people were exhausted,
its elite forces having all died in Qí and
Jìn. Thus, Yuè greatly defeated Wú,
and then besieged it for three years.
The Wú army was defeated,
and Yuè once more cornered the King of Wú on Gūsū Mountain.
The King of Wú sent Gōngsūn Xióng, who bared his upper body and approached on his knees,
to beg for peace from the King of Yuè, saying:
"This solitary subject Fūchāi dares to bare his heart:
in the past, I offended you at Kuàijī,
and Fūchāi did not dare to defy your command,
managing to make peace with you and return.
Now you, Great King, have raised your noble feet to punish this solitary subject;
I will obey your every command.
Might it be that you also wish to pardon this solitary subject's offense as at Kuàijī?"
Gōu Jiàn could not bear it
and intended to agree.
Fàn Lǐ said:
"In the affair at Kuàijī,
Heaven gave Yuè to Wú,
but Wú did not take it.
Now Heaven has given Wú to Yuè;
how can Yuè defy Heaven?
Moreover, you, Great King, have risen early and retired late,
was it not for Wú?
You have planned for twenty-two years;
can you abandon it all in one day?
Is that acceptable?
Furthermore, when Heaven gives and you do not take,
you will instead suffer the consequences.
'When cutting an axe handle, the pattern is not far'—
have you forgotten the distress at Kuàijī?"
Gōu Jiàn said:
"I wish to heed your words,
but I cannot bear to see his envoy."
Fàn Lǐ then beat the drum to advance the troops,
saying:
"The king has already entrusted governance to his officers;
envoy, leave now,
or you will incur blame."
The Wú envoy wept and departed.
Gōu Jiàn pitied him,
and sent someone to tell the King of Wú:
"I will place you at Yǒngdōng,
with a fief of one hundred families."
The King of Wú declined, saying:
"I am old,
and cannot serve you, Great King!"
He then committed suicide.
Covering his face,
he said:
"I have no face to see Zǐxū!"
The King of Yuè buried the King of Wú and executed Grand Steward Pǐ.
After Gōu Jiàn had pacified Wú,
he led his troops north across the Huái River,
and met with the feudal lords of Qí,
Jìn, and others at Xúzhōu,
presenting tribute to Zhōu.
King Yuán of Zhōu sent someone to bestow sacrificial meat upon Gōu Jiàn,
appointing him as Bà.
After Gōu Jiàn departed,
crossing south of the Huái,
he gave the land north of the Huái to Chǔ,
returned the territory Wú had seized from Sòng to Sòng,
and gave Lǔ a hundred lǐ of land east of the Sì River.
At that time,
Yuè's troops roamed freely east of the
Yangtze and Huái rivers,
all the feudal lords came to congratulate him,
and he was hailed as the Hegemon King.
Fàn Lǐ then left,
and from Qí sent a letter to Minister Zhǒng, saying:
"When the birds are all gone,
the good bow is stored away;
when the cunning hares are dead,
the hunting dog is cooked.
The King of Yuè has a long neck and a beak-like mouth;
he can share hardships with others,
but cannot share joy.
Why do you not leave?"
Zhǒng saw the letter,
and pleaded illness to avoid court.
Someone slandered Zhǒng, saying he was about to rebel,
so the King of Yuè gave Zhǒng a sword, saying:
"You taught me seven strategies to attack Wú;
I used three of them and defeated Wú.
The remaining four are with you;
go and try them for me on the former king."
Zhǒng then committed suicide.
Gōujiàn died,
and his son, King Shíyǔ, succeeded him.
King Shíyǔ died,
and his son, King Bùshòu, succeeded him.
King Bùshòu died,
and his son, King Wēng, succeeded him.
King Wēng died,
and his son, King Yì, succeeded him.
King Yì died,
and his son, King Zhīhóu, succeeded him.
King Zhīhóu died,
and his son, King Wúqiáng, succeeded him.
During King Wúqiáng's time,
Yuè raised an army to campaign north against Qí,
west against Chǔ,
contending with the Central States for supremacy.
During the era of King Wēi of Chǔ,
Yuè campaigned north against Qí,
and King Wēi of Qí sent an envoy to persuade the King of Yuè, saying:
"If Yuè does not attack Chǔ,
on a grand scale, you will not achieve kingship,
and on a minor scale, you will not attain hegemony.
I surmise that the reason Yuè refrains from attacking Chǔ
is because it has not gained the support of Jìn.
Hán and Wèi certainly will not attack Chǔ.
If Hán were to attack Chǔ,
and its army were defeated,
its generals killed,
then Yè
and Yǎngzhái would be endangered;
if Wèi, too, saw its army defeated,
its generals killed,
then Chén
and Shàngcài would be unsettled.
Thus, if the two Jìn states serve Yuè,
it would not extend to the point of their armies being defeated and generals slain—
not even the effort of making their horses sweat would be exerted.
What, then, is the importance you place on gaining Jìn's support?"
The King of Yuè replied:
"What we seek from Jìn
does not go so far as having them engage in fierce combat with drawn blades,
let alone besieging cities and towns.
We hope that Wèi will mass its troops beneath Dàliáng,
and that Qí will trial its forces in Nányáng and the land of Jǔ,
concentrating at the borders of Cháng
and Tán,
so that the region beyond Fāngchéng cannot move south,
and the area between Huái and Sì cannot advance east.
Then, the lands of Shāng, Wū,
Xī, Lì,
and Zōnghú,
along the Xià road to the left,
would be insufficient to defend against Qín,
and Jiāngnán
and Sìshàng would be inadequate to confront Yuè.
Thus, Qí,
Qín, Hán,
and Wèi would achieve their ambitions at Chǔ's expense,
and the two Jìn states would divide territory without fighting,
reaping without plowing.
If they do not act thus,
but instead wear down their blades in the mountains and rivers, serving Qí and Qín's purposes,
the strategy they rely on is so misguided—
how can they hope to kingship this way!"
The Qí envoy said:
"It is fortunate that Yuè has not perished!
I do not esteem the use of wisdom that is like the eyes,
which see fine hairs but not their own lashes.
Now, Your Majesty recognizes the miscalculations of Jìn,
but fails to see Yuè's own errors—
this is 'eye-based reasoning.'
What Your Majesty expects from Jìn
is not the exertion of their horses' sweat,
nor is it the possibility of joint forces and alliances;
you await them to divide Chǔ's forces.
But now Chǔ's forces are already divided—
what need is there to wait for Jìn?"
The King of Yuè asked:
"What then should be done?"
The envoy replied:
"Chǔ's three senior officers have deployed nine armies,
surrounding Qūwò to the north
and Wūzhōng,
stretching over 3,700 lǐ to the Wújiǎ Pass.
Jǐng Cuì's army has gathered in the north at Lǔ,
Qí, and Nányáng—
could the division be greater than this?
Moreover, what Your Majesty seeks
is to make Jìn and Chǔ fight;
if Jìn and Chǔ do not fight,
Yuè's troops will not rise—
this is knowing two and five but not ten.
If you do not attack Chǔ now,
I thereby know that Yuè will, on a grand scale, not achieve kingship,
and on a minor scale, not attain hegemony.
Fùchóu,
Páng, and Chángshā
are Chǔ's granaries;
Jìngzélíng
is Chǔ's source of timber.
If Yuè sends troops to penetrate the Wújiǎ Pass,
these four districts will no longer send tribute to Yǐng.
I have heard that
one who aims for kingship but fails to achieve it
may still attain hegemony as a fallback.
However, if one does not achieve even hegemony,
it is due to a failure in the way of kingship.
Thus, I urge Your Majesty to turn and attack Chǔ."
Thereupon, Yuè abandoned Qí and attacked Chǔ.
King Wēi of Chǔ raised an army and attacked them,
soundly defeating Yuè,
killing King Wúqiáng,
and seizing all the former Wú lands up to the Zhèjiāng River,
while also defeating Qí in the north at Xúzhōu.
Thus, Yuè disintegrated,
with various scions contending for the throne,
some becoming kings,
others lords,
dwelling along the coasts of Jiāngnán and the sea,
submitting and paying homage to Chǔ.
Seven generations later,
reaching the lord of Mǐn, Yáo,
he assisted the feudal lords in pacifying Qín.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn again appointed Yáo as King of Yuè,
to continue the Yuè lineage.
Dōngyuè
and Mǐnyuè
are all his descendants.
Fàn Lǐ served King Gōujiàn of Yuè,
enduring hardship and exerting himself fully,
devising deep strategies with Gōujiàn for over twenty years,
ultimately destroying Wú,
avenging the shame of Kuàijī,
crossing troops north over the Huái to press upon Qí
and Jìn, issuing commands to the Central States,
and honoring the Zhōu court,
whereby Gōujiàn achieved hegemony,
and Fàn Lǐ was titled Supreme General.
Upon returning to the state,
Fàn Lǐ believed that under a great reputation,
it is difficult to remain long,
and moreover, that Gōujiàn's character allowed sharing hardships
but not enduring peace,
so he wrote a letter resigning to Gōujiàn, saying:
"I have heard that when the ruler worries, the minister labors;
when the ruler is disgraced, the minister dies.
In the past, my lord suffered disgrace at Kuàijī—
the reason I did not die then
was for this endeavor.
Now that the shame has been avenged,
I request to follow through with the execution due at Kuàijī."
Gōujiàn said:
"I will share the state with you and rule it together.
If not,
I will have you executed."
Fàn Lǐ said:
"The ruler issues commands,
the minister follows his will."
Thereupon, he packed his light treasures, pearls, and jades,
and with his private followers, sailed away by sea,
never to return.
Thus, Gōujiàn designated Kuàijī Mountain as Fàn Lǐ's fief.
Fàn Lǐ sailed across the sea to Qí,
changed his name,
and called himself Chīyí Zǐpí.
He farmed by the seaside,
toiling diligently with his own hands,
working with his sons to manage their livelihood.
Before long,
they had accumulated wealth amounting to hundreds of thousands.
The people of Qí heard of his wisdom,
and made him chancellor.
Fàn Lǐ sighed deeply and said:
"As a commoner, I have amassed a fortune of a thousand gold pieces;
as an official, I have reached the rank of chancellor.
