This is the pinnacle for a man of humble origins.
To long enjoy such honor and fame
is inauspicious."
So he returned the seal of office,
distributed all his wealth,
giving it to close friends and fellow villagers,
and carrying only his most valuable treasures,
he left quietly
and settled in Táo.
He believed this to be the center of the world,
where trade routes for goods converged,
and one could make a living and become wealthy.
Thus, he called himself Táo Zhū Gōng.
Again, he and his sons engaged in farming and animal husbandry,
storing and selling goods,
waiting for the right time to trade,
seeking profits of ten percent.
Not long after,
he amassed assets worth millions.
The world acclaimed him as Táo Zhū Gōng.
Zhū Gōng lived in Táo,
where his youngest son was born.
When the youngest son came of age,
Zhū Gōng's middle son killed someone
and was imprisoned in Chǔ.
Zhū Gōng said:
"To die for murder
is the due penalty.
However, I have heard that the son of a wealthy man does not die in the marketplace."
He instructed his youngest son to go and see to the matter.
So he packed a thousand yì of gold,
placed it in a coarse container,
and loaded it onto an ox cart.
As he was about to send his youngest son,
Zhū Gōng's eldest son insisted on going,
but Zhū Gōng refused.
The eldest son said:
"The eldest son of a family is its steward.
Now that my younger brother has committed a crime,
if you, Father, do not send me,
but instead send my youngest brother,
it means I am unworthy."
He threatened to take his own life.
His mother pleaded on his behalf:
"If we send the youngest son now,
it may not save the middle son,
and we would first lose the eldest son for no reason.
What then?"
Zhū Gōng had no choice but to send the eldest son,
giving him a letter to deliver to his old friend Zhuāng Shēng.
He said:
"When you arrive, present the thousand gold to Zhuāng Shēng,
and follow his instructions.
Be careful not to dispute his actions."
The eldest son set out,
also taking several hundred gold pieces of his own.
Upon reaching Chǔ,
he found Zhuāng Shēng's home outside the city walls,
overgrown with weeds up to the door,
a place of great poverty.
Nevertheless, the eldest son delivered the letter and presented the thousand gold,
as his father had instructed.
Zhuāng Shēng said:
"You should leave quickly now,
and be sure not to stay!
Once your brother is released,
do not ask how it happened."
After the eldest son left,
he did not bid farewell to Zhuāng Shēng but stayed privately,
using his own gold to bribe influential nobles in Chǔ.
Although Zhuāng Shēng lived in poverty,
he was known throughout the country for his integrity and honesty,
and everyone from the King of Chǔ down revered him as a teacher.
When Zhū Gōng sent the gold,
Zhuāng Shēng had no intention of keeping it,
but planned to return it after the matter was resolved, as a mark of trust.
So when the gold arrived,
he said to his wife:
"This is Zhū Gōng's gold.
If I should fall ill and die unexpectedly,
be sure to return it later;
do not touch it."
But Zhū Gōng's eldest son did not understand his intent,
thinking he had no particular plan.
Zhuāng Shēng found an opportunity to see the King of Chǔ,
and said:
"A certain star is in a certain position,
which is harmful to Chǔ."
The King of Chǔ, who trusted Zhuāng Shēng deeply,
said:
"What should be done now?"
Zhuāng Shēng replied:
"Only through virtuous acts can it be averted."
The King of Chǔ said:
"You may rest, sir,
I will carry it out."
The king then ordered his officials to seal the treasury.
The Chǔ nobles were surprised and informed Zhū Gōng's eldest son:
"The king is about to issue a pardon."
He asked:
"How do you know?"
They replied:
"Whenever the king is to pardon,
he always seals the treasury.
Last evening, the king sent men to seal it."
The eldest son thought that with the pardon,
his brother would surely be released,
and it would be a waste to leave the thousand gold with Zhuāng Shēng for nothing,
so he went to see Zhuāng Shēng again.
Zhuāng Shēng was startled and said:
"Why have you not left?"
The eldest son replied:
"Not yet.
Initially, I came for my brother's sake;
now that he is about to be pardoned,
I came to bid you farewell."
Zhuāng Shēng understood that he wanted the gold back,
and said:
"You may go inside and take the gold yourself."
The eldest son went in, took the gold, and left,
feeling pleased with himself.
Zhuāng Shēng felt humiliated at being tricked by the young man,
so he went to see the King of Chǔ and said:
"I previously spoke of the star's matter,
and you, sire, said you would cultivate virtue in response.
Now, after I left,
the streets are abuzz with talk that the son of the wealthy Zhū Gōng from Táo killed someone and is imprisoned in Chǔ,
and his family has bribed your attendants with large sums of gold.
Thus, your pardon is not out of concern for Chǔ,
but because of Zhū Gōng's son."
The King of Chǔ was enraged and said:
"Though I may lack virtue,
how could I show favor because of Zhū Gōng's son!"
He ordered the execution of Zhū Gōng's son,
and the following day issued the pardon.
The eldest son ultimately brought his brother's body home.
Upon arrival,
his mother and the townspeople all mourned deeply,
but Zhū Gōng alone laughed,
saying:
"I knew all along that he would get his brother killed!
It is not that he did not love his brother,
but that he could not bear to part with wealth.
He grew up with me in hardship,
witnessing struggle,
and knowing how hard it is to make a living,
so he values wealth too much.
As for the youngest son,
he was born into wealth,
riding fine carriages and chasing hares,
never knowing where wealth comes from,
so he parts with it lightly,
without regret.
That is why I originally wanted to send the youngest son—
precisely because he could let go of wealth.
But the elder son could not,
and thus ended up causing his brother's death.
Such is the way of things,
and there is no need for sorrow.
Day and night, I have been expecting the arrival of the body."
Thus, Fàn Lǐ moved three times,
and achieved fame throughout the world.
He did not leave places without reason;
wherever he settled, he became renowned.
He eventually grew old and died in Táo,
hence the world remembers him as Táo Zhū Gōng.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Great indeed were the achievements of Yǔ,
who channeled the nine rivers,
stabilized the nine provinces,
so that to this day the various Xia regions remain peaceful.
As for his descendant Gōu Jiàn,
he toiled his body and tormented his thoughts,
ultimately destroying the powerful Wú.
He marched north to display his military might in the Central States,
honoring the Zhōu royal house,
and was acclaimed as a Hegemon King.
Can Gōu Jiàn not be called worthy!
Truly, he inherited Yǔ's lingering legacy.
Fàn Lǐ relocated three times, each time with honor and renown,
his name enduring through later generations.
When ministers and rulers are like this,
how could they not achieve illustriousness!
Duke Huán of Zhèng, Yǒu,
was the youngest son of King Lì of Zhōu and the half-brother of King Xuān.
In the twenty-second year of King Xuān's reign,
Yǒu was first enfeoffed in Zhèng.
After thirty-three years of rule,
the common people all found him convenient and loved him.
King Yōu appointed him as Minister over the Masses.
He harmonized and gathered the Zhōu people,
and the Zhōu people were all pleased.
Between the Yellow River and the Luò River,
people cherished his memory.
After serving as Minister over the Masses for one year,
due to King Yōu's favor for Queen Bāo,
the royal house's governance became increasingly corrupt,
and some feudal lords rebelled against it.
Thereupon, Duke Huán asked Grand Historian Bó:
"The royal house is fraught with troubles;
where can I escape death?"
Grand Historian Bó replied:
"Only the eastern lands of Luò,
south of the Yellow River and Jì River, are habitable."
The Duke said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"The land is near Guó
and Kuài. The rulers of Guó and
Kuài are greedy and fond of profit,
so the people are not attached to them.
Now you serve as Minister over the Masses,
and the people all love you.
If you sincerely request to reside there,
the rulers of Guó and Kuài, seeing you in power,
will readily cede land to you.
If you truly settle there,
the people of Guó and Kuài will all become your people."
The Duke said:
"I wish to go south to the riverbank;
how about that?"
He replied:
"In the past, Zhù Róng served as fire official for Gāoxīn Shì;
his achievements were great,
yet among the Zhōu, none of his descendants rose to prominence—
Chǔ is his descendant.
When Zhōu declines,
Chǔ is sure to rise.
If Chǔ rises, it will not benefit Zhèng."
The Duke said:
"I wish to reside in the west;
how about that?"
He replied:
"The people there are greedy and fond of profit,
making it difficult to reside long."
The Duke said:
"When Zhōu declines,
which states will rise?"
He replied:
"Qí,
Qín, Jìn,
and Chǔ, perhaps?
Now Qí,
of the Jiāng surname,
are descendants of Bó Yí,
who assisted Yáo in regulating ceremonies.
Qín, of the Yíng surname,
are descendants of Bó Yì,
who assisted Shùn in pacifying all creatures.
As for the ancestors of Chǔ,
they all once had achievements under heaven.
After King Wǔ of Zhōu defeated Zhòu,
King Chéng enfeoffed Shū Yú in Táng.
His land is rugged and perilous;
thus, with virtue and the decline of Zhōu concurrent,
they are also sure to rise."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he finally advised the king,
eastward moving his people east of Luò,
and Guó
and Kuài indeed offered ten cities,
eventually establishing a state there.
Two years later,
the Quǎnróng killed King Yōu at the foot of Lí Mountain,
and also killed Duke Huán.
The people of Zhèng jointly established his son Juétū,
who became Duke Wǔ.
In the tenth year of Duke Wǔ,
he married the daughter of the Marquis of Shēn as his wife,
called Wǔ Jiāng.
She bore the crown prince Wùshēng,
whose birth was difficult.
After he was born,
the lady did not love him.
Later, she bore a younger son, Shū Duàn.
Duàn's birth was easy,
and the lady loved him.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Duke Wǔ fell ill.
The lady petitioned the duke,
wishing to establish Duàn as crown prince;
the duke did not listen.
That year,
Duke Wǔ died,
and Wùshēng ascended,
becoming Duke Zhuāng.
In the first year of Duke Zhuāng,
he enfeoffed his brother Duàn at Jīng,
titled Tàishū.
Jì Zhòng said:
"Jīng is larger than the capital;
it is not suitable for enfeoffing a cadet."
Duke Zhuāng said:
"Wǔ Jiāng desires it;
I dare not deny her."
When Duàn arrived at Jīng,
he repaired armor and weapons,
conspiring with his mother Wǔ Jiāng to attack Zhèng.
In the twenty-second year,
Duàn indeed attacked Zhèng,
with Wǔ Jiāng serving as an inside agent.
Duke Zhuāng dispatched troops to attack Duàn;
Duàn fled.
They attacked Jīng;
the people of Jīng rebelled against Duàn,
and Duàn fled to Yān.
Yān fell,
and Duàn fled to Gòng.
Thereupon, Duke Zhuāng exiled his mother Wǔ Jiāng to Chéngyǐng,
swearing an oath:
"Not until the Yellow Springs
shall we meet again."
After over a year,
he regretted it and missed his mother.
Kǎoshū of Yǐnggǔ had a tribute for the duke;
the duke bestowed food upon him.
Kǎoshū said:
"I have a mother;
I beg to give this food Your Majesty bestowed to my mother."
Duke Zhuāng said:
"I miss my mother greatly,
but I detest breaking my oath;
what can I do?"
Kǎoshū said:
"Dig a tunnel down to the Yellow Springs,
and then you can meet."
Thereupon, he followed this advice,
and saw his mother.
In the 24th year,
Duke Mù of Sòng died,
and Prince Féng fled to Zhèng.
Zhèng invaded Zhōu territory,
seizing grain.
In the 25th year,
Zhōu Xū of Wèi assassinated his ruler Duke Huán and proclaimed himself,
joining Sòng in attacking Zhèng,
due to Féng's presence.
In the 27th year,
Zhèng first paid court to King Huān of Zhōu.
The king was angry about the grain seizure,
and did not treat them with proper ceremony.
In the 29th year,
Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng, angered by Zhōu's discourtesy,
exchanged territories with Lǔ - Bēng
and Xǔtián.
In the 33rd year,
Sòng killed Kǒng Fù.
In the 37th year,
Duke Zhuāng stopped attending court at Zhōu,
so King Huān of Zhōu led Chén,
Cài, Guó,
and Wèi to attack Zhèng.
Duke Zhuāng, with Jì Zhòng
and Gāo Qúmí, raised troops for self-defense,
and the royal army was badly defeated.
Zhù Dān shot and hit the king's arm.
Zhù Dān requested to pursue them,
but the Earl of Zhèng stopped him,
saying:
"To offend an elder is already difficult,
how dare we oppress the Son of Heaven?"
So they stopped.
That night, he sent Jì Zhòng to inquire about the king's injury.
In the 38th year,
the Northern Róng attacked Qí,
and Qí sent for help;
Zhèng dispatched Crown Prince Hū with troops to rescue Qí.
Duke Xī of Qí wanted to give him a wife,
but Hū declined, saying:
"We are a small state,
not a match for Qí."
At that time, Jì Zhòng was with him
and urged him to accept,
saying:
"The ruler has many favored consorts,
and without strong support, the crown prince may not be established,
for all three princes could become ruler."
The so-called three princes were
Crown Prince Hū,
his younger brother Tū,
and the next younger brother Wěi.
In the 43rd year,
Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng died.
Earlier, Jì Zhòng had been greatly favored by Duke Zhuāng,
who made him a minister;
the duke had him marry a woman from Dèng,
who bore Crown Prince Hū,
so Jì Zhòng established him,
becoming Duke Zhāo.
Duke Zhuāng also married a woman from the Yōng clan of Sòng,
who bore Duke Lì Tū.
The Yōng clan was favored in Sòng.
When Duke Zhuāng of Sòng heard that Jì Zhòng had established Hū,
he sent someone to lure Jì Zhòng, seized him,
and said:
"If you don't establish Tū,
you will die."
He also seized Tū to demand bribes.
Jì Zhòng agreed with Sòng
and made a covenant with them.
He took Tū back
and established him.
When Duke Zhāo Hū heard that Jì Zhòng, under Sòng's coercion, was establishing his brother Tū,
on the day Dìnghài in September,
Hū fled to Wèi.
On Jìhài,
Tū arrived in Zhèng
and was established as Duke Lì.
In the 4th year of Duke Lì,
Jì Zhòng monopolized state affairs.
Duke Lì was troubled by this
and secretly had his son-in-law Yōng Jiū try to kill Jì Zhòng.
Jiū's wife,
who was Jì Zhòng's daughter,
found out
and asked her mother:
"Who is closer, father or husband?"
Her mother said:
"A father is one only,
but any man can be a husband."
The daughter then informed Jì Zhòng,
who instead killed Yōng Jiū
and displayed his corpse in the market.
Duke Lì could do nothing to Jì Zhòng,
and angrily said of Jiū:
"To consult a woman about such plans,
death was indeed fitting!"
In summer, Duke Lì went to live in the border town of Lì.
Jì Zhòng welcomed Duke Zhāo Hū back,
and on the day Yǐhài in June,
he re-entered Zhèng
and resumed the throne.
In autumn,
Duke Lì Tū of Zhèng, with the help of the people of Lì, killed its senior official Shàn Bó
and then settled there.
When the feudal lords heard of Duke Lì's flight,
they attacked Zhèng
but withdrew without success.
Sòng gave Duke Lì considerable troops,
allowing him to defend himself at Lì,
so Zhèng consequently did not attack Lì.
In the 2nd year of Duke Zhāo,
since the time Duke Zhāo was crown prince,
his father Duke Zhuāng had wanted to make Gāo Qúmí a minister,
but Crown Prince Hū disliked him,
yet Duke Zhuāng did not listen,
and eventually appointed Qúmí as minister.
When Duke Zhāo ascended the throne,
Qúmí feared he would kill him,
so on the day Xīnmǎo in the tenth month, winter,
Qúmí went hunting with Duke Zhāo
and shot and killed him in the wilds.
Jì Zhòng and Qúmí dared not bring Duke Lì back,
so they established Duke Zhāo's younger brother Wěi as ruler,
known as Zǐ Wěi,
with no posthumous title.
In the first year of Zǐ Wěi, in the seventh month,
Duke Xiāng of Qí met with feudal lords at Shǒuzhǐ,
and Zǐ Wěi of Zhèng attended,
with Gāo Qúmí as assistant,
accompanying him, while Jì Zhòng pleaded illness and did not go.
The reason was that
when Duke Xiāng of Qí was still a prince,
he had once fought with Zǐ Wěi,
and they became enemies.
At the meeting of feudal lords,
Jì Zhòng advised Zǐ Wěi not to go.
Zǐ Wěi said:
"Qí is strong,
and Duke Lì is at Lì;
if I don't go,
they will lead the feudal lords to attack us
and restore Duke Lì.
I'd better go;
why must going bring humiliation,
and how could it come to that!"
So he went.
Thus, Jì Zhòng, fearing Qí would kill him too,
pleaded illness.
When Zǐ Wěi arrived,
he did not apologize to the Marquis of Qí,
who became angry
and set up ambushers to kill Zǐ Wěi.
Gāo Qúmí escaped back,
returned and plotted with Jì Zhòng,
summoned Zǐ Wěi's younger brother Prince Yīng from Chén and established him,
known as Zhèngzǐ.
That year,
Duke Xiāng of Qí had Péngshēng get Duke Huán of Lǔ drunk and kill him by pulling him apart.
In the 8th year of Zhèngzǐ,
Guǎn Zhìfǔ and others in Qí rebelled,
assassinating their ruler Duke Xiāng.
In the 12th year,
Cháng Wàn of Sòng assassinated his ruler Duke Mǐn.
Jì Zhòng of Zhèng died.
In the fourteenth year,
the former Zheng exile Duke Li of Zheng, Tū, who was in Lì, sent men to lure and seize the Zheng senior official Fǔ Jiǎ,
demanding in exchange his return to power.
Jiǎ said:
"Spare me,
and I will kill the ruler of Zhèng for you and bring you in."
Duke Li made a covenant with him,
and then released him.
On the day Jiǎzǐ in the sixth month,
Jiǎ killed the ruler of Zhèng and his two sons and welcomed Duke Li Tū,
whereupon Tū returned from Lì and re-entered to assume the throne.
Earlier, an inner snake and an outer snake had fought at the southern gate of Zhèng,
and the inner snake died.
After six years,
Duke Li indeed returned to power.
Upon entering, he reproached his paternal uncle Yuán, saying:
"When I was exiled abroad,
you, uncle, had no intention of restoring me,
which was most extreme."
Yuán said:
"To serve one's lord without duplicity
is the duty of a minister.
Yuán knows his crime."
Thereupon, he committed suicide.
Duke Li then said to Fǔ Jiǎ:
"You, sir, served your lord with duplicity."
He then had him executed.
Jiǎ said:
"Heavy virtue goes unrequited—
how true it is!"
In the first year after Duke Li Tū's return,
Duke Huán of Qí began his hegemony.
In his fifth year,
Yān, Wèi, and King Huì of Zhōu's younger brother Tuí attacked the king,
forcing the king to flee to Wēn,
and they set up his younger brother Tuí as king.
In the sixth year,
King Huì appealed to Zhèng for help,
and Duke Li sent troops to attack the Zhōu prince Tuí,
but was not victorious.
Thereupon, he returned with King Huì of Zhōu,
and the king resided in Lì.
In the spring of the seventh year,
Duke Li of Zhèng and Guó Shū launched a surprise attack, killed Prince Tuí, and restored King Huì to Zhōu.
In the autumn,
Duke Li died,
and his son Duke Wén, Jié, ascended the throne.
Duke Li had initially reigned for four years,
then lived in exile in Lì for
seventeen years,
returned to power,
and reigned for seven more years,
making a total of twenty-eight years including his exile.
In the seventeenth year of Duke Wén,
Duke Huán of Qí used his troops to defeat Cài,
then attacked Chǔ,
reaching Shàolíng.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Duke Wén's low-ranking concubine named Yān Jí
dreamed that Heaven gave her an orchid,
saying:
"I am Bó Tiáo.
I am your ancestor.
Take this as your son,
for the orchid has the fragrance of a state."
She reported the dream to Duke Wén,
who favored her,
and gave her a plant orchid as a token.
She subsequently bore a son,
named Lán.
In the thirty-sixth year,
the Jìn prince Chóng'ěr passed through,
but Duke Wén did not treat him with courtesy.
Duke Wén's younger brother Shū Zhān said:
"Chóng'ěr is worthy,
and moreover shares our surname;
he is in distress and passing by your domain—
you cannot be discourteous."
Duke Wén said:
"Many exiled princes of states have passed through;
how can I treat them all with full courtesy!"
Zhān said:
"If you, my lord, will not treat him courteously,
then kill him;
if you do not kill him,
and he returns to his state,
he will become a worry for Zhèng."
Duke Wén did not listen.
In the spring of the thirty-seventh year,
the Jìn prince Chóng'ěr returned to his state,
and ascended the throne, becoming Duke Wén of Jìn.
In autumn, Zhèng entered Huá,
and Huá submitted,
but soon after allied with Wèi instead,
whereupon Zhèng attacked Huá.
King Xiāng of Zhōu sent Bó Fèi to plead for Huá.
Duke Wén of Zhèng resented that King Huì had been in exile in Lì,
and though Duke Wén's father, Duke Li, had restored him,
King Huì had not conferred titles and emoluments upon Duke Li.
He also resented King Xiāng for siding with Wèi and Huá,
so he did not heed King Xiāng's plea and imprisoned Bó Fèi.
The king was angered,
and together with the Dí people attacked Zhèng,
but was not victorious.
In winter, the Dí attacked King Xiāng,
who fled to Zhèng,
and Duke Wén of Zhèng settled the king at Fàn.
In the thirty-eighth year,
Duke Wén of Jìn restored King Xiāng to Chéngzhōu.
In the forty-first year,
Zhèng assisted Chǔ in attacking Jìn.
Because Duke Wén of Jìn had been treated discourteously when he passed through,
they turned against Jìn and aided Chǔ.
In the forty-third year,
Duke Wén of Jìn and Duke Mù of Qín jointly besieged Zhèng,
to punish it for aiding Chǔ in attacking Jìn,
and for the discourtesy shown when Duke Wén passed through.
Earlier, Duke Wén of Zhèng had three principal wives,
and five favored sons,
all of whom died early due to offenses.
The duke was angry,
and summarily banished all his sons.
Zǐ Lán fled to Jìn,
and followed Duke Wén of Jìn in besieging Zhèng.
At that time, Lán served Duke Wén of Jìn very diligently,
who favored and loved him,
so he privately contacted Jìn,
seeking to enter Zhèng as heir apparent.
Jìn then wanted to capture Shū Zhān to execute him.
Duke Wén of Zhèng was afraid,
and dared not speak to Shū Zhān about it.
When Zhān heard,
he said to the ruler of Zhèng:
"I advised you, my lord,
but you did not listen to me,
so Jìn has finally become a threat.
Yet the reason Jìn besieges Zhèng
is because of Zhān;
if my death can spare Zhèng,
it is Zhān's wish."
He then committed suicide.
The people of Zhèng delivered Zhān's corpse to Jìn.
Duke Wén of Jìn said:
"I must see the ruler of Zhèng once,
to humiliate him before leaving."
The people of Zhèng were troubled by this,
so they sent someone to privately tell Qín:
"Destroying Zhèng would only benefit Jìn,
which is not to Qín's advantage."
The Qín troops then withdrew.
Duke Wén of Jìn wanted to install Lán as heir apparent,
and informed Zhèng of this.
The Zhèng senior official Shí Guǐ said:
"I have heard that the Jí surname descended from the principal consort of Hòu Jì,
and their descendants are destined to rise.
Zǐ Lán's mother
is among their descendants.
Moreover, all the sons of your principal wives have died,
and among the remaining sons, none is as worthy as Lán.
Now that the siege is critical,
and Jìn is making the request,
what greater advantage could there be!"
They then agreed to Jìn's terms,
concluded a covenant,
and finally established Zǐ Lán as heir apparent,
whereupon the Jìn troops withdrew.
In the forty-fifth year,
Duke Wén died,
and his son Lán ascended the throne,
becoming Duke Mù of Zhèng.
In the spring of the first year of Duke Mù,
Duke Mù of Qín sent three generals with troops intending to launch a surprise attack on Zhèng.
When they reached Huá,
they encountered a Zhèng merchant Xián Gāo, who deceptively presented twelve oxen to慰劳 the army,
so the Qín troops turned back without reaching Zhèng,
and were defeated by Jìn at Xiáo.
Earlier, in the year Duke Wén of Zhèng died,
the Zhèng minister of works Zēng Hè had sold Zhèng's secrets to them,
which was why the Qín troops came.
In the third year,
Zhèng sent troops to follow Jìn in attacking Qín,
and defeated the Qín troops at Wāng.
In previous years, Crown Prince Shāngchén of Chǔ murdered his father King Chéng and succeeded him.
In the twenty-first year,
he joined Huà Yuán of Sòng in attacking Zhèng.
Huà Yuán slaughtered sheep to feed his soldiers,
but did not give any to his chariot driver Yáng Zhēn,
who angrily drove straight to Zhèng,
where Zhèng imprisoned Huà Yuán.
Sòng ransomed Huà Yuán,
who then also fled.
Jìn sent Zhào Chuān with troops to attack Zhèng.
In the twenty-second year,
Duke Mù of Zhèng died,
and his son Yí succeeded him,
becoming Duke Líng.
In the spring of Duke Líng's first year,
Chǔ presented a giant softshell turtle to Duke Líng.
Zǐjiā and
Zǐgōng were about to attend court when
Zǐgōng's index finger twitched,
and he said to Zǐjiā:
"On other days when my finger twitched,
I was sure to eat unusual food."
When they entered,
they saw Duke Líng serving turtle soup,
Zǐgōng laughed and said:
"Indeed!"
Duke Líng asked why he was laughing,
and he fully informed Duke Líng.
Duke Líng summoned them,
but deliberately did not give Zǐgōng any soup.
Zǐgōng was angry,
dipped his finger in it,
tasted it, and left.
The Duke was angry,
and wanted to kill Zǐgōng.
Zǐgōng and Zǐjiā plotted to act first.
In summer, they assassinated Duke Líng.
The people of Zhèng wanted to install Duke Líng's younger brother Qùjí,
but Qùjí declined, saying:
"If it must be by virtue,
then Qùjí is unworthy;
if by seniority,
then Prince Jiān is the eldest."
Jiān was
Duke Líng's half-brother,
and older than Qùjí.
Thus they installed Zǐ Jiān,
who became Duke Xiāng.
When Duke Xiāng was installed,
he intended to eliminate all of the Mù clan.
The Mù clan were
the family of the assassins of Duke Líng,
Zǐgōng's lineage.
Qùjí said:
"If the Mù clan must be removed,
I will leave with them."
So he stopped.
All were made senior officials.
In the first year of Duke Xiāng,
Chǔ was angered that Zhèng had accepted Sòng's bribe and released Huà Yuán,
and attacked Zhèng.
Zhèng turned against Chǔ,
and allied with Jìn.
In the fifth year,
Chǔ again attacked Zhèng,
and Jìn came to rescue them.
In the sixth year,
Zǐjiā died,
and the people again expelled his clan,
because of their assassination of Duke Líng.
In the seventh year,
Zhèng formed an alliance with Jìn at Yānlíng.
In the eighth year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ, because Zhèng had allied with Jìn,
came to attack,
besieging Zhèng for three months,
until Zhèng surrendered the city to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ entered through the Huáng Gate,
and Duke Xiāng of Zhèng, baring his upper body and leading a sheep, came to meet him,
saying:
"I have failed in governing the border regions,
causing Your Majesty's anger to fall upon my humble city,
which is my crime.
I dare not but obey your command.
If Your Majesty relocates me south of the River,
or gives me to the feudal lords,
I will also obey your command.
But if Your Majesty does not forget King Lì,
King Xuān,
Duke Huán, and Duke Wǔ,
and in compassion cannot bear to end their line of sacrifice,
granting me barren land,
allowing me again to serve Your Majesty,
that would be my wish,
though I dare not hope for it.
I dare to bare my heart,
and will obey your command."
King Zhuāng withdrew thirty lǐ and then encamped.
The ministers of Chǔ said:
"From Yǐng to here,
the officers and men have long toiled.
Now that we have gained the state, why abandon it?"
King Zhuāng said:
"The reason for attacking
is to subdue the disobedient.
Now they have submitted,
what more is there to seek?"
He finally departed.
Jìn heard that Chǔ was attacking Zhèng,
and sent troops to rescue Zhèng.
They came hesitating between two courses,
so were delayed,
and by the time they reached the River,
the Chǔ troops had already left.
The Jìn generals, some wanted to cross,
some wanted to return,
but eventually crossed the River.
King Zhuāng heard of this,
turned back and attacked Jìn.
Zhèng instead aided Chǔ,
and greatly defeated the Jìn army by the River.
In the tenth year,
Jìn came to attack Zhèng,
because they had turned against Jìn and allied with Chǔ.
In the eleventh year,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ attacked Sòng,
and Sòng reported the emergency to Jìn.
Duke Jǐng of Jìn wanted to send troops to rescue Sòng,
but Bó Zōng advised the Jìn ruler, saying:
"Heaven is now favoring Chǔ,
they cannot be attacked."
So they sought a brave man and found Xiè Yáng from Huò,
courtesy name Zǐhǔ,
to deceive Chǔ,
and order Sòng not to surrender.
Passing through Zhèng,
which was allied with Chǔ,
they seized Xiè Yáng and presented him to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ richly rewarded him and made an agreement,
making him reverse his message,
ordering Sòng to hasten surrender,
and after three demands, he agreed.
Then Chǔ had Xiè Yáng ascend a mobile watchtower,
ordering him to call out to Sòng.
But he broke the Chǔ agreement and conveyed his Jìn ruler's command, saying:
"Jìn is mobilizing all its troops to rescue Sòng,
though Sòng is in dire straits,
be careful not to surrender to Chǔ,
the Jìn troops are now arriving!"
King Zhuāng of Chǔ was greatly angered,
and intended to kill him.
Xiè Yáng said:
"A ruler who can issue commands acts righteously,
a minister who can receive commands acts faithfully.
I received my ruler's command to go out,
and would rather die than fail."
King Zhuāng said:
"You promised me,
then betrayed it,
where is the faithfulness?"
Xiè Yáng said:
"The reason I promised the King
was to accomplish my ruler's command."
About to die,
he turned and said to the Chǔ army:
"Let no minister forget to be loyal unto death!"
The King of Chǔ's younger brothers all advised the King to pardon him,
so he pardoned Xiè Yáng and sent him back.
Jìn ennobled him as a high minister.
In the eighteenth year,
Duke Xiāng died,
and his son Duke Dào Fèi succeeded him.
In the first year of Duke Dào,
the Duke of Xǔ spoke ill of Zhèng to Chǔ,
so Duke Dào sent his brother Gǔn to Chǔ to plead his case.
The plea was unsuccessful,
and Chǔ imprisoned Gǔn.
Then Duke Dào of Zhèng came to make peace with Jìn,
and thus allied.
Gǔn privately befriended Zǐ Fǎn of Chǔ,
and Zǐ Fǎn spoke to return Gǔn to Zhèng.
In the second year,
Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and Jìn troops came to rescue.
That year,
Duke Dào died,
and his brother Gǔn was installed,
becoming Duke Chéng.
In the third year of Duke Cheng's reign,
King Gòng of Chǔ said,
"I have shown kindness to Duke Chéng of Zhèng,"
and sent an envoy to form an alliance.
Duke Chéng secretly made a pact with him.
In autumn, when Duke Chéng paid homage to Jìn,
Jìn declared,
"Zhèng has privately made peace with Chǔ,"
and detained him.
They sent Luán Shū to attack Zhèng.
In the spring of the fourth year,
Zhèng, troubled by Jìn's siege,
had the nobleman Rú establish Duke Chéng's elder half-brother Xū as ruler.
That April,
when Jìn heard that Zhèng had installed a new ruler,
they released Duke Chéng.
When the people of Zhèng heard of Duke Chéng's return,
they killed ruler Xū
and welcomed back Duke Chéng.
The Jìn troops then withdrew.
In the tenth year,
Zhèng broke its alliance with Jìn
and allied with Chǔ.
Duke Lì of Jìn was angered,
sent troops to attack Zhèng.
King Gòng of Chǔ came to Zhèng's rescue.
Jìn and Chǔ battled at Yānlíng,
where Chǔ forces were defeated,
and Jìn archers injured King Gòng of Chǔ in the eye,
after which both sides withdrew.
In the thirteenth year,
Duke Dào of Jìn attacked Zhèng,
stationing troops along the Wěi River.
Zhèng fortified its defenses,
and Jìn again withdrew.
In the fourteenth year,
Duke Chéng died,
and his son Yùn succeeded him.
He was known as Duke Xī.
In the fifth year of Duke Xī's reign,
Zhèng's minister Zǐ Sì paid court to Duke Xī,
but the duke treated him disrespectfully.
Enraged, Zǐ Sì
had a cook poison Duke Xī to death,
announcing to the other states,
"Duke Xī died of a sudden illness."
He installed Duke Xī's son Jiā,
who was then five years old,
as Duke Jiǎn.
In the first year of Duke Jiǎn's reign,
the various nobles plotted to kill minister Zǐ Sì,
but Zǐ Sì discovered their plan
and instead had them all executed.
In the second year,
Jìn attacked Zhèng,
Zhèng formed an alliance with them,
and Jìn withdrew.
In winter, Zhèng also allied with Chǔ.
Zǐ Sì, fearing execution,
thus maintained close ties with both Jìn
and Chǔ. In the third year,
minister Zǐ Sì sought to make himself ruler,
but the noble Zǐ Kǒng had the officer Wèi Zhì kill minister Zǐ Sì and replace him.
Zǐ Kǒng then also desired to become ruler himself.
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"Zǐ Sì did what was wrong,
so he was executed;
now if you imitate him,
chaos will never cease."
Thereupon, Zǐ Kǒng heeded this and served as minister to Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng.
In the fourth year,
Jìn, angered that Zhèng had allied with Chǔ,
attacked Zhèng,
and Zhèng made a pact with them.
King Gòng of Chǔ came to Zhèng's aid,
defeating the Jìn army.
Duke Jiǎn wished to make peace with Jìn,
but Chǔ then detained a Zhèng envoy.
In the twelfth year,
Duke Jiǎn, angered by minister Zǐ Kǒng's monopolization of state power,
had him executed
and appointed Zǐ Chǎn as a high minister.
In the nineteenth year,
Duke Jiǎn went to Jìn to petition for the return of the ruler of Wèi
and enfeoffed Zǐ Chǎn with six cities.
Zǐ Chǎn declined,
accepting only three.
In the twenty-second year,
Wú sent Jìzǐ of Yánlíng to Zhèng,
who upon meeting Zǐ Chǎn treated him like an old friend,
saying to him:
"Those in power in Zhèng are extravagant,
trouble is approaching,
and governance will soon fall to you.
When you administer the state,
you must do so with ritual propriety;
otherwise,
Zhèng will collapse."
Zǐ Chǎn treated Jìzǐ with great hospitality.
In the twenty-third year,
the nobles contended for favor and killed each other,
and also sought to kill Zǐ Chǎn.
One noble admonished:
"Zǐ Chǎn is a man of benevolence;
he is the reason Zhèng survives;
do not kill him!"
So they desisted.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Zhèng sent Zǐ Chǎn to Jìn
to inquire about Duke Píng's illness.
Duke Píng said:
"Divination indicates that Shí Chén
and Tái Tái are causing this affliction,
but our historians know nothing of them;
may I ask about them?"
Zǐ Chǎn replied:
"Gāoxīnshì had two sons,
the elder named È Bó,
the younger named Shí Chén,
who lived in Kuànglín
and could not get along,
daily taking up arms to attack each other.
The later emperor, disapproving,
moved È Bó to Shāngqiū,
to preside over Chén,
and the Shāng people followed him,
hence Chén became the Shāng star.
He moved Shí Chén to Dàxià,
to preside over Shēn,
and the Táng people followed him,
serving the Xià
and Shāng dynasties; their last descendant was called Shū Yú of Táng.
When King Wǔ's consort Yì Jiāng was pregnant with the Grand Mentor,
she dreamed the emperor told her:
'I name your son Yú,
and give him Táng,
entrusting him with Shēn to prosper his descendants.'
When he was born, the character
'Yú' was on his palm,
so he was named accordingly.
When King Chéng destroyed Táng, he enfeoffed the Grand Mentor there.
Thus Shēn is the star of Jìn.
From this we see,
then Shí Chén
is the spirit of Shēn.
Formerly, Jīntiānshì had a descendant named Mèi,
who was master of Xuánmíng,
and fathered Yǔn Gé
and Tái Tái.
Tái Tái succeeded to his office,
dredged the Fén
and Táo Rivers, dammed the great marsh,
and settled Tàiyuán.
The emperor commended him,
enfeoffing him along the Fén River.
Shěn, Sì,
Rù, and Huáng indeed maintained his sacrifices.
Now Jìn dominates the Fén River region yet has extinguished them.
From this we see,
then Tái Tái
is the spirit of the Fén and Táo Rivers.
However, these two cannot harm your person.
For spirits of mountains and rivers,
one offers sacrifices during floods or droughts;
for spirits of sun, moon, and stars,
one offers sacrifices during untimely snow, frost, wind, or rain;
but your illness
stems from diet, grief, joy, or women."
Duke Píng and Shū Xiàng said:
"Excellent,
you are a gentleman of vast learning!"
They treated Zǐ Chǎn with great courtesy.
In the summer of the twenty-seventh year,
Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng paid homage to Jìn.
In winter, fearing the strength of King Líng of Chǔ,
he also paid homage to Chǔ,
with Zǐ Chǎn accompanying him.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the ruler of Zhèng fell ill,
so he sent Zǐ Chǎn to meet with the nobles,
allied with King Líng of Chǔ at Shēn,
and executed Qìng Fēng of Qí.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Duke Jiǎn died,
and his son Níng, Duke Dìng, succeeded him.
In autumn, Duke Dìng paid homage to Duke Zhāo of Jìn.
In the first year of Duke Dìng's reign,
Prince Qìjí of Chǔ assassinated his sovereign King Líng and established himself,
becoming King Píng.
Wishing to practice virtue among the feudal lords,
he returned the territory of Zhèng that King Líng had seized back to Zhèng.
In the fourth year,
Duke Zhāo of Jìn died,
and the six ministers of Jìn grew powerful,
while the ducal house declined.
Zǐchǎn said to Hán Xuānzǐ:
"Governing must be based on virtue,
do not forget the foundation of your establishment."
In the sixth year,
a fire broke out in Zhèng,
and the duke wanted to perform an exorcism.
Zǐchǎn said:
"It would be better to cultivate virtue."
In the eighth year,
Crown Prince Jiàn of Chǔ fled to Zhèng.
In the tenth year,
Crown Prince Jiàn conspired with Jìn to attack Zhèng.
Zhèng killed Jiàn,
and Jiàn's son Shèng fled to Wú.
In the eleventh year,
Duke Dìng went to Jìn.
Jìn and Zhèng conspired,
to eliminate the rebellious ministers of Zhōu,
and restore King Jìng to the Zhōu court.
In the thirteenth year,
Duke Dìng died,
and his son Duke Xiàn, named Chài, succeeded him.
Duke Xiàn died in the thirteenth year of his reign,
and his son Duke Shēng, named Shèng, succeeded him.
At this time,
the six ministers of Jìn were powerful,
and they invaded and seized territory from Zhèng,
so Zhèng became weak.
In the fifth year of Duke Shēng's reign,
Zǐchǎn, the chancellor of Zhèng, died,
and all the people of Zhèng wept,
mourning him as if they had lost a relative.
Zǐchǎn
was the youngest son of Duke Chéng of Zhèng.
He was benevolent and loved others,
and served his sovereign with loyalty and sincerity.
Confucius once passed through Zhèng,
and treated Zǐchǎn as if they were brothers.
When he heard of Zǐchǎn's death,
Confucius wept for him, saying:
"He was the legacy of ancient love!"
In the eighth year,
the Fàn and
Zhōngháng clans of Jìn rebelled against Jìn,
and appealed to Zhèng for help,
so Zhèng came to their aid.
Jìn attacked Zhèng,
and defeated the Zhèng army at Tiě.
In the fourteenth year,
Duke Jǐng of Sòng destroyed Cáo.
In the twentieth year,
Tián Cháng of Qí assassinated his sovereign Duke Jiǎn,
and Cháng became chancellor of Qí.
In the twenty-second year,
King Huì of Chǔ destroyed Chén.
Confucius died.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Zhì Bó of Jìn attacked Zhèng,
and captured nine cities.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Duke Shēng died,
and his son Duke Āi, named Yì, succeeded him.
In the eighth year of Duke Āi's reign,
the people of Zhèng assassinated Duke Āi and established Duke Shēng's younger brother Chǒu,
who became Duke Gòng.
In the third year of Duke Gòng's reign,
the three Jìn families destroyed Zhì Bó.
In the thirty-first year,
Duke Gòng died,
and his son Duke Yōu, named Jǐ, succeeded him.
In the first year of Duke Yōu's reign,
Hán Wǔzǐ attacked Zhèng,
and killed Duke Yōu.
The people of Zhèng established Duke Yōu's younger brother Tái,
who became Duke Xū.
In the fifteenth year of Duke Xū's reign,
Hán Jǐnghóu attacked Zhèng,
and captured Yōngqiū.
Zhèng fortified its capital Jīng.
In the sixteenth year,
Zhèng attacked Hán,
and defeated the Hán army at Fùshǔ.
In the twentieth year,
Hán, Zhào,
and Wèi were ranked among the feudal lords.
In the twenty-third year,
Zhèng besieged Yángzhái of Hán.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the ruler of Zhèng killed his chancellor Zǐyáng.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the faction of Zǐyáng together assassinated Duke Xū Tái and established Duke Yōu's younger brother Yǐ as ruler,
who became the ruler of Zhèng.
Two years after the ruler of Zhèng Yǐ was established,
Fùshǔ of Zhèng rebelled,
and returned to Hán.
In the eleventh year,
Hán attacked Zhèng,
and captured Yángchéng.
In the twenty-first year,
Hán Āihóu destroyed Zhèng,
and annexed its state.
The Grand Historian remarks:
There is a saying,
"Those who unite for power and profit,
when power and profit are exhausted, their relationship becomes distant,"
and Fǔxiá is an example of this.
Although Fǔxiá, by coercion and murder, brought Duke Lì into Zhèng,
Duke Lì ultimately betrayed and killed him,
how is this different from Lǐkè of Jìn?
Those who uphold integrity, like Xún Xī,
died but could not preserve Xīqí.
The origins of change,
are also due to many causes!
The ancestors of the Zhào clan
shared a common ancestry with Qín.
Down to Zhòngyǎn,
he served as charioteer for Emperor Tàiwù.
Later, his descendant Fēilián had two sons,
and he named one of them Èlái,
who served Zhòu,
and was killed by Zhōu,
his descendants became Qín.
Èlái's younger brother was named Jìshèng,
and his descendants became Zhào.
Jìshèng bore Mèng Zēng.
Mèng Zēng was favored by King Chéng of Zhōu,
and was known as Zhái Gāoláng.
Gāoláng bore Héngfù,
and Héngfù bore Zàofù.
Zàofù was favored by King Mù of Zhōu.
Zàofù selected a team of fine horses,
including Táolín's Dàolí,
Huáliú,
and Lǜ'ěr,
and presented them to King Mù.
King Mù had Zàofù drive his chariot,
and went on an inspection tour to the west,
where he met the Queen Mother of the West,
and enjoyed himself so much he forgot to return.
Then Xú Yǎnwáng rebelled,
and King Mù rode a thousand miles a day on swift horses,
attacked Xú Yǎnwáng,
and defeated him utterly.
Then he bestowed upon Zàofù the city of Zhào,
and from then on they became the Zhào clan.
From Zàofù down, six generations later, they reached Yǎnfù,
also known as Gōngzhòng,
who, during the reign of King Xuān of Zhōu, campaigned against the Róng,
serving as charioteer.
At the Battle of Qiānmǔ,
Yǎnfù rescued King Xuān.
Yǎnfù bore Shūdài.
During Shūdài's time,
King Yōu of Zhōu was unprincipled,
so he left Zhōu for Jìn,
and served Duke Wén of Jìn,
thus establishing the Zhào clan in the state of Jìn.
From Shūdài onward,
the Zhào lineage prospered even more,
and after five generations, they reached Zhào Sù.
Zhào Sù,
in the sixteenth year of Jìn Xiàngōng's reign, attacked Huò,
Wèi, and Gěng,
with Zhào Sù serving as general to attack Huò.
The Duke of Huò fled to Qí.
Jìn suffered a great drought,
and divination was performed,
revealing
"Huòtài Shān is the cause of the calamity."
Zhào Sù was sent to summon the lord of Huò from Qí,
restoring him,
to resume sacrifices to Huòtài Shān,
and Jìn's harvests recovered.
Jìn Xiàngōng granted Zhào Sù the territory of Gěng.
Sù begot Gòng Mèng,
in the first year of Lǔ Mǐngōng's reign.
Gòng Mèng begot Zhào Cuī,
styled Zǐyú.
Zhào Cuī divined serving under Jìn Xiàngōng and various princes,
none proving auspicious;
divining service under Prince Chóng'ěr,
it was auspicious, so he served Chóng'ěr.
Chóng'ěr, due to Lí Jī's rebellion, fled to Dí,
and Zhào Cuī followed.
Dí attacked Qiánggāorú,
capturing two women,
Dí gave the younger to Chóng'ěr as wife,
and the elder to Zhào Cuī, who bore Zhào Dùn.
Earlier, when Chóng'ěr was in Jìn,
Zhào Cuī's wife had also borne Zhào Tóng,
Zhào Kuò,
and Zhào Yīngqí.
Zhào Cuī followed Chóng'ěr in exile,
for nineteen years in total,
until they could return to the state.
Chóng'ěr became Jìn Wéngōng,
Zhào Cuī was made lord of Yuán,
resided in Yuán,
and administered state affairs.
Wéngōng's return and rise to hegemony
relied heavily on Zhào Cuī's strategies.
Details are recorded in Jìn's affairs.
After Zhào Cuī returned to Jìn,
his Jìn wife insisted on welcoming his Dí wife,
and made her son Dùn the heir,
with the three sons of the Jìn wife serving him as subordinates.
In the sixth year of Jìn Xiānggōng's reign,
Zhào Cuī died,
posthumously titled Chéng Jì.
Zhào Dùn succeeded Chéng Jì in administering state affairs, and two years later, Jìn Xiānggōng died,
leaving the crown prince Yí Gāo too young.
Dùn, concerned for the state's troubles,
wished to install Xiānggōng's younger brother Yōng.
Yōng was then in Qín,
and envoys were sent to bring him back.
The crown prince's mother wept day and night,
kowtowing to Zhào Dùn, saying:
"What crime did the late ruler commit,
that you abandon his rightful son and seek another lord?"
Zhào Dùn grew troubled,
fearing her clan and the ministers would attack him,
so he installed the crown prince,
who became Línggōng,
and sent troops to block those bringing Xiānggōng's brother from Qín.
Once Línggōng was established,
Zhào Dùn further consolidated control of state affairs.
After fourteen years of rule,
Línggōng grew increasingly arrogant.
Zhào Dùn repeatedly admonished him,
but Línggōng would not listen.
Once, while eating bear paw,
it was undercooked,
and he killed the cook,
carrying the body out,
which Zhào Dùn witnessed.
Línggōng, fearing because of this,
sought to kill Dùn.
Dùn, known for his benevolence,
was saved by a starving man he had once fed under a mulberry tree, who defended him,
allowing Dùn to escape.
Before he left the border,
Zhào Chuān assassinated Línggōng and installed Xiānggōng's younger brother Hēitún,
who became Chénggōng.
Zhào Dùn returned,
resuming administration of state affairs.
The gentlemen criticized Dùn
"as chief minister,
he did not leave the state in exile,
nor did he punish the assassin upon return,"
so the grand historian recorded
"Zhào Dùn assassinated his ruler."
During Jìn Jǐnggōng's reign, Zhào Dùn died,
posthumously titled Xuān Mèng,
and his son Shuò succeeded him.
Zhào Shuò,
in the third year of Jìn Jǐnggōng's reign,
commanded Jìn's lower army to rescue Zhèng,
battling King Zhuāng of Chǔ by the river.
Shuò married the sister of Jìn Chénggōng as his wife.
In the third year of Jìn Jǐnggōng's reign,
the minister Tú Àn Gǔ sought to destroy the Zhào clan.
Earlier, when Zhào Dùn was alive,
he dreamed of Shū Dài holding his waist and weeping,
very sorrowfully;
then laughing,
clapping and singing.
Dùn divined it,
the omen breaking off then turning favorable.
Zhào's historian Yuán interpreted it,
saying:
"This dream is very ominous,
not for you yourself,
but for your son,
yet it is also due to your fault.
By your grandson's time,
the Zhào lineage will decline further."
Tú Àn Gǔ,
initially favored by Línggōng,
by Jǐnggōng's time served as minister of justice,
and when planning rebellion,
prosecuted Línggōng's assassin to implicate Zhào Dùn,
announcing to all generals:
"Though Dùn did not know of it,
he remains the chief culprit.
For a subject to assassinate his ruler,
with descendants still in court,
how can crime be punished?
I request their execution."
Hán Jué said:
"When Línggōng was killed,
Zhào Dùn was abroad,
our late ruler deemed him innocent,
hence not executed.
Now you wish to kill his descendants,
this contradicts the late ruler's intent and is reckless killing.
Reckless killing is called chaos.
For ministers to undertake great affairs without the ruler's knowledge,
is to deny the ruler's authority."
Tú Àn Gǔ ignored him.
Hán Jué urged Zhào Shuò to flee.
Shuò refused,
saying:
"If you ensure the Zhào sacrifices continue,
I die without regret."
Hán Jué promised,
feigning illness and staying away.
Gǔ, without seeking permission, joined generals in attacking the Zhào clan at Xiàgōng,
killing Zhào Shuò,
Zhào Tóng,
Zhào Kuò,
Zhào Yīngqí,
exterminating their entire clan.
Zhào Shuò's wife was the sister of Duke Chéng,
and she was pregnant with a posthumous child.
She fled to the duke's palace and hid.
Zhào Shuò had a retainer named Gōngsūn Chǔjiù,
who said to Shuò's friend Chéng Yīng:
"Why not die?"
Chéng Yīng replied:
"Shuò's wife is pregnant with a posthumous child.
If by luck it is a boy,
I will serve him;
if it is a girl,
I will die slowly then."
Not long after,
Shuò's wife gave birth,
and it was a boy.
Tú'àn Gǔ heard of this,
and searched the palace.
The lady placed the child in her trousers,
praying:
"If the Zhào lineage is to perish,
then cry;
if it is not to perish,
then be silent."
When the search came,
the child made no sound.
Once they had escaped,
Chéng Yīng said to Gōngsūn Chǔjiù:
"Now that one search has failed,
they will surely search again later.
What can we do?"
Gōngsūn Chǔjiù said:
"Which is harder: raising the orphan or dying?"
Chéng Yīng said:
"Dying is easy,
raising the orphan is hard."
Gōngsūn Chǔjiù said:
"The former lord of Zhào treated you well,
you take on the difficult task,
I will take the easy one,
please let me die first."
So the two plotted to take another infant and carry it,
wrapping it in embroidered swaddling clothes,
and hid in the mountains.
Chéng Yīng went out,
falsely telling the generals:
"I, Yīng, am unworthy,
unable to raise the Zhào orphan.
Whoever can give me a thousand pieces of gold,
I will tell the location of the Zhào orphan."
The generals were all pleased,
agreed to it,
and sent troops with Chéng Yīng to attack Gōngsūn Chǔjiù.
Chǔjiù falsely said:
"What a petty man, Chéng Yīng!
In the past, during the disaster at Xiàgōng, you could not die,
and plotted with me to hide the Zhào orphan,
now you betray me.
Even if you cannot raise him,
how can you bear to sell him out!"
Holding the child, he cried out:
"Heaven, oh Heaven!
What crime has the Zhào orphan committed?
I beg you, let him live,
kill only Chǔjiù, that is enough."
The generals did not consent,
and so killed Chǔjiù and the orphan.
The generals thought the Zhào orphan was truly dead,
and all were pleased.
However, the true Zhào orphan was still alive,
and Chéng Yīng eventually hid with him in the mountains.
After fifteen years,
Duke Jìng of Jìn fell ill,
and a divination was performed,
which showed that the descendants of Dà Yè who had not prospered were causing the trouble.
Duke Jìng asked Hán Jué,
who knew the Zhào orphan was alive,
and said:
"Among the descendants of Dà Yè in Jìn whose line has been cut off,
is it not the Zhào clan?
Those from Zhōng Yǎn were all of the Yíng surname.
Zhōng Yǎn had a human face and a bird's beak,
descended to assist Emperor Dà Wù of Yīn,
and up to the Zhou Son of Heaven,
all had illustrious virtue.
Down to the times of the unprincipled Yōu and Lì kings,
Shū Dài left Zhōu for Jìn,
served the former lord Wén Hóu,
and up to Duke Chéng,
each generation had achievements,
and the line was never cut off.
Now you, my lord, alone have extinguished the Zhào lineage,
and the people of the state mourn them,
hence it appears in the turtle and stalks.
I beg you to consider this."
Duke Jìng asked:
"Does Zhào still have descendants?"
Hán Jué told him the whole truth.
Thereupon, Duke Jìng plotted with Hán Jué to establish the Zhào orphan,
summoned him, and hid him in the palace.
When the generals entered to inquire about the illness,
Duke Jìng used Hán Jué's men to pressure the generals and presented the Zhào orphan.
The orphan's name was Wǔ.
The generals had no choice,
and said:
"In the past disaster at Xiàgōng,
Tú'àn Gǔ was responsible,
falsely using your command,
and ordering the ministers.
If not for that,
who would dare to cause trouble!
If not for your illness,
we ministers would have requested to reestablish the Zhào heir.
Now that you have given the order,
it is the wish of us ministers."
Thereupon, they summoned Zhào Wǔ
and Chéng Yīng to bow to all the generals,
and then turned to join Chéng Yīng
and Zhào Wǔ in attacking Tú'àn Gǔ,
exterminating his clan.
They restored to Zhào Wǔ his fields and towns as before.
When Zhào Wǔ was capped,
and became an adult,
Chéng Yīng then bid farewell to the high officials,
and said to Zhào Wǔ:
"In the past disaster at Xiàgōng,
all were able to die.
It was not that I could not die,
but I thought to establish the Zhào heir.
Now that Zhào Wǔ is established,
an adult,
and restored to his former position,
I will go down to report to Zhào Xuān Mèng and Gōngsūn Chǔjiù."
Zhào Wǔ wept, kowtowed, and firmly pleaded,
saying:
"I, Wǔ, wish to toil to the bone to repay you until death,
how can you bear to leave me and die!"
Chéng Yīng said:
"It cannot be.
They thought I could accomplish the task,
so they died before me;
if I do not report now,
it would mean I did not complete my task."
Thereupon, he committed suicide.
Zhào Wǔ wore mourning for him for three years,
established a sacrificial estate for him,
offered sacrifices in spring and autumn,
and continued this for generations without end.
Eleven years after the Zhào clan was restored,
Duke Lì of Jìn killed his three Xì ministers.
Luán Shū, fearing he would be implicated,
then assassinated his lord Duke Lì,
and instead established Duke Xiāng's great-grandson Zhōu,
who was Duke Dào.
From this, the ministers of Jìn gradually grew stronger.
Zhào Wǔ continued the Zhào line for twenty-seven years,
when Duke Píng of Jìn was established.
In the twelfth year of Duke Píng,
Zhào Wǔ became chief minister.
In the thirteenth year,
Wú's Jìzǐ of Yánlíng was on a mission to Jìn,
and said:
"The governance of Jìn will eventually fall to the descendants of Zhào Wǔzǐ,
Hán Xuānzǐ,
and Wèi Xiànzǐ."
Zhào Wǔ died,
and was given the posthumous title Wénzǐ.
Wénzǐ begot Jǐng Shū.
During Jǐng Shū's time,
Duke Jǐng of Qí sent Yàn Yīng to Jìn,
and Yàn Yīng spoke with Jìn's Shū Xiàng.
Yīng said:
"The governance of Qí will eventually fall to the Tián clan."
Shū Xiàng also said:
"The governance of Jìn will fall to the six ministers.
The six ministers are extravagant,
and our lord cannot control them."
Zhào Jǐng Shū died,
and begot Zhào Yāng,
who was Jiǎnzǐ.
While Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was in power,
in the ninth year of Duke Qǐng of Jìn,
Jiǎnzǐ was about to assemble the feudal lords to garrison Zhōu.
The next year,
they escorted King Jìng of Zhōu back to Zhōu,
to avoid the trouble of Prince Cháo.
In the twelfth year of Duke Qǐng of Jìn,
the six ministers, according to law, executed the ducal clans Qí and
Yángshé,
divided their towns into ten counties,
and each of the six ministers appointed their own clans as the administrators.
The ducal house of Jìn grew weaker from this.
Thirteen years later,
the rebellious minister Yáng Hǔ of Lǔ fled to Zhào,
and Zhào Jiǎnzǐ accepted bribes,
treating him generously.
When Zhào Jiǎnzǐ fell ill,
remaining unconscious for five days,
his ministers all feared the worst.
The physician Biǎn Què examined him,
and upon exiting, Dǒng Ānyú inquired.
Biǎn Què said:
"His pulse is normal,
so why be alarmed!
In the past, Duke Mù of Qín once experienced this,
awakening after seven days.
On the day he awoke,
he told Gōngsūn Zhī and Zǐ Yú:
'I was greatly joyful in the emperor's abode.
The reason for my long stay
was precisely because I had learning to do.
The emperor told me:
"The state of Jìn will face great turmoil,
unsettled for five generations;
thereafter, it will become hegemonic,
but the hegemon will die before growing old;
the hegemon's son will cause the men and women of your state to have no distinctions."'
Gōngsūn Zhī wrote this down and stored it,
and thus the prophecy of Qín emerged.
The chaos of Duke Xiàn,
the hegemony of Duke Wén,
and Duke Xiāng's defeat of the Qín army at Xiáo and subsequent indulgence in debauchery—
these are events you have heard of.
Now your lord's illness is the same,
within three days he will surely recover,
and upon recovery, he will have something to say."
After two and a half days,
Jiǎnzǐ awoke.
He told his ministers:
"I was greatly joyful in the emperor's abode,
roaming the equal heaven with numerous spirits,
where grand music was played in nine movements and myriad dances performed,
unlike the music of the Three Dynasties,
its sound stirring the heart.
A bear approached to seize me,
but the emperor commanded me to shoot it,
I hit the bear,
and it died.
Then a brown bear came,
I shot it as well,
hit the brown bear,
and it died.
The emperor was very pleased,
bestowing upon me two bamboo cases,
both with duplicates.
I saw a child by the emperor's side,
and the emperor entrusted me with a Dí dog,
saying:
'When your son comes of age,
give this to him.'
The emperor told me:
'The state of Jìn will decline over generations,
ending in seven generations,
the Yíng clan will greatly defeat the Zhōu people west of Fànkuí,
yet they too will not possess it.
Now, recalling the merits of Yú Shùn,
I will bestow his descendant daughter Mèng Yáo upon your seventh-generation descendant.'"
Dǒng Ānyú received these words and wrote them down for safekeeping.
He reported Biǎn Què's words to Jiǎnzǐ,
who rewarded Biǎn Què with forty thousand mǔ of land.
Another day,
as Jiǎnzǐ was going out,
someone stood in his path,
refusing to move even when urged aside,
angering the attendants,
who prepared to strike him with blades.
The person in the path said:
"I wish to have an audience with the lord."
The attendants reported this.
Jiǎnzǐ summoned him,
saying:
"Ah,
I feel I have seen you clearly before."
The person in the path said:
"Dismiss your attendants,
I wish to speak."
Jiǎnzǐ sent the others away.
The person in the path said:
"During your illness, my lord,
I was at the emperor's side."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Indeed,
that happened.
When you saw me,
what was I doing?"
The person in the path said:
"The emperor ordered you to shoot a bear and a brown bear,
and both died."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Yes,
and what does that mean?"
The person in the path said:
"Jìn will face great calamity,
and you, my lord, will lead through it.
The emperor orders you to destroy two ministers,
for the bear and brown bear are their ancestors."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"The emperor gave me two bamboo cases with duplicates,
what does that signify?"
The person in the path said:
"Your son will conquer two states from the Dí,
both under his lineage."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I saw a child at the emperor's side,
who entrusted me with a Dí dog,
saying
'when your son grows up, give it to him'.
Why bestow a Dí dog upon the child?"
The person in the path said:
"The child
is your son.
The Dí dog
represents the ancestors of Dài.
Your son is destined to possess Dài.
And among your descendants,
one will reform governance and adopt Hú attire,
annexing two states from the Dí."
Jiǎnzǐ asked his name and offered him an official post.
The person in the path said:
"I am but a rustic,
conveying the emperor's command."
Then he vanished.
Jiǎnzǐ wrote down the words and stored them in the archives.
On another day,
Gūbù Zǐqīng visited Jiǎnzǐ,
who summoned all his sons for physiognomy.
Zǐqīng said:
"None here are fit to be general."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Will the Zhào clan then perish?"
Zǐqīng said:
"I once saw a son on the road,
who may be your child."
Jiǎnzǐ summoned his son Wú Xù.
When Wú Xù arrived,
Zǐqīng rose and said:
"This is the true general!"
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"His mother is lowly,
a Dí maidservant;
how can he be noble?"
Zǐqīng said:
"Heaven's chosen,
though lowly, shall become noble."
From then on,
Jiǎnzǐ summoned all his sons to converse with them,
and Wú Xù proved the most worthy.
Jiǎnzǐ then told his sons:
"I have hidden a treasure tally on Chángshān Mountain;
the first to find it will be rewarded."
His sons raced to Chángshān,
searched, but found nothing.
Wú Xù returned,
saying:
"I have found the tally."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Report it."
Wú Xù said:
"From Chángshān, overlooking Dài,
Dài can be taken."
Thus Jiǎnzǐ knew Wú Xù was truly worthy,
so he deposed the crown prince Bó Lǔ,
and made Wú Xù his heir.
Two years later,
in the fourteenth year of Lord Dìng of Jìn,
the Fàn and Zhōngháng families rebelled.
The following spring,
Jiǎnzǐ said to Wǔ, the governor of Hándān:
"Return the five hundred households of Wèi soldiers to me,
I will relocate them to Jìnyáng."
Wǔ agreed,
but upon returning, his elders refused,
breaking their word.
Zhào Yāng arrested Wǔ,
imprisoning him in Jìnyáng.
He then announced to the people of Hándān:
"I have personally executed Wǔ,
whom do you wish to install?"
He then killed Wǔ.
Zhào Jì and
Shè Bīn revolted in Hándān.
The Jìn ruler sent Jí Qín to besiege Hándān.
Xún Yín and
Fàn Jíshè were friends with Wǔ,
unwilling to assist Qín and plotting rebellion instead,
which Dǒng Ānyú knew.
In October,
the Fàn and Zhōngháng families attacked Zhào Yāng,
who fled to Jìnyáng,
where the Jìn people besieged him.
Fàn Jíshè and
Xún Yín's enemies, such as Wèi Xiāng, plotted to expel Xún Yín,
replacing him with Liáng Yǎofù;
expel Jíshè,
replacing him with Fàn Gāoyì.
Xún Yuè advised the Lord of Jìn:
"Your decree to ministers states,
'The instigators of rebellion shall die.'
Now three ministers initiated the rebellion, yet only Yāng is expelled,
the punishment is uneven,
I request they all be banished."
In November,
Xún Yuè,
Hán Bùníng,
and Wèi Chǐ, following the lord's order, attacked the Fàn and
Zhōngháng families,
but failed.
The Fàn and Zhōngháng families counterattacked the lord,
who struck back,
defeating and routing them.
On Dīngwèi day,
the two fled to Zhāogē.
Hán and Wèi pleaded on behalf of the Zhào family.
On the Xīnwèi day of December,
Zhào Yāng entered Jiàng,
and swore an alliance in the lord's palace.
The following year,
Zhì Bó Wénzǐ said to Zhào Yāng:
"Though Fàn and
Zhōngháng indeed rebelled,
Ānyú exposed it,
thus Ānyú was involved in the plot.
Jìn has a law:
'Instigators of rebellion shall die.'
Those two have been punished, yet Ānyú remains."
Zhào Yāng grew concerned.
Ānyú said:
"If I die,
the Zhào family will be secure,
and Jìn will be at peace,
my death is belated."
He then took his own life.
The Zhào family informed Zhì Bó,
after which the Zhào family was pacified.
Confucius heard that Zhào Jiǎnzǐ arrested Hándān Wǔ without the Jìn lord's consent,
and held Jìnyáng,
thus recording in the Spring and Autumn Annals:
"Zhào Yāng rebelled from Jìnyáng."
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ had a minister named Zhōu Shě,
who favored blunt remonstrance.
After Zhōu Shě's death,
whenever Jiǎnzǐ held court,
he often appeared displeased,
and the ministers asked for punishment.
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"The ministers are not at fault.
I've heard that a thousand sheepskins are not worth one fox's armpit fur.
When you ministers attend court,
I only hear obsequious agreements,
not Zhōu Shě's candid objections,
hence my sorrow."
Thus, Jiǎnzǐ was able to secure Zhào's territories and win the hearts of the Jìn people.
In the eighteenth year of Lord Dìng of Jìn,
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ besieged Fàn and
Zhōngháng in Zhāogē,
and Zhōngháng Wénzǐ fled to Hándān.
The next year,
Lord Líng of Wèi died.
Jiǎnzǐ and Yáng Hǔ escorted Wèi's crown prince Kuǎikuì to Wèi,
but Wèi did not admit him,
so he resided in Qī.
In the twenty-first year of Lord Dìng of Jìn,
Jiǎnzǐ captured Hándān,
and Zhōngháng Wénzǐ fled to Bórén.
Jiǎnzǐ then besieged Bórén,
and Zhōngháng Wénzǐ,
along with Fàn Zhāozǐ, fled to Qí.
Zhào eventually held Hándān and
Bórén.
The remaining lands of Fàn and Zhōngháng were incorporated into Jìn.
Zhào was nominally a Jìn minister,
but effectively controlled Jìn's power,
with fiefs rivaling those of the feudal lords.
In the thirtieth year of Lord Dìng of Jìn,
he contended with King Fūchāi of Wú for precedence at Huángchí,
with Zhào Jiǎnzǐ accompanying Lord Dìng of Jìn,
but Wú ultimately took the lead.
Lord Dìng died in his thirty-seventh year,
and Jiǎnzǐ abbreviated the three-year mourning period,
observing only one year.
That year,
King Gōujiàn of Yuè destroyed Wú.
In the eleventh year of Lord Chū of Jìn,
Zhì Bó attacked Zhèng.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was ill,
so he sent his crown prince Wúxù to lead the siege against Zhèng.
Zhì Bó, drunk,
poured wine to strike Wúxù.
Wúxù's ministers requested to die for him.
Wúxù said:
"The reason my lord appointed me
is for my ability to endure disgrace."
Yet he still resented Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó returned,
and thus advised Jiǎnzǐ,
urging him to depose Wúxù,
but Jiǎnzǐ refused.
Wúxù henceforth held a grudge against Zhì Bó.
In the seventeenth year of Lord Chū of Jìn,
Jiǎnzǐ died,
and the crown prince Wúxù succeeded him,
becoming known as Xiāngzǐ.
In the first year of Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
Yuè besieged Wú.
Xiāngzǐ reduced his mourning meals,
and sent Chǔ Lóng to inquire after the King of Wú.
Xiāngzǐ's elder sister was previously the wife of the King of Dài.
After Jiǎnzǐ was buried,
before the mourning period ended,
Xiāngzǐ went north and ascended Xiàwū Mountain,
inviting the King of Dài.
He had the cooks use copper ladles to serve the King of Dài and his attendants,
and while pouring,
secretly ordered the stewards to strike and kill the King of Dài and his officials with the ladles,
then raised troops to pacify the land of Dài.
His sister heard of this,
wept and cried out to heaven,
and killed herself by rubbing a hairpin into her throat.
The people of Dài pitied her,
naming the place of her death Mójī Mountain.
He then enfeoffed Zhōu, the son of his elder brother Bólǔ, as the Chéng Lord of Dài with the territory.
Bólǔ was
Xiāngzǐ's elder brother,
the former crown prince.
The crown prince died early,
so his son was enfeoffed.
In the fourth year of Xiāngzǐ's reign,
Zhì Bó, along with Zhào,
Hán, and Wèi, divided all the former lands of Fàn and
Zhōngháng.
Lord Chū of Jìn was enraged,
and informed Qí and
Lǔ, intending to attack the four ministers.
The four ministers feared this,
so they jointly attacked Lord Chū.
Lord Chū fled to Qí,
but died on the way.
Zhì Bó then installed Jīao, the great-grandson of Lord Zhāo,
who became known as Lord Yì of Jìn.
Zhì Bó grew even more arrogant.
He demanded land from Hán and
Wèi, and Hán,
Wèi gave it to him.
He demanded land from Zhào,
but Zhào refused,
due to the humiliation of the siege against Zhèng.
Zhì Bó was furious,
and thus led Hán and
Wèi to attack Zhào.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ, in fear,
fled to hold Jìnyáng.
Yuán Guò was passing through,
and later, arrived at the marshlands of the king,
where he saw three figures,
visible from the waist up,
but not visible from the waist down.
They gave Yuán Guò two sections of bamboo,
sealed shut.
They said:
"Take these and give them to Zhào Wúxù."
After Yuán Guò arrived,
he reported this to Xiāngzǐ.
Xiāngzǐ fasted for three days,
then personally split open the bamboo,
finding red writing that said:
"Zhào Wúxù,
I am the heavenly envoy of the Marquis of Huòtài Shān's southern slope.
On the third month, bǐngxū day,
I will enable you to turn and destroy the Zhì clan.
You shall also establish for me a hundred cities,
and I will bestow upon you the lands of the Línhú.
In later generations,
there will be a mighty king,
red and black,
with a dragon's face and a bird's beak,
thick eyebrows, mustache, and beard,
a broad chest and large bosom,
long-legged and sturdy,
left-lapped and riding a fine steed,
possessing Hézhōng entirely,
reaching to Xiūhùn and various Mò tribes,
attacking the Jin separatists to the south,
and destroying Hēigū to the north."
Xiāngzǐ bowed twice,
accepting the decree of the three spirits.
Three states attacked Jìnyáng,
and after over a year,
diverted the Fén River to flood the city,
leaving only three boards' height unsubmerged.
In the city, they hung cauldrons to cook,
and exchanged children to eat.
All the ministers had thoughts of betrayal,
and etiquette grew increasingly lax,
only Gāo Gǒng dared not neglect propriety.
Xiāngzǐ, fearful,
sent his minister Zhāng Mèngtóng at night to secretly ally with Hán
and Wèi. Hán,
Wèi conspired together,
and on the bǐngxū day of the third month,
the three states turned and destroyed the Zhì clan,
dividing their lands among themselves.
Thereupon, Xiāngzǐ distributed rewards,
with Gāo Gǒng receiving the highest.
Zhāng Mèngtóng said:
"During the crisis at Jìnyáng,
only Gǒng had no merit."
Xiāngzǐ replied:
"When Jìnyáng was in peril,
all ministers were negligent,
only Gǒng dared not forsake the rites of a subject,
hence I honor him first."
Thus, Zhào held Dài to the north,
annexed the Zhì clan to the south,
and grew stronger than Hán
and Wèi. Then, he sacrificed to the three spirits in a hundred cities,
appointing Yuán Guò to oversee the sacrifices at Huòtài Shān.
Later, he married a woman of the Kōngtóng clan,
and they had five sons.
Because Bólǔ had not been established as heir,
Xiāngzǐ refused to appoint his own son,
insisting on passing the throne to Bólǔ's son, the Lord of Dài Chéng.
The Lord Chéng died first,
so he installed the Lord Chéng's son, Huàn, as crown prince.
Xiāngzǐ reigned for thirty-three years and died,
Huàn succeeded him,
known as Xiàn Hóu.
Xiàn Hóu was young when he ascended,
ruling from Zhōngmóu.
Xiāngzǐ's younger brother, Huánzǐ, ousted Xiàn Hóu,
proclaiming himself ruler in Dài,
but died after one year.
The people said Huánzǐ's accession was not Xiāngzǐ's intent,
so they killed his son and welcomed back Xiàn Hóu to reign.
In the tenth year,
Zhōngshān Wǔ Gōng first ascended.
In the thirteenth year,
the city of Píngyì was built.
In the fifteenth year,
Xiàn Hóu died,
and his son Liè Hóu Jí succeeded.
In the first year of Liè Hóu,
Wèi Wén Hóu attacked Zhōngshān,
appointing his crown prince Jī to guard it.
In the sixth year,
Wèi, Hán,
and Zhào all established themselves as feudal lords,
posthumously honoring Xiànzǐ as Xiàn Hóu.
Liè Hóu loved music,
and told his chancellor Gōngzhòng Lián:
"I have favorites;
can I ennoble them?"
Gōngzhòng said:
"Enriching them is possible,
but ennobling them is not."
Liè Hóu said:
"Indeed.
The two Zhèng singers, Qiāng
and Shí,
I wish to grant them land,
ten thousand mǔ each."
Gōngzhòng said:
"Yes."
But did not grant it.
After a month,
Liè Hóu returned from Dài,
inquiring about the singers' land.
Gōngzhòng said:
"I am seeking,
but haven't found suitable land yet."
Shortly after,
Liè Hóu asked again.
Gōngzhòng still did not grant it,
and feigned illness to avoid court.
Fānwú Jūn came from Dài,
and said to Gōngzhòng:
"You truly value goodness,
but do not know how to uphold it.
Now you serve as chancellor of Zhào,
for four years already,
have you recommended any scholars?"
Gōngzhòng said:
"Not yet."
Fānwú Jūn said:
"Niú Chù,
Xún Xīn,
and Xú Yuè are all suitable."
Gōngzhòng then recommended these three.
At court,
Liè Hóu asked again:
"What of the singers' land?"
Gōngzhòng said:
"I am just about to select the best for them."
Niú Chù attended Liè Hóu with teachings on benevolence and righteousness,
guiding him with the way of the king,
and Liè Hóu was pleased.
The next day,
Xún Xīn attended,
advising on selecting and training talents,
appointing officials based on ability.
The following day,
Xú Yuè attended,
advocating frugality in resources,
and evaluating merits and virtues.
All that was discussed was fully implemented,
and the ruler was delighted.
Liè Hóu sent a messenger to tell the chancellor:
"The matter of the singers' land can stop."
He appointed Niú Chù as preceptor,
Xún Xīn as commandant,
Xú Yuè as interior historian,
and bestowed two sets of robes upon the chancellor.
In the ninth year,
Liè Hóu died,
and his brother Wǔ Gōng succeeded.
Wǔ Gōng reigned for thirteen years and died,
Zhào reinstated Liè Hóu's crown prince Zhāng,
known as Jìng Hóu.
That year,
Wèi Wén Hóu died.
In the first year of Jìng Hóu,
Wǔ Gōng's son Zhāo rebelled,
but failed,
and fled to Wèi.
Zhào first established its capital at Hándān.
In the second year,
defeated Qí at Língqiū.
In the third year,
rescued Wèi at Lǐnqiū,
decisively defeated the Qí army.
In the fourth year,
Wèi defeated us at Tùtái.
Built Gāngpíng to invade Wèi.
In the fifth year,
Qí and Wèi attacked Zhào on behalf of Wèi,
captured our Gāngpíng.
In the sixth year,
borrowed troops from Chǔ to attack Wèi,
captured Jípú.
In the eighth year,
captured Wèi's Huángchéng.
In the ninth year,
attacked Qí.
Qí attacked Yān,
Zhào rescued Yān.
In the tenth year,
fought Zhōngshān at Fángzǐ.
In the eleventh year,
Wèi, Hán,
and Zhào jointly destroyed Jìn,
dividing its territory.
Attacked Zhōngshān,
and fought again at Zhōngrén.
In the twelfth year,
Jìng Hóu died,
his son Chéng Hóu Zhǒng ascended the throne.
In the first year of Chéng Hóu,
Prince Shèng contended with Chéng Hóu for the throne,
causing rebellion.
In the second year, sixth month,
it snowed.
In the third year,
Tàiwùwǔ became chancellor.
Attacked Wèi,
captured seventy-three villages and towns.
Wèi defeated us at Lìn.
In the fourth year,
fought Qín at Gāo'ān,
defeated them.
In the fifth year,
attacked Qí at Juàn.
Wèi defeated us at Huái.
Attacked Zhèng,
defeated them,
gave it to Hán,
Hán gave us Chángzǐ.
In the sixth year,
Zhōngshān built the Great Wall.
Attacked Wèi,
defeated them at Ruǎnzé,
surrounded King Huì of Wèi.
In the seventh year,
invaded Qí,
reached the Great Wall.
Allied with Hán to attack Zhōu.
In the eighth year,
divided Zhōu into two with Hán.
In the ninth year,
fought Qí at Āxià.
In the tenth year,
attacked Wèi,
captured Zhēn.
In the eleventh year,
Qín attacked Wèi,
Zhào rescued them at Shí'ā.
In the twelfth year,
Qín attacked Wèi's Shǎoliáng,
Zhào rescued them.
In the thirteenth year,
Duke Xiàn of Qín sent Shǔzhǎng Guó to attack Wèi's Shǎoliáng,
captured its crown prince and
Cuó. Wèi defeated us at Kuài,
captured PíLáo.
Chéng Hóu met Hán Zhāo Hóu at Shàngdǎng.
In the fourteenth year,
allied with Hán to attack Qín.
In the fifteenth year,
assisted Wèi in attacking Qí.
In the sixteenth year,
divided Jìn with Hán
and Wèi,
enfeoffed the Jìn ruler with Duānshì.
In the seventeenth year,
Chéng Hóu met King Huì of Wèi at Géniè.
In the nineteenth year,
met with Qí
and Sòng at Pínglù,
and met with Yān at Ā.
In the twentieth year,
Wèi presented róng chuán timber,
used it to build Tántái.
In the twenty-first year,
Wèi besieged our Hándān.
In the twenty-second year,
King Huì of Wèi captured our Hándān,
Qí also defeated Wèi at Guìlíng.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Wèi returned our Hándān,
formed an alliance with Wèi on the Zhāng River.
Qín attacked our Lìn.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Chéng Hóu died.
Prince Xiè contended with Crown Prince Sù Hóu for the throne,
Xiè was defeated,
fled to Hán.
In the first year of Sù Hóu,
seized Duānshì from the Jìn ruler,
relocated him to Túnliú.
In the second year,
met King Huì of Wèi at Yīnjìn.
In the third year,
Prince Fàn attacked Hándān,
was unsuccessful and died.
In the fourth year,
paid homage to the Son of Heaven.
In the sixth year,
attacked Qí,
captured Gāotáng.
In the seventh year,
Prince Kè attacked Wèi's Shǒuyuán.
In the eleventh year,
Duke Xiào of Qín sent Lord Shāng to attack Wèi,
captured its general Prince Áng.
Zhào attacked Wèi.
In the twelfth year,
Duke Xiào of Qín died,
Lord Shāng was executed.
In the fifteenth year,
constructed the Shòulíng tomb.
King Huì of Wèi died.
In the sixteenth year,
Sù Hóu toured Dàlíng,
exited through Lùmén,
Dàwùwǔ grasped his horse and said:
"Farming is currently urgent,
if one day is not worked,
there will be no food for a hundred days."
Sù Hóu descended from his carriage and apologized.
In the seventeenth year,
besieged Wèi's Huáng,
but did not capture it.
Built the Great Wall.
In the eighteenth year,
Qí and Wèi attacked us,
we breached the river to flood them,
their troops withdrew.
In the twenty-second year,
Zhāng Yí became chancellor of Qín.
Zhào Cí fought Qín,
was defeated, Qín killed Cí west of the river,
captured our Lìn
and Líshí.
In the twenty-third year,
Hán Jǔ fought with Qí
and Wèi,
died at Sāngqiū.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Sù Hóu died.
Qín, Chǔ,
Yān, Qí,
and Wèi each sent ten thousand elite troops to attend the funeral.
His son King Wǔ Líng ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Wǔ Líng,
Yángwén Jūn Zhào Bào became chancellor.
King Xiāng of Liáng and Crown Prince Sì,
King Xuān of Hán and Crown Prince Cāng came to court at Xìngōng.
King Wǔ Líng was young,
unable to govern,
had three Erudite Instructors,
three Left and Right Error-Correctors.
When he began governing,
first consulted Féi Yì, a respected minister of the previous king,
increased his rank;
three octogenarian elders of the state,
were paid monthly respects.
In the third year,
fortified Hào.
In the fourth year,
met with Hán at Qūshǔ.
In the fifth year,
married a woman from Hán as his wife.
In the eighth year,
Hán attacked Qín,
but withdrew without victory.
The five states declared themselves kings,
but only Zhào refused,
saying:
"Without the substance,
how dare I assume the title!"
He ordered his people to address him as
"Lord".
In the ninth year,
allied with Hán and
Wèi, they attacked Qín,
but Qín defeated them,
decapitating 80,000 soldiers.
Qí defeated us at Guānzé.
In the tenth year,
Qín captured our Zhōngdū and Xīyáng.
Qí conquered Yān.
Yān's chancellor Zǐzhī became the ruler,
while the former ruler became a subject.
In the eleventh year,
the king summoned Prince Zhí from Hán,
establishing him as King of Yān,
and sent Yuèchí to escort him.
In the thirteenth year,
Qín captured our Lìn,
taking General Zhào Zhuāng prisoner.
The kings of Chǔ and Wèi came,
passing through Hándān.
In the fourteenth year,
Zhào Hé attacked Wèi.
In the sixteenth year,
King Huì of Qín died.
The king toured Dàlíng.
One day,
he dreamed of a maiden playing the zither and singing:
"How radiant the beauty,
her countenance like blooming reeds.
Fate, oh fate,
why have I not found my Yíng!"
Another day,
while drinking merrily,
he repeatedly mentioned the dream,
longing to see the figure.
Wú Guǎng heard of this,
and through the queen presented his daughter Wá Yīng.
She was Mèng Yáo.
Mèng Yáo became greatly favored by the king,
and was known as Queen Huì.
In the seventeenth year,
the king went to Jiǔmén,
built Yětái,
to observe the borders of Qí and
Zhōngshān.
In the eighteenth year,
King Wǔ of Qín and Mèng Yuè lifted a dragon-engraved red tripod,
but their knee tendons snapped and they died.
The King of Zhào sent Zhào Gù, chancellor of Dài, to welcome Prince Jì from Yān,
escorted him back,
and established him as King of Qín,
known as King Zhāo.
In the nineteenth year, spring, first month,
a grand court assembly was held at Xìn Palace.
Féi Yì was summoned to discuss state affairs,
which lasted five days.
The king campaigned north through Zhōngshān territory,
reaching Fángzǐ,
then proceeded to Dài,
north to Wúqióng,
west to the river,
and ascended Huánghuā Heights.
He summoned Lóu Huǎn for counsel, saying:
"Our former kings adapted to changing times,
expanding our southern frontier,
fortified by the barriers of Zhāng and
Fǔ rivers,
built the Great Wall,
captured Lìn and
Guōláng,
defeated the Lín people at Rěn,
yet their achievements remain incomplete.
Now Zhōngshān lies at our heart,
Yān to the north,
the Hú to the east,
to the west the Línhú,
Lóufán,
and borders with Qín and Hán,
yet we lack strong military support—
this risks our state's demise.
What should we do?
Those with renowned accomplishments
inevitably bear the burden of defying conventions.
I wish to adopt Hú attire."
Lóu Huǎn replied:
"Excellent."
But all ministers opposed it.
Then Féi Yì attended the king,
who said:
"Reflecting on the achievements of Jiǎn and
Xiāng, our predecessors,
and considering the advantages regarding the Hú and
Dí tribes—
a loyal subject
should embody filial piety, fraternal duty, and respect for hierarchy in times of favor,
and contribute to the people's welfare and ruler's benefit in times of influence.
These are the duties of a minister.
Now I intend to follow Xiāng's footsteps,
venturing into Hú and
Dí territories,
yet none in this generation comprehend it.
To weaken the enemy,
with minimal effort for great gains,
sparing the people from exhaustion,
and continuing past glories—
those achieving extraordinary feats
bear the weight of tradition's disapproval;
those with unique wisdom
endure the complaints of the stubborn.
Now I plan to teach the people Hú attire and mounted archery,
and the world will surely criticize me.
What should I do?"
Féi Yì said:
"I've heard that hesitant actions bring no achievement,
and doubtful conduct gains no fame.
Since you've resolved to bear tradition's burden,
disregard the world's criticism.
Those pursuing supreme virtue don't conform to customs,
and those achieving great deeds don't consult the masses.
In the past, Shǔn danced for the Yǒumiáo,
Yǔ bared himself in the naked kingdom—
not to indulge desires or please themselves,
but to promote virtue and accomplish goals.
Fools understand only after the fact,
while the wise foresee the unseen.
Why should you hesitate?"
The king said:
"I don't doubt Hú attire itself,
but fear the world's ridicule.
What delights the mad,
the wise mourn;
what fools laugh at,
the worthy discern.
If some follow me,
Hú attire's success may be realized.
Even if the whole world mocks me,
I will surely possess the Hú lands and Zhōngshān."
Thus, he adopted Hú attire.
He sent Wǎng Xiè to inform Lord Chéng, saying:
