"I have adopted Hú attire,
intending to wear it at court,
and wish you, Uncle, to do likewise.
The family follows the elders and the state follows the ruler—
this is the universal practice throughout history.
A son does not oppose his parents,
nor a minister his sovereign—
this is the fundamental principle of kinship.
Now that I have issued an edict to change attire, yet you refuse,
I fear it will provoke criticism from all under heaven.
Governing a state has constant principles,
with benefiting the people as the foundation;
administering governance has established norms,
with the enforcement of orders being paramount.
To illuminate virtue, one must first consider the humble,
but to implement policies, one must first gain the trust of the noble.
The intent behind adopting Hú attire now
is not for indulgence or personal pleasure;
actions have their purpose and achievements their source—
when tasks are accomplished and merits established,
only then is it commendable.
Now I fear that you, Uncle, are opposing the norms of governance,
thereby fueling criticisms against you.
Moreover, I have heard that
deeds benefiting the state are never unrighteous,
and relying on noble kin brings no disgrace to one's name.
Thus, I hope to emulate your sense of duty, Uncle,
to achieve the success of adopting Hú attire.
I have sent Xiè to visit you, Uncle,
requesting that you adopt this attire."
Lord Chéng bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"I had indeed heard of Your Majesty's adoption of Hú attire.
I am untalented,
and bedridden by illness,
unable to hasten to court to offer my views.
Since the king commands it,
I dare to respond,
and will exhaust my humble loyalty.
I say: I have heard that the Central States
are where the wise and intelligent dwell,
where all goods and resources gather,
where the sages impart teachings,
where benevolence and righteousness are practiced,
where the Shījīng, Shūjīng, rites, and music are applied,
where extraordinary skills and talents are tested,
where distant regions look to for guidance,
and where the Mányí emulate as righteous conduct.
Now, Your Majesty abandons this to adopt the attire of distant lands,
altering ancient teachings,
changing the ancient way,
opposing people's hearts,
and provoking scholars,
thereby distancing yourself from the Central States.
Thus, I urge Your Majesty to reconsider this."
The messenger reported back.
The king said:
"I had indeed heard of my uncle's illness;
I will go in person to request it."
The king then went to Lord Chéng's home
and personally made his plea,
saying:
"Attire
is for convenience of use;
rites
are for facilitating affairs.
The sages observed local customs and adapted appropriately,
establishing rites according to circumstances,
all to benefit the people and strengthen the state.
Those with cropped hair and tattooed bodies,
arms patterned and lapels left-fastened,
are the people of Ōuyuè.
Those with blackened teeth and tattooed foreheads,
fish-skin caps and hempen threads,
are from the state of Dàwú.
Thus, rites and attire differ,
yet their purpose of convenience is the same.
Customs vary, and practices change;
affairs differ, and rites adapt.
Therefore, if it truly benefits the state,
the sages do not unify practices;
if it truly facilitates affairs,
they do not standardize rites.
Confucians share one teacher, yet customs differ;
the Central States share rites, yet teachings diverge—
how much more for the practical needs of mountain valleys?
Thus, in matters of adoption or rejection,
even the wise cannot unify them;
for attire of near and far,
even sages cannot make them the same.
Remote regions have many peculiarities,
and biased scholars much debate.
To not doubt what one does not understand,
and not condemn what differs from oneself—
this is impartiality, seeking perfection for all.
Now, what you, Uncle, speak of are customs,
while what I speak of is how to shape customs.
Our state to the east has the Hé
and Bóluò rivers,
shared with Qí
and Zhōngshān,
yet we lack the means of boats and oars.
From Chángshān to Dài
and Shàngdǎng,
to the east lies the border of Yān
and Dōnghú,
and to the west that of Lóufán,
Qín, and Hán,
yet now we lack preparedness in cavalry and archery.
Thus, without boats and oars,
how shall the people dwelling by the waters
guard the Hé
and Bóluò rivers?
By changing attire for cavalry and archery,
we can prepare against Yān,
the Sānhú,
Qín, and Hán's borders.
Moreover, formerly, Lord Jiǎn did not block Jìnyáng and extended to Shàngdǎng,
and Lord Xiāng annexed the Róng and took Dài to repel the various Hú—
this is clear to both foolish and wise.
Earlier, Zhōngshān, relying on Qí's strong forces,
invaded and ravaged our lands,
captured our people,
diverted water to besiege Hào—
had it not been for the spirits of the state,
Hào would nearly have been lost.
The former king felt shame for this,
and the grievance remains unavenged.
Now, with preparedness in cavalry and archery,
nearby, we can secure the terrain of Shàngdǎng,
and afar, avenge the grievance against Zhōngshān.
Yet you, Uncle, cling to Central States' customs, opposing Lords Jiǎn
and Xiāng's intent,
detesting the name of changing attire and forgetting the shame of Hào—
this is not what I expect of you."
Lord Chéng bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"I am foolish,
and failed to grasp Your Majesty's righteousness,
daring only to voice common hearsay—
this is my fault.
Now that Your Majesty will continue Lords Jiǎn
and Xiāng's intent to fulfill the former kings' will,
how dare I not obey the command!"
He bowed twice again, touching his head to the ground.
Thereupon, he was granted Hú attire.
The next day,
he wore it to court.
Thus began the issuance of the Hú attire decree.
Zhào Wén,
Zhào Zào,
Zhōu Shào,
and Zhào Jùn all advised the king to stop the Hú attire,
claiming the old ways were better.
The king said:
"The former kings had different customs—
which antiquity should we follow?
Emperors and kings did not imitate each other—
which rites should we adhere to?
Fúxī and
Shénnóng taught without punishment,
while Huángdì,
Yáo, and Shùn punished without wrath.
By the time of the Three Dynasties,
they established laws according to the times,
and rites according to affairs.
Laws, regulations, and decrees each suited their circumstances,
and clothing, tools, and equipment each served their purposes.
Thus, rites need not be uniform,
and benefiting the state need not mimic antiquity.
Sages rose to kingship without imitating predecessors,
while Xià and Yīn declined without changing rites.
Hence, opposing antiquity should not be condemned,
and adhering to rites is not necessarily praiseworthy.
Moreover, if exotic attire indicates licentiousness,
then Zōu
and Lǔ would have no virtuous conduct;
if unusual customs make people frivolous,
then Wú
and Yuè would have no outstanding scholars.
Furthermore, what sages call attire benefits the body,
and what they call rites facilitate affairs.
The rules of conduct
and regulations of clothing
are meant to standardize the common people,
not to judge the worthy.
Thus, the common people flow with customs,
while the worthy evolve with change.
As the proverb says:
'Using books to drive a chariot does not grasp the horse's nature;
using antiquity to govern today does not understand affairs' changes.'
The merit of adhering to law
cannot surpass the age;
the study of emulating antiquity
cannot govern the present.
You have not reached this understanding."
Thereupon, he adopted Hú attire and promoted cavalry and archery.
In the twentieth year,
the king campaigned through the territory of Zhōngshān,
reaching Níngjiā;
to the west, he campaigned through the lands of the Hú tribes,
reaching Yúzhōng.
The king of the Línhú presented horses.
Upon returning, he sent Lóu Huǎn to Qín,
Qiú Yè to Hán,
Wáng Bēn to Chǔ,
Fù Dīng to Wèi,
and Zhào Jué to Qí.
Zhào Gù, the chancellor of Dài, was put in charge of the Hú tribes,
and assembled their troops.
In the twenty-first year,
he attacked Zhōngshān.
Zhào Shào commanded the right army,
Xǔ Jūn the left army,
and the prince, Zhāng, the central army,
with the king commanding them all.
Niú Jiǎn commanded the chariots and cavalry,
and Zhào Xī jointly commanded the Hú
and Dài forces. Zhào gave them the Xíng pass,
joined forces at Qǔyáng,
and captured Dānqiū,
Huáyáng,
and the Chīzhī要塞.
The king's army captured Hào,
Shíyì,
Fēnglóng,
and Dōngyuán.
Zhōngshān offered four cities for peace,
which the king accepted,
and withdrew the troops.
In the twenty-third year,
he attacked Zhōngshān.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Queen Huì died.
He sent Zhōu Shào, dressed in Hú attire, to tutor the prince Hé.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he again attacked Zhōngshān,
expanding territory north to Yān
and Dài, and west to Yúnzhōng
and Jiǔyuán.
On the wùshēn day of the fifth month in the twenty-seventh year,
a grand court assembly was held in the eastern palace,
where the state was handed over,
and Prince Hé was established as king.
After the king performed the temple rites,
he held court.
All the senior officials became his ministers,
with Féi Yì as chancellor,
and also serving as his tutor.
This was King Huìwén.
King Huìwén
was the son of Queen Huì, Wú Wá.
King Wǔlíng titled himself Zhǔfù.
Zhǔfù wanted his son to govern the state,
while he himself, dressed in Hú attire, led officers and officials northwest to campaign through Hú lands,
intending to go from Yúnzhōng
and Jiǔyuán directly south to raid Qín.
Thus, he pretended to be an envoy and entered Qín.
King Zhāo of Qín did not recognize him,
but later found his appearance remarkably imposing,
unbefitting a subject's demeanor,
and sent men to pursue him,
but Zhǔfù had already galloped away and escaped the pass.
Upon investigation,
it was discovered to be Zhǔfù.
The people of Qín were greatly alarmed.
The reason Zhǔfù entered Qín
was to personally survey the terrain
and observe the character of the King of Qín.
In the second year of King Huìwén,
Zhǔfù toured the new territories,
then went out through Dài,
and west to the Xīhé region, where he met the king of the Lóufán and assembled his troops.
In the third year,
he destroyed Zhōngshān,
and relocated its king to Fūshī.
He established Língshòu,
the northern regions became submissive,
and the road to Dài was greatly opened.
Upon returning,
he distributed rewards,
granted a great amnesty,
held feasts with drinking for five days,
and enfeoffed his eldest son Zhāng as the Lord of Ānyáng in Dài.
Zhāng was habitually arrogant
and inwardly dissatisfied with his younger brother's accession.
Zhǔfù also appointed Tián Bùlǐ as Zhāng's chancellor.
Lǐ Duì said to Féi Yì:
"Prince Zhāng is strong and ambitious,
with many partisans and great desires;
is he not likely to have selfish motives?
As for Tián Bùlǐ's character,
he is cruel and arrogant.
These two finding common cause,
they are sure to plot treachery and rebellion,
staking everything on a risky venture.
When petty men have desires,
they think lightly and plan shallowly,
seeing only the benefits and disregarding the harms;
like attracts like,
and they plunge together into disaster.
From my perspective,
it cannot be long.
You bear heavy responsibilities and hold great power,
making you the starting point of disorder,
the focus of calamity;
you will surely be the first to suffer.
The benevolent love all things, and the wise prepare for disaster before it takes form;
without benevolence or wisdom,
how can one govern a state?
Why do you not plead illness and refrain from appearing,
handing over governance to Prince Chéng?
Do not become a focus of resentment,
do not become a stepping stone to disaster."
Féi Yì said:
"That cannot be.
Previously, Zhǔfù entrusted the king to me,
saying:
'Do not change your principles,
do not alter your intentions,
remain steadfast and single-minded,
until the end of your days.'
I bowed twice, received the command, and recorded it.
Now, to fear the difficulty posed by Bùlǐ and forget my record—
what change could be greater?
To advance and receive a solemn command,
then retreat and not fulfill it—
what betrayal could be worse?
A minister who changes and betrays
cannot be tolerated by law.
As the proverb says,
'If the dead were to return to life,
the living would feel no shame.'
I have already spoken my words;
I wish to preserve my word,
how can I merely preserve my person!
Moreover, the integrity of a steadfast minister is revealed when difficulties arise,
the conduct of a loyal minister becomes clear when troubles come.
You have been kind and loyal to advise me,
nevertheless,
I have my prior commitment,
and I dare not ultimately fail it."
Lǐ Duì said:
"Very well,
do your best!
I fear I will see you only within this year."
He left in tears.
Lǐ Duì repeatedly visited Prince Chéng
to prepare for any eventuality involving Tián Bùlǐ.
Another day, Féi Yì said to Xìn Qī:
"The prince and Tián Bùlǐ are deeply worrying.
Towards me, they sound friendly but are actually malicious;
this man is neither a proper son nor a loyal minister.
I have heard that
treacherous ministers at court
are the ruin of the state;
slanderous ministers in the inner circle
are the parasites of the ruler.
This man is greedy and ambitious,
enjoying the ruler's favor internally while committing violence externally.
He forges orders to act arrogantly,
usurping authority for a moment's command;
he would not hesitate to do anything,
and disaster will soon reach the state.
Now I am worried about this,
so much that I forget to sleep at night,
and forget to eat when hungry.
We must be prepared for traitors coming and going.
From now on,
if there is any summons for the king, I must first see the messenger's face;
I will personally intercept them first,
and only if there is no issue should the king then enter."
Xìn Qī said:
"Excellent,
that I should hear this!"
In the fourth year,
when the court officials were assembled,
Lord Ānyáng also came to court.
Zhǔfù ordered the king to preside over the court,
while he himself watched from the side, observing the rituals of the ministers and royal clan.
Seeing his eldest son Zhāng looking dejected,
facing north as a subject,
submitting to his younger brother,
he pitied him in his heart.
Thereupon, he considered dividing Zhào and making Zhāng king in Dài,
but the plan was abandoned before it was decided.
Lord Fù and the king were traveling at Shāqiū,
staying in separate palaces.
Prince Zhāng then used his followers and Tián Bùlǐ to stage a rebellion,
forging an order from Lord Fù to summon the king.
Féi Yì entered first,
and was killed.
Gāo Xìn immediately fought alongside the king.
Prince Chéng and Lǐ Duì arrived from the capital,
then raised troops from four cities to enter and resist the trouble,
killing Prince Zhāng and Tián Bùlǐ,
exterminating their faction of traitors and stabilizing the royal house.
Prince Chéng became chancellor,
titled the Lord of Ānpíng,
and Lǐ Duì became Minister of Justice.
When Prince Zhāng was defeated,
he fled to Lord Fù.
Lord Fù let him in,
and Chéng and Duì thus besieged Lord Fù's palace.
After Prince Zhāng died,
Prince Chéng
and Lǐ Duì plotted, saying:
"Because of Zhāng, we have besieged Lord Fù.
If we withdraw our troops now,
our clan will be exterminated."
So they continued to besiege Lord Fù.
They ordered the people in the palace
that "the last to come out will be executed,"
and all the people in the palace came out.
Lord Fù wanted to leave but could not,
and could not get food either.
He probed for nestling birds to eat them,
and after more than three months, he starved to death in the Shāqiū Palace.
Once Lord Fù was confirmed dead,
they issued funeral announcements to the various states.
At that time, the king was young,
and Chéng and Duì monopolized power.
Fearing execution,
they had besieged Lord Fù.
Initially, Lord Fù had made his eldest son Zhāng the crown prince.
Later, he obtained Wú Wá,
loved her,
and for several years did not leave her side.
She gave birth to a son, Hé,
so he deposed Crown Prince Zhāng and established Hé as king.
When Wú Wá died,
his affection waned,
and he pitied the former crown prince,
wanting both to be kings.
Hesitant and undecided,
thus the turmoil arose,
leading to the death of both father and son,
laughed at by the world.
How tragic!
In the fifth year,
they gave Yān the territories of Mào
and Yì. In the eighth year,
they built the southern wall of Xíngtáng.
In the ninth year,
Zhào Liáng commanded troops,
joining forces with Qí to attack Hán,
reaching as far as the pass of Lǔ.
By the tenth year,
Qín proclaimed itself the Western Emperor.
In the eleventh year,
Dǒng Shū, along with the Wèi clan, attacked Sòng,
and obtained Héyáng from Wèi.
Qín took Gěngyáng.
In the twelfth year,
Zhào Liáng commanded an attack on Qí.
In the thirteenth year,
Hán Xúwéi commanded,
attacking Qí.
The princess died.
In the fourteenth year,
the chancellor of state Yuè Yì led Zhào,
Qín, Hán,
Wèi, and Yān to attack Qí,
capturing Língqiū.
They met with Qín in Zhōngyáng.
In the fifteenth year,
King Zhāo of Yān came for an audience.
Zhào, together with Hán,
Wèi, and Qín, jointly attacked Qí.
The king of Qí was defeated and fled,
and Yān alone advanced deep,
capturing Línzī.
In the sixteenth year,
Qín again joined Zhào in repeatedly attacking Qí,
and the people of Qí were troubled by this.
Sū Lì, on behalf of Qí, sent a letter to the king of Zhào, saying:
I have heard that the wise rulers of ancient times,
whose virtuous conduct was not spread throughout the land,
whose teachings and order were not fully embraced by the people,
and whose seasonal sacrifices were not frequently offered to the spirits and gods,
yet sweet dew descended,
timely rains came,
the harvests were abundant,
the people were free from epidemics,
and the masses praised them,
but the wise rulers still pondered over it.
Now, Your Majesty's virtuous deeds and efforts
have not been repeatedly surpassed by Qín;
the accumulated resentment and anger
are not inherently deeper towards Qí.
Qín and Zhào are allied states,
yet they forcibly levy troops from Hán.
Does Qín truly love Zhào?
Or do they actually hate Qí?
In extreme circumstances,
a wise ruler examines them.
Qín does not love Zhào nor hate Qí;
they wish to destroy Hán and吞并 the two Zhōu,
so they use Qí as bait for the world.
Fearing that events may not align,
they send troops to coerce Wèi
and Zhào. Afraid that the world fears them,
they offer hostages to show good faith.
Worried that the world will quickly turn against them,
they levy troops from Hán to intimidate it.
They claim to virtue and ally with states,
but in reality, they attack an undefended Hán.
I believe Qín's strategy must be as such.
Things often differ in situation but share the same peril.
Chǔ was long attacked, and Zhōngshān perished;
now Qí is long attacked, and Hán will surely perish.
If Qí is defeated,
Your Majesty and the six states will share its benefits.
If Hán perishes,
Qín will monopolize it.
If they take the two Zhōu,
and seize the sacrificial vessels from the west,
Qín will keep them for themselves.
Assessing land and calculating merits,
whose gains, Yours or Qín's, are greater?
Strategists' plans say:
"If Hán loses Sānchuān,
and Wèi loses the Jìn state,
before the market changes, disaster will have arrived."
If Yān takes all of the northern lands of Qí,
it is only three hundred lǐ from Shāqiū
and Jùlù.
Hán's Shàngdǎng is a hundred lǐ from Hándān.
If Yān and Qín plot against Your Majesty's rivers and mountains,
they are only three hundred lǐ apart to connect.
Qín's Shàngjùn is near Tíngguān,
extending to Yúzhōng for fifteen hundred lǐ.
If Qín uses three commanderies to attack Your Majesty's Shàngdǎng,
west of Yángcháng,
south of Jùzhù,
will no longer be Yours.
Crossing Jùzhù,
cutting off Chángshān and defending it,
they can connect to Yān in three hundred lǐ.
Then the horses of Dài and the hounds of Hú will not come east,
and the jade of Kūnlún will not be exported.
These three treasures will also no longer be Yours.
If Your Majesty long attacks Qí,
following powerful Qín to attack Hán,
the disaster will surely reach this extent.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
Moreover, the reason Qí is attacked
is because it serves Your Majesty;
the world aligns its actions
to plot against Your Majesty.
The covenant between Yān and Qín is formed, and troops will be sent soon.
The five states plan to divide Your Majesty's land three ways.
Qí, betraying the covenant of the five states, sacrifices itself for Your Majesty's troubles,
sending troops west to restrain powerful Qín,
causing Qín to abandon the title of emperor and seek submission,
returning Gāopíng
and Gēnróu to Wèi,
and returning Jīngfēn
and Xiānyú to Zhào.
Qí's service to Your Majesty
should be considered top-notch,
yet now it is being blamed.
I fear that in the future, those who would serve Your Majesty may not dare to commit themselves.
I hope Your Majesty will deliberate on this thoroughly.
If now Your Majesty does not join the world in attacking Qí,
the world will surely regard Your Majesty as righteous.
If Qí embraces its altars of soil and grain and serves Your Majesty wholeheartedly,
the world will all respect Your Majesty's righteousness.
If Your Majesty uses the world to befriend Qín,
and Qín becomes tyrannical,
Your Majesty can use the world to restrain it.
Thus, the fame and favor of an era will be controlled by Your Majesty.
Thereupon, Zhào halted,
and declined Qín's request not to attack Qí.
The King met with the King of Yān.
Lián Pō commanded the troops,
attacked Qí's Xīyáng,
and captured it.
In the seventeenth year,
Yuè Yì led the Zhào army to attack Wèi's Bóyáng.
However, Qín resented Zhào for not joining them in attacking Qí,
so they invaded Zhào,
capturing two of our cities.
In the eighteenth year,
Qín captured our Shíchéng.
The King went again to the eastern part of Wèi,
diverted the Hé River's waters,
and attacked the Wèi clan.
There was a great flood,
and the Zhāng River overflowed.
Wèi Rǎn came to serve as chancellor of Zhào.
In the nineteenth year,
Qín took two of our cities.
Zhào gave Wèi Bóyáng.
Zhào Shē commanded the troops,
attacked Qí's Màiqiū,
and captured it.
In the twentieth year,
Lián Pō commanded the troops,
attacking Qí.
The King met with King Zhāo of Qín west of the Hé River.
In the twenty-first year,
Zhào diverted the Zhāng River west of Wǔpíng.
In the twenty-second year,
a great plague occurred.
Prince Dān was installed as Crown Prince.
In the twenty-third year,
Lóu Chāng commanded the troops,
attacked Wèi's Jī,
but could not capture it.
In the twelfth month,
Lián Pō commanded the troops,
attacked Jī,
and captured it.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Lián Pō commanded the troops,
attacked Wèi's Fángzǐ,
captured it,
and returned after fortifying the city.
He also attacked Ānyáng,
and captured it.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Yān Zhōu commanded the troops,
attacked Chāngchéng
and Gāotáng,
capturing them.
Zhào joined Wèi in attacking Qín.
Qín's general Bái Qǐ defeated our army at Huàyáng,
capturing one of our generals.
In the twenty-sixth year,
they took the Ōudài territory from the Eastern Hú.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the Zhāng River was diverted south of Wǔpíng.
Zhào Bào was enfeoffed as the Lord of Píngyáng.
The Hé River overflowed,
causing a great flood.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Lìn Xiàngrú attacked Qí,
reaching Píngyì.
The construction of the great wall at Jiǔmén in the north was halted.
Yān's general Chéng'ān Jūn Gōngsūn Cāo assassinated his king.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Qín and Hán attacked each other,
and besieged Èyǔ.
Zhào sent Zhào Shē to command the troops,
attacked Qín,
and decisively defeated the Qín army beneath Èyǔ,
for which he was granted the title Lord Mǎfú.
In the thirty-third year,
King Huìwén died,
and Crown Prince Dān ascended the throne,
becoming King Xiàochéng.
In the first year of King Xiàochéng,
Qín attacked us,
capturing three cities.
The King of Zhào was newly enthroned,
and the Queen Dowager held the reins of power,
while Qín pressed its attacks urgently.
The Zhào house sought help from Qí,
and Qí said:
"You must send Cháng'ān Jūn as a hostage,
then we will send troops."
The Queen Dowager refused,
and the ministers strongly remonstrated.
The Queen Dowager explicitly told her attendants:
"Anyone who again mentions sending Cháng'ān Jūn as a hostage,
I will surely spit in their face."
The Left Counsellor Chù Lóng expressed his wish to see the Queen Dowager,
who awaited him with great anger.
He entered, advanced slowly and sat down,
apologizing himself:
"Your servant's feet are ailing,
and I cannot walk quickly,
so I haven't been able to see you for a long time.
I privately excused myself,
but I feared that Your Majesty's health might be suffering,
hence I wished to see you."
The Queen Dowager said:
"I rely on a carriage to get around."
He said:
"Has your appetite not diminished?"
She said:
"I only manage congee."
He said:
"Your servant lately had no desire to eat at all,
so I forced myself to walk,
three or four lǐ a day,
and gradually my appetite improved a bit,
which harmonized my body."
The Queen Dowager said:
"I cannot do that."
The Queen Dowager's displeased expression slightly eased.
The Left Counsellor said:
"Your servant's humble son Shū Qí is the youngest,
and unpromising,
but as I am declining,
I privately dote on him,
and wish he could fill a vacancy in the black-clad guards to protect the royal palace.
I risk death to inform you."
The Queen Dowager said:
"Very well.
How old is he?"
He replied:
"Fifteen years old.
Though young,
I wish to entrust him before I fill the ditches and gullies."
The Queen Dowager said:
"Do men also love their young sons?"
He replied:
"More than women do."
The Queen Dowager laughed and said:
"Women love them exceptionally more."
He replied:
"Your servant privately believes that your love for the Queen of Yān surpasses that for Cháng'ān Jūn."
The Queen Dowager said:
"You are mistaken,
it is not as much as for Cháng'ān Jūn."
The Left Counsellor said:
"When parents love their children,
they plan deeply for their future.
When you sent off the Queen of Yān,
you held her heel,
wept for her,
thinking of her going far away,
and mourned for her.
After she left,
you did not stop missing her,
yet in sacrifices you prayed, saying,
'May she never return.'
Was this not planning for the long term,
so that her descendants would succeed as kings?"
The Queen Dowager said:
"Indeed."
The Left Counsellor said:
"Now, from three generations ago,
down to the descendants of the rulers of Zhào who were enfeoffed as marquises,
do any of their successors remain?"
She said:
"None."
He said:
"Not only in Zhào,
but among the other states, are there any that remain?"
She said:
"I have not heard of any."
He said:
"This is because the disaster strikes the closer ones in their own persons,
and the farther ones in their descendants.
Is it that the sons of rulers become marquises and are no good?
It is because their positions are high without merit,
their emoluments are generous without toil,
and they possess many precious vessels.
Now you honor Cháng'ān Jūn's position,
enfeoff him with fertile lands,
give him many precious vessels,
but do not let him achieve merit for the state while there is time.
Once the mountains and hills crumble,
how will Cháng'ān Jūn establish himself in Zhào?
Your servant thinks your planning for Cháng'ān Jūn is short-sighted,
hence I believe your love for him does not match that for the Queen of Yān."
The Queen Dowager said:
"Well then,
I leave it to you to send him as you see fit."
Thereupon, they prepared a hundred chariots for Cháng'ān Jūn,
and he went as a hostage to Qí,
after which Qí sent out its troops.
Zǐ Yì heard of this,
and said:
"Even the sons of a ruler,
being of his own flesh and blood,
cannot maintain a position of honor without merit,
nor enjoy emoluments without toil,
while preserving the weight of gold and jade;
how much less can I?"
Lord Ānpíng of Qí, Tián Dān, led the army of Zhào to attack Zhōngyáng of Yān,
and captured it.
He also attacked Zhùrén of Hán,
and captured it.
In the second year,
Queen Huìwén passed away.
Tián Dān became chancellor.
In the fourth year,
the king dreamed of wearing a garment with the lapel fastened to the left,
riding a flying dragon to ascend to heaven,
but before reaching it, he fell,
and saw piles of gold and jade like mountains.
The next day,
the king summoned the diviner Gǎn to interpret it,
who said:
"Dreaming of wearing a garment with the lapel fastened to the left
signifies fragmentation.
Riding a flying dragon to heaven but falling before reaching it
means having ambition without substance.
Seeing piles of gold and jade like mountains
foretells sorrow."
Three days later,
an envoy from Féng Tíng, the governor of Shàngdǎng of Hán, arrived,
saying:
"Hán cannot hold Shàngdǎng,
and is ceding it to Qín.
Its officials and people all wish to belong to Zhào,
not wanting to serve Qín.
There are seventeen cities and towns,
which we humbly offer to Zhào,
hoping the king will bestow favors upon the officials and people."
The king was greatly pleased,
and summoned Lord Píngyáng, Bào, to inform him, saying:
"Féng Tíng offers seventeen cities and towns;
should we accept them?"
He replied:
"A sage deeply fears profit that comes without cause."
The king said:
"The people cherish my virtue;
how can it be said to be without cause?"
He replied:
"Qín has been nibbling away at the territory of Hán,
cutting it off and preventing communication,
firmly believing they would sit back and receive the land of Shàngdǎng.
The reason Hán does not cede it to Qín
is to shift the disaster onto Zhào.
Qín bears the toil while Zhào reaps the benefit;
even if a strong state cannot take it from a weak one,
how can a weak one obtain it from a strong one?
How can this not be called profit without cause!
Moreover, Qín transports grain using ox-drawn water routes and nibbles away,
with superior forces doubling their efforts in battle,
tearing apart the lands of the upper states;
their administration is effective,
and it is unwise to oppose them;
we must not accept it."
The king said:
"Now if we dispatch a million troops to attack,
it takes over a year without gaining a single city.
Now with seventeen cities and towns enriching our state,
this is a great advantage."
Zhào Bào left,
and the king summoned Lord Píngyuán and Zhào Yǔ to inform them.
They replied:
"To dispatch a million troops and attack,
spending a year without gaining a city,
now for Zhào to receive seventeen cities and towns,
this is a great advantage,
and should not be lost."
The king said:
"Good."
He then ordered Zhào Shèng to receive the land,
and informed Féng Tíng, saying:
"Our humble state's envoy, your servant Shèng,
sent by our humble ruler to deliver this message:
we confer three cities of ten thousand households on the grand administrator,
three counties of a thousand households on the magistrate,
all to be enfeoffed as marquises for generations;
officials and people all gain three ranks in nobility,
and if they can live in peace together,
each will be granted six jin of gold."
Féng Tíng wept and refused to see the envoy,
saying:
"I cannot avoid three acts of injustice:
guarding the land for my lord,
yet unable to die in defense,
this is the first injustice;
ceding it to Qín,
disobeying my lord's command,
this is the second injustice;
selling my lord's land and profiting from it,
this is the third injustice."
Zhào then sent troops to take Shàngdǎng.
General Lián Pō stationed his army at Chángpíng.
In the seventh month,
Lián Pō was dismissed and Zhào Kuò took his place as general.
The Qín forces surrounded Zhào Kuò,
and Zhào Kuò surrendered with his army,
leading to the burial of over four hundred thousand soldiers.
The king regretted not following Zhào Bào's advice,
hence the disaster at Chángpíng occurred.
The king returned,
and defied Qín,
so Qín besieged Hándān.
The magistrate of Wǔyuán, Fù Bào,
Wáng Róng,
and Sū Shè led the Yān populace to revolt and reclaim Yān territory.
Zhào enfeoffed the chancellor of Chǔ, Lord Chūnshēn, with Língqiū.
In the eighth year,
Lord Píngyuán went to Chǔ to seek aid.
Upon his return, Chǔ came to rescue,
and Lord Wújì of Wèi also came to help,
so the siege of Hándān by Qín was lifted.
In the tenth year,
Yān attacked Chāngzhuàng,
and captured it in the fifth month.
Zhào generals Yuè Chéng
and Qìng Shè attacked the Qín army under Xìn Liáng,
and defeated it.
The crown prince died.
Meanwhile, Qín attacked Western Zhōu,
and captured it.
Túfù Qí departed.
In the eleventh year,
Yuánshì was walled,
and Shàngyuán was established as a county.
Lord Wǔyáng, Zhèng Ānpíng, died,
and his land was confiscated.
In the twelfth year,
the granary in Hándān burned down.
In the fourteenth year,
Lord Píngyuán, Zhào Shèng, died.
In the fifteenth year,
the chancellor of state, Lián Pō, was enfeoffed as Lord Xìnpíng with Wèiwén.
The king of Yān ordered his chancellor Lì Fù to make a pact of friendship,
offering five hundred jin of gold for the king of Zhào's banquet,
and upon returning,
reported to the king of Yān, saying:
"The strong men of Zhào all died at Chángpíng,
and their orphans are not yet grown;
we can attack them."
The king summoned Lord Chāngguó, Yuè Jiàn, and asked him.
He replied:
"Zhào
is a state accustomed to war on all fronts,
its people are skilled in warfare;
it is not advisable to attack them."
The king said:
"I attack the few with many,
two against one;
is that feasible?"
He replied:
"No."
The king said:
"Then with five against one,
is that feasible?"
He replied:
"No."
The king of Yān was enraged.
All his ministers believed it was possible.
Yān eventually raised two armies,
with two thousand chariots,
Lì Fù leading the attack on Hào,
and Qīng Qín leading the attack on Dài.
Lián Pō, as the general of Zhào,
defeated and killed Lì Fù,
captured Qīng Qín
and Yuè Jiàn.
In the sixteenth year,
Lián Pō besieged Yān.
Yuè Chéng was appointed as the Lord of Wǔxiāng.
In the seventeenth year,
Acting Chancellor and Grand General, the Lord of Wǔxiāng, attacked Yān,
besieging its capital.
In the eighteenth year,
Yánlíng Jūn led troops following Chancellor Lord Xìnpíng to aid Wèi in attacking Yān.
Qín captured thirty-seven cities including Yúcì from us.
In the nineteenth year,
Zhào exchanged territories with Yān:
giving Lóngduì,
Fénmén,
and Línlè to Yān;
Yān gave Gě,
Wǔyáng,
and Píngshū to Zhào.
In the twentieth year,
King Zhèng of Qín first ascended the throne.
Qín captured Jìnyáng from us.
In the twenty-first year,
King Xiàochéng died.
Lián Pō commanded troops,
attacked Fányáng,
and captured it.
He sent Yuè Chéng to replace him,
Lián Pō attacked Yuè Chéng,
Yuè Chéng fled,
and Lián Pō went into exile in Wèi.
His son Yǎn ascended the throne,
known as King Dàoxiāng.
In the first year of King Dàoxiāng's reign,
extensive preparations were made against Wèi.
An attempt was made to open the route between Píngyì
and Zhōngmóu,
but it was unsuccessful.
In the second year,
Lǐ Mù commanded troops,
attacked Yān,
and captured Wǔsuì
and Fāngchéng.
Qín summoned Lord Chūnpíng,
and detained him.
Xiè Jūn spoke on his behalf to Lord Wénxìn, saying:
"Lord Chūnpíng
is greatly favored by the King of Zhào, but the court officials are jealous of him,
so they conspired together, saying,
'If Lord Chūnpíng goes to Qín,
Qín will surely detain him,'
thus they conspired to send him into Qín.
Now if you detain him,
you will be severing relations with Zhào and falling into the court officials' plot.
It would be better for you to send back Lord Chūnpíng and detain Lord Píngdū instead.
Lord Chūnpíng's words and actions are trusted by the king,
and the king will surely cede substantial territory from Zhào to ransom Lord Píngdū."
Lord Wénxìn said:
"Good."
Thereupon he sent him back.
Hángāo was fortified.
In the third year,
Páng Nuǎn commanded troops,
attacked Yān,
and captured its general Jù Xīn.
In the fourth year,
Páng Nuǎn led the elite forces of Zhào,
Chǔ, Wèi,
and Yān,
attacked Zuì in Qín,
but failed to capture it;
shifting the attack to Qí,
they captured Ráo'ān.
In the fifth year,
Fù Dǐ commanded troops,
stationed at Píngyì;
Qìng Shě commanded the forces of Dōngyáng and Héwài,
guarding the Héliáng.
In the sixth year,
Lord Cháng'ān was enfeoffed with Ráo.
Wèi gave Yè to Zhào.
In the ninth year,
Zhào attacked Yān,
capturing Líyángchéng.
Before the troops were withdrawn,
Qín attacked Yè,
and captured it.
King Dàoxiāng died,
and his son King Yōumòu, Qiān, ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Yōumòu, Qiān's reign,
Bóren was fortified.
In the second year,
Qín attacked Wǔchéng,
Hù Zhé led troops to rescue it,
the army was defeated,
and he died there.
In the third year,
Qín attacked Chìlì
and Yí'ān,
Lǐ Mù led troops and fought them at Féixià,
repelling them.
Lǐ Mù was enfeoffed as the Lord of Wǔ'ān.
In the fourth year,
Qín attacked Pānwú,
Lǐ Mù engaged them in battle,
and repelled them.
In the fifth year,
the Dài region experienced a great earthquake,
from Lèxú westward,
north to Píngyīn,
more than half of the towers, houses, and walls were destroyed,
and the ground split east to west for one hundred thirty paces.
In the sixth year,
a great famine occurred,
and the people spread a rumor, saying:
"Zhào is the cry,
Qín is the laugh.
If you think it's not true,
look at the hair growing from the ground."
In the seventh year,
the people of Qín attacked Zhào,
Zhào's Grand General Lǐ Mù
and General Sīmǎ Shàng commanded troops,
and struck back.
Lǐ Mù was executed,
Sīmǎ Shàng was dismissed,
and Zhào Cōng and Qí's general Yán Jù replaced them.
Zhào Cōng's army was defeated,
Yán Jù fled.
King Qiān surrendered.
In the tenth month of the eighth year,
Hándān became part of Qín.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I heard from Féng Wángsūn:
"King Qiān of Zhào,
his mother was a courtesan,
favored by King Dàoxiāng.
King Dàoxiāng deposed the rightful heir Jiā and established Qiān.
Qiān had always been unprincipled,
trusted slander,
thus he executed his good general Lǐ Mù,
and employed Guō Kāi."
How misguided indeed!
After Qín had captured Qiān,
the surviving high officials of Zhào together established Jiā as king,
who ruled in Dài for six years,
then Qín advanced its troops, defeated Jiā,
and subsequently annihilated Zhào, making it a commandery.
The ancestors of Wèi
were descendants of Duke Bì Gāo.
Duke Bì Gāo shared the same surname as the Zhōu.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
Gāo was enfeoffed at Bì,
thus taking the surname Bì.
Later, the enfeoffment ended,
and they became commoners,
some in the Central States,
some among the barbarian tribes.
A descendant named Bì Wàn
served Duke Xiàn of Jìn.
In the sixteenth year of Duke Xiàn,
with Zhào Sù as the charioteer
and Bì Wàn as the carriage guard,
they attacked Huò,
Gěng, and Wèi,
and destroyed them.
Gěng was granted to Zhào Sù,
and Wèi was granted to Bì Wàn,
making them senior officials.
The diviner Yǎn said:
"The descendants of Bì Wàn are sure to prosper greatly.
Wàn (meaning 'ten thousand') is a number of fullness;
Wèi is a great name.
To begin his reward with this
is Heaven opening the way for him.
The Son of Heaven rules over millions of people,
the feudal lords rule over ten-thousands of people.
Now he is named with greatness,
following the number of fullness,
he is sure to have multitudes."
Earlier, when Bì Wàn divined about serving in Jìn,
he encountered the hexagram Zhūn changing to Bǐ.
Xīn Liào interpreted it,
saying:
"Auspicious.
Zhūn signifies firmness, Bǐ signifies entry,
what could be more auspicious than this?
His line is sure to flourish and prosper."
Eleven years after Bì Wàn was enfeoffed,
Duke Xiàn of Jìn died,
and his four sons contended to succeed him,
throwing Jìn into chaos.
Yet the lineage of Bì Wàn grew even greater,
taking the name of their state as the Wèi clan.
He sired Wǔzǐ.
Wèi Wǔzǐ, along with other sons of Wèi, served Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn.
In the twenty-first year of Duke Xiàn of Jìn,
Wǔzǐ followed Chóng'ěr into exile.
After nineteen years they returned,
Chóng'ěr was established as Duke Wén of Jìn,
and he ordered Wèi Wǔzǐ to inherit the enfeoffment of the Wèi lineage,
ranking him as a senior official,
governing at Wèi.
He sired Dàozǐ.
Wèi Dàozǐ moved his seat of governance to Huò.
He sired Wèi Jiàng.
Wèi Jiàng served Duke Dào of Jìn.
In the third year of Duke Dào,
he assembled the feudal lords.
The duke's younger brother Yánggān disrupted the ranks,
and Wèi Jiàng humiliated Yánggān.
Duke Dào angrily said:
"I assembled the feudal lords to bring honor,
yet now you disgrace my brother!"
He intended to execute Wèi Jiàng.
Someone advised Duke Dào,
and Duke Dào stopped.
He eventually entrusted governance to Wèi Jiàng,
sending him to make peace with the Róng
and Dí tribes, and the Róng
and Dí became closely attached.
In the eleventh year of Duke Dào,
he said:
"Since I employed Wèi Jiàng,
over eight years,
I have nine times assembled the feudal lords,
and the Róng and Dí are at peace -
this is due to your efforts."
He awarded him musical instruments,
which Wèi Jiàng declined three times
before finally accepting them.
He moved his seat of governance to Ānyì.
When Wèi Jiàng died,
he was posthumously named Zhāozǐ.
He sired Wèi Yíng.
Yíng sired Wèi Xiànzǐ.
Xiànzǐ served Duke Zhāo of Jìn.
When Duke Zhāo died, the six ministers grew powerful,
and the ducal house declined.
In the twelfth year of Duke Qǐng of Jìn,
Hán Xuānzǐ retired due to age,
and Wèi Xiànzǐ took charge of state affairs.
The Jìn royal clans Qí
and Yángshé families were at odds;
the six ministers punished them,
taking all their cities to form ten counties,
with each of the six ministers appointing their sons as administrators.
Xiànzǐ served as a minister of Jìn alongside Zhào Jiǎnzǐ,
Zhōngháng Wénzǐ,
and Fàn Xiànzǐ.
Fourteen years later, Confucius became minister of Lǔ.
Four years after that,
due to the disorder in Jìnyáng, Zhào Jiǎnzǐ
joined with Hán
and Wèi to attack the Fàn
and Zhōngháng families.
Wèi Xiànzǐ sired Wèi Chǐ.
Wèi Chǐ joined with Zhào Yāng to attack the Fàn
and Zhōngháng families.
Wèi Chǐ's grandson was called Wèi Huánzǐ,
who together with Hán Kāngzǐ
and Zhào Xiāngzǐ attacked and destroyed Zhì Bó,
dividing his territory.
Huánzǐ's grandson was called Wénhóu, named Dū.
The first year of Wèi Wénhóu
was also the first year of Duke Líng of Qín.
He was contemporary with Hán Wǔzǐ,
Zhào Huánzǐ,
and King Wēi of Zhōu.
In his sixth year,
he walled Shàoliáng.
In his thirteenth year,
he sent Zī Jī to besiege Fán
and Páng, evacuating their people.
In his sixteenth year,
he attacked Qín,
building Línjìn and Yuánlǐ.
In his seventeenth year,
he attacked Zhōngshān,
sending Zī Jī to guard it,
with Zhào Cāngtáng as his tutor.
Zī Jī encountered Wénhóu's teacher Tián Zǐfāng at Zhāogē,
drew his carriage aside to avoid him,
and descended to pay respects.
Tián Zǐfāng did not return the courtesy.
Zī Jī then asked:
"Do the wealthy and noble act arrogantly toward others?
Or do the poor and humble act arrogantly toward others?"
Zǐfāng said:
"It is the poor and humble who act arrogantly.
If a feudal lord acts arrogantly, he will lose his state;
if a senior official acts arrogantly, he will lose his family.
As for the poor and humble,
if their actions are not in accord,
or their words are not heeded,
they can leave for Chǔ
or Yuè as easily as taking off a sandal -
how can they be compared!"
Zī Jī left displeased.
He attacked Qín to the west,
reaching Zhèng before returning,
building Luòyīn
and Héyáng.
In his twenty-second year,
Wèi, Zhào,
and Hán were ranked as feudal lords.
In his twenty-fourth year,
Qín attacked us,
reaching Yánghú.
In his twenty-fifth year,
Zī Jī sired Zī Yīng.
Wénhóu studied the classics and arts with Zǐxià,
treated Duàngān Mù as an honored guest,
and whenever he passed by his lane,
he never failed to incline his carriage rail in respect.
When Qín once intended to attack Wèi,
someone said:
"The ruler of Wèi treats worthy men with courtesy,
his people praise his benevolence,
high and low are harmonious -
he cannot be targeted."
Wénhóu thereby gained reputation among the feudal lords.
He appointed Xīmén Bào to guard Yè,
and Hénèi became known for good governance.
Marquis Wén of Wèi said to Lǐ Kè:
"You once taught me,
'When a family is poor, one thinks of a good wife;
when a state is in turmoil, one thinks of a good chancellor.'
Now the appointment lies between either Chéng or Huáng;
what are these two men like?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"I have heard that
the lowly should not counsel the noble,
the distant should not counsel the intimate.
I am outside the court gates,
and dare not presume to command."
Marquis Wén said:
"Do not decline in this matter, sir."
Lǐ Kè said:
"It is because you have not observed them closely.
Observe whom they associate with when at home;
observe how they give when wealthy;
observe whom they recommend when in office;
observe what they refrain from doing when in straits;
observe what they do not take when poor.
These five criteria are sufficient to decide it;
why wait for Kè!"
Marquis Wén said:
"You may retire to your quarters, sir;
my chancellor is decided."
Lǐ Kè hurried out
and passed by Dí Huáng's home.
Dí Huáng said:
"Today I heard the lord summoned you to consult on the chancellorship;
who was ultimately appointed?"
Lǐ Kè said:
"Wèi Chéngzǐ became chancellor."
Dí Huáng flushed with anger and said:
"Based on what I have seen and remembered,
how have I fallen short compared to Wèi Chéngzǐ?
The guard of Xīhé
was recommended by me.
When the lord worried about Yè internally,
I recommended Xīmén Bào.
When the lord planned to attack Zhōngshān,
I recommended Yuè Yáng.
After Zhōngshān was captured,
with no one to govern it,
I recommended you, sir.
When the lord's son had no tutor,
I recommended Qūhóu Fù.
How have I fallen short compared to Wèi Chéngzǐ!"
Lǐ Kè said:
"Moreover, when you recommended me to your lord,
was it to form cliques and seek high office?
The lord asked about appointing a chancellor,
'Either Chéng or Huáng,
what are these two like?'
I replied:
'It is because you have not observed them closely.
Observe whom they associate with when at home;
observe how they give when wealthy;
observe whom they recommend when in office;
observe what they refrain from doing when in straits;
observe what they do not take when poor.
These five criteria are sufficient to decide it;
why wait for Kè!'
Thus I knew Wèi Chéngzǐ would be chancellor.
And how can you compare with Wèi Chéngzǐ?
Wèi Chéngzǐ, with a stipend of a thousand zhōng,
used nine-tenths of it outside,
keeping only one-tenth for himself.
Thus from the east he attracted Bǔ Zǐxià,
Tián Zǐfāng,
Duàngān Mù.
These three men
the lord regards as teachers.
The five men you recommended
the lord treats as ministers.
How can you compare with Wèi Chéngzǐ?"
Dí Huáng stepped back, bowed twice, and said:
"I, Huáng,
am a crude man;
I spoke wrongly.
I wish to be your disciple henceforth."
In the twenty-sixth year,
Mount Guó collapsed,
blocking the river.
In the thirty-second year,
they attacked Zhèng.
They fortified Suānzǎo.
They defeated Qín at Zhù.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Qí attacked and captured our Xiānglíng.
In the thirty-sixth year,
Qín invaded our Yīnjìn.
In the thirty-eighth year,
they attacked Qín,
were defeated by us at Wǔxià,
and captured their general Shí.
That year,
Marquis Wén died,
and his son Jī succeeded him,
known as Marquis Wǔ.
In the first year of Marquis Wǔ of Wèi,
Marquis Jìng of Zhào had just ascended,
and Prince Shuò rebelled,
but was unsuccessful,
fled to Wèi,
and together with Wèi attacked Hándān,
but Wèi was defeated and withdrew.
In the second year,
they fortified Ānyì
and Wángyuán.
In the seventh year,
they attacked Qí,
reaching Sāngqiū.
In the ninth year,
the Dí defeated us at Kuài.
They sent Wú Qǐ to attack Qí,
reaching Língqiū.
King Wēi of Qí had just ascended.
In the eleventh year,
together with Hán
and Zhào, they divided the land of Jìn into three parts,
extinguishing its later line.
In the thirteenth year,
Duke Xiàn of Qín established the county of Yuèyáng.
In the fifteenth year,
they defeated Zhào at Běilìn.
In the sixteenth year,
they attacked Chǔ,
capturing Lǔyáng.
Marquis Wǔ died,
and his son Yīng succeeded him,
known as King Huì.
In the first year of King Huì,
earlier, when Marquis Wǔ died,
his son Yīng and Gōngzhōng Huǎn contended for the heir apparentship.
Gōngsūn Qí went from Sòng to Zhào,
and from Zhào to Hán,
and said to Marquis Yì of Hán:
"Yīng of Wèi and Gōngzhōng Huǎn are contending for the heir apparentship;
have you heard of it?
Now Yīng of Wèi has obtained Wáng Cuò,
controls Shàngdǎng,
and firmly holds half the state.
If we take advantage of this to eliminate him,
we can certainly crush Wèi;
we must not miss this opportunity."
Marquis Yì was pleased,
and joined forces with Marquis Chéng of Zhào to attack Wèi,
battling at Zhuózé,
where the Wèi forces were badly defeated,
and the ruler of Wèi was besieged.
Zhào said to Hán:
"Let us remove the ruler of Wèi,
install Gōngzhōng Huǎn,
take some territory and withdraw;
that would benefit us."
Hán said:
"That will not do.
If we kill the ruler of Wèi,
people will call us brutal;
if we take territory and withdraw,
people will call us greedy.
It is better to divide it into two.
If Wèi is split in two,
it will be no stronger than Sòng
or Wèi, and we will never have to worry about Wèi again."
Zhào would not listen.
Hán, displeased,
withdrew its troops by night.
The reason King Huì did not die
and his state was not divided
was that the plans of the two states did not align.
Had they followed the plan of one state,
Wèi would surely have been divided.
Hence the saying,
"If a ruler has no designated heir,
his state can be destroyed."
In the second year,
Wei defeated Hán at Mǎlíng,
and defeated Zhào at Huái.
In the third year,
Qí defeated us at Guān.
In the fifth year,
we met with Hán at Zháiyáng.
We fortified Wǔdǔ.
We were defeated by Qín.
In the sixth year,
we attacked and captured Sòng's Yítái.
In the ninth year,
we attacked and defeated Hán at Kuài.
We battled Qín at Shǎoliáng,
where our general Gōngsūn Cuó was captured,
and Páng was taken.
Duke Xiàn of Qín died,
and his son Duke Xiào ascended the throne.
In the tenth year,
we attacked and captured Zhào's Píláo.
A comet appeared.
In the twelfth year,
a star fell during the day,
and there was a sound.
In the fourteenth year,
we met with Zhào at Hào.
In the fifteenth year,
the rulers of Lǔ, Wèi,
Sòng, and Zhèng came to court.
In the sixteenth year,
we met with Duke Xiào of Qín at Dùpíng.
We invaded Sòng's Huángchí,
but Sòng retook it.
In the seventeenth year,
we battled Qín at Yuánlǐ,
and Qín took our Shǎoliáng.
We besieged Zhào's Hándān.
In the eighteenth year,
we captured Hándān.
Zhào sought help from Qí,
and Qí sent Tián Jì
and Sūn Bìn to rescue Zhào,
defeating Wei at Guìlíng.
In the nineteenth year,
the feudal lords besieged our Xiānglíng.
We built a long wall,
and fortified Gùyáng.
In the twentieth year,
we returned Hándān to Zhào,
and formed an alliance on the banks of the Zhāng River.
In the twenty-first year,
we met with Qín at Tóng.
Marquis Chéng of Zhào died.
In the twenty-eighth year,
King Wēi of Qí died.
The Lord of Zhōngshān became chancellor of Wei.
In the thirtieth year,
Wei attacked Zhào,
and Zhào urgently appealed to Qí.
King Xuān of Qí employed Sūnzǐ's strategy,
rescuing Zhào and attacking Wei.
Wei then raised a large army,
appointing Páng Juān as general,
and making Crown Prince Shēn the supreme general.
Passing by Wàihuáng,
Xúzǐ of Wàihuáng said to the crown prince:
"I have a strategy for winning every battle."
The crown prince said:
"May I hear it?"
The guest said:
"I am indeed willing to offer it."
He said:
"If you personally lead the attack on Qí,
achieve a great victory and annex Jǔ,
your wealth will not exceed possessing Wei,
and your honor will not surpass being king.
But if you do not defeat Qí in battle,
then for ten thousand generations, Wei will be lost.
This is my strategy for winning every battle."
The crown prince said:
"Very well,
I will surely follow your advice and turn back."
The guest said:
"Even if you wish to turn back, Crown Prince,
it may not be possible.
Those who urge you to attack and fight,
hoping to sip the broth, are many.
Even if you wish to turn back,
I fear it may not be possible."
The crown prince thus intended to return,
but his charioteer said:
"To turn back after setting out to battle
is the same as defeat."
The crown prince indeed battled the men of Qí,
and was defeated at Mǎlíng.
Qí captured Wei's Crown Prince Shēn,
killed General Juān,
and the army was utterly defeated.
In the thirty-first year,
Qín, Zhào,
and Qí jointly attacked us.
Qín's general, Lord Shāng, deceived our general, Prince Áng, and launched a surprise attack, capturing his army,
and defeating it.
Qín, employing Lord Shāng,
expanded its territory eastward to the river,
while Qí
and Zhào repeatedly defeated us.
Ānyì was close to Qín,
so we moved the capital to Dàliáng.
We made Prince Hè the crown prince.
In the thirty-third year,
Duke Xiào of Qín died,
and Lord Shāng fled Qín and returned to Wei.
Wei was angered
and did not admit him.
In the thirty-fifth year,
we met with King Xuān of Qí south of Píng'ē.
King Huì had repeatedly suffered military defeats,
and with humble rites and rich gifts, he sought to recruit worthy men.
Zōu Yǎn,
Chúnyú Kūn,
and Mèng Kē all came to Liáng.
King Huì of Liáng said:
"I am unworthy,
having been defeated three times in external campaigns,
with my crown prince captured,
my supreme general dead,
and the state left empty and weakened,
bringing shame to the ancestral temples and altars of my predecessors.
I am deeply ashamed of this.
You, sir, have not minded the long journey,
graciously coming to the court of my humble state.
What advice do you have to benefit my country?"
Mèng Kē said:
"Your Majesty should not speak of benefit in this way.
For if the ruler seeks benefit, then the great officers will seek benefit;
if the great officers seek benefit, then the common people will seek benefit;
when high and low contend for benefit,
the state will be in danger.
As a ruler,
one should only practice benevolence and righteousness.
Why speak of benefit!"
In the thirty-sixth year,
we again met with the King of Qí at Juàn.
That year,
King Huì died,
and his son King Xiāng ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Xiāng,
we met with the feudal lords at Xúzhōu,
where we acknowledged each other as kings.
We posthumously honored his father, King Huì, as king.
In the fifth year,
Qín defeated our army of 45,000 under Lóng Jiǎ at Diāoyīn,
and besieged our Jiāo
and Qūwò.
We ceded the land west of the river to Qín.
In the sixth year,
we met with Qín at Yīng.
Qín took our Fényīn,
Píshì,
and Jiāo. Wei attacked Chǔ,
defeating them at Xíngshān.
In the seventh year,
Wei completely surrendered Shàngjùn to Qín.
Qín captured our Púyáng.
In the eighth year,
Qín returned our Jiāo
and Qūwò.
In the twelfth year,
Chǔ defeated us at Xiānglíng.
The chief ministers of the feudal lords met with Qín's chancellor Zhāng Yí at Nièsāng.
In the thirteenth year,
Zhāng Yí became chancellor of Wei.
In Wei, a woman transformed into a man.
Qín took our Qūwò
and Píngzhōu.
In the sixteenth year,
King Xiāng died,
and his son King Āi ascended the throne.
Zhāng Yí returned to Qín.
In the first year of King Āi,
five states jointly attacked Qín,
but withdrew without victory.
In the second year,
Qí defeated us at Guānjīn.
In the fifth year,
Qín sent Chūlǐzǐ to attack and capture our Qūwò,
driving Xīshǒu to Ànmén.
In the sixth year,
Qín came to install Prince Zhèng as crown prince.
We met with Qín at Línjìn.
In the seventh year,
we attacked Qí.
Together with Qín, we attacked Yān.
In the eighth year,
we attacked Wèi,
capturing two cities in succession.
The ruler of Wèi was troubled by this.
Rú Ěr went to see the ruler of Wèi and said:
"May I request to disband Wèi's troops,
and have Chénglíng Jūn dismissed, is that acceptable?"
The ruler of Wèi said:
"If you, sir, can truly accomplish this,
I pledge that Wèi will serve you, sir, for generations."
Rú Ěr went to see Chénglíng Jūn and said:
"In the past, when Wèi attacked Zhào,
it cut off Yángcháng,
captured Èyǔ,
and nearly divided Zhào,
splitting it into two parts.
The reason Zhào did not perish
was because Wèi was the leader of the alliance.
Now Wèi is on the verge of destruction,
and is about to seek service with Qín in the west.
Rather than having Qín release Wèi,
it would be better for Wèi to release Wèi itself.
Wèi's gratitude toward Wèi would surely be endless."
Chénglíng Jūn said:
"Agreed."
Rú Ěr went to see the King of Wèi and said:
"I have a report concerning Wèi.
Wèi was originally a branch of the Zhōu house,
and though it is called a small state,
it possesses many precious vessels.
Now that the state is facing difficulties and the precious vessels have not been presented,
it is because they believe that whether Wèi is attacked or released is not decided by Your Majesty,
so even if the vessels were presented, they would not reach Your Majesty.
I privately surmise that
whoever first proposes to release Wèi will be the one to receive Wèi's favor."
After Rú Ěr left,
Chénglíng Jūn entered,
and presented his proposal to the King of Wèi.
The King of Wèi listened to his argument,
withdrew his troops,
dismissed Chénglíng Jūn,
and never saw him again.
In the ninth year,
we met with the King of Qín at Línjìn.
Zhāng Yí
and Wèi Zhāng both returned to Wèi.
The Wèi chancellor Tián Xū died,
and Chǔ was wary of Zhāng Yí,
Xīshǒu,
and Xuē Gōng.
The Chǔ chancellor Zhāo Yú said to Sū Dài:
"Now that Tián Xū has died,
I fear that one among Zhāng Yí,
Xīshǒu,
or Xuē Gōng will become chancellor of Wèi."
Dài said:
"Then whom do you wish to be chancellor, and how can it be convenient for you, sir?"
Zhāo Yú said:
"I want the crown prince to serve as his own chancellor."
Dài said:
"Allow me to go north for you,
and I will surely have him appointed."
Zhāo Yú said:
"How will you do it?"
He replied:
"You, sir, play the part of the King of Liáng,
and I will try to persuade you."
Zhāo Yú said:
"How?"
He replied:
"I, Dài, have come from Chǔ,
and Zhāo Yú is very worried,
saying:
'Now that Tián Xū has died,
I fear that one among Zhāng Yí,
Xīshǒu,
or Xuē Gōng will become chancellor of Wèi.'
Dài said:
'The King of Liáng
is a mature ruler,
and will surely not appoint Zhāng Yí as chancellor.
If Zhāng Yí becomes chancellor,
he will certainly favor Qín and neglect Wèi.
If Xīshǒu becomes chancellor,
he will certainly favor Hán and neglect Wèi.
If Xuē Gōng becomes chancellor,
he will certainly favor Qí and neglect Wèi.
The King of Liáng,
being a mature ruler,
will surely find none of them convenient.'
The king said:
'Then whom should I appoint as chancellor?'
Dài said:
'None is better than the crown prince serving as his own chancellor.
If the crown prince serves as his own chancellor,
these three men will all consider the crown prince as an unusual chancellor,
and each will strive to serve Wèi with the affairs of their own states,
wishing to obtain the chancellor's seal.
With Wèi's strength,
and the support of three states with ten thousand chariots each,
Wèi will surely be secure.
Therefore, I say none is better than the crown prince serving as his own chancellor.'"
Thereupon, he went north to see the King of Liáng,
and reported this to him.
The crown prince indeed became chancellor of Wèi.
In the tenth year,
Zhāng Yí died.
In the eleventh year,
we met with King Wǔ of Qín at Yìng.
In the twelfth year,
the crown prince paid a court visit to Qín.
Qín came to attack our Píshì,
but withdrew before capturing it.
In the fourteenth year,
Qín returned King Wǔ's queen to us.
In the sixteenth year,
Qín captured our Púfǎn,
Yángjìn,
and Fēnglíng.
In the seventeenth year,
we met with Qín at Línjìn.
Qín returned Púfǎn to us.
In the eighteenth year,
together with Qín, we attacked Chǔ.
In the twenty-first year,
together with Qí
and Hán, we defeated the Qín army at Hángǔ.
In the twenty-third year,
Qín again returned to us the territory east of the Yellow River and Fēnglíng to make peace.
King Āi died,
and his son King Zhāo ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Zhāo,
Qín captured our Xiāngchéng.
In the second year,
we battled Qín,
and the outcome was unfavorable for us.
In the third year,
we assisted Hán in attacking Qín,
and the Qín general Bái Qǐ defeated our army of 240,000 at Yīquē.
In the sixth year,
we gave Qín a territory of 400 lǐ east of the Yellow River.
Máng Mǎo gained prominence through deceit.
In the seventh year,
Qín captured 61 cities of ours, large and small.
In the eighth year,
King Zhāo of Qín declared himself Emperor of the West,
while King Mǐn of Qí declared himself Emperor of the East.
After over a month,
both reverted to calling themselves kings and abandoned the title of emperor.
In the ninth year,
Qín captured our cities of Xīnyuán
and Qūyáng.
In the tenth year,
Qí annihilated Sòng,
and the King of Sòng died in our Wēn.
In the twelfth year,
together with Qín,
Zhào, Hán,
and Yān, we attacked Qí,
defeating them west of the Jì River,
and King Mǐn fled into exile.
Yān alone entered Línzī.
We met with the King of Qín in Western Zhōu.
In the thirteenth year,
Qín captured our Ānchéng.
Their troops reached Dàliáng,
then withdrew. In the eighteenth year,
Qín captured Yǐng,
and the King of Chǔ moved the capital to Chén.
In the nineteenth year,
King Zhāo died,
and his son King Ānxī ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Ān Lí's reign,
Qin captured two of our cities.
In the second year,
they took another two cities,
stationed troops beneath Dàliáng,
Hán came to rescue us,
and we gave Qin Wēn to make peace.
In the third year,
Qin seized four of our cities,
beheading forty thousand.
In the fourth year,
Qin defeated us along with Hán
and Zhào, killing one hundred fifty thousand troops,
and drove away our general Máng Mǎo.
The Wèi general Duàngānzǐ requested to give Qin Nányáng to sue for peace.
Sū Dài said to the King of Wèi:
"The one who desires the seal is Duàngānzǐ,
and the one who desires land is Qin.
Now Your Majesty lets the land-desirer control the seal,
and lets the seal-desirer control the land;
if the land of the Wèi clan is not exhausted, it will not stop.
Moreover, to serve Qin with land
is like carrying firewood to extinguish a fire—
if the firewood is not exhausted,
the fire will not go out."
The king said:
"That is indeed so.
However,
the matter has already begun,
and cannot be changed."
In reply, he said:
"Does Your Majesty not see why the xiāo piece is valued in the board game?
When advantageous, it captures;
when not, it stops.
Now Your Majesty says
'the matter has already begun,
and cannot be changed'—
how is it that Your Majesty's use of wisdom is inferior to using the xiāo piece?"
In the ninth year,
Qin captured our Huái.
In the tenth year,
the crown prince of Qin, who was a hostage in Wèi, died.
In the eleventh year,
Qin took our Cīqiū.
King Zhāo of Qin said to his attendants:
"Are Hán and
Wèi stronger now or at the beginning?"
They replied:
"Not as strong as at the beginning."
The king said:
"Are Rú Ěr and
Wèi Qí now more capable than Mèng Cháng and
Máng Mǎo?"
They replied:
"They are not."
The king said:
"With the capability of Mèng Cháng and
Máng Mǎo,
leading strong Hán and
Wèi to attack Qin,
they still could do nothing to me.
Now with the incapable Rú Ěr and
Wèi Qí leading weak Hán and
Wèi to attack Qin,
it is clear they can do nothing to me either."
The attendants all said:
"Very true."
Zhōng Qí leaned on his qín and replied:
"Your Majesty's assessment of the world is mistaken.
At the time of the six ministers of Jìn,
the Zhì clan was the strongest,
destroyed Fàn and
Zhōngháng,
and then led the troops of Hán and
Wèi to besiege Zhào Xiāngzǐ in Jìnyáng,
diverting the Jìn River to flood Jìnyáng's walls,
leaving only three boards' height unsubmerged.
Zhì Bó was inspecting the water,
with Wèi Huánzǐ driving,
and Hán Kāngzǐ as the second rider.
Zhì Bó said:
'I did not know before that water could destroy a state,
but now I know.'
The Fén River could flood Ānyì,
and the Jiàng River could flood Píngyáng.
Wèi Huánzǐ nudged Hán Kāngzǐ with his elbow,
Hán Kāngzǐ stepped on Wèi Huánzǐ's foot,
their elbows and feet connecting in the chariot,
and thus the Zhì clan's lands were divided,
he died, his state perished,
and became the laughingstock of the world.
Now Qin's army, though strong,
cannot surpass the Zhì clan;
Hán and Wèi, though weak,
are still better off than they were under Jìnyáng.
This is the time for them to use their elbows and feet;
I hope Your Majesty will not take it lightly!"
Then the King of Qin became fearful.
Qí and
Chǔ allied to attack Wèi,
Wèi sent envoys to seek rescue from Qin,
with carriages and envoys in constant view,
yet Qin's rescue did not come.
A man of Wèi named Táng Jū,
over ninety years old,
said to the King of Wèi:
"This old minister requests to go west and persuade the King of Qin,
to have troops depart before I return."
The King of Wèi bowed twice,
then prepared a carriage and sent him off.
Táng Jū arrived,
and entered to see the King of Qin.
The King of Qin said:
"Sir, you have come all this way wearily,
it must have been very hard!
Wèi has sought help many times,
I already know of Wèi's urgency."
Táng Jū replied:
"Since Your Majesty knows Wèi's urgency yet sends no rescue,
I privately think your strategy ministers are incompetent.
Wèi,
a state of ten thousand chariots,
yet faces west to serve Qin,
calls itself an eastern vassal,
receives caps and girdles,
and offers seasonal sacrifices—
all because Qin's strength suffices as an ally.
Now the troops of Qí and
Chǔ have joined at Wèi's outskirts,
yet Qin sends no rescue;
it must be relying on Wèi not being in extreme distress.
But if it is driven to great urgency,
it will cede land and form a vertical alliance;
what rescue will Your Majesty have then?
If you wait until it is urgent to rescue it,
you will lose an eastern vassal in Wèi and strengthen two enemies, Qí and
Chǔ—what benefit is that to Your Majesty?"
Thereupon King Zhāo of Qin immediately sent troops to rescue Wèi.
The Wèi clan was stabilized again.
Zhào sent a man to tell the King of Wèi:
"Kill Fàn Cuó for me,
and I will offer seventy lǐ of land."
The King of Wèi said:
"Agreed."
He sent officials to arrest him,
surrounding but not yet killing him.
Cuó then climbed onto the roof, straddling the ridge,
and said to the envoy:
"Rather than trading my dead self,
better trade me alive.
If I die,
and Zhào does not give the king the land,
what will the king do then?
So it would be better to first settle the land cession,
then kill me."
The King of Wèi said:
"Good."
Cuó then wrote a letter to Lord Xìnlíng:
"Cuó
is the former dismissed minister of Wèi;
if Zhào uses land to have me killed and the King of Wèi complies,
what if powerful Qin follows Zhào's desire—
what will you do then?"
Lord Xìnlíng spoke to the king and had him released.
The King of Wèi, because of Qin's rescue,
wished to ally with Qin and attack Hán,
to recover former territory.
Wújì said to the King of Wèi:
"Qin shares customs with the Róng and Dí tribes,
has the heart of a tiger or wolf,
greedy, cruel, fond of profit, untrustworthy,
and ignorant of ritual, righteousness, virtue, and conduct.
If there is profit to be had,
they disregard kin and brothers,
like birds and beasts—
this is known throughout the world,
for they have not bestowed kindness or accumulated virtue.
Thus, the queen dowager was his mother,
yet she died of sorrow;
the Marquess of Ráng was his uncle,
with no greater merits,
yet he was eventually banished;
his two younger brothers were innocent,
yet he repeatedly seized their states.
Such is his treatment of relatives—
how much more for a rival state?
Now if Your Majesty joins Qin to attack Hán and draws closer to Qin's menace,
I am deeply perplexed.
If Your Majesty does not recognize this, it is unwise;
if none of your ministers inform you, it is disloyal."
Now the Hán clan relies on a woman serving a weak ruler,
with great turmoil internally,
and externally facing the troops of powerful Qín and Wèi,
does Your Majesty think it will not perish?
If Hán perishes,
Qín will possess the territory of Zhèng,
bordering Liáng and Yè,
does Your Majesty consider that safe?
Your Majesty desires to recover former lands,
but now bears the hostility of powerful Qín,
does Your Majesty see that as beneficial?
Qín is not a state without ambitions;
after Hán's demise, it will certainly turn to new ventures,
and in seeking new ventures, it will inevitably choose the easy and profitable,
and in choosing the easy and profitable, it will surely not attack Chǔ and Zhào.
Why is that?
To cross mountains and rivers,
cut through Hán's Shàngdǎng to attack strong Zhào,
would be to repeat the events of Èyǔ,
which Qín certainly will not do.
If taking the route through Hénèi,
bypassing Yè
and Zhāogē,
crossing the Zhāng and Fǔ rivers,
to engage Zhào's army in the outskirts of Hándān,
that would invite the disaster of Zhì Bó,
and Qín would not dare.
To attack Chǔ,
passing through Shègǔ,
marching three thousand lǐ,
and assaulting the fortress of Míng'è,
the march is very long,
the attack very difficult,
and Qín will not do that either.
If taking the route through Héwài,
bypassing Dàliáng,
skirting Yòu, Shàngcài,
and Shàolíng,
to engage Chǔ's army in the outskirts of Chén,
Qín would not dare.
Therefore, it is said Qín certainly will not attack Chǔ and Zhào,
nor will it attack Wèi and Qí.
After Hán perishes,
on the day its troops march out,
if not against Wèi, there will be no one else to attack.
Qín already holds Huái,
Máo, and Xīngqiū,
and has fortified Guǐjīn to approach Hénèi,
so Gòng
and Jí in Hénèi will surely be in danger;
possessing Zhèng's territory,
obtaining Yuányōng,
it could breach the Yíngzé waters to flood Dàliáng,
and Dàliáng would surely fall.
Your Majesty's envoy, on his mission, spoke ill of Ānlíngshì to Qín,
and Qín has long desired to destroy it.
Qín's Yèyáng,
Kūnyáng border Wǔyáng,
and hearing the envoy's slander,
they will follow Ānlíngshì to its demise,
circling north of Wǔyáng,
to approach Xǔ from the east,
and the southern state will be endangered,
is the state not harmed?
To despise Hán and not care for Ānlíngshì is acceptable,
but not to worry about Qín's lack of love for the southern state is wrong.
In the past,
when Qín was west of the river in Jìn,
its state was a thousand lǐ from Liáng,
separated by rivers and mountains,
with Zhōu and Hán in between.
From the campaign at Línxiāng to the present,
Qín has attacked Wèi seven times,
entered the Yòuzhōng five times,
captured all border cities,
destroyed Wéntái,
burned Chuídū,
felled forests,
slaughtered all deer,
and the state was subsequently besieged.
It also drove straight north of Liáng,
east to the outskirts of Táo and Wèi,
north to Píng and Jiān.
What was lost to Qín,
south and north of the mountains,
Héwài and Hénèi,
amounted to several dozen large counties,
and hundreds of famous cities.
When Qín was west of the river in Jìn,
a thousand lǐ from Liáng,
the calamity was such.
How much more if Qín, with no Hán,
possesses Zhèng's territory,
with no rivers or mountains to block it,
no Zhōu or Hán to separate it,
only a hundred lǐ from Dàliáng,
disaster will surely arise from this.
In the past,
the alliance did not succeed,
because Chǔ and Wèi were suspicious and Hán could not be won over.
Now Hán has been under attack for three years,
Qín pressures it to negotiate,
but Hán, recognizing its potential demise, does not comply,
instead sending a hostage to Zhào,
requesting to lead the charge for all under heaven,
so Chǔ and Zhào will surely gather troops,
all aware that Qín's desires are endless,
and it will not stop
until it has destroyed all states under heaven and subjugated the lands within the seas.
Therefore, I wish to advise Your Majesty,
to quickly accept the covenant with Chǔ and Zhào,
and by leveraging Hán's hostage to preserve Hán,
and seek the return of former lands,
Hán will surely comply.
This way, the people are not wearied and former lands are regained,
an achievement greater than jointly attacking Hán with Qín,
and avoiding the calamity of bordering powerful Qín.
To preserve Hán, secure Wèi, and benefit all under heaven,
this is also Your Majesty's opportune moment.
Connect Hán's Shàngdǎng to Gòng
and Níng, establishing a route through Ānchéng,
and levy taxes on passage,
thus Wèi effectively holds Hán's Shàngdǎng as a pledge.
Now with these taxes,
the state can be enriched sufficiently.
Hán will surely be grateful, love, respect, and fear Wèi,
and will not dare rebel against Wèi,
making Hán like a county of Wèi.
If Wèi gains Hán as a county,
Wèi, Dàliáng,
and Héwài will surely be secure.
If Hán is not preserved now,
Èrzhōu
and Ānlíng will be in danger,
Chǔ and Zhào severely defeated,
Wèi and Qí greatly fearful,
and soon all under heaven will turn west to rush into Qín, paying homage and becoming its subjects.
In the twentieth year,
Qín besieged Hándān,
and Lord Xìnlíng Wújì seized command from General Jìn Bǐ by deceit to rescue Zhào,
thus preserving Zhào.
Wújì then remained in Zhào.
In the twenty-sixth year,
King Zhāo of Qín died.
In the thirtieth year,
Wújì returned to Wèi,
leading the armies of five states to attack Qín,
defeating them at Héwài,
and driving back Méng Áo.
The Wèi crown prince Zēng was a hostage in Qín,
and Qín, angered,
intended to imprison him.
Someone advised the King of Qín on Zēng's behalf:
"Gōngsūn Xǐ surely told the Wèi chancellor,
'Request that Wèi swiftly attack Qín,
the King of Qín will be angered,
and will imprison Zēng.
The King of Wèi will also be angered,
and attack Qín,
causing Qín harm.'
Now if Your Majesty imprisons Zēng,
it would fulfill Xǐ's scheme.
So it is better to honor Zēng and reconcile with Wèi,
to sow doubt with Qí
and Hán."
Qín then released Zēng.
In the thirty-first year,
King Zhèng of Qín first ascended the throne.
In the thirty-fourth year,
King Ānxī died,
and Crown Prince Zēng succeeded him,
known as King Jǐngmǐn.
Lord Xìnlíng Wújì died.
In the first year of King Jǐngmǐn,
Qín captured twenty of our cities,
establishing the Qín's Eastern Commandery.
In the second year,
Qín captured our Zhāogē.
Wèi moved to Yěwáng.
In the third year,
Qín captured our Jí.
In the fifth year,
Qín captured our Yuán,
Pǔyáng,
and Yǎn. In the fifteenth year,
King Jǐngmǐn died,
and his son, King Jiǎ, succeeded him.
In the first year of King Jiǎ's reign,
Yān Crown Prince Dān sent Jīng Kē to assassinate the King of Qín,
but the King of Qín detected it.
In the third year,
Qín flooded Dàliáng,
captured King Jiǎ,
and subsequently destroyed Wèi, turning it into commaderies and counties.
Grand Historian comments:
"I visited the ruins of old Dàliáng,
where people in the ruins said:
'When Qín destroyed Liáng,
they channeled the Hé River's canal to flood Dàliáng.
After three months the city walls crumbled,
the king requested to surrender,
and thus Wèi was destroyed.'
Commentators all say that because Wèi did not employ Lord Xìnlíng,
the state weakened until it perished,
but I believe otherwise.
Heaven was then ordering Qín to pacify the realm,
and their enterprise was not yet complete.
Even if Wèi had obtained assistance as capable as Āhéng's,
what benefit would it have been?
Hán's ancestors shared the same surname as Zhōu,
the surname Jī.
Later descendants served Jìn,
were enfeoffed at Hányuán,
and called Lord Wǔ of Hán.
Three generations after Lord Wǔ there was Hán Jué,
who took his fief's name as the clan name Hán.
Hán Jué,
in the third year of Jìn Duke Jǐng,
when Jìn Minister of Justice Tú'àn Gǔ was about to rebel,
and execute Zhào Dùn, the assassin of Duke Líng.
Zhào Dùn had already died,
so he sought to kill his son Zhào Shuò.
Hán Jué tried to stop Gǔ,
but Gǔ would not listen.
Jué informed Zhào Shuò and urged him to flee.
Shuò said:
"If you can ensure the Zhào lineage is not extinguished,
I will die without regret."
Hán Jué promised him.
When Gǔ exterminated the Zhào clan,
Jué claimed illness and did not appear.
When Chéng Yīng
and Gōngsūn Chǔjiù hid the Zhào orphan Zhào Wǔ,
Jué knew about it.
In the eleventh year of Duke Jǐng,
Jué and Xì Kè led an army of eight hundred chariots to attack Qí,
defeated Qí Duke Qìng at Ān,
and captured Féng Chǒufù.
Then Jìn established six ministers,
and Hán Jué held one minister position,
styled as Lord Xiàn.
In the seventeenth year of Jìn Duke Jǐng,
he fell ill, and divination showed it was a haunt by unfulfilled descendants of Dàyè.
Hán Jué spoke of Zhào Chéngjì's achievements,
and that he now had no posterity,
to move Duke Jǐng.
Duke Jǐng asked:
"Does he still have heirs?"
Jué then told him about Zhào Wǔ,
and restored the former Zhào lands and towns,
continuing the Zhào lineage sacrifices.
In the seventh year of Jìn Duke Dào,
Hán Lord Xiàn was aged.
Lord Xiàn died,
and his son Lord Xuān succeeded him.
Lord Xuān moved to reside at Zhōu.
In the fourteenth year of Jìn Duke Píng,
Wú Jì Zhá visited Jìn,
and said:
"Jìn's governance will eventually pass to Hán,
Wèi, and Zhào."
In the twelfth year of Jìn Duke Qǐng,
Hán Lord Xuān together with Zhào
and Wèi divided ten counties of the Qí
and Yángshé clans.
In the fifteenth year of Jìn Duke Dìng,
Lord Xuān and Zhào Jiǎnzǐ invaded and attacked the Fàn
and Zhōngháng clans.
Lord Xuān died,
and his son Lord Zhēn succeeded.
Lord Zhēn moved to reside at Píngyáng.
Lord Zhēn died,
and his son Lord Jiǎn succeeded.
Lord Jiǎn died,
and his son Lord Zhuāng succeeded.
Lord Zhuāng died,
and his son Lord Kāng succeeded.
Lord Kāng together with Zhào Lord Xiāng
and Wèi Lord Huán defeated Zhì Bó,
divided his territory,
their lands expanded,
larger than those of other lords.
Lord Kāng died,
and his son Lord Wǔ succeeded.
In the second year of Lord Wǔ,
he attacked Zhèng,
and killed its ruler Duke Yōu.
In the sixteenth year,
Lord Wǔ died,
and his son Jǐng Hóu ascended.
In the first year of Jǐng Hóu Qián,
he attacked Zhèng,
and captured Yōngqiū.
In the second year,
Zhèng defeated us at Fùshǔ.
In the sixth year,
together with Zhào
and Wèi, they all gained ranking as feudal lords.
In the ninth year,
Zhèng besieged our Yángzhái.
Jǐng Hóu died,
and his son Liè Hóu Qǔ ascended.
In the third year of Liè Hóu,
Niè Zhèng killed Hán's minister Xiá Lěi.
In the ninth year,
Qín attacked our Yíyáng,
capturing six towns.
In the thirteenth year,
Liè Hóu died,
and his son Wén Hóu ascended.
That year, Wèi Wén Hóu died.
In the second year of Wén Hóu,
he attacked Zhèng,
capturing Yángchéng.
He attacked Sòng,
reached Péngchéng,
and captured the Sòng ruler.
In the seventh year,
he attacked Qí,
reaching Sāngqiū.
Zhèng rebelled against Jìn.
In the ninth year,
he attacked Qí,
reaching Língqiū.
In the tenth year,
Wén Hóu died,
and his son Āi Hóu ascended.
In the first year of Āi Hóu,
together with Zhào
and Wèi, they partitioned the state of Jìn.
In the second year,
they destroyed Zhèng,
and consequently moved the capital to Zhèng.
In the sixth year,
Hán Yán assassinated his ruler Āi Hóu,
and his son Yì Hóu ascended.
In the second year of Yì Hóu,
Wèi defeated us at Mǎlíng.
In the fifth year,
he met with Wèi King Huì at Zháiyáng.
In the ninth year,
Wèi defeated us at Kuài.
In the twelfth year,
Yì Hóu died,
and his son Zhāo Hóu ascended.
In the first year of Zhāo Hóu,
Qín defeated us at the Western Mountains.
In the second year,
Sòng captured our Huángchí.
Wèi captured Zhū.
In the sixth year,
he attacked Eastern Zhōu,
capturing Língguàn
and Xíngqiū.
In the eighth year,
Shēn Bùhài became chancellor of Hán,
cultivated statecraft and implemented his doctrines,
the state was thereby well-governed,
and other feudal lords did not come to invade.
In the tenth year,
Hán Jī assassinated his ruler Duke Dào.
In the eleventh year,
Zhāo Hóu went to Qín.
In the twenty-second year,
Shēn Bùhài died.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Qín came and captured our Yíyáng.
In the twenty-fifth year,
there was a drought, and the high gate was built.
Qū Yíjiù said:
"Marquis Zhāo will not pass through this gate.
Why?
