Because the timing is wrong.
What I call timing
is not about days or hours;
people inherently have favorable and unfavorable times.
Marquis Zhāo once had favorable times,
yet he did not build a high gate.
Last year Qín captured Yíyáng,
this year there is drought,
Marquis Zhāo does not use this time to relieve the people's distress,
but instead increases his extravagance.
This is what is called
'acting lavishly when times are strained'."
In the twenty-sixth year,
the high gate was completed,
Marquis Zhāo died,
and indeed did not pass through this gate.
His son King Xuānhuì ascended the throne.
In the fifth year of King Xuānhuì,
Zhāng Yí became chancellor of Qín.
In the eighth year,
Wèi defeated our general Hán Jǔ.
In the eleventh year,
the ruler assumed the title of king.
He met with Zhào at Qūshǔ.
In the fourteenth year,
Qín attacked and defeated us at Yān.
In the sixteenth year,
Qín defeated us at Xiūyú,
capturing the Hán generals Sōu
and Shēn Chāi at Zhuózé.
The Hán house was in crisis,
Gōngzhòng said to the King of Hán:
"Allied states cannot be relied upon.
Now Qín has long desired to attack Chǔ,
Your Majesty should rather seek peace with Qín through Zhāng Yí,
bribing them with one major city,
equipping armor,
and joining them in attacking Chǔ to the south.
This is a plan to exchange one for two."
The King of Hán said:
"Good."
Then he alerted Gōngzhòng for the journey,
preparing to seek an agreement with Qín in the west.
The King of Chǔ heard this and was greatly alarmed,
summoning Chén Zhěn to inform him.
Chén Zhěn said:
"Qín has long wanted to attack Chǔ,
now they additionally get one major city from Hán with equipped armor,
Qín and Hán combining forces to attack Chǔ,
this is what Qín prays and seeks for.
Now that they have obtained it,
Chǔ will certainly be attacked.
If Your Majesty follows my advice, alert the entire borders,
raise troops claiming to rescue Hán,
order the war chariots to fill the roads,
dispatch trusted envoys,
increase their chariots,
make their gifts substantial,
to make Hán believe Your Majesty is rescuing them.
Even if Hán does not heed us,
Hán will surely be grateful to Your Majesty,
and certainly not march in goose formation to come;
thus Qín and Hán will be at odds,
and even if troops arrive,
Chǔ will not suffer greatly.
If they can heed us and break peace with Qín,
Qín will surely be furious,
greatly resenting Hán.
When Hán allies with Chǔ to the south,
they will surely轻视 Qín;
轻视 Qín,
their response to Qín will surely be disrespectful:
this is how to use Qín
and Hán's troops to avert Chǔ's calamity."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Good."
Then he alerted the entire borders,
raised troops claiming to rescue Hán.
He ordered the war chariots to fill the roads,
dispatched trusted envoys,
increased their chariots,
made their gifts substantial.
He said to the King of Hán:
"Though my state is small,
I have already mobilized all forces.
I hope your great state will proceed with determination against Qín,
I will sacrifice Chǔ for Hán."
The King of Hán heard this and was greatly pleased,
so he stopped Gōngzhòng's mission.
Gōngzhòng said:
"This cannot be.
The one who truly attacks us is Qín,
the one who saves us with empty fame is Chǔ.
Your Majesty relies on Chǔ's empty fame,
and lightly breaks with powerful Qín as an enemy,
Your Majesty will surely be laughed at by the world.
Moreover, Chǔ and Hán are not brotherly states,
nor did they previously plan to attack Qín together.
Having already shown signs of attack,
they then send troops claiming to rescue Hán,
this must be Chén Zhěn's scheme.
Moreover, Your Majesty has already sent word to Qín,
now not to go through with it,
is to deceive Qín.
To lightly deceive powerful Qín and trust Chǔ's scheming minister,
I fear Your Majesty will surely regret it."
The King of Hán did not listen,
and broke with Qín.
Qín consequently was greatly angered,
added troops to attack Hán,
a great battle ensued,
but Chǔ's rescue did not reach Hán.
In the nineteenth year,
they greatly defeated us at Ànmén.
Prince Cāng was sent as a hostage to Qín to make peace.
In the twenty-first year,
we joined Qín in attacking Chǔ,
defeated the Chǔ general Qū Gài,
and decapitated eighty thousand at Dānyáng.
That year,
King Xuānhuì died,
Prince Cāng ascended the throne,
known as King Xiāng.
In the fourth year of King Xiāng,
he met with King Wǔ of Qín at Línjìn.
That autumn,
Qín sent Gān Mào to attack our Yíyáng.
In the fifth year,
Qín captured our Yíyáng,
decapitating sixty thousand.
King Wǔ of Qín died.
In the sixth year,
Qín returned Wǔsuì to us.
In the ninth year,
Qín again took our Wǔsuì.
In the tenth year,
Prince Yīng paid court to Qín and returned.
In the eleventh year,
Qín attacked us,
taking Rǎng.
We joined Qín in attacking Chǔ,
defeating the Chǔ general Táng Mò.
In the twelfth year,
Prince Yīng died.
Prince Jiù
and Prince Jǐshī contended for the heir apparent position.
At that time Jǐshī was a hostage in Chǔ.
Sū Dài said to Hán Jiù:
"Jǐshī has fled to Chǔ,
the King of Chǔ greatly wishes to install him.
Now Chǔ has over a hundred thousand troops outside Fāngchéng,
why don't you have the King of Chǔ build a city of ten thousand households next to Yōngshì,
Hán will surely raise troops to rescue it,
and you will certainly command them.
You can then use the Hán and Chǔ troops to support Jǐshī and install him,
he will surely heed you,
and will surely enfeoff you with Chǔ and Hán territories."
Hán Jiù followed this plan.
Chǔ besieged Yōngshì,
and Hán sought help from Qín.
Qín had not yet sent troops,
but sent Gōngsūn Mò into Hán.
Gōng Zhòng said:
"Do you believe Qín will rescue Hán?"
He replied:
"The King of Qín said,
'I request to march through Nánzhèng
and Lántián,
and dispatch troops against Chǔ to wait for you,'
but this likely will not come to pass."
Gōng Zhòng said:
"Do you think it will actually happen?"
He replied:
"The King of Qín will certainly follow the old strategy of Zhāng Yí.
When King Wēi of Chǔ attacked Liáng,
Zhāng Yí told the King of Qín:
'If we join Chǔ in attacking Wèi,
and Wèi is defeated and turns to Chǔ,
while Hán is naturally its ally,
then Qín will be isolated.
It would be better to send troops to intervene,
so that Wèi and Chǔ engage in a major battle,
and Qín can seize the lands west of the Yellow River and withdraw.'
Now, on the surface, they claim to support Hán,
but in reality, they are secretly friendly with Chǔ.
If you rely on Qín's intervention,
you will certainly lightly engage Chǔ in battle.
Chǔ, secretly aware that Qín is not committed,
will surely find it easy to confront you.
If you defeat Chǔ in battle,
Qín will then share the spoils with you,
benefiting from Sānchuān and then withdrawing.
If you do not defeat Chǔ,
Chǔ will block Sānchuān and defend it,
and you will be unable to save the situation.
I privately worry for you.
Sīmǎ Gěng made three trips to Yǐng,
and Gān Mào met Zhāo Yú at Shāngyú;
their talk of collecting seals
truly seems like they have an agreement."
Gōng Zhòng grew fearful,
and said:
"What should be done then?"
He replied:
"You must prioritize Hán over Qín,
and yourself over Zhāng Yí.
It would be best for you to quickly ally your state with Qí and Chǔ;
Qí and Chǔ will surely entrust their states to you.
What you detest is Zhāng Yí,
but in reality, it is not without Qín's involvement."
Thereupon, Chǔ lifted the siege of Yōngshì.
Sū Dài also said to Mǐ Róng, the younger brother of the Queen Dowager of Qín:
"Gōngshū Bóyīng fears that Qín and Chǔ might support Jǐshī,
so why don't you seek a hostage from Chǔ for Hán?
If the King of Chǔ agrees to send a hostage to Hán,
then Gōngshū Bóyīng will know that Qín and Chǔ do not concern themselves with Jǐshī,
and will certainly ally Hán with Qín and Chǔ.
Qín and Chǔ, with Hán's support, will pressure Wèi,
and Wèi will not dare to ally with Qí,
thus isolating Qí.
You then seek a hostage from Chǔ for Qín;
if Chǔ refuses,
it will create enmity with Hán.
Hán, with the support of Qí and Wèi, will besiege Chǔ,
and Chǔ will surely value you highly.
Leveraging the weight of Qín and Chǔ, you will accumulate virtue in Hán,
and Gōngshū Bóyīng will certainly treat you with the respect due to the state."
Thereupon, Jǐshī ultimately could not return to Hán.
Hán established Jiù as crown prince.
The kings of Qí and Wèi came.
In the fourteenth year,
Hán joined with Qí
and the King of Wèi to attack Qín,
marching as far as Hángǔ and encamping there.
In the sixteenth year,
Qín gave us the lands east of the Yellow River and Wǔsuì.
King Xiāng died,
and Crown Prince Jiù ascended the throne,
becoming King Xī.
In the third year of King Xī's reign,
he sent Gōngsūn Xǐ to lead Zhōu
and Wèi in an attack on Qín.
Qín defeated our army of 240,000,
and captured Xǐ at Yīquē.
In the fifth year,
Qín captured our Wǎn.
In the sixth year,
Hán ceded 200 lǐ of territory at Wǔsuì to Qín.
In the tenth year,
Qín defeated our army at Xiàshān.
In the twelfth year,
Hán met with King Zhāo of Qín in Western Zhōu and assisted Qín in attacking Qí.
Qí was defeated,
and King Mǐn fled into exile.
In the fourteenth year,
Hán met with Qín between the two Zhōu states.
In the twenty-first year,
Hán sent Bào Yuán to rescue Wèi,
but he was defeated by Qín,
and Yuán fled to Kāifēng.
In the twenty-third year,
Zhào and Wèi attacked our Huáyáng.
Hán urgently sought help from Qín,
but Qín did not send aid.
The Chancellor of Hán said to Chén Shì:
"The situation is critical;
though you are ill,
I hope you can make a one-night journey."
Chén Shì went to see the Marquis of Ráng.
The Marquis of Ráng said:
"Is the situation critical?
That is why they sent you."
Chén Shì said:
"It is not critical yet."
The Marquis of Ráng angrily said:
"How can you be entrusted with your lord's mission?
Messengers with official caps and canopies have been seen one after another,
reporting that your state is in great distress,
yet you come and say it is not critical—
why is that?"
Chén Shì said:
"If Hán were in true distress, it would change allegiance and follow others;
because it is not yet critical,
I have come again."
The Marquis of Ráng said:
"You need not see the King;
I will immediately dispatch troops to rescue Hán."
They arrived in eight days,
and defeated Zhào
and Wèi below Huáyáng.
That year,
King Xī died,
and his son King Huánhuì ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Huánhuì's reign,
Hán attacked Yān.
In the ninth year,
Qín captured our Xíng,
and built a city by the Fén River.
In the tenth year,
Qín attacked us at Tàiháng,
and our commandant of Shàngdǎng Commandery surrendered Shàngdǎng to Zhào.
In the fourteenth year,
Qín captured Zhào's Shàngdǎng,
and killed over 400,000 troops of Mǎfúzǐ at Chángpíng.
In the seventeenth year,
Qín captured our Yángchéng
and Fùshǔ.
In the twenty-second year,
King Zhāo of Qín died.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Qín captured our Chénggāo
and Xíngyáng.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Qín captured all of our Shàngdǎng.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Qín captured thirteen of our cities.
In the thirty-fourth year,
King Huánhuì died,
and his son King Ān ascended the throne.
In the fifth year of King Ān's reign,
Qín attacked Hán.
Hán was in distress,
and sent Hán Fēi as an envoy to Qín.
Qín detained Fēi,
and subsequently killed him.
In the ninth year,
Qín captured King Ān,
annexed all of his territory,
and established Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Thus, Hán perished.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Hán Jué moved Duke Jǐng of Jìn,
restored the orphan of Zhào to Zǐwǔ,
thus fulfilling the righteousness of Chéng Yīng
and Gōngsūn Chǔjiù.
This was an act of hidden virtue in the world.
As for the contributions of the Hán clan,
in Jìn, their greatness was not fully evident.
Yet, along with Zhào
and Wèi, they endured as feudal lords for over ten generations—
and rightly so!
Chén Wán was
the son of Chén Lìgōng Tuō.
When Wán was born,
the Grand Historian of Zhōu passed through Chén,
and Chén Lìgōng had him perform divination for Wán.
The hexagram obtained was Guān changing to Pǐ:
"This signifies observing the glory of the state,
and it is beneficial to be a guest of the king.
Does this mean he will replace Chén and possess the state?
Or perhaps not here but in another state?
Not in his own person,
but in his descendants.
If in another state,
it must be of the Jiāng surname.
The Jiāng surname
are descendants of the Four Peaks.
Nothing can have two greats simultaneously.
When Chén declines,
this one will flourish?"
Lìgōng was
the youngest son of Chén Wéngōng,
and his mother was a woman from Cài.
When Wéngōng died,
Lìgōng's elder brother Bào ascended the throne,
becoming Huángōng.
Huángōng and Tuō had different mothers.
When Huángōng fell ill,
people from Cài, for Tuō's sake, killed Huángōng Bào and Crown Prince Miǎn, establishing Tuō,
who became Lìgōng.
After Lìgōng was established,
he married a woman from Cài.
This woman from Cài was promiscuous with men from Cài,
frequently returning to her home state,
and Lìgōng also frequently went to Cài.
Huángōng's youngest son Lín resented Lìgōng for killing his father and brother,
so he had men from Cài lure Lìgōng out and kill him.
Lín established himself,
becoming Zhuānggōng.
Thus, Chén Wán could not ascend the throne
and became a senior official of Chén.
The reason for Lìgōng's killing
was his banishment due to promiscuity,
so the Spring and Autumn Annals says
"Men of Cài killed Chén Tuō,"
placing blame on him.
When Zhuānggōng died,
his younger brother Chǔjiù was established,
becoming Xuāngōng.
In the twenty-first year of Xuāngōng's reign,
he killed his crown prince Yùkòu.
Yùkòu and Wán were close friends,
and fearing the disaster would reach him,
Wán therefore fled to Qí.
Duke Huán of Qí wanted to make him a minister,
but Wán declined, saying:
"I am a traveling minister fortunate to be spared from carrying burdens;
this is your lordship's kindness.
I dare not assume high position."
Duke Huán made him Director of Artisans.
Yì Zhòng of Qí wanted to give his daughter in marriage to Wán,
and performed divination about it.
The prognostication said:
"This is called the phoenix flying,
with harmonious cries clanging.
The descendant of Guī
will be nurtured among Jiāng.
In five generations, they will flourish,
reaching the rank of chief minister.
After eight generations,
none can match their greatness."
He finally gave his daughter to Wán in marriage.
When Wán fled to Qí,
Duke Huán of Qí had been in power for fourteen years.
When Wán died,
he was posthumously named Jìng Zhòng.
Zhòng begot Zhì Mèngyí.
When Jìng Zhòng went to Qí,
he used the character Tián as his surname.
Tián Zhì Mèngyí begot Mǐn Mèngzhuāng.
Tián Mǐn Mèngzhuāng begot Wénzǐ Xūwú.
Tián Wénzǐ served Duke Zhuāng of Qí.
When the Jìn minister Luán Chěng rebelled in Jìn,
he came fleeing to Qí,
and Duke Zhuāng of Qí treated him as a highly honored guest.
Yàn Yīng and Tián Wénzǐ admonished against this,
but Duke Zhuāng would not listen.
When Wénzǐ died,
he was succeeded by his son Huánzǐ Wúyǔ.
Tián Huánzǐ Wúyǔ was a man of strength
and served Duke Zhuāng of Qí,
enjoying great favor.
When Wúyǔ died,
he was succeeded by his sons Wǔzǐ Kāi and Xízǐ Qǐ.
Tián Xízǐ Qǐ served Duke Jǐng of Qí as a senior official.
He collected taxes from the people using a small measure,
but distributed grain to the people using a large measure,
performing secret acts of virtue for the people,
and Duke Jǐng did not prohibit this.
Thus, the Tián clan won the hearts of the Qí populace,
their clan grew stronger,
and the people longed for the Tián clan.
Yànzǐ repeatedly admonished Duke Jǐng,
but Duke Jǐng would not listen.
Later, when Yànzǐ was sent as envoy to Jìn,
he privately told Shūxiàng:
"The government of Qí will eventually fall to the Tián clan."
After Yàn Yīng died,
the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans rebelled against Jìn.
Jìn attacked them fiercely,
and Fàn and Zhōngháng requested grain from Qí.
Tián Qǐ wanted to create disorder
and build alliances with the feudal lords,
so he persuaded Duke Jǐng, saying:
"Fàn and
Zhōngháng have repeatedly shown virtue towards Qí;
Qí cannot fail to rescue them."
Qí sent Tián Qǐ to rescue them and supplied them with grain.
When Duke Jǐng's crown prince died,
he later had a favored concubine named Ruìzǐ,
who bore a son named Tú.
When Duke Jǐng fell ill,
he ordered his ministers Guō Huìzǐ and Gāo Zhāozǐ to make Zǐ Tú the crown prince.
When Duke Jǐng died,
the two ministers Gāo and
Guō established Tú,
who became Yàn Rúzǐ.
But Tián Qǐ was displeased,
wanting to establish another son of Duke Jǐng, Yángshēng.
Yángshēng had always been friendly with Qǐ.
When Yàn Rúzǐ was established,
Yángshēng fled to Lǔ.
Tián Qǐ pretended to serve Gāo Zhāozǐ and
Guō Huìzǐ,
often accompanying them in the carriage as attendant,
saying:
"Initially, the various senior officials did not want to establish Rúzǐ.
Now that Rúzǐ is established,
you, ministers, assist him,
but the senior officials all feel endangered
and are planning rebellion."
He also deceived the senior officials, saying:
"Gāo Zhāozǐ is to be feared;
we should strike before he acts."
The various senior officials followed him.
Tián Qǐ,
Bào Mù, and the senior officials led troops into the ducal residence,
attacking Gāo Zhāozǐ.
When Zhāozǐ heard of this,
he and Guō Huìzǐ went to rescue the duke.
The duke's forces were defeated.
Tián Qǐ's men pursued Guō Huìzǐ,
who fled to Jǔ,
and they then returned and killed Gāo Zhāozǐ.
Yàn Yǔ fled to Lǔ.
Tián Qǐ sent someone to Lǔ
to welcome Yángshēng.
When Yángshēng arrived in Qí,
he was hidden in Tián Qǐ's home.
Qǐ invited the senior officials, saying:
"The mother of my son Cháng is holding a fish and bean sacrifice;
please come by chance to drink together."
They gathered to drink at the Tián residence.
Tián Qǐ placed Yángshēng in a sack
and set it in the center of the seating.
He opened the sack,
revealing Yángshēng,
and said:
"This is the ruler of Qí!"
The senior officials all bowed in obeisance.
As they were about to swear an oath to establish him,
Tián Qǐ falsely claimed:
"I and Bào Mù planned together to establish Yángshēng."
Bào Mù angrily said:
"Have the senior officials forgotten Duke Jǐng's command?"
The various senior officials wanted to reconsider,
but Yángshēng then kowtowed and said:
"If it is acceptable, then establish me;
if not, then let it be."
Bào Mù feared disaster would reach himself,
so he then said again:
"All are sons of Duke Jǐng;
why would it be unacceptable!"
Thus, they established Yángshēng at Tián Qǐ's home,
and he became Dàogōng.
They then sent someone to move Yàn Rúzǐ to Tái
and killed Rúzǐ Tú.
After Dàogōng was established,
Tián Qǐ became prime minister,
controlling the government of Qí.
In the fourth year,
Tián Qǐ died,
and his son Cháng succeeded him,
becoming Tián Chéngzǐ.
Bào Mù had a grudge against Duke Dào of Qí,
and assassinated Duke Dào.
The people of Qí jointly established his son Rén,
who became Duke Jiǎn.
Tián Cháng Chéngzǐ and Jiàn Zhǐ both served as left and right chancellors,
assisting Duke Jiǎn.
Tián Cháng resented Jiàn Zhǐ in his heart,
but Jiàn Zhǐ was favored by Duke Jiǎn,
and his power could not be removed.
Thereupon, Tián Cháng revived the policies of his father Lízǐ,
lending grain with large dou measures
and collecting it with small dou measures.
The people of Qí sang of him:
"Oh, gather the medlars,
and return to Tián Chéngzǐ!"
At court, the Qí official
Yù Yàng advised Duke Jiǎn, saying:
"Tián
and Jiàn cannot coexist;
you must choose between them."
The ruler did not listen.
Zǐ Wǒ,
a clansman of Jiàn Zhǐ,
often had conflicts with the Tián clan.
Tián Bào, a distant relative of the Tián clan, served Zǐ Wǒ and was favored.
Zǐ Wǒ said:
"I wish to exterminate all the main line of the Tián clan
and replace them with Bào as the Tián clan's head."
Bào said:
"I am but a distant member of the Tián clan."
Zǐ Wǒ did not listen.
Later, Bào told the Tián clan:
"Zǐ Wǒ intends to exterminate the Tián clan;
if the Tián clan does not act first,
disaster will befall you."
Zǐ Wǒ was residing in the duke's palace;
Tián Cháng and his three brothers rode to the duke's palace,
intending to kill Zǐ Wǒ.
Zǐ Wǒ closed the gates.
Duke Jiǎn was drinking with women in the Tántái,
and was about to attack Tián Cháng.
The Grand Historian Zǐyú said:
"Tián Cháng dares not to rebel;
he is only removing a threat."
Duke Jiǎn then stopped.
Tián Cháng left,
heard that Duke Jiǎn was angry,
feared execution,
and planned to flee.
Tián Zǐxíng said:
"Hesitation
is the ruin of affairs."
Tián Cháng then attacked Zǐ Wǒ.
Zǐ Wǒ led his followers to attack the Tián clan,
but was defeated,
and fled.
The Tián clan's followers pursued and killed Zǐ Wǒ and Jiàn Zhǐ.
Duke Jiǎn fled,
and the Tián clan's followers pursued and captured him in Xúzhōu.
Duke Jiǎn said:
"Had I heeded Yù Yàng's words earlier,
I would not have met this calamity."
The Tián clan's followers feared that Duke Jiǎn would be restored and execute them,
so they killed Duke Jiǎn.
Duke Jiǎn was killed four years after his accession.
Thereupon, Tián Cháng established Duke Jiǎn's younger brother Áo,
who became Duke Píng.
When Duke Píng ascended the throne,
Tián Cháng became chancellor.
After Tián Cháng killed Duke Jiǎn,
he feared that the other states would jointly attack him,
so he returned all the lands seized from Lǔ
and Wèi,
formed alliances to the west with Jìn,
Hán, Wèi,
and Zhào,
and opened diplomatic relations to the south with Wú
and Yuè,
cultivated achievements and distributed rewards,
and drew close to the common people,
thus restoring stability to Qí.
Tián Cháng said to Duke Píng of Qí:
"Bestowing favors is what people desire;
you, my lord, should administer that;
punishments are what people hate;
I request to administer that."
After five years of this practice,
the governance of Qí all fell into Tián Cháng's hands.
Tián Cháng then exterminated the powerful members of the Bào,
Yàn, Jiàn Zhǐ families, and the ducal clan,
and carved out for himself the territory of Qí from Ānpíng east to Lángyá,
as his own fief.
His fief was larger than the area under Duke Píng's direct rule.
Tián Cháng then selected women in Qí over seven chǐ tall for his harem,
which numbered in the hundreds,
and did not restrict the comings and goings of his guests and retainers in the harem.
By the time Tián Cháng died,
he had over seventy sons.
Tián Cháng died,
and his son Xiāngzǐ Pán succeeded him,
serving as chancellor of Qí.
Cháng was posthumously titled Chéngzǐ.
After Tián Xiāngzǐ became chancellor to Duke Xuān of Qí,
the three Jìn families killed Zhì Bó
and divided his territory.
Xiāngzǐ appointed all his brothers and clansmen as magistrates of Qí's cities and towns,
exchanged envoys with the three Jìn,
and thereby came to possess the state of Qí.
Xiāngzǐ died,
and his son Zhuāngzǐ Bái succeeded him.
Tián Zhuāngzǐ served as chancellor to Duke Xuān of Qí.
In the forty-third year of Duke Xuān,
they attacked Jìn,
destroyed Huángchéng,
and besieged Yánghú.
The next year,
they attacked Lǔ,
Gé, and Ānlíng.
The following year,
they captured a city from Lǔ.
Zhuāngzǐ died,
and his son Grand Duke Hé succeeded him.
Tián Tàigōng served as chancellor to Duke Xuān of Qí.
In the forty-eighth year of Duke Xuān,
they captured Chéng from Lǔ.
The next year,
Duke Xuān met with people of Zhèng at Xīchéng.
They attacked Wèi
and captured Wúqiū.
Duke Xuān died in his fifty-first year,
and Tián Huì rebelled from Lǐnqiū.
After Duke Xuān's death,
his son Duke Kāng Dài succeeded him.
Dài reigned for fourteen years,
indulging in wine and women,
and neglecting governance.
Tàigōng then moved Duke Kāng to the coast,
granting him one city for sustenance,
to maintain the sacrifices to his ancestors.
The next year,
Lǔ defeated Qí at Pínglù.
Three years later,
Tàigōng met with Marquis Wén of Wèi at Zhuózé,
seeking to be made a feudal lord.
Marquis Wén of Wèi then sent envoys to the Zhou Son of Heaven and the feudal lords,
requesting that Tián Hé, chancellor of Qí, be made a feudal lord.
The Zhou Son of Heaven consented.
In the nineteenth year of Duke Kāng,
Tián Hé was established as Marquis of Qí,
listed among the Zhou houses,
and began his own reign era.
Marquis Tàigōng Hé of Qí reigned for two years,
then Hé died,
and his son Duke Huán Wǔ succeeded him.
In the fifth year of Duke Huán Wǔ,
Qín and Wèi attacked Hán,
and Hán sought help from Qí.
Duke Huán of Qí summoned his ministers and consulted them:
"Is it better to rescue them early or late?"
Zōu Jì said:
"It would be better not to rescue them at all."
Duàngān Péng said:
"If we do not rescue them,
Hán will be forced to submit to Wèi;
it would be better to rescue them."
Tián Chénsī said:
"Your plan is mistaken!
When Qín and Wèi attack Hán,
Chǔ and Zhào will surely rescue them;
this is Heaven giving Yān to Qí."
Duke Huán said:
"Good."
He then secretly informed the Hán envoy and sent him back.
Hán, believing it had Qí's support,
engaged Qín
and Wèi in battle.
Chǔ and Zhào, hearing of this,
indeed raised troops to rescue them.
Qí then raised troops to attack the state of Yān,
capturing Sāngqiū.
In the sixth year,
they rescued Wèi.
Duke Huán died,
and his son King Wēi, Yīn Qí, ascended the throne.
That year,
the former Qí's Duke Kāng passed away,
leaving no heir,
so his fiefs all went to the Tián family.
In the first year of King Wēi of Qí,
the three Jìn states attacked our Língqiū, taking advantage of Qí's mourning period.
In the third year,
the three Jìn states destroyed the remnants of Jìn and divided its territory.
In the sixth year,
Lǔ invaded us,
entering Yángguān.
Jìn attacked us,
reaching Bólíng.
In the seventh year,
Wèi invaded us,
capturing Xuēlíng.
In the ninth year,
Zhào attacked us,
taking Juàn.
Since King Wēi first ascended the throne,
he did not govern,
delegating authority to his ministers,
and over nine years,
the various feudal lords repeatedly attacked,
and the people were not well-governed.
Then King Wēi summoned the governor of Jímò and said to him:
"Since you resided in Jímò,
slanderous reports have reached me daily.
Yet when I sent people to inspect Jímò,
the fields were cultivated,
the people were well-provided for,
officials had no pending matters,
and the eastern region was at peace.
This shows you did not curry favor with my attendants to seek praise."
He enfeoffed him with ten thousand households.
Summoning the governor of Ā, he said:
"Since you guarded Ā,
praise has reached my ears daily.
But when I sent envoys to inspect Ā,
the fields were not cultivated,
and the people were impoverished.
Previously when Zhào attacked Juàn,
you could not rescue it.
When Wèi took Xuēlíng,
you were unaware.
This shows you bribed my attendants to seek praise."
That day,
he had the governor of Ā boiled,
along with all the attendants who had praised him, and they were all boiled together.
Then he raised troops to attack Zhào and
Wèi to the west, defeated Wèi at Zhuózé, and besieged King Huì.
King Huì offered to present Guàn to seek reconciliation,
and the people of Zhào returned our Chángchéng.
Thereupon, the state of Qí was shaken with fear,
and no one dared to conceal wrongdoings,
all striving to be utterly sincere.
Qí became greatly well-governed.
When the feudal lords heard of this,
none dared to send troops against Qí for over twenty years.
Zōu Jìzǐ met King Wēi by playing the zither,
and King Wēi, pleased, housed him in the right chamber.
After a short while,
the king played the zither,
and Zōu Jìzǐ pushed the door open and entered, saying:
"How beautifully you play the zither!"
The king suddenly displeased,
put aside the zither and grasped his sword, saying:
"Sir, you have only glimpsed the surface without deep observation;
how do you know it is beautiful?"
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"The thick strings, deep and warm like spring,
represent the ruler;
the thin strings, crisp and clear,
represent the minister;
grasping deeply,
and releasing joyfully,
symbolizes governance;
harmonious in sound,
large and small complementing each other,
twisting yet not conflicting,
reflects the four seasons:
thus I know it is beautiful."
The king said:
"Well spoken on music."
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"Why only music?
Governing the state and pacifying the people are all within it."
The king again suddenly displeased, said:
"As for discussing the principles of the five notes,
indeed none surpass you, sir.
But as for governing the state and pacifying the people,
what have they to do with the strings of the zither?"
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"The thick strings, deep and warm like spring,
represent the ruler;
the thin strings, crisp and clear,
represent the minister;
grasping deeply and releasing joyfully,
symbolizes governance;
harmonious in sound,
large and small complementing each other,
twisting yet not conflicting,
reflects the four seasons.
What repeats without chaos
leads to prosperous governance;
what connects directly
ensures survival:
thus it is said, when the zither's tones are tuned, the world is well-governed.
Governing the state and pacifying the people
are no different from the five notes."
The king said:
"Good."
Zōu Jìzǐ met the king and in three months received the prime minister's seal.
Chúnyú Kūn saw him and said:
"Skillful in speech indeed!
I have some foolish thoughts,
and wish to present them before you."
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"I respectfully receive your instruction."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"Achieve completeness, and all prospers;
lose completeness, and all perishes."
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"I respectfully accept your command,
and will carefully never stray from your presence."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"Grease on a thorny axle
makes it smooth,
yet it cannot turn a square hole."
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"I respectfully accept your command,
and will carefully serve those around me."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"Glue on a bow's old wood
makes it united,
yet it cannot fill wide gaps."
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"I respectfully accept your command,
and will carefully attach myself to the myriad people."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"A fox fur, though worn,
cannot be patched with yellow dog skin."
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"I respectfully accept your command,
and will carefully select gentlemen,
mixing no petty men among them."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"A large cart unadjusted
cannot bear its usual load;
zithers unadjusted
cannot achieve the five notes."
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"I respectfully accept your command,
and will carefully revise laws and supervise corrupt officials."
When Chúnyú Kūn finished speaking,
he hurried out,
reached the gate,
and facing his servant, said:
"This man,
to whom I spoke five subtle words,
responded to me like an echo to sound—
this man will surely be enfeoffed before long."
After a year,
he was enfeoffed at Xiàpī,
and given the title Marquis Chéng.
In the 23rd year of King Wēi's reign,
he met with the King of Zhào at Pínglù.
In the 24th year,
he went hunting in the suburbs with the King of Wèi.
The King of Wèi asked:
"Does Your Majesty also possess treasures?"
King Wēi replied:
"I have none."
King Liáng said:
"Although my state is small,
I still have ten pearls measuring an inch in diameter that can illuminate twelve chariots in front and behind.
How can a state with ten thousand chariots have no treasures?"
King Wēi said:
"What I consider treasures is different from Your Majesty.
Among my ministers, there is one named Tánzǐ;
when I sent him to guard Nánchéng,
the people of Chǔ did not dare to invade and advance eastward,
and the twelve feudal lords of Sìshàng all came to pay homage.
Among my ministers, there is one named Fēnzǐ;
when I sent him to guard Gāotáng,
the people of Zhào did not dare to fish eastward in the river.
Among my officials, there is one named Qiánfū;
when I sent him to guard Xúzhōu,
the people of Yān made sacrifices at the northern gate,
the people of Zhào made sacrifices at the western gate,
and over seven thousand households relocated to follow him.
Among my ministers, there is one named Zhǒngshǒu;
when I assigned him to guard against thieves,
then no one would pick up lost items on the road.
These men can illuminate a thousand li,
how can they be compared to just twelve chariots!"
King Huì of Liáng felt ashamed,
and left displeased.
In the 26th year,
King Huì of Wèi besieged Hándān,
and Zhào sought help from Qí.
King Wēi of Qí summoned his ministers to discuss, saying:
"Which is better, to save Zhào or not to save it?"
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"It would be better not to save it."
Duàngān Péng said:
"Not saving them would be unjust,
and moreover, disadvantageous."
King Wēi asked:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"If the Wèi clan annexes Hándān,
what benefit would that bring to Qí?
Moreover, if we save Zhào and station troops in its suburbs,
that would mean Zhào is not attacked while Wèi remains intact.
Therefore, it would be better to attack Xiānglíng from the south to weaken Wèi,
and when Hándān is captured, take advantage of Wèi's exhaustion."
King Wēi followed his plan.
Later, Chénghóu Zōu Jì and Tián Jì were on bad terms.
Gōngsūn Yuè said to Chénghóu Jì:
"Why don't you plan an attack on Wèi,
Tián Jì will surely lead the army.
If he wins and achieves merit,
then your plan will have succeeded;
if he does not win the battle,
he will either die in the front or be defeated in the rear,
and his fate will be in your hands."
Thereupon, Chénghóu advised King Wēi,
and sent Tián Jì to attack Xiānglíng from the south.
In the tenth month,
Hándān was captured,
and Qí then raised troops to attack Wèi,
defeating them greatly at Guìlíng.
Thus, Qí became the strongest among the feudal lords,
proclaimed itself a kingdom,
and issued commands to the world.
In the 33rd year,
he put to death his senior official Móu Xīn.
In the 35th year,
Gōngsūn Yuè again said to Chénghóu Jì:
"Why don't you send someone with ten jin of gold to have a divination done in the market,
saying:
'I am a follower of Tián Jì.
I have fought three battles and won all three,
my reputation and power are known throughout the world.
I wish to undertake a great enterprise—
is it auspicious or not?'"
After the diviner came out,
he then had people arrest the one who performed the divination,
and verified his words before the king.
When Tián Jì heard of this,
he led his followers in a surprise attack on Línzī,
seeking Chénghóu,
but, failing to win, fled.
In the 36th year,
King Wēi passed away,
and his son, King Xuān Pìqiáng, ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Xuān's reign,
Qín employed Shāng Yāng.
Zhōu conferred the title of Bó upon Duke Xiào of Qín.
In the second year,
Wèi attacked Zhào.
Zhào allied with Hán,
and together they attacked Wèi.
Zhào was at a disadvantage,
and they battled at Nánliáng.
King Xuān recalled Tián Jì to his former position.
The Hán clan sought help from Qí.
King Xuān summoned his ministers to discuss, saying:
"Which is better, to save them early or late?"
Zōu Jìzǐ said:
"It would be better not to save them."
Tián Jì said:
"If we do not save them,
then Hán will be forced to submit and join Wèi;
it would be better to save them early."
Sūnzǐ said:
"If we save Hán and
Wèi before their troops are exhausted,
then we would be taking on Wèi's military force on behalf of Hán,
and instead end up taking orders from Hán.
Moreover, Wèi has the intention of destroying the state;
when Hán sees its imminent destruction,
it will surely turn eastward to plead with Qí.
If we then deeply solidify our alliance with Hán and later take advantage of Wèi's exhaustion,
we can gain substantial benefits and earn a respected reputation."
King Xuān said:
"Excellent."
He then secretly informed Hán's envoy and sent him back.
Hán, relying on Qí,
fought five battles without victory,
and eventually entrusted its state affairs to Qí from the east.
Qí then raised troops,
appointing Tián Jì and
Tián Yīng as generals,
with Sūnzǐ as military advisor,
to save Hán and
Zhào by attacking Wèi,
defeating them greatly at Mǎlíng,
killing their general Páng Juān,
and capturing the Wèi crown prince Shēn.
Afterwards, the kings of the Three Jìn all, through Tián Yīng, paid homage to the King of Qí at Bówàng,
concluded a covenant, and departed.
In the seventh year,
he met with the King of Wèi south of Píng'ē.
The following year,
they met again at Zhēn.
King Huì of Wèi passed away.
The next year,
he met with King Xiāng of Wèi at Xúzhōu,
where the feudal lords recognized each other as kings.
In the tenth year,
Chǔ besieged our Xúzhōu.
In the eleventh year,
we joined Wèi in attacking Zhào.
Zhào breached the river to flood Qí and
Wèi, and the troops withdrew.
In the eighteenth year,
King Huì of Qín proclaimed himself king.
King Xuān delighted in scholars of literature and persuasion,
such as Zōu Yǎn,
Chúnyú Kūn,
Tián Pián,
Jiē Yǔ,
Shèn Dào,
Huán Yuān, and seventy-six others,
all of whom were bestowed with official residences,
appointed as senior ministers,
and did not administer but engaged in discussions.
Thus, the scholars at Qí's Jìxià Academy flourished again,
numbering nearly a thousand.
In the nineteenth year,
King Xuān passed away,
and his son, King Mǐn Dì, ascended the throne.
In the first year of King Mǐn's reign,
Qín sent Zhāng Yí to meet with the ruling powers of the feudal lords at Nièsāng.
In the third year,
he enfeoffed Tián Yīng at Xuē.
In the fourth year,
he welcomed a bride from Qín.
In the seventh year,
he joined Sòng in attacking Wèi,
defeating them at Guānzé.
In the twelfth year,
(Qi) attacked Wei.
Chu besieged Yongshi,
and Qin defeated Qu Gai.
Su Dai said to Tian Zhěn:
"I wish to make a request of you,
which is a very sound plan.
It will benefit Chu and be advantageous to you,
bringing fortune if successful,
and also fortune if not.
Just now as I stood at the gate,
a visitor said that King of Wei told Hán Féng
and Zhāng Yí:
'Zhǔzǎo is about to fall,
and Qí troops are advancing again.
If you come to rescue me, it will be fine;
if you don't save me,
I cannot hold out.'
This is merely rhetoric.
If the troops of Qin and Han do not march east,
in little more than ten days,
Wei will turn Han to follow Qin,
Qin will expel Zhāng Yí,
and (Wei) will join with Qi and Chu,
this would mean your success."
Tián Zhěn said:
"How to make them not go east?"
The reply was:
"When Hán Féng argues for rescuing Wei,
he certainly won't tell the King of Han
'Féng thinks it's for Wei',
but will surely say
'Féng will use the troops of Qin and Han to repel Qí and Sòng in the east,
Féng will then unite the armies of three states,
taking advantage of Qū Gài's defeat,
to cut south into Chǔ territory,
thus surely recovering all our former lands.'
As for Zhāng Yí's argument for rescuing Wei,
he certainly won't tell the King of Qin
'Yí thinks it's for Wei',
but will surely say
'Yí will use the troops of Qin and Han to resist Qí and Sòng in the east,
Yí will unite the armies of three states,
taking advantage of Qū Gài's defeat,
to cut south into Chǔ territory,
nominally preserving a perishing state,
but actually attacking Sānchuān and then returning,
this is the king's enterprise.'
If you have the King of Chǔ cede territory to Hán,
and let Qín control the peace,
saying to the King of Qín
'Request to give Hán land,
and you, king, can extend to Sānchuān,
so Hán's troops gain territory from Chǔ without being used.'
What then will Hán Féng say to Qín about marching east?
He will say
'Qín gains Sānchuān without using troops,
attacks Chǔ and Hán to pressure Wèi,
so Wèi dares not look east,
thus isolating Qí.'
And what will Zhāng Yí say about marching east?
He will say
'Qín and Hán desire land and have troops in readiness,
their prestige emanates from Wèi,
so Wèi's desire not to lose Qí and Chǔ has support.'
When Wèi turns and Qín and Hán compete to serve Qí and Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ desires but does not cede land,
you make Qín and Hán gain land without using troops,
which is a great virtue.
The kings of Qín and Hán, compelled by Hán Féng
and Zhāng Yí, march east to subdue Wèi,
while you always hold the advantage to demand from Qín and Hán,
this benefits you and disadvantages Master Zhāng with ample resources."
In the thirteenth year,
King Huì of Qín died.
In the twenty-third year,
(Qí) together with Qín defeated Chǔ at Zhòngqiū.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Qín sent Lord Jīngyáng as a hostage to Qí.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Lord Jīngyáng was returned to Qín.
Lord Mèngcháng, Xuē Wén, went to Qín,
and became chancellor of Qín.
Wén fled back.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Qí together with Hán and Wèi attacked Qín,
stationing troops at Hángǔ.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Qín gave Hán the land beyond the river to make peace,
and the troops withdrew.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Zhào killed its lord father.
Qí assisted Zhào in destroying Zhōngshān.
In the thirty-sixth year,
the king became the Eastern Emperor,
and King Zhāo of Qín became the Western Emperor.
Sū Dài came from Yān,
entered Qí,
and had an audience at the eastern gate of Zhānghuā.
The King of Qí said:
"Ah,
excellent, you've come!
Qín has sent Wèi Rǎn to confer the imperial title,
what do you think?"
The reply was:
"Your Majesty's question is abrupt,
yet the trouble stems from subtlety.
I hope you accept it but refrain from using the title.
If Qín claims it,
and the world accepts it,
then you may claim it too,
without lagging behind.
Moreover, yielding the contested imperial title
does no harm.
If Qín claims it,
and the world resents it,
then you simply don't claim it,
to win over the world,
this is a great asset.
Furthermore, if the world establishes two emperors,
does the world regard Qí as superior,
or Qín?"
The king said:
"Qín."
Sū Dài said:
"If the title is abandoned,
will the world love Qí,
or Qín?"
The king said:
"Love Qí and hate Qín."
Sū Dài said:
"What is more beneficial: two emperors agreeing to attack Zhào,
or attacking the tyrannical Sòng?"
The king said:
"Attacking the tyrannical Sòng is more beneficial."
The reply was:
"The agreements are equal,
yet if you become emperor with Qín, the world will honor Qín and despise Qí;
abandoning the title, the world will love Qí and hate Qín.
Attacking Zhào is not as beneficial as attacking the tyrannical Sòng,
so I wish you would clearly abandon the title to win the world,
break the pact and reject Qín,
avoid contending for supremacy,
and in the meantime conquer Sòng.
With Sòng in possession,
Yángdì of Wèi is endangered;
with Jìxī,
Ādōng of Zhào is endangered;
with Huáiběi,
the eastern territories of Chǔ are endangered;
with Táo
and Pínglù,
Liáng's gates won't open.
Abandon the title and use the pretext of attacking the tyrannical Sòng,
your state will be weighty and your name honored,
Yān and Chǔ will be subdued by circumstance,
no one in the world will dare disobey,
this is the action of Tāng and Wǔ.
Respect Qín in name,
then make the world hate it,
this is what is called using humility to achieve honor.
I hope you consider this carefully."
Thereupon Qí abandoned the imperial title and returned to being king,
and Qín also renounced the imperial position.
In the thirty-eighth year,
they attacked Sòng.
King Zhāo of Qín angrily said:
"I love Sòng as much as I love Xīnchéng
and Yángjìn.
Hán Niè is my friend,
yet he attacks what I love -
why is this?"
Sū Dài spoke to the King of Qín on behalf of Qí:
"Hán Niè's attack on Sòng
is for Your Majesty's benefit.
If Qí becomes strong,
aided by Sòng,
Chǔ and Wèi will surely fear,
and their fear will compel them to serve Qín in the west.
Thus without troubling a single soldier,
without wounding a single officer,
you can effortlessly annex Ānyì -
this is what Hán Niè prays for from Your Majesty."
The King of Qín said:
"I worry that Qí is hard to understand.
Sometimes they align, sometimes they oppose -
what explains this behavior?"
He replied:
"How can the states under heaven make Qí predictable?
Qí has attacked Sòng,
knowing that serving Qín would provide the support of a mighty state;
if they don't serve Qín in the west, then Sòng's governance won't be secure.
The white-haired wandering scholars of the central states all accumulate wisdom hoping to separate the alliance between Qí and Qín;
those leaning on their carriages and tying their reins to ride west
include not one who speaks well of Qí,
while those leaning on their carriages and tying their reins to ride east
include not one who speaks well of Qín.
Why is this?
They all wish to prevent Qí and Qín from uniting.
How clever are Jìn and Chǔ, and how foolish are Qí and Qín!
When Jìn and Chǔ unite, they invariably scheme against Qí and Qín;
when Qí and Qín unite, they invariably plot against Jìn and Chǔ -
I beg you to use this principle to decide matters."
The King of Qín said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon Qí proceeded to attack Sòng,
the King of Sòng fled into exile,
and died at Wēn.
Qí annexed the territory north of the Huái River from Chǔ in the south,
invaded the Three Jìn in the west,
wishing to absorb the Zhōu court
and become the Son of Heaven.
The lords of the various states along the Sì River, including Zōu and Lǔ, all declared themselves subjects,
and the feudal lords were terrified.
In the thirty-ninth year,
Qín came to attack,
capturing nine of our cities in sequence.
In the fortieth year,
Yān, Qín,
Chǔ, and the Three Jìn conspired together,
each sending elite troops to attack,
defeating us west of Jì.
The king withdrew his forces and retreated.
Yān general Yuè Yì then entered Línzī,
taking all of Qí's treasured vessels and artifacts.
King Mǐn fled into exile,
going to Wèi.
The lord of Wèi vacated his palace to house him,
declaring himself a subject and providing all necessities.
King Mǐn behaved arrogantly,
so the people of Wèi offended against him.
King Mǐn departed,
fleeing to Zōu
and Lǔ, wearing a haughty expression,
but the lords of Zōu and Lǔ would not admit him,
so he fled to Jǔ.
Chǔ sent Nuò Chǐ to lead troops to rescue Qí,
whereupon he became chancellor to King Mǐn of Qí.
Nuò Chǐ then killed King Mǐn and together with Yān divided up the territory and ritual vessels Qí had seized.
After King Mǐn met his death,
his son Fǎ Zhāng changed his name and became a servant in the household of Jiǎo, the Grand Historian of Jǔ.
Grand Historian Jiǎo's daughter found Fǎ Zhāng's appearance remarkable,
considering him no ordinary person;
pitying him, she often secretly provided him with clothing and food,
and engaged in an illicit relationship with him.
After Nuò Chǐ had left Jǔ,
the people of Jǔ and Qí's exiled ministers gathered together seeking King Mǐn's son,
wishing to establish him as king.
Fǎ Zhāng feared they would execute him,
but after some time,
he dared to announce himself:
"I am King Mǐn's son."
Thereupon the people of Jǔ together established Fǎ Zhāng as king,
this being King Xiāng.
They secured the city of Jǔ and proclaimed throughout the state of Qí:
"The king has already been established in Jǔ!"
After King Xiāng was established,
he made the daughter of the Grand Historian clan his queen,
this being Queen Jūnwánghòu,
who bore a son named Jiàn.
Grand Historian Jiǎo said:
"My daughter married without a matchmaker's arrangement -
she is not of my kind,
she has defiled our lineage."
He never looked upon Queen Jūnwánghòu for the rest of his life.
Queen Jūnwánghòu was virtuous,
and did not neglect her duties as a daughter because he refused to see her.
King Xiāng remained in Jǔ for five years,
until Tián Dān from Jímò attacked and defeated the Yān army,
welcoming King Xiāng from Jǔ,
and entering Línzī.
All of Qí's former territory was restored to Qí.
Qí enfeoffed Tián Dān as Lord of Ānpíng.
In the fourteenth year,
Qín attacked our Gāng and Shòu.
In the nineteenth year,
King Xiāng died,
and his son Jiàn was established.
In the sixth year of King Jiàn's reign,
Qín attacked Zhào,
and Qí and Chǔ came to its rescue.
Qín strategized:
"If Qí and Chǔ rescue Zhào,
if they are closely allied we will withdraw our troops,
if not we will attack them."
Zhào had no food,
and requested grain from Qí,
but Qí refused.
Master Zhōu said:
"It would be better to grant their request to make Qín's troops withdraw;
if you refuse, Qín's army will not retreat,
thus Qín's strategy will succeed while Qí and Chǔ's will fail.
Moreover, Zhào serves as
a protective barrier for Qí and Chǔ,
just as teeth have lips;
when the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold.
If Zhào falls today,
tomorrow the calamity will reach Qí and Chǔ.
Furthermore, the task of rescuing Zhào
should be like carrying a leaking jar to pour water on a burning pot.
To rescue Zhào
is a highly righteous act;
to repel Qín's army
brings illustrious fame.
Righteously saving a doomed state,
and awesomely repelling mighty Qín's troops -
if you don't devote yourself to this but instead focus on hoarding grain,
those planning for the state are mistaken."
The King of Qí would not listen.
Qín defeated Zhào at Chángpíng, killing over 400,000,
and then besieged Hándān.
In the sixteenth year,
Qín destroyed Zhōu.
Queen Jūnwánghòu died.
In the twenty-third year,
Qín established the Eastern Commandery.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the king went to pay court to Qín,
and King Zhèng of Qín hosted a banquet in Xiányáng.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Qín destroyed Hán.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Qín destroyed Zhào.
In the thirty-eighth year,
Yān sent Jīng Kē to assassinate the King of Qín,
but the King of Qín detected him,
and killed Kē.
The next year,
Qín defeated Yān,
and the King of Yān fled to Liáodōng.
The following year,
Qín destroyed Wèi,
and Qín's troops stationed themselves at Lìxià.
In the forty-second year,
Qín destroyed Chǔ.
The next year,
they captured King Jiā of Dài,
and destroyed King Xǐ of Yān.
In the forty-fourth year,
the Qin army attacked Qí.
The King of Qí followed the advice of his chancellor Hòu Shèng,
and without fighting,
surrendered with his troops to Qin.
Qin captured King Jiàn,
and exiled him to Gòng.
Thus, Qí was destroyed and made into a commandery.
All under Heaven was unified under Qin,
and the King of Qin, Zhèng, established the title of Huángdì.
Initially, Queen Dowager Jūnwáng was virtuous,
served Qin with caution,
and maintained trust with the other feudal lords.
Qí was also located on the eastern coast,
while Qin attacked the Three Jìn,
Yān, and Chǔ day and night.
The five states each sought to save themselves from Qin,
so King Jiàn reigned for over forty years without suffering military attacks.
After Queen Dowager Jūnwáng died,
Hòu Shèng became chancellor of Qí.
He received much gold from Qin spies,
and often sent his guests to Qin.
Qin also gave them much gold,
and these guests all acted as double agents,
urging the king to abandon the vertical alliance and pay homage to Qin,
neglecting preparations for defense and attack,
and not aiding the five states in attacking Qin.
Thus, Qin was able to destroy the five states.
After the five states had perished,
the Qin army finally entered Línzī,
and none of the people dared to resist.
King Jiàn then surrendered,
and was exiled to Gòng.
Therefore, the people of Qí resented King Jiàn for not earlier joining the feudal lords in the vertical alliance to attack Qin,
and for listening to treacherous ministers and guests, leading to the destruction of his state.
They sang of it, saying:
"O pine, O cypress,
was it the guests who made Jiàn dwell in Gòng?"
They deplored Jiàn's use of guests without discernment.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān says:
It is said that in his later years, Confucius delighted in the "Yì".
The art of the "Yì"
is profound and far-reaching;
who but a thorough and accomplished person could pay attention to it!
Thus, when the Grand Historian of Zhōu divined for Tián Jìngzhòng Wán,
the prognostication reached ten generations later.
When Wán fled to Qí,
Yì Zhòng's divination also said the same.
That Tián Qǐ and Cháng thereby twice transgressed against their lords,
and monopolized the governance of Qí,
was not necessarily a gradual trend of events,
but rather as if they followed the omens and portents.
Confucius was born in Zōuyì, Chāngpíng Village, in Lǔ.
His ancestors were from Sòng,
named Kǒng Fángshū.
Fángshū begot Bóxià,
and Bóxià begot Shūliáng Hé.
Hé had a union with a woman of the Yán clan in the wilds and begot Confucius,
who was conceived after prayers at Níqiū.
Confucius was born in the twenty-second year of Duke Xiāng of Lǔ.
He was born with a recessed fontanel,
hence he was named Qiū.
His courtesy name was Zhòngní,
and his family name was Kǒng.
Qiū was born after Shūliáng Hé died,
and was buried at Fáng Mountain.
Fáng Mountain was east of Lǔ,
so Confucius was uncertain of his father's burial place,
as his mother had kept it secret.
As a child, Confucius played games,
often arranging sacrificial vessels,
and performing ritual gestures.
When Confucius's mother died,
he temporarily placed the coffin at the crossroad of Wǔfǔ,
acting with caution.
The mother of the carriage driver from Zōu informed Confucius of his father's burial place,
after which he went to bury them together at Fáng.
Confucius, wearing mourning,
went to a feast for scholars hosted by the Jì family.
Yánghǔ rebuffed him, saying:
"The Jì family feasts scholars,
but does not dare to feast you."
Confucius then withdrew.
At age seventeen,
Mèng Lízǐ, a senior official of Lǔ, fell ill and was dying.
He admonished his heir, Yìzǐ, saying:
"Kǒng Qiū
is a descendant of sages,
whose line ended in Sòng.
His ancestor Fùfǔ Hé initially possessed Sòng but yielded the succession to Duke Lì.
When Zhèng Kǎofǔ assisted Dukes Dài,
Wǔ, and Xuān,
with each higher appointment he became more humble.
Thus, the inscription on the tripod said:
'With one appointment, I stoop;
with two, I bow;
with three, I crouch.
I hug the wall and walk,
and none dare to insult me.
Here I cook my gruel,
here I cook my porridge,
to fill my mouth.'
Such was his humility.
I have heard that among the descendants of sages,
even if they do not reign,
there must be those who achieve distinction.
Now Kǒng Qiū is young and fond of rites—
is he not one who will achieve distinction?
After I die,
you must take him as your teacher."
After Lízǐ died,
Yìzǐ and Nángōng Jìngshū of Lǔ went to study rites with him.
That year,
Jì Wǔzǐ died,
and Píngzǐ succeeded him.
Confucius was poor and of low status.
When he grew up,
he once served as a historian for the Jì family,
managing accounts fairly,
and once as a petty official in charge of livestock, where the animals multiplied.
Thus, he became Minister of Works.
Later, he left Lǔ,
was rejected in Qí,
expelled from Sòng
and Wèi,
and trapped between Chén and Cài,
then returned to Lǔ.
Confucius was nine feet six inches tall,
and people all called him
"the tall man"
and regarded him as extraordinary.
Lǔ again treated him well,
and thus he returned to Lǔ.
Nángōng Jìngshū of Lǔ said to the Lord of Lǔ:
"I request to go to Zhōu with Confucius."
The Lord of Lǔ gave them one carriage,
two horses,
and one page to accompany them.
They went to Zhōu to inquire about rites,
and it is said they met Lǎozi.
As they departed,
Lǎozi saw them off, saying:
"I have heard that the wealthy and noble see people off with gifts,
while the benevolent see people off with words.
I cannot claim wealth or nobility,
but presume the name of a benevolent person,
and see you off with these words:
'Those who are clever and deeply perceptive yet near death
are those who like to criticize others.
Those who are broadly learned and eloquent yet endanger themselves
are those who expose others' faults.
As a son, do not be self-centered;
as a minister, do not be self-centered.'"
Confucius returned to Lǔ from Zhōu,
and his disciples gradually increased.
At that time,
Duke Píng of Jìn was licentious,
and the six ministers wielded power arbitrarily,
attacking the feudal lords in the east.
King Líng of Chǔ had strong armies,
and oppressed the Central States.
Qí was large and close to Lǔ.
Lǔ was small and weak:
if it allied with Chǔ, Jìn would be angered;
if it allied with Jìn, Chǔ would attack;
if it did not prepare against Qí,
the Qí army would invade Lǔ.
In the twentieth year of Duke Zhāo of Lǔ,
Confucius was about thirty years old.
Duke Jǐng of Qí and Yàn Yīng came to Lǔ,
and Duke Jǐng asked Confucius:
"In the past, Duke Mù of Qín had a small state in a remote location;
how did he become hegemon?"
Confucius replied:
"Qín,
though small in territory,
had great ambitions;
though remote in location,
its conduct was upright.
He personally elevated the Five Rams,
ennobling him as a senior official,
raising him from bonds and fetters,
and after speaking with him for three days,
entrusted him with governance.
With this approach,
he could have been a true king—
being hegemon was minor."
Duke Jǐng was pleased.
At the age of thirty-five, Confucius witnessed
Jì Píngzǐ and Hòu Zhāobó offending Duke Zhāo of Lǔ due to a cockfighting incident.
Duke Zhāo led troops to attack Jì Píngzǐ,
but Jì Píngzǐ joined forces with the Mèng and
Shūsūn families to attack Duke Zhāo in return.
Duke Zhāo's army was defeated,
and he fled to Qí,
where he was settled in Gānhóu by Qí.
Not long after,
chaos erupted in Lǔ.
Confucius went to Qí,
serving as a steward in the household of Gāo Zhāozǐ,
hoping to gain access to Duke Jǐng.
He discussed music with the Grand Musician of Qí,
heard the melodies of the Sháo,
studied them,
and for three months did not notice the taste of meat,
earning praise from the people of Qí.
Duke Jǐng asked Confucius about governance,
and Confucius said:
"Let the ruler be a ruler,
the minister be a minister,
the father be a father,
the son be a son."
Duke Jǐng replied:
"Excellent!
If indeed the ruler is not a ruler,
the minister not a minister,
the father not a father,
the son not a son,
even if there is grain,
how could I eat it?"
Another day, he asked Confucius about governance again,
and Confucius said:
"Governance lies in economizing resources."
Duke Jǐng was pleased,
and intended to enfeoff Confucius with the land of Níxī.
Yàn Yīng advised:
"These Ru scholars are glib and cannot be regulated by law;
arrogant and self-willed,
they are unfit to be subordinates;
they emphasize mourning and prolong grief,
bankrupting themselves with lavish burials,
which should not become a custom;
traveling to persuade and beg for loans,
they are unfit to govern a state.
Since the great sages perished and the Zhōu dynasty declined,
rituals and music have been deficient.
Now Confucius adorns himself magnificently,
elaborates on the rituals of ascent and descent,
and the nuances of etiquette,
such that generations cannot exhaust his learning,
nor a lifetime fully grasp his rites.
If you wish to use him to change Qí's customs,
it is not the way to prioritize the common people."
Afterward, Duke Jǐng received Confucius with respect
but did not inquire about rituals.
On another day,
Duke Jǐng said to Confucius:
"To treat you with the status of the Jì family,
I cannot."
He treated him somewhere between the Jì and Mèng families.
When Qí's high officials sought to harm Confucius,
he heard of it.
Duke Jǐng said:
"I am old,
and cannot employ you."
Confucius then departed,
returning to Lǔ.
At the age of forty-two, Confucius saw
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ die in Gānhóu,
and Duke Dìng ascend the throne.
In the fifth year of Duke Dìng's reign,
in summer, Jì Píngzǐ died,
and Huánzǐ succeeded him.
Jì Huánzǐ, while digging a well, unearthed an earthen jar,
inside which was something like a sheep,
and asked Zhòngní, saying
he had "found a dog."
Zhòngní replied:
"From what I have heard,
it is a sheep.
I have heard that
the monsters of wood and stone are Kuí
and Wǎngliǎng,
those of water are dragons
and Wǎngxiàng,
and that of earth is the fén sheep."
When Wú attacked Yuè,
destroyed Kuàijī,
and found a bone segment that filled a cart,
Wú sent an envoy to ask Zhòngní:
"Which bone is the largest?"
Zhòngní said:
"When Yǔ assembled the multitude of spirits at Mount Kuàijī,
Fángfēngshì arrived late,
and Yǔ had him killed and displayed,
his bone segment filled a cart—
this is the largest."
The Wú envoy asked:
"Who are the spirits?"
Zhòngní said:
"The spirits of mountains and rivers are sufficient to order the world;
their guardians are the spirits,
those of the state altars are the lords and marquises,
all subordinate to the king."
The envoy asked:
"What did Fángfēng guard?"
Zhòngní said:
"The lord of Wāngwǎngshì guarded Mount Fēng
and Yú,
and was of the Xí clan.
In the times of Yú,
Xià, and Shāng, he was called Jiāngwǎng,
in Zhōu, Cháng Dí,
and now is called the Great Man."
The envoy asked:
"How tall are these men?"
Zhòngní said:
"The Jiāoyáoshì are three feet tall,
the shortest of all.
The tallest do not exceed ten times that,
the extreme of measure."
Thereupon, the Wú envoy said:
"How excellent, the sage!"
Huánzǐ had a favored minister named Zhòngliáng Huái,
who had a grudge against Yáng Hǔ.
Yáng Hǔ wanted to expel Huái,
but Gōngshān Bùniǔ stopped him.
That autumn,
Huái grew even more arrogant,
and Yáng Hǔ seized him.
Huánzǐ was angered,
so Yáng Hǔ imprisoned Huánzǐ,
made a covenant with him, and then released him.
From then on, Yáng Hǔ increasingly despised the Jì family.
The Jì family also usurped the ducal house's authority,
with stewards controlling state affairs,
so that in Lǔ, from the high officials down, all transgressed the proper way.
Thus, Confucius did not take office,
but withdrew to edit the Poetry, Documents, Rites, and Music,
while his disciples grew in number,
coming from distant places,
all receiving instruction from him.
In the eighth year of Duke Dìng,
Gōngshān Bùniǔ, discontent with the Jì family,
joined Yáng Hǔ in rebellion,
seeking to depose the rightful heirs of the three Huán families,
and establish instead the illegitimate sons favored by Yáng Hǔ,
and thus seized Jì Huánzǐ.
Huánzǐ deceived them,
and managed to escape.
In the ninth year of Duke Dìng,
Yáng Hǔ was defeated,
and fled to Qí.
At that time, Confucius was fifty years old.
Gōngshān Bùniǔ, using Bì to rebel against the Jì family,
sent someone to summon Confucius.
Confucius had long followed the Way,
patiently awaiting an opportunity untested,
with none able to employ him,
and said:
"Did not King Wén and King Wǔ of Zhōu rise from Fēng and Hào to become kings?
Now though Bì is small,
perhaps it is nearly enough!"
He intended to go.
Zǐlù was displeased,
and tried to stop Confucius.
Confucius said:
"Would those who summon me do so for no reason?
If they use me,
might I not establish an Eastern Zhōu?"
Yet in the end, he did not go.
Later, Duke Dìng appointed Confucius as the Magistrate of Zhōngdū,
and within a year,
all around followed his example.
He was then promoted from Zhōngdū Magistrate to Minister of Works,
and from Minister of Works to Minister of Justice.
In the spring of the tenth year of Duke Dìng's reign,
he made peace with Qí.
In the summer, Qí Grand Master Lí Chú said to Duke Jǐng:
"Lǔ's employment of Kǒng Qiū
poses a threat to Qí."
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to propose a friendly meeting with Lǔ,
to be held at Jiāgǔ.
Duke Dìng of Lǔ intended to go cordially with a carriage.
Kǒngzǐ, acting as minister,
said:
"Your servant has heard that those who engage in civil affairs must have military preparations,
and those who engage in military affairs must have civil preparations.
In ancient times, when feudal lords left their borders,
they necessarily took officials along.
I request that you bring the Left and Right Commanders."
Duke Dìng said:
"Agreed."
So he brought the Left and Right Commanders.
Meeting the Marquis of Qí at Jiāgǔ,
they built an altar with positions,
three earthen steps,
and met each other with the rites of encounter,
bowing and yielding as they ascended.
After the ceremonies of offering and toasting were completed,
a Qí official hurried forward and said:
"I request to perform the music of the four regions."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon, banners, feathers, spears, halberds, swords, and shields arrived with drumming and noise.
Kǒngzǐ hurried forward,
ascended the steps,
not stopping at the top,
raised his sleeve, and said:
"Our two rulers are having a friendly meeting,
why is barbarian music here!
I request orders for the officials!"
The officials made them retreat,
but they did not leave,
then looked around at Yànzǐ and Duke Jǐng.
Duke Jǐng felt ashamed in his heart,
waved them away.
After a while,
a Qí official hurried forward and said:
"I request to perform the music of the palace."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Agreed."
Actors, singers, and dwarfs came forward to perform.
Kǒngzǐ hurried forward,
ascended the steps,
not stopping at the top,
and said:
"Commoners who confuse feudal lords deserve death!
I request orders for the officials!"
The officials acted according to the law,
and their hands and feet were separated.
Duke Jǐng, frightened and shaken,
knew he was inferior in righteousness,
returned greatly alarmed,
and told his ministers:
"Lǔ uses the way of gentlemen to assist its ruler,
while you alone teach me with barbarian ways,
causing me to offend the ruler of Lǔ,
what should be done about it?"
An official came forward and replied:
"When a gentleman errs, he apologizes with substance;
when a petty man errs, he apologizes with words.
If you regret it,
then apologize with substance."
Thereupon, the Marquis of Qí returned the fields of Yùn,
Wènyáng,
and Guīyīn that he had seized from Lǔ to apologize.
In the summer of the thirteenth year of Duke Dìng,
Kǒngzǐ said to Duke Dìng:
"Ministers should not store armor,
and grand masters should not have cities with walls of a hundred zhì."
He had Zhòng Yóu serve as steward for the Jì family,
intending to dismantle the three capitals.
Thereupon, the Shūsūn family first dismantled Hòu.
When the Jì family was about to dismantle Bì,
Gōngshān Bùniǔ
and Shūsūn Zhé led the people of Bì to attack Lǔ.
The duke and three sons entered the palace of the Jì family,
ascending the terrace of Wǔzǐ.
The people of Bì attacked them,
but did not overcome,
entering near the duke's side.
Kǒngzǐ ordered Shēn Jūxū
and Yuè Qí to descend and attack them,
and the people of Bì fled north.
The people of the state pursued them,
defeating them at Gūmiè.
The two men fled to Qí,
and thus Bì was dismantled.
When about to dismantle Chéng,
Gōngliǎn Chǔfǔ said to Mèngsūn:
"If Chéng is dismantled,
the people of Qí will surely reach the northern gate.
Moreover, Chéng
is the protective barrier of the Mèng family;
without Chéng, there is no Mèng family.
I will not dismantle it."
In the twelfth month,
the duke besieged Chéng,
but did not overcome it.
In the fourteenth year of Duke Dìng,
Kǒngzǐ was fifty-six years old,
serving as acting minister from the position of Grand Minister of Justice,
and had a joyful expression.
A disciple said:
"I have heard that a gentleman does not fear when calamity comes,
nor does he rejoice when fortune comes."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"There is such a saying.
But is it not also said,
'He delights in being noble yet humbling himself to others'?"
Thereupon, he executed the Lǔ grand master Shǎozhèng Mǎo who disturbed the government.
After participating in state affairs for three months,
sellers of lambs and piglets did not inflate prices;
men and women walking separated on the roads;
lost items on the roads were not picked up;
when guests from all directions arrived in the city, they did not need to seek officials,
as all were provided for until they returned.
The people of Qí heard and feared,
saying:
"If Kǒngzǐ governs, Lǔ will surely become hegemon.
If it becomes hegemon, our land being near,
we will be the first to be annexed.
Why not offer them land?"
Lí Chú said:
"Please first try to thwart him;
if thwarting fails, then offer land—
is that too late!"
Thereupon, they selected eighty beautiful women from Qí,
all dressed in embroidered robes and dancing the "Kānglè,"
and one hundred twenty fine horses,
and sent them to the ruler of Lǔ.
They displayed the female musicians and fine horses outside the south gate of Lǔ's city wall.
Jì Huánzǐ went incognito to watch repeatedly,
intending to accept them,
then advised the ruler of Lǔ to tour around the circumference road,
going to watch all day,
and neglecting government affairs.
Zǐlù said:
"Master, you may leave now."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Lǔ is now about to perform the suburban sacrifice;
if the sacrificial meat is sent to the grand masters,
then I may still stay."
Huánzǐ finally accepted the Qí female musicians,
and for three days did not attend to governance;
at the suburban sacrifice, he did not send the sacrificial meat to the grand masters.
Kǒngzǐ then departed,
staying overnight at Tún.
And Shī Jǐ saw him off,
saying:
"Master, you are without fault."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Shall I sing for you?"
He sang:
"The mouths of those women
can make one flee;
the requests of those women
can bring death and ruin.
Ah, leisurely and carefree,
I shall pass my years!"
Shī Jǐ returned,
and Huánzǐ said:
"What did Kǒngzǐ say?"
Shī Jǐ told him the truth.
Huánzǐ sighed deeply and said:
"The master blames me because of those maids!"
Kǒngzǐ then went to Wèi,
staying at the home of Yán Zhuózōu, the elder brother of Zǐlù's wife.
Duke Líng of Wèi asked Kǒngzǐ:
"What was your salary in Lǔ?"
He replied:
"I received sixty thousand measures of grain."
The people of Wèi also gave him sixty thousand measures.
After staying a short while,
someone slandered Kǒngzǐ to Duke Líng of Wèi.
Duke Líng had Gōngsūn Yújiǎ come and go to watch him.
Kǒngzǐ feared he would be accused of a crime;
after staying ten months,
he left Wèi.
When about to go to Chén,
he passed by Kuāng,
with Yán Kè as his driver,
who pointed with his whip and said:
"Previously I entered here
through that gap."
The people of Kuāng heard this,
and thought it was Yáng Hǔ of Lǔ.
Yáng Hǔ had once oppressed the Kuāng people,
so they detained Confucius.
Confucius resembled Yáng Hǔ in appearance,
and was confined for five days.
Yán Yuān arrived later,
the Master said:
"I thought you had died."
Yán Yuān said:
"While you are alive,
how would I dare to die!"
The Kuāng people detained Confucius more urgently,
and the disciples were afraid.
Confucius said:
"Since King Wén perished,
has cultural heritage not resided here?
If Heaven intended to destroy this culture,
later generations would not partake in it.
If Heaven does not destroy this culture,
what can the Kuāng people do to me!"
Confucius sent a follower to serve as a retainer to Nìng Wǔzǐ in Wèi,
then was able to leave.
Leaving, he passed through Pú.
After over a month,
he returned to Wèi,
staying at the house of Qú Bóyù.
Lord Líng's wife, named Nánzǐ,
sent someone to tell Confucius:
"All gentlemen from various states who wish to befriend our lord,
must meet our lady.
Our lady wishes to meet you."
Confucius declined,
but eventually had to see her.
The lady was behind fine silk curtains.
Confucius entered the gate,
bowed northward.
The lady bowed twice from behind the curtains,
her jade pendants making tinkling sounds.
Confucius said:
"I had not wished to see her,
but having met, I responded with propriety."
Zǐlù was displeased.
Confucius swore:
"If I have done wrong,
may Heaven reject me!
May Heaven reject me!"
After staying in Wèi over a month,
Lord Líng and his wife rode together,
with eunuch Yōng Qú as attendant,
going out, making Confucius ride in the second carriage,
parading ostentatiously through the market.
Confucius said:
"I have never seen one who loves virtue as much as he loves beauty."
Thus ashamed of this,
he left Wèi,
passing through Cáo.
That year,
Lord Dìng of Lǔ died.
Confucius left Cáo for Sòng,
practicing rituals with disciples under a large tree.
Sīmǎ Huán Tuí of Sòng wanted to kill Confucius,
and uprooted the tree.
Confucius left.
A disciple said:
"We should hurry."
Confucius said:
"Heaven endowed me with virtue,
what can Huán Tuí do to me!"
Confucius went to Zhèng,
and got separated from his disciples,
standing alone at the eastern gate of the outer wall.
Someone from Zhèng told Zǐgòng:
"There is a man at the eastern gate,
his forehead resembles Yáo's,
his neck resembles Gāo Yáo's,
his shoulders resemble Zǐchǎn's,
but from the waist down he is three inches shorter than Yǔ,
weary like a homeless dog."
Zǐgòng truthfully told Confucius.
Confucius laughed cheerfully and said:
"The physical description,
is unimportant.
But being called a homeless dog,
quite so!
Quite so!"
Confucius then went to Chén,
staying at the house of Sīchéng Zhēnzǐ.
After over a year,
King Fūchāi of Wú attacked Chén,
capturing three cities before leaving.
Zhào Yǎng attacked Zhāogē.
Chǔ besieged Cài,
and Cài moved to Wú.
Wú defeated King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè at Kuàijī.
A hawk fell on the Chén court and died,
pierced by an arrow of thornwood,
with stone arrowhead,
the arrow being one foot eight inches long.
Lord Mǐn of Chén sent a messenger to ask Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said:
"The hawk came from afar,
this is an arrow of Sùshèn.
Formerly King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
opening routes to all tribes,
making each bring local tribute,
so they would not neglect their duties.
Then Sùshèn offered thornwood arrows with stone heads,
one foot eight inches long.
The former king, wishing to display his virtue,
gave Sùshèn arrows to his eldest daughter,
married her to Yú Húgōng and enfeoffed them at Chén.
He gave precious jade to same-surname relatives,
to strengthen kinship;
gave distant tributes to different-surname relatives,
to make them not forget their service.
Thus Chén was given Sùshèn arrows."
Searching the old treasury,
they indeed found them.
Confucius stayed in Chén for three years,
while Jìn and Chǔ struggled for supremacy,
alternately attacking Chén,
and when Wú invaded Chén,
Chén was often plundered.
Confucius said:
"Let's return, let's return!
The young members of our group are ambitious but simple,
making progress without forgetting their origins."
Thus Confucius left Chén.
Passing through Pú,
he encountered Gōngshū's rebellion there,
and the Pú people detained Confucius.
Among the disciples was Gōngliáng Rú,
who followed Confucius with five personal chariots.
He was tall and virtuous,
with courage and strength,
and said:
"I previously followed our Master in trouble at Kuāng,
now we encounter trouble here again,
this is fate.
Having faced hardship twice with our Master,
I would rather fight to death."
He fought fiercely.
The Pú people feared,
and told Confucius:
"If you do not go to Wèi,
we will let you go."
Making a covenant with them,
they released Confucius through the eastern gate.
Confucius then went to Wèi.
Zǐgòng said:
"Can we break the covenant?"
Confucius said:
"It was a coerced covenant,
the spirits do not heed it."
Lord Líng of Wèi heard Confucius had come,
was pleased, and welcomed him outside the city.
He asked:
"Can Pú be attacked?"
Confucius replied:
"It can."
Lord Líng said:
"My ministers think it cannot.
Now Pú
is what Wèi relies on against Jìn and Chǔ,
for Wèi to attack it,
would that not be inadvisable?"
Confucius said:
"Their men are determined to die,
their women determined to defend Xīhé.
Those we need to attack are but four or five."
Lord Líng said:
"Good."
But he did not attack Pú.
Lord Líng was old,
neglected governance,
and did not employ Confucius.
Confucius sighed deeply and said:
"If someone would employ me,
in a month there would be results,
in three years, great achievement."
Confucius left.
Fú Xī served as the magistrate of Zhōngmóu.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ attacked Fàn and
Zhōngháng,
and assaulted Zhōngmóu.
Fú Xī rebelled,
and sent someone to summon Confucius.
Confucius intended to go.
Zǐlù said:
"I have heard from you, Master,
'A gentleman does not enter the domain of one who personally engages in wrongdoing.'
Now Fú Xī is personally using Zhōngmóu to rebel,
and you wish to go.
How can this be?"
Confucius said:
"Indeed, there is such a saying.
But is it not said that what is truly hard
cannot be worn thin by grinding;
and is it not said that what is truly white
cannot be blackened by dye?
Am I merely a bitter gourd,
that I should hang without being eaten?"
Confucius was playing the stone chimes.
A man carrying a basket passed by his gate
and said:
"How heartfelt,
this playing of the chimes!
Clanging away so insistently,
that no one understands him—then he should stop there!"
Confucius learned to play the zither from Master Xiāngzǐ,
and after ten days had not progressed further.
Master Xiāngzǐ said:
"You may advance now."
Confucius said:
"I have mastered the melody,
but not the technique yet."
After a while,
Master Xiāngzǐ said:
"You have mastered the technique,
you may advance now."
Confucius said:
"I have not grasped the spirit yet."
After a while,
Master Xiāngzǐ said:
"You have grasped the spirit,
you may advance now."
Confucius said:
"I have not perceived the man yet."
After a while,
he became solemn and deeply thoughtful,
then joyful, gazing afar as if with lofty aspirations.
He said:
"I perceive the man—
dark and swarthy,
tall and imposing,
with eyes gazing into the distance,
as if ruling over the four states.
If not King Wén, who could have composed this!"
Master Xiāngzǐ rose from his mat and bowed twice,
saying:
"My teacher did say this was 'The Composition of King Wén.'"
Since Confucius could not gain employment in Wèi,
he planned to go west to see Zhào Jiǎnzǐ.
Upon reaching the Yellow River, he heard of the deaths of Dòu Míngdú
and Shùn Huá,
and gazing at the river, he sighed:
"How magnificent the waters,
so vast and boundless!
That I cannot cross this—
it is fate!"
Zǐgòng hurried forward and asked:
"May I ask what you mean?"
Confucius said:
"Dòu Míngdú
and Shùn Huá
were worthy ministers of Jìn.
When Zhào Jiǎnzǐ had not yet achieved his ambitions,
he needed these two to govern;
but once he succeeded,
he killed them to consolidate power.
I have heard that
if you disembowel pregnant animals and kill the young, the qílín will not approach the suburbs;
if you drain the pond to catch all fish, the jiāolóng will not harmonize yīn and yáng;
if you overturn nests and destroy eggs, the fènghuáng will not soar.
Why?
Because the gentleman avoids harming his own kind.
Even birds and beasts shun what is unjust,
how much more so should I!"
So he returned and rested in Zōuxiāng,
composing "The Zōu Composition" to mourn them.
Then he went back to Wèi,
staying at the home of Qú Bóyù.
Another day,
Duke Líng asked about battle formations.
Confucius said:
"I have learned about sacrificial rites,
but not military matters."
The next day,
while speaking with Confucius,
the duke saw wild geese flying,
looked up at them,
and his attention drifted from Confucius.
Confucius then departed,
going again to Chén.
In summer,
Duke Líng of Wèi died,
and his grandson Zhé was enthroned,
becoming Duke Chū of Wèi.
In June,
Zhào Yǎng installed the crown prince Kuǎikuì in Qī.
Yáng Hǔ had the crown prince don mourning garb,
with eight men in hempen clothes,
pretending to be a welcoming party from Wèi,
entered weeping,
and thus settled there.
In winter, Cài moved to Zhōulái.
That year was the third year of Duke Āi of Lǔ,
and Confucius was sixty years old.
Qí aided Wèi in besieging Qī,
because the Wèi crown prince Kuǎikuì was there.
In summer,
the temples of Huán and Lí in Lǔ caught fire,
and Nángōng Jìngshū helped extinguish it.
Confucius, in Chén,
heard of it
and said:
"The fire must be at the temples of Huán and Lí, mustn't it?"
And indeed it was so.
In autumn,
Jì Huánzǐ fell ill,
was carried in a carriage to see the Lǔ capital,
and sighed deeply:
"This state was nearly prosperous once,
but because I offended Confucius,
it did not prosper."
Turning to his heir Kāngzǐ, he said:
"When I die,
you will surely become minister of Lǔ;
as minister,
you must summon Zhòngní."
A few days later,
Huánzǐ died,
and Kāngzǐ succeeded him.
After the burial,
he wished to summon Zhòngní.
Gōng Zhīyú said:
"Our former lord employed him but did not see it through,
and ended up being laughed at by the feudal lords.
If we employ him now
and again fail to see it through,
we will be laughed at once more."
Kāngzǐ asked:
"Then whom should we summon instead?"
He replied:
"We must summon Rǎn Qiú."
So he sent a messenger to summon Rǎn Qiú.
As Rǎn Qiú was about to leave,
Confucius said:
"The people of Lǔ are summoning Qiú—
not for a minor role,
but for a great one."
That day,
Confucius said:
"Let's return, let's return!
The young scholars of our home are ambitious and unrestrained,
weaving patterns of brilliance,
and I do not know how to shape them."
Zǐgòng knew Confucius longed to return,
and upon sending off Rǎn Qiú,
advised him:
"If employed,
