have them summon Confucius."
So it was said.
After Rǎn Qiú departed,
the next year,
Confucius moved from Chén to Cài.
Duke Zhāo of Cài was about to go to Wú,
summoned by Wú.
Previously, Duke Zhāo had deceived his ministers by moving to Zhōulái,
and now as he prepared to go again,
the ministers feared another relocation,
so Gōngsūn Piān shot and killed Duke Zhāo.
Chǔ invaded Cài.
In autumn, Duke Jǐng of Qí died.
The following year,
Confucius went from Cài to Yè.
Duke Yè asked about governance,
and Confucius said:
"Governance lies in attracting those from afar and attaching those nearby."
Another day,
Duke Yè asked Zǐlù about Confucius,
but Zǐlù did not respond.
Confucius heard of this,
and said:
"Yóu,
why did you not reply, saying
'His character is such that
he learns the Way tirelessly,
teaches others without weariness,
so fervent he forgets to eat,
so joyful he forgets sorrow,
unaware that old age is approaching'
and so forth."
Leaving Yè,
he returned to Cài.
Cháng Jū
and Jíe Nì were plowing together,
and Confucius, taking them for recluses,
sent Zǐlù to ask them about the ford.
Cháng Jū said:
"Who is that holding the reins?"
Zǐlù said:
"It is Kǒng Qiū."
He said:
"Is it Kǒng Qiū of Lǔ?"
He said:
"Yes."
He said:
"Then he knows the ford."
Jíe Nì said to Zǐlù:
"Who are you?"
He said:
"I am Zhòng Yóu."
He said:
"You,
are a follower of Kǒng Qiū?"
He said:
"Yes."
Jíe Nì said:
"The world is full of turmoil,
and who can change it?
Moreover, rather than following one who shuns certain men,
wouldn't it be better to follow those who shun the world altogether!"
And he continued harrowing without stopping.
Zǐlù reported this to Confucius,
who sighed and said:
"One cannot herd with birds and beasts.
If the Way prevailed in the world,
I would not need to change it."
Another day,
Zǐlù was traveling
and met an old man carrying a basket,
and asked:
"Have you seen my master?"
The old man said:
"You who do not toil with your limbs
and cannot distinguish the five grains,
who is your master!"
And he planted his staff and weeded.
Zǐlù reported this,
and Confucius said:
"He is a recluse."
But when he went back,
the man was gone.
After Confucius had moved to Cài for three years,
Wú attacked Chén.
Chǔ came to rescue Chén
and encamped at Chéngfù.
Hearing that Confucius was between Chén and Cài,
Chǔ sent an envoy to invite Confucius.
As Confucius was about to go and pay respects,
the ministers of Chén and Cài plotted, saying:
"Confucius is a worthy man,
and his criticisms always hit the flaws of the feudal lords.
Now he has long stayed between Chén and Cài,
and all the measures taken by our ministers run counter to Zhòngní's ideas.
Now Chǔ,
a great state,
has come to invite Confucius.
If Confucius is employed by Chǔ,
then the ministers in power in Chén and Cài will be in danger."
Thereupon, they together sent men to surround Confucius in the wilderness.
He could not proceed,
and their provisions were cut off.
His followers fell ill,
and none could rise.
Yet Confucius continued teaching, reciting, playing the zither, and singing without faltering.
Zǐlù, looking displeased, came to see him and said:
"Can a gentleman also be in dire straits?"
Confucius said:
"A gentleman remains steadfast in adversity,
while a petty man, in adversity, becomes reckless."
Zǐgòng showed a change of expression.
Confucius said:
"Cì,
do you think I am one who learns widely and remembers much?"
He said:
"Yes.
Is it not so?"
Confucius said:
"No.
I have one thread that runs through it all."
Knowing his disciples were resentful,
Confucius summoned Zǐlù and asked:
"The Odes say,
'We are not rhinoceroses nor tigers,
yet we roam the desolate wilds.'
Is my Way wrong?
Why am I in this plight?"
Zǐlù said:
"Perhaps we are not benevolent enough?
So people do not trust us.
Perhaps we are not wise enough?
So people do not follow our Way."
Confucius said:
"Is that so!
Yóu, if the benevolent were always trusted,
how could there be Bó Yí
and Shū Qí?
If the wise were always followed,
how could there be Prince Bǐgān?"
Zǐlù went out,
and Zǐgòng entered to see him.
Confucius said:
"Cì,
the Odes say,
'We are not rhinoceroses nor tigers,
yet we roam the desolate wilds.'
Is my Way wrong?
Why am I in this plight?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Master, your Way is too great,
so the world cannot accept you.
Why not lower your standards a bit?"
Confucius said:
"Cì,
a good farmer can sow but cannot guarantee a harvest,
a good craftsman can be skillful but cannot ensure everything goes smoothly.
A gentleman can cultivate his Way,
organize it with principles,
and systematize it with order,
but he cannot guarantee it will be accepted.
Now you do not cultivate your Way but seek to be accepted.
Cì, your ambition is not far-reaching!"
Zǐgòng went out,
and Yán Huí entered to see him.
Confucius said:
"Huí,
the Odes say,
'We are not rhinoceroses nor tigers,
yet we roam the desolate wilds.'
Is my Way wrong?
Why am I in this plight?"
Yán Huí said:
"Master, your Way is too great,
so the world cannot accept it.
Nevertheless,
you promote and practice it,
and what does it matter if it is not accepted?
It is precisely when not accepted that the gentleman is revealed!
If the Way is not cultivated,
that is our shame.
But if the Way is greatly cultivated and not employed,
that is the shame of the rulers.
What does it matter if it is not accepted?
It is precisely when not accepted that the gentleman is revealed!"
Confucius laughed joyfully and said:
"Is that so, son of the Yán family!
If you had much wealth,
I would be your steward."
Thereupon, he sent Zǐgòng to Chǔ.
King Zhāo of Chǔ raised an army to welcome Confucius,
and only then was he freed.
King Zhāo intended to enfeoff Confucius with seven hundred lǐ of land from the Shūshè.
The Prime Minister of Chǔ, Zǐxī, said:
"Does the king have any envoy to the feudal lords like Zǐgòng?"
The king replied:
"There is none."
"Does the king have any assistant minister like Yán Huí?"
He replied:
"There is none."
"Does the king have any commander like Zǐlù?"
He replied:
"There is none."
"Does the king have any official like Zǎi Yǔ?"
He replied:
"There is none."
"Moreover, the ancestors of Chǔ were enfeoffed by the Zhōu,
with the title of a zǐ or nán rank over fifty lǐ.
Now Kǒng Qiū expounds the laws of the Three Huáng and Five Dì,
and elucidates the achievements of Zhōu and Shào.
If the king employs him,
then how can Chǔ maintain its vast territory of several thousand lǐ for generations to come?
King Wén was in Fēng,
King Wǔ was in Hào,
yet a lord of a hundred lǐ eventually ruled the world.
Now if Kǒng Qiū gains a territorial base,
with his worthy disciples as aides,
it would not be a blessing for Chǔ."
King Zhāo then abandoned the plan.
That autumn,
King Zhāo of Chǔ died in Chéngfù.
The madman of Chǔ, Jiēyú, passed by Confucius singing:
"Oh Phoenix, oh Phoenix,
how virtue has declined!
The past cannot be remonstrated,
but the future can still be pursued.
Enough, enough,
those in power today are in peril!"
Confucius alighted,
wishing to speak with him.
But he hurried away,
and Confucius could not converse with him.
Thereupon, Confucius returned from Chǔ to Wèi.
That year,
Confucius was sixty-three years old,
which was the sixth year of Duke Āi of Lǔ.
The following year,
Wú and Lǔ met at Zēng,
and demanded a hundred sets of sacrificial animals.
Grand Steward Pǐ summoned Jì Kāngzǐ.
Kāngzǐ sent Zǐgòng to go,
and only then was the matter resolved.
Confucius said:
"The governments of Lǔ and Wèi are like brothers."
At that time,
the father of the ruler of Wèi, Zhé, could not be established,
and was abroad,
with the feudal lords repeatedly criticizing this.
And many of Confucius's disciples were serving in Wèi,
so the ruler of Wèi wished to have Confucius handle the government.
Zǐlù said:
"If the ruler of Wèi awaits you to govern,
what will you prioritize?"
Confucius said:
"It must be the rectification of names!"
Zǐlù said:
"Is that so?
How pedantic you are!
How can they be rectified?"
Confucius said:
"How uncouth you are, Yóu!
If names are not correct, speech is not smooth;
if speech is not smooth, affairs do not succeed;
if affairs do not succeed, rites and music do not flourish;
if rites and music do not flourish, punishments are not just;
if punishments are not just, the people do not know where to place hand or foot.
The gentleman ensures that what he does can be named,
and what he says can be practiced.
The gentleman, in his speech,
is simply never careless."
The next year,
Rǎn Yǒu led the army for the Jì family,
fought with Qí at Láng,
and defeated them.
Jì Kāngzǐ said:
"As for your military skills,
did you learn them?
Or are they innate?"
Rǎn Yǒu said:
"I learned them from Confucius."
Jì Kāngzǐ said:
"What kind of person is Confucius?"
He replied:
"When he is employed, it is with just cause;
when his teachings spread among the people,
they stand scrutiny by ghosts and spirits without regret.
If one seeks to attain this Way,
even if offered a thousand shè,
the Master would not consider it advantageous."
Kāngzǐ said:
"I wish to summon him;
is it possible?"
He replied:
"If you wish to summon him,
then do not let petty men hem him in,
and it will be acceptable."
Meanwhile, in Wèi, Kǒng Wénzǐ was about to attack Tàishū,
and asked for strategy from Zhòngní.
Zhòngní declined, claiming ignorance,
withdrew, ordered the carriage, and prepared to leave,
saying:
"A bird can choose its tree,
but can a tree choose a bird?"
Wénzǐ firmly stopped him.
It happened that Jì Kāngzǐ expelled Gōng Huá,
Gōng Bīn,
and Gōng Lín,
and with gifts welcomed Confucius,
so Confucius returned to Lǔ.
Confucius had left Lǔ for a total of fourteen years before returning.
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked about government,
and he replied:
"Government lies in selecting ministers."
Jì Kāngzǐ asked about government,
and he said:
"Promote the straight and set them above the crooked,
and the crooked will become straight."
Kāngzǐ was troubled by thieves,
and Confucius said:
"If you yourself were without desire,
even if you rewarded them, they would not steal."
However, Lǔ ultimately could not employ Confucius,
and Confucius also did not seek office.
In Confucius's time,
the Zhōu court was weak and the rites and music were in disarray,
and the "Book of Songs" and "Book of Documents" were incomplete.
He traced back the rites of the Three Dynasties,
compiled the "Shū Zhuàn,"
recording from the time of Táng and Yú above,
down to Duke Mù of Qín,
arranging the events in order.
He said:
"I can discuss the rites of Xià,
but Qǐ does not provide sufficient evidence.
I can discuss the rites of Yīn,
but Sòng does not provide sufficient evidence.
If there were sufficient evidence, I could verify them."
Observing the additions and omissions of Yīn and Xià,
he said:
"Even a hundred generations hence can be known,
based on the alternation of refinement and substance.
Zhōu drew from the two dynasties;
how richly cultured it was!
I follow Zhōu."
Thus the "Shū Zhuàn" and
"Lǐjì" originated from Confucius.
Confucius said to the Grand Music Master of Lǔ:
"Music can be understood.
At the start, it harmonizes;
as it unfolds, it is pure,
clear,
and continuous,
and thus completes."
"Since I returned from Wèi to Lǔ,
only then was music corrected,
and the 'Yǎ' and 'Sòng' each found their proper place."
In ancient times, there were over three thousand poems,
but by Confucius's time,
he removed duplicates,
selecting those applicable to ritual righteousness,
gathering from the times of Xiè and Hòujì above,
recounting the prosperity of Yīn and Zhōu in the middle,
down to the failings of Yōu and Lì,
beginning with domestic life.
Hence it is said:
"'Guān Jū' marks the beginning of the 'Fēng',
'Lù Míng' the beginning of the 'Xiǎo Yǎ',
'Wén Wáng' the beginning of the 'Dà Yǎ',
and 'Qīng Miào' the beginning of the 'Sòng'."
All 305 poems were set to music by Confucius,
aiming to match the tones of 'Sháo', 'Wǔ', 'Yǎ', and 'Sòng'.
Rites and music from then on could be transmitted,
to complete the Kingly Way,
and form the Six Arts.
In his later years, Confucius developed a fondness for the "Yì Jīng",
and composed commentaries on the "Tuàn",
"Xì",
"Xiàng",
"Shuō Guà",
and "Wén Yán".
He read the "Yì Jīng" so frequently
that the leather thongs binding the bamboo strips broke three times.
He said:
"If I were given a few more years,
starting from now,
I would become well-versed in the 'Yì Jīng'."
Confucius taught using the Shī Jīng, Shū Jīng, Lǐ, and Yuè,
and his disciples numbered about three thousand,
of whom seventy-two mastered the six arts.
Disciples like Yán Zhuózōu
and others who received instruction from him were very numerous.
Confucius taught four things:
culture, conduct,
loyalty, and trustworthiness.
He abstained from four things:
arbitrary opinions,
dogmatism,
stubbornness,
and egotism.
He was cautious about:
fasting, war,
and illness. He rarely spoke about profit, fate, and benevolence.
He would not enlighten anyone who was not eager to learn,
nor explain to anyone who was not anxious to understand;
if he presented one corner and they could not come back with the other three, he would not repeat himself.
In his local community,
he appeared humble as if he could not speak.
In the ancestral temple and at court,
he spoke eloquently,
though cautiously.
At court, when speaking with high-ranking officials,
he was respectful;
when speaking with lower-ranking officials,
he was affable.
Upon entering the palace gate,
he would bow forward;
when hastening forward,
he did so with wings-like grace.
When the ruler summoned him to receive guests,
his expression became alert.
When summoned by the ruler's command,
he would not wait for the carriage to be harnessed but set off on foot.
If fish was spoiled,
meat tainted,
or it was not cut properly,
he would not eat it.
If his mat was not straight,
he would not sit on it.
When eating in the presence of someone in mourning,
he never ate his fill.
On a day he had wept,
he would not sing.
Upon seeing someone in mourning clothes
or a blind person,
even if they were a child, he would invariably show a change in demeanor.
"When three are walking together,
I am sure to find a teacher among them."
"Not cultivating virtue,
not discussing learning,
hearing what is right but not moving towards it,
failing to correct one's faults—
these are what I worry about."
When he had someone sing for him,
if it was good,
he would have them repeat it, and then he would join in.
Confucius did not speak of:
the extraordinary, feats of strength,
disorder, or spirits.
Zǐgòng said:
"We can hear our Master's views on culture and learning,
but we cannot hear his views on the Way of Heaven and human nature and destiny."
Yán Yuān said with a sigh:
"The more I look up at it, the higher it appears;
the more I drill into it, the harder it becomes.
I see it in front,
and suddenly it's behind.
Our Master is skilled at leading people on step by step;
he broadens me with culture
and restrains me with ritual,
making me want to stop but unable to do so.
Having exhausted my abilities,
it seems to stand there,
distinctly before me.
Though I wish to follow it,
I can find no way to do so."
A man from Dáxiàng village said:
"How great is Confucius!
He is so learned that he cannot be identified by any one skill."
Hearing this, Confucius said:
"What shall I take up?
Shall I take up charioteering?
Or archery?
I think I'll take up charioteering."
Láo said:
"The Master said,
'Not having been employed,
I therefore acquired many arts.'"
In the spring of the fourteenth year of Duke Āi of Lǔ,
a hunt was held at Dàyě.
Shūsūn's charioteer Chú Shāng captured a beast
and considered it inauspicious.
Zhòngní saw it
and said:
"It is a qílín."
Then he took it.
He said:
"The Hé River does not produce its chart,
the Luò River does not produce its writing—
I am done for!"
When Yán Yuān died,
Confucius said:
"Heaven is destroying me!"
And when he saw the qílín during the western hunt,
he said:
"My way is at an end!"
He sighed deeply and said:
"There is no one who knows me!"
Zǐgòng asked:
"Why is there no one who knows you?"
The Master said:
"I do not complain against Heaven,
nor do I blame others.
I study what is below and comprehend what is above.
If anyone knows me, perhaps it is Heaven!"
"Those who did not lower their aspirations
nor disgrace themselves—
were they not Bó Yí
and Shū Qí?"
He said of
"Liǔxià Huì
and Shào Lián that they lowered their aspirations and disgraced themselves."
He said of
"Yú Zhòng
and Yí Yì that they lived in seclusion and spoke freely,
their conduct was pure,
and their rejection of office was a matter of expediency."
"I am different from all these;
I have no musts and no must-nots."
The Master said:
"Is it not so? Is it not so?
A gentleman regrets dying without his name being celebrated.
My way is not being put into practice;
how shall I make myself known to later ages?"
Thereupon, he composed the "Chūn Qiū" based on historical records,
beginning with Duke Yīn
and ending in the fourteenth year of Duke Āi,
covering twelve dukes.
It was rooted in Lǔ,
respectful to Zhōu,
reverent to Yīn,
and extended through the three dynasties.
Its language was concise yet its meaning profound.
Thus, though the rulers of Wú and Chǔ called themselves kings,
the "Chūn Qiū" demoted them, calling them
"viscounts";
though the meeting at Jiàntǔ actually summoned the Zhōu Son of Heaven,
the "Chūn Qiū" concealed this, saying
"The Heavenly King hunted at Héyáng"—
applying such principles to judge the contemporary age.
The principle of criticism and restraint
would later be taken up and expanded by true kings.
When the principles of the "Chūn Qiū" were put into practice,
then all rebellious ministers and villainous sons under heaven would be filled with fear.
When Confucius held office and tried cases,
his judgments could be shared with others;
he did not keep them to himself.
But when it came to composing the "Chūn Qiū",
what should be written was written,
what should be cut was cut,
and even disciples like Zǐxià could not add a single word.
When his disciples received the "Chūn Qiū",
Confucius said:
"Later generations will know me through the 'Chūn Qiū',
and they will condemn me also because of the 'Chūn Qiū'."
Next year,
Zǐlù died in Wèi.
Confucius fell ill,
Zǐgòng requested a meeting.
Confucius was supporting himself with a staff, leisurely at the gate,
and said:
"Sì,
why have you come so late?"
Confucius then sighed,
and sang:
"The Great Mountain crumbles!
The beams and pillars shatter!
The wise men wither!"
He then wept.
He said to Zǐgòng:
"The world has been without the Way for a long time now,
no one can follow my teachings.
The people of Xià bury their dead on the eastern steps,
Zhōu people on the western steps,
Yīn people between two pillars.
Last night I dreamed of sitting between two pillars at a funeral,
I am to be considered a Yīn person."
After seven days, he passed away.
Confucius was seventy-three years old,
and died on the jǐchǒu day in the fourth month of the sixteenth year of Duke Āi of Lǔ.
Duke Āi delivered a eulogy for him, saying:
"Heaven mourns below,
forbearing not to leave even an old man,
leaving only one man to serve in office,
leaving me alone in suffering.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Master Nī,
do not impose rules on yourself!"
Zǐgòng said:
"Will the Lord not be buried in Lǔ?
The Master's words are:
'When rites are lost, there is confusion,
when names are lost, there are errors.
Losing one's aspirations causes confusion,
and losing one's position results in errors.'
In life he was not employed,
in death he is eulogized,
this is not in accord with the rites.
Referring to
'one man'
is not fitting."
Confucius was buried north of Lǔ City by the Sì River,
where his disciples all mourned for three years.
When the three years of mourning were completed,
they parted ways and left,
then cried,
each returned to express their grief;
some stayed on.
Only Zǐgàn built a hut on the mound,
for a full six years,
then left.
Disciples and people of Lǔ gathered to live by the tomb, numbering over a hundred households,
and they named it Kǒnglǐ.
From generation to generation in Lǔ, people would periodically offer sacrifices at Confucius's tomb,
and scholars would discuss the rites, village drinking ceremonies, and grand archery at Confucius’s tomb.
Confucius’s tomb covered an area of one qǐng.
At the place where he had lived, the disciples established an inner hall,
and in later generations a temple was built to store Confucius’s clothes, hat, qín, chariot, and books,
lasting over two hundred years until the Hàn dynasty.
When Emperor Gāo visited Lǔ,
he offered a grand sacrifice there.
Whenever ministers of the state arrived,
they would first pay respects before proceeding to governance.
Confucius had a son named Lǐ,
styled Bóyú.
Bóyú lived to the age of fifty,
and died before Confucius.
Bóyú had a son Jí,
styled Zǐsī,
who lived to be sixty-two.
He once faced hardships in Sòng.
Zǐsī composed the "Doctrine of the Mean".
Zǐsī had a son Bái,
styled Zǐshàng,
who lived to be forty-seven.
Zǐshàng had a son Qiú,
styled Zǐjiā,
who lived to be forty-five.
Zǐjiā had a son Jī,
styled Zǐjīng,
who lived to be forty-six.
Zǐjīng had a son Chuān,
styled Zǐgāo,
who lived to be fifty-one.
Zǐgāo had a son Zǐshèn,
who lived to be fifty-seven,
and once served as Chancellor of Wèi.
Zǐshèn had a son Fù,
who lived to be fifty-seven,
served as an academician for King Shè of Chén,
and died at Chén.
Fù had a disciple Xiāng,
who lived to be fifty-seven.
Xiāng once served as an academician for Emperor Xiàohuì,
and was promoted to be the Governor of Chángshā.
He was nine feet six inches tall.
Xiāng had a son Zhōng,
who lived to be fifty-seven.
Zhōng had a son Wǔ,
Wǔ had sons Yánnián and Ānguó.
Ānguó served as an academician for the current emperor,
became the Governor of Línhuái,
but died young.
Ānguó had a son Áng,
Áng had a son Huān.
Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
The "Classic of Poetry" says:
"Noble is the lofty mountain,
we follow its footsteps."
Though one cannot reach it,
yet the heart yearns towards it.
I read the works of the Kǒng family,
and imagine what kind of person he was.
When I went to Lǔ,
I observed Zhòngní's temple and the carriages and ritual vessels,
and the students practicing the rites at their home regularly,
I was deeply moved and reluctant to leave.
In the world there have been many wise rulers and virtuous people,
at the time they were honored,
but after death they are forgotten.
Confucius was a man of the people,
and his teachings have been passed down for over ten generations,
with scholars following them.
From emperors and princes,
those in China who speak of the "Six Arts" refer to the Master,
he can truly be called the greatest sage!
Chén Shèng,
was a man from Yángchéng,
styled Shè.
Wú Guǎng,
was a man from Yángxià,
styled Shū.
When Chén Shèng was young,
he once worked as a laborer,
and stopped tilling the ridge,
sighing for a long time,
and said:
"If I become rich and noble,
let us not forget each other."
His fellow workers laughed and replied:
"You are a laborer,
how can you expect to become rich and noble?"
Chén Shèng sighed and said:
"Alas,
how can sparrows understand the ambitions of swans!"
In the first year of the Second Emperor, in July,
men from the left side of the village were conscripted to guard Yúyáng,
nine hundred men stationed in Dàzéxiāng.
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng were both selected to go on duty,
serving as commanders of the barracks.
There was a great rain,
obstructing the roads,
and they anticipated being late.
Being late, according to the law, was punishable by decapitation.
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng therefore conspired:
"Running away means death,
starting an uprising also means death,
if we are to die,
why not die for our country?"
Chén Shèng said: "The world has suffered under Qín's harshness for so long.
I have heard the Second Emperor is a young son,
not fit to rule,
the one who should have ascended was Prince Fúsū.
Fúsū was sent to command troops due to frequent remonstrations,
so the emperor stationed him outside.
It is said that despite his innocence,
the Second Emperor has killed him.
Many people have heard of his virtue,
but are unaware of his death.
Xiàng Yàn was a general for Chǔ,
often achieving merit,
cherished his soldiers,
and the people of Chǔ sympathized with him.
Some believe him dead,
others believe him missing.
Now, if we sincerely use our troops to impersonate
claiming to be Prince Fúsū or Xiàng Yàn,
and take the world by storm,
there should be many responders."
Wú Guǎng agreed.
They then consulted a diviner.
The diviner understood their intent,
and said:
"Your endeavors will all succeed, and you will achieve merit.
Yet, have you consulted the spirits through divination?"
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng were pleased,
pondered the mention of spirits,
and said:
"This is teaching us to first awe
the masses."
They then wrote in cinnabar on silk
"Chén Shèng will be king,"
and placed it in a fish caught by someone.
When the soldiers bought the fish to cook and eat,
they found the writing in the fish's belly,
and naturally found it strange.
Furthermore, they secretly had Wú Guǎng
go to a secluded shrine near the camp,
light a torch in a basket at night,
and imitate a fox's cry, shouting
"Great Chǔ rises,
Chén Shèng will be king."
The soldiers were all frightened and alarmed at night.
The next day,
the soldiers often talked among themselves,
all pointing and looking at Chén Shèng.
Wú Guǎng had always been kind to people,
and many soldiers were willing to be used by him.
When the commanding officer was drunk,
Guǎng deliberately repeatedly said
he wanted to flee,
enraging the officer,
to make him humiliate him,
thereby inciting the soldiers to anger.
The officer indeed flogged Guǎng.
As the officer's sword was drawn,
Guǎng stood up,
seized it and killed the officer.
Chén Shèng assisted him,
and they killed both officers together.
They summoned their followers and declared:
"You all encountered rain,
and have already missed the deadline;
missing the deadline means decapitation.
Even if by chance you are not executed,
those who die guarding the frontiers would still be six or seven out of ten.
Moreover, if a brave man does not die, that's all;
if he dies, he should achieve great fame.
Are kings, nobles, generals, and ministers born to their titles?"
The followers all said:
"We respectfully accept your command."
They then falsely claimed to be under Prince Fú Sū and Xiàng Yān,
following the people's desires.
They bared their right shoulders,
and proclaimed themselves Great Chǔ.
They built an altar and swore a covenant,
sacrificing with the officers' heads.
Chén Shèng appointed himself as general,
and Wú Guǎng as commandant.
They attacked Dàzéxiāng,
gathered forces and attacked Qí.
Qí fell,
so they ordered Gé Yīng from Fúlí to lead troops
to conquer the areas east of Qí.
They attacked Zhì, Cuó, Kǔ, Zhè, and Qiáo,
all of which surrendered.
As they marched, they gathered more soldiers.
By the time they reached Chén,
they had six to seven hundred chariots,
over a thousand cavalry,
and several tens of thousands of infantry.
They attacked Chén,
where the governor and magistrate of Chén
were both absent,
only the deputy defender
fought with them at the city gate.
He was defeated,
the deputy defender died,
and they entered and occupied Chén.
After a few days,
they summoned the village elders
and local leaders
to all come and discuss matters.
The village elders and leaders all said:
"General, you personally donned armor and wielded weapons,
attacked the unjust,
punished the tyrannical Qín,
and restored the state of Chǔ,
your merit deserves you to be king."
Chén Shè then established himself as king,
with the reign name Zhāng Chǔ.
At this time,
in various commanderies and counties
those suffering under Qín officials
all punished their chief officials,
killing them to respond to Chén Shè.
He then appointed Wú Shū as acting king,
to supervise the generals
in attacking Xíngyáng to the west.
He ordered Wǔ Chén, Zhāng Ěr, and Chén Yú from Chén
to conquer the land of Zhào,
and ordered Dèng Zōng from Rǔyīn
to conquer the Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
At this time,
groups of several thousand Chǔ soldiers
gathering together
were too numerous to count.
Gé Yīng
reached Dōngchéng,
and established Xiāng Qiáng as King of Chǔ.
When Yīng later heard that King Chén had already been established,
he killed Xiāng Qiáng,
and returned to report. Upon reaching Chén,
King Chén executed Gé Yīng.
King Chén ordered Zhōu Fú from Wèi to go north
and conquer the land of Wèi.
Wú Guǎng besieged Xíngyáng.
Lǐ Yóu was the governor of Sānchuān,
defending Xíngyáng,
and Wú Shū could not capture it.
King Chén summoned the country's prominent figures
to consult with them,
appointing Cài Cì, Lord of Fáng from Shàngcài,
as Grand Pillar of State.
Zhōu Wén,
a worthy man from Chén,
had once served as an astrologer in Xiàng Yān's army,
served under Lord Chūnshēn,
claimed to be versed in military affairs,
King Chén gave him a general's seal,
to attack Qín to the west.
He gathered troops along the way until reaching the pass,
with a thousand chariots,
and several hundred thousand soldiers,
reached Xì, and encamped there.
Qín ordered Zhāng Hán, the Minister of Stewards, to pardon
the convicts from Lìshān and the sons of slaves,
and mobilize them all to attack the great Chǔ army,
defeating them completely.
Zhōu Wén was defeated, fled out of the pass,
and stayed at Cáoyáng for two or three months.
Zhāng Hán pursued and defeated him,
he fled again and stayed at Miǎnchí for over ten days.
Zhāng Hán attacked and heavily defeated him.
Zhōu Wén committed suicide by cutting his throat,
and his army thus did not fight.
Wǔ Chén arrived at Hándān,
proclaimed himself King of Zhào,
with Chén Yú as Grand General,
and Zhāng Ěr and Shào Sāo as Left and Right Chancellors.
King Chén was angry,
arrested and imprisoned the families of Wǔ Chén and others,
intending to execute them.
The Pillar of State said:
"Before Qín is destroyed,
executing the families of the King of Zhào and his generals and ministers
would create another Qín for us.
It would be better to acknowledge
and establish them."
King Chén then sent an envoy
to congratulate Zhào,
moved the families of Wǔ Chén and others to the palace,
and enfeoffed Zhāng Ěr's son Zhāng Ào as Lord of Chéngdū,
urging the Zhào troops to quickly enter the pass.
The King of Zhào and his generals and ministers deliberated together, saying:
"The king ruling Zhào is not Chǔ's intention.
Once Chǔ has destroyed Qín,
they will surely attack Zhào.
The best strategy is not to send troops west,
but send an envoy north to conquer the land of Yān
to expand our own territory.
With Zhào holding the great river to the south,
and Yān and Dài to the north,
even if Chǔ defeats Qín,
they would not dare to control Zhào.
If Chǔ does not defeat Qín,
they will necessarily value Zhào.
Zhào can take advantage of Qín's weakness,
and achieve our ambition over the world."
The King of Zhào found this reasonable,
so he did not send troops west,
but dispatched
the former minor official from Shànggǔ, Hán Guǎng,
to lead troops north and conquer the land of Yān.
The former nobles and leaders of Yān said to Hán Guǎng:
"Chǔ has already established a king,
and Zhào has also established a king.
Although Yān is small,
it is also a state of ten thousand chariots;
we wish the general to establish himself as King of Yān."
Hán Guǎng said:
"My mother is in Zhào,
it cannot be done."
A man of Yān said:
"Zhào is currently worried about Qín to the west,
and concerned about Chǔ to the south.
Their strength cannot restrain us.
Moreover, with Chǔ's power,
they dare not harm the families of King Zhào's generals and ministers—
how would Zhào alone dare to harm the family of our general!"
Hán Guǎng found this reasonable,
and thus declared himself King of Yān.
After several months,
Zhào escorted the mother of the King of Yān
and his family members back to Yān.
At this time,
the number of generals seizing territories
was beyond count.
Zhōu Fú advanced northward to Dī,
where Tián Dān of Dī killed the magistrate of Dī,
proclaimed himself King of Qí,
and using Qí's forces, counterattacked Zhōu Fú.
Zhōu Fú's army scattered,
and he returned to the territory of Wèi,
intending to establish the former Lord of Nínglíng,
Jiū, a descendant of Wèi, as King of Wèi.
At that time, Jiū was with King Chén,
and could not go to Wèi.
After Wèi's territory was stabilized,
they wished to jointly establish Zhōu Fú as King of Wèi,
but Zhōu Fú refused.
After envoys went back and forth five times,
King Chén then established Lord Nínglíng Jiū as King of Wèi
and sent him to his state.
Zhōu Fú ultimately became chancellor.
Generals such as Tián Zāng
conferred and said:
"Zhōu Zhāng's army has already been defeated;
Qín troops will arrive any moment.
We have besieged the city of Xíngyáng
but cannot capture it.
When the Qín army arrives,
we will surely be badly defeated.
It would be better to leave a small force behind,
sufficient to guard Xíngyáng,
and take all elite troops to face the Qín army.
Now, the acting king is arrogant,
does not understand military strategy,
and cannot be reasoned with.
If we do not kill him,
our cause may fail."
Thereupon, they jointly forged the king's order
to execute Wú Shū,
presenting his head to King Chén.
King Chén sent an envoy
to bestow upon Tián Zāng the seal of Chǔ's Prime Minister,
appointing him as supreme general.
Tián Zāng then ordered generals such as Lǐ Guī
to guard Xíngyáng city,
while he led elite troops west to meet the Qín army
at Áocāng.
They engaged in battle;
Tián Zāng died,
and his army was defeated.
Zhāng Hán advanced his troops
to attack Lǐ Guī and others below Xíngyáng,
defeating them;
Lǐ Guī and others died.
Dèng Yuè of Yángchéng
commanded troops stationed at Tán;
Zhāng Hán's deputy general attacked and defeated him,
and Dèng Yuè's army scattered and fled to Chén.
Wǔ Xú of Zhī commanded troops stationed at Xǔ;
Zhāng Hán attacked and defeated him,
and Wǔ Xú's army all scattered and fled to Chén.
King Chén executed Dèng Yuè.
When King Chén first rose to power,
Qín Jiā of Líng, Dǒng Xiè of Zhī,
Zhū Jīshí of Fúlí, Zhèng Bù of Qǔlǘ,
Dīng Jí of Xú, and others all rose independently,
leading troops to besiege the Governor of Dōnghǎi, Qìng, at Tán.
King Chén heard of this
and sent Wǔpíngjūn Pàn as a general
to oversee the army at Tán.
Qín Jiā did not accept the command;
he appointed himself Grand Marshal,
disliking subordination to Wǔpíngjūn.
He told his officers:
"Wǔpíngjūn is young,
and knows nothing of military affairs—
do not listen to him!"
Thereupon, he forged the king's order
and killed Wǔpíngjūn Pàn.
After Zhāng Hán defeated Wǔ Xú,
he attacked Chén,
and the Pillar of State, Fángjūn, died.
Zhāng Hán then advanced to attack Zhāng Hè's army west of Chén.
King Chén went out to oversee the battle;
his army was defeated,
and Zhāng Hè died.
In the twelfth month,
King Chén went to Rǔyīn,
and on returning to Xiàchéngfù,
his charioteer Zhuāng Gǔ killed him
to surrender to Qín.
Chén Shèng was buried at Dàng,
and given the posthumous title King Yǐn.
Lǚ Chén, a former attendant of King Chén who had become a general,
organized the Cāngtóu Army,
rose from Xīnyáng,
attacked and captured Chén,
killed Zhuāng Gǔ,
and restored Chén as Chǔ.
Earlier, when King Chén arrived in Chén,
he ordered Sòng Liú of Zhī to lead troops
to pacify Nányáng
and enter Wǔguān.
After Liú had taken Nányáng,
he heard of King Chén's death,
and Nányáng returned to Qín.
Sòng Liú could not enter Wǔguān,
so he went east to Xīncài,
encountered the Qín army,
and surrendered with his troops to Qín.
Qín transported Liú to Xiányáng,
where he was torn apart by chariots as a warning.
When Qín Jiā and others heard that King Chén's army had been defeated
and he had fled,
they established Jǐng Jū as King of Chǔ,
led troops to Fāngyǔ,
and intended to attack the Qín army below Dìngtáo.
They sent Gōngsūn Qìng
as an envoy to the King of Qí,
hoping to join forces and advance together.
The King of Qí said:
"We heard King Chén was defeated in battle,
but do not know whether he is alive or dead—
how could Chǔ establish a king without consulting us!"
Gōngsūn Qìng replied:
"Qí did not consult Chǔ
when establishing a king;
why should Chǔ consult Qí to establish a king?
Moreover, Chǔ initiated the uprising,
and should command the world."
Tián Dān executed Gōngsūn Qìng.
Qín's Left and Right Colonels attacked Chén again
and captured it.
General Lǚ fled,
gathered his troops and regrouped.
He joined forces with the troops of Dāngyángjūn
Qíng Bù, the bandit from Pó,
and together they attacked Qín's Left and Right Colonels again,
defeating them at Qīngbō,
and restored Chén as Chǔ.
At that time, Xiàng Liáng established the grandson of King Huái, Xīn,
as King of Chǔ.
Chén Shèng was king for a total of six months.
Having become king,
he ruled from Chén.
heard of this,
went to Chén,
knocked on the palace gate, and said:
"I wish to see Shè."
The palace gate officer wanted to bind him.
After he repeatedly pleaded his case,
they let him go
but refused to announce him.
When King Chén came out,
he blocked the path and called out "Shè!"
King Chén heard him,
summoned him for an audience,
and took him back in the carriage.
Entering the palace,
he saw the hall's curtains and canopies;
the guest exclaimed:
"Huǒ yí!
Shè's being king is so grand!"
Chǔ people call "many" huǒ,
hence it spread throughout the land:
"Huǒ Shè became king,"
starting with Chén Shè.
The guest's comings and goings became increasingly
relaxed and informal,
and he spoke of King Chén's past circumstances.
Someone advised King Chén, saying:
"Your guest is foolish and ignorant,
indulging in reckless talk,
undermining your dignity."
King Chén executed him.
All of King Chén's old acquaintances
withdrew on their own,
and from then on, no one felt close to King Chén.
King Chén appointed Zhū Fáng as Zhōngzhèng,
Hú Wǔ as Sīguò,
to oversee the officials.
When generals returned from conquering territories,
those who did not follow orders
were imprisoned and punished,
considering harsh scrutiny as loyalty.
Those they disliked,
instead of handing over to the judiciary,
they dealt with themselves.
King Chén trusted and employed them.
The generals, for this reason, did not become close or attached to him.
This is why he failed.
Although Chén Shèng had died,
the marquises, kings, generals, and ministers he appointed
ultimately brought down the Qín,
all because Chén Shèng initiated the uprising.
When Gāozǔ was in power,
he established thirty households in Dàng to tend Chén Shè's tomb,
and to this day,
sacrifices continue.
Master Chǔ commented:
The strategic advantages of terrain
are relied upon for security;
weapons, armor, and penal laws
are used for governance.
Yet these are still not sufficient to depend on.
The ancient kings took benevolence and righteousness as their foundation,
while relying on strongholds and legal statutes
as secondary measures—
how true this is!
I have heard Jiǎ Shēng's assessment:
Duke Xiào of Qín,
holding the natural barriers of Xiáo and Hán,
and possessing the land of Yōngzhōu,
with his ministers firmly guarded it,
while eyeing the Zhōu court.
He harbored the ambition to roll up the world like a mat,
to encompass all within the universe,
to gather the four seas into a bag,
and to swallow up the eight wildernesses.
At that time,
Lord Shāng assisted him,
internally establishing laws and regulations,
focusing on farming and weaving,
and preparing defenses for battles;
externally, he promoted the Horizontal Alliance
to pit the feudal lords against each other.
Thus, the Qín people effortlessly took the lands west of the Yellow River.
After Duke Xiào passed away,
Kings Huìwén, Wǔ, and Zhāo
inherited the established enterprise,
followed the remaining strategies,
capturing Hànzhōng in the south,
seizing Bā and Shǔ in the west,
taking fertile lands in the east,
and acquiring strategically vital commanderies.
The feudal lords grew fearful,
forming alliances to plot how to weaken Qín.
They spared no precious vessels, treasures, or fertile lands
to attract the talents of the world.
They formed vertical alliances,
uniting as one.
At this time,
Qí had Mèngcháng,
Zhào had Píngyuán,
Chǔ had Chūnshēn,
and Wèi had Xìnlíng:
these four lords,
all were wise, loyal, and trustworthy,
generous and caring towards people,
and respectful of the worthy and scholars.
They organized the Vertical Alliance to counter the Horizontal Alliance,
combining the forces of Hán, Wèi, Yān, Zhào,
Sòng, Wèi, and Zhōngshān.
Then, the scholars of the six states
had people like Nìng Yuè, Xú Shàng, Sū Qín,
Dù Hè devising strategies for them,
Qí Míng, Zhōu Zuì, Chén Zhěn, Shào Gǔ,
Lóu Huǎn, Zhái Jǐng, Sū Lì,
Yuè Yì conveying their intentions,
Wú Qǐ, Sūn Bìn, Dài Tuó, Ní Liáng,
Wáng Liào, Tián Jì, Lián Pō,
Zhào Shē commanding their troops.
They once attacked Qín at the Hángu Pass
with land ten times larger
and a million-strong army.
The Qín opened the pass to lure the enemy in,
and the armies of the nine states fled
not daring to advance.
Qín did not spend a single arrow or lose a arrowhead,
yet the world was already exhausted.
Thus, the Vertical Alliance disbanded and treaties broke,
and they competed to cede land and bribe Qín.
Qín had ample strength to exploit their weaknesses,
pursuing the fleeing and defeated,
leaving a million corpses,
with blood floating shields,
taking advantage of the situation,
carving up the world,
dividing mountains and rivers,
with strong states submitting,
and weak states paying homage.
"This continued to Kings Xiàowén and Zhuāngxiāng,
who reigned briefly,
and the state saw no major events.
By the time of Shǐ Huáng,
he built upon the achievements of the previous six generations,
wielding a long whip to rule the world,
annexing the two Zhōu and eliminating the feudal lords,
ascending to the supreme position to control all directions,
using clubs and whips to chastise the world,
his might shaking the four seas.
He captured the lands of Bǎi Yuè in the south,
establishing Guìlín and Xiàng commanderies,
and the lords of Bǎi Yuè bowed their heads,
with ropes around their necks,
surrendering to low-ranking officials.
Then he sent Méng Tián north to build the Great Wall
as a defensive barrier,
pushing the Xiōngnú back over seven hundred lǐ,
so the northern tribes dared not come south
to herd horses,
and their warriors dared not draw bows to seek revenge.
Then he abolished the ways of the ancient kings,
burned the writings of the hundred schools,
to stupefy the common people.
He destroyed famous cities,
killed the outstanding and brave,
collected all the weapons in the world
and gathered them in Xiányáng,
melted down the spearheads and arrowheads,
casting them into twelve metal statues,
to weaken the people of the world.
Then he trod on Mount Huà as a wall,
used the Yellow River as a moat,
relying on a towering wall,
overlooking an unfathomable stream
for security.
With skilled generals and strong crossbows
guarding key positions,
and trusted ministers and elite troops
displaying sharp weapons to challenge any who approached.
With the world settled,
Shǐ Huáng believed in his heart
that the strength of Guānzhōng,
the thousand-lǐ impregnable city,
would be an eternal dynasty for his descendants.
After Shǐ Huáng's death,
his remaining might still shook distant customs.
Yet Chén Shè was but a son of a humble home with a broken jar for a window and a rope for a hinge,
a common laborer,
and a conscripted exile.
His talent was no more than average,
without the wisdom of Zhòngní or Mò Dí,
nor the wealth of Táo Zhū or Yī Dùn.
Stepping among the ranks,
rising from the fields,
he led weary and scattered soldiers,
commanding a few hundred men,
turned to attack Qín.
They cut trees for weapons,
raised poles as flags,
and the world gathered like clouds and responded like an echo,
carrying provisions and following like shadows,
until the heroes east of the mountains rose together
and destroyed the Qín clan.
"Moreover, the world had not grown smaller or weaker;
the land of Yōngzhōu,
the strength of Xiáo and Hán remained as before.
Chén Shè's status
was not higher than the rulers of Qí, Chǔ, Yān,
Zhào, Hán, Wèi, Sòng, Wèi, or Zhōngshān;
his farm tools and wooden spears
were no sharper than hooked halberds or long lances;
his conscripted crowd
was no match for the armies of the nine states;
in deep planning and far-sighted strategy,
the ways of marching troops and employing soldiers,
he did not compare to the scholars of the past.
Yet the outcomes differed,
and the achievements were opposite.
If one were to compare the states east of the mountains with Chén Shè in length and size, weighing their power and strength, they could not be mentioned in the same breath.
However, Qín with a small piece of land,
achieved the power of ten thousand chariots,
suppressed the eight provinces and led other states to court,
for more than one hundred years.
Then they took the world as their home,
Xiáo and Hán as their palace.
A single man's rebellion caused the fall of the ancestral temples,
and his life ended in others' hands,
becoming the laughingstock of the world,
why is this?
Benevolence and righteousness were not practiced,
and the strategy of attack and defense was different.
Since ancient times, those who received the Mandate of Heaven, and rulers who maintained tradition,
were not solely abundant in inner virtues,
but also had the assistance of outer relatives.
The rise of Xià was due to Túshān,
while Jié's exile was due to Mòxǐ.
The rise of Yīn was thanks to Yǒusōng,
Zhòu's demise was due to Bì Zhèjǐ.
The rise of Zhōu was because of Jiāng Yuán and Dà Rèn,
while King Yōu's capture was due to his indulgence in Bāosì.
Therefore, the "Yì" is based on "Qián" and "Kūn",
the "Shī" begins with "Guān Jū",
the "Shū" praises the descent of Tiān,
and the "Chūnqiū" criticizes noncompliance with proper betrothal rites.
The relationship between husband and wife,
is the greatest of human relations.
The use of ritual,
is conscientious only in marriage.
When music is harmonious, the four seasons are balanced,
the changes of yin and yang,
are the essence of all things.
Can it not be taken seriously?
People can broaden the path,
but they cannot change fate.
Indeed,
the love between spouses,
cannot be obtained by a ruler from his ministers,
nor by a father from his son,
how much less from the lower ranks!
Even after a harmonious union,
they may not produce offspring;
if they do have children,
they may not ensure their increase;
is this not fate?
Confucius seldom spoke of fate,
because it is difficult to discuss.
Without understanding the changes of the mysterious and the clear,
how can one recognize nature and fate?
The Grand Historian said:
Before Qín, the records were brief,
the details are hard to find.
When Hàn arose,
Lǚ Éxǔ became the primary empress of Gāozǔ,
her son was the crown prince.
Later, when her beauty waned and affection faded,
Consort Qī became favored,
her son Rúyì was repeatedly considered to replace the crown prince.
After Gāozǔ's death,
Empress Lǚ eliminated Qī's family,
executed King Zhào,
and only those concubines of Gāozǔ who were out of favor and distant survived unharmed.
Empress Lǚ's eldest daughter became the wife of Xuānpíng Marquis Zhāng Áo,
Áo's daughter became Empress Hòuhuì.
Due to the closeness of kin,
Lǚ Empress wished her to bear many sons,
but in the end, she had no children,
and deceitfully took a child from the concubines as her own.
When Emperor Hòuhuì died,
the empire had not been established long,
and succession was unclear.
Thus, they elevated external relatives,
ennobling the Lü clan as regents,
and made Lǚ Lù's daughter empress for the younger emperor,
intending to firmly entrench their roots,
yet it was of no benefit.
After Empress Lǚ's death,
she was buried in Chánglíng.
Lù and Chǎn feared execution,
and planned rebellion.
The ministers raised troops against them,
heaven enticed their leader,
eventually exterminating the Lǚ clan.
Only leaving Empress Hòuhuì in the Northern Palace.
They beckoned the King of Dài,
who became Emperor Xiàowén,
serving the Hàn ancestral temples.
Was this not the work of heaven?
If not the mandate of heaven, who could achieve this?
Empress Bó's father was a man from Wú,
surnamed Bó,
during the Qín era, was intimate with a female relative of the former Wèi King, Wèi Ǒu,
producing Bó Jī,
and when Bó's father died at Shānyīn,
he was buried there.
When the feudal lords rebelled against Qín,
Wèi Bào was established as King of Wèi,
and Wèi Ǒu sent her daughter into the Wèi palace.
Ǒu's agreement was supported by Xǔ Fù,
who assessed Bó Jī,
saying she would bear a heavenly son.
At that time, Xiàng Yǔ was in conflict with Hàn King at Xíngyáng,
and the world was unsettled.
Initially Bào and Hàn fought against Chǔ,
but upon hearing Xǔ Fù's words,
Bào silently rejoiced,
and turned against Hàn,
remaining neutral,
and made peace with Chǔ.
Hàn sent Cáo Cān and others to capture King Wèi Bào,
annexed his state as a commandery,
and Bó Jī was assigned to the weaving quarters.
After Bào died,
Hàn King entered the weaving quarters,
saw that Bó Jī was beautiful,
ordered her into the harem,
but she was not favored for over a year.
In her youth,
Bó Jī was close to Lady Guǎn,
Zhào Child,
making a vow:
"If any of us gain favor, let us not forget the others."
Eventually Lady Guǎn,
Zhào Child gained favor with Hàn King first.
Hàn King sat at Hénán Palace in Chénggāo Terrace,
and these two beauties laughed at Bó Jī's original vow.
The Hàn King heard them,
asked the reason,
and the two fully explained it to him.
The Hàn King's heart was moved,
and he pitied Bó Jī,
summoning and favoring her that day.
Bó Jī said:
"Last night, I dreamt of a green dragon coiled on my belly."
Gāo Emperor said:
"This is an omen of nobility,
I shall help you achieve it."
She conceived from a single encounter,
giving birth to a son,
who became King of Dài.
Afterwards Bó Jī seldom saw the exalted ancestor.
After the ancestor's death,
consorts like favored concubine Qī and others,
Empress Lǚ, enraged,
imprisoned them,
prohibiting their exit from the palace.
Due to Bó Jī's rarity,
she was allowed to leave,
accompanying her child to Dài,
as Queen Dowager of King Dài.
The Queen Dowager's brother, Bó Zhāo, also went to Dài.
King Dài reigned for seventeen years,
and when Empress Lǚ passed,
the ministers discussed succession,
distressed by the power of the Lǚ family,
all praised Bó family's benevolence and kindness,
thus welcomed King Dài,
establishing him as Emperor Xiàowén,
and the Queen Dowager was renamed Empress Dowager,
her brother Bó Zhāo was ennobled as Zhǐ Marquis.
The mother of Empress Bó had also died earlier,
buried north of Yùyáng.
They retrospectively honored Bó's father as Língwén Marquis,
placing three hundred households in the domain of Kuàijī Commandery,
with officials below the chief entrusted to guard the tomb,
sacrificial offerings conducted according to rituals.
North of Yùyáng, they also placed a Língwén Marquis Lady's park,
following the ceremony of Língwén Marquis's park.
Empress Bó, considering herself from the Weì King lineage,
having lost her parents early,
gathered prominent members from the Qín and Wèi regions,
rewarding the Wèi clan,
distributing rewards based on closeness.
The Bó family had one marquis in total.
Empress Bó later in Emperors Wéndì and Jǐngdì's second year,
died in the second year before Emperor Xiàojǐng,
buried in Nánlíng.
Since Empress Lǚ was buried in Chánglíng,
she was specifically entombed separately,
near Emperor Xiàowén's Bàlíng.
Empress Dowager Dòu,
originally from Guānjīn in Qīnghé, Zhào.
During the time of Empress Dowager Lǚ,
Concubine Dòu entered the palace as a lady from a good family to serve the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager sent palace women to the various kings,
five each,
with Concubine Dòu among them.
The family of Concubine Dòu was in Qīnghé,
wishing to be near her home in Zhào,
she asked her master to dispatch a eunuch official:
"Be sure to place me in the registers among the Zhào group."
The eunuch forgot this,
and mistakenly placed her in the Dài group.
The registers were submitted,
an edict permitted them,
and she was to proceed.
Concubine Dòu wept,
blamed the eunuch,
and didn't wish to go,
but after persuasion,
she agreed to go.
Upon reaching Dài,
King Dài favored Concubine Dòu exclusively,
and she bore a daughter, Piāo,
and later bore two sons.
However, the Queen of King Dài bore four sons.
Before King Dài was installed as emperor, the queen died.
When King Dài was enthroned as emperor,
the four sons born by the queen all succumbed to illness.
Emperor Xiàowén was enthroned for several months,
when the ministers requested to establish a crown prince,
and Concubine Dòu's eldest son was the oldest,
he was established as the crown prince.
Concubine Dòu was made the Empress,
and daughter Piāo was made the Grand Princess.
In the following year,
the younger son Wǔ was made King of Dài,
but soon he was transferred to Liáng,
where he was known as King Liáng Xiào.
Empress Dòu passed away early,
and was buried in Guānjīn.
Subsequently, Empress Dowager Bo issued an edict to the officials,
posthumously honoring Empress Dòu's father as Marquis of Ānchéng,
and her mother as Lady Ānchéng.
She ordered Qīnghé to establish a village of two hundred households,
with a governor and deputy to serve and protect it,
following the regulations of Língwén Garden.
Empress Dòu's elder brother Dòu Zhǎngjūn,
and younger brother Dòu Guǎngguó,
styled Shàojūn.
When Shàojūn was four or five years old,
his family was poor,
and he was kidnapped and sold by someone,
his family unaware of his whereabouts.
He was passed through over ten families,
reaching Yíyáng,
where his master took him to the mountains to make charcoal,
sleeping under a ridge with over a hundred people at night,
when the ridge collapsed,
crushing all the sleepers to death,
only Shàojūn escaped,
surviving.
He divined his fortune, predicting he would become a marquis in several days,
and went with his family to Cháng'ān.
Upon hearing that Empress Dòu was newly enthroned,
with her family in Guānjīn,
having the surname Dòu.
Guǎngguó, though young when he left,
remembered the county name and surname,
and had often picked mulberries with his sister and fallen,
using this as a sign,
and submitted a letter to explain himself.
Empress Dòu informed Emperor Wéndì,
who summoned him for an audience,
questioned him,
and he explained the circumstances in full,
and it was indeed the case.
He was further asked what proof he could provide,
he replied:
"When my sister left me to the west,
she bade farewell to me at the post station,
she washed me,
fed me rice,
and then left."
At this, Empress Dòu held him and wept,
tears streaming down.
The attendants on both sides all knelt on the ground and wept,
sharing in the Empress's grief.
Generously rewarded with land, houses, and money,
the brothers were ennobled,
and settled in Cháng'ān.
Marquis Jiàng,
General Guàn, and others said:
"It is fortunate for us to survive,
and now we stay in the same place as these two men.
Their origin is humble,
it would be improper not to select mentors and guests for them,
lest it mimic the great events of the Lǚ clan."
Thus elder and virtuous scholars were chosen to stay with them.
Dòu Zhǎngjūn,
and Shàojūn then became gentlemanly persons,
not daring to be arrogant in their wealth and status.
Empress Dòu fell ill,
and lost her sight.
Emperor Wéndì favored Lady Shèn of Hàndān,
and Concubine Yǐn,
both without children.
Emperor Xiàowén passed away,
and Emperor Xiàojǐng ascended.
Dòu Guǎngguó was ennobled as Marquis of Zhāngwǔ.
Zhǎngjūn had died previously,
and his son Péngzǔ was ennobled as Marquis of Nánpí.
At the time of the Wú and Chǔ rebellion,
Empress Dowager Dòu followed her nephew Dòu Yīng,
who enjoyed associating with warriors,
leading troops,
and for his military merits became Marquis Wèi Qí.
In total, three of the Dòu family became marquises.
Empress Dowager Dòu valued the teachings of Huángdì and
Lǎozi,
and neither the emperor nor the crown prince nor the various members of the Dòu family could avoid reading the "Huángdì" and
"Lǎozi",
respecting their doctrines.
Empress Dowager Dòu died six years after Emperor Xiàojǐng,
and was buried at Bàlíng.
Her will left all the gold, silver, and property of the Eastern Palace to Grand Princess Piāo.
Empress Dowager Wáng,
from Huáilǐ,
with her mother named Zāngér.
Zāngér,
granddaughter of former King of Yān, Zāng Tǔ.
Zāngér was married first to Wáng Zhòng of Huáilǐ,
bearing a son named Xìn,
and two daughters.
After Zhòng's death,
Zāngér remarried to a man of the Tián clan from Chánglíng,
bearing sons Fén,
and Shèng. Zāngér's elder daughter was married to the grandson of Jīn,
and they had a daughter,
and for this, Zāngér divined their fortunes,
presaging both daughters would be noble.
She then sought a suitable match for each,
seizing her daughter's marriage with the Jīn clan.
The Jīn clan was angered,
and refused to consent to the match,
so she placed her daughter within the palace of the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince favored and loved her,
and she bore three daughters and one son.
While pregnant with her son,
Lady Wáng dreamed of the sun entering her bosom.
She told the Crown Prince,
who said:
"This is a sign of nobility."
Before the child was born, Emperor Xiàowén died,
and Emperor Xiàojǐng ascended,
Lady Wáng bore a son.
Before this, Zāngér had also sent in her younger daughter Érxù,
who bore four sons.
When Emperor Xiàojǐng was the Crown Prince,
Empress Dowager Bo arranged a woman of the Bó family for him as a consort.
When Emperor Xiàojǐng ascended,
he made this consort the Empress, called Empress Bó.
The Empress had no children,
and held no favor.
After Empress Dowager Bo's death,
Empress Bó was deposed.
Emperor Xiàojǐng's eldest son, Róng,
was borne by Lí Jī.
Lí Jī,
was from Qí.
Róng was established as the Crown Prince.
Grand Princess Piāo had a daughter,
desiring to give her as a consort.
Lí Jī was jealous,
as the various consorts of the Emperor, all met the Emperor through Grand Princess,
finding favor and affection,
surpassing Lí Jī,
leading Lí Jī to daily resentment and anger,
she apologized to the Grand Princess,
but was denied.
The Grand Princess wished to give her to Lady Wáng,
and Lady Wáng agreed.
Angry, the Grand Princess daily spoke ill of Lí Jī to Emperor Xiàojǐng saying:
"Lí Jī, when meeting with the other noble consorts...
often had attendants curse and spit on their backs quietly,
practicing evil seductive arts."
Because of this, Emperor Xiàojǐng looked upon her with suspicion.
Emperor Jǐng once felt unwell in body,
and his heart was not at ease.
He entrusted the sons who were kings to Lì Jī,
saying:
"After I pass away,
take good care of them."
Lì Jī grew angry,
refused to consent,
and spoke disrespectfully.
Emperor Jǐng was enraged,
and harbored resentment in his heart but did not show it.
The Elder Princess daily praised the excellence of Wáng Fūrén's son,
and Emperor Jǐng also considered him virtuous.
Moreover, there was the earlier dream's omen of the sun,
so his decision remained unsettled.
Wáng Fūrén knew that the Emperor resented Lì Jī,
and while his anger had not subsided,
she secretly urged a high official to propose establishing Lì Jī as Empress.
When the Grand Usher finished reporting on affairs,
he said:
" 'A son is honored through his mother,
a mother is honored through her son.'
Now the Crown Prince's mother has no title;
she should be established as Empress."
Emperor Jǐng angrily said:
"Is this something you should say!"
Thereupon, he investigated and executed the Grand Usher,
and demoted the Crown Prince to be King of Línjiāng.
Lì Jī grew even more resentful and hateful,
unable to see the Emperor,
and died of sorrow.
Finally, Wáng Fūrén was established as Empress,
her son as Crown Prince,
and the Empress's elder brother, Xìn, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gài.
When Emperor Jǐng passed away,
the Crown Prince succeeded to the title as Emperor.
He honored the Grand Empress Dowager's mother, Zāng'ér, as Princess of Píngyuán.
Tián Fén was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔ'ān,
and Shèng as Marquis of Zhōuyáng.
Emperor Jǐng had thirteen sons;
one became Emperor,
twelve became Kings.
Ér Xǔ died early,
and her four sons all became Kings.
The eldest daughter of Empress Dowager Wáng was titled Princess Píngyáng,
the next was Princess Nángōng,
and the next was Princess Línlǜ.
Marquis of Gài, Xìn, was fond of drink.
Tián Fén
and Shèng were greedy,
and skilled in rhetoric.
Wáng Zhòng died early,
and was buried in Huáilǐ.
He was posthumously honored as Marquis Gòng,
with an estate of two hundred households established for his tomb.
When Princess of Píngyuán passed away,
she was buried with the Tián clan at Chánglíng,
and an estate comparable to that of Marquis Gòng was established.
Empress Dowager Wáng outlived Emperor Jǐng by sixteen years,
passing away in the fourth year of Yuánshuò,
and was buried with him at Yánglíng.
In total, three from Empress Dowager Wáng's family became Marquises.
Empress Wèi, styled Zǐfū,
was of humble birth.
Her family was known as the Wèi clan,
originating from the fief of the Marquis of Píngyáng.
Zǐfū was a singer for Princess Píngyáng.
When Emperor Wǔ first ascended the throne,
for several years he had no sons.
Princess Píngyáng sought over ten fine maidens from good families,
adorned and kept them at her home.
When Emperor Wǔ returned from the purification rite at Bàshàng,
he stopped by Princess Píngyáng's.
The princess presented the beauties she had gathered,
but the Emperor was not pleased.
After drinking,
when the singers came forth,
the Emperor saw them,
and was only pleased with Wèi Zǐfū.
That day,
when Emperor Wǔ rose to change clothes,
Zǐfū attended him in the dressing room,
and gained his favor.
The Emperor returned to his seat,
very joyful,
and bestowed a thousand catties of gold upon Princess Píngyáng.
The princess then presented Zǐfū to be sent into the palace.
As Zǐfū mounted the carriage,
Princess Píngyáng patted her back and said:
"Go now,
eat heartily,
and do your best!
If you become noble,
do not forget me."
After entering the palace for over a year,
she surprisingly did not receive favor again.
Emperor Wǔ selected palace women who were not to his liking,
and dismissed them to return home.
Wèi Zǐfū managed to see him,
and tearfully requested to be sent away.
The Emperor took pity on her,
favored her again,
and she then became pregnant,
her honor and favor increasing daily.
He summoned her elder brother Wèi Chángjūn and younger brother Qīng to be Palace Attendants.
Later, Zǐfū was greatly favored,
enjoying his affection,
and bore three daughters and one son in total.
The son was named Jù.
Initially,
when the Emperor was Crown Prince,
he married the daughter of the Elder Princess as his consort.
Upon being established as Emperor,
the consort was made Empress,
of the Chén family,
but she had no sons.
The Emperor's ability to become heir
was greatly aided by the Grand Elder Princess,
hence Empress Chén was arrogant and haughty.
Hearing that Wèi Zǐfū was greatly favored,
she grew furious, nearly dying several times from rage.
The Emperor became even angrier.
Empress Chén employed feminine wiles and witchcraft,
and when this was somewhat discovered,
he deposed Empress Chén,
and established Wèi Zǐfū as Empress.
Empress Chén's mother, the Grand Elder Princess,
was the elder sister of Emperor Jǐng.
She repeatedly reproached Emperor Wǔ's elder sister, Princess Píngyáng, saying:
"The Emperor would not have been established without me,
yet now he casts aside my daughter.
Why are you so ungrateful and turn your back on your roots!"
Princess Píngyáng replied:
"It is because she has no son that she was deposed."
Empress Chén sought to have a child,
spending a total of ninety million in cash on physicians,
but ultimately had no son.
After Wèi Zǐfū was established as Empress,
and Wèi Chángjūn had previously died,
Wèi Qīng was made General,
achieved merit in campaigns against the Hú,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chángpíng.
While Qīng's three sons were still in swaddling clothes,
they were all enfeoffed as Marquises.
As for Wèi Shào'ér, the so-called elder sister of Empress Wèi,
Shào'ér bore a son, Huò Qùbìng,
who for military merit was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guànjūn,
and titled General of Swift Cavalry.
Qīng was titled Grand General.
Empress Wèi's son Jù was established as Crown Prince.
The Wèi clan's branches rose through military merit,
with five becoming Marquises.
When Empress Wèi's beauty faded,
the Wáng Fūrén of Zhào gained favor,
had a son,
who became King of Qí.
Wáng Fūrén died early.
Then, Lǐ Fūrén of Zhōngshān gained favor,
had one son,
who became King of Chāngyì.
Lǐ Fūrén died early.
Her elder brother Lǐ Yánnián gained favor through music,
and was titled Harmonious Director.
The Harmonious Director
was formerly an entertainer.
The brothers were both convicted of illicit affairs,
and their clan was executed. At that time, their eldest brother Guǎnglì was General of Èrshī,
campaigning against Dàyuān,
and was not reached by the execution order.
Upon his return, though the Emperor had already exterminated the Lǐ clan,
he later pitied their family,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Hǎixī.
Two sons of other consorts became King of Yān
and King of Guǎnglíng.
Their mothers were not favored,
and died of sorrow.
After Lǐ Fūrén passed away,
then there were those like Yín Jiéyú,
who in turn gained favor.
Yet all were seen as entertainers,
not daughters of kings, marquises, or landholders,
and thus unfit to match the sovereign.
Master Chǔ added:
"When I served as a court gentleman,
I inquired of Zhōnglí Shēng, who was well-versed in the anecdotes of the Hàn dynasty.
He said: The daughter that Empress Dowager Wáng bore while still among the common people,
her father was Jīn Wángsūn.
Wángsūn had already died,
and after Emperor Jǐng passed away,
when Emperor Wǔ had just ascended the throne,
Empress Dowager Wáng was left alone.
Meanwhile, Hán Wángsūn, named Yān, had always enjoyed Emperor Wǔ's favor,
and seized an opportunity to mention that the Empress Dowager had a daughter in Chánglíng.
Emperor Wǔ said:
'Why wasn't I told earlier!'
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to first see her,
finding her at her home.
Emperor Wǔ then went in person to fetch her.
Clearing the road,
vanguard horsemen with banners exited Qíchéng Gate,
and the imperial carriage galloped to Chánglíng.
Entering the village from the west of the small market,
the village gate was closed,
but they forced it open,
and the imperial carriage went straight into this village,
halting right outside the Jīn family's gate.
He had armed cavalry surround the residence,
fearing she might flee,
and thus failing to retrieve her in person.
Immediately, he ordered his attendants and ministers to enter and call out for her.
The family members were terrified,
and the woman hid under a bed inside the house.
They supported her and brought her out the door,
ordering her to bow in reverence.
Emperor Wǔ descended from the carriage and wept, saying:
'Alas!
Elder sister,
why were you hidden so deeply!'
He decreed that a secondary carriage carry her,
turned the carriage around and raced back,
heading straight into Chánglè Palace.
Arriving at the gate, he had her name registered and an introduction made,
leading to an audience with the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager said:
'The Emperor must be tired,
where have you come from?'
The Emperor said:
'Today, I went to Chánglíng and found my sister,
and brought her here with me.'
Turning, he said:
'Pay respects to the Empress Dowager!'
The Empress Dowager said:
'Is it that woman, so-and-so?'
He replied:
'It is her.'
The Empress Dowager shed tears for her,
and the woman also knelt on the ground and wept.
Emperor Wǔ offered wine and came forward to toast her,
presenting ten million in cash,
three hundred male and female slaves,
a hundred qǐng of public fields,
and a top-grade mansion,
to bestow upon his sister.
The Empress Dowager expressed gratitude, saying:
'You have spent much for the Emperor.'
Thereupon, she summoned Princess Píngyáng,
Princess Nángōng,
and Princess Línlǜ, all three to come and pay respects to their sister,
henceforth titling her Lady Xiūchéng.
She had one son
and one daughter.
The son was titled Xiūchéng Zǐzhòng,
and the daughter became the queen of a feudal lord.
These two children were not of the Liú lineage,
which is why the Empress Dowager cherished them.
Xiūchéng Zǐzhòng was arrogant and willful,
oppressing officials and commoners alike,
causing all to suffer and resent him.
When Wèi Zǐfú was established as Empress,
her younger brother Wèi Qīng, styled Zhòngqīng,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chángpíng due to his position as Grand General.
He had four sons;
the eldest, Wèi Kàng, was the heir to the marquisate,
and as the heir, he often served in the palace,
being highly honored and favored.
His three younger brothers were all enfeoffed as marquises,
each with a fief of thirteen hundred households:
one titled Marquis of Yīn'ān,
the second Marquis of Fāgàn,
and the third Marquis of Yíchūn,
their prestige shaking the entire realm.
A folk song of the time went:
'Having a son brings no joy,
having a daughter brings no sorrow;
have you not seen Wèi Zǐfú dominating the world!'
At that time, Princess Píngyáng was widowed and living alone,
and it was customary for a marquis to marry a princess.
The princess consulted with her attendants about which marquis in Cháng'ān could be her husband,
and all said the Grand General was suitable.
The princess laughed and said:
'He came from my household,
often ordered to ride as my escort when I went out;
how could I take him as my husband?'
Her attendants and servants said:
'Now the Grand General's sister is Empress,
his three sons are marquises,
his wealth and honor shake the world;
why would you, Princess, look down on him?'
Thereupon, the princess consented.
This was relayed to the Empress,
who had it reported to Emperor Wǔ,
and an edict was issued for General Wèi to marry Princess Píngyáng.
Master Chǔ added:
A true man transforms like a dragon.
The tradition says:
'When a snake turns into a dragon,
its patterns do not change;
when a family becomes a state,
its surname does not change.'
When a man attains wealth and honor in his time,
all his faults are erased,
and he shines with glory and splendor;
how can the burdens of his poor and lowly days hinder him!
During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
he favored Lady Yǐn, the Jiéyú.
Lady Xíng was titled Xíng'é,
and everyone called her
'Xíng Hé'.
Xíng Hé held a rank equivalent to a fully two-thousand-bushel official,
Rónghuá held a rank equivalent to a two-thousand-bushel official,
and Jiéyú held a rank equivalent to a marquis.
Often, one would be promoted from Jiéyú to become Empress.
Lady Yǐn and Lady Xíng were both favored at the same time,
and an edict forbade them from meeting each other.
Lady Yǐn personally requested of Emperor Wǔ
to be allowed to see Lady Xíng,
and the Emperor permitted it.
He then had another lady adorn herself,
followed by dozens of attendants,
pretending to be Lady Xíng coming forward.
Lady Yǐn came forward and saw her,
saying:
'This is not Lady Xíng herself.'
The Emperor said:
'How can you tell?'
She replied:
'Looking at her figure and appearance,
she is not worthy to attract the sovereign.'
Thereupon, the Emperor ordered Lady Xíng to wear her old clothes,
and come forward alone.
When Lady Yǐn saw her from a distance,
she said:
'This is truly her.'
Then she lowered her head and wept,
lamenting that she was not her equal.
As the saying goes:
'A beautiful woman entering the house
becomes the enemy of the plain ones.'
Master Chǔ added:
One need not bathe in the rivers and seas,
only to remove the dirt;
a horse need not be a qíjì,
only to run well;
a scholar need not be the wisest in the world,
only to understand the Way;
a woman need not be of noble birth,
only to be chaste and good.
The tradition says:
'Whether a woman is beautiful or plain,
upon entering the house, she incites envy;
whether a scholar is worthy or unworthy,
upon entering the court, he incites jealousy.'
A beautiful woman
is the enemy of the plain ones.
Is it not so!
Lady Gōuyì's surname was Zhào,
and she was from Héjiān.
She gained the favor of Emperor Wǔ,
bearing him one son,
who was Emperor Zhāo.
Emperor Wǔ was seventy years old
when he fathered Emperor Zhāo.
When Emperor Zhāo was enthroned,
he was only five years old.
After the crown prince Wèi was deposed,
no new crown prince was appointed.
Then, King Yān, Liú Dàn, submitted a memorial,
expressing his wish to return to the capital and serve in the palace guard.
Emperor Wǔ was enraged,
and immediately beheaded his envoy at the northern palace gate.
The emperor resided at Gānquán Palace,
and summoned artists to depict Zhōu Gōng carrying the young King.
Consequently, the attendants and ministers understood that Emperor Wǔ intended to establish the youngest child as heir.
A few days later,
the emperor rebuked Gōuyì Lady.
The lady removed her hairpins and earrings, and kowtowed.
The emperor said:
"Take her away,
and send her to the Yètíng prison!"
As the lady turned back,
the emperor said:
"Hurry,
you shall not live!"
The lady died at Yúnyáng Palace.
During this time, a violent wind raised dust,
causing sorrow among the common people.
Envoys carried her coffin at night to bury her,
and marked the site.
Afterwards, the emperor was at leisure,
and asked the attendants:
"What do people say?"
The attendants replied:
"People say that although you plan to establish her son,
why do you dismiss his mother?"
The emperor said:
"Indeed.
This is not something foolish people can understand.
In ancient times, the reason nations fell into disorder
was because the ruler was young and the mother was strong.
Female rulers living alone become arrogant and obstinate,
indulge in debauchery unrestricted,
and no one can restrain them.
Have you not heard of Empress Lǚ?"
Thus, all those who bore sons by Emperor Wǔ,
had no children,
and their mothers were all reproached and killed.
How can this not be called wise and sagacious!
With foresight and far-reaching considerations,
planning for future generations,
this is beyond the understanding of shallow scholars.
The posthumous title "Wǔ"
truly is not in vain!
Chǔ Yuán King Liú Jiāo
was the youngest brother of Gāozǔ from the same mother,
styled Yóu.
Gāozǔ had four brothers,
the eldest was Bó,
who died young.
During Gāozǔ's humble beginnings,
he sought official positions,
and frequently visited his elder sister-in-law to dine with guests.
The sister-in-law was annoyed with her uncle,
and when he came with guests,
she pretended the soup was gone,
scraping the pot,
causing the guests to leave.
Later, it was seen there was still soup in the pot,
leading Gāozǔ to resent her.
When Gāozǔ became the emperor,
he enfeoffed his brothers,
but the son of Bó was not enfeoffed.
The Supreme Emperor mentioned this,
and Gāozǔ said:
"I have not forgotten to enfeoff him,
but it is because his mother is unruly."
Thus, he enfeoffed Bó's son Xìn as Marquis of Soup.
He installed his second brother Zhòng in the region of Dài.
In Gāozǔ's sixth year,
after capturing King of Chǔ Hán Xìn in Chén,
he made his brother Jiāo the King of Chǔ,
with the capital at Péngchéng.
He reigned for twenty-three years before passing,
and his son King Yí Yǐng succeeded him.
King Yí passed in his fourth year,
and his son King Wù succeeded him.
King Wù reigned for twenty years,
in winter, was implicated in illicit relations during mourning for Grand Empress Dowager Bó,
resulting in the removal of Dōnghǎi County.
In spring, Wù conspired with the King of Wú to rebel,
his chancellor Zhāng Shàng
and Grand Tutor Zhào Yíwú advised against it,
but he did not listen.
Wù then killed Shàng
and Yíwú,
raised an army to attack Liáng from the west with Wú,
breaking through Jí Bi.
Reaching the south of Chāngyì,
he battled Hàn General Zhōu Èfū.
Hàn forces cut off the Wú-Chǔ supply lines,
and the soldiers starved,
the King of Wú fled,
while the King of Chǔ Wù committed suicide,
and the army surrendered to Hàn.
After pacifying Wú and Chǔ,
Emperor Xiàojǐng wished the heir of Marquis Dé to succeed Wú,
and the heir of King Yuán to succeed Chǔ.
Empress Dowager Dòu said:
"The King of Wú
was an old man,
he ought to have been compliant with the imperial house.
Now yet led seven states to rebel,
causing chaos under heaven,
how can he have a successor!"
Wú was not permitted,
but Chǔ was allowed to have a successor.
At that time, Lǐ was the Imperial Head for Hàn.
Thereupon, he was appointed King of Chǔ,
to maintain the temple sacrifices for King Yuán,
thus becoming King Wén of Chǔ.
King Wén reigned for three years before passing,
his son King Ān Dào succeeded him.
King Ān's reign lasted twenty-two years before he passed,
and his son King Xiāng Zhù succeeded him.
King Xiāng reigned fourteen years before passing,
his son King Chún succeeded.
With King Chún's ascent,
in the second year of the Dìjié period,
an inside agent reported King Chǔ's conspiracy of rebellion,
the king committed suicide,
and the state was abolished,
becoming Péngchéng County of Hàn.
King Zhào Liú Suì's
father was Gāozǔ's middle son,
named Yǒu,
posthumously titled
"Yōu."
The Yōu King died from worry,
hence the title
"Yōu."
Empress Dowager Lǚ appointed Lǚ Lù as King of Zhào,
after one year, Empress Dowager Lǚ passed away.
The ministers executed Lǚ Lù and others in the Lǚ clan,
establishing Yōu King's son Suì as King of Zhào.
In the second year of Emperor Xiàowén's reign,
Suì's brother Bìqiáng was established,
taking Zhào's Héxiān County to form the King of Héxiān,
styled as King Wén.
He reigned thirteen years before passing,
his son King Āi Fú succeeded him.
After one year, he passed without heirs,
leaving no descendants,
the state was abolished,
and incorporated into Hàn.
Suì reigned as King of Zhào for twenty-six years,
during Emperor Xiàojǐng's reign, due to Chāo Cuò's involvement,
the Zhào King was forced to yield the Chángshān County.
Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
and King Zhào's plans allied with them to raise an army.
His chancellor Jiàndé
and Interior History Wáng Hàn advised against it,
but he did not heed.
Suì burned and killed Jiàndé
and Wáng Hàn,
mobilizing troops to station at the western border,
hoping to wait for Wú to join the west.
He sent envoys to the Xiongnu,
allying with them to attack Hàn.
Hàn dispatched Marquis Qūzhōu Lì Jì to counterattack.
King Zhào Suì returned,
held firm in Hándān,
standing against them for seven months.
Wú and Chǔ were defeated in Liáng,
unable to advance west.
Upon hearing this,
the Xiongnu halted,
refusing to enter Hàn's borders.
Luán Bù returned from the defeat in Qí,
then united forces to flood Zhào City.
Zhào City collapsed,
and King Zhào committed suicide,
leading Hándān to surrender.
Zhào Yōu King's lineage ended.
The Grand Historian remarks:
When a state is about to flourish,
there must be auspicious signs,
with gentlemen employed and petty men dismissed.
When a state is nearing its downfall,
worthy men remain hidden,
while treacherous ministers rise to prominence.
Had King Wù of Chǔ not punished Shēn Gōng,
but followed his advice,
and had Zhào appointed Fáng Yǔ Xiānshēng,
would there have been plots of usurpation and murder,
making them scorned by the world?
Ah, worthy men,
worthy men!
Unless one possesses substance within,
how can one employ them?
How profound it is that
"security and peril lie in the issuing of commands,
survival and destruction rest on the appointments made."
Truly, these words are correct!
Regarding King Jīng Liú Jiǎ,
he was a member of the Liú clan,
though his specific lineage at the initial uprising is unknown.
In the first year of King Liú of Hàn,
when he returned to pacify the Three Qín,
Liú Jiǎ served as a general,
securing the Sài region,
and followed eastward to attack Xiàng Jí.
In the fourth year of Hàn,
