when King Liú was defeated at Chénggāo,
he crossed the river north,
obtained the armies of Zhāng Ěr
and Hán Xìn,
stationed at Xiūwǔ,
deepened moats and raised high ramparts,
and sent Liú Jiǎ with twenty thousand troops,
several hundred cavalry,
to cross at Báimǎ Jīn into Chǔ territory,
burn their stockpiles,
to ruin their livelihood,
leaving nothing to supply King Xiàng's army.
Later, when Chǔ attacked Liú Jiǎ,
Jiǎ consistently fortified and refused to engage in battle,
instead maintaining mutual support with Péng Yuè.
In the fifth year of Hàn,
King Liú pursued Xiàng Jí to Gùlíng,
sending Liú Jiǎ south across the Huái to besiege Shòuchūn.
Upon returning,
he sent agents to covertly win over Chǔ's Grand Marshal Zhōu Yīn.
Zhōu Yīn rebelled against Chǔ,
assisted Liú Jiǎ in capturing Jiǔjiāng,
and welcomed the forces of King Wǔ, Qíng Bù,
all converging at Gāixià,
to jointly attack Xiàng Jí.
King Liú then ordered Liú Jiǎ to command the Jiǔjiāng troops,
and with Grand Marshal Lú Wǎn, attack southwest against the King of Línjiāng, Gòng Wèi.
After Gòng Wèi died,
Línjiāng was made into Nánjùn.
In the spring of the sixth year of Hàn,
the feudal lords gathered at Chén,
deposed King Xìn of Chǔ,
imprisoned him,
and divided his territory into two states.
At that time,
Emperor Gāozǔ's sons were young,
his brothers few,
and none particularly worthy,
so he wished to enfeoff those of the same surname to stabilize the realm,
and thus decreed:
"General Liú Jiǎ has rendered meritorious service,
and we should select clansmen fit to be made kings."
The ministers all said:
"Establish Liú Jiǎ as King of Jīng,
ruling over fifty-two cities east of the Huái;
and the emperor's younger brother Jiāo as King of Chǔ,
ruling thirty-six cities west of the Huái."
Thereupon, he enfeoffed his son Féi as King of Qí.
This began the enfeoffment of the Liú clan brothers.
In the autumn of the eleventh year of Gāozǔ,
the King of Huáinán, Qíng Bù, rebelled,
attacking Jīng from the east.
King Jīng, Liú Jiǎ, engaged him in battle,
but was defeated,
fled to Fùlíng,
and was killed by Bù's army.
Gāozǔ personally led troops to defeat Bù.
In the twelfth year,
he enfeoffed Pèi Hóu Liú Bì as King of Wú,
ruling the former territory of Jīng.
Regarding King Yān Liú Zé,
he was a distant relative of the Liú clan.
In the third year of Emperor Gāo,
Zé served as a court gentleman.
In the eleventh year of Gāo Dì,
Zé, as a general, attacked Chén Xī,
captured Wáng Huáng,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yínglíng.
During Empress Dowager Lǚ's reign,
a man from Qí named Tián Shēng, traveling and short on funds,
sought an audience with the Marquis of Yínglíng, Zé, through a stratagem.
Zé was greatly pleased with him,
and gifted him two hundred catties of gold for his livelihood.
After Tián Shēng received the gold,
he returned to Qí.
Two years later,
Zé sent someone to tell Tián Shēng:
"No more assistance."
Tián Shēng went to Cháng'ān,
but did not visit Zé;
instead, he rented a large residence,
and had his son seek to serve Zhāng Zǐqīng, the chief palace steward favored by Empress Lǚ.
After several months,
Tián Shēng's son invited Zhāng Qīng to visit,
personally preparing the feast.
Zhāng Qīng agreed to go.
Tián Shēng set up lavish curtains and furnishings,
comparable to those of a full marquis.
Zhāng Qīng was astonished.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Tián Shēng dismissed others and advised Zhāng Qīng:
"I have observed over a hundred mansions of the feudal kings,
all meritorious officials of Gāozǔ.
Now the Lǚ clan, having originally supported Gāozǔ in gaining the empire,
have immense merit,
and are close relatives of the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager is advanced in years,
the various Lǚ are weak,
and the Empress Dowager wishes to enfeoff Lǚ Chǎn as a king,
ruling Dài.
Yet she hesitates to initiate it,
fearing the ministers' opposition.
You, sir, are most favored,
respected by the ministers;
why not hint to the ministers to propose it to the Empress Dowager?
She will surely be pleased.
Once the Lǚ are enfeoffed as kings,
a marquisate of ten thousand households will be yours.
The Empress Dowager desires this,
but as a courtier,
if you do not act promptly,
I fear disaster may befall you."
Zhāng Qīng greatly agreed,
and so hinted to the ministers to speak to the Empress Dowager.
When the Empress Dowager held court,
she inquired of the ministers.
The ministers requested to enfeoff Lǚ Chǎn as King of Lǚ.
The Empress Dowager rewarded Zhāng Qīng with a thousand catties of gold,
half of which Zhāng Qīng gave to Tián Shēng.
Tián Shēng declined to accept it,
and instead advised him:
"Lǚ Chǎn is now a king,
but the ministers are not fully convinced.
Now the Marquis of Yínglíng, Zé,
a member of the Liú clan,
serves as a senior general,
yet he alone feels discontented.
If you, sir, speak to the Empress Dowager,
to enfeoff him with a dozen or so counties as a king,
once he gains the kingship,
he will leave content,
and the Lǚ kingships will be more secure."
Zhāng Qīng went in and spoke,
and the Empress Dowager agreed.
Thus, the Marquis of Yínglíng, Liú Zé, was made King of Lángyé.
The King of Lángyé then went with Tián Shēng to his fief.
Tián Shēng urged Zé to depart quickly,
without delay.
Once they passed the frontier,
the Empress Dowager indeed sent someone to pursue and stop them,
but they had already left,
and the envoy returned.
After the Empress Dowager passed away,
the King of Lángyé, Zé, said:
"The emperor is young,
the Lǚ clan holds power,
and the Liú clan is isolated and weak."
He then led his troops and conspired with the King of Qí to march west,
intending to eliminate the Lǚ clan.
Reaching Liáng,
he heard that Hàn had sent General Guàn to station at Xíngyáng,
so Zé turned his troops to guard the western border,
then swiftly advanced to Cháng'ān.
The King of Dài also arrived from Dài.
The various generals and ministers, together with the King of Lángyé, jointly established the King of Dài as the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven then transferred Zé to be King of Yān,
and returned Lángyé to Qí,
restoring its former territory.
In the second year of King Zé of Yān,
he passed away and was posthumously titled King Jìng.
He was succeeded by his son Jiā,
who became King Kāng.
When it came to his grandson Dìngguó,
he committed incest with his father King Kāng's concubine,
producing one male child.
He took his brother's wife as a concubine.
He engaged in incest with three of his children.
Dìngguó intended to execute Minister Féirú in Lìngyǐng,
but the people of Lìngyǐng reported Dìngguó,
so Dìngguó sent an emissary to capture and kill the people of Lìngyǐng by other legal methods to silence them.
By the first year of Yuánshuò,
the brothers of Lìngyǐng again submitted a memorial exposing Dìngguó's illicit acts,
leading to the revelation.
A decree was issued to the court officials,
and they all concluded, saying:
"Dìngguó's conduct is bestial,
disrupting human ethics,
defying the heavens,
deserving execution."
The emperor approved this.
Dìngguó committed suicide,
and the state was dissolved and reorganized as a commandery.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"Jīng Wáng Yān,
established since the early Hàn,
when the empire was yet to consolidate,
thus Liú Jiǎ, though of distant lineage,
was made king by strategem,
occupying the space between Jiāng and Huái.
King Liú Zé,
challenged the power of the Lǚ clan,
yet, in the end, Lǚ Zé's descendants ruled southward for three generations.
The emergence of great affairs,
was this not magnificent!”
Liú Féi, King of Qí Dàohuì,
was the eldest illegitimate son of Gāozǔ.
His mother was an outsider,
named Cáo.
In the sixth year of Gāozǔ,
Féi was made King of Qí,
ruling over seventy cities,
and all the people who could speak Qí were given to King Qí.
King Qí,
was the elder brother of Emperor Xiàohuì.
In the second year of Emperor Xiàohuì,
King Qí attended court.
Emperor Huì dined and drank with King Qí,
treating him as a family member.
Empress Dowager Lǚ was furious,
and intended to execute King Qí.
Fearful and seeing no escape,
King Qí followed the plan of his secretary Xūn,
offering the Chéngyáng Commandery,
to be the bathing township of Princess Lǔyuán.
Empress Dowager Lǚ, pleased,
allowed him to leave and return to his kingdom.
King Dàohuì reigned for twelve years,
passing away in the sixth year of Emperor Huì.
His son Xiāng ascended,
becoming King Āi.
In the first year of King Āi,
Emperor Xiàohuì died,
Empress Dowager Lǚ seized power,
and all state matters were decided by Empress Lǚ.
In the second year,
Empress Lǚ appointed her nephew Marquis Lì,
Lǚ Tái as King Lǚ,
and carved out the Jǐnán Commandery of Qí to be King Lǚ's fief.
In the third year of King Āi,
his brother Zhāng joined the imperial guards in Hàn,
and Empress Dowager Lǚ appointed him Marquis Zhūxū,
and married him to Lǚ Lù's daughter.
Four years later,
Zhāng's younger brother Xìngjū was made Marquis Dōngmóu,
both residing within the imperial guards in Cháng'ān.
In the eighth year of King Āi,
Empress Lǚ divided Qílǎngyé Commandery to establish Marquis Yínglíng Liú Zé as King Lǎngyé.
The following year,
King Zhào's friend visited the court,
and died mysteriously at the mansion.
All three kings of Zhào were deposed.
Empress Lǚ established the Lǚs as three kings,
wielding exclusive power.
At the age of twenty, Marquis Zhūxū,
strong in physique,
grew indignant that the Liú clan lacked positions.
Once, while serving Empress Lǚ at a banquet,
Empress Lǚ ordered Liú Zhāng of Zhūxū to be the wine steward.
Zhāng requested, saying:
"Minister,
being of military stock,
asks to perform wine serving under military law."
Empress Lǚ agreed:
"Allowed."
After much drinking,
Zhāng advanced, singing and dancing.
He then said:
" May I sing a song about farming for the Empress Dowager?"
Empress Lǚ laughed, saying her son:
"What do you know of farming?"
The son replied:
"Only our father knew of farming.
If born a king's son,
would he know of farming?”
Zhāng said:
"This servant knows it well."
The Empress Dowager said:
"Try speaking of farming to me."
Zhāng replied:
"Deep plowing and close planting,
setting the seedlings to grow sparse;
those not of the correct seedling,
weeding them out."
Empress Lǚ fell silent.
Not long after,
one of the Lǚs got drunk,
went missing with wine,
Zhāng pursued,
drew his sword, executed him,
returned and reported:
"One left with wine,
I acted according to the law and executed him."
All the courtiers were greatly shocked.
Having already allowed military law,
there was no recourse against him, and
thus ended the banquet.
Thereafter,
the Lǚs feared Marquis Zhūxū,
and even the ministers depended on Marquis Zhūxū,
strengthening the Liú clan.
The following year,
Empress Lǚ passed away.
Zhào King Lǚ Lù acted as Chief General,
Lǚ Chǎn as Chancellor,
both residing in Cháng'ān,
gathering troops to intimidate the ministers,
intending rebellion.
Knowing Lǚ Lù's designs,
Marquis Zhūxū Zhāng, married to Lǚ Lù's daughter,
secretly sent someone to inform his brother King Qí,
wanting him to dispatch troops westward,
with Marquis Zhūxū
and Marquis Dōngmóu as inside support,
to end the Lǚs,
and then enthrone King Qí as emperor.
When the King of Qí heard this plan,
he conspired secretly with his uncle, Sì Jūn,
Zhù Wǔ, the Director of the Palace,
and Wèi Bó, the commandant, to raise troops.
Prime Minister Zhào Píng of Qí heard of this,
and he deployed guards to protect the royal palace.
Wèi Bó deceived Zhào Píng, saying,
"The king wishes to raise troops,
but lacks the military token of Hàn as proof.
However, my lord surrounds the king,
which is indeed good.
I, Bó, request to lead troops to guard and protect the king."
Trusting him, Zhào Píng
then sent Wèi Bó to lead troops to surround the royal palace.
Once Bó commanded the troops,
he besieged the prime minister's residence.
Zhào Píng lamented,
"Alas!
The Daoist saying
'when necessary to act, failing to act
brings chaos instead'
is indeed true."
He then committed suicide.
Consequently, the King of Qí appointed Sì Jūn as prime minister,
Wèi Bó as general,
and Zhù Wǔ as internal steward,
deploying troops from all over the country.
He sent Zhù Wǔ east to deceive Prince Lángyá saying,
"The Lü clan is rebelling,
and the King of Qí is deploying troops to execute them in the west.
The King of Qí regards himself as a child,
young in age,
unversed in military affairs,
and wishes to entrust the whole state to the Great King.
The Great King has been a general under the founding emperor,
experienced in warfare.
The King of Qí dares not advance the troops,
so he sends me to invite the Great King to Líntán to discuss plans with the King of Qí,
and together lead the Qí troops westward to quell the disturbances in Guānzhōng."
Believing this,
Prince Lángyá thought it true,
and hurried to meet the King of Qí.
The King of Qí and Wèi Bó detained Prince Lángyá,
while sending Zhù Wǔ to fully mobilize the state of Lángyá and merge their forces.
Prince Liú Zé of Lángyá, having been deceived,
could not return to his state,
and thus persuaded the King of Qí, saying,
"King Daohuì of Qí was the oldest son of the Great Emperor,
speaking from the root of all matters,
and the Great King is the rightful eldest grandson of the Great Emperor,
deserving the throne.
Now the great ministers are uncertain and have not settled on a decision,
but among the Liú clan, I am the oldest,
and the ministers naturally await my decision.
Now, keeping this minister of mine here is of no use to you;
it would be better to allow me to enter Guānzhōng to plan affairs."
The King of Qí thought this reasonable,
and accordingly provided a better carriage to send Prince Lángyá off.
Once Prince Lángyá left,
Qí proceeded to mobilize forces westward and attack Lǚ State's Jìnán.
Then King Āi of Qí sent letters to the vassal princes, saying,
"The Great Emperor unified the world,
establishing kings among his sons and brothers,
King Daohuì in Qí.
After King Daohuì's passing,
Emperor Huì had Chancellor Zhang Liáng establish me as King of Qí.
After Emperor Huì's death,
Empress Dowager Lü took charge,
growing old in years,
allowing the Lü clan to usurp positions, contrary to the Great Emperor's intentions,
and kill three Zhao kings,
eradicate Liáng,
Yān, and Zhào, establishing Lü clans as rulers,
dividing the Qí state into four.
Loyal ministers advised against it,
but the upper powers were deluded and did not listen.
Now, with the Empress Dowager's passing,
the emperor is young,
unable yet to rule the world,
relying on great ministers and vassals.
Now the Lü clan once again usurps positions,
gathering troops to impose their tyranny,
threatening lords and loyal ministers,
fabricating commands to dictate the world,
endangering the ancestral temple.
Now, I lead troops to eliminate those unfit to be kings."
Hàn heard Qí was raising troops and heading west,
prompting Chancellor Lǚ Chǎn to dispatch Grand General Guàn Yīng east to attack them.
Upon reaching Xíngyáng,
Guàn Yīng planned thus:
"The Lü clan has troops stationed in Guānzhōng,
intending to imperil the Liú clan to seize power themselves.
If I defeat Qí and report back,
it would increase the strength of the Lü clan."
So he left their troops stationed in Xíngyáng,
sending envoys to notify King Qí and the vassal lords,
seeking alliance,
awaiting a Lü clan revolt to jointly execute them.
Upon hearing this, King Qí
moved west, taking back his former Jìnán district,
and stationed troops at the western border of Qí to await agreements.
Lǚ Lù and
Lǚ Chǎn attempted a revolt in Guānzhōng,
but Marquis Zhūxū and Tàiwèi Bó,
along with Chancellor Píng and others, executed them.
Marquis Zhūxū was the first to behead Lǚ Chǎn,
enabling Tàiwèi Bó and others to completely eliminate the Lü clan.
Prince Lángyá also arrived from Qí to Cháng'ān.
The ministers deliberated installing the King of Qí,
but Prince Lángyá and the ministers said:
"The King of Qí's maternal family, Sì Jūn,
is wicked and violent,
a tiger in a cap.
With the recent Lü clan's disturbance nearly throwing the world into chaos,
installing the King of Qí would be akin to reinstating the Lü clan's chaos.
The maternal family of the Dí Wáng, the Bó clan,
is noble and virtuous;
besides, the Dí Wáng is also a direct son of the Great Emperor,
present among us,
and he is the eldest.
With lineage as his foundation, it aligns naturally,
and with a virtuous person as ruler, the ministers will be at ease."
Hence, the ministers planned to welcome and install the Dí Wáng,
sending Marquis Zhūxū to inform King Qí of the execution of the Lü clan,
instructing him to disband his troops.
When General Guàn Yīng stationed in Xíngyáng
heard that Wèi Bó had originally advised King Qí's rebellion,
with the Lü clan already executed,
he ordered Qí to disband its forces,
and sent an envoy to question Wèi Bó.
Bó replied:
"In a burning house,
how could one first speak of great men and then extinguish the fire?"
He then withdrew,
trembling with fear,
unable to speak further.
There were no other words.
General Guàn scrutinized him and laughed, saying,
"People say Wèi Bó is brave,
but he is a foolish and mediocre man,
incapable of anything of note!"
Wèi Bó was thus dismissed.
Wèi Bó's father was well-known for playing the qín before the Emperor Qín.
When young, Wèi Bó
sought an audience with Qí Minister Cáo Cān,
but due to poverty, found no means to make connections,
so he often swept the entrance of Cáo Cān's retainers' residence day and night.
The minister's retainers found it strange,
suspecting something,
and observed him,
discovering it was Bó.
Bó said,
"I wish to meet the minister,
yet have no cause,
hence I swept for you,
hoping to gain an audience."
Consequently, the retainers introduced Bó to Cáo Cān,
who then made Bó a retainer.
Once he served as Cáo Cān's aide,
offering advice,
Cáo found him wise,
and spoke of him to King Daohuì of Qí,
who summoned Bó,
appointing him as Internal Steward.
Initially, King Daohuì had the authority to appoint officials.
After King Daohuì's death and the accession of King Āi,
Bó wielded great authority,
more influential than the Qí prime minister.
Once the king disbanded the troops and returned,
with Dí Wáng ascended to the throne,
he became Emperor Xiàowén.
In the first year of Emperor Xiàowén,
the territories of Chéngyáng,
Lángyá,
and Jìnán, which were partitioned by Empress Dowager's order, were returned to Qí,
and Prince Lángyá was relocated to rule Yān,
expanding the fiefdoms of Marquis Zhūxū
and Marquis Dōngmóu by two thousand households each.
That year,
King Āi of Qí passed away,
and the crown prince ascended,
becoming King Wén.
In the first year of King Wén of Qí,
the Hàn dynasty established Marquis Zhūxū as King of Chéngyáng from the Qí district,
and established Marquis Dōngmóu as King of Jìběi from the Qí Jìběi district.
In the second year,
the King of Jìběi rebelled.
The Hàn executed him,
and the territory was incorporated into Hàn.
Two years later,
Emperor Xiàowén entirely enfeoffed the seven sons of King Qídào Huì: Bàjūn and others, all as marquises.
King Qí Wén reigned for fourteen years and died,
without an heir,
the state was abolished,
and the land was incorporated into Hàn.
The following year,
Emperor Xiàowén divided Qí among the sons of King Dàohuì, appointing Xiānglǘ as King Qí with Yangxū Hóu as King of Qí.
Therefore, the remaining counties of Qí were all given to the sons of King Dàohuì:
Zhi became King of Jìběi,
Bìguāng became King of Jǐnán,
Xián became King of Zīchuān,
Áng became King of Jiāoxī,
Xióngqú became King of Jiāodōng,
along with Chéngyáng,
making seven kings in total.
In the eleventh year of King Xiào of Qí,
King Bì of Wú and
King Wù of Chǔ rebelled,
raising troops to the west,
announcing to the feudal lords that
they would punish the traitorous minister Cáo Cuò of Hàn to secure the ancestral temples.
Jiāoxī,
Jiāodōng,
Zīchuān, and
Jǐnán all unauthorizedly raised troops to join Wú and Chǔ.
They intended to ally with Qí,
but King Xiào of Qí was indecisive,
and defended the city without surrendering,
and the combined troops of the three states besieged Qí.
King Qí sent an envoy Lu Zhōng to report to the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven sent the envoy Lu Zhōng back to tell King Qí:
"Hold firmly,
our troops have now defeated Wú and Chǔ."
When the envoy Lu Zhōng arrived,
the troops of the three states surrounded Línzī several times over,
and there was no access.
The generals of the three states coerced the envoy Lu Zhōng to ally with them,
saying:
"If you return and say Hàn has been defeated,
Qí will promptly submit to the three states,
or else it will be slaughtered."
The envoy Lu Zhōng agreed,
but when he reached the city walls,
seeing King Qí,
he shouted:
"Hàn has dispatched a million troops,
making the Grand Marshall Zhōu Yǎfū defeat Wú and Chǔ,
they are now moving to aid Qí,
Qí must hold firm and not submit!"
The generals of the three states executed Lu Zhōng.
Initially, Qí was in dire straits,
secretly conspiring with the three states,
but before the pact was completed,
they heard the envoy Lu Zhōng had come from Hàn,
and rejoicing, their ministers encouraged the king not to submit to the three states.
Soon after,
the general of Hàn, Luán Bù,
and others with troops arrived in Qí,
defeated the troops of the three states,
lifting the siege of Qí.
Subsequently, it was discovered that Qí had initially conspired with the three states,
and plans were made to move troops to attack Qí.
Fearing this,
King Xiào of Qí took poison and died.
When Emperor Jǐng heard of it,
he considered Qí's stance commendable,
as any conspiracy was due to coercion,
not the king’s fault,
so he established Prince Shòu, son of Xiào King, as King of Qí,
who was then known as Yì King,
continuing Qí.
However, Kings Jiāoxī,
Jiāodōng,
Jǐnán, and
Zīchuān were all executed,
and the land incorporated into Hàn.
The King of Jìběi was moved to rule Zīchuān.
King Yì of Qí reigned for twenty-two years and died,
succeeded by his son as King Jìng,
known as King Lì.
King Lì of Qí,
whose mother was known as Jì Tàihòu,
married the daughter of her brother Jì as Queen of King Lì.
The King did not favor Jì's daughter.
Desiring to increase her family's influence,
Tàihòu sent her eldest daughter, Wengzhǔ, into the king's palace,
controlling the inner court,
not allowing her to be close to the king,
wanting him to favor Jì's daughter.
The King, however, engaged in an affair with his sister, Wengzhǔ.
An eunuch of Qí, named Xú Jiǎ,
served the Empress Dowager of Hàn.
The Empress Dowager had a favored daughter named Xiūchéng Jūn,
though not of the Liú clan,
for whom she harbored affection.
Xiūchéng Jūn had a daughter named É.
The Empress Dowager wished to marry her to a noble.
Eunuch Jiǎ requested an envoy to Qí,
persuading the king to request É.
The Empress Dowager was pleased
and sent Jiǎ to Qí.
At this time, Qí's Zhǔfù Yǎn knew of Jiǎ's mission to arrange for a future queen,
and also asked Jiǎ,
"If successful,
please remember that Yǎn's daughter wishes to join the king's inner court."
Having arrived in Qí,
Jiǎ secretly advanced this matter.
Jì Tàihòu was furious,
saying:
"The king has a queen,
the court is complete.
Moreover, Jiǎ,
a poor person from Qí,
became an eunuch out of necessity,
served Hàn,
and was of no help,
yet now attempts to disrupt the royal household!
And what of Zhǔfù Yǎn?
He desires his daughter to join the inner court!"
Xu Jiǎ was greatly troubled,
and returned to report to the Empress Dowager:
"The king is willing to marry É,
but there is an obstacle,
fearing a repeat of the Yàn king incident."
Yàn King,
engaged in incest with his son, Kun, leading to death,
losing his state,
thus warning the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager replied:
"Never mention marrying my daughter to Qí again."
This incident gradually came to the emperor’s attention.
As a result, Zhǔfù Yǎn also distanced himself from Qí.
At that time, Zhǔfù Yǎn enjoyed favor with the emperor,
wielding influence,
and suggested that:
"Qí, with Línzī's population of ten thousand households,
market revenues amounting to a thousand gold,
populous and wealthy,
larger than Cháng'ān,
ought to be governed only by the emperor’s close family.
Currently, the Qí king grows more distant in kinship."
He began to suggest:
"During Lǚ Tàihòu's time, Qí intended to rebel;
during the Wú and Chǔ times, King Xiào nearly caused turmoil.
It’s now heard that the King of Qí engages in incest with his sister."
Thus, the emperor appointed Zhǔfù Yǎn as Prime Minister of Qí,
to rectify matters.
Upon arriving in Qí, Zhǔfù Yǎn
hastily dealt with the eunuchs in the royal inner court involved in the matter with the king's sister, Wengzhǔ,
requiring confessions that implicated the king.
Being young,
and fearing severe punishment if captured by officials,
the king took poison and died,
leaving no heir.
At this time, King Zhào feared Zhǔfù Yǎn's influence in causing the dismissal of Qí,
fearing estrangement among kin.
He wrote accusing Yǎn of accepting gold and highlighting his faults.
The Emperor then imprisoned Yǎn.
Gōngsūn Hóng spoke:
"The King of Qí died from distress with no successor,
his kingdom has returned to Hàn.
Without punishing Yǎn, public expectations cannot be satisfied."
Thus, Yǎn was executed.
King Lì of Qí ruled for five years and died,
without heirs,
and the kingdom was incorporated into Hàn.
The legacy of Qídào Huì King left two states:
Chéngyáng and Zīchuān.
Zīchuān’s land was compared with Qí.
The emperor, pitying Qí,
established the tomb park of King Dàohuì in the commandery,
granting the lands east of Línzī surrounding the tomb park to Zīchuān,
to ensure the offerings for King Dàohuì's sacrifices.
The chapter on Chéngyáng Jǐngwáng,
son of Qí Dào Huìwáng,
who, with the Marquis of Zhūxū and the grand ministers, executed the various members of the Lü clan,
personally beheading Chancellor Lü Wáng Chǎn at the palace of Wèi Yāng.
After Emperor Xiàowén ascended the throne,
the Jǐngwáng was granted an increased fief of 2,000 households
and awarded a thousand jin of gold.
In the second year of Xiàowén,
the district of Chéngyáng of Qí was established with the Jǐngwáng as its ruler.
He ruled for two years and died,
his son Xǐ succeeded him,
known as the Gòng Wáng.
In the eighth year of King Gòng,
he was moved to rule Huáinán.
After four years,
he returned to rule Chéngyáng.
After a total of thirty-three years, he died,
and his son Yán succeeded him,
known as the Qǐng Wáng.
In the twenty-sixth year of King Qǐng,
his son Yì succeeded him,
known as the Jìng Wáng.
In the ninth year of Jìng Wáng, he died,
and his son Wǔ succeeded him,
known as the Huì Wáng.
In the eleventh year, Huì Wáng died,
and his son Shùn succeeded him,
known as the Huāng Wáng.
In the forty-sixth year, King Huāng died,
and his son Huī succeeded him,
known as the Dài Wáng.
In the eighth year, King Dài died,
and his son Jǐng succeeded him,
by the third year of Jiànshǐ,
he was fifteen years old,
when he died.
Jǐbèi Wáng Xìngjū,
son of Qí Dào Huìwáng,
assisted the Marquis of Dōngmóu in helping the grand ministers to execute the Lü clan,
yet his contributions were minor.
When Emperor Wéndì returned from Dài,
Xìngjū said:
"Let me enter the imperial palace with the Grand Stablemaster Yīng."
The Emperor and the ministers deposed the Young Emperor,
and together established Emperor Xiàowén.
In the second year of Xiàowén,
Xìngjū was established as Jǐbèi Wáng in the district of Jǐbèi of Qí,
simultaneously with Chéngyáng Wáng.
After two years of reign,
he rebelled. When the grand ministers executed the Lü clan,
the Marquis of Zhūxū's contributions were especially notable,
and it was promised that he would be made king of the Zhao region,
and the Marquis of Dōngmóu would be made king of the Liang region.
When Emperor Xiàowén ascended the throne,
he heard that the Zhūxū
and Dōngmóu initially intended to support the King of Qí,
hence their merits were diminished.
By the second year,
all the sons of the royal family were appointed kings,
with two territories of Qí bequeathed to Jīng and
Xìngjū.
Jīng and Xìngjū felt deprived and stripped of their contributions.
With Jīng's death,
and hearing the Xiongnu had invaded Han in great numbers,
causing the mobilization of multiple armies,
hence sending the Chancellor Guàn Yīng to strike them down,
Emperor Wéndì personally visited Taiyuan,
believing that the emperor himself should confront the Hu,
thus he raised an army to rebel in Jǐbèi.
The Emperor, upon hearing this,
halted the Chancellor and the deployment of troops,
recalling them all to Cháng'ān.
General Chái of Jípú was dispatched to smash the rebels and defeat the Jǐbèi Wáng,
resulting in the King taking his own life,
and the land fell to the Han,
becoming a district.
Thirteen years later,
in the sixteenth year of Wéndì,
a prince of Dào Huìwáng of Qí, Zhì, Marquis of Āndū, was restored as Jǐbèi Wáng.
After eleven years,
during the Wu and Chu rebellions,
Zhì stood firm,
refusing to conspire with the other marquises.
With the quelling of Wu and Chu,
Zhì was moved to rule Zīchuān.
Jǐnán Wáng Pì Guāng,
also a son of Qí Dào Huìwáng,
was inaugurated as Jǐnán Wáng in the sixteenth year of Emperor Xiàowén as Marquis of Lē.
In the eleventh year,
he revolted during the Wu and Chu rebellions.
The Han crushed and killed Pì Guāng,
and Jǐnán became a district,
with its land incorporated into Han.
Zīchuān Wáng Xián,
another son of Qí Dào Huìwáng,
was made king of Zīchuān in the sixteenth year of Emperor Wéndì as Marquis of Wǔchéng.
In the eleventh year,
he too participated in the Wu and Chu rebellion,
the Han forces crushed him,
and Xián was slain.
Subsequently, the Emperor relocated Jǐbèi Wáng Zhì to rule Zīchuān,
who was also a son of Qí Dào Huìwáng,
having previously been the Marquis of Āndū when appointed as Jǐbèi Wáng.
The Zīchuān Wáng rebelled,
without an heir,
thus relocating Jǐbèi Wáng to rule Zīchuān.
After a reign of thirty-five years, he died,
posthumously known as Yì Wáng.
His son Jiàn succeeded him
as Jìng Wáng.
After twenty years, he died,
with his son Yí succeeding him
as Qǐng Wáng.
After thirty-six years, he died,
and his son Zhōnggǔ succeeded him
as Sī Wáng.
After twenty-eight years, he died,
and his son Shàng became
Xiào Wáng.
After five years, he died,
and his son Héng succeeded him,
reigning until the third year of Jiànshǐ,
at the age of eleven,
when he died.
Jiāoxī Wáng Áng,
another son of Qí Dào Huìwáng,
became king of Jiāoxī in the sixteenth year of Emperor Wéndì as the Marquis of Chāngpíng.
In the eleventh year,
he revolted with Wu and Chu.
The Han forces defeated him,
and Áng was executed,
with the land annexed by Han,
becoming Jiāoxī District.
Jiāodōng Wáng Xióngqú,
another son of Qí Dào Huìwáng,
was made Jiāodōng Wáng in Wéndì's sixteenth year as the Marquis of Bái Shí.
In the eleventh year,
he too rebelled with Wu and Chu,
the Han army suppressed and killed Xióngqú,
and the land fell to the Han,
becoming Jiāodōng District.
The Grand Historian said:
"Among the great states ruled by princes, none surpassed Qí Dào Huìwáng.
When the internal land disputes were first stabilized,
with his offspring few,
and incensed by the example of Qin's lack of even a inch of land bestowed,
he extensively enfeoffed those of the same surname,
to fill the aspirations of the multitudes.
As later divisions occurred,
it was indeed rational and logical."
Xiāo Chancellor Hé, what of him?
He was a man of Pèi Fēng.
Under the governance of Wén Wúhài, he was retained as a subordinate official in Pèi.
When Gāozǔ was still a commoner,
Hé frequently used official business to protect Gāozǔ.
As Gāozǔ became the head of the pavilion,
Xiāo Hé constantly remained at his side.
When Gāozǔ traveled as an official to Xiányáng,
the other officials provided him with three coins,
but Hé uniquely gifted five.
The Qin commandery overseer frequently contested against him.
Hé was assigned the duty to prepare documents for the Sìshuǐ,
achieving first place.
The Qin overseer considered recommending Xiāo Hé for summons,
but Hé firmly requested to stay,
and was allowed not to proceed.
When Emperor Gāozǔ rose to become the Lord of Pèi,
Xiāo Hé often served as his assistant, overseeing affairs.
When the Lord of Pèi reached Xiányáng,
all the generals rushed to the treasuries to seize gold, silk, and valuables to divide among themselves,
but Xiāo Hé alone entered first to collect the legal codes, decrees, maps, and documents of the Qín prime minister and imperial censor, and stored them away.
When the Lord of Pèi became the King of Hàn,
he appointed Xiāo Hé as his chancellor.
King Xiàng and the other nobles slaughtered, burned Xiányáng, and departed.
The reason the King of Hàn could fully understand the strategic passes and barriers of the realm,
the number of households and population,
the locations of strength and weakness,
and the hardships and sufferings of the people,
was because Xiāo Hé had obtained all of Qín's maps and documents.
Xiāo Hé recommended Hán Xìn,
and the King of Hàn appointed Hán Xìn as Grand General.
This is recorded in the account of the "Marquis of Huáiyīn."
When the King of Hàn led his troops east to pacify the Three Qín,
Xiāo Hé, as chancellor, remained to oversee Bā and Shǔ,
pacifying, comforting, instructing, and informing the people,
ensuring the supply of military provisions.
In the second year of Hàn,
when the King of Hàn joined the nobles to attack Chǔ,
Xiāo Hé guarded Guānzhōng,
attended to the crown prince,
and administered Yuèyáng.
He established laws and regulations,
and set up ancestral temples, altars of state, palaces, and counties.
He would report these to the king for approval;
if approved, he was permitted to proceed accordingly;
if there was no time to report,
he would act as he saw fit,
and inform the king upon his return.
In managing affairs in Guānzhōng, such as calculating households for transporting supplies to the army,
even when the King of Hàn repeatedly lost troops and fled,
Xiāo Hé often mobilized soldiers from Guānzhōng
to fill the gaps immediately.
For this reason, the emperor entrusted Xiāo Hé exclusively with all matters in Guānzhōng.
In the third year of Hàn,
when the King of Hàn and Xiàng Yǔ were locked in a stalemate between Jīng and Suǒ,
the emperor repeatedly sent envoys to console the chancellor.
Advisor Bào told the chancellor:
"The king endures exposure in the field,
yet repeatedly sends envoys to console you.
This indicates he suspects you.
For your sake,
it would be best to send all your sons, grandsons, and brothers capable of bearing arms to the army's camp.
Then the emperor will surely trust you more."
So Xiāo Hé followed his advice,
and the King of Hàn was greatly pleased.
In the fifth year of Hàn,
after Xiàng Yǔ was killed,
and the realm was pacified,
rewards were conferred based on merit.
The ministers vied for credit,
and for over a year, the merits could not be decided.
Emperor Gāozǔ considered Xiāo Hé's contributions the most outstanding,
enfeoffing him as the Marquis of Cuó,
with a large fief.
The meritorious officials all said:
"We have worn armor and wielded sharp weapons,
some fighting over a hundred battles,
others several dozen engagements,
capturing cities and seizing territories,
with achievements great and small.
Yet Xiāo Hé has never known the toil of battle,
merely wielding brush and ink in discussions,
without fighting,
he is placed above us all.
Why?"
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"Do you gentlemen understand hunting?"
They replied:
"We do."
"Do you understand hunting dogs?"
They said:
"We do."
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"In hunting,
it is the dogs that chase and kill the beasts and hares,
but the one who points out where the game is, is the man.
Now, you gentlemen can only catch running game—
you are 'merit dogs.'
As for Xiāo Hé,
he points out the trail and directs the hunt,
he is the 'merit man.'
Moreover, you gentlemen followed me alone,
at most two or three of you.
But Xiāo Hé brought his entire clan of several dozen to follow me,
a contribution that cannot be forgotten."
The ministers dared not speak further.
After all the marquises had received their enfeoffments,
and it came to reporting their rankings,
all said:
"Píngyáng Hóu Cáo Cān personally sustained seventy wounds,
capturing cities and seizing territories,
his merits are the greatest,
he should rank first."
The emperor had already overruled the meritorious officials,
granting Xiāo Hé a large fief,
and regarding the ranking, he had no further objections to raise,
yet he was determined to place Xiāo Hé first.
The Marquis of Guānnèi, È Jūn, came forward and said:
"The ministers' opinions are all mistaken.
Though Cáo Cān has achievements in field battles and seizing land,
these are but temporary deeds.
The emperor and Chǔ were locked in stalemate for five years,
often losing armies and troops,
and fleeing personally several times.
Yet Xiāo Hé constantly sent troops from Guānzhōng to replenish the losses,
without awaiting the emperor's edict or summons,
and tens of thousands of troops assembled to relieve the emperor in his dire straits multiple times.
When Hàn and Chǔ held each other at Xíngyáng for years,
with the army lacking visible provisions,
Xiāo Hé transported supplies from Guānzhōng,
ensuring a continuous food supply.
Though Your Majesty repeatedly lost territories east of the mountains,
Xiāo Hé always preserved Guānzhōng intact for Your Majesty's return,
this is a merit for ten thousand generations.
Now, even if we lost a hundred like Cáo Cān,
what would Hàn lack?
Hàn would not necessarily rely on them for survival.
How can we compare momentary merits to a ten-thousand-generation achievement!
Xiāo Hé should be first,
Cáo Cān second."
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"Well said."
Thereupon, he ordered Xiāo Hé to rank first,
granting him the privilege to wear his sword and shoes in the court,
and not to hasten his steps when entering the court.
The emperor said:
"I have heard that recommending the worthy deserves the highest reward.
Though Xiāo Hé's merit is great,
it was È Jūn who made it clearer."
So, based on È Jūn's former fief as Marquis of Guānnèi, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānpíng.
That day,
over ten of Xiāo Hé's sons, brothers, and other relatives were enfeoffed,
all receiving fiefs.
Additionally, Xiāo Hé was granted two thousand more households,
because when the emperor was once a laborer in Xiányáng, Xiāo Hé alone gave him two extra coins as a farewell gift.
In the eleventh year of Hàn,
when Chén Xī rebelled,
Emperor Gāozǔ personally led the army,
reaching Hándān.
Before the campaign ended,
the Marquis of Huáiyīn plotted rebellion in Guānzhōng,
and Empress Lǚ, using Xiāo Hé's strategy,
executed the Marquis of Huáiyīn.
This is recorded in the account of the "Marquis of Huáiyīn."
When the emperor heard of the Marquis of Huáiyīn's execution,
he sent an envoy to appoint Chancellor Hé as Chancellor of State,
increasing his fief by five thousand households,
and assigning five hundred soldiers and a commandant as his guard.
All the officials congratulated him,
but Zhào Píng alone mourned.
Zhào Píng
was the former Eastern Tomb Marquis of Qín.
After Qín's fall,
he became a commoner,
poor, and grew melons east of Cháng'ān city.
His melons were delicious,
so people commonly called them
"Eastern Tomb Melons,"
named after Zhào Píng.
Zhào Píng said to the Chancellor of State:
"Disaster begins here.
The emperor is exposed abroad while you guard the capital,
yet you are not involved in battles but receive more fiefs and guards—
it is because the Marquis of Huáiyīn has just rebelled in the capital,
and the emperor suspects you.
Assigning guards to protect you
is not to honor you.
I hope you will decline the enfeoffment and not accept it,
instead contributing all your family's wealth to support the army,
then the emperor will be pleased."
The Chancellor of State followed his advice,
and Emperor Gāozǔ was greatly delighted.
In the twelfth year of Hàn, in autumn,
Qíng Bù rebelled.
The Emperor personally led troops to attack him,
repeatedly sending messengers to ask the Chancellor what he was doing.
The Chancellor, while the Emperor was at the warfront,
comforted, inspired, and encouraged the common people,
dedicating all available resources to support the army,
as during the time of Chén Xī.
A guest advised the Chancellor, saying,
"Your family will soon face destruction.
You hold the position of Chancellor,
with unmatched merit.
Can anything more be added?
When you first entered Guānzhōng,
you won the people's hearts;
it has been over ten years,
and they all support you.
You have always diligently sought harmony among the people.
The reason the Emperor frequently inquires about you
is that he fears your sway over Guānzhōng.
Why do you not purchase more land now,
offering it at low prices to tarnish your own reputation?
This would put the Emperor at ease."
Thus, the Chancellor followed this advice,
and the Emperor was greatly pleased.
After dispersing the army against Bù,
the Emperor returned, and people blocked his path with petitions,
complaining that the Chancellor had forcefully bought tens of thousands of properties from citizens at low prices.
When the Emperor arrived,
the Chancellor came to pay respects.
The Emperor laughed, saying,
"The Chancellor indeed profits from the people!"
All the petitions from the people were delivered to the Chancellor,
with the remark,
"You should apologize to the people."
The Chancellor thus made a request on behalf of the people, saying,
"The land in Cháng'ān is limited,
yet there is much unused land within Shànglín.
Allow the people to enter and cultivate it,
instead of leaving straw for wild animals to eat."
The Emperor was furious, saying,
"The Chancellor received bribes from merchants
to make requests concerning my park!"
The Chancellor was then handed to the court's officers,
imprisoned, and beaten.
Several days later,
with Wáng the Commandant in attendance,
he stepped forward and asked,
"What great crime has the Chancellor committed,
for Your Majesty to beat him so severely?"
The Emperor replied,
"I heard that Lǐ Sī, Chancellor to the First Emperor of Qín,
took credit for good deeds on behalf of the sovereign,
but took the blame for bad deeds upon himself.
Now, the Chancellor seeks the people's favor by taking gold from merchants
and requesting the use of my park,
so I punish him."
Wáng the Commandant said,
"If a duty benefits the people and he petitions for it,
that is truly the duty of a Chancellor.
Why does Your Majesty doubt the Chancellor for accepting merchant money?
Moreover, during Your Majesty's years against Chǔ,
Chén Xī,
Qíng Bù rebelled,
and Your Majesty personally led the campaign.
At that time,
the Chancellor guarded Guānzhōng;
had he moved his feet, Guānzhōng would not remain under Your Majesty.
The Chancellor did not use this opportunity for gain,
so why would he now covet merchants' gold?
Moreover, the Qín fell because faults were not heard,
and Lǐ Sī's sharing of blame
is not worth emulating.
Why would Your Majesty doubt a Chancellor's integrity?"
The Emperor was not pleased.
That day,
he sent an emissary bearing credentials to pardon the Chancellor and release him.
Although old and ill,
the Chancellor was ever respectful and careful,
entering barefoot to apologize.
The Emperor said,
"Take your rest, Chancellor!
You made the request to benefit the people regarding the park,
but I did not permit it.
I am not worse than the tyrant Jié or Zhòu,
but you are indeed a virtuous Chancellor.
I imprisoned you
to let the people hear of my mistake."
He, habitually at odds with Cáo Shēn,
fell ill,
and when Xiàohuì visited to see the ailing Chancellor,
he asked,
"If you reach a hundred years and pass,
who can succeed you?"
The Chancellor replied,
"No one knows a servant better than his master."
Xiàohuì asked,
"What about Cáo Shēn?"
The Chancellor bowed and said,
"The Emperor has found him!
I will die with no regrets!"
The Chancellor chose to live in an impoverished place, avoiding luxurious homes.
His family neglected ostentatious walls and buildings.
He said,
"If descendants are wise,
they will emulate my frugality;
if not,
they won't be tempted by powerful families."
In the second year of Xiàohuì,
Chancellor Hè passed away,
posthumously titled Wénzhōng Hóu.
Four generations later,
his descendants lost their marquisate due to crime.
The Emperor sought Hè’s descendants
to ennoble them as the Marquis of Càn, unmatched among other meritorious officials.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān says:
Chancellor Xiāo was a minor official under Qín,
undistinguished and lacking special virtues.
When Hàn rose,
under the fading light of the sun and moon,
he prudently maintained control of authority,
utilizing the people's resentment of Qín laws
to aid in founding anew.
Huái Yīn,
Qíng Bù, among others, were executed,
while Hè's accomplishments shone forth.
His position topped all ministers,
his renown lasting through the ages,
rivaling Héngyào
and Sàn Yíshēng in fame.
Cáo Shēn, Marquis of Píngyáng,
was from Pèi.
Under Qín, he served as a petty official in Pèi's prison.
Xiāo Hè was the chief official,
excelling among the county's officials.
When Gāozǔ, as Duke of Pèi, first rose,
Shēn followed as an attendant.
He commanded forces to attack Húlíng
and Fāngyǔ.
They struck Qín's garrison,
greatly defeating them.
Descending east to Xuē,
they attacked Xī near Sìshuǐ's defending army.
They attacked Húlíng again,
capturing it.
He was reassigned to guard Fāngyǔ.
When Fāngyǔ turned to Wèi,
he attacked it.
When Fēng turned to Wèi,
he attacked it.
He was granted the rank of Seven Grand Nobles.
Upon striking Qín's Sīmǎ 𡰥's army east of Táng,
they defeated them,
capturing Táng,
Húfù,
and Qíshàn Zhī places.
He again attacked west of Xiàyì,
reaching Yú,
striking Zhānghán's cavalry.
They attacked Yuánqì and Kàngfù,
being the first to scale the walls.
He was promoted to the rank of five nobles.
Heading north to relieve Ā,
they struck Zhānghán's army,
breaking through their lines,
pursuing them to Púyáng.
They attacked Dìngtáo,
capturing Línjì.
Heading south to relieve Yōngqiū,
they struck Lǐ Yóu's army,
defeating them,
killing Lǐ Yóu,
capturing a Qín marquis.
When Qín's General Zhāng Hán defeated and killed Xiàng Liáng,
Duke of Pèi and Xiàng Yǔ withdrew east.
The King of Chǔ appointed Duke of Pèi as governor of Táng county,
commanding their troops.
Shēn was then honored with the title Zhíbǔ and
named Jiànchéng Lord.
Promoted to be Qī Gōng,
he served Táng county.
Thereafter, he followed in attacking the army of the Governor of Dōngjùn,
defeating them south of Chéngwǔ.
He engaged Wáng Lí's army south of Chéngyáng,
attacked them again at Gānglǐ,
and inflicted a major defeat.
Pursuing the fleeing forces,
he advanced west to Kāifēng,
engaged Zhào Bēn's army,
defeated it,
and besieged Zhào Bēn within the city of Kāifēng.
Westward, he attacked the Qín general Yáng Xióng's army at Qūyù,
defeated it,
and captured a Qín commander and a censor each.
He was promoted to Zhíguī.
Following in the attack on Yángwǔ,
he captured Huányuán,
Gōushì,
cut off the river crossing,
turned back to attack Zhào Bēn's army north of Shī,
and defeated it.
Advancing south to attack Chōu,
he battled the Nányáng Governor Yǐ east of Yángchéng's outer walls,
broke through their formations,
captured Wǎn,
took Yǐ captive,
and fully pacified Nányáng Commandery.
Advancing west to attack Wǔguān,
Yáoguān,
he captured them.
Pressing forward to attack the Qín army south of Lántián,
and again attacking their northern flank at night,
the Qín forces were heavily defeated,
leading to their advance to Xiányáng,
and the destruction of Qín.
When Xiàng Yǔ arrived,
he made the Pèi Lord the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn enfeoffed Cān as the Marquis of Jiànchéng.
Following him to Hànzhōng,
he was promoted to general.
He followed in the campaign to pacify the Three Qín,
initially capturing Xiàbiàn,
Gùdào,
Yōng, and Tái.
He engaged Zhāng Píng's army south of Hǎozhì,
defeated it,
besieged Hǎozhì,
and captured Rǎngxiāng.
Attacking the Three Qín armies east of Rǎng and at Gāolì,
he defeated them.
Again besieging Zhāng Píng,
Zhāng Píng fled Hǎozhì.
Thereupon, he attacked the armies of Zhào Bēn
and the Neishi Bǎo,
defeating them.
Eastward, he captured Xiányáng,
renaming it Xīnchéng.
Cān led troops in defending Jǐnglíng for twenty days,
the Three Qín sent Zhāng Píng and others to attack Cān,
Cān launched a counterattack,
and heavily defeated them.
He was granted a fief at Níngqín.
Cān, as a general, led troops to besiege Zhāng Hán at Fèiqiū.
As Zhōngwèi, he followed the King of Hàn out of Línjìn Pass.
Reaching Hénèi,
capturing Xiūwǔ,
crossing Wéijīn,
he attacked Lóng Qiě
and Xiàng Tuō east at Dìngtáo,
defeating them.
Eastward, he captured Dàng,
Xiāo, and Péngchéng.
Engaging Xiàng Jí's army,
the Hàn army was heavily defeated and fled.
Cān, as Zhōngwèi, besieged and captured Yōngqiū.
Wáng Wǔ rebelled at Wàihuáng,
Chéng Chǔ rebelled at Yān,
Cān went to attack them,
and completely defeated them.
Zhùtiānhóu rebelled at Yǎnshì,
and he advanced to defeat and capture Yǎnshì.
He attacked Yǔ Yīng at Kūnyáng,
pursuing him to Shè.
Returning to attack Wǔqiáng,
he thus reached Yíngyáng.
Cān, from Hànzhōng as a general and Zhōngwèi,
followed in attacking the various nobles,
and after Xiàng Yǔ's defeat,
returned to Yíngyáng,
a total of two years.
In the second year of Emperor Gāozǔ,
he was appointed Acting Left Chancellor,
and entered to station troops in Guānzhōng.
After over a month,
the King of Wèi, Bào, rebelled,
and as Acting Left Chancellor, separately with Hán Xìn, he attacked east the Wèi general Sūn Sù's army at Dōngzhāng,
heavily defeating them.
Thereupon attacking Ānyì,
he captured the Wèi general Wáng Xiāng.
Attacking the King of Wèi at Qūyáng,
pursuing him to Wǔyuán,
he captured the King of Wèi, Bào, alive.
Capturing Píngyáng,
he seized the King of Wèi's mother, wife, and children,
fully pacifying the land of Wèi,
a total of fifty-two cities.
He was granted a fief at Píngyáng.
Thereupon, following Hán Xìn, he attacked the army of Wèi's Chancellor of State Xià Yuè east of Wū,
heavily defeating them,
and beheading Xià Yuè.
Hán Xìn and the former King of Chángshān Zhāng Ěr led troops down Jǐngxíng,
attacking Chéng'ānjūn,
while ordering Cān to return and besiege Wèi's deputy general Qī in the city of Wū.
General Qī fled,
was pursued and beheaded.
Then he led troops to the Áocāng where the King of Hàn was.
After Hán Xìn had defeated Wèi,
he became Chancellor of State,
and attacked east against Qí.
Cān, as Right Chancellor, was attached to Hán Xìn,
attacked and defeated the Qí army at Lìxià,
and thus captured Línzī.
Returning to pacify Jǐběi Commandery,
he attacked Zhù,
Tàiyīn,
Píngyuán,
Gé, and Lú.
Subsequently, following Hán Xìn, he attacked Lóng Qiě's army at Shàngjiǎmì,
heavily defeating them,
beheading Lóng Qiě,
and capturing his general Zhōu Lán.
Pacifying Qí,
he captured over seventy counties in total.
He captured the former King of Qí Tián Guǎng's chancellor Tián Guāng,
the defending chancellor Xǔ Zhāng,
and the former Qí Jiāodōng general Tián Jì.
Hán Xìn became the King of Qí,
led troops to Chén,
and together with the King of Hàn defeated Xiàng Yǔ,
while Cān remained to pacify the unsubdued in Qí.
After Xiàng Jí's death,
and the empire was settled,
the King of Hàn became emperor,
Hán Xìn was moved to be King of Chǔ,
and Qí became a commandery.
Cān returned the seal of Hàn's Chancellor.
Emperor Gāozǔ appointed his eldest son Féi as King of Qí,
and made Cān Chancellor of State of Qí.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāozǔ, he was granted the rank of Marquis,
and with the other nobles, received a split tally,
to be hereditary without end.
His fief at Píngyáng comprised ten thousand six hundred and thirty households,
and he was titled Marquis of Píngyáng,
superseding his previous fief.
As Chancellor of State of Qí, he attacked Chén Xī's general Zhāng Chūn's army,
and defeated it.
Qíng Bù rebelled,
Cān, as Chancellor of State of Qí, followed King Dàohuì in commanding 120,000 troops and chariots,
and joining Emperor Gāozǔ, attacked Qíng Bù's army,
heavily defeating it.
Advancing south to Qí,
returning to pacify Zhúyì,
Xiàng, Xiāo,
and Liú.
Cān's achievements:
in total, he subdued two states,
and 122 counties;
captured two kings,
three chancellors,
six generals,
one Grand Mò'áo,
one commandery governor,
one commander,
one marquis, and one censor each.
In the first year of Emperor Huì's reign,
he abolished the law regarding the state chancellors of feudal lords,
and instead appointed Cáo Shēn as the Chancellor of Qí.
When Cáo Shēn served as Chancellor of Qí,
Qí possessed seventy cities.
The empire was newly stabilized,
and King Dàohuì was in the prime of his youth.
Cáo Shēn summoned all the elders and scholars,
inquiring how to pacify and gather the common people.
Numerous Confucian scholars of Qí,
each expressed differing opinions,
and Cáo Shēn was uncertain which to adopt.
Hearing that in Jiāoxī there was a Gě Gōng,
who was well-versed in the teachings of Huáng-Lǎo,
he sent an envoy with generous gifts to invite him.
After meeting Gě Gōng,
Gě Gōng told him that the way of governance values clarity and tranquility, then the people will naturally stabilize,
and elaborated on this principle in detail.
Cáo Shēn then vacated the main hall,
and provided lodging for Gě Gōng there.
His governance primarily employed the techniques of Huáng-Lǎo,
thus, during his nine years as Chancellor of Qí,
the state of Qí was peaceful and well-ordered,
and he was widely praised as a worthy chancellor.
In the second year of Emperor Huì's reign,
Xiāo Hé passed away.
Upon hearing this, Cáo Shēn
told his steward to quickly prepare for travel,
saying, "I am going to become the state chancellor."
Not long after,
an envoy indeed came to summon Cáo Shēn.
As Cáo Shēn departed,
he instructed his successor as chancellor, saying:
"I entrust to you the legal and market affairs of Qí;
be careful not to disturb them."
The successor chancellor asked:
"Is there nothing greater in governance than this?"
Cáo Shēn replied:
"Not so.
The legal and market systems
are means to accommodate all.
If you disturb them now,
where will the unscrupulous find their place?
This is why I mention it first."
In his humble beginnings,
Cáo Shēn was on good terms with Xiāo Hé;
but when they became general and chancellor,
a rift developed between them.
Yet, as Xiāo Hé was nearing death,
the only worthy he recommended was Cáo Shēn.
Cáo Shēn succeeded Xiāo Hé as Chancellor of Hàn,
and in all matters, he made no changes,
strictly adhering to Xiāo Hé's established rules.
He selected officials from the commanderies and feudal states who were质朴不善文辞,
honest and稳重 elders,
and appointed them as his administrative officers.
Those among the officials who were eloquent,苛刻,
or sought fame and reputation,
he invariably dismissed.
He drank strong wine day and night.
When the high officials, subordinates, and宾客 saw that Cáo Shēn attended to no duties,
those who came all wished to speak their minds.
Upon their arrival,
Cáo Shēn would invariably offer them strong wine to drink.
During the interval,
if they attempted to speak,
he would again have them drink,
until they were drunk and departed,
never managing to broach their intended topics.
This became the常态.
The garden behind the chancellor's residence was near the officials' quarters,
where the officials drank and sang loudly every day.
His attendants disliked this,
but could do nothing about it,
so they invited Cáo Shēn to stroll in the garden,
hoping he would hear the officials' drunken singing and shouting,
and expect the chancellor to summon and reprimand them.
Instead, he fetched wine, set up mats, and drank with them,
singing and shouting in response.
When Cáo Shēn noticed people's minor faults,
he deliberately concealed and covered them up,
so there was no trouble in his administration.
Cáo Shēn's son, Cáo Zhú, served as a Grand Master of the Palace.
Emperor Huì found it strange that the chancellor handled no affairs,
and thought
"Is it because he looks down on me?"
So he said to Cáo Zhú:
"When you return home,
try to privately and casually ask your father:
'The Late Emperor has newly left his ministers,
and the Emperor is young,
yet you, as chancellor,
drink daily
and attend to no matters of state.
How can you not worry about the empire?'
But do not let on that I told you to say this."
When Cáo Zhú had his leave and returned home,
he found a moment while attending his father,
and from his own initiative advised Cáo Shēn.
Cáo Shēn grew angry,
and caned Cáo Zhú two hundred strokes,
saying:
"Hurry back to attend at court;
matters of the empire are not for you to speak of."
At the next court session,
Emperor Huì reproached Cáo Shēn, saying:
"Why did you punish Cáo Zhú?
It was I who had him advise you."
Cáo Shēn removed his official cap and apologized, saying:
"Your Majesty, consider for yourself: how do you compare in sagehood and martial prowess to the Late Emperor?"
The Emperor said:
"How dare I aspire to match the Late Emperor!"
Cáo Shēn said:
"Your Majesty, observe my abilities: how do I compare to Xiāo Hé in worthiness?"
The Emperor said:
"You seem not to equal him."
Cáo Shēn said:
"Your Majesty is right in saying so.
Moreover, the Late Emperor and Xiāo Hé settled the empire,
the laws and decrees are already clear.
Now if Your Majesty rules with ease,
and we, like Cáo Shēn, keep to our duties,
adhering to them without fail,
would that not be sufficient?"
Emperor Huì said:
"Good.
You may rest now!"
Cáo Shēn served as Chancellor of Hàn
for three years.
Upon his death, he was posthumously titled the Yì Marquis.
His son, Cáo Zhú, succeeded to the marquisate.
The common people sang of him:
"Xiāo Hé made the laws,
clear and uniform as one;
Cáo Shēn succeeded him,
guarding them without loss.
By his purity and tranquility,
the people found peace and unity."
The Píngyáng Marquis, Cáo Zhú,
served as Imperial Secretary under Empress Dowager Lǚ.
When Emperor Wén of Hàn ascended the throne,
he was dismissed to his marquisate.
He held the title for twenty-nine years until his death,
and was posthumously titled the Jìng Marquis.
His son, Cáo Qí, succeeded to the marquisate,
held it for seven years until his death,
and was posthumously titled the Jiǎn Marquis.
His son, Cáo Shí, succeeded to the marquisate.
Cáo Shí married the Princess of Píngyáng,
and they had a son, Cáo Xiāng.
Cáo Shí fell ill with a severe disease,
and returned to his fief.
He died in the twenty-third year of Emperor Wén's reign,
and was posthumously titled the Yí Marquis.
His son, Cáo Xiāng, succeeded to the marquisate.
Cáo Xiāng married the Elder Princess of Wèi,
and they had a son, Cáo Zōng.
He held the title for sixteen years until his death,
and was posthumously titled the Gòng Marquis.
His son, Cáo Zōng, succeeded to the marquisate.
In the second year of the Zhēnghé era,
Cáo Zōng was implicated in the Crown Prince's affair and died,
and the marquisate was abolished.
The Grand Historian remarks:
The reason Chancellor Cáo Shēn could achieve so many merits in攻城野战
was because he served alongside the Huáiyīn Marquis.
After Hán Xìn was destroyed,
and the various marquises accomplished their deeds,
Cáo Shēn alone claimed the fame.
As Chancellor of Hàn,
his advocacy of purity and tranquility was in accord with the Way.
And as the people had suffered under Qín's cruelty,
Cáo Shēn's policies of rest and non-action
led the entire empire to praise his excellence.
Marquis of Liǔ, Zhāng Liáng,
his ancestors were from Hán.
His grandfather Kāidì
served as chancellor to Hán Zhāohóu,
Xuānhuì Wáng,
and Xiāng'āi Wáng.
His father Píng
served as chancellor to Xī Wáng
and Dàohuì Wáng.
In the twenty-third year of Dàohuì Wáng's reign,
Píng died.
Twenty years after his death,
Qín destroyed Hán.
Liáng was young at the time,
and had not yet served Hán in office.
After Hán was defeated,
though Liáng's family had three hundred servants,
when his younger brother died, he did not bury him,
but used all the family's wealth to seek an assassin to strike the King of Qín,
to avenge Hán,
because his grandfather
and father had served as chancellors to Hán for five generations.
Liáng once studied rites in Huáiyáng.
He traveled east to meet Cāng Hǎi Jūn.
There he found a strong man,
and made an iron hammer weighing one hundred twenty catties.
When the Qín emperor traveled east,
Liáng and the assassin ambushed the Qín emperor at Bólàngshā,
but mistakenly hit the attendant's carriage.
The Qín emperor was furious,
and ordered a great search throughout the land,
urgently seeking the culprit,
all because of Zhāng Liáng.
Liáng then changed his name,
and went into hiding in Xiàpī.
Liáng once was leisurely strolling on the bridge at Xiàpī,
when an old man appeared,
dressed in coarse cloth,
came to where Liáng was,
and deliberately dropped his shoe under the bridge,
then turned to Liáng and said:
"Young man,
go down and fetch my shoe!"
Liáng was startled,
and wanted to hit him.
But because the man was old,
he restrained himself,
went down, and fetched the shoe.
The old man said:
"Put it on for me!"
Since Liáng had already fetched the shoe,
he knelt and put it on for him.
The old man extended his foot to receive it,
then laughed and left.
Liáng was greatly astonished,
and followed him with his eyes.
After the old man had gone about a li,
he returned,
and said:
"You are worth teaching, young man.
Five days from now at daybreak,
meet me here."
Liáng, finding this strange,
knelt and said:
"Yes."
Five days later at daybreak,
Liáng went.
The old man was already there first,
and angrily said:
"When meeting an elder,
why are you late?"
He left, saying:
"Meet again early five days from now."
Five days later at cockcrow,
Liáng went.
The old man was again there first,
and again angrily said:
"Late again,
why?"
He left, saying:
"Come early again five days from now."
Five days later,
Liáng went before midnight.
After a while,
the old man also came,
and happily said:
"It should be like this."
He brought out a book,
and said:
"Read this, and you will be a teacher to kings.
Ten years from now, you will rise.
Thirteen years from now, young man, you will see me north of the Jì River,
the yellow stone at the foot of Gǔchéng Mountain is me."
Then he left,
without another word,
and was never seen again.
The next day, Liáng looked at the book,
and it was the "Grand Duke's Art of War."
Liáng thus considered it extraordinary,
and often studied and recited it.
While living in Xiàpī,
he acted as a chivalrous avenger.
Xiàng Bó had once killed someone,
and followed Liáng into hiding.
Ten years later,
when Chén Shè and others raised armies,
Liáng also gathered over a hundred young men.
Jǐng Jū had declared himself Acting King of Chǔ,
and was in Liǔ.
Liáng intended to join him,
but on the way met the Lord of Pèi.
The Lord of Pèi was leading several thousand men,
conquering territories west of Xiàpī,
so Liáng joined him.
The Lord of Pèi appointed Liáng as a cavalry officer.
Liáng several times explained the "Grand Duke's Art of War" to the Lord of Pèi,
who appreciated it,
and often used his strategies.
When Liáng spoke to others about it,
none understood.
Liáng said:
"The Lord of Pèi is perhaps heaven-sent."
So he followed him,
and did not go to see Jǐng Jū.
When the Lord of Pèi went to Xuē,
he met Xiàng Liáng.
Xiàng Liáng established King Huáiwáng of Chǔ.
Liáng then advised Xiàng Liáng, saying:
"You have already established a descendant of Chǔ,
and among the princes of Hán, Héngyáng Jūn Chéng is worthy,
he could be made king,
to increase our allies."
Xiàng Liáng sent Liáng to find Hán Chéng,
and established him as King of Hán.
He appointed Liáng as Shēntú of Hán,
and with the King of Hán, he led over a thousand men westward to conquer Hán territories,
capturing several cities,
but Qín repeatedly recaptured them,
so they moved about as guerrilla forces in Yǐngchuān.
When the Lord of Pèi went south from Luòyáng through Huányuán,
Liáng led troops to follow the Lord of Pèi,
captured over ten cities of Hán,
and defeated Yáng Xióng's army.
The Lord of Pèi then ordered King Chéng of Hán to remain guarding Yángdí,
and went south with Liáng,
captured Wǎn,
and entered Wǔguān from the west.
The Lord of Pèi intended to attack the Qín army below Yáo with twenty thousand troops,
but Liáng advised:
"The Qín army is still strong,
we cannot take them lightly.
I have heard their general is a butcher's son,
and such merchants are easily moved by profit.
I hope you will temporarily remain in camp,
send men ahead,
prepare food for fifty thousand people,
and set up more banners on the mountains,
as a deceptive force,
then have Lì Yìjī take valuable treasures to bribe the Qín general."
The Qín general indeed rebelled,
and wanted to join forces and march west together to attack Xiányáng,
and the Lord of Pèi intended to agree.
Liáng said:
"This is only the general wanting to rebel,
I fear the soldiers may not follow.
If they do not follow, it will be dangerous,
it would be better to take advantage of their laxness and attack them."
The Lord of Pèi then led troops to attack the Qín army,
and heavily defeated them.
They pursued the fleeing army to Lántián,
fought again,
and the Qín troops were ultimately defeated.
Then they reached Xiányáng,
and Zǐyīng, the King of Qín, surrendered to the Lord of Pèi.
The Lord of Pei entered the Qin palace,
where palaces, tents, hounds, horses, precious treasures, and women numbered in the thousands,
and he intended to stay and reside there.
Fán Kuài advised the Lord of Pei to leave and lodge elsewhere,
but the Lord of Pei would not listen.
Liáng said:
"It is because the Qin was without virtue
that you, Lord of Pei, have been able to come here.
To rid the world of cruel bandits,
one should rely on simplicity and austerity.
Now, upon first entering Qin,
if you immediately indulge in its pleasures,
this is what is called
'aiding Jié in his tyranny.'
Moreover,
'loyal advice may grate on the ears but benefits conduct;
bitter medicine may distress the mouth but cures illness.'
I hope you will heed Fán Kuài's words."
The Lord of Pei then withdrew his army to Bàshàng.
When Xiàng Yǔ arrived at Hóngmén,
he intended to attack the Lord of Pei.
Xiàng Bó then rode by night into the Lord of Pei's camp,
privately met with Zhāng Liáng,
and wanted to take him away.
Liáng said:
"I am here to escort the Lord of Pei on behalf of the King of Hán;
now that there is an emergency,
to flee would be unjust."
He then fully informed the Lord of Pei.
The Lord of Pei was greatly alarmed,
and said:
"What should I do?"
Liáng said:
"Do you truly wish to oppose Xiàng Yǔ?"
The Lord of Pei said:
"A petty man advised me to guard the pass and not admit the other nobles,
so that I could rule all of Qin,
and thus I listened."
Liáng said:
"Do you assess that you can repel Xiàng Yǔ?"
The Lord of Pei was silent for a long while,
then said:
"Certainly not.
What should I do now?"
Liáng then firmly invited Xiàng Bó.
Xiàng Bó met with the Lord of Pei.
The Lord of Pei drank with him and offered a toast,
forming a bond of friendship and marriage.
He had Xiàng Bó fully explain that the Lord of Pei did not dare oppose Xiàng Yǔ,
and that the reason for guarding the pass
was to prepare against other bandits.
When he later met Xiàng Yǔ, the situation was resolved;
the details are recorded in the account of Xiàng Yǔ.
In the first month of the first year of Hàn,
the Lord of Pei became the King of Hàn,
ruling over Bā and Shǔ.
The King of Hàn bestowed upon Liáng a hundred yì of gold
and two dǒu of pearls,
which Liáng presented in full to Xiàng Bó.
The King of Hàn also ordered Liáng to generously gift Xiàng Bó,
asking him to request the land of Hànzhōng.
The King of Xiàng then agreed,
and thus they obtained the land of Hànzhōng.
When the King of Hàn went to his state,
Liáng escorted him to Bāozhōng,
and was then sent back to Hán.
Liáng thereupon advised the King of Hàn, saying:
"Why not burn the plank roads you have passed,
to show the world you have no intention of returning,
and thus secure the King of Xiàng's confidence?"
He then sent Liáng back.
As they traveled, they burned and destroyed the plank roads.
When Liáng reached Hán,
because King Chéng of Hán had allowed Liáng to follow the King of Hàn,
the King of Xiàng did not send Chéng to his state,
but took him east.
Liáng said to the King of Xiàng:
"The King of Hàn has burned the plank roads,
and has no intention of returning."
Then, because the King of Qí, Tián Róng, had rebelled,
he sent a letter to inform the King of Xiàng.
The King of Xiàng, therefore, had no concern about Hàn in the west,
and sent troops north to attack Qí.
The King of Xiàng ultimately refused to send the King of Hán,
instead making him a marquis,
and later killed him in Péngchéng.
Liáng fled,
and traveled in secret to rejoin the King of Hàn,
by which time the King of Hàn had already returned and pacified the Three Qín.
He again appointed Liáng as Marquis of Chéngxìn,
and Liáng followed him east to attack Chǔ.
When they reached Péngchéng,
Hàn was defeated and withdrew.
At Xiàyì,
the King of Hàn dismounted, leaned on his saddle, and asked:
"I wish to cede the lands east of the pass;
who can share in this endeavor with me?"
Liáng stepped forward and said:
"The King of Jiǔjiāng, Qíng Bù,
a fierce general of Chǔ,
has a rift with the King of Xiàng;
Péng Yuè, together with the King of Qí Tián Róng, rebelled in Liáng:
these two can be urgently employed.
And among your generals, only Hán Xìn can be entrusted with great matters,
and hold his own front.
If you wish to cede territory,
cede it to these three,
and then Chǔ can be defeated."
The King of Hàn then sent Suí Hé to persuade the King of Jiǔjiāng, Bù,
and sent others to ally with Péng Yuè.
When the King of Wèi, Bào, rebelled,
he had Hán Xìn lead troops to attack him,
thereby conquering Yān,
Dài, Qí,
and Zhào. Yet, in the end, it was the strength of these three men
that defeated Chǔ.
Zhāng Liáng was often ill,
and never led troops independently,
but always served as a strategist,
frequently accompanying the King of Hàn.
In the third year of Hàn,
Xiàng Yǔ urgently besieged the King of Hàn at Yíngyáng,
and the King of Hàn was fearful and worried,
so he consulted Lì Yìjī on how to weaken Chǔ's power.
Yìjī said:
"In ancient times, when Tāng attacked Jié,
he enfeoffed his descendants in Qǐ.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he enfeoffed his descendants in Sòng.
Now Qín has lost virtue and abandoned righteousness,
invading and attacking the states of the nobles,
extinguishing the descendants of the six states,
leaving them not even a pinpoint of land.
If Your Majesty can truly reestablish the descendants of the six states,
and once they have all received their seals,
their rulers, ministers, and common people will surely revere Your Majesty's virtue,
all turning to admire your righteousness,
and willing to become your subjects.
Once virtue and righteousness are practiced,
Your Majesty may face south and claim hegemony,
and Chǔ will surely tidy its garments and come to court."
The King of Hàn said:
"Excellent.
Hasten to carve the seals,
and you, sir, shall take them and bestow them."
Shíjī had not yet departed,
when Zhāng Liáng came from outside to pay his respects.
The King of Hàn was just eating,
and said:
"Zǐfáng, come forward!
A guest has proposed a plan for me to weaken Chǔ's power."
He then relayed Lìshēng's words in full,
and asked:
"What do you think, Zǐfáng?"
Liáng said:
"Who devised this plan for Your Majesty?
Your Majesty's cause is lost."
The King of Hàn said:
"Why so?"
Zhāng Liáng replied:
"I beg to borrow your chopsticks to strategize for you, Great King."
He then said:
"In the past, when Tāng attacked Jié and enfeoffed his descendants in Qǐ,
it was because he could control Jié's fate.
Can Your Majesty now control Xiàng Jí's fate?"
The King said:
"I cannot."
"That is the first impossibility.
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu and enfeoffed his descendants in Sòng,
it was because he could obtain Zhòu's head.
Can Your Majesty obtain Xiàng Jí's head?"
The King said:
"I cannot."
"That is the second impossibility.
When King Wǔ entered Yīn,
he honored Shāng Róng's neighborhood,
released Jīzǐ from confinement,
and built a tomb for Bǐgān.
Can Your Majesty now build tombs for sages,
honor the neighborhoods of worthies,
and pay respects at the gates of the wise?"
The King said:
"I cannot."
"That is the third impossibility.
Distributing the grain from Jùqiáo,
scattering the money from Lùtái,
to bestow upon the poor.
Can Your Majesty now scatter the treasury to bestow upon the poor?"
The King said:
"I cannot."
"That is the fourth impossibility.
After the affairs of Yīn were concluded,
war chariots were converted into carriages,
weapons were inverted,
covered with tiger skins,
to show the world that arms would no longer be used.
Can Your Majesty now abandon warfare and practice civility,
never to use arms again?"
The King said:
"I cannot."
"That is the fifth impossibility.
Resting horses on the sunny side of Huàshān,
to show they are no longer needed.
Can Your Majesty now rest horses with no further use for them?"
The King said:
"I cannot."
"That is the sixth impossibility.
Releasing oxen in the shade of Táolín,
to show that supplies will no longer be transported.
Can Your Majesty now release oxen and no longer transport supplies?"
The King said:
"I cannot."
"That is the seventh impossibility.
Moreover, the wandering scholars of the world left their relatives,
abandoned their ancestral graves,
departed from old friends,
to follow Your Majesty,
solely hoping day and night for a small piece of land.
Now if the six states are restored,
establishing the descendants of Hán,
Wèi, Yān,
Zhào, Qí,
and Chǔ,
the wandering scholars of the world will each return to serve their own lords,
follow their relatives,
and return to their old friends and ancestral graves;
with whom will Your Majesty conquer the world?
That is the eighth impossibility.
Furthermore, if only Chǔ remains unweakened,
and the six states, once established, are subjugated and follow Chǔ,
how can Your Majesty make them your subjects?
If this guest's plan is truly adopted,
Your Majesty's cause is lost."
The King of Hàn stopped eating and spat out his food,
cursing:
"That pedantic scholar,
nearly ruined your lord's affairs!"
He ordered the immediate destruction of the seals.
In the fourth year of Hàn,
when Hán Xìn defeated Qí and wished to proclaim himself King of Qí,
the King of Hàn was furious.
Zhāng Liáng persuaded the King of Hàn,
who then sent Liáng to bestow upon Hán Xìn the seal of King of Qí,
as recorded in the affairs of Huáiyīn.
That autumn,
the King of Hàn pursued Chǔ to the south of Yángxià,
but the battle was unfavorable, so he fortified Gùlíng,
and the allied lords failed to arrive as scheduled.
Liáng advised the King of Hàn,
who employed his strategy,
and the allied lords all arrived.
This is recorded in the affairs of Xiàng Jí.
In the first month of the sixth year of Hàn,
meritorious officials were enfeoffed.
Liáng had never achieved any combat merits,
but the High Emperor said:
"Formulating strategies within the tent,
deciding victory a thousand miles away,
is the merit of Zǐfáng.
Choose for yourself thirty thousand households in Qí."
Liáng said:
"When I first rose in Xiàpī,
and met with Your Highness in Liú,
it was Heaven that delivered me to Your Majesty.
Your Majesty employed my strategies,
and fortunately they occasionally succeeded;
I would be content to be enfeoffed in Liú,
and dare not accept thirty thousand households."
Thus, Zhāng Liáng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Liú,
along with Xiāo Hé and others.
The Emperor had already enfeoffed over twenty great meritorious officials,
but the rest argued day and night over their merits without resolution,
and no further enfeoffments were carried out.
The Emperor, in the Southern Palace of Luòyáng,
saw from an elevated passageway the generals often sitting together on the sand, conversing.
The Emperor asked:
"What are they discussing?"
The Marquis of Liú said:
"Does Your Majesty not know?
They are plotting rebellion."
The Emperor said:
"The world is newly stabilized;
why would they rebel?"
The Marquis of Liú said:
"Your Majesty rose from commoner status,
and with these men conquered the world.
Now that Your Majesty is the Son of Heaven,
those enfeoffed are all old acquaintances and favorites of Xiāo
and Cáo,
while those executed are all lifelong enemies.
Now the military officers calculate merits,
and find the world insufficient for universal enfeoffment;
these men fear that Your Majesty cannot enfeoff them all,
and worry that they may be suspected of past faults and executed,
hence they gather to plot rebellion."
The Emperor then worriedly said:
"What should be done about it?"
The Marquis of Liú said:
"Among those Your Highness has always disliked,
whom all officials know of,
who is the most extreme?"
The Emperor said:
"Yōngchǐ and I have a past;
he repeatedly humiliated me.
I wished to kill him,
but because of his many merits,
I could not bring myself to do it."
The Marquis of Liú said:
"Now urgently enfeoff Yōngchǐ first to show the officials;
when they see Yōngchǐ enfeoffed,
then everyone will feel assured."
Thereupon, the Emperor held a banquet,
enfeoffed Yōngchǐ as the Marquis of Shífāng,
and urgently pressed the Chancellor
and the Censor to determine merits and carry out enfeoffments.
After the banquet concluded,
all the officials joyfully said:
"Even Yōngchǐ was made a Marquis;
we have nothing to fear."
Liú Jìng advised Emperor Gāo, saying:
"Establish the capital in Guānzhōng."
The Emperor was hesitant.
The ministers around him were all from Shāndōng,
and most urged him to establish the capital in Luòyáng:
"Luòyáng has Chénggāo to the east,
Xiáo Miǎn to the west,
backs the Yellow River,
and faces the Yī and Luò rivers;
its natural defenses are sufficient to rely on."
Liú Hóu said:
"Although Luòyáng has these defenses,
its area is small,
not exceeding a few hundred lǐ,
the land is poor,
and it is vulnerable to attack from all sides;
this is not a state for military operations.
Now Guānzhōng has Xiáo and Hán to the left,
Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
fertile fields stretching a thousand lǐ,
the abundance of Bā and Shǔ to the south,
the benefits of the Hú pastures to the north,
guarded by natural barriers on three sides,
controlling the feudal lords to the east from one side alone.
When the feudal lords are at peace,
the Yellow River and Wèi River can transport supplies from across the land,
supplying the capital from the west;
if the feudal lords rebel,
we can sail downriver,
ensuring adequate transport.
This is what is called a 'golden city of a thousand lǐ,'
the land of abundance,
and Liú Jìng's advice is correct."
Thereupon, Emperor Gāo set out that very day,
and established the capital in Guānzhōng to the west.
Liú Hóu accompanied him into the pass.
Liú Hóu was often ill by nature,
practicing daoyin and abstaining from grains,
he secluded himself and did not go out for over a year.
The Emperor wanted to depose the Crown Prince,
and establish Rúyì, the son of Lady Qī, as the King of Zhào.
Many ministers remonstrated and argued against it,
but none could firmly resolve the matter.
Empress Lǚ was fearful,
and did not know what to do.
Someone said to Empress Lǚ:
"Liú Hóu is skilled at devising strategies,
and the Emperor trusts and employs him."
Empress Lǚ then sent Lǚ Zé, the Marquis of Jiànchéng, to compel Liú Hóu,
saying:
"You have always been the Emperor's strategist,
now the Emperor wishes to change the Crown Prince,
how can you rest easy on your high pillow?"
Liú Hóu said:
"Initially, the Emperor was often in dire straits,
and fortunately used my strategies.
Now the empire is at peace,
and out of affection he wishes to change the Crown Prince,
this is a matter between flesh and blood,
what use would even over a hundred of us be?"
Lǚ Zé insisted, saying:
"Devise a plan for me."
Liú Hóu said:
"This is difficult to argue with words.
