However, there are those the Emperor cannot summon,
four men in the empire.
These four men are old,
and all believe the Emperor insults others arrogantly,
so they fled and hid in the mountains,
refusing on principle to be ministers of Hàn.
Yet the Emperor holds these four in high esteem.
If you can spare no expense in gold, jade, silks, and satins,
have the Crown Prince write a letter,
with humble words and a comfortable carriage,
and send a persuasive envoy to firmly invite them,
they should come.
Once they come, treat them as guests,
and have them accompany him to court from time to time,
letting the Emperor see them,
he will surely be intrigued and ask about them.
When he asks,
and the Emperor learns these four are worthy,
that will be a help."
Thereupon, Empress Lǚ ordered Lǚ Zé to send someone with the Crown Prince's letter,
with humble words and generous gifts,
to welcome these four men.
The four men arrived,
and stayed as guests at the Marquis of Jiànchéng's residence.
In the eleventh year of Hàn,
Qíng Bù rebelled,
the Emperor was ill,
and wanted to send the Crown Prince as general,
to lead the attack against him.
The four men said to each other:
"Our purpose in coming
is to preserve the Crown Prince.
If the Crown Prince leads the troops,
the situation is perilous."
They then advised the Marquis of Jiànchéng, saying:
"If the Crown Prince leads the troops,
success will not enhance his position;
if he returns without success,
he will suffer disaster from then on.
Moreover, the generals accompanying the Crown Prince
are all veteran commanders who once pacified the empire with the Emperor,
now to have the Crown Prince lead them
is no different from setting a sheep to lead wolves;
they will not be willing to exert their full efforts,
and his failure is certain.
We have heard
'the child of a beloved mother is held,'
now Lady Qī serves day and night,
and the King of Zhào, Rúyì, is often held in front,
the Emperor says
'I will never let an unworthy son be above a beloved son,'
clearly indicating he will surely replace the Crown Prince.
Why not urgently request Empress Lǚ to seize an opportunity and weepfully tell the Emperor:
'Qíng Bù
is a fierce general of the empire,
skilled in warfare,
and the current generals are all Your Majesty's old peers,
to have the Crown Prince lead these men
is no different from setting a sheep to lead wolves,
none will obey orders,
and if Bù hears of it,
he will march westward unimpeded.
Though Your Majesty is ill,
force yourself into a carriage,
lie down and command,
and the generals will not dare not exert their full efforts.
Though Your Majesty suffers,
do it for your wife and son and push yourself.'"
Thereupon, Lǚ Zé immediately went at night to see Empress Lǚ,
who seized an opportunity to weepfully speak to the Emperor,
as the four men intended.
The Emperor said:
"I thought that boy was not fit to send,
so I shall go myself."
Thereupon, the Emperor personally led the troops east,
with the ministers remaining to guard the capital,
all seeing him off to Bàshàng.
Liú Hóu was ill,
but forced himself to rise,
and went to Qūyóu,
where he saw the Emperor and said:
"I should accompany you,
but I am gravely ill.
The Chǔ people are swift and fierce,
I hope Your Majesty will not contend with them head-on."
Then he advised the Emperor, saying:
"Appoint the Crown Prince as general,
to oversee the troops in Guānzhōng."
The Emperor said:
"Though Zǐfáng is ill,
force yourself to lie down and assist the Crown Prince."
At that time, Shūsūn Tōng was the Grand Tutor,
and Liú Hóu acted as the Junior Tutor.
In the twelfth year of Hàn,
the Emperor returned from defeating the Bù army.
His illness worsened,
and he increasingly wanted to change the Crown Prince.
Liú Hóu remonstrated,
but he did not listen,
and due to his illness, he did not attend to state affairs.
Shū Sūn the Grand Tutor spoke both ancient and modern,
risking death to defend the Crown Prince.
The Emperor pretended to agree,
yet still desired to change him.
When they reached Yān,
a banquet was set,
and the Crown Prince attended.
Four men accompanied the Crown Prince,
all over eighty,
with white beards and eyebrows,
dressed in grand attire.
The Emperor was surprised,
and asked,
"Who are they?"
The four men stepped forward to reply,
each stating his name and surname,
saying: Dōng Yuán Gōng,
Jiǎo Lǐ Xiānshēng,
Qǐ Lǐ Jì,
Xià Huáng Gōng.
The Emperor was greatly astonished,
and said,
"I sought out the gentlemen for several years,
you evaded and fled from me.
Why do you now follow my son?"
All four replied,
"Your Majesty belittles scholars and has a penchant for scolding.
We refuse to suffer such humiliation out of principle,
hence we feared and hid.
However, we heard the Crown Prince is benevolent and filial,
respectful and loves scholars,
and everyone in the world eagerly wishes to die for him.
Thus, we have come for him."
The Emperor said,
"I request that you kindly guide and protect the Crown Prince."
The four performed rituals for longevity and then
departed quickly.
The Emperor watched them leave,
and summoned Consort Qī to show her these four men, saying
"I wanted to change the Crown Prince,
but those four now support him.
His wings have already formed,
it is difficult to touch him now.
Lǚ Hòu will truly become the ruler."
Consort Qī wept,
and the Emperor said,
"Perform the Chǔ dance for me,
and I will sing a Chǔ song for you."
The song went:
"The swan soars high,
flying a thousand miles in an instant.
Its feathers fully formed,
it spans across the four seas.
Spanning across the four seas,
what can be done about it?
Though arrows and nets may be present,
where indeed can they be placed?"
He sang several verses,
Consort Qī sobbed and wept.
The Emperor got up and left,
ending the banquet.
In the end, he did not change the Crown Prince,
which was due to the influence of the four men invited by Liú Hóu.
Liú Hóu followed the Emperor to fight in Dài,
employed a brilliant strategy to capture Mǎ Yì,
and when Xiāo Hé was established as Chancellor,
he casually discussed the affairs of the world with the Emperor on numerous occasions,
but since it was not concerning the survival of the world,
it was not recorded.
Liú Hóu then declared,
"My family has served as ministers of Hán for generations.
When Hán was destroyed,
I did not cherish my wealth of ten thousand gold,
avenged Hán against the powerful Qín,
shaking the world.
Now, with a mere three-inch tongue, I am the master to the Emperor,
have been granted thousands of households,
my rank is among the lords,
this is the pinnacle for a commoner,
it is enough for me.
I wish to abandon worldly matters,
and desire to follow Chì Sōngzǐ."
Then he learned to abstain from grains,
practiced techniques of lightening the body.
When Gāo Dì passed,
Empress Lǚ appreciated Liú Hóu,
and insisted he eat,
saying:
"In one's lifetime,
it is like a white horse passing a crack,
why subject oneself to such hardship?"
Liú Hóu bowed to the Empress' will and ate.
After eight years, he passed away,
posthumously named Wén Chéng Hóu.
His son Bù Yí inherited the title.
The old man whom Zǐ Fáng initially met at the Xià Pí bridge with the "Tài Gōng Book,"
thirteen years later, as he followed Gāo Dì crossing Jìběi,
Bù Yí saw indeed a yellow stone under the Gǔchéng Mountain,
took it and worshipped it.
When Liú Hóu died,
he was buried alongside the yellow stone.
Every time he visited the tomb during winter and summer sacrifice,
he worshipped the yellow stone.
Liú Hóu Bù Yí,
in the fifth year of Emperor Xiàwén's reign, was accused of disrespect,
and his state was abolished.
The Grand Historian said:
Scholars often claim there are no ghosts or spirits,
yet speak of things.
As with the old man Liú Hóu encountered who gave him the book,
it is truly mysterious.
The numerous occasions where the Founder Emperor found himself in dire situations,
Liú Hóu always made significant contributions,
how can it not be said this was the will of Heaven?
The Emperor said:
"In devising strategies within the command tent,
determining victory a thousand miles away,
I am not equal to Zǐ Fáng."
I believe that planning a grand strategy results in a strange title of Marquis,
but upon inspecting the portrait,
his appearance was like that of a beautiful woman.
Confucius said:
"To judge by appearance alone,
one fails at Zǐ Yǔ."
Liú Hóu also said so.
Chancellor Píng of the Chén family,
was from Hù Yǒu Township in Yángwǔ.
In his youth, his family was poor,
he loved reading books,
had thirty acres of land,
and lived alone with his elder brother Bó.
Bó often farmed the land,
allowing Píng to pursue his studies and travels.
Píng was a tall and handsome person.
Someone once said to Chén Píng:
"Though you're poor, what do you eat that makes you so fat?"
His sister-in-law resented Píng for not tending to family matters,
and said:
"He eats only hulls and cores.
To have such an uncle is better to have none."
Upon hearing this,
Bó drove his wife away and abandoned her.
When Chén Píng grew up,
it was time for him to take a wife,
but wealthy families were unwilling to marry their daughters to him,
and he himself felt ashamed to marry into a poor family.
After a long time,
in Hùyǒu, there was a wealthy man named Zhāng Fù,
whose granddaughter had been married five times, and each time her husband died,
so no one dared to marry her.
Chén Píng desired to marry her.
When there was a funeral in the town,
Chén Píng, being poor,
attended to assist with the funeral duties,
arriving early and leaving late to help out.
Zhāng Fù saw him at the funeral site,
and alone, he regarded Chén Píng as exceptional;
Chén Píng also deliberately stayed late for this reason.
Zhāng Fù followed Chén Píng to his home,
which was located in a poor alley against the city wall,
with a worn-out mat serving as the door,
yet outside the door, there were many ruts from the carriages of elders.
Zhāng Fù returned home
and said to his son Zhāng Zhòng:
"I wish to give my granddaughter to Chén Píng."
Zhāng Zhòng said:
"Chén Píng is poor and does not attend to his work;
everyone in the county laughs at his behavior.
Why would you give her to him?"
Zhāng Fù said:
"How could someone as handsome as Chén Píng remain poor and lowly forever?"
In the end, he gave his granddaughter to him.
Because Chén Píng was poor,
he borrowed money for the betrothal gifts,
and gave funds for wine and meat to bring the wife into his home.
Zhāng Fù admonished his granddaughter:
"Do not, because of his poverty,
serve him without care.
Serve his elder brother as you would a father,
and serve his sister-in-law as a mother."
After Chén Píng married the Zhāng family's daughter,
his resources became more abundant,
and his social connections grew wider.
During a village festival,
Chén Píng was the butcher,
and he distributed the meat very fairly.
The elders said:
"Excellent,
how well young Chén acts as butcher!"
Chén Píng said:
"Alas,
if I could govern the world,
I would do it just like this meat!"
When Chén Shè rose and proclaimed himself king of Chén,
he sent Zhōu Fú to conquer the Wèi region,
establishing Wèi Jiù as the King of Wèi,
and they battled the Qín army at Línjì.
Chén Píng had already taken leave of his elder brother,
and followed some young men to serve King Wèi Jiù at Línjì.
The King of Wèi made him his Grand Coachman.
He advised the King of Wèi, but his counsel was not heeded;
some people slandered him,
and Chén Píng fled.
After a long time,
when Xiàng Yǔ was conquering lands up to the river,
Chén Píng went to join him,
followed him in defeating Qín,
and was granted the rank of Qīng.
When Xiàng Yǔ went east to become king of Péngchéng,
and the King of Hán returned to secure the Three Qín and move east,
the King of Yīn rebelled against Chǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ then made Chén Píng the Lord of Xìnwǔ,
leading the former followers of King Wèi Jiù who were in Chǔ,
attacked and subdued the King of Yīn, and returned.
King Xiàng sent Xiàng Hàn to appoint Chén Píng as Commandant,
awarding him twenty yì of gold.
Not long after,
the King of Hán attacked and captured Yīn.
King Xiàng was angry,
and intended to execute the officers who had pacified Yīn.
Chén Píng, fearing execution,
sealed up the gold and his seal,
sent a messenger to return them to King Xiàng,
and Chén Píng himself fled alone, carrying his sword.
While crossing the river,
the boatman saw that he was a handsome man traveling alone,
suspected he was a fleeing general,
and thought he must have gold, jade, or precious objects on him,
eyed him,
and wanted to kill Chén Píng.
Chén Píng, afraid,
took off his clothes and stripped naked to help pole the boat.
The boatman, realizing he had nothing,
stopped.
Chén Píng then reached Xiūwǔ and surrendered to Hàn,
and through Wèi Wúzhī, sought an audience with the King of Hán,
who summoned him in.
At that time, Wànshíjūn Fèn was the King of Hán's palace attendant,
received Chén Píng's request,
and brought him in for an audience.
Chén Píng and six others advanced together,
and were given food.
The King said:
"That's enough,
you may retire to your quarters."
Chén Píng said:
"I have come on business,
and what I have to say cannot wait beyond today."
Thereupon, the King of Hán spoke with him and was pleased,
asking:
"What office did you hold in Chǔ?"
He replied:
"I was a Commandant."
That very day, he appointed Chén Píng as Commandant,
made him his chariot companion,
and put him in charge of the army.
The generals were all upset,
saying:
"The king has just acquired a deserter from Chǔ,
does not know his abilities,
and immediately shares his carriage with him,
even having him oversee us, the senior officers!"
The King of Hán, hearing this,
favored Chén Píng even more.
Then he went east to attack King Xiàng.
Upon reaching Péngchéng,
they were defeated by Chǔ.
They withdrew and returned,
gathering scattered troops until they reached Yíngyáng,
where Chén Píng was made a lieutenant general,
subordinate to King Hán Xìn,
and stationed at Guǎngwǔ.
Marquis Jiàng,
Guàn Yīng, and others all slandered Chén Píng, saying:
"Although Chén Píng is a handsome man,
he is like an ornamental jade on a cap—
his inner qualities may not match.
We heard that when Chén Píng was at home,
he had an affair with his sister-in-law;
he served Wèi but was not accepted,
so he fled to Chǔ;
in Chǔ, he did not fit in,
so he fled to Hán.
Now the king honors him with high office,
and puts him in charge of the army.
We heard that Chén Píng accepts gold from the generals,
those who give more get good assignments,
those who give less get poor ones.
Chén Píng is a treacherous, fickle minister;
we hope the king will investigate him."
The King of Hán became suspicious,
summoned Wèi Wúzhī, and reproached him.
Wúzhī said:
"What I recommended was
his ability;
what Your Majesty is asking about is
his conduct.
Now, if one had the conduct of Wěishēng or Xiàojǐ but could not contribute to the outcome of victory or defeat,
how would Your Majesty have time to use him?
With Chǔ and Hán at a standoff,
I recommended a man of unusual strategies,
considering only whether his plans could truly benefit the state or not.
As for an affair with a sister-in-law and accepting gold, why should that be cause for doubt?"
The King of Hán summoned Chén Píng and reproached him:
"You served Wèi but did not succeed,
then served Chǔ and left,
and now you follow me.
Can a trustworthy man be so changeable?"
Chén Píng said:
"I served the King of Wèi,
but he did not use my advice,
so I left to serve King Xiàng.
King Xiàng does not trust people;
those he appoints and favors
are either from the Xiàng clan or his wife's brothers.
Even if there were exceptional men, he could not use them,
so I left Chǔ.
Hearing that the King of Hán could employ men,
I came to you.
I came with nothing,
and without accepting gold, I would have no means to support myself.
If my plans are worth adopting,
I hope the king will use them;
if there is nothing usable,
the gold is all here,
I will seal it and return it to the government,
and request to retire."
The King of Hán then apologized,
rewarded him richly,
appointed him as Commandant of the Central Army,
putting him in charge of all the generals.
The generals then did not dare to speak again.
After that,
the Chu forces intensified their attacks,
cutting off the Han supply routes,
and besieging King Liú Bāng in the city of Xíngyáng.
After a long time,
King Liú Bāng grew troubled by this,
and proposed to cede the territory west of Xíngyáng to make peace.
King Xiàng Yǔ did not agree.
King Liú Bāng said to Chén Píng:
"The world is in turmoil;
when will it be settled?"
Chén Píng replied:
"King Xiàng Yǔ, as a person,
is respectful and loves others;
many scholars of integrity and propriety have joined him.
But when it comes to awarding merits and granting fiefs,
he is overly cautious,
so scholars do not attach themselves to him for this reason.
Now, Your Majesty is rude and lacking in courtesy,
so scholars of integrity do not come;
however, Your Majesty is generous in granting titles and fiefs,
and thus many shameless, greedy, and dull-witted scholars have joined Hàn.
If each could discard their two shortcomings
and adopt the other's two strengths,
the world could be settled with a wave of the hand.
But Your Majesty is prone to insulting others,
and cannot attract men of integrity.
However, there are elements in Chǔ that can be disrupted.
Those steadfast ministers of King Xiàng Yǔ—Fàn Zēng,
Zhōnglí Mò,
Lóng Qiě,
Zhōu Yīn and their like—
are only a few in number.
If Your Majesty can spare tens of thousands of catties of gold,
to carry out counter-intrigue,
sowing discord among his ministers,
to make him suspicious in his heart,
King Xiàng Yǔ, being suspicious by nature and trusting slander,
will surely have them kill each other internally.
Then Hàn can raise troops to attack,
and will certainly defeat Chǔ."
King Liú Bāng thought this reasonable,
so he gave out forty thousand catties of gold
to Chén Píng,
letting him do as he pleased,
without questioning his expenditures.
Chén Píng then used large amounts of gold to spread counter-intrigue in the Chǔ army,
spreading rumors that generals like Zhōnglí Mò,
though having achieved great merits,
had never been granted lands to become kings,
and wished to ally with Hàn,
to destroy the Xiàng clan and partition their lands to rule.
Xiàng Yǔ indeed grew suspicious and distrusted Zhōnglí Mò and others.
Once King Xiàng Yǔ became suspicious,
he sent an envoy to Hàn.
King Liú Bāng prepared a grand feast
and had it presented.
Upon seeing the Chǔ envoy,
he feigned surprise and said:
"I thought you were an envoy from Fàn Zēng,
but you are an envoy from King Xiàng Yǔ!"
He then had the feast taken away,
and replaced it with poor food for the Chǔ envoy.
When the Chǔ envoy returned,
he reported everything to King Xiàng Yǔ.
King Xiàng Yǔ indeed grew highly suspicious of Fàn Zēng.
Fàn Zēng wanted to urgently capture the city of Xíngyáng,
but King Xiàng Yǔ did not trust him,
and refused to listen.
When Fàn Zēng heard that King Xiàng Yǔ suspected him,
he angrily said:
"The affairs of the world are largely settled;
let Your Majesty handle them yourself!
I wish to retire and return home!"
On his way back, before reaching Péngchéng,
he developed a boil on his back and died.
Chén Píng then had two thousand women exit the east gate of Xíngyáng at night,
and while the Chǔ forces attacked them,
Chén Píng and King Liú Bāng slipped out from the west gate under cover of darkness.
They then entered the pass,
gathered scattered troops, and headed east again.
The following year,
the Marquis of Huáiyín defeated Qí,
proclaimed himself King of Qí,
and sent an envoy to inform King Liú Bāng.
King Liú Bāng was furious and cursed,
but Chén Píng nudged him.
King Liú Bāng then understood,
and treated the Qí envoy generously,
sending Zhāng Liáng to finally establish Hán Xìn as King of Qí.
He enfeoffed Chén Píng with the district of Hùyǒu.
Using his ingenious strategies,
they eventually destroyed Chǔ.
He often accompanied as Protector of the Central Army to pacify Zāng Tú, the King of Yān.
In the sixth year of Hàn,
someone submitted a report accusing the King of Chǔ, Hán Xìn, of rebellion.
Emperor Gāo consulted his generals,
who said:
"Quickly send troops to bury that scoundrel!"
Emperor Gāo remained silent.
He asked Chén Píng,
who initially declined to comment,
saying:
"What do the generals say?"
The Emperor told him everything.
Chén Píng asked:
"Does anyone else know about this report accusing Xìn of rebellion?"
The Emperor said:
"No."
Chén Píng asked:
"Does Xìn know about it?"
The Emperor said:
"He does not."
Chén Píng said:
"How does Your Majesty's elite army compare to Chǔ's?"
The Emperor said:
"It cannot surpass it."
Chén Píng said:
"Among Your Majesty's commanders, is there anyone who can surpass Hán Xìn in using troops?"
The Emperor said:
"No one can match him."
Chén Píng said:
"Now, our troops are not as elite as Chǔ's,
and our commanders cannot match him;
if we raise an army to attack,
we would be forcing him into battle,
and I fear for Your Majesty's safety."
The Emperor said:
"What should be done then?"
Chén Píng said:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven toured the realms,
meeting the feudal lords.
In the south, there is Yúnmèng;
Your Majesty can pretend to travel to Yúnmèng,
and meet the feudal lords at Chén.
Chén is on the western border of Chǔ;
when Xìn hears that the Son of Heaven is on a friendly tour,
he will surely come to the outskirts to greet you without suspicion.
When he greets you, Your Majesty can capture him;
this is merely a task for one strong man."
Emperor Gāo thought this reasonable,
so he sent envoys to inform the feudal lords to meet at Chén,
saying, "I will travel south to Yúnmèng."
The Emperor then set out accordingly.
Before reaching Chén,
King Xìn of Chǔ indeed came to greet him on the road at the outskirts.
Emperor Gāo had prepared warriors in advance;
seeing Xìn arrive,
they immediately seized and bound him,
placing him in a following carriage.
Xìn cried out:
"Now that the world is settled,
I am indeed to be boiled!"
Emperor Gāo turned to Xìn and said:
"Be silent!
Your rebellion
is clear!"
The warriors bound his hands behind his back.
They then met the feudal lords at Chén,
and fully pacified the land of Chǔ.
Returning to Luòyáng,
he pardoned Xìn and made him Marquis of Huáiyīn,
and distributed tallies to confirm the enfeoffments of the meritorious officials.
Thereupon, he awarded Píng with a tally,
making his title hereditary without end,
as Marquis of Hùyǒu.
Píng declined, saying:
"This is not my achievement."
The Emperor said:
"I used your strategies,
to win battles and defeat enemies;
if not an achievement, what is it?"
Píng said:
"If not for Wèi Wúzhī, how could I have been recommended?"
The Emperor said:
"You, sir, can be said to not forget your roots."
He then also rewarded Wèi Wúzhī.
The following year,
he accompanied as Protector of the Central Army to attack the rebel King Xìn of Hán in Dài.
They reached Píngchéng,
where they were besieged by the Xiōngnú,
and went without food for seven days.
Emperor Gāo used Chén Píng's ingenious stratagem,
sent to the Xiōngnú Chányú's wife,
and the siege was lifted.
After Emperor Gāo escaped,
the details of the plan remained secret,
and the world never learned of it.
Gāo Dì traveled south through Qūnì.
He ascended its city wall,
gazed upon its great houses,
and said:
"Magnificent county!
As I roam the world,
I have only seen Luòyáng comparable to this."
Looking back, he asked a yùshǐ:
"How many households are in Qūnì?"
The response was:
"At the beginning of the Qin dynasty, there were over thirty thousand households.
During the wars, many perished or hid,
now five thousand households remain."
Thereupon, an edict was issued to the yùshǐ,
appointing Chén Píng as the Marquess of Qūnì,
granting him all its resources,
and removing the previous household allowances.
Later, he often served as Guard Commander,
accompanying expeditions against Chén Xī and Qíngbù.
He devised six brilliant strategies,
resulting in increased fief size,
with his fief expanded six times.
Some strategies were highly secretive,
known by none in later generations.
When Gāo Dì returned from defeating Bù's army,
he was afflicted by illness,
and traveled slowly to Cháng’ān.
When Yān Wáng Lú Wǎn rebelled,
the emperor sent Fán Kuài as the chancellor to lead troops against him.
Upon setting out,
rumors were spread disparaging Kuài.
Gāo Dì, angry, said:
"Kuài sees me ill,
hoping for my death."
Employing Chén Píng's strategy, he summoned Jiàng Hóu Zhōu Bó to receive the imperial edict beneath his bed,
and said:
"Chén Píng hasten with imperial dispatches to appoint Bó to replace Kuài as the general.
Upon arrival, execute Kuài immediately!"
After both received the edict,
racing on imperial orders but not yet reaching the army,
they deliberated:
"Fán Kuài
is the Emperor’s old ally,
with many achievements,
and also the husband of Empress Lü's sister, Lǚ Xū,
thus both kin and noble.
The Emperor, in his rage,
would execute him,
but might regret it later.
Better to imprison and bring him before the Emperor,
and let the Emperor personally decide his fate."
Before reaching the army,
they constructed a platform,
using an authority token to summon Fán Kuài.
Kuài received the edict,
and was immediately bound and placed in a caged carriage,
transported to Cháng’ān,
and Jiàng Hóu Bó was ordered to replace him as the general,
leading forces to pacify the Yān rebellion.
Upon hearing of Emperor Gāo's death,
Chén Píng feared the slander of Empress Dowager Lü and Lǚ Xū,
so he hurriedly departed.
Encountering an envoy,
he was ordered to meet with Guàn Yīng in Xíngyáng.
After receiving the edict,
he again swiftly arrived at the palace,
weeping bitterly before the funeral,
and performing state affairs in mourning.
Empress Dowager Lü was moved,
and said:
"You have labored much;
go and rest."
Fearing entrapment of slander,
he earnestly requested to be part of the palace guard.
Thus, Empress Dowager appointed him as Chief Minister
and said:
"Guide and instruct Xiàohuì."
Thereafter, Lǚ Xū was unable to act on her slanders.
When Fán Kuài arrived,
his titles and lands were restored.
In the sixth year of Emperor Xiàohuì,
Chancellor Cáo Cān passed away,
and Ànguó Hóu Wáng Líng was appointed Right Chancellor,
and Chén Píng as Left Chancellor.
Wáng Líng originally hailed from Pèi,
starting as an influential local,
whom Gāozǔ regarded as an elder in his youth.
Though less educated,
he was principled,
valuing blunt speech.
When Gāozǔ rose in Pèi,
entering Xiányáng,
Líng also amassed a group of several thousand,
residing in Nányáng,
initially unwilling to follow.
As the Hàn King returned to attack Xiàng Jí,
Líng eventually aligned his troops with Hàn.
Xiàng Yǔ captured Líng's mother, placing her in his camp,
attempting to lure Líng over.
His mother secretly sent a messenger,
tearfully saying:
"Tell Líng to loyally serve the Hàn King;
he is a great person.
Because of me, do not waver your loyalty.
I die sending this message."
She then committed suicide by the sword.
Enraged, Xiàng Wáng boiled Líng’s mother.
Líng ultimately followed the Hàn King to unify the realm.
He was able to tolerate Yōng Chí,
Gāo Dì's enemy,
hence was last to be ennobled,
becoming Ànguó Hóu.
As Ànguó Hóu was appointed Right Chancellor,
in two years,
Emperor Xiàohuì passed.
Empress Dowager Gāo wished to make the Lü clan kings,
asking Wáng Líng,
who replied:
"It is not advisable."
Asking Chén Píng,
who said:
"It is possible."
Angered, Empress Dowager faked promoting Líng to Grand Mentor,
effectively dismissing him.
Enraged, Líng claimed illness to leave,
closing his doors without attending court,
and died after seven years.
After Líng stepped down as Prime Minister,
Empress Dowager Lü appointed Píng as Right Chancellor,
making Bìiyáng Hóu Shěn Shíqí the Left Chancellor.
The Left Chancellor did not handle governance,
maintaining daily duties in the inner palace.
Shíqí was also a man from Pèi.
When the Hàn King lost west of Péngchéng,
Chǔ captured the Supreme Emperor and
Empress Lü as hostages,
and Shíqí attended Empress Lü as a retainer.
Later, he followed to defeat Xiàng Jí and became a marquess,
gaining favor with Empress Dowager Lü.
Becoming Prime Minister,
residing in the inner palace,
all officials referred to him for decisions.
Lǚ Xū often held against Chén Píng that he plotted against Fán Kuài on Gāo Dì's behalf,
repeatedly slandering:
"Chén Píng, as Chancellor, does not manage affairs,
drinks strong wine daily,
and indulges with women."
Upon hearing this, Chén Píng indulged even more.
Learning of this, Empress Dowager secretly rejoiced,
and personally confronted Lǚ Xū in front of Chén Píng,
saying: "As the saying goes,
'a daughter-in-law's words cannot be trusted.' So what should I care about your complaints?
Fear not Lǚ Xū’s slanders."
Empress Dowager Lü granted kingship to the Lü clan,
and Chén Píng pretended to go along.
Upon her death,
Píng and Grand Commandant Bó conspired,
exterminating the Lü clan,
establishing Emperor Xiàowén.
This was originally Chén Píng’s plan.
Shěn Shíqí was thus dismissed.
When Emperor Xiàowén ascended the throne,
he appointed Tài Wèi Bo, who had personally used military force to execute the Lü clan,
as he had achieved great merit.
Chén Píng wished to yield his higher position to Bo,
thus he feigned illness.
As Emperor Xiàowén had just begun his reign,
he was puzzled by Píng's illness
and questioned him.
Píng said:
"During the time of the High Ancestor,
Bo's merit was not as great as mine.
As for the execution of the Lü,
my merit was also not as great as Bo's.
I wish to relinquish my position as Right Chancellor to Bo."
Thereupon, Emperor Xiàowén appointed Marquis of Jiàng, Bo, as the Right Chancellor,
placing him in the foremost position.
Píng was moved to the position of Left Chancellor,
ranked second.
He was gifted a thousand catties of gold,
and his domain was increased by three thousand households.
After some time,
as Emperor Xiàowén became more knowledgeable and accustomed to state affairs,
he asked the Right Chancellor Bo in court:
"How many legal cases are settled in the realm in one year?"
Bo apologized, saying:
"I do not know."
He then asked:
"What is the annual balance of revenue and expenditure in the realm?"
Bo again apologized for not knowing,
sweat dampening his back,
ashamed at his inability to respond.
Then the emperor also questioned Left Chancellor Píng.
Píng replied:
"There are those responsible."
The emperor asked:
"Whom do you mean by those responsible?"
Píng said:
"If His Majesty inquires about adjudicating cases,
he should hold the Minister of Justice accountable;
if inquiring about finances,
he should hold the Minister of Revenue accountable."
The emperor said:
"Since each has their responsibilities,
then what matters are you responsible for?"
Píng apologized, saying:
"Responsible for myself!
His Majesty, unaware of my inadequacies, has appointed me to serve as a Prime Minister.
A Prime Minister
assists the Son of Heaven in regulating yin and yang,
aligning with the four seasons,
nurturing the myriad things appropriately,
externally pacifying the barbarian states and feudatories,
internally aligning with the people,
enabling the ministers and grandees to each fulfill their roles."
Emperor Xiàowén thus praised him.
The Right Chancellor was greatly ashamed,
and upon leaving, he reproached Chén Píng, saying:
"Why did you not privately instruct me in how to respond?"
Chén Píng laughed and said:
"You hold such a position
and do not know your duties?
Moreover, if His Majesty were to inquire about the number of thieves within Cháng'ān,
would you forcibly respond as well?"
Thus, Marquis of Jiàng came to realize that his abilities were far inferior to Píng's.
After a while,
Marquis of Jiàng feigned illness and requested to be relieved of his position,
leaving Chén Píng to serve as the sole Chancellor.
In the second year of Emperor Xiàowén's reign,
Chancellor Chén Píng passed away,
posthumously named Marquis Xiàn.
His son, Marquis Gòng Bù, succeeded him.
In the second year, he also passed away,
succeeded by Marquis Jiǎn Huī.
In the twenty-third year, he passed away,
succeeded by Marquis Hé.
In the twenty-third year,
Marquis Hé was punished for abducting another man's wife,
executed in the marketplace,
and his state abolished.
Initially, Chén Píng said:
"I have engaged in many covert schemes,
which are forbidden by Daoism.
Should my lineage fall into decline,
so be it,
it will never rise again,
due to the many hidden calamities I have caused."
However, later, his great-grandson Chén Zhǎng, through being an intimate relation of the Wèi clan,
desired to continue the Chén lineage,
yet was ultimately unable to do so.
The Grand Historian said:
"When Chancellor Chén Píng was young,
he was originally fond of the teachings of the Yellow Emperor and
Laozi.
Even as he carved meat on the butcher's block,
his ambitions were already far-reaching.
Amidst the turmoil between Chǔ and Wèi,
he ultimately returned to the Great Ancestor,
consistently offering extraordinary strategies,
resolving potential threats,
and alleviating the state's troubles.
During Empress Lü’s time,
though many matters were indeed troublesome,
Píng eventually extricated himself,
stabilizing the ancestral temples,
ending his life with honor,
regarded as a virtuous minister.
Is this not the epitome of starting well and ending well?
Without such discerning counsel, who else could have managed these feats?"
Marquis of Jiàng, Zhōu Bo,
hailed from Pei.
His ancestors were from Juàn,
but relocated to Pei.
Bo made his living weaving small items,
often playing the flute for funerals,
and being quite strong.
When the Great Ancestor initially rose as Duke of Pei,
Bo followed as an attendant on his campaign against Húlíng,
subjugating Fāngyǔ.
Fāngyǔ rebelled,
he engaged in battle with them,
defeating them soundly.
He attacked Fēng,
defeating the Qin forces east of Dang.
He returned his troops to Liú and Xiaō.
He again attacked Dang,
defeating it.
He took Xià Yì,
being the first to ascend the walls.
He was awarded the rank of grandee five times.
He attacked Meng and
Yu, capturing them.
He engaged the chariots and cavalry of Zhāng Hán,
serving as the rear guard. He pacified Wèi territory.
He assaulted and captured Yuàn Qì,
Dōngmín,
moving on to Lì,
capturing it.
He attacked Niè Sāng,
being the first to ascend.
He defeated the Qin forces at Ā,
routing them.
Pursuing to Púyáng,
he captured Zhēn City.
He attacked Dūguān and
Dìngtáo,
capturing and seizing Wănqú by surprise,
securing the commandery of Shānfù.
At night, he surprised and captured Línjì,
attacked Zhāng,
moving forward to Juàn,
defeating it.
He defeated Lǐ Yóu’s army below Yōngqiū.
He attacked Kāifēng,
being the first to reach the city defenses.
Later, Zhāng Hán defeated and killed Xiàng Liáng.
Duke of Pei along with Xiàng Yǔ led troops east to Dàng.
From initially rising at Pei to returning to Dàng,
it took a year and two months.
King Huái of Chu enfeoffed Pei Gong with the title of Marquis of Wǔ'ān,
appointing him as governor of Dàng Prefecture.
Pei Gong appointed Bo as the Commander of Tiger Warriors,
leading forces with Pei Gong to pacify Wèi territory.
He attacked the Eastern Garrison Commander at Chéngwǔ,
defeating him.
He engaged the army of Wáng Lí,
defeating him.
He attacked Chángshè,
being the first to ascend.
He attacked Yǐngyáng and
Gōushì,
severing the ferry at Hé.
He engaged Zhào Bèn’s army at Shīběi.
He attacked Nányáng, defeating General Yǐ.
He captured Wǔguān and
Yáoguān.
He defeated the Qin forces at Lántián,
reaching Xiányáng,
extinguishing Qin.
When Xiàng Yǔ arrived,
he appointed Pèi Gōng as the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn granted the title of Marquis of Wēiwǔ to Bó.
Following him into Hànzhōng,
he was appointed as a general.
He returned to pacify Sān Qín,
and upon reaching Qín,
he was granted the fief of Huái Dé.
He attacked Huáilǐ,
Hǎo Zhí,
achieving great success. He defeated Zhào Bì,
and the Interior Commandant retreated to Xiányáng,
gaining the advantage. He advanced northward to Qī.
He defeated Zhāng Píng and
Yáo Áng's forces.
He pacified Qiān to the west.
Returning down to Méi,
and Pínyáng.
He besieged Zhāng Hán at the abandoned Qiu.
He destroyed the western chancellor.
He struck the bandits of Bā's army,
and defeated them.
He attacked Shàngguī.
Moving eastward, he guarded Yáoguān.
Turning to strike Xiàng Jí.
He attacked Qū Nì,
achieving significant success. He returned to guard Áo Cāng,
pursuing Xiàng Jí.
Since Jí had already died,
he then moved east to secure the Chǔ territories, Sìshuǐ,
and Dōnghǎi Commanderies,
altogether obtaining twenty-two counties.
He returned to guard Luòyáng,
and Lèyáng,
granting joint fiefdom with the Prince of Yǐngyīn, Zhōnglí.
As a general, he followed Gāo Dì to attack the rebel King of Yān, Zāng Tú,
easily defeating him.
The soldiers he led often took on the role of occupying main pathways.
He was granted the rank of marquis,
permanently inheriting the privilege.
He received food from 8,180 households in Jiàng,
and was titled Marquis of Jiàng.
As a general, he followed Gāo Dì to attack the rebel King of Hán, Xìn, at Dài,
and subdued the people of Huò.
Previously reaching Wǔquán,
he attacked the Hú cavalry,
defeating them north of Wǔquán.
He then turned to attack the army of Hán Xìn at Tóngdī,
defeating them.
Returning, he subdued six cities of Tàiyuán.
He struck Hán Xìn's Hú cavalry under Jìnyáng,
defeating them,
and captured Jìnyáng.
Later, he attacked Hán Xìn's forces at Shāshí,
defeating them,
pursuing them north for eighty lǐ.
He returned to attack three cities of Lóufán,
then struck the Hú cavalry again under Píngchéng,
his troops frequently taking key routes.
Bó was promoted to Grand Commandant.
He attacked Chén Xī,
and ransacked Mǎ Yì.
His soldiers beheaded Xī's General Chéngmá Chī.
He struck the forces of Hán Xìn,
Chén Xī,
and Zhào Lì at Lóufán,
defeating them.
He captured Xī's general Sòng Zuì,
and the garrison commander of Yànmén, Hùn.
He then turned to capture the governor of Yúnzhōng, Sù,
the chancellor Jī Sì,
and general Xūn.
He secured the Yànmén Commandery with seventeen counties,
the Yúnzhōng Commandery with twelve counties.
He consequently attacked Xī at Língqiū again,
defeating him,
and beheaded Xī,
capturing Xī's chancellor Chéng Zòng,
General Chén Wǔ,
and Commandant Gāo Sì.
He secured nine counties in the Dài Commandery.
King Lú Wǎn of Yān rebelled,
and Bó, as prime minister, replaced Fán Kuāi to lead,
striking Jì,
capturing Wǎn's chief general Dǐ,
chancellor Yǎn,
garrison commander Xíng,
Grand Commandant Ruò,
and Grand Tutor Shī,
ransacking Hún Dū.
He defeated Wǎn's forces at Shànglán,
and again defeated them at Jǔyáng.
He pursued him to the Great Wall,
securing Shànggù with twelve counties,
Yòu Běipíng with sixteen counties,
Liáoxī,
and Liáodōng with twenty-nine counties,
Yúyáng with twenty-two counties.
Following Gāo Dì's orders, he secured one prime minister,
two chancellors,
three generals, and
three two-thousand-stone officials;
separately he defeated two armies,
captured three towns,
secured five commanderies,
seventy-nine counties,
capturing one chancellor and
one chief general.
Bó was simple, strong, and sincere in character,
and Gāo Dì considered him reliable for major affairs.
Bó was not fond of literature,
and whenever he summoned scholars,
he sat facing east and criticized them,
saying, "Hurry and speak for me."
His bluntness towards scholarship was like this.
After pacifying Yān and returning,
Gāo Zǔ had already passed away,
and he served the Filial and Benevolent Emperor as a feudal lord.
In the sixth year of the Filial and Benevolent Emperor's reign,
the Grand Commandant's office was established,
and Bó was appointed as Grand Commandant.
After ten years,
Empress Lü passed away.
Lǚ Lù, as the King of Zhào, became Grand General of Hàn,
Lǚ Chǎn became prime minister of Hàn,
holding power over Hàn,
and sought to endanger the Liú family.
Bó as Grand Commandant
was unable to enter the military gate.
Chén Píng as prime minister
was unable to act on his responsibilities.
Thereupon, Bó and Píng conspired,
ultimately executing the Lǚ clan and establishing the Filial and Civil Emperor.
Their account is in the "Empress Lü" and
"Filial and Civil" records.
Once the Civil Emperor was established,
Bó was appointed right prime minister,
rewarded with five thousand jin of gold,
and a fief of ten thousand households.
After more than a month,
someone advised Bó,
saying, "You have executed the Lǚ clan,
established the King of Dài,
your power intimidates the world,
and you have received rich awards,
occupying a prestigious position,
if you stay long, disaster will befall you."
Bó was frightened,
and felt endangered,
so he resigned and requested to return the prime minister’s seal.
The Emperor permitted it.
Over a year later,
the prime minister Píng died,
and the Emperor restored Bó as prime minister.
After more than ten months,
the Emperor said,
“Previously I decreed the marquises to go to their states,
and some have not yet departed,
I regard the responsibility of the prime minister highly,
let him lead by example.”
Thus, he exempted the prime ministry to retire to his state.
Over a year passed.
Whenever the governor and commander of Hedong visited Jiang County,
Jiàng Hóu Bó was fearful of being executed,
so he always wore armor
and had his family members hold weapons when meeting him.
Later, someone wrote a memorial accusing him of treason,
and he was sent to the court jailer.
The court jailer sent the matter to Chang’an,
to arrest and investigate Bó.
Bó was terrified,
not knowing what to say.
The officials gradually insulted and humiliated him.
Bó gave a thousand gold pieces to the prison guards,
and the guards then wrote on the back of a document to show him,
saying,
"Use the princess as a witness."
The mentioned princess
was Emperor Xiaowen’s daughter,
whom Bó's eldest son Shèngzhī had married,
thus the prison guards advised him to call her as a witness.
Bó, with his additional titles and rewards,
gave them all to Bó Zhāo.
When the situation became urgent,
Bó Zhāo spoke to Empress Dowager Bó,
and the Empress Dowager also thought there was no matter of rebellion.
During Emperor Wen’s court,
the Empress Dowager lightly mentioned this to Emperor Wen,
saying:
"Jiàng Hóu once held the imperial seal,
commanded troops in the northern army,
and if he didn’t rebel at that time,
how could he possibly seek to rebel now in a small county!"
Emperor Wen, after seeing Jiàng Hóu’s prison plea,
then apologized, saying:
"The officials are investigating and will release him."
Thus, he sent an envoy with a token to pardon Jiàng Hóu,
restoring his title and lands.
After Jiàng Hóu was released,
he said:
"I once led an army of a million,
yet I didn’t know the power of the jailers!"
Jiàng Hóu returned to his state.
In the eleventh year of Emperor Xiaowen, he passed away,
posthumously named Wǔ Hóu.
His son Shèngzhī succeeded him as marquis.
After six years,
he married the princess,
but they were not compatible,
resulting in him killing someone,
and the state was abolished.
After a year,
Emperor Wen selected capable sons of Jiàng Hóu, and Zhì Xiànzhě Hé Nèi Shôu Yǎfu was selected,
bestowed the title of Tiáo Hóu,
continuing the line of Jiàng Hóu.
When Tiáo Hóu Yǎfu was still not a marquis but Hé Nèi governor,
Xǔ Fù predicted,
saying:
"You will be marquis in three years.
In eight years you'll be a general and minister,
holding the state's power,
esteemed and revered,
unmatched among ministers.
In nine years, you will starve to death."
Yǎfu laughed, saying:
"My brother has already succeeded my father as marquis,
should something happen,
the son should inherit,
what could lead me to become marquis?
Yet should I become esteemed as Xǔ Fù says,
why would I starve?
Show me."
Xǔ Fù pointed to his mouth, saying:
"There will be something entering causing death by starvation."
After three years,
his brother Jiàng Hóu Shèngzhī committed a crime,
and Emperor Xiaowen chose among Jiàng Hóu's capable sons,
all recommending Yǎfu,
thus granting Yǎfu Tiáo Hóu,
continuing Jiàng Hóu’s line.
Six years after Emperor Wen,
the Xiongnu invaded the borders.
Liu Li, the head of the Liu clan, was appointed general,
stationed at Ba Shang;
Zhù Zī Hóu Xú Lì as general,
at Jí Gate;
Yǎfu, governor of Hé Neì, as general,
stationed at Xì Lǐu:
to prepare for the Hu.
The emperor personally visited the troops.
At Ba Shang and Jí Gate troops,
he rode straight in,
greeted by generals and officers on horseback.
Later, he went to Xì Lǐu troops,
where soldiers and officers wore armor,
sharp weapons ready,
bows drawn,
fully armed.
The emperor's vanguard arrived,
but was denied entry.
The vanguard said:
"The emperor is about to arrive!"
The army gate commandant said:
"The general orders state
'In the army, we hear the general’s orders,
not the emperor’s decrees'."
Soon after,
the emperor arrived,
again denied entry.
The emperor sent an envoy to give the general orders:
"I wish to enter to inspect the troops."
Yǎfu then conveyed orders to open the camp gate.
The camp gate officers and soldiers told the accompanying carriages and cavalry:
"The general's agreements,
entering the army must be slow."
The emperor then proceeded slowly.
Arriving at the camp,
General Yǎfu, bearing arms, saluted and said:
"Armored soldiers do not bow,
please observe military courtesy."
The emperor was moved,
changing demeanor and stance,
sending someone to respectfully thank him:
"The emperor respectfully rewards the general."
After the formalities, he departed.
After exiting the camp gate,
all ministers were astonished.
Emperor Wen said:
"Ah,
this truly is a general!
Earlier, the Ba Shang and Jí Gate troops
were like child's play,
their generals could be easily overtaken and captured.
But as for Yǎfu,
how could one possibly defy him!"
The praise continued for a long time.
Over a month later,
all three armies were disbanded.
Yǎfu was appointed as Zhongwei.
When Emperor Xiaowen was about to pass,
he admonished Crown Prince, saying:
"In case of emergencies,
Zhōu Yǎfu can truly be entrusted with commanding troops."
After Emperor Wen passed,
Yǎfu was appointed as a general of chariots and cavalry.
In the third year of Emperor Xiaojing,
Wu and Chu rebelled.
Yǎfu, then Zhongwei, became Taiwei,
and marched east to attack Wu and Chu.
He requested, saying:
"The Chu armies are swift and unencumbered,
hard to confront head-on.
I request to use Liang to cut off their supply route,
only then can they be controlled."
The emperor permitted it.
The Grand Commandant gathered troops at Yíngyáng,
while Wú was besieging Liáng.
Liáng was in danger,
and requested assistance.
The Grand Commandant led troops northeast towards Chāngyì,
fortified defenses and stood guard.
Liáng sent emissaries daily to request aid from the Grand Commandant,
but he assessed the situation
and refused to advance.
Liáng reported to Jǐngdì,
who sent an order to rescue Liáng.
The Grand Commandant did not comply,
maintaining strong defenses and did not engage,
instead dispatching light cavalry under Gōng Gāo Hóu and others to cut Wú and Chǔ’s supply lines.
Wú's forces, lacking provisions,
were hungry and frequently attempted to provoke a battle,
but never succeeded.
One night, there was panic in their camp,
with troops attacking each other in chaos,
even reaching the Grand Commandant's tent.
The Grand Commandant remained lying down and did not rise.
After a while,
order was restored.
Later, Wú troops fled towards the southeastern corner of the fortress,
and the Grand Commandant prepared defenses in the northwest.
Indeed, their elite troops eventually fled northwest,
and could not break through.
Wú soldiers were starving,
so they withdrew.
The Grand Commandant deployed elite troops in pursuit,
utterly defeating them.
Wú King Bì abandoned his army,
fleeing with several thousand valiant warriors,
and took refuge in Dāntú south of the Yangtze River.
Hàn forces exploited their victory,
capturing all of them,
forcing their surrender,
and placing a bounty of a thousand measures of gold on Wú King Bì.
After a little more than a month,
Yuè people beheaded Wú King and reported it.
In total, after three months of combat,
Wú and Chǔ were defeated and pacified.
Consequently, the various generals finally recognized the Grand Commandant's strategy as the correct one.
Because of this, King Xiào of Liáng and the Grand Commandant had disagreements.
Returning,
the Grand Commandant was reinstated.
Five years later,
he was promoted to Chancellor,
and Jǐngdì highly esteemed him.
When Jǐngdì deposed Crown Prince Lì,
the Chancellor firmly opposed it,
but to no avail.
This led Jǐngdì to distance himself from him.
And whenever King Xiào of Liáng came to court,
he always spoke to Empress Dowager Dòu about Tiáo Hóu's shortcomings.
Empress Dowager Dòu said,
"The Empress's brother, Wáng Xìn, should be made a marquis."
Jǐngdì responded,
"Initially, during the time of the late Emperor, Nánpí,
and Zhāngwǔ Marquises were not made marquises;
it was only after I ascended the throne that they were enfeoffed.
Xìn has not yet been enfeoffed."
Empress Dowager Dòu said,
"Rulers act according to the times.
During the time of Lord Dòu Zhǎng,
he was never enfeoffed,
it was only after his death that his son Péngzǔ was granted nobility.
I regret it deeply.
The Emperor should swiftly enfeoff Xìn!"
Jǐngdì replied,
"I request a discussion with the Chancellor."
The Chancellor discussed it,
Yàfū said,
"As the Emperor Gāo made a covenant,
'None who are not of the Liú clan shall be kings,
no one without merit shall be marquis,
otherwise,
the whole world shall unite to attack them.'
Though Xìn is the Empress's brother,
he has no merit.
Making him a marquis
violates the covenant."
Jǐngdì fell silent and ceased the matter.
Later, when several Xiongnu kings including Wéi Xú and Lú surrendered,
Jǐngdì wanted to enfeoff them to encourage future defectors.
Chancellor Yàfū said,
"If they betray their lord and surrender to Your Majesty,
if Your Majesty enfeoffs them,
how can you expect ministers to remain loyal?"
Jǐngdì said,
"The Chancellor's advice is not applicable."
Thus, all of them were enfeoffed as ranked marquises.
Yàfū then claimed illness.
In the third year of Jǐngdì’s reign,
he was relieved of his chancellorship due to illness.
Shortly thereafter,
Jǐngdì was in the inner palace,
summoning Tiáo Hóu,
and provided a meal.
A large piece of meat was set alone,
without any sliced meat,
nor was a meat knife provided.
Tiáo Hóu felt discontented,
and asked an attendant for a knife.
Jǐngdì watched and laughed, saying,
"Is this not sufficient for you?"
Tiáo Hóu removed his crown and apologized.
The emperor stood up,
and Tiáo Hóu promptly withdrew.
Jǐngdì followed him with his eyes as he left,
and said,
"This discontented one is not a servant to a young ruler!"
Not long after,
Tiáo Hóu’s son purchased five hundred sumptuous ceremonial armor sets intended for burial from the imperial workshops.
He pressed the artisans without paying them.
The artisans, learning he illicitly purchased government property,
became angry and reported the incident,
implicating Tiáo Hóu in the matter.
When the report reached the emperor,
an investigation was launched.
Officials interrogated Tiáo Hóu,
but he remained silent.
Jǐngdì scolded him, saying,
"Heed me not!"
Summoning him to the Tingwei.
The Tingwei interrogated, asking,
"Do you intend to rebel?"
Yàfū replied,
"The items I bought were for burial,
how can one speak of rebellion?"
When questioned,
someone said,
"Even if you do not wish to rebel in this world,
you might wish to do so in the next."
The officials pressed him more aggressively.
Initially, when officials came to arrest Tiáo Hóu,
he intended to commit suicide,
but his wife stopped him.
As a result, he did not die,
but was taken to the Tingwei.
There, he refused to eat for five days,
vomiting blood and dying.
His state was eliminated.
After a year,
Jǐngdì re-enfeoffed Jìang Hóu Bó's son Jiān as Marquis of Píngqū,
continuing Jìang Hóu's line.
He died in the nineteenth year,
posthumously titled as Gòng Hóu.
His son Jiàndé succeeded as Marquis,
serving as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince for thirteen years.
He was involved in an issue with the Zhoù gold,
and in the fifth year of Yuándǐng,
he was convicted,
and his state was abolished.
Thus, Tiáo Hóu indeed starved to death.
After his death,
Jǐngdì then enfeoffed Wáng Xìn as Marquis of Gài.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"Jìang Hóu Zhōu Bó, when he was a mere commoner,
was a simple and unrefined man,
his talents no more than average.
However, when he assisted Emperor Gāozǔ in settling the realm,
holding high office as a general,
when the Lǚ clan sought to cause chaos,
Bó safeguarded the nation in peril,
restoring order.
Though Yī Yǐn and Duke of Zhōu,
what could surpass this?
Yàfū, in his use of military force,
held firm authority,
wielding a sharp blade,
how could Ráng Jū surpass him?
Self-satisfied in achievement and reluctant to learn,
steadfast but lacking humility,
he ultimately met a tragic end.
What a lamentable fate!
The martial Xiào King of Liáng was,
the son of Emperor Xiàowén,
sharing the same mother with Emperor Xiàojǐng.
Their mother was Empress Dowager Dòu."
In the winter of the thirty-fifth year,
he again attended court.
He submitted a memorial wishing to remain,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Returning to his kingdom,
he felt disconsolate and unhappy.
While hunting north at Liángshān,
someone presented an ox,
with a foot growing out of its back,
which King Xiào found ominous.
In mid-June,
he fell ill with fever,
and died after six days,
posthumously titled King Xiào.
King Xiào was kind and filial;
whenever he heard that the Empress Dowager was ill,
he could not eat,
nor rest peacefully,
and often wished to stay in Cháng'ān to attend to her.
The Empress Dowager also loved him.
Upon hearing of the King of Liáng's death,
Empress Dowager Dòu wept in extreme grief,
refusing to eat,
saying:
"The Emperor has indeed killed my son!"
Emperor Jǐng, grieved and fearful,
did not know what to do.
Consulting with the Elder Princess,
he divided Liáng into five kingdoms,
enfeoffing all five sons of King Xiào as kings,
and granting the five daughters towns for their bathing expenses.
This was reported to the Empress Dowager,
who then became pleased,
and ate an extra meal for the emperor.
King Xiào's eldest son, Mǎi, became King of Liáng,
known as King Gòng;
his son Míng became King of Jìchuān;
his son Pénglí became King of Jìdōng;
his son Dìng became King of Shānyáng;
his son Bùshí became King of Jìyīn.
Before King Xiào died,
his wealth amounted to hundreds of millions,
beyond calculation.
After his death,
the treasury still contained over four hundred thousand catties of gold,
with other assets to match.
In the third year of King Gòng of Liáng,
Emperor Jǐng passed away.
King Gòng reigned for seven years and died,
succeeded by his son Xiāng,
known as King Píng.
In the fourteenth year of King Píng Xiāng of Liáng,
his mother was called Empress Dowager Chén.
King Gòng's mother was called Empress Dowager Lǐ.
Empress Dowager Lǐ
was King Píng's paternal grandmother.
King Píng's queen bore the surname Rén,
called Queen Rén.
Queen Rén was greatly favored by King Píng Xiāng.
Earlier, during King Xiào's lifetime,
there was a léi zūn vessel,
worth a thousand pieces of gold.
King Xiào instructed his descendants
to carefully preserve the léi zūn,
and not give it to anyone.
Queen Rén heard of it and desired the léi zūn.
King Píng's grandmother, Empress Dowager Lǐ, said:
"The former king commanded
that the léi zūn not be given to anyone.
Even if other things are worth a hundred million,
you may indulge freely."
Queen Rén desperately wanted it.
King Píng Xiāng directly ordered someone to open the treasury and take the léi zūn,
bestowing it upon Queen Rén.
Empress Dowager Lǐ was furious;
when Hàn envoys came,
she intended to speak out,
but King Píng Xiāng and Queen Rén intercepted and stopped her,
closing the gates.
Empress Dowager Lǐ struggled at the gate,
injuring her fingers,
and thus could not meet the Hàn envoys.
Empress Dowager Lǐ also privately engaged in illicit relations with the Chief Food Officer and the court official Yǐn Bà, among others.
The king and Queen Rén used this to have people dissuade Empress Dowager Lǐ,
who, being involved in immoral conduct herself,
let it be.
Later, she fell ill and died.
During her illness,
Queen Rén never inquired about her health;
after her death, she did not observe mourning.
During the Yuánshuò era,
a man from Suīyáng named Lèi Gànfǎn,
whose father had been insulted by someone,
was riding in the same carriage as a guest of the Governor of Huáiyáng.
When the governor's guest got out of the carriage,
Lèi Gànfǎn killed his enemy in the carriage and fled.
The Governor of Huáiyáng was angered
and reprimanded the Liáng officials of two-thousand-dan rank.
Officials below two-thousand-dan rank pursued Fǎn urgently,
arresting his relatives.
Fǎn, knowing state secrets,
submitted a report of irregularities,
detailing the dispute between the king and his grandmother over the vessel.
At that time, the Chancellor and others learned of it
and sought to harm the senior officials of Liáng;
the document reached the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven ordered officials to investigate,
and it was confirmed.
The high officials requested that Xiāng be deposed as a commoner.
The Son of Heaven said:
"Empress Dowager Lǐ engaged in immoral conduct,
and King Xiāng of Liáng lacked good mentors,
thus leading him into impropriety."
He then reduced Liáng by eight cities,
and displayed Queen Rén's head in the market.
Liáng was left with ten cities.
Xiāng reigned for thirty-nine years and died,
posthumously titled King Píng.
His son Wúshāng succeeded as King of Liáng.
As for King Míng of Jìchuān,
he was a son of King Xiào of Liáng,
enfeoffed as King of Jìchuān in the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng's middle period, from his title as Marquis of Huányì.
After seven years,
he was accused of shooting and killing his Commandant of the Central Guard,
and the Hàn authorities requested his execution.
The Son of Heaven could not bear to kill him,
but deposed him as a commoner,
exiling him to Fánglíng,
and his territory was incorporated into Hàn as a commandery.
As for King Pénglí of Jìdōng,
he was a son of King Xiào of Liáng,
enfeoffed as King of Jìdōng in the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng's middle period.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Pénglí, being arrogant and violent,
lacked the demeanor of a ruler,
and at dusk would privately go with his slaves
and dozens of fugitive youths to rob and kill people,
taking their belongings for pleasure.
Over a hundred murders were discovered,
and the whole kingdom knew of it,
daring not to travel at night.
The sons of the victims submitted reports.
The Hàn authorities requested his execution,
but the emperor could not bear it,
deposing him as a commoner,
and exiling him to Shàngyōng,
his territory incorporated into Hàn,
as Dàhé Commandery.
As for King Āi Dìng of Shānyáng,
he was a son of King Xiào of Liáng,
enfeoffed as King of Shānyáng in the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng's middle period.
He died after nine years,
without a son,
so his kingdom was abolished,
and the territory incorporated into Hàn,
as Shānyáng Commandery.
As for King Āi Bùshí of Jìyīn,
he was a son of King Xiào of Liáng,
enfeoffed as King of Jìyīn in the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng's middle period.
He died after one year,
without a son,
so his kingdom was abolished,
and the territory incorporated into Hàn,
as Jìyīn Commandery.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Although King Xiào of Liáng, due to familial affection,
was enfeoffed with fertile lands,
yet encountering the prosperity of the Hàn house,
and the people's wealth,
he was able to amass great riches,
expand his palaces,
and have carriages and attire rivaling the Son of Heaven's.
But this was indeed presumptuous.
Mr. Chǔ added:
When I served as a court attendant,
I heard this story from elderly officials in the palace who enjoyed recounting such tales.
I privately believe that the resentment of Liáng Xiàowáng,
and his intention to commit wrongful acts,
stemmed from these circumstances.
The Empress Dowager,
being a female ruler,
out of affection for her youngest son,
wished to make the King of Liáng the crown prince.
The ministers failed to timely articulate the reasons against it,
instead flattering and focusing on trivial matters,
seeking personal favor to receive rewards—
this was not the conduct of loyal officials.
If they had been as upright as Dòu Yīng, the Marquis of Wèijī,
how could subsequent disasters have occurred?
When Emperor Jǐng met with the king privately,
and they drank in attendance upon the Empress Dowager,
Emperor Jǐng said:
"After a thousand autumns and ten thousand years, I will pass the throne to you."
The Empress Dowager was delighted.
But Dòu Yīng, standing before them,
knelt and declared:
"By the laws of Hàn,
the throne passes to the son or rightful grandson.
How can Your Majesty pass it to a younger brother,
willfully violating the covenant of Emperor Gāo?"
At this, Emperor Jǐng fell silent.
The Empress Dowager was displeased.
Thus, when King Chéng stood under a tree with his young brother,
plucked a paulownia leaf, and gave it to him,
saying:
"I enfeoff you with this,"
the Duke of Zhōu, upon hearing of it,
came to see the king and said:
"The Son of Heaven enfeoffing his brother
is most commendable."
King Chéng replied:
"I was only joking."
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"A ruler should not make improper moves,
nor should he speak in jest.
What is said must be carried out."
Thereupon, he enfeoffed the younger brother with the territory of Yìng County.
From then on, King Chéng never dared to speak jestingly for the rest of his life;
his words were always followed by action.
The "Classic of Filial Piety" states:
"Do not speak against the law,
do not act against the Way."
These are the wise words of the sages.
Now, the emperor should not have made such promises to the King of Liáng.
The King of Liáng, backed by the weight of the Empress Dowager's authority,
had long been arrogant and unruly.
Repeatedly hearing Emperor Jǐng's promises
that after millennia he would pass the throne to him,
yet seeing no fulfillment,
moreover, when feudal lords came to court to see the Son of Heaven,
by Hàn law, they were to have only four audiences.
Upon arrival,
a minor audience;
on the first day of the first month,
presenting furs and jade pendants to celebrate the new year,
a formal audience;
three days later,
a banquet held for the king,
bestowing gold, coins, and goods;
two days after that,
another minor audience,
before departure.
In all, their stay in Cháng'ān did not exceed twenty days.
A minor audience meant
a private meeting within the palace gates,
drinking in the inner chambers,
not a place ordinary officials could enter.
But when the King of Liáng came to court in the west,
he stayed on,
for almost half a year.
Inside, he rode in the same carriage as the emperor;
outside, he shared the same chariot.
To raise expectations with grand words yet not fulfill them,
leading to grievances,
plots of rebellion,
and then to worry about the consequences—
is that not misguided?
Unless one is a truly virtuous person,
one does not understand yielding and humility.
According to the current rituals and laws of Hàn,
those coming to court to celebrate the new year
usually include one king and four marquises together,
once every ten years or so.
Yet the King of Liáng often came to court year after year,
and stayed long.
As the saying goes,
"A spoiled child is unfilial"—
this is not harsh criticism.
Therefore, for feudal kings, good tutors should be appointed,
and chancellors who speak loyal words,
such as Jí Àn,
Hán Chángrú, and others,
daring to admonish directly and firmly—
how could troubles arise then?
He reigned for forty-two years and died,
whereupon his son, Prince Āi Chāng, succeeded him.
After one year, he died,
and his son Kūnchǐ became the King of Zhōngshān.
The kings of these two states were originally sons of Lady Jiǎ.
King Dìng of Chángshā, Fā,
whose mother was Táng Jī,
formerly a maidservant of Chéng Jī.
When Emperor Jǐng summoned Chéng Jī,
she was avoiding something,
unwilling to attend,
so she dressed her maidservant Táng'ér and sent her in at night.
The emperor was drunk and unaware,
mistaking her for Chéng Jī and favored her,
resulting in pregnancy.
Only later did he realize it was not Chéng Jī.
When the child was born,
he was named Fā.
In the second year of the Qián era of Emperor Jǐng, he was made King of Chángshā as an imperial son.
Because his mother was of low status,
and not favored,
he was enfeoffed in a low-lying, damp, and poor kingdom.
He reigned for twenty-seven years and died,
and his son King Kāng Yōng succeeded him.
After twenty-eight years,
he died, and his son Fùjū became King of Chángshā.
The king of this state was originally the son of Táng Jī.
King Huì of Guǎngchuān, Yuè,
in the second year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng, was made King of Guǎngchuān as an imperial son.
He reigned for twelve years and died,
and his son Qí became king.
Qí had a favored minister named Sāng Jù.
Later, when Jù committed a crime,
and the king wanted to execute him,
Jù fled,
so the king captured his clan.
Jù resented the king,
and submitted a report accusing King Qí of incest with his siblings.
From then on,
King Qí repeatedly submitted reports accusing Hàn ministers and favored officials like Suǒ Zhōng.
King Kāng of Jiāodōng, Jì,
in the second year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng, was made King of Jiāodōng as an imperial son.
He reigned for twenty-eight years and died.
When the King of Huáinán plotted rebellion,
Jì secretly heard of it,
and privately prepared chariots, arrows, and defenses,
awaiting Huáinán's uprising.
When officials investigated Huáinán's case,
his involvement was revealed.
Jì was the closest to the emperor,
who was grieved by this,
and Jì fell ill and died,
not daring to appoint an heir.
The emperor learned of this.
Jì had an eldest son named Xián,
whose mother was not favored;
and a younger son named Qìng,
whose mother was loved and favored.
Jì often wished to establish him,
but it was improper,
and due to his own faults,
he never spoke of it.
The emperor pitied him,
and made Xián King of Jiāodōng to continue King Kāng's line,
while enfeoffing Qìng in the former Héngshān territory,
as King of Lìù'ān.
King Xián of Jiāodōng reigned for fourteen years and died,
posthumously titled Prince Āi.
His son Qìng became king.
King Qìng of Lìù'ān,
in the second year of the Yuánshòu era, was made King of Lìù'ān as the son of King Kāng of Jiāodōng.
Prince Āi of Qīnghé, Chéng,
in the third year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng, was made King of Qīnghé as an imperial son.
He reigned for twelve years and died,
leaving no heir,
so the kingdom was abolished,
its land incorporated into Hàn,
becoming Qīnghé Commandery.
King Xiàn of Chángshān, Shùn,
in the fifth year of the Zhōng era of Emperor Jǐng, was made King of Chángshān as an imperial son.
Shùn was the closest to the emperor,
being Emperor Jǐng's youngest son,
but he was arrogant, lazy, and promiscuous,
frequently breaking laws,
though the emperor often pardoned him.
He reigned for thirty-two years and died,
and his heir apparent Bó succeeded him as king.
Initially,
King Xiàn Shùn had an unloved concubine who bore his eldest son Tuō.
Because his mother was not favored,
Tuō also did not gain the king's favor.
The queen, Xiū, bore the heir apparent Bó.
The king had many concubines,
and his favored ones bore sons Píng
and Shāng,
so the queen was rarely favored.
When King Xiàn was gravely ill,
his favored concubines often attended him,
while the queen, out of jealousy, seldom attended,
often returning to her quarters.
When medicine was presented,
the heir apparent Bó neither tasted it himself
nor stayed to attend the illness.
After the king died,
the queen
and heir apparent only then arrived.
King Xiàn never regarded his eldest son Tuō as worthy,
and upon his death,
left him no share of wealth.
A courtier advised the heir apparent
and queen
to let all sons share the wealth with Tuō,
but the heir apparent
and queen refused.
When the heir apparent succeeded,
he did not care for Tuō.
Tuō resented the queen
and heir apparent.
When Hàn envoys observed King Xiàn's funeral,
Tuō reported that during the king's illness,
the queen
and heir apparent did not attend him,
and after his death,
within six days, they left their posts,
with heir apparent Bó engaging in illicit affairs,
drinking and gambling,
playing the zhù,
riding with women,
circling the city and passing through markets,
and visiting prisons to see prisoners.
The emperor sent the senior minister Qián to investigate the queen and question King Bó,
requesting the arrest of Bó's accomplices and witnesses,
but the king hid them.
When officials urgently sought to capture Bó,
he had people beat and torture them,
and arbitrarily released prisoners suspected by Hàn.
The officials requested the execution of Queen Xiū and King Bó.
The emperor, considering Xiū's longstanding misconduct
and that Tuō had framed her,
and that Bó lacked proper mentors,
could not bear to execute them.
The officials requested the deposition of Queen Xiū
and the exile of King Bó with his family to Fánglíng,
which the emperor approved.
Bó reigned for several months,
was moved to Fánglíng,
and the kingdom was extinguished.
Over a month later,
the emperor, due to closeness,
ordered the officials:
"King Xiàn of Chángshān died early,
his consorts were discordant,
heirs and concubines accused and contended,
leading to injustice and the kingdom's fall;
I deeply pity this.
Let 30,000 households be enfeoffed to King Xiàn's son Píng,
as King of Zhēndìng;
and 30,000 households to his son Shāng,
as King of Sìshuǐ."
King Píng of Zhēndìng,
in the fourth year of the Yuándǐng era, was made King of Zhēndìng as the son of King Xiàn of Chángshān.
King Sī of Sìshuǐ, Shāng,
in the fourth year of the Yuándǐng era, was made King of Sìshuǐ as the son of King Xiàn of Chángshān.
He reigned for eleven years and died,
and his son Prince Āi Ānshì succeeded him.
After eleven years, he died,
leaving no son.
The emperor, pitying the extinction of Sìshuǐ's line,
then made Ānshì's younger brother Hè King of Sìshuǐ.
The kings of these four states were originally sons of Lady Wáng Érxū.
Later, Hàn further enfeoffed their collateral sons as kings of Lìù'ān
and Sìshuǐ, two states.
In all, the descendants of Érxū
now number six kings.
The Grand Historian remarks:
During Emperor Gāozǔ's time, all feudal lords collected taxes,
and could appoint officials below the position of Nèishǐ themselves.
Only for the Hàn court did they appoint the Chancellor,
with a gold seal.
The feudal lords themselves appointed their Yùshǐ,
Tíngwèizhèng,
and Bóshì,
modeling themselves after the Son of Heaven.
After the rebellion of Wú and Chǔ,
through the reigns of the Five Clans and Kings,
the Hàn court appointed the two-thousand-shí officials for them,
removing
"Chéngxiàng"
and calling it
"Xiàng",
with a silver seal.
The feudal lords only received rental taxes,
their power taken away.
After that, some of the impoverished feudal lords even rode in ox carts.
"Great Marshal Chén Qùbì, risking death, bows repeatedly to submit a memorial to His Majesty the Emperor:
Your Majesty has overestimated me,
appointing Chén Qùbì to await punishment amidst the ranks.
I should focus solely on border defense concerns,
with my bones exposed in the wilderness, unable to repay,
yet I dare to consider other matters to trouble those in charge,
truly seeing that Your Majesty worries and toils for the world,
pities the common people to the point of forgetting yourself,
reducing meals and cutting back on music,
decreasing the number of court attendants.
The imperial princes, blessed by heaven,
are able to wear robes and perform bows,
yet to this day have no titles, positions, or tutorial officials.
Your Majesty is modest and yielding, not attending to this,
while the ministers privately hope,
but dare not overstep their duties to speak.
I secretly cannot contain my loyal heart,
and risk death to wish that Your Majesty orders the responsible officials,
to establish the positions of the imperial princes during this auspicious midsummer time.
I only hope Your Majesty will kindly consider.
Chén Qùbì, risking death, bows repeatedly to report to His Majesty the Emperor."
On the yǐhài day of the third month,
Acting Imperial Secretary Chén Guāng, serving as Shàngshū Lìng, presented the memorial at Wèiyāng Palace.
The edict said:
"Refer to the Imperial Secretary."
On the sixth year, third month, wùshēn being the first day,
yǐhài,
Acting Imperial Secretary Chén Guāng, serving as Shàngshū Lìng,
and Assistant Chén Fēi,
upon the document reaching the Imperial Secretary,
stated:
"Chancellor Chén Qīngdí,
Imperial Secretary Grandee Chén Tāng,
Grand Master of Ceremonies Chén Chōng,
Grand Herald Chén Xī,
and Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent Chén Ān, acting as Director of the Imperial Clan, risk death to memorialize:
Great Marshal Qùbì submitted a memorial saying:
'Your Majesty has overestimated me,
appointing Chén Qùbì to await punishment amidst the ranks.
I should focus solely on border defense concerns,
with my bones exposed in the wilderness, unable to repay,
yet I dare to consider other matters to trouble those in charge,
truly seeing that Your Majesty worries and toils for the world,
pities the common people to the point of forgetting yourself,
reducing meals and cutting back on music,
decreasing the number of court attendants.
The imperial princes, blessed by heaven,
are able to wear robes and perform bows,
yet to this day have no titles, positions, or tutorial officials.
Your Majesty is modest and yielding, not attending to this,
while the ministers privately hope,
but dare not overstep their duties to speak.
I secretly cannot contain my loyal heart,
and risk death to wish that Your Majesty orders the responsible officials,
to establish the positions of the imperial princes during this auspicious midsummer time.
I only hope Your Majesty will kindly consider.'
The edict said
'Refer to the Imperial Secretary'.
We carefully deliberated with the fully two-thousand-shí officials,
two-thousand-shí official Chén Hè, and others:
In ancient times, land was divided to establish states,
and feudal lords were set up to serve the Son of Heaven,
in order to honor the ancestral temple and value the altars of land and grain.
Now Chén Qùbì's memorial,
not forgetting his duty,
thereby proclaims grace,
and speaks of the Son of Heaven humbling himself to toil for the world,
concerned that the imperial princes have no titles or positions.
We, Qīngdí,
Tāng, and others, should uphold righteousness and adhere to our duties,
but are foolish and unable to manage affairs.
Now during this auspicious midsummer time,
we, Qīngdí,
Tāng, and others, risk death to request the establishment of the imperial princes Chén Hóng,
Chén Dàn,
and Chén Xū as feudal kings.
We risk death to request the names of the states to be established."
The edict said:
"I have heard that Zhōu enfeoffed eight hundred,
with the Jī surname all ranked,
some as zǐ,
nán, or attached territories.
The Rites
say 'A branch son does not sacrifice.'
It is said that establishing feudal lords is to value the altars of land and grain,
but I have not heard of this.
Moreover, heaven did not create the people for the ruler.
I lack virtue,
and the realm is not yet harmonized,
yet to force uneducated ones to rule connected cities,
how would that encourage my ministers?
Let it be reconsidered to enfeoff them as lièhóu."
On the bǐngzǐ day of the third month,
the memorial was presented at Wèiyāng Palace.
"Chancellor Chén Qīngdí,
Imperial Secretary Grandee Chén Tāng, risk death to state:
We carefully deliberated with Lièhóu Chén Yīngqí,
fully two-thousand-shí and two-thousand-shí official Chén Hè,
Grandee Remonstrant and Bóshì Chén Ān, and others, saying:
We have humbly heard that Zhōu enfeoffed eight hundred,
with the Jī surname all ranked,
serving the Son of Heaven.
Kāng Shū was honored due to his ancestors,
and Bó Qín was established because of the Duke of Zhōu,
all becoming feudal lords of established states,
with assistants as tutors.
All officials upheld the laws,
each adhering to their duties,
and the state's system was complete.
We humbly believe that establishing feudal lords to value the altars of land and grain means
that all feudal lords under heaven each perform their duties in offering tribute and sacrifices.
Branch sons cannot perform sacrifices to the ancestral temple,
as is proper in the rites.
Enfeoffment makes them guard the border states,
which is how emperors and kings support virtue and spread transformation.
Your Majesty upholds heaven's mandate,
brightly opening the sagely lineage,
honoring the worthy and highlighting achievements,
reviving the extinct and continuing the severed.
Continuing Xiāo Wénzhōng's line in Cuó,
praising and encouraging ministers like Píngjīn Hóu.
Clarifying the order of the six relations,
illuminating the categories of heavenly bestowal,
allowing feudal kings and enfeeffed lords to extend personal grace to divide lands among their sons and brothers,
granting titles and honorably establishing over a hundred states.
But to enfeoff the imperial princes as lièhóu,
would mean the noble and humble transgress,
ranks lose order,
and it cannot be handed down for ten thousand generations.
We request to establish Chén Hóng,
Chén Dàn,
Chén Xū as feudal kings."
On the bǐngzǐ day of the third month,
the memorial was presented at Wèiyāng Palace.
The edict said:
"Kāng Shū had ten relatives but only he was honored,
because virtue was praised.
The Duke of Zhōu sacrificed to heaven in the suburbs,
so Lǔ had white male and
red purebred animals.
Other lords had non-pure-colored ones,
showing the difference between worthy and unworthy.
'Look up to the high mountain,
strive towards the great path',
I greatly admire this.
Therefore, to restrain the immature,
enfeoffing them as lièhóu is acceptable."
On the day Wùyín in the fourth month,
a memorial was submitted to the Wèiyāng Palace.
"We, your subjects, the Chancellor Qīng Dí
and the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Tāng, venture to state at the risk of our lives:
We, Qīng Dí and others, along with the marquises,
officials of two-thousand-dan rank,
Grand Masters of Remonstrance,
and Erudite Qìng and others, have deliberated:
We venture to memorialize at the risk of our lives to request the enfeoffment of the imperial princes as feudal kings.
The imperial decree stated:
'Kāng Shū had ten relatives, yet he alone was honored,
to commend his virtue.
The Duke of Zhōu performed sacrifices to Heaven in the suburbs,
hence Lǔ had white male and
red purebred sacrificial animals.
Other lords did not have such offerings,
showing the distinction between the worthy and unworthy.
"I look up to the high mountain,
I aspire to the great path,"
We greatly admire this.
Therefore, to restrain the immature,
enfeoffing them as marquises is acceptable.'
We, your subjects Qīng Dí,
Tāng,
and Erudite Jiàng Xíng and others, have humbly learned that Kāng Shū had ten relatives,
King Wǔ succeeded to the throne,
the Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng,
and eight of them were enfeoffed as great states due to the honor of their ancestors.
Kāng Shū was young in years,
the Duke of Zhōu held the position of one of the Three Dukes,
and Bó Qín held the state of Lǔ,
likely because at the time of their enfeoffment,
they had not yet reached adulthood.
Later, Kāng Shū defended against the rebellion of Lù Fù,
and Bó Qín quelled the Huáiyí rebellion.
In ancient times, the Five Emperors had different systems,
the Zhōu dynasty had five ranks of nobility,
