the Spring and Autumn period had three ranks,
all arranged according to the times to order honor and humility.
Emperor Gāo brought order from chaos and returned to correctness,
manifested supreme virtue,
stabilized the realm,
enfeoffed feudal lords,
with two ranks of nobility.
Imperial princes were sometimes enfeoffed as feudal kings while still in swaddling clothes,
to serve the Son of Heaven,
as an eternal model,
which cannot be changed.
Your Majesty personally practices benevolence and righteousness,
embodies and acts with sage virtue,
combining civil and martial virtues inwardly and outwardly.
You manifest acts of kindness and filial piety,
and broaden the path for the worthy and capable.
Internally, you commend the virtuous,
externally, you punish the strong and violent.
You reach the Northern Sea,
penetrate the Yuèzhī in the west,
the Xiōngnú,
and the Western Regions,
with the whole country supplying the armies.
The expenses for vehicles and equipment,
are not levied from the people.
You empty the stores of the imperial treasury to reward the commanders,
open the prohibited granaries to relieve the poor,
and reduce the garrison troops by half.
The rulers of the hundred barbarian tribes,
all turn to your influence,
receiving your grace and expressing satisfaction.
Distant regions with different customs,
send repeated translations to pay court,
your grace extends beyond the borders.
Thus, rare beasts arrive,
auspicious grains flourish,
and Heaven's response is very clear.
Now, the collateral sons of feudal lords are enfeoffed as feudal kings,
while the imperial princes are made marquises,
we, your subjects Qīng Dí,
Tāng and others, have secretly and carefully considered this,
and all believe it disrupts the order of honor and humility,
causing disappointment throughout the land,
which is not permissible.
We request to enfeoff our subjects Hóng,
Dàn,
and Xū as feudal kings."
On the day Guǐwèi in the fourth month,
the memorial was submitted to the Wèiyāng Palace,
but it was retained in the palace and not issued.
"We, your subjects, the Chancellor Qīng Dí,
the Grand Coachman Hè,
the Grand Minister of Ceremonies Chōng acting as Imperial Censor-in-Chief,
and the Junior Tutor of the Crown Prince Ān acting as Director of the Imperial Clan, venture to state at the risk of our lives:
We, Qīng Dí and others, previously memorialized that the Grand Marshal Qùbì submitted a memorial stating,
the imperial princes have no titles or positions,
we respectfully, along with the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Tāng,
officials of fully two-thousand-dan rank,
two-thousand-dan rank officials,
Grand Masters of Remonstrance,
and Erudite Qìng and others, venture at the risk of our lives to request the enfeoffment of the imperial princes Hóng and others as feudal kings.
Your Majesty declined in civil and martial matters,
personally criticized yourself,
and mentioned the imperial princes' lack of education.
The deliberations of your ministers,
where Confucian scholars expound their doctrines,
sometimes confuse their minds.
Your Majesty firmly declined and did not consent,
enfeoffing the imperial princes as marquises.
We, Qīng Dí and others, secretly deliberated with the marquis Shòuchéng and twenty-six others,
and all said that it disrupts the order of honor and humility.
Emperor Gāo established the empire,
becoming the Great Ancestor of Hàn,
enfeoffing his sons and grandsons,
to broaden the branches and supports.
The laws and institutions of the former emperors should not be changed,
to proclaim the utmost honor.
We request to order the court historians to select an auspicious day,
prepare the rituals and ceremonies for submission,
the imperial censors to submit the maps,
all else as in previous precedents."
The imperial decree stated:
"Approved."
On the day Bǐngshēn in the fourth month,
a memorial was submitted to the Wèiyāng Palace.
"I, your subject, the Grand Coachman Hè acting as Imperial Censor-in-Chief, venture to state at the risk of my life:
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies Chōng reported that divination selected the twenty-eighth day of the fourth month, Yǐsì,
as suitable for enfeoffing feudal kings.
I venture to submit the maps at the risk of my life,
requesting the names for the states to be established.
The rituals and ceremonies will be submitted separately.
I venture to request at the risk of my life."
The imperial decree stated:
"Enfeoff the prince Hóng as King of Qí,
Dàn as King of Yān,
and Xū as King of Guǎnglíng."
On the day Dīngyǒu in the fourth month,
a memorial was submitted to the Wèiyāng Palace.
In the sixth year, the fourth month began on Wùyín, the new moon day,
Guǐmǎo,
the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Tāng issued the decree to the Chancellor,
the Chancellor issued it to the fully two-thousand-dan rank officials,
the two-thousand-dan rank officials issued it to the commandery governors
and feudal chancellors,
the documents were executed by those responsible as applicable.
In accordance with the statutes and ordinances.
"On the day Yǐsì in the fourth month of the sixth year,
the Emperor sent the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Tāng to the temple to enfeoff his son Hóng as King of Qí.
He said: Ah,
young son Hóng,
receive this green altar!
We inherit from our ancestors,
following antiquity to establish your state,
enfeoffing you in the eastern land,
for generations to be a bulwark and support of Hàn.
Ah, remember this!
Revere Our decree,
for the Mandate is not constant.
If one loves virtue,
one can manifest brightness.
If one does not plan for righteousness,
it causes the noble to neglect.
Devote your heart fully,
sincerely hold to the mean,
and Heaven's favor will be eternal.
If you have faults and do not improve,
then disaster will come to your state,
and harm to your person.
Ah,
protect the state and nurture the people,
can you not be reverent!
Let the King be warned."
The above is the decree for the King of Qí.
Bó Yí and
Shū Qí
were the two sons of the Lord of Gūzhú.
Their father wished to establish Shū Qí as his heir,
but when the father died,
Shū Qí yielded to Bó Yí.
Bó Yí said:
"It was our father's command."
Thereupon he fled and left.
Shū Qí likewise refused to take the throne and fled.
The people of the state installed their middle brother.
Thereupon Bó Yí and
Shū Qí heard that Xībó Chāng was good at caring for the elderly,
so why not go and join him?
When they arrived,
Xībó had died,
and King Wǔ was carrying the wooden spirit tablet,
proclaiming him King Wén,
and marching east to attack Zhòu.
Bó Yí and
Shū Qí grasped the horse's reins and remonstrated, saying:
"Your father has died and is not yet buried,
yet you take up arms—
can this be called filial?
As a subject to assassinate your sovereign—
can this be called benevolent?"
The attendants wished to strike them down.
Tàigōng said:
"These are righteous men."
He helped them up and sent them away.
After King Wǔ had quelled the turmoil in Yīn,
all under heaven pledged allegiance to Zhōu,
but Bó Yí and
Shū Qí were ashamed of this,
and on principle would not eat the grain of Zhōu,
so they hid on Shǒuyáng Mountain,
gathering ferns to eat.
When they were starving and near death,
they composed a song.
Its words said:
"We climb that western mountain,
and pick its ferns.
Replacing violence with violence,
they do not realize their error.
Shénnóng, Yú, and Xià have suddenly vanished—
where shall we turn?
Alas, we go to our death,
our fate is衰败!"
Thereupon they starved to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain.
From this perspective,
is it resentment or not?
Some say:
"The Way of Heaven is impartial,
yet it often sides with the good."
As for Bó Yí and
Shū Qí,
can they be called good men or not?
They accumulated benevolence and purified their conduct to such an extent, yet starved to death!
Moreover, among the seventy disciples,
Zhòngní singled out Yán Yuān as fond of learning.
Yet Huí was often in want,
not even having enough chaff and husks to eat,
and died prematurely.
How does Heaven reward the good?
What is it like?
Robber Zhí daily killed the innocent,
ate human livers,
was cruel and tyrannical,
gathered a band of several thousand to rampage across the land,
yet he died of old age.
By what virtue did he follow?
These are particularly clear and evident cases.
As for recent times,
those whose conduct is improper,
who deliberately violate taboos,
yet enjoy comfort and pleasure all their lives,
with wealth and influence lasting for generations without end—
or those who choose their steps carefully,
speak only at the right time,
do not take shortcuts in their actions,
and do not express indignation except in the cause of justice,
yet encounter disaster and misfortune—
such cases are too numerous to count.
I am deeply perplexed by this.
If this is the so-called Way of Heaven,
is it right or wrong?
The Master said:
"Those who follow different ways do not take counsel together,"
each follows his own aspirations.
Therefore it is said:
"If wealth and honor were attainable,
even as a lowly carriage driver,
I would do it.
If they are not attainable,
I follow what I love."
"When the year grows cold,
then we know the pine and cypress are the last to wither."
When the whole world is turbid,
then the pure scholar appears.
Is it because they value what others despise,
and despise what others value?
"The gentleman hates the thought of dying without his name being celebrated."
Master Jiǎ said:
"The greedy die for wealth,
the martyrs die for fame,
the vainglorious die for power,
the common people cling to life."
"Like brightness illuminates like,
like kinds seek each other out."
"Clouds follow the dragon,
wind follows the tiger,
the sage arises and all things become visible."
Though Bó Yí and
Shū Qí were worthy,
it was through the Master that their names became more illustrious.
Though Yán Yuān was devoted to learning,
he attached himself to the horse's tail and his deeds became more manifest.
Hermits in mountain caves,
their choices of timing are like this—
their kind often perish nameless and uncelebrated,
how sad!
Commoners in alleyways
who wish to cultivate their conduct and establish their names—
unless they attach themselves to men of high standing,
how can their fame be transmitted to later ages?
Guǎn Zhòng, named Yíwú,
was a man of Yǐngshàng.
In his youth he often associated with Bào Shūyá,
and Bào Shū recognized his worth.
Guǎn Zhòng was poor and hard-pressed,
and often took advantage of Bào Shū,
but Bào Shū always treated him well,
and never complained about it.
Later, Bào Shū served Prince Xiǎobái of Qí,
while Guǎn Zhòng served Prince Jiǔ.
When Xiǎobái was established as Duke Huán,
Prince Jiǔ died,
and Guǎn Zhòng was imprisoned.
Bào Shū then recommended Guǎn Zhòng.
After Guǎn Zhòng was employed,
he administered the government of Qí,
and Duke Huán of Qí became hegemon,
nine times assembling the feudal lords,
and unifying all under heaven—
this was due to Guǎn Zhòng's strategies.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"When I was first in distress,
I once did business with Bào Shū,
and when dividing the profits I took more for myself—
Bào Shū did not consider me greedy,
for he knew I was poor.
I once planned affairs for Bào Shū but made them worse—
Bào Shū did not consider me foolish,
for he knew the times were sometimes favorable, sometimes not.
I once held office three times and was dismissed three times by my lord—
Bào Shū did not consider me incompetent,
for he knew I had not met with the right time.
I once fought three battles and fled three times—
Bào Shū did not consider me cowardly,
for he knew I had an old mother.
When Prince Jiǔ was defeated,
Zhào Hū died for him,
while I endured the shame of imprisonment—
Bào Shū did not consider me shameless,
for he knew I was not ashamed of small matters but ashamed that my achievements and fame were not manifest to the world.
Those who gave me life are my parents,
but he who knows me is Bào Zǐ."
After Bào Shū had recommended Guǎn Zhòng,
he placed himself beneath him.
His descendants enjoyed hereditary emoluments in Qí for generations,
with fiefs for over ten generations,
and were often famous great officers.
The world praises not so much Guǎn Zhòng's worth as Bào Shū's ability to recognize men.
When Guǎn Zhòng assumed the administration and became chancellor of Qí,
with that tiny state of Qí situated by the sea,
he facilitated trade and accumulated wealth,
enriching the state and strengthening its military,
aligning with the customs and preferences of the people.
Therefore, he is quoted as saying:
"When granaries are full, the people understand propriety and moderation;
when they are well-fed and clothed, they know honor and shame.
If the ruler observes proper measures, the six relationships will be secure.
If the four cardinal principles are not upheld,
the state will perish.
Issue orders as if from the source of a flowing stream,
making them conform to the people's hearts."
Thus, his policies were humble and easy to implement.
What the people desired,
he accordingly provided;
what the people rejected,
he accordingly removed.
In his governance,
he excelled at turning calamity into blessing,
and transforming defeat into success.
He valued the balance of priorities,
and was cautious in weighing decisions.
Duke Huán was truly angered by Shào Jī,
and attacked Cài to the south;
Guǎn Zhòng used this to launch a campaign against Chǔ,
reproaching them for not offering tribute of bundled thatch to the Zhōu court.
Duke Huán indeed campaigned north against the Shān Róng,
and Guǎn Zhòng thereby had Yān restore the governance of Shào Gōng.
At the meeting in Kē,
Duke Huán intended to break the covenant with Cáo Mèi,
but Guǎn Zhòng used the situation to establish trust,
and from then on, the feudal lords turned to Qí.
Hence it is said:
"To know that giving is taking—
that is the treasure of governance."
Guǎn Zhòng's wealth rivaled that of the ducal house,
with three returns and
a reversed stand for cups,
yet the people of Qí did not consider him extravagant.
After Guǎn Zhòng's death,
Qí continued to follow his policies,
often dominating among the feudal lords.
Over a hundred years later, there was Yàn Zǐ.
Yàn Píngzhòng Yīng
was a man from Yíwéi in Lái.
He served under Duke Líng,
Duke Zhuāng,
and Duke Jǐng of Qí,
and was esteemed in Qí for his frugality and diligent efforts.
Once he became chancellor of Qí,
he did not eat more than one meat dish,
and his concubines did not wear silk.
At court,
when the ruler spoke to him,
he responded with upright words;
when not spoken to,
he conducted himself with upright actions.
When the state was well-ordered,
he followed commands;
when it was not,
he weighed them carefully.
Through this, he gained renown among the feudal lords for three generations.
Yuè Shífù was a worthy man
imprisoned in fetters.
When Yàn Zǐ went out,
he encountered him on the road,
untied his left trace horse to ransom him,
and brought him home.
Without thanking him,
Yàn Zǐ entered his inner chamber.
After some time,
Yuè Shífù requested to sever ties.
Yàn Zǐ was startled,
straightened his clothes and cap, and apologized, saying:
"Although I, Yīng, am not benevolent,
I rescued you from distress;
why do you seek to break off so quickly?"
Shífù said:
"Not so.
I have heard that a gentleman may be misunderstood by those who do not know him but trusted by those who do.
When I was in fetters,
they did not know me.
Since you, sir, were moved to ransom me,
that means you know me;
yet to know me and show no courtesy—
it would surely be better to remain in fetters."
Yàn Zǐ then invited him in as an honored guest.
When Yàn Zǐ was chancellor of Qí,
as he went out, his charioteer's wife watched her husband through a crack in the gate.
Her husband, driving for the chancellor,
holding a large canopy,
whipping the team of four horses,
was buoyant in spirit,
very self-satisfied.
When he returned home,
his wife requested to leave him.
The husband asked the reason.
The wife said:
"Yàn Zǐ is not even six chǐ tall,
yet as chancellor of Qí,
his name is renowned among the feudal lords.
Today I observed him going out,
his thoughts profound,
always humble.
Now you are eight chǐ tall,
yet you serve as a servant driving a chariot,
and you seem so content with yourself,
that is why I wish to leave."
Thereafter, the husband restrained his pride.
Yàn Zǐ, surprised, asked him about it,
and the charioteer truthfully replied.
Yàn Zǐ recommended him for the position of senior official.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I have read Guǎn's "Mùmín,"
"Shān Gāo,"
"Chéng Mǎ,"
"Qīng Zhòng,"
"Jiǔ Fǔ,"
and the "Yànzǐ Chūnqiū,"
how detailed their words are!
Having seen their writings,
I wished to observe their deeds,
hence I compiled their biographies.
As for their books,
they are widely available in the world,
so I do not discuss them here,
but rather their anecdotes.
Guǎn Zhòng is what the world calls a worthy minister,
yet Confucius belittled him.
Was it because, with the Way of Zhōu in decline,
and Duke Huán being capable,
he did not urge him to become a true king,
but only to hegemony?
As the saying goes,
"To follow and promote their virtues,
to correct and save them from faults,
so that above and below can be close."
Is this not what is said of Guǎn Zhòng?
When Yàn Zǐ threw himself over Duke Zhuāng's corpse and wept,
completing the rites before leaving,
was this not what is called
"seeing what is right and not doing it is cowardice"
indeed?
As for his remonstrance,
braving the ruler's displeasure,
this is what is called
"in office, think of loyalty;
out of office, think of making amends"
indeed!
If Yàn Zǐ were still alive,
even if I had to hold the whip for him,
I would rejoice and admire him.
Lǎo Zǐ
was a man from Qǔrén Lane, Lì Village, Kǔ County, in Chǔ,
surnamed Lǐ,
named Ěr,
styled Dān,
and served as the historian in charge of the imperial archives of Zhōu.
Confucius went to Zhōu,
intending to ask Lǎo Zǐ about the rites.
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"What you speak of—
the men and their bones have long decayed,
only their words remain.
Moreover, a gentleman, when the time is right, rides in a carriage;
when it is not, he drifts like the tumbleweed.
I have heard that
a good merchant hides his treasures as if empty,
a gentleman of great virtue appears as if foolish.
Rid yourself of arrogance and many desires,
pretentious airs and excessive ambitions—
these are of no benefit to you.
What I have to tell you,
is just this."
Confucius left,
and said to his disciples:
"Birds,
I know they can fly;
fish, I know they can swim;
beasts, I know they can run.
For runners, I can set nets;
for swimmers, I can use lines;
for flyers, I can make arrows.
But as for the dragon,
I cannot know how it rides the wind and clouds to ascend to heaven.
Today I met Lǎo Zǐ—
is he not like a dragon!"
Lǎo Zǐ cultivated the Dào and Dé,
his teachings focusing on self-concealment and anonymity.
He resided in Zhōu for a long time,
witnessed its decline,
and then departed.
Upon reaching the pass,
the guardian of the pass, Yǐn Xǐ, said:
"You are about to withdraw into seclusion,
I insist you write a book for me."
Thereupon, Lǎo Zǐ wrote a book in two parts,
expounding the meaning of the Dào and Dé in over five thousand words, and then left,
with none knowing his final whereabouts.
Some say:
Lǎo Lái Zǐ was also a man of Chǔ,
author of fifteen essays,
discussing the application of Dàoist principles,
and was a contemporary of Kǒng Zǐ, it is said.
It is said that Lǎo Zǐ lived over one hundred and sixty years,
some say over two hundred years,
due to his cultivation of the Dào and nurturing longevity.
One hundred and twenty-nine years after Kǒng Zǐ's death,
the historian of Zhōu, Tài Shǐ Dān, met with Duke Xiàn of Qín and said:
"Initially, Qín and Zhōu were united,
united for five hundred years then separated,
after seventy years of separation, a hegemon king will arise."
Some say Dān was Lǎo Zǐ,
others say not,
the world does not know the truth of it.
Lǎo Zǐ
was a recluse gentleman.
Lǎo Zǐ's son was named Zōng,
Zōng became a general of Wèi,
and was enfeoffed at Duàn Gān.
Zōng's son was Zhù,
Zhù's son was Gōng,
Gōng's great-great-grandson was Jiǎ,
Jiǎ served under Emperor Wén of Hàn.
Jiǎ's son, Xiè, was the Grand Tutor to King Áng of Jiāo Xī,
thus establishing their family in Qí.
Those in the world who study Lǎo Zǐ's teachings often disparage Confucianism,
and Confucianism likewise disparages Lǎo Zǐ.
"Those who follow different Dàos do not take counsel together,"
is this not referring to such a case?
Lǐ Ěr advocated non-action leading to self-transformation,
and clarity and stillness leading to self-correction.
Zhuāng Zǐ
was a man of Méng,
named Zhōu.
Zhōu once served as an official in charge of the lacquer garden in Méng,
contemporary with King Huì of Liáng
and King Xuān of Qí.
His learning encompassed all without exception,
yet its essence fundamentally derived from the words of Lǎo Zǐ.
Thus, his writings amount to over one hundred thousand words,
mostly consisting of fables.
He composed "The Old Fisherman,"
"Robber Zhí,"
"Breaking into Trunks,"
to criticize the followers of Kǒng Zǐ,
and to elucidate the methods of Lǎo Zǐ.
Works like "Wèi Lěi Xū"
and "Kàng Sāng Zǐ"
are all empty words without factual basis.
Yet he was skilled at composing texts and arranging words,
pointing out matters and analogizing emotions,
using them to attack Confucianism
and Mohism, such that even the learned of his time could not defend themselves.
His words are vast and self-indulgent, suiting his own purposes,
thus even kings and nobles could not employ him.
King Wēi of Chǔ heard of Zhuāng Zhōu's worth,
sent an envoy with rich gifts to invite him,
promising to make him chancellor.
Zhuāng Zhōu laughed and said to the envoy of Chǔ:
"A thousand pieces of gold
are substantial profit;
the position of chancellor
is a respected office.
But have you not seen the sacrificial ox used in suburban sacrifices?
It is fed for several years,
clothed in embroidered silk,
and then taken into the great temple.
At that moment,
even if it wishes to be a lone piglet,
could it attain that?
You should leave quickly,
do not defile me.
I would rather amuse myself in the muddy ditches
than be constrained by the ruler of a state.
I will never hold office,
to satisfy my own aspirations."
Shēn Bù Hài
was a man of Jīng,
formerly a low-ranking official of Zhèng.
He studied statecraft to seek favor with Hán Zhāo Hóu,
who employed him as chancellor.
Internally, he cultivated governance and education,
externally, he dealt with the various feudal lords,
for fifteen years.
Throughout Shēn Zǐ's lifetime,
the state was well-ordered and the military strong,
with no one invading Hán.
Shēn Zǐ's learning was rooted in Huáng-Lǎo but emphasized xíngmíng.
He authored two essays,
titled "Shēn Zǐ."
Hán Fēi
was a scion of the Hán nobility.
He favored the studies of xíngmíng, laws, and methods,
yet his teachings ultimately derived from Huáng-Lǎo.
Fēi had a stutter
and could not speak well,
but was skilled at writing.
He and Lǐ Sī both studied under Xún Qīng,
and Sī considered himself inferior to Fēi.
Fēi, seeing Hán's weakening,
repeatedly admonished the King of Hán in writing,
but the King of Hán could not employ him.
Thereupon, Hán Fēi lamented that the state's governance did not focus on clarifying its laws and systems,
wielding authority to control its ministers,
enriching the state and strengthening the military, yet seeking to employ the worthy,
while instead promoting frivolous parasites over those with solid achievements.
He believed that Confucians used culture to disrupt laws,
while knights-errant used force to violate prohibitions.
In times of peace, the state honored those with reputations,
in times of crisis, it used armored warriors.
Now, those nurtured are not those used,
those used are not those nurtured.
Grieving that integrity and honesty were not tolerated by corrupt officials,
and observing the changes in past successes and failures,
he thus wrote "Solitary Indignation,"
"The Five Vermin,"
"Inner and Outer Storehouses,"
"Forest of Persuasions,"
and "The Difficulties of Persuasion," totaling over one hundred thousand words.
Yet Hán Fēi understood the difficulties of persuasion,
and wrote "The Difficulties of Persuasion" in great detail,
but ultimately died in Qín,
unable to save himself.
"The Difficulties of Persuasion" states:
Generally, the difficulty of persuasion
lies not in the difficulty of my knowledge being sufficient to persuade;
nor in the difficulty of my eloquence being able to clarify my intent;
nor in the difficulty of my daring to be unrestrained and exhaustive.
Generally, the difficulty of persuasion
lies in knowing the mind of the persuaded,
so that my persuasion can match it.
If the persuaded is motivated by a desire for high reputation,
but you persuade him with substantial profit,
then you will be seen as lowly and base,
and will certainly be rejected and distanced.
If the persuaded is motivated by substantial profit,
but you persuade him with high reputation,
then you will be seen as unrealistic and detached from reality,
and will certainly not be accepted.
If the persuaded secretly seeks substantial profit but overtly seeks high reputation,
and you persuade him with high reputation,
then he will overtly accept you but secretly distance you;
if you persuade him with substantial profit,
then he will covertly use your words but overtly reject you.
This is something one must understand.
Affairs succeed through secrecy,
and fail through leakage.
It is not necessarily that the person himself leaked it,
but if his words touch upon what is concealed,
in such cases, he is in danger.
If a noble has faults,
and the persuader explicitly speaks of what is good to expose his evils,
then he is in danger.
If the favor is not yet deep but one speaks to the utmost of his knowledge,
and if the advice is followed with success, the credit is forgotten;
if the advice is not followed and leads to failure, he is suspected—
in such cases, he is in danger.
If a noble has a plan and wishes to claim the merit for himself,
and the persuader is aware of it,
then he is in danger.
If the noble openly undertakes something,
yet actually does it for another reason,
and the persuader is aware of it,
then he is in danger.
To force someone to do what he absolutely will not do,
or to stop him from what he cannot cease doing,
endangers oneself.
Hence it is said:
If you discuss great men with him,
he thinks you are driving a wedge between you;
if you discuss petty men,
he thinks you are trafficking in power.
If you talk about his favorites,
he thinks you are seeking leverage;
if you talk about those he hates,
he thinks you are testing him.
If you make your words concise,
he thinks you ignorant and puts you down;
if you speak broadly and eloquently,
he finds it lengthy and tedious.
If you conform to the matter and state your ideas,
he says you are timid and not thorough;
if you consider matters broadly and freely,
he says you are crude and arrogant.
These are the difficulties of persuasion,
which one must not be unaware of.
The essence of all persuasion
lies in knowing how to embellish what the listener respects
and conceal what he finds shameful.
If he is confident in his own plans,
do not use his failures to corner him;
if he is proud of his decisiveness,
do not anger him by opposing it;
if he boasts of his strength,
do not challenge him with difficulties.
When planning different matters that align with his schemes,
or praising different people who share his conduct,
do so with embellishment that causes no harm.
If there is a shared mistake,
then clearly embellish it as no mistake.
Only when great loyalty meets no resistance,
and words encounter no rejection,
can one then fully express one's wisdom.
This is how to become close and trusted,
and to know the difficulty of exhausting one's knowledge.
After gaining time and long duration,
when the favor has become deep,
and deep plans are made without suspicion,
and debates occur without offense,
then one can clarify the advantages and disadvantages to achieve merit,
and directly point out right and wrong to refine one's character.
Maintaining this mutual stance,
is the success of persuasion.
Yǐ Yǐn worked as a cook,
Bǎi Lǐ Xī as a captive,
both thereby sought to approach their superiors.
Thus these two men,
both sages,
still could not avoid demeaning themselves to engage with the world in such lowly ways—
this is not what the capable official would devise.
In Sòng, there was a rich man,
whose wall collapsed due to rain.
His son said,
"If not repaired, there will be thieves,"
and his neighbor's father said the same.
That evening, he indeed lost much property,
and the family highly trusted their son but suspected the neighbor's father.
Long ago, Zhèng Wǔ Gōng wanted to attack Hú,
so he married his daughter to its ruler.
Then he asked his ministers:
"I wish to use troops;
whom should we attack?"
Guān Qí Sī said:
"Hú can be attacked."
Wǔ Gōng then executed Guān Qí Sī,
saying:
"Hú
is our brother state;
you speak of attacking it,
why?"
The ruler of Hú heard this
and thought Zhèng was friendly, so did not prepare against it.
Zhèng attacked Hú by surprise
and captured it.
These two persuaders,
their knowledge was correct in both cases,
yet the severe one was executed,
the mild one was suspected.
It is not that knowing is difficult,
but applying that knowledge is hard.
Long ago, Mí Zǐ Xiá was loved by the ruler of Wèi.
By Wèi law,
stealing the ruler's carriage warranted punishment by amputation.
Later, Mí Zǐ's mother fell ill;
someone heard,
went to tell him at night,
and Mí Zǐ pretended to command the ruler's carriage to go out.
The ruler heard and praised him:
"How filial!
For his mother's sake, he risked amputation!"
When with the ruler in the orchard,
Mí Zǐ ate a peach and found it sweet,
so offered the unfinished half to the ruler.
The ruler said:
"He loves me!
Forgetting his own taste to think of me!"
When Mí Zǐ's looks faded and favor waned,
he offended the ruler.
The ruler said:
"He once pretended to command my carriage,
and once gave me his leftover peach."
Thus Mí Zǐ's conduct had not changed from the start,
yet earlier he was praised and later condemned—
such is the extreme shift in love and hate.
So if loved by the ruler,
one's wisdom fits and brings closer ties;
if hated by the ruler,
one's offenses fit and bring greater distance.
Therefore, the persuader must assess the ruler's love or hate before speaking.
The dragon, as a creature,
can be tamed and ridden.
But under its throat are reverse scales a foot wide;
if a person touches them,
it will surely kill.
The ruler also has reverse scales;
the persuader who can avoid touching them
is nearly successful.
Someone transmitted Hán Fēi's writings to Qín.
The King of Qín saw the books "Gū Fèn"
and "Wǔ Dù",
and said:
"Alas,
if I could meet this man and befriend him,
I would die without regret!"
Lǐ Sī said:
"These are books by Hán Fēi."
Qín then urgently attacked Hán.
The King of Hán had not employed Fēi at first,
but in crisis,
sent Fēi as envoy to Qín.
The King of Qín was pleased with him
but did not yet trust or employ him.
Lǐ Sī and Yáo Jiǎ, envying him,
slandered him:
"Hán Fēi
is a noble scion of Hán.
Now Your Majesty wishes to annex the states;
Fēi will ultimately side with Hán, not Qín—
this is human nature.
If you do not employ him now,
keeping him long and then sending him back,
this is leaving a trouble for yourself;
better to execute him for some offense."
The king agreed,
and had officials try Fēi.
Lǐ Sī sent someone to give Fēi poison,
forcing him to suicide.
Fēi wished to plead his case,
but could not get an audience.
The king later regretted it,
sent someone to pardon him,
but Fēi was already dead.
Shēn Zǐ
and Hán Zǐ both wrote books
passed down to later ages,
studied by many scholars.
I alone lament that Hán Zǐ, who wrote "Shuì Nán" on the difficulties of persuasion, could not save himself.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Lǎo Zǐ valued the Way,
emptiness and non-being,
and responding to transformations through non-action,
thus his writings are described as subtle and difficult to comprehend.
Zhuāng Zǐ disseminated the Way and its virtue,
expounding freely,
yet his essentials also returned to nature.
Shēn Zǐ urged self-humiliation,
applying it to names and realities.
Hán Zǐ drew the line,
cut to the heart of matters,
and clarified right and wrong,
but his extremes were cruel and lacking in kindness.
All originated from the ideas of the Way and its virtue,
yet Lǎo Zǐ was the most profound.
Sīmǎ Rángjū
was a descendant of Tián Wán.
During the time of Duke Jǐng of Qí,
Jìn attacked Ā
and Zhēn, while Yān invaded the region north of the Yellow River,
and the Qí army suffered a major defeat.
Duke Jǐng was troubled by this.
Yàn Yīng then recommended Tián Rángjū, saying:
"Although Rángjū is a member of a cadet branch of the Tián clan,
he is a man whose civil virtues can win over the masses,
and whose military prowess can intimidate the enemy.
I hope you will try him."
Duke Jǐng summoned Rángjū,
discussed military affairs with him,
and was greatly pleased,
appointing him as a general
to lead troops to resist the armies of Yān and Jìn.
Rángjū said:
"Your subject has always been of low status.
You have promoted me from among the common people,
placing me above the grand masters.
The soldiers are not yet attached to me,
the common people do not trust me,
and I am insignificant and my authority light.
I wish to have one of your favored ministers,
someone respected by the state,
to serve as army supervisor;
only then will it be feasible."
Thereupon, Duke Jǐng agreed
and sent Zhuāng Jiǎ to go.
After Rángjū took his leave,
he made an appointment with Zhuāng Jiǎ, saying:
"We will meet at the army gate at noon tomorrow."
Rángjū first galloped to the army,
set up a gnomon and water clock, and waited for Jiǎ.
Jiǎ, being arrogant and privileged by nature,
thought that since he was supervising his own army,
he was not in a great hurry;
his relatives and retainers saw him off,
and he stayed to drink with them.
At noon, Jiǎ had not arrived.
Rángjū then toppled the gnomon and broke the water clock,
entered the camp, mobilized the troops,
and announced the regulations.
Once the regulations were set,
by evening,
Zhuāng Jiǎ finally arrived.
Rángjū said:
"Why are you late?"
Jiǎ apologized, saying:
"My colleagues and relatives were seeing me off,
so I was detained."
Rángjū said:
"A general, from the day he receives his command, forgets his family;
when facing the army and its regulations, he forgets his kin;
in the urgency of beating the drum, he forgets his own person.
Now the enemy state has deeply invaded,
the realm is in turmoil,
soldiers are exposed on the borders,
the ruler cannot sleep peacefully,
nor eat with relish,
the lives of the common people all hang on you—
what do you mean by seeing people off!"
He summoned the army judge and asked:
"What does military law say about arriving after the appointed time?"
The reply was:
"He should be beheaded."
Zhuāng Jiǎ was terrified,
sent someone galloping to report to Duke Jǐng,
and begged for rescue.
Before the messenger had gone
and returned,
Rángjū then beheaded Zhuāng Jiǎ and displayed his head to the three armies.
All the officers and soldiers of the three armies trembled with fear.
Some time later,
Duke Jǐng sent an envoy with credentials to pardon Jiǎ,
who galloped into the army camp.
Rángjū said:
"A general in the field
may not always accept the orders of his ruler."
He asked the army judge:
"What is the law regarding galloping into the three armies?"
The judge said:
"He should be beheaded."
The envoy was greatly afraid.
Rángjū said:
"The ruler's envoy cannot be killed."
So he beheaded the envoy's attendant,
cut down the left shaft of his chariot,
and killed the left-side horse of his team,
displaying them to the three armies.
He sent the envoy back to report,
and then set out.
Regarding the soldiers' encampments, wells, stoves, food and drink, and care for the sick and medicine,
he personally oversaw and comforted them.
He took all the provisions and grain allocated to the general and shared them with the soldiers,
personally dividing the food equally with them,
giving special attention to the weakest among them.
Three days later, he drilled the troops.
The sick all requested to march,
vying eagerly to go forth and fight for him.
When the Jìn army heard of this,
they withdrew and left.
When the Yān army heard of it,
they crossed the river and disbanded.
Thereupon, he pursued and attacked them,
recovered all the lost territory within the borders, and led the troops back.
Before reaching the capital,
he disbanded the troops,
lifted the restrictions,
swore oaths, and only then entered the city.
Duke Jǐng and the various ministers greeted him at the suburbs,
conducted the rituals to reward the army,
and only then returned to rest.
After meeting Rángjū,
he honored him as Grand Marshal.
From then on, the Tián clan grew increasingly respected in Qí.
Later, Grand Masters of the Bào clan,
Gāo, and Guó factions grew jealous of him
and slandered him to Duke Jǐng.
Duke Jǐng dismissed Rángjū,
and Jū fell ill and died.
Tián Qǐ
and Tián Bào and their followers henceforth bore a grudge against the Gāo
and Guó clans, among others.
Later, when Tián Cháng killed Duke Jiǎn,
he exterminated the entire clans of the Gāo
and Guó families.
By the time of Cháng's great-grandson Hé,
he consequently established himself as King Wēi of Qí,
wielding military power and authority,
greatly emulating the methods of Rángjū,
and the various feudal lords came to pay homage to Qí.
King Wēi of Qí commanded his ministers to compile and discuss the ancient "Sīmǎ Art of War" and included Rángjū's methods within it,
thus naming it "Sīmǎ Rángjū's Art of War."
The Grand Historian remarks:
I have read the "Sīmǎ Art of War,"
broad in scope and profound,
and even the campaigns of the Three Dynasties
could not fully exhaust its principles,
and as for its literary style,
it is also somewhat laudable.
As for Rángjū,
merely leading troops for a small state,
how could he have had the leisure to match the courteous decorum of the "Sīmǎ Art of War"?
Since the world already has much of the "Sīmǎ Art of War,"
for this reason, I do not discuss it,
but instead write the biography of Rángjū.
Sūnzǐ Wǔ was a man of Qí.
He was presented to the King of Wú, Hélǘ,
through his military strategy.
Hélǘ said,
"I have thoroughly read your thirteen chapters on warfare.
Could you conduct a small drill to demonstrate your command of troops?"
Sūnzǐ replied,
"Yes."
Hélǘ asked,
"Can it be tested with women?"
Sūnzǐ said,
"Yes."
Thus, permission was granted,
and the beautiful women from the palace were brought out,
totaling one hundred and eighty.
Sūnzǐ divided them into two teams,
appointing the king's two favorite concubines as team leaders,
and had them all hold halberds.
He commanded them,
"Do you know your heart, left and right hands, and back?"
The women replied,
"We do."
Sūnzǐ said,
"When I say 'forward,' look at your heart;
'left,' look at your left hand;
'right,' look at your right hand;
'back,' look at your back."
The women said,
"Yes."
After the rules were announced,
axes and executioner's blocks were set up,
and the orders were repeated three to five times.
Then, the drum was beaten for 'right,'
but the women burst into laughter.
Sūnzǐ said,
"If the rules are unclear and the orders not familiar,
it is the fault of the general."
He repeated the orders three to five times and beat the drum for 'left,'
but the women laughed again.
Sūnzǐ said,
"If the rules are unclear and the orders not familiar,
it is the fault of the general;
but if they are clear and not followed,
it is the fault of the officers."
He then intended to execute the two team leaders.
The King of Wú, watching from the terrace,
saw that his beloved concubines were about to be executed
and was greatly alarmed.
He hastily sent a messenger to order,
"I now know the general's ability to command troops.
Without these two concubines,
my food would be tasteless.
I beg you not to execute them."
Sūnzǐ said,
"I have received the command to serve as general.
When the general is in the army,
he may not always obey the sovereign's orders."
He then executed the two team leaders as a warning.
Using the next in line as team leaders,
he beat the drum again.
The women moved left, right, forward, and back, kneeling and rising, all in accordance with the rules and measures,
without daring to make a sound.
Sūnzǐ then sent a messenger to report to the king,
"The troops are now well-disciplined.
Your Majesty may inspect them.
You can use them as you wish,
even to march through fire and water."
The King of Wú said,
"General, you may retire to your quarters.
I do not wish to inspect them."
Sūnzǐ said,
"The king only appreciates words
but cannot apply them in practice."
Thus, Hélǘ knew that Sūnzǐ could command troops
and eventually appointed him as general.
He defeated the powerful Chǔ in the west,
entered Yǐng,
intimidated Qí and Jìn in the north,
and made his name renowned among the feudal lords,
in which Sūnzǐ played a significant role.
After Sūn Wǔ's death,
over a hundred years later, there was Sūn Bìn.
Bìn was born between Ā and Juàn,
and he was a descendant of Sūn Wǔ.
Sūn Bìn once studied military strategy with Páng Juān.
After Páng Juān entered the service of Wèi,
he became General under King Huì,
but he believed his own ability was inferior to Sūn Bìn's.
So he secretly summoned Sūn Bìn.
When Bìn arrived,
Páng Juān, fearing Bìn's superiority,
grew jealous
and had him punished by having his feet cut off and his face tattooed,
intending to hide him from the world.
When an envoy from Qí came to Liáng,
Sūn Bìn, as a convict, secretly met with him
and persuaded the Qí envoy.
The Qí envoy, considering him extraordinary,
secretly took him to Qí.
The Qí general Tián Jì treated him well as a guest.
Jì often raced horses with the noble sons of Qí, betting heavily.
Sūnzǐ noticed that their horses' speeds were quite close,
with horses of upper,
middle, and lower classes.
So Sūnzǐ said to Tián Jì,
"Just bet heavily,
and I can make you win."
Tián Jì believed him
and raced with the king and the noble sons for a thousand pieces of gold.
Before the race,
Sūnzǐ said,
"Now, use your lower-class horse against their upper-class,
your upper-class against their middle-class,
and your middle-class against their lower-class."
After the three rounds,
Tián Jì lost one but won two,
ultimately winning the king's thousand pieces of gold.
Thereupon, Jì recommended Sūnzǐ to King Wēi.
King Wēi consulted him on military strategy
and thus regarded him as a teacher.
Later, Wèi attacked Zhào,
and Zhào, in distress,
sought help from Qí.
King Wēi of Qí wanted to appoint Sūn Bìn as general,
but Bìn declined, saying,
"A mutilated man is not suitable."
So Tián Jì was made general instead,
with Sūnzǐ as military advisor,
staying in a supply wagon,
devising strategies.
Tián Jì intended to lead troops to Zhào,
but Sūnzǐ said,
"To untangle a mess, one should not tug recklessly;
to stop a fight, one should not join in the fray.
Strike at their vital point and attack their weakness;
when their situation is constrained and movement hindered,
they will resolve it themselves.
Now Liáng and Zhào are attacking each other;
their swift troops and sharp soldiers must be exhausted abroad,
while the old and weak are weary at home.
You'd better lead your troops swiftly to Dàliáng,
seize its thoroughfares,
and strike where they are empty.
They will surely abandon Zhào to save themselves.
Thus, with one move, we lift the siege of Zhào and exploit Wèi's weakness."
Tián Jì followed this advice.
Wèi indeed left Hándān
and fought Qí at Guìlíng,
where the Liáng army was severely defeated.
Thirteen years later,
Wei and Zhao attacked Hán,
and Hán urgently sought aid from Qí.
Qí sent Tián Jì to lead troops,
heading straight for Dàliáng.
Wei general Páng Juān heard this,
withdrew from Hán and returned,
but the Qí army had already advanced westward.
Sūnzǐ said to Tián Jì:
"The soldiers of the Three Jìn have always been fierce and brave, looking down on Qí,
and Qí is reputed to be timid.
A skilled warrior guides the situation to his advantage.
According to military strategy,
marching a hundred lǐ for gain will exhaust the top general,
marching fifty lǐ for gain only half the army arrives.
Have the Qí army build a hundred thousand cooking stoves upon entering Wei territory,
fifty thousand the next day,
and thirty thousand the day after."
After three days of pursuit, Páng Juān
was greatly pleased,
saying:
"I always knew the Qí army was timid.
Three days into our territory,
more than half their soldiers have deserted."
He then abandoned his infantry,
and with his light, elite troops marched double-time in pursuit.
Sūnzǐ calculated their march,
estimating they'd reach Mǎlíng at dusk.
The Mǎlíng path was narrow,
with many obstacles on both sides,
suitable for an ambush.
He stripped a large tree of bark and wrote:
"Páng Juān dies beneath this tree."
He then stationed ten thousand skilled Qí archers
in ambush along the road,
commanding:
"Shoot together when you see fire at dusk."
Páng Juān indeed arrived at the tree that night,
saw the writing,
lit a torch to read it.
Before finishing,
the ten thousand arrows of Qí fired simultaneously,
throwing the Wei army into chaos.
Knowing he was outwitted and defeated,
Páng Juān cut his own throat,
saying:
"Thus I make that runt famous!"
Qí then crushed his army in victory,
capturing Wei crown prince Shēn and returning.
Sūn Bìn thus gained fame throughout the land,
and his military strategies were passed down through generations.
Wú Qǐ
was from Wèi,
and fond of military strategy.
He once studied under Zēngzǐ,
serving the ruler of Lǔ.
When Qí attacked Lǔ,
Lǔ wanted to make Wú Qǐ general,
but he had married a Qí woman,
so Lǔ doubted him.
Wú Qǐ, seeking fame,
killed his wife
to prove he wasn't aligned with Qí.
Lǔ then made him general.
He attacked Qí
and defeated them soundly.
Some in Lǔ spoke against Wú Qǐ:
"Wú Qǐ's character
is suspicious and cruel.
In his youth,
his family had substantial wealth,
but failing to secure an official post,
he bankrupted his family.
His villagers mocked him,
so he killed over thirty who slandered him,
then left east through Wèi's outer gate.
Parting from his mother,
he bit his arm and vowed:
'Unless I become a high minister,
I won't return to Wèi.'
He then studied under Zēngzǐ.
Soon after,
his mother died,
yet he never returned.
Zēngzǐ despised this,
and cut ties with him.
Wú Qǐ went to Lǔ,
studied military strategy to serve its ruler.
The ruler doubted him,
so he killed his wife to become general.
Lǔ is a small state;
gaining a victory reputation
will make other states target it.
Moreover, Lǔ and Wèi are brotherly states;
employing Wú Qǐ
means abandoning Wèi."
The ruler of Lǔ thus doubted him,
and dismissed Wú Qǐ.
Hearing of Wèi Wénhóu's virtue,
Wú Qǐ wished to serve him.
Wénhóu asked Lǐ Kè:
"What kind of man is Wú Qǐ?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"He is greedy and fond of women,
but in warfare, even Sīmǎ Rángjū couldn't surpass him."
So Wèi Wénhóu made him general,
attacked Qín,
and captured five cities.
As general,
Wú Qǐ shared food and clothing with the lowest soldiers.
He slept without mats,
marched without riding,
personally carried provisions,
sharing hardships with his men.
When a soldier had a boil,
Wú Qǐ sucked the pus.
The soldier's mother wept upon hearing.
Someone asked:
"Your son is a soldier,
and the general himself sucked his boil.
Why weep?"
She said:
"Not so.
Years ago, Lord Wú sucked his father's boil,
his father fought without retreating,
and died in battle.
Now Lord Wú sucks his son's boil,
I don't know where he'll die.
That's why I weep."
Wénhóu, seeing Wú Qǐ's military skill,
integrity,
and ability to win hearts,
made him governor of Xīhé,
to defend against Qín
and Hán.
After Wèi Wénhóu died,
Wú Qǐ served his son Wǔhóu.
Wǔhóu sailed down the Xī Hé,
midstream,
turned and said to Wú Qǐ:
"How magnificent, these secure mountains and rivers—
they are Wèi's treasures!"
Wú Qǐ replied:
"It lies in virtue, not in terrain.
In the past, the Sānmiáo clan had Dòngtíng on the left,
Pénglí on the right,
but lacking virtue and righteousness,
Yǔ destroyed them.
Xià Jié's domain
had Hé Jì on the left,
Tài Huà on the right,
Yīquē to the south,
Yángcháng to the north,
yet his rule was unkind,
so Tāng exiled him.
Yīn Zhòu's state
had Mèngmén on the left,
Tàiháng on the right,
Cháng Shān to the north,
the great river flowing south,
yet his rule was virtueless,
so King Wǔ killed him.
Thus,
it lies in virtue, not in terrain.
If you neglect virtue,
even those in your boat may become enemies."
Wǔhóu said:
"Well said."
Wú Qǐ served as the governor of Xīhé,
enjoying great fame and reputation.
When the state of Wèi appointed a chancellor,
it was Tián Wén who received the position.
Wú Qǐ was displeased,
and said to Tián Wén:
"May I discuss our achievements with you,
is that acceptable?"
Tián Wén replied:
"It is."
Qǐ said:
"In commanding the three armies,
making soldiers willing to die in battle,
and causing enemy states not to dare plot against us,
how do you compare to me?"
Wén said:
"I am not your equal."
Qǐ said:
"In managing the百官,
winning the affection of the people,
and filling the state treasury,
how do you compare to me?"
Wén said:
"I am not your equal."
Qǐ said:
"In guarding Xīhé so that Qín troops dare not advance eastward,
and making Hán and Zhào submit like guests,
how do you compare to me?"
Wén said:
"I am not your equal."
Qǐ said:
"In these three aspects,
you are all beneath me,
yet your position is above mine,
why is that?"
Wén said:
"The ruler is young and the state unstable,
the ministers are not yet loyal,
the common people are distrustful,
at such a time,
should the responsibility be entrusted to you?
Or to me?"
Qǐ remained silent for a long time,
then said:
"It should be entrusted to you."
Wén said:
"This is precisely why I am above you."
Wú Qǐ then realized he was not Tián Wén's equal.
After Tián Wén's death,
Gōng Shū became chancellor,
married a princess of Wèi,
and sought to harm Wú Qǐ.
Gōng Shū's servant said:
"Qǐ can be easily removed."
Gōng Shū asked:
"How?"
The servant replied:
"Wú Qǐ is a man of integrity who values his reputation.
You should first speak to Marquis Wǔ saying:
'Wú Qǐ is a worthy man,
but your state is small,
and borders the powerful Qín,
I fear he may not wish to stay.'
Marquis Wǔ will then ask:
'What should be done?'
You can then tell Marquis Wǔ:
'Test him by offering a princess in marriage,
if he intends to stay he will certainly accept,
if not he will definitely decline.
Use this to gauge his intentions.'
Then invite Wú Qǐ to your home,
and have the princess display anger and contempt toward you.
When Wú Qǐ sees the princess disrespecting the chancellor,
he will certainly decline the marriage."
When Wú Qǐ witnessed the princess disparaging the Wèi chancellor,
he indeed declined Marquis Wǔ's offer.
Marquis Wǔ became suspicious and lost trust in him.
Fearing punishment,
Wú Qǐ departed,
and went to Chǔ.
King Dào of Chǔ had long heard of Qǐ's worthiness,
and upon his arrival made him chancellor.
He clarified laws and examined decrees,
eliminated unnecessary officials,
abolished privileges for distant royal relatives,
to support and train fighting men.
His focus was on strengthening the military,
and refuting the rhetoric of纵横 strategists.
Thereupon he pacified the Bǎi Yuè in the south;
annexed Chén and Cài in the north,
and repelled the Three Jìn;
attacking Qín in the west.
The feudal lords feared Chǔ's growing power.
Thus the noble relatives of Chǔ all sought to harm Wú Qǐ.
When King Dào died,
the royal family and ministers rebelled and attacked Wú Qǐ,
who fled and threw himself upon the king's corpse.
Those attacking Qǐ consequently shot and stabbed him,
also hitting King Dào's body.
After King Dào was buried,
the crown prince ascended the throne,
and ordered the prime minister to execute all who had shot Wú Qǐ and hit the king's corpse.
Over seventy families were exterminated for their involvement in shooting Qǐ.
Grand Historian Simǎ Qiān said:
When people discuss military matters,
they all speak of Master Sūn's thirteen chapters,
and Wú Qǐ's Art of War,
which are widely available,
so I will not discuss them,
but rather their practical actions and implementations.
As the saying goes:
"Those who can do may not be able to speak,
those who can speak may not be able to do."
Sūn Zǐ's strategies against Páng Juān were brilliant,
yet he could not save himself from punishment earlier.
Wú Qǐ advised Marquis Wǔ that circumstances are less important than virtue,
yet when implementing policies in Chǔ,
he brought about his own demise through harshness and lack of compassion.
How lamentable!
Wǔ Zǐxū
was a man of Chǔ,
named Yún.
Yún's father was Wǔ Shē.
Yún's elder brother was Wǔ Shàng.
Their ancestor was Wǔ Jǔ,
who served King Zhuāng of Chǔ with honest counsel,
gaining prominence,
thus his descendants became renowned in Chǔ.
King Píng of Chǔ had a crown prince named Jiàn,
appointing Wǔ Shē as Grand Tutor,
and Fèi Wújì as Junior Tutor.
Wújì was not loyal to Crown Prince Jiàn.
King Píng sent Wújì to fetch a bride for the prince from Qín,
the Qín woman being beautiful,
Wújì hurried back to report to King Píng:
"The Qín woman is exquisitely beautiful,
Your Majesty should take her for yourself,
and find another bride for the crown prince."
King Píng then took the Qín woman for himself and doted on her exceedingly,
begetting a son named Zhěn.
He found another bride for the crown prince.
Having ingratiated himself with King Píng through the Qín woman,
Wújì left the crown prince's service to attend the king.
Fearing that if King Píng died and the crown prince ascended,
he would be killed,
he began slandering Crown Prince Jiàn.
Jiàn's mother,
being a woman from Cài,
was not favored by King Píng.
King Píng gradually distanced himself from Jiàn,
sending him to guard Chéngfù,
to prepare border defenses.
Soon after,
Wújì again spoke day and night to the king about the crown prince's faults:
"Because of the Qín woman affair,
the crown prince cannot help but resent you,
I hope Your Majesty will take precautions.
Since residing in Chéngfù,
commanding troops,
and forming alliances with other states,
he plans to return and stage a rebellion."
King Píng then summoned Grand Tutor Wǔ Shē for interrogation.
Knowing Wújì had slandered the crown prince to the king,
Shē said:
"Why would Your Majesty trust a slanderous petty official and estrange your own flesh and blood?"
Wújì said:
"If Your Majesty does not act now,
his plan will succeed.
You will be captured."
Enraged,
King Píng imprisoned Wǔ Shē,
and sent Chéngfù's military commander Fèn Yáng to kill the crown prince.
Before arriving,
Fèn Yáng sent someone to warn the crown prince:
"Leave quickly,
or you will be executed."
Crown Prince Jiàn fled to Sòng.
Wú Jì spoke to King Píng, saying:
"Wǔ Shē has two sons,
both worthy;
if not executed, they will become a worry for Chǔ.
We can use their father as hostage to summon them,
otherwise they will bring disaster to Chǔ."
The king sent an envoy to tell Wǔ Shē:
"If you can bring your two sons here, you live;
if not, you die."
Wǔ Shē said:
"Shàng is benevolent,
he will surely come if called.
Yún is resolute, fierce, and able to endure disgrace,
capable of great achievements;
when he sees that coming means capture together,
he certainly will not come."
The king did not listen,
and sent someone to summon the two sons, saying:
"Come,
and I will spare your father;
do not come,
and I will kill Shē now."
Wǔ Shàng wanted to go,
but Yún said:
"Chǔ summons us brothers,
not because they want to spare our father,
but fearing that any escapees would cause future trouble,
so they use our father as a hostage,
deceptively calling for his two sons.
If the two sons go,
then father and sons will all die.
What good is that to our father's death?
Going would only prevent the revenge from being achieved.
It would be better to flee to another state,
borrow strength to wash away our father's shame;
to perish together
is futile."
Wǔ Shàng said:
"I know that going will not ultimately save our father's life.
Yet I would regret not going when father summoned us hoping for life,
and later being unable to clear the shame,
ending up laughed at by the world."
He told Yún:
"You may leave!
You can avenge our father's death,
I will return to die."
Once Shàng was captured,
the envoys went to arrest Wǔ Xū.
Wǔ Xū strung his bow and aimed an arrow at the envoys,
who dared not advance,
and Wǔ Xū thus escaped.
Hearing that Crown Prince Jiàn was in Sòng,
he went to follow him.
When Shē heard of Zǐ Xū's escape,
he said:
"The rulers and ministers of Chǔ will soon suffer from war."
When Wǔ Shàng reached Chǔ,
Chǔ executed both Shē and Shàng.
After Wǔ Xū arrived in Sòng,
Sòng was in the turmoil of the Huá clan's rebellion,
so he fled with Crown Prince Jiàn to Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng treated them very well.
Crown Prince Jiàn then went to Jìn,
where Duke Qìng of Jìn said:
"Since the Crown Prince is on good terms with Zhèng,
and Zhèng trusts him,
if the Crown Prince can be our insider,
while we attack from outside,
we will surely destroy Zhèng.
After destroying Zhèng, we will enfeoff the Crown Prince."
The Crown Prince then returned to Zhèng.
Before the plan could be coordinated,
it happened that he privately intended to kill one of his followers,
who learned of the plot,
and reported it to Zhèng.
Duke Dìng of Zhèng and Zǐ Chǎn executed Crown Prince Jiàn.
Jiàn had a son named Shèng.
Wǔ Xū, fearful,
fled with Shèng to Wú.
Arriving at Zhāo Guān,
the guards at Zhāo Guān tried to capture them.
Wǔ Xū then fled on foot alone with Shèng,
barely escaping.
Pursuers were close behind.
Reaching a river,
there was an old fisherman in a boat on the river,
who, knowing Wǔ Xū's desperation,
ferried him across.
After crossing,
Wǔ Xū untied his sword and said:
"This sword is worth a hundred gold pieces,
I give it to you, father."
The old man said:
"By Chǔ's law,
capturing Wǔ Xū brings a reward of fifty thousand dàn of grain,
and the nobility of Zhí Guī,
how could it compare to a mere hundred-gold sword!"
He did not accept it.
Before reaching Wú, Wǔ Xū fell ill,
stopped midway,
and begged for food.
Upon reaching Wú,
King Liáo of Wú was in power,
with Prince Guāng as general.
Wǔ Xū then sought an audience with the King of Wú through Prince Guāng.
After some time,
as the border town of Zhōng Lí in Chǔ and the border town of Bēi Liáng in Wú both raised silkworms,
two girls argued over mulberry leaves and fought,
leading to great anger,
escalating until the two states raised armies against each other.
Wú sent Prince Guāng to attack Chǔ,
capturing its Zhōng Lí
and Jū Cháo before returning.
Wǔ Zǐ Xū advised King Liáo of Wú:
"Chǔ can be defeated.
I hope you will send Prince Guāng again."
Prince Guāng said to the King of Wú:
"That Wǔ Xū's father and brother were killed in Chǔ,
and he urges you to attack Chǔ,
is only to avenge his own grudge.
Attacking Chǔ now may not lead to its defeat."
Wǔ Xū realized that Prince Guāng had ambitions within,
wanting to kill the king and establish himself,
and was not to be persuaded with external affairs,
so he recommended Zhuān Zhū to Prince Guāng,
then withdrew and farmed in the countryside with Crown Prince Jiàn's son, Shèng.
Five years later, King Píng of Chǔ died.
Earlier, the daughter of Qín whom King Píng had taken from Crown Prince Jiàn bore a son, Zhěn,
and when King Píng died,
Zhěn eventually succeeded him,
becoming King Zhāo.
King Liáo of Wú, taking advantage of Chǔ's mourning,
sent two princes with troops to raid Chǔ.
Chǔ dispatched troops to cut off the Wú army's retreat,
preventing their return.
With Wú's interior left undefended,
Prince Guāng ordered Zhuān Zhū to assassinate King Liáo of Wú and established himself,
becoming King Hé Lú of Wú.
Once Hé Lú was established,
and his ambitions realized,
he summoned Wǔ Yún to serve as a diplomat,
and consulted him on state affairs.
When Chǔ executed its high officials Xì Wǎn
and Bó Zhōu Lí,
Bó Zhōu Lí's grandson, Bó Pǐ, fled to Wú,
and Wú also appointed Pǐ as a senior official.
The two princes previously sent by King Liáo to lead troops against Chǔ,
cut off from retreat, could not return.
Later, hearing that Hé Lú had killed King Liáo and taken the throne,
they surrendered with their troops to Chǔ,
and Chǔ enfeoffed them in Shū.
In the third year of Hé Lú's reign,
he raised an army and, with Wǔ Xū
and Bó Pǐ, attacked Chǔ,
capturing Shū,
and thus captured the two former Wú generals who had rebelled.
Intending to press on to Yǐng,
General Sūn Wǔ said:
"The people are weary,
it is not feasible yet,
we should wait."
So they returned.
In the fourth year,
Wú attacked Chǔ,
seizing Lù and Qián.
In the fifth year,
they attacked Yuè,
and defeated it.
In the sixth year,
King Zhāo of Chǔ sent Prince Náng Wǎ to lead troops against Wú.
Wú sent Wǔ Yún to meet the attack,
decisively defeating the Chǔ army at Yù Zhāng,
and capturing Chǔ's Jū Cháo.
In the ninth year,
King Hé Lǘ of Wú said to Wǔ Zǐ Xū and
Sūn Wǔ:
"Initially, you said Yǐng could not be entered,
but now how does it seem?"
The two men replied:
"Chǔ's general Náng Wǎ is greedy,
and both Táng and
Cài resent him.
If Your Majesty wishes to greatly attack them,
you must first win over Táng and
Cài to succeed."
Hé Lǘ heeded their advice,
mobilized all forces along with Táng and
Cài to attack Chǔ,
facing Chǔ across the Hàn River in battle formation.
The Wú king's brother Fū Gài requested to lead troops in the campaign,
but the king refused,
so he took his own five thousand men and attacked Chǔ general Zǐ Cháng.
Zǐ Cháng was defeated and fled,
seeking refuge in Zhèng.
Thereupon Wú advanced victoriously,
fighting five battles,
and reached Yǐng.
On the day Jǐ Mǎo,
King Zhāo of Chǔ fled.
On the day Gēng Chén,
the King of Wú entered Yǐng.
King Zhāo fled into exile,
entering Yún Mèng;
bandits attacked the king,
and he fled to Yún.
Yún's duke's brother Huái said:
"King Píng killed my father,
so I kill his son -
isn't that fitting!"
Yún's duke, fearing his brother would kill the king,
fled with the king to Suí.
Wú troops surrounded Suí,
saying to its people:
"All descendants of Zhōu in Hànchuān,
Chǔ has exterminated them."
The people of Suí wanted to kill the king,
but Prince Qí hid him,
presenting himself as king instead.
When Suí divined about surrendering the king to Wú,
it was inauspicious,
so they declined Wú's demand for the king.
Earlier, Wǔ Yún and Shēn Bāo Xū had been friends.
When Yún was fleeing,
he told Bāo Xū:
"I will surely destroy Chǔ."
Bāo Xū replied:
"I will surely preserve it."
When Wú troops entered Yǐng,
Wǔ Zǐ Xū sought King Zhāo.
Failing to find him,
he excavated King Píng of Chǔ's tomb,
exhumed his corpse,
whipped it three hundred times,
and only then stopped.
Shēn Bāo Xū fled to the mountains,
sending someone to tell Zǐ Xū:
"Your vengeance,
is it not excessive!
I have heard that
numerous men can overcome Heaven,
but Heaven's decree can also destroy men.
You were formerly King Píng's minister,
personally served him facing north as subject,
yet now you desecrate a dead man -
is this not the ultimate in defying Heaven's way!"
Wǔ Zǐ Xū said:
"Tell Shēn Bāo Xū for me that
my day is late and my road long,
so I must act contrary and perverse."
Thereupon Shēn Bāo Xū went to Qín to report the emergency,
seeking help from Qín.
Qín refused.
Bāo Xū stood in the Qín court,
weeping day and night,
for seven days and nights without ceasing his cries.
Duke Āi of Qín took pity on him,
saying:
"Though Chǔ is without virtue,
to have such a minister -
can we not preserve it!"
He then sent five hundred chariots to rescue Chǔ and attack Wú.
In the sixth month,
they defeated Wú troops at Jì.
Meanwhile, the Wú king had long remained in Chǔ seeking King Zhāo,
and Hé Lǘ's brother Fū Gài fled back home,
proclaiming himself king.
Hearing this,
Hé Lǘ abandoned Chǔ and returned,
attacking his brother Fū Gài.
Fū Gài was defeated and fled,
ultimately seeking refuge in Chǔ.
King Zhāo of Chǔ, seeing Wú had internal strife,
returned to Yǐng.
He enfeoffed Fū Gài at Táng Xī,
establishing the Táng Xī clan.
Chǔ again battled Wú,
defeated Wú,
and the Wú king withdrew.
Two years later,
Hé Lǘ sent Crown Prince Fū Chāi to lead troops against Chǔ,
capturing Pó.
Chǔ, fearing Wú would launch another major attack,
abandoned Yǐng,
moving the capital to Ruò.
At this time,
through the strategies of Wǔ Zǐ Xū and
Sūn Wǔ,
Wú crushed powerful Chǔ in the west,
intimidated Qí and Jìn in the north,
and subdued Yuè people in the south.
Four years later,
Confucius became minister of Lǔ.
Five years after that,
Wú attacked Yuè.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè counterattacked,
defeating Wú at Gū Sū,
wounding Hé Lǘ's finger,
and the army retreated.
Hé Lǘ, ill from the wound and near death,
told Crown Prince Fū Chāi:
"Do you forget Gōu Jiàn killed your father?"
Fū Chāi replied:
"I dare not forget."
That evening,
Hé Lǘ died.
After Fū Chāi ascended the throne,
he appointed Bó Pǐ as Grand Steward,
and practiced warfare and archery.
Two years later he attacked Yuè,
defeating Yuè at Fū Jiāo.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè then retreated with his remaining five thousand troops to Kuài Jī Mountain,
sending Minister Wén Zhǒng with rich gifts to Wú Grand Steward Pǐ to seek peace,
offering to submit his state as vassal.
The Wú king was about to agree.
Wǔ Zǐ Xū admonished:
"King of Yuè is a man who endures hardship.
If you don't eliminate him now,
you will surely regret it later."
The Wú king disregarded him,
following Grand Steward Pǐ's counsel,
and made peace with Yuè.
Five years later,
the Wú king heard that Duke Jǐng of Qí had died and ministers were contending for favor,
with the new ruler weak,
so he raised troops to attack Qí northward.
Wǔ Zǐ Xū admonished:
"Gōu Jiàn eats plain food,
mourns the dead and cares for the sick,
intending to use his people.
If this man doesn't die,
he will surely become Wú's calamity.
Now Wú having Yuè
is like a person having heartburn.
Yet you prioritize Qí over Yuè -
is this not mistaken!"
The Wú king disregarded him,
attacked Qí,
decisively defeated Qí's army at Ài Líng,
then intimidated the rulers of Zōu and Lǔ before returning.
He increasingly distanced himself from Zǐ Xū's counsel.
Four years later,
the King of Wú planned to attack Qí in the north.
Yuè King Gōu Jiàn, adopting Zǐ Gòng's strategy,
led his troops to assist Wú
and presented precious treasures to Grand Steward Pǐ.
Since Grand Steward Pǐ had repeatedly accepted bribes from Yuè,
he became exceptionally fond and trusting of Yuè,
speaking on their behalf day and night to the King of Wú.
The King of Wú trusted and employed Pǐ's plans.
Wǔ Zǐ Xū remonstrated, saying:
"Yuè is
a disease in our heart and belly.
Now you trust their empty, deceitful words and covet Qí.
Even if we conquer Qí,
it would be like a stony field,
useless to us.
Moreover, the 'Announcement of Pán Gēng' states:
'Those who are rebellious and disrespectful,
cut off and exterminate them,
leave none to propagate,
do not let them spread their seed in this land.'
This is why Shāng rose to power.
I hope you will abandon Qí and deal with Yuè first;
if not,
you will regret it when it's too late."
But the King of Wú did not listen
and sent Zǐ Xū to Qí.
Before departing,
Zǐ Xū told his son:
"I have repeatedly advised the king,
but he does not heed me.
I now foresee the fall of Wú.
For you to perish with Wú
would be of no benefit."
He then entrusted his son to Bào Mù of Qí
and returned to report to Wú.
Grand Steward Pǐ of Wú, bearing a grudge against Zǐ Xū,
slandered him, saying:
"Zǐ Xū is by nature harsh, violent,
lacking in kindness,
suspicious, and treacherous.
His resentment may bring deep calamity.
Previously, when you wished to attack Qí,
Zǐ Xū deemed it unfeasible,
yet you proceeded and achieved great success.
Zǐ Xū felt ashamed that his counsel was unused,
and thus harbored resentment.
Now that you plan to attack Qí again,
Zǐ Xū obstinately and forcefully remonstrates,
obstructing and undermining affairs,
merely hoping for Wú's defeat to prove his own strategies right.
Now that you personally lead the campaign,
mobilizing all military force in the state against Qí,
and Zǐ Xū's advice is rejected,
he feigns illness,
pretending to be too sick to go.
You must be prepared,
for he could easily start trouble.
Moreover, I sent someone to spy on him;
when he went to Qí,
he entrusted his son to the Bào clan of Qí.
As a subject,
discontent at home,
he relies on foreign lords abroad,
considering himself a strategist of the former king,
now unused,
he is constantly disgruntled and resentful.
I urge you to deal with him early."
The King of Wú said:
"Even without your words,
I would have suspected him."
He then sent an envoy to present Wǔ Zǐ Xū with the sword Zhǔ Lòu,
saying:
"Use this to die."
Wǔ Zǐ Xū looked up to heaven and sighed:
"Alas!
The slanderer Pǐ is causing chaos,
and the king instead executes me.
I made your father a hegemon.
Before you were established,
when the princes contended for the throne,
I risked death to plead for you before the former king,
almost failing to secure your position.
Once you were established,
you wished to divide Wú and give me part,
which I dared not expect.
Yet now you listen to flattering ministers and kill an elder."
Then he told his retainer:
"Be sure to plant catalpa trees on my grave,
so they can be used for instruments,
and gouge out my eyes to hang over the eastern gate of Wú,
to watch the Yuè invaders enter and destroy Wú."
He then cut his own throat and died.
The King of Wú, hearing of this, was enraged,
took Zǐ Xū's corpse, stuffed it into a leather sack,
and cast it into the river.
The people of Wú pitied him,
built a shrine by the river,
and named the mountain Xū Shān.
After executing Wǔ Zǐ Xū,
the King of Wú attacked Qí.
The Bào clan of Qí killed their ruler, Duke Dào, and installed Yáng Shēng.
The King of Wú sought to punish the usurpers,
but failed and withdrew.
Two years later,
he summoned the rulers of Lǔ and Wèi to meet at Tuó Gāo.
The next year,
he convened a grand northern assembly of lords at Huáng Chí,
to command respect from the Zhōu court.
Yuè King Gōu Jiàn launched a surprise attack, killed the crown prince of Wú,
and defeated the Wú army.
The King of Wú, hearing this,
returned,
sending envoys with rich gifts to make peace with Yuè.
Nine years later,
Yuè King Gōu Jiàn ultimately destroyed Wú,
killing King Fū Chāi;
and executed Grand Steward Pǐ,
for his disloyalty to his lord,
accepting heavy bribes from abroad,
and colluding with the enemy.
Shèng, the son of the former Chǔ Crown Prince Jiàn, with whom Wǔ Zǐ Xū had initially fled,
was in Wú.
During the reign of Wú King Fū Chāi,
King Huì of Chǔ wanted to recall Shèng to Chǔ.
Shè Gōng advised against it:
"Shèng is fond of bravery and secretly seeks daring men;
he likely has private motives!"
King Huì did not listen.
He summoned Shèng,
settled him in the border town of Yān in Chǔ,
and titled him Lord Bái.
Lord Bái returned to Chǔ three years before Wú executed Zǐ Xū.
After Lord Bái Shèng returned to Chǔ,
he resented Zhèng for killing his father,
and secretly nurtured daring men to seek revenge against Zhèng.
Five years after returning to Chǔ,
he requested to attack Zhèng,
and Chǔ's Prime Minister Zǐ Xī agreed.
Before the troops were dispatched, Jìn attacked Zhèng,
and Zhèng sought help from Chǔ.
Chǔ sent Zǐ Xī to rescue them,
who made a pact and returned.
Lord Bái Shèng angrily said:
"My enemy is not Zhèng,
but Zǐ Xī."
Shèng sharpened his sword himself;
someone asked him:
"What for?"
Shèng said:
"To kill Zǐ Xī."
Zǐ Xī heard this,
laughed, and said:
"Shèng is like an egg;
what can he do?"
Four years later,
Lord Bái Shèng and Shí Qǐ launched a surprise attack, killing Chǔ Prime Minister Zǐ Xī
and Minister of War Zǐ Qí at court.
Shí Qǐ said:
"If we don't kill the king,
it won't do."
They then forced the king to go to the Gāo Mansion.
Shí Qǐ's follower Qū Gù carried King Huì of Chǔ on his back and fled to Lady Zhāo's palace.
Shè Gōng, hearing of Lord Bái's rebellion,
led his men to attack Lord Bái.
Lord Bái's followers were defeated,
fled into the mountains,
where he committed suicide.
They captured Shí Qǐ,
and asked where Lord Bái's corpse was,
threatening to boil him alive if he didn't tell.
Shí Qǐ said:
"If the affair succeeded, I'd be a minister;
if it failed, being boiled alive
is only fitting."
He never revealed the corpse's location.
They then boiled Shí Qǐ alive,
and sought to restore King Huì to the throne.
The Grand Historian remarks:
How profound is the venom of resentment in men!
Even a sovereign cannot impose it upon his ministers,
let alone among peers!
Had Wǔ Zǐxū chosen to die with his father Wǔ Shē,
how would he have differed from an ant?
By forsaking minor righteousness
to avenge a great disgrace,
his name endured through later generations—
how poignant!
When Zǐxū was stranded by the river,
begging for food along the way,
was there even a moment his ambition forgot Yǐng?
Thus, through endurance he achieved merit and fame:
who but a stalwart man could have accomplished this?
Had Bái Gōng not set himself up as lord,
his achievements and strategies would still be beyond telling!
Confucius said,
"Those who mastered the teachings through personal study numbered seventy-seven,"
all being men of exceptional talents.
In virtuous conduct:
Yán Yuān,
Mǐn Zǐqiān,
Rǎn Bóniú,
Zhònggōng.
In governmental affairs:
Rǎn Yǒu,
Jìlù.
In speech and diplomacy:
Zǎi Wǒ,
Zǐgòng.
In cultural scholarship:
Zǐyóu,
Zǐxià.
Shī (Zǐzhāng) was eccentric,
Shēn (Zēngzǐ) was dull,
Chái (Gāochāi) was simple,
Yóu (Zǐlù) was rash,
Huí (Yán Yuān) was often in want.
Cì (Zǐgòng) disobeyed fate to engage in trade,
yet his estimations were often accurate.
Those whom Confucius revered and served:
in Zhōu, Lǎozi;
in Wèi,
Qú Bóyù;
in Qí,
Yàn Píngzhòng;
in Chǔ,
Lǎo Láizi;
in Zhèng,
Zǐchǎn;
in Lǔ,
Mèng Gōngchuò.
He repeatedly praised Zāng Wénzhòng,
Liǔxià Huì,
Tóngtí Bóhuá,
and Jièshān Zǐrán,
though Confucius lived after them all,
not being their contemporary.
Yán Huí,
a man of Lǔ,
styled Zǐyuān,
was thirty years younger than Confucius.
When Yán Yuān asked about benevolence,
Confucius said,
"Master yourself and return to propriety,
and all under heaven will attribute benevolence to you."
Confucius said,
"How worthy is Huí!
With a single bamboo bowl of rice,
a single gourd dipper of drink,
dwelling in a humble alley,
others could not have endured such hardship,
yet Huí never altered his joy."
"Huí appears dull;
but observing his private conduct,
he sufficiently elaborates on teachings—
Huí is not dull."
"When employed, to act;
when cast aside, to withdraw—
only you and I have this capacity!"
At twenty-nine,
Huí's hair turned entirely white,
and he died young.
Confucius wept bitterly for him,
saying,
"Since I had Huí,
my disciples have grown closer."
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked,
"Which of your disciples loves learning?"
Confucius replied,
"There was Yán Huí who loved learning,
never transferring his anger,
never repeating a fault.
Unfortunately, his life was cut short—
now there is none."
Mǐn Sǔn, styled Zǐqiān,
was fifteen years younger than Confucius.
Confucius said,
"How filial is Mǐn Zǐqiān!
No one finds fault with the words of his parents and brothers."
He refused to serve high ministers,
nor accept the salary of corrupt rulers.
"If anyone seeks me again,
I shall surely be north of the Wèn River."
Rǎn Gēng, styled Bóniú.
Confucius considered him virtuous in conduct.
When Bóniú fell gravely ill,
Confucius visited him,
reaching through the window to grasp his hand,
saying,
"It is fate!
That such a man should have such a disease—
it is fate!"
Rǎn Yōng, styled Zhònggōng.
When Zhònggōng asked about governance,
Confucius said,
"When going forth, act as if receiving an honored guest;
when employing the people, act as if presiding over a great sacrifice.
Let there be no resentment in the state,
no resentment in the household."
Confucius regarded Zhònggōng as virtuous in conduct,
saying,
"Yōng is fit to face south" (i.e., to rule).
Zhònggōng's father
was a lowly man.
Confucius said,
"If the offspring of a plow ox is reddish with proper horns,
though one may wish not to use it,
would the mountains and rivers reject it?"
Rǎn Qiú, styled Zǐyǒu,
was twenty-nine years younger than Confucius.
He served as steward to the Jì family.
Jì Kāngzǐ asked Confucius,
"Is Rǎn Qiú benevolent?"
He replied,
"In a town of a thousand households
or a family with a hundred chariots,
Qiú could be entrusted to manage its taxes.
As for benevolence, I do not know."
He asked again,
"Is Zǐlù benevolent?"
Confucius replied,
"The same as Qiú."
Qiú asked,
"Upon hearing something, should one act immediately?"
The Master said,
"Act immediately."
Zǐlù asked,
"Upon hearing something, should one act immediately?"
The Master said,
"While your father and elder brothers live,
how can you act immediately upon hearing something?"
Zǐhuá found this strange,
"Daring to ask: why different answers to the same question?"
Confucius said,
"Qiú is hesitant,
so I urged him forward.
Yóu (Zǐlù) surpasses others in daring,
so I restrained him."
Zhòng Yóu, styled Zǐlù,
was a man of Biàn.
He was nine years younger than Confucius.
Zǐlù was coarse by nature,
fond of courage and strength,
upright in ambition,
wearing a rooster-crested cap,
sporting a boar-tooth adornment,
and once bullied Confucius.
Confucius gradually guided him with ritual,
until Zǐlù later donned scholarly attire, presented gifts,
and through other disciples requested to become a follower.
Zǐlù asked about governance,
Confucius said,
"Lead them personally,
labor with them."
He asked for more.
The reply:
"Never weary."
Zǐlù asked:
"Does a noble man value courage?"
Confucius replied:
"Righteousness is of the highest importance.
If a noble man loves courage without righteousness, he will create chaos;
if a petty man loves courage without righteousness, he becomes a robber."
When Zǐlù learned something,
if he had not yet been able to put it into practice,
he would fear learning something new.
Confucius said:
"One who can decide a legal case with only a partial statement
must be Yóu (Zǐlù)!"
"Yóu's fondness for courage exceeds mine,
but there is nowhere to get the material (to temper it)."
"As for Yóu,
he will not die a natural death."
"To wear a shabby gown padded with old silk floss and stand with those wearing fox and badger furs without feeling ashamed
- this must be Yóu!"
"Yóu has ascended the hall,
but has not yet entered the inner chamber."
Jì Kāngzǐ asked:
"Is Zhòng Yóu benevolent?"
Confucius said:
"He can be entrusted with managing the military levies of a state of a thousand chariots,
but I do not know about his benevolence."
Zǐlù enjoyed accompanying Confucius in his travels,
encountering Cháng Jū,
Jié Nì,
and the old man carrying a weed basket.
When Zǐlù served as steward to the Jì family,
Jì Sūn asked:
"Can Zǐlù be called a great minister?"
Confucius said:
"He can be called a qualified minister."
When Zǐlù became magistrate of Pú,
he took leave of Confucius.
Confucius said:
"Pú has many strong men,
and is difficult to govern.
However, I tell you:
with reverence and respect,
you can control courage;
with tolerance and uprightness,
you can win over the masses;
with reverence, uprightness, and calmness,
you can serve your superiors well."
Earlier,
Duke Líng of Wèi had a favored concubine named Nánzǐ.
The duke's heir apparent, Kuìkuì, offended Nánzǐ,
and fearing execution, fled.
When Duke Líng died, his wife wanted to install Prince Yǐng.
Yǐng refused,
saying:
"The son of the exiled heir apparent, Zhé, is here."
Thereupon Wèi established Zhé as ruler,
known as Duke Chū.
Duke Chū had ruled for twelve years,
while his father Kuìkuì remained abroad,
unable to return.
Zǐlù served as district magistrate for Kǒng Kuī, a senior minister of Wèi.
Kuìkuì then conspired with Kǒng Kuī to rebel,
