plotting to enter Kǒng Kuī's residence,
and subsequently attacked Duke Chū with his followers.
Duke Chū fled to Lǔ,
while Kuìkuì entered and assumed power,
becoming Duke Zhuāng.
While Kǒng Kuī was rebelling,
Zǐlù was outside,
heard the news and rushed there.
He met Zǐgāo leaving the city gate of Wèi,
who said to Zǐlù:
"Duke Chū has left,
and the gates are already closed,
you should turn back,
don't pointlessly suffer disaster."
Zǐlù said:
"One who eats his lord's food does not avoid his difficulties."
Zǐgāo then left.
When a messenger entered the city,
the city gate opened,
and Zǐlù followed him in.
He went to see Kuìkuì,
who was with Kǒng Kuī on a terrace.
Zǐlù said:
"Why does my lord employ Kǒng Kuī?
Please let me capture and kill him."
Kuìkuì would not listen.
Thereupon Zǐlù wanted to set fire to the terrace,
Kuìkuì grew afraid,
and sent down Shí Qǐ
and Hú Yǎn to attack Zǐlù,
who struck and broke Zǐlù's cap string.
Zǐlù said:
"A noble man may die, but his cap should not be removed."
He then tied his cap string and died.
When Confucius heard about the turmoil in Wèi,
he said:
"Alas,
Yóu has died!"
And indeed he had died.
Therefore Confucius said:
"Since I got Yóu,
malicious words no longer reached my ears."
At that time, Zǐgòng was on a mission to Qí for Lǔ.
Zǎi Yǔ, styled Zǐwǒ,
was glib-tongued and skilled in debate.
After receiving instruction,
he asked:
"Isn't the three-year mourning period too long?
If a noble man does not practice rites for three years,
the rites will deteriorate;
if he does not practice music for three years,
music will collapse.
When the old grain is finished,
and the new grain has been harvested,
and the fire-drill has made its annual change,
one year should be enough."
The Master said:
"Would you feel at ease doing so?"
He replied:
"Yes."
"If you feel at ease, then do it.
When a noble man is in mourning,
he finds no sweetness in fine food,
no joy in hearing music,
therefore he does not do these things."
After Zǎi Wǒ left,
the Master said:
"Yǔ is without benevolence!
A child is held in its parents' arms for three years after birth.
The three-year mourning period
is the universal principle throughout the world."
Zǎi Yǔ was sleeping during the day.
The Master said:
"Rotten wood cannot be carved;
a wall of dried dung cannot be plastered."
When Zǎi Wǒ asked about the virtue of the Five Emperors,
the Master said:
"Yǔ is not the right person (to discuss this with)."
When Zǎi Wǒ served as magistrate of Línzī,
he joined Tián Cháng in rebellion,
which led to the extermination of his clan,
something Confucius felt ashamed of.
Duānmù Cì,
a man of Wèi,
styled Zǐgòng,
was thirty-one years younger than Confucius.
Zǐgòng was glib-tongued and skilled in speech,
and Confucius often curtailed his arguments.
He asked him:
"Who is superior, you or Huí?"
He replied:
"How dare Cì compare himself with Huí!
Huí hears one point and understands ten;
Cì hears one point and understands only two."
After Zǐgòng had received instruction,
he asked:
"What kind of person is Cì?"
Confucius said:
"You are a vessel."
He asked:
"What kind of vessel?"
He replied:
"A húliǎn (ritual vessel)."
Chén Zǐqín asked Zǐgòng:
"From whom did Zhòngní learn?"
Zǐgòng said:
"The Way of King Wén and King Wǔ has not fallen to the ground;
it exists in people.
The worthy recognize its major aspects,
the unworthy recognize its minor aspects,
but no one is without something of the Way of Wén and Wǔ.
From whom would our Master not learn?
And why would he need a constant teacher?"
He asked further:
"Whenever Confucius goes to a state, he invariably learns about its government.
Does he seek this information,
or is it given to him?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Our Master acquires it through being cordial, upright, courteous, temperate, and deferential.
Our Master's way of seeking it
is different from other people's way of seeking it."
Zǐgòng asked:
"To be wealthy yet not arrogant,
to be poor yet not obsequious,
what would you say of this?"
Confucius replied:
"That is acceptable;
but it is not as good as being poor yet delighting in the Way,
or wealthy yet loving the rites."
Tián Cháng wished to stage a rebellion in Qí,
but feared the Gāo,
Guó, Bào,
and Yàn families, so he shifted his troops intending to attack Lǔ.
When Confucius heard of this,
he said to his disciples:
"Now Lǔ,
is where our ancestors' graves are located,
the state of our parents.
With the state in such peril,
why has none of you ventured forth?"
Zǐlù requested to go,
but Confucius stopped him.
Zǐzhāng,
Zǐshí requested to go,
but Confucius did not consent.
Zǐgòng requested to go,
and Confucius approved.
So he went,
arriving in Qí,
and persuaded Tián Cháng, saying:
"Your campaign against Lǔ is mistaken.
Now Lǔ,
is a state difficult to attack,
its walls are thin and low,
its land narrow and marshy,
its ruler foolish and unkind,
its ministers hypocritical and useless,
and its people and soldiers detest warfare,
so it is not advisable to fight them.
You would do better to attack Wú.
Now Wú,
has high and thick walls,
vast and deep territory,
new and sturdy armor,
well-selected and well-fed troops,
with elite soldiers and fine weaponry all within,
and has appointed wise ministers to guard it,
making it an easy target."
Tián Cháng flushed with anger and said:
"What you consider difficult,
others find easy;
what you consider easy,
others find difficult.
And you advise me thus,
why?"
Zǐgòng said:
"I have heard that
those with internal worries should attack the strong,
those with external worries should attack the weak.
Now your worries lie within.
I hear you have attempted three times to gain enfeoffment but failed each time,
because some ministers do not obey you.
Now if you destroy Lǔ to expand Qí,
victory will make your ruler arrogant,
conquering a state will elevate other ministers,
yet your own achievements will not be recognized,
so your relationship with the ruler will grow distant daily.
Thus you would inflate the ruler's pride above,
and indulge the ministers below,
seeking to accomplish great things—
this is difficult.
For when the ruler is arrogant, he becomes arbitrary;
when ministers are arrogant, they contend for power.
Thus you would have estrangement from the ruler above,
and conflicts with ministers below.
In such a situation,
your position in Qí would be precarious.
Therefore I said you should attack Wú instead.
If you attack Wú and do not win,
the people will die abroad,
ministers will be weakened at home,
then you would have no strong ministerial rivals above,
and no blame from the people below,
leaving you alone to control Qí with the isolated ruler."
Tián Cháng said:
"Good.
However,
my troops are already directed at Lǔ,
to withdraw and turn to Wú,
the ministers would suspect me,
what then?"
Zǐgòng said:
"You halt the troops and do not attack,
I request to go as envoy to the King of Wú,
to have him rescue Lǔ and attack Qí,
then you can meet them with your forces."
Tián Cháng agreed,
and sent Zǐgòng south to see the King of Wú.
He persuaded him, saying:
"I have heard that
a true king does not let states perish,
a hegemon has no powerful rivals,
a weight of thousand jūn can be shifted by adding a few zhū.
Now with the mighty Qí of ten thousand chariets annexing the small Lǔ of a thousand chariets,
it contends for strength with Wú,
I secretly fear for Your Majesty.
Moreover, to rescue Lǔ
brings illustrious fame;
to attack Qí
brings great benefit.
By pacifying the lords along the Sì River,
punishing the violent Qí to subdue the powerful Jìn,
no benefit could be greater.
In name, preserving the perishing Lǔ,
in reality, weakening the strong Qí,
no wise man would hesitate."
The King of Wú said:
"Good.
However,
I once fought Yuè,
and cornered them at Kuàijī.
The King of Yuè suffers personally to nurture his men,
intending revenge against me.
Wait till I subdue Yuè, then I will heed you."
Zǐgòng said:
"Yuè's strength is no match for Lǔ,
Wú's power no match for Qí,
if you abandon Qí to attack Yuè,
then Qí will have already pacified Lǔ.
Moreover, you claim to preserve perishing states and continue severed lines,
yet attacking small Yuè while fearing strong Qí
is not courage.
The courageous do not avoid difficulties,
the benevolent do not abandon the distressed,
the wise do not miss opportunities,
the kingly do not let states perish,
thereby establishing their righteousness.
Now preserving Yuè shows benevolence to the lords,
rescuing Lǔ and attacking Qí,
imposing awe on Jìn,
the lords will surely come in succession to pay homage to Wú,
and your hegemon's cause will be achieved.
And if you must resent Yuè,
I request to go east to see the King of Yuè,
to have him send troops to follow you,
thus emptying Yuè in reality,
while in name having it join the lords in the campaign."
The King of Wú was greatly pleased,
and sent Zǐgòng to Yuè.
The King of Yuè cleared the path and welcomed him at the outskirts,
personally escorted him to his residence, and asked:
"This is a barbaric state,
why has the Grand Master dignified us with your honorable presence?"
Zǐgòng replied:
"Recently, I persuaded the King of Wú to save Lǔ and attack Qí,
but his intention is set on it yet he fears Yuè,
saying
'Wait until I conquer Yuè, then it can be done.'
In this way,
he will certainly destroy Yuè.
Moreover, having no intention of retaliating against others yet making them suspicious of you
is clumsy;
having the intention to retaliate against others,
and letting them know about it,
is perilous;
when affairs have not yet begun but are heard of first,
it is dangerous.
These three are great calamities in undertaking actions."
Gōujiàn bowed his head and paid respects twice, saying:
"I once did not measure my strength,
and thus battled with Wú,
was trapped at Kuàijī,
the pain penetrated my bone marrow,
day and night my lips are parched and tongue dry,
only wishing to follow in the footsteps of the King of Wú and die,
that is my desire."
Then he asked Zǐgòng for advice.
Zǐgòng said:
"The King of Wú is fierce and violent by nature,
his ministers cannot endure it;
the state is exhausted from frequent wars,
the soldiers cannot bear it;
the common people resent their superiors,
high officials have internal strife;
Zǐxū died due to his remonstrance,
while Grand Steward Pǐ holds power,
indulging the ruler's faults to secure his own interests:
this is governance that ruins a state.
If now you truly send soldiers to assist him to fulfill his ambition,
offer precious treasures to please his heart,
use humble words to show respect in etiquette,
he will certainly attack Qí.
If he does not win the battle,
it will be your blessing.
If he wins the battle,
he will surely lead his troops to confront Jìn,
I request to go north to meet the ruler of Jìn,
and have him join in attacking Wú,
weakening Wú is certain.
When his elite troops are exhausted in Qí,
and his heavy armor is trapped in Jìn,
then you can take advantage of his weakness,
this will surely destroy Wú."
The King of Yuè was greatly pleased,
and agreed.
He offered Zǐgòng a hundred yì of gold,
one sword,
and two fine spears.
Zǐgòng did not accept them,
and then departed.
He reported to the King of Wú, saying:
"I respectfully conveyed your words to the King of Yuè,
the King of Yuè was greatly terrified,
saying:
'I am unfortunate,
having lost my ancestors at a young age,
internally not knowing my own measure,
offended Wú and incurred punishment,
my army defeated and myself disgraced,
stranded at Kuàijī,
my state reduced to ruins and wilderness,
relying on your great king's grace,
I am able to serve with sacrificial vessels and maintain sacrifices,
I dare not forget even in death,
how would I dare to contemplate any schemes!'"
Five days later,
Yuè sent Minister Zhǒng to bow and speak to the King of Wú:
"The humble servant of the Eastern Sea, solitary Gōujiàn's envoy, your servant Zhǒng,
dares to address the lower officials and inquire of your attendants.
Now I have privately heard that your great king is about to rise for a righteous cause,
to punish the strong and save the weak,
subdue the violent Qí and pacify the Zhōu court,
I request to mobilize all the three thousand soldiers within our borders,
and I myself ask to don armor and take up arms,
to be the first to receive arrows and stones.
Thus, through the humble servant Zhǒng of Yuè, I present heirloom treasures stored by my ancestors,
twenty sets of armor,
Fūqūlú spears,
Bùguāng swords,
to congratulate your military officers."
The King of Wú was greatly pleased,
and told Zǐgòng:
"The King of Yuè wishes to personally follow me to attack Qí,
is that acceptable?"
Zǐgòng said:
"It is not acceptable.
To empty someone's state,
take all their people,
and also have their ruler accompany you,
is unjust.
You should accept their gifts,
approve their troops,
but decline their ruler."
The King of Wú agreed,
and then declined the King of Yuè.
Thereupon, the King of Wú mobilized the troops of nine commanderies to attack Qí.
Zǐgòng then left for Jìn,
and said to the ruler of Jìn:
"I have heard that,
if plans are not set in advance, one cannot respond to emergencies,
if troops are not prepared beforehand, one cannot defeat the enemy.
Now Qí and Wú are about to battle,
if they fight and do not win,
Yuè will surely cause chaos for them;
if they battle Qí and win,
they will certainly lead their troops to confront Jìn."
The ruler of Jìn was greatly alarmed,
saying:
"What should be done about it?"
Zǐgòng said:
"Train your troops and let them rest, waiting for them."
The ruler of Jìn agreed.
Zǐgòng left and went to Lǔ.
The King of Wú indeed battled the men of Qí at Àilíng,
decisively defeated the Qí army,
captured the weapons of seven generals and did not return,
indeed led his troops to confront Jìn,
and encountered the men of Jìn at Huángchí.
Wú and Jìn contended for supremacy.
The men of Jìn attacked them,
and greatly defeated the Wú army.
The King of Yuè heard of this,
crossed the river and attacked Wú,
encamping seven lǐ from the city.
The King of Wú heard of this,
left Jìn and returned,
and battled Yuè at Wǔhú.
After three battles without victory,
the city gates could not be held,
Yuè then besieged the royal palace,
killed Fūchāi and executed his chancellor.
Three years after destroying Wú,
he faced east and became hegemon.
Thus, with one journey of Zǐgòng,
he preserved Lǔ,
threw Qí into chaos,
destroyed Wú,
strengthened Jìn and made Yuè a hegemon.
With one mission by Zǐgòng,
he caused the powers to break each other,
within ten years,
five states each underwent changes.
Zǐgòng was fond of buying low and selling high,
and converting goods according to the times.
He liked to praise others' virtues,
but could not conceal others' faults.
He served as chancellor of Lǔ and Wèi,
accumulated a fortune of a thousand gold at home,
and eventually died in Qí.
Yán Yǎn,
a man of Wú,
courtesy name Zǐyóu.
He was forty-five years younger than Confucius.
After Zǐyóu had received his education,
he became the magistrate of Wǔchéng.
When Confucius passed by,
he heard the sound of stringed instruments and singing.
Confucius smiled and said:
"Why use a butcher's knife for a chicken?"
Zǐyóu said:
"In the past, I heard from you, Master,
that when a gentleman learns the Way, he loves others,
and when a common person learns the Way, he is easier to employ."
Confucius said:
"My disciples,
Yǎn's words are correct.
What I said earlier was just a joke."
Confucius considered Zǐyóu well-versed in literature.
Bǔ Shāng, courtesy name Zǐxià.
He was forty-four years younger than Confucius.
Zǐxià asked:
"'Her artful smile, with its dimples;
her beautiful eyes, so bright;
the plain ground with colors to set them off' —
what does this mean?"
The Master said:
"The painting comes after the plain groundwork."
Zǐxià said:
"Does ritual come afterwards?"
Confucius said:
"It is Shāng who can begin to discuss the Odes with me."
Zǐgòng asked:
"Who is superior, Shī or Shāng?"
The Master said:
"Shī goes too far,
and Shāng does not go far enough."
"Then is Shī better?"
He said:
"To go too far is as bad as not to go far enough."
The Master said to Zǐxià:
"Be a nobleman scholar,
not a petty man scholar."
After Confucius passed away,
Zǐxià lived at Xīhé and taught,
becoming the teacher of Lord Wèi Wén.
When his son died,
he wept until he lost his eyesight.
Zhuānsūn Shī,
a man from Chén,
styled Zǐzhāng.
He was forty-eight years younger than Confucius.
Zǐzhāng asked about seeking an official salary.
Confucius said:
"Hear much and set aside what is doubtful,
speak cautiously of the rest,
then you will have few occasions for blame.
See much and set aside what seems perilous,
act cautiously with the rest,
then you will have few occasions for regret.
With few occasions for blame in speech,
and few occasions for regret in action,
salary will be found within."
Another day, when following between Chén and Cài,
in distress, he asked about conduct.
Confucius said:
"Be loyal and trustworthy in speech,
sincere and respectful in action,
and you will get along even in barbarian states.
If you are not loyal and trustworthy in speech,
nor sincere and respectful in action,
how can you get along even in your own neighborhood?
Standing, see these principles ranged before you;
in your carriage, see them resting on the crossbar —
then you may proceed."
Zǐzhāng wrote this on his girdle.
Zǐzhāng asked:
"What must a scholar be like to be called distinguished?"
Confucius said:
"What do you mean
by 'distinguished'?"
Zǐzhāng replied:
"To be famous in the state,
and famous in the clan."
Confucius said:
"That is fame,
not distinction.
The distinguished man is
upright in character and fond of righteousness,
examines people's words and observes their expressions,
and is mindful to defer to others.
Such a man will be distinguished in the state and in the clan.
The famous man,
assuming an appearance of benevolence while his actions belie it,
and self-assured without doubt,
will be famous in the state and in the clan."
Zēng Shēn,
a man from Nánwǔchéng,
styled Zǐyú.
He was forty-six years younger than Confucius.
Confucius considered him capable of understanding the Way of Filial Piety,
so he taught him.
He composed the "Classic of Filial Piety".
He died in Lǔ.
Dāntái Mièmíng,
a man from Wǔchéng,
styled Zǐyǔ.
He was thirty-nine years younger than Confucius.
His appearance was very ugly.
He wished to serve Confucius,
but Confucius thought him lacking in talent.
After he had been accepted as a pupil,
he withdrew and cultivated his conduct,
never taking shortcuts,
and never visiting high officials without public business.
Traveling south to the river,
he had three hundred disciples following him,
establishing rules for giving and taking, advancing and withdrawing,
and his reputation spread among the feudal lords.
Confucius heard of this,
and said:
"I judged by speech,
and erred with Zǎiyǔ;
I judged by appearance,
and erred with Zǐyǔ."
Fú Bùqí, styled Zǐjiàn.
He was thirty years younger than Confucius.
Confucius said of him,
"Zǐjiàn is a nobleman indeed!
If there were no noblemen in Lǔ,
how could he have acquired this?"
When Zǐjiàn was steward of Shànfù,
he reported back to Confucius,
saying:
"In this district, there are five men more worthy than Bùqí,
who taught me how to govern."
Confucius said:
"It is a pity that Bùqí governs only a small place;
if he governed something larger, he would come close to it."
Yuán Xiàn, styled Zǐsī.
Zǐsī asked about disgrace.
Confucius said:
"When the state has the Way,
take salary. When the state is without the Way,
taking salary is disgraceful."
Zǐsī said:
"If one refrains from boasting, resentment, covetousness, and desire,
can this be called benevolence?"
Confucius said:
"This can be called difficult,
but I do not know about benevolence."
After Confucius died,
Yuán Xiàn went to live in the marshes.
When Zǐgòng was prime minister of Wèi,
with a train of four-horse carriages,
he pushed through weeds into a poor alley,
to visit and thank Yuán Xiàn.
Xiàn, in worn-out clothes and cap, came to see Zǐgòng.
Zǐgòng felt ashamed for him,
and said:
"Are you ill, Master?"
Yuán Xiàn said:
"I have heard that
lack of wealth is called poverty,
but learning the Way and failing to practice it is called illness.
As for me,
I am poor,
not ill."
Zǐgòng was ashamed,
and left displeased,
regretting his words for the rest of his life.
Gōngyě Cháng,
a man from Qí,
styled Zǐcháng.
Confucius said:
"Cháng is fit to be given a wife;
though he has been in bonds,
it was not through any fault of his."
He gave him his own daughter in marriage.
Nángōng Kuò, styled Zǐróng.
Someone asked Confucius:
"Yì was skilled in archery,
Ào was adept at naval warfare,
yet both died unnatural deaths;
while Yǔ and Jì personally engaged in farming and gained the world?"
Confucius did not reply.
After the questioner left,
Confucius said:
"What a superior man this person is!
What a man of high virtue this person is!"
"When the state is well-governed;
he is not cast aside;
when the state is ill-governed,
he escapes punishment and execution."
He repeatedly recited
"the flaw in the white jade scepter,"
and gave his elder brother's daughter to him in marriage.
Gōngxī Āi, courtesy name Jìcì.
Confucius said:
"When there's no moral conduct in the world,
many become household officials,
serving in the cities;
only Jìcì never took office."
Zēng Diǎn, courtesy name Xī.
While attending upon Confucius,
Confucius said:
"Tell me your aspirations."
Diǎn said:
"When spring clothes are ready,
with five or six capped gentlemen,
and six or seven young boys,
bathing in the Yí River,
enjoying the breeze at the Wǔyú altar,
and returning home singing."
Confucius sighed and said:
"I agree with Diǎn!"
Yán Wúyóu, courtesy name Lù.
Lù
was Yán Huí's father,
father and son each served Confucius at different times.
When Yán Huí died,
Yán Lù was poor,
and asked Confucius for his carriage to use for the burial.
Confucius said:
"Talented or not,
each speaks of his own son.
When Lǐ died,
he had a coffin but no outer coffin,
I didn't go on foot to provide him an outer coffin,
because having served as a senior official,
I cannot go on foot."
Shāng Qú,
from Lǔ,
courtesy name Zǐmù.
Twenty-nine years younger than Confucius.
Confucius transmitted the "Yì" to Qú,
Qú transmitted it to the Chǔ person Hánbì Zǐhóng,
Hóng transmitted it to the Jiāngdōng person Jiǎo Zǐyōng Cī,
Cī transmitted it to the Yān person Zhōu Zǐjiā Shù,
Shù transmitted it to the Chúnyú person Guāng Zǐchéng Yǔ,
Yǔ transmitted it to the Qí person Tián Zǐzhuāng Hé,
Hé transmitted it to the Dōngwǔ person Wáng Zǐzhōng Tóng,
Tóng transmitted it to the Zīchuān person Yáng Hé.
Hé during Yuánshuò era became a Han grand master for his mastery of the "Yì".
Gāo Chái, courtesy name Zǐgāo,
thirty years younger than Confucius.
Zǐgāo's height didn't reach five chǐ,
he studied under Confucius,
Confucius considered him dull.
Zǐlù made Zǐgāo steward of Fèihòu,
Confucius said:
"You're ruining another man's son!"
Zǐlù said:
"There are common people there,
there are altars of soil and grain there,
why must one study books to be considered learned!"
Confucius said:
"This is why I dislike glib talkers."
Qīdiāo Kāi, courtesy name Zǐkāi.
Confucius urged Kāi to take office,
he replied:
"I'm not yet confident in my ability for this."
Confucius was pleased.
Gōngbó Liáo, courtesy name Zǐzhōu.
Zhōu accused Zǐlù before Jìsūn,
Zǐfú Jǐngbó reported this to Confucius,
saying:
"Our master certainly has doubts,
regarding Liáo,
my strength can still have him executed in the marketplace."
Confucius said:
"If the Way is to prevail,
it's fate;
if the Way is to fall,
it's fate.
What can Gōngbó Liáo do about fate!"
Sīmǎ Gēng, courtesy name Zǐniú.
Niú was talkative and impetuous.
He asked Confucius about benevolence,
Confucius said:
"The benevolent are hesitant in speech."
He said:
"Being hesitant in speech,
can this be called benevolence?"
The Master said:
"Doing it is difficult,
how can speaking about it not be hesitant!"
He asked about the superior man,
the Master said:
"The superior man neither worries nor fears."
He said:
"Neither worrying nor fearing,
can this be called a superior man?"
The Master said:
"When introspection reveals no guilt,
what is there to worry or fear!"
Fán Xū, courtesy name Zǐchí.
Thirty-six years younger than Confucius.
Fán Chí requested to learn farming,
Confucius said:
"I'm not as good as an old farmer."
He requested to learn gardening,
Confucius said:
"I'm not as good as an old gardener."
After Fán Chí left,
Confucius said:
"What a small-minded man Fán Xū is!
If superiors love ritual,
then none among the people will dare be disrespectful;
if superiors love righteousness,
then none among the people will dare be disobedient;
if superiors love trustworthiness,
then none among the people will dare be insincere.
When it is thus,
then people from all directions will come carrying their children on their backs,
why would one need farming!"
Fán Chí asked about benevolence,
the Master said:
"Love people."
He asked about wisdom,
the Master said:
"Know people."
Yǒu Ruò was forty-three years younger than Confucius.
Yǒu Ruò said:
"In the application of ritual,
harmony is valued;
this is what made the way of former kings beautiful.
In matters small and great following this,
there are cases where it doesn't work;
knowing harmony and pursuing harmony alone,
without regulating it with ritual,
also cannot be done."
"Trustworthiness close to righteousness
makes words fulfillable;
reverence close to ritual
keeps one far from shame and disgrace;
not losing attachment to one's kin,
can also be worthy of esteem."
After Confucius passed away,
his disciples missed him deeply.
There was Yǒu Ruò, who resembled Confucius in appearance,
so the disciples jointly regarded him as their teacher,
serving him as they had during the Master's time.
One day,
a disciple came forward and asked:
"In the past, when the Master was about to go out,
he had a disciple bring rain gear,
and it indeed rained afterward.
The disciple asked:
'How did you know, Master?'
The Master said:
'Doesn't the Book of Songs say?
"When the moon passes through the constellation Bì,
it brings pouring rain."
Did the moon not lodge in Bì last night?'
Another day,
the moon lodged in Bì,
but it did not rain after all.
Shāng Qú was older but had no sons,
and his mother sought a wife for him.
Confucius sent him to Qí,
and Qú's mother pleaded with him.
Confucius said:
'Do not worry;
after Qú turns forty, he will have five sons.'
And so it turned out.
May I ask how the Master knew this?'
Yǒu Ruò remained silent and had no response.
The disciples rose and said:
'Step down, Master Yǒu;
this is not your seat!'
Gōngxī Chì, styled Zǐhuá,
was forty-two years younger than Confucius.
When Zǐhuá was sent on a mission to Qí,
Rǎn Yǒu requested grain for his mother.
Confucius said:
'Give her a fǔ.'
He asked for more,
and Confucius said:
'Give her a yǔ.'
Rǎnzǐ instead gave her five bǐng of grain.
Confucius said:
'When Chì went to Qí,
he rode fat horses
and wore light furs.
I have heard that a gentleman relieves the needy, not enriches the wealthy.'
Wūmǎ Shī, styled Zǐqí,
was thirty years younger than Confucius.
Chén Sībài asked Confucius:
'Does Duke Zhāo of Lǔ understand the rites?'
Confucius said:
'He understands the rites.'
Afterward, Chén Sībài bowed to Wūmǎ Qí and said:
'I have heard that a gentleman is not partial;
is a gentleman also partial?
The ruler of Lǔ married a woman from Wú as his wife,
naming her Mèngzǐ.
Mèngzǐ's surname was Jī,
and it was taboo to mention the same surname,
so she was called Mèngzǐ.
If the ruler of Lǔ understands the rites,
who does not?'
Shī reported this to Confucius,
and Confucius said:
'I am fortunate;
if I have faults,
others are sure to know them.
A minister cannot speak of the faults of his ruler or parents;
to conceal them
is in accordance with the rites.'
Liáng Zhān, styled Shūyú,
was twenty-nine years younger than Confucius.
Yán Xìng, styled Zǐliǔ,
was forty-six years younger than Confucius.
Rǎn Rú, styled Zǐlǔ,
was fifty years younger than Confucius.
Cáo Xù, styled Zǐxún,
was fifty years younger than Confucius.
Bó Qián, styled Zǐxī,
was fifty years younger than Confucius.
Gōngsūn Lóng, styled Zǐshí,
was fifty-three years younger than Confucius.
From Zǐshí and above, there are thirty-five individuals
whose ages and names are recorded and who are known through texts and traditions for their learning.
The remaining forty-two,
whose ages are unknown and who do not appear in texts, are listed below:
Rǎn Jì, styled Zǐchǎn.
Gōngzǔ Gōuzī, styled Zǐzhī.
Qín Zǔ, styled Zǐnán.
Qīdiāo Chǐ, styled Zǐliǎn.
Yán Gāo, styled Zǐjiāo.
Qīdiāo Túfù.
Rǎngsì Chì, styled Zǐtú.
Shāng Zé.
Shízuò Shǔ, styled Zǐmíng.
Rèn Bùqí, styled Xuǎn.
Gōngliáng Rú, styled Zǐzhèng.
Hòu Chǔ, styled Zǐlǐ.
Qín Rǎn, styled Kāi.
Gōngxià Shǒu, styled Chéng.
Xīróng Zhēn, styled Zǐxī.
Gōngjiān Dìng, styled Zǐzhōng.
Yán Zǔ, styled Xiāng.
Qiāo Shàn, styled Zǐjiā.
Gōujǐng Jiāng.
Hǎnfǔ Hēi, styled Zǐsuǒ.
Qín Shāng, styled Zǐpī.
Shēn Dǎng, styled Zhōu.
Yán Zhīpú, styled Shū.
Róng Qí, styled Zǐqí.
Xiàn Chéng, styled Zǐqí.
Zuǒrén Yǐng, styled Xíng.
Yàn Jí, styled Sī.
Zhèng Guó, styled Zǐtú.
Qín Fēi, styled Zǐzhī.
Shī Zhīcháng, styled Zǐhéng.
Yán Kuài, styled Zǐshēng.
Bùshū Chéng, styled Zǐchē.
Yuán Kàngjí.
Yuè Kài, styled Zǐshēng.
Lián Jié, styled Yōng.
Shūzhòng Huì, styled Zǐqī.
Yán Hé, styled Rǎn.
Dí Hēi, styled Xī.
Bāng Xùn, styled Zǐliǎn.
Kǒng Zhōng.
Gōngxī Yúrú, styled Zǐshàng.
Gōngxī Zhēn, styled Zǐshàng.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Scholars often speak of the seventy disciples,
where those who praise them may exaggerate their merits,
and those who criticize them may undervalue their true worth.
Since we have not seen their appearances,
to discuss the records of the disciples,
the ancient texts from the Confucian school are the most reliable.
I have compiled the names and details of the disciples based on the questions and answers in the Analects, arranging them into this chapter,
omitting those that are doubtful.
Lord Shāng was
a son of the collateral line of the ruling house of Wèi,
named Yāng, with the surname Gōngsūn,
and his ancestors originally bore the surname Jī.
Yāng was fond of the study of punishment and name from a young age,
and served as a household aide
to the minister of Wèi, Gōngshū Cuò.
Gōngshū Cuò recognized his worth,
but had not yet recommended him.
It happened that Cuò fell ill,
and King Huì of Wèi personally went to inquire about his illness,
saying: "If your illness proves fatal,
what will become of the state?"
Gōngshū replied:
"My household aide Gōngsūn Yāng,
though young in years,
has extraordinary talent.
I hope Your Majesty will entrust the state
to him and heed his counsel."
The king remained silent.
As the king was about to leave,
Cuò dismissed his attendants and said:
"If Your Majesty does not intend to employ Yāng,
you must kill him,
and not allow him to leave the state."
The king assented and departed.
Gōngshū Cuò summoned Yāng and apologized:
"Just now the king asked
who could serve as minister,
and I mentioned you,
but the king's expression showed disapproval.
I then prioritized my lord before my subject,
and therefore told the king that if he would not use Yāng,
he should kill him.
The king agreed.
You must leave quickly,
or you will be captured."
Yāng said:
"Since that king would not heed your advice to employ me,
how could he heed your advice to kill me?"
In the end, he did not leave.
After King Huì had departed,
he said to his attendants:
"Gōngshū is gravely ill,
how pitiable,
to suggest that I entrust the state to Gōngsūn Yāng,
is that not absurd!"
After Gōngshū's death,
Gōngsūn Yāng heard that
Duke Xiào of Qín had issued an order throughout the state
seeking worthy men,
intending to continue the achievements of Duke Mù,
and recover the lost territories in the east.
Thereupon, he went west to Qín,
and through the favor of Duke Xiào's favored minister Jǐng Jiān,
sought an audience with Duke Xiào.
After Duke Xiào met with Wèi Yāng,
they conversed at length,
but Duke Xiào dozed off from time to time,
and did not listen.
After the audience, Duke Xiào angrily said to Jǐng Jiān:
"Your guest is but a braggart,
how could he be of any use!"
Jǐng Jiān reproached Wèi Yāng for this.
Wèi Yāng said:
"I expounded the Way of the Emperors to the duke,
but his mind was not enlightened."
Five days later,
he again requested to see Yāng.
Yāng again met Duke Xiào,
and the conversation went somewhat better,
yet still did not meet the duke's expectations.
After the audience, Duke Xiào again reproached Jǐng Jiān,
and Jǐng Jiān in turn reproached Yāng.
Yāng said:
"I expounded the Way of the Kings to the duke,
but it did not reach him.
Please request another audience for me."
Yāng again met Duke Xiào,
and Duke Xiào thought well of him
but did not employ him.
The audience ended and he left.
Duke Xiào said to Jǐng Jiān:
"Your guest is good,
and one can converse with him."
Yāng said:
"I expounded the Way of the Hegemons to the duke,
and his mind inclined to employ it.
If he truly sees me again,
I know what to do."
Wèi Yāng again met Duke Xiào.
The duke conversed with him,
unconsciously moving his knees forward on the mat.
They talked for several days without tiring.
Jǐng Jiān said:
"How did you manage to please my lord?
My lord is exceedingly delighted."
Yāng said:
"I expounded the ways of emperors and kings to him,
comparing them to the Three Dynasties,
but the lord said:
'That is too long ago,
I cannot wait.
Moreover, a worthy ruler
should make his name illustrious throughout the world in his own lifetime;
how can I languish waiting for decades or centuries
to achieve the status of emperor or king?'
Therefore, I used the methods of strengthening the state to persuade the lord,
and he was greatly pleased.
Yet it will be difficult
to compare in virtue to the Shāng and Zhōu."
After Duke Xiào employed Wèi Yāng,
Yāng wished to reform the laws,
but feared the world would criticize him.
Wèi Yāng said: "Hesitant action wins no fame,
hesitant undertakings achieve no merit.
Moreover, those who act superior to others
are inevitably condemned by the world;
those with uniquely wise plans
are inevitably mocked by the people.
The foolish do not understand things even when accomplished,
the wise perceive things before they sprout.
One cannot discuss beginnings with the people,
but can share success with them.
Those who discuss supreme virtue
do not conform to custom;
those who achieve great merit
do not consult the multitude.
Therefore, if a sage can strengthen the state,
he does not model on the old ways;
if he can benefit the people,
he does not follow established rites."
Duke Xiào said: "Good."
Gān Lóng said:
"Not so.
The sage teaches without changing the people,
the wise govern without altering the laws.
Teaching according to the people
brings success without toil;
governing by following the laws
makes officials familiar and people content."
Wèi Yāng said:
"What Lóng says
is the talk of the common world."
Ordinary people are comfortable with old customs,
scholars are immersed in what they have heard.
With these two, one can hold office
and maintain laws well enough,
but they are not fit to discuss what lies beyond the laws.
The Three Dynasties ruled with different rites,
the Five Hegemons dominated with different laws.
The wise make laws,
the foolish are controlled by them;
the worthy change rites,
the unworthy are constrained by them."
Dù Zhì said:
"Without a hundredfold benefit,
do not change the law;
without a tenfold gain,
do not alter implements.
Following antiquity avoids error,
adhering to rites avoids deviation."
Wèi Yāng said:
"Governing the world does not follow a single way,
benefiting the state does not imitate antiquity.
Thus, Tāng and Wǔ did not follow antiquity yet became kings,
while Xià and Shāng did not change their rites yet perished.
Those who oppose antiquity should not be faulted,
and those who adhere to rites do not deserve praise."
Duke Xiào said: "Good."
He appointed Wèi Yāng as left庶長,
and finally established the orders for law reform.
He ordered the people to be grouped in fives and tens,
mutually supervising and sharing collective responsibility.
Those who failed to report crimes were cut in half at the waist;
those who reported crimes
received the same reward as for beheading an enemy;
those who concealed crimes
were punished the same as surrendering to the enemy.
Households with two or more adult males
that did not separate
had their taxes doubled.
Those with military merits
each received high ranks according to their achievements;
those who engaged in private fights
were punished in varying degrees of severity.
Devoting effort to fundamental occupations,
farming and weaving—
those who produced much grain and cloth
were exempted from corvée labor.
Those engaged in secondary profits or who were idle and poor
were all enslaved together with their families.
Members of the royal clan who have no military merits to their credit
shall not be entered into the registry.
To clarify distinctions between the noble and the humble,
ranks and positions were defined by grades,
and each was allotted fields and residences according to their rank.
Servants and clothing were also assigned based on family status.
Those with achievements were honored and glorified,
while those without merits,
even if wealthy, were not allowed to display extravagance.
After the ordinances were prepared,
but before they were promulgated,
fearing the people would not trust them,
a three-zhang tall wooden pole was erected
at the south gate of the capital's market,
and the people were summoned, promising ten jin of gold to anyone who could move it to the north gate.
The people found it strange,
and no one dared to move it.
He then announced:
"Anyone who can move it will be given fifty jin of gold."
One person moved it,
and he was promptly given fifty jin of gold,
to demonstrate that there would be no deception.
Finally, the ordinances were issued.
After the ordinances had been in effect among the people for a year,
thousands of Qin people came to the capital to complain about the inconvenience of the new laws.
At that time, the crown prince violated the law.
Wèi Yāng said:
"If the laws are not enforced,
it is because those above violate them."
He intended to punish the crown prince.
However, the crown prince, being the heir to the ruler,
could not be subjected to corporal punishment,
so his tutor, Gōngzǐ Qián, was punished in his place,
and his instructor, Gōngsūn Gǔ, was tattooed.
The next day,
the people of Qin all complied with the ordinances.
After ten years of implementation,
the Qin people were greatly pleased,
lost items were not picked up on the roads,
there were no bandits in the mountains,
and every household had enough to live in abundance.
The people became brave in public warfare,
but timid in private fights,
and the villages and cities were well-governed.
Some of the Qin people who had initially complained about the ordinances
came to say they were convenient,
but Wèi Yāng said,
"These are all people who disrupt transformation,"
and he relocated them all to border towns.
After that, no one dared to discuss the ordinances.
Subsequently, Yāng was appointed as Dàliángzào.
He led troops to besiege Wei's Ānyì,
and forced its surrender.
After three years,
he built palace towers and courtyards
in Xiányáng,
and Qin moved its capital from Yōng to there.
He also prohibited
fathers and sons, brothers from living together in the same room.
Moreover, he consolidated small towns and villages
into counties,
appointing magistrates and assistants,
making a total of thirty-one counties.
He opened up field boundaries and removed borders,
equalizing taxes.
He standardized dou, buckets, weights, measures, and length units.
After four years of implementation,
Gōngzǐ Qián again violated the agreement,
and his nose was cut off.
After five years,
the Qin people became wealthy and strong,
the Son of Heaven sent sacrificial meat to Duke Xiào,
and the feudal lords all came to congratulate him.
The following year,
Qí defeated the Wei army at Mǎlíng,
capturing their crown prince Shēn,
and killing General Páng Juān.
The next year,
Wèi Yāng advised Duke Xiào, saying:
"The relationship between Qin and Wei
is like a person having a disease in the heart or abdomen;
if Wei does not annex Qin,
then Qin will annex Wei.
Why is that?
Wei is located west of the ridges and narrow passes,
with its capital at Ānyì,
bordering Qin by the river,
and exclusively controlling the advantages east of the mountains.
When advantageous, they invade Qin to the west;
when disadvantaged, they expand eastward.
Now, with Your Lordship's wisdom and sageliness,
the state thrives because of it.
Moreover, Wei in previous years
was severely defeated by Qí,
and the feudal lords have turned against it;
we can take this opportunity to attack Wei.
Wei cannot withstand Qin,
and will surely move eastward.
If they move east,
Qin will occupy the solidity of the rivers and mountains,
facing east to control the feudal lords;
this is the enterprise of a king."
Duke Xiào agreed,
and sent Wèi Yāng to lead troops and attack Wei.
Wei sent Gōngzǐ Áng to lead troops against him.
When the armies faced each other,
Wèi Yāng sent a letter to the Wei general Gōngzǐ Áng, saying:
"I was once friendly with you, sir,
now we are both generals of two states;
I cannot bear to attack you.
I would like to meet with you face to face,
conclude a covenant,
drink joyfully and withdraw troops,
to bring peace to Qin and Wei."
Wei's Gōngzǐ Áng thought it was reasonable.
After the meeting and covenant, while drinking,
Wèi Yāng had hidden armored soldiers
who ambushed and captured Wei's Gōngzǐ Áng,
then attacked his army,
defeating it entirely and returning to Qin.
Wei King Huì's army
had been repeatedly defeated by Qí and Qin,
the state was depleted,
and its territory daily diminished;
fearing,
he sent an envoy to cede the land west of the river
and offer it to Qin
to make peace.
Thereupon, Wei left Ānyì,
and moved its capital to Dàliáng.
King Huì of Liáng said:
"I regret not following Gōngshū Cuò's advice."
After Wèi Yāng defeated Wei and returned,
Qin enfeoffed him with fifteen towns in Yū and Shāng,
and he was titled Lord Shāng.
Lord Shāng served as Qin's chancellor for ten years,
and many of the royal clan and noble relatives
harbored resentment towards him.
Zhào Liáng went to see Lord Shāng.
Lord Shāng said:
"The reason I can see you is through Méng Lángāo;
now I wish to befriend you,
is that possible?"
Zhào Liáng said:
"I dare not wish for that.
Confucius once said:
'Recommending the worthy leads to the advancement of those who are supported;
gathering the unworthy causes kings to retreat.'
I am unworthy,
so I dare not accept your command.
I have heard it said:
'To occupy a position that is not rightfully yours is called coveting position;
to hold a name that is not rightfully yours is called coveting fame.'
If I listen to your righteousness,
I fear I would be coveting position and fame.
Therefore, I dare not heed your command."
Lord Shāng said:
"Are you, sir, displeased with my governance of Qin?"
Zhào Liáng said:
"To listen to oneself is called acuity,
to look inward is called clarity,
to overcome oneself is called strength.
Emperor Shun once said:
'Humility is exalted.'
You would do better to follow the way of Emperor Shun,
and not ask me."
Lord Shāng said:
"Initially, Qin had the customs of the Róng and Dí tribes,
with no distinction between father and son,
living together in the same room.
Now I have changed their teachings,
establishing distinctions between men and women,
and built grand palace towers,
making it as splendid as Lǔ and Wèi.
As you observe my governance of Qin,
how does it compare to the worthiness of the Five Rams Grandee?"
Zhào Liáng said:
"The skins of a thousand sheep
are not as good as the armpit fur of one fox;
the assents of a thousand people
are not as good as the straightforward words of one scholar.
King Wǔ prospered because of straightforward speech,
while King Zhòu of Yīn perished because of silence.
If you do not disapprove of King Wǔ,
then I ask to speak honestly all day
without being punished, may I?"
Lord Shāng said:
"There is a saying:
Pleasant words are flowers,
sincere words are fruits,
bitter words are medicine,
sweet words are sickness.
If you, sir, would indeed speak honestly with me all day,
that would be my medicine.
I would serve you,
so why should you decline!"
Zhào Liáng said:
"Now, the Minister of Five Rams,
was a humble man from Chǔ.
Hearing of Duke Mù of Qín's virtue
he wished to see him,
but had no means for the journey,
so he sold himself to a Qín traveler,
wearing coarse clothes and feeding oxen.
After one year,
Duke Mù recognized his worth,
raised him from beneath the oxen's mouth,
and elevated him above the common people,
so that none in Qín dared oppose him.
As Qín's minister for six or seven years,
he campaigned east against Zhèng,
thrice established Jìn's rulers,
and once saved Chǔ from calamity.
His teachings spread within the borders,
and the Bā people brought tribute;
his virtue extended to the feudal lords,
so the Eight Tribes submitted.
Yóu Yú, hearing of him,
knocked at the pass requesting audience.
When the Minister of Five Rams governed Qín,
he never rode in a carriage when weary,
never used a canopy in heat,
traveling through the state
without chariot escort,
without bearing arms.
His achievements were recorded in the archives,
his virtuous conduct passed to later ages.
When the Minister of Five Rams died,
men and women of Qín wept,
children ceased their singing,
rice-pounders hushed their pestle songs.
Such was the virtue of the Minister of Five Rams!
Now you, sir, in visiting the King of Qín,
used the favorite Jǐng Jiàn as patron -
this is no way to build reputation.
Governing Qín
without regard for the people's welfare,
erecting grand palace gates,
this is no way to achieve merit.
Tattooing the crown prince's tutors,
harming people with harsh punishments -
this stores resentment and breeds disaster.
Example transforms people more deeply than commands;
people imitate superiors faster than obeying orders.
Yet you establish perverse policies,
this is no way to educate.
You assume the title 'The Solitary One',
daily disciplining Qín's noble scions.
The Book of Songs says:
'Even field mice have their forms,
but men without propriety;
men without propriety,
why not quickly die?'
Judging by the Songs,
this promises no longevity.
Young Lord Qián
has barred his gate eight years now;
you executed Zhù Huān
and tattooed Gōngsūn Gǔ.
The Book of Songs says:
'Gaining men, one prospers;
losing men, one falls.'
These several matters
win you no followers.
When you go out,
dozens of follower carriages,
chariots laden with armor,
strong men with fused ribs as guards,
spear and halberd bearers
running alongside.
Lacking any one preparation,
you firmly stay inside.
The Book of Documents says:
'Relying on virtue, one flourishes;
relying on force, one perishes.'
Your danger is like morning dew,
yet you seek extended life?
Why not return the fifteen cities,
tend gardens in the countryside,
urge the King to honor recluses,
support elders and orphans,
respect fathers and elders,
reward the meritorious,
honor the virtuous -
then you might find some safety.
If you still covet Shāngwū's wealth,
cherish Qín's harsh governance,
accumulate people's resentment,
should the King suddenly depart
and leave the court,
those in Qín who would seize you -
would they be few?
Your ruin awaits on tiptoe."
Lord Shāng did not heed him.
Five months later, Duke Xiào of Qín died,
the crown prince succeeded.
Young Lord Qián's faction accused Lord Shāng of plotting rebellion,
officials were sent to arrest him.
Lord Shāng fled to the pass,
wanting to lodge at an inn.
The innkeeper didn't recognize him as Lord Shāng,
saying:
"By Lord Shāng's law,
hosting guests without identification
brings punishment."
Lord Shāng sighed deeply:
"Alas! The harm of my laws has reached this point!"
He left for Wèi.
The Wèi people resented his deception of Young Lord Áng
and defeat of Wèi's army,
so they refused him.
Lord Shāng wanted to go to another state.
The Wèi people said:
"Lord Shāng is Qín's fugitive.
Qín is strong, and their fugitive entering Wèi -
not returning him is unacceptable."
So they sent him back to Qín.
After Lord Shāng reentered Qín,
he fled to Shāng City,
raising troops from his fief
to attack Zhèng northward.
Qín dispatched troops against Lord Shāng,
killing him at Miǎnchí in Zhèng.
King Huì of Qín had Lord Shāng torn apart by chariots
as warning, proclaiming:
"Let none rebel like Shāng Yāng!"
Then he exterminated Lord Shāng's family.
Grand Historian remarks:
Lord Shāng
was inherently harsh by nature.
Examining his desire to serve Duke Xiào
with kingly arts,
he promoted empty theories -
not his true substance.
Moreover, he rose through a favorite's help,
and when employed,
punished Young Lord Qián,
deceived Wèi's general Áng,
disregarded Zhào Liáng's advice -
all sufficient to demonstrate
Lord Shāng's lack of compassion.
I have read Lord Shāng's writings on opening barriers
and farming-warfare,
similar to his actual conduct.
That he finally incurred infamy in Qín -
there was reason indeed!
Sū Qín
was from Luòyáng in Eastern Zhōu.
He studied in Qí to the east,
learning from Master Guǐgǔ.
Traveling for several years,
he returned in great poverty.
Brothers, sisters-in-law, wife and concubines all secretly laughed at him,
saying:
"Our Zhōu custom
values managing property,
excelling in crafts and trade,
pursuing twenty percent profit.
Now you abandon fundamentals for glib talk -
your poverty is only fitting!"
Hearing this, Sū Qín felt ashamed
and wounded,
so he secluded himself,
taking out all his books to study.
He said:
"A scholar who has bowed his head over books
yet cannot gain honor -
what use are many books?"
Thereupon he found the Zhōu book "Yīnfú",
pored over it intently.
After a year,
he developed strategies of assessment,
saying:
"This can persuade contemporary rulers."
He sought to persuade King Xiǎn of Zhōu.
The King's attendants knew Sū Qín well
and thought little of him.
They distrusted him.
Then he went west to Qín.
Duke Xiào of Qín had died.
He advised King Huì, saying:
"Qín is a state fortified on all sides,
embraced by mountains and girded by the Wèi River,
with strategic passes and rivers to the east,
Hànzhōng to the west,
Bā and Shǔ to the south,
Dài and Mǎ to the north—
this is the storehouse of nature.
With Qín's numerous soldiers and people,
and the training in military tactics,
you can swallow the whole world,
proclaim yourself emperor and rule."
The King of Qín replied:
"When feathers are not yet fully grown,
one cannot fly high;
when civil administration is not yet clear,
one cannot annex others."
Just then, he had executed Shāng Yāng,
detested debaters,
and did not employ him.
So he went east to Zhào.
Marquis Sù of Zhào had appointed his younger brother Chéng as chancellor,
titled Fèngyáng Lord.
Fèngyáng Lord did not like him.
He left to travel to Yān,
and after over a year, he gained an audience.
He advised Marquis Wén of Yān, saying:
"Yān has Cháoxiǎn and
Liáodōng to the east,
Línhú and
Lóufán to the north,
Yúnzhōng and
Jiǔyuán to the west,
Hūtuó and
Yìshuǐ to the south,
with a territory over two thousand li square,
armored troops numbering several hundred thousand,
six hundred chariots,
six thousand cavalry horses,
and grain supplies lasting several years.
To the south, it has the abundance of Jiéshí and
Yànmén,
to the north, the benefits of dates and chestnuts—
even if the people do not farm, they have enough from dates and chestnuts.
This is what is called the storehouse of nature.
"As for living in peace without troubles,
without seeing armies destroyed and generals killed,
none surpasses Yān.
Does Your Majesty know why this is so?
The reason Yān is not invaded by bandits or burdened with armor and weapons
is because Zhào acts as a shield to its south.
Qín and Zhào fought five battles,
with Qín winning twice and Zhào three times.
Qín and Zhào wear each other out,
while you, King, with a whole Yān, control the aftermath—
this is why Yān is free from invaders.
Moreover, if Qín attacks Yān,
it must cross Yúnzhōng and
Jiǔyuán,
pass through Dài and
Shànggǔ,
covering thousands of li of land.
Even if they capture Yān's cities,
Qín's plans surely cannot hold them.
Thus, Qín's inability to harm Yān is clear.
Now, if Zhào attacks Yān,
issuing orders and commands,
in less than ten days, several hundred thousand troops could be stationed at Dōngyuán.
Crossing the Hūtuó River,
fording the Yìshuǐ,
in less than four or five days, they would reach the capital.
Therefore, I say: when Qín attacks Yān,
the battle is fought a thousand li away;
when Zhào attacks Yān,
the battle is within a hundred li.
To not worry about a threat within a hundred li but fear one a thousand li away—
no strategy is more mistaken than this.
Hence, I hope Your Majesty will ally closely with Zhào,
uniting the world as one,
then Yān will surely have no troubles."
Marquis Wén said:
"Your words are reasonable,
but my state is small,
pressed by powerful Zhào to the west,
and close to Qí to the south.
Qí and Zhào are strong states.
If you insist on forming a vertical alliance to secure Yān,
I pledge my state to follow."
Thereupon, he provided Sū Qín with carriages, horses, gold, and silk to go to Zhào.
But Fèngyáng Lord had already died,
so he took the chance to advise Marquis Sù of Zhào, saying:
"All the ministers, officials, and common scholars of the world
admire Your Lordship's righteous conduct,
and have long wished to offer advice and loyalty before you.
However,
Fèngyáng Lord was jealous, and you did not handle affairs,
so guests and traveling scholars dared not exert themselves in your presence.
Now that Fèngyáng Lord has passed away,
you have once again drawn close to scholars and people,
hence I dare to present my humble thoughts."
"In my opinion, for your strategy,
nothing is better than settling the people and avoiding troubles,
and not burdening the people with affairs.
The foundation of settling the people
lies in choosing alliances.
If alliances are well-chosen, the people are secure;
if not, the people will never be secure.
Let me speak of external threats:
If Qí and Qín are both enemies, the people cannot be secure;
relying on Qín to attack Qí, the people cannot be secure;
relying on Qí to attack Qín, the people cannot be secure.
So, plotting against other rulers,
attacking other states,
often suffers from using words to sever others' alliances.
I hope you will be careful not to let such words pass your lips.
Let me distinguish black from white,
to differentiate the opposing forces.
If you truly heed my advice,
Yān will surely present lands of furs, dogs, and horses;
Qí will surely offer seas of fish and salt;
Chǔ will surely contribute gardens of oranges and pomelos;
Hán,
Wèi, and Zhōngshān can all be made to provide tributes for upkeep,
and your noble relatives and elders can all receive marquis titles.
Partitioning lands and embracing profits—
this is what the Five Hegemons sought through destroying armies and capturing generals;
enfeoffing marquises and honoring relatives—
this is what Tāng and Wǔ fought for through deposing and killing.
Now you can sit high and have both,
this is what I wish for you."
"Now if you align with Qín,
then Qín will surely weaken Hán and
Wèi; if with Qí,
then Qí will surely weaken Chǔ and
Wèi. If Wèi is weakened, it will cede Héwài;
if Hán is weakened, it will offer Yíyáng.
If Yíyáng is offered, the connection to Shàngjùn is cut;
if Héwài is ceded, the route is blocked;
if Chǔ is weakened, there is no support.
These three strategies
must be carefully considered."
"If Qín takes Zhǐdào,
then Nányāng is endangered;
if it coerces Hán and encircles Zhōu,
then Zhào will have to take up arms itself;
if it occupies Wèi and seizes Juǎn,
then Qí will surely submit to Qín.
Once Qín achieves its desires east of the mountains,
it will surely raise troops against Zhào.
When Qín's armor crosses the river and passes Zhāng,
occupying Pānwú,
then battle will surely be fought beneath Hándān.
This is what I worry about for you."
"At present,
among the states east of the mountains, none is stronger than Zhào.
Zhào's territory spans over two thousand li square,
with armored troops numbering several hundred thousand,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry horses,
and grain supplies lasting several years.
To the west, it has Chángshān,
to the south, the Hé and Zhāng rivers,
to the east, the Qīnghé River,
to the north, the state of Yān.
Yān is inherently weak,
not worth fearing.
Of all the states in the world, none is more threatening to Qín than Zhào,
yet Qín dares not raise troops to attack Zhào.
Why?
It fears that Hán and
Wèi will scheme behind it.
Thus, Hán and
Wèi are the southern shield of Zhào.
When Qín attacks Hán and
Wèi,
there are no great mountains or rivers to limit it;
it gradually nibbles away at them,
approaching their capitals before stopping.
If Hán and Wèi cannot withstand Qín,
they will surely submit to Qín.
Without the restraint of Hán and
Wèi,
disaster will surely strike Zhào.
This is what I worry about for you."
"I have heard that Yáo did not possess the land of three families,
Shùn did not have a foot of territory,
yet they came to possess the empire;
Yǔ did not have a gathering of a hundred men,
yet he became king over the feudal lords;
the soldiers of Tāng and Wǔ did not exceed three thousand,
their chariots no more than three hundred,
their troops no more than thirty thousand,
yet they were established as Sons of Heaven:
truly, they had grasped the Way.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler externally assesses the strength and weakness of his enemies,
internally measures the worthiness or unworthiness of his officers and soldiers,
and without waiting for the two armies to face each other, the key to victory or defeat, survival or destruction, is already formed in his breast—
how could he be swayed by the words of the multitude and decide matters in the dark!
"I have privately examined the maps of the empire,
and the territories of the feudal lords are five times that of Qín,
I estimate the troops of the feudal lords to be ten times those of Qín.
If the six states unite as one,
combining their strength to face west and attack Qín,
Qín is sure to be defeated.
Yet now we face west and serve it,
being subjugated by Qín.
To crush others versus being crushed by others,
to make others one's ministers versus being minister to others—
how can these be spoken of in the same breath!
"Those advocates of the horizontal alliance [to Qín],
all desire to cut off the lands of the feudal lords to give to Qín.
When Qín succeeds,
they will have high towers and pavilions,
beautiful palaces and chambers,
listen to the sounds of yú and sè,
before them tower gates and canopied chariots,
behind them are tall, lovely beauties,
yet when the state suffers from Qín's menace, they do not share its worries.
Hence, these horizontal alliance advocates day and night strive to use Qín's power to intimidate the feudal lords, seeking to have land ceded,
so I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
"I have heard that an enlightened ruler cuts off doubts and discards slanders,
removes the traces of rumors,
blocks the gate of factionalism,
thus plans for honoring the ruler, expanding territory, and strengthening the military can be laid out before him with loyalty.
Therefore, I privately plan for Your Majesty,
that nothing is better than uniting Hán,
Wèi, Qí,
Chǔ, Yān,
and Zhào in a vertical alliance of kinship,
to rebel against Qín.
Have the generals and ministers of the empire meet on the banks of the Huán River,
exchange hostages,
and swear an oath by slitting a white horse's throat.
The covenant would say:
'If Qín attacks Chǔ,
Qí and Wèi each shall send elite troops to assist,
Hán shall cut off its supply route,
Zhào shall cross the Hé and Zhāng rivers,
Yān shall guard north of Chángshān.
If Qín attacks Hán or Wèi,
then Chǔ shall cut off its rear,
Qí shall send elite troops to assist,
Zhào shall cross the Hé and Zhāng rivers,
Yān shall guard Yúnzhōng.
If Qín attacks Qí,
then Chǔ shall cut off its rear,
Hán shall guard Chénggāo,
Wèi shall block its path,
Zhào shall cross the Hé and Zhāng rivers
and Bóguān,
Yān shall send elite troops to assist.
If Qín attacks Yān,
then Zhào shall guard Chángshān,
Chǔ shall station troops at Wǔguān,
Qí shall cross the Bó Sea,
Hán and Wèi shall both send elite troops to assist.
If Qín attacks Zhào,
then Hán shall station troops at Yíyáng,
Chǔ at Wǔguān,
Wèi north of the Hé River,
Qí shall cross the Qīng River,
Yān shall send elite troops to assist.
Should any feudal lord fail to abide by the covenant,
the armies of the five states shall jointly attack him.'
If the six states form a vertical alliance to resist Qín,
then Qín's armor surely will not dare venture beyond Hángǔ Pass to harm the lands east of the mountains.
Thus,
the enterprise of a hegemon and king will be achieved."
The King of Zhào said:
"I am young in years,
and my establishment of the state is recent,
never having had the chance to hear long-term strategies for the altars of grain and soil.
Now you, esteemed guest, have the intent to preserve the empire,
and pacify the feudal lords,
I respectfully commit my state to follow."
Thereupon, he prepared a hundred carriages,
a thousand yì of gold,
a hundred pairs of white jade discs,
a thousand bolts of brocade and embroidery,
to make a pact with the feudal lords.
At that time, the Zhou Son of Heaven sent the sacrificial meat of King Wén and King Wǔ to King Huì of Qín.
King Huì sent Xīshǒu to attack Wèi,
captured General Lóng Jiǎ,
took Diāoyīn of Wèi,
and intended to march eastward.
Sū Qín, fearing that Qín's troops would reach Zhào,
then provoked Zhāng Yí,
sending him into Qín.
Thereupon, he persuaded King Xuān of Hán, saying:
"Hán has to the north the strongholds of Gǒng
and Chénggāo,
to the west the passes of Yíyáng
and Shāngbǎn,
to the east Wǎn,
Ráng, and the Wěi River,
to the south Xíngshān,
with a territory of over nine hundred lǐ,
armored troops numbering several hundred thousand,
and the empire's strongest bows and crossbows all come from Hán.
The Xīzǐ,
Shǎofǔ Shílì,
and Jùlái types
all can shoot beyond six hundred paces.
Hán's soldiers, drawing with their feet to shoot,
can fire a hundred times without pause,
at a distance piercing through shields and chests,
at close range piercing through hearts.
The swords and halberds of Hán's soldiers all come from Míngshān,
Tángxī,
Mòyáng,
Héfù,
Dèngshī,
Wǎnféng,
Lóngyuān,
and Tài'ē,
all can on land cut down oxen and horses,
in water sever swans and wild geese,
against the enemy they slash through strong armor and iron curtains,
leather arm-guards and shields,
all are fully equipped.
With the courage of Hán's soldiers,
clad in strong armor,
treading powerful crossbows,
girded with sharp swords,
one man can stand against a hundred—
this is no empty boast.
Given Hán's strength and Your Majesty's worthiness,
yet to face west and serve Qín,
submitting with arms tied,
bringing shame to the altars of grain and soil and becoming a laughingstock of the empire—
nothing is worse than this.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider it.
"If Your Majesty serves Qín,
Qín will surely demand Yíyáng
and Chénggāo.
This year you yield them,
next year it will again demand more land to cede.
To give means having no land left to offer,
not to give means abandoning previous efforts and suffering later calamity.
Moreover, Your Majesty's land is finite, while Qín's demands are endless—
to meet endless demands with finite land
is what is called buying resentment and incurring disaster;
without fighting, your land is already diminished.
I have heard a common saying:
'Rather be the beak of a chicken,
than the rump of an ox.'
Now to face west, arms tied, and serve Qín as a minister,
how is that different from being the ox's rump?
With Your Majesty's worthiness,
and the support of Hán's strong troops,
yet to bear the name of an ox's rump—
I privately feel shame for Your Majesty."
Thereupon, the King of Hán suddenly changed countenance,
rolled up his sleeves and glared in anger,
pressed his sword, looked up to heaven, and sighed deeply, saying:
"Though I am unworthy,
I certainly cannot serve Qín.
Now you, my lord, have instructed me with the teachings of the King of Zhào,
I respectfully offer my state to follow."
He further advised King Xiāng of Wèi:
"Your Majesty's territory
to the south includes Hóng Gōu,
Chén, Rǔnán,
Xǔ, Yǎn,
Kūnyáng,
Shàolíng,
Wǔyáng,
Xīndū,
Xīnxī,
to the east lies Huái,
Yǐng, Zhǔzǎo,
Wúxū,
to the west is bounded by the Great Wall,
to the north encompasses Héwài,
Juǎn, Yǎn,
Suānzǎo,
spanning a thousand lǐ in extent.
Though the place may seem small,
yet the number of fields, cottages, and huts
leaves no room for grazing.
The multitude of people,
the abundance of chariots and horses,
ceaselessly moving day and night,
rumbling and bustling,
as if with the numbers of three armies.
I privately estimate Your Majesty's state is not inferior to Chǔ.
Yet those persuaders alarm Your Majesty into allying with the fierce tiger-like Qín to invade the world,
until suddenly Qín's menace arises,
disregarding its calamity.
To leverage the power of strong Qín to internally coerce one's own ruler,
no crime is greater than this.
Wèi is a powerful state in the world;
Your Majesty is a worthy king in the world.
Now you intend to face west and serve Qín,
proclaim yourself an eastern vassal,
build an imperial palace,
accept caps and sashes,
offer seasonal sacrifices,
I am privately ashamed for Your Majesty.
"I heard King Gōujiàn of Yuè, with three thousand weary soldiers,
captured Fūchāi at Gānsuì;
King Wǔ of Zhōu with three thousand troops,
three hundred armored chariots,
subdued Zhòu at Mùyě;
was it because their soldiers were numerous?
Truly, they could exert their might.
Now I privately hear of Your Majesty's forces:
two hundred thousand warriors,
two hundred thousand green-turbaned troops,
two hundred thousand assault fighters,
one hundred thousand laborers,
six hundred chariots,
five thousand cavalry.
This far surpasses King Gōujiàn of Yuè
and King Wǔ,
yet now you heed the words of your ministers and wish to submit to Qín.
Serving Qín inevitably means ceding land to show sincerity,
so before the army is even used, the state is already weakened.
All ministers who advocate serving Qín
are treacherous men,
not loyal subjects.
As subjects,
they cut their ruler's land to seek foreign ties,
stealing momentary merit without regard for the consequences,
breaking the public good to build private power,
externally leveraging strong Qín's might to internally coerce their ruler,
seeking land cession,
I urge Your Majesty to examine this closely.
"The Zhōu Shū says:
'If threads are unbroken,
how can vines be managed?
If tiny sprouts aren't cut,
they'll require an axe handle.'
If earlier plans aren't settled,
great troubles will follow,
what can be done then?
If Your Majesty truly heeds me,
the six states allied in kinship,
focused and united in purpose,
then surely there will be no menace from strong Qín.
Thus, my humble king of Zhào sent me to offer this simple plan,
presenting a clear covenant,
awaiting Your Majesty's decree to command it."
The King of Wèi said:
"I am unworthy,
and have never heard such enlightened teaching.
Now you, sir, with Zhào king's decree command it,
I respectfully commit my state to follow."
Then he went east to persuade King Xuān of Qí:
"Qí has Tài Shān to the south,
Lángyá to the east,
Qīnghé to the west,
Bó Hǎi to the north,
this is what's called a state fortified on four sides.
Qí's territory spans over two thousand lǐ,
armored troops number in the hundreds of thousands,
grain piles like hills.
The finest of three armies,
the forces of five families,
advance like sharp arrows,
fight like thunderbolts,
disperse like wind and rain.
Even if there's military service,
they've never doubled Tài Shān,
crossed Qīnghé,
or waded Bó Hǎi.
In Línzī alone, there are seventy thousand households,
I privately estimate,
no less than three men per household,
three times seven is two hundred ten thousand,
without recruiting from distant counties,
Línzī's soldiers alone are firmly two hundred ten thousand.
Línzī is exceedingly wealthy and substantial,
its people all play yú, strum sè,
pluck qín, strike zhù,
fight cocks, race dogs,
play liùbó, kick tàjū.
On Línzī's roads,
chariot hubs clash,
shoulders rub together,
joined lapels form curtains,
raised sleeves make canopies,
waved sweat becomes rain,
homes prosperous, people well-off,
ambitions high, spirits soaring.
With Your Majesty's worthiness and Qí's strength,
none in the world can match you.
Yet now you face west to serve Qín,
I am privately ashamed for Your Majesty.
"Moreover, the reason Hán
and Wèi deeply fear Qín
is because they share borders with Qín.
When troops march out to confront each other,
within ten days the fate of victory or survival is decided.
If Hán and Wèi fight and defeat Qín,
their forces are half depleted,
their borders undefended;
if they fight and lose,
then their state's peril follows immediately.
Hence, Hán
and Wèi's reason for heavily engaging Qín in battle
yet lightly submitting as subjects.
Now if Qín attacks Qí, it's not so.
Beyond Hán
and Wèi's lands,
passing through Wèi's Yángjìn route,
traversing the narrows of Gāngfù,
chariots cannot run parallel,
cavalry cannot ride abreast,
a hundred men guarding the pass,
a thousand dare not cross.
Even if Qín wishes to advance deeply,
it glances back like a wolf,
fearing Hán
and Wèi might scheme behind it.
Thus, it hesitates with empty threats,
arrogant yet not daring to advance,
so Qín's inability to harm Qí is also clear.
"Not deeply considering that Qín can do nothing to Qí,
yet wishing to face west and serve it,
this is your ministers' faulty strategy.
Now, without the name of serving Qín, you can have the reality of a strong state,
I therefore wish Your Majesty to slightly consider and plan for it."
The King of Qí said:
"I am not clever,
residing remotely by the sea,
a state at the eastern end of the impoverished road,
and have never heard such remaining teachings.
Now you, with Zhào king's decree commanding it,
I respectfully commit my state to follow."
Then he went southwest to persuade King Wēi of Chǔ, saying:
"Chǔ is
the most powerful state in the world;
and you, Great King, are the worthiest ruler under heaven.
To the west, you possess Qiánzhōng
and Wū Prefecture,
to the east Xiàzhōu
and Hǎiyáng,
to the south Dòngtíng
and Cāngwú,
and to the north Xíngsài
and Xúnyáng.
Your territory spans over five thousand lǐ,
you command a million armored troops,
a thousand chariots,
and ten thousand cavalry,
with grain reserves to last ten years.
These are the foundations for a hegemon or true king.
With Chǔ's strength and your wisdom,
no one in the world can withstand you.
Yet now you wish to face west and serve Qín,
then all the feudal lords will face west and pay homage beneath the Zhāngtái Palace.
"No state is more threatened by Qín than Chǔ.
When Chǔ is strong, Qín is weak;
when Qín is strong, Chǔ is weak—
their positions are irreconcilable.
Therefore, for your strategy, Great King,
nothing is better than forming a vertical alliance to isolate Qín.
If you do not join the alliance,
Qín will surely raise two armies:
one to exit Wǔ Pass,
another to descend upon Qiánzhōng,
and then Yānyǐng will be shaken.
"I have heard that governing should be done before chaos arises,
and actions taken before events occur.
To worry only after disaster strikes
is too late.
Thus, I urge you, Great King, to consider this early and carefully.
"If you truly heed my advice,
I will request that the states east of the mountains offer seasonal tributes,
following your brilliant decree,
entrusting their altars of land and grain,
and serving their ancestral temples,
training soldiers and sharpening weapons,
all for your use as you command.
If you can adopt my humble plan,
then from Hán,
Wèi, Qí,
Yān, Zhào,
and Wèi, exquisite music and beautiful women will fill your inner palace,
and fine camels and horses from Yān and Dài will stock your outer stables.
Thus, with vertical alliance success, Chǔ will rule as king;
with horizontal alliance success, Qín will become emperor.
Now to abandon the path of hegemon and true king,
and bear the name of serving others,
I privately believe is not worthy of you, Great King.
"That Qín
is a state of tigers and wolves,
with a heart to devour the world.
Qín is the enemy of all under heaven.
Those advocating horizontal alliances want to carve up the feudal lords' lands to serve Qín,
which is what is called nurturing an enemy and serving a foe.
As ministers,
they cut their own lord's territory to ally with the strong, wolf-like Qín,
invading the world,
until suddenly Qín's menace comes,
and they ignore the disaster.
Using the might of powerful Qín abroad to coerce their lord at home,
seeking to carve land,
is the height of treason and disloyalty,
with no greater offense.
So with vertical alliance, the feudal lords cede land to serve Chǔ;
with horizontal alliance, Chǔ cedes land to serve Qín.
These two strategies are vastly different;
which one will you choose, Great King?
Therefore, my humble king of Zhào has sent me to present this foolish plan,
offering a clear covenant,
awaiting your command."
King of Chǔ said:
"My state borders Qín to the west,
and Qín has intentions to seize Bā and Shǔ and annex Hànzhōng.
Qín is a state of tigers and wolves,
not to be trusted.
And Hán,
Wèi, pressured by Qín's threat,
cannot be deeply conspired with,
for deep conspiracy might lead to traitors turning to Qín,
so before plans are launched, the state would already be in danger.
I reckon that with Chǔ facing Qín alone,
I see no victory;
internally, consulting my ministers,
they are unreliable.
I lie restless on my mat,
eat without tasting food,
my heart swaying like a hanging banner with nowhere to settle.
Now you, sir, wish to unify the world,
gather the feudal lords,
and save endangered states;
I respectfully offer my state to follow."
Thus, the six states formed a vertical alliance and united their strength.
Sū Qín became the head of the vertical alliance,
and served as chancellor of the six states.
Returning north to report to the King of Zhào,
he passed through Luòyáng,
with chariots, cavalry, and baggage trains,
the feudal lords sending numerous envoys to see him off,
resembling a king's entourage.
King Xiǎn of Zhōu heard and feared,
cleared the roads,
and sent men to greet him at the outskirts.
Sū Qín's brothers, wife, and sisters-in-law dared not look directly at him,
bowing low to serve him food.
Sū Qín laughed and said to his sister-in-law:
"Why so arrogant before and so respectful now?"
His sister-in-law wriggled and crawled,
pressing her face to the ground in apology, saying:
"It's because you, young master, now have high rank and much gold."
Sū Qín sighed deeply and said:
"This same person,
in wealth and honor, even relatives fear him;
in poverty and lowliness, they scorn him—
how much more so with ordinary people!
Had I owned two qǐng of land near the walls of Luòyáng,
how could I have worn the seals of six states' chancellors!"
Thereupon, he distributed a thousand pieces of gold to reward his clan and friends.
Earlier, when Sū Qín went to Yān,
he borrowed a hundred coins from someone for funds,
and upon gaining wealth and honor,
repaid him with a hundred gold pieces.
He repaid all who had shown him kindness.
One follower alone had not been rewarded,
so he came forward to speak.
Sū Qín said:
"I have not forgotten you.
When you accompanied me to Yān,
you repeatedly wanted to leave me by the Yì River,
at that time,
I was in dire straits,
so I had high hopes of you,
hence I put you off.
Now you have your reward too."
After Sū Qín secured the vertical alliance of the six states,
he returned to Zhào,
where King Sù of Zhào enfeoffed him as Lord Wǔ'ān,
and he cast the vertical covenant document at Qín.
For fifteen years, Qín troops dared not peek beyond Hángǔ Pass.
Later, Qín sent Xī Shǒu to deceive Qí
and Wèi into jointly attacking Zhào,
aiming to break the vertical alliance.
When Qí and Wèi attacked Zhào,
the King of Zhào reproached Sū Qín.
Sū Qín, afraid,
requested to be sent to Yān,
vowing to repay Qí.
After Sū Qín left Zhào, the vertical alliance dissolved.
King Huì of Qín gave his daughter as wife to the Yān crown prince.
That year,
Lord Wén died,
the crown prince ascended,
becoming King Yì of Yān.
Soon after King Yì's accession,
King Xuān of Qí took advantage of Yān's mourning to attack,
capturing ten cities.
King Yì said to Sū Qín:
"Previously, you came to Yān,
and the late king supported you to visit Zhào,
leading to the six-state alliance.
Now Qí first attacked Zhào,
then came to Yān,
because of you, we become the laughingstock of the world.
Can you recover the invaded land for Yān?"
Sū Qín was greatly ashamed,
and said:
"I will retrieve it for you, Great King."
Sū Qín appeared before the King of Qí,
bowed twice,
lowered his head in congratulation,
then raised it in condolence.
The King of Qí said:
"Why do congratulations and condolences follow each other so swiftly?"
Sū Qín replied:
"I have heard that a starving person refrains from eating crow's beak despite hunger
because filling the belly with it shares the same calamity as dying of starvation.
Now, though Yān is small and weak,
it is the young son-in-law of the King of Qín.
Your Majesty covets its ten cities and will long be at enmity with powerful Qín.
If you now let weak Yān lead the way while strong Qín attacks from behind,
attracting the elite troops of the world,
that would be like eating crow's beak."
The King of Qí's countenance changed gravely as he said:
"What then should be done?"
Sū Qín said:
"I have heard that those skilled in managing affairs in ancient times
turned disaster into blessing,
and transformed failure into success.
If Your Majesty truly follows my plan,
immediately return Yān's ten cities.
Yān, gaining ten cities without cause,
will surely rejoice;
the King of Qín, knowing they were returned because of him,
will also rejoice.
This is what is called abandoning an enemy to gain a steadfast friendship.
When both Yān
and Qín serve Qí,
then Your Majesty's commands to the world
will have none who dare not listen.
Thus, you attach Qín with empty words
and win the world with ten cities.
This is the enterprise of a hegemon king."
The King said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he returned Yān's ten cities.
There were those who slandered Sū Qín, saying:
"He is a fickle minister who sells out his state to the left and right,
and will stir up rebellion."
Sū Qín feared being blamed upon his return,
and that the King of Yān would not restore his position.
Sū Qín went to see the King of Yān and said:
a humble man from Dōngzhōu,
had not an inch of merit,
yet you personally honored me in the temple and received me at court.
Now that I have repelled Qí's troops for you and gained ten cities,
I should be closer to you.
Yet upon my return, you do not reinstate me,
surely because someone has damaged my credibility with you.
My lack of credibility
is your blessing.
I have heard that loyalty and trustworthiness
are for one's own sake;
ambition and striving
are for the sake of others.
Moreover, when I persuaded the King of Qí,
it was certainly not to deceive him.
I left my old mother in Dōngzhōu,
firmly abandoning self-interest to pursue ambition.
Suppose you had someone as filial as Zēng Shēn,
as incorruptible as Bó Yí,
as trustworthy as Wěi Shēng.
Having these three serve you,
how would that be?"
The King said:
"That would suffice."
Sū Qín said:
"As filial as Zēng Shēn,
he would not leave his parents for even a night away,
