so how could you make him travel a thousand miles to serve a endangered king of weak Yān?
As incorruptible as Bó Yí,
he refused to be heir to the lord of Gūzhú,
would not serve King Wǔ of Zhōu,
and starved to death at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain without accepting a fief.
With such integrity,
how could you make him travel a thousand miles to strive ambitiously in Qí?
As trustworthy as Wěi Shēng,
he waited under a bridge for a woman,
and when she didn't come,
he stayed until the water rose,
clinging to a pillar and dying.
With such trustworthiness,
how could you make him travel a thousand miles to repel Qí's strong troops?
Thus, I am one who offends his superior precisely through loyalty and trustworthiness."
The King of Yān said:
"It's just that you are not loyal and trustworthy;
how could one offend by being loyal and trustworthy?"
Sū Qín said:
"Not so.
I heard of a traveler who served far away while his wife had an affair,
and when her husband was about to return,
her lover worried,
but the wife said,
'Do not worry,
I have prepared poisoned wine for him.'
After three days,
the husband indeed arrived,
and the wife had the concubine serve him the poisoned wine.
The concubine wanted to say the wine was poisoned,
but feared she'd be driven out by the mistress;
if she didn't speak,
she feared the master would be killed.
So she pretended to stumble and spilled the wine.
The master was furious
and whipped her fifty times.
Thus, the concubine, by stumbling once and spilling the wine,
saved the master above,
and the mistress below,
yet she could not avoid the whipping—
where then is the innocence of loyalty and trustworthiness?
My fault,
unfortunately, resembles this!"
The King of Yān said:
"Sir, resume your former post."
And treated him even more generously.
King Yì's mother,
the wife of Wén Hóu,
had a secret affair with Sū Qín.
The King of Yān knew of it,
yet treated him even better.
Sū Qín, fearing execution,
then advised the King of Yān:
"My presence in Yān does not enhance its importance,
but in Qí, Yān will surely gain weight."
The King of Yān said:
"Do as you see fit, sir."
Thereupon, Sū Qín pretended to have offended Yān and fled to Qí,
where King Xuān of Qí made him a visiting minister.
When King Xuān of Qí died,
King Mǐn ascended the throne,
and Sū Qín persuaded him to hold lavish funerals to display filial piety,
and build high palaces and vast parks to show his pride,
intending to exhaust Qí for Yān's benefit.
When King Yì of Yān died,
Yān Kuài succeeded as king.
Later, many Qí ministers vied with Sū Qín for favor,
and someone was sent to assassinate him;
he did not die immediately,
but was severely wounded and fled.
The King of Qí sent men to find the assassin,
but failed.
As Sū Qín was dying,
he said to the King of Qí:
"When I die,
have me torn apart by chariots and displayed in the market,
announcing
'Sū Qín plotted rebellion in Qí for Yān.'
This way, my assassin will surely be found."
Following his words,
the killer of Sū Qín indeed came forward,
and the King of Qí thus executed him.
Yān, upon hearing this, said:
"How extreme—
for Qí to avenge Sir Sū like this!"
After Sū Qín died,
his affairs were greatly exposed.
When Qí later heard of it,
they then resented and became angry with Yān.
Yān was very fearful.
Sū Qín's younger brother was named Dài,
and Dài's younger brother was Sū Lì.
Seeing their elder brother's success,
they both also studied.
When Sū Qín died,
Dài then sought an audience with the King of Yān,
wishing to follow the old precedent.
He said:
"Your servant,
is a humble man from Dōngzhōu.
I have privately heard that Your Majesty's righteousness is very lofty,
and though I am unwise,
I have set aside my hoe and plow to seek an audience with Your Majesty.
When I reached Hándān,
what I saw fell short of what I had heard in Dōngzhōu,
and I privately felt disappointed in my aspirations.
But upon arriving at the Yān court,
and observing Your Majesty's assembled ministers and lower officials,
I see that Your Majesty is an enlightened ruler of the world."
The King of Yān said:
"What do you mean by an enlightened ruler?"
He replied:
"I have heard that an enlightened ruler strives to hear about his faults,
and does not wish to hear about his virtues.
I beg to state Your Majesty's faults.
Now Qí
and Zhào
are Yān's enemies;
while Chǔ
and Wèi
are Yān's allied states.
Now Your Majesty supports enemies to attack allied states,
which is not beneficial to Yān.
If Your Majesty considers this yourself,
this is an error in strategy,
and if no one informs you of it,
they are not loyal ministers."
The King said:
"Indeed, Qí is my enemy,
whom I wish to attack,
but I am only concerned that our state is weak and our strength insufficient.
If you can use Yān to attack Qí,
then I will entrust the entire state to you."
He replied:
"In all, there are seven warring states in the world,
and Yān is among the weak.
Fighting alone is impossible,
but allying with someone will always bring weight.
Allying with Chǔ to the south,
Chǔ gains weight;
allying with Qín to the west,
Qín gains weight;
allying with Hán
and Wèi in the center, Hán
and Wèi gain weight.
And if the state you ally with gains weight,
this will surely make Your Majesty weighty as well.
Now as for Qí,
their ruler is arrogant and self-willed.
They have attacked Chǔ to the south for five years,
exhausting their stored resources;
they have troubled Qín to the west for three years,
leaving their soldiers weary and depleted;
they have fought with the people of Yān to the north,
destroying three armies,
and capturing two generals.
Yet with their remaining troops, they have turned south to raise a great army of five thousand chariots against Sòng,
and enveloped twelve feudal lords.
This shows their ruler's desires are excessive,
and their people's strength is exhausted.
How can they be worth taking!
Moreover, I have heard that
frequent warfare wearies the people,
and prolonged campaigns exhaust the troops."
The King of Yān said:
"I have heard that Qí has the clear Jì River
and the muddy Hé River which can serve as strong defenses,
and the Long Wall
and Jùfáng which are sufficient as barriers.
Is this truly so?"
He replied:
"If the timing of heaven is not with them,
even with the clear Jì
and muddy Hé,
how can they serve as strong defenses!
If the people's strength is weary and depleted,
even with the Long Wall
and Jùfáng,
how can they serve as barriers!
Moreover, in the past, west of the Jì they did not raise armies,
in order to guard against Zhào;
north of the Hé they did not raise armies,
in order to guard against Yān.
Now west of the Jì and north of the Hé are fully mobilized,
and the interior is exhausted.
An arrogant ruler inevitably loves profit,
and ministers of a doomed state are inevitably greedy for wealth.
If Your Majesty can unstintingly send your sons, brothers, and maternal relatives as hostages,
and offer precious pearls, jades, and silks to serve their attendants,
they will feel grateful to Yān and lightly destroy Sòng,
then Qí can be vanquished."
The King of Yān said:
"I ultimately accept your counsel as if it were a mandate from heaven."
Yān then sent a son as a hostage to Qí.
And Sū Lì, through the Yān hostage, sought an audience with the King of Qí.
The King of Qí resented Sū Qín,
and wanted to imprison Sū Lì.
The Yān hostage interceded for him,
and eventually Sū Lì offered his services as a minister of Qí.
The Yān chancellor Zǐ Zhī was related by marriage to Sū Dài,
and wishing to gain power in Yān,
he sent Sū Dài to attend the hostage in Qí.
Qí sent Dài back to report to Yān,
and King Kuài of Yān asked:
"Is the King of Qí likely to become hegemon?"
He said:
"No."
The King asked:
"Why not?"
He said:
"He does not trust his ministers."
Thereupon, King Kuài of Yān exclusively entrusted power to Zǐ Zhī,
and later abdicated the throne to him,
causing great chaos in Yān.
Qí attacked Yān,
killing King Kuài
and Zǐ Zhī.
Yān established King Zhāo,
and Sū Dài
and Sū Lì then did not dare enter Yān,
both eventually returning to Qí,
where Qí treated them well.
When Sū Dài passed through Wèi,
Wèi arrested Dài on behalf of Yān.
Qí sent someone to tell the King of Wèi:
"Qí requests to grant the land of Sòng to Lord Jīngyáng,
but Qín will certainly not accept.
It is not that Qín does not benefit from having Qí's favor and obtaining the land of Sòng,
but they do not trust the King of Qí and Master Sū.
Now that Qí and Wèi are so severely at odds,
Qí will not deceive Qín.
If Qín trusts Qí,
Qí and Qín will unite,
and Lord Jīngyáng will have the land of Sòng,
which is not beneficial to Wèi.
Therefore, Your Majesty should rather send Master Sū east,
and Qín will surely suspect Qí and not trust Master Sū.
If Qí and Qín do not unite,
and there is no change in the world,
the conditions for attacking Qí will take shape."
Thereupon, they released Sū Dài.
Dài went to Sòng,
and Sòng treated him well.
When Qí attacked Sòng,
and Sòng was in crisis,
Sū Dài then sent a letter to King Zhāo of Yān, saying:
"To be ranked among the ten-thousand-chariot states yet send a hostage to Qí,
is to have a low name and light authority;
to support a ten-thousand-chariot state in helping Qí attack Sòng,
wearies the people and wastes resources;
to destroy Sòng,
and devastate Chǔ's Huáiběi,
strengthens great Qí,
empowering an enemy and harming one's own state:
these three are all great failures for a state.
Yet Your Majesty carries them out,
intending to gain trust from Qí.
But Qí adds distrust towards Your Majesty,
and fears Yān even more,
which is an error in Your Majesty's strategy.
Now, with Sòng added to Huáiběi,
it would be a strong ten-thousand-chariot state,
and if Qí annexes it,
that is adding one Qí.
The northern barbarian lands of seven hundred lǐ,
plus Lǔ
and Wèi, would be a strong ten-thousand-chariot state,
and if Qí annexes them,
that is adding two Qí.
With the strength of one Qí,
Yān would still be apprehensive and unable to withstand it,
but now with three Qí pressing upon Yān,
the disaster will surely be great."
Nevertheless,
the wise man in conducting affairs
turns misfortune into blessing
and converts failure into success.
The purple of Qí
was faded plain silk,
yet its price was tenfold;
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè dwelt on Kuài Jī Mountain,
yet he destroyed powerful Wú and became hegemon of the world:
these both are cases of turning misfortune into blessing
and converting failure into success.
Now if Your Majesty wishes to turn misfortune into blessing
and convert failure into success,
then nothing is better than to encourage the hegemony of Qí and honor it,
sending envoys to form an alliance at the court of Zhōu,
burn the tallies of Qín,
and declare:
"The highest strategy
is to destroy Qín;
the next
must be to permanently ostracize it."
Qín, facing ostracism while awaiting destruction,
will surely distress the King of Qín.
Qín has attacked the feudal lords for five generations,
and now is beneath Qí;
if the King of Qín's ambition could exhaust Qí,
he would not hesitate to stake the state for achievement.
Then why does Your Majesty not send persuaders to say these words to the King of Qín:
"Yān
and Zhào destroyed Sòng to fatten Qí,
honoring it and placing themselves beneath it,
not because it benefited Yān and Zhào.
Yān and Zhào act against their benefit due to circumstances
because they do not trust the King of Qín.
Then why does Your Majesty not send trustworthy men to win over Yān
and Zhào, ordering Lord Jīng Yáng
and Lord Gāo Líng to go first to Yān
and Zhào? If Qín changes,
they can be held as hostages,
then Yān
and Zhào will trust Qín.
Let Qín be the Western Emperor,
Yān the Northern Emperor,
Zhào the Central Emperor,
establishing three emperors to command the world.
If Hán and Wèi do not obey, then Qín attacks them;
if Qí does not obey, then Yān
and Zhào attack it;
who in the world would dare not obey?
When the world submits and obeys,
then drive Hán
and Wèi to attack Qí,
saying:
'You must return the land of Sòng
and restore to Chǔ the territory north of the Huái River.'
Returning the land of Sòng
and restoring to Chǔ the territory north of the Huái
is beneficial to Yān and Zhào;
establishing three emperors together
is what Yān and Zhào desire.
Gaining actual benefit
and achieving desired honor,
Yān and Zhào would cast off Qí like discarding worn sandals.
Now if we do not win over Yān
and Zhào, Qí's hegemony will surely succeed.
If the feudal lords praise Qí and Your Majesty does not follow,
the state will be attacked;
if the feudal lords praise Qí and Your Majesty follows them,
your name will be debased.
Now by winning over Yān
and Zhào, the state is secure and your name honored;
by not winning over Yān
and Zhào, the state is endangered and your name debased.
To abandon honor and security for danger and debasement
is not what a wise man does."
When the King of Qín hears such persuasion,
it will surely feel like a stab to his heart.
Then why does Your Majesty not send persuaders to use these words to persuade Qín?
Qín will certainly be won over,
and Qí will surely be attacked.
To win over Qín
is to build a strong alliance;
to attack Qí
is to pursue correct benefit.
Honoring strong alliances
and striving for correct benefit
is the task of a sage king.
King Zhāo of Yān approved of this letter,
saying:
"My ancestors once showed kindness to the Sū family,
but Sū left Yān during the rebellion of Zǐ Zhī.
If Yān wishes to take revenge on Qí,
no one but Sū will do."
Thereupon he summoned Sū Dài,
treated him well again,
and plotted with him to attack Qí.
They eventually destroyed Qí,
and King Mǐn fled.
After a long time,
Qín summoned the King of Yān,
and the King of Yān wished to go.
Sū Dài cautioned the King of Yān, saying:
"Chǔ obtained Zhǐ yet the state perished,
Qí obtained Sòng yet the state perished.
Why is it that Qí and Chǔ, despite having Zhǐ
and Sòng, had to serve Qín?
Why?
It is because those who achieve merit
become Qín's deep enemies.
When Qín seeks to take the world,
it does not act with righteousness,
but with violence.
Qín's acts of violence
are openly declared to the world.
"It declared to Chǔ:
'The armor from Shǔ territory
boards ships floating on the Mín River,
riding the summer floods down the Yangtze,
reaching Yǐng in five days.
The armor from Hàn Zhōng
boards ships departing from Bā,
riding the summer floods down the Hàn River,
reaching Wǔ Zhǔ in four days.
I mass armor east of Wǎn descending to Suí;
the wise have no time to plan,
the brave no time to rage,
I am like shooting a falcon.
Does the King wish to wait for the world's forces to attack Hán Gǔ?
Is that not too late!'"
The King of Chǔ for this reason
served Qín for seventeen years.
"Qín openly declared to Hán:
'I arise from Shǎo Qū,
and in one day cut off Tài Háng.
I arise from Yí Yáng and strike Píng Yáng,
in two days nothing is not set in motion.
I pass through the two Zhōu and strike Zhèng,
in five days the state is taken.'"
The Hán house considered this true,
therefore served Qín.
"Qín openly declared to Wèi:
'I raise Ān Yì,
block Nǚ Jǐ,
the Hán house's Tài Yuán rolls up.
I take Zhǐ,
pass through Nán Yáng,
seal Jì,
encircle the two Zhōu.
Riding the summer floods,
floating light boats,
strong crossbows in front,
sharp spears behind,
breach the Yíng Pass,
Wèi loses Dà Liáng;
breach the White Horse Pass,
Wèi loses Wài Huáng
and Jì Yáng;
breach the Sù Xū Pass,
Wèi loses Xū
and Dùn Qiū.
Attack by land and strike Hé Nèi,
attack by water and destroy Dà Liáng.'"
The Wèi house considered this true,
therefore served Qín.
"Qín wished to attack Ān Yì,
but feared Qí would rescue it,
so it entrusted Sòng to Qí.
Saying:
'The King of Sòng is without virtue,
making a wooden figure in my likeness,
shooting its face.
My lands are cut off, my troops distant,
I cannot attack.
If the King can destroy Sòng and possess it,
it is as if I obtained it myself.'"
Having obtained Ān Yì,
blocked Nǚ Jǐ,
it then blamed Qí for destroying Sòng.
"When Qin intended to attack Hán,
fearing other states would rescue it,
they abandoned Qí to the world.
Saying:
'The King of Qí made four agreements with me,
yet deceived me four times,
and three times mustered the world to attack me.
With Qí there is no Qín,
with Qín there is no Qí,
we must attack them,
we must destroy them.'
After capturing Yíyáng,
Shǎoqū,
obtaining Lìn,
Líshí,
they thus made destroying Qí a crime against the world.
"When Qin wanted to attack Wèi and valued Chǔ,
they abandoned Nányáng to Chǔ.
Saying:
'I have already broken with Hán.
Destroy Jūnlíng,
block Ménɡ'è,
if it benefits Chǔ,
I consider it as my own.'
Wèi abandoned its allies and allied with Qín,
thus making blocking Ménɡ'è a crime against Chǔ.
"When troops were trapped in Línzhōng,
valuing Yān,
Zhào, they abandoned Jiāodōng to Yān,
and Jìxī to Zhào.
After making peace with Wèi,
reaching Prince Yán,
they followed Xīshǒu's campaign to attack Zhào.
"When troops were wounded at Qiáoshí,
and defeated at Yánɡmǎ,
they valued Wèi,
abandoning Yè,
Cài to Wèi.
After making peace with Zhào,
they coerced Wèi,
but Wèi refused to cede territory.
In distress, they sent the queen dowager's brother, the Marquis of Ránɡ, to make peace,
in victory, they deceived both uncle and mother.
"To those going to Yān they said
'take Jiāodōng',
to those going to Zhào they said
'take Jìxī',
to those going to Wèi they said
'take Yè,
Cài',
to those going to Chǔ they said
'block Ménɡ'è',
to those going to Qí they said
'take Sòng'.
Such words inevitably circulate in cycles,
using troops like swatting flies,
mothers cannot control them,
uncles cannot restrain them.
"In the battle of Lónɡ Jiǎ,
the battle of Ànmén,
the battle of Fēnɡlínɡ,
the battle of Gāoshānɡ,
the battle of Zhào Zhuānɡ,
Qín killed millions of people from the Three Jìn,
now the survivors are all orphans of those killed by Qín.
West of the Hé River,
the lands of Shànɡluò,
the disasters of Sānchuān and the Jìn state,
half of the Three Jìn,
such is the magnitude of Qín's calamity.
Yet those in Yān,
Zhào who favor Qín,
all urge their lords to compete in serving Qín,
this is what I greatly fear."
King Zhāo of Yān did not act.
Sū Dài regained importance in Yān.
Yān sent envoys to form alliances among the feudal lords for vertical cooperation as in Sū Qín's time,
some joined, some did not,
and from then on, the world honored the Sū family's vertical alliance.
Dài and Lì both died of old age,
their fame renowned among the feudal lords.
Grand Historian Simǎ said:
The three Sū Qín brothers,
all traveled persuading feudal lords to achieve fame,
their methods excelled in adaptability.
Yet Sū Qín died due to counter-espionage,
the world laughed at him together,
忌讳 learning his techniques.
However, worldly tales about Sū Qín vary greatly,
events of different times similar to his were all attributed to him.
Sū Qín rose from the alleys,
united six states in vertical alliance,
this shows his wisdom surpassed others.
Therefore I record his deeds,
arrange them chronologically,
so he does not solely bear ill repute.
Zhānɡ Yí,
was a man of Wèi.
Initially, he studied with Sū Qín under Master Guǐgǔ,
learning strategies,
Sū Qín considered himself inferior to Zhānɡ Yí.
After studying, Zhānɡ Yí traveled persuading feudal lords.
Once drinking with the Chǔ prime minister,
later the prime minister lost a jade disc,
his followers suspected Zhānɡ Yí,
saying:
"Yí is poor and without integrity,
he must have stolen the prime minister's disc."
They seized Zhānɡ Yí together,
flogged him hundreds of times,
but he did not confess,
and they released him.
His wife said:
"Alas!
If you hadn't studied and traveled persuading,
how would you suffer this humiliation?"
Zhānɡ Yí asked his wife:
"See if my tongue is still there?"
His wife laughed and said:
"It is."
Yí said:
"That is enough."
After Sū Qín persuaded the King of Zhào and secured the vertical alliance,
he feared Qín would attack the feudal lords,
breaking the pact and causing betrayal,
and thought no one could be used in Qín,
so he secretly prompted Zhānɡ Yí, saying:
"You were once close to Sū Qín,
now he holds power,
why not visit him,
to achieve your aspirations?"
Zhānɡ Yí then went to Zhào,
seeking an audience with Sū Qín.
Sū Qín instructed his guards not to admit him,
and kept him waiting for days.
Eventually he received him,
seated him in the lower hall,
fed him servants' food.
Then he reproached him repeatedly:
"With your talent,
you've brought yourself to such hardship and shame.
I could easily speak for your wealth and honor,
but you're not worth recruiting."
He dismissed him.
Zhānɡ Yí had come,
thinking they were old friends,
seeking advancement,
but was instead humiliated,
enraged, he thought no feudal lord was worth serving,
only Qín could torment Zhào,
so he went to Qín.
Later, Sū Qín told his retainer:
"Zhānɡ Yí,
is a worthy man of the world,
I am likely inferior to him.
Now I am fortunate to be employed first,
but the one who can wield power in Qín,
is only Zhānɡ Yí.
However, he is poor,
with no means to advance.
I feared he'd be content with small gains and not succeed,
so I summoned and humiliated him,
to stir his determination.
You secretly provide for him."
He then spoke to the King of Zhào,
procuring gold, coins, carriages, and horses,
sent someone to subtly follow Zhānɡ Yí,
share his lodging,
gradually befriend him,
providing carriages, horses, and money,
whatever he needed,
was supplied,
without his knowledge.
Thus Zhānɡ Yí managed to see King Huì of Qín.
King Huì made him a guest minister,
consulting him on attacking the feudal lords.
Sū Qín's retainer then bid farewell to depart,
Zhāng Yí said:
"Thanks to you, I attained prominence,
and was just about to repay your kindness,
why are you leaving?"
The retainer said:
"I did not recognize your talent,
it was Sū Jūn who recognized you.
Sū Jūn feared that Qín would attack Zhào and break the vertical alliance,
believing that no one but you could gain power in Qín,
so he deliberately provoked your anger,
sent me to secretly provide you with funds,
all part of Sū Jūn's strategy.
Now you have been employed,
I request to return and report."
Zhāng Yí said:
"Alas,
I was within his scheme yet unaware,
I am clearly not as astute as Sū Jūn!
I have only recently been employed,
how could I plot against Zhào?
Please convey my gratitude to Sū Jūn,
while Sū Jūn is alive,
how would Yí dare speak against him.
Moreover, with Sū Jūn present,
how could Yí possibly achieve anything!"
After Zhāng Yí became chancellor of Qín,
he issued a proclamation to the Chǔ chancellor saying:
"When I previously drank with you,
I did not steal your jade disc,
yet you had me flogged.
You'd better guard your state well,
for I intend to steal your cities!"
Jū and Shǔ attacked each other,
each coming to Qín to report their emergency.
King Huì of Qín wanted to send troops to attack Shǔ,
but considered the route dangerous, narrow and difficult to reach,
and Hán was also invading Qín,
King Huì of Qín wanted to attack Hán first,
then attack Shǔ later,
but feared this would be disadvantageous,
wanted to attack Shǔ first,
but feared Hán would attack Qín when it was weakened,
he hesitated and couldn't decide.
Sīmǎ Cuò and Zhāng Yí debated before King Huì,
Sīmǎ Cuò wanted to attack Shǔ,
Zhāng Yí said:
"It would be better to attack Hán."
The King said:
"Please let me hear your reasoning."
Yí said:
"Befriend Wèi and maintain good relations with Chǔ,
send troops to Sānchuān,
block the Shígǔ pass,
guard against the Túnliú route,
have Wèi cut off Nányáng,
have Chǔ approach Nánzhèng,
while Qín attacks Xīnchéng,
Yíyáng,
to approach the suburbs of the two Zhōu domains,
punish the Zhōu king for his crimes,
invade the territories of Chǔ,
and Wèi.
When Zhōu realizes it cannot save itself,
the nine tripods and precious vessels will surely be surrendered.
By possessing the nine tripods,
and examining the maps and records,
holding the Son of Heaven to command the world,
no one under heaven would dare disobey,
this is the way to kingly achievement.
Now as for Shǔ,
it is a western remote state of the Róng and Dí kind,
exhausting troops and wearying the masses would not bring fame,
gaining its land would not bring benefit.
I hear that those contending for fame do so at court,
those contending for profit do so in the marketplace.
Now Sānchuān,
and the Zhōu court,
are the court and marketplace of the world,
yet Your Majesty does not contend there,
but instead contends with the Róng and Dí,
this is far from the path to kingly achievement."
Sīmǎ Cuò said:
"Not so.
I have heard that,
those who want to enrich the state must expand its territory,
those who want to strengthen the army must enrich its people,
those who want to become king must broaden his virtue,
when these three resources are complete, kingship follows.
Now Your Majesty's territory is small and people poor,
so I wish to start with what is easier.
Now Shǔ,
is a western remote state,
and the leader of the Róng and Dí,
having the turmoil of a Jié or Zhòu.
Using Qín to attack it,
is like sending wolves and jackals after a flock of sheep.
Gaining its land is enough to expand the state,
taking its wealth is enough to enrich the people and repair arms,
without harming the masses yet they will already submit.
Conquering one state without the world considering it violent,
exhausting the benefits of the Western Sea without the world considering it greedy,
this way we achieve both name and substance at one stroke,
and also gain the name of stopping violence and quelling chaos.
Now attacking Hán,
and coercing the Son of Heaven,
brings an evil name,
and may not necessarily bring benefit,
plus having the name of unrighteousness,
attacking what the world does not want attacked,
is dangerous.
Let me explain the reason:
Zhōu is the ancestral temple of the world;
Qí is an ally of Hán.
When Zhōu knows it will lose the nine tripods,
and Hán knows it will lose Sānchuān,
they will combine forces and unite strategies,
relying on Qí,
and Zhào while seeking resolution with Chǔ,
and Wèi, giving the tripods to Chǔ,
and territory to Wèi,
Your Majesty will be unable to stop it.
This is what I call dangerous.
It would be better to attack Shǔ and be done."
King Huì said:
"Good,
I will follow your advice."
Finally he raised troops to attack Shǔ,
in the tenth month,
captured it,
thus pacifying Shǔ,
demoted the King of Shǔ to a lower title of Hóu,
and appointed Chén Zhuāng as chancellor of Shǔ.
After Shǔ became subordinate to Qín,
Qín became increasingly powerful,
wealthy and substantial,
and looked down upon the other states.
In the tenth year of King Huì of Qín,
he sent Prince Huá with Zhāng Yí to besiege Púyáng,
and subdued it.
Yí then suggested that Qín return it to Wèi,
and sent Prince Yóu as hostage to Wèi.
Yí then persuaded the King of Wèi saying:
"The King of Qín has treated you very generously,
Wèi cannot respond without courtesy."
Wèi therefore presented Shàngjùn,
and Shǎoliáng,
to thank King Huì of Qín.
King Huì then made Zhāng Yí his chancellor,
and renamed Shǎoliáng as Xiàyáng.
Yí served as Qín's chancellor for four years,
and established King Huì as Hegemon King.
After one year,
he served as Qín general,
and captured Shǎn.
Built the Shàngjùn fortress.
Two years later,
he was sent to meet with the chancellors of Qí,
and Chǔ at Nièsāng.
After returning east he was dismissed as chancellor,
became chancellor of Wèi to serve Qín's interests,
wanting to make Wèi submit to Qín first so other states would follow.
The King of Wèi refused to listen to Yí.
The King of Qín was angry,
attacked and captured Qūwò,
Píngzhōu from Wèi,
and again secretly treated Zhāng Yí even more generously.
Zhāng Yí was ashamed,
having nothing to report upon return.
He stayed in Wèi for four years until King Xiāng of Wèi died,
and King Āi succeeded.
Zhāng Yí again persuaded King Āi,
but King Āi wouldn't listen.
Thereupon Zhāng Yí secretly ordered Qín to attack Wèi.
Wèi fought with Qín,
and was defeated.
The following year,
Qí again came and defeated Wèi at Guānjīn.
Qín once more intended to attack Wèi,
first defeating Hán Shēnchā's army,
beheading eighty thousand soldiers,
causing the feudal lords to tremble with fear.
Then Zhāng Yí again persuaded King of Wèi, saying:
"Wèi's territory does not extend a thousand lǐ,
its soldiers do not exceed three hundred thousand.
The land is flat on all sides,
with feudal lords accessible from every direction like spokes meeting at a hub,
without the barriers of famous mountains or great rivers.
From Zhèng to Liáng is over two hundred lǐ,
whether by chariot or on foot,
one arrives without expending much effort.
Liáng borders Chǔ to the south,
Hán to the west,
Zhào to the north,
and Qí to the east,
with soldiers garrisoning all four directions,
those guarding the watchtowers and barriers number no less than one hundred thousand.
Liáng's geographical situation
is inherently a battlefield.
If Liáng allies with Chǔ to the south but not with Qí,
then Qí will attack from the east;
if allying with Qí to the east but not with Zhào,
then Zhào will attack from the north;
if not in harmony with Hán,
then Hán will attack from the west;
if not close with Chǔ,
then Chǔ will attack from the south:
this is what is called the path to being torn apart.
"Moreover, those among the feudal lords who form alliances,
do so to secure the state, honor the ruler, strengthen the military, and gain fame.
Now the alliance unites the world,
swearing to be as brothers,
sacrificing a white horse to swear an oath above the Huánshuǐ,
to solidify their bond.
Yet even blood brothers born of the same parents
still contend over wealth,
and to rely on the deceitful and fickle remnants of Sū Qín's schemes,
their impossibility of success is also clear.
"If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
Qín will send troops to attack Héwài,
occupy Juǎn,
Yǎn, Yān,
Suānzǎo,
coerce Wèi and take Yángjìn,
then Zhào cannot go south,
and if Zhào cannot go south, Liáng cannot go north,
if Liáng cannot go north, the alliance route is cut off,
and with the alliance route cut off, Your Majesty's state wishing to avoid danger would be impossible.
If Qín subdues Hán and attacks Liáng,
Hán being timid towards Qín,
Qín and Hán united as one,
Liáng's downfall can be awaited momentarily.
This is what I worry about for Your Majesty.
"Planning for Your Majesty,
nothing is better than serving Qín.
Serving Qín then Chǔ,
Hán will not dare to act;
without the troubles of Chǔ,
Hán,
then Your Majesty can rest high on the pillow and sleep,
the state will surely have no worries.
"Moreover, whom Qín wishes to weaken is none other than Chǔ,
and who can weaken Chǔ is none other than Liáng.
Although Chǔ has the reputation of being rich and large, it is actually empty;
its soldiers though numerous,
are prone to flee and be easily defeated,
unable to hold firm in battle.
Mobilize all of Liáng's troops to attack Chǔ from the south,
victory is certain.
Carve up Chǔ to benefit Liáng,
diminish Chǔ to please Qín,
transferring misfortune and securing the state,
this is a good course of action.
If Your Majesty does not listen to me,
when Qín sends armored troops east to attack,
even if you wish to serve Qín,
it will be impossible.
"Moreover, those advocating alliances often use bold words but are rarely trustworthy,
persuading one feudal lord to achieve enfeoffment as a marquis,
hence the itinerant talkers of the world all day and night clutch their wrists, glare, and gnash their teeth speaking of the advantages of alliances,
to persuade the rulers.
The rulers admire their eloquence and are swayed by their arguments,
how can they not be dazzled?
"I have heard that,
accumulated feathers can sink a boat,
a multitude of light things can break an axle,
numerous mouths can melt metal,
accumulated slanders can dissolve bones,
therefore I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider and decide on a plan,
and allow me to retire and leave Wèi."
King Āi then renounced the alliance covenant and through Yí sought peace with Qín.
Zhāng Yí returned,
and again became chancellor of Qín.
Three years later, Wèi again turned against Qín to join the alliance.
Qín attacked Wèi,
capturing Qūwò.
The next year,
Wèi again served Qín.
Qín wanted to attack Qí,
but Qí and Chǔ were allied and friendly,
so Zhāng Yí went to become chancellor of Chǔ.
King Huái of Chǔ heard Zhāng Yí was coming,
vacated the best lodging and hosted him there personally.
Saying:
"This is a remote and humble state,
what would you teach me?"
Yí persuaded the King of Chǔ, saying:
"If Your Majesty truly listens to me,
close the passes and sever the covenant with Qí,
I will request to present the land of Shāngwū, six hundred lǐ,
have Qín women become Your Majesty's humble servants,
with Qín and Chǔ marrying and giving in marriage,
long becoming brotherly states.
This weakens Qí in the north and benefits Qín in the west,
no plan is more advantageous than this."
The King of Chǔ was greatly pleased and agreed.
All ministers congratulated him,
only Chén Zhěn mourned it.
The King of Chǔ angrily said:
"I, the solitary one, without raising an army or sending troops, gained six hundred lǐ of land,
all ministers congratulate me,
yet you alone mourn,
why?"
Chén Zhěn replied:
"Not so,
from my perspective,
the land of Shāngwū cannot be obtained, and Qí and Qín will unite,
if Qí and Qín unite, then calamity is sure to come."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Is there an explanation?"
Chén Zhěn replied:
"The reason Qín values Chǔ
is because it has Qí.
Now closing the passes and severing the covenant with Qí,
then Chǔ is isolated.
Why would Qín covet an isolated state,
and give it six hundred lǐ of Shāngwū land?
When Zhāng Yí returns to Qín,
he is sure to betray Your Majesty,
this would cut off relations with Qí in the north,
create trouble with Qín in the west,
and the troops of both states are sure to come together.
Those skilled at planning for Your Majesty
would secretly ally with Qí while openly breaking,
sending someone to follow Zhāng Yí.
If he gives us the land,
breaking with Qí is not late;
if he does not give us the land,
then secretly ally and plan accordingly."
The King of Chǔ said:
"I hope Master Chén will shut his mouth and speak no more,
and wait for me to obtain the land."
Then he bestowed the chancellor's seal upon Zhāng Yí,
richly rewarding him.
Thereupon he closed the passes and severed the covenant with Qí,
sending a general to follow Zhāng Yí.
Zhāng Yí arrived in Qín,
pretending to have fallen from his carriage by losing the handstrap,
and did not attend court for three months.
The King of Chǔ heard of this,
and said:
"Does Yí think I have not severed relations with Qí thoroughly enough?"
He then sent a brave warrior to Sòng,
borrowing Sòng's credentials,
to go north and insult the King of Qí.
The King of Qí was greatly angered,
broke off his alliance and submitted to Qín.
With Qín and Qí's relations restored,
Zhāng Yí then attended court,
and said to the Chǔ envoy:
"I have a fief of six lǐ,
which I wish to present to His Majesty's attendants."
The Chǔ envoy said:
"I received orders from my king
regarding the land of Shāngwū covering six hundred lǐ,
I have not heard of six lǐ."
He returned and reported to the King of Chǔ,
who was furious,
and sent troops to attack Qín.
Chén Zhěn said:
"May Zhěn speak openly?
Attacking them is not as good as ceding land to bribe Qín instead,
and joining forces with them to attack Qí.
This way we give land to Qín,
but seek compensation from Qí,
and the king's state may still survive."
The King of Chǔ did not listen,
and finally sent troops, ordering General Qū Gài to attack Qín.
Qín and Qí jointly attacked Chǔ,
decapitating eighty thousand,
killing Qū Gài,
and subsequently seized the lands of Dānyáng
and Hànzhōng.
Chǔ again sent more troops to raid Qín,
reaching Lántián,
where a great battle occurred,
and Chǔ was severely defeated,
so Chǔ ceded two cities to make peace with Qín.
Qín demanded that Chǔ give up the land of Qiánzhōng,
wishing to exchange it for territory beyond Wǔguān.
The King of Chǔ said:
"I do not wish to exchange lands,
but I wish to obtain Zhāng Yí and will offer the land of Qiánzhōng."
The King of Qín wanted to send him,
but could not bear to say it.
Zhāng Yí then requested to go.
King Huì said:
"That King of Chǔ is angry that you failed to deliver the land of Shāngwū,
and he is determined to have his revenge on you."
Zhāng Yí said:
"Qín is strong and Chǔ is weak,
and I am on good terms with Jìn Shàng,
who serves Lady Zhèng Xiù of Chǔ,
and whatever she says is followed.
Moreover, I go as an envoy of the king with his credentials to Chǔ,
how would Chǔ dare to harm me?
Even if they kill me and Qín thereby gains the land of Qiánzhōng,
it would be my highest wish."
So he was sent to Chǔ.
King Huái of Chǔ, upon his arrival, imprisoned Zhāng Yí,
and intended to kill him.
Jìn Shàng said to Zhèng Xiù:
"Do you know that you are falling out of favor with the king?"
Zhèng Xiù said:
"Why?"
Jìn Shàng said:
"The King of Qín greatly loves Zhāng Yí and does not wish to let him go,
now he plans to bribe Chǔ with the six counties of Shàngyōng,
send beauties to marry into Chǔ,
and include skilled singers from the palace as maids.
The King of Chǔ values land and respects Qín,
so the Qín women will surely become noble and you, madam, will be cast aside.
It would be better to speak on his behalf and have him released."
Thereupon, Zhèng Xiù day and night said to King Huái:
"Ministers each serve their own lord.
Now the land has not yet been given to Qín,
and Qín has sent Zhāng Yí here,
showing great respect for the king.
If the king, without proper courtesy, kills Zhāng Yí,
Qín will surely be furious and attack Chǔ.
I beg to move with our children to Jiāngnán,
to avoid being slaughtered by Qín."
King Huái regretted his decision,
pardoned Zhāng Yí,
and treated him with the same great courtesy as before.
After Zhāng Yí was released,
before he had left,
he heard of Sū Qín's death,
and then persuaded the King of Chǔ, saying:
"The land of Qín covers half the world,
its soldiers can oppose four states,
protected by natural barriers and girded by rivers,
with four fortified passes making it secure.
It has over a million fierce warriors,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
and grain stores piled like mountains.
Its laws and decrees are clear,
its soldiers face hardship calmly and are willing to die,
its ruler is wise and strict,
its generals are intelligent and martial.
Even without sending out troops,
they could sweep over the perilous Chángshān,
and surely break the backbone of the world;
any state that submits later will be the first to perish.
Moreover, those advocating the vertical alliance
are no different from driving a flock of sheep to attack a fierce tiger;
it is clear that a tiger and sheep cannot match each other.
Now if the king does not side with the tiger but with the sheep,
I secretly believe your strategy is mistaken.
"Throughout the world, the powerful states
are none but Qín and Chǔ,
none but Chǔ and Qín.
If these two states contend,
their situation is such that they cannot coexist.
If the king does not ally with Qín,
Qín will send troops to occupy Yíyáng,
and the upper lands of Hán will be cut off.
They will descend to Hédōng,
seize Chénggāo,
and Hán will surely submit,
while Liáng will follow like the wind.
With Qín attacking Chǔ from the west,
and Hán, Liáng attacking from the north,
how can the state avoid danger?
"Moreover, the vertical alliance gathers the weak to attack the strongest,
without assessing the enemy and lightly going to war,
impoverishing the state with frequent military campaigns—
this is the way to danger and destruction.
I have heard that
if your troops are inferior, do not challenge;
if your grain is inferior, do not prolong the fight.
Those promoting the vertical alliance use ornate but empty rhetoric,
exalting the ruler's integrity,
speaking only of its benefits and not its harms,
until suddenly the disaster from Qín arrives,
and it is too late to act.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
"To the west, Qín has Bā and Shǔ,
where large ships store grain,
starting from Wènshān,
floating down the river,
over three thousand lǐ to Chǔ.
Boats carry soldiers,
each boat holding fifty men and three months' provisions,
floating downstream,
traveling over three hundred lǐ a day.
Although the distance is great,
it does not exhaust the strength of oxen or horses,
and in less than ten days they can reach Hánguān.
If Hánguān is alarmed,
then all territories east of it will fortify their cities,
and Qiánzhōng
and Wūjùn will no longer belong to the king.
If Qín sends troops out of Wǔguān,
attacking southward,
then the northern territories will be cut off.
When Qín's troops attack Chǔ,
the crisis will occur within three months,
while Chǔ awaits help from the other states,
which will take over half a year,
such that the situations cannot meet.
To rely on the rescue of weak states
and forget the threat of strong Qín—
this is what I worry about for Your Majesty.
"Your Majesty once fought against the Wú people,
winning three out of five battles,
but your frontline troops were exhausted;
barely holding onto new cities,
the surviving people suffered.
I have heard that great achievements easily lead to danger,
and when the people are exhausted, they resent their superiors.
To cling to easily endangered achievements and defy the will of strong Qín—
I secretly fear for Your Majesty's safety.
"The reason why Qin has not sent troops through Hángǔ Pass for fifteen years to attack Qí
and Zhào is because
it secretly plots to unite the world under its will.
Chǔ once engaged in conflict with Qin,
battling in Hànzhōng,
where the Chǔ people were defeated,
with over seventy marquises and holders of the guī jade insignia perishing,
leading to the loss of Hànzhōng.
The King of Chǔ was greatly enraged,
raised an army to attack Qin,
and fought at Lántián.
This is what is called two tigers fighting each other.
When Qin and Chǔ exhaust each other, Hán and Wèi can fully control the aftermath,
no strategy is more perilous than this.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
"If Qin sends troops down to attack Yángjìn in Wèi,
it will surely block the vital passage of the world.
If Your Majesty mobilizes all your forces to attack Sòng,
within a few months Sòng can be captured,
and after taking Sòng, advancing eastward,
then all twelve states of Sìshàng will belong to Your Majesty.
"Throughout the world, the one who used faithful alliances to strengthen vertical kinship was Sū Qín,
who was enfeoffed as the Lord of Wǔ'ān,
served as chancellor of Yān,
but then secretly plotted with the King of Yān to defeat and divide Qí's territory;
he then feigned guilt and fled to Qí,
where the King of Qí accepted and made him chancellor;
after two years, this was discovered,
and the King of Qí was furious,
having Sū Qín torn apart by chariots in the market.
With such a deceitful man as Sū Qín,
attempting to manage the world,
and unify the feudal lords,
his failure was evident.
"Now Qin and Chǔ share borders,
and are naturally countries with close ties.
If Your Majesty truly listens to your servant,
I request that the Qin crown prince be sent as a hostage to Chǔ,
and the Chǔ crown prince as a hostage to Qin,
and offer a Qin woman as a humble servant for Your Majesty,
presenting a city of ten thousand households as a fief for bathing,
establishing a lasting fraternal state,
with no mutual attacks for life.
I believe no plan is more advantageous than this."
Thereupon, the King of Chǔ, having obtained Zhāng Yí and reluctant to cede Qiánzhōng land to Qin again,
intended to agree.
Qū Yuán said:
"Previously, Your Majesty was deceived by Zhāng Yí;
when Zhāng Yí arrived,
I thought Your Majesty would boil him;
now even if you cannot bear to kill him,
listening to his evil words
is not acceptable."
King Huái said:
"Agreeing with Yí to regain Qiánzhōng
is a great benefit.
To betray him later
is not acceptable."
Thus, he finally agreed with Zhāng Yí,
and allied with Qin.
Zhāng Yí left Chǔ,
and then went to Hán,
persuading the King of Hán, saying:
"Hán's land is treacherous and mountainous,
what the five grains produce,
is not beans but wheat,
and the people's food is mostly bean meals and vegetable soup.
If one harvest fails,
the people are not satisfied with chaff and husks.
The land does not exceed nine hundred lǐ,
with not enough food for two years.
Estimating Your Majesty's troops,
all together do not exceed three hundred thousand,
including laborers and porters.
Excluding those guarding outposts and fortresses,
the visible troops are no more than two hundred thousand.
Qin has over a million armored soldiers,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
with warriors leaping bareheaded, piercing cheeks and brandishing halberds,
too numerous to count.
The excellence of Qin's horses,
the multitude of its soldiers,
those galloping three xún between hoof falls,
are beyond measure.
The eastern states' soldiers clad in armor and helmets to join battle,
while Qin men discard armor and charge bare-chested at the enemy,
left hand carrying heads,
right hand clutching live captives.
Comparing Qin's troops with those of the eastern states,
is like Mèng Bēn against a coward;
pressing with heavy force,
is like Wū Huò against an infant.
Using warriors like Mèng Bēn
and Wū Huò to attack a weak, resisting state,
is no different from hanging a thousand jūn weight on a bird's egg,
inevitably with no chance of survival.
"The ministers and feudal lords do not consider their limited land,
but listen to the sweet words of coalition advocates,
colluding to embellish each other,
all fervently saying
'follow my plan to strengthen and dominate the world.'
Disregarding the long-term interests of the state for momentary persuasion,
misleading the ruler,
there is no greater fault than this.
"If Your Majesty does not serve Qin,
Qin will send troops to occupy Yíyáng,
severing Hán's upper lands,
taking Chénggāo to the east,
and Xíngyáng,
then the Hóngtái Palace
and Sānglín Gardens will not be Your Majesty's.
Blocking Chénggāo,
cutting off the upper lands,
will divide Your Majesty's state.
Serving Qin first ensures safety,
not serving it brings danger.
To create disaster yet seek fortunate reward,
with shallow plans and deep enmity,
opposing Qin and aligning with Chǔ,
even if you wish not to perish,
it will be impossible.
"Thus, for Your Majesty's strategy,
nothing is better than aligning with Qin.
What Qin desires most is to weaken Chǔ,
and none can weaken Chǔ better than Hán.
Not that Hán is stronger than Chǔ,
but its geographical position makes it so.
If now you turn west to serve Qin and attack Chǔ,
the King of Qin will surely be pleased.
Attacking Chǔ to gain its land,
turning disaster into pleasing Qin,
no plan is more advantageous than this."
The King of Hán followed Yí's plan.
Zhāng Yí returned to report,
and Qín King Huì enfeoffed Yí with five cities,
bestowing the title Lord Wǔxìn.
He sent Zhāng Yí east to persuade King Mǐn of Qí, saying:
"No state in the world is stronger than Qí,
with ministers and clans abundant, wealthy, and joyful.
Yet those planning for Your Majesty
all offer temporary advice,
disregarding benefits for a hundred generations.
Those advocating alliances to Your Majesty
surely say
'Qí has strong Zhào to the west,
and Hán and Liáng to the south.
Qí, a sea-backed state,
vast in land and populous,
with strong troops and brave soldiers,
even a hundred Qins
could do nothing to Qí.'
Your Majesty praises their words without considering the reality.
These advocates form cliques and collude,
all believing alliances are feasible.
I have heard that
Qí and Lǔ fought three times, with Lǔ winning all,
yet Lǔ faced peril and destruction afterward,
having the name of victory,
but the reality of a ruined state.
Why is that?
Because Qí was large and Lǔ small.
Now the relation between Qin and Qí
is like that between Qí and Lǔ.
Qin and Zhào battled by the Hézhāng River,
with Zhào winning twice against Qin;
they fought beneath Pānwú,
and Zhào won again.
After four battles,
Zhào lost hundreds of thousands of soldiers,
leaving Hándān barely standing,
having the name of victory but a broken state.
Why is that?
Because Qin is strong and Zhào weak.
"Now Qín and Chǔ have intermarried through the exchange of daughters,
becoming brotherly states.
Hán presented Yíyáng;
Liáng surrendered Héwài;
Zhào came to pay homage at Miǎnchí,
ceding Héjiān to serve Qín.
If Your Majesty does not submit to Qín,
Qín will drive Hán and Liáng to attack the southern territories of Qí,
mobilize all of Zhào's troops to cross the Qīng Hé,
advance toward Bóguān,
and then Línzī
and Jímò will no longer belong to the king.
Once the state is attacked,
even if you wish to serve Qín,
it will be impossible.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this."
The King of Qí replied:
"Qí is remote and uncultured,
secluded east of the sea,
and has never heard of long-term benefits for the state."
He then agreed to Zhāng Yí's proposal.
Zhāng Yí departed
and went west to persuade the King of Zhào, saying:
"My humble ruler, the King of Qín, has sent me to present a foolish plan to Your Majesty.
Your Majesty rallied the world to resist Qín,
causing Qín's troops not to dare exit Hángǔ Pass for fifteen years.
Your Majesty's prestige spread throughout Shāndōng,
making my state fearful and submissive.
We mended armor and sharpened weapons,
repaired chariots and cavalry,
practiced riding and archery,
worked hard at farming and storing grain,
guarded our borders,
living anxiously and timidly,
not daring to make a move,
solely because Your Majesty might intend to reprimand us.
"Now, thanks to Your Majesty's power,
you conquered Bā and Shǔ,
annexed Hànzhōng,
surrounded the two Zhōu domains,
moved the Nine Tripods,
and guarded the ferry at Báimǎ.
Although Qín is remote,
our hearts have long been filled with resentment and anger.
Now Qín has worn-out armor and depleted troops
stationed at Miǎnchí,
wishing to cross the Hé and Yuè Zhāng rivers,
occupy Pānwú,
and converge beneath Hándān.
We hope to engage in battle on the jiǎzǐ day,
to rectify the affairs of the tyrant Zhòu of Yīn,
and respectfully send me to inform Your Majesty's attendants first.
"In all this, what Your Majesty believes in regarding the vertical alliance relies on Sū Qín.
Sū Qín deluded the feudal lords,
turning right into wrong,
and wrong into right,
attempting to rebel against Qí,
which led to him being torn apart by chariots in the market.
Thus, the impossibility of unifying the world is clear.
Now Chǔ and Qín are brotherly states,
while Hán and Liáng proclaim themselves eastern vassals,
and Qí has offered its fish and salt lands,
severing Zhào's right arm.
To fight someone with a severed right arm,
losing allies and left isolated,
and still hope to avoid danger—
how could that be possible?
"Now Qín is dispatching three generals:
one army will block Wǔdào,
order Qí to send troops across the Qīng Hé,
and station east of Hándān;
another army will be stationed at Chénggāo,
driving Hán and Liáng's forces to Héwài;
and a third army will be at Miǎnchí.
They plan to unite the four states to attack Zhào,
and once Zhào is defeated,
its land will surely be divided into four.
Therefore, I dare not conceal my intentions,
but inform Your Majesty's attendants first.
I privately advise Your Majesty
to meet with the King of Qín at Miǎnchí,
face to face to forge an agreement,
and request a ceasefire with no attack.
I hope Your Majesty will decide on this plan."
The King of Zhào said:
"During the previous king's time,
Fèngyáng Jūn monopolized power and influence,
deceiving the former king,
solely controlling state affairs,
while I, the orphaned ruler, was under the tutelage of mentors,
not involved in state planning.
After the former king passed away,
I was young,
newly ascended to the sacrifices,
and inwardly doubtful,
believing that adhering to the vertical alliance and not serving Qín
was not in the state's long-term interest.
Thus, I intended to change my mind and reconsider,
ceding territory to apologize for past errors and serve Qín.
I was just about to prepare carriages and hasten the journey
when I fortunately heard the envoy's clear instruction."
The King of Zhào agreed with Zhāng Yí,
and Zhāng Yí then left.
He went north to Yān,
and persuaded King Zhāo of Yān, saying:
"Your Majesty's closest ally is none other than Zhào.
Formerly, Zhào Xiāngzǐ once married his sister to the King of Dài,
intending to annex Dài.
He arranged to meet the King of Dài at the fort of Gōuzhù.
He then had craftsmen make a golden ladle,
with a long handle,
so it could be used to strike someone.
While drinking with the King of Dài,
he secretly instructed the cook, saying:
'When the drinking is merry and enjoyable,
serve a hot broth,
and use the reversed ladle to strike him.'
So when the drinking became merry,
and hot broth was served,
the cook came forward to pour,
and using the reversed ladle, struck the King of Dài,
killing him,
his brains spilling on the ground.
His sister heard of this,
then sharpened her hairpin and stabbed herself,
hence to this day there is Mójī Mountain.
The death of the King of Dài
is known throughout the world.
"The King of Zhào's cruelty and lack of kinship,
as Your Majesty clearly sees,
how can he be considered trustworthy?
Zhào raised troops to attack Yān,
twice besieging Yān's capital and coercing Your Majesty,
forcing you to cede ten cities in apology.
Now the King of Zhào has already paid homage at Miǎnchí,
offering Héjiān to serve Qín.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín now,
Qín will send troops to Yúnzhōng
and Jiǔyuán,
driving Zhào to attack Yān,
and then the Yì Shuǐ
and Chángchéng will no longer belong to Your Majesty.
"Moreover, nowadays Zhào is to Qín like a commandery or county,
not daring to recklessly raise troops for attack.
If now you serve Qín,
the King of Qín will surely be pleased,
and Zhào will not dare act rashly.
Thus, you will have the support of a powerful Qín to the west,
and no threat from Qí and Zhào to the south.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this."
The King of Yān said:
"I, the orphaned ruler, am a barbarian in a remote land,
and though a grown man, I am as naive as an infant,
my words not fit to adopt proper strategies.
Now that you, honored guest, have kindly instructed me,
I will submit to Qín and serve it,
offering five cities at the foot of Héng Shān."
The King of Yān heeded Yí.
Yí returned to report,
but before reaching Xiányáng, King Huì of Qín passed away,
and King Wǔ ascended the throne.
King Wǔ had disliked Zhāng Yí since his time as crown prince,
and upon his accession,
many ministers slandered Zhāng Yí, saying:
"He is untrustworthy,
betraying the state to curry favor.
If Qín reemploys him,
I fear we will become the laughingstock of the world."
The feudal lords heard that Zhāng Yí had fallen out with King Wǔ,
so they all abandoned the horizontal alliance,
and restored the vertical alliance.
In the first year of King Wǔ of Qín,
the ministers ceaselessly spoke ill of Zhāng Yí day and night,
and then a reproach from Qí also arrived.
Zhāng Yí feared execution,
so he took the opportunity to say to King Wǔ of Qín:
"I have a humble plan,
which I wish to offer."
The king said:
"What is it?"
He replied:
"For the sake of Qín's state,
if there is a major upheaval in the east,
then Your Majesty can seize much land.
Now I hear the King of Qí despises me greatly;
wherever I am,
he is sure to raise an army and attack it.
Therefore, I wish to offer my unworthy self to go to Liáng,
and Qí will surely raise troops to attack Liáng.
When the armies of Liáng and Qí are locked in battle beneath the city walls and cannot disengage,
Your Majesty can take that opportunity to attack Hán,
enter Sānchuān,
send troops through Hángǔ Pass without engaging in battle,
approach Zhōu,
and the sacrificial vessels will surely be yielded.
Holding the Son of Heaven,
controlling the maps and registers,
this is the kingly enterprise."
The King of Qín thought it reasonable,
so he prepared thirty chariots
and sent Zhāng Yí to Liáng.
Qí indeed raised an army to attack it.
King Āi of Liáng was frightened.
Zhāng Yí said:
"Your Majesty, do not worry;
allow me to make the Qí troops withdraw."
He then sent his retainer Féng Xǐ to Chǔ,
borrowing an envoy to go to Qí,
and said to the King of Qí:
"Your Majesty greatly despises Zhāng Yí;
however,
you have also deeply entrusted Yí to Qín!"
The King of Qí said:
"I despise Yí;
wherever he is,
I must raise an army to attack it—
how have I entrusted him?"
He replied:
"This is precisely how Your Majesty has entrusted Yí.
When Yí left,
he certainly made a pact with the King of Qín, saying:
'For the king's strategy,
if there is a major upheaval in the east,
then the king can seize much land.
Now the King of Qí despises me greatly;
wherever I am,
he will surely raise an army to attack it.
Therefore, I wish to offer my unworthy self to go to Liáng,
and Qí will surely raise troops to attack it.
When the armies of Qí and Liáng are locked in battle beneath the city walls and cannot disengage,
the king can take that opportunity to attack Hán,
enter Sānchuān,
send troops through Hángǔ Pass without engaging in battle,
approach Zhōu,
and the sacrificial vessels will surely be yielded.
Holding the Son of Heaven,
controlling the maps and registers,
this is the kingly enterprise.'
The King of Qín thought it reasonable,
so he prepared thirty chariots and sent him to Liáng.
Now that Yí has entered Liáng,
Your Majesty indeed attacked it;
this means you internally exhaust your state and externally attack an allied country,
broadening neighboring enemies to bring pressure upon yourself,
and fulfilling Yí's credibility with the King of Qín.
This is what I call
'entrusting Yí'
The King of Qí said:
"Good."
He then ordered the troops to withdraw.
Zhāng Yí served as chancellor of Wèi for one year
and died in Wèi.
Chén Zhěn was
a wandering persuader.
He and Zhāng Yí both served King Huì of Qín,
both were honored and esteemed,
and competed for favor.
Zhāng Yí spoke ill of Chén Zhěn to the King of Qín, saying:
"Zhěn heavily bribes and lightly serves between Qín and Chǔ,
intending to conduct state relations.
Now Chǔ does not show more goodwill to Qín but favors Zhěn;
Zhěn acts for his own benefit and does little for Your Majesty.
Moreover, Zhěn wishes to leave Qín for Chǔ—
why does Your Majesty not heed this?"
The king said to Chén Zhěn:
"I hear you wish to leave Qín for Chǔ—
is this true?"
Zhěn said:
"Yes."
The king said:
"Yí's words indeed proved true."
Zhěn said:
"Not only Yí knows this,
but all who travel the roads know it.
In the past, Zǐxū was loyal to his lord, and all under heaven contended to have him as a minister;
Zēng Shēn was filial to his parents, and all under heaven wished to have him as a son.
Thus, if maidservants sold within the village lanes find buyers,
they are good maidservants;
if a divorced woman remarries in her hometown,
she is a good woman.
Now if I, Zhěn, am not loyal to my lord,
why would Chǔ consider me loyal?
Being loyal yet cast aside,
if I do not go to Chǔ, where else should I go?"
The king found his words reasonable,
and thus treated him well.
After staying in Qín for a year,
King Huì of Qín finally made Zhāng Yí chancellor,
and Chén Zhěn fled to Chǔ.
Chǔ did not highly esteem him,
but sent Chén Zhěn on a mission to Qín.
Passing through Liáng,
he wished to see Xī Shǒu.
Xī Shǒu declined to see him.
Zhěn said:
"I have come on business;
if you, sir, do not see me,
I will depart,
and cannot wait for another day."
Xī Shǒu then saw him.
Chén Zhěn said:
"Why do you, sir, enjoy drinking so much?"
Xī Shǒu said:
"I have nothing to do."
He said:
"May I make you overwhelmed with affairs?"
He said:
"How?"
He said:
"Tián Xū has arranged an alliance of the various states,
but the King of Chǔ doubts him,
and does not trust it.
You, sir, say to the king:
'I have old ties with the kings of Yān
and Zhào;
they have sent messengers several times,
saying,
"Since there is no urgent matter, why not meet?"
I wish to request permission from Your Majesty to go.'
Even if the king permits you,
ask not to take many chariots—
just thirty chariots,
which can be displayed in the courtyard,
openly announced to Yān
and Zhào."
When the envoys of Yān and Zhào heard this,
they rushed in chariots to inform their kings,
who sent people to welcome Xī Shǒu.
The King of Chǔ heard this and was greatly angered,
saying:
"Tián Xū made a pact with me,
yet Xī Shǒu goes to Yān
and Zhào—this is deceiving me."
In anger, he did not heed Tián Xū's affairs.
When Qí heard that Xī Shǒu was heading north,
they sent someone to entrust matters to him.
Xī Shǒu then set out,
and the affairs of the three states all came under his control.
Zhěn then proceeded to Qín.
Hán and Wèi attacked each other,
and the conflict remained unresolved for a full year.
Qín King Huì wished to intervene,
so he consulted his attendants.
Some suggested it was advantageous to rescue them,
while others argued it was better not to,
leaving King Huì unable to decide.
Just then, Chén Zhěn happened to arrive in Qín,
and King Huì said:
"Since you left me for Chǔ,
have you missed me?"
Chén Zhěn replied:
"Has Your Majesty heard of the Yuè man Zhuāng Xì?"
The king said:
"I have not."
Chén Zhěn continued:
"Zhuāng Xì, a man of Yuè, served in Chǔ holding the position of zhíguī,
and after some time fell ill.
The King of Chǔ said:
'Xì was originally a lowly commoner from Yuè,
now serving in Chǔ as a zhíguī,
enjoying wealth and honor;
does he still miss Yuè?'
A court attendant replied:
'Generally, when people miss their homeland,
it shows when they are ill.
If he misses Yuè, he will speak in the Yuè accent;
if not, he will speak in the Chǔ accent.'
The king sent someone to listen,
and he was still using the Yuè accent.
Now, although I have been cast out to Chǔ,
how could I not have the heart of Qín!"
King Huì said:
"Well said.
Now Hán and Wèi are attacking each other,
and the conflict has lasted a year without resolution;
some tell me it is advantageous to rescue them,
others say it is not,
and I cannot decide.
I hope that, in addition to advising your lord,
you will also advise me."
Chén Zhěn replied:
"Has Your Majesty ever heard of Biàn Zhuāngzǐ stabbing tigers?
Zhuāngzǐ wanted to stab a tiger,
but a servant at the inn stopped him,
saying:
'Two tigers are about to eat an ox;
when the food is tasty, they will surely fight,
and fighting will lead to a struggle,
in which the larger will be injured
and the smaller will die.
Then, if you strike the injured one,
with one move you can gain the fame of killing two tigers.'
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ thought this reasonable,
and stood waiting.
After a while,
the two tigers indeed fought,
the larger was injured,
and the smaller died.
Zhuāngzǐ then stabbed the injured one,
and with one move achieved the feat of two tigers.
Now Hán and Wèi are attacking each other,
and the conflict has lasted a year without resolution;
surely the larger state will be injured,
and the smaller state will perish.
If you attack the injured one,
with one move you can gain both outcomes.
This is similar to Zhuāngzǐ stabbing the tigers.
My lord and Your Majesty are no different in this regard."
King Huì said:
"Well said."
In the end, he did not intervene.
The larger state was indeed injured,
the smaller state perished,
Qín raised troops and attacked,
achieving a great victory.
This was Chén Zhěn's strategy.
Xī Shǒu
was from Yīnjìn in Wèi,
his given name was Yǎn,
and his surname was Gōngsūn.
He did not get along with Zhāng Yí.
When Zhāng Yí went to Wèi for Qín,
the King of Wèi made Zhāng Yí his chancellor.
Xī Shǒu saw this as unfavorable,
so he sent someone to tell Hán's Gōngshū:
"Zhāng Yí has already allied Qín and Wèi,
and he has said:
'Wèi will attack Nányáng,
and Qín will attack Sānchuān.'
The reason the King of Wèi values Zhāng Yí
is that he wants to acquire Hán's territory.
Moreover, Hán's Nányáng is already targeted;
why not cede a small part to me to credit Yǎn,
so that the alliance between Qín and Wèi can be broken?
Then Wèi will surely turn against Qín and abandon Yí,
ally with Hán, and make me chancellor."
Gōngshū found this advantageous,
so he entrusted it to Xī Shǒu as an achievement.
Xī Shǒu indeed became chancellor of Wèi.
Zhāng Yí left.
The Lord of Yìqú paid a visit to Wèi.
Xī Shǒu heard that Zhāng Yí had become chancellor of Qín again,
and he felt threatened.
Xī Shǒu then said to the Lord of Yìqú:
"The road is long, and I may not see you again,
so let me tell you something important."
He said:
"If the central states are at peace,
Qín will burn and plunder your state;
if there is conflict,
Qín will send envoys with heavy bribes to win your favor."
Later, five states attacked Qín.
It happened that Chén Zhěn said to the King of Qín:
"The Lord of Yìqú
is a worthy ruler among the barbarians;
it would be best to bribe him to appease his ambitions."
The King of Qín said:
"Well said."
So he sent a thousand rolls of embroidered silk
and a hundred women to the Lord of Yìqú.
The Lord of Yìqú gathered his ministers and plotted:
"Is this what Gōngsūn Yǎn meant?"
Then he raised troops and attacked Qín by surprise,
defeating the Qín forces at Lǐbó.
After Zhāng Yí had died,
Xī Shǒu entered Qín and became chancellor.
He once wore the seals of five states as chancellor,
serving as the alliance leader.
Grand Historian Simǎ said:
The three Jìn states produced many strategists and tacticians;
those who advocated alliances to strengthen Qín were mostly from the three Jìn.
Zhāng Yí's actions were more extreme than Sū Qín's,
yet the world detests Sū Qín
because he died first,
and Yí exposed his faults to promote his own ideas,
establishing his horizontal alliance doctrine.
In summary,
these two were truly treacherous and dangerous men!
Chūlǐzǐ,
named Jí,
was the younger brother of Qín King Huì,
born of a different mother.
His mother
was a woman from Hán.
Chūlǐzǐ was witty and highly intelligent,
and the people of Qín called him the "Wisdom Sack."
In the eighth year of Qín King Huì's reign,
Chūlǐzǐ was granted the rank of Yòugèng,
sent to lead troops and attack Qǔwò,
driving out all its people,
capturing the city,
and incorporating the land into Qín.
In the twenty-fifth year of Qín King Huì,
Chūlǐzǐ was sent as general to attack Zhào,
capturing Zhào general Zhuāng Bào,
and seizing Lìn.
The following year,
he assisted Wèi Zhāng in attacking Chǔ,
defeated Chǔ general Qū Gài,
and took the land of Hànzhōng.
Qín enfeoffed Chūlǐzǐ,
bestowing the title Lord Yán.
When Qín King Huì died,
Crown Prince King Wǔ ascended,
expelled Zhāng Yí and Wèi Zhāng,
and appointed Chūlǐzǐ and Gān Mào as left and right chancellors.
Qín sent Gān Mào to attack Hán,
capturing Yíyáng.
They sent Chūlǐzǐ with a hundred chariots into Zhōu.
Zhōu sent soldiers to welcome him,
showing great respect.
The King of Chǔ was angered,
reprimanded Zhōu,
for honoring the Qín guest so highly.
Yóu Téng spoke to the King of Chǔ on behalf of Zhōu:
"When Zhì Bó attacked Qiúyóu,
he presented them with large chariots,
then followed with troops,
and Qiúyóu was thus destroyed.
Why?
Because they were unprepared.
When Duke Huán of Qí attacked Cài,
he claimed it was to punish Chǔ,
but in reality, he was attacking Cài.
Now the state of Qín,
a nation of tigers and wolves,
sent Chūlǐzǐ with a hundred chariots into Zhōu,
and Zhōu treated them as it had Qiúyóu and Cài,
thus placing long halberds in front,
and strong crossbows behind,
nominally to guard against illness,
but in reality to imprison them.
Moreover, how could Zhōu not worry about its altars of grain and soil?
It fears that one day it will perish and cause Your Majesty concern."
The King of Chǔ was then pleased.
When King Wǔ of Qín died,
King Zhāo ascended the throne,
and Chūlǐzǐ became even more respected.
In the first year of King Zhāo,
Chūlǐzǐ was about to attack Pú.
The defender of Pú was afraid,
and sought out Hú Yǎn.
Hú Yǎn spoke to Chūlǐzǐ on behalf of Pú:
"Your attack on Pú,
is it for Qín?
Or for Wèi?
If it is for Wèi, then it is good,
but if for Qín, it is not beneficial.
The reason Wèi remains Wèi,
is because of Pú.
Now if you attack Pú and it falls to Wèi,
Wèi will certainly break and follow it.
Wèi lost the land west of the Hé River and had no means to regain it,
because its military was weak.
Now if you merge Wèi with Pú,
Wèi will surely become strong.
When Wèi becomes strong,
the land west of the Hé River will be in danger.
Moreover, the King of Qín will observe your actions,
if they harm Qín and benefit Wèi,
the king will surely hold you accountable."
Chūlǐzǐ said:
"What should be done?"
Hú Yǎn said:
"You should abandon Pú and not attack it,
allow me to go in and speak on your behalf,
to show virtue to the Lord of Wèi."
Chūlǐzǐ said:
"Good."
Hú Yǎn entered Pú,
and said to its defender:
"Chūlǐzǐ knows the weakness of Pú,
he says he will certainly capture Pú.
But I can make him abandon Pú and not attack."
The defender of Pú was afraid,
and bowed twice, saying:
"I beg you to intercede."
Then he offered three hundred jīn of gold,
saying:
"If the Qín troops withdraw,
I will certainly speak of you to the Lord of Wèi,
and have you face south as a ruler."
Thus Hú Yǎn received gold from Pú to elevate himself in Wèi.
Thereupon, he lifted the siege of Pú and left.
He turned back to attack Píshì,
but Píshì had not surrendered,
so he left again.
In the seventh year of King Zhāo,
Chūlǐzǐ died,
and was buried east of Zhāngtái in southern Wèi.
He said:
"A hundred years from now,
there will be an imperial palace on either side of my tomb."
Chūlǐzǐ's tomb was located in Chūlǐ, Yīnxiāng, south of Wèi, west of King Zhāo's temple,
hence he was commonly called Chūlǐzǐ.
By the time Hàn rose,
the Chánglè Palace was to its east,
the Wèiyāng Palace to its west,
and the armory was directly facing his tomb.
The people of Qín had a saying:
"For strength, Rén Bǐ;
for wisdom, Chūlǐ."
As for Gān Mào,
he was from Xiàcài.
He served under Historian Jǔ of Xiàcài,
studying the arts of the hundred schools.
Through Zhāng Yí
and Chūlǐzǐ, he sought an audience with King Huì of Qín.
The king was pleased upon meeting him,
made him a general, and sent him to assist Wèi
Zhāng in capturing the land of Hànzhōng.
When King Huì died,
King Wǔ ascended the throne.
Zhāng Yí and Wèi Zhāng left,
heading east to Wèi.
Marquis Huī of Shǔ and Chancellor Zhuàng rebelled,
and Qín sent Gān Mào to pacify Shǔ.
Upon his return,
Gān Mào was made Left Chancellor,
and Chūlǐzǐ was made Right Chancellor.
In the third year of King Wǔ of Qín,
he said to Gān Mào:
"I wish to have a carriage pass through Sānchuān,
to spy on the Zhōu court,
so that I may die without regret."
Gān Mào said:
"Allow me to go to Wèi,
to form an alliance to attack Hán,
and let Xiàng Shòu assist me."
When Gān Mào arrived,
he said to Xiàng Shòu:
"You return,
and tell the king, 'Wèi has agreed with me,
but I hope the king will not attack yet.'
If this succeeds,
all credit will be yours."
Xiàng Shòu returned,
and reported to the king,
who welcomed Gān Mào at Xìrǎng.
When Gān Mào arrived,
the king asked for the reason.
He replied:
"Yíyáng
is a large county,
and Shàngdǎng and Nányáng have stored supplies there for a long time.
It is called a county,
but in reality, it is a commandery.
Now, Your Majesty faces multiple dangers,
marching a thousand lǐ to attack it,
which is difficult.
In the past, when Zēng Shēn was in Fèi,
a man of Lǔ with the same name as Zēng Shēn killed someone,
and someone told his mother, 'Zēng Shēn has killed a man,'
but his mother continued weaving calmly.
After a while,
another person came and said, 'Zēng Shēn has killed a man,'
and his mother still wove calmly.
Soon, another person came and said, 'Zēng Shēn has killed a man,'
and his mother threw down the shuttle, left the loom,
climbed over the wall, and fled.
Now, with Zēng Shēn's virtue and his mother's trust in him,
when three people cast doubt,
his mother became afraid.
Now, my virtue is not equal to Zēng Shēn's,
and Your Majesty's trust in me is not like Zēng Shēn's mother's trust in him,
yet those who doubt me are not just three,
I fear that Your Majesty will also throw down the shuttle.
When Zhāng Yí first annexed the lands of Bā and Shǔ in the west,
opened up the territory beyond the western Hé River in the north,
and captured Shàngyōng in the south,
the world did not praise Zhāng Yí but credited the former king.
When Marquis Wén of Wèi ordered Yuè Yáng to attack Zhōngshān,
it took three years to capture it.
When Yuè Yáng returned to discuss his merits,
Marquis Wén showed him a chest full of slanderous letters.
Yuè Yáng bowed twice and kowtowed, saying:
'This is not my achievement,
but the strength of my lord.'
Now I,
am a minister in a foreign land.
Chūlǐzǐ and Gōngsūn Shì both hold influence over Hán and will criticize me,
and if Your Majesty listens to them,
it will mean you have deceived the King of Wèi and I will incur the resentment of Gōngzhòng Chǐ."
The king said:
"I will not listen to them,
let us make an oath."
He then sent Chancellor Gān Mào to lead troops to attack Yíyáng.
After five months without success,
Chūlǐzǐ and Gōngsūn Shì indeed opposed it.
King Wǔ summoned Gān Mào,
intending to withdraw the troops.
Gān Mào said:
"The oath at Xìrǎng remains."
The king said:
"It does."
Thereupon, he mobilized all his troops,
and sent Gān Mào to attack.
They beheaded sixty thousand,
and finally captured Yíyáng.
King Xiāng of Hán sent Gōngzhòng Chǐ to apologize,
and made peace with Qín.
King Wǔ eventually reached Zhōu,
and died there.
His younger brother ascended the throne,
becoming King Zhāo.
The king's mother, Queen Dowager Xuān,
was a woman of Chǔ.
King Huái of Chǔ resented Qín for previously defeating Chǔ at Dānyáng while Hán did not come to the rescue,
so he sent troops to besiege Yōngshì in Hán.
Hán sent Gōngzhòng Chǐ to urgently seek help from Qín.
King Zhāo of Qín had newly ascended,
and the queen dowager, being from Chǔ,
was unwilling to send aid.
Gōngzhòng then approached Gān Mào,
who spoke to King Zhāo of Qín on behalf of Hán:
"Gōngzhòng is able to resist Chǔ
only because he expects rescue from Qín."
Now that Yōngshì is under siege,
and the Qín army does not descend from Xiáo,
Lord Zhòng will lift his head and not attend court,
while Lord Shū will ally the state south with Chǔ.
If Chǔ and Hán unite as one,
the Wèi clan would not dare disobey,
then the situation for attacking Qín will take shape.
I wonder, is it more beneficial to sit and wait to be attacked or to attack others?"
The King of Qín said:
"Good."
Then he sent troops down from Xiáo to rescue Hán.
The Chǔ forces withdrew.
Qín sent Xiàng Shòu to pacify Yíyáng,
and had Chūlǐzǐ and Gān Mào attack Wèi's Píshì.
Xiàng Shòu was
a maternal relative of Queen Dowager Xuān,
and had grown up with King Zhāo from childhood,
so he was entrusted with office.
When Xiàng Shòu went to Chǔ,
Chǔ, hearing that Qín honored Xiàng Shòu,
treated him with great respect.
Xiàng Shòu guarded Yíyáng for Qín,
intending to attack Hán.
Hán's Lord Zhòng sent Sū Dài to tell Xiàng Shòu:
"A cornered beast will overturn the carriage.
If you crush Hán,
humiliating Lord Zhòng,
and Lord Zhòng rallies his state to again serve Qín,
he would think it certain to earn a fief. Now you give Chǔ land at Jiěkǒu,
and enfeoff the junior minister with Dùyáng.
If Qín and Chǔ ally,
and again attack Hán,
Hán will surely perish.
If Hán perishes,
Lord Zhòng will personally lead his private followers to oppose Qín.
I hope you will consider this carefully."
Xiàng Shòu said:
"My uniting Qín and Chǔ is not to confront Hán;
you should petition Lord Zhòng on my behalf,
saying that the alliance between Qín and Hán can be restored."
Sū Dài replied:
"I wish to have a word with you.
It is said that one is honored by honoring what makes one honorable.
The king's affection for you
is not equal to that for Gōngsūn Shì;
his recognition of your wisdom and ability
is not equal to that for Gān Mào.
Now these two men are both not close to Qín's affairs,
yet you alone with the king decide state matters—why?
They have reasons for their loss.
Gōngsūn Shì sides with Hán,
and Gān Mào sides with Wèi,
so the king does not trust them.
Now Qín and Chǔ contend for power, and you side with Chǔ,
this is the same path as Gōngsūn Shì and Gān Mào;
how do you differ?
People all say Chǔ is fickle,
yet you insist on its ruin,
this is bringing blame upon yourself.
If you instead advise the king to adapt to changes,
and befriend Hán to guard against Chǔ,
then there will be no trouble.
The Hán clan will surely first entrust the state to Gōngsūn Shì and later assign it to Gān Mào.
Hán
is your enemy.
Now you speak of befriending Hán to guard against Chǔ,
this is recommending externally without avoiding enemies."
Xiàng Shòu said:
"Yes,
I very much wish to ally with Hán."
The reply was:
"Gān Mào promised Lord Zhòng Wǔsuì,
and to return the people of Yíyáng,
but now you merely take it for yourself,
making it very difficult."
Xiàng Shòu said:
"Then what to do?
Can Wǔsuì never be obtained?"
The reply was:
"Why don't you use Qín's influence to seek Yǐngchuān from Chǔ for Hán?
This is land held in trust by Hán.
If you seek and obtain it,
it shows your orders are heeded in Chǔ and you grace Hán with the land.
If you seek and fail,
it means the enmity between Hán and Chǔ remains unresolved and both will turn to Qín.
While Qín and Chǔ contend for power,
you can gradually win over Chǔ to secure Hán,
this benefits Qín."
Xiàng Shòu said:
"How?"
The reply was:
"This is a good plan.
Gān Mào wants to use Wèi to take Qí,
Gōngsūn Shì wants to use Hán to take Qí.
Now you take Yíyáng as an achievement,
secure Chǔ and Hán to stabilize them,
and condemn Qí and Wèi's crimes,
thus leaving Gōngsūn Shì and Gān Mào with nothing to do."
Gān Mào eventually persuaded King Zhāo of Qín,
to return Wǔsuì to Hán.
Xiàng Shòu and Gōngsūn Shì contested this,
but could not succeed.
Xiàng Shòu and Gōngsūn Shì hence bore a grudge,
slandering Gān Mào,
who, in fear,
halted the attack on Wèi's Púbǎn,
and fled.
Chūlǐzǐ negotiated with Wèi,
and withdrew the troops.
When Gān Mào fled Qín for Qí,
he met Sū Dài.
Dài was on a mission to Qín for Qí.
Gān Mào said:
"I have offended Qín,
and fled in fear,
with no place to shelter.
I heard of a poor man's daughter and a rich man's daughter weaving together,
the poor man's daughter said:
'I have no means to buy candles,
and your candlelight fortunately has surplus,
you can share your surplus light with me,
without diminishing your brightness and we both gain convenience.'
Now I am in distress and you are envoys to Qín and in power.
My wife and children are there,
I hope you can lend your surplus light to aid them."
Sū Dài agreed.
Then he went on his mission to Qín.
Afterward,
he persuaded the King of Qín, saying:
"Gān Mào
is no ordinary scholar.
His residence in Qín
spanned generations of high status.
From the Xiáo Pass to the Ghost Valley,
he knows the terrain's perils and ease intimately.
If he allies Qí with Hán and Wèi to plot against Qín,
it would not benefit Qín."
The King of Qín said:
"Then what to do?"
Sū Dài said:
"Your Majesty should honor him with heavy gifts,
generous emoluments to welcome him back,
so that when he comes, place him in Ghost Valley,
and never let him leave for life."
The King of Qín said:
"Good."
Then he conferred on him the title of Senior Minister,
and sent a minister's seal to welcome him from Qí.
Gān Mào did not go.
Sū Dài said to King Mǐn of Qí:
"Now Gān Mào
is a worthy man.
Now Qín has awarded him Senior Minister,
and sent a minister's seal to welcome him.
Gān Mào is grateful for your kindness,
and wishes to be your servant,
so he declined and did not go.
How will you honor him?"
The King of Qí said:
"Good."
Then he made him a Senior Minister and kept him.
Qín thereupon restored Gān Mào's family property to win over Qí.
Qí sent Gān Mào to Chǔ,
where King Huái of Chǔ had newly allied with Qín through marriage and was joyous.
