When Qín heard Gān Mào was in Chǔ,
they sent a messenger to tell the King of Chǔ:
"We hope you will send Gān Mào to Qín."
The King of Chǔ asked Fàn Xuān:
"I wish to appoint a minister in Qín,
who is suitable?"
The reply was:
"I am not qualified to know."
The King of Chǔ said:
"I wish to make Gān Mào minister,
is that acceptable?"
The reply was:
"No.
That Shǐ Jǔ,
was a gatekeeper in Xiàcài,
in great matters did not serve his lord well,
in small matters did not manage his household,
known to the world for his shamelessness and lack of integrity,
yet Gān Mào served him obediently.
So with King Huì's wisdom,
King Wǔ's discernment,
and Zhāng Yí's eloquence,
Gān Mào served them,
holding ten offices without fault.
Truly, Mào is a worthy man,
but he should not be minister in Qín.
For Qín to have a worthy minister
is not to Chǔ's benefit."
Moreover, the king previously employed Zhào Huá in Yuè,
which led to internal turmoil and the calamity of Zhāng Yì,
causing Yuè to fall into chaos.
Thus, Chu fortified the southern pass of Lìmén and established the Jiangdōng commandery.
The reason for the king's achievements reaching this extent
was due to Yuè's disorder while Chǔ remained stable.
Now, the king knows how to employ such strategies in Yuè but neglects to apply them in Qín.
I consider this a grave oversight by the king.
If the king wishes to install a chancellor in Qín,
then none would be more suitable than Xiàng Shòu.
For Xiàng Shòu, in relation to the king of Qín,
is close;
they shared clothes in youth,
and rode together in chariots as they grew,
handling affairs.
If the king ensures Xiàng Shòu becomes chancellor in Qín,
it will benefit the state of Chǔ."
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to request that Qín appoint Xiàng Shòu as chancellor.
Qín ultimately made Xiàng Shòu chancellor.
But Gān Mào never managed to return to Qín,
dying in Wèi.
Gān Mào had a grandson named Gān Luó.
Gān Luó
was the grandson of Gān Mào.
After Gān Mào's death,
Gān Luó, at the age of twelve,
served under Wénxìn Hóu Lǚ Bùwéi, the chancellor of Qín.
Qín Shǐ Huángdì sent Gāngchéng Jūn Cài Zé to Yān,
and after three years, King Xǐ of Yān sent Crown Prince Dān to Qín as a hostage.
Qín dispatched Zhāng Táng to serve as chancellor in Yān,
intending to ally with Yān to attack Zhào and expand the Héjiān territory.
Zhāng Táng said to Wénxìn Hóu:
"I once attacked Zhào for King Zhāo of Qín,
and Zhào holds a grudge against me,
saying:
'Whoever captures Táng will be rewarded with a hundred lǐ of land.'
Now, going to Yān must pass through Zhào,
so I cannot make the journey."
Wénxìn Hóu was displeased
but had no means to compel him.
Gān Luó asked:
"Why is my lord so deeply displeased?"
Wénxìn Hóu replied:
"I had Gāngchéng Jūn Cài Zé serve in Yān for three years,
and Crown Prince Dān of Yān has already entered as a hostage.
Yet when I personally asked Zhāng Qīng to be chancellor in Yān, he refused to go."
Gān Luó said:
"Allow me to persuade him to go."
Wénxìn Hóu scolded:
"Away with you!
I personally requested it and he refused;
how can you make him go?"
Gān Luó replied:
"The great Xiàng Tuó became Confucius' teacher at seven.
Now I am already twelve years old;
my lord should test me—
why scold so hastily?"
Thereupon, Gān Luó visited Zhāng Qīng and said:
"How does your merit compare to Wǔ'ān Jūn's?"
Zhāng Qīng said:
"Wǔ'ān Jūn thwarted the powerful Chǔ in the south,
intimidated Yān and Zhào in the north,
winning battles and capturing lands,
destroying cities and razing towns—
too many to count.
My merits do not match his."
Gān Luó asked:
"When Yìng Hóu was employed in Qín,
was his authority greater than Wénxìn Hóu's?"
Zhāng Qīng said:
"Yìng Hóu's authority was not as great as Wénxìn Hóu's."
Gān Luó said:
"Do you clearly know that it is not as great?"
He replied:
"I know it."
Gān Luó said:
"When Yìng Hóu wished to attack Zhào,
Wǔ'ān Jūn opposed it,
and just seven lǐ from Xiányáng, he died at Dùyóu.
Now Wénxìn Hóu personally asks you to be chancellor in Yān, yet you refuse to go.
I do not know where you will meet your end."
Zhāng Táng said:
"I shall go, following the boy's advice."
He ordered preparations for the journey.
When the departure date was set,
Gān Luó said to Wénxìn Hóu:
"Lend me five chariots,
and let me go ahead to inform Zhào."
Wénxìn Hóu then entered and reported to Shǐ Huáng:
"The grandson of the late Gān Mào, Gān Luó,
though young in years,
is from a renowned family,
known among the feudal lords.
Earlier, Zhāng Táng feigned illness and refused to go,
but Gān Luó persuaded him, and he is now going.
He now wishes to first report to Zhào;
I request permission to send him."
Shǐ Huáng summoned him for an audience
and dispatched Gān Luó to Zhào.
King Xiāng of Zhào welcomed Gān Luó at the outskirts.
Gān Luó persuaded the king of Zhào, saying:
"Has the king heard that Crown Prince Dān of Yān has entered Qín as a hostage?"
He replied:
"I have heard it."
Gān Luó asked:
"Has the king heard that Zhāng Táng is becoming chancellor in Yān?"
He replied:
"I have heard it."
"Crown Prince Dān entering Qín
means Yān does not deceive Qín.
Zhāng Táng becoming chancellor in Yān
means Qín does not deceive Yān.
With Yān and Qín not deceiving each other,
an attack on Zhào
would be perilous.
The reason Yān and Qín do not deceive each other
is their intent to attack Zhào and expand Héjiān.
Your Majesty should instead grant me five cities to expand Héjiān,
whereupon I will request the return of Crown Prince Dān of Yān,
and you can ally with strong Zhào to attack weak Yān."
The king of Zhào immediately ceded five cities to expand Héjiān.
Qín returned Crown Prince Dān of Yān.
Zhào attacked Yān,
gaining thirty cities from Shànggǔ,
and allowed Qín to have eleven of them.
Gān Luó returned to report to Qín,
and was enfeoffed as a senior minister,
with the former lands and residences of Gān Mào restored to him.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Chūlǐzǐ was esteemed due to kinship,
which is natural,
yet the people of Qín praised his wisdom,
so I have recorded it somewhat.
Gān Mào rose from the alleys of Xiàcài,
gaining renown among the feudal lords,
and strengthened both Qí and Chǔ.
Gān Luó was young,
yet he devised a remarkable stratagem,
earning fame for later generations.
Though not a deeply virtuous gentleman,
he was indeed a strategist of the Warring States period.
In the era of Qín's strength,
the world especially favored cunning tactics.
Ráng Hóu, named Wèi Rǎn,
was the younger brother of King Zhāo of Qín's mother, Queen Dowager Xuān.
His ancestors were from Chǔ,
of the Mǐ clan.
When King Wǔ of Qín died,
having no son,
his younger brother was enthroned as King Zhāo.
King Zhāo's mother was originally titled Mǐ Bāzǐ,
and upon King Zhāo's accession,
Mǐ Bāzǐ was titled Queen Dowager Xuān.
Queen Dowager Xuān was not King Wǔ's mother.
King Wǔ's mother was titled Queen Huìwén,
who died before King Wǔ.
Queen Dowager Xuān had two younger brothers:
the elder, from a different father, was Ráng Hóu,
of the Wèi clan,
named Rǎn;
the younger, from the same father, was Mǐ Róng,
who became Huáyáng Jūn.
King Zhāo's full brothers were Gāolíng Jūn
and Jīngyáng Jūn.
Among them, Wèi Rǎn was the most capable,
serving in office since the times of King Huì and King Wǔ.
When King Wǔ died,
his brothers contended for the throne,
but only Wèi Rǎn had the strength to establish King Zhāo.
Upon King Zhāo's accession,
he appointed Rǎn as a general
to guard Xiányáng.
He suppressed the rebellion of Jì Jūn,
expelled King Wǔ's queen to Wèi,
and eliminated all of King Zhāo's dissenting brothers,
shaking Qín with his authority.
King Zhāo being young,
Queen Dowager Xuān governed herself,
entrusting administration to Wèi Rǎn.
In the seventh year of King Zhāo,
Chūlǐzǐ died,
and Jīngyáng Jūn was sent as a hostage to Qí.
The Zhào official Lóu Huǎn came to serve as chancellor of Qín,
which was unfavorable to Zhào,
so they sent Qiú Yè to Qín,
requesting that Wèi Rǎn be made chancellor of Qín.
When Qiú Yè was about to depart,
his retainer Sòng Gōng said to him:
"If Qin does not heed you,
Lóu Huǎn will surely resent you.
You should instead say to Lóu Huǎn, 'I will plead for you not to press Qin urgently.'
When the King of Qin sees that Zhào's request to make Wèi Rǎn chancellor is not urgent,
he will not listen to you.
If you speak and the matter fails,
you will have done a favor to Lóu Zǐ;
if it succeeds,
Wèi Rǎn will be grateful to you."
Thereupon, Qiú Yè followed this advice.
And indeed, Qin dismissed Lóu Huǎn and made Wèi Rǎn chancellor of Qin.
(He) wanted to execute Lǚ Lǐ,
so Lǚ Lǐ fled to Qí.
In the fourteenth year of King Zhāo,
Wèi Rǎn recommended Bái Qǐ,
sending him to replace Xiàng Shòu as general to attack Hán and Wèi,
defeating them at Yīquē,
beheading 240,000,
and capturing the Wèi general Gōngsūn Xǐ.
The next year,
they also took Yuān and Yè from Chǔ.
Wèi Rǎn pleaded illness and resigned as chancellor,
making the guest minister Shòu Zhú chancellor.
The year after that,
Zhú was dismissed,
and Rǎn was made chancellor again,
whereupon he was enfeoffed in Rǎng,
and additionally granted Táo,
with the title Marquis of Rǎng.
Four years after the Marquis of Rǎng's enfeoffment,
he served as a general of Qin to attack Wèi.
Wèi presented 400 li east of the Hé.
They captured Wèi's Hénèi,
taking over sixty cities large and small.
In the nineteenth year of King Zhāo,
Qin proclaimed itself the Western Emperor,
and Qí proclaimed itself the Eastern Emperor.
After over a month,
Lǚ Lǐ came,
and both Qí and Qin resumed calling themselves kings.
Wèi Rǎn again became chancellor of Qin,
and was dismissed after six years.
Two years after his dismissal,
he again became chancellor of Qin.
Four years later,
he sent Bái Qǐ to capture Yǐng from Chǔ,
and Qin established the Nán Commandery.
Then he enfeoffed Bái Qǐ as Lord Wǔ'ān.
Bái Qǐ was
the one recommended and employed by the Marquis of Rǎng,
and they were on good terms.
At this time, the wealth of the Marquis of Rǎng
surpassed that of the royal house.
In the thirty-second year of King Zhāo,
the Marquis of Rǎng served as chancellor of state,
leading troops to attack Wèi,
driving away Máng Mǎo,
entering Běi Zhái,
and then besieging Dàliáng.
The Wèi senior official Xū Gǔ persuaded the Marquis of Rǎng, saying:
"I have heard a senior official of Wèi say to the King of Wèi:
'In the past, King Huì of Liáng attacked Zhào,
was victorious at Sānliáng,
and captured Hándān;
yet the Zhào clan did not cede territory,
and Hándān was restored.
The men of Qí attacked Wèi,
captured the old capital,
and killed Zǐ Liáng;
yet the men of Wèi did not cede territory,
and the old lands were returned.
The reason Wèi and Zhào preserved their states with strong armies and their lands were not annexed by the feudal lords
is that they were able to endure hardship and valued not giving up land.
Sòng and Zhōngshān repeatedly fought and ceded land,
and their states perished as a result.
I believe that Wèi and Zhào should be emulated,
and Sòng and Zhōngshān should serve as warnings.
Qin
is a greedy and violent state,
and cannot be trusted.
It nibbles away at the Wèi clan,
and has already taken all of Jìn,
defeated Bào Zǐ,
and taken eight counties,
yet before the land was fully handed over,
its troops were sent out again.
How can Qin ever be satisfied!
Now it has again driven away Máng Mǎo,
entered Běi Zhái,
not daring to attack Liáng,
but rather to coerce the king into ceding more land.
Your Majesty must not listen.
Now if you, King, turn your back on Chǔ and Zhào to make peace with Qin,
Chǔ and Zhào will be angry and abandon you,
and compete with you in serving Qin;
Qin will surely accept them.
If Qin uses the troops of Chǔ and Zhào to attack Liáng again,
then the state will inevitably perish.
I hope Your Majesty will certainly not make peace.
If you wish to make peace,
cede a little and provide hostages;
otherwise,
you will surely be deceived.'
This is what I heard in Wèi,
and I hope you, King, will consider matters accordingly.
The 'Zhōu Shū' says, 'The mandate is not constant,'
meaning that fortune cannot be frequent.
Defeating Bào Zǐ
and taking eight counties
was not due to the excellence of military strength,
nor to the cleverness of strategy,
but largely to heavenly fortune.
Now driving away Máng Mǎo again,
entering Běi Zhái,
and attacking Dàliáng
is to treat heavenly fortune as constant;
the wise do not do so.
I have heard that Wèi has mobilized all its able-bodied men from a hundred counties to defend Dàliáng,
and I estimate no fewer than 300,000.
With 300,000 men guarding Liáng's seven-ren walls,
I believe even Tāng and Wǔ resurrected
would find it hard to capture.
To lightly turn one's back on the troops of Chǔ and Zhào,
assault seven-ren walls,
and fight 300,000 men,
determined to capture it,
I believe from the beginning of heaven and earth until now,
such a thing has never occurred.
If you attack and fail to capture it,
the Qin troops will be exhausted,
Táo Yì will be lost,
and all previous achievements will be wasted.
Now the Wèi clan is hesitant,
and can be won over with a small cession of land.
I hope you will, before the troops of Chǔ and Zhào reach Liáng,
quickly win over Wèi with a small cession.
Wèi, being hesitant, will see advantage in a small cession,
and will surely desire it;
then you will achieve your wish.
Chǔ and Zhào will be angry that Wèi made peace before them,
and will surely compete in serving Qin;
the alliance will thus dissolve,
and you can choose later.
Moreover, must you gain land by force?
If Jìn is partitioned,
Qin troops need not attack,
and Wèi will surely offer Jiàng and Ānyì.
Also, open two routes for Táo,
almost all of the former Sòng,
and Wèi will surely offer Shànfù.
Qin troops can be preserved,
and you will control them;
what can you not obtain,
what can you not accomplish!
I hope you will consider this carefully and not act dangerously."
The Marquis of Rǎng said:
"Well said."
Then he lifted the siege of Liáng.
The next year,
Wèi turned against Qin,
and allied closely with Qí.
Qin sent the Marquis of Rǎng to attack Wèi,
beheading 40,000,
driving away the Wèi general Bào Yuān,
and capturing three counties of Wèi.
The Marquis of Rǎng was granted additional fiefs.
The next year,
the Marquis of Rǎng, along with Bái Qǐ and the guest minister Hú Yáng, again attacked Zhào, Hán, and Wèi,
defeated Máng Mǎo at Huáyáng,
beheaded 100,000,
and took Juàn, Càiyáng, and Chángshè from Wèi,
and Guānjīn from the Zhào clan.
And they gave Guānjīn to Zhào,
strengthened Zhào with troops,
to attack Qí.
King Xiāng of Qí feared,
and sent Sū Dài to secretly send a letter to the Marquis of Rǎng on behalf of Qí, saying:
"I have heard travelers say, 'Qin will strengthen Zhào with 40,000 armored troops to attack Qí.'
I assuredly told the king of my humble state, 'The King of Qin is wise and skilled in strategy,
the Marquis of Rǎng is intelligent and experienced in affairs,
he will surely not strengthen Zhào with 40,000 armored troops to attack Qí.'
Why is that?
The alliance of the Three Jìn
is Qin's deep-seated enemy.
They betray each other a hundred times,
deceive each other a hundred times,
yet it is not considered untrustworthy,
nor is it considered unrighteous.
Now to defeat Qí and fatten Zhào.
Zhào,
being Qin's deep-seated enemy,
is not beneficial to Qin.
This is the first reason."
The strategists of Qín,
must say 'Destroy Qí,
exhaust Jìn and Chǔ,
and then dominate with the victory over Jìn and Chǔ.'
Now Qí,
is a weakened state;
to attack Qí with the forces of the realm,
is like using a thousand-jūn crossbow to burst an abscess;
it is bound to perish,
but how could it exhaust Jìn and Chǔ?
This is the second point.
If Qín sends few troops,
then Jìn and Chǔ will not be trustful;
if it sends many troops,
then Jìn and Chǔ will be controlled by Qín.
Qí, in fear,
if not fleeing to Qín,
will surely flee to Jìn and Chǔ.
This is the third point.
If Qín carves up Qí to feed Jìn and Chǔ,
and Jìn and Chǔ press with troops,
Qín will instead face enemies.
This is the fourth point.
Thus, Jìn and Chǔ use Qín to scheme against Qí,
and use Qí to scheme against Qín;
why are Jìn and Chǔ so wise and Qín and Qí so foolish?
This is the fifth point.
Therefore, by obtaining Ānyì and managing it well,
one can surely avoid calamity.
With Qín holding Ānyì,
the Hán clan will certainly lose Shàngdǎng.
To seize the vital region of the realm,
compared to sending troops and fearing their inability to return,
which is more beneficial?
Hence I say that the King of Qín is astute and well-versed in strategy,
and the Marquis of Ráng is wise and experienced in affairs;
they will certainly not reinforce Zhào with forty thousand armored troops to attack Qí."
Thereupon, the Marquis of Ráng did not proceed,
but led the troops back.
In the thirty-sixth year of King Zhāo,
the Chancellor, the Marquis of Ráng, recommended the guest minister Zào,
wanting to attack Qí and seize Gǎng and Shòu,
to expand his fief of Táo.
Then Fàn Jū of Wèi, who called himself Master Zhāng Lù,
criticized the Marquis of Ráng's campaign against Qí,
as it meant crossing the Three Jìn to attack Qí,
and seized this moment to persuade King Zhāo of Qín.
King Zhāo then employed Fàn Jū.
Fàn Jū spoke of Queen Dowager Xuān's autocracy,
the Marquis of Ráng's arbitrary power over the feudal lords,
and the extravagance of the likes of the Lord of Jīngyáng and the Lord of Gāolíng,
whose wealth surpassed the royal house.
Thereupon, King Zhāo of Qín awakened,
dismissed the Chancellor,
and ordered the Lord of Jīngyáng and his kind to leave the pass,
and go to their fiefs.
When the Marquis of Ráng left the pass,
his baggage carts numbered over a thousand.
The Marquis of Ráng died in Táo,
and was buried there.
Qín later recovered Táo and made it a prefecture.
The Grand Historian remarks:
The Marquis of Ráng,
was the own uncle of King Zhāo.
And the reason Qín could expand eastward,
weaken the feudal lords,
once claim the title of Emperor over the realm,
with all under heaven bowing westward in homage,
was due to the Marquis of Ráng's achievements.
Yet when he reached the peak of nobility and overflowed with wealth,
a single man's persuasion,
broke his position and stripped his power, leading to his death in sorrow—
how much more so for a minister from a foreign land?
Bái Qǐ
was a man of Méi.
He excelled in using troops
and served King Zhāo of Qín.
In the thirteenth year of King Zhāo,
Bái Qǐ became a Left Shùzhǎng,
leading an attack on Xīnchéng of Hán.
That year,
the Marquis of Ráng became Chancellor of Qín,
recommending Rèn Bǐ to be Governor of Hànzhōng.
The next year,
Bái Qǐ became a Left Gèng,
attacked Hán and Wèi at Yīquē,
beheaded 240,000,
captured their general Gōngsūn Xǐ,
and took five cities.
Qǐ was promoted to Guówèi.
Crossing the river, he took Hán's territory east of Ānyì,
reaching Gànhé.
The next year,
Bái Qǐ became a Grand Liángzào.
He attacked Wèi,
captured it,
and took sixty-one cities, large and small.
The next year,
Qǐ and the guest minister Cuò attacked Yuánchéng,
and captured it.
Five years later,
Bái Qǐ attacked Zhào,
capturing Guānglángchéng.
Seven years later,
Bái Qǐ attacked Chǔ,
capturing five cities including Yān and Dèng.
The next year,
he attacked Chǔ,
captured Yǐng,
burned Yílíng,
then advanced east to Jìnglíng.
The King of Chǔ fled from Yǐng,
going east to move the capital to Chén.
Qín made Yǐng the Nán Prefecture.
Bái Qǐ was promoted to Lord Wǔ'ān.
Lord Wǔ'ān thereby took Chǔ,
pacifying the prefectures of Wū and Qiánzhōng.
In the thirty-fourth year of King Zhāo,
Bái Qǐ attacked Wèi, captured Huáyáng,
drove away Máng Mǎo, and captured generals of the Three Jìn,
beheading 130,000.
Fighting Zhào's general Jiǎ Yǎn,
he drowned 20,000 of his soldiers in the river.
In the forty-third year of King Zhāo,
Bái Qǐ attacked Hán's Xíngchéng,
captured five cities,
and beheaded 50,000.
In the forty-fourth year,
Bái Qǐ attacked the Tàiháng route in Nányáng,
and cut it off.
In the forty-fifth year,
he attacked Hán's Yěwáng.
Yěwáng surrendered to Qín,
cutting off the route to Shàngdǎng.
Its governor Féng Tíng discussed with the people, saying:
"The route to Zhèng is already cut,
Hán surely cannot protect us as its people.
Qín troops advance daily,
Hán cannot respond,
it's better to give Shàngdǎng to Zhào.
If Zhào accepts us,
Qín will be angered,
and surely attack Zhào.
Zhào, facing attack,
will surely ally with Hán.
If Hán and Zhào unite,
they can resist Qín."
Thereupon, he sent a messenger to report to Zhào.
King Xiàochéng of Zhào deliberated with Lord Píngyáng and Lord Píngyuán.
Lord Píngyáng said:
"It's better not to accept.
If we accept it,
the disaster will outweigh the gain."
Lord Píngyuán said:
"To obtain a prefecture for no reason,
it is convenient to accept it."
Zhào accepted it,
and enfeoffed Féng Tíng as Lord Huáyáng.
In the forty-sixth year,
Qín attacked Hán's Gōushì
and Lìn, capturing them.
In the forty-seventh year,
Qín sent Left Shùzhǎng Wáng Hé to attack Hán,
taking Shàngdǎng.
The people of Shàngdǎng fled to Zhào.
The Zhào army was at Chángpíng,
to receive and protect the people of Shàngdǎng.
In April,
Hé thus attacked Zhào.
Zhào sent Lián Pō to command.
Zhào army soldiers encountered Qín scouts,
and the Qín scouts beheaded Zhào's deputy general Jiā.
In June,
they breached the Zhào army,
taking two Zhàng positions and four officers.
In July,
the Zhào army built fortifications and defended them.
Qín attacked their fortifications again,
captured two officers,
defeated their formation,
and seized the western fortifications.
Lián Pō held firm in his defenses awaiting Qín,
Qín repeatedly challenged to battle,
but the Zhào troops did not come out.
The King of Zhào repeatedly reprimanded him for this.
Meanwhile, the Qín chancellor, the Marquis of Yìng, sent agents to spend a thousand gold in Zhào for counter-intrigue,
saying:
"What Qín fears,
is only that Mǎfú's son Zhào Kuò commands;
Lián Pō is easy to deal with,
and will soon surrender."
The King of Zhào, angered by Lián Pō's army suffering heavy losses,
repeated defeats,
and his further fortification of defenses without daring to engage in battle,
and upon hearing the slanderous rumors spread by Qín,
thus sent Zhào Kuò to replace Lián Pō as general to attack Qín.
When Qín heard that the son of Mǎfú was commanding,
they secretly appointed Wǔ'ān Jūn Bái Qǐ as supreme general.
Wáng Hé was made deputy general,
and an order was issued in the army that anyone who dared reveal Bái Qǐ was commanding would be executed.
When Zhào Kuò arrived,
he immediately sent troops to attack the Qín army.
The Qín army feigned defeat and retreated,
deploying two flanking forces to ambush them.
The Zhào army pursued in victory,
chasing them right up to the Qín fortifications.
The walls were坚固 and they could not break in,
while a Qín force of 25,000 cut off the Zhào army's retreat,
and another force of 5,000 cavalry severed the lines between Zhào's fortifications,
splitting the Zhào army in two,
and cutting off their supply route.
Then Qín sent out light troops to attack them.
The Zhào army fared poorly in battle,
so they built fortifications and held firm,
awaiting rescue.
When the King of Qín heard that Zhào's supply route was cut,
he personally went to Hénèi,
granted one rank of nobility to each commoner,
and mobilized all those aged fifteen and above to go to Chángpíng,
to block Zhào's reinforcements and supplies.
By the ninth month,
the Zhào soldiers had gone without food for forty-six days,
and they were secretly killing and eating each other.
They attacked the Qín encampments,
trying to break out.
Forming four units,
they attempted four or five times,
but could not escape.
Their general Zhào Kuò led elite troops in personal combat,
and the Qín army shot and killed Zhào Kuò.
Kuò's army was defeated,
and 400,000 soldiers surrendered to Wǔ'ān Jūn.
Wǔ'ān Jūn calculated, saying:
"Previously, Qín had already captured Shàngdǎng,
but the people of Shàngdǎng were not happy to be under Qín and turned to Zhào.
These Zhào soldiers are fickle.
If we do not kill them all,
I fear they will rebel."
So he deceitfully had them all buried alive,
sparing only 240 of the younger ones to return to Zhào.
In total, 450,000 were captured and beheaded.
The people of Zhào were greatly shaken.
In the tenth month of the forty-eighth year,
Qín once again pacified Shàngdǎng Prefecture.
Qín divided its army into two:
Wáng Hé attacked Píláo,
and captured it;
Sīmǎ Gěng secured Tàiyuán.
Hán and Zhào grew fearful,
and sent Sū Dài with generous gifts to persuade Qín's chancellor Yìnghóu, saying:
"Has Wǔ'ān Jūn captured the son of Mǎfú?"
He replied:
"Yes."
He asked further:
"And will he besiege Hándān next?"
He said:
"Yes."
"If Zhào falls, then the King of Qín will rule all,
and Wǔ'ān Jūn will become one of the Three Excellencies.
The cities Wǔ'ān Jūn has captured for Qín through battle number over seventy,
securing Yān, Yǐng, and Hànzhōng in the south,
and capturing Zhào Kuò's army in the north.
Even the achievements of Zhōu, Shào, and Lǚ Wàng would not surpass this.
Now if Zhào perishes,
and the King of Qín rules,
then Wǔ'ān Jūn will surely be among the Three Excellencies.
Can you accept being beneath him?
Even if you have no desire to be under him,
it would be unavoidable.
Qín once attacked Hán,
besieged Xíngqiū,
and pressured Shàngdǎng,
yet the people of Shàngdǎng all defected to Zhào.
The world has long been unwilling to be subjects of Qín.
Now if Zhào is destroyed,
its northern territories will go to Yān,
the eastern to Qí,
the southern to Hán and Wèi,
then how many people would you gain, my lord?
So it would be better to seize this chance to accept their ceded land for peace,
and not let it add to Wǔ'ān Jūn's achievements."
Thereupon, Yìnghóu spoke to the King of Qín, saying:
"The Qín troops are weary,
I request permission to accept the ceded land from Hán and Zhào for peace,
and let our soldiers rest."
The king agreed,
and accepted Yuānyōng from Hán and six cities from Zhào for peace.
In the first month,
all troops were withdrawn.
When Wǔ'ān Jūn heard of this,
from then on he bore a grudge against Yìnghóu.
In the ninth month of that year,
Qín again dispatched troops,
sending Wǔdàfū Wáng Líng to attack Zhào's Hándān.
At that time, Wǔ'ān Jūn was ill,
and unable to travel.
In the first month of the forty-ninth year,
Líng attacked Hándān,
with little success,
so Qín sent more troops to support Líng.
Líng's army lost five regiments.
When Wǔ'ān Jūn recovered from his illness,
the King of Qín wanted to send him to replace Líng as commander.
Wǔ'ān Jūn stated:
"Hándān is truly not easy to attack.
Moreover, reinforcements from the other states are arriving daily,
and those states have long held grudges against Qín.
Although we defeated the army at Chángpíng,
over half of Qín's own soldiers perished,
and the country is drained.
To traverse mountains and rivers to contend for another's capital,
with Zhào resisting from within,
and the other states attacking from without,
the defeat of Qín's army is certain.
It cannot be done."
The King of Qín gave the order himself,
but he did not go;
then he sent Yìnghóu to urge him,
but Wǔ'ān Jūn firmly declined and would not go,
claiming illness.
The King of Qín sent Wáng Hé to replace Líng as commander,
and for eight or nine months they besieged Hándān,
but could not capture it.
Chǔ sent Chūnshēn Jūn and the Lord of Wèi with several hundred thousand troops to attack the Qín army,
and the Qín army suffered heavy losses.
Wǔ'ān Jūn remarked:
"Qín did not heed my advice,
and now see what has happened!"
When the King of Qín heard this,
he was enraged,
and forcibly ordered Wǔ'ān Jūn to rise,
but Wǔ'ān Jūn then claimed his illness was critical.
Yìnghóu went to urge him,
but he would not rise.
Thereupon, he was stripped of his rank and made a common soldier,
and exiled to Yīnmì.
Wǔ'ān Jūn was ill,
and unable to travel.
After three months,
the other states pressed their attack on the Qín army urgently,
and the Qín army repeatedly retreated,
with messengers arriving daily.
The King of Qín then sent men to expel Bái Qǐ,
not allowing him to remain in Xiányáng.
After Wǔ'ān Jūn set out,
ten lǐ west of Xiányáng's city gate,
he reached Dùyóu.
King Zhāo of Qín and Yìnghóu, along with his ministers, deliberated, saying:
"Bái Qǐ in his exile,
still seems discontent and resentful,
with more to say."
The King of Qín then sent a messenger to grant him a sword,
to take his own life.
Wǔ'ān Jūn drew the sword and was about to cut his throat,
saying:
"What crime have I committed against heaven to come to this?"
After a long while,
he said:
"I surely deserve death.
At the battle of Chángpíng,
hundreds of thousands of Zhào soldiers surrendered,
and I deceitfully had them all buried alive.
That is reason enough to die."
Thereupon, he committed suicide.
Wǔ'ān Jūn died
in the eleventh month of the fiftieth year of King Zhāo of Qín.
He died though not guilty of any crime,
and the people of Qín pitied him,
with villages and towns everywhere making sacrifices to him.
Wáng Jiǎn
was a man of Dōngxiāng in Pínyáng.
From youth, he loved military affairs,
and served Qín Shǐ Huáng.
In the eleventh year of Shǐ Huáng,
Jiǎn led an attack on Zhào's Yānyǔ,
defeated it,
and captured nine cities.
In the eighteenth year,
Jiǎn led an attack on Zhào.
After over a year,
he finally conquered Zhào,
the King of Zhào surrendered,
and all of Zhào's territory was secured and made into prefectures.
The following year,
the state of Yān sent Jīng Kē to assassinate the King of Qín,
and the King of Qín dispatched Wáng Jiǎn to attack Yān.
King Xǐ of Yān fled to Liáodōng,
and Jiǎn then pacified Yān's capital Jì and returned.
Qín sent Jiǎn's son Wáng Bēn to attack Jīng (Chǔ),
and the Jīng army was defeated.
He then turned to attack Wèi,
and the King of Wèi surrendered,
thus securing the territory of Wèi.
After Qín Shǐhuáng had destroyed the three Jìn states,
forced the King of Yān to flee,
and repeatedly defeated the Jīng army,
the Qín general Lǐ Xìn,
young, robust, and brave,
once pursued Crown Prince Dān of Yān with several thousand troops to the Yǎnshuǐ River,
finally capturing Dān,
and Shǐhuáng considered him worthy and courageous.
So Shǐhuáng asked Lǐ Xìn:
"I wish to attack and conquer Jīng;
in your estimation, how many men would suffice?"
Lǐ Xìn said:
"No more than two hundred thousand men."
Shǐhuáng asked Wáng Jiǎn,
and Wáng Jiǎn said:
"Nothing less than six hundred thousand men will do."
Shǐhuáng said:
"General Wáng has grown old;
how timid he is!
General Lǐ is decisive, robust, and brave;
his words are correct."
So he sent Lǐ Xìn and Méng Tián with two hundred thousand men south to attack Jīng.
Wáng Jiǎn's advice was not heeded,
so he pleaded illness,
and retired to his hometown of Pínyáng.
Lǐ Xìn attacked Píngyǔ,
Méng Tián attacked Qǐn,
and they heavily defeated the Jīng army.
Xìn then attacked Yānyǐng,
captured it,
and then led his troops westward,
joining Méng Tián at Chéngfù.
The men of Jīng followed them closely,
not resting day or night for three days,
heavily defeated Lǐ Xìn's army,
broke through two fortifications,
killed seven commandants,
and the Qín army fled.
Shǐhuáng heard of this,
was greatly angered,
personally rushed to Pínyáng,
and apologized to Wáng Jiǎn, saying:
"Because I did not adopt your strategy,
Lǐ Xìn has indeed brought disgrace upon the Qín army.
Now I hear the Jīng troops are advancing westward daily;
though you are ill,
can you bear to abandon me?"
Wáng Jiǎn said:
"If Your Majesty must use me,
nothing less than six hundred thousand men will do."
Shǐhuáng said:
"I will follow your strategy."
So Wáng Jiǎn led an army of six hundred thousand men,
and Shǐhuáng personally saw him off at Bàshàng.
As Wáng Jiǎn departed,
he requested numerous fine fields, houses, gardens, and ponds.
Shǐhuáng said:
"General, you may go;
why worry about poverty?"
Wáng Jiǎn said:
"To serve as a general for the great king,
yet never be enfeoffed as a marquis for my merits,
so while Your Majesty favors me,
I seize the moment to request gardens and ponds as estates for my descendants."
Shǐhuáng laughed heartily.
After Wáng Jiǎn passed through the pass,
he sent messengers back five times to request more good fields.
Someone said:
"General, your begging
is rather excessive."
Wáng Jiǎn said:
"Not so.
The King of Qín is suspicious and distrustful of others.
Now he has emptied the state of its armored soldiers and entrusted them solely to me.
If I do not repeatedly request fields and houses as estates for my descendants to show my steadfastness,
would it not make the King of Qín sit and doubt me?"
Wáng Jiǎn indeed replaced Lǐ Xìn to attack Jīng.
Jīng, hearing that Wáng Jiǎn was coming with reinforced troops,
mobilized all the troops in the state to resist Qín.
When Wáng Jiǎn arrived,
he fortified his positions and defended them,
refusing to engage in battle.
The Jīng troops repeatedly came out to challenge him,
but he never emerged.
Wáng Jiǎn daily allowed his soldiers to rest and bathe,
provided them with good food and drink, and cared for them,
personally eating the same meals as his soldiers.
After a long time,
Wáng Jiǎn sent someone to ask if the army was engaging in games.
The reply was:
"They are throwing stones and leaping."
Then Wáng Jiǎn said:
"The soldiers are ready for use."
As Jīng repeatedly challenged but Qín did not respond,
they withdrew eastward.
Jiǎn then mobilized his troops to pursue them,
ordering strong men to attack,
and heavily defeated the Jīng army.
Reaching Qínán,
they killed their general Xiàng Yàn,
and the Jīng troops fled in defeat.
Qín then took advantage of the victory to conquer and secure the cities and lands of Jīng.
Over a year later,
they captured King Fúchú of Jīng,
and finally pacified the land of Jīng, turning it into commanderies and counties.
Then they campaigned south to subdue the lords of Bǎiyuè.
And Wáng Jiǎn's son Wáng Bēn,
together with Lǐ Xìn, defeated and secured the lands of Yān and Qí.
In the twenty-sixth year of Qín Shǐhuáng,
he unified all under heaven,
with the Wáng and Méng families contributing greatly to the achievement,
their fame extending to later generations.
During the time of Qín Èrshì,
Wáng Jiǎn and his son Bēn had already died,
and the Méng family was exterminated.
When Chén Shèng rebelled against Qín,
Qín sent Wáng Jiǎn's grandson Wáng Lí to attack Zhào,
besieging the King of Zhào and Zhāng Ĕr in the city of Jùlù.
Someone said:
"Wáng Lí
is a famous general of Qín.
Now leading the strong army of Qín,
he attacks the newly established Zhào;
he will surely capture it."
A guest said:
"Not so.
A general from a family that has served for three generations is bound to be defeated.
Why is that?
Because they have killed too many,
and their descendants suffer the ill omens.
Now Wáng Lí is already the third generation of generals."
Not long after,
Xiàng Yǔ came to rescue Zhào,
attacked the Qín army,
and indeed captured Wáng Lí,
and Wáng Lí's army then surrendered to the feudal lords.
The Grand Historian remarks:
As the common saying goes, "A foot may be too short,
an inch may be long enough."
Bái Qǐ could assess the enemy and adapt to changes,
devising endless surprises,
his fame shaking the world,
yet he could not save himself from trouble with Yìnghóu.
Wáng Jiǎn served as a general for Qín,
pacifying the six states,
and at that time,
Jiǎn was a veteran general,
whom Shǐhuáng regarded as a teacher,
yet he could not assist Qín in establishing virtue,
nor consolidate its foundations,
but instead went along to gain favor,
until the end of his life.
And his grandson Wáng Lí was captured by Xiàng Yǔ;
was that not fitting?
Each had his shortcomings.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I read the book of Mèngzǐ,
and when I came to King Huì of Liáng asking
"How can I benefit my state?"
I never failed to put the book down and sigh.
I said: Alas,
benefit is truly the beginning of disorder!
The Master seldom spoke of benefit
because he always guarded against its source.
Hence it is said,
"To act based on benefit
invites much resentment."
From the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
how do the harms of craving benefit differ!
Mèng Kē
was a man of Zōu.
He studied under a disciple of Zǐsī.
Having mastered the Way,
he traveled to serve King Xuān of Qí,
but the king could not employ him.
He went to Liáng,
but King Huì of Liáng did not act on his words,
considering them impractical and detached from reality.
At that time,
Qín employed Lord Shāng,
enriching the state and strengthening its military;
Chǔ and Wèi employed Wú Qǐ,
achieving victories and weakening enemies;
King Wēi
and King Xuān of Qí employed Sunzi,
Tián Jì, and their followers,
causing the feudal lords to face east and pay homage to Qí.
The world was focused on vertical and horizontal alliances,
valuing military conquests,
yet Mèng Kē spoke of the virtues of Táng,
Yú, and the Three Dynasties,
so he did not find acceptance wherever he went.
He withdrew and, with Wàn Zhāng and others, compiled the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*,
expounding the ideas of Zhòngní,
and authored the seven chapters of *Mèngzǐ*.
Later, there were figures like Zōuzǐ.
In Qí, there were three Zōuzǐ.
The first was Zōu Jì,
who approached King Wēi by playing the qín,
and thus became involved in state affairs,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chéng and received the seal of chancellor,
preceding Mèngzǐ.
The next was Zōu Yǎn,
who came after Mèngzǐ.
Zōu Yǎn observed that rulers were becoming increasingly decadent and extravagant,
failing to uphold virtue,
unlike the self-cultivation described in the *Greater Odes*,
which should extend to the common people.
He deeply studied the waxing and waning of yīn and yáng and created esoteric and mystical theories,
writing works like *Zhōng Shǐ*
and *Dà Shèng*, totaling over a hundred thousand words.
His words were grandiose and unorthodox,
always starting with small verifiable things,
extrapolating to larger scales,
reaching the boundless.
He began with the present era, going back to Huángdì,
as commonly studied by scholars,
broadly correlating with the rise and fall of ages,
and recording omens and systems,
extrapolating further back,
to before heaven and earth were born,
into obscurity that cannot be traced or verified.
He first listed the famous mountains, great rivers,
accessible valleys, birds, and beasts of the Central States,
what grew in the water and soil,
and the treasures of various species,
then extrapolated from these
to what lay beyond the seas, unseen by people.
He cited the time since the separation of heaven and earth,
the transitions of the Five Virtues,
each governance having its appropriateness,
with corresponding omens as such.
He believed that what the Ruists called the Central States
constituted only one eighty-first part of the world.
The Central States are named Chìxiàn Shénzhōu.
Within Chìxiàn Shénzhōu, there are nine provinces,
as Yǔ arranged them,
but these do not count as the full number of provinces.
Beyond the Central States, there are nine regions like Chìxiàn Shénzhōu,
which are the so-called nine provinces.
These are surrounded by minor seas,
where people and animals cannot communicate with each other,
forming isolated areas,
each constituting one province.
There are nine such regions,
surrounded by a great ocean beyond,
at the edge of heaven and earth.
His methods were all of this kind.
However, in essence,
they always emphasized benevolence, righteousness, and frugality,
and the application of relationships between ruler and subject, superior and inferior, and the six family relations,
though starting broadly.
When feudal lords and nobles first encountered his methods,
they were awed and inclined to transform,
but later could not implement them.
Thus, Zōuzǐ was highly regarded in Qí.
He went to Liáng,
where King Huì greeted him at the outskirts,
observing the rites of host and guest.
He went to Zhào,
where Lord Píngyuán walked sideways and dusted off mats for him.
In Yān,
King Zhāo wielded a broom to clear the path,
requested a seat among the disciples to receive instruction,
built the Jiéshí Palace,
and personally went to study under him.
He authored *Zhǔ Yùn*.
His travels among the feudal lords earned him such respect and courtesy;
how could this be compared to Zhòngní suffering hunger in Chén and Cài,
or Mèng Kē's hardships in Qí and Liáng?
Thus, King Wǔ attacked Zhòu with benevolence and righteousness and became king,
while Bó Yí starved and refused to eat the grain of Zhōu;
when Duke Líng of Wèi inquired about battle formations,
Confucius did not answer;
when King Huì of Liáng planned to attack Zhào,
Mèng Kē spoke of King Tài leaving Bīn.
How could they have intended to flatter the world and seek mere conformity?
Trying to fit a square peg into a round hole—
how could it enter?
Some say
that Yī Yǐn carried a tripod and urged Tāng to become king,
and Bǎilǐ Xī fed oxen under a cart, yet Duke Mù used him to achieve hegemony;
they first found common ground,
then guided them to the great Way.
Though Zōu Yǎn's words were unorthodox,
might they also have had the intent of the "ox and tripod"?
From Zōu Yǎn and the Jìxià scholars of Qí,
such as Chúnyú Kūn,
Shèn Dào,
Huán Yuān,
Jiē Zǐ,
Tián Pián,
Zōu Shì, and others,
each wrote books on governance and chaos,
to appeal to the rulers of the time,
too numerous to fully recount!
Chúnyú Kūn
was a man of Qí.
He was widely learned and had a strong memory,
with no fixed master in his studies.
In his remonstrations and persuasions,
he admired the character of Yàn Yīng,
yet focused on discerning intentions and observing expressions.
A guest introduced Kūn to King Huì of Liáng,
and the king dismissed his attendants,
sitting alone to receive him twice,
but Kūn remained silent throughout.
The king found it strange,
and reproached the guest, saying:
"You praised Master Chúnyú,
saying even Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng were不及,
yet when he met me,
I gained nothing.
Am I unworthy of his words?
Why is this?"
The guest relayed this to Kūn.
Kūn said:
"Indeed.
The first time I saw the king,
his mind was on hunting;
the second time I saw him,
his mind was on music:
that is why I remained silent."
The guest reported this fully to the king,
who was greatly astonished,
and said:
"Alas,
Master Chúnyú is truly a sage!
Before Master Chúnyú's first visit,
someone had presented a fine horse,
and I had not yet seen it,
when the master arrived.
Before his second visit,
someone had presented a singer,
and I had not yet tested them,
when the master came again.
Though I dismissed others,
my private thoughts were on those matters,
it is true."
Later, when Chúnyú Kūn had an audience,
they spoke continuously for three days and nights without tiring.
King Huì wished to treat him with the position of a minister or chancellor,
but Kūn declined and left.
Thereupon, he was sent off with a comfortable carriage drawn by four horses,
bundles of silk with added jade,
and a hundred yì of gold.
He never held office for life.
Shèn Dào
was a man of Zhào.
Tián Pián
and Jiē Zǐ
were men of Qí.
Huán Yuān
was a man of Chǔ.
They all studied the techniques of the Yellow Emperor and Lǎozi's Way and Virtue,
and thus elucidated and systematized their essential ideas.
Hence, Shèn Dào wrote twelve essays,
Huán Yuān wrote upper and lower chapters,
and Tián Pián
and Jiē Zǐ also had their respective discourses.
Zōu Shì,
a descendant of the various Zōu families in Qí,
also extensively adopted Zōu Yǎn's techniques in composing his writings.
Thereupon, the King of Qí commended him,
and from Chúnyú Kūn onward,
all were appointed as ranked grand officers,
building mansions along the broad avenues,
with towering gates and spacious houses,
honoring and favoring them.
They attracted guests and retainers from all the feudal lords under heaven,
proclaiming that Qí could gather the worthy scholars of the world.
Xún Qīng,
a man of Zhào.
At the age of fifty, he first came to Qí to study.
Zōu Yǎn's techniques were grandiose and eloquently debated;
Shì's writings were ornate but difficult to apply;
Chúnyú Kūn, after long association with them,
occasionally gained insightful words.
Thus, the people of Qí praised them, saying:
"Yǎn who discourses on heaven,
Shì who carves dragons,
and Kūn with his glib tongue."
When Tián Pián and his like had all died by the time of King Xiāng of Qí,
Xún Qīng was the most senior teacher.
Qí still cultivated the vacancies among the ranked grand officers,
and Xún Qīng three times served as the libationer.
When someone in Qí slandered Xún Qīng,
he then went to Chǔ,
where Lord Chūnshēn appointed him as the magistrate of Lánlíng.
After Lord Chūnshēn's death, Xún Qīng was dismissed from office,
and thus made his home in Lánlíng.
Lǐ Sī once studied as his disciple,
and later became chancellor of Qín.
Xún Qīng detested the governance of the corrupt world,
where ruined states and chaotic rulers followed one another,
not following the great Way but preoccupied with shamans and sorcerers,
believing in omens and auspices,
despising petty and rigid Confucians,
and like Zhuāng Zhōu, who with his wit confused customs,
thus he examined the rise and fall of the practices of Confucianism,
Mohism, and the Way and its Virtue,
sequentially composing tens of thousands of words before his death.
He was then buried in Lánlíng.
In Zhào, there was also Gōngsūn Lǒng, who debated hardness and whiteness, sameness and difference,
and Jùzǐ with his discourses;
in Wèi, there was Lǐ Kuī,
who taught the full use of land's resources;
in Chǔ, there were Shīzǐ
and Chánglú;
and in Ā, there was Yùzǐ.
From Mèngzǐ to Yùzǐ,
their books were widely available in the world,
so their biographies are not discussed here.
Mò Dí,
a senior officer of Sòng,
excelled in defense and protection,
and advocated frugality in expenditures.
Some say he was contemporary with Confucius,
others say he lived after him.
Lord Mèngcháng was named Wén,
of the Tián clan.
Wén's father was Lord Jìngguō Tián Yīng,
who
was the youngest son of King Wēi of Qí and the half-brother of King Xuān of Qí.
Tián Yīng had held office and wielded power since the time of King Wēi,
joining Marquis Chéng Zōu Jì and Tián Jì in leading troops to rescue Hán and attack Wèi.
Marquis Chéng and Tián Jì vied for favor,
and Marquis Chéng betrayed Tián Jì.
Tián Jì, in fear,
attacked a border town of Qí,
but was unsuccessful,
and fled into exile.
It happened that King Wēi died,
and King Xuān ascended the throne,
learning that Marquis Chéng had betrayed Tián Jì,
he recalled Tián Jì and appointed him as a general.
In the second year of King Xuān's reign,
Tián Jì, along with Sūn Bìn
and Tián Yīng, attacked Wèi,
defeating them at Mǎlíng,
capturing Wèi's crown prince Shēn and killing Wèi's general Páng Juān.
In the seventh year of King Xuān's reign,
Tián Yīng was sent as an envoy to Hán
and Wèi, and Hán,
Wèi submitted to Qí.
Yīng met with Marquis Zhāo of Hán
and King Huì of Wèi south of Dōng'ē with King Xuān of Qí,
concluded a covenant, and departed.
The following year,
he again met with King Huì of Liáng at Juàn.
That year,
King Huì of Liáng died.
In the ninth year of King Xuān's reign,
Tián Yīng became chancellor of Qí.
King Xuān of Qí met with King Xiāng of Wèi at Xúzhōu, and each recognized the other as king.
King Wēi of Chǔ heard of this,
and was angered at Tián Yīng.
The next year,
Chǔ attacked and defeated the Qí army at Xúzhōu,
and sent someone to expel Tián Yīng.
Tián Yīng sent Zhāng Chǒu to persuade King Wēi of Chǔ,
and King Wēi desisted.
Tián Yīng served as chancellor of Qí for eleven years,
then King Xuān died,
and King Mǐn ascended the throne.
In the third year of his reign,
he enfeoffed Tián Yīng at Xuē.
Initially,
Tián Yīng had over forty sons,
and a lowly concubine bore a son named Wén,
who was born on the fifth day of the fifth month.
Yīng told the mother:
"Do not raise him."
The mother secretly raised him and kept him alive.
When he grew up,
his mother, through his brothers, presented her son Wén to Tián Yīng.
Tián Yīng angrily said to the mother:
"I ordered you to abandon this child,
yet you dared to let him live;
why?"
Wén kowtowed,
and then said:
"My lord, what is the reason
for not raising a child born in the fifth month?"
Yīng said:
"A child born in the fifth month,
when grown, will be as tall as the door,
and will bring harm to his parents."
Wén said:
"Is human life bestowed by heaven?
Or is it bestowed by the door?"
Yīng was silent.
Wén said:
"If it is bestowed by heaven,
what is there to worry about?
If it is bestowed by the door,
then simply raise the height of the door;
who could reach it then!"
Yīng said:
"Enough, my son."
After some time,
Wén seized an opportunity to ask his father Yīng:
"What is the son of a son called?"
He replied:
"A grandson."
"What is the grandson of a grandson called?"
He replied:
"A great-grandson."
"What is the grandson of a great-grandson called?"
He replied:
"I do not know."
Wén said:
"You have wielded power and served as chancellor of Qí,
through three kings now,
yet Qí's territory has not expanded, while your private family has amassed wealth of ten thousand gold,
and among your followers, not one worthy is seen.
I have heard that a general's household must produce generals,
a chancellor's household must produce chancellors.
Now, your rear palace treads on fine silks while scholars cannot even have coarse garments,
your servants and concubines have surplus fine grain and meat while scholars are not satisfied with dregs and husks.
Now you still hoard and accumulate treasures,
intending to bequeath them to someone you do not even know,
while forgetting the affairs of the state are daily declining;
I secretly find this strange."
Thereupon, Yīng began to treat Wén with respect,
putting him in charge of hosting guests.
Guests increasingly came,
and his reputation became known among the feudal lords.
The feudal lords all sent messengers to request Lord Xuē Tián Yīng to make Wén his heir,
and Yīng agreed.
When Yīng died,
he was posthumously titled Lord Jìngguō.
And Wén indeed succeeded him at Xuē,
becoming Lord Mèngcháng.
Lord Mèngcháng was in Xuē,
where he summoned feudal lords' guests and fugitives who had committed crimes,
all of whom came to Lord Mèngcháng.
He abandoned his estate to generously host them,
thus winning over the scholars of the world.
He had several thousand retainers,
treating them all equally regardless of status, just like himself.
When Lord Mèngcháng received guests and conversed with them seated,
there was always a scribe behind a screen,
whose duty was to record his conversations with guests,
asking about their relatives' residences.
After a guest left,
Lord Mèngcháng would send envoys to inquire after them
and present gifts to their relatives.
Once, Lord Mèngcháng was hosting guests at an evening meal,
when someone blocked the light of the fire.
A guest became angry,
thinking the rice portions were unequal,
and stopped eating to take his leave.
Lord Mèngcháng stood up,
took his own rice to compare it.
The guest felt ashamed
and committed suicide by cutting his throat.
Because of this, many scholars came to Lord Mèngcháng.
He did not discriminate among his guests,
treating them all well,
so each believed Lord Mèngcháng was close to them.
King Zhāo of Qín heard of his virtue,
so he first sent Lord Jīngyáng as a hostage to Qí,
in order to request a meeting with Lord Mèngcháng.
When Lord Mèngcháng was about to go to Qín,
none of his guests wanted him to go,
and they remonstrated, but he wouldn't listen.
Sū Dài said to him:
"This morning, as I came from outside,
I saw a wooden figurine and a clay figurine talking to each other.
The wooden figurine said:
'If it rains,
you will be ruined.'
The clay figurine replied:
'I was born from clay,
so if ruined, I'll return to clay.
But if it rains now,
you will be washed away,
with no one knowing where you'll end up.'
Now Qín is
a nation of tigers and wolves,
and you wish to go there.
If you cannot return,
wouldn't you be laughed at by the clay figurine?"
So Lord Mèngcháng stopped.
In the twenty-fifth year of King Mǐn of Qí,
he finally sent Lord Mèngcháng to Qín,
and King Zhāo appointed him as Qín's chancellor.
Someone advised King Zhāo of Qín, saying:
"Lord Mèngcháng is virtuous,
and moreover, he is of the Qí royal clan.
Now as Qín's chancellor,
he will surely put Qí's interests before Qín's,
and Qín will be in danger."
So King Zhāo of Qín stopped him
and imprisoned Lord Mèngcháng,
plotting to kill him.
Lord Mèngcháng sent someone to bribe King Zhāo's favored consort to intercede.
The consort said:
"I wish to have your lord's white fox fur coat."
At that time, Lord Mèngcháng had one white fox fur coat,
worth a thousand pieces of gold,
unmatched in the world,
but he had already presented it to King Zhāo upon entering Qín,
and had no other such coat.
Lord Mèngcháng was troubled by this,
and asked all his guests,
but none could respond.
The lowest-seated guest, who was skilled in dog-like theft,
said:
"I can get the white fox fur coat."
So that night, he acted like a dog
to enter the Qín palace treasury,
retrieved the presented white fox fur coat,
and offered it to the king's consort.
The consort spoke to King Zhāo on his behalf,
and King Zhāo released Lord Mèngcháng.
Once free,
he immediately galloped away,
altered his travel documents,
changed his name to pass through the checkpoint.
At midnight, he reached Hángǔ Pass.
King Zhāo of Qín later regretted releasing Lord Mèngcháng,
and upon finding he had left,
sent men on fast horses to pursue him.
When Lord Mèngcháng arrived at the pass,
the rule was to let guests out only at cockcrow,
and fearing pursuit would catch up,
a guest seated in the lower ranks, who could imitate a rooster's crow,
made all the roosters crow together,
so they issued the documents and left.
Shortly after they left,
Qín's pursuers indeed reached the pass,
but since Lord Mèngcháng had already exited,
they turned back.
Initially, when Lord Mèngcháng included these two men among his guests,
the guests were all ashamed of them,
but when Lord Mèngcháng faced trouble in Qín,
it was these two who rescued him.
After this,
all the guests were convinced.
Lord Mèngcháng passed through Zhào,
where Lord Píngyuán of Zhào hosted him.
The people of Zhào, hearing of Lord Mèngcháng's virtue,
came out to see him,
and laughed, saying:
"We thought Lord Xuē would be imposing,
but now we see him,
he's just a small man."
Lord Mèngcháng heard this
and was enraged. His accompanying guests descended,
hacked and killed several hundred people,
and wiped out an entire county before leaving.
King Mǐn of Qí felt insecure,
having sent Lord Mèngcháng away.
When Lord Mèngcháng returned,
he was made chancellor of Qí,
taking charge of governance.
Lord Mèngcháng held a grudge against Qín,
and planned to use Qí to help Hán
and Wèi attack Chǔ,
then join Hán
and Wèi in attacking Qín,
borrowing troops and provisions from Western Zhōu.
Sū Dài, on behalf of Western Zhōu, said to him:
"You have used Qí to help Hán
and Wèi attack Chǔ for nine years,
taking Wǎn
and Yè northward to strengthen Hán
and Wèi, and now you attack Qín to further empower them.
If Hán and Wèi have no worries from Chǔ in the south,
and no threats from Qín in the west,
then Qí will be in danger.
Hán and Wèi will surely despise Qí and fear Qín,
and I fear for your safety.
You'd better have our humble state deeply align with Qín,
while you refrain from attacking,
and don't borrow troops or provisions.
You can approach Hángǔ Pass without attacking,
and let our state convey your intent to King Zhāo of Qín, saying:
'Lord Xuē will not weaken Qín to strengthen Hán
and Wèi. His attack on Qín
is to urge you, King, to have the King of Chǔ cede the eastern lands to Qí,
and for Qín to release King Huái of Chǔ as a peace offering.'
If you let our state offer this benefit to Qín,
Qín can avoid defeat and use the eastern lands to extricate itself,
which Qín will surely desire.
If the King of Chǔ is released,
he will be grateful to Qí.
Qí gaining the eastern lands will grow stronger,
and Lord Xuē will have no worries for generations.
Qín will not be greatly weakened,
and located west of the Three Jìn,
the Three Jìn will surely value Qí."
Lord Xuē said:
"Good."
So he ordered Hán
and Wèi to congratulate Qín,
stopped the three states from attacking,
and did not borrow troops or provisions from Western Zhōu.
At that time,
King Huái of Chǔ had entered Qín,
and Qín detained him,
so they wanted to secure his release.
However, Qín did not ultimately release King Huái of Chǔ.
Lord Mèngcháng served as chancellor of Qí,
and his retainer Wèi Zǐ was responsible for collecting the tax revenues from his fief for Lord Mèngcháng.
He returned three times without delivering a single payment.
Lord Mèngcháng questioned him about it,
and he replied:
"There was a worthy man,
and I secretly lent it to him,
which is why I did not deliver the payment."
Lord Mèngcháng became angry and dismissed Wèi Zǐ.
After several years,
someone slandered Lord Mèngcháng to King Mǐn of Qí, saying:
"Lord Mèngcháng is about to stage a rebellion."
When Tián Jiǎ attempted to kidnap King Mǐn,
King Mǐn suspected Lord Mèngcháng was involved,
so Lord Mèngcháng fled.
The worthy man to whom Wèi Zǐ had given the grain heard of this,
and submitted a letter stating that Lord Mèngcháng was not plotting a rebellion,
offering to pledge with his own life,
and then cut his own throat at the palace gate to prove Lord Mèngcháng's innocence.
King Mǐn was shocked,
and upon investigating and verifying the matter,
found that Lord Mèngcháng indeed had no rebellious intentions,
so he summoned Lord Mèngcháng back.
Lord Mèngcháng then pleaded illness,
and retired to his fief in Xuē.
King Mǐn permitted this.
Later,
the exiled Qín general Lǚ Lǐ became chancellor of Qí,
intending to put Sū Dài in a difficult position.
Sū Dài then said to Lord Mèngcháng:
"Zhōu Zuì was treated most generously in Qí,
yet the King of Qí expelled him,
and listens to Qīn Fú making Lǚ Lǐ chancellor,
because he wants to ally with Qín.
If Qí and Qín unite,
then Qīn Fú and Lǚ Lǐ will become powerful.
If they are employed,
both Qí and Qín will surely轻视 you.
You would be better off quickly sending troops north,
advancing into Zhào to make peace with Qín
and Wèi, recalling Zhōu Zuì to enhance your reputation,
thereby reversing the King of Qí's trust,
and also preventing changes under heaven.
Without Qín,
all under heaven will gather around Qí,
Qīn Fú will surely flee,
and then with whom will the King of Qí govern his state?"
So Lord Mèngcháng followed his advice,
and Lǚ Lǐ grew jealous and hostile towards Lord Mèngcháng.
Lord Mèngcháng feared this,
and sent a letter to the Qín chancellor Ránhóu Wèi Rǎn, saying:
"I hear that Qín wants to use Lǚ Lǐ to win over Qí.
Qí is a powerful state under heaven,
and you will surely be轻视.
If Qí and Qín join forces to pressure the Three Jìn,
Lǚ Lǐ will certainly become chancellor of both,
and this would mean you are helping Qí to strengthen Lǚ Lǐ.
If Qí avoids attack from all under heaven,
its enmity towards you will surely deepen.
You would be better off urging the King of Qín to attack Qí.
If Qí is defeated,
I will request that the conquered territory be enfeoffed to you.
With Qí broken,
Qín will fear Jìn's strength,
and will surely value you to win over Jìn.
Jìn, exhausted by Qí and fearing Qín,
will surely value you to win over Qín.
Thus, by destroying Qí you achieve merit,
and by controlling Jìn you gain weight;
this way, you destroy Qí to secure your fief,
with both Qín and Jìn valuing you.
If Qí is not defeated,
and Lǚ Lǐ is reappointed,
you will surely be in great distress."
So Ránhóu advised King Zhāo of Qín to attack Qí,
and Lǚ Lǐ fled.
Later, King Mǐn of Qí destroyed Sòng,
became even more arrogant,
and wanted to remove Lord Mèngcháng.
Lord Mèngcháng grew afraid,
and went to Wèi.
King Zhāo of Wèi made him chancellor,
and he allied with Qín
and Zhào in the west, joining with Yān to attack and defeat Qí.
King Mǐn of Qí fled to Jǔ,
and died there.
King Xiāng of Qí ascended the throne,
and Lord Mèngcháng remained neutral among the states,
belonging to none.
King Xiāng of Qí, newly enthroned,
feared Lord Mèngcháng,
so he made peace with him,
and renewed friendly relations with Lord Xuē.
When Wén (Lord Mèngcháng) died,
he was posthumously honored as Lord Mèngcháng.
His sons contended for the succession,
and Qí and Wèi together destroyed Xuē.
Lord Mèngcháng's line was cut off without an heir.
Earlier,
Féng Xuān heard that Lord Mèngcháng enjoyed hosting guests,
so he went to see him wearing straw sandals.
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"You have honored me from afar,
what instruction do you have for Wén?"
Féng Xuān said:
"I heard that you appreciate scholars,
and so I, a poor man, have come to you."
Lord Mèngcháng placed him in the guesthouse for ten days,
then asked the guesthouse manager:
"What has the guest been doing?"
The manager replied:
"Mr. Féng is very poor,
with only a sword,
and its hilt wrapped in straw.
He plucked his sword and sang,
'Long sword, let's go back,
for food here has no fish.'"
Lord Mèngcháng moved him to the better quarters,
where he had fish to eat.
After five days,
he asked the guesthouse manager again.
The manager replied:
"The guest again plucked his sword and sang,
'Long sword, let's go back,
for going out has no carriage.'"
Lord Mèngcháng moved him to the best quarters,
where he could ride in a carriage when going out.
After another five days,
Lord Mèngcháng asked the guesthouse manager once more.
The manager replied:
"The gentleman again plucked his sword and sang,
'Long sword, let's go back,
for I have no means to support a family.'"
Lord Mèngcháng was displeased.
After a year had passed,
Féng Xuān had said nothing more.
At that time, Lord Mèngcháng was chancellor of Qí,
enfeoffed with ten thousand households in Xuē.
He had three thousand retainers,
and the income from his fief was insufficient to support them,
so he sent someone to lend money in Xuē.
Over a year passed with no repayment,
and many borrowers could not pay the interest,
so the support for the retainers was about to be cut off.
Lord Mèngcháng worried about this,
and asked his attendants:
"Who can be sent to collect the debts in Xuē?"
The guesthouse manager said:
"The guest in the best quarters, Mr. Féng, has a very eloquent appearance and demeanor,
he is an honorable man,
with no other skills,
so he might be suitable to send to collect debts."
Lord Mèngcháng then summoned Féng Xuān and requested of him:
"My guests, unaware of my unworthiness,
have kindly come to me, numbering over three thousand.
The income from my fief is not enough to support them,
so I lent out money at interest in Xuē.
Xuē has had no harvest this year,
and the people are largely unable to pay the interest.
Now I fear the guests' provisions will be insufficient;
I hope you, sir, will collect the debts for me."
Féng Xuān said:
"Very well."
He took his leave and set off,
arriving in Xuē,
where he summoned all those who had borrowed money from Lord Mèngcháng to a meeting,
collecting one hundred thousand in interest.
Then he brewed much wine,
bought fattened oxen,
and summoned all the borrowers,
those who could pay the interest and those who could not alike,
all bringing their loan contracts to verify them.
Together they held a feast,
slaughtering oxen and setting out wine daily.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he held the contracts as before to verify them,
setting deadlines with those who could pay the interest;
for those too poor to pay,
he took their contracts and burned them.
He said:
"Lord Mèngcháng lent money to help those without means to establish their livelihoods;
the reason for seeking interest was due to having no means to support his guests.
Now those who are well-off are given deadlines,
and for the poor, the contracts are burned to cancel the debts.
Everyone, eat and drink heartily.
With such a lord,
how could you betray him!"
All present rose
and bowed twice.
Lord Mèngcháng heard that Féng Huān had burned the debt contracts,
and angrily sent a messenger to summon Huān.
When Huān arrived,
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"I, Wén, have three thousand retainers,
so I borrowed money in Xuē.
My fiefdom's revenue is small,
and the people still mostly fail to pay their interest on time,
so I fear there may be insufficient provisions for my guests.
Therefore, I asked you, sir, to collect the debts.
I heard that after you obtained money,
you immediately used it to prepare cattle and wine in abundance and burned the debt contracts.
Why?"
Féng Huān replied:
"Indeed.
Without preparing ample cattle and wine, I could not gather everyone completely,
and had no way to know who had surplus or shortage.
Those with surplus,
I set a final deadline for them.
For those with insufficient means,
even if I pressed them for ten years,
the interest would only grow more,
and in desperation, they would flee and abandon their debts.
If pressed urgently,
they would ultimately have no way to repay,
which above would make you appear greedy and uncaring toward the common people,
and below would give them a reputation for rebelling and defaulting.
This is not the way to encourage the people and enhance your reputation.
Burning the useless, empty debt contracts,
and discarding the uncollectible fictitious accounts,
makes the people of Xuē cherish you and spreads your good name.
Why do you have any doubts about this!"
Lord Mèngcháng then clapped his hands and thanked him.
The King of Qí, misled by slanders from Qín
and Chǔ,
believed that Lord Mèngcháng's fame surpassed his own and that he monopolized the power of the state of Qí,
so he deposed Lord Mèngcháng.
When the retainers saw Lord Mèngcháng deposed,
they all left.
Féng Huān said:
"Lend me a carriage fit
to enter Qín,
and I will surely make you esteemed in the state and your fiefdom expanded.
May I?"
Lord Mèngcháng then prepared a carriage and gifts and sent him off.
Féng Huān went west and persuaded the King of Qín, saying:
"The wandering scholars of the world who lean on their carriage rails and tighten their reins to enter Qín from the west
all desire to strengthen Qín and weaken Qí;
those who lean on their carriage rails and tighten their reins to enter Qí from the east
all desire to strengthen Qí and weaken Qín.
These are two rival states,
and by nature, they cannot both stand as the dominant power;
the one that becomes dominant will win the world."
The King of Qín knelt upright and asked him:
"How can Qín avoid being the weaker one?"
Féng Huān said:
"Has Your Majesty heard that Qí has deposed Lord Mèngcháng?"
The King of Qín said:
"I have heard of it."
Féng Huān said:
"It was Lord Mèngcháng who made Qí respected throughout the world.
Now the King of Qí has deposed him due to slanders,
so he must be resentful
and will surely turn against Qí;
if he turns against Qí and comes to Qín,
then the secrets of Qí's state affairs,
and the sincerity of its human relations,
will all be delivered to Qín.
The land of Qí can be obtained,
and not just that—you could become the dominant power!
You should quickly send envoys with gifts to secretly welcome Lord Mèngcháng;
do not miss this opportunity.
If Qí realizes its mistake
and reinstates Lord Mèngcháng,
then the balance of power between the two states will be uncertain."
The King of Qín was greatly pleased,
and sent ten carriages with a hundred yì of gold to welcome Lord Mèngcháng.
Féng Huān took his leave, claiming to go ahead,
and upon reaching Qí,
persuaded the King of Qí, saying:
"The wandering scholars of the world who lean on their carriage rails and tighten their reins to enter Qí from the east
all desire to strengthen Qí and weaken Qín;
those who lean on their carriage rails and tighten their reins to enter Qín from the west
all desire to strengthen Qín and weaken Qí.
Now Qín and Qí are rival states;
if Qín is strong, then Qí is weak,
and by nature, they cannot both be dominant.
Now I have privately heard that Qín has sent envoys with ten carriages carrying a hundred yì of gold to welcome Lord Mèngcháng.
If Lord Mèngcháng does not go west, all is well;
but if he goes west to become chancellor of Qín, the world will rally to him,
Qín will be the dominant power and Qí the weaker,
and then Línzī
and Jímò
will be in danger.
Why does Your Majesty not preempt the Qín envoys before they arrive,
reinstate Lord Mèngcháng,
and further increase his fiefdom to apologize to him?
Lord Mèngcháng will surely be pleased and accept it.
Though Qín is a strong state,
how can it ask for another's chancellor and welcome him away?
This will thwart Qín's scheme
and foil its plan for hegemony."
The King of Qí said:
"Good."
Then he sent men to the border to await the Qín envoys.
Just as the Qín envoys' carriages entered Qí territory,
the messengers raced back to report it.
The king summoned Lord Mèngcháng and restored him to his position as chancellor,
returning his original fiefdom
and adding a thousand households to it.
When the Qín envoys heard that Lord Mèngcháng had been reinstated as chancellor of Qí,
they turned their carriages around and left.
Since the King of Qí had deposed Lord Mèngcháng due to slanders,
all the retainers had left.
Later, when he was summoned and reinstated,
Féng Huān went to welcome him.
Before they arrived,
Lord Mèngcháng sighed deeply and said:
"I have always enjoyed having guests,
and never dared to neglect any of them,
hosting over three thousand retainers,
as you, sir, know.
When they saw me deposed in a single day,
they all turned their backs on me and left,
with no one showing concern for me.
Now, thanks to you, sir, I have regained my position,
but what face do those guests have to see me again?
If any of them come to see me again,
I will surely spit in their faces and greatly humiliate them."
Féng Huān tied the reins and bowed.
Lord Mèngcháng got off the carriage to receive him,
saying:
"Are you, sir, apologizing on behalf of the guests?"
Féng Huān said:
"Not to apologize for the guests,
but because your words are mistaken.
All things have their inevitable end,
and all affairs have their inherent nature.
Do you understand this?"
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"I am foolish and do not know what you mean."
Féng Huān said:
"The living must die;
that is the inevitable end of all things.
The wealthy and noble have many followers,
while the poor and lowly have few friends;
that is the inherent nature of affairs.
Have you not observed those who rush to the market at dawn?
In the early morning,
they jostle shoulder-to-shoulder to squeeze through the gate and enter;
after nightfall,
those passing by the market swing their arms without a glance.
It is not that they love dawn and hate dusk,
but that what they hope to find is no longer there.
Now that you lost your position,
the guests all left;
this is no reason to resent them, as it would only cut off the path for future guests.
I hope you will treat guests as before."
Lord Mèngcháng bowed twice and said:
"I respectfully obey your command.
Having heard your words,
how dare I not accept your instruction?"
The Grand Historian remarks:
I once passed through Xuē,
and found that the local customs included many violent and unruly youths among the common people,
unlike in Zōu
and Lǔ.
When I asked the reason,
it was said:
"Lord Mèngcháng recruited bold and chivalrous men from all over the world,
and over sixty thousand households of troublemakers entered Xuē."
The world's tradition that Lord Mèngcháng took pride in hosting guests
is not unfounded.
Lord Píngyuán, Zhào Shèng,
was a noble son of Zhào.
Among the sons, Shèng was the most worthy,
fond of guests,
and several thousand guests came to him.
Lord Píngyuán served as chancellor under King Wén of Zhào and King Chéng of Zhào,
was removed from the chancellorship three times,
and reinstated three times,
and was enfeoffed in Dōngwǔchéng.
Lord Píngyuán's mansion had an upper story overlooking commoners' homes.
One of these households had a lame man,
who limped while fetching water.
A beautiful concubine of Lord Píngyuán, residing in the upper story,
looked down and saw him,
and laughed heartily at him.
The next day,
the lame man came to Lord Píngyuán's gate,
and pleaded:
"I have heard that you, my lord, delight in scholars,
and that scholars travel thousands of li without considering it far to come to you,
because you value scholars and hold women in low regard.
I unfortunately suffer from a crippling ailment,
yet your concubine in the rear chambers looked down and laughed at me.
I wish to have the head of the one who laughed at me."
Lord Píngyuán laughed and replied:
"Very well."
After the lame man left,
Lord Píngyuán laughed and said:
"Look at this fellow,
wanting to kill my beautiful concubine over a single laugh,
isn't that going too far!"
In the end, he did not kill her.
After a little over a year,
more than half of the guests, followers, and retainers had gradually withdrawn and left.
Lord Píngyuán found this strange,
and said:
"I, Shèng, have never dared to be discourteous in how I treat you all,
so why are so many leaving?"
One of his followers came forward and replied:
"It is because you did not kill the one who laughed at the lame man,
they believe you cherish beauty and belittle scholars,
so the scholars are leaving."
Thereupon, Lord Píngyuán beheaded the concubine who had laughed at the lame man,
personally went to the lame man's door to present it,
and apologized to him.
After that, his followers gradually returned.
At that time, Qí had Mèngcháng,
Wèi had Xìnlíng,
and Chǔ had Chūnshēn,
so they vied to outdo each other in treating scholars well.
When Qín besieged Hándān,
Zhào sent Lord Píngyuán to seek aid,
to form an alliance with Chǔ,
planning to take twenty of his guests and followers who were brave, strong, and skilled in both civil and military arts along.
Lord Píngyuán said:
"If we can achieve victory through civil means,
that would be best.
If civil means cannot secure victory,
then we will smear blood in the grand hall,
and must secure the alliance before returning.
We need not seek men from outside,
taking from among our guests and followers is sufficient."
He found nineteen men,
but there were no more suitable candidates,
leaving him unable to make up the twenty.
Among his followers was a man named Máo Suì,
who came forward and recommended himself to Lord Píngyuán, saying:
"I have heard you are going to form an alliance with Chǔ,
planning to take twenty guests and followers along,
without seeking from outside.
Now you are one short,
I hope you will take me to fill the number and go."
Lord Píngyuán said:
"How many years have you, sir, been here under my roof?"
Máo Suì said:
"Three years now."
Lord Píngyuán said:
"A worthy scholar in the world,
is like an awl in a bag—
its tip immediately shows.
Now you, sir, have been here under my roof for three years,
yet none around me have praised or spoken of you,
and I have heard nothing of you,
this means you have nothing to offer.
You are not capable,
sir, stay behind."
Máo Suì said:
"I am only asking today to be placed in the bag.
Had I been in the bag earlier,
I would have pierced through and emerged entirely,
not just shown the tip."
Lord Píngyuán eventually took Máo Suì along.
The nineteen men exchanged glances and laughed at him, but did not reject him.
By the time Máo Suì reached Chǔ,
after discussions with the nineteen men,
they were all convinced by him.
Lord Píngyuán negotiated the alliance with Chǔ,
explaining its advantages and disadvantages,
speaking from sunrise
until noon without reaching a decision.
The nineteen men said to Máo Suì:
"Sir, go up."
Máo Suì gripped his sword and ascended the steps,
saying to Lord Píngyuán:
"The advantages and disadvantages of the alliance
can be decided in two words.
Today, you spoke of the alliance at sunrise,
yet by noon it's undecided,
why?"
The King of Chǔ said to Lord Píngyuán:
"Who is this man?"
Lord Píngyuán said:
"He is my retainer."
The King of Chǔ shouted:
"Why don't you step down!
I am speaking with your lord,
what are you doing here!"
Máo Suì gripped his sword and stepped forward, saying:
"The reason you shout at me, King,
is because of Chǔ's multitude.
But now within ten paces,
you cannot rely on Chǔ's multitude,
your life hangs in my hands.
My lord is before you,
why do you shout?
Moreover, I have heard that Tāng ruled the world with seventy li of land,
and King Wén made the feudal lords submit with a hundred li of territory—
was it because their soldiers were numerous?
Truly, it was because they could leverage their position and exert their might.
Now Chǔ has five thousand li of land,
and a million halberd-bearing troops,
these are the resources of a hegemon.
With Chǔ's strength,
no one under heaven can withstand it.
Bái Qǐ,
a mere youngster,
led tens of thousands of troops,
raised an army to battle Chǔ,
in one battle captured Yānyǐng,
in a second burned Yílíng,
and in a third humiliated your ancestors.
This is a hatred for a hundred generations, and a shame for Zhào,
yet you, King, feel no disgrace.
The alliance is for Chǔ's sake,
not for Zhào's.
My lord is before you,
why do you shout?"
The King of Chǔ said:
"Yes, yes,
truly as you say, sir,
I respectfully pledge my state to the alliance."
Máo Suì said:
"Is the alliance settled?"
The King of Chǔ said:
"It is settled."
Máo Suì said to the King's attendants:
"Bring the blood of a chicken, dog, and horse."
Máo Suì held a bronze basin and knelt, presenting it to the King of Chǔ, saying:
"You, King, should smear the blood to confirm the alliance,
next my lord,
then me."
Thus, the alliance was settled in the hall.
Máo Suì, holding the basin of blood in his left hand, gestured with his right to the nineteen men, saying:
"You all smear this blood below the hall.
You are mediocre,
what are called those who rely on others to accomplish things."
After Lord Píngyuán had secured the alliance and returned,
arriving back in Zhào,
he said:
"I, Shèng, dare not judge scholars again.
I have judged scholars, at most a thousand,
at least several hundred,
and thought I had not missed any under heaven,
yet now I missed Máo Suì.
Máo Suì went once to Chǔ,
and made Zhào weightier than the Nine Tripods and the Great Bell.
Máo Suì, with his three-inch tongue,
proved stronger than a million troops.
I dare not judge scholars again."
Thus, he regarded Máo Suì as a top guest.
Lord Píngyuán had already returned to Zhào,
and the Chǔ state sent Lord Chūnshēn to lead troops to rescue Zhào,
while Lord Xìnlíng of Wèi also seized Jìn Bǐ's army by subterfuge to go and save Zhào,
but none had arrived yet.
Qín urgently besieged Hándān,
Hándān was in dire straits,
and on the verge of surrender,
Lord Píngyuán was deeply troubled by this.
Lǐ Tóng, son of an official at the Hándān guesthouse, advised Lord Píngyuán, saying:
"Aren't you worried about Zhào's demise?"
Lord Píngyuán replied:
"If Zhào falls, I, Shèng, will become a captive—
how could I not be worried?"
Lǐ Tóng said:
"The people of Hándān
burn bones for fuel and exchange children to eat—
one could call this desperate.
Yet your rear palace numbers in the hundreds,
maids and concubines clad in fine silks,
with surplus fine grains and meat,
while the people lack even whole coarse garments,
and aren't satisfied with chaff and dregs.
The people are exhausted, weapons depleted,
some whittle wood into spears and arrows,
yet your vessels, bells, and chimes remain as they are.
If Qín destroys Zhào,
how would you keep these?
If Zhào is preserved,
why worry about not having them?
Now if you truly can have your ladies and below join the ranks of the soldiers,
sharing tasks and working together,
distributing all your household's possessions to feast the troops,
soldiers in their peril and hardship
would easily feel grateful."
Thereupon, Lord Píngyuán followed his advice
and gathered three thousand daring warriors.
Lǐ Tóng then led these three thousand men against the Qín army,
forcing the Qín forces to retreat thirty lǐ.
It so happened that rescue forces from Chǔ
and Wèi arrived,
and the Qín troops thus withdrew,
Hándān was preserved.
