Lǐ Tóng died in battle,
and his father was enfeoffed as Lǐ Hóu.
Yú Qīng wanted to use Lord Xìnlíng's role in saving Hándān to seek a fief for Lord Píngyuán.
Gōngsūn Lóng heard of this,
and drove overnight to see Lord Píngyuán, saying:
"I, Lóng, have heard that Yú Qīng intends to use Lord Xìnlíng's preservation of Hándān to seek a fief for you—
is this true?"
Lord Píngyuán said:
"Yes."
Lóng said:
"This is highly inappropriate.
Moreover, the king elevated you to be chancellor of Zhào
not because your wisdom and ability were unmatched in Zhào.
Ceding Dōngwǔchéng to enfeoff you
was not because you had merit,
but rather because the state's people lacked achievement,
and it was due to your status as a relative.
You accepted the chancellor's seal without declining for lack of ability,
took the land without mentioning lack of merit,
also considering yourself a relative.
Now if Lord Xìnlíng saved Hándān and you seek a fief,
it would be a relative receiving a city while the state's people measure merit.
This is highly inappropriate.
Furthermore, Yú Qīng holds both advantages:
if successful,
he holds the right tally to claim credit;
if not,
he gains a reputation for gratitude from you.
You must not listen to him."
Lord Píngyuán then did not heed Yú Qīng.
Lord Píngyuán died in the fifteenth year of King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
His descendants succeeded him,
and eventually perished along with Zhào.
Lord Píngyuán treated Gōngsūn Lóng generously.
Gōngsūn Lóng was skilled in the debate on hardness and whiteness,
but when Zōu Yǎn passed through Zhào speaking of the ultimate Way,
he discredited Gōngsūn Lóng.
As for Yú Qīng,
he was a wandering persuader.
He trod in straw sandals, carrying a bamboo hat, to persuade King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
At the first audience,
he was awarded a hundred yì of gold,
a pair of white jade discs;
at the second,
he was made senior minister of Zhào,
hence titled Yú Qīng.
When Qín and Zhào battled at Chángpíng,
Zhào was defeated,
losing a commandant.
The king summoned Lóu Chāng and Yú Qīng, saying:
"Our army is defeated in battle,
the commandant is dead again,
I plan to have them arm up and charge—
what do you think?"
Lóu Chāng said:
"It's no use,
better send an important envoy to seek peace."
Yú Qīng said:
"Chāng suggests peace
thinking that without it, the army will surely be crushed.
But the power to decide peace lies with Qín.
And in your view of Qín,
does it want to destroy Zhào's army or not?"
The king said:
"Qín has spared no effort,
and surely aims to crush our army."
Yú Qīng said:
"If you heed me,
send envoys with valuable treasures to ally with Chǔ
and Wèi; Chǔ
and Wèi, desiring your treasures,
will surely admit our envoys.
If Zhào's envoy enters Chǔ
and Wèi, Qín will suspect a united front among the states,
and will surely fear.
Thus,
peace can be negotiated."
The king did not listen,
but had Lord Píngyáng seek peace,
sending Zhèng Zhū into Qín.
Qín admitted him.
The king summoned Yú Qīng, saying:
"I had Lord Píngyáng seek peace with Qín,
and Qín has admitted Zhèng Zhū—
what do you think?"
Yú Qīng replied:
"You will not achieve peace,
and the army will surely be crushed.
All under heaven congratulating the victors are in Qín.
Zhèng Zhū,
an eminent man,
entering Qín,
the king of Qín and Marquis Yìng will surely display him prominently to show the world.
Chǔ and Wèi, thinking Zhào has made peace,
will not rescue you.
When Qín knows no one will save you,
peace cannot be achieved."
Marquis Yìng indeed displayed Zhèng Zhū to those congratulating Qín's victory,
and ultimately refused peace.
Zhào suffered a great defeat at Chángpíng,
Hándān was besieged,
and they became the laugh of the world.
After Qín lifted the siege of Hándān,
the king of Zhào went to court Qín,
sent Zhào Hǎo to settle affairs with Qín,
ceding six counties for peace.
Yú Qīng said to the king:
"Did Qín attack you
and withdraw because weary,
or does it still have strength to advance but
spares you and does not attack?"
The king said:
"Qín attacked us
with all its might,
surely it withdrew due to weariness."
Yú Qīng said:
"Qín used its strength to attack what it could not take,
grew weary and withdrew;
if you now give it what its strength could not take,
you aid Qín in attacking yourself.
Next year when Qín attacks again,
you will have no rescue."
The king told Zhào Hǎo Yú Qīng's words.
Zhào Hǎo said:
"Can Yú Qīng truly gauge the extent of Qín's strength?
If he truly knows Qín's strength cannot advance further,
and we don't give this tiny land,
letting Qín attack again next year,
might you not have to cede inner territories for peace then?"
The king said:
"I'll listen to you and cede,
but can you ensure Qín won't attack me again next year?"
Zhào Hǎo replied:
"This is not something I dare guarantee.
In the past, the three Jìn states' relations with Qín
were friendly.
Now Qín is on good terms with Hán
and Wèi but attacks you,
meaning your service to Qín must be worse than Hán's
and Wèi's.
Now I am helping you resolve the attack due to betrayed kinship,
open borders, exchange currency,
and align with Hán
and Wèi; if by next year you alone are attacked by Qín,
it must be because your service to Qín lags behind Hán's
and Wèi's.
This is not something I dare guarantee."
The king informed Yú Qīng of this.
Yú Qīng replied:
"Hǎo said
'If we do not make peace,
next year Qin will attack Your Majesty again,
and won't Your Majesty have to cede territory from your heartland to make peace?'
Now if we make peace,
Hǎo again cannot guarantee that Qin will not attack again.
Even if we cede six cities now,
what good would it do!
When they attack again next year,
we would again have to cede what we cannot afford and make peace,
this is a strategy of self-destruction,
better not to make peace at all.
Although Qin is skilled at attacking,
they cannot take six counties;
although Zhào cannot defend well,
in the end we would not lose six cities.
When Qin grows weary and withdraws,
their troops will certainly be exhausted.
We could use the six cities to win over the world to attack the exhausted Qin,
thus what we lose to the world we would recover from Qin.
Our state would still benefit,
how does this compare to sitting idly and ceding territory,
weakening ourselves to strengthen Qin?
Now Hǎo says
'The reason Qin is friendly with Hán and
Wèi while attacking Zhào,
must be because Your Majesty serves Qin less well than Hán and
Wèi do',
this would make Your Majesty serve Qin with six cities every year,
and soon you would be sitting idly until your cities are exhausted.
Next year when Qin again demands territory,
will Your Majesty give it to them?
If not,
this would abandon previous efforts and provoke Qin's wrath;
if you give it,
then there would be no land left to give.
As the saying goes
'The strong are good at attacking,
the weak cannot defend'.
Now if we sit back and obey Qin,
Qin troops would not be exhausted yet gain much territory,
this would strengthen Qin and weaken Zhào.
To feed the ever-stronger Qin by cutting from the ever-weaker Zhào,
their demands would certainly never stop.
Moreover, Your Majesty's land is finite while Qin's demands are endless,
to satisfy endless demands with finite land,
the situation would inevitably lead to Zhào's demise."
King of Zhào had not yet decided on a plan,
when Lóu Huǎn arrived from Qin,
the King of Zhào consulted Lóu Huǎn about it,
saying:
"To give Qin land or not to give,
which is more auspicious?"
Huǎn declined politely saying:
"This is not something your subject can know."
The king said:
"Even so,
try to speak your personal opinion."
Lóu Huǎn replied:
"Has Your Majesty heard about Gōngfǔ Wénbó's mother?
Gōngfǔ Wénbó served in Lǔ,
fell ill and died,
two women killed themselves in their rooms for him.
When his mother heard this,
she did not weep.
Her steward said:
'How can there be someone who doesn't weep when her son dies?'
His mother said:
'Confucius,
a worthy man,
was driven out of Lǔ,
yet this man did not follow him.
Now that he's dead, two women have killed themselves for him,
this must mean he treated elders poorly but treated women well.'
So from the mother's perspective,
she was a worthy mother;
from the wife's perspective,
she would inevitably be considered a jealous wife.
Thus the same words,
spoken by different people change people's minds.
Now I have newly arrived from Qin, if I say not to give,
that would not be strategic,
if I say to give,
I fear Your Majesty would think I am acting for Qin:
therefore I dare not respond.
But if I may plan for Your Majesty,
it would be better to give."
The king said:
"Very well."
When Yú Qīng heard this,
he went to see the king and said:
"This is deceptive talk,
Your Majesty must be careful not to give!"
When Lóu Huǎn heard this,
he went to see the king.
The king again told Lóu Huǎn what Yú Qīng had said.
Lóu Huǎn replied:
"Not so.
Yú Qīng understands one aspect,
but not the other.
When Qín and Zhào conflict, all under heaven rejoice,
why?
They say
'We will rely on the strong and exploit the weak'.
Now that Zhào troops are trapped by Qin,
all under heaven who congratulate the victor will certainly side with Qin.
Therefore it would be better to quickly cede territory to make peace,
to confuse the world and appease Qin's heart.
Otherwise,
the world will take advantage of Qin's anger,
and exploit Zhào's exhaustion,
to carve it up.
When Zhào is about to perish,
how can it scheme against Qin?
Therefore I say Yú Qīng understands one aspect,
but not the other.
I hope Your Majesty will decide based on this,
and consider no other plans."
When Yú Qīng heard this,
he went to see the king and said:
"How dangerous is Lóu Zǐ's strategy for Qin!
This would further alert the world,
so how could it appease Qin's heart?
Why doesn't he mention that it shows Zhào's weakness to the world?
Moreover, when I say not to give,
I don't mean simply not to give.
Qin demands six cities from Your Majesty,
and Your Majesty should use these six cities to bribe Qí.
Qí is Qin's bitter enemy,
if they receive Your Majesty's six cities,
and join forces to attack Qin from the west,
Qí will listen to Your Majesty
before the words are finished.
Then what Your Majesty loses to Qí, you would recover from Qin.
And the deep enmity of Qí and
Zhào can be avenged,
while showing the world what you are capable of.
If Your Majesty announces this,
before troops even approach the border,
I foresee Qin sending heavy bribes to Zhào and instead seeking peace with Your Majesty.
If we follow Qin's peace offer,
when Hán and Wèi hear of it,
they will certainly greatly respect Your Majesty;
respecting Your Majesty,
they will certainly produce precious treasures to win Your Majesty's favor first.
Thus with one move Your Majesty would establish close relations with three states,
and reverse positions with Qin."
The King of Zhào said:
"Excellent."
Then he sent Yú Qīng east to see the King of Qí,
to plan against Qin with him.
Before Yú Qīng returned,
Qin's envoy was already in Zhào.
When Lóu Huǎn heard this,
he fled.
Zhào then enfeoffed Yú Qīng with one city.
Some time later,
Wèi requested to form a vertical alliance.
King Xiàochéng of Zhào summoned Yú Qīng to plan.
He visited Píngyuán Jūn,
Píngyuán Jūn said:
"I hope you will advocate the vertical alliance."
Yú Qīng entered to see the king.
The king said:
"Wèi has requested to form a vertical alliance."
He replied:
"Wèi is mistaken."
The king said:
"We have not yet agreed to it."
He replied:
"Your Majesty is mistaken."
The king said:
"Wèi requests an alliance,
you say Wèi is mistaken,
We have not agreed,
yet you say We are mistaken,
then can the vertical alliance never be formed?"
He replied:
"Your subject has heard that when small states work with large states,
if there is benefit, the large state receives the blessing,
if there is failure, the small state receives the disaster."
Now Wèi, as a small state, is requesting disaster,
while Your Majesty, as a large state, is declining blessing,
therefore your subject says Your Majesty is mistaken,
and Wèi is also mistaken.
I privately believe the vertical alliance is advantageous."
The king said:
"Excellent."
Then he united with Wèi in the vertical alliance.
Yú Qīng, for the sake of Wèi Qí's cause,
did not value the seal of a marquis with ten thousand households or the insignia of a minister and chancellor,
but fled with Wèi Qí in secret,
eventually leaving Zhào,
and found himself stranded in Liáng.
After Wèi Qí died,
Yú Qīng, feeling disheartened,
took to writing books,
drawing from the ancient "Spring and Autumn Annals" above,
and observing recent eras below,
titled "Integrity and Righteousness,"
"Titles and Designations,"
"Conjecture and Deliberation,"
and "Political Strategies,"
eight chapters in total.
They critiqued the successes and failures of the state,
and the world passed them down as "The Spring and Autumn Annals of Master Yú."
The Grand Historian remarks:
Lord Píngyuán
was an elegant and noble gentleman in a turbulent world,
yet he failed to grasp the greater picture.
As the common saying goes,
"Profit clouds wisdom,"
Lord Píngyuán greedily accepted Féng Tíng's deceitful advice,
leading Zhào to lose over four hundred thousand troops at Chángpíng,
and Hándān nearly fell.
Yú Qīng, in assessing events and weighing circumstances,
devised strategies for Zhào—
how masterful he was!
But when he could not bear to abandon Wèi Qí,
he ended up stranded in Dàliáng.
Even an ordinary person would know this was unwise,
let alone a man of virtue?
Yet had Yú Qīng not faced hardship and sorrow,
he might not have written books to make his name known to posterity.
Lord Wèi Wújì
was the youngest son of King Wèi Zhāo and the half-brother of King Wèi Ānlí.
After King Zhāo passed away,
King Ānlí ascended the throne,
and enfeoffed the lord as the Lord of Xìnlíng.
At that time, Fàn Jū had fled Wèi and become chancellor of Qín,
and due to his grudge against Wèi Qí,
Qín troops besieged Dàliáng,
defeated Wèi at Huáyáng's foot,
and routed Máng Mǎo.
The King of Wèi and the lord were deeply concerned.
The lord was benevolent and treated scholars with humility;
regardless of their ability, he welcomed them courteously and with respect,
never flaunting his wealth or status arrogantly.
Thus, scholars from thousands of miles around competed to join him,
amassing three thousand retainers.
At that time,
the feudal lords, recognizing the lord's virtue
and his many followers,
dared not plot military action against Wèi for over a decade.
Once, while the lord was playing a board game with the King of Wèi,
a beacon fire was reported from the northern border,
saying
"Zhào invaders are coming,
about to cross the border."
The king stopped the game,
intending to summon his ministers for counsel.
The lord halted him, saying:
"The King of Zhào is merely hunting,
not invading."
They resumed the game as before.
The king remained anxious,
his mind not on the game.
After a short while,
another report came from the north:
"The King of Zhào was only hunting,
not invading."
The king, astonished,
asked:
"How did you know this, my lord?"
The lord replied:
"One of my retainers has deep insight into the King of Zhào's private affairs;
whatever the king does,
the retainer reports to me,
so I knew."
From then on, the king feared the lord's wisdom and capability,
and dared not entrust him with state affairs.
In Wèi, there was a recluse named Hóu Yíng,
seventy years old,
poor,
serving as a gatekeeper at Yímén in Dàliáng.
The lord heard of him,
went to visit,
and wished to bestow generous gifts.
Hóu Yíng declined,
saying:
"I have cultivated my character and upheld integrity for decades;
I will not accept your wealth due to my poverty as a gatekeeper."
So the lord hosted a grand banquet for his guests.
Once seated,
he took his carriage and retinue,
left the left seat empty,
and personally went to welcome Hóu Yíng at Yímén.
Hóu Yíng, in worn clothes and hat,
straightaway mounted the carriage and took the honored seat,
without yielding,
to test the lord.
The lord held the reins even more respectfully.
Hóu Yíng then said to the lord:
"I have a friend in the market butcher shop;
I wish to trouble your carriage to visit him."
The lord drove the carriage into the market,
where Hóu Yíng got down to see his friend Zhū Hài,
deliberately standing long,
chatting with his friend,
while subtly observing the lord.
The lord's expression grew even gentler.
At that moment,
Wèi's generals, ministers, nobles, and guests filled the hall,
waiting for the lord to toast.
Market onlookers watched the lord holding the reins,
and his attendants secretly cursed Hóu Yíng.
Seeing the lord's composure unchanged,
Hóu Yíng finally bid farewell and returned to the carriage.
At the lord's home,
he seated Hóu Yíng in the place of honor,
introduced him to all the guests,
who were all astonished.
As the wine flowed freely,
the lord stood up
and toasted Hóu Yíng.
Hóu Yíng then said to the lord:
"Today, I have put you through enough, my lord.
I am but a lowly gatekeeper at Yímén,
yet you personally troubled your carriage
to welcome me before the crowd.
It was improper to go further,
but you deliberately did so.
I wished to enhance your reputation,
so I made your carriage wait long in the market,
passing by friends to observe you,
and you grew more humble.
The market people see me as a petty man,
but they see you as a noble who honors scholars."
After the banquet ended,
Hóu Yíng became a top retainer.
Hóu Yíng told the lord:
"The butcher I visited, Zhū Hài,
is a worthy man,
unknown to the world,
so he hides among butchers."
The lord repeatedly visited him,
but Zhū Hài never thanked him,
which puzzled the lord.
In the twentieth year of King Wèi Ānlí's reign,
after King Qín Zhāo had defeated Zhào's army at Chángpíng,
he advanced to besiege Hándān.
The lord's sister was the wife of Lord Píngyuán, brother of King Zhào Huìwén,
and she sent repeated letters to the King of Wèi and the lord,
pleading for rescue from Wèi.
The king sent General Jìn Bǐ with a hundred thousand troops to save Zhào.
The King of Qín sent an envoy to warn the King of Wèi:
"I will take Zhào soon;
if any state dares to rescue it,
after I conquer Zhào,
I will turn my troops to attack them first."
The King of Wèi, frightened,
ordered Jìn Bǐ to halt,
stationing the army at Yè,
nominally to rescue Zhào,
but actually hesitating to see how things would unfold.
Lord Píngyuán's envoys hurried to Wèi one after another,
reproaching Lord Wèi:
"The reason I allied with you through marriage
was your high sense of duty,
believing you would help others in distress.
Now Hándān is about to fall to Qín, yet Wèi's rescue does not come—
where is your reputation for aiding the troubled?
Even if you despise me,
abandoning me to surrender to Qín,
do you not pity your own sister?"
The lord was deeply troubled,
pleaded repeatedly with the King of Wèi,
and sent persuaders to argue every angle.
But the king, fearing Qín,
refused to listen.
The lord, seeing he could not sway the king,
resolved not to let Zhào perish alone,
gathered his retainers,
prepared over a hundred chariots and riders,
and planned to lead them against the Qín army,
dying with Zhào.
Passing by the Yí Gate,
he saw Hóu Shēng,
and fully explained the situation of why he intended to die fighting the Qín army.
After bidding farewell and departing,
Hóu Shēng said:
"Gōngzǐ, do your best,
this old servant cannot follow you."
Gōngzǐ traveled several lǐ,
feeling unhappy,
and said:
"The way I treated Hóu Shēng was thorough enough,
and the whole world knows it.
Now I am about to die, yet Hóu Shēng did not have a single word to send me off.
Could it be that I have made some mistake?"
He turned his carriage around and returned,
to question Hóu Shēng.
Hóu Shēng laughed and said:
"I knew you would return, Gōngzǐ."
He continued:
"Gōngzǐ delights in scholars,
and your reputation is known throughout the land.
Now that you face calamity,
with no other plan but to rush against the Qín army,
it is like throwing meat at a starving tiger—
what achievement could there be?
What use then for retainers?
However, you have treated me generously, Gōngzǐ,
and when you left, I did not see you off,
so I knew you would resent it and return."
Gōngzǐ bowed twice,
and then asked for advice.
Hóu Shēng then sent others away and spoke privately,
saying:
"Yíng has heard that the tally for Jìn Bǐ's army is always kept in the king's bedchamber,
and Rú Jī, being the most favored,
can enter and leave the king's bedchamber,
and has the means to steal it.
Yíng has heard that Rú Jī's father was killed by someone,
and Rú Jī sought revenge for three years,
yet from the king down, all who tried to find her father's murderer
could not succeed.
Rú Jī wept before you, Gōngzǐ,
and you sent a retainer to behead her enemy,
respectfully presenting it to Rú Jī.
Rú Jī would be willing to die for you, Gōngzǐ,
without any refusal,
but has not yet found a way.
If you truly ask Rú Jī once,
she is sure to consent,
then you can obtain the tiger tally and take command of Jìn Bǐ's army,
rescue Zhào in the north and repel Qín in the west—
this would be a feat worthy of the Five Hegemons."
Gōngzǐ followed his plan,
and asked Rú Jī.
Rú Jī indeed stole the military tally for Jìn Bǐ's army and gave it to Gōngzǐ.
As Gōngzǐ was leaving,
Hóu Shēng said:
"A general in the field
may not always accept his sovereign's orders
if it benefits the state.
Even if you match the tally, Gōngzǐ,
if Jìn Bǐ does not hand over the troops to you and instead requests confirmation,
the situation will surely be perilous.
My friend, the butcher Zhū Hài, can go with you;
this man is a man of great strength.
If Jìn Bǐ obeys,
very good;
if he does not,
have Zhū Hài strike him down."
At this, Gōngzǐ wept.
Hóu Shēng said:
"Are you afraid to die, Gōngzǐ?
Why are you weeping?"
Gōngzǐ said:
"Jìn Bǐ is a seasoned general, fierce and formidable;
I fear he will not obey,
and we will have to kill him—
that is why I weep,
how could it be fear of death?"
So Gōngzǐ invited Zhū Hài.
Zhū Hài laughed and said:
"I am but a butcher who wields a knife in the marketplace,
yet you, Gōngzǐ, have personally shown me kindness time and again.
The reason I have not repaid you
is that I considered petty courtesies of no use.
Now that you are in urgent need,
this is the time for me to offer my life."
Thereupon, he went with Gōngzǐ.
Gōngzǐ went to thank Hóu Shēng.
Hóu Shēng said:
"I ought to accompany you,
but I am too old and cannot.
I will count the days of your journey,
and on the day you reach Jìn Bǐ's army,
I will face north and cut my throat,
to see you off."
Gōngzǐ then departed.
Arriving at Yè,
he forged the King of Wèi's order to replace Jìn Bǐ.
Jìn Bǐ matched the tally,
but grew suspicious,
raised his hand, looked at Gōngzǐ, and said:
"Now I command a host of a hundred thousand,
stationed at the border—
a heavy responsibility of the state.
Yet you come alone in a single carriage to replace me;
what does this mean?"
He intended not to comply.
Zhū Hài concealed a forty-catty iron hammer in his sleeve,
and struck Jìn Bǐ dead with it.
Gōngzǐ then took command of Jìn Bǐ's army.
He marshaled the troops and issued an order to the army:
"If both father and son are in the army,
the father may return;
if both brothers are in the army,
the elder brother may return;
if one is an only son without brothers,
he may return to support his family."
Thus, he selected eighty thousand elite troops,
advanced, and attacked the Qín army.
The Qín forces withdrew,
and he thereby saved Hándān,
preserving Zhào.
The King of Zhào and Píngyuán Jūn personally greeted Gōngzǐ at the border,
with Píngyuán Jūn carrying an arrow quiver and leading the way for Gōngzǐ.
The King of Zhào bowed twice and said:
"Since ancient times, no worthy man has ever surpassed you, Gōngzǐ."
At that time,
Píngyuán Jūn did not dare compare himself to others.
When Gōngzǐ parted from Hóu Shēng,
and reached the army,
Hóu Shēng indeed faced north and cut his throat.
The King of Wèi was furious that Gōngzǐ had stolen his military tally
and forged his order to kill Jìn Bǐ,
and Gōngzǐ was also aware of this.
After repelling Qín and saving Zhào,
he sent a general to lead the army back to Wèi,
while he alone remained in Zhào with his retainers.
King Xiàochéng of Zhào, grateful to Gōngzǐ for seizing Jìn Bǐ's troops and saving Zhào,
consulted with Píngyuán Jūn,
and decided to enfeoff Gōngzǐ with five cities.
When Gōngzǐ heard this,
he became proud and wore a self-congratulatory expression.
A retainer advised Gōngzǐ, saying:
"Some things should not be forgotten,
and some should not be remembered.
If someone has shown you kindness, Gōngzǐ,
you should not forget it;
but if you have shown kindness to others,
I hope you will forget it.
Moreover, you forged the King of Wèi's order,
seized Jìn Bǐ's troops to save Zhào—
to Zhào, you have merit,
but to Wèi, you cannot be considered a loyal subject.
For you to be proud and claim credit for it—
I privately believe it is not fitting for you, Gōngzǐ."
Thereupon, Gōngzǐ immediately reproached himself,
as if he had no place to hide.
The King of Zhào swept the grounds and personally welcomed him,
performing the rites of a host,
and led Gōngzǐ to the western steps.
Gōngzǐ stepped aside, declining and yielding,
and ascended by the eastern steps.
He confessed his faults,
saying he had betrayed Wèi,
and had no merit toward Zhào.
The King of Zhào served him wine until evening,
but could not bring himself to offer the five cities,
because of Gōngzǐ's humility.
In the end, Gōngzǐ remained in Zhào.
The King of Zhào granted Hào to Gōngzǐ as a fief for his sustenance,
and Wèi also restored Xìnlíng to Gōngzǐ.
Gōngzǐ stayed in Zhào.
The young lord heard that in Zhào there was a recluse, Máo Gōng, hiding among gamblers,
and Xuē Gōng hiding among ale sellers.
The young lord wished to meet these two men,
but they concealed themselves and refused to see him.
Upon learning their whereabouts,
he quietly went on foot to accompany and befriend these two men,
and they were very happy together.
Lord Píngyuán heard of this,
and said to his wife:
"Initially, I heard that your brother, the young lord, was peerless under heaven,
but now I hear
that he recklessly associates with gamblers and ale sellers.
The young lord is but a fool."
The wife reported this to the young lord.
The young lord then bade farewell to the lady and prepared to leave,
saying:
"At first, I heard that Lord Píngyuán was worthy,
so I defied the King of Wèi to rescue Zhào,
in order to honor Lord Píngyuán.
But Lord Píngyuán's socializing
is merely for show,
not for seeking true scholars.
When I was in Dàliáng,
I often heard of the worthiness of these two men.
Upon coming to Zhào,
I feared I might not get to see them.
Even with me associating with them,
I still worried they might not want me;
now Lord Píngyuán actually considers it shameful.
He is not worth associating with."
So he packed to leave.
The wife relayed all this to Lord Píngyuán.
Lord Píngyuán then took off his cap and apologized,
firmly urging the young lord to stay.
When Lord Píngyuán's followers heard of this,
half of them left him to join the young lord.
Scholars from across the land returned to the young lord,
and he outshone Lord Píngyuán in attracting guests.
The young lord remained in Zhào for ten years without returning.
Qín, hearing that the young lord was in Zhào,
day and night sent troops east to attack Wèi.
The King of Wèi grew anxious,
and sent envoys to invite the young lord back.
Fearing the king's anger,
the young lord warned his followers:
"Anyone who dares to communicate with the King of Wèi's envoy
will die."
All his guests had turned their backs on Wèi for Zhào,
and none dared advise the young lord to return.
Máo Gōng and
Xuē Gōng went to see the young lord and said:
"The reason you are esteemed in Zhào,
and renowned among the feudal lords,
is solely because Wèi exists.
Now Qín attacks Wèi;
if Wèi is in crisis and you show no concern,
should Qín destroy Dàliáng and level the ancestral temples of your late king,
what face would you have to stand under heaven?"
Before they finished speaking,
the young lord immediately changed countenance,
ordered his carriage to be readied hastily to return and rescue Wèi.
The King of Wèi met the young lord,
they wept together,
and he bestowed the seal of supreme general upon the young lord,
who then assumed command.
In the thirtieth year of King Ānxī of Wèi,
the young lord sent envoys to inform all the feudal lords.
Upon hearing that the young lord was commanding,
each sent generals with troops to aid Wèi.
The young lord led the armies of five states to defeat the Qín forces beyond the Yellow River,
and drove back Méng Áo.
Then, pursuing the victory, he chased the Qín army to Hángǔ Pass,
suppressing Qín's troops,
so that they dared not emerge.
At that time,
the young lord's might shook the world,
and guests from various states presented texts on military strategy,
all of which the young lord endorsed with his name,
hence the common world refers to it as "The Young Lord of Wèi's Art of War."
The King of Qín, troubled by this,
spent ten thousand catties of gold in Wèi,
seeking out followers of Jìn Bǐ,
ordering them to slander the young lord to the King of Wèi, saying:
"The young lord has been in exile for ten years;
now as Wèi's general,
the feudal lords' armies all follow him.
They only hear of the Young Lord of Wèi,
not of the King of Wèi.
The young lord also wishes to seize this moment to face south and proclaim himself king;
the feudal lords, fearing his power,
are about to jointly install him."
Qín repeatedly used counter-espionage,
feigning congratulations on the young lord's imminent enthronement as King of Wèi.
The King of Wèi heard these slanders daily,
and could not help but believe them.
Eventually, he sent someone to replace the young lord as general.
Knowing he was again dismissed due to slander,
the young lord pleaded illness and ceased attending court,
spending nights drinking with his guests,
consuming strong wine,
and frequently keeping company with women.
For four years, he indulged in revelry day and night,
until he finally died from alcohol-related illness.
That year,
King Ānxī of Wèi also passed away.
Upon hearing of the young lord's death,
Qín sent Méng Áo to attack Wèi,
capturing twenty cities,
and initially established the Dōng Commandery.
Afterwards, Qín gradually nibbled away at Wèi,
and in eighteen years, captured the King of Wèi,
slaughtering Dàliáng.
When Emperor Gāozǔ was still young and obscure,
he often heard of the young lord's worthiness.
After ascending the throne as Son of Heaven,
whenever he passed through Dàliáng,
he always made sacrifices to the young lord.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāozǔ's reign,
upon returning from the campaign against Qíng Bù,
he established five households to guard the young lord's tomb,
ensuring that through generations, sacrifices would be offered to the young lord in all four seasons.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I passed by the ruins of Dàliáng,
and inquired about the so-called Yí Gate.
The Yí Gate
is the eastern gate of the city.
There have been other young lords under heaven who delighted in scholars,
but the way the Lord of Xìnlíng associated with recluses in caves and dens,
not ashamed to befriend those beneath him,
there is reason for it.
His fame crowned him among the feudal lords,
and it was not without substance.
Emperor Gāozǔ, whenever passing by, ordered the people to maintain sacrifices without end.
Lord Chūnshēn
was a man of Chǔ,
named Xiē,
of the Huáng clan.
Well-traveled and learned,
he served King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ.
King Qǐngxiāng, considering Xiē eloquent,
sent him on a mission to Qín.
King Zhāo of Qín ordered Bái Qǐ to attack Hán
and Wèi, defeating them at Huáyáng,
and capturing Wèi's general Máng Mǎo.
Hán and Wèi submitted and served Qín.
King Zhāo of Qín was about to order Bái Qǐ, along with Hán
and Wèi, to jointly attack Chǔ,
but before the campaign began,
the Chǔ envoy Huáng Xiē happened to arrive in Qín,
and learned of Qín's plans.
At that time,
Qín had previously sent Bái Qǐ to attack Chǔ,
capturing the commanderies of Wū
and Qiánzhōng,
seizing Yānyǐng,
and advancing east to Jìnglíng.
King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ moved eastward, establishing his capital at Chén County.
Huáng Xiē, reflecting on how King Huái of Chǔ had been lured by Qín into visiting their court,
only to be deceived,
and detained until his death in Qín,
and considering that King Qǐngxiāng
was his son,
whom Qín looked down upon,
feared that Qín might raise an army and destroy Chǔ in one move.
Xiē then submitted a memorial to persuade King Zhāo of Qín, saying:
Under heaven, none are mightier than Qín
and Chǔ. Now I hear Your Majesty intends to attack Chǔ.
This is like two tigers fighting each other.
When two tigers fight, even a worn-out dog can exploit their exhaustion.
It would be better to maintain good relations with Chǔ.
Allow me to explain my reasoning:
I have heard that when things reach an extreme, they reverse,
as with winter and summer;
when carried to the utmost, danger arises,
as with piling up chess pieces.
Now the territory of your great state
spans two borders across the realm,
a scale unprecedented since the beginning of humanity,
never before seen for a land of ten thousand chariots.
The former emperors King Wén
and King Zhuāng themselves,
for three generations, carefully avoided connecting territories with Qí,
to sever the crucial alliances.
Now Your Majesty sent Shèng Qiáo to handle affairs in Hán,
and Shèng Qiáo incorporated their land into Qín,
thus without deploying armor,
without exerting military might,
you gained a hundred lǐ of territory.
Your Majesty may be called capable indeed.
You further raised arms to attack Wèi,
blockaded the gates of Dàliáng,
captured Hénèi,
seized Yān,
Suānzǎo,
Xū, and Táo,
entered Xíng,
while Wèi's troops hovered like clouds but dared not rescue.
Your achievements are numerous indeed.
You rested your troops and gave the people respite,
then after two years resumed campaigns;
also annexed Pú,
Yǎn, Shǒu,
and Yuán, approaching Rén
and Píngqiū,
forcing Huáng and Jìyáng to defend their walls until the Wèi clan submitted;
you further cut off the north of Púlì,
channeling the strategic points between Qí and Qín,
severing the spine between Chǔ and Zhào,
while the states under heaven gathered five times, assembled six, yet dared not intervene.
Your Majesty's might has reached its peak.
If Your Majesty can maintain achievements and uphold authority,
curb the desire for conquest and enrich the grounds of benevolence and righteousness,
ensuring no future troubles,
then the Three Kings would not suffice to be four,
nor the Five Hegemons to be six.
But if you rely on the multitude of your forces,
lean on the strength of your weapons,
and ride the prestige of crushing Wèi
to forcibly subjugate the lords under heaven,
I fear there will be future troubles.
The Book of Songs says:
"Nothing is without a beginning,
but few reach the end."
The Book of Changes says:
"The fox crosses water,
wetting its tail."
This means beginnings are easy,
but endings are difficult.
How do we know this is so?
Long ago, the Zhì clan saw the benefit of attacking Zhào but overlooked the disaster at Yúcì;
Wú saw the advantage of attacking Qí but ignored the defeat at Gānsuì.
These two states
did not lack great achievements,
but were blinded by immediate gains and careless of later perils.
Wú trusted Yuè,
proceeded to attack Qí,
and after defeating the Qí people at Àilíng,
returned only to be captured by the King of Yuè at Sānzhǔ's shore.
The Zhì clan trusted Hán
and Wèi,
proceeded to attack Zhào,
besieged Jìnyáng city,
and were on the verge of victory,
when Hán and Wèi betrayed them,
killing Zhì Bó Yáo beneath Záotái.
Now Your Majesty resents Chǔ for remaining unbroken,
but forgets that destroying Chǔ would strengthen Hán
and Wèi;
I consider this unwise for Your Majesty.
The Book of Songs says:
"The great martial [king] keeps distant dwellings and does not tread there."
From this perspective,
Chǔ is a support;
neighboring states are foes.
The Book of Songs says:
"The nimble hare,
meets the hound and is caught.
Others have intentions,
I ponder and measure them."
Now Your Majesty, midway, trusts that Hán
and Wèi are well-disposed toward you.
This is exactly like Wú's trust in Yuè.
I have heard that
enemies cannot be indulged,
opportunities cannot be lost.
I fear that Hán
and Wèi, with humble words to remove troubles, actually intend to deceive your great state.
Why is that?
Your Majesty has no multi-generational virtue with Hán
and Wèi, but rather accumulated resentment over generations.
For Hán
and Wèi, fathers and sons, brothers, have died in succession under Qín for nearly ten generations.
Their states are devastated,
their altars of grain and soil ruined,
their ancestral temples destroyed.
Bellies ripped open, intestines severed,
necks broken, jaws shattered,
heads and bodies separated,
bones exposed in marshes,
skulls fallen,
visible across the borders,
fathers and sons, old and weak, bound and helpless, becoming captives in droves along the roads.
Spirits and ghosts alone and sorrowful,
with no sacrifices offered.
The people find life unbearable,
clans scatter and disperse,
those wandering in exile as slaves and concubines
fill the land.
Thus, if Hán
and Wèi do not perish,
they are a worry for Qín's altars of grain and soil.
Now if you assist them in attacking Chǔ,
is that not a mistake?!
Moreover, how will Your Majesty deploy troops to attack Chǔ?
Will you seek passage through your enemy states Hán
and Wèi?
On the day the troops set out, you would worry about their return,
thus providing military resources to your enemy states Hán
and Wèi.
If you do not seek passage through your enemy states Hán
and Wèi, you must attack the right bank of the Suí River.
The right bank of the Suí River
is all vast rivers and great waters,
forests, mountains, streams, and valleys,
barren land.
Even if you possess it,
it does not count as gaining territory.
Thus, you would have the name of destroying Chǔ but not the reality of gaining land.
Furthermore, when you attack Chǔ,
the four states will surely all raise troops in response.
When Qín and Chǔ's troops engage and cannot disengage,
Wèi will likely attack Liú,
Fāngyǔ,
Zhì, Húlíng,
Dàng, Xiāo,
and Xiàng, so the former Sòng will be completely taken.
The Qí people will attack Chǔ from the south,
and Sìshàng will surely be captured.
These are all plains accessible in all directions,
fertile lands,
yet you would let others attack them alone.
By defeating Chǔ, you would fatten Hán
and Wèi in the central states and strengthen Qí.
The strength of Hán and Wèi
would be sufficient to rival Qín.
Qí, with the Sì River as its southern border,
the sea to the east,
the river to the north,
and no rear worries,
would become, under heaven, no state stronger than Qí
and Wèi. Qí
and Wèi, gaining land and preserving advantages while cautiously serving your officials,
within a year,
may not yet claim the title of emperor,
but they would have more than enough power to prevent Your Majesty from becoming one.
With the vastness of Your Majesty's territory,
the multitude of your people,
and the strength of your arms and armor,
to initiate an action that would incur the enmity of Chǔ,
while delaying and allowing Hán
and Wèi to honor Qí with the imperial title,
would be a miscalculation on Your Majesty's part.
In my consideration for Your Majesty,
nothing is better than befriending Chǔ.
If Qín and Chǔ unite as one to confront Hán,
Hán will surely fold its hands in submission.
Your Majesty can then deploy the natural barriers of the Eastern Mountains,
and harness the advantages of the winding river,
and Hán will become a marquis within the pass.
If so, and Your Majesty stations a hundred thousand troops to guard Zhèng,
the Liáng clan will be terrified,
Xǔ and Yānlíng will fortify their cities,
while Shàngcài
and Zhàolíng will be cut off from communication.
In this way, Wèi too will become a marquis within the pass.
Once Your Majesty befriends Chǔ,
and the two rulers of ten thousand chariots within the pass focus their lands toward Qí,
the right territory of Qí can be taken with a mere gesture.
Your Majesty's land will then stretch from one sea to the other,
controlling all under heaven,
so that Yān
and Zhào will be isolated from Qí
and Chǔ, and Qí
and Chǔ from Yān
and Zhào.
Then, by threatening Yān
and Zhào, and directly shaking Qí
and Chǔ, these four states will submit without even needing to be struck.
King Zhāo said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he halted Bái Qǐ and apologized to Hán
and Wèi. He sent envoys with gifts to Chǔ,
forming an alliance.
Huáng Xiē accepted the agreement and returned to Chǔ.
Chǔ sent Xiē and the crown prince Wán to Qín as hostages,
where they were detained for several years.
When King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ fell ill,
the crown prince could not return.
As the crown prince of Chǔ was on good terms with Yìnghóu, the chancellor of Qín,
Huáng Xiē then persuaded Yìnghóu, saying:
"Is the chancellor truly well-disposed toward the crown prince of Chǔ?"
Yìnghóu replied:
"Yes."
Xiē said:
"Now the king of Chǔ fears he may not recover from his illness.
It would be better for Qín to return his crown prince.
If the crown prince ascends the throne,
he will surely serve Qín diligently and be eternally grateful to the chancellor,
thus strengthening ties with an allied state and securing the heir to ten thousand chariots.
If he is not returned,
he is but a commoner in Xiányáng;
if Chǔ appoints another crown prince,
he will certainly not serve Qín.
To lose an ally and sever harmony with a state of ten thousand chariots
is not a wise plan.
I hope the chancellor will consider this carefully."
Yìnghóu reported this to the king of Qín.
The king of Qín said:
"Let the crown prince's tutor of Chǔ first go to inquire about the king of Chǔ's illness,
and we will decide after he returns."
Huáng Xiē devised a plan for the crown prince of Chǔ, saying:
"Qín's detention of the crown prince
is to seek advantage.
Now, the crown prince lacks the means to benefit Qín,
and I am deeply concerned.
Moreover, Yángwén Jūn has two sons at court.
If the king passes away,
and the crown prince is absent,
Yángwén Jūn's son is sure to be established as successor,
and the crown prince will lose the ancestral temple.
It would be better to flee Qín,
and leave with the envoy;
I will stay behind,
and face death in your stead."
The crown prince of Chǔ then changed into the envoy's attire and drove out of the pass as his coachman,
while Huáng Xiē guarded the residence,
often feigning illness.
Estimating that the crown prince was already far away
and beyond Qín's pursuit,
Xiē then confessed to King Zhāo of Qín:
"The crown prince of Chǔ has returned,
and is now far off.
I deserve death,
and beg to be executed."
King Zhāo was enraged
and intended to let him commit suicide.
Yìnghóu said:
"Xiē, as a subject,
sacrificed himself for his lord.
If the crown prince becomes king,
he will surely employ Xiē.
Thus, it would be better to pardon him and send him back,
to foster goodwill with Chǔ."
Qín then sent Huáng Xiē away.
Three months after Xiē's return to Chǔ,
King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ died,
and the crown prince Wán ascended the throne,
becoming King Kǎoliè.
In the first year of King Kǎoliè's reign,
he appointed Huáng Xiē as chancellor,
enfeoffed him as Chūnshēn Jūn,
and granted him twelve counties north of the Huái River.
Fifteen years later,
Huáng Xiē advised the king of Chǔ, saying:
"The land north of the Huái borders Qí,
and the situation is urgent.
I request that it be made into a commandery for convenience."
Thereupon, he offered the twelve counties north of the Huái,
and asked to be enfeoffed in Jiāngdōng.
King Kǎoliè agreed.
Chūnshēn Jūn then built a city on the old ruins of Wú,
making it his capital.
After Chūnshēn Jūn became chancellor of Chǔ,
at that time, Qí had Mèngcháng Jūn,
Zhào had Píngyuán Jūn,
and Wèi had Xìnlíng Jūn,
all vying to treat scholars with humility,
recruiting guests,
to compete with each other,
and assist their states in holding power.
In the fourth year of Chūnshēn Jūn's chancellorship of Chǔ,
Qín defeated Zhào's army at Chángpíng, with over four hundred thousand casualties.
In the fifth year,
they besieged Hándān.
Hándān appealed to Chǔ for help,
and Chǔ sent Chūnshēn Jūn to lead troops to its rescue.
The Qín forces then withdrew,
and Chūnshēn Jūn returned.
In the eighth year of his chancellorship,
he led a northern campaign for Chǔ, destroying Lǔ,
and appointed Xún Qīng as magistrate of Lánlíng.
At that time,
Chǔ became strong again.
Zhào's Píngyuán Jūn sent an envoy to Chūnshēn Jūn,
who housed him in the finest quarters.
The Zhào envoy wished to boast before Chǔ,
wearing a tortoiseshell hairpin,
and adorning his sword scabbard with pearls and jade,
he requested to meet Chūnshēn Jūn's guests.
Chūnshēn Jūn had over three thousand guests,
and his top guests all wore pearl-embedded shoes to meet the Zhào envoy,
who was greatly ashamed.
In the fourteenth year of Chūnshēn Jūn's chancellorship,
King Zhuāngxiāng of Qín ascended the throne,
appointed Lǚ Bùwéi as chancellor,
and enfeoffed him as Wénxìn Hóu.
They annexed Eastern Zhōu.
In the twenty-second year of his chancellorship,
the feudal lords, troubled by Qín's incessant attacks,
formed a vertical alliance,
and marched west to attack Qín,
with the king of Chǔ as the alliance leader,
and Chūnshēn Jūn in charge.
When they reached Hángǔ Pass,
Qín sent troops to attack,
and the allied forces were defeated and fled.
King Kǎoliè of Chǔ blamed Chūnshēn Jūn,
who consequently became increasingly estranged.
A guest from Guānjīn named Zhū Yīng
said to Chūnshēn Jūn:
"Everyone thinks Chǔ is strong, but you have weakened it;
but I do not see it that way.
In the previous king's time, we were on good terms with Qín for twenty years, and they did not attack Chǔ.
Why?
For Qín to cross the Miǎn'ài Pass to attack Chǔ
was inconvenient;
to borrow the route through the two Zhōu states,
bypassing Hán
and Wèi to attack Chǔ,
was not feasible.
Now it is different.
Wèi may fall any day,
and cannot protect Xǔ
and Yānlíng,
so it will likely cede them to Qín.
With Qín troops only a hundred and sixty lǐ from Chén,
from what I observe,
I foresee Qín
and Chǔ in constant conflict."
Thereupon, Chǔ moved its capital from Chén to Shòuchūn;
and Qín moved Wèi to Yěwáng,
establishing the Eastern Commandery.
Chūnshēn Jūn then went to his fief in Wú,
and continued to perform his duties as chancellor.
King Kǎoliè of Chǔ had no son,
and Chūnshēn Jūn was troubled by this.
He sought women likely to bear children to present to the king,
and there were very many,
but in the end, none bore a son.
Lǐ Yuán of Zhào, bringing his younger sister,
intended to present her to the King of Chǔ.
Hearing that the king was not able to have children,
he feared she would not retain favor for long.
Lǐ Yuán sought to serve Chūnshēn Jūn as a retainer,
and after a while requested leave to return home,
deliberately missing the deadline.
Upon his return, he paid a visit,
and Chūnshēn Jūn asked him about the situation.
He replied:
"The King of Qí sent an envoy to seek my younger sister,
and I drank with his envoy,
hence I missed the deadline."
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"Has the betrothal gift been sent?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"May I see her?"
He said:
"Yes."
Thereupon, Lǐ Yuán presented his younger sister,
and she soon became favored by Chūnshēn Jūn.
Knowing she was pregnant,
Lǐ Yuán then plotted with his younger sister.
Lǐ Yuán's younger sister seized an opportunity to persuade Chūnshēn Jūn, saying:
"The King of Chǔ honors and favors you,
surpassing even his own brothers.
Now you have been in Chǔ for over twenty years,
yet the king has no son.
When he passes away, they will set up one of his brothers instead,
and if Chǔ establishes a new ruler,
each will honor their own former intimates.
How then can you long retain favor?
And that is not all;
you have been honored and in power for a long time,
and have often been disrespectful to the king's brothers.
If a brother is truly established,
disaster will befall you.
How then will you preserve your ministerial seal and fief in Jiāngdōng?
Now I know myself to be with child,
and no one else knows.
I have been favored by you for only a short time.
If truly, using your influence, you present me to the King of Chǔ,
the king is sure to favor me.
If I, relying on heaven, bear a son,
then it will be your son who becomes king,
and all of Chǔ can be yours.
How does that compare with facing unforeseeable crimes yourself?"
Chūnshēn Jūn greatly agreed with her,
and sent Lǐ Yuán's younger sister away,
carefully housing her and then speaking of her to the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ summoned her in and favored her,
and she subsequently bore a son,
who was made crown prince,
and Lǐ Yuán's younger sister was made queen.
The King of Chǔ honored Lǐ Yuán,
and Yuán came into power.
After Lǐ Yuán had presented his younger sister,
and she was established as queen,
with her son as crown prince,
he feared Chūnshēn Jūn might leak the secret and grow even more arrogant,
so he secretly raised assassins,
intending to kill Chūnshēn Jūn to silence him,
and many in the state knew about it.
In the twenty-fifth year of Chūnshēn Jūn's chancellorship,
King Kǎoliè of Chǔ fell ill.
Zhū Yīng said to Chūnshēn Jūn:
"There are unforeseen blessings in the world,
and also unforeseen disasters.
Now you live in an unforeseeable age,
serving an unforeseeable lord.
How can you not have an unforeseeable man?"
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"What is an unforeseen blessing?"
He said:
"You have been chancellor of Chǔ for over twenty years,
though called chancellor,
you are in fact the King of Chǔ.
Now the King of Chǔ is ill,
and may pass away at any moment.
You will then be chancellor to a young sovereign,
and could thus act as regent and rule the state,
like Yī Yǐn
or the Duke of Zhōu.
When the king grows up, you return the government,
or else you might face south and call yourself sovereign, possessing Chǔ.
This is what is called an unforeseen blessing."
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"What is an unforeseen disaster?"
He said:
"Lǐ Yuán does not govern the state but is your enemy.
He does not raise an army but has long been raising assassins.
When the King of Chǔ dies,
Lǐ Yuán is sure to enter first, seize power, and kill you to silence you.
This is what is called an unforeseen disaster."
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"What is an unforeseeable man?"
He replied:
"You appoint me as a court gentleman.
When the King of Chǔ dies,
Lǐ Yuán is sure to enter first,
and I will kill Lǐ Yuán for you.
This is what is called an unforeseeable man."
Chūnshēn Jūn said:
"Put aside such thoughts.
Lǐ Yuán
is a weak man,
and I am on good terms with him.
How could it come to this!"
Zhū Yīng, knowing his advice would not be heeded,
and fearing disaster would reach him,
fled.
Seventeen days later,
King Kǎoliè of Chǔ died.
Lǐ Yuán indeed entered first,
and stationed assassins inside the棘门 (thorn gate).
When Chūnshēn Jūn entered the棘门,
Yuán's assassins flanked and stabbed Chūnshēn Jūn,
cut off his head,
and threw it outside the棘门.
Thereupon, he sent officers to exterminate Chūnshēn Jūn's entire family.
And the son born of Lǐ Yuán's younger sister, who had first been favored by Chūnshēn Jūn and was with child when she entered the king's presence, was then established,
becoming King Yōu of Chǔ.
In that year,
Qín Shǐ Huángdì had been on the throne for nine years.
Lào Ǎi also caused turmoil in Qín,
was discovered, and his three clans were exterminated,
while Lǚ Bùwéi was dismissed.
Grand Historian says:
I went to Chǔ,
and saw the old city of Chūnshēn Jūn.
How magnificent were its palaces!
Initially, when Chūnshēn Jūn persuaded King Zhāo of Qín,
and risked his life to send the crown prince of Chǔ back,
how clear was his wisdom!
Later, he was controlled by Lǐ Yuán,
and how deluded he was.
As the saying goes:
"To act when you should, and not act,
brings disorder upon yourself."
Was this not the case with Chūnshēn Jūn ignoring Zhū Yīng?
Fàn Jū
was a man of Wèi, styled Shū.
He traveled around persuading various feudal lords,
wishing to serve the King of Wèi,
but his family was poor and he had no means to support himself,
so he first served Xū Gǔ, a grandee of Wèi.
Xū Gǔ was sent by King Zhāo of Wèi
on a mission to Qí,
and Fàn Jū accompanied him.
They stayed for several months,
without receiving a reply.
King Xiāng of Qí heard of Jū's eloquence,
and sent someone to grant Jū ten jīn of gold
along with oxen and wine.
Jū declined
and did not dare accept.
Xū Gǔ learned of this,
was greatly angered,
thinking that Jū had revealed Wèi's secrets to Qí,
hence receiving these gifts.
He made Jū accept the oxen and wine,
but return the gold.
After returning,
he was resentful towards Jū,
and reported it to the chancellor of Wèi.
The chancellor of Wèi,
a scion of the Wèi ruling family, was called Wèi Qí.
Wèi Qí was greatly angered,
and had his retainers flog Jū,
breaking his ribs and knocking out his teeth.
Jū pretended to be dead,
so they rolled him up in a mat,
and placed him in the latrine.
Guests who were drinking and drunk,
took turns urinating on Jū,
intending to humiliate him as a warning to others,
to prevent any reckless talk.
Suī spoke from inside the reed mat to the guard, saying:
"If you can get me out,
I will surely reward you handsomely."
The guard then requested
to take out and discard the dead body from the reed mat.
He said:
"Lord Wèi Qí is drunk,
it can be done."
Fàn Suī managed to escape.
Later, Wèi Qí regretted it,
and summoned him again to search for him.
A man from Wèi, Zhèng Ānpíng, heard about this,
and then took Fàn Suī and fled,
going into hiding,
changing his name to Zhāng Lù.
At this time,
King Zhāo of Qín sent his receptionist Wáng Jǐ to Wèi.
Zhèng Ānpíng pretended to be a soldier,
serving Wáng Jǐ.
Wáng Jǐ asked:
"Is there any worthy person in Wèi
who can go west with me?"
Zhèng Ānpíng said:
"There is a Mr. Zhāng Lù in my neighborhood,
who wishes to meet you,
to discuss matters of the world.
This man has enemies,
and dares not meet during the day."
Wáng Jǐ said: "Bring him along at night."
Zhèng Ānpíng and Zhāng Lù at night
met Wáng Jǐ.
Before their conversation concluded,
Wáng Jǐ recognized Fàn Suī's worth,
and said to him:
"Sir, wait for me
south of Sāntíng."
They made a private agreement and parted.
Wáng Jǐ bid farewell to Wèi and left,
picking up Fàn Suī on the way into Qín.
When they reached Hú,
they saw chariots and cavalry approaching from the west.
Fàn Suī asked:
"Who is that coming?"
Wáng Jǐ replied:
"The Prime Minister of Qín, Ráng Hóu,
is touring the eastern counties and towns."
Fàn Suī said:
"I've heard that Ráng Hóu monopolizes power in Qín,
and dislikes admitting guest scholars from other states.
This might bring me humiliation,
I'd rather hide in the chariot for now."
Shortly after,
Ráng Hóu indeed arrived,
greeted Wáng Jǐ,
and standing by his chariot, asked:
"What changes have occurred east of the pass?"
The reply was:
"None."
He then said to Wáng Jǐ:
"You haven't brought any guest scholars from other states with you, have you?
They are of no benefit,
only disrupt states."
Wáng Jǐ said: "I wouldn't dare."
They then parted.
Fàn Suī said:
"I've heard Ráng Hóu is a wise man,
but he is slow to catch on.
Earlier, he suspected someone was in the chariot,
but forgot to search it."
Thereupon, Fàn Suī got off the chariot and ran,
saying:
"He will surely regret it."
After traveling over ten lǐ,
indeed, horsemen were sent back
to search the chariot.
Finding no guest, they gave up.
Wáng Jǐ then entered Xiányáng with Fàn Suī.
After reporting his mission,
he then said:
"In Wèi, there is a Mr. Zhāng Lù,
a master debater of the world.
He says
'The state of the King of Qín is as precarious as a pile of eggs,
but with me, it can be secure.
However, this cannot be conveyed in writing.'
Therefore, I brought him here."
The King of Qín did not believe it,
had him lodged and provided with coarse food,
and kept waiting for over a year.
At that time,
King Zhāo had been on the throne for thirty-six years.
He had captured Yānyǐng from Chǔ in the south,
and King Huái of Chǔ died imprisoned in Qín.
In the east, Qín had defeated Qí.
King Mǐn had once declared himself emperor,
but later renounced the title.
Qín repeatedly troubled the Three Jìn states.
He was weary of the debaters of the world,
and trusted none of them.
Ráng Hóu and Huáyáng Jūn
were brothers of King Zhāo's mother, Queen Dowager Xuān,
while Jīngyáng Jūn and Gāolíng Jūn
were King Zhāo's full brothers.
Ráng Hóu served as chancellor,
and the three others took turns as generals,
possessing fiefdoms.
Due to the Queen Dowager's influence,
their private wealth surpassed that of the royal house.
When Ráng Hóu was a general of Qín,
he intended to cross Hán and Wèi
to attack Qí's Gāngshòu,
aiming to expand his fief in Táo.
Fàn Suī then submitted a memorial, saying:
I have heard that an enlightened ruler establishes governance such that
those with achievements must be rewarded,
those with ability must be given office,
those with great labor receive ample emoluments,
those with numerous merits attain high ranks,
and those who can govern many hold great offices.
Thus, the incapable dare not assume positions,
and the capable cannot be hidden.
If my words are deemed acceptable,
I hope you will act
to further benefit your way;
if my words are deemed unacceptable,
keeping me here long is pointless.
As the saying goes: "A mediocre ruler rewards those he loves
and punishes those he dislikes;
an enlightened ruler is not so,
rewards are given only for merit,
and punishments are meted only for crimes."
Now, my chest is not sufficient
to serve as a chopping block,
and my waist is not fit for the axe,
how would I dare to test the king with uncertain matters!
Even if you consider me a lowly person
and treat me lightly with disrespect,
do you not value the recommender who shows no duplicity to the king?
Moreover, I have heard that Zhōu had Dǐ'è,
Sòng had Jiélǜ,
Liáng had Xuánlí,
Chǔ had Hépǔ,
these four treasures,
born from the earth,
missed by fine craftsmen,
yet became renowned vessels of the world.
Then, those discarded by sage kings,
can they not also enrich the state?
I have heard that those good at enriching their families
take from the state,
those good at enriching the state
take from the feudal lords.
When the world has an enlightened ruler,
the feudal lords cannot monopolize wealth.
Why?
Because it divides the glory.
A good physician knows the life and death of a patient,
and a sage ruler understands matters of success and failure.
If beneficial, he acts;
if harmful, he desists;
if doubtful, he tests slightly.
Even if Shùn and Yǔ were reborn,
they could not change this.
The deepest words,
I dare not put in writing;
the shallow ones are not worth hearing.
Perhaps I am foolish
and do not align with the king's heart?
Or is it that those who speak of me are lowly
and not to be trusted?
If not for these reasons,
I wish to be granted a little time
during your leisure for sightseeing,
to behold your countenance.
If one word proves ineffective,
I ask to be executed by the axe.
Thereupon, King Zhāo of Qín was greatly pleased,
thanked Wáng Jǐ,
and sent a relay carriage to summon Fàn Suī.
Thus, Fàn Suī was able to have an audience at the detached palace,
pretending not to know the inner corridors
and entering them.
When the king arrived,
the eunuch became angry and chased him away,
saying:
"The king is coming!"
Fàn Suī feigned ignorance and said:
"How can Qín have a king?
Qín only has the Queen Dowager and Ráng Hóu."
intending to provoke King Zhāo's anger.
When King Zhāo arrived,
hearing that he had argued with a eunuch,
he then extended a welcome,
apologizing:
"I should have personally received your instructions long ago,
but the matter of Yìqú was urgent,
I had to consult the Queen Dowager day and night;
now that the Yìqú affair is concluded,
I am finally able to receive your guidance.
I am privately regretful for my dullness,
and respectfully observe the rites of host and guest."
Fàn Jū declined modestly.
Those who witnessed Fàn Jū's audience that day
all among the ministers could not help but look awed and change expression.
The King of Qín dismissed his attendants,
leaving the palace empty and devoid of others.
The King of Qín knelt and requested:
"What instruction has the gentleman to favor me with?"
Fàn Jū said: "Yes, yes."
After a pause,
the King of Qín knelt again and asked:
"What instruction has the gentleman to favor me with?"
Fàn Jū said: "Yes, yes."
This happened three times.
The King of Qín knelt and said:
"Does the gentleman ultimately not favor me with instruction?"
Fàn Jū said: "I dare not be so.
I have heard that in the past,
when Lǚ Shàng met King Wén,
he was but a fisherman
angling by the Wèi River.
In that situation,
their acquaintance was distant.
Once he persuaded
and was appointed Grand Tutor,
taken in the carriage back together,
it was because his words were profound.
Thus King Wén achieved success through Lǚ Shàng
and eventually ruled the world.
Had King Wén kept Lǚ Shàng at a distance
and not engaged in deep conversation,
then Zhōu would have lacked the virtue of a Son of Heaven,
and King Wén and King Wǔ would have had none to accomplish
their royal enterprise.
Now I am a minister traveling from afar,
my acquaintance with you is distant,
and what I wish to present
all concerns rectifying the ruler's affairs,
touching upon matters between flesh and blood,
I wish to offer my simple loyalty
but do not know Your Majesty's heart.
This is why
despite Your Majesty's three inquiries, I dared not respond.
It is not that I fear something and dare not speak.
I know that if I speak today,
I may be executed tomorrow,
yet I do not dare to avoid it.
If Your Majesty truly acts on my words,
death is not enough to be my worry,
exile is not enough to be my concern,
lacquering my body to become leprous
or disheveling my hair to appear insane
is not enough to be my shame.
Moreover, even the sages like the Five Emperors died,
the benevolent like the Three Kings died,
the worthy like the Five Hegemons died,
the strong like Wū Huò and Rén Bǐ died,
the brave like Chéng Jīng, Mèng Bēn,
Wáng Qìngjì, and Xià Yù died.
Death
is something no man can avoid.
Facing an inevitable fate,
if I can offer the slightest benefit to Qín,
that is my greatest wish,
what worry do I have then!
Wǔ Zǐxū was smuggled out in a sack
through Zhāo Pass,
traveling by night and hiding by day,
reaching Língshuǐ,
with nothing to feed himself,
crawling on his knees, creeping forward,
kowtowing and baring his flesh,
drumming his belly and playing the chí,
begging for food in the markets of Wú,
yet he eventually revived the state of Wú,
making Hé Lǘ a hegemon.
If I could fully strategize like Wǔ Zǐxū,
even if imprisoned,
never to see the light again,
that would mean my advice was implemented,
what worry would I have?
Jīzǐ and Jiēyú lacquered their bodies to appear leprous,
disheveled their hair to seem insane,
yet it brought no benefit to their lords.
If I could act like Jīzǐ,
and benefit the lord I consider worthy,
that would be my great honor,
what shame would I have?
What I fear
is only that after my death,
the world seeing my utmost loyalty
leading to my death,
would thus shut their mouths and bind their feet,
none willing to turn towards Qín.
You, above, fear the sternness of the Queen Dowager,
below, are deluded by the demeanor of treacherous ministers,
residing deep within the palace,
never leaving the care of nurses,
perpetually confused,
with none to expose the treachery.
At worst, the ancestral temple may be overthrown,
at least, you yourself may be isolated and endangered,
this is what I fear.
As for matters of poverty and disgrace,
the worries of death and exile,
I do not dare to fear them.
If my death brings order to Qín,
then my death is worthier than my life."
The King of Qín knelt and said:
"What words are these, sir!
The state of Qín is remote and isolated,
I am foolish and unworthy,
yet you have graciously condescended to come here,
this is Heaven using me to trouble you, sir,
to preserve the ancestral temple of the former kings.
That I may receive instruction from you, sir,
is how Heaven favors you, sir,
and does not abandon this orphan.
How can you speak such words!
Matters, whether great or small,
from above involving the Queen Dowager,
to below concerning the great ministers,
I wish you to instruct me fully on all,
without doubting me."
Fàn Jū bowed,
and the King of Qín also bowed.
Fàn Jū said:
"Your Majesty's state,
secured by barriers on all four sides,
with Gānquán and Gǔkǒu to the north,
bordered by the Jīng and Wèi rivers to the south,
Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
passes and slopes to the left,
with a million fierce warriors,
a thousand war chariots,
advantageous for launching attacks,
or retreating to defend when not,
this is the land of a true king.
The people are timid in private fights
but brave in public battles,
these are the people of a true king.
You possess both these advantages.
With the bravery of Qín's soldiers,
the multitude of its chariots and cavalry,
to deal with the feudal lords,
is like unleashing a Hán Lǔ hound
to chase a lame rabbit;
the hegemony of a true king is attainable,
yet none of your ministers are fit for their positions.
For fifteen years now, you have closed the passes,
not daring to show military ambition east of the mountains,
this is because the Marquis of Ráng was not loyal in his counsel for Qín,
and Your Majesty's strategy has been flawed."
The King of Qín knelt and said:
"I wish to hear about the flawed strategy."
However, there were many eavesdroppers around,
Fàn Jū grew fearful,
not daring to speak of internal matters yet,
he first spoke of external affairs,
to gauge the King of Qín's reactions.
Thereupon he advanced and said:
"The Marquis of Ráng crossing Hán and Wèi
to attack Qí's Gāng and Shòu,
is not a sound plan.
Sending a small force
would not suffice to harm Qí,
sending a large force
would harm Qín.
I surmise Your Majesty's plan
was to send a small force
and fully employ the troops of Hán and Wèi,
but that is unjust.
Now seeing that your allied states are not close,
is it permissible to cross others' states to attack?
That is a careless strategy.
Moreover, in the past, King Mǐn of Qí attacked Chǔ in the south,
defeated armies and killed generals,
again expanding territory by a thousand lǐ,
yet Qí gained not an inch of land,
not that they did not desire land,
but the circumstances made it impossible to hold.
The feudal lords saw Qí's exhaustion and weakness,
the discord between ruler and ministers,
raised armies and attacked Qí,
greatly defeating it.
When officers were humiliated and soldiers exhausted,
all blamed their king, saying:
'Who devised this strategy?'
The king replied:
'Wénzǐ did.'
The ministers rebelled,
and Wénzǐ fled.
Thus the reason Qí suffered great defeat
was because it attacked Chǔ
only to enrich Hán and Wèi.
This is what is called lending weapons to bandits
and supplying provisions to thieves.
Your Majesty should befriend distant states
and attack nearby ones,
for every inch gained becomes Your Majesty's inch,
every foot gained becomes Your Majesty's foot.
Now to abandon this and attack distant states
—is that not mistaken?
Moreover, in the past
the state of Zhōngshān covered five hundred li square,
yet Zhào alone devoured it,
achieving merit, establishing fame, and securing benefits,
with none under heaven able to harm it.
Now Hán and Wèi, located in the central states
and being the pivot of all under heaven—
if Your Majesty wishes to become hegemon,
you must befriend the central states to control this pivot,
thereby intimidating Chǔ and Zhào.
If Chǔ is strong, attach to Zhào;
if Zhào is strong, attach to Chǔ.
When both Chǔ and Zhào are attached,
Qí will surely fear.
When Qí fears,
it will surely use humble words and generous gifts to serve Qín.
Once Qí is attached,
Hán and Wèi can then be captured."
King Zhāo said:
"I have long wished to befriend Wèi,
but Wèi is a fickle state,
and I have been unable to befriend it.
May I ask how to befriend Wèi?"
Fànjū replied:
"Your Majesty should use humble words and generous gifts to serve it;
if that fails,
then cede territory to bribe it;
if that fails,
then raise troops and attack it."
The king said:
"I respectfully heed your advice."
Thereupon he appointed Fànjū as a guest minister,
to plan military affairs.
Eventually he followed Fànjū's plan,
sending the fifth-rank official Wǎn to attack Wèi,
capturing Huái.
Two years later, they captured Xíngqiū.
The guest minister Fànjū
again advised King Zhāo, saying:
"The territories of Qín and Hán
intertwine like embroidery.
Qín's possession of Hán
is like a tree having woodworms,
or a person suffering from a heart ailment.
If all under heaven remains unchanged, so be it;
but if change occurs,
what greater threat to Qín could there be than Hán?
Your Majesty should subdue Hán."
King Zhāo said:
"I indeed wish to subdue Hán,
but Hán does not comply.
What should be done about it?"
Fànjū replied:
"How could Hán not comply?
If Your Majesty sends troops to attack Yíngyáng,
then the routes to Gǒng and Chénggāo will be cut off;
if you sever the Tàiháng road to the north,
then the army from Shàngdǎng cannot descend.
Once Your Majesty raises troops to attack Yíngyáng,
their state will be severed into three parts.
When Hán sees it must perish,
how could it not comply?
If Hán complies,
then hegemonic plans can be considered."
The king said: "Good."
And he prepared to send an envoy to Hán.
As Fànjū grew increasingly favored,
having advised for several years,
he requested a private audience and said:
"When I lived east of the mountains,
I heard of Qí having Tiánwén,
but not of its having a king;
I heard of Qín having the Queen Dowager, Ránghóu,
Huáyáng, Gāolíng, and Jīngyáng,
but not of its having a king.
To control the state is to be king,
to wield benefits and harms is to be king,
to command the power of life and death is to be king.
Now the Queen Dowager acts arbitrarily without regard,
Ránghóu sends envoys without reporting,
Huáyáng and Jīngyáng punish and decide without restraint,
Gāolíng advances or retreats without seeking permission.
With these four nobles all present,
for the state not to be in peril has never happened.
To be subordinate to these four nobles
is what is called having no king.
Then how can authority not be undermined,
and how can orders now come from the king?
I have heard that those skilled in governing
internally consolidate their authority
and externally reinforce their power.
Ránghóu's envoys
wield the king's authority,
decide matters among the feudal lords,
distribute tallies across the land,
launch campaigns against other states,
with none daring to disobey.
Victories in battle and captured territories
bring benefits to Táo,
while the state's exhaustion is imposed on the feudal lords;
defeats in battle
create resentment among the common people,
and disaster falls upon the altars of soil and grain.
The Odes say:
'When the tree's fruit is abundant,
its branches split;
when its branches split,
its heart is injured;
when its cities are enlarged,
its state is endangered;
when its ministers are exalted,
its ruler is debased.'
Cuīzhù and Nàochǐ controlled Qí,
shot the king's thigh,
pulled out the king's sinews,
hung him on the temple beam,
where he died overnight.
Lǐduì controlled Zhào,
imprisoned the king's father at Shāqiū,
where he starved to death after a hundred days.
Now I hear that in Qín the Queen Dowager
and Ránghóu hold power,
assisted by Gāolíng, Huáyáng, and Jīngyáng,
ultimately ignoring the king of Qín—
these are also of the same kind as Nàochǐ and Lǐduì.
Moreover, the reason the three dynasties perished
was because the rulers delegated governance entirely,
indulging in drink, galloping, and hunting,
and not attending to state affairs.
Those to whom they delegated power
envied the worthy and capable,
controlled subordinates and deceived superiors,
to serve their private interests,
without planning for their ruler,
while the ruler remained unawakened,
thus losing their states.
Now from officials of rank and above to the highest ministers,
down to Your Majesty's attendants,
there are none who are not the chancellor's men.
Seeing Your Majesty standing alone at court,
I secretly fear for you,
that after ten thousand generations,
those who will possess Qín
will not be Your Majesty's descendants."
King Zhāo, hearing this, was greatly alarmed,
and said:
"Well said."
Thereupon he deposed the Queen Dowager,
and exiled Ránghóu, Gāolíng, Huáyáng,
and Jīngyáng beyond the pass.
The king of Qín then appointed Fànjū as chancellor.
He confiscated Ránghóu's seal,
sending him back to Táo,
ordering the local officials to provide carts and oxen for the move,
numbering over a thousand carriages.
At the pass, the guards inspected his treasure vessels,
and the rare and exotic treasures
exceeded those of the royal house.
Qín enfeoffed Fànjū with Yìng,
bestowing the title Marquess of Yìng.
At this time,
it was the forty-first year of King Zhāo of Qín.
After Fànjū became Qín's chancellor,
he was known in Qín as Zhānglù,
while Wèi remained unaware,
believing Fànjū had long been dead.
When Wèi heard Qín was about to campaign east against Hán and Wèi,
Wèi sent Xūjiǎ to Qín.
Fànjū, learning of this,
went in disguise,
wearing worn clothes, and strolled casually to the guesthouse,
meeting Xūjiǎ.
Xūjiǎ, seeing him, exclaimed in surprise:
"Is Fànshū truly unharmed?"
Fànjū said: "Yes."
Xūjiǎ laughed and said:
"Has Fànshū come to persuade Qín?"
He replied: "No.
Some time ago, I offended the Chancellor of Wèi,
so I fled here,
how dare I offer advice!"
Xū Jiǎ asked: "What are you doing now, Uncle?"
Fàn Jū said: "I work as a hired laborer for others."
Xū Jiǎ felt pity for him,
stayed and shared food and drink with him,
saying: "To think Uncle Fàn has fallen into such hardship!"
Then he took out one of his silk robes
and gave it to him.
Xū Jiǎ then asked:
"The Qín Chancellor, Lord Zhāng,
do you know him?
I've heard he is favored by the king,
and all matters under heaven are decided by the Chancellor.
Now whether my mission succeeds or fails depends on Lord Zhāng.
Do you happen to have any acquaintances familiar with the Chancellor?"
Fàn Jū said:
"My host knows him well.
I too can gain an audience,
I request to arrange a meeting for you with Lord Zhāng."
Xū Jiǎ said:
"My horse is sick,
my carriage axle is broken,
unless it's a large carriage with a team of four horses,
I certainly won't go out."
Fàn Jū said:
"I am willing to
borrow a large carriage with a team of four horses from my host for you."
Fàn Jū returned
to fetch a large carriage with a team of four horses,
and for Xū Jiǎ
he drove it himself,
entering the Qín Chancellor's residence.
Those in the residence who saw them from afar,
anyone who recognized him avoided and hid.
Xū Jiǎ found it strange.
Upon reaching the Chancellor's door,
he said to Xū Jiǎ:
"Wait for me,
I will go in first to announce you to the Chancellor."
Xū Jiǎ waited at the gate,
holding the carriage for a long time,
then asked the gatekeeper:
"Why hasn't Uncle Fàn come out?"
The gatekeeper said:
"There is no Uncle Fàn."
Xū Jiǎ said:
"The one who rode
in with me earlier."
The gatekeeper said:
"That is our Chancellor, Lord Zhāng."
Xū Jiǎ was greatly shocked,
realizing he had been deceived,
then bared his upper body and knelt,
apologizing through the gatekeeper.
Thereupon, Fàn Jū, with lavish curtains and canopies,
and many attendants,
received him.
Xū Jiǎ kowtowed
and spoke of deserving death,
saying: "I never imagined you could rise so high to the clouds yourself,
I dare not read the books of the world again,
nor dare I participate in the affairs of the world.
I deserve the punishment of boiling cauldron,
I beg to banish myself to the lands of the Hú and Mò barbarians,
my life or death is in your hands!"
Fàn Jū said:
"How many crimes do you have?"
He replied:
"If you plucked out all my hair to count my crimes,
it still wouldn't be enough."
Fàn Jū said:
"You have three crimes.
In the past, during the time of King Zhāo of Chǔ,
when Shēn Bāoxū repelled the Wú army for Chǔ,
the King of Chǔ offered him a fief of five thousand households in Jīng,
but Bāoxū declined and did not accept,
because
his ancestral graves were in Jīng.
Now my ancestors' graves are also in Wèi,
yet you previously suspected me of having ulterior motives towards Qí
and slandered me to Wèi Qí,
that is your first crime.
When Wèi Qí humiliated me in the latrine,
you did not stop him,
that is the second crime.
Moreover, when drunk, you urinated on me,
how could you be so cruel?
That is the third crime.
However, the reason you are spared death
is because of the silk robe you gave, showing lingering affection,
and the sentiment of an old friend,
so I release you."
Then he dismissed him.
He went in and reported to King Zhāo,
and sent Xū Jiǎ back.
Xū Jiǎ took leave of Fàn Jū,
Fàn Jū prepared a grand feast,
inviting all the envoys from various states,
seating them in the hall,
with abundant food and drink.
But he seated Xū Jiǎ in the courtyard below,
placed chopped beans and fodder before him,
and ordered two tattooed convicts to flank him
and force-feed him like a horse.
He admonished him, saying:
"Tell the King of Wèi for me,
to quickly bring me Wèi Qí's head!
Otherwise,
I will massacre Dàliáng."
Xū Jiǎ returned,
and reported this to Wèi Qí.
Wèi Qí was terrified, fled to Zhào,
and hid in the residence of Lord Píngyuán.
After Fàn Jū became Chancellor,
Wáng Jī said to Fàn Jū:
"There are three unpredictable things,
and three unavoidable things.
If the royal carriage one day halts late (the king dies),
that is the first unpredictable thing.
If you, sir, suddenly pass away,
that is the second unpredictable thing.
If I, your servant, suddenly die and fill a ditch,
that is the third unpredictable thing.
If the royal carriage one day halts late,
though you may regret regarding me,
there is nothing to be done.
If you, sir, suddenly pass away,
though you may regret regarding me, there is also nothing to be done.
If I, your servant, suddenly die and fill a ditch,
though you may regret regarding me, there is also nothing to be done."
Fàn Jū was displeased,
so he went in and spoke to the king, saying:
"Without Wáng Jī's loyalty,
no one could have brought me inside Hángǔ Pass;
without Your Majesty's wisdom and virtue,
no one could have honored me.
Now my official rank has reached Chancellor,
my nobility is among the marquises,
yet Wáng Jī's position remains only that of a receptionist,
which does not reflect his merit in bringing me in."
King Zhāo summoned Wáng Jī,
appointed him as Governor of Hédōng,
exempt from reporting for three years.
He also recommended Zhèng Ānpíng,
and King Zhāo made him a general.
Fàn Jū then distributed his family's wealth and goods,
fully repaying all those who had helped him in times of hardship,
repaying even the kindness of a single meal,
and avenging the slightest grievance.
Fàn Jū served as Chancellor of Qín for two years,
in the forty-second year of King Zhāo of Qín,
when they marched east to attack Hán's Shǎoqū
and Gāopíng, and captured them.
King Zhāo of Qín heard that Wèi Qí
was at Lord Píngyuán's place,
and wishing to surely avenge Fàn Jū's grudge,
he feigned friendship
and sent a letter to Lord Píngyuán, saying:
"I have heard of your high righteousness,
and wish to be friends with you as commoners,
if you would honor me with a visit,
I would like to share ten days of drinking with you."
Lord Píngyuán feared Qín,
and thought it genuine,
so he went to Qín to see King Zhāo.
King Zhāo drank with Lord Píngyuán for several days,
then said to Lord Píngyuán:
"In the past, King Wén of Zhōu obtained Lǚ Shàng
and regarded him as Tàigōng,
Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Yíwú
and regarded him as Zhòngfù,
now Lord Fàn is also my Shūfù.
