Lord Fàn's enemy is in your household,
I wish you to send someone to bring his head here;
otherwise,
I will not let you leave the pass."
Lord Píngyuán said:
"When noblemen form friendships,
it is for times of lowliness;
when the wealthy form friendships,
it is for times of poverty.
As for Wèi Qí,
he is my friend,
and if he were here,
I certainly would not hand him over,
and now he is not even at my place."
King Zhāo then sent a letter to the King of Zhào, saying:
"Your Majesty's younger brother is in Qín,
and Fàn Jūn's enemy Wèi Qí
is at the home of Lord Píngyuán.
Send someone quickly to bring his head;
otherwise,
I will raise troops to attack Zhào,
and will not release Your Majesty's brother from the pass."
King Xiàochéng of Zhào then dispatched soldiers
to surround Lord Píngyuán's home.
In desperation,
Wèi Qí fled out at night,
and went to see the Zhào chancellor Yú Qīng.
Yú Qīng judged that the King of Zhào could ultimately not be persuaded,
so he resigned his chancellor seal,
and fled with Wèi Qí, traveling discreetly.
Considering that none of the feudal lords
could be relied on in this crisis,
they then fled again to Dàliáng,
wishing to rely on Lord Xìnlíng
to escape to Chǔ.
When Lord Xìnlíng heard of this,
fearing Qín,
he hesitated and was unwilling to see them,
saying: "What kind of man is Yú Qīng?"
At that time, Hóu Yíng was beside him,
and said:
"It is truly hard to know a person,
and knowing people is also not easy.
Now Yú Qīng, wearing straw sandals and carrying a bamboo hat,
upon first meeting the King of Zhào,
was bestowed a pair of white jade discs,
and a hundred yì of gold;
at the second meeting,
he was appointed senior minister;
at the third meeting,
he finally received the chancellor seal,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis with ten thousand households.
At that time,
everyone in the world vied to know him.
Now Wèi Qí, in dire straits,
came to Yú Qīng.
Yú Qīng did not dare
to cling to the honor of high rank and emolument,
but resigned his chancellor seal,
gave up his marquisate of ten thousand households, and traveled discreetly.
He came to you, my lord, in his urgency to help a scholar in distress,
and you, my lord, say 'What kind of man?'
It is truly hard to know a person,
and knowing people is also not easy!"
Lord Xìnlíng was greatly ashamed,
and drove out to the countryside to welcome them.
When Wèi Qí heard that Lord Xìnlíng
had initially been reluctant to see him,
in anger he cut his own throat.
The King of Zhào heard of this,
and finally took his head and gave it to Qín.
King Zhāo of Qín then released Lord Píngyuán to return to Zhào.
In the forty-third year of King Zhāo,
Qín attacked Fénxíng of Hán and captured it,
then built a city at Guǎngwǔ on the river.
Five years later,
King Zhāo employed the stratagem of Marquis Yìng,
spreading false rumors to sow discord in Zhào.
Zhào, for this reason,
ordered Mǎfúzǐ
to replace Lián Pō as general.
Qín heavily defeated Zhào at Chángpíng,
and then besieged Hándān.
Later, he had a rift with Lord Wǔ'ān Bái Qǐ,
and spoke against him, causing his death.
He appointed Zhèng Ānpíng,
and sent him to attack Zhào.
Zhèng Ānpíng was besieged by Zhào,
and in desperation,
surrendered to Zhào with twenty thousand troops.
Marquis Yìng laid on a straw mat
to ask for punishment.
According to Qín law,
one who recommends someone and the recommended person proves unworthy
shall be punished according to the same crime.
Thus Marquis Yìng's crime
warranted the arrest of his three clans.
King Zhāo of Qín, fearing to hurt Marquis Yìng's feelings,
then issued an order throughout the state:
"Whoever dares to speak of the matter of Zhèng Ānpíng
shall be punished with the same crime."
Moreover, he increased the gifts of food to Chancellor Marquis Yìng
daily more generously,
to soothe his feelings.
Two years later,
Wáng Jī, as governor of Hédōng,
colluded with the feudal lords,
and was executed for his crime.
And Marquis Yìng grew daily more displeased.
King Zhāo, at court, sighed,
and Marquis Yìng stepped forward and said:
"Your servant has heard
'When the ruler worries, the ministers are disgraced;
when the ruler is disgraced, the ministers die.'
Now that Your Majesty worries in the midst of court,
I dare to ask for my crime."
King Zhāo said:
"I have heard that in Chǔ the iron swords are sharp
but the entertainers are unskilled.
If the iron swords are sharp,
then the warriors are brave;
if the entertainers are unskilled,
then the thoughts are far-reaching.
With far-reaching thoughts
and commanding brave warriors,
I fear that Chǔ is planning against Qín.
If things are not prepared in advance,
one cannot respond to sudden events.
Now that Lord Wǔ'ān is already dead,
and Zhèng Ānpíng and others have rebelled,
with no good generals within and many enemy states without,
I therefore worry."
He wished to stimulate Marquis Yìng.
Marquis Yìng was afraid,
and did not know what to do.
Cài Zé heard of this,
and went to Qín.
Cài Zé
was a man of Yān.
He traveled to study and sought office among the feudal lords,
large and small, very many,
but did not meet with success.
Then he went to Táng Jǔ for a physiognomy,
saying:
"I have heard that you, sir, read the face of Lǐ Duì,
saying
'Within a hundred days
you will hold the reins of state,'
is that true?"
He said:
"It is true."
He said:
"What about someone like me?"
Táng Jǔ looked at him carefully and laughed, saying:
"You, sir, have a turned-up nose,
broad shoulders,
a prominent forehead,
a sunken nose bridge,
and hunched knees.
I have heard that sages have no fixed appearance,
perhaps that describes you, sir?"
Cài Zé knew Táng Jǔ was teasing him, so he said:
"Wealth and honor I already possess by nature,
what I do not know is my lifespan,
I wish to hear it."
Táng Jǔ said:
"Your lifespan, sir,
from now on is forty-three years."
Cài Zé laughed, thanked him, and left,
saying to his carriage driver:
"I shall eat fine rice and meat,
gallop on a swift horse,
carry the golden seal of office,
tie the purple ribbon at my waist,
bow and defer before my sovereign,
enjoy the wealth and honor of eating meat,
forty-three years is enough."
He went to Zhào,
but was expelled.
He went to Hán and Wèi,
and had his cauldron and tripod robbed on the road.
Hearing that Marquis Yìng
had appointed Zhèng Ānpíng and Wáng Jī,
who both committed heavy crimes in Qín,
and that Marquis Yìng was inwardly ashamed,
Cài Zé then went west to enter Qín.
When he was about to see King Zhāo,
he had someone spread words to provoke Marquis Yìng, saying:
"The Yān guest Cài Zé,
is a man of outstanding talent, great eloquence, and wisdom in the world.
Once he sees the King of Qín,
the King of Qín is sure to distress you, sir,
and take away your position."
Marquis Yìng heard this and said:
"The affairs of the Five Emperors and Three Dynasties,
the theories of the Hundred Schools, I already know them;
the debates of many mouths,
I have crushed them all.
How can this man distress me
and take away my position?"
He sent someone to summon Cài Zé.
When Cài Zé entered,
he merely bowed to Yìnghóu.
Yìnghóu was already displeased,
and upon seeing him,
his manner was arrogant,
so Yìnghóu reproached him, saying:
"You have publicly declared
that you wish to replace me as the chancellor of Qín,
is there such a thing?"
He replied: "Yes."
Yìnghóu said: "I would like to hear your explanation."
Cài Zé said:
"Alas, how slow you are to see!
The sequence of the four seasons
is such that when one completes its task, it departs.
When a person's body is robust and strong,
with agile hands and feet,
sharp ears and eyes,
and a wise and intelligent mind,
is that not the aspiration of a scholar?"
Yìnghóu said: "Yes."
Cài Zé said:
"To embody benevolence and uphold righteousness,
practice the Way and bestow virtue,
achieving one's ambitions under heaven,
so that all under heaven cherish, rejoice, respect, love, and honor them,
all wishing to make them sovereign—
is that not the goal of eloquence and wisdom?"
Yìnghóu said: "Yes."
Cài Zé continued:
"Wealth, honor, prominence, and glory,
bringing order to all things,
enabling each to find its proper place;
a life of longevity,
living out one's natural years without premature death or injury;
the world continuing its legacy,
preserving its achievements,
passing them on endlessly;
reputation and reality both pure,
influence flowing for a thousand miles,
praised generation after generation without end,
enduring as long as heaven and earth—
is that not the manifestation of virtue
and what the sages called
auspicious and good deeds?"
Yìnghóu said: "Yes."
Cài Zé said:
"As for Shāng Jūn of Qín,
Wú Qǐ of Chǔ,
and the minister Wén Zhǒng of Yuè,
would their final outcomes be desirable?"
Yìnghóu knew that Cài Zé intended to corner him with arguments,
so he responded evasively:
"Why would they not be?
When Gōngsūn Yǎng served Duke Xiào,
he devoted himself entirely without second thoughts,
acting solely for the public good with no regard for private interests;
he established punishments
to suppress treachery and evil,
faithfully rewarding and penalizing
to achieve order;
baring his heart,
he bore resentment and blame,
deceived his old friend,
captured Prince Áng of Wèi,
secured the altars of Qín,
benefited the common people,
and ultimately captured enemy generals and defeated foes for Qín,
expanding territory by a thousand miles.
When Wú Qǐ served King Dào,
he prevented private interests
from harming the public good,
and slander from obscuring loyalty,
never accepting words just for agreement,
nor actions merely for approval,
not changing his conduct in the face of danger,
upholding righteousness without avoiding hardship,
thus making his lord a hegemon
and the state powerful,
never shirking misfortune or peril.
When Minister Wén Zhǒng served the King of Yuè,
even when the lord was in distress and humiliated,
he remained utterly loyal without slackening;
even when the lord faced ruin,
he exerted all his ability without desertion;
he did not boast of his successes,
nor grow arrogant or negligent in wealth and honor.
These three men
truly reached the pinnacle of righteousness
and the peak of loyalty.
Thus, a gentleman faces death for righteousness,
regarding it as returning home;
better to die with honor than live in disgrace.
A scholar may indeed sacrifice himself to achieve fame;
wherever righteousness lies,
even death brings no regret.
Why would they not be desirable?"
Cài Zé said:
"A sage ruler and worthy ministers
are the greatest blessing to the world;
an enlightened sovereign and fitting officials
are the fortune of the state;
a kind father and filial son,
a faithful husband and chaste wife
are the blessing of a family.
Yet Bǐ Gān was loyal
but could not preserve Yīn,
Zǐ Xū was wise
but could not保全 Wú,
Shēn Shēng was filial
but Jìn fell into chaos.
All had loyal ministers and filial sons,
yet their states were destroyed or in turmoil—
why?
Because there were no enlightened rulers or worthy fathers
to heed them,
so the world regarded their lords and fathers with scorn
and pitied their ministers and sons.
Now, Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng
as ministers were righteous;
their lords were not.
Thus, the world praises the three for their achievements
but sees no virtue in their fate;
would they aspire to die without meeting the right era?
If only through death
can one establish loyalty and fame,
then Wēizǐ would lack benevolence,
Confucius lack sagacity,
and Guǎn Zhòng lack greatness.
When one achieves merits,
is it not hoping for completion and preservation?
To have both life and reputation intact
is the best.
To have a reputation worthy of emulation
but lose one's life
is the next best.
To have a reputation marred by disgrace
while preserving one's life
is the worst."
At this, Yìnghóu expressed agreement.
Seizing a slight opportunity,
Cài Zé then said:
"Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng,
as ministers who were loyal and achieved merits,
may be admirable,
but Hóng Yāo serving King Wén,
and the Duke of Zhōu assisting King Chéng—
were they not also loyal and sage?
Judging by the ruler-minister relationship,
how do Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng
compare to Hóng Yāo and the Duke of Zhōu in desirability?"
Yìnghóu said:
"Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng
do not measure up."
Cài Zé said:
"Then, is your lord, in his kindness, benevolence, and employment of the loyal,
his sincerity toward old acquaintances,
his virtue and wisdom in bonding with men of principle,
and his righteousness in not betraying meritorious officials,
comparable to Duke Xiào of Qín, King Dào of Chǔ, or the King of Yuè?"
Yìnghóu said: "I am not sure."
Cài Zé said:
"In your lord's closeness to loyal ministers,
he does not surpass Duke Xiào of Qín,
King Dào of Chǔ, or the King of Yuè,
while your wisdom and ability
in securing the lord's safety, reforming governance,
bringing order from chaos, strengthening the military,
resolving crises and overcoming difficulties,
expanding territory, cultivating grains,
enriching the state, satisfying families,
empowering the sovereign,
honoring the altars of state,
glorifying the ancestral temple,
ensuring none under heaven dare deceive or offend your lord,
whose majesty shakes the realm,
whose achievements shine for ten thousand miles,
whose fame and glory spread far and wide—
how do you compare to Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng?"
Yìnghóu said: "I do not measure up."
Cài Zé said:
"Now, your lord's closeness to loyal ministers
and remembrance of old ties
is not like that of Duke Xiào, King Dào, or Gōu Jiàn,
and your achievements, favor, trust, and intimacy
also fall short of Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng,
yet your emolument and position
are more noble and powerful,
your personal wealth greater than those three,
and you have not retired—
I fear your calamity may surpass theirs;
I am deeply concerned for your danger."
As the saying goes,
'When the sun reaches its zenith, it must decline;
when the moon becomes full, it must wane.'
When things flourish, they then decay—
this is the constant principle of heaven and earth.
To advance or retreat, to expand or contract,
changing with the times,
is the constant way of the sage.
Therefore, 'When the state has the Way, serve in office;
when the state is without the Way, withdraw into seclusion.'
The sage said,
'The flying dragon is in the heavens;
it is beneficial to see the great man.'
'Wealth and honor obtained through unrighteousness
are to me as floating clouds.'
Now, your grudges have been avenged
and your kindnesses repaid,
your ambitions have been fulfilled,
yet you do not change your plans—
I secretly believe this is not what you should choose.
Moreover, the kingfisher, the swan,
the rhinoceros, and the elephant
are situated in circumstances that are not
distant from death,
yet the reason they die
is because they are deluded by bait.
The wisdom of Sū Qín and Zhì Bó
was not insufficient to avoid disgrace and keep death at bay,
yet the reason they died
was because they were deluded by insatiable greed for profit.
Therefore, the sage established rituals
to moderate desires,
taking from the people with measure,
employing them according to the season,
using them with restraint,
so that ambitions are not excessive,
conduct is not arrogant,
always walking together with the Way
and not losing it,
thus the world carries on without end.
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí
assembled the feudal lords nine times,
unifying and rectifying the world,
but at the meeting of Kuíqiū,
he had an arrogant and self-satisfied ambition,
and nine states rebelled against him.
King Fūchāi of Wú had troops unmatched in the world,
brave and strong, he looked down upon the feudal lords,
overpowered Qí and Jìn,
and thus was killed and his state perished.
Xià Yù and Tàishǐ Jiào
shouted and terrified the three armies,
yet they died at the hands of common men.
These all rode the peak of prosperity
and did not turn back to reason,
not dwelling in humility and retreat,
the peril of not practicing frugality and restraint.
Now, Lord Shāng for Duke Xiào of Qín
clarified laws and decrees,
prohibited the roots of evil,
honored ranks and necessarily rewarded,
punished crimes without fail,
standardized weights,
rectified measures,
adjusted the light and heavy,
abolished the field boundaries,
to stabilize the livelihoods of the people
and unify their customs,
encouraged the people to farm
and utilize the land,
each household without dual occupations,
exerting effort in farming and storing up,
practicing the arts of war and formation,
so that when the army moved
the territory expanded,
when the army rested the state grew rich,
thus Qín was unmatched in the world,
established awe among the feudal lords,
and accomplished the enterprise of Qín.
His achievements were already complete,
yet he was torn apart by chariots.
The territory of Chǔ spanned several thousand lǐ,
with a million halberd-bearing soldiers,
Bái Qǐ led a force of several tens of thousands to battle Chǔ,
in one campaign he took Yānyǐng and burned Yílíng,
in a second campaign he annexed Shǔ and Hàn to the south.
Moreover, he crossed Hán and Wèi
to attack the powerful Zhào,
in the north he buried the troops of Mǎfú,
slaughtering over four hundred thousand men,
exterminating them beneath Chángpíng,
where blood flowed to form rivers,
the seething sound like thunder,
then he advanced to besiege Hándān,
enabling Qín to possess imperial enterprise.
Chǔ and Zhào were powerful states of the world
and enemies of Qín,
yet after this, Chǔ and Zhào
all trembled and did not dare attack Qín,
due to the momentum of Bái Qǐ.
Personally, he subdued over seventy cities,
his achievements were already complete,
yet he was given a sword to die at Dùyóu.
Wú Qǐ for King Dào of Chǔ established laws,
humbled and reduced the authority of the great ministers,
dismissed the incompetent,
abolished the useless,
cut redundant officials,
blocked private solicitations,
unified the customs of Chǔ,
prohibited wandering people,
refined the scholars of farming and war,
subdued Yángyuè in the south,
annexed Chén and Cài in the north,
shattered the horizontal alliances
and dispersed the vertical ones,
so that the itinerant persuaders had no opening for their words,
prohibited factions to encourage the common people,
stabilized the governance of Chǔ,
his troops shook the world,
his might subdued the feudal lords.
His achievements were already complete,
yet he was ultimately torn limb from limb.
Great Fū Zhòng devised deep plans and long-term strategies for the King of Yuè,
averted the peril of Kuàijī,
turning perishing into survival,
and disgrace into honor,
reclaimed wasteland to establish cities,
opened lands to grow grain,
led the scholars of the four directions,
focused the strength of high and low,
assisted the worthy Gōu Jiàn,
avenged the enmity against Fūchāi,
finally captured powerful Wú,
enabling Yuè to become hegemon.
His achievements were clear and trustworthy,
yet Gōu Jiàn ultimately betrayed and killed him.
These four men,
did not leave after their achievements were complete,
and disaster reached them thus.
This is what is called being extended
but unable to contract,
going forward but unable to return.
Fàn Lǐ understood this,
transcended and avoided the world,
long becoming Lord Táo Zhū.
Do you not observe the gamblers?
Some want to make large bets,
some want to share the winnings—
these are all well known to you.
Now you serve as chancellor of Qín,
devising strategies without leaving your mat,
planning without leaving the court,
controlling the feudal lords from your seat,
benefiting and extending to Sānchuān,
enriching Yíyáng,
cutting through the perils of Yángcháng,
blocking the paths of Tàiháng,
moreover severing the routes of Fàn and Zhōngháng,
so that the six states cannot form a vertical alliance,
building plank roads for a thousand lǐ,
connecting to Shǔ and Hàn,
making the world fear Qín,
Qín's desires are achieved,
your achievements have reached their peak,
this is also the time for Qín to share the winnings.
If you do not withdraw now,
then you will be like Lord Shāng,
Lord Bái, Wú Qǐ, and Great Fū Zhòng.
I have heard,
'Those who look into water see the reflection of their face;
those who look into people know good and ill fortune.'
The Shū says,
'Beneath the summit of success,
one cannot dwell for long.'
With the disaster of these four men,
why would you remain in such a position?
Why do you not at this time
return the chancellor's seal,
yield to the worthy and hand it over,
withdraw to dwell among cliffs and observe the streams,
you will surely have the integrity of Bó Yí,
long remain as Lord Yìng,
called 'the solitary one' for generations,
and possess the humility of Xǔ Yóu
and Yánlíng Jìzǐ,
the longevity of Qiáo and Sōng—
how does this compare to ending in disaster?
So why would you remain in such a position?
If you endure but cannot leave of your own accord,
hesitate and cannot decide for yourself,
you will surely have the disaster of these four men.
The Yì says,
'The dragon at the zenith has regrets,'
this speaks of those who rise
but cannot descend,
are extended but cannot contract,
who go forward but cannot return of their own accord.
I hope you will deeply consider this!"
Lord Yìng said, "Good."
I have heard
the saying: "If one desires but does not know when to stop and be content,
one loses what one desires;
if one possesses but does not know contentment and limits,
one loses what one possesses."
I am fortunate to receive your guidance,
and I humbly accept your instruction."
Thereupon, he invited him to take a seat,
treating him as an honored guest.
A few days later,
he entered the court
and spoke to King Zhāo of Qín, saying:
"A newcomer from east of the mountains named Cài Zé
is a skilled debater
well-versed in the affairs of the Three Sovereigns,
the achievements of the Five Hegemons,
and the changes in worldly customs.
He is fully capable of entrusting with the governance of Qín.
I have seen many people,
but none compare to him;
I am not his equal.
I dare to bring this to your attention."
King Zhāo of Qín summoned him for an audience,
spoke with him,
and was greatly pleased,
appointing him as a guest minister.
Marquis Yìng then pleaded illness
and requested to return his ministerial seal.
King Zhāo urged Marquis Yìng to remain,
but Marquis Yìng claimed to be critically ill.
Fàn Jū was relieved of his ministerial post,
and King Zhāo, newly fond of Cài Zé's strategies,
appointed him as the chancellor of Qín,
leading to the eastern annexation of the Zhōu court.
Cài Zé served as chancellor of Qín for several months
when some people spoke ill of him.
Fearing execution,
he pleaded illness and returned the ministerial seal,
receiving the title Lord Gāngchéng.
He remained in Qín for over ten years,
serving under King Zhāo, King Xiàowén, and King Zhuāngxiāng,
and finally under the First Emperor.
He was sent as an envoy to Yān on behalf of Qín,
and within three years, Yān sent
its Crown Prince Dān to Qín as a hostage.
Grand Historian comments:
Hán Zǐ said,
"Long sleeves are good for dancing,
abundant money is good for trading,"
and truly, this saying is apt!
Fàn Jū and Cài Zé
were what the world calls versatile debaters,
yet they roamed persuading the feudal lords
until their hair turned white without meeting success,
not because their strategies were poor,
but because the support they received was insufficient.
When these two men traveled and entered Qín,
they successively attained high ministerial ranks,
leaving their achievements for the world to see,
which was indeed due to the difference in the strength of the states.
Yet scholars also depend on chance encounters;
many worthy individuals like these two
never fully realize their ambitions—
how can one recount them all?
But had these two not faced hardship,
how could they have been spurred to action?
Yuè Yì's
ancestor was named Yuè Yáng.
Yuè Yáng served as a general under Marquis Wén of Wèi,
conquering Zhōngshān,
for which Marquis Wén of Wèi enfeoffed him with Língshòu.
After Yuè Yáng's death,
he was buried in Língshòu,
and his descendants settled there.
Zhōngshān was restored as a state,
but by the time of King Wǔlíng of Zhào, it was conquered again,
and among Yuè's later descendants was Yuè Yì.
Yuè Yì was talented
and fond of military affairs,
recommended by the people of Zhào.
When King Wǔlíng of Zhào faced the Shāqiū rebellion,
Yuè Yì left Zhào for Wèi.
Hearing that King Zhāo of Yān, due to the rebellion of Zǐ Zhī, had been badly defeated by Qí,
bore a grudge against Qí,
and never forgot to seek revenge for a single day,
though Yān was a small state,
remote and isolated,
unable to overcome Qí by force,
King Zhāo humbled himself and treated scholars with respect,
first honoring Guō Wěi
to attract the worthy.
Yuè Yì was then sent as an envoy to Yān by King Zhāo of Wèi,
and the King of Yān received him with the礼节 of a guest.
Yuè Yì declined the honor,
but eventually pledged his service as a subject,
and King Zhāo of Yān appointed him as deputy minister,
a position he held for a long time.
At that time,
King Mǐn of Qí was powerful,
having defeated Chǔ's minister Táng Mò at Chóngqiū in the south,
crushed the Three Jìn at Guānjīn in the west,
then allied with the Three Jìn to attack Qín,
helped Zhào destroy Zhōngshān,
conquered Sòng,
and expanded his territory by over a thousand lǐ.
He vied with King Zhāo of Qín for the title of emperor,
but later relinquished it.
The feudal lords all wished to turn away from Qín and submit to Qí.
King Mǐn became arrogant,
and the people could not endure it.
Thus, King Zhāo of Yān inquired about attacking Qí.
Yuè Yì replied:
"Qí,
with its legacy of a hegemon state,
vast land and numerous people,
is not easy to attack alone.
If Your Majesty must attack it,
it would be best to ally with Zhào, Chǔ,
and Wèi."
Thereupon, he sent Yuè Yì to make a pact with King Huìwén of Zhào,
while separately allying with Chǔ
and Wèi, and having Zhào persuade Qín of the benefits of attacking Qí.
The feudal lords, resentful of King Mǐn of Qí's arrogance and tyranny,
all vied to form a coalition with Yān to attack Qí.
Yuè Yì returned to report,
and King Zhāo of Yān mobilized all his troops,
appointing Yuè Yì as supreme general,
while King Huìwén of Zhào conferred upon him the seal of chancellor.
Yuè Yì then commanded the combined forces of Zhào,
Chǔ, Hán,
Wèi, and Yān to attack Qí,
defeating them west of the Jì River.
The forces of the other states withdrew and returned,
but Yuè Yì alone pursued with the Yān army,
advancing to Línzī.
After King Mǐn of Qí's defeat west of the Jì River,
he fled
and sought refuge in Jǔ.
Yuè Yì remained to pacify Qí,
while the Qí forces defended their cities.
Yuè Yì attacked and entered Línzī,
seizing all of Qí's treasures, goods, and ritual vessels to send to Yān.
King Zhāo of Yān was greatly pleased,
personally traveling to the Jì River to reward the troops,
bestowing rewards and feasting the soldiers,
enfeoffing Yuè Yì with Chāngguó,
and bestowing the title Lord Chāngguó.
King Zhāo of Yān then gathered the spoils from Qí and returned,
while sending Yuè Yì with troops to subdue the remaining Qí cities that had not surrendered.
Yuè Yì remained to pacify Qí for five years,
capturing over seventy Qí cities,
all organized as commanderies and districts under Yān's control,
with only Jǔ
and Jímò holding out.
Then, King Zhāo of Yān died,
and his son succeeded him as King Huì of Yān.
King Huì had borne a grudge against Yuè Yì since his time as crown prince,
and upon his accession,
Tián Dān of Qí, hearing of this,
spread counter-intrigue in Yān,
saying:
"Only two Qí cities remain uncaptured.
The reason they have not been taken sooner
is that Yuè Yì has a rift with the new King of Yān
and wishes to prolong the campaign in Qí,
aiming to rule Qí himself.
What Qí fears
is only that another general will come."
Thus, King Huì of Yān already suspected Yuè Yì,
and upon hearing Qí's counter-intrigue,
sent Qí Jié to replace him as general,
recalling Yuè Yì.
Yuè Yì, knowing that King Huì's replacement was ill-intentioned,
feared execution,
and thus went west to surrender to Zhào.
Zhào enfeoffed him with Guānjīn,
bestowing the title Lord Wàngzhū.
They honored and favored Yuè Yì to unsettle Yān
and Qí.
Later, Tián Dān of Qí battled Qí Jié,
indeed setting a ruse to deceive the Yān army,
defeating Qí Jié at Jímò,
then turning to pursue the Yān forces,
driving them north to the river,
recapturing all of Qí's cities,
and welcoming King Xiāng from Jǔ,
returning to Línzī.
King Huì of Yān regretted having sent Qì Jié to replace Yuè Yì,
which led to the defeat of his army, loss of his general, and the fall of Qí;
he also resented Yuè Yì for surrendering to Zhào,
fearing that Zhào would employ Yuè Yì to exploit Yān's weakness and attack Yān.
King Huì of Yān then sent a messenger to reproach Yuè Yì,
and to apologize, saying:
"The late king entrusted the entire state to you, General,
and you, General, defeated Qí for Yān,
avenging the late king's enemy,
shaking the whole world with your deeds.
How could I dare forget your achievements for even a single day!
It happened that the late king passed away,
and I had just ascended the throne,
when my advisors misled me.
My sending Qì Jié to replace you, General,
was because you had long been exposed to the hardships of campaign,
so I recalled you to rest awhile
and discuss affairs.
But you, General, misunderstood,
thinking there was a rift between us,
and so abandoned Yān and went to Zhào.
For your own plans, this may be acceptable,
but how does it repay the late king's intent in treating you so well?"
Yuè Yì replied in a letter to King Huì of Yān, saying:
I, unworthy as I am,
could not carry out the king's command
to satisfy the wishes of your attendants,
fearing it would tarnish the late king's wisdom
and harm your righteousness,
so I fled to Zhào.
Now you send someone to accuse me of crimes,
and I fear your attendants do not understand the reason the late king favored and trusted me,
nor do they know my heart in serving the late king,
hence I dare to respond by letter.
I have heard that wise and sage rulers do not bestow emoluments on their personal favorites,
but reward those with great achievements,
and appoint those whose abilities match the tasks.
Thus, to examine capability and confer office
is the mark of a successful ruler;
to assess conduct and form friendships
is the way of a scholar establishing his name.
I privately observed the late king's actions
and saw that he had ambitions surpassing ordinary rulers,
so I borrowed credentials from Wèi
and presented myself to be examined in Yān.
The late king, in his excessive favor,
placed me among his guests,
elevated me above his ministers,
without consulting his kinsmen,
and made me Assistant Minister.
I, unaware of my own limitations,
thought that by obeying orders and accepting instructions,
I might fortunately avoid offense,
so I accepted the command without declining.
The late king commanded me, saying:
"I have deep-seated resentment and fury towards Qí,
and despite our weakness,
I wish to make conquering Qí our mission."
I replied:
"Qí,
inheriting the legacy of a hegemonic state and the remnants of great victories,
is well-trained in arms and armor,
experienced in warfare and attack.
If you wish to attack it,
you must ally with the world to plan it.
To ally with the world against it,
none is better than forming a pact with Zhào.
Moreover, Huáiběi
and the land of Sòng,
are desired by Chǔ and Wèi.
If Zhào agrees and we form a covenant of four states to attack it,
Qí can be greatly defeated."
The late king agreed,
and provided credentials to send me south as an envoy to Zhào.
Upon my return with the response,
he raised troops to strike Qí.
By the way of Heaven
and the late king's spirit,
the lands north of the Yellow River followed the late king and were raised to the Jì River's edge.
The army at the Jì River, commanded to attack Qí,
greatly defeated the people of Qí.
With light-footed soldiers and sharp troops,
we drove straight to their capital.
The king of Qí fled to Jǔ,
barely escaping with his life;
pearls, jade, treasures, chariots, armor, and precious vessels were all collected and brought to Yān.
Qí's vessels were displayed at Níngtái,
the Dàlǚ bell was set up at Yuányīng,
the former tripods returned to the Lìshì,
and the plantings at Jìqiū were from the bamboos of Wèn,
such that since the time of the Five Hegemons,
no achievement has matched that of the late king.
The late king, feeling his ambitions satisfied,
divided the land to enfeoff me,
allowing me to rank with the lords of small states.
I, unaware of my own limitations,
thought that by obeying orders and accepting instructions,
I might fortunately avoid offense,
and thus accepted the command without declining.
I have heard that wise and sage rulers,
once they establish achievements, do not let them fade,
so they are recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals;
foresighted scholars,
once they achieve fame, do not let it be destroyed,
so they are praised by later generations.
As for the late king's avenging of grievances and wiping away of shame,
vanquishing a powerful state of ten thousand chariots,
and collecting eight centuries of accumulated treasures,
until the day he left his ministers,
his teachings had not declined,
and his ministers in charge of governance,
by cultivating laws and decrees,
being cautious with the collateral lines,
and extending benefits to the common people and slaves,
all could serve as lessons for later generations.
I have heard that
those who are good at starting things are not necessarily good at finishing them,
and those who are good at beginnings are not necessarily good at endings.
In the past, Wǔ Zǐxū's advice was heeded by Hé Lǘ,
and the king of Wú extended his reach to Yǐng;
Fū Chāi did not agree with him,
gave him a leather sack and floated him down the river.
The king of Wú did not realize that following earlier advice could lead to achievements,
so he drowned Zǐxū without regret;
Zǐxū did not foresee early that his lord's measure was different,
and thus ended up in the river without changing.
To save myself and achieve merit,
thereby illuminating the late king's deeds,
is my best plan.
To incur slander and disgrace,
ruining the late king's name,
is what I greatly fear.
Facing an unforeseeable crime,
and seeking profit from misfortune,
is something righteousness does not permit me to do.
I have heard that noble men of old,
even when ending friendships, did not use harsh words;
loyal ministers leaving a state
do not clear their names.
Though I am unworthy,
I have often received teachings from noble men.
I fear that your attendants, influenced by those close to you,
may not understand the actions of one kept at a distance,
so I dare to present this letter for your consideration,
hoping that you, O King, will take note.
Thereupon, the king of Yān again made Yuè Yì's son Yuè Jiān the Lord of Chāngguó;
and Yuè Yì traveled back and forth, renewing ties with Yān,
and both Yān and Zhào regarded him as a guest minister.
Yuè Yì died in Zhào.
Yuè Jiān resided in Yān for over thirty years,
when King Xǐ of Yān adopted the plan of his minister Lì Fù
to attack Zhào,
and consulted the Lord of Chāngguó, Yuè Jiān.
Yuè Jiān said:
"Zhào,
a state fought over on four fronts,
has a people accustomed to war;
it is not advisable to attack it."
The king of Yān did not listen,
and proceeded to attack Zhào.
Zhào sent Lián Pō to attack them,
who greatly defeated Lì Fù's army at Hào,
capturing Lì Fù
and Yuè Chéng.
Yuè Chéng
was a clansman of Yuè Jiān.
Thereupon, Yuè Jiān fled to Zhào,
and Zhào then besieged Yān.
Yān heavily ceded territory to make peace with Zhào,
and Zhào then withdrew and left.
The King of Yān regretted not having employed Yuè Xián,
who was already in Zhào.
So he sent a letter to Yuè Xián, saying:
"During the reign of King Zhòu,
Jīzǐ was not employed,
yet he persistently remonstrated without cease,
hoping the king would listen;
Shāng Róng was not successful,
and suffered personal humiliation,
hoping for a change.
Only when the people's will was not heeded,
and prisoners were released on their own,
did these two gentlemen retreat into seclusion.
Thus, King Zhòu bore the burden of tyranny like Jié,
while the two gentlemen did not lose their reputation for loyalty and sagacity.
Why is that?
Because they had exhausted their efforts in concern.
Now, although I am foolish,
I am not as tyrannical as King Zhòu;
and though the people of Yān are disorderly,
they are not as extreme as the people of Yīn.
If there are disputes within the household,
they should not be fully aired
to the neighbors.
These two points,
I do not think you should adopt, my lord."
Yuè Xián and
Yuè Chéng resented Yān for not following their advice,
and both eventually remained in Zhào.
Zhào enfeoffed Yuè Chéng as Lord Wǔxiāng.
The following year,
Yuè Chéng and
Lián Pō besieged Yān for Zhào,
but Yān offered heavy bribes for peace,
and the siege was lifted.
Five years later,
King Xiàochéng of Zhào died.
King Xiāng sent Yuè Chéng to replace Lián Pō.
Lián Pō attacked Yuè Chéng,
who fled,
and Lián Pō went into exile in Wèi.
Sixteen years later, Qín destroyed Zhào.
More than twenty years after that,
Emperor Gāo passed through Zhào,
and asked:
"Does Yuè Yì have any descendants?"
The reply was:
"There is Yuè Shū."
Emperor Gāo enfeoffed him at Yuèqīng,
with the title Lord Huàchéng.
Lord Huàchéng
was the grandson of Yuè Yì.
And among the Yuè clan, there were Yuè Xiá Gōng
and Yuè Chén Gōng.
When Zhào was about to be destroyed by Qín,
they fled to Gāomì in Qí.
Yuè Chén Gōng was skilled in expounding the teachings of Huángdì
and Lǎozi,
becoming renowned in Qí,
and was called a virtuous teacher.
The Grand Historian comments:
When Kuǎi Tōng of Qí and Zhǔfǔ Yǎn read Yuè Yì's letter in reply to the King of Yān,
they never failed to put down the scroll and weep.
Yuè Chén Gōng studied the teachings of Huángdì
and Lǎozi;
his original teacher was known as Héshàng Zhàngrén,
but his origins are unknown.
Héshàng Zhàngrén taught Ānqīshēng,
Ānqīshēng taught Máo Xì Gōng,
Máo Xì Gōng taught Yuè Xiá Gōng,
Yuè Xiá Gōng taught Yuè Chén Gōng,
and Yuè Chén Gōng taught Gài Gōng.
Gài Gōng taught in Gāomì
and Jiāoxī in Qí,
and was the teacher of Chancellor Cáo.
Lián Pō
was an excellent general of Zhào.
In the sixteenth year of King Huìwén of Zhào,
Lián Pō, as a general of Zhào, attacked Qí,
defeated them decisively,
captured Yángjìn,
and was appointed Senior Minister,
renowned among the feudal lords for his courage.
Lìn Xiàngrú
was a man of Zhào,
and served as a retainer to Miào Xián, the Chief Eunuch of Zhào.
During the reign of King Huìwén of Zhào,
he obtained the Hé Shì Bì from Chǔ.
King Zhāo of Qín heard of this,
and sent a letter to the King of Zhào,
offering fifteen cities in exchange for the jade.
The King of Zhào consulted with General Lián Pō and his ministers:
If they gave it to Qín,
they feared they might not get the cities,
and would be deceived;
if they did not give it,
they worried about Qín's army attacking.
Unable to decide on a plan,
they sought someone who could be sent to respond to Qín,
but found no one.
Chief Eunuch Miào Xián said:
"My retainer Lìn Xiàngrú can be sent."
The king asked:
"How do you know?"
He replied:
"I once committed a crime,
and secretly planned to flee to Yān.
My retainer Xiàngrú stopped me,
saying:
'How do you know the King of Yān?'
I told him:
'I once accompanied the king to meet the King of Yān at the border,
and the King of Yān privately grasped my hand,
saying
"I wish to befriend you."
That's how I know,
so I intended to go.'
Xiàngrú said to me:
'Since Zhào is strong and Yān weak,
and you are favored by the King of Zhào,
the King of Yān wishes to befriend you.
Now if you flee from Zhào to Yān,
Yān, fearing Zhào,
would certainly not dare to keep you,
but would bind you and return you to Zhào.
You would do better to bare your upper body and prostrate on the execution block to ask for punishment;
then you might fortunately be pardoned.'
I followed his advice,
and Your Majesty also graciously pardoned me.
I privately consider him a brave man,
with wisdom and strategy,
fit to be sent."
Thereupon, the king summoned him,
and asked Lìn Xiàngrú:
"The King of Qín offers fifteen cities for my jade;
should I give it?"
Xiàngrú said:
"Qín is strong and Zhào weak;
we cannot refuse."
The king said:
"If they take my jade
and do not give me the cities,
what then?"
Xiàngrú said:
"If Qín requests the jade with cities and Zhào refuses,
the fault lies with Zhào.
If Zhào gives the jade and Qín does not give the cities,
the fault lies with Qín.
Weighing these two options,
it is better to agree and place the fault on Qín."
The king said:
"Who can be sent?"
Xiàngrú said:
"If Your Majesty has no one else,
I wish to take the jade and go on this mission.
If the cities go to Zhào, the jade stays in Qín;
if the cities do not come,
I will ensure the jade returns intact to Zhào."
The King of Zhào then sent Xiàngrú west to Qín with the jade.
The King of Qín sat in the Zhāngtái Palace to receive Lìn Xiàngrú,
who presented the jade disk to the King of Qín.
The King of Qín was overjoyed,
and passed it around to his concubines and attendants for them to see;
they all shouted "Long live the king!"
Lìn Xiàngrú saw that the King of Qín had no intention of compensating Zhào with cities,
so he stepped forward and said:
"There is a flaw in the jade,
allow me to show it to Your Majesty."
The king handed him the jade,
whereupon Lìn Xiàngrú, holding it, stepped back and stood still,
leaning against a pillar,
his hair bristling with rage,
and said to the King of Qín:
"Your Majesty desired to obtain the jade disk,
and sent a messenger with a letter to the King of Zhào.
The King of Zhào summoned all his ministers to deliberate,
and they all said,
'Qín is greedy,
and relying on its strength,
seeks the jade with empty promises;
we fear we will not actually receive the cities in return.'
They deliberated and did not wish to give the jade to Qín.
But I believed that even commoners do not deceive each other,
let alone great states!
Moreover, for the sake of a single jade disk to oppose the mighty Qín's goodwill,
would not be right.
Thereupon the King of Zhào fasted for five days,
and then sent me to present the jade disk,
personally bowing to send off the letter in the court.
Why?
To honor the prestige of a great state and show respect.
Now that I have arrived,
Your Majesty receives me in an ordinary hall,
with very arrogant etiquette;
having obtained the jade,
you pass it among your concubines,
to amuse yourselves at my expense.
I observe that Your Majesty has no intention of compensating the King of Zhào with cities,
so I have taken back the jade.
If Your Majesty insists on pressing me,
my head shall now shatter together with the jade against this pillar!"
Lìn Xiàngrú, holding the jade, glanced at the pillar,
intending to dash the jade against it.
The King of Qín, fearing he would break the jade,
apologized and earnestly pleaded,
summoned the official in charge to consult the map,
and pointed out fifteen cities from here onward to give to Zhào.
Lìn Xiàngrú reckoned that the King of Qín was only pretending to give Zhào the cities as a deception,
and that in reality, they would not be obtained,
so he said to the King of Qín:
"The Héshì Jade Disk
is a treasure renowned throughout the world.
The King of Zhào, in awe,
did not dare not to offer it.
When the King of Zhào sent the jade,
he fasted for five days.
Now, Your Majesty should also fast for five days,
and set up the nine宾 ceremony in the court,
then I would dare to present the jade."
The King of Qín considered this,
and realizing he could not seize it by force,
agreed to fast for five days,
and housed Lìn Xiàngrú at the Guǎngchéng Lodge.
Lìn Xiàngrú reckoned that even if the King of Qín fasted,
he would certainly break the promise and not compensate the cities,
so he had his attendant dress in coarse clothing,
conceal the jade on his person,
and flee by a small path,
returning the jade to Zhào.
After the King of Qín had fasted for five days,
he set up the nine宾 ceremony in the court
and ushered in the Zhào ambassador Lìn Xiàngrú.
Lìn Xiàngrú arrived
and said to the King of Qín:
"From Duke Mù onward, Qín has had over twenty rulers,
yet none has ever steadfastly kept a covenant.
I truly feared being deceived by Your Majesty and failing Zhào,
so I have had someone take the jade back,
and it has already reached Zhào by now.
Moreover, Qín is strong and Zhào is weak.
If Your Majesty were to send a single envoy to Zhào,
Zhào would immediately send the jade here.
Now, with Qín's strength, if you first cut off fifteen cities to give to Zhào,
how would Zhào dare to keep the jade and offend Your Majesty?
I know that the crime of deceiving Your Majesty deserves death,
so I request to be thrown into the cauldron.
I only ask that Your Majesty and your ministers carefully consider this."
The King of Qín and his ministers looked at each other and gasped.
Some attendants wanted to drag Lìn Xiàngrú away,
but the King of Qín then said:
"Now if we kill Lìn Xiàngrú,
we still will not obtain the jade,
and it will sever the friendly relations between Qín and Zhào.
It would be better to treat him generously
and send him back to Zhào.
Would the King of Zhào dare deceive Qín over a jade disk!"
Finally, he received Lìn Xiàngrú in court,
completed the ceremonies, and sent him back.
After Lìn Xiàngrú returned,
the King of Zhào considered him a worthy senior official who had not disgraced his state before the feudal lords,
and appointed him as Senior Minister.
Qín did not give the cities to Zhào,
and Zhào ultimately did not give the jade to Qín.
After that, Qín attacked Zhào
and captured Shíchéng.
The following year,
it attacked Zhào again,
killing twenty thousand men.
The King of Qín sent an envoy to inform the King of Zhào,
wishing to meet with him for a friendly gathering at Miǎnchí west of the Yellow River.
The King of Zhào, fearing Qín,
wished not to go.
Lián Pō
and Lìn Xiàngrú advised:
"If Your Majesty does not go,
it will show that Zhào is weak and cowardly."
The King of Zhào then proceeded,
accompanied by Lìn Xiàngrú.
Lián Pō saw them off to the border,
and bade farewell to the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, on this journey,
I estimate the travel and the duration of the meeting ceremonies
will take no more than thirty days to return.
If you do not return in thirty days,
I request that we establish the crown prince as king,
to thwart Qín's ambitions."
The king agreed,
and then met with the King of Qín at Miǎnchí.
The King of Qín, feasting and drunk,
said:
"I have privately heard that the King of Zhào is fond of music;
please play the sè."
The King of Zhào played the sè.
The Qín historian came forward and recorded:
"On such-and-such date,
the King of Qín feasted with the King of Zhào
and commanded the King of Zhào to play the sè."
Lìn Xiàngrú came forward and said:
"The King of Zhào has privately heard that the King of Qín is skilled in Qín music;
I request that you perform on the pot for us,
for mutual entertainment."
The King of Qín grew angry
and refused.
Thereupon Lìn Xiàngrú came forward with the pot,
and kneeling, requested the King of Qín.
The King of Qín would not strike the pot.
Lìn Xiàngrú said:
"Within five paces,
I can bespatter Your Majesty with the blood from my neck!"
The attendants wanted to cut down Lìn Xiàngrú,
but he glared and shouted at them,
causing them to retreat.
Thereupon the King of Qín, displeased,
struck the pot once.
Lìn Xiàngrú turned and summoned the Zhào historian to record:
"On such-and-such date,
the King of Qín struck the pot for the King of Zhào."
The Qín ministers said:
"We request that Zhào offer fifteen cities to the King of Qín as a birthday gift."
Lìn Xiàngrú also said:
"We request that Qín offer its capital Xiányáng to the King of Zhào as a birthday gift."
The King of Qín completed the feast
but ultimately could not gain the upper hand over Zhào.
Zhào had also heavily deployed troops in preparation against Qín,
so Qín did not dare to act.
After returning to the state,
due to Lìn Xiàngrú's great merit,
he was appointed as senior minister,
ranking above Lián Pō.
Lián Pō said:
"As a general of Zhào,
I have achieved great merits in攻城野战,
while Lìn Xiàngrú merely contributed through rhetoric,
yet he ranks above me.
Moreover, Xiàngrú was originally a lowly man,
I feel ashamed,
and cannot bear to be beneath him."
He declared:
"If I meet Xiàngrú,
I will surely humiliate him."
Xiàngrú heard this,
and refused to meet with him.
Whenever attending court,
Xiàngrú often claimed illness,
not wishing to compete for precedence with Lián Pō.
Later when Xiàngrú went out,
and saw Lián Pō approaching,
he would steer his carriage aside to avoid him.
Thereupon his retainers jointly remonstrated:
"The reason we left our relatives to serve you,
was solely because we admired your noble righteousness.
Now you and Lián Pō hold equal rank,
yet when he speaks ill and you fear and hide from him,
your fear is excessive.
Even ordinary men would be ashamed of this,
let alone a general and minister!
We are unworthy,
and request to take our leave."
Lìn Xiàngrú firmly stopped them,
saying:
"In your view, how does General Lián compare to the King of Qín?"
They replied:
"He is not equal."
Xiàngrú said:
"With the King of Qín's authority,
I publicly rebuked him in court,
and humiliated his ministers.
Though I am incompetent,
would I alone fear General Lián?
But I consider this:
the reason mighty Qín dares not attack Zhào,
is solely because both of us are here.
If two tigers fight,
inevitably neither will survive.
The reason I act this way,
is to put the state's urgency before personal grudges."
Lián Pō heard this,
bared his upper body and carried brambles,
and through intermediaries went to Lìn Xiàngrú's gate to apologize.
Saying:
"I am a crude and lowly man,
who did not know the general was so magnanimous."
Finally they became friends,
sworn to death.
That year,
Lián Pō attacked Qí eastward,
defeating one of its armies.
After two years,
Lián Pō again attacked Qí's Jī,
capturing it.
Three years later,
Lián Pō attacked Wèi's Fánglíng
and Ānyáng,
capturing them.
Four years later,
Lìn Xiàngrú led troops to attack Qí,
but halted at Píngyì.
The next year,
Zhào Shē defeated the Qín army at Yānyǔ.
Zhào Shē
was an official in Zhào's land department.
When collecting taxes, Lord Píngyuán's household refused to pay,
Shē enforced the law against them,
executing nine of Lord Píngyuán's stewards.
Lord Píngyuán was enraged,
and intended to kill Shē.
Shē thereupon persuaded him:
"You are a noble scion of Zhào,
if your household evades public duty, the law weakens,
if the law weakens, the state weakens,
if the state weakens, other states will attack,
if other states attack, Zhào will perish,
how then could you maintain this wealth?
With your nobility,
if you uphold public duty according to law, all will be equitable,
if all are equitable, the state strengthens,
if the state strengthens, Zhào is secure,
and you as a noble relative,
would you be lightly regarded by the world?"
Lord Píngyuán considered him worthy,
and recommended him to the king.
The king employed him to manage state taxes,
state taxes became well-regulated,
the people prospered and treasuries were full.
When Qín attacked Hán,
stationing troops at Yānyǔ,
the king summoned Lián Pō and asked:
"Can we rescue them?"
He replied:
"The road is long, perilous and narrow,
rescue is difficult."
He also summoned Yuè Chéng and asked him,
Yuè Chéng's reply matched Lián Pō's.
He then summoned and asked Zhào Shē,
Shē replied:
"Though the road is long and narrow,
it's like two rats fighting in a hole -
the braver general wins."
The king then ordered Zhào Shē to lead troops,
to rescue them.
The army marched thirty lǐ from Hándān,
and he ordered the troops:
"Anyone advising on military matters will die."
The Qín army camped west of Wǔ'ān,
their drums and shouts drilling troops
shook all the roof tiles in Wǔ'ān.
A scout in the army urged urgently rescuing Wǔ'ān,
Zhào Shē immediately beheaded him.
He fortified defenses,
remaining stationary for twenty-eight days,
further increasing fortifications.
When a Qín spy entered,
Zhào Shē treated him well and sent him back.
The spy reported to the Qín general,
who greatly rejoiced:
"They halted thirty lǐ from their capital,
and increased fortifications -
Yānyǔ is no longer Zhào territory."
After sending away the Qín spy,
Zhào Shē lightened gear and advanced rapidly,
reaching in two days and one night,
stationing skilled archers fifty lǐ from Yānyǔ.
Once camp was fortified,
the Qín forces learned of it,
and came in full armor.
Soldier Xǔ Lì requested to advise on military matters,
Zhào Shē said:
"Let him in."
Xǔ Lì said:
"The Qín forces didn't expect Zhào troops here,
their advancing morale is high,
general must densely array formations to await them.
Otherwise,
we will surely be defeated."
Zhào Shē said:
"I accept your advice."
Xǔ Lì said:
"I request execution by axe."
Zhào Shē said:
"Await later orders in Hándān."
Xǔ Lì again requested to advise,
saying:
"Whoever first occupies the north mountain wins,
latecomers lose."
Zhào Shē agreed,
immediately sending ten thousand troops to seize it.
Qín troops arrived later,
failed to capture the hill in contention,
Zhào Shē unleashed troops attacking them,
decisively defeating the Qín army.
The Qín forces scattered and fled,
thus lifting the siege of Yānyǔ before returning.
King Wén of Zhào bestowed upon Shē the title Lord Mǎfú,
appointing Xǔ Lì as commandant.
Thus Zhào Shē
held equal rank with Lián Pō and Lìn Xiàngrú.
Four years later,
King Huìwén of Zhào died,
and his son King Xiàochéng ascended the throne.
In the seventh year of his reign,
Qín and Zhào armies confronted each other at Chángpíng.
By then, Zhào Shē had already died,
and Lìn Xiàngrú was gravely ill.
Zhào sent Lián Pō to command the attack against Qín,
but Qín repeatedly defeated the Zhào army,
so the Zhào forces fortified their positions and refused to engage in battle.
Qín repeatedly challenged them to fight,
but Lián Pō would not comply.
The King of Zhào believed Qín's spies.
Qín's spies said:
"What Qín fears
is only that Mǎfújūn Zhào Shē's son Zhào Kuò might be appointed as general."
The King of Zhào therefore made Kuò the general,
replacing Lián Pō.
Lìn Xiàngrú said:
"Your Majesty is appointing Kuò based on reputation,
which is like gluing the tuning pegs when playing the sè.
Kuò can only read his father's books on military strategy,
but does not know how to adapt to changing circumstances."
The King of Zhào did not listen,
and thus appointed him.
Zhào Kuò had studied military strategy since youth,
discussing warfare,
believing that no one in the world could match him.
He once discussed military affairs with his father Shē,
and though Shē could not refute him,
he did not consider him good.
Kuò's mother asked Shē the reason,
and Shē said:
"Warfare
is a matter of life and death,
yet Kuò speaks of it lightly.
If Zhào does not make Kuò a general, that's fine;
but if he must be appointed,
the one who will destroy the Zhào army will surely be Kuò."
When Kuò was about to depart,
his mother submitted a letter to the king, saying:
"Kuò should not be made a general."
The king said:
"Why?"
She replied:
"When I first served his father,
he was then a general.
Those he personally served food and drink numbered in the tens,
those he treated as friends numbered in the hundreds,
and all the rewards from Your Majesty and the royal family he gave to his officers and officials.
From the day he received his commission,
he never inquired about family affairs.
Now that Kuò has suddenly become a general,
he faces east to receive his officers,
and none of them dare look up at him.
The gold and silk bestowed by Your Majesty
he takes home to store,
and daily looks for advantageous fields and houses to buy.
What does Your Majesty think of him compared to his father?
Father and son have different mindsets;
I hope Your Majesty will not send him."
The king said:
"Set this aside, mother,
I have already decided."
Kuò's mother then said:
"If Your Majesty ultimately sends him,
and if he proves unworthy,
may I not be implicated?"
The king promised.
After Zhào Kuò replaced Lián Pō,
he completely changed the regulations
and replaced the military officers.
When the Qín general Bái Qǐ heard this,
he deployed surprise troops,
feigned defeat and retreat,
cut off their supply routes,
divided their army into two,
causing the soldiers to lose morale.
After more than forty days,
the army starved,
and Zhào Kuò led elite troops to personally engage in combat.
The Qín army shot and killed Zhào Kuò.
Kuò's army was defeated,
and hundreds of thousands of troops surrendered to Qín,
who buried them all alive.
The total number of casualties for Zhào before and after was four hundred and fifty thousand.
The following year,
Qín troops besieged Hándān,
for over a year,
nearly causing its fall.
Thanks to the rescue by the states of Chǔ
and Wèi,
the siege of Hándān was lifted.
The King of Zhào, because of Kuò's mother's prior words,
ultimately did not execute her.
Five years after the siege of Hándān was lifted,
Yān, following Lì Fù's strategy,
said
"Zhào's strong men were all lost at Chángpíng,
and their orphans have not yet grown,"
and raised an army to attack Zhào.
Zhào sent Lián Pō as general,
who attacked and heavily defeated the Yān army at Hào,
killed Lì Fù,
and then besieged Yān.
Yān ceded five cities to seek peace,
and Zhào agreed.
Zhào enfeoffed Lián Pō as Lord Xìnpíng with Wèiwén,
and made him acting chancellor.
When Lián Pō was dismissed from Chángpíng and returned,
in his time of lost influence,
all his former clients left.
When he was reappointed as general,
the clients returned.
Lián Pō said:
"Guests, leave!"
A client said:
"Alas!
Why do you see this so late?
The world interacts like a market;
when you have power,
we follow you;
when you have no power, we leave.
This is the natural way of things;
what is there to resent?"
After six years,
Zhào sent Lián Pō to attack Fányáng of Wèi,
and he captured it.
King Xiàochéng of Zhào died,
and his son King Dàoxiāng ascended the throne,
appointing Yuè Chéng to replace Lián Pō.
Lián Pō was angry,
attacked Yuè Chéng,
and Yuè Chéng fled.
Lián Pō then fled to Dàliáng of Wèi.
The following year,
Zhào appointed Lǐ Mù as general to attack Yān,
capturing Wǔsuì
and Fāngchéng.
Lián Pō stayed in Liáng for a long time,
but Wèi did not trust or employ him.
As Zhào was repeatedly hard-pressed by Qín troops,
the King of Zhào thought of regaining Lián Pō's services,
and Lián Pō also wished to serve Zhào again.
The King of Zhào sent an envoy to see if Lián Pō was still usable.
Lián Pō's enemy Guō Kāi gave the envoy much gold
to slander him.
When the Zhào envoy saw Lián Pō,
Lián Pō ate a dǒu of rice in one meal,
ten catties of meat,
donned armor, and mounted his horse
to show he was still fit for service.
The Zhào envoy returned and reported to the king:
"General Lián, though old,
still eats heartily,
but while sitting with me,
he defecated three times in a short while."
The king thought him too old,
and thus did not summon him.
Chǔ heard that Lián Pō was in Wèi,
and secretly sent someone to welcome him.
Once Lián Pō became a general of Chǔ,
he achieved no merits,
saying:
"I wish to command Zhào men."
Lián Pō eventually died in Shòuchūn.
Lǐ Mù was
a fine general stationed at Zhào's northern frontier.
He often resided in Dài and Yànmén,
guarding against the Xiōngnú.
He appointed officials based on expediency,
diverting all market taxes to his headquarters,
to cover military expenses.
He had several cattle slaughtered daily to feast his troops,
drilled them in archery and cavalry skills,
maintained vigilant beacon fires,
deployed numerous spies,
and treated his soldiers generously.
He established this regulation:
"When the Xiōngnú come raiding,
quickly retreat to defensive positions.
Anyone who dares capture enemies will be executed."
Whenever the Xiōngnú invaded,
beacon fires would alert them,
and they'd immediately retreat to safety,
not daring to engage in battle.
This continued for several years,
with no losses incurred.
However, the Xiōngnú considered Lǐ Mù cowardly,
and even Zhào's frontier troops thought their general timid.
The King of Zhào reprimanded Lǐ Mù,
but Lǐ Mù persisted in his ways.
The King grew angry,
recalled him,
and appointed another general in his place.
Over a year later,
whenever the Xiōngnú came,
the new general would engage them.
In these battles,
they suffered repeated defeats,
with heavy casualties,
making farming and herding impossible along the border.
They requested Lǐ Mù's return.
Lǐ Mù shut his door and refused to emerge,
firmly claiming illness.
The King of Zhào then forcibly reinstated him to command the troops.
Lǐ Mù said:
"If Your Majesty must employ me,
I will only follow my previous methods,
then dare I accept the command."
The King agreed.
When Lǐ Mù arrived,
he maintained his former regulations.
For several years, the Xiōngnú gained nothing.
They still thought him cowardly.
The frontier soldiers received daily rewards without fighting,
and all yearned for a battle.
Thereupon, he selected 1,300 chariots,
13,000 cavalry horses,
50,000 elite soldiers worth a hundred gold each,
and 100,000 archers,
drilling them all in combat.
He then released livestock widely,
filling the fields with people.
When the Xiōngnú raided in small numbers,
he feigned defeat,
sacrificing several thousand men.
The Chányú heard of this,
and led a massive force to invade.
Lǐ Mù deployed many unusual formations,
extending left and right wings to attack them,
crushing and killing over 100,000 Xiōngnú cavalry.
He annihilated the Dān,
defeated the Dōnghú,
subdued the Línhú,
and sent the Chányú fleeing.
For over ten years after,
the Xiōngnú dared not approach Zhào's border cities.
In the first year of Zhào Dàoxiāng Wáng's reign,
after Lián Pō had fled to Wèi,
Zhào sent Lǐ Mù to attack Yān,
capturing Wǔsuì
and Fāngchéng.
Two years later,
Páng Xuān defeated the Yān army,
killing Jù Xīn.
Seven years later,
Qín defeated and killed Zhào's general Hù Zhé at Wǔsuì,
beheading 100,000.
Zhào then appointed Lǐ Mù as Grand General,
to attack the Qín army at Yí'ān,
where he crushed them,
routing Qín's general Huán Yǐ.
He was enfeoffed as Lord Wǔ'ān.
Three years later,
when Qín attacked Pānwú,
Lǐ Mù defeated the Qín army,
repelling Hán
and Wèi to the south.
In the seventh year of Zhào Wáng Qiān's reign,
Qín sent Wáng Jiǎn to attack Zhào,
and Zhào dispatched Lǐ Mù
and Sīmǎ Shàng to defend.
Qín bribed the King of Zhào's favorite, Guō Kāi, with much gold,
to sow discord,
claiming that Lǐ Mù
and Sīmǎ Shàng intended to rebel.
The King of Zhào then sent Zhào Cōng and Qí's general Yán Jù to replace Lǐ Mù.
Lǐ Mù refused the order,
so Zhào sent men to secretly capture him,
and executed him.
They dismissed Sīmǎ Shàng.
Three months later,
Wáng Jiǎn pressed a fierce attack on Zhào,
crushing and killing Zhào Cōng,
capturing King Qiān of Zhào and his general Yán Jù,
and thus destroyed Zhào.
The Grand Historian remarks:
To know death is inevitable makes one brave;
it's not that dying is hard,
but facing death rightly is difficult.
When Lìn Xiàngrú held the jade and glared at the pillar,
and shouted at the King of Qín's attendants,
he risked nothing more than execution,
yet some men would be too timid to act.
Xiàngrú, rousing his courage,
awed the enemy state with his authority,
and later yielded to Lián Pō,
his fame weighty as Tài Shān.
In his exercise of wisdom and courage,
he may be said to have combined both!
Tián Dān was
a distant relative of the Tián clan in Qí.
During King Mǐn's time,
he served as a minor official in Línzī's market,
unnoticed.
When Yān sent Yuè Yì to attack and defeat Qí,
King Mǐn of Qí fled,
later taking refuge in Jǔ City.
The Yān army swept through Qí,
and Tián Dān retreated to Ānpíng,
ordering his clansmen to cut the ends of their chariot axles and fit them with iron caps.
When the Yān army attacked Ānpíng,
the walls crumbled,
the people of Qí fled,
scrambling for the roads,
their chariots breaking as axle ends snapped,
and they were captured by Yān.
Only Tián Dān's clan, due to the iron caps, escaped,
retreating east to hold Jímò.
After Yān had subdued all other Qí cities,
only Jǔ
and Jímò remained unyielding.
The Yān army, hearing the King of Qí was in Jǔ,
concentrated their attack there.
After Nào Chǐ killed King Mǐn in Jǔ,
they held firm,
resisting the Yān army,
for years without falling.
Yān then turned east to besiege Jímò,
where the city's chief went out to fight,
and died in defeat.
The townspeople together recommended Tián Dān,
saying:
"At the battle of Ānpíng,
Tián Dān's clan was saved by the iron caps,
showing military expertise."
They appointed him general,
to defend Jímò against Yān.
Soon after,
King Zhāo of Yān died,
and King Huì ascended,
who had a rift with Yuè Yì.
Tián Dān, hearing this,
spread discord in Yān,
declaring:
"The King of Qí is dead,
and only two cities remain uncaptured.
Yuè Yì fears execution and dares not return,
using the campaign against Qí as a pretext,
while actually intending to keep his troops and rule Qí as king.
The people of Qí have not yet submitted,
so he's delaying the attack on Jímò to await his chance.
What the Qí people fear
is that another general will come,
and then Jímò will be destroyed."
The King of Yān believed this,
and sent Qí Jié to replace Yuè Yì.
Yuè Yì thus returned to Zhào,
and the officers and soldiers of Yān were resentful.
Then Tián Dān ordered the people in the city to always make offerings to their ancestors in the courtyards when eating,
causing flocks of birds to soar, dance, and descend to feed in the city.
The Yān people found this strange.
Tián Dān then declared:
"A deity has descended to instruct me."
He then commanded the people in the city:
"There will be a divine being who shall be our teacher."
One soldier said:
"Can I serve as the teacher?"
and then turned to run away.
Tián Dān then rose,
led him back,
seated him facing east,
and served him as a teacher.
The soldier said:
"I deceived you, my lord,
I truly have no ability."
Tián Dān said:
"Say no more!"
and thus took him as his teacher.
Whenever he issued orders and regulations,
he always referred to the divine teacher.
He then proclaimed:
"I only fear that the Yān army will cut off the noses of the captured Qí soldiers,
place them in the front lines,
and fight against us;
then Jímò will be defeated."
The Yān people heard this,
and acted accordingly.
When the people in the city saw that all the surrendered Qí soldiers had their noses cut off,
they were enraged,
stood firm in defense,
fearing only to be captured.
Tián Dān also spread counter-intelligence, saying:
"I fear that the Yān people will dig up the graves outside our city,
desecrating our ancestors;
it would be heartbreaking."
The Yān army dug up all the graves,
and burned the dead.
When the people of Jímò saw this from the city walls,
they all wept,
and were eager to go out and fight,
their fury increasing tenfold.
Tián Dān knew that the soldiers could be used,
so he personally carried construction tools,
shared the labor with the soldiers,
had his wives and concubines join the ranks,
and distributed all food and drink to feast the troops.
He ordered the armored soldiers to hide,
and had the elderly, weak, and women man the walls,
then sent an envoy to arrange surrender with Yān,
and the Yān army all cheered "Wànsuì."
Tián Dān also collected gold from the people,
obtaining a thousand yì,
and ordered the wealthy of Jímò to present it to the Yān general,
saying:
"Jímò is about to surrender,
we hope you will not plunder our families and wives,
and allow us to live in peace."
The Yān general was greatly pleased,
and agreed.
The Yān army thus became even more lax.
Tián Dān then gathered over a thousand oxen from the city,
dressed them in crimson silk,
painted with multicolored dragon patterns,
tied sharp blades to their horns,
and tied oil-soaked reeds to their tails,
setting the ends on fire.
Dozens of openings were made in the city walls,
and at night the oxen were released,
with five thousand warriors following behind.
The ox tails grew hot,
and the oxen charged furiously into the Yān army,
which was greatly startled in the night.
The torchlight from the ox tails was dazzlingly bright,
and the Yān army saw what appeared to be dragon patterns,
and all those touched were killed or wounded.
The five thousand men then advanced silently to attack,
while those in the city shouted and followed,
with the old and weak beating bronze vessels to make noise,
the sound shaking heaven and earth.
The Yān army was terrified,
defeated and fled.
The Qí people then killed their general Qí Jié.
The Yān army was thrown into chaos and fled,
while the Qí pursued the fleeing enemy,
and all the cities and towns they passed rebelled against Yān and returned to Tián Dān,
his forces growing daily,
and riding on the momentum of victory,
Yān was defeated and destroyed day by day,
until they reached the river,
and over seventy cities of Qí were restored to Qí.
They then welcomed King Xiāng from Jǔ,
and he entered Línzī to govern.
King Xiāng enfeoffed Tián Dān,
bestowing the title Lord Ānpíng.
The Grand Historian remarks:
In war, one engages with orthodox tactics,
and prevails with unorthodox strategies.
Those who excel at it
produce unorthodox moves endlessly.
The orthodox and unorthodox mutually generate each other,
like a ring without end.
At first, be like a maiden,
causing the enemy to open his door;
later, be like a fleeing hare,
making the enemy unable to resist:
this describes Tián Dān!
Earlier,
when Nào Chǐ killed King Mǐn,
the people of Jǔ sought King Mǐn's son Fǎ Zhāng,
and found him at the home of Grand Historian Jiǎo,
where he was working as a gardener.
Jiǎo's daughter pitied him and treated him well.
Later, Fǎ Zhāng privately told her his feelings,
and she then became intimate with him.
When the people of Jǔ together established Fǎ Zhāng as King of Qí,
and used Jǔ to resist Yān,
the daughter of the Grand Historian clan then became queen,
known as
"Queen Jūnwáng."
When Yān first invaded Qí,
hearing that Wáng Zhú of Huàyì was virtuous,
they ordered the army:
"Do not enter within thirty lǐ of Huàyì,"
out of respect for Wáng Zhú.
Later, they sent a messenger to tell Zhú:
"Many in Qí praise your righteousness,
we appoint you as a general,
and grant you a fief of ten thousand households."
Zhú firmly declined.
The Yān people said:
"If you do not comply,
we will lead our army to massacre Huàyì."
Wáng Zhú said:
"A loyal minister does not serve two rulers,
a chaste woman does not marry two husbands.
The King of Qí did not heed my advice,
so I withdrew to farm in the countryside.
Now that the state is destroyed and lost,
I cannot preserve it;
and now you coerce me with troops to be your general,
that is to aid a tyrant in his violence.
Rather than live without righteousness,
it is better to be boiled alive!"
He then hung his neck on a tree branch,
and with a forceful struggle, broke his neck and died.
The lost officials of Qí heard of this,
and said:
"Wáng Zhú,
a commoner,
righteously refused to submit to Yān,
how much more should those in office and receiving salaries do so!"
They then gathered and went to Jǔ,
sought out the princes,
and established one as King Xiāng.
Lǔ Zhòng Lián,
was a man of Qí.
He delighted in remarkable and unconventional strategies,
but refused to hold office or take up appointments,
preferring to uphold high principles.
He traveled to Zhào.
During the time of King Xiàochéng of Zhào,
the King of Qín sent Bái Qǐ to defeat the Zhào army at Chángpíng, killing over four hundred thousand before and after,
and the Qín troops then advanced east to besiege Hándān.
The King of Zhào was afraid,
and the rescue forces from the other states did not dare to attack the Qín army.
King Ānlí of Wèi sent General Jìn Bǐ to rescue Zhào,
but he feared Qín,
and halted at Dàngyīn without advancing.
The King of Wèi sent the guest general Xīnyuán Yǎn to sneak into Hándān,
and through Lord Píngyuán, he said to the King of Zhào:
"The reason Qín urgently besieges Zhào is that
previously, they contended with King Mǐn of Qí for supremacy and both declared themselves emperors,
but later gave up the title;
now Qí has grown weaker,
and currently only Qín dominates the world,
so this is not necessarily about coveting Hándān,
their intention is to seek again to become emperor.
If Zhào sincerely sends an envoy to honor King Zhāo of Qín as emperor,
Qín will surely be pleased,
and withdraw its troops."
Lord Píngyuán hesitated and could not decide.
At this time, Lǔ Zhònglián happened to be traveling in Zhào,
when Qín besieged Zhào.
Hearing that Wèi's general wanted to make Zhào honor Qín as emperor,
he went to see Lord Píngyuán, saying:
"What is to be done about the situation?"
Lord Píngyuán replied:
"How dare Shèng speak of affairs!
Previously we lost four hundred thousand troops abroad,
and now we are besieged within Hándān with no means of escape.
The King of Wèi sent visiting general Xīnyuán Yǎn to make Zhào acknowledge Qín as emperor,
and now this man is here.
How dare Shèng speak of affairs!"
Lǔ Zhònglián said:
"I initially considered you to be a worthy lord of the realm,
but only now do I realize you are not a worthy lord of the realm.
Where is the visitor from Liáng, Xīnyuán Yǎn?
I beg to reprimand him on your behalf and send him back."
Lord Píngyuán said:
"Shèng requests to introduce him to meet you, sir."
Lord Píngyuán then went to see Xīnyuán Yǎn, saying:
"There is a gentleman Lǔ Zhònglián from the eastern state,
now this man is here,
Shèng requests to introduce him,
to make acquaintance with the general."
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"I have heard of gentleman Lǔ Zhònglián,
a noble scholar of Qí state.
Yǎn is a mere servant,
on a mission with official duties,
I do not wish to meet gentleman Lǔ Zhònglián."
Lord Píngyuán said:
"Shèng has already revealed it."
Xīnyuán Yǎn consented.
Lǔ Lián met Xīnyuán Yǎn but remained silent.
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"I observe that those staying in this besieged city
all have requests of Lord Píngyuán;
now observing your jade-like countenance,
you appear to have no requests of Lord Píngyuán,
why do you remain long in this besieged city without leaving?"
Lǔ Zhònglián said:
"The world considers Bào Jiāo as one who died without followers to praise him,
but this is all wrong.
Common people don't understand,
thinking he acted only for himself.
That Qín
is a state that discards ritual and righteousness while exalting military achievements,
using power to command its officers,
treating its people like captives.
If they presumptuously become emperor,
and mistakenly govern the world,
then Lián would rather tread the Eastern Sea and die
than bear being their subject.
The reason I seek to see the general
is to wish to help Zhào."
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"How will you help them, sir?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"I will make Liáng and Yān assist them,
while Qí and Chǔ will certainly help."
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"As for Yān, I believe they will follow;
but as for Liáng,
I am from Liáng myself,
how can you, sir, make Liáng assist them?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"Liáng has not yet witnessed the harm of Qín declaring itself emperor.
If Liáng saw the harm of Qín declaring itself emperor,
then it would certainly help Zhào."
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"What harm would come from Qín declaring itself emperor?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"Formerly, King Wēi of Qí practiced benevolence and righteousness,
leading the feudal lords to pay homage to Zhōu.
Zhōu was poor and weak,
yet none of the feudal lords paid homage,
only Qí alone paid homage.
After over a year,
King Liè of Zhōu died,
Qí arrived late,
Zhōu was angry,
and sent a message to Qí saying:
'Heaven collapses and earth splits,
the Son of Heaven has left his mat.
The eastern vassal Yīn Qí arrived late,
he should be beheaded.'
King Wēi of Qí flared up in anger:
'Bah!
Your mother was a slave!'
He ultimately became the laughingstock of the world.
Thus while alive he paid homage to Zhōu,
but when dead he cursed it,
truly unable to bear their demands.
That Son of Heaven was like that,
it's nothing strange."
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"Sir, have you not seen servants?
When ten men follow one man,
is it because their strength is inferior or wisdom lacking?
It is because they fear him."
Lǔ Zhònglián said:
"Alas!
Is Liáng compared to Qín like a servant?"
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"Yes."
Lǔ Zhònglián said:
"I will make the King of Qín boil and mince the King of Liáng."
Xīnyuán Yǎn looked displeased,
saying:
"Ah,
your words go too far, sir!
How can you, sir, make the King of Qín boil and mince the King of Liáng?"
Lǔ Zhònglián said:
"Certainly,
I will explain.
Formerly, Jiǔ Hóu,
È Hóu,
and King Wén
were the three ministers of Zhòu.
Jiǔ Hóu had a beautiful daughter,
and presented her to Zhòu,
but Zhòu considered her ugly,
so he minced Jiǔ Hóu.
È Hóu strongly disputed this,
arguing vehemently,
so he dried È Hóu's flesh.
King Wén heard of this,
sighed deeply,
so he was confined in the Yǒulǐ prison for a hundred days,
intending to make him die.
Why is it that when all are called kings,
they end up in places of dried flesh and mincemeat?
When King Mǐn of Qí went to Lǔ,
Yíwéizi followed holding the whip,
and said to the people of Lǔ:
'How will you receive our lord?'
The people of Lǔ said:
'We will receive your lord with ten grand sacrificial offerings.'
Yíwéizi said:
'Where did you get this ritual to receive our lord?
That lord of ours
is the Son of Heaven.
When the Son of Heaven tours,
feudal lords vacate their palaces,
hand over the keys,
arrange their garments and hold the tables,
serve meals below the hall,
and only after the Son of Heaven has eaten
do they withdraw to attend court.'
The people of Lǔ locked their gates,
and refused him entry.
Unable to enter Lǔ,
he planned to go to Xuē,
passing through Zōu.
At that time,
the lord of Zōu had died,
and King Mǐn wished to pay condolences,
Yíwéizi said to the orphaned heir of Zōu:
'When the Son of Heaven condoles,
the host must move the coffin to the opposite position,
set it facing north with the south behind,
then the Son of Heaven faces south to condole.'
The ministers of Zōu said:
'If it must be like this,
we would rather fall on our swords and die.'
So he ultimately dared not enter Zōu.
The ministers of Zōu and Lǔ,
while alive could not properly serve their lords,
when dead could not provide proper funeral clothes,
yet when they wanted to perform Son of Heaven rituals in Zōu
and Lǔ, the ministers of Zōu
and Lǔ refused them entry.
Now Qín is a state of ten thousand chariots,
Liáng is also a state of ten thousand chariots.
Both occupy states of ten thousand chariots,
each has the name of king,
yet seeing them win one battle,
you wish to follow and make them emperor -
this makes the ministers of the Three Jìn inferior to the servants of Zōu
and Lǔ.
Moreover, if Qín becomes emperor without restraint,
it will replace the ministers of feudal lords.
They will remove those they consider unworthy and install those they consider worthy,
remove those they hate and install those they love.
They will also make their daughters and slandering concubines feudal lords' consorts,
residing in Liáng's palaces.
How could the King of Liáng peacefully remain as before?
And how could you, general, retain your former favor?"
Thereupon Xīnyuán Yǎn rose,
bowed twice and apologized, saying:
"At first I took you, sir, for an ordinary man,
but today I have come to know you as a scholar of the empire.
I beg to take my leave,
and dare not speak again of making Qín an emperor."
When the Qín generals heard of this,
they withdrew their army fifty lǐ.
It so happened that Lord Wújì of Wèi seized Jìn Bǐ's army to rescue Zhào,
attacked the Qín army,
and the Qín army then withdrew and departed.
Thereupon Lord Píngyuán wished to enfeoff Lǔ Lián,
