but Lǔ Lián declined the offer three times,
and ultimately refused to accept.
Lord Píngyuán then set out wine,
and when the drinking was at its height, he came forward,
presenting a thousand pieces of gold as a longevity gift to Lǔ Lián.
Lǔ Lián laughed and said:
"What is valued in the scholars of the empire
is their ability to resolve troubles, dispel difficulties, and untangle chaos without seeking reward.
If there is any seeking of reward,
that is the business of merchants,
and Lián cannot bear to do such a thing."
Thereupon he took leave of Lord Píngyuán and departed,
never to be seen again for the rest of his life.
More than twenty years later,
a Yān general captured Liáochéng,
but someone from Liáochéng slandered him to Yān,
and the Yān general, fearing execution,
thus guarded and held Liáochéng,
not daring to return.
Tián Dān of Qí attacked Liáochéng for over a year,
with many soldiers dying yet Liáochéng not falling.
Lǔ Lián then wrote a letter,
tied it to an arrow and shot it into the city,
addressing the Yān general.
The letter said:
I have heard that
the wise do not oppose the times and abandon advantage,
the brave do not shrink from death and destroy their reputation,
and the loyal ministers do not put themselves before their lord.
Now you act on a moment's anger,
disregarding that the King of Yān is without his minister—
this is not loyalty;
to cause your own death and the loss of Liáochéng,
with your might not trusted by Qí—
this is not bravery;
with achievements ruined and reputation destroyed,
and no praise from later generations—
this is not wisdom.
Those who possess these three faults will not be employed by the lords of the age,
nor recorded by persuasive scholars.
Therefore, the wise do not reconsider their plans twice,
and the brave do not fear death.
Now life and death, honor and disgrace,
nobility and baseness, respect and humility—
this moment will not come again.
I hope you will consider this in detail and not follow the common way.
Moreover, Chǔ attacked Qí's Nányáng,
Wèi attacked Pínglù,
yet Qí had no intention to face south in resistance,
believing that the harm of losing Nányáng was small
compared to the great advantage of gaining Jìběi,
and thus settled on this plan after careful consideration.
Now the Qín troops have moved down,
and Wèi dares not look eastward;
the situation of Héng Qín is established,
and Chǔ's position is precarious;
Qí abandoned Nányáng,
cut off the right territory,
and secured Jìběi—
this plan is still being pursued.
Moreover, Qí's resolve concerning Liáochéng is firm,
so do not reconsider.
Now both Chǔ and Wèi have withdrawn from Qí,
and Yān's rescue does not come.
With the full force of Qí's army,
and no threats from the rest of the empire,
to hold out in Liáochéng against a year-long siege's exhaustion,
then I foresee that you will not succeed.
Furthermore, Yān is in great turmoil,
with its ruler and ministers having lost their strategy,
and high and low alike confused.
Lì Fù with a host of a hundred thousand suffered five defeats abroad,
and a state of ten thousand chariots was besieged by Zhào,
with territory reduced and the ruler distressed,
becoming a laughingstock of the empire.
The state is exhausted and disasters abound,
and the people have nowhere to place their loyalty.
Now you, with the weary people of Liáochéng, resist the full force of Qí's army—
this is a defense like Mò Dí's.
Eating human flesh and using bones for fuel,
yet the soldiers have no thought of turning outward—
this is an army like Sūn Bìn's.
This can be seen by the whole empire.
Even so,
for your sake,
it would be better to preserve your chariots and armor and return to Yān.
With chariots and armor intact upon returning to Yān,
the King of Yān will surely be pleased;
returning to your state with your person safe,
the officers and people will welcome you like parents,
and your friends will roll up their sleeves and speak of you in the world,
making your achievements clear.
Above, you can assist the orphaned lord to control his ministers,
below, nourish the common people to supply persuasive scholars,
rectify the state and reform customs,
and establish merit and fame.
Or, if you have no such intention, then abandon Yān and ignore the world,
and travel east to Qí?
There, land would be apportioned and a fief confirmed,
making you as rich as in Táo
and Wèi, called 'the solitary one' for generations,
existing long with Qí—
this is another plan.
These two plans
bring clear fame and substantial gain.
I hope you will consider them in detail and carefully choose one.
Moreover, I have heard that
those who fuss over minor points of integrity cannot achieve glorious fame,
and those who detest small shames cannot accomplish great deeds.
In the past, Guǎn Yíwú shot Duke Huán and hit his belt hook—
that was treason;
he failed to die for Prince Jiǔ—
that was cowardice;
he was bound in fetters—
that was disgrace.
With such three behaviors,
lords of the age would not employ him, and his village would not associate with him.
Had Guǎnzǐ remained imprisoned and not been released,
dying without returning to Qí,
then his name would not have escaped being that of a disgraced man with base conduct.
Even slaves would be ashamed to share his name,
let alone the世俗!
Thus Guǎnzǐ was not ashamed to be in bonds but ashamed that the empire was not well-governed;
he was not ashamed of not dying for Prince Jiǔ but ashamed that his might was not trusted among the feudal lords.
So he overcame the faults of those three behaviors and became the leader of the Five Hegemons,
with his name towering over the empire and his light shining on neighboring states.
Cáozǐ was a general of Lǔ,
fought three battles and fled three times,
losing five hundred lǐ of territory.
Had Cáozǐ then resolved not to look back,
decided not to turn around,
cut his throat and died,
then his name would not have escaped being that of a defeated general captured in war.
But Cáozǐ set aside the shame of three defeats,
and retired to plan with the ruler of Lǔ.
When Duke Huán assembled the empire in court,
gathering the feudal lords,
Cáozǐ, relying on the duty of his single sword,
pressed Duke Huán's heart on the altar platform,
his countenance unchanged,
his words unperturbed,
and recovered in one morning what was lost in three battles,
shaking the empire,
startling the feudal lords,
and extending his might to Wú
and Yuè.
These two men
were not incapable of achieving minor integrity and practicing small points of honor,
but they considered that to kill themselves and destroy their bodies,
cutting off their line and ending their posterity,
without establishing merit and fame,
was not wise.
Therefore, they dismissed the resentment of impulsive anger,
to establish a name for life;
they abandoned the integrity of indignant stubbornness,
to set a merit for generations.
Thus their achievements compete with the flow of the Three Kings,
and their names endure as long as heaven and earth.
I hope you will choose one of these and act upon it.
When the Yān general saw Lǔ Lián's letter,
he wept for three days,
wavering and unable to decide.
He wished to return to Yān,
but there was already a rift,
and he feared execution;
he wished to surrender to Qí,
but he had killed and captured many from Qí,
and feared being humiliated after surrendering.
He sighed deeply and said:
"Rather than be killed by others,
I would rather kill myself."
Thereupon he committed suicide.
Liáochéng fell into chaos,
and Tián Dān then massacred Liáochéng.
Returning, he spoke of Lǔ Lián,
wishing to ennoble him.
But Lǔ Lián fled and hid on the seacoast,
saying:
"I would rather be poor and lowly,
lightly regarding the world and following my own will, than to enjoy wealth and honor and be subservient to others."
Zōu Yáng was
a man of Qí.
He traveled to Liáng,
and associated with such men as the venerable Zhuāng Jì, a former man of Wú,
and Méi Shēng of Huáiyīn.
He presented a letter of advice but found himself between Yáng Shèng
and Gōngsūn Guǐ.
Shèng and others envied Zōu Yáng,
and slandered him to Liáng Xiàowáng.
The Xiàowáng was angered,
handed him over to the officials,
and was about to have him killed.
Zōu Yáng, as a traveling visitor,
was captured due to slander,
and fearing death while bearing false accusations,
then submitted a letter from prison, saying:
Your servant has heard that loyalty is always rewarded,
and trust never doubted,
and I always believed it to be so,
but these are mere empty words.
In the past, Jīng Kē admired the righteousness of Yān Dān,
and a white rainbow pierced the sun,
yet the crown prince feared him;
when Mr. Wèi planned the Chángpíng campaign for Qín,
Venus eclipsed the Pleiades,
yet King Zhāo doubted him.
That their essence moved heaven and earth, yet their sincerity was not understood by the two rulers,
is this not lamentable!
Now, your servant has exhausted loyalty and sincerity,
fully presenting my views in the hope they would be known,
but those around you were not discerning,
and I was finally subjected to official interrogation,
doubted by the world.
This is like making Jīng Kē
and Mr. Wèi rise again,
yet Yān
and Qín remain unenlightened.
I hope Your Majesty will examine this carefully.
In the past, Biàn Hé presented a treasure,
and the King of Chǔ had his feet cut off;
Lǐ Sī exhausted his loyalty,
yet Hú Hài executed him.
Thus, Jīzǐ feigned madness,
and Jiē Yú withdrew from the world,
fearing to encounter such misfortune.
I hope Your Majesty will consider the intent of Biàn Hé
and Lǐ Sī,
and then the judgments of the King of Chǔ
and Hú Hài,
so as not to let your servant be laughed at by Jīzǐ
and Jiē Yú.
Your servant heard of Bǐ Gān having his heart cut out,
and Zǐ Xū being stuffed into a leather sack,
and initially did not believe it,
but now I know it to be true.
I hope Your Majesty will examine this carefully,
and show a little compassion.
A proverb says:
"Some meet with white hair as if new acquaintances,
while others meet with covered carriages as old friends."
Why is that?
It is a matter of understanding or not understanding.
Thus, in the past, Fán Wūjī fled from Qín to Yān,
and lent his head to Jīng Kē for the service of Dān;
Wáng Shē left Qí for Wèi,
and cut his own throat at the city wall to repel Qí and preserve Wèi.
Now Wáng Shē
and Fán Wūjī were not new to Qí
and Qín but old to Yān
and Wèi;
the reason they left two states and died for two rulers
was that their actions matched their aspirations and they infinitely admired righteousness.
Thus, Sū Qīn was distrusted by the world,
yet became a Wěi Shēng for Yān;
Bái Guī lost six cities in battle,
yet captured Zhōngshān for Wèi.
Why?
Because there truly was mutual understanding.
When Sū Qīn served as minister of Yān,
the people of Yān slandered him to the king,
but the king grasped his sword in anger,
and fed him swift steeds;
when Bái Guī became prominent in Zhōngshān,
the people of Zhōngshān slandered him to Marquis Wén of Wèi,
yet the marquis presented him with a luminous jade disk.
Why?
Because the two rulers and two ministers,
baring their hearts and livers, trusted each other—
how could they be swayed by floating words!
Thus, whether a woman is beautiful or ugly,
upon entering the palace, she is envied;
whether a scholar is worthy or unworthy,
upon entering the court, he is resented.
In the past, Sīmǎ Xǐ had his kneecaps removed in Sòng,
yet finally became minister of Zhōngshān;
Fàn Jū had his ribs broken and teeth knocked out in Wèi,
yet finally became Marquis of Yìng.
These two men,
both held firm to their inevitable plans,
abandoned the selfishness of cliques,
and maintained solitary positions,
thus they could not avoid envious people.
Therefore, Shēntú Dí drowned himself in the river,
and Xú Yǎn carried a stone into the sea.
Not tolerated by the world,
they would not improperly gain anything for righteousness' sake,
nor form cliques in court
to sway the ruler's mind.
Thus, Bǎilǐ Xī begged for food on the road,
yet Duke Mù entrusted him with governance;
Nìng Qī fed his ox under a cart,
yet Duke Huán appointed him to the state.
These two men,
did they rely on official connections at court,
or borrow praise from those around,
before the two rulers employed them?
Their hearts were moved,
their actions aligned,
bonded like glue and lacquer,
even brothers could not separate them—
how could they be confused by the mouths of the many?
Thus, listening partially gives rise to treachery,
and relying solely leads to chaos.
In the past, Lǔ listened to Jì Sūn's words and expelled Confucius,
and Sòng believed Zǐ Hǎn's scheme and imprisoned Mò Dí.
With the eloquence of Confucius
and Mò Dí,
they could not escape slander and flattery,
and the two states were thereby endangered.
Why?
Because many mouths can melt metal,
and accumulated slanders dissolve bones.
Thus, Qín employed the tribesman Yóu Yú and dominated the central states,
and Qí employed the Yuè man Méng and strengthened under Wēi
and Xuān. These two states,
were they constrained by customs,
dragged by the times,
or tied to biased words?
They listened broadly and observed comprehensively,
leaving their names to the age.
Thus, when intentions align, even Hú and Yuè become brothers,
as with Yóu Yú
and the Yuè man Méng;
when not aligned,
even flesh and blood are expelled and not taken back,
as with Zhū, Xiàng,
Guǎn, and Cài.
Now if a ruler truly could adopt the righteousness of Qí
and Qín,
and reject the judgments of Sòng
and Lǔ,
then the Five Hegemons would not be worth praising,
and the Three Kings' deeds would be easy to accomplish.
Thus, the sage kings, awakening,
discarded the heart of Zǐ Zhī,
and could not be pleased by Tián Cháng's worth;
they enfeoffed Bǐ Gān's descendants,
and repaired the grave of the pregnant woman,
thus their achievements were restored to the world.
Why?
Because their desire for goodness was insatiable.
Now Duke Wén of Jìn cherished his enemy,
and strongly hegemonized the feudal lords;
Duke Huán of Qí employed his foe,
and unified and corrected the world.
Why?
Because of compassionate kindness and earnest sincerity,
genuinely applied in their hearts,
which cannot be borrowed with empty words.
As for the Qin state employing the laws of Shāng Yāng,
weakening Hán
and Wèi in the east, and making its armies the strongest under heaven,
yet he ultimately suffered death by dismemberment;
Yuè adopting the strategies of Minister Wén Zhǒng,
conquering powerful Wú,
and becoming hegemon of the Central States,
yet he was eventually executed.
Therefore, Sūn Shū'áo thrice resigned from the ministerial post without regret,
and Zǐzhòng of Wòlíng declined the position of one of the Three Dukes to water gardens for others.
If a ruler today could truly rid himself of an arrogant heart,
harbor intentions that can be reciprocated,
lay open his innermost thoughts,
reveal his true feelings,
bare his liver and gall,
bestow generous virtue,
and share both adversity and prosperity to the end,
sparing no generosity towards men of talent,
then even Jié's dog could be made to bark at Yáo,
and Zhí's follower could be induced to assassinate Xǔ Yóu;
how much more so when one wields the authority of a sovereign with ten thousand chariots,
and possesses the resources of a sage king?
If so, then the drowning of Jīng Kē's seven clans,
and the burning of Yāolí's wife and children,
would hardly be worth mentioning!
I have heard that if a bright moon pearl
or a night-shining jade
is thrown at someone in the dark on the road,
there is no one who does not clutch his sword and glare askance.
Why is that?
Because they appear without reason.
A gnarled tree root,
twisted and irregular,
can become a vessel for a sovereign.
Why is that?
Because those around him have first prepared and adorned it.
Thus, when something comes before one without cause,
even if it is the pearl of the Marquis of Suí
or a night-shining jade,
it will only incur resentment and not be appreciated.
But if someone first speaks on its behalf,
then even a withered tree or decayed stump can achieve merit and not be forgotten.
Now, the scholars of the world who live in poverty and seclusion,
dwelling in humble circumstances,
though they may possess the wisdom of Yáo
and Shùn,
the eloquence of Yī Yǐn
and Guǎn Zhòng,
and the intentions of Lóng Péng
and Bǐ Gān,
and wish to devote their loyalty to the ruler of the time,
yet lack any prior preparation or adornment,
even if they exhaust their mental efforts
and seek to demonstrate their loyalty and sincerity,
to assist the ruler in governance,
the ruler will inevitably show signs of clutching his sword and glaring askance.
This prevents the common scholars from having the advantage of being like the withered tree or decayed stump.
Therefore, a sage king governs the world and guides customs,
transforming alone as if on a potter's wheel,
unswayed by base and chaotic words,
and not swayed by the many voices.
Thus, the First Emperor of Qín trusted the words of his attendant Méng Jiā,
believed in Jīng Kē's story,
and was almost assassinated by a hidden dagger;
while King Wén of Zhōu hunted in the Jīng
and Wèi rivers, took Lǚ Shàng back in his carriage,
and thereby became king over the world.
So Qín trusted those close to him and nearly met death,
while Zhōu employed a chance encounter and became king.
Why is that?
Because the latter could transcend constraining words,
and range beyond conventional discussions,
viewing alone the bright and expansive Way.
Now, if a ruler is immersed in flattering words,
constrained by the influences of the inner court,
causing unbridled scholars to share the same trough as oxen and inferior horses,
this is why Bào Jiāo resented the world and would not linger for the joys of wealth and honor.
I have heard that those who enter court in full attire do not defile righteousness for profit,
and those who sharpen their reputation do not harm their conduct for desires.
Thus, Zēngzǐ would not enter a district named "Surpassing Mother,"
and Mòzǐ turned his carriage back from a town called "Morning Song."
Now, if one wishes to make the broad-minded scholars of the world
cower under the power of authority,
be controlled by the nobility of position and influence,
so they distort themselves and soil their conduct to serve flatterers and seek closeness to those around the ruler,
then scholars would rather die in hiding in caves and marshes,
how could there be any who would exert their loyalty and sincerity and hasten to your court?
The letter was presented to King Xiào of Liáng,
who had him released,
and he eventually became a honored guest.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Though Lǔ Lián's intentions did not align with the great righteousness,
I admire that from his position as a commoner,
he was untrammeled and followed his will,
unbending before the feudal lords,
discoursing in his time,
and challenging the power of ministers and chancellors.
Though Zōu Yáng's words were not humble,
his drawing of analogies and connecting categories
has much that is moving,
and he can be said to have been upright and unyielding.
Therefore, I have appended his story in the biographies.
Qū Yuán,
named Píng,
was a clansman of the Chǔ royal family.
He served as a senior official under King Huái of Chǔ.
He was widely learned and had a strong memory,
well-versed in order and chaos,
and skilled in rhetoric.
At court, he would discuss state affairs with the king,
issuing decrees;
outside, he received guests
and responded to the feudal lords.
The king trusted him greatly.
Senior Official
was of the same rank as him,
and competing for favor, he envied Qū Yuán's ability.
King Huái had Qū Yuán draft ordinances,
and Qū Píng was working on a draft that was not yet finalized.
Senior Official saw it
and tried to take it,
but Qū Píng refused,
so he slandered him, saying:
"Your Majesty had Qū Píng draft ordinances,
and everyone knows it.
Every time a decree is issued,
Píng boasts of his achievement,
saying that
'no one but me could do it.'"
The king became angry and distanced himself from Qū Píng.
Qū Píng grieved that the king's hearing was not clear,
that slander and flattery obscured his vision,
that evil and crookedness harmed the public good,
and that the upright were not tolerated,
so in sorrow and deep contemplation
he composed the "Lí Sāo."
"Lí Sāo"
means "encountering sorrow."
Heaven
is the origin of humans;
parents
are the foundation of humans.
When in distress,
one turns back to the foundation.
Thus, in toil, suffering, and exhaustion,
one never fails to cry out to Heaven;
in pain and anguish,
one never fails to call upon parents.
Qū Píng walked the straight path and acted with integrity,
exhausting his loyalty and wisdom
to serve his ruler,
yet slanderers came between them;
he can be said to have been in distress.
Trusted yet suspected,
loyal yet slandered,
how could he not feel resentment?
Qū Yuán's composition of the "Lí Sāo"
arose from this resentment.
The "Guó Fēng" expresses love
but not licentiousness;
the "Xiǎo Yǎ" expresses complaint and criticism
but not sedition.
As for the "Lí Sāo,"
it may be said to combine both.
It speaks of Emperor Kù above,
mentions Duke Huán of Qí below,
and recounts Tāng and Wǔ in the middle,
to satirize contemporary affairs.
It elucidates the breadth and loftiness of virtue and morality,
and the coherence of order and chaos,
leaving nothing unrevealed.
Its language is concise,
its words subtle,
its intent pure,
its conduct upright.
Its references may be small
but their meaning is immense;
the examples are near
but the significance is far-reaching.
His intent being pure,
he often referred to fragrant things.
His conduct being upright,
he would not allow himself to drift even in death.
Though immersed in filth and mire,
he shed his skin in the midst of corruption,
floating beyond the dust of the world,
untainted by the grime of the age,
spotless though stained, unsoiled.
Extending this intent,
it can contend in brightness with the sun and moon.
Qū Yuán had already been dismissed from office.
After that, Qín intended to attack Qí.
Qí and Chǔ were in an alliance and friendly relations,
which troubled King Huì of Qín,
so he ordered Zhāng Yí to pretend to leave Qín,
bringing generous gifts and presenting himself to serve Chǔ,
saying:
"Qín deeply hates Qí.
Since Qí and Chǔ are allied and friendly,
if Chǔ can truly break off with Qí,
Qín is willing to offer the territories of Shāng
and Wū, six hundred lǐ in total."
King Huái of Chǔ, greedy, believed Zhāng Yí,
and thus severed ties with Qí,
sending an envoy to Qín to receive the land.
Zhāng Yí deceived him,
saying:
"I agreed with the king on six lǐ,
not six hundred lǐ."
The Chǔ envoy left in anger,
returning to report to King Huái.
King Huái was enraged,
and raised a large army to attack Qín.
Qín sent troops to counterattack,
decisively defeating the Chǔ army at Dān and Xī,
decapitating eighty thousand,
capturing the Chǔ general Qū Gài,
and subsequently seizing the Hànzhōng territory from Chǔ.
King Huái then mobilized all the troops in the state
to advance deep and attack Qín,
engaging in battle at Lántián.
Wèi, hearing of this,
raided Chǔ as far as Dèng.
The Chǔ troops, frightened,
withdrew from Qín.
Meanwhile, Qí, angered, ultimately did not rescue Chǔ,
leaving Chǔ in great distress.
The following year,
Qín ceded the Hànzhōng territory to Chǔ
to make peace.
The King of Chǔ said:
"I do not desire the land,
but wish to capture Zhāng Yí to satisfy my heart."
Zhāng Yí, upon hearing this,
said:
"With one me equivalent to the Hànzhōng territory,
I request to go to Chǔ."
Upon arriving in Chǔ,
he again used generous bribes on the influential official Jìn Shàng,
and arranged deceptive arguments with King Huái's
favored consort Zhèng Xiù.
King Huái ultimately listened to Zhèng Xiù,
and once again released Zhāng Yí.
At this time, Qū Yuán had already been estranged,
no longer in office,
and was on a mission to Qí.
Upon his return,
he advised King Huái, saying:
"Why not kill Zhāng Yí?"
King Huái regretted it,
but pursuing Zhāng Yí, he failed to catch up.
After that, the feudal lords jointly attacked Chǔ,
greatly defeating it,
and killed its general Táng Mò.
At that time, King Zhāo of Qín
was married into the Chǔ royal family,
and wished to meet with King Huái.
King Huái intended to go,
but Qū Yuán said:
"Qín is a state of tigers and wolves,
not to be trusted.
It would be better not to go."
King Huái's youngest son Zǐ Lán urged the king to go:
"How can we reject Qín's goodwill!"
King Huái eventually went.
Entering Wǔguān,
Qín ambushed and cut off his retreat,
thus detaining King Huái,
demanding the cession of territory.
King Huái, enraged,
refused.
He fled to Zhào,
but Zhào did not admit him.
Returning to Qín,
he eventually died there and was brought back for burial.
His eldest son, King Qǐngxiāng,
ascended the throne,
appointing his younger brother Zǐ Lán as Lìng Yǐn.
The people of Chǔ blamed Zǐ Lán
for persuading King Huái to enter Qín
and not return.
Qū Yuán deeply resented this,
and although exiled,
he longed for Chǔ,
his heart tied to King Huái,
never ceasing to hope for return,
wishing for the king to awaken,
and for customs to be reformed.
His desire to preserve the king and revive the state, seeking to turn things around,
was expressed repeatedly in his writings.
Yet, in the end, there was no alternative,
so he could not return,
ultimately revealing that King Huái
never came to understand.
Whether a ruler is foolish or wise, worthy or unworthy,
none does not seek loyalty to serve himself,
or promote the worthy to assist himself.
Yet, the fall of states and ruin of families follow one another,
and sagely rulers and well-governed states are not seen for generations,
because those called loyal are not loyal,
and those called worthy are not worthy.
King Huái, not understanding the duty of loyal ministers,
was thus deluded internally by Zhèng Xiù,
deceived externally by Zhāng Yí,
estranged Qū Yuán,
and trusted Shàngguān Dàfū and Lìng Yǐn Zǐ Lán.
His troops were defeated, his territory reduced,
he lost six commanderies,
died abroad in Qín,
and became a laughingstock to the world.
This is the calamity of not knowing men.
The "Yì" says:
"The well is drained, none drink from it,
for it grieves my heart;
it can be drawn from. If the king were enlightened,
all would receive its blessing."
If the king is not enlightened,
how can he bring blessings?
Lìng Yǐn Zǐ Lán, hearing of this,
was greatly angered,
and finally had Shàngguān Dàfū
slander Qū Yuán before King Qǐngxiāng,
who, enraged, banished him.
Qū Yuán came to the riverbank,
with disheveled hair, chanting by the marshes.
His face was haggard,
his form emaciated.
A fisherman saw him and asked:
"Are you not the Sānlǘ Dàfū?
What brings you here?"
Qū Yuán said: "The whole world is muddy,
yet I alone am clear;
all men are drunk,
yet I alone am sober.
Therefore, I am exiled."
The fisherman said:
"The sage
is not constrained by things
but can move with the world.
Since the whole world is muddy,
why not go with the flow and stir the waves?
Since all men are drunk,
why not eat the dregs and drink the weak wine?
Why hold gems and jades,
only to bring about your own exile?"
Qū Yuán said:
"I have heard:
after washing the hair, one must dust the hat;
after bathing, one must shake the clothes.
How can a man, with his pure self,
bear to be soiled by external filth?
I would rather plunge into the flowing waters
and be buried in the bellies of river fish,
than let my spotless purity
be sullied by the world's grime!"
Thereupon, he composed the rhapsody "Huái Shā."
Its verses said:
Warm is the midsummer,
lush are the plants and trees.
My heart grieves with endless sorrow,
as I hurry to the southern land.
My gaze is dim and distant,
all is silent and obscure.
Wrongs entangled, sorrows twisted,
long suffering in distress;
weighing my feelings, testing my will,
I bow and restrain myself.
To carve square into round,
yet the constant measure remains;
to change one's original course,
is despised by the noble.
Mark the plan, follow the line,
the former rule unchanged;
upright within, substantial and firm,
praised by the great.
If the skilled carpenter does not carve,
who can discern his straight rule?"
In the fifty-sixth year of King Zhāoxiāng of Qín,
he passed away.
The crown prince Ān Guójūn ascended as king,
with Huáyáng Fūrén becoming queen,
and Zǐchǔ designated as crown prince.
Zhào also escorted Zǐchǔ's wife
and his son Zhèng back to Qín.
The Qín king reigned for one year and died,
posthumously titled King Xiàowén.
Crown Prince Zǐchǔ succeeded him,
known as King Zhuāngxiāng.
King Zhuāngxiāng's nominal mother Huáyáng Hòu
became Queen Dowager Huáyáng,
while his birth mother Xià Jī
was honored as Queen Dowager Xià.
In the first year of King Zhuāngxiāng's reign,
Lǚ Bùwéi was appointed chancellor,
enfeoffed as Marquis Wénxìn,
with a fief of 100,000 households in Luòyáng, Hénán.
After three years on the throne, King Zhuāngxiāng died,
and Crown Prince Zhèng ascended as king,
honoring Lǚ Bùwéi as chancellor of state,
addressing him
as "Second Father".
The Qín king being young,
the queen dowager
frequently engaged in secret affairs with Lǚ Bùwéi.
Lǚ Bùwéi possessed ten thousand servants.
At that time,
Wèi had Lord Xìnlíng,
Chǔ had Lord Chūnshēn,
Zhào had Lord Píngyuán,
Qí had Lord Mèngcháng,
all known for humbly receiving guests to compete for influence.
Lǚ Bùwéi, ashamed that mighty Qín
fell short in this regard,
also recruited scholars,
treating them generously,
until he hosted three thousand retainers.
At this time
many persuasive scholars among the feudal lords,
such as Xún Qīng and his peers,
published books circulating everywhere.
Lǚ Bùwéi then had his guests
each write their knowledge,
compiling their discussions into
the Eight Observations, Six Discourses,
and Twelve Annals,
totaling over two hundred thousand words.
Believing it encompassed all matters of heaven and earth,
all things past and present,
it was titled "The Spring and Autumn Annals of Lǚ".
Displayed at the Xiányáng market gate,
with a thousand gold pieces hung above it,
he invited roaming scholars and guests from various states
to claim the gold if they could add or remove a single character.
As the First Emperor grew older,
the queen dowager's promiscuity continued.
Fearing discovery
would bring disaster upon himself,
Lǚ Bùwéi secretly sought a man with large genitals named Lào Ǎi
to be his retainer,
occasionally arranging performances
where Ǎi moved a wooden wheel with his penis,
ensuring the queen dowager heard of it,
to tempt her.
Upon hearing,
she indeed desired him privately.
Lǚ Bùwéi then presented Lào Ǎi,
falsely having him accused of a castration offense.
Lǚ Bùwéi secretly told the queen dowager:
"He can pretend to be castrated,
then serve in the palace."
The queen dowager secretly bribed the official in charge of castration heavily,
who fake sentenced him,
plucking his beard and eyebrows to pose as a eunuch,
thus enabling him to attend the queen dowager.
She privately consorted with him,
deeply enamored.
When she became pregnant,
fearing discovery,
she feigned divination
requiring seclusion,
moving to the Yōng palace.
Lào Ǎi often accompanied her,
receiving lavish rewards,
with all matters decided by him.
Lào Ǎi had several thousand servants,
and over a thousand guests sought positions as his retainers.
In the seventh year of the First Emperor,
King Zhuāngxiāng's mother, Queen Dowager Xià, died.
King Xiàowén's queen, known as Queen Dowager Huáyáng,
was buried with King Xiàowén at the Shòu tomb.
Queen Dowager Xià's son King Zhuāngxiāng was buried at Zhǐyáng,
so Queen Dowager Xià was separately interred east of Dù,
saying
"Eastward I gaze upon my son,
westward upon my husband.
A hundred years hence,
a city of ten thousand households shall rise beside me."
In the ninth year of the First Emperor,
someone reported that Lào Ǎi was not truly a eunuch,
often engaging in illicit relations with the queen dowager,
fathering two sons,
all concealed.
He plotted with the queen dowager,
"When the king dies,
our son shall succeed."
Thereupon the Qín king ordered an investigation,
uncovering the full truth,
implicating Chancellor Lǚ Bùwéi.
In September,
Lào Ǎi's three clans were executed,
the two sons born to the queen dowager killed,
and she was moved to Yōng.
All of Lào Ǎi's retainers had their families confiscated
and were exiled to Shǔ.
The king intended to execute the chancellor,
but due to his great service to the previous king,
and many guests and persuaders
pleading on his behalf,
he could not bear to punish him.
In the tenth year of the Qín king, October,
Chancellor Lǚ Bùwéi was dismissed.
After Qí native Máo Jiāo persuaded the Qín king,
he brought the queen dowager back from Yōng,
returning her to Xiányáng,
while sending Marquis Wénxìn
to his fief in Hénán.
Over a year later,
guests, envoys, and visitors from various states
constantly traveled the roads,
seeking audience with Marquis Wénxìn.
The Qín king, fearing rebellion,
sent him a letter stating:
"What merit have you for Qín?
Qín enfeoffed you in Hénán,
with a fief of 100,000 households.
What kinship have you with Qín?
Yet you're called 'Second Father'.
You and your family
shall move to Shǔ!"
Lǚ Bùwéi, feeling increasingly threatened,
fearing execution,
drank poison and died.
With both Lǚ Bùwéi and Lào Ǎi dead, the Qín king's anger subsided,
and he recalled Lào Ǎi's retainers exiled to Shǔ.
In the nineteenth year of the First Emperor,
the queen dowager died,
posthumously titled Empress Dowager,
buried with King Zhuāngxiāng in Yáng.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Lǚ Bùwéi and Lào Ǎi rose to prominence,
with Lǚ Bùwéi enfeoffed as Marquis Wénxìn.
When someone reported Lào Ǎi,
he learned of it.
The Qín king verified with attendants,
but took no action yet.
When the king went to the suburban sacrifice at Yōng,
Lào Ǎi, fearing
disaster, conspired with his faction,
forged the queen dowager's seal
to mobilize troops and rebel at the Qínián Palace.
Officers were sent to attack Ǎi,
who fled after defeat,
was pursued and killed at Hàozhì,
and his clan exterminated.
Thus Lǚ Bùwéi was dismissed.
As for what Confucius called "being notorious",
did he mean someone like Lǚ?
Cáo Mèi
was a man of Lǔ
who served Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ
with his courage and strength.
Duke Zhuāng favored physical prowess.
Cáo Mèi, as a Lǔ general,
fought against Qí
and suffered three defeats.
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ, afraid,
offered the territory of Suìyì for peace.
Yet he still kept Cáo Mèi as general.
Duke Huán of Qí agreed to meet with Lǔ
at Kē to form an alliance.
After Duke Huán and Duke Zhuāng swore the covenant on the platform,
Cáo Mèi seized a dagger and threatened Duke Huán of Qí,
with none of Duke Huán's attendants daring to move,
and asked:
"What do you intend to do?"
Cáo Mèi said: "Qí is strong and Lǔ is weak,
yet your great state has invaded Lǔ quite severely.
Now the walls of Lǔ's capital are crumbling
and press close to Qí's borders—
you should consider this."
Duke Huán then agreed to return all
the lands Qí had seized from Lǔ.
After the agreement was made,
Cáo Mèi threw down his dagger,
descended the platform,
took his place facing north among the ministers,
his expression unchanged,
and his speech as composed as ever.
Duke Huán grew angry
and wanted to break the agreement.
Guǎn Zhòng said: "That cannot be.
To seek petty gains for momentary satisfaction,
to abandon trust among the feudal lords,
and to lose the support of the world—
it is better to give them the land."
Thereupon Duke Huán
proceeded to cede the invaded territories of Lǔ,
and all the lands lost by Cáo Mèi in three battles
were restored to Lǔ.
One hundred and sixty-seven years later,
there occurred the affair of Zhuān Zhū in Wú.
Zhuān Zhū
was a man of Tángyì in Wú.
When Wǔ Zǐxū fled Chǔ and went to Wú,
he recognized Zhuān Zhū's abilities.
After Wǔ Zǐxū met with King Liáo of Wú,
he persuaded him of the advantages of attacking Chǔ.
Prince Guāng of Wú said: "That Wǔ
Yún's father and elder brother both died in Chǔ,
and now Yún advocates attacking Chǔ—
he seeks to avenge his personal grudge,
not to benefit Wú."
The King of Wú then halted the plan.
Wǔ Zǐxū, knowing that Prince Guāng intended
to kill King Liáo of Wú,
said: "That Guāng has ambitions within the state;
he cannot be persuaded with external affairs."
So he introduced Zhuān Zhū to Prince Guāng.
Guāng's father was King Zhūfán of Wú.
Zhūfán had three younger brothers:
the next was Yúzhài,
then Yímò,
and finally Jìzǐ Zhá.
Zhūfán, knowing Jìzǐ Zhá was worthy,
did not appoint an heir apparent,
but passed the throne successively to his three brothers,
hoping to eventually give the state to Jìzǐ Zhá.
After Zhūfán died,
it passed to Yúzhài.
When Yúzhài died,
it passed to Yímò.
When Yímò died,
it should have passed to Jìzǐ Zhá;
but Jìzǐ Zhá fled and refused to take the throne,
so the people of Wú made Yímò's son Liáo king.
Prince Guāng said:
"If succession is by brotherly order,
then Jìzǐ should be king;
if it must be by sons,
then I am the true legitimate heir,
and should be king."
Thus, he secretly nurtured strategists to seek the throne.
Once Guāng obtained Zhuān Zhū,
he treated him well as a guest.
In the ninth year, King Píng of Chǔ died.
In spring,
King Liáo of Wú sought to take advantage of Chǔ's mourning,
sending his two younger brothers, Prince Gàiyú and Shǔyōng,
to lead troops and besiege Qián of Chǔ;
he sent Yánlíng Jìzǐ
to Jìn,
to observe the changes
among the feudal lords.
Chǔ dispatched troops to cut off the retreat of Wú's generals Gàiyú and Shǔyōng,
and the Wú army could not return.
Thereupon Prince Guāng said to Zhuān Zhū:
"This opportunity must not be lost;
if we do not seek, what will we gain!
Moreover, I am the true royal heir,
and should be king;
even if Jìzǐ returns,
he will not depose me."
Zhuān Zhū said:
"King Liáo can be killed.
His mother is old and his sons young,
and his two brothers are leading troops against Chǔ,
with Chǔ cutting off their retreat.
Currently, Wú
is externally strained by Chǔ,
and internally empty of loyal ministers—
he can do nothing to us."
Prince Guāng bowed his head and said:
"My life
is your life."
On the day Bǐngzǐ of the fourth month,
Guāng hid armored soldiers in a cellar room,
and prepared a banquet to invite King Liáo.
King Liáo had soldiers line up
from the palace to Guāng's home,
with guards at every door, step, and corridor, all relatives of King Liáo.
They stood in pairs attending,
all holding long pikes.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Prince Guāng feigned a foot ailment,
entered the cellar room,
and had Zhuān Zhū place a dagger in the belly of a roasted fish
and present it.
When he reached the king,
Zhuān Zhū split the fish,
and with the dagger stabbed King Liáo,
who died instantly.
The attendants also killed Zhuān Zhū,
and the king's men fell into chaos.
Prince Guāng released his hidden soldiers
to attack King Liáo's followers,
exterminating them all,
then made himself king,
becoming Hé Lǘ.
Hé Lǘ enfeoffed Zhuān Zhū's son
as a high minister.
More than seventy years later,
there occurred the affair of Yù Ràng in Jìn.
Yù Ràng
was a man of Jìn,
who had formerly served the Fàn clan
and the Zhōngháng clan,
but gained no fame.
He left and served Zhì Bó,
who greatly honored and favored him.
When Zhì Bó attacked Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
Zhào Xiāngzǐ allied with Hán and Wèi
to plot Zhì Bó's destruction,
and after eliminating Zhì Bó,
they divided his territory into three.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ bore the deepest grudge against Zhì Bó,
lacquering his skull
to make a drinking vessel.
Yù Ràng fled into the mountains,
saying: "Alas!
A man dies for one who knows his worth;
a woman adorns herself for one who pleases her.
Now Zhì Bó knew me,
I must die to avenge him,
to repay Zhì Bó,
so my spirit will feel no shame."
He then changed his name and disguised as a convict,
entering the palace to plaster the latrine,
hiding a dagger inside,
intending to assassinate Xiāngzǐ.
When Xiāngzǐ went to the latrine,
his heart stirred,
and he seized and questioned the convict plastering the latrine—
it was Yù Ràng,
holding a weapon inside,
saying:
"I wish to avenge Zhì Bó!"
The attendants wanted to execute him.
Xiāngzǐ said: "He is a righteous man;
I will simply avoid him.
Moreover, Zhì Bó died without heirs,
yet his minister seeks to avenge him—
this is a worthy man of the world."
He finally released him.
After a short while,
Yù Ràng lacquered his body to cause sores,
swallowed charcoal to hoarsen his voice,
making his appearance unrecognizable,
and begged in the market.
His wife did not recognize him.
He met his friend while walking,
and the friend recognized him,
saying:
"Aren't you Yù Ràng?"
He replied:
"I am."
His friend wept for him, saying:
"With your talent,
if you pledged yourself and served Xiāngzǐ as a minister,
Xiāngzǐ would surely favor you.
Once favored,
you could then do as you wished—
wouldn't that be easier?
Why mutilate your body and suffer,
seeking to take revenge on Xiāngzǐ—
isn't that too difficult!"
Yù Ràng said:
"Having pledged my allegiance to serve a master,
and then seeking to kill him,
would be harboring duplicity in serving one's lord.
Moreover, what I am doing is extremely difficult!
Yet the reason I undertake this
is to shame those throughout the world and future generations who, as ministers, serve their lords with divided loyalties."
After he left, shortly after,
Xiāngzǐ was about to go out,
and Yù Ràng hid under the bridge he was due to cross.
When Xiāngzǐ reached the bridge,
his horse became startled,
and Xiāngzǐ said, "This must be Yù Ràng."
He sent someone to inquire,
and it was indeed Yù Ràng.
Thereupon, Xiāngzǐ enumerated Yù Ràng's deeds, saying:
"Did you not once serve the Fàn and Zhōngháng families?
Zhì Bó exterminated them all,
yet you did not seek revenge for them,
but instead pledged your service to Zhì Bó.
Now Zhì Bó is also dead,
so why alone do you seek such deep revenge for him?"
Yù Ràng replied:
"When I served the Fàn and Zhōngháng families,
they treated me as an ordinary man,
so I repaid them as an ordinary man would.
As for Zhì Bó,
he treated me as a man of the state,
so I repay him as a man of the state would."
Xiāngzǐ sighed deeply, wept, and said:
"Alas, Master Yù!
Your deeds for Zhì Bó
have already made your name,
and I, the unworthy one, have spared you,
which should be enough.
You must now consider your own fate,
I will not release you again!"
He ordered soldiers to surround him.
Yù Ràng said:
"I have heard that an enlightened ruler
does not conceal others' virtues,
and a loyal minister has the duty to die for his reputation.
Previously, you generously spared me,
and all under heaven praised your worthiness.
In today's matter,
I am resolved to accept execution,
but I wish to ask for your garment
to strike it,
thereby expressing my intent for revenge,
so that even in death, I will have no regret.
This is not something I dare to expect,
but I venture to bare my innermost thoughts!"
Moved by his sense of duty, Xiāngzǐ
then sent an attendant to bring a garment to Yù Ràng.
Yù Ràng drew his sword, leaped three times,
and struck the garment,
saying, "Now I can report to Zhì Bó below!"
Thereupon, he fell on his sword and committed suicide.
On the day of his death,
the noble-minded of the state of Zhào heard of it,
and all wept for him.
More than forty years later,
in Zhǐ, there occurred the affair of Niè Zhèng.
Niè Zhèng
was a native of Shēnjǐng Lane in Zhǐ.
Having killed a man and fled from enemies,
he went with his mother and elder sister to Qí,
where he made his living as a butcher.
After some time,
Yán Zhòngzǐ of Púyáng,
who served Hán Āihóu,
had a grudge against Xiá Lěi, the chancellor of Hán.
Fearing execution, Yán Zhòngzǐ
fled,
traveling to seek someone
who could take revenge on Xiá Lěi.
He came to Qí,
where some people of Qí said that Niè Zhèng was a brave and fierce man,
hiding from enemies among butchers.
Yán Zhòngzǐ went to his door to request an audience,
repeatedly returning,
and then prepared wine
and personally toasted Niè Zhèng's mother.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Yán Zhòngzǐ presented
a hundred yì of gold,
stepping forward to toast Niè Zhèng's mother's longevity.
Niè Zhèng, surprised by the generosity,
firmly declined Yán Zhòngzǐ's offer.
Yán Zhòngzǐ insisted on giving it,
but Niè Zhèng declined, saying:
"I am fortunate to have an aged mother,
my family is poor,
and I wander as a guest, working as a dog butcher,
so I can obtain sweet and delicate food morning and night
to support my parent.
With my parent's provisions already sufficient,
I dare not accept your gift."
Yán Zhòngzǐ dismissed the others
and then said to Niè Zhèng:
"I have an enemy,
and I have traveled among many feudal lords;
but upon coming to Qí,
I privately heard that your sense of duty is very high,
hence I offer a hundred pieces of gold,
intending it as coarse provisions for your esteemed mother,
to be able to share joy with you,
how would I dare to have any expectations from it!"
Niè Zhèng said: "The reason I lower my ambitions
and demean myself living among the market butchers
is solely to luckily support my aged mother;
while my mother lives,
I dare not pledge my life to anyone."
Yán Zhòngzǐ firmly pressed,
but Niè Zhèng ultimately refused to accept.
Nevertheless, Yán Zhòngzǐ finally observed the rites of host and guest
and departed.
After some time,
Niè Zhèng's mother died.
After she was buried,
and the mourning period ended,
Niè Zhèng said: "Alas!
I am but a man of the marketplace,
wielding a knife as a butcher;
yet Yán Zhòngzǐ
is a minister among the feudal lords,
who did not consider a thousand lǐ too far,
but humbly came with his carriage to befriend me.
How I treated him was extremely shallow and meager,
without any great deed to match his regard,
yet Yán Zhòngzǐ presented a hundred pieces of gold for my parent's longevity,
and though I did not accept it,
this shows he alone deeply understood me.
For a worthy man
to, out of indignation over a slight,
befriend and trust a poor and obscure person,
how could I, Zhèng, alone remain silent and do nothing!
Moreover, he previously invited me,
and I declined only because of my aged mother;
now my mother has ended her natural lifespan,
I shall be used by one who knows me."
Thereupon, he went west to Púyáng,
saw Yán Zhòngzǐ, and said:
"The reason I did not agree with you before
was solely that my parent was alive;
now, unfortunately, my mother has ended her natural lifespan.
Whom does you wish to take revenge on?
Allow me to undertake the task!"
Yán Zhòngzǐ fully informed him, saying:
"My enemy is Chancellor Xiá Lěi of Hán,
and Xiá Lěi is also the younger uncle of the ruler of Hán;
his clan is numerous,
and his residence is heavily guarded with soldiers.
I wanted to send someone to assassinate him,
but none could accomplish it.
Now, you fortunately do not refuse,
I ask to increase your carriage, riders, and strong men
to assist you."
Niè Zhèng said: "Between Hán and Wèi,
the distance is not very great;
now to kill the chancellor,
who is also a relative of the state's ruler,
in this situation, many people cannot be used;
with many people, it's impossible to avoid mishaps,
mishaps lead to information leakage,
and if information leaks, the entire state of Hán
will become your enemy,
would that not be perilous!"
So he declined the carriage, riders, and followers,
and Niè Zhèng took his leave and went alone.
Carrying his sword, he went to Hán.
Chancellor Xiá Lěi of Hán
was just sitting in his hall,
with many guards holding spears and halberds.
Niè Zhèng went straight in,
ascended the steps, and assassinated Xiá Lěi.
The attendants were thrown into great chaos.
Niè Zhèng shouted loudly,
killed several tens of those he struck,
then skinned his face, gouged out his eyes,
disemboweled himself,
and thus died.
Hán took Niè Zhèng's corpse
and exposed it in the market,
offering a reward for information, but no one knew who he was.
Thereupon, Hán offered a reward throughout the districts,
promising a thousand pieces of gold to anyone who could name the killer of Chancellor Xiá Lěi.
For a long time, no one knew.
Zhèng's elder sister Róng heard
that someone had assassinated the Hán chancellor,
but the assassin was not caught,
and the state did not know his name or surname.
His corpse was exposed with a thousand gold bounty for identification.
She then lamented in distress:
"Could it be my brother? Alas, Yán Zhòngzǐ knew my brother!"
She immediately set out,
went to Hán, and reached the marketplace,
where the deceased indeed turned out to be Zhèng.
She leaned over the corpse and wept with extreme grief,
saying:
"This is the one called Niè Zhèng from Shēn Jǐng Lane in Zhǐ."
Passersby and the crowd in the market all said:
"This man brutally murdered our state's chancellor,
and the king has posted a thousand gold reward for his identity.
Have you not heard, madam?
How dare you come to identify him?"
Róng responded to them: "I have heard.
However, the reason Zhèng endured disgrace and abandoned himself among the market vendors
was that our elderly mother was fortunately still alive and well,
and I had not yet married.
Now that our parent has passed away from natural causes,
and I have married,
Yán Zhòngzǐ recognized and lifted my brother from his plight and disgrace
to befriend him, showing profound kindness.
What could be done!
A nobleman naturally dies for one who understands him.
Now, because I am still alive,
he severely mutilated himself to sever any leads,
so how could I, fearing execution,
ultimately let my worthy brother's name be obliterated!"
She greatly astonished the people in the Hán market.
Then, she cried out to heaven three times,
and ultimately died of sorrow and distress beside Zhèng's body.
When Jìn, Chǔ, Qí, and Wèi heard of this,
they all said:
"Not only was Zhèng capable,
but his sister was also a woman of fierce integrity.
Had Zhèng truly known
that his sister lacked a tolerant and enduring will,
and would not shrink from the hardship of exposing her remains,
but would brave dangers over a thousand miles
to spread his name,
leading to both sister and brother being executed in the Hán market,
he might not have dared
to pledge himself to Yán Zhòngzǐ.
Yán Zhòngzǐ can indeed be said to have known men well
and been able to win over scholars!"
More than two hundred and twenty years later,
there was the affair of Jīng Kē in Qín.
Jīng Kē
was a man of Wèi.
His ancestors were from Qí,
but moved to Wèi,
where the people of Wèi called him Qìng Qīng.
When he went to Yān,
the people of Yān called him Jīng Qīng.
Jīng Qīng was fond of reading books and fencing,
and he tried to persuade Lord Yuán of Wèi with his strategies,
but Lord Yuán of Wèi did not employ him.
Later, Qín attacked Wèi,
established the Eastern Commandery,
and moved the collateral relatives of Lord Yuán of Wèi to Yěwáng.
Jīng Kē once traveled and passed through Yúcì,
where he discussed swordsmanship with Gài Niè,
and Gài Niè became angry and glared at him.
Jīng Kē left,
and someone suggested calling Jīng Qīng back.
Gài Niè said: "Earlier, when I discussed swordsmanship with him,
there were points where he fell short,
and I glared at him;
try going to find him,
but he ought to have left,
not daring to stay."
He sent a messenger to Jīng Kē's host,
and Jīng Qīng had already harnessed his carriage and left Yúcì.
The messenger returned and reported,
and Gài Niè said:
"He was sure to leave;
my earlier glare intimidated him!"
Jīng Kē traveled in Hándān,
where Lǔ Jūjiàn was playing a board game with Jīng Kē and they disputed over a move.
Lǔ Jūjiàn became angry and shouted at him,
but Jīng Kē silently fled away,
and they never met again.
After Jīng Kē arrived in Yān,
he befriended a Yān dog butcher
and the skilled zhu player Gāo Jiànlí.
Jīng Kē was fond of drink,
and daily with the dog butcher and Gāo Jiànlí
he drank in the Yān market.
Once they were drunk,
Gāo Jiànlí would play the zhu,
and Jīng Kē would harmonize and sing
in the marketplace,
enjoying themselves together.
After a while, they would weep together,
as if no one else were around.
Although Jīng Kē associated with drinkers,
his character was deep and thoughtful, and he loved books;
in all the feudal states he visited,
he fully associated with their worthy and heroic elders.
When he went to Yān,
the Yān recluse Master Tián Guāng
also treated him well,
knowing he was no ordinary man.
After a short while,
it happened that Crown Prince Dān of Yān, who had been a hostage in Qín,
fled back to Yān.
Crown Prince Dān of Yān had previously been a hostage in Zhào,
and the King of Qín, Zhèng, was born in Zhào,
so in their youth he and Dān were friends.
When Zhèng was established as King of Qín,
Dān became a hostage in Qín.
The King of Qín's treatment of Crown Prince Dān of Yān was not good,
so Dān resented it and fled back.
Upon returning, he sought
a way to take revenge on the King of Qín,
but his state was small,
and its strength insufficient.
Afterwards, Qín daily sent troops east of the mountains
to attack Qí, Chǔ, and the Three Jìn,
gradually nibbling away at the feudal states,
and were about to reach Yān,
so the rulers and ministers of Yān all feared the disaster's arrival.
Crown Prince Dān was troubled by this
and consulted his tutor Jū Wǔ.
Wǔ replied:
"Qín's territory spans the world,
threatening Hán, Wèi, and Zhào.
To the north, it has the strongholds of Gānquán and Gǔkǒu,
to the south, the fertile lands of the Jīng and Wèi rivers,
it monopolizes the riches of Bā and Hàn,
with the mountains of Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
and the strategic passes of Guān and Xiáo to the left.
Its people are numerous and its soldiers fierce,
with ample weapons and armor.
If it intends to act,
then south of the Great Wall,
north of the Yì River,
nothing will remain unsettled.
How can we, over the grievance of being humiliated,
think to strike against its scales?"
Dān said: "Then what course should we take?"
He replied: "Allow me to ponder it further."
After a while,
the Qín general Fán Yújī offended the King of Qín,
fled to Yān,
and the Crown Prince took him in and provided lodging.
Jū Wǔ admonished:
"This is not acceptable.
Given the King of Qín's tyranny
and accumulated anger towards Yān,
it is enough to make one tremble,
and even more so if he hears where General Fán is?
This is what is called
'placing meat in the path of a starving tiger'—
disaster is inevitable!
Even with advisors like Guǎn or Yàn,
they could not devise a plan for this.
I urge Your Highness to quickly send General Fán
into the Xiōngnú to eliminate the cause.
Then, seek alliances west with the Three Jìn,
south with Qí and Chǔ,
and negotiate north with the Chányú,
after which we can make plans."
The Crown Prince said: "The Grand Tutor's plan
would take a long time,
and my mind is troubled,
fearing I cannot wait even a moment.
Moreover, it's not just that;
General Fán is destitute throughout the world,
and has entrusted himself to me.
I will not, under pressure from powerful Qín,
abandon a friend I pity,
casting him to the Xiōngnú.
This would be the time for my life to end.
I ask the Grand Tutor to reconsider."
Jū Wǔ said:
"To pursue safety through dangerous actions,
seek fortune by creating disaster,
with shallow plans and deep resentment,
clinging to a new friendship with one man,
ignoring the great harm to the state—
this is what is called
'nourishing resentment and aiding disaster'."
If a goose feather were to be burned over a stove's charcoal,
it would surely be incinerated without a trace.
Moreover, with the fierce and predatory Qin,
acting out its resentful and violent rage,
how could words suffice to describe it!
In Yan, there is a Master Tián Guāng,
whose character is marked by profound wisdom and deep-seated courage,
and with whom one can discuss strategies.
The Crown Prince said:
"I wish through the Grand Tutor to be introduced to Master Tián;
would that be possible?"
Jū Wǔ replied:
"Respectfully, as you command."
He went to see Master Tián Guāng,
conveying that "the Crown Prince wishes to consult you on matters of state."
Tián Guāng said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
Then he went to visit him.
The Crown Prince greeted him personally,
stepping backward to guide the way,
and knelt to dust off the mat.
Once Tián Guāng was seated,
with no attendants around,
the Crown Prince moved from his mat
and pleaded:
"Yan and Qin cannot coexist;
I beg you, Sir, to give this your attention."
Tián Guāng said:
"I have heard that when the steed Qíjì is in its prime,
it can gallop a thousand li in a day;
but when it grows old,
even a nag can outrun it.
Now, you have heard of my prime,
but do not know that my vigor has already faded.
Nevertheless,
though I dare not undertake state affairs myself,
my good friend Jīng Qīng can be entrusted with the task."
The Crown Prince said:
"May I, through you, be introduced to Jīng Qīng?
Would that be possible?"
Tián Guāng said:
"Respectfully, as you command."
He rose immediately,
and hurried out.
The Crown Prince saw him to the gate,
cautioning him:
"What I have confided and what you have discussed
are matters of grave importance to the state;
I implore you, Sir, not to divulge them!"
Tián Guāng bowed his head and smiled, saying:
"Understood."
Hunched over, he went to see Jīng Qīng,
and said: "You and I are close friends,
and all in Yan know it.
Now, the Crown Prince has heard of my prime,
unaware that my body is no longer up to the task,
and graciously instructed me, saying
'Yan and Qin cannot coexist;
I beg you, Sir, to give this your attention.'
I made bold, considering myself not an outsider,
to recommend you to the Crown Prince,
and hope you will visit him at the palace."
Jīng Kē said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
Tián Guāng said:
"I have heard that a person of honor in their conduct
should not give others cause for doubt.
Now, the Crown Prince warned me,
'What we have discussed are matters of grave importance to the state;
I implore you, Sir, not to divulge them'—
this shows the Crown Prince doubts me.
To act in a way that invites suspicion
is not the mark of a principled knight-errant."
He intended to kill himself to inspire Jīng Qīng,
saying:
"I urge you to hasten to the Crown Prince,
and tell him I am dead,
to prove my silence."
Thereupon, he cut his throat and died.
Jīng Kē then went to see the Crown Prince,
informing him of Tián Guāng's death
and conveying his words.
The Crown Prince bowed twice and knelt,
crawling on his knees with tears streaming,
and after a while, spoke:
"My caution to Master Tián not to speak
was meant to ensure the success of our great plan.
Now that Master Tián has died
to prove his silence,
how could that have been my intention!"
Once Jīng Kē was seated,
the Crown Prince moved from his mat, kowtowed, and said:
"Master Tián, unaware of my unworthiness,
enabled me to come before you and dare to speak my mind;
this is Heaven's pity on Yan
and its refusal to abandon this orphan.
Now, Qin has a greedy and covetous heart,
and its desires know no bounds.
Not until it has consumed all the land under heaven
and made every king its subject
will its ambition be satisfied.
Already, Qin has captured the King of Hán
and annexed all his territory.
Moreover, it has raised armies to campaign south against Chǔ
and threaten Zhào in the north;
Wáng Jiǎn leads a host of several hundred thousand
to the Zhāng and Yè regions,
while Lǐ Xìn advances from Tàiyuán and Yúnzhōng.
If Zhào cannot withstand Qin,
it will surely submit,
and once it submits, disaster will befall Yan.
Yan is small and weak,
repeatedly battered by war,
and now, even mustering the entire state
would be insufficient to oppose Qin.
The other states are subservient to Qin,
and none dare form an alliance.
In my humble and foolish plan,
I believe that if we could find a truly courageous man from across the land
to send as an envoy to Qin,
luring them with great gains;
the King of Qin is greedy,
and under such circumstances, he would surely grant an audience.
If we could then seize the King of Qin
and force him to return all the lands seized from the other states,
as Cáo Mèi did with Duke Huán of Qí,
that would be ideal;
if not,
we should assassinate him then and there.
With Qin's great generals commanding troops abroad
and turmoil at home,
ruler and ministers would suspect each other,
and in the ensuing chaos, the other states could
form an alliance,
and Qin's defeat would be certain.
This is my highest hope,
yet I knew not to whom to entrust this mission—
I beg you, Jīng Qīng, to consider it."
After a long silence,
Jīng Kē said:
"This is a matter of grave importance to the state;
I am but a humble and inferior man,
and fear I may not be fit for the task."
The Crown Prince approached, kowtowed,
and insisted, urging him not to decline,
until at last he consented.
Thereupon, Jīng Qīng was honored as a High Minister,
and lodged in the finest quarters.
The Crown Prince visited him daily,
provided him with sumptuous feasts,
presented rare objects intermittently,
and indulged Jīng Kē's every desire with carriages, horses, and beautiful women,
all to please and satisfy him.
After some time,
Jīng Kē showed no intention of setting out.
Meanwhile, the Qin general Wáng Jiǎn conquered Zhào,
captured the King of Zhào,
and annexed all its territory,
then advanced northward to seize lands
up to the southern border of Yan.
Crown Prince Dān grew fearful
and pleaded with Jīng Kē:
"The Qin army may cross the Yì River any day now;
and though I wish to keep you by my side forever,
how could that be possible!"
Jīng Kē said: "Even without your words,
I intended to request an audience.
But if I go now
without a token of trust,
I will not be able to get close to the King of Qin.
Now, General Fán, the King of Qin has offered a thousand catties of gold
and a fief of ten thousand households for his head.
If we could obtain General Fán's head
along with the map of Yān's Dūkàng region,
and present them to the King of Qin,
he would surely be pleased to receive me,
and then I would have a means to carry out our plan."
The Crown Prince said:
"General Fán, in his desperation, came to seek refuge with me,
and I cannot bear to for my own personal reasons
to harm the feelings of an honorable man;
I beg you to consider another plan!"
Jīng Kē, knowing the Crown Prince's reluctance,
then went privately to see Fán Wūqí and said:
"Qin's treatment of you, General, has been utterly ruthless—
your parents and entire clan
have been executed or enslaved.
Now, I hear they offer a thousand catties of gold
and a fief of ten thousand households for your head;
what do you intend to do?"
Fán Wūqī looked up to the sky, heaved a deep sigh,
and said with tears streaming down:
"Every time I think of it,
the pain penetrates my very marrow,
but I just don't know what plan to devise!"
Jīng Kē said:
"Now I have a proposal
that can both resolve the crisis of Yān
and avenge you, General.
What do you think?"
Fán Wūqī stepped forward and asked:
"What is it?"
Jīng Kē replied:
"I wish to have your head to present to the King of Qín.
The King of Qín will surely be pleased to receive me.
With my left hand I'll grab his sleeve,
and with my right hand I'll stab his chest.
Then your vengeance will be achieved,
and the shame of Yān being bullied will be wiped away.
Would you be willing, General?"
Fán Wūqī bared one shoulder and gripped his wrist,
stepping forward to say:
"This is what I grit my teeth over day and night,
gnawing at my heart.
Only now have I heard your guidance!"
Thereupon he cut his own throat.
When the Crown Prince heard of this,
he rushed to the scene,
threw himself on the body and wept,
overcome with grief.
Since it was beyond remedy,
he then placed Fán Wūqī's head in a box and sealed it.
Thereupon the Crown Prince prepared in advance to seek the sharpest dagger in the land,
and obtained the dagger of Xú Fūrén of Zhào.
He bought it for a hundred pieces of gold,
and had a craftsman temper it with poison.
When tested on a person,
if it drew even a thread of blood,
the person would die instantly.
Then he packed it to give to Jīng Kē.
In Yān there was a brave man named Qín Wǔyáng,
who at thirteen years old
had killed someone,
and no one dared to look him in the eye.
So he was appointed as Jīng Kē's assistant.
Jīng Kē was waiting for someone,
wanting to go together;
that person lived far away and hadn't arrived yet,
so he was preparing for the journey.
After a while,
before setting out,
the Crown Prince grew impatient with the delay,
suspecting he had changed his mind,
and urged him again, saying:
"The day is almost over.
Are you still intending to go, Jīng Kē?
Allow me to send Qín Wǔyáng first."
Jīng Kē was angered and rebuked the Crown Prince:
"Why are you sending me off like this?
To go and not return is the act of a fool!
Moreover, I'm taking a mere dagger into the unpredictable might of Qín.
The reason I've delayed
is to wait for my companion to go with me.
Now that you're impatient with me,
I bid you farewell!"
Then he set out.
The Crown Prince and those guests
who knew of the matter
all dressed in white mourning clothes to see him off.
When they reached the banks of the Yì River,
after the farewell ceremony,
as he was about to take the road,
Gāo Jiànlí played the zhù,
and Jīng Kē sang in harmony,
in a mournful, altered key,
moving all the men to tears.
Then he stepped forward and sang:
"The wind sighs cold o'er Yì River's shore;
the brave man leaves, to return no more!"
He followed with a passionate, high-pitched tune,
and all the men stared with wide eyes,
their hair standing on end under their caps.
Thereupon Jīng Kē mounted the carriage and departed,
never once looking back.
He then arrived in Qín,
bearing gifts worth a thousand pieces of gold,
and lavishly presented them to Méng Jiā, the king's favored attendant.
Méng Jiā spoke to the King of Qín on his behalf, saying:
"The King of Yān truly trembles at Your Majesty's might,
and dares not raise arms against your officers.
He wishes to make his whole country your subject,
ranking among the other lords,
offering tribute like a prefecture,
so that he may preserve
the ancestral temple of his predecessors.
Fearful, he dares not state this himself,
but has respectfully beheaded Fán Wūqī,
and presents the map of Dūkàng in Yān,
sealed in a box.
The King of Yān bowed in his court to send it off,
and sent a messenger to inform Your Majesty.
It awaits your command."
The King of Qín heard this,
was greatly pleased,
and donned his court robes,
arranged the nine-tiered ceremonial guard,
and received the Yān envoy in the Xiányáng Palace.
Jīng Kē carried the box with Fán Wūqī's head,
while Qín Wǔyáng held the case with the map,
and they advanced in order.
When they reached the steps,
Qín Wǔyáng turned pale and trembled with fear,
which puzzled the ministers.
Jīng Kē turned and smiled at Wǔyáng,
then stepped forward to apologize:
"He is a rustic from the northern barbarian lands,
who has never seen the Son of Heaven,
hence his terror.
I beg Your Majesty to indulge him a little,
so that he may complete his mission before you."
The King of Qín said to Jīng Kē: "Bring me the map that Wǔyáng holds."
Jīng Kē took the map and presented it.
The King of Qín unrolled the map,
and when it was fully open, the dagger was revealed.
Jīng Kē then seized the King of Qín's sleeve with his left hand,
while with his right hand he grasped the dagger
and stabbed at him.
Before it reached him,
the King of Qín, startled,
jerked back and rose,
tearing his sleeve.
He tried to draw his sword,
but it was long,
and he grasped the scabbard.
In his panic,
the sword was stuck, so he couldn't draw it immediately.
Jīng Kē chased the King of Qín,
who ran around a pillar.
The ministers were all stunned;
taken completely by surprise,
they lost all composure.
According to Qín law,
those ministers serving in the hall
could not carry any weapons;
all guards armed with weapons were stationed below the hall,
and could not ascend without a summons.
In the urgency of the moment,
there was no time to call the guards,
so Jīng Kē was able to pursue the King of Qín.
In their desperate panic,
having nothing to strike Jīng Kē with,
they used their hands to grapple with him.
At that moment, the royal physician Xià Wújū
threw the medicine bag he was carrying at Jīng Kē.
As the King of Qín was running around the pillar,
in sudden panic,
not knowing what to do,
his attendants shouted: "Your Majesty, push your sword to your back!"
He did so,
and thus drew it to strike Jīng Kē,
severing his left thigh.
Jīng Kē, disabled,
then threw his dagger at the King of Qín,
but missed,
hitting a bronze pillar.
The King of Qín struck Jīng Kē again,
wounding him eight times.
Jīng Kē knew he had failed,
leaned against the pillar and laughed,
then sat with legs sprawled and cursed:
"The reason I failed
is that I wanted to capture you alive,
to force a pact to report to the Crown Prince."
Thereupon the attendants rushed forward and killed Jīng Kē,
and the King of Qín was displeased for a long while.
Later, when rewarding achievements,
he distributed rewards to the ministers and those involved accordingly,
and awarded Xià Wújū two hundred yì of gold,
saying:
"Wújū cared for me,
for he threw his medicine bag at Jīng Kē."
Thereupon the King of Qín grew furious,
dispatched more troops to Zhào,
and ordered Wáng Jiǎn's army to attack Yān.
In the tenth month, they captured Jì City.
The King of Yān, Xǐ, Crown Prince Dān, and others
led all their elite troops east to seek refuge in Liáodōng.
The Qín general Lǐ Xìn pursued the King of Yān
relentlessly,
and the King of Dài, Jiā, sent a letter to the King of Yān, Xǐ, saying:
"The reason Qín pursues Yān so urgently
is because of Crown Prince Dān.
If you now kill Dān and present him to the King of Qín,
the King of Qín is sure to relent,
and your state may luckily survive."
Afterwards, Lǐ Xìn pursued Dān,
who hid in the Yǎn River,
so the King of Yān sent an envoy to behead Crown Prince Dān,
intending to offer him to Qín.
Qín again advanced troops to attack them.
Five years later,
Qín finally destroyed Yān,
capturing the King of Yān Xǐ.
The next year,
Qín unified the world,
establishing the title of Huángdì.
Thereupon Qín expelled
the followers of Crown Prince Dān and Jīng Kē,
who all fled.
Gāo Jiànlí changed his name
and became a hired laborer,
hiding while working in Sòngzǐ.
After a long time, suffering from hard labor,
he heard a guest in his master's hall
playing the zhù,
and lingered, unable to leave.
He often remarked:
"That playing has both good and bad points."
Attendants reported this to their master,
saying:
"That laborer actually understands music,
secretly commenting on what's right and wrong."
The master summoned him to come forward
and play the zhù,
and all present praised his skill,
rewarding him with wine.
But Gāo Jiànlí thought of hiding forever
in fear and poverty with no end,
so he withdrew,
took out his zhù from his luggage and his fine clothes,
changed his appearance, and came forward.
All the seated guests were astonished,
descended to treat him as an equal,
and considered him an honored guest.
When he played the zhù and sang,
no guest left without shedding tears.
The people of Sòngzǐ took turns hosting him as a guest,
and this reached Qín Shǐ Huáng's ears.
Qín Shǐ Huáng summoned him for an audience,
and someone who recognized him
said:
"It's Gāo Jiànlí."
The Qín emperor, valuing his skill with the zhù, heavily pardoned him,
but had his eyes blinded.
When made to play the zhù,
he never failed to earn praise.
Gradually, he was allowed closer,
so Gāo Jiànlí placed lead inside his zhù,
and when again permitted near,
he raised the zhù to strike Qín Shǐ Huáng,
but missed.
Thereupon, he executed Gāo Jiànlí,
and for the rest of his life never again approached people from the various states.
Lǔ Jūjiàn, having heard
of Jīng Kē's assassination attempt on the King of Qín,
privately said: "Alas!
What a pity he didn't master the art of swordplay!
How greatly I misjudged the man!
Previously, I scolded him,
and he must have thought me less than human!"
Grand Historian comments:
When the world speaks of Jīng Kē,
those who recount Crown Prince Dān's fate
with "heaven rained grain,
horses grew horns"
go too far.
Also, claims that Jīng Kē wounded the King of Qín
are all untrue.
Previously, Gōngsūn Jìgōng and Mr. Dǒng
associated with Xià Wúqiě,
knew the full story,
and told me thus.
From Cáo Mèi to Jīng Kē, these five men,
whether their righteous deeds succeeded or not,
their intentions were clearly noble,
not betraying their aspirations,
their names enduring through later ages—how could this be in vain!
Lǐ Sī
was from Shàngcài in Chǔ.
In his youth,
he served as a minor clerk in the commandery,
and saw rats in the office restroom eating filth,
approaching people and dogs,
frequently frightened.
When Lǐ Sī entered a granary,
he observed the rats there,
eating stored grain,
living under large eaves,
untroubled by people or dogs.
Thereupon, Lǐ Sī sighed and said:
"Whether a man is worthy or not is like these rats—
it depends on where he positions himself!"
So he studied under Xún Qīng
the methods of emperors and kings.
After completing his studies,
he reckoned the King of Chǔ not worth serving,
and the six states all weak,
with no opportunity to achieve merit,
he wished to go west to Qín.
Taking leave of Xún Qīng, he said:
"I've heard one must not delay when the time is right;
now is when the myriad chariots contend,
and traveling advisers decide affairs.
Currently, the King of Qín desires to devour the world,
ruling as emperor,
this is the time for commoners to gallop
and the season for itinerant persuaders.
To remain in lowly positions without ambition
is like beasts viewing meat,
having human faces but barely able to walk.
Thus, no shame is greater than lowliness,
and no sorrow deeper than poverty.
Long dwelling in humble stations,
in hardship and distress,
condemning the world and despising profit,
pretending to inaction—
this is not the true nature of scholars.
Therefore, I will go west to persuade the King of Qín."
Arriving in Qín,
he encountered King Zhuāngxiāng's death,
so Lǐ Sī sought to become a retainer
of the Qín chancellor, Marquis Wénxìn Lǚ Bùwéi;
Bùwéi esteemed him,
appointing him as a court gentleman.
Thus, Lǐ Sī gained opportunity to advise,
saying to the King of Qín:
"Those who wait on others
miss their opportunities.
Those who achieve great merit
seize upon cracks and conflicts
and act ruthlessly.
In the past, during Duke Mù of Qín's hegemony,
he never annexed the six states eastward—
why?
The feudal lords were still numerous,
and the virtue of Zhōu had not yet declined,
so the Five Hegemons arose successively,
each honoring the Zhōu court.
Since Duke Xiào of Qín,
the Zhōu court has declined,
feudal lords annexed each other,
east of the pass becoming six states,
and Qín, riding victory to command the feudal lords,
has lasted six generations.
Now the feudal lords submit to Qín
like commanderies and counties.
With Qín's strength
and Your Majesty's worthiness,
it's as easy as sweeping dust from a stove,
enough to annihilate the feudal lords,
achieve imperial enterprise,
unify the world under one rule—
this is the opportunity of ten thousand generations.
If we delay and don't act urgently,
and the feudal lords regain strength,
forming vertical alliances,
even with Huángdì's wisdom,
we couldn't annex them."
The King of Qín then appointed Lǐ Sī as Chief Clerk,
heeding his plans,
secretly sending strategists carrying gold and jade
to persuade the feudal lords.
Prominent figures among the feudal lords
who could be swayed by wealth
were richly bribed and won over;
those unwilling
were stabbed with sharp swords.
After sowing discord among their rulers and ministers,
the King of Qín would send his best generals
to follow up.
The King of Qín appointed Lǐ Sī as a Guest Minister.
Meanwhile, a man of Hán named Zhèng Guó
came to spy on Qín,
by constructing the Zhùgài Canal,
but was eventually discovered.
Qín's imperial clan and high officials
all advised the King of Qín:
"Those from other states who come to serve Qín
mostly act for their own rulers,
spying in Qín under the guise of travel;
we request the expulsion of all foreigners."
Lǐ Sī was also among those slated for expulsion.
So Lǐ Sī submitted a memorial saying:
I have heard that officials are discussing the expulsion of foreigners,
and I privately consider this to be a mistake.
In the past, Duke Mù sought talents,
obtaining Yóuyú from the west among the Róng,
securing Bǎilǐ Xī from the east in Wǎn,
welcoming Jiǎn Shū from Sòng,
and attracting Pī Bào and Gōngsūn Zhī from Jìn.
These five individuals,
though not born in Qín,
were employed by Duke Mù,
leading to the annexation of twenty states,
and thus he dominated the Western Róng.
Duke Xiào employed the laws of Shāng Yāng,
transforming customs and practices,
resulting in a prosperous and thriving populace,
a wealthy and powerful state,
the people gladly served,
the feudal lords submitted willingly,
they captured the armies of Chǔ and Wèi,
seized a thousand lǐ of territory,
and to this day, the state remains strong and well-governed.
King Huì adopted Zhāng Yí's strategies,
capturing the land of Sānchuān,
annexing Bā and Shǔ to the west,
acquiring Shàngjùn in the north,
taking Hànzhōng in the south,
encompassing the Nine Yí tribes,
controlling Yān and Yǐng,
securing the strategic Chénggāo in the east,
partitioning fertile lands,
thereby breaking up the alliance of the six states,
forcing them to serve Qín from the west,
with achievements lasting to the present.
King Zhāo obtained Fàn Jū,
dismissed the Marquis of Ráng,
expelled Huáyáng,
strengthened the royal house,
blocked private factions,
gradually encroached upon the feudal lords,
enabling Qín to accomplish imperial ambitions.
These four rulers,
all achieved success through the contributions of foreigners.
From this perspective,
how have foreigners failed Qín!
Had these four rulers rejected foreigners
and not admitted them,
spurned scholars and not employed them,
it would have left the state without the reality of wealth and benefit
and Qín without the reputation of strength and greatness.
Now, Your Majesty acquires jade from Kūnlún,
possesses the treasures of Suí and Hé,
hangs pearls as bright as the moon,
wields the Tài'ē sword,
rides the Xiānlí horses,
erects banners with kingfisher feathers,
and sets up drums made from alligator skin.
These numerous treasures,
not a single one is produced in Qín,
yet Your Majesty delights in them;
why is that?
If only what is produced in Qín is acceptable,
then night-shining jade disks would not adorn the court,
rhinoceros and ivory artifacts would not be for amusement,
women from Zhèng and Wèi would not fill the harem,
fine steeds like Juétí would not stock the outer stables,
gold and tin from Jiāngnán would not be used,
and cinnabar and azurite from Western Shǔ would not be for pigments.
All that adorns the harem, fills the ranks,
pleases the heart, and delights the senses,
if it must come from Qín to be acceptable,
then hairpins with Wǎn pearls,
earrings with dangling gems,
robes of Ā-gauze,
and embroidered ornaments would not be presented before you,
and the elegant, charming, and graceful
women of Zhào would not stand by your side.
Beating earthen jars, tapping pottery, strumming zithers, and slapping thighs,
with boisterous singing to please the ears,
is truly the music of Qín;
while the tunes of "Zhèng," "Wèi," "Sāngjiān,"
"Zhāo," "Yú," "Wǔ," and "Xiàng,"
are the music of other states.
Now, abandoning the beating of jars and pottery
for "Zhèng" and "Wèi,"
setting aside the zither for "Zhāo" and "Yú,"
why is this so?
For immediate pleasure,
and suitability for enjoyment.
Yet in selecting people, it is not so.
Without asking if they are suitable or not,
without considering right or wrong,
those not from Qín are dismissed,
and foreigners are expelled.
This shows that what is valued
lies in beauty, music, pearls, and jade,
while what is轻视 lies in the people.
