This is not the way to rule the world
and control the feudal lords.
I have heard that broad lands yield abundant grain,
a large state has a numerous population,
and strong soldiers make brave warriors.
Thus, Mount Tài does not reject soil,
hence it achieves its greatness;
rivers and seas do not disdain small streams,
hence they attain their depth;
a true king does not spurn the masses,
hence he manifests his virtue.
Therefore, the land knows no boundaries,
the people no foreign states,
the four seasons are full and beautiful,
spirits and gods bestow blessings,
this is why the Five Emperors and Three Kings
were invincible.
Now, to abandon the common people
to aid rival states,
to reject guests
to empower the feudal lords,
causing the scholars of the world to withdraw
and not dare to look westward,
to halt and not enter Qín,
this is what is called
"arming the enemy and provisioning the thieves."
Things not produced in Qín,
many are precious;
scholars not born in Qín,
yet many wish to be loyal.
Now, expelling foreigners to aid rival states,
reducing your own people to benefit your foes,
weakening yourself internally
while creating enemies externally among the feudal lords,
to hope for the state to be free from danger,
is impossible.
The King of Qín then rescinded the order to expel foreigners,
restored Lǐ Sī to his post,
and ultimately adopted his strategies.
He rose to the position of Commandant of Justice.
Over twenty years later,
they finally unified the world,
honored the ruler as emperor,
and appointed Lǐ Sī as chancellor.
They dismantled the walls of commanderies and counties,
melted down their weapons,
to show they would not be used again.
Ensuring Qín had not an inch of enfeoffed land,
not establishing sons or brothers as kings,
nor making meritorious officials feudal lords,
so that future generations would be free from the troubles of war and conflict.
In the thirty-fourth year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
a banquet was held at the Xiányáng Palace,
where the Erudite Chief Zhōu Qīngchén and others
praised the emperor's might and virtue.
A man from Qí, Chúnyú Yuè, came forward
and admonished, saying:
"I have heard that
the kings of Yīn and Zhōu ruled for over a thousand years,
enfeoffing their sons, brothers, and meritorious officials
to serve as supporting branches.
Now, Your Majesty possesses the world,
yet your sons and brothers are commoners.
Should there suddenly be troubles like Tián Cháng or the Six Ministers,
with no assistants or supporters,
how could you be rescued?
Affairs not modeled on antiquity
yet able to last long—I have never heard of such.
Now, Zhōu Qīngchén and others flatter to your face
to exaggerate Your Majesty's errors,
they are not loyal ministers."
The emperor referred his proposal to the chancellor.
The chancellor refuted his argument,
dismissed his words,
and then submitted a memorial, saying:
"In ancient times, the world was fragmented and chaotic,
unable to achieve unity,
hence the feudal lords arose together,
their words all invoking the past to harm the present,
embellishing empty talk to confuse reality,
each praising their private studies,
to criticize what the ruler has established.
Now, Your Majesty has unified the world,
distinguished right from wrong and established a single authority;
yet private scholars collude
to oppose the laws and teachings,
as soon as decrees are issued,
they immediately critique them based on their private studies,
inwardly disapproving in their hearts,
outwardly discussing in the alleys,
criticizing the ruler to gain fame,
differing from the norm to appear superior,
leading the masses to create slander."
If such practices are not prohibited,
then the ruler's authority will decline from above,
and factions will form below.
It is expedient to prohibit them.
I request that all those possessing literature of the "Odes", "Documents",
and the Hundred Schools' doctrines,
be cleansed and removed.
Upon the order's arrival, if they do not remove them within thirty days,
they shall be tattooed and made city-wall laborers.
What is not to be removed
are books on medicine, divination, and agriculture.
If there are those who wish to study,
they should take officials as their teachers."
The First Emperor approved his proposal,
collecting and removing the "Odes", "Documents",
and the Hundred Schools' doctrines to keep the common people ignorant,
so that the world could not use the past to criticize the present.
He clarified laws and regulations,
established statutes and orders,
all originating from the First Emperor.
He unified the writing system.
He built detached palaces and lodges,
spreading throughout the realm.
The following year,
he again toured the provinces,
repelling the barbarians on all frontiers,
in all of which Lǐ Sī played a significant role.
Lǐ Sī's eldest son, Yóu, served as governor of Sānchuān,
all his sons married Qin princesses,
and his daughters all married Qin princes.
When Sānchuān governor Lǐ Yóu
returned to Xiányáng on leave,
Lǐ Sī hosted a banquet at home,
all the officials came to toast him,
carriages and horsemen at his gate
numbered in the thousands.
Lǐ Sī sighed deeply and said:
"Alas!
I heard from Master Xún
'Things should not reach excessive prosperity.'
I, Sī, was but a commoner from Shàngcài,
a black-headed commoner from the alleys,
yet His Majesty, unaware of my mediocrity,
has promoted me to this position.
Currently, no minister's rank surpasses mine,
one could say I've reached the peak of wealth and honor.
When things reach their peak, they decline,
I do not know where my carriage will finally rest!"
In the tenth month of the thirty-seventh year of the First Emperor,
he traveled to Kuàijī,
along the coast,
north reaching Lángyá.
Chancellor Lǐ Sī and the Prefect of the Central Carriage Office Zhào Gāo,
who also acted as the Seal Office Prefect, all accompanied him.
The First Emperor had over twenty sons,
the eldest Fú Sū
had frequently remonstrated directly with the emperor,
so the emperor sent him to supervise troops in Shàngjùn,
with Méng Tián as general.
The youngest son Hú Hài was favored,
he requested to accompany the tour,
and the emperor permitted it.
The other sons did not accompany them.
That year in the seventh month,
the First Emperor reached Shāqiū,
fell gravely ill,
and ordered Zhào Gāo to write a letter bestowing upon Prince Fú Sū, saying:
"Entrust the troops to Méng Tián,
and return to Xiányáng for the funeral and burial."
The letter was already sealed,
but not yet given to the messenger,
when the First Emperor passed away.
The letter and seal were both in Zhào Gāo's possession,
only the son Hú Hài, Chancellor Lǐ Sī, Zhào Gāo,
and five or six favored eunuchs knew of the First Emperor's death,
the other officials were unaware.
Lǐ Sī believed that since the emperor died outside the capital,
and there was no confirmed crown prince,
he kept it secret.
They placed the First Emperor's body
in the cooling carriage,
officials continued to submit memorials
and provide meals as usual,
the eunuchs would respond to memorials
from within the cooling carriage.
Zhào Gāo then kept the sealed letter intended for Fú Sū,
and said to Prince Hú Hài:
"The emperor has passed away,
with no edict enfeoffing any princes
but only a letter for the eldest son.
When the eldest son arrives,
he will immediately be established as emperor,
while you will have not an inch of land,
what will you do about it?"
Hú Hài said:
"It is so.
I have heard that
an enlightened ruler understands his ministers,
an enlightened father understands his sons.
My father passed away without enfeoffing his sons,
what is there to say!"
Zhào Gāo said: "Not so.
Now the power over the realm,
life and death lies with you, Gāo, and the chancellor,
I hope you will consider it.
Moreover, to make others one's subjects or be subject to others,
to control others or be controlled by others,
how can they be spoken of in the same breath!"
Hú Hài said:
"To depose an elder brother and establish a younger,
is unrighteous;
to disobey my father's decree and fear death,
is unfilial;
with shallow ability and meager talent,
to forcibly rely on others' achievements,
is incompetence:
These three violate virtue,
the world will not submit,
I would face peril,
the state would lose its sacrifices."
Gāo said:
"I heard that Tāng and Wǔ killed their lords,
yet the world praised their righteousness,
they were not considered disloyal.
The ruler of Wèi killed his father,
yet Wèi recorded his virtue,
Confucius documented it,
not considering it unfilial.
In great undertakings, one need not be scrupulous in small matters;
in abundant virtue, one need not decline;
different localities have their own ways
and officials have different achievements.
So to care for the small and forget the great
will surely bring harm later;
to hesitate and doubt
will surely bring regret later.
Decisive and daring action
makes even ghosts and spirits avoid you,
leading to later success.
I hope you will follow through!"
Hú Hài sighed deeply and said:
"Now the great journey has not yet begun,
the funeral rites are not concluded,
how can we trouble the chancellor with this matter!"
Zhào Gāo said:
"The time, the time,
there is no leisure for lengthy planning!
Carrying provisions and leaping on horses,
we only fear being too late!"
After Hú Hài accepted Gāo's words,
Gāo said:
"If we do not consult the chancellor,
I fear the matter will not succeed,
I ask to discuss it with the chancellor on your behalf."
Gāo then said to Chancellor Lǐ Sī:
"The emperor has passed away,
he left a letter for the eldest son,
to return to Xiányáng for the funeral and be established as successor.
The letter has not been sent,
now the emperor has died,
and no one knows of it.
The letter for the eldest son and the seal
are both with Hú Hài,
determining the crown prince lies with you, my lord, and Gāo.
What shall we do?"
Lǐ Sī said:
"How can you speak such subversive words!
This is not something a minister should discuss!"
Gāo said:
"My lord, consider yourself: how do you compare to Méng Tián in ability?
In high achievements, how do you compare to Méng Tián?
In far-sighted planning without error, how do you compare to Méng Tián?
In being without resentment in the world,
how do you compare to Méng Tián?
In being long-known and trusted by the eldest son,
how do you compare to Méng Tián?"
Lǐ Sī said:
"In these five aspects I am inferior to Méng Tián,
why do you press me so deeply?"
Gāo said:
"I, Gāo, was but a menial servant in the inner palace,
fortunately able through clerical skills
to enter the Qin palace,
managing affairs for over twenty years,
I have never seen a Qin chancellor dismissed
or a meritorious minister enfeoffed
who lasted to the second generation,
all ultimately were executed and perished.
The emperor has over twenty sons,
all known to you."
The eldest son is resolute and brave in war,
trusting others and inspiring his men,
upon ascending the throne
will surely appoint Méng Tián as chancellor.
You, my lord, will ultimately not return to your hometown clutching the marquis's seal,
this is clear.
I, Gāo, received the edict to teach Hú Hài,
having him study legal matters for several years,
and have never observed any faults.
He is benevolent and deeply kind,
values people over wealth,
sharp in mind though hesitant in speech,
treats scholars with utmost courtesy and respect.
Among all the sons of Qín, none can match him,
thus he is fit to be the heir.
You should consider and decide this."
Lǐ Sī said:
"You should return to your post!
I, Sī, follow the sovereign's decree,
obey the will of Heaven.
What decision is there to make?"
Zhào Gāo said:
"Security can turn into peril,
peril can become security.
If security and peril are unsettled,
how can one honor the sage?"
Lǐ Sī said:
"I, Sī,
was but a commoner from the alleys of Shàngcài,
honored by the emperor's promotion to chancellor,
enfeoffed as a marquis,
with descendants all holding high positions
and substantial emoluments.
Thus, I am entrusted with matters of survival, danger, and security,
a duty placed upon me.
How could I betray that!
A loyal minister does not avoid death for a chance at righteousness,
a filial son does not shirk toil and face danger.
A subject should merely adhere to his duties.
Please say no more,
or you will cause me offense."
Zhào Gāo said:
"I have heard that sages are not constant in their movements,
but adapt to change and follow the times,
seeing the end to know the root,
observing the direction to foresee the outcome.
This is inherent in all things;
how can there be a constant way?
Now, the power and fate of the empire hang on Hú Hài,
and I can achieve my aims.
Moreover, to control the center from the outside
is called confusion,
to control the top from below
is called treachery.
Thus, when autumn frost falls, grass and flowers wither;
when waters stir, all things arise.
This is the inevitable effect.
Why are you so slow to see it?"
Lǐ Sī said:
"I have heard that when Jìn changed its heir,
three generations knew no peace;
when Duke Huán of Qí and his brothers contended for the throne,
they died violent deaths;
when Zhòu killed his kin,
and ignored remonstrance,
his state became ruins,
endangering the altars of grain and soil:
these three acts defied Heaven,
and their ancestral temples received no sacrifices.
I am but a man;
how could I plot such things!"
Zhào Gāo said:
"When above and below are in harmony,
it can last long;
when inside and outside are as one,
affairs have no duplicity.
If you heed my plan,
you will long hold your marquisate,
be called 'the solitary one' for generations,
surely enjoy the longevity of Qiáo and Sōng,
and the wisdom of Confucius and Mòzǐ.
Now, to abandon this and not follow,
disaster will extend to your descendants,
enough to chill the heart.
The wise turn calamity into blessing;
what will you choose?"
Lǐ Sī then looked up to heaven and sighed,
shedding tears with a deep breath, saying:
"Alas!
Alone in this chaotic time,
since I cannot die,
where else can I entrust my fate?"
Thereupon, Lǐ Sī obeyed Zhào Gāo.
Zhào Gāo then reported to Hú Hài, saying:
"I request to carry the bright command of the crown prince
to inform the chancellor,
and Chancellor Lǐ Sī dares not disobey the order!"
Thereupon, they conspired together,
forging a decree from the First Emperor
to the chancellor,
establishing Hú Hài as crown prince.
They further wrote a letter bestowing upon the eldest son Fú Sū, saying:
"I tour the empire,
praying at famous mountains and various shrines
to prolong my life.
Now, Fú Sū, with General Méng Tián,
leads a host of several hundred thousand troops
garrisoning the border,
for over ten years,
yet has not advanced forward,
with many soldiers lost,
without an inch of achievement.
Instead, he repeatedly sends memorials
bluntly slandering my actions,
resentful for not being recalled as crown prince,
grumbling day and night.
Fú Sū, as a son, is unfilial;
he is granted a sword to take his own life!
General Méng Tián, residing abroad with Fú Sū,
failed to correct him,
and must have known of his schemes.
As a subject, he is disloyal;
he is granted death,
and his troops are to be handed over to Vice General Wáng Lí."
They sealed the letter with the emperor's seal,
and sent an envoy of Hú Hài to deliver it
to Fú Sū in Shàngjùn.
When the envoy arrived,
the letter was opened,
Fú Sū wept, entered his inner chamber,
and intended to kill himself.
Méng Tián stopped Fú Sū, saying:
"His Majesty is abroad,
and has not established a crown prince.
He sent me with three hundred thousand troops to guard the border,
with you, young master, as supervisor.
This is a weighty responsibility for the empire.
Now, a single envoy comes,
and you immediately kill yourself.
How do you know it is not a fraud?
I beg you to request confirmation;
after reconfirming, then die,
and it would not be too late."
The envoy repeatedly urged him.
Fú Sū, being benevolent by nature,
said to Méng Tián:
"If a father bestows death upon his son,
how can one request again!"
Thereupon, he killed himself.
Méng Tián refused to die,
so the envoy handed him over to the officials,
and he was imprisoned in Yángzhōu.
The envoy returned to report,
and Hú Hài, Lǐ Sī, and Zhào Gāo were greatly pleased.
Upon reaching Xiányáng,
they held the funeral,
and the crown prince was established as the Second Emperor.
Zhào Gāo was appointed as Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace,
often attending the emperor and wielding power.
When the Second Emperor was at leisure,
he summoned Zhào Gāo to discuss affairs,
saying to him: "A person's life in this world,
is like driving six steeds
through a crack in a wall.
Since I now rule the empire,
I wish to indulge all that pleases my ears and eyes,
exhaust all that delights my heart and mind,
to calm the ancestral temple and please the myriad families,
long possess the empire,
and live out my years.
Is this way possible?"
Zhào Gāo said:
"This is what a wise ruler can accomplish,
but a foolish and disorderly ruler would prohibit it.
I beg to speak,
not daring to avoid execution by axe,
hoping Your Majesty will pay slight attention.
The Shāqiū plot,
is suspected by all the princes and high officials.
Moreover, the princes are all your elder brothers,
and the high officials were appointed by the late emperor.
Now that Your Majesty has newly ascended,
these men are discontent and不服,
and I fear they may rebel.
Furthermore, Méng Tián is dead,
but Méng Yì leads troops abroad.
I tremble with fear,
only worried it will not end well.
How can Your Majesty indulge in such pleasures?"
The Second Emperor said:
"What is to be done?"
Zhào Gāo said:
"Enforce strict laws and severe punishments,
so that those who are guilty are implicated and executed,
extending to the confiscation of their clans,
eliminating senior ministers and distancing blood relatives;
enrich the poor,
and elevate the humble.
Completely remove the former ministers of the late emperor,
and replace them with those whom Your Majesty trusts
and keeps close.
Then the hidden virtue will belong to Your Majesty,
harm will be eradicated and treacherous schemes blocked,
all officials will be bathed in your grace,
receiving abundant kindness,
and Your Majesty can then rest easy and indulge your desires,
enjoying favor and pleasure.
No plan is better than this."
The Second Emperor agreed with Zhào Gāo's words,
and thus revised the laws.
As a result, when officials and various princes
were accused of crimes,
they were handed over to Zhào Gāo,
who ordered their interrogation and punishment.
He executed senior ministers like Méng Yì and others,
twelve princes were publicly executed in Xiányáng's market,
ten princesses were torn apart at Dù,
their property confiscated by the state,
and those implicated
were too numerous to count.
Prince Gāo wanted to flee,
but feared his clan would be seized,
so he submitted a memorial saying:
"When the late emperor was in good health,
I was given food upon entering court,
and rode in imperial carriages when leaving.
Robes from the imperial wardrobe,
I received as gifts;
fine horses from the imperial stables,
I was granted.
I should have followed in death
but failed to do so,
making me an unfilial son,
and an disloyal minister.
The disloyal cannot establish a name in this world,
so I request to follow in death,
wishing to be buried at the foot of Lìshān.
I beg Your Majesty to take pity on me."
When the memorial was presented,
Hú Hài was greatly pleased,
summoned Zhào Gāo to show it to him,
and said:
"Can this be considered urgent?"
Zhào Gāo replied:
"When ministers worry about death
and have no leisure,
how can they plot any rebellion!"
Hú Hài approved his request,
granting a hundred thousand coins for his burial.
Laws, decrees, and punishments
became increasingly harsh,
causing all officials to feel personally endangered,
and many desired to rebel.
Moreover, the construction of the Ēpáng Palace commenced,
along with the Straight Road and the Imperial Highway,
taxes grew heavier,
and military conscription never ceased.
Thus, Chǔ conscripts Chén Shèng,
Wú Guǎng, and others started a rebellion,
rising in the area east of the mountains,
with outstanding figures establishing themselves,
proclaiming themselves as marquises and kings,
rebelling against Qín,
their troops reached Hóngmén before retreating.
Lǐ Sī repeatedly sought an opportunity
to remonstrate,
but the Second Emperor would not permit it.
Instead, the Second Emperor questioned Lǐ Sī, saying:
"I have a private opinion
and have heard something from Hán Fēizǐ,
which says
'When Yáo possessed the empire,
his hall's foundation was only three feet high,
the rafters were untrimmed wood,
the thatch was uncut,
even an inn's lodging was no less comfortable than this.
In winter, he wore deerskin,
in summer, hemp cloth,
ate coarse grains,
and vegetable soup,
ate from earthen bowls,
drank from earthen vessels,
even a gatekeeper's sustenance was no worse than this.
Yǔ dredged the Lóngmén mountain,
opened up the Dàxià region,
channeled the nine rivers,
curved the nine embankments,
diverted stagnant waters to the sea,
until his thighs had no hair,
his shins were bare,
his hands and feet calloused,
his face and complexion dark,
and thus he died abroad,
buried at Kuàijī,
the toil of a slave or prisoner
was no more intense than this.'
So then, what is valued in possessing the empire
is surely not to torment the body and weary the spirit,
residing in an inn's lodging,
eating a gatekeeper's fare,
and laboring like a slave or prisoner, is it?
This is what inferior people strive for,
not what the worthy pursue.
When a worthy person possesses the empire,
it is solely to use the empire for his own comfort,
this is why possessing the empire is valued.
Those called worthy persons
must be able to stabilize the empire
and govern the myriad people,
but if one cannot even benefit oneself,
how can one govern the empire!
Therefore, I wish to fulfill my desires and broaden my wants,
long enjoy the empire without harm,
how can this be done?"
Lǐ Sī's son, Lǐ Yóu, was governor of Sānchuān,
and when the bandits Wú Guǎng and others
advanced westward seizing territory,
he passed by but could not stop them.
After Zhāng Hán defeated and pursued Wú Guǎng's forces,
investigators repeatedly examined Sānchuān,
reprimanding Lǐ Sī
for holding the position of one of the Three Excellencies,
yet allowing bandits to act so freely.
Lǐ Sī, fearful,
and valuing his rank and emolument,
unsure what to do,
catered to the Second Emperor's wishes,
seeking to gain favor,
and responded with a memorial saying:
A worthy ruler
must be one who can fully uphold the Way
and practice the methods of supervision and accountability.
Through supervision and accountability,
then ministers dare not fail to exhaust their abilities
in serving their ruler.
This establishes the distinction between ruler and minister,
clarifies the duty between superior and inferior,
so that all in the empire, worthy or not,
dare not fail to exert their utmost
in their duties to serve their ruler.
Thus, the ruler alone controls the empire
and is controlled by none.
He can reach the ultimate in pleasure,
a worthy and enlightened ruler indeed,
should he not examine this!
Therefore, Shěn Bùhài said
"To possess the empire
and not be self-indulgent,
is called making the empire one's shackles,"
for no other reason
than failing to supervise and hold accountable,
and instead laboring personally
for the people of the empire,
like Yáo and Yǔ did,
hence it is called 'shackles.'
If one does not cultivate the enlightened methods of Shěn Bùhài and Hán Fēi,
practice the way of supervision and accountability,
and solely use the empire for self-comfort,
but merely strives to torment the body and weary the spirit,
sacrificing oneself for the common people,
then one is but a servant to the black-haired people,
not one who possesses the empire,
what is there to value!
To have others sacrifice for oneself,
then one is noble and others are base;
to sacrifice oneself for others,
then one is base and others are noble.
Thus, those who sacrifice for others are base,
and those for whom others sacrifice are noble,
from ancient times to the present,
it has never been otherwise.
In ancient times, the reason for honoring the worthy
was because they were noble;
and the reason for despising the unworthy
was because they were base.
Yet Yáo and Yǔ sacrificed themselves for the empire,
and if we follow and honor them for that,
then we lose the original intent of honoring the worthy,
which can be called a great error.
To call it 'shackles,' is that not fitting?
It is the fault of failing to supervise and hold accountable.
Hence Hán Fēizǐ said,
"A doting mother may have a wayward son,
while a strict household has no unruly servants."
Why is that?
It is because severe penalties are invariably imposed.
Thus, under Lord Shāng's laws,
those who dumped ashes on the road were punished.
Now dumping ashes
is a minor offense,
yet being punished for it
is a heavy penalty.
Only an enlightened ruler
can rigorously supervise even minor crimes.
If minor offenses are deeply supervised,
how much more so for serious crimes?
Thus, the people dare not transgress.
Therefore, Hán Fēizǐ said
"A few feet of cloth or silk,
ordinary people won't let go;
molten gold worth a hundred yì,
even the robber Zhí wouldn't grab"
not because ordinary people value it highly
or the small gain is profound,
nor because the robber Zhí's desires are shallow;
nor is it that the robber Zhí's actions
consider a hundred yì lightly.
Grabbing would mean instant punishment for his hands,
so the robber Zhí doesn't grab the hundred yì;
but if penalties aren't consistently enforced,
then ordinary people won't relinquish a few feet.
Thus, a city wall five zhàng high,
even Lóu Jì wouldn't lightly scale;
while Mount Tài stands a hundred rèn tall,
lame sheep graze upon it.
If Lóu Jì finds a five-zhàng barrier difficult,
how could a lame sheep find a hundred-rèn height easy?
The steepness of the precipice differs.
The reason enlightened rulers and sage kings can
long remain in尊贵之位,
perpetually hold weighty authority,
and exclusively monopolize the world's benefits
is not due to some different way,
but because they can independently decide
and meticulously supervise accountability,
ensuring severe punishments,
so the world dares not offend.
Now if one doesn't pursue what prevents offenses,
but engages in what makes doting mothers ruin sons,
then they fail to comprehend the sage's discourse.
If one cannot implement the sage's methods,
then aside from being enslaved by the world,
what else can they do?
Is this not lamentable!
Moreover, if frugal, righteous, and benevolent persons
stand in court,
then wanton amusements cease;
if remonstrating and principled ministers
are at one's side,
then dissolute ambitions are curtailed;
if the conduct of staunch martyrs
is prominent in the world,
then excessive pleasures are abandoned.
Hence, an enlightened ruler can exclude these three,
and solely wield the ruler's techniques
to control obedient ministers,
and refine clear laws,
thus achieving personal尊贵 and weighty authority.
All worthy rulers
must necessarily oppose worldly customs,
abolish what they dislike,
and establish what they desire,
so that in life they enjoy尊贵 and authority,
and in death
receive wise and enlightened posthumous titles.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler decides independently,
so power doesn't reside with ministers.
Only then can they obliterate the path of benevolence and righteousness,
silence the mouths of persuasive orators,
thwart the actions of martyrs,
block hearing and obscure sight,
internally seeing and hearing alone,
so externally
they cannot be swayed by benevolence and righteousness
or martyrs' conduct,
and internally cannot be robbed by remonstrance
or contentious debates.
Thus, they can resolutely act alone
with a willful heart
and none dare oppose.
Only then can it be said
they understand the methods of Shēn and Hán,
and practice Lord Shāng's laws.
With laws practiced and methods clear,
the world in chaos is unheard of.
Hence it is said
"The kingly way is simple and easy to grasp."
Only an enlightened ruler can implement it.
Thus,
if the essence of supervision and accountability is realized,
then ministers harbor no evil,
if ministers harbor no evil, the world is at peace,
if the world is at peace, the ruler is威严 and尊贵,
if the ruler is威严 and尊贵,
then supervision and accountability are certain,
if supervision and accountability are certain,
then desired outcomes are achieved,
if desired outcomes are achieved, the state prospers,
if the state prospers, the ruler's pleasures abound.
Thus, with the method of supervision and accountability in place,
all desires are fulfilled.
Ministers and common people
struggle to avoid faults,
how dare they plot changes?
Then the imperial way is complete,
and it can be said
one understands the ruler-minister relationship.
Even if Shēn and Hán were reborn,
they could add nothing.
The memorial presented,
Èrshì was pleased.
Thereupon, supervision and accountability
intensified in severity,
and those who taxed the people heavily
were considered enlightened officials.
Èrshì said: "If so, then it can be said
supervision and accountability are achieved."
The punished filled half the roads,
and the dead piled up daily in the markets.
Those who killed many
were deemed loyal ministers.
Èrshì said: "If so, then it can be said
supervision and accountability are achieved."
Earlier,
when Zhào Gāo was Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace,
he killed many and settled numerous private grudges,
fearing that ministers at court
would report and slander him,
so he advised Èrshì:
"The reason the Son of Heaven is尊贵
is that only his voice is heard,
and no minister sees his face,
hence titled 'Zhèn'.
Moreover, Your Majesty is young,
not necessarily versed in all matters,
now sitting in court,
if reproofs or promotions are improper,
your shortcomings are exposed to ministers,
not a way to display divinity to the world.
Better if Your Majesty remains deeply in the forbidden quarters,
with me and court attendants well-versed in law awaiting matters,
so when affairs arise, there's a way to assess them.
Thus, ministers won't dare report uncertain matters,
and the world will acclaim a sage ruler."
Èrshì adopted his plan,
ceased sitting in court to see ministers,
and stayed in the forbidden quarters.
Zhào Gāo often attended, handling affairs,
all matters decided by Zhào Gāo.
Gāo heard Lǐ Sī had commented on this,
so he visited the Chancellor saying:
"Bandits east of the pass are numerous,
now the Emperor urgently
increases conscription to build the Ēpáng Palace,
gathering useless dogs and horses.
I wish to remonstrate,
but my position is lowly.
This is truly Your Lordship's duty,
why not remonstrate?"
Lǐ Sī said:
"Indeed,
I've long intended to speak.
But now the Emperor doesn't hold court,
stays deep in the palace,
when I have something to say, it can't be conveyed,
and I've no opportunity for an audience."
Zhào Gāo told him: "If you truly can remonstrate,
I'll request the Emperor to find a moment for you."
Thereupon, Zhào Gāo waited
until Èrshì was feasting and merry,
with women present,
then had someone inform the Chancellor:
"His Majesty is free now,
you may report matters."
The Chancellor reached the palace gate
requesting audience,
this happened thrice.
Èrshì angrily said:
"I often have many free days,
but the Chancellor doesn't come.
When I'm privately feasting,
he immediately comes seeking audience.
Does the Chancellor look down on me?
Or intend to embarrass me?"
Zhào Gāo then said: "This is dangerous!
The Shāqiū plot, the Chancellor was involved in it."
Now that Your Majesty has ascended as emperor,
yet the chancellor's status has not been elevated,
this indicates his intention to expect enfeoffment
and become a king.
Moreover, had Your Majesty not inquired,
I would not dare speak.
The chancellor's eldest son Lǐ Yóu
serves as governor of Sānchuān,
while the Chǔ bandits like Chén Shèng
are all sons of counties adjacent to the chancellor's,
hence the Chǔ bandits operate openly,
passing through Sānchuān,
where the city guards refuse to attack them.
I have heard of documents exchanged between them,
but lacking concrete evidence,
I dared not report it.
Furthermore, with the chancellor operating externally,
his power surpasses Your Majesty's."
The Second Emperor found this reasonable.
He intended to investigate the chancellor,
but fearing insufficient evidence,
sent someone to examine
the circumstances of the Sānchuān governor's collusion with bandits.
Lǐ Sī heard of this.
At that time, the Second Emperor was at Gānquán,
watching wrestling and comedian performances.
Unable to gain audience,
Lǐ Sī submitted a memorial criticizing Zhào Gāo:
"I have heard that
when ministers suspect their ruler,
it invariably endangers the state;
when concubines suspect their husband,
it invariably endangers the household.
Now there is a high official
who monopolizes advantages and harms for Your Majesty,
no different from Your Majesty himself,
which is highly inappropriate.
Formerly, Sīchéng Zǐhǎn served as minister of Sòng,
personally administering punishments,
using authority to implement them,
and within a year usurped his ruler.
Tián Cháng served as minister to Duke Jiǎn,
his rank unmatched in the state,
his private wealth equal to the treasury's,
dispensing favors and virtue,
gaining support from the common people below,
and winning over officials above,
secretly seizing Qí state,
killing Zǎi Yǔ in the courtyard,
then assassinating Duke Jiǎn in court,
finally possessing Qí state.
This is clearly known throughout the land.
Now Zhào Gāo harbors devious intentions,
and dangerous rebellious conduct,
like Zǐhǎn's ministry in Sòng;
his private wealth
resembles the Tián clan's in Qí.
Combining the rebellious ways of Tián Cháng and Zǐhǎn
while usurping Your Majesty's authority,
his ambition resembles
Hán Jì's service as minister to Hán Ān.
If Your Majesty doesn't plan,
I fear he will stage a rebellion."
The Second Emperor said:
"Why so?
This Zhào Gāo,
though originally a eunuch,
doesn't indulge recklessly in safety,
nor changes heart in danger,
maintains pure conduct and cultivates goodness,
achieving his position through self-discipline,
advanced through loyalty,
maintaining position through trustworthiness,
I truly consider him worthy,
yet you suspect him - why?
Moreover, I lost my predecessor young,
lacking knowledge,
unpracticed in governing people,
while you are aged,
fearing severance from the world.
If I don't rely on Lord Zhào,
whom should I trust?
Besides, Lord Zhào is refined, incorruptible and vigorous,
understanding human sentiments below,
able to suit me above,
you should not doubt him."
Lǐ Sī said:
"Not so.
This Zhào Gāo,
originally a lowly man,
ignorant of principles,
insatiably greedy,
ceaselessly pursuing profit,
positioned next to the sovereign,
boundlessly seeking desires,
therefore I say he is dangerous."
The Second Emperor, previously trusting Zhào Gāo,
feared Lǐ Sī would kill him,
so privately informed Zhào Gāo.
Gāo said:
"The chancellor only worries about me,
if I die,
the chancellor will attempt what Tián Cháng did."
Thereupon the Second Emperor said:[106"Let Lǐ Sī be handed over to the court steward!"
Zhào Gāo investigated Lǐ Sī.
Lǐ Sī was bound and restrained,
imprisoned in jail,
sighing to heaven:
"Alas, how tragic!
What strategy can one employ with an unprincipled ruler!
Formerly, Jié killed Guān Lóngpáng,
Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān,
King Fūchāi of Wú killed Wǔ Zǐxū.
These three ministers,
were they not loyal?
Yet unavoidably died,
dying for misplaced loyalty.
Now my wisdom falls short of these three,
while the Second Emperor's lack of principle exceeds Jié,
Zhòu, and Fūchāi,
my death through loyalty is fitting.
Moreover, isn't the Second Emperor's rule chaotic!
Recently executing his brothers to自立,
killing loyal ministers while elevating lowly men,
constructing the Ēpáng Palace,
imposing levies throughout the land.
It's not that I didn't remonstrate,
but he wouldn't listen.
All ancient sage kings
moderated their eating and drinking,
limited their vehicles and utensils,
restrained their palaces and rooms,
issuing decrees and undertaking projects,
prohibiting excessive expenses without public benefit,
thus achieving lasting stability.
Now he commits atrocities against brothers,
disregarding the consequences;
persecutes loyal ministers,
unmindful of the calamity;
builds enormous palaces,
heavily taxing the land,
sparing no expense:
these three practices implemented,
the land refuses obedience.
Now rebels already control half the empire,
yet his mind remains unawakened,
with Zhào Gāo as assistant,
I will surely see invaders reach Xiányáng,
with deer roaming the court."
Thereupon the Second Emperor ordered Gāo
to investigate the chancellor's case,
determine crimes,
interrogate Sī about conspiring with his son Yóu,
arresting all clan members and guests.
Zhào Gāo interrogated Sī,
administering over a thousand beatings,
until unbearable pain
forced false confession.
Sī refrained from suicide
due to confidence in his eloquence,
his achievements,
and actual lack of rebellious intent,
hoping to memorialize his case,
hoping the Second Emperor would awaken and pardon him.
Lǐ Sī thus submitted a prison memorial:
"As chancellor governing the people,
I have served over thirty years.
Encountering Qín's narrow territory.
During former kings' time, Qín's lands
measured barely a thousand lǐ,
with troops numbering tens of thousands.
I exhausted my modest talents,
diligently upholding laws and decrees,
secretly deploying strategists,
providing them gold and jade,
sending them to lobby feudal lords,
covertly strengthening armor and weapons,
refining administration and education,
appointing combatants as officials,
honoring meritorious ministers,
enriching their ranks and emoluments,
thus finally intimidating Hán and weakening Wèi,
destroying Yān and Zhào,
eliminating Qí and Chǔ,
ultimately annexing the six states,
capturing their kings,
establishing Qín as Son of Heaven.
This is my first crime."
The land was not without breadth,
and in the north, they drove out the Hú and Mò tribes,
while in the south, they pacified the Bǎiyuè,
demonstrating Qín's strength.
This is the second crime.
Honoring high officials,
enriching their ranks and positions,
to secure their loyalty.
This is the third crime.
Establishing the altars of soil and grain,
repairing the ancestral temples,
to manifest the sovereign's virtue.
This is the fourth crime.
Revising the systems,
standardizing measures, volumes, and written scripts,
and promulgating them throughout the land,
to establish Qín's reputation.
This is the fifth crime.
Building imperial highways,
promoting tours and inspections,
to display the sovereign's achievements.
This is the sixth crime.
Mitigating punishments,
reducing taxes and levies,
to fulfill the sovereign's desire to win the people's hearts,
so that all subjects support the sovereign,
remembering him even in death.
This is the seventh crime.
A minister who acts thus,
has long deserved death for his crimes.
Fortunately, the emperor allowed me to exert my abilities fully,
enabling me to survive until now.
I beg Your Majesty to consider this!"
The memorial was submitted,
but Zhào Gāo had the officials discard it
without presenting it,
saying:
"How can a prisoner submit a memorial!"
Zhào Gāo sent over ten of his associates to pose as imperial censors, court ushers, and palace attendants,
taking turns to interrogate Lǐ Sī repeatedly.
When Lǐ Sī answered truthfully,
they would have him beaten again.
Later, when Èrshì sent someone to verify Lǐ Sī's case,
Lǐ Sī, thinking it was the same as before,
ultimately dared not change his statement,
and pleaded guilty.
When the verdict was presented to the emperor,
Èrshì exclaimed joyfully:
"Without Zhào Jūn,
I would have been betrayed by the chancellor."
By the time the envoy sent by Èrshì
to investigate the governor of Sānchuān
arrived,
Xiàng Liáng had already attacked and killed him.
When the envoy returned,
coinciding with the chancellor being handed over to the officials,
Zhào Gāo fabricated
evidence of rebellion.
In the seventh month of the second year of Èrshì,
Lǐ Sī was subjected to the five punishments in full,
sentenced to be cut in half at the waist in the market of Xiányáng.
As Lǐ Sī was led out of prison,
he and his middle son were bound together;
he turned to his son and said:
"I wish I could again go with you, leading a yellow dog,
out the east gate of Shàngcài to chase crafty hares—
but how could that be possible now?"
Thereupon, father and son wept together,
and his three clans were exterminated.
After Lǐ Sī's death,
Èrshì appointed Zhào Gāo as Central Chancellor,
and all matters, great or small, were decided by Gāo.
Knowing his own power was immense,
Gāo presented a deer,
calling it a horse.
Èrshì asked his attendants:
"Isn't this a deer?"
The attendants all replied, "It is a horse."
Èrshì was startled,
thinking himself confused,
so he summoned the Grand Diviner,
ordering a hexagram to be cast.
The Grand Diviner said:
"Your Majesty, during the spring and autumn suburban sacrifices,
when offering to the ancestral temples and spirits,
the purification and fasting were not properly observed,
hence this confusion.
You should follow the way of great virtue
and observe purification and fasting clearly."
Thereupon, he entered the Shànglín Park
to fast and purify.
While hunting daily,
a passerby entered the Shànglín Park,
and Èrshì personally shot and killed him.
Zhào Gāo instructed his son-in-law,
the magistrate of Xiányáng, Yán Lè, to impeach
for moving an unknown murderer's body
into Shànglín.
Gāo then advised Èrshì:
"For the Son of Heaven to unjustly
kill an innocent person,
this is forbidden by the High God;
the spirits will not accept offerings,
and Heaven will send down calamities.
You should leave the palace to avert this."
Èrshì then went out
to reside at the Wàngyí Palace.
After three days, Zhào Gāo forged an edict to the guards,
ordering them to dress in plain clothes and bear arms,
facing inward,
and entered to tell Èrshì:
"The rebel armies from east of the mountains have arrived in force!"
Èrshì climbed up to look
and saw them,
became terrified,
and Gāo seized the moment to force him to commit suicide.
Gāo took the imperial seal and wore it himself,
but none of the officials or attendants would follow him;
when he ascended the hall,
the hall nearly collapsed three times.
Realizing that Heaven did not grant him favor,
and the ministers did not consent,
he summoned the First Emperor's younger brother,
and handed him the seal.
Zǐ Yīng ascended the throne,
but was troubled by this,
so he claimed illness and did not attend to affairs,
conspiring with the eunuch Hán Tán and his son
to assassinate Gāo.
When Gāo came to pay respects,
inquiring about his health,
he was summoned inside,
and Hán Tán was ordered to stab him to death,
exterminating his three clans.
Zǐ Yīng reigned for three months
when Péi Gōng's army entered through Wǔguān,
reaching Xiányáng.
All the ministers and officials defected,
offering no resistance.
Zǐ Yīng, with his wife and children,
tied their own necks with silk cords,
and surrendered by the side of the Zhǐdào.
Péi Gōng then handed them over to his officials.
When Xiàng Yǔ arrived, he executed them.
Thus, the empire was lost.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Lǐ Sī rose from common origins to serve various feudal lords,
then entered to serve Qín,
seizing opportunities,
assisted the First Emperor,
and ultimately helped complete the imperial enterprise.
As one of the Three Dukes,
he can be said to have been honored and employed.
Though he understood the essence of the Six Arts,
he did not strive to clarify governance
to remedy his sovereign's shortcomings;
clinging to high rank and emolument,
he flattered and complied for expedience,
enforced harsh authority and cruel punishments,
heeded Gāo's evil counsel,
and set aside the rightful heir for a lesser son.
When the feudal lords had already rebelled,
only then did he think to remonstrate and contend—
was that not too late!
Many consider Lǐ Sī utterly loyal
and yet died by the five punishments,
but examining the root,
it differs from common opinion.
Otherwise,
his achievements might have ranked with those of Zhōu and Shào.
Méng Tián—
his ancestors were from Qí.
Tián's grandfather, Méng Ào,
served King Zhāoxiāng of Qín from Qí,
rising to Senior Minister.
In the first year of King Zhuāngxiāng of Qín,
Méng Ào served as a Qín general,
attacked Hán,
captured Chénggāo and Xíngyáng,
and established the Sānchuān Commandery.
In the second year,
Méng Ào attacked Zhào,
capturing thirty-seven cities.
In the third year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
Méng Ào attacked Hán,
capturing thirteen cities.
In the fifth year,
Méng Ào attacked Wèi,
capturing twenty cities,
and established the Dōngjùn commandery.
In the seventh year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
Méng Ào died.
Ào's son was named Wǔ,
and Wǔ's son was named Tián.
Tián once studied law and classical literature.
In the twenty-third year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
Méng Wǔ served as a lieutenant general of Qín,
and together with Wáng Jiǎn attacked Chǔ,
routing them decisively,
and killing Xiàng Yàn.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Méng Wǔ attacked Chǔ,
capturing the king of Chǔ.
Méng Tián had a younger brother named Yì.
In the twenty-sixth year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
Méng Tián, owing to his family heritage, became a general of Qín,
attacked Qí,
routing them decisively,
and was appointed as Nèishǐ.
After Qín had unified the world,
he then sent Méng Tián with three hundred thousand troops north to drive out the Róng and Dí tribes,
recovering the territory south of the Yellow River.
He built the Great Wall,
following the terrain,
using it to create strategic fortresses,
starting from Líntáo,
reaching Liáodōng,
stretching over ten thousand lǐ.
Thereupon, they crossed the Yellow River,
occupied Yángshān,
and meandered northward.
His troops were exposed in the field for over ten years,
stationed in Shàngjùn.
At that time, Méng Tián's might shook the Xiōngnú.
Qín Shǐ Huáng greatly honored and favored the Méng family,
trusting and regarding them as worthy.
And he kept Méng Yì close,
appointing him to the position of Shàngqīng,
when going out, Yì would accompany him in his carriage,
when entering, he would be in the emperor's presence.
Tián handled external affairs while Yì often advised internally,
both were known for their loyalty and trustworthiness,
thus even the various generals and ministers dared not contend with them.
There was one Zhào Gāo,
a distant relative of the Zhào clan.
Zhào Gāo and his several brothers,
were all born in the hidden palace,
their mother had been punished and executed,
their lineage was lowly and humble for generations.
The King of Qín heard that Gāo was strong and capable,
well-versed in penal law,
and promoted him to be Zhōngchēfǔ Lìng.
Gāo then privately attended to the young prince Hú Hài,
teaching him how to decide legal cases.
Gāo committed a serious crime,
and the King of Qín ordered Méng Yì to judge him according to the law.
Yì did not dare to bend the law,
sentenced Gāo to death,
and removed him from the roster of eunuchs.
The emperor, because Gāo was diligent in his duties,
pardoned him,
and restored his office and title.
Qín Shǐ Huáng wished to tour the world,
via Jiǔyuán,
straight to Gānquán,
so he sent Méng Tián to build a road,
from Jiǔyuán to Gānquán,
leveling mountains and filling valleys,
The road was not completed.
In the winter of the thirty-seventh year of Qín Shǐ Huáng,
he traveled to visit Kuàijī,
along the coast,
heading north to Lángyá.
On the way, he fell ill,
and sent Méng Yì back to pray to the mountains and rivers,
before Yì could return.
Qín Shǐ Huáng reached Shāqiū and passed away,
it was kept secret,
and none of the ministers knew.
At that time, the chancellor Lǐ Sī, the young prince Hú Hài, and Zhōngchēfǔ Lìng Zhào Gāo were often in attendance.
Gāo had long enjoyed favor with Hú Hài,
and wished to establish him as heir,
and also resented Méng Yì for judging him by law and not siding with him,
thus he harbored treacherous intentions,
and conspired with Chancellor Lǐ Sī and the young prince Hú Hài,
to establish Hú Hài as crown prince.
Once the crown prince was established,
they sent a messenger to bestow death upon the young prince Fú Sū and Méng Tián for their crimes.
After Fú Sū died,
Méng Tián was suspicious and requested verification.
The messenger handed Méng Tián over to the officials,
and he was replaced.
Hú Hài appointed a retainer of Lǐ Sī as army supervisor.
The messenger returned and reported,
Hú Hài, having heard that Fú Sū was dead,
wished to release Méng Tián.
But Zhào Gāo feared that the Méng family would regain nobility and power,
and held a grudge against them.
When Yì returned,
Zhào Gāo, pretending to offer loyal advice to Hú Hài,
wishing to destroy the Méng family,
said:
"I have heard that the late emperor long wished to promote a worthy and establish a crown prince,
but Yì advised against it, saying 'It cannot be.'
If he knew the worthy yet delayed establishing him,
then he is disloyal and deceiving his lord.
In my humble opinion,
it would be better to execute him."
Hú Hài listened and imprisoned Méng Yì in Dài.
Earlier, he had already imprisoned Méng Tián in Yángzhōu.
When the funeral procession reached Xiányáng,
and after the burial,
the crown prince ascended as the Second Emperor,
and Zhào Gāo, being close to him,
day and night slandered the Méng family,
seeking their faults,
and impeaching them.
Zǐ Yīng remonstrated, saying:
"I have heard that the former King of Zhào, Qiān, killed his good general Lǐ Mù and employed Yán Jù,
the King of Yān, Xǐ, secretly employed the schemes of Jīng Kē and betrayed the covenant with Qín,
the King of Qí, Jiàn, killed his long-time loyal ministers and adopted the advice of Hòu Shèng.
These three rulers,
each, by altering the old ways, lost their states and brought disaster upon themselves.
Now the Méng family,
are Qín's great ministers and strategists,
yet the ruler wishes to suddenly discard them,
I privately consider this improper.
I have heard that those who think lightly cannot govern a state,
and those who rely solely on their own wisdom cannot preserve their lord.
To kill loyal ministers and establish those without integrity,
this internally causes the ministers to distrust and externally causes the fighters to become disheartened,
I privately consider this improper."
Hú Hài did not listen.
And he sent the censor Qū Gōng by relay carriage to Dài,
instructing Méng Yì:
"The late lord wished to establish a crown prince, and you, sir, made it difficult.
Now the chancellor considers you disloyal,
and the crime extends to your clan.
I cannot bear this,
so I bestow upon you death,
which is already very fortunate.
You should consider this!"
Yì replied:
"If it is said that I failed to understand the late lord's intention,
then since I entered service young,
and followed his favor until the end of his life,
I could be said to have known his will.
If it is said that I did not know the crown prince's ability,
then the crown prince alone accompanied him,
traveling throughout the world,
far surpassing the other princes,
I had no doubts.
The late lord's decision to appoint the crown prince,
was the result of years of consideration,
how would I dare to advise against it,
how would I dare to scheme against it!
I do not dare to embellish my words to avoid death,
but I am ashamed to tarnish the late lord's name,
I hope you, sir, will consider this,
and let me die knowing the true reason.
Moreover, to follow and achieve completeness,
is what the Way values;
to punish and kill,
In the past, Duke Mù of Qín killed the three good men and died,
and blamed Bǎilǐ Xī for crimes he did not commit,
thus he was given the posthumous title 'Mù' (meaning 'erroneous').
King Xiāng of Zhào killed the martial lord Bái Qǐ.
King Píng of Chǔ killed Wǔ Shē.
King Fūchāi of Wú killed Wǔ Zǐxū.
These four rulers,
all committed great errors,
and the world condemned them,
considering them unenlightened rulers,
and thus they were recorded as such among the feudal lords.
Therefore it is said, 'Those who govern by the Way do not kill the innocent,
and do not punish the guiltless.'
I hope you, sir, will take heed!"
The messenger knew Hú Hài's intention,
did not listen to Méng Yì's words,
and executed him.
The Second Emperor again sent an envoy to Yángzhōu,
commanding Méng Tián:
"Your offenses are numerous,
and your younger brother Méng Yì has committed grave crimes,
so the law extends to you as the Prefect of the Capital."
Tián replied:
"From my ancestors,
down to their descendants,
we have accumulated merit and trustworthiness in Qín for three generations.
Now I command over three hundred thousand troops,
and though my body is imprisoned,
my power is sufficient to rebel,
yet I know I must die while upholding righteousness,
not daring to disgrace my ancestors' teachings,
so as not to forget the former ruler.
In the past, when King Chéng of Zhōu first ascended the throne,
still in swaddling clothes,
the Duke of Zhōu, Dàn, carried the king to court,
and eventually stabilized the realm.
When King Chéng fell gravely ill,
the Duke of Zhōu cut his own nails and sank them into the river,
saying:
'The king is not yet aware,
so I, Dàn, am handling affairs.
If there is crime and calamity,
let Dàn bear the ill omens.'
He then wrote this down and stored it in the archives,
which can be called trustworthy.
When the king could govern the state,
treacherous ministers said:
'The Duke of Zhōu, Dàn, has long desired to rebel.
If Your Majesty does not prepare,
great trouble will surely arise.'
The king became enraged,
and the Duke of Zhōu fled to Chǔ.
King Chéng inspected the archives,
found the Duke of Zhōu's sunken-nail document,
and wept, saying:
'Who said the Duke of Zhōu wanted to rebel!'
He executed the slanderer and recalled the Duke of Zhōu.
Thus, the 'Zhōu Shū' says: 'Must cross-reference and verify.'
Now my clan,
for generations without disloyalty,
yet ends up like this—
this must be due to treacherous ministers rebelling and causing chaos,
the way of internal subversion.
King Chéng erred but recovered and ultimately prospered;
Jié executed Guān Lóngpáng,
Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān without remorse,
and upon their deaths, their states perished.
Therefore, I say faults can be rectified and remonstrance can awaken.
Examining through cross-verification
is the method of the sagely above.
All my words,
are not to seek exemption from blame,
but to remonstrate even unto death,
hoping Your Majesty considers following the Way for the myriad people."
The envoy said:
"I have received the edict to carry out the law upon the general,
and dare not report the general's words to the emperor."
Méng Tián sighed deeply:
"What crime have I committed against heaven,
to die without fault?"
After a long while,
he slowly said:
"My crime indeed warrants death.
From Líntáo connecting to Liáodōng,
building walls and moats over ten thousand lǐ,
how could it not have severed the earth's veins?
This is my crime."
He then took poison and killed himself.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I traveled to the northern border,
returning via the Straight Road,
and observed the fortifications Méng Tián built for Qín's Great Wall,
cutting through mountains and filling valleys,
opening the Straight Road—
truly he took the people's labor lightly.
When Qín first annihilated the feudal lords,
the hearts of the realm were unsettled,
the wounded had not recovered,
and Tián, as a famed general,
did not forcefully remonstrate at this time,
to relieve the people's distress,
support the aged and orphaned, and strive for harmony among the masses.
Instead, he flattered and pursued achievements,
leading to his and his brother's execution—
was it not fitting?
Why blame the earth's veins?
Zhāng Ěr
was from Dàliáng.
In his youth,
he became a retainer of Lord Wújì of Wèi.
Zhāng Ěr once fled and wandered to Wàihuáng.
A rich man's daughter there was very beautiful,
married to a common laborer,
fled from her husband,
and went to her father's guest.
The guest, who knew Zhāng Ěr well,
said to the girl:
"If you must seek a worthy husband,
follow Zhāng Ěr."
The girl listened,
finally requested a divorce,
and married Zhāng Ěr.
At that time, Zhāng Ěr had escaped and was wandering,
and the girl's family generously provided for him,
enabling Zhāng Ěr to attract guests from afar.
He then became an official in Wèi as the magistrate of Wàihuáng.
His reputation for worthiness grew from this.
Chén Yú
was also from Dàliáng,
fond of Confucian teachings,
and frequently traveled to Kǔxíng in Zhào.
The wealthy Gōngchéng family married their daughter to him,
knowing Chén Yú was no ordinary man.
Yú was young,
and served Zhāng Ěr like a father;
the two formed a life-and-death friendship.
When Qín destroyed Dàliáng,
Zhāng Ěr's home was in Wàihuáng.
When Emperor Gāozǔ was a commoner,
he often accompanied Zhāng Ěr in travels,
staying for months as a guest.
A few years after Qín destroyed Wèi,
having heard of these two as famous scholars of Wèi,
offered a reward of a thousand gold for Zhāng Ěr,
and five hundred for Chén Yú.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú then changed their names,
went together to Chén,
and worked as village gatekeepers to support themselves.
The two faced each other.
A local officer once faulted and caned Chén Yú,
and Chén Yú wanted to rise up,
but Zhāng Ěr stepped on him,
making him endure the caning.
After the officer left,
Zhāng Ěr led Chén Yú under a mulberry tree and admonished him:
"What did I initially tell you?
Now, for a small insult, you would die fighting an officer?"
Chén Yú agreed.
Qín's edict sought the two,
but they instead used their gatekeeper roles to issue orders in the village.
When Chén Shè rose in Qí,
entering Chén,
his troops numbered tens of thousands.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú paid respects to Chén Shè.
Shè and his attendants had often heard of Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú's worth,
never having met them,
and were overjoyed upon meeting.
The local elite and elders of Chén then advised Chén Shè:
"General, you don armor and wield weapons,
leading troops to punish the tyrannical Qín,
restore the state of Chǔ,
revive the fallen and continue the severed,
your merit and virtue deserve kingship.
Moreover, to oversee all the generals under heaven,
not becoming king is not feasible.
We hope you establish yourself as King of Chǔ."
Chén Shè consulted the two,
who replied:
"Qín, being without virtue,
destroyed others' states,
annihilated their altars,
ended their posterity,
exhausted the people's strength,
and depleted their wealth.
You, General, bold and resolute,
risked certain death without regard for your life,
to rid the world of its scourge.
Now, upon reaching Chén, if you proclaim yourself king,
you show the world selfishness.
We urge you not to become king yet,
but quickly lead troops westward,
send men to reestablish the six states' descendants,
building your own faction,
to increase Qín's enemies.
More enemies divide their strength,
and with allies, your army strengthens.
Thus, in the wilds, no battles will be fought,
in counties, no cities defended,
as you punish tyrannical Qín,
occupy Xiányáng and command the feudal lords.
The lords, restored from ruin,
will be won over by your virtue,
and thus imperial achievement will be realized.
If you alone king in Chén,
I fear the world will dissolve."
Chén Shè did not listen,
and proclaimed himself king.
Chén Yú then advised King Chén again, saying:
"Your Majesty has raised Liáng and Chǔ to march west,
focusing on entering the pass,
but has not yet secured Héběi.
I have traveled in Zhào before,
knowing its prominent figures and terrain,
and wish to request special troops to campaign north and capture Zhào's territory."
Thereupon, King Chén appointed his old acquaintance Wǔ Chén of Chén as general,
Shào Sāo as army supervisor,
and Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú as left and right colonels,
granting them three thousand soldiers,
to campaign north and capture Zhào's territory.
Wǔ Chén and others crossed the river from Báimǎ,
reaching various counties,
where they persuaded the local leaders, saying:
"Qín's chaotic governance and cruel punishments have devastated the world,
for decades now.
In the north, there is the labor of the Great Wall,
in the south, the garrisoning of the Five Ridges,
turmoil inside and out,
the common people exhausted and impoverished,
taxes collected by headcount and gathered with dustpans,
to supply military expenses,
wealth depleted and strength exhausted,
the people having no means to live.
Compounded by harsh laws and severe punishments,
families under heaven cannot live in peace.
King Chén raised his arm to initiate for all under heaven,
ruling over the land of Chǔ,
spanning two thousand lǐ square,
with none failing to respond,
each household acting on its own anger,
each person fighting for themselves,
each avenging their grievances and attacking their enemies,
counties killing their magistrates and assistants,
commanderies killing their governors and commanders.
Now he has established Great Chǔ,
ruling from Chén,
sending Wú Guǎng and Zhōu Wén leading a million troops west to attack Qín.
In such a time, failing to achieve the feat of becoming a marquis
is not the mark of an outstanding man.
Gentlemen, please consider this together!
For all under heaven share the same mind and have long suffered under Qín.
Using the strength of all under heaven to attack the unprincipled ruler,
avenge the grievances of fathers and brothers, and accomplish the feat of carving out land and possessing territory—
this is the moment for men of ambition."
The prominent figures all agreed with his words.
They then proceeded to gather troops,
gaining tens of thousands of men,
and hailed Wǔ Chén as Lord Wǔxìn.
They captured ten cities in Zhào,
while the rest defended their cities,
unwilling to surrender.
They then led troops northeast to attack Fànyáng.
Kuǎi Tōng of Fànyáng advised the magistrate of Fànyáng, saying:
"I have privately heard of your impending death,
hence I come to mourn.
Nevertheless,
I congratulate you for meeting me and gaining life."
The magistrate of Fànyáng said:
"Why do you mourn me?"
He replied:
"Qín's laws are severe,
and you have been magistrate of Fànyáng for ten years,
killing people's fathers,
orphaning people's sons,
cutting off people's feet,
and tattooing people's faces,
beyond count.
Yet no kind father or filial son has dared to thrust a blade into your belly,
only for fear of Qín's laws.
Now the world is in great chaos,
Qín's laws are unenforceable,
so kind fathers and filial sons will thrust blades into your belly to make their names,
which is why I mourn you.
Now the feudal lords have rebelled against Qín,
and Lord Wǔxìn's troops are about to arrive.
If you stubbornly defend Fànyáng,
the young men will all compete to kill you
and surrender to Lord Wǔxìn.
If you quickly send me to see Lord Wǔxìn,
you can turn disaster into blessing,
and it must be now."
The magistrate of Fànyáng then sent Kuǎi Tōng to see Lord Wǔxìn, saying:
"You insist on winning battles before capturing land,
taking by force before securing cities;
I humbly believe this is mistaken.
If you truly follow my plan,
you can make cities surrender without attack,
capture land without battle,
and stabilize a thousand lǐ with a proclamation.
Is that acceptable?"
Lord Wǔxìn said:
"What do you mean?"
Kuǎi Tōng said:
"Now, the magistrate of Fànyáng should be organizing his soldiers for defense and battle,
but he is timid and fears death,
greedy and values wealth and honor,
so he wishes to surrender first,
but fears you will consider him an official appointed by Qín
and execute him as in the previous ten cities.
Yet now the young men of Fànyáng are also about to kill their magistrate
and use the city to resist you.
Why not grant me a marquis seal
to appoint the magistrate of Fànyáng?
Then the magistrate will surrender the city to you,
and the young men will not dare kill their magistrate.
Have the magistrate of Fànyáng ride in a red-wheeled, ornate carriage,
driving through the outskirts of Yān and Zhào.
When the outskirts of Yān and Zhào see this,
they will all say, 'This is the magistrate of Fànyáng,
the first to surrender,'
and they will be pleased;
the cities of Yān and Zhào can then surrender without battle.
This is what I mean by stabilizing a thousand lǐ with a proclamation."
Lord Wǔxìn followed his plan,
thus sending Kuǎi Tōng to bestow a marquis seal upon the magistrate of Fànyáng.
When the land of Zhào heard of this,
over thirty cities surrendered without battle.
Upon reaching Hándān,
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú heard that Zhōu Zhāng's army had entered the pass,
reaching Xì before retreating;
they also heard that many generals campaigning for King Chén
had been slandered, found guilty, and executed,
and resented that King Chén had not used their strategies or made them generals but only colonels.
They then advised Wǔ Chén, saying:
"King Chén rose from Qí,
and upon reaching Chén, became king,
not necessarily establishing the descendants of the six states.
Now, General, with three thousand men, you have captured dozens of cities in Zhào,
standing alone in Héběi;
without becoming king, you cannot secure it.
Moreover, King Chén listens to slander,
and if we return to report,
I fear we cannot escape disaster.
It would be better to set up his brothers;
if not,
then establish a descendant of Zhào.
General, do not miss the opportunity;
the moment allows not a breath's delay."
Wǔ Chén heeded them,
and thus was established as King of Zhào.
He appointed Chén Yú as grand general,
Zhāng Ěr as right chancellor,
and Shào Sāo as left chancellor.
They sent someone to report to King Chén,
who was greatly angered
and wanted to execute the entire families of Wǔ Chén and others,
then send troops to attack Zhào.
King Chén's chancellor, Lord Fángjūn, admonished him, saying:
"Qín is not yet destroyed, and to execute the families of Wǔ Chén and others
is to create another Qín.
It would be better to congratulate them accordingly
and have them quickly lead troops west to attack Qín."
King Chén agreed,
followed his advice,
moved the families of Wǔ Chén and others to the palace,
and enfeoffed Zhāng Ěr's son Zhāng Áo as Lord of Chéngdū.
King Chén sent an envoy to congratulate Zhào,
ordering them to quickly send troops west into the pass.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú advised Wǔ Chén, saying:
"Your Majesty rules Zhào,
which is not Chǔ's intention;
they only congratulate you as a stratagem.
Once Chǔ has destroyed Qín,
they will surely send troops against Zhào.
We hope Your Majesty will not send troops west,
but campaign north to Yān and Dài,
and south to capture Hénèi to expand your territory.
With Zhào holding the great river in the south,
and Yān and Dài in the north,
even if Chǔ defeats Qín,
they will not dare control Zhào."
The King of Zhào thought this reasonable,
so he did not send troops west,
but sent Hán Guǎng to campaign against Yān,
Lǐ Liáng against Chángshān,
and Zhāng Yǎn against Shàngdǎng.
When Hán Guǎng reached Yān,
the people of Yān thereupon established Guǎng as King of Yān.
The King of Zhào then with Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú campaigned north to the border of Yān.
The King of Zhào went out incognito,
and was captured by the Yān army.
The Yān general imprisoned him,
wanting to divide Zhào's land in half
before returning the king.
Envoys were sent,
but Yān repeatedly killed them to demand land.
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú were troubled by this.
A laborer soldier said to his housemates:
"I will go to Yān for you
and bring back the King of Zhào in our carriage."
Everyone in the quarters laughed and said: "Over ten envoys have been sent before,
and each time they died.
How can you possibly bring back the king?"
He then rushed to the Yān army camp.
The Yān general received him,
and he asked the Yān general:
"Do you know what I desire?"
The Yān general said: "You wish to obtain the king of Zhào."
He said: "Do you know what kind of men Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú are?"
The Yān general said: "They are worthy men."
He said:
"Do you know what their ambitions are?"
The general said:
"They wish to have their king back."
The Zhào groom then laughed and said:
"You do not understand what these two men truly desire.
Wǔ Chén, Zhāng Ěr, and Chén Yú conquered dozens of cities in Zhào with horsewhips in hand,
yet each of them also desires to face south and proclaim themselves king.
How could they be content to remain ministers and chancellors forever?
The relationship between minister and sovereign cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
Considering the situation was just stabilizing,
they did not yet dare to divide into three and become kings,
so they temporarily established Wǔ Chén as king based on seniority,
to secure the hearts of Zhào.
Now that Zhào's territory is pacified,
these two also wish to divide Zhào and become kings themselves,
but the time is not yet right.
Now you have imprisoned the king of Zhào.
These two ostensibly seek the king of Zhào,
but in reality want Yān to kill him,
so they can divide Zhào and establish themselves.
With one Zhào alone, it is still easy to overcome Yān,
let alone with two worthy kings supporting each other,
and condemning you for the crime of killing the king—
it would be easy to destroy Yān."
The Yān general thought this reasonable,
so he returned the king of Zhào,
and the groom served as charioteer on their return.
Lǐ Liáng had already pacified Chángshān,
and returned to report.
The king of Zhào again sent Lǐ Liáng to capture Tàiyuán.
When he reached Shíyì,
Qín troops blocked Jǐngxíng,
preventing his advance.
A Qín general falsely claimed that Èrshì had sent a letter to Lǐ Liáng,
unsealed,
saying:
"Lǐ Liáng once served me and achieved prominence and favor.
If Lǐ Liáng can truly turn against Zhào for Qín,
I will pardon his crimes,
and honor him."
Lǐ Liáng received the letter,
but was skeptical and did not believe it.
He then returned to Hándān,
to request more troops.
Before arriving,
he encountered the elder sister of the king of Zhào returning from a banquet on the road,
accompanied by over a hundred cavalry.
Lǐ Liáng saw her from afar,
mistaking her for the king,
and knelt in reverence by the roadside.
The king's sister was drunk,
and did not recognize him as a general,
so she sent a cavalryman to dismiss Lǐ Liáng.
Lǐ Liáng had always been esteemed,
and when he rose,
he felt ashamed before his officers.
One of his officers said:
"All under heaven have rebelled against Qín,
and those with ability rise first.
Moreover, the king of Zhào has always been beneath you in status,
yet now this woman does not even dismount her carriage for you.
I request we pursue and kill her."
Lǐ Liáng had already received the Qín letter,
and was inclined to betray Zhào,
but had not decided yet.
Angered by this incident,
he sent men to pursue and kill the king's sister on the road,
then led his troops to attack Hándān.
Hándān was unaware,
and he ultimately killed Wǔ Chén and Shào Sāo.
Many people in Zhào served as eyes and ears for Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú,
so they managed to escape.
They gathered their troops,
obtaining tens of thousands of men.
A guest advised Zhāng Ěr:
"You two gentlemen are travelers here,
and wish to attach yourselves to Zhào—
that is difficult.
Only by establishing a descendant of Zhào,
and supporting him with righteousness,
can you achieve merit."
They then found Zhào Xiē,
and established him as king of Zhào,
residing in Xìndū.
Lǐ Liáng advanced to attack Chén Yú,
but Chén Yú defeated Lǐ Liáng,
and Lǐ Liáng fled to join Zhāng Hán.
Zhāng Hán led his troops to Hándān,
relocated all its people to Hénèi,
and razed its city walls.
Zhāng Ěr and King Zhào Xiē fled into the city of Jùlù,
where Wáng Lí besieged them.
Chén Yú went north to gather troops from Chángshān,
obtaining tens of thousands of men,
and stationed his army north of Jùlù.
Zhāng Hán stationed his army at Jíyuán south of Jùlù,
building a walled road connecting to the river,
to supply Wáng Lí.
Wáng Lí had ample troops and provisions,
and urgently attacked Jùlù.
Jùlù was short on food and troops,
and Zhāng Ěr repeatedly sent messengers to summon Chén Yú,
but Chén Yú estimated his own troops were too few,
and no match for Qín,
so he did not dare to advance.
After several months,
Zhāng Ěr grew furious,
and resented Chén Yú.
He sent Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé to reproach Chén Yú:
"Initially, you and I were sworn friends,
yet now the king and I face imminent death,
while you hold tens of thousands of troops,
unwilling to come to our aid.
Where is our pledge to die for each other?
If you must keep your word,
why not join us in fighting the Qín army to the death?
Moreover, there is still a one or two in ten chance of survival."
Chén Yú said:
"I estimate that advancing would ultimately fail to save Zhào,
and only result in the total loss of our army.
Moreover, the reason I do not join you in death
is that I wish to avenge Zhào and you, Zhāng Jūn, against Qín.
If we must all die now,
it would be like throwing meat to a starving tiger—
what good would that do?"
Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé said:
"The situation is critical,
and we must die together to establish trust.
How can we consider future concerns!"
Chén Yú said:
"I believe my death would be futile.
If you insist on your words."
He then ordered five thousand men under Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé to test the Qín army first,
but they all perished upon arrival.
At that time,
Yān, Qí, and Chǔ heard of Zhào's crisis,
and all came to rescue.
Zhāng Áo also went north to gather troops from Dài,
obtaining over ten thousand men, and came,
all camping near Chén Yú,
but not daring to attack Qín.
Xiàng Yǔ's troops repeatedly cut off Zhāng Hán's walled road,
and Wáng Lí's army ran short of food.
Xiàng Yǔ then led all his troops across the river,
and defeated Zhāng Hán.
Zhāng Hán withdrew his troops,
and the allied armies of the nobles then dared to attack the Qín forces besieging Jùlù,
capturing Wáng Lí.
Shè Jiàn committed suicide.
The preservation of Jùlù in the end
was due to the strength of Chǔ.
Thereupon, King Zhào Xiē and Zhāng Ěr were able to leave Jùlù,
and thanked the nobles.
Zhāng Ěr met with Chén Yú,
reproaching him for not rescuing Zhào,
and asking about the whereabouts of Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé.
Chén Yú angrily said:
"Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé demanded that I die with them,
so I sent them with five thousand men to test the Qín army first,
and they all perished without returning."
Zhāng Ěr did not believe it,
thinking Chén Yú had killed them,
and repeatedly questioned Chén Yú.
Chén Yú angrily said:
"I never expected you to distrust me so deeply!
Do you think I cling heavily to my command?"
He then took off his seal and ribbon,
and pushed them to Zhāng Ěr.
Zhāng Ěr was also startled and did not accept.
Chén Yú stood up to go to the restroom.
A guest advised Zhāng Ěr:
"I have heard, 'When Heaven gives, if you do not take,
you will instead suffer misfortune.'
Now General Chén gives you his seal,
if you do not accept it,
it goes against Heaven and is inauspicious.
Take it quickly!"
Zhāng Ěr then wore the seal,
and took command of Chén Yú's troops.
When Chén Yú returned,
he also resented that Zhāng Ěr had not declined,
so he hurriedly left.
Zhāng Ěr thus took over his army.
Chén Yú alone went with several hundred of his close followers to fish and hunt in the marshes by the river.
From then on, Chén Yú and Zhāng Ěr became estranged.
King Xiè of Zhào returned to reside in Xìndū.
Zhāng Ěr followed Xiàng Yǔ and the other nobles into the Pass.
In the second month of the first year of Hàn,
Xiàng Yǔ established the feudal kings,
and since Zhāng Ěr was well-traveled in social circles,
many people spoke on his behalf,
while Xiàng Yǔ had also often heard of Zhāng Ěr's worthiness,
so he partitioned Zhào and established Zhāng Ěr as King of Chángshān,
ruling from Xìndū.
Xìndū was renamed Xiāngguó.
Chén Yú's retainers repeatedly urged Xiàng Yǔ, saying:
"Chén Yú and Zhāng Ěr were equally meritorious for Zhào."
Xiàng Yǔ, because Chén Yú had not followed him into the Pass,
and hearing he was at Nánpí,
enfeoffed him with the three counties around Nánpí,
while moving King Xiè of Zhào to rule over Dài.
When Zhāng Ěr went to his state,
Chén Yú grew increasingly angry,
saying: "Zhāng Ěr and I had equal merit,
yet now Zhāng Ěr is made king,
while I remain merely a marquis—
this shows Xiàng Yǔ's unfairness."
When Tián Róng, King of Qí, rebelled against Chǔ,
Chén Yú sent Xià Yuè to persuade Tián Róng, saying:
"Xiàng Yǔ, as arbiter of the empire, is unjust,
enfeoffing all his generals with good territories
while moving former kings to poor lands—
now the King of Zhào is made to dwell in Dài!
I hope you will lend me troops,
requesting to use Nánpí as a protective screen."
Tián Róng, wishing to build an alliance with Zhào to oppose Chǔ,
sent troops to follow Chén Yú.
Chén Yú then mobilized all troops from the three counties to attack Zhāng Ěr, King of Chángshān.
Zhāng Ěr was defeated and fled,
and considering that there was no noble he could turn to,
said:
"The King of Hàn and I have an old friendship,
and though Xiàng Yǔ is strong,
he established me,
I wish to go to Chǔ."
Master Gān said:
"When the King of Hàn entered the Pass,
the five planets converged at the Eastern Well.
The Eastern Well
corresponds to Qín's region.
He who arrives first is bound to become hegemon.
Though Chǔ is strong now,
it will eventually belong to Hàn."
So Zhāng Ěr fled to Hàn.
The King of Hàn had also returned to pacify the Three Qín,
and was then besieging Zhāng Hán at Fèiqiū.
Zhāng Ěr had an audience with the King of Hàn,
who treated him generously.
After Chén Yú defeated Zhāng Ěr,
he recovered all of Zhào's territory,
welcomed the King of Zhào back from Dài,
and restored him as King of Zhào.
The King of Zhào, grateful to Chén Yú,
established him as King of Dài.
Chén Yú, considering the King of Zhào weak
and the state newly stabilized,
did not go to his kingdom,
but remained as assistant to the King of Zhào,
sending Xià Yuè to guard Dài as chancellor.
In the second year of Hàn,
when Hàn attacked Chǔ in the east,
it sent an envoy to inform Zhào,
wishing to fight together.
Chén Yú said: "Only if Hàn kills Zhāng Ěr will I join."
Thereupon the King of Hàn found a man who resembled Zhāng Ěr, executed him,
and sent his head to Chén Yú.
Chén Yú then sent troops to assist Hàn.
When Hàn was defeated west of Péngchéng,
Chén Yú also realized Zhāng Ěr was not dead,
and immediately turned against Hàn.
In the third year of Hàn,
after Hán Xìn had pacified Wèi territory,
he sent Zhāng Ěr with Hán Xìn to attack and defeat Zhào at Jǐngxíng,
executing Chén Yú at the Zhī River,
and pursuing and killing King Xiè of Zhào at Xiāngguó.
Hàn established Zhāng Ěr as King of Zhào.
In the fifth year of Hàn,
Zhāng Ěr died,
posthumously titled King Jǐng.
His son Zhāng Áo succeeded him as King of Zhào.
Emperor Gāozǔ's eldest daughter, Princess Lǔyuán, became the queen of Zhāng Áo, King of Zhào.
In the seventh year of Hàn,
Emperor Gāozǔ passed through Zhào from Píngchéng,
and the King of Zhào, from morning till night, bared his arms and served as shield-bearer,
personally presenting food,
with very humble etiquette,
as befitting a son-in-law.
Emperor Gāozǔ sat sprawled and cursed,
treating him with great disrespect.
Guàn Gāo and Zhào Wǔ, chancellors of Zhào, both over sixty years old,
who were former retainers of Zhāng Ěr,
being men of spirit all their lives,
became angry and said:
"Our king is a weakling!"
They advised the king, saying: "When all the heroes in the world rose together,
the capable were established first.
Now our king serves Emperor Gāozǔ with utmost respect,
yet Emperor Gāozǔ shows no courtesy—
we request to kill him for you!"
Zhāng Áo bit his finger until it bled,
saying:
"How wrong your words are!
Moreover, our predecessors lost the state,
