and only through Emperor Gāozǔ was it restored;
his grace flows to his descendants,
every tiny bit is due to Emperor Gāozǔ's strength.
I hope you will not speak of this again."
Guàn Gāo, Zhào Wǔ, and more than ten others said to each other:
"It is we who are at fault.
Our king is a noble man
who does not betray virtue.
Moreover, we cannot tolerate insult in the name of righteousness;
now we resent Emperor Gāozǔ for insulting our king,
so we wish to kill him—
why should we implicate our king?
If the deed succeeds, credit goes to the king;
if it fails, we alone will bear the consequences."
In the eighth year of Hàn,
when the Emperor returned from Dōngyuán,
passing through Zhào, Guàn Gāo and others hid men in Bǎirén,
planning to ambush him in a side room.
The Emperor, passing through, wished to stay overnight,
but his heart stirred,
and he asked:
"What is the name of this county?"
They replied:
"Bǎirén."
"Bǎirén—
means 'pressured by men'!"
He did not stay and left.
In the ninth year of Hàn,
Guàn Gāo's enemy learned of the plot
and reported it to the authorities.
Thereupon the Emperor arrested both the King of Zhào and Guàn Gāo and others.
More than ten men vied to commit suicide,
but Guàn Gāo alone angrily scolded them:
"Who told you to do this?
Now the king truly had no part in the plot,
yet he is arrested along with us;
if you all die,
who will clear the king of rebellion?"
So they were transported in a prison cart, sealed and delivered,
and went with the king to Cháng'ān.
They tried Zhāng Áo for his crime.
The Emperor decreed that all officials and guests of Zhào who dared follow the king would be executed with their clans.
Guàn Gāo and his guest Mèng Shū, along with more than ten others,
all shaved their heads and wore fetters,
becoming the king's household slaves,
and followed him.
When Guàn Gāo arrived,
during the trial,
he said:
"We alone did it;
the king truly knew nothing."
The officials tortured him with thousands of blows,
pierced and cut him,
until there was no place on his body left unharmed,
yet he never spoke differently.
Empress Lǚ repeatedly stated that because King Zhāng was married to Princess Lǔyuán,
he should not have been involved in this.
The Emperor angrily said:
"If Zhāng Áo held the empire,
would he lack women like your daughter?"
He did not listen.
When the court minister reported Guàn Gāo's testimony,
the Emperor said: "He is a stalwart man!
Who knows him?
Inquire privately of him."
Xiè Gōng, a grand master, said:
"He is from my hometown,
and I have long known him.
He is truly one who, for the sake of honor in Zhào, does not break his promise."
The Emperor sent Xiè Gōng, bearing his credentials, to question him before the carriage.
Guàn Gāo looked up and said:
"Is that you, Xiè Gōng?"
Xiè Gōng comforted him as in their past friendship,
and spoke with him,
asking if King Zhāng had truly been involved in the plot.
Guàn Gāo said: "Do not all people naturally love their parents, wives, and children?
Now my three clans are condemned to death—
would I trade my kin for the king?
But the truth is that the king did not rebel;
we alone did it."
He explained in detail the original intent and how the king was unaware of the situation.
Thereupon Xiè Gōng entered,
and fully reported the situation.
The Emperor then pardoned King Zhào.
The Emperor, admiring Guàn Gāo's character as a man who could stand by his promises,
sent Xiè Gōng to fully inform him,
saying:
"King Zhāng has already been released."
Consequently, he pardoned Guàn Gāo.
Guàn Gāo joyfully said: "Has my king truly been released?"
Xiè Gōng said: "Yes."
Xiè Gōng said: "The Emperor thinks highly of you, sir,
and therefore has pardoned you, sir."
Guàn Gāo said:
"The reason I did not die, leaving not a single remnant of myself,
was to clear King Zhāng of rebellion.
Now that the king has been released,
my responsibility has been fulfilled,
and I die without regret.
Moreover, how could a subject who bears the name of one who plotted regicide and murder
have the face to serve the Emperor again!
Even if the Emperor did not kill me,
would I not feel shame in my heart?"
He then threw back his head and broke his neck,
and thus died.
At this time,
his name became known throughout the empire.
After Zhāng Ào was released,
because he had married the Princess of Lǔyuán,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xuānpíng.
Thereupon, the Emperor esteemed the various guests of King Zhāng;
those who had followed King Zhāng into the Pass as slaves with iron collars
all became chancellors of feudal lords or commandery governors.
By the time of Emperor Huì of Hàn, Empress Dowager Gāo, Emperor Wén, and Emperor Jǐng,
the sons and grandsons of King Zhāng's guests all attained the rank of two thousand piculs.
Zhāng Ào
died in the sixth year of Empress Dowager Gāo's reign.
His son Yǎn became King of Lǔyuán.
Because his mother was a daughter of Empress Lǚ,
Empress Lǚ enfeoffed him as King of Lǔyuán.
As King Yuán was young,
and had few brothers,
two other sons of Zhāng Ào by different consorts were enfeoffed:
Shòu as Marquis of Lèchāng,
and Chǐ as Marquis of Xìndū.
When Empress Dowager Gāo passed away,
the various Lǚs acted without principle;
the high officials executed them,
and deposed the King of Lǔyuán, the Marquis of Lèchāng, and the Marquis of Xìndū.
When Emperor Wén of Hàn ascended the throne,
he re-enfeoffed the former King of Lǔyuán, Yǎn, as Marquis of Nángōng,
to continue the Zhāng family line.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú
are praised by tradition as worthy men;
their guests and servants
were all outstanding talents of the empire,
and in whichever state they resided, none failed to attain the positions of ministers or chancellors.
Yet when Zhāng Ěr and Chén Yú first lived in humble circumstances,
they pledged faith to each other unto death—
how could they have been concerned with other considerations?
But when they came to possess states and contend for power,
they ended up destroying each other.
Why was the sincerity of their mutual admiration and support in earlier times
so violently betrayed later?
Was it not because their friendship was based on power and profit?
Though their reputations were high,
and their followers numerous,
their course was surely different from that of Tàibó and Jìzǐ of Yánlíng.
Wèi Bào
was a scion of the former Wèi royal house.
His elder brother Wèi Jiù,
was enfeoffed as Lord of Nínglíng during the time of Wèi.
When Qín destroyed Wèi,
Jiù was relocated and made a commoner.
When Chén Shèng rose and proclaimed himself king,
Jiù went to join him.
King Chén sent Zhōu Fú, a man of Wèi, to campaign through the territory of Wèi.
After the land of Wèi was subdued,
the people wished to establish Zhōu Fú as King of Wèi.
Zhōu Fú said:
"When the empire is in chaos,
then loyal ministers appear.
Now the whole empire has rebelled against Qín;
in righteousness, we must establish a descendant of the King of Wèi."
Qí and Zhào each sent envoys with fifty chariots,
to establish Zhōu Fú as King of Wèi.
Fú declined and would not accept,
but welcomed Wèi Jiù from Chén.
After five attempts,
King Chén finally sent Jiù to be established as King of Wèi.
After Zhāng Hán had defeated King Chén,
he advanced his troops and attacked the King of Wèi at Línjì.
The King of Wèi then sent Zhōu Fú to go and seek aid from Qí and Chǔ.
Qí and Chǔ sent Xiàng Tuō and Tián Bā to lead troops following Fú to rescue Wèi.
Zhāng Hán then attacked, defeated, and killed the armies of Zhōu Fú and others,
besieging Línjì.
Jiù made an agreement with his people to surrender.
Once the agreement was settled,
Jiù burned himself to death.
Wèi Bào fled to Chǔ.
King Huái of Chǔ gave Wèi Bào several thousand men,
to campaign again through the territory of Wèi.
After Xiàng Yǔ had defeated Qín,
and accepted Zhāng Hán's surrender,
Bào captured more than twenty cities of Wèi,
and was established as King of Wèi.
Bào led elite troops to follow Xiàng Yǔ into the Pass.
In the first year of Hàn,
when Xiàng Yǔ enfeoffed the various lords,
wishing to possess the land of Liáng,
he moved King Wèi Bào to Hédōng,
making Píngyáng his capital,
and titled him King of Western Wèi.
When the King of Hàn returned to pacify the Three Qín,
and crossed Línjìn,
King Wèi Bào submitted his state to him,
and then followed him to attack Chǔ at Péngchéng.
When Hàn was defeated,
and returned to Xíngyáng,
Bào requested to return home to see his ailing parent.
Upon reaching his state,
he immediately blocked the river crossings and rebelled against Hàn.
When the King of Hàn heard that Wèi Bào had rebelled,
he was at the time worried about Chǔ in the east,
and had no time to attack,
so he said to Lì Shēng:
"Go and persuade Wèi Bào with soothing words.
If you can make him submit,
I will enfeoff you with ten thousand households."
Lì Shēng tried to persuade Bào.
Bào declined, saying:
"A human life in this world
is like a white steed flashing past a crack.
Now the King of Hàn is arrogant and insults others,
cursing the feudal lords and ministers as if they were slaves,
without any regard for the rituals of superior and inferior.
I cannot bear to see him again."
Thereupon, the King of Hàn sent Hán Xìn to attack and capture Bào in Hédōng,
and had him escorted to Xíngyáng,
converting Bào's state into a commanery.
The King of Hàn ordered Bào to guard Xíngyáng.
When Chǔ besieged it fiercely,
Zhōu Kē then killed Wèi Bào.
Péng Yuè
was a man of Chāngyì,
courtesy name Zhòng.
He often fished in the Jùyě Marsh,
and became a bandit leader.
When Chén Shèng and Xiàng Liáng rose in rebellion,
some young men said to Yuè:
"Many heroes are rising against Qín;
you, Zhòng, could come
and emulate them."
Péng Yuè said:
"Two dragons are just beginning to fight;
let us wait a while."
After more than a year had passed,
the young men in the marsh gathered a group of over a hundred men,
and went to follow Péng Yuè,
saying:
"We ask you, Zhòng, to be our chief."
Yuè declined, saying: "I do not wish to join you, gentlemen."
The young men insistently pleaded,
and he then agreed.
He set a meeting time for sunrise the next day,
stating that those late would be executed.
At sunrise the next day,
over ten men were late,
with the latest arriving by noon.
Thereupon Yuè apologized, saying:
"I am old,
and you gentlemen insisted on making me your chief.
Now we set a time, and many are late;
it is impossible to execute all of them,
so only the very last one will be executed."
He ordered the squad leader to behead him.
Everyone laughed and said:
"How can it come to this?
We beg you, we won't dare be late again."
Thereupon Yuè dragged one man out and beheaded him,
set up an altar to make offerings,
and then gave orders to his followers.
His followers were all greatly shocked,
feared Yuè,
and dared not look up at him.
He then proceeded to seize territory,
gathering scattered soldiers from the various lords,
and obtained over a thousand men.
When the Lord of Pei advanced north from Dàng to attack Chāngyì,
Péng Yuè assisted him.
Chāngyì had not yet fallen,
when the Lord of Pei led his troops westward.
Péng Yuè also stationed his forces in the Jùyě marshes,
gathering scattered soldiers from Wèi.
After Xiàng Jí entered the pass,
enfeoffed the various nobles as kings,
and returned east,
Péng Yuè's ten-thousand-strong force had no allegiance.
In the autumn of the first year of Hàn,
Tián Róng, the King of Qí, rebelled against King Xiàng,
so Hàn sent an envoy to bestow upon Péng Yuè the seal of a general,
ordering him to capture Jìyīn and attack Chǔ.
Chǔ commanded Xiāo Gōng Jiǎo to lead troops against Yuè,
but Yuè heavily defeated the Chǔ army.
In the spring of the second year of the King of Hàn,
he joined King Bào of Wèi and other nobles to attack Chǔ from the east,
and Péng Yuè led his thirty-thousand-strong force to join Hàn at Wàihuáng.
The King of Hàn said:
"General Péng has captured over ten cities in Wèi territory,
and urgently wishes to establish a descendant of Wèi.
Now King Bào of Western Wèi is also a cousin of King Jiù of Wèi,
truly a Wèi descendant."
Thereupon, he appointed Péng Yuè as Chancellor of Wèi,
granting him autonomous command of his troops,
to pacify the Liáng region.
When the King of Hàn was defeated at Péngchéng and retreated westward,
Péng Yuè lost all the cities he had captured,
and alone led his troops north to station by the Yellow River.
In the third year of the King of Hàn,
Péng Yuè frequently operated as Hàn's mobile force,
attacking Chǔ
and cutting off their supply lines in Liáng.
In the winter of the fourth year of Hàn,
while King Xiàng and the King of Hàn were stalemated at Xíngyáng,
Péng Yuè captured seventeen cities including Suīyáng and Wàihuáng.
Upon hearing this,
King Xiàng ordered Cáo Jiù to defend Chénggāo,
while he himself went east to recapture the cities taken by Péng Yuè,
all of which returned to Chǔ control.
Yuè led his troops north to Gǔchéng.
In the autumn of the fifth year of Hàn,
as King Xiàng moved south to Yángjiǎ,
Péng Yuè again captured over twenty cities near Chāngyì,
obtaining more than a hundred thousand hú of grain,
which he supplied to the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn, having been defeated, sent an envoy to summon Péng Yuè to combine forces against Chǔ.
Yuè said:
"Wèi territory has only recently been pacified,
and still fears Chǔ,
so I cannot leave."
When the King of Hàn pursued Chǔ,
he was defeated by Xiàng Jí at Gùlíng.
He then said to the Marquis of Liú:
"The nobles' troops do not follow me;
what should I do?"
The Marquis of Liú replied:
"Hán Xìn's establishment as King of Qí was not Your Majesty's original intention,
and Xìn himself feels insecure.
Péng Yuè originally pacified Liáng,
with great achievements,
and initially, because of Wèi Bào,
you appointed Péng Yuè as Chancellor of Wèi.
Now Bào has died without an heir,
and moreover, Yuè also wishes to be king,
yet Your Majesty has not promptly decided.
Make an agreement with these two states:
if we defeat Chǔ,
then from north of Suīyáng to Gǔchéng,
all shall be granted to Chancellor Péng as king;
and from east of Chén to the sea,
to King Qí Xìn.
King Qí Xìn's home is in Chǔ,
so he desires to regain his former territory.
If Your Majesty can cede these lands to these two men,
they can be summoned now;
if not,
the outcome is uncertain."
Thereupon, the King of Hàn sent envoys to Péng Yuè,
following the Marquis of Liú's strategy.
When the envoy arrived,
Péng Yuè led all his troops to join at Gāixià,
and they subsequently defeated Chǔ.
In the fifth year, after Xiàng Jí's death, in spring,
Péng Yuè was established as King of Liáng,
with his capital at Dìngtáo.
In the sixth year,
he paid court at Chén.
In the ninth
and tenth years,
he came to court at Cháng'ān.
In the autumn of the tenth year,
when Chén Xī rebelled in Dài,
Emperor Gāo personally went to suppress it,
reaching Hándān,
and summoned troops from the King of Liáng.
The King of Liáng pleaded illness,
sending a general with troops to Hándān.
Emperor Gāo was angered,
and sent someone to reprimand the King of Liáng.
The King of Liáng grew fearful
and intended to go in person to apologize.
His general Hù Zhé said:
"If you did not go initially,
but go after being reprimanded,
you will be captured upon going.
It would be better to raise troops and rebel."
The King of Liáng did not listen,
and continued to claim illness.
The King of Liáng became angry with his Grand Coachman,
and wanted to execute him.
The Grand Coachman fled to Hàn,
and reported that the King of Liáng and Hù Zhé were plotting rebellion.
Thereupon, the Emperor sent agents to surprise the King of Liáng,
who was unaware,
captured him,
and imprisoned him in Luòyáng.
The officials investigated and found evidence of rebellion complete,
and requested judgment according to the law.
The Emperor pardoned him but reduced him to commoner status,
exiling him to Qīngyī in Shǔ.
While traveling west to Zhèng,
he met Empress Lǚ coming from Cháng'ān,
who was heading to Luòyáng,
and encountered King Péng on the road.
King Péng wept before Empress Lǚ,
proclaiming his innocence,
and wishing to be settled in his former territory of Chāngyì.
Empress Lǚ agreed,
and traveled east with him to Luòyáng.
Empress Lǚ reported to the Emperor:
"King Péng is a mighty warrior,
and now moving him to Shǔ
leaves a future trouble;
it would be better to execute him.
I have carefully brought him with me."
Thereupon, Empress Lǚ ordered her retainer to accuse Péng Yuè of plotting rebellion again.
The Commandant of Justice Wáng Tiánkāi petitioned for his execution and the extermination of his clan.
The Emperor approved,
and thus exterminated Yuè's clan,
abolishing his kingdom.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Although Wèi Bào and Péng Yuè were originally of humble status,
they swept across a thousand lǐ,
faced south and called themselves 'the solitary one',
and their victories in bloody battles were daily heard.
Yet they harbored rebellious intentions,
and upon defeat,
instead of dying, were captured and imprisoned,
suffering execution.
Why?
Even those of medium talent or above would be ashamed of such conduct,
let alone kings!
They had no other reason
than that their wisdom and strategy surpassed others,
but they only feared for their own lives.
Once they grasped even a small measure of power,
they rose like clouds and transformed like dragons,
wishing to fulfill their ambitions.
Therefore, they did not refuse even imprisonment.
Qíng Bù was a man of Lù,
of the Yīng family.
During Qín times, he was a commoner.
In his youth,
a physiognomist told him:
"You will be punished and then become a king."
When he reached adulthood,
he was convicted and tattooed.
Bù laughed joyfully and said:
"Someone read my face and said I would be punished and then become king;
could this be it?"
Those who heard this
all mocked him together.
After Bù was sentenced and sent to Lìshān,
where the convicts numbered in the hundreds of thousands,
he associated with the leaders and heroes among them,
and eventually led his companions
to flee to the river and become bandits.
When Chén Shèng rose in rebellion,
Bù went to see Lord Fān,
and with his followers rebelled against Qín,
gathering several thousand troops.
Lord Fān gave him his daughter in marriage.
After Zhāng Hán destroyed Chén Shèng
and defeated Lǚ Chén's army,
Bù led his troops north to attack the Qín left and right colonels,
defeating them at Qīngbō,
then led his troops eastward.
Upon hearing that Xiàng Liáng had secured Jiāngdōng and Kuàijī,
he crossed the river and headed west.
Chén Yīng, considering the Xiàng family's generations as Chǔ generals,
then placed his troops under Xiàng Liáng's command,
crossing south of the Huái River.
Yīng Bù and General Pú also assigned their forces to Xiàng Liáng.
As Xiàng Liáng crossed the Huái westward,
he attacked Jǐng Jū and Qín Jiā, among others,
with Yīng Bù often leading the charge.
When Xiàng Liáng reached Xuē,
he learned that King Chén was confirmed dead,
so he established King Huái of Chǔ.
Xiàng Liáng was titled Lord Wǔxìn,
and Yīng Bù became Lord Dāngyáng.
After Xiàng Liáng was defeated and died in Dìngtáo,
King Huái moved the capital to Péngchéng,
and the various generals, including Yīng Bù, all gathered and defended Péngchéng.
At that time,
Qín urgently besieged Zhào,
and Zhào repeatedly sent envoys requesting aid.
King Huái appointed Sòng Yì as supreme general,
Fàn Zēng as junior general,
Xiàng Jí as second general,
with Yīng Bù and General Pú both serving as generals,
all under Sòng Yì's command,
to rescue Zhào in the north.
When Xiàng Jí killed Sòng Yì by the river,
King Huái consequently appointed Jí as supreme general,
and all generals came under Xiàng Jí's authority.
Xiàng Jí sent Yīng Bù to cross the river first and attack Qín,
and as Bù repeatedly gained advantages,
Jí then led all his troops across the river to follow him,
ultimately defeating the Qín army
and forcing Zhāng Hán and others to surrender.
The Chǔ forces were often victorious,
their achievements surpassing those of the other lords.
The reason the armies of the various lords submitted to Chǔ
was that Yīng Bù repeatedly defeated larger forces with fewer troops.
When Xiàng Jí led his troops west to Xīn'ān,
he again ordered Yīng Bù and others to attack and bury alive over two hundred thousand of Zhāng Hán's Qín soldiers at night.
Arriving at the pass,
they were unable to enter,
so he again sent Yīng Bù and others to first break through the defenders at the pass via bypaths,
thus gaining entry and reaching Xiányáng,
with Yīng Bù consistently serving as the vanguard.
When King Xiàng enfeoffed his generals,
he established Bù as the King of Jiǔjiāng,
with his capital at Lù.
In the fourth month of the first year of Hàn,
the various lords disbanded their forces under the command,
each returning to their own states.
The Xiàng clan installed King Huái as the Righteous Emperor,
moving his capital to Chángshā,
then secretly ordered the King of Jiǔjiāng, Yīng Bù, and others to attack him.
In the eighth month of that year,
Bù sent his generals to assault the Righteous Emperor,
pursuing and killing him in Chēn County.
In the second year of Hàn,
the King of Qí, Tián Róng, rebelled against Chǔ,
and King Xiàng went to attack Qí,
requesting troops from Jiǔjiāng.
The King of Jiǔjiāng, Yīng Bù, pleaded illness and did not go,
sending a general with several thousand men instead.
When Hàn defeated Chǔ at Péngchéng,
Bù again claimed illness and did not assist Chǔ.
King Xiàng thus resented Bù,
repeatedly sending envoys to reprimand and summon him,
making Bù increasingly fearful,
and he dared not go.
King Xiàng was then concerned about Qí and Zhào in the north,
and worried about Hàn in the west,
with his only ally being the King of Jiǔjiāng,
and moreover, he valued Bù's abilities,
wishing to employ him closely,
so for that reason, he did not attack.
In the third year of Hàn,
the King of Hàn attacked Chǔ,
engaging in a major battle at Péngchéng,
but was unsuccessful,
retreating through Liáng territory,
reaching Yú,
where he said to his attendants:
"People like them
are not worth discussing the affairs of the world with."
The court attendant Suí Hé stepped forward and said:
"I do not understand what Your Majesty means."
The King of Hàn said:
"Who can go as my envoy to Huáinán,
to persuade them to send troops and turn against Chǔ,
delaying King Xiàng in Qí for several months,
so that my conquest of the world can be fully assured?"
Suí Hé said:
"I request to be sent as envoy."
He then went with twenty men,
dispatched to Huáinán. Upon arrival,
through the Grand Steward's hosting,
he waited three days without an audience.
Suí Hé then persuaded the Grand Steward, saying:
"If the King does not see me,
it must be because he considers Chǔ strong
and Hàn weak,
which is precisely why I am here as envoy.
If I am granted an audience,
and my words are correct,
that is what the King wishes to hear;
if they are wrong,
then let me and my twenty men be executed in the market of Huáinán,
to demonstrate the King's betrayal of Hàn and alliance with Chǔ."
The Grand Steward then spoke to the King,
and the King received him.
Suí Hé said: "The King of Hàn has sent me to respectfully present a letter to Your Majesty's attendant,
and I privately wonder why Your Majesty is so close to Chǔ."
The King of Huáinán said: "I face north and serve them as a subject."
Suí Hé said:
"Your Majesty and King Xiàng are both ranked as feudal lords,
yet you face north and serve him,
surely because you consider Chǔ strong,
and thus entrust your state to it.
When King Xiàng attacked Qí,
he carried building planks himself,
leading the soldiers from the front.
Your Majesty should have mobilized all the forces of Huáinán,
personally leading them,
to serve as the vanguard of the Chǔ army.
Yet you only sent four thousand men to aid Chǔ.
Is facing north and serving another
truly like this?
When the King of Hàn battled at Péngchéng,
and King Xiàng had not yet left Qí,
Your Majesty should have rallied Huáinán's troops to cross the Huái River,
fighting day and night beneath Péngchéng.
Yet with Your Majesty commanding ten thousand troops,
not a single one crossed the Huái;
you idly watched to see who would win.
Is entrusting one's state to another
truly like this?
Your Majesty upholds an empty allegiance to Chǔ,
yet seeks to deeply entrust yourself—
I privately believe this is not advisable for Your Majesty.
However, the reason you do not betray Chǔ
is that you consider Hàn weak.
Although Chǔ's forces are strong,
the world burdens them with a reputation for injustice,
because they broke the covenant and killed the Righteous Emperor.
Moreover, King Chǔ relies on his victories to bolster his strength,
while the King of Hàn gathers the feudal lords,
returning to defend Chénggāo and Xíngyáng,
transporting grain from Shǔ and Hàn,
digging deep trenches and building strong fortifications,
deploying troops to guard the borders and passes.
When the Chǔ forces turn back,
passing through Liáng territory,
they penetrate eight or nine hundred lǐ into enemy land,
unable to engage in battle if they wish,
and lacking the strength to capture cities;
the old and weak transport provisions from a thousand lǐ away.
When Chǔ troops reach Xíngyáng and Chénggāo,
Hàn holds firm and does not move,
so they cannot advance to attack,
nor can they retreat to resolve the situation.
Thus, it is said that Chǔ's forces are not reliable.
If Chǔ were to defeat Hàn,
the feudal lords would feel endangered and fearful, aiding each other.
Chǔ's strength
would only suffice to provoke the armies of the world.
Therefore, Chǔ is inferior to Hàn,
a situation easily seen.
Now, Your Majesty does not side with the fully secure Hàn but entrusts yourself to the perilous Chǔ—
I am privately puzzled on Your Majesty's behalf.
I do not claim that Huáinán's troops are enough to destroy Chǔ.
But if Your Majesty sends troops and turns against Chǔ,
King Xiàng will surely be detained;
detained for several months,
Hàn's conquest of the world can be completely assured.
I request that Your Majesty take up arms and return to Hàn,
and the King of Hàn will surely grant you land and enfeoffment,
let alone Huáinán—
Huáinán will undoubtedly remain yours.
Thus, the King of Hàn respectfully sent me to offer this humble plan,
hoping Your Majesty will consider it."
The King of Huáinán said: "I will follow your command."
He secretly agreed to betray Chǔ and join Hàn,
but did not dare reveal it.
A Chǔ envoy was present,
urgently demanding that Yīng Bù send troops,
staying at the guesthouse.
Suí Hé entered directly,
sat in the seat above the Chǔ envoy,
and said:
"The King of Jiǔjiāng has already pledged allegiance to Hàn;
how can Chǔ demand troops from him?"
Bù was taken aback.
The Chǔ envoy rose to leave.
Hé Yīn advised Bù, saying:
"The matter is already set,
you should kill the Chǔ envoy immediately,
do not let him return,
and swiftly join Hàn to combine forces."
Bù said: "As the envoy instructs,
I shall raise troops and attack them."
Thereupon, he killed the envoy,
and raised an army to attack Chǔ.
Chǔ sent Xiàng Shēng and Lóng Qiě to attack Huáinán,
while King Xiàng remained to attack Xiàyì.
After several months,
Lóng Qiě attacked Huáinán,
defeating Bù's army.
Bù wanted to lead his troops to join Hàn,
but feared King Chǔ would kill him,
so he secretly traveled with Hé and returned to Hàn together.
When the King of Huáinán arrived,
the Emperor was sitting on a couch washing his feet,
and summoned Bù for an audience.
Bù was greatly enraged,
regretted coming,
and wanted to commit suicide.
Upon leaving and going to his residence,
the tents, provisions, food, drink, and attendants were like those of the King of Hàn.
Bù then became exceedingly overjoyed.
Thereupon, he sent someone into Jiǔjiāng.
Chǔ had already sent Xiàng Bó to take over the Jiǔjiāng troops,
and killed all of Bù's wife and children.
Bù's envoy managed to gather some old acquaintances and favored ministers,
leading several thousand troops to join Hàn.
Hàn further distributed troops to Bù and advanced north with him,
gathering forces until reaching Chénggāo.
In the seventh month of the fourth year,
Bù was established as King of Huáinán,
and joined in attacking Xiàng Jí.
In the fifth year of Hàn,
Bù sent people into Jiǔjiāng,
capturing several counties.
In the sixth year,
Bù and Liú Jiǎ entered Jiǔjiāng,
persuading Grand Marshal Zhōu Yīn,
who rebelled against Chǔ,
then raised the Jiǔjiāng troops to join Hàn in attacking Chǔ,
defeating them at Gāixià.
After Xiàng Jí died,
and the realm was pacified,
the Emperor held a banquet.
The Emperor belittled Suí Hé's contributions,
calling Hé a pedantic scholar,
asking what use a pedantic scholar was to the realm.
Suí Hé knelt and said:
"When Your Majesty led troops to attack Péngchéng,
before the King of Chǔ had left Qí,
if Your Majesty had dispatched fifty thousand infantry,
and five thousand cavalry,
could you have taken Huáinán?"
The Emperor said:
"No."
Suí Hé said:
"Your Majesty sent me with twenty envoys to Huáinán,
and upon arrival,
achieved Your Majesty's intent.
How is my merit not superior to fifty thousand infantry and five thousand cavalry?
Yet Your Majesty calls me a pedantic scholar,
saying of what use is a pedantic scholar to the realm,
why is that?"
The Emperor said: "I was just considering your merit."
Then he appointed Suí Hé as Protector of the Army.
Bù then received the tally as King of Huáinán,
with his capital at Lù,
and the commaneries of Jiǔjiāng, Lújiāng, Héngshān, and Yùzhāng all under Bù's rule.
In the seventh year,
he paid court at Chén.
In the eighth year,
he paid court at Luòyáng.
In the ninth year,
he paid court at Cháng'ān.
In the eleventh year,
Empress Gāo executed the Marquis of Huáiyīn,
causing Bù to become fearful.
In the summer,
Hàn executed King of Liáng Péng Yuè,
made him into mincemeat,
and distributed the mincemeat to all the nobles.
When it reached Huáinán,
the King of Huáinán was hunting,
saw the mincemeat,
and became greatly terrified,
secretly ordering his men to gather troops,
and watch for alerts in neighboring commaneries.
A favored concubine of Bù fell ill,
and requested to see a doctor.
The doctor's house was opposite that of the Palace Grandee Fèi Hè.
The concubine visited the doctor's house several times,
and Fèi Hè, considering himself an attendant,
gave generous gifts,
and drank with the concubine at the doctor's house.
When the concubine served the King,
during casual conversation,
she praised Hè as an honorable man.
The King angrily said:
"How do you know of him?"
She explained the situation in detail.
The King suspected she had an affair with him.
Hè became fearful,
and claimed illness.
The King grew angrier,
and wanted to arrest Hè.
Hè reported a matter of rebellion,
and rode a relay carriage to Cháng'ān.
Bù sent men to pursue him,
but failed to catch him.
When Hè arrived,
he reported the rebellion,
stating that Bù had signs of plotting rebellion,
and should be executed before it starts.
The Emperor read his letter,
and discussed it with Chancellor Xiāo.
The Chancellor said:
"I fear it may be false accusation due to enmity.
I request to detain Hè,
and send someone to secretly investigate the King of Huáinán."
When the King of Huáinán Bù saw that Hè had fled accused of a crime,
and reported rebellion,
he already suspected Hè had revealed state secrets;
when Hàn envoys arrived again,
and investigations were made,
he then executed Hè's family,
and raised troops in rebellion.
When the rebellion was reported,
the Emperor pardoned Fèi Hè,
and appointed him as a general.
The Emperor summoned his generals and asked:
"Bù has rebelled,
what should be done about it?"
All said:
"Send troops to attack him,
bury the scoundrel,
what can he do!"
The Marquis of Rǔyīn, Téng Gōng, summoned the former Chǔ Prime Minister to ask him.
The Prime Minister said:
"It is natural that he rebels."
Téng Gōng said: "The Emperor granted him land to make him a king,
bestowed titles to honor him,
established him as a sovereign facing south with ten thousand chariots,
why does he rebel?"
The Prime Minister said: "Last year, Péng Yuè was killed,
the year before, Hán Xìn was killed.
These three men
were of equal merit and standing.
He fears disaster will befall him,
hence he rebels."
Téng Gōng reported to the Emperor, saying:
"My guest, the former Chǔ Prime Minister, Lord Xuē,
is a man with strategic plans,
you may consult him."
The Emperor then summoned and questioned Lord Xuē.
Lord Xuē replied: "Bù's rebellion is not surprising.
If Bù adopts the superior strategy,[170 then Shāndōng will not belong to Hàn;
if he adopts the middle strategy,
the outcome of victory or defeat is uncertain;
if he adopts the inferior strategy,
Your Majesty can rest easy on your pillow."
The Emperor said:
"What is the superior strategy?"
The Prime Minister replied:
"Take Wú to the east,
take Chǔ to the west,
annex Qí and take Lǔ,
issue proclamations to Yān and Zhào,
firmly hold his territory,
then Shāndōng will not belong to Hàn."
"What is the middle strategy?"
"Take Wú to the east,
take Chǔ to the west,
annex Hán and take Wèi,
seize the grain at Áo Yú,
block the pass at Chénggāo,
then the outcome of victory or defeat is uncertain."
"What is the inferior strategy?"
"Take Wú to the east,
take Xiàcài to the west,
shift importance to Yuè,
and himself retreat to Chángshā,
then Your Majesty can rest easy on your pillow,
and Hàn will have no troubles."
The Emperor said:
"What strategy will he adopt?"
The Prime Minister replied: "He will adopt the inferior strategy."
The Emperor said:
"Why do you discard the superior and middle strategies and say he'll adopt the inferior one?"
The Prime Minister said:
"Yīng Bù was originally a convict from Lìshān,
who made himself a ruler of ten thousand chariots,
all for his own sake,
without considering the welfare of the people for generations to come.
Therefore, I say he will adopt the inferior strategy."
The Emperor said: "Good."
He enfeoffed Lord Xuē with a thousand households.
Then he established his son Liǔ as the King of Huáinán.
The Emperor thereupon raised an army and personally led it east to attack Bù.
When Bù first rebelled,
he said to his generals:
"The Emperor is old,
weary of warfare,
and surely cannot come himself.
If he sends his generals,
the only ones to fear are Huáiyīn and Péng Yuè,
but now they are both dead.
The rest are not worth fearing."
So he rebelled.
It turned out exactly as Lord Xuē had predicted.
Bù attacked Jīng to the east,
and the King of Jīng, Liú Jiǎ, fled and died at Fùlíng.
Bù seized all his troops,
crossed the Huái River, and attacked Chǔ.
Chǔ sent troops to fight him between Xú and Tóng,
dividing into three armies,
intending to use mutual rescue as a surprise tactic.
Someone advised the Chǔ general:
"Bù is skilled in using troops,
and the people have always feared him.
Moreover, according to military strategy,
when feudal lords fight on their own land, it is called 'scattered ground.'
Now we are divided into three parts;
if he defeats one of our armies,
the others will flee.
How can they rescue each other!"
The advice was not heeded.
Bù indeed defeated one army,
and the other two scattered and fled.
Then he went west,
and encountered the Emperor's troops west of Qí,
at Huìzhuì.
Bù's troops were very elite,
so the Emperor fortified Yōng City,
and saw that Bù's army was deployed in formation like Xiàng Jí's army,
which displeased him.
When they saw each other,
the Emperor shouted to Bù from a distance:
"Why go to the trouble of rebelling?"
Bù said:
"I want to be emperor, that's all."
The Emperor angrily cursed him,
and a great battle ensued.
Bù's army was defeated and fled,
crossing the Huái River.
He made several stands to fight,
but was unsuccessful,
and fled to Jiāngnán with over a hundred men.
Bù had previously married into the family of the Lord of Pó,
so because of this, the King of Chángshā, Āi, sent someone to deceive Bù,
pretending to flee with him,
luring him to Yuè,
so Bù trusted him and followed him to Póyáng.
A man of Póyáng killed Bù in a farmer's field in Zīxiāng,
and thus Yīng Bù was destroyed.
The Emperor's son Liǔ was established as the King of Huáinán,
Bēn Hè was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Qīsī,
and many of the generals were enfeoffed for their merits.
The Grand Historian remarks:
As for Yīng Bù,
were his ancestors from Yīng and Lù, which Chǔ destroyed as seen in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
descendants of Gāo Yáo?
He suffered corporal punishment,
yet how suddenly he rose to power!
The Xiàng family killed people by the tens of thousands,
and Bù was often the chief perpetrator of atrocities.
His achievements surpassed those of other feudal lords,
and thus he became a king,
yet he could not avoid being severely punished by the world.
The disaster originated from his beloved concubine,
jealousy bred calamity,
and in the end, it destroyed his state!
Hán Xìn, Marquis of Huáiyīn,
was a man of Huáinyīn.
When he was still a commoner,
he was poor and without reputable conduct,
so he could not be recommended for office,
nor could he make a living by trade,
often depending on others for meals,
and many people disliked him.
He frequently relied on the village chief of Xiàxiāng in Nánchāng for meals,
but after several months,
the village chief's wife grew tired of him,
so she cooked early and ate in bed.
When mealtime came and Xìn arrived,
she did not prepare food for him.
Xìn understood her intention,
was angry,
and finally left for good.
Xìn was fishing under the city wall,
and some old women were washing silk.
One of them, seeing Xìn hungry,
gave him food,
and continued to do so for dozens of days until the washing ended.
Xìn was pleased
and said to the washing woman:
"I will surely repay you generously someday."
The woman angrily said:
"A real man cannot feed himself;
I pity you, young noble, and give you food,
how could I expect repayment!"
A young man from the Huáiyīn slaughterhouse insulted Xìn,
saying:
"Though you are tall and big,
like to wear sword and knife,
you are cowardly at heart."
And he publicly humiliated him, saying:
"If you are not afraid to die,
stab me;
if you are afraid to die,
crawl between my legs."
Thereupon, Xìn looked at him carefully,
bent down, and crawled between his legs,
creeping on the ground.
Everyone in the market laughed at Xìn,
thinking him a coward.
When Xiàng Liáng crossed the Huái River,
Xìn joined him with his sword,
serving under his command,
but was unknown.
After Xiàng Liáng was defeated,
he followed Xiàng Yǔ,
who made him a gentleman of the palace.
He several times tried to advise Xiàng Yǔ on strategy,
but Yǔ did not employ him.
When the King of Hàn entered Shǔ,
Xìn left Chǔ and joined Hàn,
still unknown,
and was made a minor official.
He committed an offense punishable by decapitation;
thirteen of his companions had already been executed,
and when it was Xìn's turn,
he looked up
and happened to see Lord Téng,
saying: "Does the King not wish to conquer the world?
Why behead a strong man!"
Lord Téng found his words remarkable,
and his appearance impressive,
so he released him without execution.
He spoke with him,
and was greatly pleased.
He reported to the King,
who appointed him Commandant of Grain Supplies,
but the King did not yet find him extraordinary.
Xìn spoke with Xiāo Hé several times,
and Hé thought him remarkable.
When they reached Nánzhèng,
dozens of generals deserted along the way,
and Xìn estimated that Hé had already recommended him to the King several times,
but the King did not employ him,
so he too deserted.
When Hé heard that Xìn had left,
without time to report it,
he personally pursued him.
Someone reported to the King:
"Chancellor Hé has deserted."
The King was greatly enraged,
as if he had lost his right and left hands.
After a day or two,
Hé came to see the King,
who was both angry and pleased,
and scolded Hé:
"You deserted—
why?"
Hé said: "I did not dare to desert;
I was pursuing a deserter."
The King said:
"Who were you pursuing?"
Hé said:
"Hán Xìn."
The emperor scolded again, saying:
"Of the dozens of generals who have fled,
you pursued none of them;
yet you chased after Hán Xìn,
which is deceitful."
Xiāo Hé replied:
"Other generals are easily found.
But as for someone like Hán Xìn,
he is unparalleled in the nation.
If Your Majesty intends to rule over Hànzhōng long-term,
then Hán Xìn is of no use;
but if you wish to contend for the empire,
there is no one but Hán Xìn to strategize with.
It depends on what Your Majesty's plan decides."
The king said: "I too wish to head east;
how can I gloomily remain here long?"
Xiāo Hé said:
"If Your Majesty's plan is set on going east,
and you can employ Hán Xìn,
then he will stay;
if you cannot use him,
he will eventually flee."
The king said: "For your sake, I'll make him a general."
Xiāo Hé said:
"Even as a general,
Hán Xìn will certainly not stay."
The king said:
"Then as a grand general."
Xiāo Hé said: "Excellent."
Thereupon, the king wished to summon Hán Xìn to appoint him.
Xiāo Hé said:
"Your Majesty is usually arrogant and discourteous;
now appointing a grand general as if calling a child
is precisely why Hán Xìn left.
If Your Majesty must appoint him,
choose an auspicious day,
fast and purify yourself,
set up an altar and grounds,
and prepare the ceremonies—
only then will it be acceptable."
The king agreed.
The generals were all pleased,
each thinking themselves to have become grand general.
When it came to the appointment,
it was Hán Xìn,
and the entire army was astonished.
After Hán Xìn's appointment ceremony concluded,
he took the seat of honor.
The king said:
"The chancellor has repeatedly spoken of you, General;
what strategies do you have to advise me?"
Hán Xìn expressed gratitude,
then asked the king:
"Now, heading east to contend for power over the empire,
is it not against King Xiàng?"
The Hàn king said:
"Yes."
Hán Xìn said:
"Does Your Majesty consider yourself braver, fiercer, kinder, or stronger than King Xiàng?"
The Hàn king was silent for a long while,
then said:
"I am not his equal."
Hán Xìn bowed twice and congratulated him:
"Even I, Xìn, believe Your Majesty is not his equal.
However, I once served him,
allow me to speak of King Xiàng's character.
King Xiàng roars fiercely,
terrifying thousands,
yet he cannot entrust tasks to capable generals;
this is merely the courage of a common man.
King Xiàng appears respectful and compassionate toward others,
speaking gently;
when someone is ill,
he weeps and shares his food and drink;
but when it comes to rewarding those with merit deserving titles,
he wears out the seals' edges,
grudging giving them away;
this is what is called the kindness of a woman.
Though King Xiàng dominates the empire and subjugates the nobles,
he does not reside in Guānzhōng but makes Péngchéng his capital.
He violated the covenant with the Righteous Emperor,
enfeoffing his favorites as kings,
causing discontent among the nobles.
Seeing King Xiàng banish the Righteous Emperor to Jiāngnán,
the nobles also expelled their own lords and seized the best lands for themselves.
Wherever King Xiàng passes, nothing escapes destruction;
the empire harbors much resentment,
the people do not support him,
but are merely coerced by his might.
Though nominally a hegemon,
he has truly lost the hearts of the empire.
Thus, his strength can easily weaken.
Now if Your Majesty can indeed reverse his ways:
employ the brave and martial of the empire,
who could you not conquer!
Enfeoff cities and towns to meritorious subjects,
who would not submit!
Lead righteous troops with soldiers longing to return east,
Moreover, the three Qín kings served as Qín generals,
leading Qín's sons and brothers for years,
with countless deaths under their command;
they also deceived their troops into surrendering to the nobles;
reaching Xīn'ān,
King Xiàng treacherously buried over 200,000 surrendered Qín soldiers,
only Sīmǎ Xīn, Dǒng Yì, and Zhāng Hán escaping;
the Qín elders and brothers resent these three,
their hatred piercing to the marrow.
Now Chǔ forcibly enfeoffs these three with its might,
but the Qín people feel no affection for them.
When Your Majesty entered Wǔguān,
you harmed not a hair,
abolished Qín's harsh laws,
and made a pact with the Qín people,
with only three statutes;
the Qín people all desire Your Majesty to rule over Qín.
According to the covenant among the nobles,
Your Majesty should rule Guānzhōng,
which all in Guānzhōng know.
Your Majesty, deprived of your rightful position, entered Hànzhōng,
leaving every Qín person resentful.
Now if Your Majesty raises troops eastward,
the three Qín regions can be secured with a proclamation."
Thereupon, the Hàn king was overjoyed,
feeling he had found Hán Xìn too late.
He thus followed Hán Xìn's strategies,
deploying the generals to their assaults.
In the eighth month,
the Hàn king raised troops eastward, emerging at Chéncāng,
and pacified the three Qín regions.
In the second year of Hàn,
he exited the pass,
subdued Wèi and Hénán,
and the kings of Hán and Yīn surrendered.
He allied with Qí and Zhào to attack Chǔ together.
In the fourth month,
they reached Péngchéng,
where the Hàn forces were defeated and scattered, retreating.
Hán Xìn regrouped his troops and joined the Hàn king at Xíngyáng,
again defeating Chǔ between Jīng and Suǒ,
thus preventing the Chǔ army from advancing west.
After Hàn's defeat and retreat from Péngchéng,
King Sāi Xīn and King Zhái Yì fled Hàn and surrendered to Chǔ,
while Qí and Zhào also rebelled against Hàn and made peace with Chǔ.
In the sixth month,
King Bào of Wèi requested leave to visit his ailing mother;
upon reaching his state,
he immediately sealed off Héguan and rebelled against Hàn,
making a pact with Chǔ.
The Hàn king sent Lì Shēng to persuade Bào,
but without success.
That eighth month,
Hán Xìn was appointed left chancellor
to attack Wèi.
King Bào of Wèi massed troops at Púbǎn,
blocking Línjìn;
Hán Xìn then created decoy forces,
arraying boats as if to cross at Línjìn,
while secretly sending troops from Xiàyáng to cross using wooden barrels,
and launched a surprise attack on Ānyì.
King Bào of Wèi was shocked,
led his troops to confront Hán Xìn,
and was captured by Hán Xìn,
securing Wèi as the Hédōng commandery.
The Hàn king sent Zhāng Ěr to accompany Hán Xìn,
leading troops eastward,
then north to attack Zhào and Dài.
In the intercalary ninth month,
they defeated the Dài army,
capturing Xià Yuè at Yānyǔ.
After Hán Xìn conquered Wèi and defeated Dài,
Hàn repeatedly took his elite troops,
sending them to Xíngyáng to resist Chǔ.
Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr, with tens of thousands of troops,
intended to march east down Jǐngxíng to attack Zhào.
The king of Zhào and Chéng'ān Jūn Chén Yú, hearing of Hàn's impending attack,
gathered troops at the Jǐngxíng Pass,
claiming 200,000.
Guǎngwǔ Jūn Lǐ Zuǒjū advised Chéng'ān Jūn:
"I hear Hán general Hán Xìn crossed the Western River,
captured the king of Wèi,
seized Xià Yuè,
recently bloodied Yānyǔ,
and now is aided by Zhāng Ěr,
plotting to take Zhào;
this is riding victory's momentum to fight far from home,
their edge is unstoppable.
I've heard supplying grain over a thousand lǐ
leaves soldiers hungry;
gathering firewood before cooking
means troops seldom eat their fill.
Now the Jǐngxíng road
is too narrow for chariots to run parallel,
cavalry cannot form columns;
marching hundreds of lǐ,
their supply situation surely lags behind."
I hope you will lend me thirty thousand elite troops,
to cut off their supply routes from a bypath;
you should deepen the moats and heighten the ramparts,
strengthen the camp and do not engage in battle.
They will be unable to advance and fight,
unable to retreat and return,
while my elite troops cut off their rear,
leaving them nothing to plunder in the countryside,
within ten days at most,
the heads of the two generals can be delivered before your banner.
I hope you will consider my plan.
Otherwise,
you will surely be captured by these two men."
Lord Chéng'ān,
being a Confucian scholar,
often claimed that righteous armies do not employ deceitful strategies or unexpected tactics,
saying:
"I have heard that in the art of war, with ten times the force one should surround the enemy,
with double the force one should engage in battle.
Now Hán Xìn's troops are said to number tens of thousands,
but in reality, they are no more than a few thousand.
Having marched a thousand lǐ to attack us,
they are already exhausted.
If we avoid battle now,
when faced with greater forces later,
how will we withstand them!
Then the feudal lords will say we are cowardly,
and will lightly come to attack us."
He did not heed the strategy of Guǎngwǔ Jūn,
and Guǎngwǔ Jūn's plan was not used.
Hán Xìn sent spies to observe,
and upon learning that his plan was not adopted,
they returned to report,
whereupon he was greatly pleased,
and dared to lead his troops down.
Thirty lǐ from the entrance of Jǐngxíng Pass,
he halted and encamped.
At midnight, he issued orders,
selecting two thousand light cavalry,
each carrying a red banner,
to take a bypath and conceal themselves in the mountains to observe the Zhào army,
instructing them:
"When the Zhào army sees us retreat,
they will certainly empty their fortifications to pursue us,
then swiftly enter the Zhào camp,
pull down the Zhào banners,
and raise the Hàn red banners."
He ordered his deputy generals to distribute a meal,
saying:
"Today, after defeating Zhào, we will feast together!"
None of the generals believed him,
but they pretended to agree,
saying:
"Yes."
He then said to the military officers:
"The Zhào army has already taken a favorable position for their camp,
and since they have not yet seen my general's flags and drums,
they are unwilling to attack our vanguard,
fearing we might turn back upon reaching difficult terrain."
Hán Xìn then sent ten thousand troops ahead,
who marched out
and deployed with their backs to the river.
The Zhào army saw this and laughed heartily.
At dawn,
Hán Xìn raised the general's flags and drums,
and marched out of Jǐngxíng Pass with drums beating,
whereupon the Zhào army opened their fortifications and attacked,
and a great battle ensued for a long time.
Then Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr pretended to abandon their drums and flags,
and fled to the army by the river.
The riverbank army opened ranks to let them in,
and then fought fiercely again.
The Zhào army indeed emptied their fortifications to compete for the Hàn drums and flags,
pursuing Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr.
Once Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr entered the riverbank army,
the troops all fought desperately,
and could not be defeated.
The two thousand elite cavalry Hán Xìn had sent out,
waiting for the Zhào army to leave their fortifications empty in pursuit of gain,
galloped into the Zhào camp,
pulled down all the Zhào banners,
and raised two thousand Hàn red banners.
The Zhào army, already unable to win,
and failing to capture Hán Xìn and others,
wanted to return to their fortifications,
but found them full of Hàn red banners,
and were greatly shocked,
thinking that the Hàn army had already captured the Zhào king and generals,
whereupon the troops fell into chaos,
and fled.
Even though the Zhào generals beheaded some,
they could not stop the rout.
Then the Hàn troops launched a major attack,
decisively defeating and capturing the Zhào army,
beheading Lord Chéng'ān at the Chí River,
and capturing King Xiē of Zhào.
Hán Xìn then ordered his troops not to kill Guǎngwǔ Jūn,
offering a thousand pieces of gold to anyone who could capture him alive.
Thus, someone bound Guǎngwǔ Jūn and brought him before the banner,
whereupon Hán Xìn untied his bonds,
seated him facing east,
faced him from the west,
and treated him as a teacher.
The generals presented the heads and captives,
and after the celebrations,
they asked Hán Xìn:
"According to the art of war, one should deploy with hills to the right and rear,
and water to the front and left,
yet today you ordered us to deploy with our backs to the river,
saying we would feast after defeating Zhào,
and we were not convinced.
Yet we ultimately won,
what strategy was this?"
Hán Xìn said:
"This is in the art of war,
but you gentlemen failed to notice it.
Does not the art of war say
'Place them in a fatal position to ensure their survival,
put them in a hopeless situation to preserve their lives'?
Moreover, I have not had the time to train and win the loyalty of the officers and men,
this is what is called 'driving market people to fight,'
and under such circumstances, unless they are placed in a fatal position,
making each man fight for his own life;
if given a chance to survive,
they would all flee,
how could they be used then!"
The generals all expressed admiration, saying:
"Excellent.
This is beyond our reach."
Then Hán Xìn asked Guǎngwǔ Jūn:
"I wish to attack Yān to the north,
and campaign against Qí to the east,
how can I achieve success?"
Guǎngwǔ Jūn declined, saying:
"I have heard that a general of a defeated army
should not speak of courage,
a minister of a fallen state
should not plan for survival.
Now that I am a captive of defeat and ruin,
how can I be worthy of deliberating on great matters!"
Hán Xìn said:
"I have heard that Bǎilǐ Xī, while in Yú, witnessed its fall,
but in Qín, helped it achieve hegemony,
not because he was foolish in Yú and wise in Qín,
but because his advice was heeded or not,
and he was employed or not.
If Lord Chéng'ān had followed your strategy,
someone like me would have been captured already.
It is precisely because he did not use your counsel
that I am able to serve you now."
He then pressed further:
"I sincerely submit to your guidance,
I hope you will not decline."
Guǎngwǔ Jūn said:
"I have heard that the wise, after a thousand considerations,
must have one oversight;
the foolish, after a thousand considerations,
must have one insight.
Hence it is said, 'The words of a madman,
the sage may choose.'
I fear my strategy may not be worthy of use,
but I wish to offer my humble loyalty.
Lord Chéng'ān had strategies for winning every battle,
yet he lost them in one morning,
his army defeated at Hào,
and he himself died at the Chí River.
Now you, General, have crossed the Western River,
captured the King of Wèi,
seized Xià Yuè at Yānyǔ,
in one move taken Jǐngxíng,
and in less than a morning shattered the two hundred thousand troops of Zhào,
executing Lord Chéng'ān.
Your fame is known throughout the land,
your might shakes the world,
so that farmers leave their plows and tools,
dress finely and eat well,
listening attentively for your commands.
Such is your strength, General.
However, your troops are weary and exhausted,
and in reality, hard to employ.
If you now lead these tired and worn-out soldiers,
to confront Yān's strong fortifications,
you may wish to fight but fear prolonged effort will not take them,
your true situation exposed and momentum lost,
days dragged out and supplies exhausted,
while weak Yān remains unsubdued,
and Qí will surely fortify its borders to strengthen itself.
If Yān and Qí hold out against you,
then the balance between Liú and Xiàng will remain undecided.
Such are your weaknesses, General.
In my foolish opinion,
I privately believe this would be a mistake.
Therefore, those skilled in war do not use their weaknesses to attack the enemy's strengths,
but use their strengths to attack the enemy's weaknesses."
Hán Xìn said:
"Then what course should be taken?"
Guǎngwǔ Jūn replied: "For the present, in planning for you, General,
nothing is better than resting your troops and keeping your armor sheathed,
pacifying Zhào and comforting its orphans,
within a hundred lǐ,
cattle and wine arrive daily,
to feast the officers and release the soldiers from service,
facing north toward the road to Yān,
and then sending an eloquent envoy bearing a short letter,
displaying your strengths to Yān,
Yān will certainly not dare to refuse compliance.
Once Yān has submitted,
have a persuasive envoy go east to inform Qí,
Qí is bound to follow like the wind and submit,
even if there are wise men,
they will not know how to plan for Qí.
If this is done,
then all under heaven can be schemed for.
In warfare, there is indeed a principle of first making a display and then following with substance,
this is what it means."
Hán Xìn said:
"Excellent."
He followed this strategy,
dispatched an envoy to Yān,
and Yān submitted like grass bending in the wind.
Then he sent an envoy to report to Hàn,
and requested that Zhāng Ě be made King of Zhào,
to pacify and govern that state.
The King of Hàn approved it,
and thus established Zhāng Ě as King of Zhào.
Chǔ repeatedly sent surprise troops across the river to attack Zhào,
King Ě of Zhào and Hán Xìn went back and forth to rescue Zhào,
while securing the cities and towns of Zhào,
and sending troops to Hàn.
Chǔ was then urgently besieging the King of Hàn at Xíngyáng,
the King of Hàn went out southward,
to between Wǎn and Yè,
obtained Qíng Bù,
fled into Chénggāo,
and Chǔ again urgently besieged him.
In the sixth month,
the King of Hàn left Chénggāo,
crossed the river eastward,
accompanied only by Lord Téng,
and went to the army of Zhāng Ě at Xiūwǔ.
Upon arrival,
they lodged at a relay station.
At dawn, claiming to be an envoy of Hàn,
he galloped into the Zhào encampment.
Zhāng Ě and Hán Xìn had not yet risen,
so he entered their sleeping quarters, took their seals and tallies,
used the commander's flag to summon the generals,
and reassigned their positions.
When Xìn and Ě arose,
they then realized the King of Hàn had come,
and were greatly astonished.
The King of Hàn took command of both their armies,
immediately ordered Zhāng Ě to prepare the defense of Zhào territory,
appointed Hán Xìn as Chancellor of State,
and gathered the Zhào troops that had not yet been dispatched to attack Qí.
Xìn led his troops east,
before crossing at Píngyuán,
he heard that the King of Hàn had sent Lì Yìjī to persuade Qí to surrender,
and Hán Xìn wanted to stop.
Kuǎi Tōng, an eloquent man from Fànyáng, advised Xìn, saying:
"General, you received an edict to attack Qí,
yet Hàn separately sent a covert envoy to subdue Qí,
is there an edict ordering you to stop, General?
How can you not proceed!
Moreover, Lì Shēng is but one scholar,
leaning on his carriage rail, wagging his three-inch tongue,
he subdued over seventy cities of Qí,
while you, General, leading tens of thousands of troops,
took over a year to capture just over fifty cities of Zhào,
having been a general for several years,
are you反而不如一个竖儒之功吗？"
Thereupon, Xìn agreed with him,
followed his plan,
and thus crossed the river.
Qí, having already heeded Lì Shēng,
stayed to indulge in drinking,
and relaxed their defenses against Hàn.
Xìn thereupon launched a surprise attack on the Qí army at Lìxià,
and advanced to Línzī.
King Tián Guǎng of Qí, believing Lì Shēng had betrayed him,
had him boiled alive,
and fled to Gāomì,
sending an envoy to Chǔ to request rescue.
Hán Xìn, having secured Línzī,
then pursued Guǎng east to the west of Gāomì.
Chǔ also sent Lóng Jū to command,
claiming two hundred thousand troops,
to rescue Qí.
King Guǎng of Qí and Lóng Jū combined their armies to engage Xìn in battle,
before they joined combat.
Someone advised Lóng Jū, saying:
"The Hàn troops are fighting far from home, desperate in battle,
their vanguard cannot be withstood.
Qí and Chǔ are fighting on their own territory,
their soldiers are easily defeated and scattered.
It would be better to fortify deeply,
and have the King of Qí send his trusted ministers to recruit the lost cities,
when the lost cities hear their king is present,
and Chǔ has come to rescue,
they will certainly turn against Hàn.
The Hàn troops are guests residing two thousand lǐ away,
if all the Qí cities turn against them,
their situation will leave them with no means to obtain food,
and they could be made to surrender without a fight."
Lóng Jū said:
"I have always known Hán Xìn's character,
he is easy to deal with.
Moreover, to rescue Qí and make them surrender without fighting,
what merit would I have?
If we fight and defeat him now,
we can gain half of Qí,
why stop!"
Thus they engaged in battle,
facing Xìn across the Wéi River.
Hán Xìn then had men prepare over ten thousand bags overnight,
filled them with sand,
blocked the upper stream,
led half his army across,
attacked Lóng Jū,
feigned defeat,
and retreated.
Lóng Jū indeed said joyfully:
"I always knew Xìn was timid."
He then pursued Xìn across the river.
Xìn had men break the sandbag dam,
and the water rushed down in great force.
Most of Lóng Jū's army could not cross,
Xìn immediately launched a fierce attack,
and killed Lóng Jū.
Lóng Jū's army east of the river scattered and fled,
and King Guǎng of Qí escaped.
Xìn then pursued the fleeing forces to Chéngyáng,
capturing all the Chǔ soldiers.
In the fourth year of Hàn,
he thus subdued and pacified all of Qí.
He sent a message to the King of Hàn, saying:
"Qí is deceitful and fickle,
a state of repeated reversals,
bordering Chǔ to the south,
if a proxy king is not established to pacify it,
the situation will remain unstable.
I wish to act as proxy king for convenience."
At that time,
Chǔ was urgently besieging the King of Hàn at Xíngyáng,
when Hán Xìn's envoy arrived, the King opened the letter,
and flew into a rage, cursing:
"I am trapped here,
day and night hoping for you to come assist me,
yet you want to set yourself up as king!"
Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng stepped on the King of Hàn's foot,
and whispered in his ear:
"Hàn is currently at a disadvantage,
can we prevent Xìn from making himself king?
It would be better to establish him accordingly,
treat him well,
and let him guard the area himself.
Otherwise,
trouble may arise."
The King of Hàn also realized this,
and thus continued cursing:
"A true man, having pacified the feudal lords,
should be a real king,
what need for a proxy!"
He then sent Zhāng Liáng to establish Xìn as King of Qí,
and summoned his troops to attack Chǔ.
With Chǔ having lost Lóng Jū,
King Xiàng grew fearful,
and sent Wǔ Shè, a man from Xūyí, to persuade King Xìn of Qí, saying:
"All under heaven have long suffered under Qín,
and joined forces to attack Qín.
After Qín was defeated,
merits were calculated and lands divided,
territories were allotted and kings established,
to give rest to the officers and soldiers.
Now the King of Hàn has again raised troops and moved east,
invading others' shares,
seizing others' lands,
having already destroyed the Three Qín,
leading troops out of the pass,
gathering the armies of the feudal lords to attack Chǔ in the east,
his intention is not to stop until he has devoured all under heaven,
his insatiability is extreme to this degree.
Moreover, the King of Hàn cannot be trusted,
he has been in King Xiàng's grasp several times,
King Xiàng took pity and spared him,
yet once he escaped,
he immediately broke the agreement,
and attacked King Xiàng again,
his untrustworthiness is such."
Now although you consider yourself to have a deep friendship with the King of Hàn,
exerting your strength and leading troops for him,
you will ultimately be captured by him.
The reason you have survived until now
is because King Xiàng still exists.
In the current affairs of the two kings,
the power lies with you.
If you side with the right, the King of Hàn will win;
if you side with the left, King Xiàng will win.
If King Xiàng perishes today,
then next he will come for you.
Since you have a past connection with King Xiàng,
why not turn against Hàn and ally with Chǔ,
dividing the world into three parts to rule?"
If you let this opportunity pass,
and insist on sticking with Hàn to attack Chǔ,
is this how a wise man should act?"
Hán Xìn declined, saying:
"I served King Xiàng,
my position was no higher than a court gentleman,
my duty merely holding a halberd,
my advice went unheeded,
my strategies unused,
so I turned against Chǔ and joined Hàn.
The King of Hàn bestowed upon me the seal of Supreme General,
gave me command of tens of thousands of troops,
took off his own clothes to dress me,
offered his own food to feed me,
listened to my words and used my plans,
thus I have reached this position.
When someone trusts and favors me so deeply,
it would be inauspicious to betray him,
and I would not change this even if I die.
Please convey my apologies to King Xiàng!"
After Wǔ Shè had left,
Kuǎi Tōng of Qí, knowing that the fate of the world lay with Hán Xìn,
wished to move him with an extraordinary strategy,
and approached Hán Xìn with physiognomy, saying:
"I have studied the art of reading faces."
Hán Xìn asked, "How do you read people, sir?"
He replied:
"Nobility or baseness lies in bone structure,
joy or sorrow in facial expression,
success or failure in decisiveness.
Using these to assess,
one is never mistaken."
Hán Xìn said:
"Good.
What do you read in me, sir?"
He replied, "I wish for a moment alone."
Xìn said, "My attendants may leave."
Tōng said:
"Judging by your face,
you will not exceed the rank of marquis,
and even that is precarious.
But judging by your back,
your nobility is beyond words."
Hán Xìn asked, "What does that mean?"
Kuǎi Tōng said:
"When the uprising first began,
heroes and stalwarts raised their banners and called,
men of talent gathered like clouds and mist,
crowding like fish scales,
swift as fire and wind.
At that time,
the only concern was overthrowing Qín.
Now Chǔ and Hàn contend,
causing the innocent people of the world to suffer grievously,
fathers and sons lying exposed in the fields,
beyond counting.
The men of Chǔ rose from Péngchéng,
fought and pursued northward,
reaching Yíngyáng,
sweeping forward with advantage,
their might shaking the world.
Yet their troops are trapped between Jīng and Suǒ,
halted at the western hills unable to advance,
for three years now.
The King of Hàn leads hundreds of thousands of troops,
holding Gǒng and Luò,
using the natural barriers of mountains and rivers,
fighting several battles a day,
gaining not an inch of ground,
defeated and unsupported,
defeated at Yíngyáng,
wounded at Chénggāo,
fleeing between Wǎn and Yè—
this is what is called both wisdom and courage being exhausted.
Their sharpness blunted by perilous passes,
their provisions drained from the stores,
the people exhausted and resentful,
wavering with no one to rely on.
In my estimation,
only a sage of the world can end this calamity.
Now the fates of both lords hang on you.
If you side with Hàn, Hàn wins;
if you join Chǔ, Chǔ wins.
I wish to lay bare my heart,
offer my innermost thoughts,
and present my humble plan,
though I fear you may not use it.
If you truly heed my advice,
it would be best to let both survive to their benefit,
dividing the world into three,
standing like the legs of a tripod,
so that none dare move first.
With your sagacity,
and your armed multitude,
holding strong Qí,
leading Yān and Zhào,
striking at undefended areas to control the rear,
following the people's desires,
appealing westwards for their welfare,
then the world will respond like wind and echo,
and who would dare not obey!
Divide the great and weaken the strong,
establishing feudal lords;
once they are established,
the world will submit and virtue will be attributed to Qí.
Securing Qí's ancient lands,
with territories of Jiāo and Sì,
treating the lords with virtue,
humbly bowing and yielding,
then the kings of the world will come in succession to court Qí.
I have heard that if Heaven gives and you do not take,
you will suffer misfortune;
if the time comes and you do not act,
you will incur disaster.
I urge you to consider this deeply."
Hán Xìn said:
"The King of Hàn has treated me most generously,
letting me ride in his carriage,
dressing me in his clothes,
feeding me with his food.
I have heard that
he who rides another's carriage shares their burdens,
he who wears another's clothes shares their worries,
he who eats another's food dies for their cause.
How can I turn to profit and betray righteousness!"
Kuǎi Shēng said: "You think yourself loyal to the King of Hàn,
wishing to establish an eternal enterprise,
but I privately believe you are mistaken.
Initially, King Chángshān and Lord Chéng'ān were commoners,
sworn to die for each other,
yet later quarreled over the matter of Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé,
and became resentful.
King Chángshān betrayed King Xiàng,
carrying Xiàng Yīng's head in flight,
and fled to the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn lent him troops to march east,
killing Lord Chéng'ān south of the Chí River,
head and feet separated,
finally laughed at by the world.
These two were
the closest friends in the world,
yet ended up capturing each other—why?
Because trouble arises from many desires and the human heart is hard to fathom.
Now you wish to act with loyalty and trust towards the King of Hàn,
but your bond cannot be stronger than theirs was,
and the matters between you are greater than Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé.
So I believe that if you think the King of Hàn will not endanger you,
you are also mistaken.
Wén Zhǒng and Fàn Lǐ preserved dying Yuè,
made Gōu Jiàn hegemon,
achieved merit and fame but met their deaths.
When the wild game is finished, the hounds are cooked.
In terms of friendship,
yours is not like that of Zhāng Ěr and Lord Chéng'ān;
in terms of loyalty and trust,
yours does not exceed that of Wén Zhǒng and Fàn Lǐ towards Gōu Jiàn.
These two cases
are enough for reflection.
I urge you to consider deeply.
Moreover, I have heard that he whose bravery and strategy shake his lord is in danger,
and he whose merit overshadows the world receives no reward.
Let me speak of your achievements and strategies:
You crossed the Western River,
captured the King of Wèi,
seized Xià Yuè,
led troops down Jǐngxíng,
executed Lord Chéng'ān,
subdued Zhào,
intimidated Yān,
secured Qí,
crushed the Chǔ army of two hundred thousand in the south,
killed Lóng Jū in the east,
and reported westwards—
this is what is called unmatched merit in the world,
and strategies unheard of in generations.
Now you bear the awe that shakes your lord,
hold merit that cannot be rewarded,
if you return to Chǔ,
the men of Chǔ will not trust you;
if you return to Hàn,
the men of Hàn will be terrified:
where can you go with this?
In the position of a subject yet with power that shakes your lord,
renowned throughout the world, I fear for your safety."
Hán Xìn declined, saying:
"Sir, please rest for now.
I will consider it."
A few days later,
Kuǎi Tōng again persuaded him, saying:
"Listening is the sign of affairs,
planning is the pivot of matters.
Those who mishear plans and lose opportunities yet remain secure for long
are rare indeed.
One who never errs in listening
cannot be confused by words;
one whose plans never mistake fundamentals and details
cannot be disordered by arguments.
He who follows menial duties
loses the power of a sovereign;
he who guards a meager salary
misses the position of a minister.
Thus, the wise decide with resolution,
while doubt is the harm of affairs.
To scrutinize trivial calculations
yet neglect the great destiny of the world—
even if wisdom truly knows it,
but dares not act on the decision,
this is the calamity of all endeavors.

The arrangements were set,
awaiting reports from Xì.
One of his retainers had offended Hán Xìn,
so Xìn imprisoned him,
intending to execute him.
The retainer's younger brother submitted a report of unusual events,
informing Empress Lǚ that Xìn intended to rebel.
Empress Lǚ wanted to summon him,
but feared his faction wouldn't comply,
so she conspired with Chancellor Xiāo Hé,
deceiving people into believing someone came from the emperor,
claiming Xì had been captured and killed,
with all marquises and ministers offering congratulations.
The chancellor deceived Xìn, saying:
"Though ill,
force yourself to come congratulate."
Xìn entered,
where Empress Lǚ had warriors bind him,
and executed him in the bell room of Chánglè Palace.
As Xìn was about to be executed,
he said:
"I regret not following Kuǎi Tōng's strategy,
thus being deceived by women and children,
is this not Heaven's will!"
Then Xìn's three clans were exterminated.
Emperor Gāozǔ had returned from Xì's army,
arriving to find
Xìn dead,
both pleased and pitying him,
asked:
"What were Xìn's last words?"
Empress Lǚ said:
"Xìn said he regretted not using Kuǎi Tōng's plan."
Emperor Gāozǔ said: "That's the debater from Qí."
He then ordered Qí to arrest Kuǎi Tōng,
who upon arrival
was asked by the emperor:
"Did you advise the Marquis of Huáiyīn to rebel?"
He replied: "Yes,
I certainly advised him.
That fool didn't use my strategy,
thus bringing about his own destruction here.
Had that fool used my plan,
how could Your Majesty have destroyed him!"
The emperor angrily said: "Boil him."
Tōng said:
"Alas, boiling is unjust!"
The emperor said:
"You advised Hán Xìn to rebel,
what injustice?"
He replied:
"When Qín's laws collapsed and order relaxed,
the east was in great turmoil,
different surnames arose together,
talented men gathered like crows.
Qín lost its deer,
and all under heaven chased it,
so those with great talent and swift feet caught it first.
Zhí's dog barks at Yáo,
not because Yáo is unvirtuous,
but because the dog barks at anyone not its master.
At that time,
I only knew Hán Xìn,
not Your Majesty.
Moreover, many under heaven sharpened weapons wishing to achieve what you did,
but lacked the strength.
Could they all be boiled?"
Emperor Gāozǔ said: "Let him go."
Thus pardoned Tōng's crime.
Grand Historian Simǎ Qiān said:
When I visited Huáiyīn,
the locals told me
that even as a commoner,
Hán Xìn's ambitions differed from others.
When his mother died,
he was too poor for burial,
yet sought high, open land,
where ten thousand households could be placed around it.
I saw his mother's grave,
and indeed it was so. Had Hán Xìn learned humility,
not boasting of his achievements,
not flaunting his abilities,
he might have been nearly perfect,
his merit for Hàn comparable to the Duke of Zhōu, Duke of Shào, or Grand Duke Wàng,
receiving sacrifices for generations.
Instead of pursuing this,
with the empire already settled,
he plotted rebellion,
exterminating his clan,
was this not fitting!
King Xìn of Hán
was the grandson of King Xiāng of Hán's concubine,
standing eight feet five inches tall.
When Xiàng Liáng established King Huái's descendant as King of Chǔ,
Yān, Qí, Zhào, and Wèi already had kings,
only Hán lacked an heir,
so he made Héngyáng Jūn Chéng, a Hán noble, King of Hán,
hoping to pacify former Hán territory.
After Xiàng Liáng's defeat and death at Dìngtáo,
Chéng fled to King Huái.
Pei Gōng attacked Yángchéng,
sending Zhāng Liáng as Hán's Minister over the Masses to subdue former Hán lands,
finding Xìn,
making him a Hán general,
leading troops with Pei Gōng into Wǔguān.
When Pei Gōng became King of Hàn,
Xìn followed to Hànzhōng,
then advised the King of Hàn:
"King Xiàng placed his generals in nearby lands,
while you alone dwell distantly here,
this is a demotion.
Our soldiers are all from the east,
standing on tiptoe, longing to return.
Use their keenness heading east
to contend for the empire."
The King of Hàn pacified the Three Qín,
then promised Xìn to be King of Hán,
first appointing him Grand Commandant of Hán,
leading troops to conquer Hán territory.
When Xiàng Jí enfeoffed various kings to their states,
King Chéng of Hán, having achieved no merit by not following,
was not sent to his state,
instead made a marquis.
Hearing Hàn sent Xìn to conquer Hán lands,
he ordered former Wú magistrate Zhèng Chāng, whom Xiàng Jí knew from Wú travels, as King of Hán to resist Hàn.
In Hàn's second year,
Xìn conquered over ten Hán cities.
When the King of Hàn reached Hénán,
Xìn urgently attacked King Chāng of Hán at Yángchéng.
Chāng surrendered,
and the King of Hàn made Xìn King of Hán,
often leading Hán troops in his service.
In the third year,
the King of Hàn left Xíngyáng,
with King Xìn of Hán, Zhōu Kē, etc. guarding Xíngyáng.
When Chǔ defeated them at Xíngyáng,
Xìn surrendered to Chǔ,
but later escaped,
returning to Hàn,
who reinstated him as King of Hán,
finally following to defeat Xiàng Jí,
stabilizing the empire.
In spring of the fifth year,
he received the tally as King of Hán,
ruling Yǐngchuān.
Next spring,
the emperor, considering Xìn's military talent,
and his kingdom's proximity to Gǒng and Luò in the north,
pressured by Wǎn and Yè in the south,
with Huáiyáng to the east,
all areas with strong troops,
ordered King Xìn of Hán moved to rule north of Tàiyuán,
to defend against the Hú,
capital at Jìnyáng.
Xìn memorialized:
"The state borders the frontier,
with Xiōngnú frequently invading.
Jìnyáng is far from the passes,
request to govern from Mǎyì."
The emperor approved,
so Xìn moved to Mǎyì.
In autumn,
Mòdú of Xiōngnú heavily besieged Xìn,
who sent multiple envoys seeking peace.
Hàn sent reinforcements,
suspecting Xìn's frequent communications
indicated divided loyalty,
sent messengers to reprimand him.
Fearing execution,
Xìn allied with Xiōngnú to attack Hàn,
rebelling, surrendering Mǎyì to the Hú,
attacking Tàiyuán.
In winter of the seventh year,
the emperor personally attacked,
defeating Xìn's army at Tóngdī,
executing his general Wáng Xǐ.
Xìn fled to Xiōngnú.
(His general Mǎnqiū Chén from Báitǔ, Wáng Huáng, etc. made Zhào Lì, descendant of Zhào, king,
gathering Xìn's scattered troops,
conspiring with Xìn and Mòdú to attack Hàn.
Xiōngnú sent left and right wise kings with over ten thousand cavalry with Wáng Huáng, etc., stationed south of Guǎngwǔ,
reaching Jìnyáng,
battling Hàn troops,
where Hàn heavily defeated them,
pursuing to Líshí,
defeating them again.
Xiōngnú regrouped northwest of Lóufán,
Hàn ordered chariots and cavalry to defeat Xiōngnú.)
Chén Xī,
a man of Liáng,
in his youth often expressed admiration for the Lord of Wèi;
when he became a general guarding the border,
he attracted guests and treated scholars with respect,
but his reputation exceeded reality.
Zhōu Chāng suspected him,
and flaws and faults arose considerably,
fearing disaster would befall him,
wicked men offered counsel,
leading him to sink into unrighteousness.
Alas, how tragic!
Indeed, the depth to which the success or failure of a plan affects a person is profound!
Tián Dān,
a man of Dí,
was from the Tián clan of the former kings of Qí.
Dān's cousin Tián Róng,
and Róng's younger brother Tián Héng,
were all influential,
their clan strong,
and able to win people's support.
When Chén Shè first rose and proclaimed himself king of Chǔ,
he sent Zhōu Fú to conquer and pacify the land of Wèi,
reaching north to Dí,
where Dí defended its city.
Tián Dān pretended to bind his slave,
and followed some young men to the court,
intending to report and execute the slave.
When he saw the magistrate of Dí,
he took the opportunity to strike and kill the magistrate,
then summoned the influential officials and their sons, saying:
"The feudal lords have all rebelled against Qín and established themselves;
Qí,
an ancient established state,
and I, Dān,
of the Tián clan,
should be king."
Thereupon, he proclaimed himself King of Qí,
and raised troops to attack Zhōu Fú.
Zhōu Fú's army withdrew and left,
and Tián Dān then led his troops east to conquer and pacify the land of Qí.
The Qín general Zhāng Hán besieged King Jiù of Wèi at Línjì,
and the situation was critical.
The King of Wèi sought rescue from Qí,
and the King of Qí, Tián Dān, led troops to save Wèi.
Zhāng Hán attacked at night with silent troops,
routed the armies of Qí and Wèi,
and killed Tián Dān at Jì.
Dān's younger brother Tián Róng gathered Dān's remaining troops and fled east to Dōng'ē.
The people of Qí, hearing of King Tián Dān's death,
then established Tián Jiǎ, the younger brother of the former King Jiàn of Qí, as King of Qí,
with Tián Jiǎo as chancellor,
and Tián Jiàn as general,
to resist the feudal lords.
When Tián Róng fled to Dōng'ē,
Zhāng Hán pursued and besieged him.
Xiàng Liáng, hearing of Tián Róng's crisis,
led troops to attack and defeat Zhāng Hán's army at Dōng'ē.
Zhāng Hán fled west,
and Xiàng Liáng pursued him.
But Tián Róng was angered by Qí's establishment of Jiǎ,
so he led his troops back,
