attacked and drove out King Jiǎ of Qí.
Jiǎ fled to Chǔ.
The Qí chancellor Jiǎo fled to Zhào;
Jiǎo's younger brother Tián Jiàn had previously gone to Zhào for rescue,
and thus stayed there, not daring to return.
Tián Róng then established Tián Dān's son Shì as King of Qí,
with Róng as his chancellor,
and Tián Héng as general,
pacifying the land of Qí.
After Xiàng Liáng pursued Zhāng Hán,
Zhāng Hán's forces grew stronger,
and Xiàng Liáng sent messengers to inform Zhào and Qí,
to send troops for a joint attack on Zhāng Hán.
Tián Róng said:
"If Chǔ kills Tián Jiǎ,
and Zhào kills Tián Jiǎo and Tián Jiàn,
then I will send troops."
King Huái of Chǔ said:
"Tián Jiǎ is the king of an allied state,
who, in dire straits, came to me;
killing him would be unjust."
Zhào also refused to kill Tián Jiǎo and Tián Jiàn to bargain with Qí.
Qí said: "If a viper bites your hand, cut off the hand;
if it bites your foot, cut off the foot.
Why?
Because it endangers the body.
Now Tián Jiǎ, Tián Jiǎo, and Tián Jiàn are to Chǔ and Zhào,
not even as close as hands or feet;
why not kill them?
Moreover, if Qín regains power under heaven,
then the graves of those in authority will be desecrated."
Chǔ and Zhào did not listen,
and Qí, angered,
ultimately refused to send troops.
Zhāng Hán indeed defeated and killed Xiàng Liáng,
routed the Chǔ army,
which fled east,
and Zhāng Hán crossed the river to besiege Zhào at Jùlù.
Xiàng Yǔ went to rescue Zhào,
and from this bore a grudge against Tián Róng.
After Xiàng Yǔ saved Zhào,
accepted the surrender of Zhāng Hán and others,
marched west to slaughter Xiányáng,
destroyed Qín, and established feudal kings,
he moved King Tián Shì of Qí to become King of Jiāodōng,
ruling from Jímò.
The Qí general Tián Dū had followed to rescue Zhào,
and thus entered the pass,
so he was made King of Qí,
ruling from Línzī.
The grandson of the former King Jiàn of Qí, Tián Ān,
while Xiàng Yǔ was crossing the river to rescue Zhào,
captured several cities in Jìběi,
led his troops to surrender to Xiàng Yǔ,
and Xiàng Yǔ made Tián Ān King of Jìběi,
ruling from Bóyáng.
Tián Róng, for having failed Xiàng Liáng by not sending troops to aid Chǔ and Zhào against Qín,
was not made a king;
the Zhào general Chén Yú also lost his position,
and was not made a king:
both men held a grudge against King Xiàng.
After King Xiàng returned,
the feudal lords went to their respective states,
and Tián Róng sent troops to aid Chén Yú,
ordering him to rebel in Zhào's territory,
while Róng also raised troops to resist and attack Tián Dū,
who fled to Chǔ.
Tián Róng detained King Shì of Qí,
not allowing him to go to Jiāodōng.
Shì's attendants said:
"King Xiàng is strong and violent,
and you, King, are assigned to Jiāodōng;
if you do not go to your state,
you will surely be in danger."
Shì feared,
and fled to his state.
Tián Róng, angered,
pursued and killed King Shì of Qí at Jímò,
then turned to attack and kill King Ān of Jìběi.
Thereupon, Tián Róng proclaimed himself King of Qí,
annexing all three Qí territories.
King Xiàng heard of this,
was greatly angered,
and launched a northern campaign against Qí.
King Tián Róng of Qí was defeated,
fled to Píngyuán,
where the people of Píngyuán killed Róng.
King Xiàng then burned and razed the cities of Qí,
slaughtering all in his path.
The people of Qí gathered and rebelled against him.
Róng's younger brother Héng,
gathered Qí's scattered troops,
numbering tens of thousands,
and counterattacked Xiàng Yǔ at Chéngyáng.
Meanwhile, King Hàn led the feudal lords to defeat Chǔ,
and entered Péngchéng.
Xiàng Yǔ, hearing of this,
released Qí and returned,
attacking Hàn at Péngchéng,
then engaging in continuous battles with Hàn,
confronting each other at Xíngyáng.
Thus, Tián Héng was able to recover Qí's cities,
establishing Tián Róng's son Guǎng as King of Qí,
with Héng as chancellor,
holding full control of the state's administration,
where all affairs, great and small, were decided by the chancellor.
Héng stabilized Qí for three years,
when King Hàn sent Lì Shēng to persuade King Guǎng of Qí and his chancellor Héng to surrender.
Héng found it reasonable,
and disbanded his defenses at Lìxià.
The Hàn general Hán Xìn led troops east to attack Qí.
Qí had initially stationed Huà Wúshāng and Tián Xiě at Lìxià to resist Hàn,
but when the Hàn envoy arrived,
they ceased defensive preparations,
indulged in drinking,
and sent envoys to make peace with Hàn.
The Hàn general Hán Xìn, having pacified Zhào and Yān,
followed Kuǎi Tōng's strategy,
crossed Píngyuán,
surprised and defeated Qí's defenses at Lìxià,
and entered Línzī.
King Guǎng of Qí and Chancellor Héng, enraged,
believed Lì Shēng had betrayed them,
and boiled Lì Shēng to death.
King Guǎng of Qí fled east to Gāomì,
while Chancellor Tián Héng fled to Bóyáng.
Acting Chancellor Tián Guāng defended Chéngyáng,
and General Tián Jì stationed his army at Jiāodōng.
Chǔ sent Lóng Jū to rescue Qí,
and the King of Qí joined forces with him at Gāomì.
Hàn general Hán Xìn, along with Cáo Shēn, defeated and killed Lóng Jū,
and captured King Guǎng of Qí.
Hàn general Guàn Yīng pursued and captured Qí's Acting Chancellor Tián Guāng.
At Bóyáng,
when Héng heard that the King of Qí had died,
he proclaimed himself King of Qí,
turned back to attack Yīng,
but Yīng defeated Héng's army at Yíngxià.
Tián Héng fled to Liáng,
and submitted to Péng Yuè.
Péng Yuè was then occupying the land of Liáng,
remaining neutral,
sometimes siding with Hàn,
sometimes with Chǔ.
After Hán Xìn had killed Lóng Jū,
he ordered Cáo Shēn to advance and defeat and kill Tián Jì at Jiāodōng,
and sent Guàn Yīng to defeat and kill Qí general Tián Xī at Qiānshèng.
Hán Xìn thus pacified Qí,
and requested to establish himself as Acting King of Qí,
which Hàn granted.
Over a year later,
Hàn destroyed Xiàng Jí,
and the King of Hàn was enthroned as Emperor,
appointing Péng Yuè as King of Liáng.
Tián Héng, fearing execution,
went with over five hundred of his followers to the sea,
residing on an island.
Emperor Gāo heard of this,
and thought that since the Tián Héng brothers had originally stabilized Qí,
and many worthy men of Qí had joined them,
if they remained at large in the sea,
they might cause trouble later.
So he sent an envoy to pardon Tián Héng and summon him.
Tián Héng declined, saying:
"I boiled Your Majesty's envoy Lì Shēng,
and now hear that his brother Lì Shāng is a capable general of Hàn.
I am afraid,
and dare not obey the summons.
I beg to remain a commoner,
guarding the island in the sea."
When the envoy returned and reported,
Emperor Gāo then commanded Commandant of the Palace Guard Lì Shāng:
"When King Tián Héng of Qí arrives,
if anyone among his men or horses dares to move, their clan will be exterminated!"
He then sent another envoy with credentials to inform Héng of the command to Shāng,
saying:
"If Tián Héng comes,
at best he will be made a king,
at least a marquis;
if he does not come,
troops will be sent to punish him."
Tián Héng then went with two of his followers by post carriage to Luòyáng.
When they were thirty lǐ away,
at the Shīxiāng relay station,
Héng said to the envoy:
"A subject meeting the Son of Heaven should bathe and cleanse himself."
He stopped and stayed.
He told his followers:
"I once faced south as a king like the King of Hàn,
but now he is the Son of Heaven,
and I am a fugitive facing north to serve him—
this shame is already great enough.
Moreover, I boiled a man's elder brother,
and would serve the same lord side by side with his younger brother.
Even if he fears the Emperor's command
and dares not move against me,
how could I not feel ashamed in my heart?
Besides, the reason His Majesty wishes to see me
is merely to see my face.
Now His Majesty is in Luòyáng.
If you cut off my head
and gallop thirty lǐ,
my features will not yet have decayed,
and can still be viewed."
He then cut his own throat,
ordered his followers to present his head,
and follow the envoy to gallop and report to Emperor Gāo.
Emperor Gāo said:
"Alas!
There is reason for this!
Rising from common cloth,
three brothers successively became kings—
how could they not be worthy!"
He shed tears for him,
appointed his two followers as commandants,
dispatched two thousand soldiers,
and buried Tián Héng with royal rites.
After the burial,
the two followers dug holes beside his tomb,
cut their own throats,
and followed him in death.
Emperor Gāo heard of this,
was greatly surprised,
and considered Tián Héng's followers all worthy.
Hearing that the remaining five hundred were still in the sea,
he sent an envoy to summon them.
Upon arrival, they heard of Tián Héng's death,
and all committed suicide.
Thus it was known that the Tián Héng brothers could win the allegiance of men.
The Grand Historian remarks:
How profound were Kuǎi Tōng's schemes,
which threw Qí into chaos and made Huáiyīn arrogant,
leading to the downfall of these two men!
Kuǎi Tōng
was skilled in persuasive debate,
discussed the stratagems of the Warring States,
and compiled eighty-one chapters.
Tōng was a friend of the Qí man Ānqī Shēng,
who once offered his services to Xiàng Yǔ,
but Xiàng Yǔ did not employ his strategies.
Later, when Xiàng Yǔ wanted to enfeoff these two,
they steadfastly refused to accept,
and fled.
Tián Héng's high integrity,
and his followers' admiration for righteousness leading them to die for him—
is this not the utmost worthiness!
I therefore recorded their stories.
It is not that there were no skilled painters,
yet none could depict them—
why?
Fán Kuài, Marquis of Wǔyáng,
was from Pèi.
He made his living by butchering dogs,
and went into hiding with Emperor Gāozǔ.
He first followed Gāozǔ in rising at Fēng,
and captured Pèi.
When Gāozǔ became the Duke of Pèi,
he appointed Kuài as a retainer.
He followed in attacking Húlíng and Fāngyǔ,
then returned to defend Fēng,
attacked the Sìshuǐ inspector at Fēng,
and defeated him.
He again pacified Pèi to the east,
and defeated the Sìshuǐ governor west of Xuē.
He fought a Sīmǎ east of Dàng,
repelled the enemy,
cut off fifteen heads,
and was awarded the rank of Guó Dàfū.
Often accompanying him,
when the Duke of Pèi attacked Zhāng Hán's army at Púyáng,
he was first to mount the wall in assaulting the city,
cut off twenty-three heads,
and was awarded the rank of Liè Dàfū.
Again often accompanying him,
he attacked Chéngyáng,
and was first to mount the wall.
He captured Hùyǒu,
defeated Lǐ Yóu's army,
cut off sixteen heads,
and was awarded the Shàngjiān rank.
He followed in attacking and besieging the Dōngjùn governor and commandant at Chéngwǔ,
repelled the enemy,
cut off fourteen heads,
captured eleven prisoners,
and was awarded the rank of Wǔ Dàfū.
He followed in attacking the Qín army,
emerging south of Bó.
The Héjiān governor's army was at Gānglǐ,
and he defeated it.
He defeated Zhào Bēn's army north of Kāifēng,
repelling the enemy and being first to mount the wall,
killed one marquis,
sixty-eight heads,
captured twenty-seven prisoners,
and was awarded the rank of Qīng.
He followed in defeating Yáng Xióng's army at Qūyù.
He attacked Wǎnlíng,
was first to mount the wall,
cut off eight heads,
captured forty-four prisoners,
and was awarded the title Xiánchéng Jūn.
He followed in attacking Chángshè and Huányuán,
cut off the river crossing,
attacked the Qín army east at Shī,
and south at Chōu.
He defeated the Nányáng governor Yǐ at Yángchéng.
He attacked eastward to Wǎnchéng,
being the first to ascend its walls.
Advancing west to Lì,
he repelled the enemy,
beheading twenty-four men,
and capturing forty prisoners,
for which he was generously enfeoffed.
Attacking Wǔguān,
he reached Bàshàng,
beheaded one commandant,
took ten heads,
captured one hundred forty-six prisoners,
and received the surrender of twenty-nine hundred soldiers.
Xiàng Yǔ was at Xìxià,
intending to attack Pèi Gōng.
Pèi Gōng, accompanied by over a hundred cavalry, met Xiàng Yǔ through Xiàng Bó's introduction,
apologizing for the matter of closing the passes.
After Xiàng Yǔ had feasted his troops,
and was intoxicated,
Yàfù plotted to kill Pèi Gōng,
ordering Xiàng Zhuāng to draw his sword and dance in their midst,
intending to strike Pèi Gōng.
Xiàng Bó repeatedly shielded him with his shoulders.
At that time, only Pèi Gōng and Zhāng Liáng were seated inside,
while Fán Kuài was outside the camp.
Hearing the situation was critical,
he took an iron shield and entered the camp.
The camp guards tried to stop Kuài,
but he barged straight in,
standing beneath the tent.
Xiàng Yǔ stared at him,
asking who he was.
Zhāng Liáng said:
"He is Fán Kuài, Pèi Gōng's assistant charioteer."
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"A mighty warrior."
He bestowed upon him a cup of wine and a pig's shoulder.
After drinking the wine,
Kuài drew his sword, cut the meat, and ate it all.
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"Can you drink more?"
Kuài said:
"I do not even shun death,
let alone a mere cup of wine!
Moreover, Pèi Gōng entered and pacified Xiányáng first,
stationed his troops at Bàshàng,
awaiting Your Highness.
Today, upon your arrival,
you listen to the words of petty men,
creating a rift with Pèi Gōng.
I fear the empire will disintegrate,
and hearts will doubt Your Highness."
Xiàng Yǔ fell silent.
Pèi Gōng went to the latrine,
signaling Fán Kuài to leave.
Once outside,
Pèi Gōng left his chariots and cavalry behind,
mounted a single horse alone,
and with Fán Kuài and three others following on foot,
they took a mountain path back to the army at Bàshàng,
sending Zhāng Liáng to apologize to Xiàng Yǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ then let the matter rest,
no longer intending to execute Pèi Gōng.
Had it not been for Fán Kuài rushing into the camp that day to reprimand Xiàng Yǔ,
Pèi Gōng's affairs would have nearly been doomed.
The next day,
Xiàng Yǔ entered and slaughtered Xiányáng,
establishing Pèi Gōng as the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn enfeoffed Kuài as a ranked marquis,
bestowing the title Marquis of Línwǔ.
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Interior,
following the king into Hànzhōng.
Upon returning to pacify the Three Qín,
he separately attacked the west administrator north of Báishuǐ,
engaging Yōng's light chariots and cavalry south of Yōng,
and defeating them.
He followed in attacking Yōng and Tái cities,
being the first to ascend. Attacking Zhāng Píng's army at Hàozhì,
assaulting the city,
he was first to ascend and break the enemy formation,
beheading one county magistrate and one assistant each,
taking eleven heads,
and capturing twenty men,
being promoted to Chief of Cavalry Gentlemen of the Interior.
Following to attack Qín's chariots and cavalry east of Rǎng,
he repelled the enemy,
and was promoted to general.
Attacking Zhào Bēn,
he captured Méi,
Huáilǐ,
Liǔzhōng, and Xiányáng;
flooding Fèiqiū,
he achieved the highest merit.
Upon reaching Yuèyáng,
he was granted the estate of Fánxiāng in Dù as his domain.
Following to attack Xiàng Jí,
he slaughtered Zhǔzǎo.
He defeated the armies of Wáng Wǔ and Chéng Chù at Wàihuáng.
Attacked Zōu,
Xuē,
and Lǔ. Xiáqiū. Xiàng Yǔ defeated the King of Hàn at Péngchéng,
retaking all the lands of Lǔ and Liáng.
Kuài returned to Xíngyáng,
was granted an additional two thousand households in Píngyīn,
and as a general, defended Guǎngwǔ.
After one year,
Xiàng Yǔ withdrew eastward.
He followed Emperor Gāozǔ to attack Xiàng Jí,
capturing Yángxià,
and capturing four thousand soldiers of Chǔ's General Zhōu.
Surrounding Xiàng Jí at Chén,
he heavily defeated him.
Slaughtered Húlíng.
After Xiàng Jí died,
and the King of Hàn became emperor,
due to Kuài's merits in steadfast defense and combat,
he was granted an additional eight hundred households.
He followed Emperor Gāozǔ to attack the rebellious King of Yān Zāng Tú,
captured Tú,
and pacified Yān.
The King of Chǔ Hán Xìn rebelled,
Kuài followed to Chén,
captured Xìn,
and pacified Chǔ.
He was further enfeoffed as a ranked marquis,
sharing tallies with the feudal lords,
with the title hereditary forever,
his domain at Wǔyáng,
titled Marquis of Wǔyáng,
canceling previous domains.
As a general, he followed Emperor Gāozǔ to attack the rebellious King of Hán Hán Xìn in Dài.
From Huòrén onward to Yúnzhōng,
he pacified it together with the Marquis of Jiàng and others,
and was granted an additional fifteen hundred households.
Then attacking the armies of Chén Xī and Mánqiū Chén,
he fought at Xiāngguó,
defeated Bóirén,
being first to ascend,
accepted surrender and pacified twenty-seven counties in Qīnghé and Chángshān in total,
destroyed Dōngyuán,
and was promoted to Left Counselor-in-Chief.
Defeated and captured Qí Wú Áng's
and Yīn Pān's armies at Wúzhōng and Guǎngchāng.
Defeated Chén Xī's separate general, the Hú rén Wáng Huáng's army south of Dài,
then attacked Hán Xìn's army at Cānhé.
The troops under his command beheaded Hán Xìn,
defeated Chén Xī's Hú cavalry at Hénggǔ,
beheaded General Zhào Jì,
captured Dài's Counselor-in-Chief Féng Liáng, Commandant Sūn Fèn,
Grand General Wáng Huáng, generals,
Grand Diviner, Grand Coachman Xiè Fú, and ten others.
Together with other generals, he pacified seventy-three towns and villages in Dài.
Later, the King of Yān Lú Wǎn rebelled,
Kuài, as Chancellor of State, attacked Lú Wǎn,
defeated his chancellor south of Dǐjì,
pacified Yān,
totaling eighteen counties,
and fifty-one towns and villages.
He was granted an additional thirteen hundred households,
fixing his domain at Wǔyáng with fifty-four hundred households.
In following campaigns,
he beheaded one hundred seventy-six men,
captured two hundred eighty-eight prisoners.
In separate campaigns,
he defeated seven armies,
captured five cities,
pacified six commanderies,
fifty-two counties,
captured one chancellor,
twelve generals,
and eleven officials ranked from two thousand piculs down to three hundred piculs.
Kuài married Lǚ Xū, the younger sister of Empress Lǚ,
and had a son named Kàng,
thus he was the closest among all the generals.
Previously, when Qíng Bù rebelled,
Emperor Gāozǔ was severely ill,
detesting to see people,
lying in the forbidden chambers,
ordering the gatekeepers not to admit any ministers.
Ministers like the Marquis of Jiàng and the Marquis of Guàn dared not enter.
After over ten days,
Kuài pushed open the door and entered directly,
with ministers following him.
The emperor was lying alone, pillowing on a eunuch.
A man from Zhào named Fāng Yǔ Gōng
said to the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Zhōu Chāng:
"Your clerk, Zhào Yáo,
though young in years,
is a man of extraordinary talent.
You must treat him exceptionally,
for he is likely to replace you in your position."
Zhōu Chāng laughed and said:
"Yáo is young,
merely a petty clerk.
How could he possibly achieve such a thing!"
Not long after,
Zhào Yáo was in attendance upon Emperor Gāozǔ.
The Emperor was privately unhappy,
singing mournful songs,
and his ministers did not understand the reason for His Majesty's demeanor.
Zhào Yáo stepped forward and inquired, saying:
"Is Your Majesty's unhappiness
not due to the young age of the King of Zhào
and the discord between Lady Qī and Empress Lǚ?
Are you concerned that after ten thousand years
the King of Zhào will be able to preserve himself?"
Emperor Gāozǔ said: "Indeed.
I privately worry about this,
and do not know what course to take."
Yáo said:
"Your Majesty should specifically appoint for the King of Zhào
a noble and powerful chancellor,
one whom Empress Lǚ, the Crown Prince, and the ministers
have always respected and feared,
then it can be done."
Emperor Gāozǔ said: "Indeed.
I have thought of this and wish to do so,
but among my ministers, who is suitable?"
Yáo said: "The Imperial Censor-in-Chief Zhōu Chāng,
this man is resolute, enduring, sincere, and upright,
and moreover, Empress Lǚ, the Crown Prince, and the great ministers
have always respected and feared him.
Only Chāng is suitable."
Emperor Gāozǔ said: "Good."
Thereupon, he summoned Zhōu Chāng,
and said to him: "I wish to impose upon you, sir,
you must force yourself
to serve as chancellor for me to the King of Zhào."
Zhōu Chāng wept and said:
"I first rose to follow Your Majesty,
how can you abandon me midway
among the feudal lords?"
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"I am fully aware that this is a demotion,
but I am privately concerned for the King of Zhào,
and believe there is no one else but you, sir.
You have no choice but to force yourself to go!"
Thereupon, he transferred the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Zhōu Chāng
to be Chancellor of Zhào.
After he had been gone for some time,
Emperor Gāozǔ held the seal of the Imperial Censor-in-Chief
and toyed with it, saying:
"Who is fit to be Imperial Censor-in-Chief?"
He looked intently at Zhào Yáo,
and said:
"No one can replace Yáo."
Thereupon, he appointed Zhào Yáo as Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
Yáo had previously earned military merits and had a food fief,
and as Imperial Censor-in-Chief
he followed in attacking Chén Xī and achieved merit,
being enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiāngyì.
When Emperor Gāozǔ passed away,
Empress Dowager Lǚ sent an envoy to summon the King of Zhào,
but his chancellor Zhōu Chāng made the king
claim illness and not go.
The envoy returned three times,
and Zhōu Chāng firmly refused to send
the King of Zhào.
Thereupon, Empress Gāo became troubled by this,
and sent an envoy to summon Zhōu Chāng.
When Zhōu Chāng arrived,
he paid his respects to Empress Gāo,
who angrily scolded Zhōu Chāng, saying:
"Do you not know that I resent the Qī clan?
And yet you do not send the King of Zhào, why?"
After Chāng had been summoned,
Empress Gāo sent an envoy to summon the King of Zhào,
and the King of Zhào indeed came.
Within a month or so after reaching Cháng'ān,
he drank poison and died.
Zhōu Chāng then pleaded illness and did not attend court audiences,
and died three years later.
Five years after that,
Empress Gāo heard that
the Imperial Censor-in-Chief, Marquis of Jiāngyì, Zhào Yáo,
had previously devised the plan during Emperor Gāozǔ's time to secure the position of the King of Zhào, Rúyì,
so she charged Yáo with a crime,
and appointed Rén Áo, Marquis of Guǎng'ē, as Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
Rén Áo
was formerly a prison officer in Pèi.
Emperor Gāozǔ once avoided an official,
and the officer imprisoned Empress Lǚ,
treating her disrespectfully.
Rén Áo had always been on good terms with Gāozǔ,
and in anger,
he attacked and injured the officer in charge of Empress Lǚ.
When Gāozǔ first rose up,
Áo followed as a retainer and became an imperial censor,
guarding Fèng for two years.
When Gāozǔ was established as King of Hàn,
and attacked Xiàng Jí in the east,
Áo was promoted to Governor of Shàngdǎng.
When Chén Xī rebelled,
Áo firmly held his position,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guǎng'ē,
with a fief of one thousand eight hundred households.
During Empress Gāo's time, he served as Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
After three years, he was dismissed,
and Píngyáng Hóu Cáo Zhú was made Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
When Empress Gāo passed away,
he did not join the great ministers
in collectively executing Lǚ Lù and others.
He was dismissed,
and Zhāng Cāng, Chancellor of Huáinán, was made Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
Cāng, together with the Marquis of Jiàng and others, honored
and established the King of Dài as Emperor Wén of Hàn.
In the fourth year,
the Chancellor Guàn Yīng died,
and Zhāng Cāng became Chancellor.
From the rise of the Hàn dynasty to the time of Emperor Wén, over twenty years had passed,
coinciding with the initial stabilization of the empire,
and the generals, ministers, and high officials were all military officers.
When Zhāng Cāng was Minister of Calculations,
he systematized the pitch standards and calendar.
Because Gāozǔ first arrived at Bàshàng in the tenth month,
following the former Qín practice
of using the tenth month as the start of the year,
he did not change it.
Calculating the cycle of the Five Virtues,
he believed that the Hàn dynasty corresponded to
the time of the Water Virtue,
and thus continued to honor black as before.
He blew the pitch pipes to tune the music,
incorporating it into the sounds,
and used it to standardize the laws and decrees.
As for the various artisans, he established standard measures for the empire.
When he became Chancellor,
he finally completed these tasks,
so when the Hàn scholars speak of
pitch standards and the calendar,
they trace it back to Zhāng Cāng.
Cāng was originally fond of books,
there was nothing he did not read,
nothing he did not comprehend,
and he was especially skilled in pitch standards and the calendar.
Zhāng Cāng felt indebted to Wáng Líng.
Wáng Líng was the Marquis of Ānguó.
When Cāng became noble,
he often served Wáng Líng as a father.
After Wáng Líng's death,
when Cāng was Chancellor,
on his days off,
he would always first visit Wáng Líng's wife,
present food,
and only then dare return home.
Cāng served as Chancellor for over ten years,
when a man from Lǔ named Gōngsūn Chén submitted a memorial
stating that the Hàn dynasty corresponded to the Earth Virtue,
and its omen would be the appearance of a yellow dragon.
The edict referred the discussion to Zhāng Cāng,
but Zhāng Cāng considered it incorrect,
and it was dismissed.
Later, a yellow dragon appeared in Chéngjì,
whereupon Emperor Wén summoned Gōngsūn Chén
and made him a Erudite,
drafting the calendar system for the Earth Virtue,
and changing the reign era.
Chancellor Zhāng, because of this, voluntarily resigned,
pleading illness and claiming old age.
Cāng appointed a man as Central Captain,
who greatly engaged in corrupt practices for profit,
and the Emperor reprimanded Cāng for this,
so Cāng then pleaded illness and was dismissed.
Cāng served as Chancellor for fifteen years before being dismissed.
In the fifth year of the former era of Emperor Jǐng, Cāng died,
and was posthumously titled Marquis Wén.
His son, Marquis Kāng, succeeded him,
and died after eight years.
His son Lèi succeeded as Marquis,
and after eight years,
was convicted of disrespect
for taking his seat after attending the funeral of a feudal lord,
and his marquisate was abolished.
The Grandee Remonstrant Zhèng Hóng was dismissed from office due to an offense,
and Kuāng Jūn became the Grandee Remonstrant.
A little over a year later,
Chancellor Wéi died,
and Kuāng Jūn succeeded him as Chancellor,
being enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lè'ān.
Within ten years,
he reached the position of Chancellor without ever leaving the gates of Cháng'ān—
was this not meeting the right time and fate indeed!
The Grand Historian remarks:
Deeply considering how scholars who travel for office reach the point of being enfeoffed as marquises,
it is very rare.
Yet many reach the Grandee Remonstrant and then leave.
Those who serve as Grandee are next in line for Chancellor,
and in their hearts, they hope and wish for the Chancellor to pass away.
Some even secretly slander and harm each other,
wanting to replace him.
However, some guard the position for a long time without attaining it,
while others hold it for a short time and gain it,
reaching enfeoffment as a marquis—
truly, it is fate!
The Grandee Remonstrant, Zhèng Jūn, guarded it for several years without success,
while Kuāng Jūn held it for less than a year,
and when Chancellor Wéi died,
he immediately replaced him.
How could this be achieved by wisdom or cunning?
Many possess outstanding and sagely talents,
yet those trapped in adversity and unable to succeed are numerous indeed.
Lì Shēng Yìjī
was a native of Gāoyáng in Chénliú.
He loved reading books,
but his family was poor and destitute,
with no means to make a living for food and clothing,
so he worked as a gatekeeper for the village.
However, the worthy and powerful in the county
did not dare to order him about,
and everyone in the county called him the "mad scholar."
When Chén Shèng, Xiàng Liáng, and others rose up,
dozens of generals
passed through Gāoyáng while conquering territories,
and Lì Shēng heard that their commanders
were all petty, fond of strict rituals, and self-opinionated,
unable to listen to grand and tolerant words.
So Lì Shēng deeply concealed himself.
Later, he heard that Péi Gōng was leading troops
to seize lands near the outskirts of Chénliú,
and a cavalryman under Péi Gōng's command
happened to be a fellow villager of Lì Shēng.
Péi Gōng often inquired
about the worthy scholars and heroes in the city.
When the cavalryman returned,
Lì Shēng met him and said:
"I have heard that Péi Gōng is arrogant
and looks down on others,
but he has great strategies.
This is truly whom I wish to follow and accompany.
Do not precede me in introducing me.
If you see Péi Gōng,
tell him,
'In my village, there is a Lì Shēng,
over sixty years old,
eight feet tall,
whom everyone calls the mad scholar,
but he says of himself that he is not mad.'"
The cavalryman said:
"Péi Gōng does not like Confucians.
When guests come wearing Confucian hats,
Péi Gōng often takes off their hats
and urinates in them.
When speaking with people,
he often curses loudly.
You cannot persuade him as a Confucian scholar."
Lì Shēng said, "Just say it."
The cavalryman calmly spoke as Lì Shēng had instructed.
When Péi Gōng arrived at the relay station in Gāoyáng,
he sent someone to summon Lì Shēng.
Lì Shēng arrived,
entered to pay his respects,
and Péi Gōng was sitting arrogantly on the bed
having two women wash his feet
while he received Lì Shēng.
Lì Shēng entered,
made a deep bow without kneeling,
and said:
"Do you wish to help Qín attack the other lords,
or do you wish to lead the lords to defeat Qín?"
Péi Gōng cursed, "You petty Confucian!
The world has suffered together under Qín for a long time,
so the lords join forces to attack Qín.
How can you say
I am helping Qín attack the lords?"
Lì Shēng said:
"If you are determined to gather followers and raise a righteous army
to punish the unprincipled Qín,
you should not receive an elder with such arrogance."
Thereupon, Péi Gōng stopped the foot-washing,
stood up, straightened his clothes,
and invited Lì Shēng to the seat of honor, apologizing to him.
Lì Shēng then spoke about
the time of the vertical and horizontal alliances of the Six States.
Péi Gōng was pleased,
rewarded Lì Shēng with food,
and asked:
"What strategy should we adopt?"
Lì Shēng said:
"You have raised a motley crowd,
gathered scattered and disordered troops,
numbering less than ten thousand,
and wish to directly invade strong Qín—
this is what is called probing the tiger's mouth.
Now, Chénliú
is a hub of the world,
a place where all roads converge,
and currently, its city has stored much grain.
I am on good terms with its magistrate,
and I request to be sent to him
to make him surrender to you.
If he does not listen,
you can raise troops to attack it,
and I will act as your insider."
Thereupon, he sent Lì Shēng on his mission,
and Péi Gōng led his troops to follow him,
thus capturing Chénliú.
He honored Lì Yìjī as Lord Guǎngyě.
Lì Shēng recommended his younger brother Lì Shāng,
who was made a general leading several thousand troops
to follow Péi Gōng in conquering lands to the southwest.
Lì Shēng often served as a persuader,
riding to various lords as an envoy.
In the autumn of the third year of Hàn,
Xiàng Yǔ attacked Hàn,
capturing Yíngyáng,
and the Hàn troops retreated to defend Gǒng
and Luò.
The Chǔ people heard that Huáiyín Hóu had defeated Zhào,
and Péng Yuè had rebelled several times in Liáng territory,
so they divided their forces to rescue them.
Huáiyín Hóu was just then attacking Qí to the east,
and the King of Hàn was repeatedly trapped
in Yíngyáng and Chénggāo.
He planned to abandon
the area east of Chénggāo,
stationing troops in Gǒng and Luò
to resist Chǔ.
Lì Shēng then said:
"I have heard that those who know the heaven of heaven
can accomplish royal deeds;
those who do not know the heaven of heaven
cannot accomplish royal deeds.
A king regards the people as his heaven,
and the people regard food as their heaven.
Now, Áo Granary has long been a hub for grain transport in the world,
and I have heard that beneath it, there are vast stores of grain.
The Chǔ people captured Yíngyáng,
but did not firmly hold Áo Granary;
instead, they withdrew eastward,
leaving only conscripted soldiers to guard Chénggāo.
This is heaven's way of aiding Hàn.
Right now, Chǔ is vulnerable to attack,
yet Hàn is instead retreating,
forfeiting this advantage on its own.
I secretly believe this is a mistake.
Moreover, two heroes cannot stand together;
if Chǔ and Hàn remain deadlocked for long,
the common people will be agitated,
the whole land will be shaken,
farmers will abandon their plows,
weaving women will leave their looms,
and the hearts of the world will have no anchor.
I urge you to quickly advance your troops again,
recapture Yíngyáng,
seize the grain in Áo Granary,
secure the strategic points of Chénggāo,
block the Tàiháng Pass road,
guard the Fēihú Pass entrance,
hold the ferry at Báimǎ,
to show the other lords
the tangible advantage of our position,
then the world will know where to turn.
Currently, Yān and Zhào are already pacified,
only Qí has not yet surrendered.
Now Tián Guǎng holds the vast territory of Qí,
and Tián Jiān leads a host of two hundred thousand troops,
stationed at Lìchéng.
The Tian clan's lineage is strong,
backed by the sea and guarded by the Ji and Yellow Rivers,
bordering Chu to the south,
its people are cunning and deceitful.
Even if Your Majesty dispatches hundreds of thousands of troops,
it cannot be conquered in a short time.
I request to carry your wise edict and persuade the King of Qí,
making him a vassal of Hàn
and declaring himself an eastern protector."
The Emperor said: "Good."
He then followed this plan,
again guarding the Áo Granary,
and sent Lì Shēng to persuade the King of Qí, saying:
"Does the King know where the world's allegiance lies?"
The King said: "I do not."
He said:
"If the King knows where the world's allegiance lies,
then the state of Qí can be secured and possessed;
if he does not know where the world's allegiance lies,
then Qí cannot be preserved."
The King of Qí said:
"Where does the world's allegiance lie?"
He said:
"With Hàn."
The King said:
"How does the Master justify this?"
He replied:
"The King of Hàn and King Xiàng joined forces
to attack Qín from the west,
agreeing that whoever entered Xiányáng first would rule it.
The King of Hàn entered Xiányáng first,
but King Xiàng broke the promise and did not grant it to him,
instead making him king in Hànzhōng.
King Xiàng moved and killed the Righteous Emperor,
and when the King of Hàn heard of it,
he raised troops from Shǔ and Hàn to attack the Three Qín,
marched through the pass
to demand an account for the Righteous Emperor's fate,
gathered the world's soldiers,
and established the descendants of feudal lords.
When a city surrendered, he enfeoffed its general as a marquis;
when spoils were obtained, he shared them with his men;
he shared benefits with all under heaven,
so heroes and talents gladly served him.
Armies from feudal lords arrived from all directions,
and grain from Shǔ and Hàn
came down the river in great fleets.
King Xiàng bears the name of breaking promises,
and the guilt of killing the Righteous Emperor;
he records no one's merits,
forgets no one's faults;
those who win battles receive no rewards,
those who capture cities gain no fiefs;
none but the Xiàng clan hold power;
when carving seals for others,
he wears them smooth
yet will not bestow them;
when spoils are taken in攻城,
he hoards them without rewarding:
thus, the world rebels against him,
talents resent him,
and none will serve him.
Therefore, the world's scholars turn to the King of Hàn,
and this can be foreseen while sitting still.
The King of Hàn started from Shǔ and Hàn,
pacified the Three Qín;
crossed west of the Yellow River,
and enlisted troops from Shàngdǎng;
descended Jǐngxíng,
and executed Lord Chéng'ān;
defeated Northern Wèi,
capturing thirty-two cities:
this is like the army of Chīyóu,
not mere human strength,
but heaven's blessing.
Now he holds the grain of the Áo Granary,
blocks the strategic point of Chénggāo,
guards the ferry at Báimǎ,
secures the slopes of the Tàiháng Mountains,
and guards the entrance of Fēihú;
those who submit later to the rule of heaven will perish first.
If the King swiftly submits to the King of Hàn,
the state of Qí can be preserved;
if not,
danger and destruction await immediately."
Tián Guǎng found this reasonable,
so he heeded Lì Shēng,
disbanded the defenses and preparations at Lìxià,
and spent days drinking freely with Lì Shēng.
When the Marquis of Huáiyīn heard that Lì Shēng
had persuaded over seventy cities of Qí to surrender with ease,
he crossed troops by night at Píngyuán
to attack Qí.
King Tián Guǎng of Qí, upon hearing the Hàn army's arrival,
thought Lì Shēng had betrayed him,
and said: "If you can stop the Hàn army,
I will spare you;
if not,
I will boil you alive!"
Lì Shēng said:
"He who undertakes great deeds does not fret over trifles,
and one of great virtue does not shy from responsibility.
I will not speak further for you!"
King Qí then boiled Lì Shēng alive,
and led his troops eastward in flight.
In the twelfth year of Hàn,
Marquis of Qǔzhōu, Lì Shāng,
as chancellor,
led troops to attack Qíng Bù with merit.
Emperor Gāozǔ enumerated the merits of marquises and功臣,
and remembered Lì Yìjī.
Lì Yìjī's son, Jiè, had repeatedly led troops,
but his achievements were not sufficient for a marquisate.
The Emperor, for his father's sake,
enfeoffed Jiè as Marquis of Gāoliáng.
Later, his fief was changed to Wǔsuì,
and it passed down for three generations.
In the first year of Yuánshòu,
Marquis of Wǔsuì, Píng,
was convicted of forging an edict
to obtain a hundred catties of gold from the King of Héngshān,
sentenced to public execution,
but he fell ill and died,
and the marquisate was abolished.
Lù Jiǎ
was a man of Chǔ.
He followed Emperor Gāozǔ as a retainer to pacify the world,
known as an eloquent debater,
staying by his side,
often sent on missions to feudal lords.
During Emperor Gāozǔ's time,
when the central plains were newly stabilized,
Wèi Tuó pacified Nányuè,
and thus declared himself its king.
Emperor Gāozǔ sent Lù Jiǎ to bestow
Wèi Tuó with the seal as King of Nányuè.
When Lord Lù arrived,
Wèi Tuó, with his hair tied in a knot, sat arrogantly with legs spread to receive him.
Lord Lù then advised him, saying:
"You are a man of the central plains,
with relatives, brothers, and ancestral graves in Zhēndìng.
Now you rebel against your innate nature,
abandoning cap and belt,
wishing to use this tiny Yuè
to rival the Son of Heaven as an enemy state—
disaster will soon befall you.
Moreover, when Qín lost its governance,
feudal lords and heroes rose together,
yet only the King of Hàn first entered the pass,
occupying Xiányáng.
Xiàng Yǔ broke the agreement,
proclaiming himself Hegemon King of Western Chǔ,
with all feudal lords under him,
he could be called supremely powerful.
Yet the King of Hàn rose from Bā and Shǔ,
wielding authority over the world,
compelling the feudal lords,
and eventually executed Xiàng Yǔ, destroying him.
Within five years,
the realm was pacified—
this was not human effort,
but heaven's establishment.
The Son of Heaven heard that
you, Great King, rule Nányuè,
yet do not aid the world in punishing the violent and rebellious;
the generals and ministers wished to move troops to execute you,
but the Son of Heaven, pitying
the people's recent toils and sufferings,
thus temporarily halted them,
sending me to confer the king's seal upon you,
dividing the tally and establishing diplomatic relations.
You, Great King, should
welcome me at the outskirts,
face north and declare yourself a subject,
yet instead, with this newly formed, unstable Yuè,
you stubbornly resist here.
If Hàn truly hears of this,
it will dig up and burn your ancestors' graves,
exterminate your clan,
and send a lieutenant general with a hundred thousand troops
to approach Yuè—
then Yuè would kill you and surrender to Hàn,
as easy as turning a hand."
Thereupon, Wèi Tuó abruptly rose from his seat,
apologizing to Lord Lù, saying:
"Having lived among the barbarians for long,
I have greatly neglected etiquette and righteousness."
Then he asked Lord Lù:
"Who is more worthy, I or Xiāo Hé, Cáo Shēn,
and Hán Xìn?"
Lord Lù said: "You, Great King, seem more worthy."
He asked again: "Who is more worthy, I or the Emperor?"
Lord Píngyuán was an eloquent and articulate man,
known for his integrity, austerity, and unyielding uprightness,
residing in Cháng'ān.
He never acted in improper compliance,
upholding righteousness without seeking favor.
The Marquis of Pìyáng engaged in improper conduct,
yet gained the favor of Empress Dowager Lǚ.
At that time, the Marquis of Pìyáng wished to befriend Lord Píngyuán,
but Lord Píngyuán refused to meet him.
When Lord Píngyuán's mother passed away,
Lù Jiǎ, who had long been on good terms with Lord Píngyuán,
paid him a visit.
Lord Píngyuán's family was impoverished,
lacking the means to hold a funeral,
and was borrowing mourning attire and supplies.
Lù Jiǎ urged Lord Píngyuán to proceed with the funeral.
Lù Jiǎ then went to see the Marquis of Pìyáng,
congratulating him, saying:
"Lord Píngyuán's mother has died."
The Marquis of Pìyáng replied:
"Lord Píngyuán's mother has died—
why are you congratulating me?"
Lù Jiǎ said: "Previously,
you, my lord, wished to befriend Lord Píngyuán,
but he, out of righteousness, would not befriend you,
because of his mother.
Now that his mother has died,
if you sincerely provide a generous funeral offering,
then he will be willing to die for you."
The Marquis of Pìyáng then presented
a hundred pieces of gold as a condolence gift.
Due to the Marquis of Pìyáng's influence,
the marquises and nobles contributed a total of five hundred pieces of gold in condolences.
The Marquis of Pìyáng enjoyed the favor of Empress Dowager Lǚ,
but someone slandered him to Emperor Huì of Hàn,
who became enraged,
had him imprisoned,
and intended to execute him.
Empress Dowager Lǚ felt ashamed,
unable to speak on his behalf.
Many ministers resented the Marquis of Pìyáng's conduct,
wishing to see him executed.
The Marquis of Pìyáng, in desperation,
sent someone to seek an audience with Lord Píngyuán.
Lord Píngyuán declined, saying:
"The legal matter is urgent,
I dare not meet you."
Instead, he sought an audience with Hóng Jírú, a favored courtier of Emperor Huì,
and persuaded him, saying:
"The reason for your favor with the Emperor
is known throughout the land.
Now, the Marquis of Pìyáng, favored by the Empress Dowager,
has been imprisoned,
and rumors on the streets say that you slandered him,
wanting him killed.
If the Marquis of Pìyáng is executed today,
tomorrow the Empress Dowager, harboring anger,
will also have you executed.
Why not bare your shoulders
and plead for the Marquis of Pìyáng before the Emperor?
If the Emperor heeds you and releases the Marquis of Pìyáng,
the Empress Dowager will be greatly pleased.
Both sovereigns will favor you,
and your wealth and status will double."
Hóng Jírú, greatly alarmed,
followed his plan,
spoke to the Emperor,
and indeed secured the Marquis of Pìyáng's release.
While imprisoned, the Marquis of Pìyáng had wished to see Lord Píngyuán,
but Lord Píngyuán refused to meet him,
leading the Marquis to believe he had been betrayed, and he was furious.
Upon his successful release,
he was greatly astonished.
When Empress Dowager Lǚ passed away,
the ministers exterminated the Lǚ clan,
and though the Marquis of Pìyáng had deep ties to them,
he was ultimately spared.
The strategies that saved him
were all due to the efforts of Lù Jiǎ and Lord Píngyuán.
During the reign of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
Liú Zhǎng, the Prince of Huáinán, killed the Marquis of Pìyáng,
because of his association with the Lǚ clan.
Emperor Wén learned that his retainer, Lord Píngyuán,
had devised plans,
and sent officials to arrest and prosecute him.
Upon hearing the officials had arrived at his door,
Lord Píngyuán intended to take his own life.
His sons and subordinates all said:
"The outcome is uncertain,
why rush to suicide?"
Lord Píngyuán replied:
"If I die, the calamity ends,
and will not extend to you."
He then slit his own throat.
Emperor Wén, upon hearing this, lamented,
saying: "I had no intention of killing him."
He then summoned his son,
appointing him as a Grand Master of the Palace.
Sent on a mission to the Xiōngnú,
the Chányú treated him disrespectfully,
so he cursed the Chányú,
and ultimately died among the Xiōngnú.
Earlier, when Pei Gōng led his troops past Chénliú,
Lì Shēng hurried to the army gate and presented his card, saying:
"I am Lì Yìjī, a humble man of Gāoyáng,
who has privately heard that Pei Gōng endures exposure,
leading troops to assist Chǔ in punishing the unrighteous.
I respectfully wish to labor for your followers,
hoping for an audience,
to verbally strategize advantageous matters for the realm."
The messenger entered to report,
while Pei Gōng was washing,
and asked the messenger:
"What kind of man is he?"
The messenger replied:
"In appearance, he resembles a great scholar,
wearing scholar's robes,
with a tilted cap."
Pei Gōng said:
"Decline for me,
saying I am occupied with the affairs of the realm,
and have no time to meet scholars."
The messenger went out and apologized, saying:
"Pei Gōng respectfully declines, sir,
as he is occupied with the affairs of the realm,
and has no time to meet scholars."
Lì Shēng glared, pressed his sword, and scolded the messenger:
"Go!
Report back to Pei Gōng,
I am the drunkard of Gāoyáng,
not a scholar!"
The messenger, terrified, dropped the name card,
knelt to pick it up,
then ran back,
and re-entered to report:
"The guest
is a mighty warrior of the realm,
who scolded me,
and I was so frightened
that I dropped the card.
He said,
'Go!
Report back,
your lord is the drunkard of Gāoyáng!'"
Pei Gōng quickly wiped his feet, grabbed a spear, and said:
"Invite the guest in!"
Lì Shēng entered,
bowed to Pei Gōng, and said:
"You have endured much hardship,
with clothes and hat exposed to the elements,
leading troops to assist Chǔ in punishing the unrighteous.
Why do you not take pride in this?
I wished to discuss matters with you,
yet you said,
'I am occupied with the affairs of the realm,
and have no time to meet scholars.'
If you wish to accomplish great deeds and achieve great merits for the realm,
yet judge by appearance alone,
I fear you will lose the capable men of the realm.
Moreover, I reckon your wisdom falls short of mine,
and your courage also falls short.
If you seek to conquer the realm yet refuse to meet me,
I privately believe you are making a mistake."
Pei Gōng apologized, saying:
"Earlier, I heard of your appearance,
but now I understand your intent."
He then invited him to sit,
and asked how to seize the realm.
Lì Shēng said:
"If you wish to achieve great merit,
it is best to halt at Chénliú.
Chénliú is
a strategic stronghold of the realm,
a convergence point for troops,
with granaries storing tens of millions of dàn of grain,
and its city defenses are very strong.
I have long been on good terms with its magistrate,
and wish to persuade him on your behalf.
If he does not heed me,
I will kill him for you,
and capture Chénliú.
With the people of Chénliú under your command,
holding its city,
and consuming its stored grain,
you can rally the allied forces of the realm;
once the allied forces are formed,
you can roam the realm unhindered,
with none able to harm you."
Pei Gōng said:
"I respectfully heed your advice."
Thereupon, Lì Shēng went to see the magistrate of Chénliú at night,
and persuaded him, saying:
"The Qín dynasty, having lost the Way, faces rebellion from all under heaven.
If you, sir, join with the forces opposing it, you could achieve great merit.
But now you alone fortify the city and stubbornly defend the doomed Qín,
I secretly fear for your safety."
The magistrate of Chénliú replied:
"The laws of Qín are extremely severe,
one must not speak recklessly.
Those who speak recklessly will be exterminated.
I cannot respond to you.
What you, sir, teach me
does not align with my intentions.
I beg you not to speak of it again."
Lì Shēng stayed overnight to sleep there,
and at midnight, beheaded the magistrate of Chénliú.
He crossed over the city wall and went down to report to Peì Gōng.
Peì Gōng led his troops to attack the city,
hung the magistrate's head on a long pole to show the people on the city walls,
and said:
"Quickly surrender!
Your magistrate's head is already severed!
From now on, those who delay surrendering will be beheaded first!"
Thereupon, the people of Chénliú, seeing their magistrate was dead,
then followed one another down to surrender to Peì Gōng.
Peì Gōng lodged at the southern gate tower of Chénliú,
utilized the weapons from its armory,
consumed its stored grain,
stayed for three months,
and gathered followers numbering in the tens of thousands,
then went on to defeat Qín.
Grand Historian comments:
The texts about Lì Shēng passed down in the world
mostly say that the King of Hàn had already captured the Three Qín,
was moving east to attack Xiàng Jí,
and had stationed his army between Gǒng and Luò,
when Lì Shēng, dressed in Confucian robes, went to persuade the King of Hàn.
But this is incorrect.
From the time before Peì Gōng entered the Pass,
when he parted with Xiàng Yǔ and reached Gāoyáng,
he had already obtained the services of Lì Shēng and his brothers.
I have read twelve chapters of Lù Shēng's "New Discourses",
and he was indeed a master debater of his time.
As for the gentleman of Píngyuán, he was a good friend of mine,
therefore I am able to discuss this in detail.
Fù Kuān, Marquis of Yánglíng,
followed as a cavalry general of the fifth rank from Wèi,
served as a retainer,
and started from Héngyáng.
He followed in attacking Ānyáng and Gānglǐ,
attacked Zhào Bēn's army at Kāifēng,
and also attacked Yáng Xióng at Qūyù and Yángwǔ,
beheading twelve ranks,
and was granted the title of Qīng.
He followed to Bàshàng.
When Peì Gōng was established as King of Hàn,
the King of Hàn granted Kuān the title Lord of Gòngdé.
He followed into Hànzhōng,
and was then made General of the Right Cavalry.
He followed in pacifying the Three Qín,
and was granted the estate of Diāoyīn.
He followed in attacking Xiàng Jí,
waited at Huái,
and was granted the title Marquis of Tōngdé.
He followed in attacking Xiàng Guān,
Zhōu Lán, and Lóng Qiē,
and the troops under his command beheaded one general at Áo,
increasing his estate.
Attached to Huáiyīn,
he attacked and defeated the Qí army at Lìxià,
and attacked Tián Jiě.
Attached to Chancellor Cān,
he devastated Bó,
further increasing his estate.
Thereby pacifying the Qí region,
he received a tally dividing the command, hereditary without end,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yánglíng,
with twenty-six hundred households,
excluding previous estates.
He served as Right Chancellor of Qí,
guarding Qí.
After five years, he became Chancellor of Qí.
In the fourth month,
he attacked Chén Xī,
attached to Grand Commandant Bó,
and as Chancellor replaced Chancellor Kuài in attacking Xī.
In the first month,
he was transferred to be Chancellor of Dài,
commanding the garrison.
After two years,
he became Chancellor of Dài,
commanding the garrison.
He died in the fifth year of Emperor Huì's reign,
posthumously titled Marquis Jǐng.
His son, the refined Marquis Jīng, succeeded,
and died after twenty-four years.
His son, the respectful Marquis Zé, succeeded,
and died after twelve years.
His son, Marquis Yǎn, succeeded,
and in the thirty-first year,
was implicated in plotting rebellion with the King of Huáinán,
died,
and his fief was abolished.
Jìn Xī, Marquis of Xìnwǔ,
followed as a Zhōngjuān,
starting from Yuānqú.
He attacked Jìyáng.
Defeated Lǐ Yóu's army.
Attacked the Qín army south of Bó and northeast of Kāifēng,
beheading one commander of a thousand cavalry,
fifty-seven ranks,
and capturing seventy-three prisoners,
was granted the title Lord of Línpíng.
Fought again north of Lántián,
beheading two Chariot司马,
one Cavalry Leader,
twenty-eight ranks,
and capturing fifty-seven prisoners.
Reached Bàshàng.
When Peì Gōng was established as King of Hàn,
he granted Xī the title Marquis of Jiànwǔ,
and promoted him to Commandant of Cavalry.
He followed in pacifying the Three Qín.
Separately, he went west to attack Zhāng Píng's army in Lǒngxī,
defeated it,
pacified six counties in Lǒngxī,
and the troops under his command beheaded four each of Chariot司马 and Hòu,
and twelve Cavalry Leaders.
He followed east to attack Chǔ,
reaching Péngchéng.
The Hàn army was defeated and returned,
defended Yōngqiū,
then went to attack the rebel Wáng Wǔ and others.
Secured the Liáng region,
and as a separate commander attacked Xíng Shuō's army south of Zī,
defeated it,
personally captured two of Shuō's Commandants,
twelve司马 and Hòu,
and received the surrender of 4,180 officers and men.
Defeated the Chǔ army east of Xíngyáng.
In the third year,
he was granted an estate of 4,200 households.
Separately went to Hénèi,
attacked Zhào general Bèn Hǎo's army at Zhāogē,
defeated it,
and the troops under his command captured two cavalry generals,
and 250 chariots and horses.
Followed in attacking east from Ānyáng,
to Jípú,
capturing seven counties.
Separately attacked and defeated the Zhào army,
capturing two of its司马,
four Hòu,
and receiving the surrender of 2,400 officers and men.
Followed in capturing Hándān.
Separately captured Píngyáng,
personally beheaded the defending chancellor,
and the troops under his command beheaded one each of the military governor and commandery governor,
and received the surrender of Yè.
Followed in attacking Zhāogē and Hándān,
and separately attacked and defeated the Zhào army,
receiving the surrender of six counties in the Hándān commandery.
Returned the army to Áocāng,
defeated Xiàng Jí's army south of Chénggāo,
attacked and severed the Chǔ supply route,
from Xíngyáng to Xiāngyì.
Defeated Xiàng Guān's army at Lǔ.
Secured territory east to Zēng, Tán, and Xiàpī,
and south to Qí and Zhúyì.
Attacked Xiàng Hàn below Jìyáng.
Returned to attack Xiàng Jí at Chén,
and defeated him.
Separately pacified Jiānglíng,
receiving the surrender of eight officials from the Zhùguó and Grand司马 down,
personally captured the King of Jiānglíng,
delivered him alive to Luòyáng,
thereby pacifying the Nán commandery.
Followed to Chén,
captured the King of Chǔ, Xìn,
received a tally dividing the command, hereditary without end,
was granted a fixed estate of 4,600 households,
and titled Marquis of Xìnwǔ.
He followed as a Cavalry Commandant to attack Dai,
assailed Hán Xìn beneath Píngchéng's walls,
and withdrew his troops to Dōngyuán.
Having rendered service,
he was promoted to Chariot and Cavalry General,
commanding the chariot and cavalry forces of Liáng,
Zhào, Qí, Yān, and Chǔ,
separately attacked Chén Xī's chancellor Chǎng,
defeated him,
and thereupon subdued Qūnì.
He followed to attack Qíng Bù with merit,
and was further enfeoffed with a fixed estate of five thousand three hundred households.
In total, he beheaded ninety men,
captured one hundred thirty-two persons;
separately defeated fourteen armies,
induced fifty-nine cities to surrender,
pacified one commandery and one kingdom each,
and twenty-three counties;
captured one king and one Pillar of State each,
and thirty-nine officials ranked from two thousand piculs down to five hundred piculs.
In the fifth year of Empress Dowager's reign,
Jìn Xī died,
and was posthumously titled Marquis Sù.
His son Tǐng succeeded to the marquisate.
In the twenty-first year,
due to employing state subjects beyond regulations,
in the third year after Emperor Wén of Hàn's accession,
he was stripped of his marquisate,
and the fief was abolished.
Marquis Kǎichéng, Sào, was a man of Pèi,
of the surname Zhōu.
He often served as Gāozǔ's carriage attendant,
following as a Retainer from their rise at Pèi.
Reaching Bàshàng, west to Bàshàng,
to Hàn,
west into Shǔ, returning to pacify the Three Qín,
he was granted Chíyáng as his estate.
Eastward, he cut off the elevated passage,
followed the emperor out crossing Píngyīn,
encountered the troops of Huáiyīn Hóu at Xiāngguó,
where the army sometimes succeeded and sometimes failed,
yet he never harbored a heart to leave the emperor.
Thus, Sào was made Marquis Xìnwǔ,
with an estate of three thousand three hundred households.
In the twelfth year of Gāozǔ,
Sào was made Marquis Kǎichéng,
replacing his previous estate.
The emperor wished to personally attack Chén Xī,
Marquis Kǎichéng wept and said:
"In the past, when Qín attacked and conquered the world,
the emperor never personally campaigned.
Now Your Majesty often personally campaigns,
does this mean there is no one else to send?"
The emperor considered this as "affection for me,"
granting him the privilege to enter palace gates without hastening,
and immunity from death penalty if he killed someone.
By the fifth year of Emperor Wén's reign,
Sào died of old age,
and was posthumously titled Marquis Zhēn.
His son Chāng succeeded to the marquisate,
but committed a crime,
and the fief was abolished.
By the second year of the Zhōng era under Emperor Jǐng,
Sào's son Jū was enfeoffed as marquis.
By the third year of the Yuándǐng era,
Jū served as Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
committed a crime,
and the fief was abolished.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Marquis Yánglíng Fù Kuān and Marquis Xìnwǔ Jìn Xī
both held high ranks,
followed Gāozǔ from east of the mountains,
attacked Xiàng Jí,
slaughtered famous generals,
defeated armies and subdued cities by the tens,
yet never suffered hardship or disgrace,
this too was Heaven's grant.
Marquis Kǎichéng Zhōu Sào maintained
a firm and upright heart,
and his person was never doubted,
whenever the emperor intended to go somewhere,
he never failed to shed tears,
this is how one with a wounded heart behaves,
he may be called a sincere and earnest gentleman.
Liú Jìng
was a man of Qí.
In the fifth year of Hàn,
garrisoning Lǒngxī,
passing Luòyáng,
where Emperor Gāozǔ was then residing.
Lóu Jìng took off his harness,
wore his sheepskin coat,
and visited General Yú of Qí, saying:
"I wish to see the emperor
to discuss advantageous matters."
General Yú wanted to give him fine clothes,
but Lóu Jìng said:
"If I wear silk,
I'll see him in silk;
if I wear coarse cloth,
I'll see him in coarse cloth:
I dare not change my clothes."
Thereupon General Yú went in to inform the emperor.
The emperor summoned him for an audience,
and bestowed food upon him.
Afterward, the emperor asked Lóu Jìng,
and Lóu Jìng expounded:
"Your Majesty capitalizes at Luòyáng,
is it not wishing to rival the glory of the Zhōu house?"
The emperor said: "Yes."
Lóu Jìng said:
"Your Majesty's acquisition of the world
differs from that of the Zhōu house.
The ancestors of Zhōu began with Hòu Jì,
whom Yáo enfeoffed at Tái,
accumulating virtue and good deeds for over ten generations.
Gōng Liú avoided Jié and dwelled at Bīn.
The Great King, due to the attacks of the Dí,
left Bīn,
and with horsewhip in hand settled at Qí,
where the people contended to follow him.
When King Wén became the Earl of the West,
settling the dispute between Yú and Ruì,
he began to receive the Mandate,
Lǚ Wàng and Bó Yí came from the seashores
to submit to him.
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and without prior agreement, eight hundred lords
gathered at Mèngjīn,
all saying Zhòu could be attacked,
and thus they destroyed Yīn.
When King Chéng ascended the throne,
the Duke of Zhōu and others assisted as regents,
then built the secondary capital at Luòyì,
considering it the center of the world,
where lords from all directions presented tribute,
and the distances were equal,
so that with virtue it was easy to rule,
and without virtue it was easy to perish.
All who dwelled here
wished to make Zhōu focus
on attracting people through virtue,
not wanting to rely on dangerous barriers,
lest later generations become arrogant and extravagant
and oppress the people.
When Zhōu was at its peak,
the world was harmonious,
the four barbarians turned to its influence,
admiring its righteousness and embracing its virtue,
attached and jointly served the Son of Heaven,
without stationing a single soldier,
without fighting a single battle,
the people of the eight barbarian tribes and great states
all submitted,
and offered their tribute.
When Zhōu declined,
it split into two,
and none in the world paid court,
which Zhōu could not control.
Not because its virtue was thin,
but because its strategic position was weak.
Now Your Majesty rose from Fēng and Pèi,
gathered three thousand troops,
with which you directly advanced
and swept through Shǔ and Hàn,
pacified the Three Qín,
fought Xiàng Yǔ at Xíngyáng,
contended for the pass at Chénggāo,
fought seventy major battles,
forty minor battles,
causing the people of the world
to have their livers and brains spilled on the ground,
fathers and sons exposing their bones in the wilderness,
too numerous to count,
the sound of weeping not yet ceased,
the wounded not yet risen,
and yet you wish to rival
the prosperity of the times of Chéng and Kāng,
I privately believe it is not comparable.
Moreover, the land of Qín is backed by mountains and girded by rivers,
fortified by four passes,
so that in sudden emergency,
a million troops can be assembled.
Relying on Qín's foundations,
and utilizing its rich and fertile land,
this is what is called the 'Storehouse of Heaven'.
Your Majesty entered the Hánguān Pass and established the capital there;
though the lands east of the mountains are in turmoil,
the former territory of Qín can be entirely secured and held.
When contending with others,
if one does not grip their throat
and press upon their back,
one cannot achieve complete victory.
Now if Your Majesty enters the pass and makes it the capital,
controlling the former lands of Qín,
this is also like gripping the throat of the empire
and pressing upon its back."
Emperor Gāo questioned his ministers,
who were all men from east of the mountains;
they vied to argue that the Zhōu dynasty ruled for several hundred years,
while Qín fell after only two generations,
so it would be better to establish the capital at Zhōu.
The Emperor was doubtful and unable to decide.
Only when Liú Hóu clearly stated
the advantages of entering the pass
did he that very day have his carriage head west
to establish the capital within the pass.
Thereupon the Emperor said:
"The one who originally proposed making the Qín lands the capital was Lóu Jìng,
and 'Lóu' means 'Liú'."
He bestowed upon him the surname Liú,
appointed him as a Lángzhōng,
and honored him as Fèngchūn Jūn.
In the seventh year of Hàn,
Hán King Xìn rebelled,
and Emperor Gāo personally went to attack him.
Upon reaching Jìnyáng,
he heard that Xìn and the Xiōngnú
intended to jointly attack Hàn;
the Emperor was greatly enraged
and sent envoys to the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú concealed their strong men
and fat oxen and horses,
showing only the old and weak along with emaciated livestock.
Ten groups of envoys returned,
all reporting that the Xiōngnú could be attacked.
The Emperor sent Liú Jìng again as an envoy to the Xiōngnú;
upon returning he reported:
"When two states attack each other,
they ought to boast and display their strengths.
Now when I went,
I only saw the thin, weak, old, and frail;
this must mean they wish to show weakness,
concealing elite troops to gain advantage.
In my foolish opinion, the Xiōngnú should not be attacked."
At that time, the Hàn troops
had already crossed Jūzhù,
and over two hundred thousand soldiers had commenced their march.
The Emperor angrily scolded Liú Jìng, saying:
"You Qí slave!
You obtained office through mere talk,
and now you recklessly speak to discourage my army!"
He had Jìng shackled and imprisoned at Guǎngwù.
The army then proceeded,
reaching Píngchéng,
where the Xiōngnú indeed deployed elite troops
and besieged Emperor Gāo at Báidēng,
from which he escaped only after seven days.
Emperor Gāo returned to Guǎngwù,
pardoned Jìng,
and said:
"I failed to heed your advice,
thus suffering hardship at Píngchéng.
I have executed all ten of the previous envoys
who said we could attack."
He then enfeoffed Jìng with two thousand households,
making him a Guānnèi Hóu,
with the title Jiànxìn Hóu.
After Emperor Gāo withdrew from Píngchéng and returned,
Hán King Xìn fled to the Hú.
At that time, Mòdú was the Chányú,
his military was strong,
commanding three hundred thousand archers,
and they repeatedly harassed the northern border.
The Emperor was troubled by this
and consulted Liú Jìng.
Liú Jìng said:
"The empire has only recently been pacified,
the soldiers are weary from war,
so it is not possible to subdue them by force.
Mòdú killed his father and took his place,
took his father's consorts as wives,
and relies on might to assert authority,
so he cannot be persuaded with benevolence and righteousness.
The only way is to devise a long-term plan
so that his descendants will become subjects,
but I fear Your Majesty may not be able to do it."
The Emperor said: "If it is truly feasible,
why would I be unable!
But how should it be done?"
Liú Jìng replied:
"If Your Majesty could truly
give your eldest legitimate daughter in marriage to him,
bestowing generous gifts,
he, knowing she is the Hàn's legitimate daughter
sent with rich offerings,
the barbarians would surely admire
and make her Yānzhī,
and any son born would become the crown prince, succeeding as Chányú.
Why?
Because they covet Hàn's valuable gifts.
Your Majesty could from time to time send them what Hàn has in surplus and they lack,
and have eloquent scholars subtly instruct them
in ritual etiquette.
While Mòdú lives,
he would be your son-in-law;
after his death,
your grandson would be Chányú.
Has one ever heard of a grandson
daring to treat his grandfather as an equal?
Thus, we can subdue them without warfare,
gradually making them subjects.
If Your Majesty cannot send the eldest princess,
but orders a woman from the imperial clan
or the rear palace to pretend to be the princess;
he would also know,
and would not honor or be close to her,
rendering it useless."
Emperor Gāo said: "Excellent."
He intended to send the eldest princess.
Empress Lǚ wept day and night,
saying:
"I have only the crown prince and one daughter;
how can you abandon her to the Xiōngnú!"
In the end, the Emperor could not send the eldest princess,
but took a daughter of a commoner family
named as the eldest princess,
and gave her in marriage to the Chányú.
He sent Liú Jìng to conclude the peace and kinship treaty.
When Liú Jìng returned from the Xiōngnú,
he took the opportunity to say:
"The Xiōngnú kings of Báiyáng and Lóufán
in Hénán,
are as close as seven hundred lǐ to Cháng'ān,
and light cavalry can reach Qínzhōng
in a day and a night.
Qínzhōng has recently been devastated,
its population is sparse,
the land is fertile,
and it can be further populated.
When the feudal lords first rose,
none could have succeeded without the various Tián clans of Qí,
and the Zhāo, Qū, and Jǐng clans of Chǔ.
Now although Your Majesty has the capital within the pass,
there are truly few people.
To the north, we are close to Hú raids,
to the east, there are the powerful clans of the six states,
and if turmoil arises one day,
Your Majesty may not be able to rest easy.
I wish for Your Majesty to relocate the various Tián clans of Qí,
the Zhāo, Qū, and Jǐng of Chǔ,
the descendants of Yān, Zhào, Hán, and Wèi,
along with renowned and powerful families, to settle within the pass.
In times of peace,
they can guard against the Hú;
if the feudal lords rebel,
they are sufficient to lead an eastern campaign.
This is the method of strengthening the root and weakening the branches."
The Emperor said: "Excellent."
He then sent Liú Jìng to relocate over a hundred thousand people as proposed
to within the pass.
Shūsūn Tōng
was a man of Xuē.
During the Qín dynasty, he was recruited for his literary talent,
serving as an expectant academician.
After several years,
when Chén Shèng rose east of the mountains,
an envoy reported it,
and the Second Emperor summoned the academicians
and various scholars to ask:
"The Chǔ garrison soldiers have attacked Qí
and entered Chén;
what is your view on this?"
Over thirty academicians and scholars
came forward and said:
"As subjects, one must not lead troops;
to lead troops is to rebel,
a crime punishable by death without pardon.
We urge Your Majesty to quickly send troops to attack them."
The Second Emperor was angered, his countenance changing.
Shūsūn Tóng stepped forward and said:
"These scholars are all wrong.
Now the empire is united as one family,
the walls of commanderies and counties have been dismantled,
their weapons melted down,
showing the world they will not be used again.
Moreover, with an enlightened ruler above,
and laws and decrees established below,
ensuring everyone fulfills their duties,
and all regions converge like spokes to a hub,
how dare there be rebels!
These are merely bands of robbers
engaging in petty theft and pilfering,
hardly worth mentioning.
The commandery governors and captains are now capturing and prosecuting them,
there is nothing to worry about."
The Second Emperor was pleased and said: "Good."
He then questioned all the scholars,
some of whom said it was rebellion,
others called it banditry.
Thereupon, the Second Emperor ordered the imperial censors to investigate
and had those scholars who spoke of rebellion
handed over to the officials,
for uttering inappropriate words.
Those who spoke of banditry
were all dismissed.
He then bestowed upon Shūsūn Tóng twenty bolts of silk,
a set of clothing,
and appointed him as an Erudite.
After Shūsūn Tóng left the palace,
and returned to his residence,
the scholars said:
"Sir, why did you speak so flatteringly?"
Tóng replied: "You gentlemen don't understand;
I barely escaped the tiger's mouth!"
He then fled,
going to Xuē,
which had already surrendered to Chǔ.
When Xiàng Liáng came to Xuē,
Shūsūn Tóng followed him.
After their defeat at Dìngtáo,
he followed King Huái.
When King Huái became the Righteous Emperor,
and moved to Chángshā,
Shūsūn Tóng remained and served King Xiàng.
In the second year of Hàn,
when the King of Hàn entered Péngchéng with five feudal lords,
Shūsūn Tóng surrendered to the King of Hàn.
The King of Hàn was defeated and moved west,
and Tóng ultimately followed Hàn.
Shūsūn Tóng wore Confucian robes,
which the King of Hàn disliked;
so he changed his attire,
donning short garments,
in the style of Chǔ,
and the King of Hàn was pleased.
When Shūsūn Tóng surrendered to Hàn,
he brought over a hundred Confucian disciples with him,
yet Tóng did not recommend any of them,
instead exclusively recommending former bandits and brave men.
His disciples secretly complained, saying:
"We have served you, sir, for several years,
and were fortunate to follow you in surrendering to Hàn,
but now you do not recommend us,
only speaking of great rogues;
why is that?"
Shūsūn Tóng heard this,
and then told them:
"The King of Hàn is currently braving arrows and stones
to contend for the empire;
can you scholars fight?
Therefore, I first recommend
those who can behead generals and capture flags.
You scholars, wait for me,
I will not forget you."
The King of Hàn appointed Shūsūn Tóng as an Erudite,
bestowing the title Jìsì Jūn.
In the fifth year of Hàn,
after unifying the empire,
the feudal lords collectively honored the King of Hàn
as emperor at Dìngtáo,
and Shūsūn Tóng established the ceremonial protocols and titles.
Emperor Gāo abolished all
the harsh rituals and laws of Qín,
making them simple and easy.
The ministers, while drinking,
vied over their merits,
some drunkenly shouting recklessly,
drawing swords and striking pillars,
which troubled Emperor Gāo.
Shūsūn Tóng knew that the emperor
was increasingly annoyed by this,
and advised him, saying:
"Confucians are difficult to employ
in gaining power,
but can be used in maintaining it.
I wish to summon scholars from Lǔ,
to work with my disciples in establishing court rituals."
Emperor Gāo said: "Won't it be too difficult?"
Shūsūn Tóng said:
"The Five Emperors had different music,
the Three Kings had different rites.
Rites are
based on the times and human sentiments,
providing structure and refinement.
Thus, the rites of Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu
with their known adaptations and modifications
show they did not simply repeat each other.
I wish to selectively adopt ancient rites
and blend them with Qín rituals to create new ones."
The emperor said: "You may try it,
make it easy to understand,
and gauge what I can manage to implement."
Thereupon, Shūsūn Tóng sent
for over thirty scholars from Lǔ.
Two scholars from Lǔ refused to go,
saying: "You have served nearly ten masters,
always flattering to gain favor and wealth.
Now the empire is newly stabilized,
the dead are not yet buried,
the wounded not yet recovered,
and you already wish to establish rites and music.
The foundation of rites and music
requires a century of accumulated virtue before they can flourish.
We cannot bear to do what you do.
What you do does not conform to antiquity,
we will not go.
Go on your way,
do not taint us!"
Shūsūn Tóng laughed and said:
"You are truly pedantic scholars,
unaware of the changes of the times."
Then he went west with those summoned,
thirty men,
along with the emperor's attendants who were scholars
and his own disciples, over a hundred people,
to set up straw markers and flags in the open field.
After practicing for over a month,
Shūsūn Tóng said: "Your Majesty may come and observe."
The emperor observed, had them perform the rituals,
and said:
"I can do this."
He then ordered the ministers to practice,
for the assembly in the tenth month.
In the seventh year of Hàn,
when the Chánglè Palace was completed,
the feudal lords and ministers all attended court
in the tenth month. The ceremony:
Before dawn,
the ushers managed the rites,
guiding them in order through the palace gates,
the courtyard arrayed with chariots and cavalry
and foot soldiers guarding the palace,
with weapons displayed and flags raised.
The command "Hasten" was passed along.
Attendants lined the steps of the hall,
hundreds of men on the steps.
Meritorious officials, marquises, generals, and military officers
were arrayed in order to the west,
facing east;
civil officials from the chancellor down
were arrayed to the east,
facing west.
The master of ceremonies set up the nine宾 protocol, with heralds relaying messages.
Then the emperor was carried in his palanquin from the chamber,
all officials holding their posts announced the alert,
guiding the feudal kings and those below
down to officials of six hundred piculs salary
to offer congratulations in order.
From the feudal kings down, none were not awed and solemnly respectful.
When the rites concluded,
a ceremonial wine was served.
All those seated in the hall bowed their heads low,
rising to offer toasts according to rank and seniority.
After nine rounds of wine,
the usher announced "Cease drinking."
The censors enforcing the rules
immediately removed
those who did not follow the ceremony.
Throughout the court assembly and drinking,
no one dared to be noisy or breach etiquette.
Thereupon, Emperor Gāo said:
"Only today do I realize
the honor of being emperor."
He then appointed Shūsūn Tóng as Grand Master of Ceremonies,
bestowing five hundred catties of gold.
When an opportunity arose,
he indeed spoke as Zhū Jiā had intended.
The emperor then pardoned Jì Bù.
At that time,
all the nobles greatly admired Jì Bù for his ability
to transform firmness into gentleness,
and Zhū Jiā also became renowned in his time for this.
Jì Bù was summoned for an audience,
offered his thanks,
and the emperor appointed him as a Langzhong.
During Emperor Hui’s reign,
he served as a General of the Palace Guard.
The Chányú once sent a letter insulting Empress Lǚ,
which was disrespectful,
causing Empress Lǚ great anger.
She summoned the generals to discuss it.
The Supreme General Fán Kuài said:
"I wish to lead a hundred thousand troops,
to march unopposed through the Xiōngnú lands."
All the generals flattered Empress Lǚ’s wishes,
saying
"Yes."
Jì Bù said:
"Fán Kuài deserves to be beheaded!
The late Emperor Gāo led over four hundred thousand troops,
yet was trapped at Píngchéng.
Now how can Kuài, with a hundred thousand troops,
march unopposed through the Xiōngnú lands?
This is blatant deception!
Moreover, the Qín dynasty’s troubles with the Hú
led to the uprisings of Chén Shèng and others.
To this day, the wounds have not healed,
yet Kuài flatters to your face,
seeking to destabilize the empire."
At this, the entire court was terrified,
and the Empress Dowager dismissed the court,
never again discussing the campaign against the Xiōngnú.
Jì Bù served as Governor of Hédōng.
During Emperor Wén’s reign,
someone spoke of his worthiness,
so Emperor Wén summoned him,
intending to make him Imperial Censor.
But then others spoke of his boldness,
saying he was difficult to approach when drunk.
Upon arrival,
he stayed at the guesthouse for a month,
and was dismissed without an audience.
Jì Bù then addressed the emperor:
"I, without merit, undeservedly enjoyed your favor,
serving in Hédōng awaiting punishment.
Your Majesty summoned me without cause,
surely because someone praised me to you;
now that I have come,
I receive no assignment,
and am dismissed to leave,
surely because someone has slandered me.
If Your Majesty summons me based on one person’s praise,
and dismisses me based on one person’s slander,
I fear that those with insight in the empire,
hearing of this,
will find a way to see through Your Majesty."
The emperor fell silent, ashamed,
and after a long while said:
"Hédōng is a vital commandery to me,
hence I specially summoned you, that is all."
Bù took his leave and returned to his post.
A man of Chǔ, Cáo Qiūshēng, was a persuasive speaker
who often sought influence and money.
He served the noble Zhào Tóng and others,
and was friendly with Dòu Chángjūn.
Jì Bù heard of this
and sent a letter advising Chángjūn:
"I hear Cáo Qiūshēng is not a gentleman;
do not associate with him."
When Cáo Qiūshēng returned,
he wanted a letter of introduction to visit Jì Bù.
Dòu Chángjūn said: "General Jì dislikes you, sir;
you should not go."
He persistently requested the letter,
and then went.
He sent someone ahead with the letter;
Jì Bù indeed became furious, awaiting Cáo Qiūshēng.
When Cáo Qiūshēng arrived,
he immediately bowed to Jì Bù and said:
"In Chǔ, there is a proverb:
'Better to get one promise from Jì Bù
than a hundred pieces of gold.'
How did you, sir, gain such a reputation
between Liáng and Chǔ?
Moreover, I am from Chǔ,
and you, sir, are also from Chǔ.
If I travel promoting your name throughout the empire,
would that not be significant?
Why do you, sir, reject me so deeply!"
Jì Bù then became very pleased,
invited him in,
hosted him for several months,
treated him as an honored guest,
and sent him off with generous gifts.
The reason Jì Bù’s fame grew even more
was because Cáo Qiūshēng promoted him.
Jì Bù’s younger brother, Jì Xīn,
had a spirit that overshadowed Guānzhōng.
He treated others with respect and caution,
was a chivalrous man,
and across thousands of miles,
scholars all vied to die for him.
He once killed a man,
fled to Wú,
and hid with Yuán Sī.
He served Yuán Sī as an elder,
and treated Guàn Fū, Jí Fú, and others as younger brothers.
He once served as a Central Major,
and even Zhì Dū, the Commandant of the Capital,
dared not treat him without respect.
Young men often
secretly used his name to act.
At that time, Jì Xīn was famous for his courage,
and Bù for his promises,
both well-known throughout Guānzhōng.
Jì Bù’s maternal uncle, Dīng Gōng,
was a general of Chǔ.
Dīng Gōng, under Xiàng Yǔ,
pursued and cornered Emperor Gāo west of Péngchéng.
In close combat,
Emperor Gāo, in desperation,
turned to Dīng Gōng and said:
"Should two worthy men oppress each other!"
Thereupon, Dīng Gōng led his troops back,
and the King of Hàn escaped.
After Xiàng Yǔ was destroyed,
Dīng Gōng went to pay respects to Emperor Gāo.
Emperor Gāo had Dīng Gōng executed in the army as an example,
saying:
"Dīng Gōng was disloyal as a subject of King Xiàng;
