it was Dīng Gōng
who caused King Xiàng to lose the empire."
He then beheaded Dīng Gōng,
saying:
"Let no subject in later generations imitate Dīng Gōng!"
Luán Bù
was from Liáng.
When King Péng Yuè of Liáng was still a commoner,
he once traveled with Bù.
In poverty,
he hired himself out in Qí,
working as a bartender’s assistant.
After several years,
Péng Yuè left to become a bandit in Jùyě,
while Bù was kidnapped and sold into slavery
in Yān.
He avenged his master’s enemy,
and the Yān general Zāng Tú
recommended him as a Commandant.
When Zāng Tú later became King of Yān,
he appointed Bù as a general.
After Zāng Tú rebelled,
Hàn attacked Yān,
and captured Bù.
King Péng Yuè of Liáng heard of this,
and spoke to the emperor,
requesting to ransom Bù to serve as a Grand Master of Liáng.
Sent on a mission to Qí,
before his return,
Hàn summoned Péng Yuè,
accused him of plotting rebellion,
and exterminated his three clans.
Soon after, Péng Yuè’s head was displayed in Luòyáng,
with an edict:
"Anyone daring to view or collect it
will be arrested immediately."
Bù returned from Qí,
reported his mission below Péng Yuè’s head,
sacrificed and wept for him.
Officials arrested Bù and reported it.
The emperor summoned Bù,
scolded him:
"Are you plotting rebellion with Péng Yuè?
I forbade anyone to collect his head,
yet you alone sacrificed and wept for him,
clearly conspiring with Yuè.
Hurry, boil him alive."
When the rebellion of Wú and Chǔ was reported,
Cháo Cuò said to his assistant officials:
"That Yuán Àng has accepted much gold and valuables from the King of Wú,
deliberately covering up for him,
claiming he would not rebel.
Now he has indeed rebelled,
I request to investigate Àng
who must have known about the plot."
The assistant officials said:
"Before the affair broke out,
investigating him could have prevented it.
Now the armies are marching westward,
what good would investigating do!
Moreover, Yuán Àng probably had no part in the plot."
Cháo Cuò hesitated without reaching a decision.
Someone informed Yuán Àng about this,
who became fearful,
and visited Dòu Yīng at night,
explaining the reasons for Wú's rebellion,
wishing to go before the Emperor
to testify in person.
Dòu Yīng spoke to the Emperor,
who then summoned Yuán Àng for an audience.
Cháo Cuò was present in front,
and when Àng requested others to withdraw
for a private audience,
Cuò had to leave, deeply resenting it.
Yuán Àng detailed the circumstances of Wú's rebellion,
stating it was because of Cuò,
urging that only by hastily executing Cuò to appease Wú
could their troops be disbanded.
His account is fully recorded in "The Affairs of Wú."
The Emperor appointed Yuán Àng as Tàicháng,
and Dòu Yīng as Grand General.
These two had always been on good terms.
When Wú rebelled,
the prominent elders from the mausoleum towns
and worthy officials in Cháng'ān vied to attach themselves to them,
with hundreds of carriages following daily.
After Cháo Cuò was executed,
Yuán Àng, as Tàicháng, was sent as envoy to Wú.
The King of Wú wanted to make him a general,
but he refused.
Intending to kill him,
the king sent a commandant with five hundred men
to surround and guard Àng in the army camp.
Back when Yuán Àng was Chancellor of Wú,
he had a retinue officer who
secretly favored Àng's maid,
which Àng knew about,
but did not expose,
treating him as before.
Someone informed the retinue officer,
saying
"The lord knows you are involved with his attendant,"
so he fled home.
Yuán Àng personally rode after him,
then bestowed the maid upon him,
and reinstated him as retinue officer.
When Yuán Àng was detained in Wú,
this retinue officer happened to be
the Major Simǎ guarding Àng,
who used all his savings
to buy two dàn of strong
wine.
Taking advantage of the cold weather,
when the soldiers were hungry and thirsty,
they got drunk, and the southwestern corner guards all lay down,
the Simǎ led Yuán Àng out at night,
saying:
"You may leave now,
the King of Wú plans to execute you at dawn."
Àng, disbelieving, said:
"Who are you, sir?"
The Simǎ said: "I am the former retinue officer
who coveted your maid."
Àng then expressed surprised gratitude:
"You have family, sir,
I cannot implicate you."
The Simǎ said: "Just go,
I will also flee,
hiding my family;
do not worry!"
He then cut open the tent with a knife,
leading the way out through the path of drunken soldiers.
The Simǎ parted ways with him,
Yuán Àng removed the tassels from his envoy's insignia
and concealed it,
walking with a staff,
covered seven or eight lǐ on foot,
at dawn,
encountered Liáng cavalry,
mounted a horse and rode away,
thus returning to report.
After Wú and Chǔ were defeated,
the Emperor appointed the Yuánwáng's son, Pínglù Hóu
Lǐ as King of Chǔ,
with Yuán Àng as Chancellor of Chǔ.
He once submitted memorials with advice,
but they were not heeded.
Yuán Àng retired due to illness
and lived at home,
mixing with the locals,
engaging in cockfighting and dog racing.
When Luòyáng's Jù Mèng once visited Yuán Àng,
Àng treated him well.
A wealthy man from Ānlíng said to Àng:
"I hear Jù Mèng is a gambler,
why does a general associate with him?"
Àng said: "Though Jù Mèng gambles,
when his mother died,
over a thousand carriages of guests attended the funeral,
showing he has exceptional qualities.
Moreover, everyone faces emergencies.
If one urgently knocks on your door,
not using family as an excuse,
nor avoiding matters of life and death,
those the world looks up to
are only Jì Xīn and Jù Mèng.
Now you usually have several riders with you,
but in an emergency,
would they be reliable!"
He scolded the rich man,
and broke off relations.
The gentlemen heard of this,
all praising Yuán Àng.
Though Yuán Àng lived at home,
Emperor Jǐng would often send messengers
to consult him on strategies.
The King of Liáng
wanted to be designated heir,
Yuán Àng advised against it,
and the matter was dropped.
The King of Liáng thus bore a grudge against Àng,
and once sent an assassin to kill him.
The assassin reached Guānzhōng,
inquired about Yuán Àng,
and everyone praised him
unanimously.
He then met Yuán Àng and said:
"I received gold from the King of Liáng to assassinate you,
but you are a worthy man,
I cannot bring myself to do it.
However, there are over ten more assassins after you,
be prepared!"
Yuán Àng felt troubled,
and his home experienced many strange occurrences,
so he went to a diviner
for a reading.
On his return,
the later group of Liáng assassins
indeed ambushed and killed Àng outside the Ānlíng city gate.
Cháo Cuò was
a man from Yǐngchuān.
He studied Shēn and Shāng's legalist doctrines
from Zhǎng Huī Xiān in Zhǐ,
along with Luòyáng's Sòng Mèng and Liú Lǐ as classmates.
Due to his literary learning,
he became a Tàicháng Archivist.
Cuò was stern, upright, and severe
in character.
During Emperor Wén's reign,
no one in the empire studied the Shàngshū,
only hearing that Jǐnán's Fú Shēng,
a former Qín Erudite,
studied the Shàngshū,
but being over ninety years old,
too elderly to summon,
the Emperor ordered the Tàicháng
to send someone to learn from him.
The Tàicháng sent Cuò
to study the Shàngshū with Fú Shēng.
Upon returning,
he presented memorials on advantageous policies,
citing the Shū in his arguments.
He was appointed as Gentleman of the Household to the Heir Apparent,
Gate Master,
and Household Steward.
His eloquence won him the Heir Apparent's favor,
who called him
"the Wisdom Sack."
He repeatedly submitted memorials to Emperor Wén,
advocating reducing the feudal lords' power,
and revising laws and decrees.
Though he submitted dozens of memorials,
Emperor Wén did not adopt them,
but admired his talent,
promoting him to Grand Master of the Palace.
At that time,
the Heir Apparent favored Cuò's strategies,
but Yuán Àng and other senior meritorious officials mostly disliked Cuò.
Emperor Jǐng assumed the throne,
and appointed Cuò as the Minister of the Palace.
Cuò often requested private audiences to discuss affairs,
and these were always granted,
earning him such favor that it overshadowed the nine ministers,
with many laws and decrees being revised.
Chancellor Shéntú Jiā was displeased at heart,
but lacked the means to harm him.
The Minister of the Palace's office was situated
within the grounds of the Supreme Ancestor Temple,
with its gate facing east,
which was inconvenient,
so Cuò had two gates pierced through facing south,
breaching the temple's outer wall.
When Chancellor Jiā heard of this,
he was greatly enraged,
and intended to use this fault
to submit a memorial requesting Cuò's execution.
Upon learning of this,
Cuò immediately sought a private audience that very night,
and fully explained the matter to the Emperor.
When the Chancellor presented his report,
he cited Cuò's unauthorized breach of the temple wall
to create a gate,
and requested that he be handed over to the Commandant of Justice for execution.
The Emperor said:
"This is not the temple wall itself,
but the wall of the outer grounds,
so it does not warrant legal punishment."
The Chancellor apologized.
After court was dismissed,
he angrily said to his Chief Clerk:
"I should have beheaded him first and then reported it,
but instead I made a request first,
and was outmaneuvered by that boy,
truly a mistake."
The Chancellor then fell ill and died.
Because of this, Cuò became even more esteemed.
He was promoted to Grandee of the Censorate,
and accused the feudal lords of their offenses,
proposing to reduce their territories
and confiscate their branch commanderies.
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor ordered the high officials,
marquises, and imperial clan to assemble for discussion,
and none dared to oppose,
except for Dòu Yīng, who argued against it,
thus creating a rift between him and Cuò.
Cuò had revised thirty chapters of laws,
and the feudal lords were all in an uproar, detesting Cháo Cuò.
Cuò's father heard of this,
and came from Yǐngchuān,
saying to Cuò:
"The Emperor has newly ascended the throne,
and you, sir, hold power in governance,
encroaching upon and reducing the feudal lords' lands,
separating and alienating kin from their own flesh and blood,
so that many people gossip and resent you, sir.
Why is this?"
Cháo Cuò said: "It is inevitable.
If not done this way,
the Son of Heaven will not be honored,
and the imperial temple will not be secure."
Cuò's father said: "The Liú clan may be secure,
but the Cháo clan is in peril.
I leave you, sir, and return home!"
Thereupon, he drank poison and died,
saying:
"I cannot bear to see disaster befall me."
More than ten days after his death,
the seven states of Wú and Chǔ indeed rebelled,
under the pretext of executing Cuò.
When Dòu Yīng and Yuán Àng presented their counsel,
the Emperor ordered Cháo Cuò to don his court robes
and be executed at the Eastern Market.
After Cháo Cuò had died,
the Gentleman of the Palace, Dèng Gōng,
serving as a Commandant,
led troops against the armies of Wú and Chǔ.
Upon his return,
he submitted a report on military affairs,
and had an audience with the Emperor.
The Emperor asked him:
"On your way from the army,
did you hear that Cuò had died,
and have Wú and Chǔ ceased their rebellion?"
Dèng Gōng replied:
"The King of Wú had been planning rebellion for decades;
his anger over the land reduction was merely a pretext,
using the execution of Cuò as a name,
but his true intent was not against Cuò.
Moreover, I fear
that the scholars of the empire will be silenced,
and dare not speak out again!"
The Emperor said: "Why so?"
Dèng Gōng said:
"Cháo Cuò feared that the feudal lords were too powerful
to be controlled,
so he proposed reducing their territories
to strengthen the capital,
a benefit for all generations.
Yet when the plan began to be implemented,
he abruptly suffered execution,
internally blocking the mouths of loyal ministers,
and externally avenging the feudal lords.
I privately believe this was not a course for Your Majesty to take."
Thereupon, Emperor Jǐng remained silent for a long while,
then said:
"Your words are good,
and I too regret it."
He then appointed Dèng Gōng as Commandant of Chéngyáng.
Dèng Gōng
was a man of Chénggù,
and had many ingenious strategies.
During the Jiànyuán era,
when the Emperor summoned worthy and talented men,
the high officials recommended Dèng Gōng,
who at the time was dismissed from office,
and he was reinstated directly as one of the nine ministers.
After one year,
he again resigned due to illness and returned home.
His son, Zhāng, through his studies of the teachings of Huángdì and Lǎozǐ,
became prominent among the dignitaries.
Grand Historian Simǎ Qiān said:
Although Yuán Àng was not fond of learning,
he was skilled at adapting to circumstances,
with a benevolent heart as his essence,
and he upheld righteousness with fervor.
Encountering the early reign of Emperor Wén,
his talents met the times.
As the era changed,
and with his advice regarding Wú and Chǔ,
though his counsel was followed,
it ultimately did not achieve full success.
He loved fame and flaunted his worth,
and in the end was ruined by reputation.
When Cháo Cuò served as Household Grandee,
he frequently advised on affairs
but was not heeded;
later, when he wielded power exclusively,
he implemented many changes.
When the feudal lords raised difficulties,
he did not urgently seek to rectify and save the situation,
but aimed to settle private grudges,
and instead lost his life.
As the saying goes,
"To alter the ancient and disrupt the constant,
one does not die then perish,"
does this not refer to the likes of Cuò!
The Commandant of Justice, Zhāng Shìzhī,
was a man of Dǔyáng, styled Jì.
He had an elder brother, Zhòng, with whom he lived together.
He became a Cavalry Attendant by wealth,
serving Emperor Wén of Hàn,
but for ten years received no promotion,
and remained unknown.
Shìzhī said:
"A long official career
has diminished my brother's wealth,
without success."
He intended to resign and return home.
The Leader of the Palace Attendants, Yuán Àng, recognizing his worth,
regretted his departure,
so requested that Shìzhī be transferred to fill a post as Gentleman of the Palace.
After Shìzhī had attended court,
he took the opportunity to present matters of expediency.
Emperor Wén said: "Keep it humble;
do not be too lofty in discussion,
but let it be practicable now."
Thereupon, Shìzhī spoke of affairs between Qín and Hàn times,
on why Qín was lost
and Hàn rose, for a long time.
Emperor Wén praised him,
and appointed Shìzhī as Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace.
Shìzhī accompanied the Emperor on an excursion,
ascending the Tiger Enclosure.
The Emperor asked the Superintendent of the Shanglin Park about the registers of birds and beasts,
posing over ten questions,
but the Superintendent looked left and right,
and could not answer any.
The Keeper of the Tiger Enclosure, from the side, answered on behalf of the Superintendent
all the Emperor's questions about the animal registers in great detail,
wishing to display his ability
to respond fluently and endlessly.
Emperor Wén said:
"Should not officials be like this?
The Superintendent is worthless!"
He then ordered Shìzhī
to appoint the Keeper as Prefect of the Shanglin Park.
Shìzhī advanced after a moment and said:
"What does Your Majesty think of personages like Marquis Jiàng, Zhōu Bó?"
The Emperor said: "He is a respectable elder."
He asked again:
"What kind of person is Marquis of Dōngyáng, Zhāng Xiàngrú?"
The Emperor again said:
"A respectable elder."
Zhāng Shìzhī said:
"Now, Jiàng Hóu and the Marquis of Dōngyáng are called respectable elders,
yet these two men, when discussing matters,
could hardly get their words out.
How could they imitate this village official's glib tongue and quick responses!
Moreover, the Qín dynasty, by employing clerks skilled with the pen and knife,
saw officials compete to surpass each other in harshness and severity,
taking pride in their meticulous investigations.
However, the flaw in this was that it was merely superficial formality,
lacking any genuine compassion.
Consequently, they never heard of their own faults,
leading to decline until the era of the Second Emperor,
when the empire crumbled like loose earth.
Now, if Your Majesty promotes this village official over others because of his eloquence,
I fear the whole empire will follow this trend,
striving only for clever speech
without substance.
Furthermore, the influence from above on those below
is swifter than shadow and echo;
thus, every action and decision must be made with utmost care."
Emperor Wén said: "Well said."
He then stopped the appointment of the village official.
The Emperor mounted his carriage,
summoned Shìzhī to share the carriage as his companion,
and they proceeded slowly.
He asked Shìzhī about the failings of the Qín dynasty.
Shìzhī provided a detailed and honest account.
Upon reaching the palace,
the Emperor appointed Shìzhī as the Commander of the Public Carriages.
Soon after,
the Crown Prince and the King of Liáng entered the court together in the same carriage
and failed to dismount at the Simǎ Gate.
Thereupon, Shìzhī pursued and stopped the Crown Prince and the King of Liáng,
preventing them from entering
the palace gate.
He then impeached them for not dismounting at the public gate, an act of disrespect,
and submitted a memorial to the throne.
When Empress Dowager Bó heard of this,
Emperor Wén removed his crown
and apologized, saying:
"I have failed to teach my sons properly."
Empress Dowager Bó then sent a messenger bearing an edict
to pardon the Crown Prince and the King of Liáng,
after which they were allowed to enter.
From this, Emperor Wén regarded Shìzhī as extraordinary,
and appointed him as a Grand Master of the Palace.
Not long after,
he was promoted to Commandant of the Palace Guards.
He accompanied the Emperor on an excursion to Bàlíng,
where they stood at the northern edge overlooking the side.
At that time, Lady Shèn was in attendance.
The Emperor pointed out the road to Xīnfēng to Lady Shèn,
saying:
"That is the road that leads to Hándān."
He had Lady Shèn play the sè,
while he himself leaned against the instrument and sang,
his mood somber and filled with sorrow.
Turning to his ministers, he said:
"Alas!
If one were to use the stones of the northern mountains for the outer coffin,
and bind it with hempen cord and lacquer,
filling the gaps with lacquer and flax,
could it ever be disturbed!"
Those in attendance all said: "Excellent."
Shìzhī stepped forward and said:
"If there is something desirable inside it,
even if you seal it with the metal of South Mountain, there will still be cracks;
but if there is nothing desirable inside,
even without a stone outer coffin,
what is there to worry about!"
Emperor Wén praised his words.
After this, he appointed Shìzhī as the Commandant of Justice.
Some time later,
the Emperor was passing through
the Middle Wèi Bridge,
when a man emerged from under the bridge,
startling the horses of the imperial carriage.
The Emperor then sent horsemen to arrest him
and handed him over to the Commandant of Justice.
Shìzhī conducted the interrogation.
The man said:
"I am a countryman who came to the capital.
Hearing the clearing of the road for the imperial procession,
I hid under the bridge.
After a long time,
thinking the procession had passed,
I came out,
saw the imperial carriage and horsemen,
and ran away."
The Commandant of Justice presented his judgment:
the man had violated the imperial procession clearance,
and the penalty was a fine.
Emperor Wén angrily said:
"This man personally startled my horse.
Luckily my horses are gentle;
if they had been other horses,
surely I would have been thrown and injured!
And yet the Commandant of Justice only sentences him to a fine!"
Shìzhī said:
"The law is something that the Son of Heaven shares with all under heaven.
Now, the law stipulates this penalty,
yet if we make it heavier,
the law will no longer be trusted by the people.
Moreover, at the moment it happened,
if Your Majesty had immediately ordered him executed,
that would have been the end of it.
But since he has been handed over to the Commandant of Justice,
and the Commandant of Justice
is the balance of justice for all under heaven,
if that balance is once tilted,
then all under heaven in applying the law
will either lighten or加重 penalties arbitrarily,
and how then will the people know where to place their hands and feet?
I beg Your Majesty to consider this."
After a long silence,
the Emperor said:
"The Commandant of Justice's judgment is correct."
Later, someone stole
a jade ring from in front of the throne in the Gāo Temple. The thief was caught,
and Emperor Wén, enraged,
handed him over to the Commandant of Justice for judgment.
Shìzhī, according to the law against stealing
objects used in the imperial ancestral temples, prepared a memorial,
recommending the sentence of execution in the marketplace.
The Emperor was greatly angered and said: "This man is utterly without principle,
daring to steal artifacts from the temple of a previous emperor.
I handed him over to the Commandant of Justice
intending to have his clan exterminated,
yet you, based on the law, memorialize this sentence.
This does not fulfill my intent
to honor and continue the ancestral temple."
Shìzhī removed his cap, kowtowed, and apologized, saying:
"The law stipulates this penalty, and it is sufficient.
Moreover, crimes may be of equal level,
yet distinctions are made based on the degree of defiance.
Now, if we exterminate the clan for stealing a temple artifact,
what if, by one chance in ten thousand,
some foolish commoner were to take a handful of earth from the Chánglíng tomb mound—
how would Your Majesty加重 the penalty then?"
After some time,
Emperor Wén discussed it with the Empress Dowager,
and then approved the Commandant of Justice's judgment.
At that time,
the Commandant of the Capital, Tiáohóu Zhōu Yàfū, and the Chancellor of Liáng,
Shāndūhóu Wáng Tiánkāi,
seeing that Shìzhī upheld fair judgments,
became close friends with him.
Commandant of Justice Zhāng thereby became praised throughout the empire.
Later, when Emperor Wén passed away,
and Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
Shìzhī grew fearful
and pleaded illness.
He wished to resign and leave,
but feared severe punishment might follow;
he considered presenting himself to apologize,
but did not know what would come of it.
Following Wáng Shēng's advice,
he eventually went to apologize,
and Emperor Jǐng did not reproach him.
Wáng Shēng
was skilled in the teachings of the Yellow Emperor and Lǎozi,
and was a recluse scholar.
He was once summoned to the court,
where all the three lords and nine ministers were gathered standing.
Wáng Shēng, being an old man,
said,
"My sock has come untied,"
and turning to Commandant of Justice Zhāng, said:
"Tie my sock for me!"
Shìzhī knelt and tied it for him.
After this was done,
someone asked Wáng Shēng:
"Why did you single out and publicly humiliate
Commandant of Justice Zhāng,
making him kneel to tie your sock?"
Wáng Shēng replied:
"I am old and of little worth,
and I considered that I could ultimately be of no help to Commandant of Justice Zhāng.
Commandant of Justice Zhāng is now a famous minister of the empire,
so I deliberately humiliated him slightly,
making him kneel to tie my sock,
in order to enhance his reputation."
When the officials heard this,
they esteemed Wáng Shēng and respected Commandant of Justice Zhāng all the more.
Commandant Zhāng served Emperor Jǐng
for over a year,
then became chancellor to the Prince of Huáinán,
still due to his past faults.
After some time,
Zhāng Shìzhī passed away.
His son named Zhāng Zhì,
courtesy name Chánggōng,
rose to the rank of Grand Master,
but was dismissed.
Because he could not ingratiate himself with the times,
he never held office again for life.
Féng Táng,
his grandfather was from Zhào.
His father moved to Dài.
After Hàn's rise, they relocated to Ānlíng.
Féng Táng was known for filial piety,
serving as Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace under Emperor Wén.
When Emperor Wén passed by in his carriage,
he asked Féng Táng:
"Venerable sir, how come you're a gentleman?
Where is your home?"
Féng Táng answered fully and truthfully.
Emperor Wén said:
"When I lived in Dài,
my Provisioner-in-Chief Gāo Qū often told me
of the worthiness of Zhào's Lǐ Qí,
who fought beneath Jùlù.
Now whenever I eat,
my thoughts always turn to Jùlù.
Do you know about it?"
Féng Táng replied:
"He was still not as good as Lián Pō and Lǐ Mù as generals."
The Emperor asked: "Why?"
Féng Táng said:
"When my grandfather was in Zhào,
he served as an officer captain,
and was friends with Lǐ Mù.
My father was formerly chancellor of Dài,
and was friends with Zhào's general Lǐ Qí,
knowing his character."
Upon hearing about Lián Pō and
Lǐ Mù's qualities,
the Emperor was greatly pleased, and slapping his thigh said:
"Alas!
If only I had Lián Pō and Lǐ Mù as my generals now,
would I worry about the Xiōngnú!"
Féng Táng said: "Your servant begs pardon!
Even if Your Majesty obtained Lián Pō and Lǐ Mù,
you couldn't use them."
The Emperor grew angry,
rose and entered the palace.
After a long while,
he summoned Féng Táng and reproached him:
"Why did you insult me publicly,
couldn't you find a private moment?"
Féng Táng apologized:
"This humble man knows no restraint."
At that time,
the Xiōngnú had recently invaded on a large scale,
killing the Commandant of Běidì, Áng.
The Emperor concerned about the barbarian raids,
finally asked Féng Táng again:
"How do you know I couldn't
use Lián Pō and Lǐ Mù?"
Féng Táng replied: "Your servant has heard
that when ancient kings dispatched generals,
they knelt and pushed the chariot wheels,
saying, 'Within the threshold,
I decide;
beyond the threshold,
the general decides.'
Military merits
and rewards
were all determined externally,
reported upon return.
This was no empty talk.
My grandfather said,
when Lǐ Mù served as Zhào's general guarding the border,
the taxes from the army markets
he all used to feast his officers,
rewards decided externally,
without interference from the court.
Entrusted with authority
and expected to achieve success,
thus Lǐ Mù could fully employ his wisdom and ability,
dispatched selected chariots numbering thirteen hundred,
mounted archers thirteen thousand,
elite soldiers worth a hundred gold pieces one hundred thousand,
thereby driving the Chányú north,
defeating the Dōnghú,
annihilating the Dànlín,
suppressing powerful Qín to the west,
and supporting Hán and Wèi to the south.
At that time,
Zhào nearly achieved hegemony.
Later, when King Qiān of Zhào ascended,
his mother was a courtesan.
Upon King Qiān's accession,
he employed Guō Kāi's slanders,
finally executed Lǐ Mù,
and ordered Yán Jù to replace him.
Thus the army was defeated, soldiers fled,
and they were captured and destroyed by Qín.
Now I've privately heard that Wèi Shǎng as governor of Yúnzhōng,
uses all army market taxes to feast his officers,
spends his personal funds,
butchers an ox every five days,
to feast guests, army officers, and retainers,
thus the Xiōngnú keep their distance,
not approaching Yúnzhōng's passes.
Once when the enemy invaded,
Shǎng led chariots and cavalry to attack them,
killing very many.
Now these soldiers are all commoners' sons,
rising from the fields to join the army,
how would they know official registers and tallies?
They fight strenuously all day,
beheading and capturing enemies,
reporting merits to headquarters, but if one word doesn't match,
the clerks punish them by law.
Their rewards go unfulfilled
while officials' strict law application prevails.
I am foolish,
but believe Your Majesty's laws are too precise,
rewards too light,
punishments too heavy.
Moreover, Governor Wèi Shǎng of Yúnzhōng was accused
of misreporting six enemy heads in his merit claim,
Your Majesty handed him to the officials,
stripped his rank,
and sentenced him to penal servitude.
From this perspective,
even if Your Majesty obtained Lián Pō,
Lǐ Mù,
you couldn't use them.
I am truly foolish,
offending taboos, deserving death! Deserving death!"
Emperor Wén was pleased.
That day he ordered Féng Táng to bear the tally
and pardon Wèi Shǎng,
reinstating him as governor of Yúnzhōng,
and appointed Féng Táng as Commandant of Chariots and Cavalry,
overseeing chariot warriors of the capital commandant and commanderies.
In the seventh year,
when Emperor Jǐng ascended,
he made Féng Táng chancellor of Chǔ,
but was later dismissed.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended,
seeking worthy and talented men,
Féng Táng was recommended.
Féng Táng was then over ninety years old,
unable to serve again,
so his son Féng Suì was made a gentleman.
Suì, courtesy name Wángsūn,
was also an extraordinary man,
and friendly with me.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Master Zhāng Jì's words about elders,
upholding law without flattery;
Master Féng's discourse on generals,
how profound! How profound!
As the saying goes,
"If you don't know the man,
look at his friends."
What these two gentlemen praised
could be displayed in the court temples.
The Book of Documents says,
"Without partiality, without faction,
the kingly way is vast;
without faction, without partiality,
the kingly way is level."
Masters Zhāng Jì and Féng approximated this.
Wànshí Jūn was named Fèn,
his father was from Zhào,
of the Shí family.
After Zhào's fall,
they moved to Wēn.
When Emperor Gāo attacked Xiàng Jí eastward,
passing through Hénèi,
Fèn was then fifteen,
serving as a minor clerk,
attending upon Emperor Gāo.
Emperor Gāo spoke with him,
admiring his respectfulness,
asked: "What family do you have?"
He replied:
"Fèn only has a mother,
unfortunately blind.
The family is poor.
There is an elder sister,
who can play the zither."
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"Will you follow me?"
The reply was:
"I wish to exert my full effort."
Thereupon, Emperor Gāozǔ summoned his elder sister to be a Měirén,
appointed Fèn as Zhōngjuān,
receiving documents and audiences,
and moved his family to Cháng'ān,
in the Zhōngqī Lǐ,
because his sister had become a Měirén.
His official career lasted until Emperor Wén's time,
accumulating merits and labors
until he reached the position of Dàzhōng Dàfū.
He had no literary learning,
yet his respectfulness and caution were unmatched.
During Emperor Wén's reign,
Dōngyáng Hóu Zhāng Xiàngrú
served as Tàizǐ Tàifù,
but was dismissed.
When selecting someone suitable to be the Tutor,
all recommended Fèn,
and Fèn became Tàizǐ Tàifù.
When Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
he appointed him as one of the Jiǔqīng;
being too close to the emperor, he felt intimidated by him,
so he transferred Fèn to be the Chancellor of a feudal state.
Fèn's eldest son was Jiàn,
the second son Jiǎ,
the third son Yǐ,
and the youngest son Qìng,
all known for their gentle conduct, filial piety, and respectfulness,
and their official ranks all reached
two thousand dàn.
Thereupon, Emperor Jǐng said:
"Lord Shí and his four sons all hold two thousand dàn,
such honor and favor upon a subject are gathered at his door."
He thus titled Fèn as Wànshí Jūn.
In the later years of Emperor Jǐng,
Wànshí Jūn retired on the salary of a Shàngdàfū
to his home,
attending court as a minister on seasonal occasions.
When passing through palace gates,
Wànshí Jūn would always dismount from his carriage and hasten on foot,
and upon seeing the imperial horses, he would bow in his carriage.
When his sons or grandsons serving as minor officials
returned home to visit,
Wànshí Jūn would always receive them in court attire,
without addressing them by name.
If his descendants committed faults,
he would not scold them,
but would sit aside,
facing the table without eating.
Then his sons would reproach each other,
and through the elders,
they would bared their upper bodies to firmly apologize,
and only after they corrected themselves,
would he relent.
When his grown-up descendants were by his side,
even at leisure, he would always wear his official cap,
appearing solemn and proper.
His servants were cheerful,
yet strictly respectful.
When the emperor bestowed food at his home,
he would always kowtow and prostrate himself before eating it,
as if in the emperor's presence.
In observing mourning,
he was deeply sorrowful and grieved.
His descendants followed his teachings,
behaving similarly.
Wànshí Jūn's family was renowned throughout the commanderies and states for filial piety and respectfulness,
even the Confucian scholars of Qí and Lǔ, known for their substantial conduct,
all considered themselves inferior.
In the second year of the Jiànyuán era,
Lángzhōnglìng Wáng Zāng
was convicted due to literary matters.
The Empress Dowager believed
that Confucian scholars
were more about embellishment than substance,
whereas Wànshí Jūn's family spoke little
but practiced diligently,
so she appointed his eldest son Jiàn
as Lángzhōnglìng,
and his youngest son Qìng as Nèishǐ.
Jiàn grew old and gray-haired,
while Wànshí Jūn was still in good health.
Jiàn, as Lángzhōnglìng,
every five days on his washing day off
would return home to visit his parent,
enter his father's quarters,
secretly ask the attendants,
take his parent's undergarments and chamber pot liners,
personally wash them,
and return them to the attendants,
not daring to let Wànshí Jūn know,
and this became his routine.
Jiàn, as Lángzhōnglìng,
when there were matters to discuss,
would dismiss others and speak freely,
with utmost sincerity;
but at court appearances,
he seemed as if he could not speak.
Therefore, the emperor personally honored and respected him.
Wànshí Jūn moved to reside
in Líng Lǐ.
Once, Nèishǐ Qìng returned drunk,
and entered the outer gate without dismounting from his carriage.
Wànshí Jūn heard of this,
and refused to eat.
Qìng became fearful,
bared his upper body to apologize,
but was not forgiven.
The whole clan and his elder brother Jiàn
bared their upper bodies,
and Wànshí Jūn reproached, saying:
"The Nèishǐ is an honored man,
entering the village,
the elders of the village all flee and hide,
yet the Nèishǐ sits in his carriage composed as usual,
how fitting indeed!"
Only then did he dismiss Qìng's apology.
Thereafter, Qìng and all the younger family members
upon entering the village gate,
would hasten on foot to their home.
Wànshí Jūn passed away in the fifth year of the Yuánshuò era.
His eldest son, Lángzhōnglìng Jiàn,
wept in mourning with deep sorrow,
needing a cane to walk.
A little over a year later,
Jiàn also died.
All his descendants were filial,
but Jiàn was the most so,
even more than Wànshí Jūn.
Jiàn, as Lángzhōnglìng,
when submitting written reports,
after the matters were decided,
Jiàn would read them and
say:
"A mistake in writing!
The character 'horse'
should have five strokes for the tail,
but here it has only four,
one short.
The emperor would have me condemned to death!"
He was extremely fearful.
His cautiousness
was like this in all matters.
Wànshí Jūn's youngest son Qìng
served as Tàipú,
driving the imperial carriage out,
the emperor asked how many horses
were in the carriage,
Qìng used his whip to count the horses, and after finishing,
raised his hand and said:
"Six horses."
Qìng was the most straightforward among the sons,
yet he still acted this way.
As Chancellor of Qí,
the entire state of Qí admired his family's conduct,
and without much speaking,
Qí was greatly well-governed,
so they erected a stone shrine for the Chancellor.
In the first year of the Yuánshòu era,
the emperor established the Crown Prince,
and selected among the ministers one suitable to be the Tutor,
Qìng was promoted from Governor of Pèi
to Tàizǐ Tàifù,
and after seven years, he was promoted to Yùshǐ Dàfū.
In the autumn of the fifth year of the Yuándǐng era,
the Chancellor was found guilty,
and dismissed.
An imperial decree to the Yùshǐ stated:
"Wànshí Jūn was honored by the late emperor,
and his descendants are filial,
let Yùshǐ Dàfū Qìng
be appointed Chancellor,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Mùqiū."
At that time, Hàn was campaigning in the south against
the two Yuè states,
attacking Korea in the east,
pursuing the Xiōngnú in the north,
and civilizing Dàyuān in the west,
and the central plains were full of activities.
The Son of Heaven toured the realm,
restored ancient shrines,
performed imperial sacrifices,
and promoted rituals and music.
With the state treasury running low,
Sāng Hóngyáng and others generated revenue,
while Wáng Wēnshū's faction enforced harsh laws.
Ér Kuān and his peers advanced through literary scholarship to become the Nine Ministers,
taking turns in wielding power.
Matters were no longer decided by the Chancellor;
the Chancellor remained merely sincere and cautious.
After nine years in office,
he had been unable to offer any corrective advice.
Once he attempted to prosecute the emperor's close attendant Suǒ Zhōng
and the Nine Minister Xián Xuān for their crimes,
but failed to subdue them,
instead incurring blame himself,
and had to redeem his offense.
In the fourth year of Yuánfēng,
two million displaced people from east of the pass,
including four hundred thousand unregistered,
prompted the high officials to deliberate
and propose relocating them to the borders
as a solution.
The emperor, considering the Chancellor old and overcautious,
incapable of participating in the debate,
granted him leave to retire,
and instead investigated those from the Imperial Secretary down
who had supported the proposal.
Ashamed of his inadequacy,
the Chancellor submitted a memorial saying:
"I am fortunate to have served as Chancellor, though unworthily,
but being inept, I have failed to assist in governance.
With cities and granaries empty,
and many people displaced,
I deserve execution by the axe,
yet His Majesty cannot bear to enforce the law.
I wish to return my seal as Marquis and Chancellor,
beg to retire with my bones,
and make way for the worthy."
The Son of Heaven replied:
"The granaries are already empty,
the people impoverished and wandering;
you proposed moving them,
causing unrest and instability,
endangering them,
and now you resign from office—
to which difficulty do you wish to return peace?"
With this written reprimand to Qìng, he felt deeply ashamed,
and thus resumed his duties.
Qìng was meticulous and cautious in documents,
yet lacked any grand strategy
to speak for the common people.
Over three years later,
in the second year of Tàichū,
Chancellor Qìng passed away,
posthumously honored as the Tranquil Marquis.
His middle son Dé, whom Qìng cherished and employed,
was appointed by the emperor as heir,
succeeding to the marquisate.
Later, as Grand Ceremonialist,
he was convicted of a crime deserving death,
but redeemed himself and was reduced to commoner status.
While Qìng served as Chancellor,
his sons and grandsons in official posts
reached the rank of two thousand bushels, thirteen in total.
After Qìng's death,
they gradually left office due to offenses,
and their filial devotion and caution declined further.
The Marquis of Jiànlíng, Wèi Wǎn,
was from Dàlíng in Dài.
Wǎn started as a acrobatic charioteer
to become a court gentleman,
serving Emperor Wén,
and by merit
advanced to General of the Household.
He was sincere and cautious without ulterior motives.
When Emperor Jǐng was crown prince,
he summoned the emperor's attendants to drink,
but Wǎn pleaded illness and did not attend.
As Emperor Wén lay dying,
he instructed Emperor Jǐng:
"Wǎn is a man of integrity;
treat him well."
After Emperor Wén's death,
Emperor Jǐng ascended the throne,
and for over a year did not reproach Wǎn,
who grew daily more diligent in his caution.
When Emperor Jǐng visited the Shanglin Park,
he ordered the General of the Household to accompany him in his carriage,
and upon return asked:
"Do you know why you were chosen to ride with me?"
Wǎn replied:
"I, a mere chariot warrior, was fortunate to advance by merit to General of the Household;
I do not know the reason."
The emperor asked: "When I was crown prince and summoned you,
you refused to come—
why?"
He answered: "A capital offense—I was truly ill!"
The emperor bestowed a sword upon him.
Wǎn said:
"The late emperor gifted me six swords in total;
I dare not accept this decree."
The emperor said:
"Swords are often exchanged among people;
have you kept them all this time?"
Wǎn replied: "They are all here."
The emperor had them fetched—
the swords were still sheathed,
never having been worn.
If court gentlemen were reprimanded,
he often took the blame himself,
not contending with other generals;
if there was merit,
he always yielded it to others.
The emperor considered him upright,
loyal and without hidden agendas,
thus appointing Wǎn
as Tutor to the King of Héjiān.
During the rebellion of Wú and Chǔ,
he was commanded to lead troops,
directing Héjiān's forces against them
with success,
and was promoted to Commandant of the Capital.
Three years later,
for military merit,
in the sixth year of Emperor Jǐng's reign, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiànlíng.
The following year,
the emperor deposed the crown prince,
and executed Lì Qīng and his faction.
Deeming Wǎn a man of integrity,
he could not bear to involve him,
so granted him leave to retire,
and had Zhì Dū arrest and try the Lì clan.
After this,
the emperor established the King of Jiāodōng as crown prince,
recalled Wǎn,
and appointed him Tutor to the Crown Prince.
After some time,
he was promoted to Imperial Secretary.
Five years later,
he succeeded Táohóu Shě as Chancellor,
reporting affairs in court strictly according to his duties.
Yet from his first post to the chancellorship,
he never had anything notable to say.
The emperor considered him honest and kind,
fit to assist a young ruler,
honored and favored him,
with abundant rewards.
After three years as Chancellor,
Emperor Jǐng passed away,
and Emperor Wǔ ascended.
In the Jiànyuán era,
because during Emperor Jǐng's illness
many officials and prisoners
had been unjustly convicted,
and the Chancellor had failed in his duties,
he was dismissed.
Later, Wǎn died,
and his son Xìn succeeded him.
Convicted of inferior gold tribute,
he lost his marquisate.
The Marquis of Sāi, Zhí Bùyí,
was from Nányáng.
As a court gentleman,
he served Emperor Wén.
A colleague in his quarters,
on leave home,
mistakenly took another gentleman's gold.
Later, the owner noticed,
and wrongly suspected Bùyí,
who apologized and admitted to it,
buying gold to repay.
When the colleague returned
and gave back the gold,
the former gold-loser was greatly ashamed,
and this earned Bùyí a reputation for integrity.
Emperor Wén praised and promoted him,
gradually advancing him to Grand Master of the Palace.
At court appearances,
some slandered him:
"Bùyí is very handsome,
but alas, how he excels at seducing his brothers' wives!"
Hearing this,
Bùyí said:
"But I have no elder brother."
Yet he never tried to clear his name.
During the rebellion of Wú and Chǔ,
Bù Yí, as a two-thousand-bushel official,
led troops to suppress it.
In the first year of the later period of Emperor Jǐng's reign,
he was appointed as Grand Secretary.
The emperor, recognizing his merits during the Wú-Chǔ conflict,
enfeoffed Bù Yí as the Marquis of Sài.
During the Jiànyuán era of Emperor Wǔ,
he and Chancellor Wǎn were both dismissed
due to faults.
Bù Yí studied the teachings of the Lǎo Zǐ.
Wherever he served,
he performed his duties as usual,
yet he feared others might detect his official demeanor.
He disliked building a reputation,
and was regarded as a virtuous elder.
After Bù Yí's death,
his son Xiàng Rú succeeded him.
His grandson Wàng,
lost the marquisate due to a violation involving sacrificial gold.
The Commandant of the Palace, Zhōu Wén,
named Rén,
was originally from Rènchéng.
He gained recognition as a physician.
When Emperor Jǐng was the crown prince,
he was appointed as a retainer,
and through accumulated merits, gradually advanced,
reaching the position of Grand Master of the Palace
during Emperor Wén's reign.
When Emperor Jǐng first ascended the throne,
he appointed Rén as Commandant of the Palace.
Rén was discreet and reserved,
often wearing patched clothes and soiled
trousers,
intentionally appearing unkempt,
which earned him favor.
When Emperor Jǐng entered private chambers,
or engaged in secret amusements in the rear palace,
Rén was often by his side.
Until Emperor Jǐng's death,
Rén remained as Commandant of the Palace,
never speaking out of turn.
When the emperor inquired about others,
Rén would say:
"Your Majesty should observe them yourself."
Yet he never slandered anyone.
For this, Emperor Jǐng visited his home twice.
His family moved to Yánglíng.
He received many gifts from the emperor,
but often declined them,
daring not to accept.
Gifts from nobles and ministers
were never accepted.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended,
he regarded Rén as a minister of the previous emperor
and respected him.
Rén then retired due to illness,
receiving a two-thousand-bushel pension to retire,
and his descendants all attained high offices.
The Grand Secretary Zhāng Shū,
named Ōu,
was the illegitimate son of Marquis Ānqiū, Shuō.
During Emperor Wén's reign,
he served the crown prince
with expertise in legalist doctrines.
Though Ōu studied legalist teachings,
he was a man of virtue.
Respected during Emperor Jǐng's time,
he often served as one of the Nine Ministers.
By the fourth year of Yuánshuò under Emperor Wǔ,
when Hán Ān Guó was dismissed,
Ōu was appointed Grand Secretary by decree.
Throughout his official career,
he never prosecuted anyone,
serving solely with sincerity as a virtuous elder.
His subordinates, seeing him as such,
dared not deceive him greatly.
When presenting legal cases to the emperor,
if there was room for dismissal,
he dismissed them;
if not, reluctantly,
he would face the emperor with tears
and seal the documents.
Such was his compassion.
In old age and severe illness,
he requested retirement.
The emperor then issued a decree to release him,
granting him a senior grand master's pension to retire at home.
His home was in Yánglíng.
His descendants all attained high offices.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Confucius once said,
"The noble person wishes to be slow in speech
and diligent in action,"
does this not refer to Wàn Shí, Jiànlíng, and Zhāng Shū?
Thus, their teaching was achieved without severity
and order maintained without strictness.
The Marquis of Sài was subtly cunning,
and Zhōu Wén engaged in flattery, which noble persons criticize
for being close to sycophancy.
Yet these can still be called sincere and virtuous gentlemen!
Tián Shū
was from Xíngchéng in Zhào.
His ancestors
were descendants of the Tián clan of Qí.
Shū enjoyed swordsmanship
and studied the arts of Huáng-Lǎo
under the tutelage of Lè Jùgōng.
Shū was stern, incorruptible, and self-assured,
fond of associating with dignitaries.
The people of Zhào recommended him to Chancellor Zhào Wǔ of Zhào,
who introduced him to King Zhào, Zhāng Áo,
and the king appointed him as a court gentleman.
After several years,
being straightforward, honest, and fair,
the king esteemed him,
but had not yet promoted him.
When Chén Xī rebelled in Dài,
in the seventh year of Hàn,
Emperor Gāozǔ went to suppress him,
passing through Zhào,
where King Zhào, Zhāng Áo, personally served him meals,
showing utmost respect,
yet the emperor sat sprawled and insulted him.
At this, Chancellor Zhào Wǔ
and dozens of others grew furious,
saying to King Zhāng:
"Your Majesty has served the emperor with full courtesy,
yet he treats you thus.
We request to start a rebellion."
The king bit his finger until it bled,
saying:
"Our ancestors lost the kingdom;
without His Majesty,
we would be like worms emerging from corpses.
How can you speak like this!
Do not say such things again!"
Then Guàn Gāo and others said: "The king is a virtuous elder
who does not betray virtue."
Ultimately, they privately plotted to assassinate the emperor.
When the plot was discovered,
Hàn issued an order to arrest King Zhào
and the rebellious ministers.
Thus, Zhào Wǔ and others committed suicide,
only Guàn Gāo was captured.
At that time, Hàn decreed:
"Anyone in Zhào who dares to follow the king
will be punished with the extermination of three clans."
Only Mèng Shū, Tián Shū, and over ten others
donned red convict clothes, shaved their heads, and wore metal collars,
claiming to be the king's slaves,
and followed King Zhào Áo to Cháng'ān.
When Guàn Gāo's case was clarified,
King Zhào Áo was released,
demoted to Marquis of Xuānpíng,
and then recommended Tián Shū
and over ten others.
The emperor summoned and interviewed them all;
in conversation,
no court minister surpassed them,
pleasing the emperor,
who appointed them all as commandery administrators
and chancellor to the nobles.
Shū served as administrator of Hànzhōng
for over ten years,
until Empress Dowager Gāo's death,
when the Lǚ clan rebelled,
the ministers suppressed them,
and established Emperor Wén.
After Emperor Wén ascended,
he summoned Tián Shū and asked:
"Do you know the virtuous elders of the realm?"
Shū replied:
"How could I know them all!"
The emperor said:
"You, sir,
are a virtuous elder,
you should know."
Shū kowtowed and said:
"The former administrator of Yúnzhōng, Mèng Shū,
is a virtuous elder."
At that time, Mèng Shū had been dismissed
due to major raids and pillaging by the enemy in the frontier,
with Yúnzhōng suffering the most.
The Emperor said: "The late emperor placed Mèng Shū in Yúnzhōng
for over ten years.
The barbarians once invaded,
and Mèng Shū failed to hold firm,
needlessly causing several hundred soldiers to die in battle.
Does a virtuous elder deliberately cause men's deaths?
Why do you, sir, say Mèng Shū is a virtuous elder?"
Shǔ kowtowed and replied:
"This is precisely why Mèng Shū
is a virtuous elder.
When Guàn Gāo and others plotted rebellion,
an imperial decree was issued from above,
stating that anyone in Zhào who dared follow King Zhāng
would be punished with the extermination of three clans.
Yet Mèng Shū shaved his head and wore a metal collar,
following King Zhāng Áo wherever he was,
willing to die for him.
How could he have known then he would become governor of Yúnzhōng!
When Hàn and Chǔ contended,
the soldiers were weary and exhausted.
The Xiōngnú leader Mòdú
had recently subjugated the northern tribes,
and came to harass the border.
Mèng Shū knew the soldiers were weary,
and could not bear to order them forth,
yet the soldiers vied to mount the walls
and die fighting the enemy,
like sons for their fathers,
younger brothers for their elders.
Thus, several hundred men died.
How could Mèng Shū have deliberately driven them to battle!
This is why Shū is a virtuous elder."
Then the Emperor said: "How worthy is Mèng Shū!"
He summoned Mèng Shū again
and appointed him governor of Yúnzhōng.
Several years later,
Shǔ was dismissed from office for breaking the law.
When King Xiào of Liáng
had the former Wú chancellor, Yuán Àng, assassinated,
Emperor Jǐng summoned Tián Shǔ
to investigate Liáng,
and he obtained all the facts,
returning to report.
Emperor Jǐng asked: "Is Liáng guilty of this?"
Shǔ replied: "I deserve death! It is true."
The Emperor said:
"Where is the evidence?"
Tián Shǔ said:
"Your Majesty should not pursue the matter of Liáng."
The Emperor asked: "Why?"
He said:
"If King Liáng is not executed,
the laws of Hàn will not be upheld;
if he is executed,
the Empress Dowager will find no flavor in her food,
nor rest peacefully in her bed,
and this worry will fall upon Your Majesty."
Emperor Jǐng greatly esteemed him for this,
and appointed him chancellor of Lǔ.
When the chancellor first arrived in Lǔ,
the people petitioned him directly,
with over a hundred accusing the king of taking their belongings.
Tián Shǔ took their twenty leaders,
flogged each fifty strokes,
and the rest twenty strokes each,
angrily saying:
"Is the king not your lord?
How dare you speak against your lord!"
The King of Lǔ heard this and was deeply ashamed,
drawing money from the central treasury
to have the chancellor compensate them.
The chancellor said:
"Your Majesty took it yourself,
yet have the chancellor compensate them;
this would make the king the wrongdoer
and the chancellor the virtuous.
The chancellor will not take part in the compensation."
Thereupon, the king compensated them all himself.
The King of Lǔ enjoyed hunting,
and the chancellor often accompanied him into the park.
The king would urge the chancellor to rest at the lodge,
but when the chancellor went out,
he often sat exposed
waiting outside the park.
The king repeatedly sent people to urge the chancellor to rest,
but he never did,
saying:
"My king is exposed in the park,
how can I alone rest in the lodge!"
Because of this, the King of Lǔ seldom went on major outings.
Several years later,
Shǔ died in office.
Lǔ offered a hundred catties of gold
for sacrifices in his honor,
but his youngest son, Rén, declined,
saying:
"I will not tarnish my father's name
for a hundred catties of gold."
Rén, being strong and fit, became a retainer of General Wèi
and several times followed him to battle the Xiōngnú.
General Wèi recommended Rén,
and Rén became a gentleman of the palace.
After a few years,
he rose to the two-thousand-picul rank as senior secretary to the chancellor,
but lost the position.
Later, he was sent to investigate and report on the three Hé regions.
When the Emperor toured east,
Rén presented his report eloquently,
pleasing the Emperor,
who appointed him commandant of the capital area.
Over a month later,
the Emperor promoted him to imperial secretary.
Several years later, he was implicated in the crown prince's affair.
At that time, the left chancellor himself led troops,
ordering the imperial secretary Tián Rén to take charge
of guarding the city gates.
He was accused of allowing the crown prince to escape,
handed over to the officials, and executed.
Rén had raised troops,
and the magistrate of Chánglíng, Chē Qiānqiū, reported Rén's treachery,
leading to Rén's execution and the extermination of his clan.
Xíngchéng is now in the state of Zhōngshān.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Confucius said,
"He who dwells in a state will surely learn of its governance,"
was he not speaking of Tián Shǔ!
Righteous, he did not forget the worthy;
he illuminated the virtues of an enlightened ruler
to rectify faults.
Rén was a friend of mine,
hence I have discussed them together.
Master Chǔ says:
When I was a gentleman,
I heard that Tián Rén was formerly good friends with Rèn Ān.
Rèn Ān
was from Xíngyáng.
Orphaned young and impoverished,
he drove a carriage for someone to Cháng'ān,
and stayed,
seeking a minor official post,
but found no opportunity.
He then registered as a resident.
Wǔgōng,
a small town on the western border of Fúfēng,
is near the mountains at Gǔkǒu, where the Shǔ path is cut.
Ān thought Wǔgōng a small town,
without powerful families,
making it easier to rise high,
so he stayed,
replacing someone as a constable and watchman.
Later, he became a station master.
When the townsfolk went out hunting,
Rèn Ān often distributed deer, game, and rabbits for others,
assigning tasks to the old, young, strong, and weak appropriately,
and everyone was pleased,
saying:
"No harm done,
Rèn Shǎoqīng allocates fairly,
and is wise and strategic."
The next day, they gathered again,
with several hundred participants.
Rèn Shǎoqīng asked:
"Why hasn't so-and-so come?"
All were amazed at his quick notice.
Later, he was appointed village elder,
recommended for being close to the people,
and sent out as a three-hundred-picul magistrate,
governing the people.
He was dismissed for failing to prepare the tents during an imperial tour,
and removed from office.
He then became a retainer of General Wèi,
met Tián Rén,
and both were retainers,
living at the gate,
united in heart and affection.
These two were poor,
with no money to bribe the general's steward,
who made them tend the ill-tempered biting horses.
The two shared a bed,
and Rén whispered:
"How ignorant the steward is!"
Rèn Ān said:
"If the general himself does not know men,
what of the steward!"
When General Wèi
took these two past Princess Píngyáng's estate,
the princess's steward made them sit at the same mat as the riding slaves to eat,
whereupon the two drew their knives, cut the mat, and sat separately.
The steward found it strange and disliked them,
but none dared reprimand them.
Subsequently, an imperial edict was issued to select household retainers of generals to serve as court gentlemen.
The general chose the wealthiest among his retainers,
ordering them to prepare saddled horses, crimson robes, and jade-adorned
swords,
intending to present them to the emperor.
It happened that the worthy senior official Shàofǔ Zhào Yǔ came to visit General Wèi,
who called forth his recommended retainers to show them to Zhào Yǔ.
Zhào Yǔ questioned them one by one,
and found none of the dozen or so men to be experienced or strategically astute.
Zhào Yǔ said:
"I have heard that
beneath a general's gate, there must be those of a general's caliber.
The tradition says, 'If you do not know the ruler, look at whom he employs;
if you do not know the son, look at whom he befriends.'
Now the edict calls for recommending the general's retainers
to observe the general's ability to attract worthy men of civil and martial talents.
Yet you merely select sons of the wealthy to present,
who lack wisdom and strategy,
like wooden dolls dressed in fine embroidery—
what can be done about this?"
Thereupon, Zhào Yǔ summoned all over a hundred of General Wèi's retainers,
questioning them sequentially,
and identified Tián Rén and Rén Ān,
saying:
"Only these two will do;
the rest are unusable."
General Wèi, seeing that these two were poor,
felt displeased.
After Zhào Yǔ left,
he said to the two:
"Each of you prepare your own saddled horses and new crimson robes."
The two replied:
"Our families are poor and lack the means to do so."
The general angrily said:
"Now that your own families are poor,
why say such things?
You seem resentful as if shifting your virtue onto me—
why is that?"
The general had no choice
but to submit their names to the emperor.
An edict summoned General Wèi's retainers for an audience,
and these two came forward.
The emperor inquired about their abilities and had them rank each other.
Tián Rén responded:
"Holding the drumstick at the army gate,
inspiring officers to gladly die in battle,
I am not as good as Rén Ān."
Rén Ān replied:
"Resolving doubts,
determining right and wrong,
distinguishing administrative duties,
and ensuring the common people hold no resentment—
I am not as good as Tián Rén."
Emperor Wǔ laughed heartily and said:
"Excellent."
He appointed Rén Ān to oversee the Northern Army,
and sent Tián Rén to guard the border granaries along the Yellow River.
These two men made their names known throughout the land.
Later, Rén Ān was appointed as Governor of Yìzhōu,
and Tián Rén as Senior Secretary to the Chancellor.
Tián Rén submitted a memorial stating:
"Many commandery governors across the empire engage in corrupt practices for profit,
especially in Sānhé.
I request to first investigate and impeach those in Sānhé.
The governors of Sānhé all rely on powerful palace insiders
and have kinship with the Three Excellencies,
fearing nothing.
We should first rectify Sānhé to warn corrupt officials nationwide."
At that time, the governors of Hénán and Hénèi were both relatives of the Yùshǐ Dàfū Dù,
and the governor of Hédōng was a descendant of the Chancellor Shí.
At that time, nine members of the Shí clan held positions of two thousand piculs,
at the peak of their power and prestige.
Tián Rén repeatedly memorialized about this.
Excellency Dù and the Shí clan sent someone to apologize,
saying to Tián Shàoqīng:
"We dare not make any statements,
but hope Shàoqīng does not falsely accuse or defame us."
After Tián Rén investigated Sānhé,
all three governors were handed over to the officials and executed.
When Tián Rén returned to report,
Emperor Wǔ was pleased,
considering him capable of fearing no powerful opposition,
and appointed him as the Chancellor's Rectifier,
whose authority shook the empire.
Later, when the Crown Prince was involved in military affairs,
the Chancellor personally led troops,
ordering the Rectifier to guard the city gates.
The Rectifier, considering the Crown Prince's blood relation to the emperor,
and that father and son should not be forced into conflict,
left his post and passed by the imperial tombs.
At that time, Emperor Wǔ was at Gānquán,
and sent the Yùshǐ Dàfū Bào Jūn
to reprimand the Chancellor,
"Why did you let the Crown Prince escape?"
The Chancellor replied,
"I ordered the Rectifier to guard the city gates, but he released the Crown Prince."
A memorial was sent to inform the emperor,
requesting the arrest of the Rectifier.
The Rectifier was handed over to the officials
and executed.
At that time, Rén Ān was the Northern Army Emissary and Protector of the Army.
The Crown Prince positioned his troops outside the Southern Gate of the Northern Army,
summoned Rén Ān,
and gave him the tally, ordering him to dispatch troops.
Rén Ān bowed and received the tally,
entered the camp,
and closed the gates, not sending out troops.
When Emperor Wǔ heard of this,
he thought Rén Ān was feigning compliance,
not assisting in the matter,
asking why.
Rén Ān had caned and humiliated a minor official in charge of funds in the Northern Army,
who submitted a memorial stating
that Rén Ān had received the Crown Prince's tally
and said,
"I hope to get the fresh and good ones from him."
The memorial reached the emperor,
and Emperor Wǔ said:
"This is a crafty old official.
Seeing the military conflict arise,
he wanted to sit back and watch the outcome,
intending to side with the winner—
he had a divided heart.
Rén Ān has committed numerous capital offenses,
but I often spared him.
Now he harbors deceit
and disloyal intentions."
Rén Ān was handed over to the officials
and executed.
For when the moon is full, it wanes;
when things reach their peak, they decline—
this is the constant way of heaven and earth.
Those who know advancement but not retreat,
long enjoying wealth and honor,
accumulate calamities that become hauntings.
Thus, when Fàn Lǐ left Yuè,
declining official posts,
his name was passed down to later ages,
remembered for millennia—
how could others match this?
Let those who come after take careful heed.
Biǎn Què
was a man from Zhèng in Bóhǎi Commandery,
whose surname was Qín,
and personal name Yuèrén.
In his youth, he was the chief of a guesthouse.
A guest named Chángsāng Jūn passed through,
and Biǎn Què alone found him extraordinary,
always treating him with respect.
Chángsāng Jūn also knew Biǎn Què was no ordinary man.
After over ten years of interaction,
he called Biǎn Què for a private talk,
and during a quiet moment said:
"I have secret prescriptions,
but I am old
and wish to pass them to you.
Do not reveal them."
Biǎn Què said:
"I respectfully agree."
Then he took medicine from his bosom and gave it to Biǎn Què:
"Take this with water from above the pond,
and in thirty days, you will perceive the unseen."
He then gave all his secret prescription books to Biǎn Què.
Suddenly, he vanished—
likely not a mortal being.
Biǎn Què followed his words and took the medicine for thirty days,
gaining the ability to see people through walls.
Using this to examine illnesses,
he could see all the obstructions in the five organs,
though he only used pulse diagnosis as a pretext.
He practiced medicine sometimes in Qí,
sometimes in Zhào.
In Zhào, he was known as Biǎn Què.
During the reign of Jìn Zhāogōng,
the senior officials were powerful while the ducal clan was weak.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ served as a senior official,
monopolizing state affairs.
When Jiǎnzǐ fell ill
and remained unconscious for five days,
the officials all grew fearful,
so they summoned Biǎn Què.
Biǎn Què entered to examine the illness,
and upon exiting,
Dǒng Ānyú asked Biǎn Què about it.
Biǎn Què said:
"His pulse is normal,
so why the astonishment?
In the past, Qín Mùgōng once experienced this,
and after seven days he awoke.
On the day he awoke,
he told Gōngsūn Zhī and Zǐyú:
'I visited the emperor's abode and was greatly delighted.
The reason I stayed so long
was because I had something to learn there.
The emperor told me:
"The state of Jìn will face great turmoil,
unsettled for five generations.
Afterward, it will produce a hegemon,
who will die before growing old.
The hegemon's son will cause men and women in your state to have no distinctions."'
Gōngsūn Zhī recorded this and stored it away,
and the Qín strategies thus emerged.
The chaos of Duke Xiàn,
the hegemony of Duke Wén,
and Duke Xiāng's defeat of the Qín army at Xiáo followed by indulgence in debauchery—
these are things you have heard of.
Now your lord's illness is the same,
within three days he will surely awaken,
and upon awakening, he will have something to say."
After two and a half days,
Jiǎnzǐ awoke
and addressed the officials:
"I visited the emperor's abode and was greatly delighted,
roaming with all the spirits in the heavens,
where magnificent music played nine times and myriad dances performed—
unlike the music of the three dynasties,
its sounds stirred the heart.
A bear appeared and tried to seize me,
but the emperor ordered me to shoot it,
I hit the bear,
and it died.
Then a brown bear came,
I shot it as well,
hit the brown bear,
and it died.
The emperor was very pleased
and bestowed upon me two bamboo cases,
both with duplicates.
I saw a child by the emperor's side,
and the emperor entrusted me with a Dí dog,
saying:
'When your son reaches maturity, give this to him.'
The emperor also told me:
'The state of Jìn will decline over generations,
and perish after seven.
The Yíng clan will greatly defeat the Zhōu people west of Fànkuí,
yet they too will not possess it.'"
Dǒng Ānyú received these words,
recorded and stored them.
He relayed Biǎn Què's words to Jiǎnzǐ,
who then granted Biǎn Què forty thousand mǔ of land.
Later, Biǎn Què passed through Guó.
The crown prince of Guó had died,
and Biǎn Què arrived at the palace gate of Guó,
asking a chamberlain fond of remedies:
"What illness did the crown prince have,
that the state conducted excessive exorcisms over all other matters?"
The chamberlain replied:
"The crown prince suffered from irregular blood and vital energy,
intertwined and unable to disperse,
erupting violently outward,
thus causing internal harm.
His spirit could not restrain the evil energy,
which accumulated without release,
leading to yang relaxation and yin tension,
hence a sudden collapse and death."
Biǎn Què asked:
"When did he die?"
The reply:
"From cockcrow until now."
He asked:
"Has the body been encoffined?"
Answer:
"Not yet,
he has been dead for less than half a day."
"Inform them that I, Qín Yuèrén from the Bó Hǎi area of Qí,
residing in Zhèng,
have not yet had the honor to pay respects in person.
Hearing of the crown prince's unfortunate death,
I can revive him."
The chamberlain said:
"Sir, are you not deceiving us?
How can you claim the crown prince can be revived!
I have heard that in ancient times,
there was a physician Yú Fū
who treated illnesses not with decoctions or wines,
stone needles or traction,
massage, cautery, or poultices,
but with one touch revealing the illness's response,
following the transport points of the five organs,
he would cut skin and part muscles,
unblock vessels and tie tendons,
hold the marrow and brain,
cleanse the diaphragm and grasp the membranes,
wash the intestines and stomach,
rinse the five organs,
refining essence and transforming the body.
If your methods could match this,
then the crown prince might be revived;
if not and you still claim to revive him,
you couldn't even tell it to a babbling infant."
After a long while,
Biǎn Què looked up and sighed:
"Your approach to medicine
is like viewing the sky through a tube,
or observing patterns through a crack.
My methods
do not rely solely on pulse-taking, observation, listening, or inquiry
to identify the illness's location.
Hearing of the illness's yang aspect,
I deduce its yin;
hearing of its yin,
I deduce its yang.
The illness manifests in major signs,
and within a thousand lǐ,
my determinations are numerous,
not to be doubted.
If you doubt my words,
try examining the crown prince—
you should hear ringing in his ears and flaring nostrils,
and along his thighs to the groin,
it should still be warm."
Upon hearing Biǎn Què's words,
the chamberlain's eyes stared unblinkingly,
his tongue stuck out and wouldn't retract,
so he went in to report to the ruler of Guó.
The ruler, greatly startled,
came out to meet Biǎn Què at the central gate,
saying:
"I have long privately heard of your noble virtue,
yet never had the chance to pay respects.
Now that you pass through our small state,
fortunately you aid us—
this humble servant of a remote state is most grateful.
With you, there is life;
without you, abandonment to fill the ditches,
eternal departure without return."
Before he finished speaking,
he choked with sobs, chest heaving,
spirit scattered and distraught,
tears streaming continuously,
dazed with eyelids heavy,
grief beyond self-control,
his countenance altered.
Biǎn Què said:
"The crown prince's illness
is what is called
'corpse syncope.'
When yang enters the yin,
agitating the stomach's wrappings,
affecting the meridians and collaterals,
separating down to the triple burner
and bladder,
so yang pulses descend,
yin pulses rise in contention,
blocking the meeting energy,
yin ascending while yang turns inward,
downward and inward drumming without rising,
upward and outward cut off and unresponsive,
above, severed yang collaterals,
below, broken yin connections,
with yin broken and yang severed,
complexion faded and pulses chaotic,
hence the body lies still as if dead.
The crown prince is not dead.
When yang enters the yin at the organ barriers, there is life;
when yin enters the yang at the organ barriers, there is death.
All these occurrences
are sudden attacks during syncope of the five organs.
A skilled physician can address them,
while a clumsy one may hesitate and fail."
Biǎn Què then had his disciple Zǐ Yáng sharpen needles and grind stones,
to perform acupuncture at the three yáng and five confluence points.
After a short while,
the crown prince revived.
He then had Zǐ Bào prepare a fifty-percent moxibustion treatment,
using the eight-reduction formula to blend and boil it,
and applied moxibustion alternately under both armpits.
The crown prince sat up.
Further adjusting the yīn and yáng balance,
he merely took the decoction for twenty days and recovered as before.
Hence, the whole world regarded Biǎn Què as capable of raising the dead.
Biǎn Què said:
"Yuè Rén is not able to raise the dead;
this one was destined to live,
Yuè Rén merely enabled him to rise."
Biǎn Què visited Qí,
and Qí Huán Hóu received him as a guest.
Entering the court for an audience,
he said:
"You have an illness in the skin's texture;
if not treated, it will deepen."
Huán Hóu said:
"I have no illness."
Biǎn Què left,
and Huán Hóu said to his attendants:
"Physicians are fond of profit,
wanting to claim credit for treating the non-ill."
Five days later,
Biǎn Què saw him again,
saying:
"You have an illness in the blood vessels;
if not treated, I fear it will deepen."
Huán Hóu said:
"I have no illness."
Biǎn Què left,
and Huán Hóu was displeased.
Five days later,
Biǎn Què saw him again,
saying:
"You have an illness between the intestines and stomach;
if not treated, it will deepen."
Huán Hóu did not respond.
Biǎn Què left,
and Huán Hóu was displeased.
Five days later,
Biǎn Què saw him again,
but upon sighting Huán Hóu, he retreated and fled.
Huán Hóu sent someone to ask the reason.
Biǎn Què said:
"When the illness resides in the skin's texture,
it can be reached by decoctions and moxibustion;
in the blood vessels,
it can be reached by needles and stones;
when it is in the intestines and stomach,
it can be reached by medicinal wines;
but when it is in the bone marrow,
even the Director of Fate can do nothing about it.
Now it is in the bone marrow,
therefore I have no more requests to make."
Five days later,
Huán Hóu fell ill,
and sent someone to summon Biǎn Què,
but Biǎn Què had already fled.
Huán Hóu then died.
If a sage foresees the subtle signs,
enabling a good physician to act early,
then the illness can be cured,
and the body can be saved.
What people worry about
is having many illnesses;
and what physicians worry about
is having few methods.
Hence, there are six cases of incurable illnesses:
arrogance and willfulness without regard for reason,
is the first incurable;
valuing wealth lightly and the body heavily,
is the second incurable;
inability to regulate clothing and food,
is the third incurable;
imbalance of yīn and yáng,
with unstable visceral energy,
is the fourth incurable;
physical weakness preventing medication intake,
is the fifth incurable;
believing in shamans rather than physicians,
is the sixth incurable.
If any one of these is present,
then it is severely difficult to treat.
Biǎn Què was renowned throughout the land.
Passing through Hándān,
hearing that women were esteemed there,
he became a specialist in women's diseases;
passing through Luòyáng,
hearing that the Zhōu people cherished the elderly,
he became a specialist in ear, eye, and paralysis ailments;
arriving in Xiányáng,
hearing that the Qín people loved children,
he became a pediatrician:
adapting to local customs.
The Qín Grand Physician Lǐ Xī, knowing his own skills were inferior to Biǎn Què's,
had him assassinated.
To this day, those in the world who speak of pulse diagnosis
trace it back to Biǎn Què.
The Grand Granary Master,
was the chief of the Qí state granary,
a man of Línzī,
with the surname Chúnyú,
and given name Yì.
From youth, he delighted in medical arts.
In the eighth year of Empress Dowager Lǚ's reign,
he further studied under Yáng Qìng, a Gōngchéng from Yuánlǐ in the same commandery.
Qìng was over seventy years old,
had no sons,
made Yì discard all his old formulas,
and instead gave him all his secret prescriptions,
transmitting the pulse books of Huángdì
and Biǎn Què,
diagnosing illnesses by the five colors,
knowing life and death in people,
resolving doubts,
determining treatability,
and discussions on medicinals,
all very refined.
After studying for three years,
he treated people's illnesses,
determining life and death with frequent accuracy.
However, he traveled among the feudal lords,
not settling down at home,
and sometimes refused to treat patients,
so many sick families resented him.
In the fourth year of Emperor Wén's reign,
someone submitted a report accusing Yì,
and for his criminal penalty, he was to be escorted west to Cháng'ān.
Yì had five daughters,
who followed him weeping.
Yì grew angry,
and scolded them:
"Having borne children but no sons,
in times of crisis, there is no one to rely on!"
Thereupon, his youngest daughter Tí Yíng, saddened by her father's words,
followed her father west.
She submitted a petition stating:
"My father served as an official,
praised in Qí for his integrity and fairness,
now he faces punishment for breaking the law.
I deeply grieve that the dead cannot live again and the punished cannot be restored,
even if they wish to reform and start anew,
there is no way to do so,
ultimately impossible.
I wish to offer myself as a government slave,
to redeem my father's punishment,
enabling him to reform and start anew."
The petition reached the emperor,
who was moved by her intent,
and that year, the corporal punishment laws were abolished.
Yì was at home,
when an edict summoned him to inquire about how many people he had treated, verifying life and death outcomes,
and who they were by name.
The edict asked the former Grand Granary Chief Chén Yì:
"What are your specialized skills,
and what illnesses can you treat?
Do you have any books on them or not?
From whom did you receive your learning?
How many years did you study?
Have you had verified cases,
from which counties and villages were the people?
What illnesses did they have?
After medical treatment,
what were the conditions of their illnesses like?
Answer in full detail."
Chén Yì replied:
From my youth,
I had an interest in medicine,
but most of the remedies I tried from medical texts proved ineffective.
Until the eighth year of Empress Lü's reign,
I met my teacher, Gōngchéng Yáng Qìng from Yuánlǐ in Línzī.
Yáng Qìng was over seventy years old,
and I was able to meet and serve him.
He said to me:
"Discard all your formula books,
for they are incorrect.
I possess pulse texts passed down from ancient masters, from Huángdì
and Biǎn Què,
which use the five colors to diagnose illness,
determine whether a person will live or die,
resolve uncertainties,
and decide what is treatable,
along with texts on pharmaceutical theory,
all extremely refined.
My household is wealthy,
and I am fond of you, sir,
so I wish to teach you all my secret formula texts."
I, Chún Yù Yì, immediately replied:
"I am most fortunate;
this is beyond what I dared hope for."
I then stepped back from my mat, bowed twice in reverence,
and received from him the pulse texts: the Upper and Lower Classics,
Five Colors Diagnosis,
Unusual Breathing Techniques,
Assessing Yīn-Yáng External Changes,
Pharmaceutical Theory,
Stone Spirit,
and the forbidden texts on connecting yīn and yáng.
I received, studied, interpreted, and tested them
for about a year.
The following year, I began applying them,
and they proved effective,
though I was not yet proficient.
After serving him for about three years in total,
I started treating people,
diagnosing illnesses and determining life and death,
with successful results,
becoming skilled.
Now Yáng Qìng has been dead for about ten years,
and I have completed my three years of study,
being thirty-nine years old.
The Attendant Censor of Qí, Chéng, complained of having a headache,
and I, Chún Yù Yì, felt his pulse,
then told him:
"Your illness is severe,
and I cannot speak of it openly."
After leaving,
I privately told his younger brother, Chāng:
"This illness is an internal abscess,
developing within the intestines and stomach.
In five days, it will swell into a carbuncle,
and in eight days, he will vomit pus and die."
Chéng's illness resulted from drinking alcohol and engaging in intimate relations.
Chéng indeed died as predicted.
The reason I knew Chéng's illness
was that when I palpated his pulse,
I detected liver energy.
The liver energy was turbid and still,
indicating an internal blockage disease.
The Pulse Method states:
"A pulse that is long and stringy,
and does not change with the four seasons,
means the illness resides in the liver.
If harmonious, it is a channel illness;
if changing, the collateral vessels are affected."
When the channel illness is harmonious,
the illness arises from within the sinews and marrow.
If the pulse changes and ceases, with a rushing pulse,
the illness results from alcohol and intimate relations.
The reason I knew he would swell in five days
and die vomiting pus in eight days
was that when I felt his pulse,
the Shàoyáng channel was beginning to change.
A changing pulse indicates a channel illness;
when the illness passes through a person,
the person will depart.
The collateral vessels govern the illness;
at that time,
the Shàoyáng channel was blocked at the first point,
so there was internal heat but pus had not yet formed.
By the fifth point,
it reached the boundary of Shàoyáng,
and by the eighth day,
he would vomit pus and die.
Thus, at the second point, pus formed,
reaching the boundary where the carbuncle swelled,
and when it fully drained, he died.
Heat rising then scorched the Yángmíng channel,
corroding the flowing collaterals.
When the flowing collaterals are agitated, knotted pulses emerge;
when knotted pulses emerge, decay and dissolution occur,
hence the collaterals intersect.
The heat energy had already ascended,
reaching the head and causing movement,
thus the headache.
The second son of the King of Qí, an infant child, fell ill,
and I, Chún Yù Yì, was summoned to diagnose his pulse.
I reported:
"It is a diaphragm energy illness.
