The illness causes irritability and fullness,
inability to eat,
and occasional vomiting of foam.
The illness resulted from heart-worry,
and frequent suppression of food and drink."
I then prepared a Descending Energy Decoction for him to drink.
On the first day, his energy descended;
on the second day, he could eat;
on the third day, he recovered.
The reason I knew the child's illness
was that upon diagnosing his pulse,
it was heart energy,
turbulent, agitated, and channel-related,
indicating a collateral yáng illness.
The Pulse Method states:
"A pulse that comes rapidly, departs with difficulty, and is irregular
means the illness resides in the heart."
When the whole body is hot
and the pulse is exuberant,
it is double yáng.
Double yáng
afflicts the heart governor.
Thus, irritability, fullness, and inability to eat indicate the collateral vessels are affected;
if the collateral vessels are affected, blood rises and exits,
and if blood rises and exits, death follows.
This arose from a sorrowful heart,
the illness resulting from worry.
The Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace of Qí, Xún, fell ill,
and all the physicians believed it was reversal entering the center,
so they needled him.
I, Chún Yù Yì, diagnosed him
and said:
"It is gushing shàn,
which prevents one from passing urine or stool."
Xún said:
"I have been unable to pass urine or stool for three days."
I had him drink Fire-Regulating Decoction;
after one dose, he could pass urine and stool,
after two doses, he had a large bowel movement,
and after three doses, he recovered.
The illness resulted from internal causes.
The reason I knew Xún's illness
was that when I felt his pulse,
the right mouth pulse was rapid,
and the pulse lacked the energy of the five organs,
with the right mouth pulse being large and rapid.
Rapidity indicates heat in the middle and lower parts, causing gushing;
the left corresponds to the lower,
the right to the upper,
and neither responded to the five organs,
hence it was called gushing shàn.
There was internal heat,
so the urine was red.
The chief steward of the Central Palace in Qí, named Xìn, fell ill.
I, Yì, entered to examine his pulse
and informed him:
"It is the energy of a heat illness.
However, with summer sweating,
the pulse has somewhat diminished,
so you will not die."
I said:
"This illness was contracted when you bathed in flowing water and felt extreme cold,
which then turned to heat."
Xìn said:
"Yes,
indeed! Last winter,
I was sent by the king to Chǔ,
reaching the Yángzhōu River in Jǔ County,
where the bridge of Jǔ was quite damaged.
I was holding the chariot's shaft, not intending to cross yet,
when the horses startled,
and I fell immediately,
plunging into the water,
nearly dying.
The officials came promptly to rescue Xìn,
pulling me out of the water,
with my clothes completely soaked.
After a short while, my body felt cold,
then became as hot as fire,
and to this day, I cannot bear the cold."
I, Yì, then prepared a liquid decoction with a fire formula to expel the heat.
After one dose, the sweating ceased;
after two doses, the heat dissipated;
after three doses, the illness was cured.
He then took the medicine,
and within twenty days,
he was free of illness.
The reason I knew Xìn's illness
was that when I felt his pulse,
it was solely yīn.
The pulse method states:
"In heat illnesses, if yīn and yáng intersect, death occurs."
Upon examination, they did not intersect,
but were solely yīn.
When it is solely yīn,
the pulse follows a clear pattern and leads to recovery;
even if the heat is not entirely gone,
the patient can still survive.
The kidney energy occasionally appears turbid,
and at the Tàiyīn pulse opening, it is sparse,
indicating water energy.
The kidneys inherently govern water,
so I knew from this.
If treatment were delayed even briefly,
it would turn into alternating chills and fever.
The Queen Dowager of Qí fell ill,
summoning me, Yì, to examine her pulse.
I said:
"Wind dàn has invaded the bladder,
making it difficult to pass urine or feces,
and the urine is red."
I, Yì, administered a fire formula decoction,
and after one dose, she could urinate and defecate;
after two doses, the illness was cured,
and her urine returned to normal.
The illness resulted from sweating profusely while bathing.
Bathing means
removing clothes and drying sweat.
The reason I knew the Queen Dowager's illness
is that I, Yì, examined her pulse,
feeling the Tàiyīn opening,
which was moist, indicating wind energy.
The pulse method states:
"If deep, it is large and firm;
if floating, it is large and tight,
indicating the illness resides in the kidneys."
But the kidney pulse felt contrary to this,
being large and agitated.
Large indicates
bladder energy;
agitated means
there is heat inside, causing red urine.
Cáo Shānfū from Zhāngwǔ Lane in Qí fell ill,
and I, Yì, examined his pulse,
saying:
"It is lung consumption dàn,
accompanied by alternating chills and fever."
I then told his family:
"He will die,
it is incurable.
Attend to his care,
this is not a case for medical treatment."
The rule states:
"After three days, he will become manic,
rising recklessly to walk,
wanting to run;
after five days, he will die."
He died exactly as predicted.
Shānfū's illness resulted from great anger followed by sexual intercourse.
The reason I knew Shānfū's illness
is that I, Yì, felt his pulse,
which indicated lung energy heat.
The pulse method states:
"Uneven and unsteady,
the form is depleted."
This is due to the five viscera being affected through meridians from high and distant counts,
so when felt, it was uneven and intermittent.
Uneven means
blood does not reside in its place;
intermittent means
irregular beats occur together,
suddenly agitated, suddenly large.
This indicates the two collateral pulses are severed,
hence incurable and fatal.
The reason for the added chills and fever
is that the person's vitality is seized.
Vitality seizure means
the form is depleted;
when the form is depleted,
it is not suitable for moxibustion, stone needles, or potent medicines.
Before I, Yì, went to diagnose him,
the royal physician of Qí had first examined Shānfū's illness,
applying moxibustion at the foot Shàoyáng pulse opening
and administering Bànxià pills,
causing the patient to have violent diarrhea,
leaving the abdomen empty;
then moxibustion was applied to the Shàoyīn pulse,
which severely damaged the liver's rigidity and cut deeply,
thus further depleting the patient's energy,
leading to the added chills and fever.
The reason he became manic after three days
is that one liver collateral connects and gathers below the breast at the Yángmíng,
so when the collateral is severed,
it opens the Yángmíng pulse,
and when the Yángmíng pulse is injured,
it causes manic running.
The reason he died after five days
is that the liver and heart are five units apart,
so it is said that in five days, it ends,
and when it ends, death occurs.
Pān Mǎnrú, the commandant of Qí, had an illness with lower abdominal pain,
and I, Yì, examined his pulse,
saying:
"It is a accumulated jiă mass."
I, Yì, then told the grand coachman of Qí, Ráo,
and the internal historian, Yáo:
"If the commandant does not stop his internal activities,
he will die in thirty days."
After more than twenty days,
he died with bloody urine.
The illness resulted from alcohol and internal activities.
The reason I knew Pān Mǎnrú's illness
is that I, Yì, felt his pulse as deep, small, and weak,
with sudden gatherings,
indicating spleen energy.
The right pulse opening's energy was tight and small,
showing jiă energy.
Multiplying in sequence,
he died in thirty days.
If all three yīn pulses beat together,
it follows the rule;
if not all beat together,
the decision lies in a shorter period;
if one beat is intermittent,
it is nearer.
Thus, his three yīn pulses beat together,
and he died with bloody urine as before.
Zhào Zhāng, the chancellor of the Marquis of Yángxū, fell ill,
summoning me, Yì.
All the physicians thought it was internal cold,
but I, Yì, examined his pulse and said:
"It is tòng wind."
Tòng wind means
whatever is eaten or drunk is regurgitated immediately without retention.
The rule states:
"Death in five days,"
but he died only after ten days.
The illness resulted from alcohol.
The reason I knew Zhào Zhāng's illness
is that I, Yì, felt his pulse,
which came smoothly,
indicating internal wind energy.
That food and drink are regurgitated immediately without retention
should, by rule, lead to death in five days,
according to the previous boundary method.
He died only after ten days
because
he was fond of congee,
so his central organs were substantial,
and because they were substantial, he exceeded the deadline.
The master's saying goes:
"Those who retain grain exceed the deadline;
those who do not retain grain fall short of it."
The King of Jìběi fell ill,
summoned me, Yì, to examine his pulse,
and I said:
"Wind reversal with chest fullness."
I then prepared a medicinal wine,
after consuming three dàn of it,
the illness was cured.
It was caused by sweating and lying prostrate on the ground.
The reason I knew the King of Jìběi's illness
was that when I felt his pulse,
it indicated wind energy,
and the heart pulse was turbid.
According to medical principles,
"when it excessively enters his yang,
yang energy depletes and yin energy enters."
When yin energy enters and expands,
then cold energy rises and hot energy descends,
hence the chest fullness.
As for sweating and lying prostrate on the ground,
when feeling his pulse,
the energy was yin.
Yin energy
inevitably causes the illness to enter internally,
manifesting as dripping water.
The wife of the Minister of Works of Qí's Běigōng, named Chūyú, fell ill,
all physicians believed it was wind entering internally,
with the illness rooted in the lungs,
so they needled her foot Shàoyáng pulse.
I examined her pulse
and said:
"The illness is qi hernia,
lodged in the bladder,
making urination and defecation difficult,
with dark urine.
When exposed to cold energy, it causes enuresis,
and makes the abdomen swell."
Chūyú's illness resulted from wanting to urinate but being unable to,
followed by sexual intercourse.
The reason I knew Chūyú's illness
was that her pulse felt large and solid,
its arrival difficult,
which is the movement of the Juéyīn channel.
A pulse that arrives with difficulty
indicates hernia qi lodged in the bladder.
The reason for abdominal swelling
is that the collaterals of the Juéyīn channel knot in the lower abdomen.
When the Juéyīn channel is impaired, the pulse knots and moves,
and movement causes abdominal swelling.
I then applied moxibustion to her foot Juéyīn pulse,
once on each side,
immediately stopping enuresis and clearing the urine,
and relieving the lower abdominal pain.
I then changed to a fire formula decoction for her to drink,
and in three days the hernia qi dispersed,
and she recovered.
The nanny of the King of Jìběi complained of hot feet and oppression,
I told her:
"It is heat reversal."
Then I needled the center of her soles three times each,
pressing without drawing blood,
and the illness quickly resolved.
It was caused by drinking to extreme drunkenness.
The King of Jìběi summoned me to examine the pulses of his attending maidens,
coming to the maiden Shù,
Shù appeared without illness.
I told the Chief of the Yongxiang:
"Shù has a spleen injury,
cannot be overworked,
by principle, she will vomit blood and die in spring."
I said to the King:
"What skills does the talented maiden Shù have?"
The King said:
"She is fond of methods,
highly skilled,
innovative in applying techniques,
last year bought from the common market,
for four million seven hundred thousand cash,
among four companions."
The King asked:
"Could she be ill?"
I replied:
"Shù is seriously ill,
under the principle of fatal illness."
The King summoned to see her,
her complexion unchanged,
thought it not so,
and did not sell her to the feudal lords.
Come spring,
Shù served with a sword following the King to the restroom,
the King left,
Shù remained behind,
the King sent someone to summon her,
she immediately collapsed in the restroom,
vomited blood and died.
Her illness resulted from flowing sweat.
Flowing sweat
indicates an internally severe illness by principle,
with glossy hair and radiant complexion,
and pulse not weakened,
this is also an illness of internal blockage.
The Grandee of Qí had a tooth decay illness,
I applied moxibustion to his left Great Yángmíng pulse,
then prepared a bitter参 decoction,
gargling three shēng daily,
after five or six days,
the illness was cured.
It was caused by wind,
and sleeping with an open mouth,
eating without rinsing.
The beauty of the King of Zīchuān was pregnant but not delivering,
summoned me.
I went,
gave her a pinch of làngdàng medicine,
to drink with wine,
and she promptly delivered.
I again examined her pulse,
and the pulse was agitated.
Agitation indicates residual illness,
so I gave her a dose of saltpeter,
causing bleeding,
with blood like beans, about five or six specks.
The servant of the Chancellor of Qí's retainer entered the palace at court,
I saw him eating outside the women's quarters,
and observed illness in his complexion.
I then informed the eunuch Píng.
Píng was fond of pulse diagnosis,
studied under me,
I showed him the retainer's servant's illness,
and told him:
"This is an injury to the spleen energy,
by spring, diaphragm blockage will occur,
unable to eat or drink,
by principle, he will die from bloody diarrhea in summer."
The eunuch Píng went and told the Chancellor:
"Your retainer's servant is ill,
seriously ill,
with days to his death."
The Chancellor asked:
"How do you know?"
He said:
"When you entered the palace at court,
your retainer's servant was eating outside the women's quarters,
Píng and I, Cānggōng, stood by,
and he showed me, saying,
such illness leads to death."
The Chancellor then summoned the retainer and asked:
"Is your servant ill or not?"
The retainer said:
"The servant is not ill,
has no bodily pain."
Come spring, he indeed fell ill,
by the fourth month,
had bloody diarrhea and died.
The reason I knew the servant's illness
was that spleen energy circulates through the five organs,
injured areas intersect,
hence the complexion of spleen injury,
looking sallow and withered,
upon close inspection, like the hue of dead blue.
Other physicians did not know,
thought it was a major parasite,
unaware of the spleen injury.
The reason for death in spring
is that stomach energy is yellow,
yellow represents earth energy,
earth cannot overcome wood,
hence death in spring.
The reason for death in summer
is according to pulse principles:
"Severe illness with a smooth and clear pulse is called internal blockage,"
in internal blockage illness,
one does not feel the pain,
the heart is anxious but without suffering.
If another illness is added,
death occurs in mid-spring;
if recovery is smooth,
it lasts a season.
The reason he died in the fourth month
is that when examined, his recovery was smooth.
Smooth recovery
means the person was still plump.
The servant's illness resulted from frequent sweating,
being heated by fire and then going out into strong wind.
The King of Zīchuān fell ill,
summoned me, Yì, to diagnose his pulse,
and said:
"I have a heavy sensation rising upwards,
with headache and body fever,
making me feel irritable and stifled."
I immediately applied cold water to his head,
and needled the Foot Yángmíng meridian,
three points on each side,
and the illness quickly subsided.
The illness was caused by lying down with wet hair after washing it.
The diagnosis was as before;
the reason for the uprising reversal,
was heat from the head reaching the shoulders.
At the home of Huáng Chángqīng, brother of the Yellow Concubine of the King of Qí, wine was served to summon guests,
and I, Yì, was summoned.
All the guests were seated,
but food had not yet been served.
I saw the Queen's younger brother Sòng Jiàn,
and told him:
"You are ill.
Four or five days ago,
you had pain in your waist and ribs, unable to bend or straighten up,
and also could not pass urine.
If not treated urgently,
the illness will enter and soak the kidneys.
Before it lodges in the five viscera,
treat it urgently.
The illness is now lodging in the kidney's moisture,
this is what is called
'Kidney Impediment'
Sòng Jiàn said:
"Indeed,
I, Jiàn, did have pain in the waist and spine.
Four or five days ago,
it was raining,
the various sons-in-law of the Huáng family saw a foundation stone under my house,
and started playing with it,
I also wanted to imitate them,
but when I tried, I couldn't lift it,
so I put it back down.
By evening, my waist and spine hurt,
I couldn't urinate,
and it hasn't healed until now."
Jiàn's illness was caused by his fondness for lifting heavy objects.
The reason I knew about Jiàn's illness
was that I observed his complexion;
the Tàiyáng area was dry,
and the kidney region up to the border below the waist was about forty percent withered,
so I knew it had started four or five days ago.
I then prepared a softening decoction for him to take,
and in about eighteen days, the illness was cured.
Hán Nǚ, an attendant of the King of Jìběi, had pain in her waist and back,
with alternating chills and fever,
and all the physicians thought it was a case of chills and fever.
I diagnosed her pulse,
and said:
"Internal cold,
causing menstruation not to flow."
I immediately applied medication by fumigation,
and it quickly flowed down,
the illness was cured.
The illness was caused by desiring a man but not being able to have one.
The reason I knew about Hán Nǚ's illness
was that when diagnosing her pulse,
palpating it,
the kidney pulse was choppy and discontinuous.
Being choppy and discontinuous means
it comes with difficulty,
and is hard, hence menstruation does not flow.
The liver pulse was taut,
emerging from the left opening,
so it was said she desired a man but could not have one.
In Línzī, at Fàn Village, a woman named Bó Wú was seriously ill,
and all the physicians thought it was severe chills and fever,
and she would die,
incurable.
I diagnosed her pulse,
and said:
"It's a worm accumulation."
The worm accumulation as an illness
causes enlarged abdomen,
the upper skin yellow and coarse,
and upon palpation, it feels uneasy.
I gave her a pinch of yuán huā to drink,
and immediately worms came out, about several shēng,
the illness was cured,
and in thirty days she was as before.
The worm illness was caused by cold dampness;
the cold damp qi stagnated severely and did not disperse,
transforming into worms.
The reason I knew Bó Wú's illness
was that upon palpating her pulse,
and feeling her chi skin,
her chi was rough like thorns,
yet her body hair and hair were beautiful and abundant,
which is a sign of worm qi.
Her complexion being lustrous
indicated no evil qi in the central organs or serious illness.
The Marshal of Qí, Chúnyú, fell ill,
I palpated his pulse,
and told him:
"You should have a reversal wind illness.
The symptoms of reversal wind
are that food and drink, upon passing the throat, immediately pass out from below.
The illness was caused by eating full and then running quickly."
Marshal Chúnyú said:
"I went to the king's palace and ate horse liver,
ate very full,
saw wine coming,
immediately left and ran,
hurried quickly home,
and then had diarrhea dozens of times."
I told him:
"Prepare a fire-aligned rice water drink for him,
and in seven or eight days he should recover."
At the time, physician Qín Xìn was nearby;
after I left,
Xìn said to the Attendant Guard on the left and right:
"What does Yì think Marshal Chúnyú's illness is?"
They said:
"He thinks it's reversal wind,
and can be treated."
Xìn then laughed and said:
"He doesn't know.
Marshal Chúnyú's illness,
by rule, should result in death after nine days."
But after nine days, he did not die;
his family summoned me again.
I went to inquire about him,
and it was exactly as I had diagnosed.
I then prepared a fire-aligned rice water,
had him take it,
and in seven or eight days the illness was cured.
The reason I knew
was that when diagnosing his pulse,
palpating it,
it fully matched the method.
His illness was favorable,
so he did not die.
Pò Shí, a Gentleman of the Palace of Qí, fell ill,
I diagnosed his pulse,
and told him:
"The lung is injured,
incurable,
you will die by passing blood in urine after ten days, on Dīnghài day."
Then after eleven days,
he passed blood in urine and died.
Pò Shí's illness
was caused by falling from a horse onto a stiff rock.
The reason I knew Pò Shí's illness
was that upon palpating his pulse,
I detected the lung's yin qi,
which came scattered,
arriving through several pathways but not unified.
And his complexion also corresponded to it.
The reason I knew he fell from a horse
was that upon palpation, I found a turning yin pulse.
The turning yin pulse enters the virtual interior,
and rides the lung pulse.
When the lung pulse is scattered,
the complexion necessarily changes accordingly.
The reason he did not die within the predicted period
is as the teacher said:
"If the patient can take grain, they exceed the period;
if they cannot take grain, they do not reach the period."
This person was fond of millet,
millet governs the lung,
so he exceeded the period.
The reason he passed blood in urine
is as the pulse diagnosis method says:
"If the patient tends to enjoy shady places, they die favorably;
if they tend to enjoy sunny places, they die adversely."
This person liked to be quiet by himself,
not agitated,
and also sat peacefully for long times,
leaning on a table to sleep,
so the blood discharged downward.
The personal physician Suì of the King of Qí fell ill,
and prepared the five minerals himself to take.
I, Yì, happened to pass by him,
and Suì said to me:
"I, unworthy, am ill,
I am fortunate that you diagnose me, Suì."
I, the minister, immediately diagnosed him,
and informed him:
"Your illness is internal heat.
The theory states
'For internal heat with no urination,
one must not take the five minerals.'
Mineral-based medicines are potent and harsh,
since taking them you have not been able to urinate frequently,
quickly stop taking them.
The complexion indicates an abscess will develop."
Suì said:
"Biǎn Què said
'Use yīn stones to treat yīn illnesses,
use yáng stones to treat yáng illnesses.'
Now medicinal stones have formulations matching yīn and yáng, water and fire,
so for internal heat,
one should use yīn stones and gentle formulations to treat it;
for internal cold,
one should use yáng stones and strong formulations to treat it."
I, the minister, said:
"Your reasoning is far from correct.
Although Biǎn Què spoke thus,
one must still carefully diagnose,
establish measures,
set standards,
apply balances,
integrate the methods for assessing complexion and pulse, exterior and interior, excess and deficiency, compliance and defiance,
correlate these with the patient's activity, rest, and breathing patterns,
only then can one discuss treatment.
The theory states
'When a yáng disease resides internally,
and a yīn manifestation appears externally,
do not add harsh medicines or stone needles.'
For if harsh medicines enter the center,
then the pathogenic factors are repelled,
and the stagnant qi becomes deeper.
The diagnostic method states
'When two yīn correspond externally,
and one yáng connects internally,
one must not use strong medicines.'
If strong medicines enter, they stir the yáng,
the yīn illness further declines,
the yáng illness becomes more pronounced,
pathogenic factors spread,
causing severe distress at the transport points,
and angrily erupting into abscesses."
A hundred or so days after I warned him,
indeed an abscess developed above his breast,
entered the supraclavicular fossa,
and he died. This refers to the general principles of medical theory,
there must be guiding principles.
If an unskilled doctor fails to master any one aspect,
the patterns and principles of yīn and yáng are lost.
When the King of Qí was formerly the Hóu of Yángxū,
he was severely ill,
all the physicians considered it Júe (reversal).
I, the minister, felt his pulse,
and diagnosed it as Bì (blockage),
its root below the right rib,
large like an overturned cup,
causing panting,
rebellious qi, and inability to eat.
I immediately used a fire-formulation decoction and had him drink it,
in six days the qi descended;
then I had him change to pill medicine,
after another six days,
the illness was cured.
The illness was acquired internally.
At the time of diagnosis, I could not explain its channel theory in detail,
but largely recognized where the disease was located.
I, the minister, once diagnosed Chéng Kāifāng from Wǔdū Lane in Ānyáng,
Kāifāng himself claimed to have no illness,
I told him he suffered from Tà Fēng illness,
in three years his four limbs would not obey him,
would make him mute,
and muteness would lead to death.
Now I hear his four limbs are unusable,
he is mute but not yet dead.
The illness was acquired from frequently drinking alcohol and encountering great wind qi.
The reason I knew Chéng Kāifāng's illness,
upon diagnosis,
his pulse method, the Qí Hāi, stated:
"When the visceral qi are contrary, death."
Upon palpation,
I found the kidney pulse contrary to the lung,
the rule says:
"Death in three years."
Gōngchéng Xiàng Chǔ from Bǎn Lane in Ānlíng fell ill,
I, the minister, felt his pulse,
and said:
"Mǔ Shàn (male hernia)."
Mǔ Shàn is below the diaphragm,
connecting upward to the lung.
The illness was acquired internally.
I instructed him:
"Be careful not to do strenuous labor,
if you do strenuous labor you will certainly vomit blood and die."
Chǔ later played Cùjū (kickball),
suffered a waist Júe and cold,
sweated profusely,
and then vomited blood.
I, the minister, examined him again,
and said:
"You will die tomorrow evening."
He died then.
The illness was acquired internally.
The reason I knew Xiàng Chǔ's illness,
upon palpating his pulse I found Fān Yáng.
Fān Yáng entering the xū lǐ,
meant Chǔ would die the next day.
One Fān and one Luò,
indicates Mǔ Shàn.
I, the minister, said:
In other cases where I diagnosed, predicted life and death, and treated many illnesses,
over time I have largely forgotten them,
cannot remember them all,
and dare not report them.
They asked me, Yì:
"Among the illnesses you diagnose and treat,
many have the same name but different diagnoses,
some die, some do not die,
why is that?"
I replied:
"Illness names are often similar,
and cannot be known [just by name],
therefore the ancient sages created pulse methods,
to establish measures,
set standards,
suspend balances,
apply the marking line,
harmonize yīn and yáng,
distinguish people's pulses and name them individually,
correlating with Heaven and Earth,
integrating with the person,
thus differentiating the hundred illnesses to distinguish them,
those with skill can distinguish them,
those without skill conflate them.
However, the pulse methods are not infallibly verifiable,
when diagnosing sick people, use measures to differentiate them,
then one can distinguish those with the same name,
and determine the primary location of the illness.
Now, the cases I, Yì, have diagnosed,
all have diagnostic records.
The reason I can distinguish them is,
the methods I received from my teacher had just been mastered,
my teacher died,
therefore I recorded my diagnoses in records,
predicting life and death,
observing successes and failures in relation to pulse methods,
hence I still know them today."
They asked me, Yì:
"When you predict whether an illness will result in life or death,
sometimes it doesn't match the predicted timing,
what is the reason?"
I replied:
"These are all due to lack of moderation in diet and emotions,
or sometimes inappropriate medication,
or sometimes inappropriate acupuncture and moxibustion,
therefore they do not die within the predicted period."
They asked Chún Yì:
"You are capable of knowing life and death from illness,
discussing the appropriate use of medicine.
Have any feudal lords, kings, or great ministers ever consulted you?
And when King Wén was ill,
why didn't he seek your diagnosis and treatment?"
Chún Yì replied:
"The King of Zhào,
the King of Jiāoxī,
the King of Jǐnán,
and the King of Wú all sent people to summon me,
but I dared not go.
When King Wén was ill,
my family was poor,
and though I wished to treat people,
I truly feared officials would restrict me with appointments,
so I moved my household registration,
neglected my family livelihood,
and traveled around the country,
long seeking those skilled in medical arts.
I studied under several teachers,
fully learning their essential techniques,
comprehending their medical texts,
and interpreting their theories.
While residing in the domain of the Marquis of Yángxū,
I served the Marquis.
When he went to court,
I accompanied him to Cháng'ān,
thus gaining the opportunity to diagnose illnesses like that of Xiàng Chǔ of Ānlíng."
They asked Chún Yì:
"Do you know why King Wén's illness became terminal?"
Chún Yì replied:
"I did not see King Wén's illness,
but I privately heard he suffered from asthma,
headaches,
and blurred vision.
In my judgment,
I considered it not an illness.
I believed his obesity and accumulated essence,
with his body unable to move freely,
and muscles unable to support bones,
caused the asthma,
which shouldn't have been medically treated.
The pulse method states:
'At twenty, the pulse energy should be active;
at thirty, it should move swiftly;
at forty, one should sit calmly;
at fifty, one should rest peacefully;
at sixty and above, the energy should be deeply conserved.'
King Wén was not yet twenty,
when his pulse energy should have been active but was instead slow,
not aligning with the natural order of the four seasons.
Later I heard physicians used moxibustion, worsening his condition—
this was an error in diagnosing the illness.
In my analysis,
I believe his vital energy struggled while pathogenic energy invaded,
a condition a young person couldn't recover from,
hence he died.
Regarding what's called 'energy',
one should regulate diet,
choose calm days,
walk or ride to broaden the spirit,
thereby conditioning muscles, bones, flesh, blood, and vessels,
to release pent-up energy.
So at twenty years,
this is called
'the easily altered',
where the method shouldn't involve stone needles or moxibustion,
as such treatments would drive the energy away."
They asked Chún Yì:
"From whom did Teacher Qìng receive his knowledge?
Was he known among the feudal lords of Qí?"
He replied:
"I don't know who Qìng studied under.
Qìng's family was wealthy,
and he was skilled in medicine,
but unwilling to treat people,
likely why he wasn't known.
Qìng also told me:
'Be careful not to let my descendants know you're learning my methods.'"
They asked Chún Yì:
"What did Teacher Qìng see in you to favor you
and want to teach you all his methods?"
He replied:
"I hadn't heard of Teacher Qìng's medical skills being exceptional.
I came to know Qìng because
in my youth I enjoyed various medical arts,
I tested his methods,
and they were highly effective,
refined and excellent.
I heard Gōngsūn Guāng of Tánglǐ in Zīchuān was skilled in ancient formulas,
so I went to visit him.
I was able to meet and serve him,
receiving methods of transforming yin-yang and oral transmissions,
which I fully recorded.
When I wanted to learn all his refined formulas,
Gōngsūn Guāng said:
'My methods are exhausted;
I'm not withholding from you.
I am already aged,
with nothing more to teach.
These are the wonderful formulas I received in my youth,
all given to you—
do not teach them to others.'
I said:
'To serve before you
and receive these forbidden formulas
is my great fortune.
I would rather die than recklessly transmit them.'
After some time,
while Gōngsūn Guāng was at leisure,
I deeply discussed medical formulas with him,
and he recognized my words as refined through generations.
Teacher Guāng joyfully said:
'You will surely become a national master physician.
All my skilled acquaintances are distant;
my sibling lives in Línzī,
excelling in medical formulas—
I am not his equal.
His methods are extraordinary,
unheard of in this world.
In my middle years,
I wished to learn his methods,
but Yáng Zhōngqiàn refused,
saying
"You are not the right person."
Let us go see him together;
he will recognize your passion for medicine.
He is also elderly now,
and his family is wealthy.'
Before we could go,
Qìng's son Yīn came presenting horses,
and through Teacher Guāng's introduction to the king,
I thus became acquainted with Yīn.
Guāng also commended me to Yīn, saying:
'Yì loves medical arts;
you must treat him respectfully,
for he is a sage scholar.'
He then wrote a letter recommending me to Yáng Qìng,
thus I came to know Qìng.
I served Qìng diligently,
which is why he favored me."
They asked Chún Yì:
"Have officials or commoners ever studied your methods,
and did any completely master them?
Who were they and from where?"
He replied:
"Sòng Yì from Línzī.
He studied
the five diagnostic methods under me
for over a year.
The King of Jǐběi sent his royal physicians Gāo Qí
and Wáng Yǔ to study;
I taught them the pathways of meridians and extraordinary collaterals,
discussing the locations of acupoints,
and the flow of energy—upward, downward, inward, outward, pathogenic, normal, adverse, and smooth—
for appropriate stone needle use,
determining acupuncture and moxibustion sites,
for over a year.
The King of Zīchuān sent his granary official Féng Xìn to correct his methods;
I taught him massage techniques and their directions,
discussed medicinal methods,
determined the five flavors and preparation of balanced decoctions.
Dù Xìn, steward of the household of the Marquis of Gāoyǒng,
fond of pulse diagnosis,
came to study;
I taught him the upper and lower classics, pulse diagnosis, and the five diagnostics,
for over two years.
Táng Ān from Zhàolǐ in Línzī came to study;
I taught him the five diagnostics, upper and lower meridians,
extraordinary variations,
and the correspondence of yin-yang with the four seasons' cycles—
before he completed his studies,
he was appointed as the King of Qí's attending physician."
They asked Chún Yì:
"In diagnosing illness and determining life or death,
can you be entirely error-free?"
Chún Yì replied:
"When I treat patients,
I always first feel their pulse,
then treat them.
Those with deteriorating, adverse conditions are untreatable;
only those with smooth conditions can be treated.
If one's mind isn't precise in pulse reading,
the anticipated outcome of life or death based on treatability
may sometimes be mistaken—
I cannot be entirely error-free."
Those who can behead or capture a Grand General
shall be rewarded with five thousand catties of gold,
and enfeoffed with ten thousand households;
for a Lieutenant General,
three thousand catties,
and enfeoffed with five thousand households;
for an Assistant General,
two thousand catties,
and enfeoffed with two thousand households;
for officials of two thousand shi rank,
one thousand catties,
and enfeoffed with one thousand households;
for those of one thousand shi rank,
five hundred catties,
and enfeoffed with five hundred households:
all shall be made Marquis.
For those who surrender with their troops or cities,
a force of ten thousand men
or a city of ten thousand households
shall be treated as capturing a Grand General;
five thousand men or households,
as a Lieutenant General;
three thousand men or households,
as an Assistant General;
one thousand men or households,
as a two thousand shi official;
minor officials shall all receive titles and gold according to their rank.
Other rewards shall be doubled according to military law.
Those who already have titles and fiefs
shall have them increased, not replaced.
I hope the various kings will clearly inform their officers,
so none dare deceive them.
My wealth and resources are abundant throughout the land,
not necessarily drawn only from Wú,
and the various kings may use them day and night without exhaustion.
If there are those deserving rewards, inform me,
and I will send them accordingly.
Respectfully submitted."
When the rebellion memorials of the Seven States reached the Emperor,
he sent Tàiwèi Tiáohóu Zhōu Yàfū with thirty-six generals
to attack Wú and Chǔ;
sent Qūzhōuhóu Lì Jì to attack Zhào;
General Luán Bù to attack Qí;
and Grand General Dòu Yīng to station at Yíngyáng,
overseeing the troops of Qí and Zhào.
When the rebellion of Wú and Chǔ was reported,
before the troops were dispatched
and Dòu Yīng had not yet left,
he mentioned the former Wú Chancellor Yuán Àng.
Àng was then residing at home,
and an edict summoned him for an audience.
The Emperor was at the time coordinating troops and calculating military provisions with Cháo Cuò,
and asked Yuán Àng: "You once served as Chancellor of Wú,
do you know the character of Tián Lùbó, a minister of Wú?
Now that Wú and Chǔ have rebelled,
what is your view?"
He replied: "There is no need to worry,
they will be defeated now."
The Emperor said:
"The King of Wú mines mountains to mint coins,
boils seawater for salt,
entices the brave and ambitious of the land,
and launches his endeavor in old age.
If so, would he act without a perfect plan?
How can you say they are incapable?"
Yuán Àng replied: "Wú may have the advantages of copper and salt,
but how could they truly attract the brave and ambitious!
If Wú really had such men,
they would assist the king in righteousness,
and not rebel.
Those Wú has enticed are all unruly youths,
fugitives and corrupt coiners,
hence they follow in rebellion together."
Cháo Cuò said:
"Yuán Àng's assessment is sound."
The Emperor asked: "What strategy do you propose?"
Àng replied: "I wish for the attendants to withdraw."
The Emperor dismissed others,
leaving only Cuò present.
Àng said: "What I have to say,
should not be known by other ministers."
So Cuò was also dismissed.
Cuò hurriedly retreated to the eastern wing,
deeply resentful.
The Emperor finally asked Àng,
who replied:
"Wú and Chǔ have exchanged letters,
stating
'The sons and brothers of Emperor Gāozǔ each had their allotted lands,
now the treacherous minister Cháo Cuò arbitrarily faults the feudal lords,
seizing their territories.'
Thus, under the pretext of rebellion,
they march west to jointly eliminate Cháo Cuò,
restore their former lands, and cease.
The current plan is solely to behead Cháo Cuò,
send envoys to pardon the seven states of Wú and Chǔ,
restore their seized territories,
and then the armies can disband without bloodshed."
The Emperor remained silent for a long time,
then said:
"If it truly is as you say,
I would not spare one person to appease the world."
Àng said: "My humble plan offers no alternative,
I urge Your Majesty to consider it carefully."
He then appointed Àng as Tàicháng,
and the King of Wú's nephew Déhóu as Zōngzhèng.
Àng prepared for his journey.
Over ten days later,
the Emperor sent the Commandant of the Central Guard to summon Cuò,
deceiving him into a carriage to the eastern market.
Cuò, dressed in court robes, was beheaded at the eastern market.
Then he sent Yuán Àng to honor the ancestral temple,
and Zōngzhèng to assist the relatives,
instructing them to inform Wú as per Àng's strategy.
Upon arrival in Wú,
the Wú and Chǔ troops had already attacked Liáng's fortifications.
Zōngzhèng, due to kinship ties,
entered first to see,
urging the King of Wú to kneel and receive the decree.
The King of Wú, hearing of Yuán Àng's arrival,
knew he intended to persuade him,
laughed and responded:
"I have already become the Eastern Emperor,
whom should I kneel to?"
He refused to see Àng and detained him in the army,
intending to force him to lead troops.
Àng refused,
so they had him surrounded and guarded,
and planned to kill him,
but Àng managed to escape at night,
fleeing on foot,
heading to the Liáng army,
and eventually returned to report.
Tiáohóu, riding a six-horse relay carriage,
assembled troops at Yíngyáng.
Upon reaching Luòyáng,
he saw Jù Mèng,
and joyfully said:
"With the seven states in rebellion,
I traveled by relay to here,
not expecting to remain unscathed.
I thought the feudal lords had already secured Jù Mèng,
but Jù Mèng has not moved.
Now that I hold Yíngyáng,
there is nothing to worry about to the east."
Reaching Huáiyáng,
he asked his father Jiǎnghóu's former guest, Commandant Dèng:
"What strategy should we adopt?"
The guest said:
"The Wú troops are very sharp,
hard to confront directly.
The Chǔ troops are light,
unable to last long.
Currently, for the general's plan,
it would be best to lead troops northeast to fortify Chāngyì,
abandoning Liáng to Wú,
so Wú will concentrate its elite to attack it.
The general should dig deep moats and build high ramparts,
sending light troops to cut off the Huái-Sì River mouth,
blocking Wú's supply route.
When Wú and Liáng exhaust each other and provisions run out,
then use your full strength to control their weariness,
and defeating Wú is certain."
Tiáohóu said:
"Good."
He followed this plan,
thus fortifying south of Chāngyì,
and light troops cut off Wú's supply route.
When the King of Wú first launched the campaign,
his minister Tián Lùbó served as Grand General.
Tián Lùbó said:
"If the troops mass and march west,
without any surprise routes,
it will be hard to achieve success.
I wish to take fifty thousand men,
separately advance along the Jiāng and Huái rivers upstream,
capture Huáinán and Chángshā,
enter Wǔguān,
and rendezvous with the Great King,
which would also be a clever move."
I wish to take fifty thousand men,
separately advance along the Jiāng and Huái rivers upstream,
capture Huáinán and Chángshā,
enter Wǔguān,
and rendezvous with the Great King,
which would also be a clever move."
When Huáinán King Liú Ān's plot to rebel was discovered,
he was prosecuted.
During the king's previous court visit,
Wǔ'ān Hóu (Tián Fén) was Grand Commandant
and welcomed the king at Bàshàng,
telling him:
"The Emperor has no crown prince yet.
Your Highness, being the most virtuous
and a grandson of Gāozǔ,
should the imperial carriage rest late (if the Emperor passes away),
who else should ascend the throne but you!"
The Huáinán King was greatly pleased
and bestowed generous gifts of gold and valuables.
The Emperor had disapproved of Wǔ'ān since the time of Wèijī's case,
only tolerating him for the Empress Dowager's sake.
Upon hearing about the Huáinán King's bribery,
the Emperor said:
"Were Wǔ'ān Hóu still alive,
he would have been executed along with his clan."
The Grand Historian comments:
Both Wèijī and Wǔ'ān gained prominence through imperial kinship,
while Guàn Fū rose to fame by a single decisive stratagem.
Wèijī's advancement came from the Wú-Chǔ rebellion,
Wǔ'ān's elevation occurred during the transition between reigns.
Yet Wèijī truly failed to understand changing times,
and Guàn Fū, lacking tact, was insolent.
The two supporting each other
led to their calamity.
Wǔ'ān, relying on his status, loved power,
harbored grievances over a cup of wine,
and framed those two worthy men.
Alas, how lamentable!
Transferring anger onto others,
his own life was not prolonged.
Unsupported by the masses,
he ultimately faced vilification.
Alas, how lamentable!
Such is the origin of disaster!
The Imperial Secretary Hán Ānguó
was from Chéng'ān in Liáng,
later moving to Suīyáng.
He studied the "Hán Fēizǐ"
and eclectic theories under Master Tián of Zōu.
Serving Liáng King Xiào as Grand Master of the Palace,
when Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
King Xiào appointed Ānguó and Zhāng Yǔ as generals
to defend against Wú forces at the eastern border.
Zhāng Yǔ fought fiercely,
while Ānguó maintained caution,
thus preventing Wú from crossing Liáng.
After Wú and Chǔ were defeated,
Ānguó
and Zhāng Yǔ gained renown.
Liáng King Xiào,
being Emperor Jǐng's younger brother by the same mother,
was dearly loved by Empress Dowager Dòu,
who allowed him to personally request his chancellor
and two-thousand-dan officials,
coming and going freely in amusement,
usurping imperial privileges.
The Emperor learned of this
and disapproved.
The Empress Dowager, aware of the Emperor's displeasure,
became angry with Liáng's envoys,
refusing audience
and investigating the king's conduct.
When Hán Ānguó served as Liáng's envoy,
he tearfully said to the Grand Princess:
"Why does the Empress Dowager fail to recognize
Liáng King's loyalty as subject
and filial piety as son?
Previously when Wú,
Chǔ, Qí,
and Zhào—seven states—rebelled,
all lands east of Hángu Pass united westward,
yet only Liáng stood firm through hardship.
The king, mindful of the Empress Dowager
and Emperor in the capital,
while the nobles caused chaos,
shed tears with every word,
kneeling to send us six officers
leading troops to repel Wú and Chǔ,
preventing their westward advance,
leading to their eventual defeat—
all due to Liáng King's efforts.
Now the Empress Dowager criticizes him for minor breaches of etiquette.
Liáng King's father and brothers were all emperors,
accustomed to grandeur,
hence clearing roads when going out,
announcing alerts when entering,
with chariots and banners all bestowed by the Emperor,
intending to impress remote counties,
galloping through the realm,
boasting to the nobles,
letting all under heaven know
the Empress Dowager and Emperor's love for him.
Now when Liáng's envoys come,
they are immediately investigated.
The king, fearful,
weeps day and night, longing
yet uncertain what to do.
How can the Empress Dowager ignore
Liáng King's filial devotion
and ministerial loyalty?"
The Grand Princess reported this fully to the Empress Dowager,
who joyfully said:
"Speak of this to the Emperor."
When told,
the Emperor's heart was eased,
and he removed his cap to apologize to the Empress Dowager:
"I failed to guide my brother,
causing Your Majesty worry."
He then received all Liáng's envoys,
rewarding them richly.
Thereafter, the Liáng King grew closer in favor,
and the Empress Dowager
and Grand Princess further rewarded Ānguó with valuables worth over a thousand gold.
His fame thus spread,
establishing connections with Hàn.
Later, Ānguó was convicted of a crime and punished,
where jailer Tián Jiǎ insulted him.
Ānguó said:
"Can dead ashes not reignite?"
Tián Jiǎ retorted:
"If they do, I'll piss on them."
Not long after,
when the position of Liáng Neishi became vacant,
Hàn appointed Ānguó as Liáng Neishi,
promoting him from convict to two-thousand-dan official.
Tián Jiǎ fled.
Ānguó declared:
"If Jiǎ doesn't report for duty,
I'll exterminate his clan."
Jiǎ then bared his upper body to apologize.
Ānguó laughed:
"You can piss now!
Are you worth troubling with?"
Ultimately, he treated him well.
When the Liáng Neishi position was vacant,
King Xiào had newly acquired Gōngsūn Guǐ from Qí,
favored him,
and wished to request him as Neishi.
Empress Dowager Dòu, hearing this,
instead commanded the king to appoint Ānguó as Neishi.
Gōngsūn Guǐ and
Yáng Shèng persuaded King Xiào to seek appointment as crown prince and request additional territory from the emperor.
Fearing that the Hàn ministers would not consent,
they secretly sent assassins to kill influential Hàn advisors involved in policymaking.
After the former Prime Minister of Wú, Yuán Àng, was murdered,
Emperor Jǐng learned of Guǐ and
Shèng's schemes.
He dispatched envoys to arrest Guǐ and
Shèng, demanding their capture at all costs.
Ten groups of Hàn envoys arrived in Liáng,
and the entire state, from the prime minister down, conducted a massive search,
yet after over a month, they remained unfound.
When the Neishi Hán Ànguó heard that Guǐ and
Shèng were hiding at King Xiào's residence,
he entered and tearfully addressed the king:
"When the ruler is disgraced, the ministers should die.
Your Highness lacks loyal ministers,
hence affairs have become chaotic to this extent.
Now that Guǐ and
Shèng cannot be found,
I beg to resign and request death."
The king replied,
"Why go this far?"
Ànguó shed tears and said,
"Your Highness, consider your relationship with the emperor:
how does it compare to that between Tàishàng Huáng and Emperor Gāo, or the emperor and Línjiāng King?"
King Xiào answered,
"It is not as close."
Ànguó continued,
"Though Tàishàng and
Línjiāng were close father-son relationships,
Emperor Gāo declared,
'It is I who seized the empire with a three-foot sword,'
so Tàishàng Huáng ultimately could not govern and
resided in Yuèyáng.
Línjiāng King,
the rightful eldest son and crown prince,
due to a single fault in speech,
was deposed and made king of Línjiāng;
over a matter of palace walls,
he eventually took his own life in the commandant's office.
Why?
Because governing the empire must not allow personal feelings to disrupt public duty.
As the saying goes:
'Though one has a biological father,
how can one know he is not a tiger?
Though one has a biological brother,
how can one know he is not a wolf?'
Now Your Highness ranks among the feudal lords,
yet you delight in the empty words of treacherous ministers,
violate imperial prohibitions,
and distort clear laws.
The Son of Heaven, for the sake of the Empress Dowager,
cannot bear to bring you to justice.
The Empress Dowager weeps day and night,
hoping Your Highness will reform yourself,
but you remain unawakened.
If the Empress Dowager's carriage were to suddenly halt (i.e., she passes away),
whom could you rely on then?"
Before he finished speaking,
King Xiào wept profusely and
apologized to Ànguó:
"I will now produce Guǐ and
Shèng."
Guǐ and Shèng committed suicide.
The Hàn envoys returned to report,
and the matters concerning Liáng were all resolved,
thanks to Ànguó's efforts.
Thereafter, Emperor Jǐng and
the Empress Dowager held Ànguó in even higher esteem.
After King Xiào's death,
King Gǒng succeeded to the throne,
and Ànguó was dismissed from office due to legal offenses,
staying at home.
During the Jiànyuán era,
Wǔ'ān Hóu Tián Fén served as Grand Commandant of Hàn,
wielding power through imperial favor and nobility.
Ànguó sent Fén gifts worth five hundred catties of gold.
Fén spoke of Ànguó to the Empress Dowager,
and the Son of Heaven, having long heard of his worthiness,
summoned him to appoint as Commandant of Běidì,
later promoting him to Grand Minister of Agriculture.
When Mǐnyuè and
Dōngyuè attacked each other,
Ànguó and the Grand Herald Wáng Huī were sent to lead troops.
Before reaching Yuè,
Yuè killed its king and surrendered,
so the Hàn forces withdrew.
In the sixth year of Jiànyuán,
Wǔ'ān Hóu became Chancellor,
and Ànguó was made Imperial Secretary.
The Xiōngnú came to request a marriage alliance,
and the Son of Heaven sought opinions.
The Grand Herald Wáng Huī,
a man of Yān,
had served multiple times as a border official,
well-versed in the affairs of the barbarians.
He argued:
"When Hàn forms marriage alliances with the Xiōngnú,
they typically break the treaty within a few years.
It would be better not to agree
and instead launch a military campaign against them."
Ànguó said:
"Fighting a war over a thousand lǐ,
the army gains no advantage.
Now the Xiōngnú rely on their swift horses,
harbor the hearts of beasts,
move like migrating birds,
and are difficult to control.
Gaining their land does not expand our territory meaningfully,
having their people does not strengthen us significantly,
since ancient times, they have not been subjugated as subjects.
For Hàn to contend for profit over thousands of lǐ,
our men and horses would be exhausted,
and the enemy would exploit our weakness with their full strength.
Moreover, at the extreme range of a strong crossbow,
its arrow cannot pierce the thin silk of Lǔ;
at the tail end of a gusting wind,
its force cannot lift a goose feather.
Not that they lack strength initially,
but their force wanes at the end.
Attacking is not advisable;
it is better to form a marriage alliance."
Most ministers in the discussion sided with Ànguó,
so the emperor approved the alliance.
The following year,
which was the first year of Yuánguāng,
the wealthy Mǎyì man from Yànmén, Niè Wēngyī, through the Grand Herald Wáng Huī, said to the emperor:
"The Xiōngnú have just formed a marriage alliance,
trusting our border regions;
they can be lured with profit."
He secretly sent Niè Wēngyī as a spy,
who fled to the Xiōngnú
and told the Chányú:
"I can behead the magistrates and officials of Mǎyì
and surrender the city,
so you can seize all its wealth."
The Chányú, fond and trusting of him,
believed it to be true,
and agreed with Niè Wēngyī.
Niè Wēngyī then returned,
deceptively beheaded prisoners condemned to death,
and hung their heads on the Mǎyì city walls,
showing the Chányú's envoys as proof.
He said:
"The senior officials of Mǎyì are dead;
you can come quickly."
Thereupon, the Chányú breached the frontier with over a hundred thousand cavalry,
entering through Wǔzhōu Pass.
At that time,
Hàn had埋伏ed over three hundred thousand chariots, cavalry, and infantry,
hidden in the valleys near Mǎyì.
Commandant of the Guard Lǐ Guǎng was the Valiant Cavalry General,
Supervisor of the Imperial Carriages Gōngsūn Hè was the Light Charlot General,
Grand Herald Wáng Huī was the Garrison General,
Grand Master of Palace Counsel Lǐ Xī was the Infantry General.
Imperial Secretary Hán Ànguó was the Army Protector General,
and all generals were under his command.
They planned to attack when the Chányú entered Mǎyì.
Wáng Huī,
Lǐ Xī, and
Lǐ Guǎng separately advanced from Dài to strike the enemy's supply train.
Thus, the Chányú entered Hàn's Great Wall at Wǔzhōu Pass.
When they were over a hundred lǐ from Mǎyì,
they plundered along the way,
but only saw livestock in the fields,
with not a person in sight.
The Chányú grew suspicious,
attacked a beacon tower,
and captured a Wǔzhōu commandant's clerk.
He intended to interrogate the clerk.
The clerk said:
"Tens of thousands of Hàn troops are埋伏ed under Mǎyì."
The Chányú turned to his attendants and said:
"I was nearly betrayed by Hàn!"
He then led his troops back.
Once outside the frontier,
he said:
"My capture of the clerk
was heaven's will."
He appointed the clerk
"Heavenly King."
Word spread below the frontier that the Chányú had withdrawn.
The Hàn troops pursued to the frontier,
but realizing they could not catch up,
withdrew.
Wáng Huī and others with thirty thousand troops,
hearing that the Chányú had not engaged with Hàn forces,
calculated that attacking the supply train
would inevitably lead to battle with the Chányú's elite troops,
and the Hàn army would likely be defeated,
so they used their discretion to withdraw,
and none achieved merit.
The emperor was angry that Wáng Huī had not attacked the Xiōngnú's supply train,
and had arbitrarily led his troops to withdraw.
Huī said:
"Initially, it was agreed that once the enemy entered Mǎyì City,
and our troops engaged with the Chányú,
then I would attack their supply train,
which could yield gains.
Now the Chányú, having learned of this,
turned back before reaching the city,
and I, with thirty thousand men, was no match for him;
it would only have brought disgrace.
I knew full well that returning would mean my execution,
but it has preserved His Majesty's thirty thousand soldiers."
Thereupon, Huī was handed over to the Commandant of Justice.
The Commandant of Justice found Huī guilty of hesitating and flinching,
and he was sentenced to death.
Huī privately gave a thousand pieces of gold to Chancellor Tián Fén.
Fén did not dare speak to the emperor about it,
but said to the Empress Dowager:
"Wáng Huī was the first to propose the Mǎyì affair,
and now, since it did not succeed, to execute Huī
would be to avenge the Xiōngnú."
When the emperor visited the Empress Dowager,
she relayed the chancellor's words to him.
The emperor said:
"The one who first initiated the Mǎyì affair
was Huī.
Therefore, I mobilized several hundred thousand troops from across the empire,
following his advice,
to carry this out.
Even if we could not capture the Chányú,
had Huī's troops attacked his supply train,
we might still have gained considerably,
to comfort the hearts of the officers.
Now, if I do not execute Huī,
I shall have no way to apologize to the empire."
Thereupon, upon hearing this,
Huī committed suicide.
Ān Guó was a man of great strategy,
his wisdom sufficient to adapt to the times and achieve success,
yet he was also of a loyal and honest nature.
He was greedy and fond of wealth.
Those he recommended were all incorruptible men,
superior to himself.
In Liáng, he recommended Hú Suì,
Zāng Gù,
and Zhì Tuō,
all renowned scholars of the empire,
and gentlemen also praised and admired him for this,
with only the Son of Heaven considering him a vessel of the state.
Ān Guó served as Grandee of the Palace for over four years;
when Chancellor Tián Fén died,
Ān Guó acted as chancellor,
but while leading the procession, he fell from his carriage and became lame.
The Son of Heaven deliberated on appointing a chancellor,
wishing to use Ān Guó,
but sent an envoy to see him;
finding him very lame,
he instead appointed Píngjí Hóu Xuē Zé as chancellor.
Ān Guó was dismissed due to illness for several months;
when his lameness improved,
the emperor reappointed him as Commandant of the Palace.
Over a year later,
he was transferred to be Commandant of the Guards.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Wèi Qīng attacked the Xiōngnú,
marching out from Shànggǔ,
and defeated the barbarians at Lóngchéng.
General Lǐ Guǎng was captured by the Xiōngnú,
but escaped;
Gōngsūn Áo lost a great number of soldiers:
all deserved execution,
but they ransomed themselves to become commoners.
The following year,
the Xiōngnú invaded the border on a large scale,
killing the Grand Administrator of Liáoxī,
and entering Yànmén,
where they killed or captured several thousand people.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Wèi Qīng attacked them,
marching out from Yànmén.
Commandant of the Guards Ān Guó served as General of the Skilled Soldiers,
stationed at Yúyáng.
Ān Guó captured a live prisoner,
who said the Xiōngnú had gone far away.
He then submitted a report saying it was the farming season,
and requested to temporarily disband the army's garrison.
A little over a month after the garrison was disbanded,
the Xiōngnú invaded Shànggǔ
and Yúyáng on a large scale.
Ān Guó's fort had only over seven hundred men;
he went out to engage them in battle,
but was defeated,
and retreated back into the fort.
The Xiōngnú captured over a thousand people and livestock before leaving.
When the Son of Heaven heard of this,
he was angry and sent an envoy to reprimand Ān Guó.
He transferred Ān Guó further east,
to station at Yòuběipíng.
At that time, Xiōngnú prisoners said they would invade the eastern region.
Ān Guó initially served as Grandee of the Palace and Army Supervisor,
but later was gradually marginalized and distanced,
and demoted;
while newly favored young generals like Wèi Qīng achieved merit,
becoming increasingly honored.
Ān Guó, being marginalized and distant,
remained silent;
and as a garrison commander, he was deceived by the Xiōngnú,
suffering heavy losses,
he felt deeply ashamed.
Though fortunate to be dismissed and return,
he was then transferred further east to garrison,
and felt disheartened and unhappy.
After several months,
he fell ill, vomited blood, and died.
Ān Guó died in the second year of the Yuánshuò era.
The Grand Historian remarks:
I, together with Hú Suì, established the calendar and pitch-standards,
and observed the righteousness of Hán Chángrú,
and the profound integrity and hidden kindness of Hú Suì.
The world says that in Liáng there were many men of virtue;
this is not untrue!
Hú Suì's office reached to the Chamberlain of the Palace,
and the Son of Heaven was about to rely on him to become the Hàn chancellor,
when he happened to pass away.
Otherwise,
with Hú Suì's inner integrity and cultivated conduct,
he would have been a gentleman who served with utmost dedication.
General Lǐ Guǎng
was a man of Chéngjì in Lǒngxī.
His ancestor was named Lǐ Xìn,
who served as a general in the Qín era,
and pursued and captured Crown Prince Dān of Yān.
Originally from Huáilǐ,
they moved to Chéngjì.
The Lǐ family for generations practiced archery.
In the fourteenth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
the Xiōngnú invaded on a large scale at Xiāoguān,
and Guǎng, as a son of a good family, joined the army to attack the barbarians;
excelling in mounted archery,
he killed and captured many enemy,
and became a Palace Attendant of the Hàn.
His cousin Lǐ Cài also served as an Attendant,
and both were Imperial Cavalry Guards,
with a salary of eight hundred shi.
Once, while accompanying the emperor on an excursion,
he performed feats of charging through barriers, breaking through passes, and fighting fierce beasts,
and Emperor Wén said:
"What a pity,
you have not met the right time!
If you had lived in the era of Emperor Gāo,
a marquis with ten thousand households would have been nothing to speak of!"
When Emperor Jǐng first ascended the throne,
Guǎng became the Commandant of Lǒngxī,
and was transferred to be Commandant of the Cavalry Attendants.
During the rebellion of Wú and Chǔ,
Guǎng served as Commandant of the Elite Cavalry,
and followed Grand Commandant Zhōu Yàfū to attack the armies of Wú and Chǔ,
capturing their flags,
and achieving fame for his merits at Chāngyì.
Because the King of Liáng had conferred on Guǎng the seal of a general,
upon his return, he was not rewarded.
He was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Shànggǔ,
where the Xiōngnú engaged him in battle daily.
The Chamberlain for the Dependent States, Gōngsūn Húnyé, said to the emperor with tears:
"Lǐ Guǎng's talent and spirit
are unmatched in the empire;
he relies on his own ability,
and frequently engages the enemy in battle;
I fear he may be lost."
Thereupon, he was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Shàngjùn.
Later, Guǎng served in turn as Grand Administrator of various border commanaderies,
including Shàngjùn.
He had served as Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī,
Běidì,
Yànmén,
Dàijùn,
and Yúnzhōng,
and was renowned in all for his fierce fighting.
When the virtue of the Xià dynasty declined,
Gōngliú lost his position as Minister of Millet,
adopted the customs of the Western Róng,
and established his capital at Bīn.
More than three hundred years later,
the Róng and Dí tribes attacked Great King Dǎnfù,
who fled to the foot of Mount Qí,
and all the people of Bīn followed Dǎnfù to establish a settlement there,
founding Zhōu.
Over a hundred years later,
Zhōu's Western Lord Chāng attacked the Quǎnyí tribe.
More than ten years after that,
King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu and built the city of Luòyì,
then returned to reside at Fēnghào,
expelling the Róng and Yí tribes north of the
Jīng and Luò rivers,
requiring them to pay tribute at appointed times,
designating them as
"the Wild Tribute."
Over two hundred years later,
the way of Zhōu declined,
and King Mù attacked the Quǎnróng,
capturing four white wolves and four white deer to bring back.
From then on,
the Wild Tribute ceased to come.
Thereupon, Zhōu established the penal code of the "Fǔ Xíng."
More than two hundred years after King Mù,
King Yōu of Zhōu, because of his favor for his consort Bāosì,
had a rift with the Marquis of Shēn.
The Marquis of Shēn, in anger, joined with the Quǎnróng to attack and kill King Yōu of Zhōu at the foot of Líshān,
then seized Zhōu's Jiāohù,
and settled between the Jīng and Wèi rivers,
invading and harassing the Central States.
Duke Xiāng of Qín came to Zhōu's rescue,
whereupon King Píng of Zhōu left Fēnghào and moved east to Luòyì.
At that time,
Duke Xiāng of Qín attacked the Róng as far as Qí,
and began to be ranked among the feudal lords.
Sixty-five years later,
the Shānróng crossed Yān to attack Qí,
and Duke Xí of Qí fought them in the outskirts of Qí.
Forty-four years later,
the Shānróng attacked Yān.
Yān appealed urgently to Qí for help,
and Duke Huán of Qí marched north to attack the Shānróng,
who then fled.
Over twenty years later,
the Róng and Dí reached Luòyì,
attacking King Xiāng of Zhōu,
who fled to the city of Fàn in Zhèng.
Earlier, King Xiāng of Zhōu, wishing to attack Zhèng,
had taken a woman of the Róng and Dí as his queen,
and joined forces with the Róng and Dí to attack Zhèng.
Later, he deposed the Dí queen,
who bore a grudge,
and King Xiāng's stepmother, known as Queen Huì,
had a son named Zǐdài,
whom she wished to install
—so Queen Huì, along with the Dí queen
and Zǐdài, acted as insiders,
opening the way for the Róng and Dí,
who thus gained entry,
defeated and drove out King Xiāng of Zhōu,
and set up Zǐdài as the Son of Heaven.
Thereupon, some of the Róng and Dí settled at Lùhún,
reaching east to Wèi,
plundering and brutalizing the Central States.
The Central States loathed them,
so the poets sang,
"The Róng and Dí are answered,"
"We smote the Xiǎnyǔn,
reaching Tàiyuán,"
"Out chariots roll mightily,
fortifying that northern region."
After King Xiāng of Zhōu had lived in exile for four years,
he sent a messenger to appeal urgently to Jìn.
Duke Wén of Jìn, newly established,
wishing to cultivate hegemonic rule,
raised troops to attack and drive out the Róng and Dí,
executed Zǐdài,
and welcomed back King Xiāng of Zhōu,
who resided in Luòyì.
At that time,
Qín and Jìn were powerful states.
Duke Wén of Jìn repelled the Róng and Dí,
who settled between the
Yín and Luò rivers west of the Yellow River,
called the Chìdí
and Báidí.
Duke Mù of Qín, having obtained Yóuyú,
saw eight states of the Western Róng submit to Qín,
so from west of Lǒng there were the Miánzhū,
Gǔnróng,
Dí, and Huán róng,
and north of Qí, Liángshān,
Jīng, and Qī were the Yìqú,
Dàlì,
Wūzhī,
and Qúyǎn róng.
North of Jìn were the Línhú
and Lóufán róng,
and north of Yān were the Dōnghú
and Shānróng.
They each lived scattered in valleys,
having their own chiefs,
with groups gathering here and there totaling over a hundred Róng tribes,
yet none could unite the others.
More than a hundred years later,
Duke Dào of Jìn sent Wèi Jiàng to make peace with the Róng and Dí,
who then paid court to Jìn.
Over a hundred years later,
Lord Xiāng of Zhào crossed Jūzhù and conquered and annexed Dài to confront the Hú and Mò.
After he, along with Hán and Wèi, destroyed Zhì Bó,
they divided the land of Jìn among themselves,
so Zhào held Dài
and north of Jūzhù,
while Wèi held Héxī
and Shàngjùn,
bordering the Róng.
Later, the Yìqú Róng built walls to defend themselves,
but Qín gradually nibbled away at them,
until under King Huì,
he captured twenty-five cities of Yìqú.
King Huì attacked Wèi,
and Wèi ceded all of Xīhé and Shàngjùn to Qín.
During the reign of King Zhāo of Qín,
the king of the Yìqú Ròng had an affair with Queen Dowager Xuān,
and they had two sons.
Queen Dowager Xuān deceitfully killed the Yìqú king at Gānquán,
then raised troops to attack and destroy Yìqú.
Thereupon, Qín possessed Lǒngxī,
Běidì,
and Shàngjùn,
building a long wall to resist the Hú.
Meanwhile, King Wǔlíng of Zhào also changed customs to adopt Hú dress,
practicing cavalry archery,
and defeated the Línhú
and Lóufán in the north.
He built a long wall,
from Dài along the Yīnshān,
to Gāoquē as a barrier.
And established Yúnzhōng,
Yànmén,
and Dài commanderies.
Later, Yān had a capable general named Qín Kāi,
who was a hostage among the Hú,
and the Hú trusted him greatly.
He returned to launch a surprise attack, defeating and driving out the Dōnghú,
who retreated over a thousand li.
The Qín Wǔyáng who attempted to assassinate the King of Qín with Jīng Kē
was Qín Kāi's grandson.
Yān also built a long wall,
from Zàoyáng to Xiāngpíng.
Establishing Shànggǔ,
Yúyáng,
Yòuběipíng,
Liáoxī,
and Liáodōng commanderies to resist the Hú.
At that time,
there were seven warring states of civilized dress,
and three of them bordered the Xiōngnú.
Later, when Lǐ Mù was a general of Zhào,
the Xiōngnú did not dare to enter Zhào's borders.
Later, Qín destroyed the six states,
and the First Emperor sent Méng Tián to lead a host of a hundred thousand north to attack the Hú,
recovering all the land south of the river.
Using the river as a barrier,
he built forty-four county towns along the river,
and relocated conscripts to populate them.
He opened a straight road,
from Jiǔyuán to Yúnyáng,
and fortified the mountain passes and valleys along the border that could be repaired,
stretching over ten thousand li from Líntáo to Liáodōng.
He also crossed the river to occupy Yángshān and Běijiǎ.
At that time,
the Dōnghú were strong and the Yuèzhī were powerful.
The Xiōngnú chanyu was named Tóumàn,
who, unable to overcome Qín,
moved north.
Over ten years later, Méng Tián died,
the feudal lords rebelled against Qín,
and the Central States were in turmoil,
so all the conscripts Qín had relocated to garrison the borders left,
and thus the Xiōngnú had room to relax,
gradually crossing back south of the river to border the Central States at the old fortifications.
The Chányú had a crown prince named Mòdú.
Later, he had a beloved Yānzhī,
who gave birth to a younger son.
The Chányú wished to depose Mòdú and establish the younger son instead,
so he sent Mòdú as a hostage to the Yuèzhī.
After Mòdú had been sent as a hostage to the Yuèzhī,
Tóumàn urgently attacked the Yuèzhī.
The Yuèzhī wanted to kill Mòdú,
but Mòdú stole their finest horse,
mounted it, and fled back.
Tóumàn considered him brave,
and ordered him to command ten thousand cavalry.
Mòdú then made a whistling arrow,
and trained his cavalry in shooting,
issuing the order:
"Whoever does not shoot at whatever the whistling arrow shoots at,
will be executed."
When hunting birds and animals,
if anyone did not shoot at what the whistling arrow shot,
he was immediately executed.
After a while, Mòdú used the whistling arrow to shoot his own fine horse;
among his attendants, some did not dare to shoot,
and Mòdú immediately executed those who did not shoot the fine horse.
After some time,
he again used the whistling arrow to shoot his beloved wife;
among his attendants, some were quite fearful
and did not dare to shoot,
and Mòdú again executed them.
After some time,
Mòdú went out hunting
and used the whistling arrow to shoot the Chányú's fine horse;
all his attendants shot at it.
Thereupon, Mòdú knew that all his attendants could be used.
While accompanying his father Chányú Tóumàn on a hunt,
he shot Tóumàn with the whistling arrow,
and his attendants also all followed the whistling arrow and shot and killed Chányú Tóumàn.
Then he executed all his stepmother, younger brother, and ministers who would not obey.
Mòdú established himself as Chányú.
After Mòdú had established himself,
at that time the Dōnghú were powerful and prosperous,
and upon hearing that Mòdú had killed his father and made himself Chányú,
they sent an envoy to tell Mòdú
that they wanted to obtain the thousand-mile horse that Tóumàn had owned.
Mòdú asked his ministers,
and the ministers all said:
"The thousand-mile horse
is a treasure of the Xiōngnú;
do not give it."
Mòdú said:
"How can we, as a neighboring state, begrudge a single horse?"
So he gave them the thousand-mile horse.
After some time,
the Dōnghú thought that Mòdú feared them,
and sent an envoy to tell Mòdú
that they wanted to obtain one of the Chányú's Yānzhī.
Mòdú again asked his attendants,
and they were all angry, saying:
"The Dōnghú are without principle,
to actually ask for a Yānzhī!
We request to attack them."
Mòdú said:
"How can we, as a neighboring state, begrudge a single woman?"
So he took his beloved Yānzhī and gave her to the Dōnghú.
The king of the Dōnghú became increasingly arrogant,
and invaded westward.
Between them and the Xiōngnú,
there was a deserted land,
uninhabited,
over a thousand lǐ,
where each lived on their border as Ōutuō.
The Dōnghú sent an envoy to tell Mòdú:
"The deserted land beyond the Ōutuō that borders us and the Xiōngnú,
the Xiōngnú cannot reach it,
I wish to possess it."
Mòdú asked his ministers,
and some ministers said:
"This is deserted land;
it can be given to them,
or not given."
At this, Mòdú was greatly angered and said:
"Land
is the foundation of a state;
how can it be given away!"
All those who had said to give it
were executed.
Mòdú mounted his horse,
and ordered that anyone in the state who lagged behind would be executed,
then he headed east and launched a surprise attack on the Dōnghú.
The Dōnghú had initially looked down on Mòdú,
and were unprepared.
When Mòdú arrived with his troops,
he attacked, completely defeating and destroying the king of the Dōnghú,
and captured his people and livestock.
After returning,
he attacked westward and drove away the Yuèzhī,
annexed Lóufán to the south,
and the Báiyáng Hénán king.
He fully recovered all the Xiōngnú lands that Qín had taken through Méng Tián's campaigns,
along the old Hénán frontier passes with Hàn,
reaching Zhāonuó
and Fūshī,
then invaded Yān
and Dài. At that time, the Hàn armies and Xiàng Yǔ were contending with each other,
and the Central States were exhausted by warfare,
so because of this, Mòdú was able to strengthen himself,
commanding over three hundred thousand archers.
From Chúnwéi to Tóumàn, over a thousand years had passed,
sometimes large, sometimes small,
separating and scattering,
for a long time,
and their generational succession cannot be clearly ordered.
However, by the time of Mòdú, the Xiōngnú were at their most powerful and great,
completely subjugating the northern barbarians,
and in the south becoming a rival state to the Central States,
and their generational succession of state offices and titles can be recorded.
They established Left and Right Wise Kings,
Left and Right Gǔlí Kings,
Left and Right Great Generals,
Left and Right Great Commandants,
Left and Right Great Dānghù,
Left and Right Gǔdūhóu.
The Xiōngnú call "wise"
"Túqí",
so they often made the crown prince the Left Túqí King.
From the Left and Right Wise Kings down to the Dānghù,
the larger [commands] had ten thousand cavalry,
the smaller several thousand,
altogether twenty-four chiefs,
established with the title
"Ten Thousand Cavalry".
All the great ministers held hereditary offices.
The Hūyǎn clan,
the Lán clan,
and later the Xūbǔ clan,
these three clans were their noble lineages.
All the kings and generals of the left side dwell in the eastern region,
directly from Shànggǔ onward,
connecting east with Huìmò
and Cháoxiǎn;
the kings and generals of the right side dwell in the western region,
directly from Shàngjùn westward,
connecting with the Yuèzhī,
Dī,
and Qiāng;
and the court of the Chányú is directly opposite Dài
and Yúnzhōng:
each has their allotted lands,
moving according to water and grass.
And the Left and Right Wise Kings,
Left and Right Gǔlí Kings are the greatest,
with the Left and Right Gǔdūhóu assisting in governance.
Each of the twenty-four chiefs also established their own Thousand Leaders,
Hundred Leaders,
Ten Leaders,
Lesser Deputy Kings,
Chancellors, Frontier Commandants,
Dānghù,
and Qiěqú officials.
Some Han envoys remarked:
"The Xiongnu customarily disrespect the elderly."
Zhōngháng Yuè refuted the Han envoys, saying:
"In Han custom, when conscripts are called up for garrison duty,
do not their elderly parents strip themselves of warm clothing and rich food to provide provisions for those departing on garrison duty?"
The Han envoy said:
"True."
Zhōngháng Yuè said:
"The Xiongnu explicitly regard warfare as their primary affair,
and since their elderly and weak cannot fight,
they give their rich food and drink to the strong and healthy,
so as to secure their own defense.
In this way, fathers and sons can long preserve each other.
How can you say the Xiongnu belittle the old?"
The Han envoy said:
"Xiongnu fathers and sons even sleep under the same felt tent.
When a father dies,
the son marries his stepmother;
when a brother dies,
the surviving brothers take his wives as their own.
They lack the adornments of caps and sashes,
and the rituals of court etiquette."
Zhōngháng Yuè said:
"The customs of the Xiongnu
involve people eating the meat of livestock,
drinking their milk,
and wearing their skins;
the livestock feed on grass and water,
moving with the seasons.
Thus, in urgent times, the people are practiced in riding and archery,
and in peaceful times, they enjoy tranquility,
their laws are simple,
and easily followed.
The relationship between ruler and subject is straightforward,
and the governance of the entire state is as coordinated as one body.
When fathers, sons, or brothers die,
taking their wives as one's own
prevents the loss of lineage.
Therefore, even if the Xiongnu experience turmoil,
they always establish a successor from the ancestral line.
Now, in China, though you ostensibly avoid marrying the wives of fathers and brothers,
when kinship ties weaken, you kill each other,
even to the point of changing dynasties,
all stemming from such issues.
Moreover, the flaws of ritual righteousness
lead to mutual resentment between high and low,
and the extreme pursuit of housing
inevitably exhausts the people's strength.
Forcing people to farm and weave for clothing and food,
and building walls for self-defense,
means that in emergencies, the people are unskilled in warfare,
and in peacetime, they are worn out by labor.
Alas, you people of earthen houses,
do not bother with many words—
let your endless chattering and posturing;
what use are your caps after all?"
From then on,
whenever Han envoys wished to debate,
Zhōngháng Yuè would say:
"Han envoys, no more words.
Just ensure that the silk, floss, grain, and yeast that Han delivers to the Xiongnu
are of adequate quantity,
and of good quality—that is all.
What need is there for talk?
If the provisions provided are complete and good, then it is settled;
if not,
if they are poor and inferior,
then wait for the autumn harvest,
and we will trample your crops with our cavalry."
Day and night, he taught the Chányú how to assess advantages and disadvantages.
In the fourteenth year of Emperor Wén of Han,
the Xiongnu Chányú led 140,000 cavalry into Zhāonà
and Xiāoguān,
killed the Commandant of Běidì, Áng,
plundered many people and livestock,
and advanced to Péngyáng.
They sent surprise troops to burn the Huízhōng Palace,
and their scouts reached Yōng and Gānquán.
Thereupon, Emperor Wén appointed Zhōu Shě, the Commandant of the Capital,
and Zhāng Wǔ, the Chief of the Gentlemen-of-the-Palace, as generals,
mobilized a thousand chariots,
and a hundred thousand cavalry,
stationing them near Cháng'ān to guard against the Hu invaders.
And he appointed Marquis Chāng Lǚ Qīng as General of Shàngjùn,
Marquis Níng Wèi Sù as General of Běidì,
Marquis Lónglǘ Zhōu Zào as General of Lǒngxī,
Marquis Dōngyáng Zhāng Xiàngrú as Grand General,
Marquis Chéng Dǒng Chì as Vanguard General,
and massively dispatched chariots and cavalry to attack the Hu.
The Chányú remained within the borders for over a month before leaving,
and the Han forces chased them out of the frontier but then turned back,
unable to inflict any casualties.
The Xiongnu grew increasingly arrogant,
invading the borders yearly,
killing and capturing many people and livestock,
with Yúnzhōng
and Liáodōng suffering the most,
and over ten thousand people affected in Dàijùn.
Han was troubled by this,
and sent an envoy with a letter to the Xiongnu.
The Chányú also sent a Dānghù to reply and apologize,
and again discussed matters of peace through marriage.
In the second year of the later period of Emperor Wén,
he sent an envoy with a letter to the Xiongnu, stating:
"The Emperor respectfully inquires after the well-being of the Great Chányú of the Xiongnu.
The envoy Dānghù Qiějū Diāoqúnán
and Gentleman-of-the-Palace Hán Liáo presented us with two horses,
which have arrived,
and we respectfully accept them.
The late Emperor decreed:
North of the Great Wall,
the nations that draw the bow
are under the command of the Chányú;
inside the Great Wall,
the households of caps and sashes
are governed by us.
Let the myriad people farm, weave, hunt, and shoot for their clothing and food,
so that fathers and sons are not separated,
subjects and rulers live in peace,
and all are free from violence and rebellion.
