Now we hear that wicked people, greedy for the profits of aggression,
have betrayed righteousness and broken treaties,
forgetting the lives of the myriad people,
and estranging the harmony between the two rulers—
but these events are in the past.
The letter says:
'The two states have made peace through marriage,
the two rulers are pleased,
arms are laid aside, troops rested, horses nurtured,
and generations flourish in joy,
embarking anew in tranquility.'
We greatly approve of this.
Sages renew themselves daily,
reforming and starting afresh,
so that the old may rest,
the young may grow,
each preserving their lives and living out their natural years.
We and the Chányú both follow this path,
complying with heaven and caring for the people,
passing it down through generations,
applying it endlessly,
so that all under heaven may benefit.
Han and the Xiongnu are neighboring states,
with the Xiongnu residing in the northern lands,
where it is cold, and the killing frost comes early,
so we have ordered officials to send the Chányú grain, yeast, gold, silk, floss, and other goods annually in fixed amounts.
Now all under heaven is greatly peaceful,
the myriad people are joyful,
and we and the Chányú act as parents to them.
Reflecting on past events,
trivial matters
and miscalculations by advisors
should not be enough to break the harmony between brothers.
We hear that heaven does not cover partially,
nor does earth bear loads unevenly.
We and the Chányú should cast aside past minor grievances,
both treading the great path,
discarding previous wrongs,
to plan for the long term,
making the people of both states like one family.
The innocent myriad people,
down to the fish and turtles,
up to the flying birds,
and all creatures that walk, peck, breathe, or crawl,
none fail to seek safety and benefit while avoiding danger.
Thus, those who come are not turned away—
this is the way of heaven.
Let us both set aside the past:
we shall pardon the fugitives and captives,
and the Chányú shall not mention Zhāng Ní and others.
We hear that the ancient emperors and kings
made clear covenants and did not break their word.
May the Chányú keep this in mind;
with all under heaven greatly peaceful,
after peace through marriage,
Han will not be the first to err.
May the Chányú consider this."
After the Chányú had agreed to peace through marriage,
an edict was issued to the Imperial Secretary, stating:
"The Great Chányú of the Xiongnu has sent us a letter,
stating that peace through marriage is settled,
and that fugitives are not enough to increase population or expand territory.
The Xiongnu shall not enter the frontier,
and Han shall not go beyond it.
Those who violate the current covenant shall be executed,
so that we may long remain close,
with no future blame,
and mutual benefit.
We have agreed to this.
Let it be proclaimed throughout the land,
so that all may clearly know."
Four years later,
the old Shàngqízhōu Chányú died,
and his son Jūnchén became Chányú.
Upon ascension,
Emperor Xiàowén renewed the peace and kinship with the Xiōngnú.
Zhōngháng Yuè once again served them.
After Jūnchén Chányú ruled for four years,
the Xiōngnú broke off peace and kinship again,
launching a major raid into Shàngjùn,
and Yúnzhōng with thirty thousand cavalry each,
causing significant casualties before retreating.
In response, Hàn deployed three generals to garrison the northern territories,
with Dài at Gōuzhù,
Zhào at Fēihúkǒu,
and fortified the borders to guard against the Xiōngnú invaders.
Moreover, three generals were stationed,
with armies at Cháng'ān's western Xìliǔ,
Jímén north of Wèi,
and Bàshàng as a defense against the Xiōngnú.
When the Xiōngnú cavalry invaded the Gōuzhù border of Dài,
beacon fires communicated to Gānquán,
and Cháng'ān.
After several months,
Hàn troops reached the border,
the Xiōngnú also withdrew far from the frontier,
and the Hàn troops were disbanded.
Over a year later,
Emperor Xiàowén passed away,
and Emperor Xiàojǐng ascended the throne.
King Zhào then secretly sent people to the Xiōngnú.
During the rebellion of Wú and Chǔ,
they intended to ally with Zhào to plot an invasion.
Hàn besieged and crushed Zhào,
and the Xiōngnú ceased their actions.
After this,
Emperor Xiàojǐng once again established peace and kinship with the Xiōngnú,
opened trade through borders,
provided gifts to the Xiōngnú,
sent princesses,
as per old agreements.
Throughout Xiàojǐng's time,
there were minor border thefts,
but no major invasions.
When the current emperor ascended,
peace treaties and constraints were clarified,
relations were made cordial,
trade through borders was facilitated,
and ample provisions were given.
From the Chányú downward, all were friendly towards Hàn,
frequently visiting below the Great Wall.
Hàn used a local from Mǎyì, Niè Wēngyī, who with treachery betrayed by offering goods to the Xiōngnú,
deceitfully proposed selling Mǎyì City to lure the Chányú.
Believing him,
and coveting Mǎyì's wealth,
the Chányú led a hundred thousand cavalry into Wǔzhōu Pass.
Hàn had over 300,000 soldiers ambushed beside Mǎyì, with
Censor-in-chief Hán Ānguó leading as guardian general,
overseeing four generals to trap the Chányú.
As the Chányú entered Hàn's borders,
but was still over 100 li from Mǎyì,
he saw livestock roaming fields without herdsmen,
which was suspicious,
and thus he attacked a pavilion.
At this moment, Commander Yàn Mén was patrolling,
saw the incursion,
and protected this pavilion,
aware of Hàn's ruse,
which the Chányú understood,
intending to kill him,
but the commander informed the Chányú of Hàn troop positions.
The Chányú, greatly alarmed, said,
“I already suspected this.”
He then withdrew his troops.
Upon leaving, he said,
“To have captured the commander,
it was fate;
fate destined him to speak.”
He honored the commander as
"Tiānwáng" (Heavenly King).
Hàn troops awaited the Chányú at Mǎyì in vain,
so gained nothing as the Chányú did not arrive.
Due to Garrison General Wáng Huī’s proposal of the military plot without advancing,
he was executed.
After this,
the Xiōngnú severed peace and kinship,
attacking frontier fortifications,
frequently raiding Hàn borders,
beyond count.
Nevertheless, Xiōngnú greed,
delighting in border commerce,
desiring Hàn goods,
led Hàn to maintain trading without break to curb them.
Five years after the Mǎyì campaign,
Hàn dispatched four generals each with ten thousand cavalry to strike Xiōngnú under border trade.
General Wèi Qīng departed from Shànggǔ, reaching Lóng City,
capturing 700 Xiōngnú.
Gōngsūn Hé left Yúnzhōng, having no gains.
Gōngsūn Áo left Dài Command,
was defeated by the Xiōngnú, losing over 7,000 men.
Lǐ Guǎng departed Yànmén,
was defeated by the Xiōngnú,
and captured alive,
but later escaped and returned.
Hàn imprisoned Áo and
Guǎng, redeeming them to commoner status.
That winter,
the Xiōngnú frequently raided borders,
particularly in Yúyáng.
Hàn stationed General Hán Ānguó at Yúyáng to guard against the Xiōngnú.
In the following autumn,
twenty thousand Xiōngnú cavalry invaded Hàn,
killing Liáoxī's governor,
capturing over 2,000 people.
The Xiōngnú also invaded, defeating Yúyáng's governor's army of over 1,000,
besieged General Ānguó,
whose 1,000 cavalry nearly exhausted,
met rescue from Yàn,
leading the Xiōngnú to retreat.
The Xiōngnú invaded Yànmén again,
killing over 1,000 people.
Therefore, Hàn sent General Wèi Qīng with 30,000 cavalry out of Yànmén,
Lǐ Xī from Dài Command,
to strike the Xiōngnú.
Captured prisoners numbered in thousands.
The following year,
Wèi Qīng again left from Yúnzhōng westward to Lǒngxī,
struck Xiōngnú's Loufán and
Bài Yáng kings at Henan,
capturing several thousand Xiōngnú,
and over 1 million cattle and sheep.
Thus Hàn seized the Henan lands,
built Shuòfāng,
repaired the old Qin-era barriers constructed by Méng Tián,
securing by the river.
Hàn also abandoned Shànggǔ's Shíbì County, creating Yáng lands to give to the Xiōngnú.
That year was Hàn's second year of Yuánshuò.
The subsequent winter,
Jūnchén Chányú died.
Jūnchén Chányú's younger brother Zuǒgǔlí King Yīzhīxu, self-established as Chányú,
attacked and defeated Jūnchén Chányú's Crown Prince at Shàn.
The prince fled to Hàn,
and was titled Marquis Shè'ān by Hàn,
dying within months.
After Yīzhīxu Chányú was established,
that summer,
tens of thousands of Xiōngnú cavalry invaded, killing Dài Command’s governor Gōng Yǒu,
capturing over 1,000 people.
That autumn,
the Xiōngnú invaded Yànmén again,
killing over 1,000 people.
In the following year,
the Xiōngnú invaded Dài Command again,
Dìngxiāng,
Shàngjùn,
with 30,000 cavalry each,
causing thousands of casualties.
The Xiōngnú Right Wise King resented Hàn for seizing Henan lands and constructing Shuòfāng,
frequently raiding,
looting borders,
intruding into Henan,
disturbing Shuòfāng,
killing and capturing many officials and civilians.
In the following spring,
Hàn appointed Wèi Qīng as Grand General,
leading six generals,
over 100,000 troops,
to launch from Shuòfāng and
Gāoquē to strike the Xiōngnú.
The Right Wise King believed Hàn's army impossible to reach,
indulging drunkenly,
until Hàn troops advanced over 600-700 li beyond the frontier,
and surrounded the Right Wise King by night.
The Right Wise King, shocked,
escaped himself,
with elite cavalry gradually following.
Hàn captured 15,000 men and women of the Right Wise King's group,
and over a dozen lesser kings.
That autumn,
ten thousand Xiōngnú cavalry invaded, killing Dài Command Officer Zhū Yīng,
capturing over 1,000 people.
In the spring of the following year,
the Han dynasty again dispatched the Grand General Wèi Qīng,
leading six generals,
with over a hundred thousand cavalry troops,
who once more set out from Dìngxiāng several hundred li to attack the Xiōngnú,
capturing and beheading a total of more than nineteen thousand enemies.
However, the Han also lost two generals,
and over three thousand cavalry troops.
Right General Jiàn managed to escape with his life,
but Former General Marquis of Xī, Zhào Xìn, met with unfavorable circumstances in battle
and surrendered to the Xiōngnú.
Zhào Xìn
was originally a minor Xiōngnú king
who had surrendered to the Han,
and the Han enfeoffed him as Marquis of Xī.
As Former General, he joined forces with the Right General but advanced separately;
encountering the Chányú's troops alone,
his army was completely wiped out.
After the Chányú obtained Marquis of Xī,
he appointed him as Zìcì King,
gave him his elder sister as a wife,
and consulted with him on plans against the Han.
Zhào Xìn advised the Chányú to move further north beyond the desert,
to lure and exhaust the Han troops,
waiting until they were at their limit to attack them,
and not to approach the frontier fortresses.
The Chányú followed his plan.
The following year,
ten thousand Xiōngnú cavalry invaded Shànggǔ,
killing several hundred people.
In the spring of the next year,
the Han sent Piàoqí General Qùbìng with ten thousand cavalry out of Lǒngxī,
passing beyond Yānzhī Shān over a thousand li,
to attack the Xiōngnú,
capturing and beheading over eighteen thousand enemies,
and seizing the golden idol used by the Xiūtú King for worshipping heaven.
That summer,
Piàoqí General again joined Marquis Héqí with tens of thousands of cavalry out of Lǒngxī
and Běidì for two thousand li,
attacking the Xiōngnú.
Passing through Jūyán,
they assaulted Qílián Shān,
capturing over thirty thousand Xiōngnú,
and more than seventy minor kings and below.
At that time, the Xiōngnú also invaded Dài Jùn
and Yànmén,
killing and capturing several hundred people.
The Han sent Marquis Bówàng and General Lǐ Guǎng out of Yòuběipíng,
to attack the Xiōngnú's Zuǒxián King.
The Zuǒxián King surrounded General Lǐ,
whose forces numbered about four thousand men,
and were nearly annihilated,
yet they killed and captured more than their own number.
Just then, Marquis Bówàng's relief forces arrived,
and General Lǐ managed to escape.
The Han lost several thousand men;
Marquis Héqí arrived later than the scheduled time with Piàoqí General,
and both he and Marquis Bówàng were sentenced to death,
but redeemed themselves to become commoners.
That autumn,
the Chányú, angered that the Húnyé King and
Xiūtú King, stationed in the west, had lost tens of thousands of men killed or captured by the Han,
intended to summon and execute them.
The Húnyé King and Xiūtú King, fearing for their lives,
plotted to surrender to the Han,
and the Han sent Piàoqí General to welcome them.
The Húnyé King killed the Xiūtú King,
and leading their combined forces, surrendered to the Han.
In all, over forty thousand people,
claimed to be a hundred thousand.
With the Han having obtained the Húnyé King,
then Lǒngxī,
Běidì,
and Héxī saw increasingly fewer Xiōngnú raids.
Poor people from Guāndōng were relocated to the lands taken from the Xiōngnú south of the river
and Xīnqínzhōng to populate them,
and the garrison troops west of Běidì were reduced by half.
The following year,
the Xiōngnú invaded Yòuběipíng
and Dìngxiāng with tens of thousands of cavalry each,
killing and capturing over a thousand people before leaving.
In the spring of the next year,
the Han strategized, saying,
"Marquis of Xī, Zhào Xìn, advised the Chányú,
to station north of the desert,
believing the Han troops could not reach there."
They then fed grain to their horses and dispatched a hundred thousand cavalry,
with privately supported followers totaling a hundred forty thousand horses,
not including the grain and heavy supplies.
Ordering Grand General Qīng
and Piàoqí General Qùbìng to divide the army equally,
the Grand General set out from Dìngxiāng,
and Piàoqí General from Dài,
both agreeing to cross the desert and attack the Xiōngnú.
The Chányú, hearing of this,
moved his supplies to a distance,
and awaited with elite troops north of the desert.
Engaging the Han Grand General in battle for one day,
as dusk fell,
a great wind arose,
and the Han troops deployed left and right wings to surround the Chányú.
The Chányú judged that his forces could not match the Han troops,
so he broke through the Han encirclement with several hundred robust cavalry and fled northwest.
The Han troops pursued at night but could not catch him.
They marched, beheading and capturing nineteen thousand Xiōngnú,
and advanced north to Tiányán Shān and Zhào Xìn's city before returning.
As the Chányú fled,
his troops often intermingled with the Han soldiers while following him.
The Chányú was long separated from his main force,
and his Right Gūlǐ King, thinking the Chányú dead,
proclaimed himself Chányú.
When the true Chányú regained his followers,
the Right Gūlǐ King then abandoned his title of Chányú,
and resumed being the Right Gūlǐ King.
The Han Piàoqí General, advancing over two thousand li from Dài,
engaged the Zuǒxián King in battle,
and the Han troops captured and beheaded over seventy thousand Xiōngnú,
causing the Zuǒxián King and his generals to flee.
Piàoqí General conducted a fēng sacrifice at Lángjūxū Shān,
a shàn sacrifice at Gūyǎn,
and reached the Hànhǎi before returning.
After this, the Xiōngnú fled far away,
and there was no royal court south of the desert.
The Han crossed the river from Shuòfāng west to Língjū,
often digging canals to establish farmland,
with officials and soldiers numbering fifty to sixty thousand,
gradually nibbling away,
until their territory connected with the Xiōngnú to the north.
Initially,
when the two Han generals launched a major campaign to surround the Chányú,
they killed or captured eighty to ninety thousand,
but the Han also lost tens of thousands of soldiers to death,
and over a hundred thousand Han horses died.
Although the Xiōngnú were weakened,
and had gone far away,
the Han also had few horses,
and could not launch another expedition.
The Xiōngnú, following Zhào Xìn's strategy,
sent an envoy to the Han,
with friendly words requesting héqīn.
The Son of Heaven put the matter to discussion;
some advocated héqīn,
others suggested subjugating them.
Chancellor Chief Clerk Rèn Chǎng said:
"The Xiōngnú have recently been defeated,
and are in distress; it would be appropriate to make them outer subjects,
having them pay court at the border."
The Han sent Rèn Chǎng to the Chányú.
The Chányú, hearing Rèn Chǎng's proposal,
was greatly angered,
and detained him without sending him back.
Prior to this, the Han had also detained some Xiōngnú envoys who had surrendered,
and the Chányú likewise detained Han envoys in retaliation.
The Han was again gathering troops and horses,
when Piàoqí General Qùbìng fell ill and died,
so for a long time, the Han did not attack the northern Hú.
Several years later,
Chányú Yīzhìxié died after reigning for thirteen years,
and his son Wūwéi was established as Chányú.
This year
was the third year of the Yuándǐng era of the Han.
When Chányú Wūwéi was established,
the Han Son of Heaven began touring the commanderies and counties.
Afterwards, the Han was busy conquering the two Yuè in the south,
and did not attack the Xiōngnú,
nor did the Xiōngnú invade the border.
Three years after Chányú Wūwéi's accession,
the Han had already destroyed Nányuè,
and sent the former Grand Coachman Hè with fifteen thousand cavalry out of Jiǔyuán for over two thousand li,
reaching Fújújǐng before returning,
without seeing a single Xiōngnú.
The Han also sent the former Marquis Cóngpiào, Zhào Pònú, with ten thousand cavalry out of Língjū for several thousand li,
reaching the Xiōnghé Shuǐ before returning,
also without seeing a single Xiōngnú.
At that time, the Son of Heaven was touring the border regions,
reaching Shuòfāng,
where he marshaled 180,000 cavalry to display military might,
and sent Guō Jí to convey a message to the Chányú.
When Guō Jí arrived among the Xiōngnú,
the Xiōngnú official in charge of guests inquired about his mission,
but Guō Jí, with humble courtesy and pleasant words,
said:
"I will speak directly when I see the Chányú."
The Chányú received Guō Jí,
and Guō Jí declared:
"The head of the King of Nányuè now hangs on the northern gate of Hàn.
If the Chányú can advance and fight Hàn,
the Son of Heaven himself will await with troops at the border;
if the Chányú cannot,
then turn south and submit to Hàn as a subject.
Why merely flee afar,
hiding in the bitter cold, waterless grasslands north of the desert,
to no avail?"
As soon as he finished speaking, the Chányú flew into a rage,
immediately beheaded the official who had received the guest,
and detained Guō Jí, preventing his return,
exiling him to the northern sea.
Yet the Chányú ultimately refused to raid Hàn's borders,
instead resting and nurturing his men and horses,
practicing archery and hunting,
and frequently sending envoys to Hàn,
using sweet words and fine rhetoric to seek a peace marriage alliance.
Hàn sent Wáng Wū and others to spy on the Xiōngnú.
By Xiōngnú law,
Hàn envoys could not enter the yurt unless they removed their credentials and had their faces tattooed with ink.
Wáng Wū,
being from Běidì,
was familiar with barbarian customs,
so he removed his credentials,
tattooed his face,
and gained entry to the yurt.
The Chányú took a liking to him,
feigned agreement with sweet words,
and promised to send his crown prince to Hàn as a hostage,
in exchange for a peace marriage alliance.
Hàn then sent Yáng Xìn to the Xiōngnú.
At that time, Hàn had conquered Huìmò and
Cháoxiǎn in the east, establishing commanderies,
and in the west set up the Jiǔquán Commandery to block the route between the Hú and Qiāng peoples.
Hàn also opened communications with Yuèzhī and
Dàxià in the west,
and gave a princess in marriage to the King of Wūsūn,
to split the Xiōngnú's western allies.
Furthermore, they expanded northern farmlands to Xiánléi as a barrier,
yet the Xiōngnú never dared to protest.
That year,
Marquis Xìn died,
and Hàn's ministers believed the Xiōngnú had weakened enough
to be subjugated.
Yáng Xìn was rigid and stubborn by nature,
not a high-ranking official,
so the Chányú did not favor him.
When the Chányú summoned him,
he refused to remove his credentials,
so the Chányú received Yáng Xìn seated outside the yurt.
After the audience,
Yáng Xìn persuaded him:
"If you desire peace marriage,
send the Chányú's crown prince as a hostage to Hàn."
The Chányú replied:
"That was not the old agreement.
Under the old pact,
Hàn regularly sent princesses,
provided silk, food, and goods of certain grades,
to cement peace,
and the Xiōngnú did not harass the border.
Now you wish to reverse this,
demanding my crown prince as a hostage—
that is hopeless."
Xiōngnú custom held that
if a Hàn envoy was not a high-ranking courtier,
but a Confucian scholar,
they would try to out-argue him to break his debate;
if he was young,
they would assume he intended to provoke,
and crush his spirit.
Whenever Hàn sent envoys to the Xiōngnú,
the Xiōngnú would retaliate in kind.
If Hàn detained a Xiōngnú envoy,
the Xiōngnú would also detain a Hàn envoy,
only stopping when they achieved parity.
After Yáng Xìn returned,
Hàn sent Wáng Wū again,
and the Chányú once more used sweet words to deceive him,
wanting to obtain more wealth from Hàn,
falsely telling Wáng Wū:
"I wish to go to Hàn to see the Son of Heaven,
and personally swear a brotherhood pact."
Wáng Wū reported this to Hàn,
and Hàn built a residence for the Chányú in Cháng'ān.
The Xiōngnú said:
"Unless Hàn sends a noble envoy,
I will not speak sincerely."
When the Xiōngnú sent a noble to Hàn,
he fell ill; Hàn provided medicine,
hoping to cure him,
but he unfortunately died.
Hàn then sent Lù Chōngguó, bearing a two-thousand-picul official seal, as an envoy,
to escort the funeral procession,
conducting a lavish burial worth thousands of gold,
declaring
"This was a Hàn noble."
The Chányú, however, believed Hàn had killed his noble envoy,
so he detained Lù Chōngguó and would not let him return.
All that had been said
was merely empty deception by the Chányú to Wáng Wū,
with no real intention to go to Hàn or send his crown prince as a hostage.
Thereafter, the Xiōngnú repeatedly sent surprise troops to raid the border.
Hàn then appointed Guō Chāng as General Bá Hú,
and stationed him with Marquess Zhuóyě east of Shuòfāng,
to guard against the Hú.
Lù Chōngguó was detained among the Xiōngnú for three years,
until the Chányú died.
Wūwéi Chányú had reigned for ten years when he died,
and his son Wūshīlú succeeded him as Chányú.
Being young,
he was called the Boy Chányú.
This was the sixth year of the Yuánfēng era.
From then on,
the Chányú moved further northwest,
with his left flank forces facing Yúnzhōng,
and the right flank facing Jiǔquán and
Dūnhúang Commanderies.
After the Boy Chányú ascended,
Hàn sent two envoys,
one to condole with the Chányú,
the other with the Right Wise King,
aiming to sow discord in their state.
When the envoys entered Xiōngnú territory,
the Xiōngnú escorted them all to the Chányú.
The Chányú, enraged, detained all the Hàn envoys.
In total, over ten groups of Hàn envoys were held by the Xiōngnú,
and whenever Xiōngnú envoys came to Hàn,
Hàn likewise detained them as retaliation,
only stopping when balance was achieved.
That year,
Hàn sent General Èrshī Guǎnglì west to attack Dàyuān,
and ordered General Yīn Yú Áo to build the Shòuxiáng Fortress.
That winter,
the Xiōngnú suffered heavy snow,
and many livestock died of hunger and cold.
The Boy Chányú, being young,
was fond of killing and warfare,
causing much unrest among his people.
The Left Great Commander wanted to kill the Chányú,
and secretly informed Hàn:
"I intend to kill the Chányú and surrender to Hàn,
but Hàn is far;
if troops come to welcome me,
I will act."
Initially, upon hearing this,
Hàn built the Shòuxiáng Fortress,
yet still considered it too distant.
The following spring,
Hàn sent Marquess Zhuóyě Pònú with over 20,000 cavalry out of Shuòfāng, over 2,000 li northwest,
planning to reach the Jūnjī Mountains and return.
When Marquess Zhuóyě returned as scheduled,
the Left Great Commander's plot was discovered before he could act,
and the Chányú executed him,
then dispatched left flank troops to attack Zhuóyě.
Marquess Zhuóyě captured several thousand enemies in his campaigns.
On his return, 400 li from Shòuxiáng Fortress,
80,000 Xiōngnú cavalry surrounded him.
Marquess Zhuóyě went out at night to fetch water,
was captured by Xiōngnú scouts,
and taken alive,
leading to a fierce attack on his army.
In the army, Guō Zòng served as protector,
and King Wéi as leader;
they conspired together, saying:
"The other officers fear being executed for losing their general,
so no one urges a return."
Thus, the army was annihilated by the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú Boy Chányú was overjoyed,
and sent surprise troops to attack Shòuxiáng Fortress.
Failing to capture it,
they raided the border and withdrew.
The next year,
the Chányú intended to personally attack Shòuxiáng Fortress,
but before arriving,
he fell ill and died.
The Boy Chányú reigned for three years before his death.
His son being too young,
the Xiōngnú installed his uncle, the Right Wise King Gōulíhú, brother of Wūwéi Chányú, as the new Chányú.
This was the third year of the Tàichū era.
When Húlǐhú Chányú ascended the throne,
the Han envoy, the Imperial Household Grandee Xú Zìwéi, ventured several hundred li beyond the Five Plains frontier,
the farthest point over a thousand li away,
constructing fortresses and a line of watchtowers reaching Lúqú,
while dispatching the Flying Cavalry General Hán Yuè
and Chángpíng Hóu Wèi Kàng to station troops nearby,
and ordering the Commandant of Strong Crossbows Lù Bódé to build fortifications at Lake Jūyán.
That autumn,
the Xiōngnú invaded Dìngxiāng
and Yúnzhōng on a large scale,
killing or capturing several thousand people,
defeating officials of two-thousand-dan rank, and then withdrawing,
destroying the fortresses and watchtower lines built by the Imperial Household Grandee along the way.
They also sent the Right Worthy King to invade Jiǔquán
and Zhāngyè,
capturing several thousand people.
Fortunately, Rèn Wén attacked and rescued them,
recovering all that had been lost before the enemy withdrew.
That year,
the Ershi General conquered Dàyuān,
beheading its king and returning.
The Xiōngnú tried to intercept him,
but could not reach him.
That winter,
they planned to attack Shòuxiáng City,
but the Chányú fell ill and died.
Húlǐhú Chányú reigned for only one year before his death.
The Xiōngnú then enthroned his younger brother, the Left Grand Commander Qiědīhóu, as Chányú.
After the Han had conquered Dàyuān,
its prestige shook foreign states.
The Son of Heaven intended to press the Hú into submission,
and thus issued an edict stating:
"Emperor Gāo left me the worry of Píngchéng,
and during Empress Gāo's time, the Chányú's letter was utterly rebellious.
In the past, Duke Xiāng of Qí avenged a grievance from nine generations back,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals praised this."
This was the fourth year of the Tàichū era.
After Qiědīhóu Chányú ascended the throne,
he repatriated all Han envoys who had not surrendered.
Lù Chōngguó and others were thus able to return.
The Chányú, newly enthroned,
feared a Han attack,
and thus declared himself
"I am a son,
how dare I aspire to equal the Han Son of Heaven!
The Han Son of Heaven
is my elder."
The Han sent the Court Gentleman Su Wu with generous gifts to bribe the Chányú.
The Chányú grew increasingly arrogant,
his demeanor quite disrespectful,
contrary to Han expectations.
The following year,
Zhuóyě Hóu Pò Nú managed to escape and return to Han.
The year after that,
the Han dispatched the Ershi General Lǐ Guǎnglì with thirty thousand cavalry out of Jiǔquán,
attacking the Right Worthy King at Tiānshān,
capturing over ten thousand Hú heads and prisoners before returning.
The Xiōngnú heavily surrounded the Ershi General,
who barely escaped.
Han troops suffered sixty to seventy percent casualties.
The Han again sent the General of Yīnwū Gōngsūn Áo out from Xīhé,
to rendezvous with the Commandant of Strong Crossbows at Zhuōtú Mountain,
but achieved nothing.
They also dispatched the Cavalry Commandant Lǐ Líng leading five thousand infantry and cavalry,
advancing over a thousand li north of Jūyán,
where he encountered the Chányú,
engaged in battle,
and inflicted over ten thousand casualties,
but with his troops and supplies exhausted,
and attempting to disengage and return,
the Xiōngnú surrounded Lǐ Líng,
who surrendered to the Xiōngnú,
his army thus annihilated,
with only four hundred men returning.
The Chányú then honored Lǐ Líng,
giving him his daughter in marriage.
Two years later,
the Han again sent the Ershi General leading sixty thousand cavalry
and one hundred thousand infantry,
out from Shuòfāng.
The Commandant of Strong Crossbows Lù Bódé led over ten thousand men,
to join the Ershi General.
The Flying Cavalry General Gōngsūn Yuè led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry,
out from Wǔyuán.
The General of Yīnwū Gōngsūn Áo led ten thousand cavalry and thirty thousand infantry,
out from Yànmén.
The Xiōngnú, upon hearing this,
moved all their heavy supplies far north of the Yúwú River,
while the Chányú awaited with one hundred thousand cavalry south of the river,
engaging the Ershi General in battle.
The Ershi General then disengaged and withdrew,
fighting the Chányú continuously for over ten days.
The Ershi General learned that his family had been executed due to accusations of witchcraft,
and thus surrendered with his forces to the Xiōngnú,
with only one or two men in a thousand managing to return.
The Flying Cavalry General Gōngsūn Yuè achieved nothing.
The General of Yīnwū Gōngsūn Áo fought the Left Worthy King,
was unsuccessful,
and withdrew.
That year, the Han troops sent against the Xiōngnú could not speak of their achievements in terms of scale,
as their merits were not substantial.
An edict was issued to arrest the Grand Physician Líng Suí Dàn,
who had reported the extermination of the Ershi General's family,
leading Guǎnglì to surrender to the Xiōngnú.
The Grand Historian remarks:
When Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
the events of the Yǐn and Huán periods were clearly recorded,
but by the Dìng and Āi periods, they became subtle,
because writing about contemporary events involved no praise,
reflecting cautious and restrained language.
Common discussions about the Xiōngnú
suffer from seeking momentary advantage,
and striving to flatter and adopt such views,
to favor biased opinions,
without considering both sides;
commanders rely on China's vastness,
their spirits roused,
and rulers base decisions on this,
hence achievements are not profound.
Although Yáo was virtuous,
he could not accomplish his enterprises alone,
until he obtained Yǔ, and the nine provinces were pacified.
To revive the sagely tradition,
it lies solely in selecting and appointing generals and ministers!
It lies solely in selecting and appointing generals and ministers!
The Grand General Wèi Qīng
was from Píngyáng.
His father, Zhèng Jì,
was a minor official
serving in the household of the Marquis of Píngyáng,
and had an affair with the marquis' concubine Wèi Āo,
giving birth to Qīng.
Qīng's elder brother from the same mother was Wèi Zhǎngzǐ,
and his elder sister Wèi Zǐfú gained the favor of the Son of Heaven from the household of Princess Píngyáng,
so he assumed the surname Wèi.
His courtesy name was Zhòngqīng.
Zhǎngzǐ's courtesy name was changed to Zhǎngjūn.
Their mother was called Wèi Āo.
Āo's eldest daughter was Wèi Rú,
the second daughter was Shào'ér,
and the third daughter was Zǐfú.
Later, Zǐfú's younger brothers Bù
and Guǎng also assumed the surname Wèi.
Qīng belonged to the marquis' household,
and in his youth returned to his father,
who made him tend sheep.
His stepbrothers treated him as a slave,
not counting him among their brothers.
Once, Qīng followed someone to the Gānquán Palace detention house,
where a convict in a metal collar physiognomized him, saying:
"You are a noble man,
destined to become a marquis."
Qīng laughed and said:
"Born as a person's slave,
if I can avoid whipping and scolding, that's enough—
how could I attain enfeoffment as a marquis!"
When Qīng grew up,
he became a cavalryman in the marquis' household,
attending Princess Píngyáng.
In the spring of the second year of the Jiànyuán era,
Qīng's sister Zǐfú entered the palace and gained the emperor's favor.
The empress,
daughter of the Grand Princess of Tángyì,
had no sons
and was jealous. The Grand Princess, hearing that Wèi Zǐfú was favored
and pregnant,
grew jealous
and had Qīng arrested.
Qīng was then serving at Jiànzhāng Palace,
unknown to most.
The Grand Princess captured and imprisoned Qīng,
intending to kill him.
His friend, the Cavalry Court Gentleman Gōngsūn Áo, went with strong men to rescue him,
thus saving his life.
The emperor, upon hearing of this,
summoned Qīng to be the Supervisor of Jiànzhāng Palace,
and a Palace Attendant,
and along with his maternal brothers, he was honored,
receiving gifts worth a thousand gold within days.
Rú became the wife of the Grand Coachman Gōngsūn Hè.
Shào'ér had previously been involved with Chén Zhǎng,
and the emperor summoned and honored Zhǎng.
Gōngsūn Áo thereby became more esteemed.
Zǐfú was made a Lady.
Qīng was appointed Grand Master of the Palace.
In the fifth year of Yuánguāng,
Wèi Qīng served as General of Chariots and Cavalry,
attacking the Xiōngnú,
and marched out from Shànggǔ;
the Grand Coachman Gōngsūn Hè served as General of Light Chariots,
and marched out from Yúnzhōng;
the Grand Master of Palace Leisure Gōngsūn Áo served as General of Cavalry,
and marched out from Dàijùn;
the Commandant of the Palace Guard Lǐ Guǎng served as General of Valiant Cavalry,
and marched out from Yànmén:
each army had ten thousand cavalry.
Wèi Qīng reached Lóngchéng,
and beheaded or captured several hundred enemies.
General of Cavalry Áo lost seven thousand cavalry;
Commandant of the Palace Guard Lǐ Guǎng was captured by the enemy,
but managed to escape and return:
both deserved execution,
but were ransomed to become commoners.
Hè also achieved no merit.
In the spring of the first year of Yuánshuò,
Lady Wèi bore a son,
and was established as Empress.
That autumn,
Wèi Qīng served as General of Chariots and Cavalry,
marched out from Yànmén,
and with thirty thousand cavalry attacked the Xiōngnú,
beheading or capturing several thousand enemies.
The next year,
the Xiōngnú invaded and killed the Grand Administrator of Liáoxī,
captured over two thousand people from Yúyáng,
and defeated General Hán's army.
Hàn ordered General Lǐ Xī to attack them,
marching out from Dài;
and ordered General of Chariots and Cavalry Wèi Qīng to march out from west of Yúnzhōng to Gāoquē.
They then captured the land south of the river,
reaching as far as Lǒngxī,
capturing several thousand enemies,
and seizing hundreds of thousands of livestock,
routing the White Sheep
and Lóufán kings.
They then established the land south of the river as Shuòfāng Commandery.
Wèi Qīng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chángpíng with three thousand eight hundred households.
Wèi Qīng's Colonel Sū Jiàn had merit,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Pínglíng with one thousand one hundred households.
He was sent to build Shuòfāng City.
Wèi Qīng's Colonel Zhāng Cìgōng had merit,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Àntóu.
The Son of Heaven said:
"The Xiōngnú defy the natural order,
disrupt human relations,
oppress the elders and abuse the aged,
devote themselves to theft and robbery,
practice deceit among the various barbarians,
plot and borrow troops,
and repeatedly cause border troubles.
Therefore, we raised an army and dispatched generals
to punish their crimes.
Does the Book of Songs not say,
'We smote the Xiǎnyǔn,
reaching Tàiyuán,'
'The chariots set out in grandeur,
building that city in Shuòfāng.'
Now General of Chariots and Cavalry Wèi Qīng crossed the Western River to Gāoquē,
captured two thousand three hundred enemy heads,
completely seized their chariots, supplies, and livestock as spoils,
and has already been enfeoffed as a ranked marquis.
He then pacified the land south of the river to the west,
inspected the old fortress at Yúxī,
crossed Zǐ Ridge,
bridged the Northern River,
subdued Púní,
defeated Fúlí,
beheaded light and sharp troops,
captured three thousand seventy-one spies and scouts,
interrogated prisoners and captured chieftains,
drove over a million horses, cattle, and sheep,
and returned with armor and weapons intact.
We increase Wèi Qīng's fief by three thousand households."
The next year,
the Xiōngnú invaded and killed the Grand Administrator of Dàijùn, Yǒu,
and captured over a thousand people from Yànmén.
The next year,
the Xiōngnú greatly invaded Dài,
Dìngxiāng,
and Shàngjùn,
killing or capturing several thousand Hàn people.
The next year,
in the spring of the fifth year of Yuánshuò,
Hàn ordered General of Chariots and Cavalry Wèi Qīng to lead thirty thousand cavalry,
and march out from Gāoquē;
Commandant of the Palace Guard Sū Jiàn served as General of Agile Cavalry,
the Left Neishi Lǐ Jǔ served as General of Strong Crossbows,
the Grand Coachman Gōngsūn Hè served as General of Cavalry,
the Chancellor of Dài Lǐ Cài served as General of Light Chariots,
all under the command of the General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and together marched out from Shuòfāng;
the Grand Herald Lǐ Xī
and Marquis of Àntóu Zhāng Cìgōng served as generals,
and marched out from Yòuběipíng:
all attacked the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú Wise King of the Right faced Wèi Qīng and others' troops,
thinking the Hàn troops could not reach this place,
and drank until drunk.
The Hàn troops arrived at night,
surrounded the Wise King of the Right,
the Wise King of the Right was startled,
fled at night,
alone with his beloved concubine and several hundred strong cavalry galloping away,
breaking through the encirclement and fleeing north.
Hàn's Colonel of Light Cavalry Guō Chéng and others pursued for several hundred li,
but could not catch up,
capturing over ten subordinate kings of the Wise King of the Right,
over fifteen thousand men and women,
and livestock numbering in the tens of millions,
then led the troops back.
Upon reaching the frontier,
the Son of Heaven sent an emissary holding the seal of the Grand General,
and right in the army appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry Wèi Qīng as Grand General,
all generals then placed their troops under the Grand General's command,
the Grand General established his authority and returned.
The Son of Heaven said:
"Grand General Qīng personally led the warriors,
the army achieved great victory,
capturing over ten Xiōngnú kings,
we increase Wèi Qīng's fief by six thousand households."
And enfeoffed Wèi Qīng's son Wèi Kàng as Marquis of Yíchūn,
Wèi Qīng's son Wèi Bùyí as Marquis of Yīn'ān,
Wèi Qīng's son Wèi Dēng as Marquis of Fāgān.
Wèi Qīng firmly declined, saying:
"Your subject is fortunate to serve in the army despite his faults,
relying on Your Majesty's divine power,
the army achieved great victory,
all due to the efforts of the various colonels in battle.
Your Majesty has already graciously increased your subject Qīng's fief.
Your subject Qīng's sons are still in swaddling clothes,
having performed no toil or service,
yet Your Majesty graciously grants them land enfeoffing them as three marquises,
this is not how your subject, serving in the army despite his faults, intends to encourage the warriors to fight hard.
How dare Kàng and the other two accept enfeoffment!"
The Son of Heaven said:
"I have not forgotten the merits of the various colonels,
and will certainly consider them now."
Then he decreed to the Censor:
"Commandant of the Central Army Gōngsūn Áo three times followed the Grand General to attack the Xiōngnú,
often protecting the army,
assisting the troops to capture a king,
enfeoff Áo as Marquis of Héqí with one thousand five hundred households.
Commandant Hán Yuè followed the Grand General out of Yǔhún,
reached the court of the Xiōngnú Wise King of the Right,
fought bravely under the command to capture a king,
enfeoff Yuè as Marquis of Lóng'é with one thousand three hundred households.
General of Cavalry Gōngsūn Hè followed the Grand General and captured a king,
enfeoff Hè as Marquis of Nánjiào with one thousand three hundred households.
General of Light Chariots Lǐ Cài twice followed the Grand General and captured a king,
enfeoff Cài as Marquis of Lè'ān with one thousand six hundred households.
Colonel Lǐ Shuò,
Colonel Zhào Bùyú,
Colonel Gōngsūn Róngnú,
each three times followed the Grand General and captured a king,
enfeoff Shuò as Marquis of Shèzhǐ with one thousand three hundred households,
enfeoff Bùyú as Marquis of Suíchéng with one thousand three hundred households,
enfeoff Róngnú as Marquis of Cóngpíng with one thousand three hundred households.
General Lǐ Jǔ,
Lǐ Xī, and Colonel Dòu Rúyì had merit,
granted the title of Marquis within the Pass,
each with a revenue fief of three hundred households."
That autumn,
the Xiōngnú invaded Dài,
and killed Commandant Zhū Yīng.
In the spring of the following year,
General-in-Chief Qīng set out from Dìngxiāng,
with Marquis Héqí Áo serving as Central General,
Grand Coachman Hè as Left General,
Marquis Xī Zhào Xìn as Vanguard General,
Commandant of the Palace Guards Sū Jiàn as Right General,
Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace Lǐ Guǎng as Rear General,
and Right Interior Secretary Lǐ Jǔ as General of Strong Crossbows,
all under the command of the General-in-Chief,
who returned after beheading several thousand enemy troops.
Over a month later,
they all set out again from Dìngxiāng to attack the Xiōngnú,
beheading or capturing over ten thousand men.
Right General Jiàn
and Vanguard General Xìn, combining their forces of over three thousand cavalry,
alone encountered the Chányú's troops,
fought with them for more than a day,
and the Hàn soldiers were nearly wiped out.
Vanguard General, originally a Hú man,
had surrendered and been made a Marquis Xī,
but when pressed hard,
the Xiōngnú lured him,
so he led his remaining cavalry, about eight hundred,
to flee and surrender to the Chányú.
Right General Sū Jiàn lost his entire army,
only managing to escape alone,
and returned on his own to the General-in-Chief.
The General-in-Chief consulted his rectifier Hóng,
Chief Clerk Ān,
and Court Counselor Zhōu Bà, among others:
"What should be done with Jiàn?"
Bà said:
"Since the General-in-Chief began his campaigns,
he has never executed a deputy general.
Now Jiàn has abandoned his army;
he should be executed to demonstrate the General's authority."
Hóng and Ān said:
"Not so.
According to the Art of War,
'A small force that stands firm
becomes the prey of a large force.'
Now Jiàn faced the Chányú's tens of thousands with only a few thousand men,
fought fiercely for over a day,
until his troops were exhausted,
yet he dared not harbor disloyalty,
and returned on his own.
To execute him upon his return
would signal to others that there is no intention of returning.
He should not be executed."
The General-in-Chief said:
"I, Qīng, am fortunate to serve with a close relationship to the throne, performing duties in the army;
I do not worry about lacking authority,
yet Bà advises me to assert my authority,
which greatly contradicts my intentions as a subject.
Moreover, although my duties might include executing generals,
given my honored and favored position, I dare not arbitrarily exercise the power of execution beyond the borders.
Instead, I shall send him back to the Son of Heaven,
and let the Son of Heaven decide his fate himself.
In this way, it can be seen that as a subject, I dare not monopolize authority;
is that not appropriate?"
The military officials all said,
"Well said."
So they imprisoned Jiàn and sent him to the emperor's temporary residence.
They then entered the frontier passes and disbanded the troops.
That year,
the General-in-Chief's nephew Huò Qùbìng,
aged eighteen,
favored, served as the Son of Heaven's attendant.
Skilled in archery and horsemanship,
he twice followed the General-in-Chief,
receiving an edict to lead brave warriors,
and was appointed as Colonel of Swift Cavalry,
taking eight hundred light and daring cavalry straight ahead, leaving the main army hundreds of miles behind to seek advantage,
and beheading or capturing enemies beyond the expected count.
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven said:
"Colonel of Swift Cavalry Qùbìng has beheaded or captured two thousand and twenty-eight enemies,
and along with a chancellor,
and a Dānghù, beheaded the Chányú's granduncle Jíruòhóu Chǎn,
captured alive his uncle Luógūbǐ,
twice achieving the foremost military merit,
so I enfeoff Qùbìng as Marquis of Champion with one thousand six hundred households."
The Administrator of Shànggǔ Hǎo Xián, having followed the General-in-Chief four times,
captured and beheaded over two thousand enemies,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhònglì with one thousand one hundred households.
That year,
two generals lost their armies,
and a Marquis Xī was lost,
so military achievements were not abundant,
thus the General-in-Chief received no additional enfeeffment.
When Right General Jiàn arrived,
the Son of Heaven did not execute him,
pardoning his crime,
allowing him to redeem himself as a commoner.
After the General-in-Chief returned,
he was awarded a thousand catties of gold.
At that time, Lady Wáng was favored by the Emperor,
and Nìng Chéng advised the General-in-Chief, saying:
"The reason you, General, though your achievements are not exceedingly great,
enjoy a fief of ten thousand households,
and your three sons are all marquises,
is solely due to the Empress's influence.
Now Lady Wáng is favored, yet her clan has not attained wealth and honor;
I hope you, General, will offer the thousand catties of gold you received as a gift to Lady Wáng's relatives."
The General-in-Chief then gave five hundred catties of gold as a gift.
When the Son of Heaven heard of this,
he asked the General-in-Chief,
who told the truth,
and the Emperor then appointed Nìng Chéng as Governor of Dōnghǎi.
Zhāng Qiān followed the General-in-Chief,
having previously been an envoy to Dàxià,
stayed long among the Xiōngnú,
guided the army,
knew places with good water and pasture,
so the army did not suffer from hunger or thirst;
for his earlier merit of missions to distant lands,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis Bówàng.
Three years after Marquis of Champion Qùbìng was enfeoffed,
in the spring of the second year of Yuánshòu,
Marquis of Champion Qùbìng was appointed as General of Swift Cavalry,
leading ten thousand cavalry out of Lǒngxī,
and achieved merit.
The Son of Heaven said:
"General of Swift Cavalry led his warriors across Wūlì,
attacked Sùpú,
forded Húnú,
passed through five kingdoms,
not seizing those intimidated by the baggage trains and crowds,
hoping to capture the Chányú's son.
He fought for six days,
traversed over a thousand miles beyond Yānzhī Shān,
engaged in close combat,
killed the King of Zhélán,
beheaded the King of Lúhú,
annihilated fully armored troops,
captured the son of Húnyé and his chancellor,
commandant,
beheading or capturing over eight thousand enemies,
and seized the golden statue for worshiping heaven of Xiūchú,
so I increase Qùbìng's enfeeffment by two thousand households."
That summer,
the Swift Cavalry General and Marquis Héqí Ào both set out from Běidì,
taking different routes;
Marquis of Bówàng Zhāng Qiān and
the Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace Lǐ Guǎng both set out from Yòuběipíng,
taking different routes,
all to attack the Xiōngnú.
The Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace, leading four thousand cavalry, arrived first,
while the Marquis of Bówàng, leading ten thousand cavalry, arrived later.
The Xiōngnú Left Worthy King led tens of thousands of cavalry to surround the Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace,
who fought them for two days,
with over half his men killed,
though the enemy casualties were even greater.
When the Marquis of Bówàng arrived,
the Xiōngnú troops withdrew.
The Marquis of Bówàng was charged with delaying his advance,
sentenced to death,
but redeemed himself to become a commoner.
Meanwhile, the Swift Cavalry General set out from Běidì,
advanced deep into enemy territory,
and lost contact with Marquis Héqí,
failing to rendezvous.
The Swift Cavalry General crossed Jūyán and reached Qílián Mountain,
capturing many enemy leaders and soldiers.
The Son of Heaven said:
"The Swift Cavalry General crossed Jūyán,
passed through Xiǎo Yuèzhī,
attacked Qílián Mountain,
captured King Qiútú,
with 2,500 of his followers surrendering,
beheaded 30,200 enemies,
captured five kings,
the mothers of five kings,
the Chányú's consort,
fifty-nine princes,
chancellors,
generals,
Dānghù officials,
and commandants—sixty-three in total,
reducing the enemy's forces by about thirty percent.
I grant Huò Qùbìng an additional five thousand households.
I bestow upon the commandants who followed him to Xiǎo Yuèzhī the rank of Left庶長.
Eagle Attack Sima Pò nú, following the Swift Cavalry General again, beheaded King Sù Pú,
captured King Jī Jū,
with a cavalry commander capturing a king,
a king's mother—one each,
forty-one individuals from princes downward,
and 3,330 prisoners.
The vanguard captured 1,400 prisoners;
I grant Pò nú 1,500 households and enfeoff him as Marquis Cóng Piào.
Commandant Gōu Wáng Gāo Bùshí,
following the Swift Cavalry General, captured King Hūyútú's prince and eleven others below him,
and 1,768 prisoners;
I grant Bùshí 1,100 households and enfeoff him as Marquis Yí Guàn.
Commandant Pú Duō has rendered meritorious service,
and is enfeoffed as Marquis Huī Qú."
Marquis Héqí Ào was charged with delaying and failing to rendezvous with the Swift Cavalry General,
sentenced to death,
but redeemed himself to become a commoner.
The veteran generals' troops, horses, and weapons were also inferior to those of the Swift Cavalry General;
the Swift Cavalry General often selected the best,
and he dared to advance deep,
often leading elite cavalry ahead of the main army.
His army also had heavenly fortune,
never facing dire straits.
However, the veteran generals often faced setbacks and missed opportunities.
Thus, the Swift Cavalry General grew increasingly favored and esteemed,
on par with the Great General.
That autumn,
the Chányú was angered that King Húnxié, stationed in the west, had been repeatedly defeated by Hàn,
losing tens of thousands of men,
due to the Swift Cavalry General's forces.
The Chányú, enraged,
intended to summon and execute King Húnxié.
King Húnxié, along with King Xiūchú and others, plotted to surrender to Hàn,
sending men first to the border to arrange it.
At that time, the Grand Herald Lǐ Xī was fortifying positions along the river,
and upon encountering King Húnxié's envoy,
he immediately sent a fast carriage to report it.
The Son of Heaven, upon hearing this,
feared it might be a feigned surrender to attack the border,
so he ordered the Swift Cavalry General to lead troops to meet them.
After the Swift Cavalry General crossed the river,
he and King Húnxié's forces sighted each other.
Many of King Húnxié's subordinate commanders, upon seeing the Hàn army, wished not to surrender,
and some fled.
The Swift Cavalry General then galloped in to meet King Húnxié,
beheading eight thousand of those who intended to flee,
and then sent King Húnxié alone by fast carriage to the imperial headquarters,
leading all his followers across the river.
Tens of thousands surrendered,
claiming to be a hundred thousand.
Upon reaching Cháng'ān,
the Son of Heaven bestowed rewards worth several hundred million.
He enfeoffed King Húnxié with ten thousand households,
making him Marquis of Luòyīn.
He enfeoffed his subordinate king Hūdúní as Marquis Xiàmó,
Yīng Bì as Marquis Huī Qú,
Qín Lí as Marquis Hé Qí,
and the Grand Dānghù Tóng Lí as Marquis Chánglè.
Then the Son of Heaven praised the Swift Cavalry General's achievements, saying:
"The Swift Cavalry General Qùbìng led his army to attack the Xiōngnú's Western Region King Húnxié,
and the king and his people all fled to us.
He supplied them with army rations,
and led over ten thousand archers,
executing the fierce and unruly,
capturing over eight thousand enemy heads,
and subjugating thirty-two kings from foreign lands.
His warriors remained uninjured,
and the hundred thousand masses were all pacified and subdued.
Through his diligent efforts,
extending to the river frontiers,
there is nearly no more worry,
and peace is now long-lasting.
I grant the Swift Cavalry General an additional 1,700 households."
He reduced the garrison soldiers in Lǒngxī,
Běidì,
and Shàngjùn by half,
to ease the corvée burdens across the land.
Shortly after,
he resettled the surrendered people along the borders of five commanderies outside the old barriers,
all south of the river,
allowing them to keep their native customs,
as dependent states.
The following year,
the Xiōngnú invaded Yòuběipíng
and Dìngxiāng,
killing or capturing over a thousand Hàn people.
The next year,
the Son of Heaven discussed with his generals:
"Marquis Xī Zhào Xìn has advised the Chányú,
often believing that Hàn troops cannot cross the desert lightly and linger.
Now, if we send a large force,
we are sure to achieve our goal."
This was the fourth year of the Yuánshòu era.
In the spring of the fourth year of Yuánshòu,
the Emperor ordered the Great General Wèi Qīng
and the Swift Cavalry General Huò Qùbìng to each lead fifty thousand cavalry,
with infantry and supply troops following in the tens of thousands,
and all the soldiers daring to fight fiercely and advance deep were assigned to the Swift Cavalry General.
The Swift Cavalry General initially set out from Dìngxiāng,
to face the Chányú.
But prisoners revealed the Chányú had gone east,
so he was redirected to set out from Dàijùn,
while the Great General set out from Dìngxiāng.
The Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace was the Front General,
the Grand Coachman was the Left General,
the Master of Titles Zhào Shíjī was the Right General,
and Marquis of Píngyáng Cáo Xiāng was the Rear General,
all under the Great General.
Once the troops crossed the desert,
totaling fifty thousand cavalry,
they, along with the Swift Cavalry General, all attacked the Xiōngnú Chányú.
Zhào Xìn advised the Chányú:
"The Hàn troops have crossed the desert,
their men and horses are exhausted,
and the Xiōngnú can easily capture them."
So, they moved all their heavy supplies far north,
and awaited with elite troops north of the desert.
It happened that the Great General's army emerged over a thousand lǐ beyond the frontier,
and found the Chányú's troops arrayed and waiting.
Thereupon, the Great General ordered armored vehicles to form a circular camp,
and sent five thousand cavalry to engage the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú also sent out about ten thousand cavalry.
As the sun was setting,
a strong wind arose,
sand and gravel striking faces,
and the two armies lost sight of each other.
The Hàn then extended their left and right wings to encircle the Chányú.
The Chányú saw the Hàn troops were numerous,
and their men and horses still strong,
so the battle turned unfavorable for the Xiōngnú.
Near dusk,
the Chányú mounted a six-horse chariot,
with several hundred elite cavalry,
and broke through the Hàn encirclement, galloping northwest.
By then, it was dark,
and the Hàn and Xiōngnú forces were entangled in chaos,
inflicting heavy casualties on each other.
The Hàn army's left wing captured prisoners who said the Chányú had left before nightfall,
so the Hàn army dispatched light cavalry to pursue him overnight,
with the Great General's army following behind.
The Xiōngnú troops also scattered and fled.
At dawn,
they had advanced over two hundred lǐ,
without catching the Chányú,
but captured and beheaded over ten thousand enemies.
They then reached Tiányán Mountain and Zhào Xìn's city,
where they seized the Xiōngnú's stored grain to feed the army.
The army stayed one day and then returned,
burning the remaining grain in the city before heading back.
When the Grand General was to rendezvous with the Chányú,
the former General Guǎng and
the Right General Shíjī's troops separately followed the eastern route,
but lost their way,
and attacked the Chányú later.
The Grand General led his forces back across the desert's southern edge,
where he then encountered the former General and
the Right General.
The Grand General intended to send envoys to report back,
ordering the Chief Clerk to interrogate former General Guǎng with written charges,
and Guǎng committed suicide.
When the Right General arrived,
he was handed over to the officials,
and ransomed himself to become a commoner.
The Grand General's army entered the frontier pass,
having altogether beheaded or captured 19,000 enemy.
At that time, the Xiōngnú masses had lost their Chányú for over ten days,
and the Right Gūlǐwáng, hearing of this,
proclaimed himself Chányú.
The Chányú later regained his followers,
and the Right King then relinquished the title of Chányú.
The Swift Cavalry General also led 50,000 cavalry,
with supply wagons equal to those of the Grand General's army,
but had no subordinate generals.
He fully appointed Lǐ Gǎn and others as senior colonels,
acting as subordinate generals,
and marched from Dài
and Yòuběipíng over a thousand lǐ,
directly confronting the left flank forces,
and the achievements in beheading and capturing enemies already surpassed those of the Grand General.
After the army returned,
the Son of Heaven said:
"Swift Cavalry General Qùbìng led his troops,
personally commanding the captured Xūnyù warriors,
with lightly carried provisions,
crossed the great desert,
forded and captured Zhāngqú,
to execute Bǐchēqí,
turned to attack the Left Great General,
beheading him and capturing his banners and drums,
traversed Líhóu.
Crossed Gōnglǘ,
captured Túntóuwáng,
Hánwáng, and another, three kings in total,
along with generals,
chancellors,
Dānghù,
and commandants, eighty-three in all,
sealed Lángjūxū Mountain,
performed the fēng sacrifice at Gūyǎn,
and ascended to the Hànhǎi.
Captured 70,443 enemies and leaders,
with army losses reduced by thirty percent,
procuring food from the enemy,
marching exceptionally far without exhausting provisions,
I add 5,800 households to enfeoff the Swift Cavalry General."
Yòuběipíng Grand Administrator Lù Bódé, attached to the Swift Cavalry General,
rendezvoused at Yǔchéng,
not missing the deadline,
followed to Táoyú Mountain,
beheading and capturing 2,700 enemies,
and with 1,600 households, enfeoffed Bódé as Fúlí Marquis.
Běidì Commandant Xíng Shān, following the Swift Cavalry General, captured a king,
and with 1,200 households, enfeoffed Shān as Yìyáng Marquis.
Former Guīyì Yīnchúnwáng Fù Lùzhī,
Lóuzhuānwáng Yī Jíjiān both followed the Swift Cavalry General with merit,
and with 1,300 households, enfeoffed Fù Lùzhī as Zhuàng Marquis,
with 1,800 households, enfeoffed Yī Jíjiān as Zhònglì Marquis.
Cóngpiáo Marquis Pòná,
Chāngwǔ Marquis Ānjī followed the Swift Cavalry General with merit,
each granted an additional 300 households.
Colonel Gǎn captured banners and drums,
was made Guānnèi Marquis,
with a fief of 200 households.
Colonel Zìwéi was awarded the rank of Dàshùzhǎng.
Army officers and soldiers who became officials,
received abundant rewards.
But the Grand General did not receive additional enfeeffment,
and none of his army officers or soldiers were enfeoffed as marquises.
When the two armies exited the frontier pass,
the pass recorded a total of 140,000 official and private horses,
but fewer than 30,000 returned through the pass.
Then the position of Grand Marshal was additionally established,
and both the Grand General
and Swift Cavalry General were made Grand Marshals.
A decree was fixed,
ordering that the Swift Cavalry General's rank and emolument be equal to the Grand General's.
From then on,
the Grand General Qīng daily declined,
while the Swift Cavalry General increasingly rose in honor.
Many former followers and retainers of the Grand General left to serve the Swift Cavalry General,
and often obtained offices and titles,
only Rèn Ān refused.
The Swift Cavalry General was a person of few words and not leaky,
possessing courage and daring to undertake responsibilities.
The Son of Heaven once wished to teach him the military strategies of Sūn and Wú,
to which he replied:
"It depends on how the strategy is,
not necessarily to study ancient military tactics."
The Son of Heaven built a mansion for him,
and ordered the Swift Cavalry General to view it,
to which he replied:
"The Xiōngnú have not yet been destroyed,
I have no use for a home."
From this, the Emperor increasingly valued and loved him.
However, since youth he served in the palace,
was noble, and did not attend to his soldiers.
When he went on campaign,
and upon return,
the heavy carts leftover discarded fine grains and meat,
while some soldiers went hungry.
When outside the frontier pass,
when troops were short of food,
some could not even stand,
yet the Swift Cavalry General still had fields leveled for playing Cùjū.
Matters were often like this.
The Grand General was benevolent, kind, and retiring,
using gentleness to ingratiate himself with the Emperor,
yet he was not praised by the world.
The Swift Cavalry General, three years after his campaign in the fourth year,
died in the sixth year of Yuánshòu.
The Son of Heaven mourned him,
dispatched the Dependent State's Black Armor Army,
arrayed from Cháng'ān to Màolíng,
and built his tomb in the likeness of Qílián Mountain.
Posthumously titled him,
combining martial and territorial expansion as Jǐnghuán Marquis.
His son Shàn succeeded to the marquisate.
Shàn was young,
styled Zǐhóu,
and the Emperor loved him,
hoping that when he grew strong, he would command him.
After six years,
in the first year of Yuánfēng,
Shàn died,
posthumously titled Āi Marquis.
He had no son,
the line ended, and the fief was abolished.
After the Swift Cavalry General's death,
the Grand General's eldest son, Yìchūn Marquis Kàng, lost his marquisate due to legal offense.
Five years later,
Kàng's two younger brothers,
Yīn'ān Marquis Bùyí and Fāgàn Marquis Dēng, both lost their marquisates due to the Zhòujīn offense.
Two years after losing their marquisates,
the Champion Marquis's fief was abolished.
Four years later,
the Grand General Qīng died,
posthumously titled Liè Marquis.
His son Kàng succeeded as Chángpíng Marquis.
From the time the Grand General besieged the Chányú,
fourteen years later he died.
Ultimately, he did not attack the Xiōngnú again,
because the Hàn horses were few,
and they were concurrently suppressing the two Yuè in the south,
attacking Cháoxiǎn in the east,
and striking the Qiāng
and Southwestern Barbarians,
hence they long did not attack the Hú.
Because the Grand General had the honor of marrying the Princess of Píngyáng,
Chángpíng Marquis Kàng succeeded to the marquisate.
Six years later,
he lost his marquisate due to legal offense.
Listed to the left are the two Grand Generals and various subordinate generals' names:
Foremost is Grand General Qīng,
who in total launched seven attacks against the Xiōngnú,
beheading or capturing over 50,000 enemies.
Once battled the Chányú,
recovered the land south of the river,
and thus established the Shuòfāng Commandery,
twice received additional enfeeffment,
totaling 11,800 households.
Enfeoffed three sons as marquises,
with 1,300 households per marquis.
Combined,
15,700 households.
His colonels and subordinate generals who were enfeoffed as marquises for following the Grand General numbered nine.
His subordinate generals and colonels who later became generals numbered fourteen.
Among the subordinate generals was Lǐ Guǎng,
who has his own biography.
Those without biographies are:
General Guō Chāng
was a native of Yúnzhōng.
He served as a Colonel under the Grand General.
In the fourth year of the Yuánfēng era,
he was appointed as the General for Uprooting the Hú, with the title of Grand Master of the Palace,
and stationed in Shuòfāng.
He returned to attack the Kūnmíng,
but achieved no merit,
and his seal was taken away.
General Xún Zhì,
a native of Guǎngwǔ in Tàiyuán,
was recognized for his driving skills,
served as a Palace Attendant,
and became a Colonel,
frequently following the Grand General.
In the third year of the Yuánfēng era, as a Left General, he attacked Cháoxiān,
but achieved no merit.
He was executed for arresting the Towered Ship General in accordance with the law.
As for the Swift Cavalry General Huò Qùbìng,
he went on six campaigns against the Xiōngnú in total,
four of them as a general,
decapitating or capturing over 110,000 enemies.
When Prince Húnyé surrendered with tens of thousands of followers,
he thus opened up the lands west of the river, establishing Jiǔquán,
and the western regions saw fewer Hú raids.
He was enfeoffed four times,
totaling 15,100 households.
Among his officers who achieved merit and became marquises, there were six in total,
and two later became generals.
General Lù Bódé,
a native of Píngzhōu,
served as the Grand Administrator of Right Běipíng under the Swift Cavalry General and achieved merit,
becoming the Marquis of Fúlí.
After the Swift Cavalry General's death,
Bódé, as Commandant of the Guards, became the Wave-Subduing General,
attacked and defeated Nányuè,
and gained additional enfeoffment.
Later, he lost his marquisate due to legal offenses.
He served as Commandant of the Strong Crossbows,
stationed in Jūyán,
where he died.
General Zhào Pònú,
originally from Jiǔyuán,
once fled to the Xiōngnú,
but later returned to Hàn,
serving as a Major under the Swift Cavalry General.
He achieved merit during the campaign from Běidì,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis Following the Swift Cavalry.
He lost his marquisate due to the ceremonial gold offense.
A year later,
he became the Xiōnghé General,
attacked the Hú up to the Xiōngnú River,
but achieved no merit.
Two years later,
he attacked and captured the King of Lóulán,
and was again enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhuóyě.
Six years later,
as the Jūnjī General,
he led 20,000 cavalry to attack the Left Wise King of the Xiōngnú.
The Left Wise King engaged him in battle,
surrounding Pònú with 80,000 cavalry;
Pònú was captured alive by the enemy,
and his army was wiped out.
He lived among the Xiōngnú for ten years,
then fled back to Hàn with his crown prince Ān Guó.
Later, he was implicated in witchcraft accusations,
and his clan was executed.
Since the rise of the Wèi family,
the Grand General Wèi Qīng was the first enfeoffed,
and later his branches became five marquises.
In just twenty-four years, all five marquisates were stripped,
and no one from the Wèi family remained a marquis.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Sū Jiàn told me:
"I once admonished the Grand General that he held the highest respect,
yet the worthy officials of the world did not praise him for it.
I hoped the General would observe how ancient famous commanders attracted and selected worthy men,
and strive to do so.
The Grand General apologized and said:
'Since the days of Wèi Qí
and Wǔ'ān entertaining guests lavishly,
the Son of Heaven has often gnashed his teeth in anger.
To draw close to scholars and officials,
attracting the worthy and rejecting the unworthy—
that is the prerogative of the ruler.
A subject's duty is merely to uphold the laws and fulfill his responsibilities;
why should he engage in attracting scholars!'"
The Swift Cavalry General also followed this principle,
such was their approach to being generals.
Chancellor Gōngsūn Hóng,
a native of Xuē County in the kingdom of Zīchuān in Qí,
courtesy name Jì.
In his youth, he served as a prison officer in Xuē,
committed an offense,
and was dismissed. His family was poor,
so he herded pigs by the sea.
Over forty years old,
he then studied the Spring and Autumn Annals and various doctrines.
He supported his stepmother with filial piety and respect.
In the first year of the Jiànyuán era,
the Son of Heaven had just ascended the throne,
and summoned worthy, virtuous, and literary scholars.
At that time, Hóng was sixty years old,
and was recommended as a Erudite for his worthiness and virtue.
Sent on a mission to the Xiōngnú,
upon his return report,
it did not meet the Emperor's expectations,
the Emperor was angered,
considering him incompetent,
so Hóng pleaded illness and returned home dismissed.
In the fifth year of the Yuánguāng era,
an edict summoned literary scholars,
and the kingdom of Zīchuān again recommended Gōngsūn Hóng.
Hóng declined and apologized to his countrymen, saying:
"I have already once gone west in response to the command,
and was dismissed and returned due to incompetence;
I wish you would recommend someone else."
His countrymen firmly recommended Hóng,
and Hóng went to the Minister of Ceremonies.
The Minister of Ceremonies ordered the recommended Confucian scholars to each present policy responses,
over a hundred men,
Hóng's ranking was at the bottom.
When the responses were presented,
the Son of Heaven promoted Hóng's response to first place.
Summoned for an audience,
his appearance was very handsome,
and he was appointed as an Erudite.
At that time, the road to the southwestern tribes was being opened,
and commaderies established,
causing hardship for the people of Bā and Shǔ,
so an edict sent Hóng to inspect it.
Upon his return report,
he strongly criticized the southwestern tribes as useless,
but the Emperor did not listen.
Hóng was a man of broad and extraordinary knowledge,
often stating that the ruler's flaw is a lack of breadth and grandeur,
while the subject's flaw is a lack of frugality.
Hóng used cloth quilts,
and did not eat more than one meat dish.
When his stepmother died,
he observed the three-year mourning period.
In court discussions,
he would present the main points,
letting the ruler choose for himself,
unwilling to confront or argue in court.
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven observed his conduct as sincere and generous,
his arguments ample,
well-versed in legal statutes and administrative affairs,
and further adorned with Confucian principles,
so the Emperor greatly delighted in him.
Within two years,
he rose to Left Interior Secretary.
When Hóng presented matters,
if there was disagreement,
he did not argue in court.
Once he and the Commandant of the Nobility Jí Àn requested a private audience;
Jí Àn spoke first,
Hóng followed up,
and the Emperor was often pleased,
listening to all they said,
thus Hóng grew increasingly close and honored.
He once made agreements with the high officials in discussions,
but when before the Emperor,
he would betray those agreements to comply with the Emperor's wishes.
Jí Àn confronted Hóng in court, saying:
"Men of Qí are often deceitful and insincere;
initially you joined us in making this proposal,
now you betray it all,
disloyal."
The Emperor asked Hóng.
Hóng apologized and said:
"Those who know me consider me loyal,
those who do not know me consider me disloyal."
The Emperor agreed with Hóng's words.
When the favored courtiers nearby often slandered Hóng,
the Emperor treated him even more generously.
The Methods of the Sīmǎ states:
"Though a state may be large,
if it is fond of war it will surely perish;
though the world may be at peace,
if it forgets war it will surely be endangered."
When the world is at peace,
the Son of Heaven holds grand reviews,
conducting spring hunts and autumn drills,
while the feudal lords train their troops in spring
and drill their soldiers in autumn,
all to ensure they do not forget war.
Moreover, anger is a contrary virtue,
weapons are instruments of ill omen,
and contention is a petty matter.
In ancient times, when a ruler gave vent to his anger, corpses would surely fall and blood flow,
thus the sage kings were cautious in such actions.
Those who insist on victory and exhaust military affairs
have never failed to regret it.
In the past, the Qín Emperor wielded the might of his victories,
gnawing away at the world like a silkworm,
swallowing up the Warring States,
unifying all within the seas,
achieving merits equal to the Three Dynasties.
Yet striving for victory without cease,
he desired to attack the Xiōngnú.
Lǐ Sī admonished him, saying:
"This will not do.
The Xiōngnú have no walled cities to dwell in,
nor storehouses to guard;
they move like birds taking flight,
making them difficult to capture and control.
If we send light troops deep into their territory,
our provisions will surely be cut off;
if we follow with supply trains,
the burden will be too great to accomplish the task.
Gaining their land would not suffice to establish control,
and encountering their people, we could not conscript and garrison them.
Victory would necessitate their slaughter,
which is not the way of a parent to the people.
Exhausting the Middle Kingdom
to gratify ourselves against the Xiōngnú
is not a sound strategy."
The Qín Emperor did not listen,
and so sent Méng Tián to lead troops against the Hú,
opening up a thousand lǐ of territory,
making the river his border.
The land was but marshes and salt flats,
where the five grains would not grow.
Thereupon he conscripted all able-bodied men of the realm to guard the Northern River.
For over a decade, his troops were exposed in the field,
and the dead were beyond counting,
yet in the end they could not cross the river to the north.
Was this due to insufficient manpower
or inadequate weapons and armor?
It was because the circumstances made it impossible.
He further made the whole realm transport fodder and grain,
starting from the coastal commanleries of Huáng,
Chuí, and Lángyá,
conveying them to the Northern River,
at a rate where thirty zhōng yielded but one shí.
Men toiled at farming yet could not produce enough grain supplies,
women spun and wove yet could not provide enough tents and curtains.
The common people were exhausted and impoverished,
orphans, widows, the old, and the weak could not support one another,
and the dead lined the roads,
marking the beginning of the realm's rebellion against Qín.
When Emperor Gāo secured the realm,
he campaigned along the border
and, hearing that the Xiōngnú had gathered beyond Dàigǔ, sought to attack them.
Censor Chéng Jìn admonished him:
"This will not do.
The nature of the Xiōngnú
is to gather like beasts and scatter like birds;
pursuing them is like striking at a shadow.
Now for Your Majesty, in your great virtue, to attack the Xiōngnú,
I privately fear the danger."
Emperor Gāo did not listen,
and proceeded north to Dàigǔ,
where indeed he was besieged at Píngchéng.
Emperor Gāo deeply regretted this,
and so sent Liú Jìng to negotiate a peace and marriage alliance,
after which the world forgot the affairs of war.
Thus the Art of War states:
"To raise an army of a hundred thousand
costs a thousand pieces of gold daily."
Now Qín often amassed troops and exposed hundreds of thousands of soldiers,
and though they achieved the feat of crushing armies, killing generals, and capturing the Chányú,
it only served to deepen enmity and hatred,
insufficient to repay the realm's expenses.
Above, it depleted the treasuries;
below, it exhausted the common people.
To find satisfaction in foreign lands
is not a sound undertaking.
That the Xiōngnú are difficult to control
is not a matter of one era alone.
Raiding and plundering
are their way of life;
it is their inherent nature.
From Yú, Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu times onward,
they were surely not regulated or supervised,
but treated as beasts and livestock,
not regarded as human.
If those above do not observe the traditions of Yú, Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu,
but instead follow the errors of recent times,
this is what I greatly fear,
and what the common people bitterly suffer.
Moreover, prolonged warfare gives rise to turmoil,
and bitter hardship leads to altered plans.
Thus the border people become exhausted, sorrowful, and disaffected,
while officers and officials grow suspicious and collude with outsiders,
hence Wèi Tuó
and Zhāng Hán were able to pursue their private interests.
The reason Qín's governance failed
was that authority was divided between these two men;
this demonstrates the effect of gain and loss.
Therefore, the Zhōu Shū states:
"Safety and danger lie in the issuing of commands,
survival and perish in their employment."
I hope Your Majesty will examine this in detail,
and devote some attention to careful consideration.
At that time, Xú Lè of Zhào
and Yán Ān of Qí both submitted memorials on affairs of the world,
each addressing one matter.
Xú Lè said:
I have heard that the calamity of the realm lies in collapse from within,
not in fragmentation from without;
this holds true for both ancient and modern times.
What is meant by collapse from within?
The end of Qín exemplifies it.
Chén Shè lacked the dignity of a thousand-chariot lord,
not an inch of territory,
was not descended from kings, dukes, great men, or renowned clans,
had no reputation in his village,
possessed not the virtue of a Confucius,
Mòzǐ, or Zēngzǐ,
nor the wealth of a Táo Zhū
or Yī Dùn;
yet rising from a poor alley,
brandishing thorn-tipped staves,
baring his arm and shouting, he drew the world to follow like the wind.
What is the reason for this?
The people were distressed, yet the ruler showed no compassion;
those below resented, yet those above remained unaware;
customs were already corrupt, yet governance went unreformed.
These three factors were what Chén Shè capitalized on.
This is called collapse from within.
Thus it is said the calamity of the realm lies in collapse from within.
What is meant by fragmentation from without?
The armies of Wú, Chǔ,
Qí, and Zhào exemplify it.
The Seven States plotted great rebellion,
each styling themselves lords of ten thousand chariots,
fielding armored troops numbering in the hundreds of thousands,
their might sufficient to overawe their domains,
their wealth enough to motivate their officers and people.
Yet they could not seize an inch of land to the west and were themselves captured in the central plains.
What is the reason for this?
Not that their authority was lighter than a commoner's or their troops weaker than Chén Shè's,
but at that time,
the former emperor's virtuous influence had not waned, and the people were content with their land and customs;
thus the feudal lords had no support beyond their borders.
This is called fragmentation from without.
Thus it is said the calamity of the realm does not lie in fragmentation from without.
From this perspective,
if the realm truly faces the momentum of collapse from within,
even a commoner in dire straits may become the chief villain endangering the world,
as Chén Shè did.
How much more so if the lords of the Three Jìn survive!
Though the realm may not be greatly well-governed,
if it truly lacks the momentum of collapse from within,
even with powerful states and strong armies, one may be captured before one can turn around,
as with Wú, Chǔ,
Qí, and Zhào.
How much less could ministers and common people cause rebellion!
These two forms
are the clear essentials of safety and danger,
which worthy rulers should heed and deeply examine.
Recently, the five grains in Guāndōng have failed to yield,
the harvest has not recovered,
the people are largely impoverished,
compounded by border conflicts.
Examining this through reasoning and patterns,
it is evident that the people may become unsettled in their homes.
Being unsettled makes them prone to unrest.
Such unrest
signals a trend toward collapse.
Thus, a wise ruler alone perceives the roots of all transformations,
understands the pivots of safety and danger,
and cultivates governance from the court,
eradicating troubles before they take form.
The essence
lies in ensuring the realm avoids the momentum of collapse.
Hence, even with a powerful state and strong army,
if Your Majesty chases after fleeing beasts,
shoots at flying birds,
expands hunting parks for excursions,
indulges in extravagant sights,
and pursues the extremes of galloping pleasures,
it may seem effortless.
The sounds of bells, strings, and flutes never cease in your ears,
the intimacies of curtains and the laughter of jesters and dwarfs never lack before you,
