yet the realm harbors no lingering worries.
Why must fame rival Tāng and Wǔ,
customs match those of Chéng and Kāng!
Nevertheless,
I humbly believe that with Your Majesty's innate sageliness,
generous and benevolent nature,
and sincere dedication to the realm's affairs,
equaling the fame of Tāng and Wǔ would not be difficult,
and the customs of Chéng and Kāng could be revived.
Once these two aspects are established,
then you will possess the substance of secure honor,
spread a renowned reputation in the present age,
draw the world close and subdue the four barbarians,
leaving a legacy of grace and virtue to flourish for generations.
Facing south, leaning on the screen, adjusting sleeves to salute the nobles,
this is what Your Majesty should embody.
I have heard that aiming for kingship, even if not fully achieved,
its remnants suffice to bring stability.
With stability, what could Your Majesty not obtain,
what could you not accomplish,
what campaign would not succeed!
Yán Ān submitted a memorial stating:
I have heard that the Zhōu dynasty held the realm,
ruling for over three hundred years,
with its peak under Chéng and Kāng,
when punishments were set aside unused for over forty years.
As it declined,
it also lasted over three hundred years,
hence the Five Hegemons arose in succession.
The Five Hegemons
often assisted the Son of Heaven in promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
punishing the violent and restraining the wicked,
rectifying the land,
to honor the Son of Heaven.
After the Five Hegemons passed,
no sages continued their work,
the Son of Heaven grew isolated and weak,
and his commands were not heeded.
The feudal lords acted arbitrarily,
the strong oppressed the weak,
the many abused the few,
Tián Cháng usurped Qí,
the six ministers divided Jìn,
leading to the Warring States period,
marking the beginning of the people's suffering.
Then, strong states focused on attack,
weak states prepared for defense,
forming vertical and horizontal alliances,
with chariots clashing hubs,
armor breeding lice,
and the people having nowhere to appeal.
By the time of the Qín king,
he devoured the world like a silkworm,
annexing the Warring States,
proclaiming himself emperor,
governing the land's administration,
demolishing the cities of the feudal lords,
melting their weapons,
casting them into bell stands,
to show they would not be reused.
The common people were spared the Warring States era,
encountering an enlightened Son of Heaven,
each feeling reborn.
Had Qín relaxed its penalties,
lightened taxes,
reduced corvée labor,
valued benevolence and righteousness,
despised power and profit,
promoted sincerity and honesty,
discouraged cunning and craft,
transformed customs and practices,
and spread this throughout the land,
then generations would surely have been secure.
But Qín did not follow this path and clung to old ways,
advancing the cunning and power-hungry,
while pushing aside the sincere and faithful;
with harsh laws and severe governance,
flatterers abounded,
daily hearing of its own excellence,
its ambitions expanded and mind grew reckless.
Wishing to display might beyond the seas,
it sent Méng Tián to lead troops north against the Hú,
expanding territory and pushing borders,
garrisoning at the Northern River,
with endless supply transports trailing behind.
Also, it sent Commandant Tú Suī with naval forces south to attack the Bǎiyuè,
ordering Jiàn Lù to dig canals for grain transport,
penetrating deep into Yuè territory,
where the Yuè people fled.
Dragging on for long,
supplies ran out,
the Yuè attacked,
and the Qín forces were badly defeated.
Qín then sent Wèi Tuó to lead troops garrisoning Yuè.
At that time,
Qín's troubles were entangled with the Hú in the north,
and bogged down with Yuè in the south,
stationing troops in useless lands,
unable to advance or retreat.
After over a decade,
men bore armor,
women hauled supplies,
suffering beyond endurance,
hanging themselves on roadside trees,
with corpses in sight everywhere.
When the Qín emperor died,
the realm rebelled widely.
Chén Shèng
and Wú Guǎng rose in Chén,
Wǔ Chén
and Zhāng Ěr in Zhào,
Xiàng Liáng in Wú,
Tián Dān in Qí,
Jǐng Jū in Yǐng,
Zhōu Fú in Wèi,
Hán Guǎng in Yān,
with bold figures emerging from remote mountains and valleys,
too numerous to record.
Yet none were descendants of dukes or marquises,
nor high-ranking officials.
Without an inch of power,
they rose from alleys,
wielding thorny sticks,
moving with the times,
rising together without consultation,
gathering without prior agreement,
expanding lands and advancing,
until becoming hegemons or kings,
all driven by the era's circumstances.
Qín, honored as Son of Heaven,
rich with the entire realm,
saw its lineage extinguished and sacrifices ended,
all due to the calamity of warmongering.
Thus, Zhōu failed through weakness,
Qín failed through strength,
each a disaster of inflexibility.
Now there is a desire to summon the southern barbarians,
have the Yèláng pay court,
subdue the Qiāngbó,
conquer the Huìzhōu region,
build cities and towns,
penetrate deep into Xiōngnú territory,
and burn their Lóngchéng city.
Advisors praise these plans.
These are benefits for ministers,
but not sound strategies for the empire.
Currently, the central states suffer no alarm even from barking dogs,
yet we burden ourselves with defenses in distant lands,
depleting the state's resources—
this is no way to nurture the people.
Pursuing endless desires,
indulging in personal satisfaction,
and incurring the hatred of the Xiōngnú—
this is no way to secure the borders.
Once conflict is ignited, it becomes inextricable;
when wars cease, they soon reignite.
Those nearby endure hardship and suffering,
while those far away live in fear and panic—
this is no way to achieve lasting stability.
Now across the empire, armor is forged and swords sharpened,
arrows straightened and bowstrings stocked,
with continuous transport of supplies—
no end in sight,
a shared concern throughout the land.
Prolonged warfare leads to upheaval,
and complex affairs give rise to troubles.
Today, some outer commanderies span nearly a thousand miles,
with dozens of cities in rows,
their terrain and territories controlled,
exerting pressure on the feudal lords—
this is not to the imperial house's advantage.
Looking back, the downfall of Qí and Jìn occurred
when the ducal houses were weakened and diminished,
and the six ministers grew overly powerful;
observing Qín's demise,
it resulted from harsh laws and severe governance,
and insatiable expansionist desires.
Now the authority of commandery governors
is no less weighty than that of the six ministers;
their lands nearly a thousand miles,
far surpassing the resources of alleys and lanes;
their armor, weapons, and equipment
go beyond the utility of thorn-tipped spears.
Should a crisis of ages befall,
the consequences would be too dire to name.
The memorial was presented to the Son of Heaven,
who summoned the three men for an audience,
saying to them:
"Where have you all been?
How regrettably late our meeting is!"
Thereupon, the emperor appointed Zhǔfù Yǎn,
Xú Yuè,
and Yán Ān as court gentlemen.
Yǎn had several audiences,
submitting memorials on state affairs.
By decree, he was appointed as a receptionist,
then promoted to grand master of the palace.
Within a year, Yǎn was promoted four times.
Yǎn advised the emperor, saying:
"In ancient times, feudal lords held no more than a hundred li,
making it easy to control their strength or weakness.
Now some lords possess dozens of connected cities,
with territories spanning a thousand li.
In peacetime, they grow arrogant and prone to decadence;
in crisis, they leverage their strength to ally against the capital.
If we reduce their lands by law now,
rebellious tendencies will sprout,
as seen previously with Cháo Cuò.
Currently, feudal lords may have a dozen or more sons,
but only the heir succeeds to the title,
while the others, though flesh and blood,
receive not an inch of land.
This obscures the way of benevolence and filial duty.
I urge Your Majesty to permit the lords to extend grace by enfeoffing their sons and brothers,
granting them land and titles.
They will each rejoice in having their wishes fulfilled,
while the throne bestows virtue,
effectively dividing their states—
weakening them gradually without formal reduction."
The emperor followed his advice.
He further counseled:
"With Màolíng newly established,
powerful families that monopolize wealth,
and troublemakers among the people
can all be relocated to Màolíng,
thereby strengthening the capital internally
and eliminating cunning elements externally—
this is what is called removing harm without execution."
The emperor again adopted his plan.
In the honoring of Empress Wèi
and the exposure of King Yàn Dìngguó's secret affairs,
Yǎn played a contributing role.
High officials feared his words,
bribing him with accumulations of a thousand gold.
Someone admonished Yǎn, saying:
"You are too overbearing."
Zhǔfù replied:
"I have traveled and studied for over forty years since youth,
yet achieved no personal success,
my parents did not acknowledge me as a son,
my brothers would not take me in,
and friends abandoned me.
I have long been in distress.
Moreover, a true man, if unable to dine from five tripods in life,
may as well be cooked in them in death.
I see the road ahead long as dusk falls,
so I act contrary and impose harsh measures."
Yǎn strongly advocated that Shuòfāng's land was fertile,
protected externally by the river,
where Méng Tián built a city to expel the Xiōngnú,
internally reducing the need for transport and garrison supplies,
expanding the central states,
and forming the foundation for destroying the Hú.
The emperor considered his proposal,
referred it to the ministers for discussion,
but all voiced objections.
Gōngsūn Hóng said:
"In Qín times, three hundred thousand men were often conscripted to build north of the river,
yet it was never completed,
and eventually abandoned."
Zhǔfù Yǎn fervently argued its advantages,
and the emperor ultimately adopted his plan,
establishing Shuòfāng Commandery.
In the second year of Yuánshuò,
Zhǔfù reported that the King of Qí indulged in debauchery and aberrant conduct,
so the emperor appointed him as chancellor of Qí.
Upon reaching Qí,
he summoned all his brothers and associates,
distributed five hundred gold among them,
and rebuked them:
"When I was poor initially,
my brothers gave me no food or clothing,
nor did friends welcome me through their gates;
now that I am chancellor of Qí,
some of you greet me from a thousand li away.
I sever ties with you all;
do not enter Yǎn's door again!"
He then had someone hint to the king about his affair with his sister,
leading the king to believe he could not escape guilt,
fearing he might share King Yàn's fate of being condemned to death,
so he took his own life.
The officials reported this.
When Zhǔfù was still a commoner,
he once traveled in Yān
and Zhào; after rising to high status,
he exposed Yān's affairs.
The King of Zhào feared he would become a threat to the state,
intending to memorialize about his secret activities,
but with Yǎn in a central position,
did not dare to act.
When Yǎn became chancellor of Qí
and passed through the frontier,
the king immediately had someone submit a memorial,
accusing Zhǔfù Yǎn of accepting bribes from feudal lords,
resulting in many of their sons and brothers being enfeoffed.
After the King of Qí's suicide,
the emperor was enraged upon hearing,
believing Zhǔfù had coerced the king into killing himself,
so he summoned him for judicial investigation.
Zhǔfù admitted to taking gold from the lords
but denied coercing the king to suicide.
The emperor considered sparing him,
but at that time, Gōngsūn Hóng was imperial secretary,
and he stated:
"The King of Qí died without an heir,
his state abolished into a commandery,
incorporated into Hàn.
Zhǔfù Yǎn is the primary culprit;
if Your Majesty does not execute him,
there will be no way to answer to the empire."
Thus, Zhǔfù Yǎn was executed along with his clan.
When Zhǔfù was at the peak of favor,
his followers numbered in the thousands,
yet when he and his clan were killed,
not one came to collect his body—
only Xiáo Kǒngchē buried him.
The Son of Heaven later heard of this
and considered Kǒngchē a noble man.
Yīngqí succeeded to the throne,
and immediately concealed the seal of his predecessor Emperor Wǔ.
During Yīngqí's service in the imperial guard in Cháng'ān,
he had taken a wife from the Jiū family of Hándān,
who bore him a son named Xīng.
Upon his accession,
he petitioned to appoint Lady Jiū as queen
and Xīng as heir apparent.
The Hàn court repeatedly sent envoys to persuade Yīngqí,
but he preferred exercising absolute power over life and death at will,
fearing that if he went to court he would be constrained by Hàn laws,
treated as a domestic feudal lord,
so he persistently pleaded illness
and never attended court.
He sent his son Cìgōng to serve in the imperial guard instead.
When Yīngqí died,
he was posthumously titled King Míng.
The crown prince Xīng succeeded him,
with his mother becoming queen dowager.
Before becoming Yīngqí's consort,
the queen dowager had been involved with Ān Guóshàojì from Bàlíng.
After Yīngqí's death,
in the fourth year of Yuándǐng,
the Hàn court sent Ān Guóshàojì to persuade the king
and queen dowager to attend court,
to be treated as domestic feudal lords;
they also dispatched eloquent scholar and Grand Master of Remonstrance Zhōng Jūn to deliver their message,
with warriors like Wèi Chén to assist where needed,
while Commandant of the Guards Lù Bódé stationed troops at Guìyáng,
awaiting the envoys.
The king being young
and the queen dowager being from central China,
who had previously been involved with Ān Guóshàojì,
resumed their illicit relationship during his mission.
Many in the kingdom knew of this,
and most did not support the queen dowager.
Fearing unrest,
and wishing to rely on Hàn authority,
she repeatedly urged the king and his officials to seek incorporation into Hàn.
Through the envoys, they submitted a petition
requesting to be treated as domestic feudal lords,
to attend court once every three years,
and to have border checkpoints removed.
The Son of Heaven approved,
granting the chancellor Lǚ Jiā a silver seal,
along with seals for the interior史,
commandant,
and grand tutor;
the rest they could appoint themselves.
The former punishments of tattooing and nose amputation were abolished,
Hàn laws were adopted,
and they were treated as domestic feudal lords.
The envoys remained to pacify the region.
The king and queen dowager prepared heavy luggage and supplies,
making ready for their court attendance.
Chancellor Lǚ Jiā was advanced in years,
having served three kings,
with over seventy clansmen holding high offices,
his sons all marrying the king's daughters,
his daughters all wedding the king's brothers and clansmen,
and he was connected to the King of Cāngwú.
He held great influence in the kingdom,
trusted by the Yuè people,
with many informants,
enjoying more popular support than the king.
When the king petitioned,
Lǚ Jiā repeatedly advised against it,
but the king would not listen.
He developed rebellious intentions,
often pleading illness to avoid meeting Hàn envoys.
The envoys focused on Jiā,
yet lacked the power to eliminate him.
The king and queen dowager, fearing Jiā might act first,
arranged a banquet,
leveraging the authority of the Hàn envoys,
plotting to kill Jiā and his faction.
The envoys faced east,
the queen dowager south,
the king north,
Chancellor Jiā
and high ministers all faced west,
seated and drinking.
Jiā's brother, a general,
stationed troops outside the palace.
As wine was served,
the queen dowager said to Jiā:
"Nányuè's incorporation benefits the state,
yet you, Chancellor, find it troublesome;
why is that?"
intending to provoke the envoys.
The envoys hesitated, leaning on their staffs,
and ultimately dared not act.
Jiā, sensing something amiss,
stood up and left.
The queen dowager, enraged,
wanted to spear Jiā,
but the king stopped her.
Jiā then exited,
shared his brother's troops and returned to his residence,
claimed illness,
and refused to see the king or envoys.
He secretly conspired with officials to rebel.
The king had never intended to kill Jiā,
and Jiā knew it,
hence the rebellion was delayed for months.
The queen dowager's immoral conduct
left her without popular support,
and though she wished to eliminate Jiā alone,
she lacked the strength.
The Son of Heaven heard that Jiā defied the king,
and that the king and queen dowager were too weak to control him,
while the envoys were timid and indecisive.
Believing that the king
and queen dowager had submitted to Hàn,
and only Lǚ Jiā was causing trouble,
he deemed it unnecessary to mobilize a large army,
intending to send Zhuāng Cān with two thousand men on a mission.
Cān said:
"If going peacefully,
a few men suffice;
if with force,
two thousand are insufficient."
He declined, unable to go,
and the emperor did not press him.
Jiá stalwart and former Jìběi chancellor Hán Qiānqiū fervently said:
"With such a small Yuè,
and the king
and queen dowager responding,
only Chancellor Lǚ Jiā poses a threat;
I request two hundred brave men
to surely behead Jiā and report back."
So the Son of Heaven sent Qiānqiū and the queen dowager's brother Jiū Lè with two thousand men,
entering Yuè territory.
Lǚ Jiā then rebelled,
proclaiming to the kingdom:
"The king is young.
The queen dowager,
a central Chinese,
has illicit relations with the envoys,
solely intent on incorporation,
taking all the former king's treasures to offer the Son of Heaven to curry favor,
leading many followers,
who upon reaching Cháng'ān,
will be enslaved and sold.
She seeks immediate escape for her own gain,
with no regard for the Zhào lineage's altars
or plans for eternity."
He and his brother led troops to attack and kill the king,
queen dowager, and Hàn envoys.
They informed the King of Cāngwú and various commanderies and counties,
establishing the elder son of King Míng by his Yuè wife, the Marquis of Shùyáng Jiàndé, as king.
As Hán Qiānqiū's troops advanced,
they captured several small towns.
Thereafter, Yuè openly provided roads and supplies,
but forty lǐ from Pānyú,
Yuè forces attacked Qiānqiū and others,
annihilating them.
They sent a box containing the Hàn envoys' credentials to the border,
with hypocritical words of apology,
and deployed troops to guard strategic points.
The Son of Heaven then said:
"Though Hán Qiānqiū achieved no success,
he was the vanguard's finest."
He enfeoffed his son Yánnián as Marquis of Chéng'ān.
Jiū Lè,
whose sister was queen dowager
and first desired to submit to Hàn,
had his son Guǎngdé enfeoffed as Marquis of Lóngkàng.
An amnesty was declared:
"The Son of Heaven is humble,
the feudal lords exert force,
criticizing ministers for not punishing rebels.
Now Lǚ Jiā,
Jiàndé, and others rebel,
establishing themselves comfortably,
I order convicts and a hundred thousand troops from the tower ships south of the Jiāng and Huái to campaign against them."
In autumn of the fifth year of Yuándǐng,
Commandant of the Guards Lù Bódé was appointed General Fúbō,
marching from Guìyáng,
descending the Huì River;
Chief of the Nobles Yáng Pú was made General Lóuchuán,
marching from Yùzhāng,
descending Héngpǔ;
two former Yuè marquises who had submitted were appointed Generals Gēchuán and Xiàlì,
marching from Línglíng,
one descending the Lí River,
the other reaching Cāngwú;
they sent the Marquis of Chíyì to mobilize convicts from Bā and Shǔ,
raising troops from Yèláng,
descending the Zāngkē River:
all to converge at Pānyú.
By the sixth year of the Jiànyuán era,
Mǐnyuè attacked Nányuè.
Nányuè abided by the Son of Heaven's covenant,
not daring to launch an attack without authorization and instead reported it.
The Emperor dispatched Grand Herald Wáng Huī to march from Yùzhāng,
and Grand Minister of Agriculture Hán Ānguó to set out from Kuàijī,
both serving as generals.
Before the troops had crossed the mountains,
King Yǐng of Mǐnyuè dispatched forces to hold the strategic points.
His younger brother, Yúshàn, then conspired with his chancellor and
clan members, saying:
"The king launched an attack on Nányuè without authorization,
without seeking permission,
hence the Son of Heaven's troops have come to punish him.
Now the Hàn forces are numerous and strong;
even if we were fortunate enough to defeat them now,
more would come later,
until our state is ultimately destroyed.
Let us now kill the king to apologize to the Son of Heaven.
If the Son of Heaven heeds us,
and withdraws his troops,
then surely our state will remain intact;
if he does not listen,
then we shall fight with all our might;
if we cannot win,
we shall flee to the sea."
All said,
"Good."
They immediately stabbed the king to death,
and sent an envoy to present his head to the Grand Herald.
The Grand Herald said:
"The reason we came was to punish the king.
Now that the king's head has arrived,
and an apology has been made,
we can achieve our goal without fighting,
which is most advantageous."
He then, acting on his own authority, halted the troops and informed the Grand Minister of Agriculture's army,
and sent an envoy to swiftly report to the Son of Heaven with the king's head.
An edict was issued to withdraw the two generals' troops,
stating:
"Yǐng and others were the chief culprits,
only Wúzhū's grandson, the Yáo Lord Chǒu, was not involved in the plot."
He then sent a Gentleman of the Palace to establish Chǒu as the Yuèyáo King,
to uphold the ancestral sacrifices of Mǐnyuè.
Yúshàn, having killed Yǐng,
wielded authority throughout the state,
and most of the people pledged allegiance to him,
so he secretly proclaimed himself king.
The Yáo King was unable to correct the people's stance and uphold righteousness.
When the Son of Heaven heard of this,
he considered it not worth mobilizing troops again for Yúshàn,
and said:
"Yúshàn repeatedly plotted rebellion with Yǐng,
but later took the lead in killing Yǐng,
so our troops were spared the toil."
Thus, he established Yúshàn as the King of Dōngyuè,
to coexist with the Yáo King.
By the fifth year of the Yuándǐng era,
Nányuè rebelled,
and the King of Dōngyuè, Yúshàn, submitted a memorial,
requesting to follow the Towered Ship General with eight thousand soldiers to attack Lǚ Jiā and others.
When his troops reached Jiēyáng,
he used rough seas and winds as an excuse,
and did not proceed,
maintaining an ambivalent stance,
while secretly aiding Nányuè.
By the time Hàn destroyed Pānyú,
he had not arrived.
At that time, the Towered Ship General Yáng Pú sent an envoy to submit a memorial,
wishing to lead his troops to attack Dōngyuè.
The Emperor said the soldiers were weary and exhausted,
and did not permit it,
withdrawing the troops instead,
ordering the various colonels to station at Méilǐng in Yùzhāng and await orders.
In the autumn of the sixth year of Yuándǐng,
Yúshàn heard that the Towered Ship General had requested to punish him,
and that Hàn troops were approaching the border,
about to advance,
so he rebelled,
dispatching troops to block the Hàn routes.
He appointed the general Zōu Lì and others as
"Swallow-Hàn Generals,"
who entered Báishā,
Wǔlín,
and Méilǐng,
killing three Hàn colonels.
At that time, Hàn had sent the Grand Minister of Agriculture Zhāng Chéng and
the former Marquis of Shānzhōu, Chǐ, to command the garrison,
but they dared not attack,
instead retreating to safer positions,
and both were executed for cowardice.
Yúshàn engraved
"Emperor Wǔ"
on a seal and proclaimed himself emperor,
deceiving his people,
with false claims.
The Son of Heaven dispatched the Cross-Sea General Hán Yuè to set out from Gōuzhāng,
sailing from the east;
the Towered Ship General Yáng Pú set out from Wǔlín;
the Commandant of the Capital Wáng Wēnshū set out from Méilǐng;
the Yuè Marquis served as the Spear Boat and
Rapids Descent General,
setting out from Ruòyé and
Báishā.
In the winter of the first year of Yuánfēng,
they all entered Dōngyuè.
Dōngyuè had long stationed troops at strategic points,
appointing the Northern Pacification General to guard Wǔlín,
who defeated several colonels of the Towered Ship army,
killing senior officers.
The Towered Ship General led Qiántáng's Yuán Zhōnggǔ to behead the Northern Pacification General,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yù'ér.
Before his own troops arrived.
The former Yuè Yǎn Marquis Wú Yáng, who had previously been in Hàn,
was sent back by Hàn to persuade Yúshàn,
but Yúshàn would not listen.
When the Cross-Sea General arrived first,
the Yuè Yǎn Marquis Wú Yáng rebelled with seven hundred men from his fief,
attacking the Yuè army at Hànyáng.
Following the lead of the Marquis of Jiànchéng, Áo,
and his followers,
he conspired with the Yáo King Jūgǔ, saying:
"Yúshàn is the chief culprit,
who has coerced and controlled us.
Now the Hàn troops have arrived,
numerous and strong;
if we plot to kill Yúshàn,
and surrender to the generals ourselves,
we might侥幸 escape."
So they together killed Yúshàn,
and surrendered with their followers to the Cross-Sea General.
Thus, the Yáo King Jūgǔ was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngchéng,
with ten thousand households;
the Marquis of Jiànchéng, Áo, was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Kāilíng;
the Yuè Yǎn Marquis Wú Yáng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Běishí;
the Cross-Sea General Yuè was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Àndào;
and the Cross-Sea Colonel Fú was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Liáoyīng.
Fú was
the son of the Gong King of Chéngyáng,
formerly the Marquis of Hǎicháng,
who had lost his marquisate due to legal offenses.
Though he had no previous military achievements,
he was enfeoffed due to his imperial clan status.
The other generals had no achievements,
and were not enfeoffed.
The Dōngyuè general Duō Jūn,
when the Hàn troops arrived,
abandoned his army and surrendered,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wúxī.
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven said that Dōngyuè was narrow and rugged,
and the Mǐnyuè people were fierce,
frequently rebellious,
so he ordered the military officials to relocate all the people to the area between the Huái and Yangtze Rivers.
Thus, the land of Dōngyuè was left empty.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Though Yuè were barbarians,
could it be that their ancestors had once performed great deeds and virtues for the people?
How long-lasting they were!
Through several generations, they often served as kings and lords,
and Gōu Jiàn once claimed hegemony.
Yet Yúshàn went so far as to commit great treason,
leading to the destruction of the state and the relocation of the people.
Still, a descendant of their ancestors, the Yáo King Jūgǔ and others, were enfeoffed as marquises with ten thousand households,
from this we know that the Yuè people, generation after generation, served as dukes and marquises.
This is perhaps the lingering influence of Yǔ.
As for the King of Cháoxiǎn, Mǎn,
he was originally from Yān.
From the time when Yān was intact, it had once annexed Zhēnfān and
Cháoxiǎn,
establishing officials there,
and building fortresses.
When Qín destroyed Yān,
it became part of the outer frontier of Liáodōng.
When Hàn rose,
due to its remoteness and difficulty to defend,
they restored the old Liáodōng frontier,
with the Pèi River as the boundary,
belonging to Yān.
When the King of Yān, Lú Wǎn, rebelled,
and fled to the Xiōngnú,
Mǎn became a fugitive,
gathering a band of over a thousand followers,
adopting barbarian attire with topknots and heading east out of the frontier,
crossing the Pèi River,
and settling in the old Qín empty lands of the upper and lower fortresses,
gradually subjugating the barbarians of Zhēnfān and
Cháoxiǎn, as well as former Yān and
Qí fugitives, and ruling over them,
establishing his capital at Wángxiǎn.
During the reigns of Emperor Huì and
Empress Dowager Gāo, when the realm was first stabilized,
the Governor of Liáodōng made an agreement with Wèi Mǎn to serve as an outer vassal,
guarding against the barbarian tribes beyond the frontier,
and preventing them from raiding the border;
if the chieftains of the various barbarian tribes wished to come and see the Son of Heaven,
they were not to be hindered.
This was reported upward,
and the emperor approved it.
Consequently, Wèi Mǎn was able to use military might and wealth to invade and subdue the neighboring small settlements.
Zhēnpān and
Líntún all came to submit and become dependencies,
covering an area of several thousand li.
The rule passed from son to grandson, reaching Yòu Qú,
who enticed an increasing number of Han deserters,
and moreover had never come to see the emperor;
the many states near Zhēnpān wished to send letters and see the Son of Heaven,
but he also blocked and hindered them, preventing communication.
In the second year of Yuánfēng,
the Han envoy Shè Hé went to admonish and instruct Yòu Qú,
but he ultimately refused to obey the imperial decree.
Hé left and reached the border,
arriving at the Pèi River.
He had his driver assassinate the Korean lieutenant king named Zhǎng who was escorting Hé.
He then crossed the river immediately,
galloped into the frontier pass,
and returned to report to the Son of Heaven, saying,
"I killed a Korean general."
The emperor, considering the name honorable,
did not interrogate him,
and appointed Hé as the Commandant of the Eastern Division of Liáodōng.
Korea resented Hé,
and dispatched troops to attack and kill him.
The Son of Heaven recruited convicts to attack Korea.
That autumn,
he sent Towered Ship General Yáng Pú to set out from Qí and cross the Bó Sea;
with fifty thousand troops,
and Left General Xún Zhì to march out from Liáodōng:
to chastise Yòu Qú.
Yòu Qú dispatched troops to hold the strategic points.
Left General's Colonel Duō led the Liáodōng troops in a rash advance,
was defeated and scattered,
and most fled back.
For violating military law, he was executed.
Towered Ship General led seven thousand Qí troops and arrived first at Wángxiǎn.
Yòu Qú defended the city,
and upon observing that the Towered Ship army was small,
he immediately left the city to attack the Towered Ship forces.
The Towered Ship army was defeated, scattered, and fled.
General Yáng Pú lost his troops,
and hid in the mountains for over ten days,
gradually seeking to gather his scattered soldiers,
and they regrouped.
Left General attacked the Korean army west of the Pèi River,
but was unable to break through to the front.
The Son of Heaven, because the two generals had not achieved success,
then sent Wèi Shān to go and, relying on military might, instruct Yòu Qú.
Yòu Qú, upon seeing the envoy, kowtowed and apologized:
"I wish to surrender,
but I fear the two generals will deceitfully kill me;
now that I see the trustworthy credentials,
I beg to submit and surrender."
He sent his crown prince to enter and apologize,
presenting five thousand horses,
and provisions for the army.
The retinue numbered over ten thousand people,
carrying weapons.
As they were about to cross the Pèi River,
the envoy and Left General suspected they were planning a mutiny,
saying that since the crown prince had already submitted and surrendered,
he should order his men not to carry weapons.
The crown prince also suspected that the envoy and Left General would deceitfully kill him,
so he did not cross the Pèi River,
but instead turned back.
Shān returned and reported to the Son of Heaven,
and the Son of Heaven executed Shān.
Left General defeated the army on the Pèi River,
then advanced,
reaching the city walls,
and besieged the northwest.
Towered Ship also went to join him,
stationing south of the city.
Yòu Qú then firmly defended the city,
and for several months it could not be taken.
Left General had long served in the palace,
favored, leading Yān and Dài troops,
fierce, riding on victory,
his army was mostly arrogant.
Towered Ship led Qí troops,
who had gone to sea,
and had already suffered many defeats and losses;
having previously fought Yòu Qú,
they were trapped, humiliated, and lost soldiers,
the soldiers were all fearful,
the general's heart was ashamed.
In besieging Yòu Qú,
he often maintained a conciliatory stance.
Left General urgently attacked him,
and the Korean ministers then secretly sent people to privately arrange surrender with Towered Ship,
going back and forth in discussions,
but they had not yet decided.
Left General repeatedly arranged battle dates with Towered Ship,
but Towered Ship wanted to quickly conclude his agreement,
and did not join him;
Left General also sent people to seek an opportunity to make Korea surrender,
but Korea refused,
their hearts attached to Towered Ship:
because of this, the two generals were at odds.
Left General thought that Towered Ship had previously committed the crime of losing his army,
and now was privately friendly with Korea yet they did not surrender,
suspecting he had rebellious plans,
but did not dare act.
The Son of Heaven said the generals were incompetent,
and previously had sent Wèi Shān to instruct Yòu Qú to surrender,
Yòu Qú sent his crown prince,
but Shān, as envoy, could not make a decisive judgment,
and his plans with Left General were mutually mistaken,
ultimately ruining the agreement.
Now the two generals besieged the city,
but were again at odds,
so for a long time no decision was reached.
He sent Jǐnán Prefect Gōngsūn Suì to go and rectify the situation,
with authority to act as he saw fit.
Suì arrived,
and Left General said:
"Korea should have been taken long ago,
the reason it has not been taken has a cause."
He said Towered Ship repeatedly missed arranged meetings,
and fully informed Suì of what he had long suspected,
saying:
"If we do not act now like this,
I fear it will become a great disaster,
not only Towered Ship,
but he may even join with Korea to destroy our army."
Suì also thought this was so,
and using his credentials summoned Towered Ship General to enter Left General's camp to discuss matters,
then ordered Left General's subordinates to arrest Towered Ship General,
and merged his army,
reporting this to the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven executed Suì.
Left General, having merged the two armies,
urgently attacked Korea.
The Korean Chancellor Lù Rén,
Chancellor Hán Yīn,
Níxī Chancellor Cān,
and General Wáng Jiá plotted together, saying:
"At first we wished to surrender to Towered Ship,
but Towered Ship is now arrested,
only Left General commands the merged army,
the battle grows more urgent,
I fear we cannot withstand it,
and the king still refuses to surrender."
Yīn, Jiá,
and Lù Rén all fled and surrendered to Han.
Lù Rén died on the way.
In the summer of the third year of Yuánfēng,
Níxī Chancellor Cān then sent someone to kill the Korean King Yòu Qú and come to surrender.
Wángxiǎn city had not yet fallen,
so Yòu Qú's minister Chéng Sǐ rebelled again,
and again attacked the officials.
Left General sent Yòu Qú's son Cháng Jiàng,
and Chancellor Lù Rén's son Zuì to instruct and inform the people,
executed Chéng Sǐ,
and thus finally pacified Korea,
establishing four commanderies.
He enfeoffed Cān as Marquis of Huàqīng,
Yīn as Marquis of Díjū,
Jiá as Marquis of Píngzhōu,
and Cháng Jiàng as Marquis of Jī.
Zuì, because his father died and he had considerable merit,
was made Marquis of Nièyáng.
Left General was summoned to court,
and for contending over merit and mutual jealousy,
and erroneous plans,
was executed in the marketplace.
Towered Ship General was also charged for arriving with his troops at Lièkǒu,
where he should have waited for Left General,
but presumptuously advanced rashly,
suffering many losses,
deserving execution,
but redeemed himself to become a commoner.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Yòuqú relied on his stronghold,
and his state lost its ancestral sacrifices.
Shè Hé falsely claimed merit,
becoming the instigator of military action.
The Towered-ship general was narrow-minded,
and encountered disaster, incurring blame.
Regretting the loss of Pānyú,
he was instead suspected of treason.
Xún Zhì contended for credit,
and along with [Guō] Suì, was executed.
With both armies' [commanders] executed,
none of the commanders and leaders were enfeoffed as marquises.
The chieftains of the southwestern Yi numbered by the tens,
with Yèláng the largest;
west of them, tribes like Mímò numbered by the tens,
with Diān the largest;
north from Diān, the chieftains numbered by the tens,
with Qióngdū the largest:
These all wore their hair in mallet-shaped knots,
cultivated fields,
and had walled towns and settlements.
Beyond them, from west of Tóngshī eastward,
north to Yèyú,
were named Xī,
and Kūnmíng,
who all braided their hair,
moved about with their livestock,
having no permanent abode,
no chieftains,
their territory stretching perhaps several thousand li.
Northeast from Xī,
the chieftains numbered by the tens,
with Xǐ and Zuódū the largest;
northeast from Zuó,
the chieftains numbered by the tens,
with Ránmáng the largest.
Their customs varied, some being settled,
some migratory,
located west of Shǔ.
Northeast from Ránmáng,
the chieftains numbered by the tens,
with Báimǎ the largest,
all being of the Dī kind.
These were all the Man and Yi tribes southwest beyond Bā and Shǔ.
Beginning in the time of King Wēi of Chǔ,
he sent General Zhuāng Qiāo to lead troops up the river,
conquering Bā,
and the region west of Qiánzhōng.
Zhuāng Qiāo was
a descendant of the former King Zhuāng of Chǔ.
Qiāo reached Diānchí Lake,
three hundred li square,
with flat land around it,
fertile and rich for several thousand li,
and by military might pacified and attached it to Chǔ.
He wished to return and report,
but then Qín attacked and seized Chǔ's Bā
and Qiánzhōng commanderies,
blocking the route,
so he turned back,
and with his followers became king of Diān,
changing his dress,
following their customs,
in order to rule them.
In the Qín era, Cháng È roughly opened the Five-Foot Road,
and officials were somewhat established in these various states.
After more than ten years,
Qín fell.
When Hàn arose,
they all abandoned these states and reopened the old Shǔ frontier.
People of Bā and Shǔ sometimes slipped out to trade,
obtaining their Zuó horses,
Bó slaves,
and yaks,
thereby making Bā and Shǔ prosperous.
In the sixth year of the Jiànyuán era,
the Grand Coach Wáng Huī attacked Eastern Yuè,
and Eastern Yuè killed its king Yǐng in response.
Huī, using military authority, sent Pānyáng Magistrate Táng Méng to subtly inform Southern Yuè [of Hàn's intentions].
Southern Yuè served Méng Shǔ's jujube paste,
Méng asked where it came from,
and they said,
"By the northwestern Zāngkē route,
the Zāngkē River is several li wide,
emerging below the walls of Pānyú."
Méng returned to Cháng'ān,
and asked Shǔ merchants,
the merchants said:
"Only Shǔ produces jujube paste,
many secretly take it to sell in Yèláng.
Yèláng
borders the Zāngkē River,
the river is over a hundred paces wide,
sufficient for sailing boats.
Southern Yuè uses wealth and goods to subjugate Yèláng,
west to Tóngshī,
but still cannot command them as subjects."
Méng then submitted a memorial advising the Emperor:
"The King of Southern Yuè uses the yellow-canopied carriage and left-tasseled banner,
his territory stretches over ten thousand li east to west,
nominally an outer subject,
but actually the master of one province.
Now, to go via Chángshā
and Yùzhāng,
the waterways are largely cut off,
making travel difficult.
I have privately heard that Yèláng possesses elite troops,
numbering over a hundred thousand,
floating boats on the Zāngkē River,
taking them by surprise,
this would be a clever stratagem to control Yuè.
Truly, with Hàn's strength,
and Bā and Shǔ's abundance,
opening the road to Yèláng,
establishing officials there,
would be very easy."
The Emperor approved.
He then appointed Méng as a General of the Gentlemen of the Palace,
leading a thousand men,
with over ten thousand provision carriers,
entering from the Bā-Shǔ Zuó Pass,
and thus met Yèláng Hóu Duō Tóng.
Méng bestowed rich gifts,
explained with authority and virtue,
agreed to establish officials,
making his son a magistrate.
The small towns near Yèláng all coveted Hàn's silks,
and thinking the Hàn roads perilous,
that they could never ultimately possess them,
provisionally accepted Méng's terms.
He returned and reported,
and it was then made into Qiánwèi Commandery.
They conscripted Bā and Shǔ laborers to build roads,
from Bódào pointing towards the Zāngkē River.
The Shǔ man Sīmǎ Xiàngrú also said the western Yi's Qióng
and Zuó could be made into a commandery.
He sent Xiàngrú as a General of the Gentlemen of the Palace to inform them,
all like the southern Yi,
establishing one Chief Commandant,
over ten counties,
attached to Shǔ.
At that time,
the four commanderies of Bā and Shǔ opened roads to the southwestern Yi,
garrisoning and transporting supplies.
After several years,
the roads were impassable,
soldiers were exhausted, starving, or dead from exposure and damp;
the southwestern Yi also rebelled repeatedly,
troops were raised to attack them,
wasting resources without success.
The Emperor was troubled,
and sent Gōngsūn Hóng to investigate.
He returned and reported,
saying it was inadvisable.
When Hóng became Imperial Secretary,
they were then building Shuòfāng to control the river and expel the Hú,
Hóng thus repeatedly spoke of the harm of the southwestern Yi,
that it could be suspended for now,
to focus efforts on the Xiōngnú.
The Emperor suspended the western Yi [project],
only establishing two counties and one Chief Commandant for the southern Yi and Yèláng,
gradually ordering Qiánwèi to secure itself.
In the first year of the Yuánshòu era,
Marquis Bówàng Zhāng Qiān, returning from his mission to Dàxià,
said that while in Dàxià he saw Shǔ cloth,
Qiōng bamboo,
and staffs, and asked where they came from,
they said
"from Shēndú country to the southeast,
perhaps several thousand li away,
obtained from Shǔ merchants' markets."
Some had heard that some two thousand li west of Qióng was Shēndú country.
Qiān thus strongly advocated that Dàxià, southwest of Hàn,
admired the Middle Kingdom,
but was troubled by the Xiōngnú blocking the route,
truly, if Shǔ were connected,
the route to Shēndú country would be convenient and near,
beneficial and harmless.
Thereupon the Son of Heaven ordered Wáng Rányú,
Bó Shǐchāng,
Lǚ Yuèrén, and others,
to be sent secretly out west of the western Yi,
aiming to seek Shēndú country.
They reached Diān,
and Diān King Cháng Qiāng detained them,
sending over ten batches west to seek the route.
After more than a year,
all were blocked by Kūnmíng,
none could reach Shēndú country.
When King Xiào of Liáng passed away,
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú returned home,
but his family was poor,
with no means to support himself.
He had long been on good terms with the magistrate of Línqióng, Wáng Jí,
who said:
"Chángqīng, you have long traveled in official posts without success,
yet you come to visit me."
Thereupon, Xiàngrú went
and lodged at the capital inn.
The magistrate of Línqióng feigned reverence,
visiting Xiàngrú daily as if paying court.
Initially, Xiàngrú still received him,
but later claimed illness,
sending his attendants to decline Jí,
yet Jí grew even more respectful and solemn.
In Línqióng, there were many wealthy men,
with Zhuó Wángsūn having eight hundred household servants,
and Chéng Zhèng also several hundred.
The two men then said to each other:
"The magistrate has an honored guest;
let us prepare a feast and invite him."
They also invited the magistrate.
When the magistrate arrived,
the guests at the Zhuó residence numbered in the hundreds.
By midday,
they requested the presence of Sīmǎ Chángqīng,
but Chángqīng declined due to illness and could not come.
The magistrate of Línqióng dared not eat,
and went personally to fetch Xiàngrú.
Xiàngrú had no choice
but to force himself to go,
and his arrival captivated the entire assembly.
As the wine flowed freely,
the magistrate of Línqióng came forward with a zither and said:
"I have privately heard that Chángqīng is fond of this;
I wish you would amuse yourself with it."
Xiàngrú declined politely,
but then played a couple of tunes.
At that time, Zhuó Wángsūn had a daughter, Wénjūn, recently widowed,
who loved music.
Therefore, Xiàngrú, feigning mutual respect with the magistrate,
used the zither's melody to woo her.
When Xiàngrú came to Línqióng,
he was accompanied by carriages and horsemen,
appearing dignified, leisurely, and exceedingly elegant.
And when he drank at the Zhuó residence
and played the zither,
Wénjūn secretly peeped at him through a door,
her heart delighted and fond of him,
yet fearing she might not be a match.
After the feast ended,
Xiàngrú then sent someone to richly reward Wénjūn's attendants to convey his deep affection.
Wénjūn fled at night to Xiàngrú,
and Xiàngrú then galloped away with her back to Chéngdū.
Their home stood empty with only four bare walls.
Zhuó Wángsūn was greatly angered and said:
"My daughter is utterly without virtue,
but I cannot bear to kill her,
nor will I give her a single coin."
Some people tried to persuade Wángsūn,
but he would not listen.
After a while, Wénjūn grew unhappy,
saying:
"Chángqīng, let us just go to Línqióng together;
even borrowing from my brothers would suffice for a living.
Why must we torment ourselves like this!"
Xiàngrú went with her to Línqióng,
sold all their carriages and horses,
bought a tavern to sell wine,
and had Wénjūn tend the counter.
Xiàngrú himself wore short breeches,
working alongside the servants,
washing utensils in the market.
Zhuó Wángsūn heard of this and was ashamed,
shutting his doors and not going out.
His brothers and elders then advised Wángsūn, saying:
"You have one son and two daughters;
what you lack is not wealth.
Now Wénjūn has already given herself to Sīmǎ Chángqīng;
Chángqīng, though weary of wandering,
and poor,
his talent is worthy of reliance.
Moreover, he is a guest of the magistrate;
why must you shame him so!"
Zhuó Wángsūn had no choice,
and gave Wénjūn a hundred servants,
a million cash,
and the clothing and belongings from her wedding.
Wénjūn then returned with Xiàngrú to Chéngdū,
bought fields and a house,
and became wealthy.
After some time had passed,
Yáng Déyì from Shǔ served as the supervisor of hounds,
attending the emperor.
The emperor read the "Rhapsody of Zǐxū" and praised it,
saying:
"How I wish I could have lived at the same time as this man!"
Déyì said:
"My fellow townsman Sīmǎ Xiàngrú claims to have written this rhapsody."
The emperor was astonished,
and summoned Xiàngrú for questioning.
Xiàngrú said:
"It is so.
But this concerns the affairs of the feudal lords,
not worthy of much note.
Allow me to compose a rhapsody on the imperial hunts,
and present it when completed."
The emperor consented,
ordering the Secretary to provide brushes and slips.
Xiàngrú used
"Zǐxū,"
meaning empty words,
to represent Chǔ's praise;
"Mr. Wūyǒu,"
meaning there is no such thing,
to pose Qí's rebuttal;
and "Lord Wúshì,"
meaning no such man,
to elucidate the righteousness of the Son of Heaven.
Thus, he fictitiously employed these three personas in his composition,
to extol the parks and hunting grounds of the emperor and feudal lords.
The final chapter returns to the theme of frugality,
thereby offering subtle admonition.
When presented to the emperor,
the emperor was greatly pleased.
The text reads:
The envoy Zǐxū of Chǔ was sent to Qí,
and the King of Qí mobilized all the gentlemen within his borders,
mustering a host of carriages and horsemen,
to go hunting with the envoy.
After the hunt,
Zǐxū visited and boasted to Mr. Wūyǒu,
with Lord Wúshì also present.
When they were seated,
Mr. Wūyǒu asked:
"Was the hunt enjoyable today?"
Zǐxū said:
"Enjoyable."
"Did you bag much game?"
He said:
"Little."
"Then what was enjoyable about it?"
He said:
"I enjoyed the King of Qí's attempt to impress me with his multitude of carriages and horsemen,
while I responded with tales of Yúnmèng."
He said:
"Might I hear of it?"
Zǐxū said:
"Certainly.
The king drove a thousand chariots,
selected ten thousand riders on foot,
and hunted by the seashore.
Ranks of soldiers filled the marshes,
nets covered the mountains,
trapping hares and crushing deer,
shooting elk and snaring unicorns.
They raced over the salt flats,
slicing fresh game and staining the wheels.
Hitting the mark often and capturing much,
he boasted and took credit.
Turning to me, he said:
'Does Chǔ also have plains and vast marshes for hunting and pleasure like these?
How does the King of Chǔ's hunt compare with mine?'
I alighted from the carriage and replied:
am a humble man of Chǔ,
fortunate to have served in the palace guard for over ten years,
occasionally accompanying the king on outings,
roaming in the rear gardens,
observing what is there and what is not,
yet I have not seen it all,
how could I possibly speak of the outer marshes!'
The King of Qí said:
'Even so,
briefly tell me what you have heard and seen.'
"I replied:
'Yes, yes.
I have heard that Chǔ has seven marshes,
and I have seen one of them,
but have not witnessed the others.
What I have seen
is merely the smallest of them,
called Yúnmèng.
Yúnmèng
covers an area of nine hundred lǐ square,
and within it, there are mountains.
These mountains wind and twist, lofty and dense;
they rise high and precipitous;
their peaks are jagged and uneven,
obscuring the sun and moon;
they intertwine and tangle,
reaching up to the blue clouds;
with sloping and undulating terrain,
they descend to connect with the rivers.
The soil is of cinnabar, azure, ochre, and white clay,
orpiment and white quartz,
tin, jadeite, gold, and silver,
all colors dazzling and brilliant,
shining like dragon scales.
The stones include red jade and rose quartz,
Línmín and Kūnwú jades,
Jiānlè and dark whetstones,
Ruǎnshí and Wǔfū stones.
To the east, there are gardens of orchids and thoroughwort,
Zhǐruò and Shègān,
Qiōngqióng and sweet flag,
Jiānglí and Míwú,
sugarcane and Bóqiě.
To the south, there are plains and vast marshes,
with rising and falling slopes,
stretching far and wide,
bordered by the great river,
and bounded by the Wū Mountains.
In the high and dry areas grow Zhēn, Sī, Bāo, and Lì plants,
Bìsuō and green Fán.
In the low and damp areas grow Zānglàng, Jiān, and Jiā reeds,
Dōngqiáng and Diāohú,
lotus roots, Gū, and reeds,
Ānlú and Xuānyù,
where countless creatures dwell,
too numerous to depict fully.
To the west, there are gushing springs and clear pools,
with rushing waters pushing forward;
on the surface bloom lotuses and water lilies,
while beneath lie giant rocks and white sand.
Within them dwell divine turtles, flood dragons, and tuó crocodiles,
hawksbill turtles and softshell turtles.
To the north, there are shaded forests with giant trees,
Pián, Nán, Yù, and Zhāng trees,
cinnamon, pepper, and magnolia,
Nièlí and Zhūyáng,
Zhā pears, Yǐng plums, and chestnuts,
fragrant oranges and pomelos.
In the trees above are red apes and Wèi náo,
Yuānchú, peacocks, and luan birds,
Téngyuǎn and Yègān.
Below are white tigers and black leopards,
Mànyán, Chū, and Àn beasts,
rhinoceroses, elephants, and wild oxen,
Qióngqí and Mànyán.
" 'Then he sent men like Zhuān Zhū
to wrestle with these beasts by hand.
The King of Chǔ then harnessed trained piebald steeds,
rode in a carriage adorned with carved jade,
waved flags made of fish whiskers on curved poles,
trailed banners studded with bright moon pearls,
raised the mighty halberds of Gànjiàng,
held on the left a carved bow from Wūhào,
and on the right, strong arrows from Xià's quiver:
Yángzǐ rode as attendant,
Xiān'ē served as charioteer;
before the pace had fully quickened,
they already overwhelmed the cunning beasts,
trampled Qiōngqióng,
kicked Jùxū,
outran wild horses and overran Táotú,
mounted the swift Yífēng and shot roaming Qí steeds;
swift as lightning and sudden as a gust,
they moved like thunder and arrived like a blaze,
like meteors streaking and thunderbolts striking,
not a single arrow shot in vain,
each hit sure to split an eye socket,
piercing chests and reaching armpits,
severing the heart's connections,
capturing beasts like rainfall,
covering the grass and obscuring the ground.
Then the King of Chǔ reined in his pace and wandered leisurely,
soaring and drifting at ease,
gazing upon the shaded forests,
observing the fierce rage of the warriors,
and the terror of the wild beasts,
intercepting the exhausted and accepting surrenders,
fully witnessing the transformations of all creatures.
" 'Then the graceful maidens of Zhèng,
clad in fine silk and hemp,
draped in linen and white gauze,
adorned with delicate silks,
and veiled in mist-like crepe;
with layered folds and gathered pleats,
winding and twisting,
deep and winding like valleys;
fluttering and flowing,
lifting hems and tapered edges,
with flying sashes and dangling tassels;
swaying gracefully and elegantly,
rustling softly as they moved,
brushing against orchids below,
sweeping feather canopies above,
adorned with kingfisher plumes and lush decorations,
entwined with jade-tasseled ribbons;
ethereal and elusive,
as if immortals in a vision.
" 'Then they joined in hunting in the orchid gardens,
climbing gracefully up the golden embankment,
netting kingfishers,
shooting Jùnyí birds,
releasing fine arrows,
deploying slender silk lines,
capturing white swans,
snaring wild geese in pairs,
bringing down a pair of cāng birds,
and adding black cranes.
After resting, they set out again,
boating on the clear pools;
floating in painted boats,
raising cassia oars,
spreading emerald canopies,
erecting feather covers,
catching hawksbill turtles in nets,
angling for purple cowries;
beating golden drums,
playing sounding flutes,
boatmen singing,
voices echoing clearly,
startling water creatures,
waves boiling like a flood,
springs gushing forth,
surging waters converging,
stones clashing against each other,
rumbling and crashing loudly,
like the sound of thunder,
heard from hundreds of lǐ away.
" 'When the hunt was about to end,
they struck the spirit drums,
lit beacon fires,
carriages formed lines,
riders assembled in ranks,
proceeding in continuous streams,
moving in orderly and endless rows.
Then the King of Chǔ ascended the Yángyún Tower,
resting in inaction,
serene and self-possessed,
and only after the blend of peony spices was prepared did he partake of it.
Unlike Your Majesty, who gallops all day without dismounting from the carriage,
slicing meat and roasting it on the wheels,
considering it entertainment.
In my humble opinion, [171 Qí is likely not as refined.'
At this, the king fell silent and had no response to my words."
Master Wūyǒu said:
"What an excessive statement this is!
You have not considered a thousand lǐ too far,
but come to grace the state of Qí with your presence.
The king has mobilized all the gentlemen within his borders,
and prepared a multitude of chariots and cavalry,
to go out hunting,
wishing to join forces in achieving captures,
to amuse you, sir.
How can this be called boasting!
Inquiring about what the land of Chǔ may or may not have,
I wished to hear about the glorious achievements of your great state,
and the remaining discourses of you, sir.
Now you, sir, do not praise the abundant virtue of the King of Chǔ,
but instead extol Yúnmèng to elevate it,
extravagantly speaking of excessive pleasures and displaying lavish extravagance.
I privately believe this is not something you, sir, should adopt.
If what you say were indeed true,
it would certainly not be to the credit of the state of Chǔ.
If these things exist and you speak of them,
you are publicizing your lord's faults;
if they do not exist and you speak of them,
you are harming your own credibility, sir.
To publicize your lord's faults and injure private righteousness—
neither of these two courses is acceptable.
Yet you, sir, proceed with them,
which will surely lead to being轻视 in Qí and becoming a burden in Chǔ.
Moreover, Qí has the great sea to the east,
Lángyá to the south,
views from Chéngshān,
hunts at Zhīfú,
floats on Bóxiè,
wanders through Mèngzhū,
borders with Sùshèn diagonally,
and has Yánggǔ as its boundary to the right.
We hunt in autumn at Qīngqiū,
roam freely beyond the seas,
and could swallow eight or nine places like Yúnmèng,
without them even causing the slightest discomfort in our chest.
As for the extraordinary and magnificent,
the exotic and diverse,
rare and strange birds and beasts,
myriad kinds gathering like fish scales,
filling its lands so fully
that they cannot be fully recorded,
even Yǔ could not name them all,
nor could Qì count them.
Yet, holding a position among the feudal lords,
we dare not speak of the joys of amusement
or the vastness of our parks and preserves;
and since you, sir, are a guest,
the king declined to respond.
Why should we trouble to give a useless reply!"
Master Wúshì gōng smiled and said:
"Chǔ may be at fault,
but Qí has not exactly been correct either.
The reason for requiring feudal lords to present tribute
is not for the sake of wealth and valuables,
but to allow them to report on their governance;
and the demarcation of borders
is not merely for defense,
but to prevent excess.
Now Qí is ranked as an eastern vassal,
yet privately associates with Sùshèn beyond its borders,
detracting from the state and overstepping limits,
crossing the sea to hunt—
this cannot be considered righteous.
Moreover, the arguments of both gentlemen
do not strive to clarify the duty between sovereign and subject nor rectify the rites of feudal lords,
but merely contend over the pleasures of hunting
and the size of parks and preserves,
trying to outdo each other in extravagance
and surpass in wanton excess.
This cannot serve to spread fame and enhance reputation,
but rather is fit only to贬低 one's lord and harm oneself.
Besides, how can the affairs of Qí and Chǔ be worth mentioning!
You have not witnessed true grandeur,
have you not heard of the sovereign's Shànglín Park?
"To the left is Cāngwú,
to the right the western extremes,
the Dān River flows past its south,
the Zǐyuān runs through its north;
it begins and ends with the Bà and Chǎn,
receives the Jīng and Wèi as they flow in and out;
the Fēng, Hào, Liáo, and Jué
wind and meander,
circulating within its bounds.
Vast are the eight rivers dividing their streams,
facing away from each other in different forms.
East, west, south, and north,
they race back and forth,
emerging from the que towers of pepper-topped hills,
flowing through the banks of deep marshes,
passing through forests of cassia trees,
crossing expansive wild plains.
Swiftly they merge into a浑流,
follow the slopes downward,
rushing toward narrow gorges' mouths.
Striking against towering rocks,
dashing against piled-up banks,
boiling up in sudden fury,
surging and splashing wildly,
swirling deep and gushing fiercely,
横流 and turning back upon themselves,
whirling and churning coldly,
roaring and misting heavily,
arching like clouds and twisting,
蜿蜒 and coiling intricately,
waves surging toward low-lying pools,
rustling down over shallows,
battering cliffs and assaulting barriers,
奔腾 and scattering abundantly,
approaching islets and pouring into valleys,
plunging and tumbling down,
deeply and obscurely,
with a pounding, booming thunder,
bubbling and gurgling endlessly,
seething like a boiling cauldron,
racing waves leaping with foam,
swiftly and smoothly rushing,
far-reaching and long-remembered,
then falling into寂漻 silence,
spreading forth in eternal return.
Thereafter, vast and expansive, overflowing widely,
calmly soaring and slowly circling,
gleaming brightly and shining brilliantly,
they flow east into the great lake,
spreading and filling the pools and ponds.
Here then are jiāo dragons and red chī serpents,
gèngméng and chánlí fish,
yúyōng and qiántuō,
yúyú and qūnà,
raising their fins and lifting their tails,
shaking their scales and flapping their 'wings',
dwelling hidden in the deep rocks;
fish and turtles make joyous sounds,
and myriad creatures abound,
bright moon-pearls
glitter along the river's edge,
Shǔ stone and yellow ruǎn jade,
water-crystals piled in heaps,
glistening and sparkling brilliantly,
their colors radiant and dazzling,
accumulate in masses within.
Wild swans and sù swans, bǎo birds,
gē geese and zhǔyù,
jiāocī and huánmù,
fánwù and yōngqú, zhēn
cí ducks and jiāolú cormorants,
flock and float upon its surface.
Drifting freely and spreading widely,
following the wind, calm and gentle,
rocking and swaying with the waves,
sheltering among the grassy islets,
nibbling on water plants and algae,
chewing on water chestnuts and lotus roots.
"Thus, the lofty mountains rise steeply,
towering and jagged,
with deep forests and giant trees,
rugged cliffs and uneven peaks,
Jiǔzōng,
Jiéniè,
the Southern Mountains stand majestic,
with rocky slopes and precipitous ledges,
undulating and steep,
where valleys converge and gorges connect,
winding streams and ditches,
vast and gaping,
hills and separate isles,
towering and rugged,
mounds and hollows rise abruptly,
layered and densely packed,
ascending and descending in waves,
slopes and ponds stretch endlessly,
waters flow and merge abundantly,
spreading across the level plains,
marshlands stretch for a thousand miles,
all cultivated and managed.
Covered with green huì orchids,
draped with jiānglí herbs,
mixed with míwú fragrance,
interwoven with liúyí blossoms.
Densely knotted lǚ grass,
clustered lìsuō reeds,
jiēchē, hénglán,
gǎoběn, shègān,
zǐjiāng, ránghé,
zhēn, chéng, ruò, sūn,
xiānzhī, huánglì,
jiǎng, zhù, qīngfán,
spreading widely in the vast marshes,
extending across the great plains,
lush and sprawling far and wide,
swaying with the wind,
emitting intense fragrances,
rich and aromatic,
myriad scents diffuse,
permeating and spreading,
overwhelming and potent.
"Thus, gazing all around and observing broadly,
the view is blurred and indistinct,
vast and bewildering,
with no beginning to be seen,
no edge to discern.
The sun rises in the eastern pool,
sets in the western slope.
In the south, growth thrives even in deep winter,
waters surge and waves leap;
beasts include yōngmáo, mòmáo,
shěnniú, zhǔmí,
red-headed and round-foreheaded creatures,
qióngqí, elephants, and rhinoceroses.
In the north, even midsummer brings freezing cold that cracks the earth,
one wades through ice and lifts river waters,
beasts include qílín, jiǎoduān,
táotú, tuótuó,
qióngqióng, tuóxī,
juétí, lǘ, luó.
"Thus, detached palaces and separate lodges,
cover mountains and span valleys,
with high corridors extending in four directions,
double-tiered halls and winding pavilions,
ornate rafters and jade-like finials,
covered pathways interconnected,
verandas encircling for leisurely walks,
long routes requiring overnight stays.
Leveling peaks to build halls,
layering terraces in rising tiers,
with rock chambers and deep rooms,
looking down into obscurity with nothing visible,
reaching up to touch the sky by climbing rafters,
shooting stars pass through inner doors,
curving rainbows drape over balustrades.
Green dragons coil in the eastern wing,
elephant-drawn carriages move gracefully in the western clear space,
immortal beings rest in secluded towers,
figures like Wòquán bask in the southern eaves,
sweet springs gush in pure chambers,
flowing streams pass through the central courtyard.
Massive stones line the cliffs,
steep rocks leaning precariously,
towering and jagged,
carved and precipitous,
with méiguī jade and green lín gems,
coral growing in clusters,
mǐn jade spreading broadly,
patterned and scaly in appearance,
red xiá jade streaked and mottled,
interspersed among them,
hanging tassels of wǎnyǎn jades,
where the Héshì jade emerges.
"Thus, lújú ripen in summer,
huánggān, chéng, còu,
pípá, rǎnshì,
shì, nài, hòupò,
yǐngzǎo, yángméi,
yīngtáo, pútáo,
yǐnfū, yùdì,
tātà, lìzhī,
spread across the rear palaces,
arrayed in the northern gardens.
They extend over hills and mounds,
descend to the plains,
waving emerald leaves,
shaking purple stems,
blooming with red flowers,
displaying vibrant blossoms,
radiant and magnificent,
illuminating the vast wilderness.
Shātáng, lì, zhū,
huáfàn, pínglú,
liúluò, xūyú,
rénpín, bìnglǘ,
chántán, mùlán,
yùzhāng, nǚzhēn,
towering a thousand rèn high,
vast enough to encircle with arms,
with straight and soaring branches,
fruits and leaves luxuriantly dense,
clustered together and leaning in groups,
twisted and interconnected,
intricately tangled and winding,
robust and grandly overlapping,
dangling branches swaying gently,
falling petals fluttering down,
lush and rustling,
gracefully following the wind,
with sounds like soughing and sighing,
resembling the tones of metal and stone instruments,
the music of pipes and flutes.
Varied and uneven,
they encircle the rear palaces,
densely gathered and layered,
covering mountains and lining valleys,
following slopes down to moist lowlands,
with no end in sight,
and no limit to their expanse.
"Thus, black apes and white females,
wèi, jué, fēilěi,
zhì, tiáo, qúróu,
chánhú, hùgǔ,
perch and dwell among them;
long cries and mournful calls,
fluttering and crossing paths,
nimbly leaping between branches,
perching atop the highest tips.
Then they cross broken bridges,
leap over unusual thickets,
grasp hanging vines,
dart through sparse gaps,
scattered and varied,
roaming wildly to distant places.
"Such spots as these
number in the thousands.
Here, amusement and travel come and go,
lodging in palaces and resting in lodges,
kitchens need not be moved,
the rear palace remains in place,
all officials are fully equipped.
"Thus, from autumn through winter,
the Son of Heaven conducts grand hunts.
Riding carved ivory carriages,
drawn by six jade-like dragons,
trailing rainbow banners,
waving cloud-emblazoned flags,
with leather-covered vans ahead,
and guided processions behind;
Sūn Shǔ holding the reins,
Wèi Gōng riding alongside,
attendants following in all directions,
emerging from among the four guard formations.
Drums beat sternly,
hunters are unleashed,
using rivers as enclosures,
Mount Tài as a lookout,
chariots and cavalry thunder forth,
shaking the heavens and moving the earth,
advancing in scattered formations,
splitting up to pursue separately,
spreading far and wide,
along hills and across marshes,
like clouds spreading and rain falling.
"They bred pí leopards,
wrestled with chái wolves,
handled bears and pí bears,
trod upon wild sheep,
wore helmets adorned with hé bird feathers,
clad in white tiger trousers,
draped in patterned Bīn robes,
straddled wild horses.
They scaled the perilous heights of three peaks,
descended the rugged slopes of rocky terrain,
traversed steep cliffs and ventured into danger,
crossed ravines and waded through waters.
They pushed aside the feilían beast,
played with the xièzhì creature,
confronted the xiáhā monster,
struck the měngshì beast,
ensnared the yǎoniǎo steed,
shot the great fēngshǐ boar.
Arrows never struck without purpose,
piercing throats and shattering skulls;
bows never loosed in vain,
each shot felling its target with a cry.
Thus, the imperial carriage slowed its pace, meandering,
soaring and gliding back and forth,
observing the maneuvers of the troops,
surveying the changing tactics of the commanders.
Then, with sudden acceleration,
they swiftly vanished into the distance,
scattering light birds,
trampling cunning beasts,
overtaking white deer,
outrunning agile hares,
surpassing red lightning,
leaving brilliance behind,
pursuing monstrous creatures,
venturing beyond the cosmos,
drawing the Fánruò bow,
nocking white-feathered arrows,
shooting wandering owls,
striking flying jù beasts,
selecting targets before releasing,
hitting vital spots with precision,
bowstrings and arrows parting ways,
each shot felling its prey.
"Then, raising their whips, they ascended skyward,
riding the startled winds,
traversing the terrifying gusts,
mounting the void,
uniting with the divine,
trampling black cranes,
disrupting kūn chickens,
capturing peacocks and luán birds,
hastening jùnyì fowl,
brushing past yī birds,
seizing phoenixes,
intercepting yuānchú fledglings,
enveloping jiāomíng birds.
"When the path ended and the road ran out,
they turned the carriage and returned.
Wandering freely and aimlessly,
they descended and gathered at the northern boundary,
heading straight onward,
then quietly turning back toward home.
They passed Shíguān,
traversed Fēngluán,
went by Zhīquè,
gazed upon Lùhán,
descended to Tánglí,
rested at Yíchūn,
galloped west to Xuānqǔ,
washed at Niúshǒu,
ascended Lóngtái,
paused at Xìliǔ,
observing the diligence and strategies of the officials,
tallying the hunters' catches.
The tracks of chariots and soldiers crisscrossed,
the hooves of riders trampled the ground,
the footprints of the people were everywhere,
along with the exhausted and weary,
the terrified and subdued,
those who died without a wound,
lying in heaps and disorder,
filling pits and valleys,
covering plains and marshes.
"Then, in leisurely play and relaxation,
they set a feast at the Hàotiān Tower,
performed music in the vast courtyard,
struck bells of a thousand shí,
erected giant bells of ten thousand shí;
raised emerald banners,
set up drums of divine tuó lizards.
They performed the dances of Táotángshì,
listened to the songs of Gětiānshì,
with a thousand voices singing,
ten thousand joining in chorus,
mountains and hills trembling from the sound,
rivers and valleys rippling with waves.
Music from Bā, Yú, Sòng, and Cài,
Yúzhē from Huáinán,
Wénchéng and Diān songs,
performed in succession by groups,
golden drums alternating in rhythm,
clashing and resonating loudly,
piercing the heart and startling the ears.
The melodies of Jīng, Wú, Zhèng, and Wèi,
the music of Sháo, Huò, Wǔ, and Xiàng,
indulgent and extravagant tunes,
Yānyǐng's vibrant performances,
Jíchǔ's stirring winds,
comedians and dwarves,
singers from Dīdī,
all there to delight the senses and gladden the heart,
with dazzling splendor in front,
and exquisite beauties behind.
"As for those like Qīngqín and Fúfēi,
utterly unique and aloof from the mundane,
elegant and enchanting,
adorned with refined grace,
graceful and delicate,
softly swaying and gentle,
charming and slender;
they trailed single-silk gowns,
ethereal and finely tailored,
moving with light steps,
in attire distinct from the world;
their fragrance rich and profound,
intensely aromatic and pure;
their bright teeth gleaming,
their smiles radiantly fitting;
their long eyebrows arched delicately,
their sidelong glances tender and distant;
their beauty captivating the soul,
bringing joy to the heart beside them.
"Then, amid wine and music's climax,
the Son of Heaven grew pensive,
as if sensing a loss.
He said:
'Alas,
this is too extravagant!
I, in my leisure from governance,
with no pressing duties to fill the days,
follow the Way of Heaven in hunting,
taking rest here at times,
yet fear that future generations may pursue luxury,
advancing without return,
which is not the way to establish a legacy for successors and perpetuate the tradition.'
So, he ended the feast and halted the hunt,
commanding the officials:
'Lands that can be cultivated,
let all become farmlands,
to support the common people;
dismantle walls and fill moats,
so that mountain and marsh dwellers may come and go.
Fill ponds and lakes without restrictions,
leave palaces and towers unoccupied.
Open granaries to relieve the poor,
supplement what is lacking,
care for the widowed and solitary,
support the orphaned and alone.
Issue benevolent decrees,
reduce punishments,
reform institutions,
change ceremonial colors,
correct the calendar,
and make a new beginning with all under heaven.'
"Then, having chosen an auspicious day and fasted,
he donned court attire,
rode in the imperial carriage,
raised embroidered banners,
rang jade bells,
roamed in the park of the Six Arts,
galloped along the path of benevolence and righteousness,
surveyed the forest of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
shot with the 'Lí Shǒu' melody,
combined with the 'Zōu Yú' tune,
aimed at dark cranes,
erected shield and axe,
mounted cloud-like nets,
covered the various 'Yǎ' odes,
lamented with 'Fá Tán',
rejoiced with 'Lè Xū',
cultivated demeanor in the garden of the Rites,
soared in the field of the Documents,
expounded the way of the Changes,
released strange beasts,
ascended the Bright Hall,
sat in the Pure Temple,
allowed ministers their freedom,
reported successes and failures,
and within the four seas,
none failed to receive benefits.
At this time,
the world was greatly pleased,
listening to the wind's direction,
transforming with the flow,
sighing deeply, they revived the Way and moved toward righteousness,
punishments were set aside unused,
virtue surpassed that of the Three Sovereigns,
achievements exceeded those of the Five Emperors.
Thus,
such hunting is indeed delightful.
"But if one exposes oneself all day, galloping about,
exhausting the spirit and straining the body,
wearing out carriages and horses,
depleting the energy of soldiers,
wasting the wealth of the treasury,
without bestowing generous kindness,
focusing solely on personal pleasure,
disregarding the masses,
forgetting the governance of the state,
and coveting the capture of pheasants and hares,
then the benevolent would not follow such a path.
From this perspective,
the affairs of Qí and Chǔ,
are they not lamentable!
Their territories do not exceed a thousand lǐ,
yet their parks occupy nine hundred,
so that vegetation cannot be cultivated,
and the people have nothing to eat.
For feudal lords, though minor,
to delight in the extravagance of a ten-thousand-chariot ruler,
I fear the people will suffer from their excesses."
At this, the two men changed countenance, looking dismayed,
as if lost in thought,
and retreating from their mats, they said:
"We, being ignorant and uncultured,
did not know the taboos,
but today we have been instructed,
and we respectfully heed your command."
The rhapsody was presented,
and the Son of Heaven appointed him as a court gentleman.
Wúshìgōng spoke of the vastness of the Son of Heaven's Shànglín Park,
its mountains, valleys, streams, and myriad things,
and Zǐxū described the abundance of Chǔ's Yúnmèng,
exaggerating beyond reality,
and not upholding moral principles,
so it was edited to extract the essentials,
returning to the correct path for discussion.
Xiàngrú served as a court gentleman for several years,
when Táng Méng was sent to open communications with Yèláng and the western Bó region,
mobilizing a thousand officials and soldiers from Bā and Shǔ,
with the commanderies additionally dispatching over ten thousand for transport by land and water,
using military law to execute their chieftains,
causing great alarm among the people of Bā and Shǔ.
The Emperor, hearing of this,
sent Xiàngrú to reprimand Táng Méng,
and to inform the people of Bā and Shǔ that this was not the Emperor's intention.
The proclamation said:
To the Grand Administrators of Bā and Shǔ:
The barbarians have long acted on their own without being punished,
often invading the borders,
troubling the officials.
Since His Majesty ascended the throne,
he has comforted the world,
pacified the Central States.
Then he raised armies and sent troops,
campaigning north against the Xiōngnú,
terrifying the Chányú,
who crossed his arms in submission,
knelt and begged for peace.
Kāngjú and the Western Regions,
through multiple interpreters, requested audience,
bowing their heads to offer tribute.
Turning the army eastward,
Mǐnyuè attacked each other.
To the right, comforting Pānyú,
its crown prince entered the court.
The rulers of the southern tribes,
the chiefs of the western Bó,
often presented tribute duties,
not daring to neglect,
stretching their necks and rising on tiptoe,
eagerly vying to submit to righteousness,
wishing to become subjects,
but the roads are long,
mountains and rivers obstructive and deep,
preventing them from coming personally.
Those who were disobedient have been punished,
yet the good have not been rewarded,
so we sent a Central General to receive them as guests,
mobilizing five hundred scholars and commoners each from Bā and Shǔ,
to present silks and coins,
protecting the envoys without incident,
avoiding military affairs,
and the perils of battle.
Now we hear that they have instead invoked military conscription,
frightening the youth,
worrying the elders,
and the commanderies have arbitrarily undertaken grain transport,
all contrary to His Majesty's intent.
Those conscripted sometimes flee or kill themselves,
which is also not the duty of subjects.
The men of the border commanderies,
upon seeing beacon fires raised and signals burned,
all string their bows and gallop,
bear arms and run,
sweating profusely in succession,
fearing only to be last,
facing naked blades,
braving flying arrows,
righteously not looking back,
resolved not to retreat,
each heart filled with fury,
as if avenging personal grudges.
Do they delight in death and hate life,
or are they not registered citizens,
differing from Bā and Shǔ in allegiance?
They plan deeply and consider far,
urgently address the state's difficulties,
and delight in fulfilling their duties as subjects.
Thus, some receive enfeeffment with split tallies,
are ennobled with divided jades,
attain the rank of full marquis,
reside in eastern mansions,
leaving illustrious titles to posterity,
passing lands to sons and grandsons,
their actions most loyal and respectful,
their positions very secure and comfortable,
their fame spreading endlessly,
their achievements shining unfading.
Therefore, worthy men and gentlemen,
spill their brains on the central plains,
moisten wild grass with their fat without regret.
Now, conscripted to present coins to the southern tribes,
they instead kill themselves,
or flee and face execution,
dying nameless,
deemed most foolish,
shaming their parents,
laughed at by the world.
How vastly different human measures are!
Is it not far indeed!
Yet this is not solely the fault of the conscripts;
their elders failed to teach them first,
the youth lacked careful guidance;
lacking integrity and shame,
customs are not long-lasting and sincere.
Their suffering punishment and execution,
is it not fitting!
His Majesty grieves that the envoys and officials act thus,
mourns that foolish commoners behave so,
hence sending trusted envoys to clarify to the people the matter of conscription,
while enumerating the crimes of disloyalty leading to death,
reproaching the village elders for their failure in instruction.
Now during farming season,
to heavily burden the people,
we have personally informed nearby counties,
but fear those in remote valleys, mountains, and marshes may not fully hear,
so upon this proclamation's arrival,
hasten to disseminate it to counties and districts,
ensuring all know His Majesty's intent,
and do not neglect it."
Xiàngrú returned to report.
Táng Méng had already roughly connected with Yèláng,
and thereby opened the route to the southwestern tribes,
mobilizing soldiers from Bā,
Shǔ, and Guǎnghàn,
with tens of thousands of laborers.
After two years of road construction,
the road was not completed,
many soldiers and laborers died,
and the cost amounted to hundreds of millions.
Many people of Shǔ and Han officials spoke of its inconvenience.
At that time, the chieftains of Qióng and Zuó heard that the southern tribes had contact with Hàn,
receiving many rewards,
and most wished to become inner vassals,
requesting officials,
comparable to the southern tribes.
The Son of Heaven asked Xiàngrú,
Xiàngrú said:
"Qióng,
Zuó, Rǎn,
and Máng are close to Shǔ,
and the routes are easy to open,
having been connected as commanderies and counties in Qín times,
but discontinued when Hàn rose.
If we truly reconnect them now,
establishing commanderies and counties,
it would be better than with the southern tribes."
The Son of Heaven agreed,
and appointed Xiàngrú as Imperial Court General,
bearing credentials to go as envoy.
Deputy envoys Wáng Rányú,
Hú Chōngguó,
and Lǚ Yuèrén sped in four-horse carriages,
