using gifts from Bā and Shǔ officials to bribe the western tribes.
Arriving in Shǔ,
the Shǔ governor and below greeted them in the suburbs,
the county magistrate bearing crossbow arrows to lead the way,
which the people of Shǔ considered an honor.
Thereupon, Zhuō Wángsūn,
and the gentlemen of Línqióng all presented oxen and wine through their followers to foster goodwill.
Zhuō Wángsūn sighed with emotion,
regretting that he had let his daughter marry Sīmǎ Zhǎngqīng too late,
and generously divided property with his daughter,
equal to that of his sons.
Sīmǎ Zhǎngqīng then roughly pacified the western tribes,
with the chieftains of Qióng, Zuó,
Rǎn, Máng,
and Sīyú all requesting to become inner vassals.
Border passes were removed,
the frontiers expanded,
west to Mò
and Ruòshuǐ,
south to Zāngkē as the boundary,
opening the Língguān route,
and bridging the Sūnshuǐ to connect to Qióngdū.
He returned to report to the Son of Heaven,
who was greatly pleased.
When Xiàngrú was on his mission,
many Shǔ elders said opening the southwestern tribes was useless,
and even high ministers thought so.
Xiàngrú wished to remonstrate,
but having already proposed it,
he dared not,
so he wrote a text,
using the Shǔ elders as a pretext,
and himself refuting them,
to subtly advise the Son of Heaven,
and also to clarify his mission's intent,
letting the people know the Son of Heaven's will.
The text said:
Since Hàn's rise, seventy-eight years have passed,
with virtue flourishing through six reigns,
military might abundant,
deep grace vast,
all living things moistened,
overflowing beyond the borders.
Then he ordered an envoy to campaign west,
pushing back along the currents,
where the wind reached,
none failed to yield.
Thereby making Rǎn submit and Máng follow,
pacifying Zuó and preserving Qióng,
conquering Sīyú,
raising Bāomǎn,
turning the chariots back,
heading east to report,
arriving at Shǔ's capital.
Twenty-seven elders, senior officials, and gentry,
solemnly came to visit.
After greetings,
they advanced saying:
"We hear that regarding barbarians,
the principle is to loosely control without severing ties.
Now exhausting three commanderies' men,
opening the road to Yèláng,
for three years now,
the task remains unfinished,
soldiers weary,
the people unsupported,
and now adding the western tribes,
the people's strength depleted,
fearing it cannot be completed,
this also burdens the envoy,
we worry for you.
Moreover, Qióng,
Zuó, and Xībó coexisted with the central states,
for many years,
beyond record.
The benevolent could not attract them by virtue,
the strong could not annex them by force,
perhaps it is impossible!
Now dividing our people to join barbarians,
exhausting our resources for useless endeavors,
we, ignorant and narrow-minded,
do not understand the purpose."
The envoy said:
"How can you say this?
If it were as you say,
then Shǔ would not change dress nor Bā transform customs.
I dislike hearing such talk.
But this matter is significant,
beyond ordinary observation.
My journey is urgent,
no time for details,
but let me briefly outline it.
"For the world must have extraordinary people,
then extraordinary deeds;
with extraordinary deeds,
then extraordinary achievements.
The extraordinary,
naturally differ from the ordinary.
Thus, the start of the extraordinary,
frightens the common people;
when it succeeds,
the world is at peace.
"In the past, floodwaters surged forth,
overflowing widely,
people moved up and down,
unsettled and insecure.
The Xiàhòu clan grieved over it,
and blocked the floods,
diverting rivers and dredging streams,
draining swamps and relieving disasters,
directing them east to the sea,
and the world was eternally tranquil.
In that toil,
were only the people involved?
Minds troubled by worries, bodies enduring labor,
hands calloused, no fine hair,
skin growing no down.
Thus, glorious achievements shine endlessly,
renown spreads to this day.
"Moreover, when a virtuous sovereign ascends the throne,
how could he merely be preoccupied with trivial matters,
constrained by formalities and bound by customs,
following recited texts and practiced traditions,
seeking only contemporary approval?
He must elevate grand discourses and profound deliberations,
establish foundations and perpetuate traditions,
setting models for ten thousand generations.
Thus he ranges widely, embracing all inclusively,
and diligently contemplates matching heaven and earth.
Does not the Book of Songs say:
'Under the vast heaven,
there is no land that is not the king's;
within the borders of the land,
there are none who are not the king's subjects.'
Therefore, within the six directions,
beyond the eight boundaries,
wherever moisture spreads and overflows,
if any living creature fails to be moistened by this grace,
the virtuous sovereign considers it shameful.
Now within our bounded territories,
among the civilized people,
all have obtained excellent blessings,
with none omitted or left behind.
But in countries of the barbarians with different customs,
in distant lands of alien peoples,
where boats and carriages cannot reach,
and human footprints rarely tread,
where governance and教化 have not been extended,
and transforming influence remains faint,
internally they violate righteousness and encroach upon propriety at the borders,
externally they commit wicked deeds recklessly,
murdering and overthrowing their superiors.
Ruler and minister exchange positions,
the noble and humble lose proper order,
fathers and brothers suffer unjustly,
young orphans become slaves,
bound and weeping,
they turn inward with resentment,
saying
'We have heard that in the Middle Kingdom there is perfect benevolence,
where virtue flows abundantly and grace is universal,
where nothing fails to find its proper place,
why now are we alone abandoned?'
They stand on tiptoe with longing,
like parched land yearning for rain.
Even cruel men would shed tears at this,
how much more should the supremely sage,
how could he refrain from action?
Therefore, we dispatched troops northward to punish the strong Hú,
and sent envoys speeding south to reprimand the powerful Yuè.
Virtue blows like wind to the four directions,
rulers from both regions gather like fish scales, looking up to the flow,
those wishing to receive our commands number in the hundreds of millions.
Thus we established passes at Mò
and Ruò, marked the boundaries at Zāngkē,
carved paths through Líng Mountain,
and built bridges at Sūn Plateau.
We created the way of道德,
and extended the tradition of benevolence and righteousness.
We shall broadly bestow kindness and widely extend beneficence,
pacifying from afar and driving long,
so that the distant are not shut out,
and the deeply obstructed and benighted may shine with brightness,
thus laying aside armor and weapons here,
and ceasing punitive campaigns there.
Far and near become one body,
within and without share in blessings,
is this not prosperity?
To rescue the people from drowning,
to uphold the sovereign's excellent virtue,
to reverse the decline of decadent ages,
to continue the severed enterprise of the Zhōu house,
this is the urgent task of the Son of Heaven.
Though the common people may toil,
how can we possibly desist?
"Moreover, royal affairs invariably begin with anxiety and diligence,
and end in ease and pleasure.
Thus the signs of receiving the Mandate,
are precisely found herein.
We shall soon enhance the fēng sacrifice at Tài Shān,
and add the shì ceremony at Liángfù,
make the harmonious bells resound,
raise songs of music and praise,
above equal the Five Emperors,
below surpass the Three Sovereigns.
Though viewers have not yet seen the direction,
and listeners have not yet heard the sounds,
like the jiāomíng already soaring in the vast skies,
while netters still stare at the marshes.
How lamentable!"
Thereupon the various grand masters were dazed, losing what they had intended to present and forgetting their means of advancement,
sighing in unison they exclaimed:
"Truly admirable is the virtue of Hàn,
this is what we humble men wished to hear.
Though the common people may be weary,
we beg to lead them by our own example."
Confused and with no place to go,
they withdrew step by step and took their leave.
Later, someone submitted a memorial accusing Xiàngrú of accepting bribes during his mission,
and he lost his official position.
After about a year,
he was recalled to serve as a court gentleman.
Xiàngrú stammered but excelled at writing.
He often suffered from diabetes.
He married into the Zhuō family,
and was wealthy.
In his official career advancement,
he never willingly involved himself in affairs of state with the high ministers,
pleading illness he lived in leisure,
not coveting official posts or titles.
He often accompanied the emperor to Chángyáng for hunting,
at that time the emperor particularly enjoyed personally attacking bears and boars,
chasing wild animals,
Xiàngrú submitted a memorial advising against this.
Its text said:
Your servant hears that among things of the same kind there are those with exceptional abilities,
thus for strength we speak of Wūhuò,
for swiftness we mention Qìngjì,
for courage we look to Bēn
and Yù. In my foolish opinion,
I privately believe that if this is true for humans,
it should also be so for beasts.
Now Your Majesty delights in traversing dangerous terrain,
shooting fierce animals,
should you suddenly encounter a beast of extraordinary ability,
startled in an untenable position,
invading the pure dust of the imperial carriage train,
with the carriage unable to turn around,
and people having no time to employ their skills,
even if you had the abilities of Wūhuò
or Péngméng,
their strength would be useless,
and every dead tree and rotten stump would become hazardous.
This would be like having the Hú and Yuè rise from beneath your wheels,
and the Qiāng and Yí adjacent to your carriage,
is this not perilous?
Even if all were perfectly safe without mishap,
still this is fundamentally not what the Son of Heaven should approach.
Moreover, clearing the road before proceeding,
and galloping only on the middle path,
even then there are occasional accidents with bridles and bits,
how much more when traversing through overgrown weeds,
galloping over hills and mounds,
with the pleasure of pursuing game ahead but no mind for potential dangers within,
wouldn't disaster then be hard to avoid?
To treat lightly the importance of the myriad chariots without considering safety,
yet to find amusement in paths that offer one chance in ten thousand of danger,
your servant privately believes this is not what Your Majesty should choose.
For the clear-sighted see far ahead before things sprout, and the wise avoid danger before it takes form,
calamities inherently hide in obscurity and subtlety, and erupt from what people overlook.
Thus the common saying goes
"Those with a thousand gold in household wealth
do not sit under the eaves."
These words, though small,
can illustrate greater principles.
I hope Your Majesty will consider and examine this carefully.
The emperor approved of his advice.
Returning, he passed by Yíchūn Palace,
Xiàngrú presented a rhapsody lamenting the Second Emperor's misdeeds.
Its text said:
I climb the long slope, winding and steep,
and enter abruptly the towering layered palaces.
I approach the winding river's sandy isle,
and gaze upon the Nán Mountains' jagged peaks.
The profound depths of the steep deep mountains,
the penetrating valleys, deep and vast.
The rushing waters, swiftly converging, forever flowing away,
pouring onto the plain's broad expanse.
I observe the dense profusion of numerous trees,
and view the lush growth of bamboos and woods.
Eastward I speed to the earthen hill,
northward I ford the stony shallows.
Reining in, I linger leisurely,
then pass by, mourning the Second Emperor.
In conducting himself without caution,
he lost his state and forfeited power.
Trusting slander without awakening,
his ancestral temple was utterly destroyed.
Alas, how sorrowful!
In his conduct finding no proper way,
his grave lies desolate and unkempt,
his soul wanders homeless with no offerings.
Far and remote, cut off and disordered,
the longer lasting, the more decayed.
His essence, ethereal and fleeting, drifts away,
soaring to the nine heavens, forever departing.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Xiàngrú was appointed as the Prefect of the Filial and Cultured Park.
The Son of Heaven, having admired the tales of Zǐxū,
Xiàngrú noticed the emperor's fondness for the ways of immortals,
and thus said:
"The events of the Shanglin Park are not yet worthy of praise,
for there are even more extravagant ones.
I once composed the 'Rhapsody of the Great Man,'
but it remains unfinished;
I request to complete it and present it to you."
Xiàngrú believed that the accounts of immortals dwelling in mountains and marshes,
with their emaciated appearances,
did not align with the emperor's idea of immortality,
so he proceeded to finish the "Rhapsody of the Great Man."
Its verses read:
In the world, there is a great man,
residing in the central realm.
His abode spans ten thousand miles,
yet he finds it insufficient for a brief stay.
Grieving the narrow constraints of the mundane world,
he lightly ascends to wander afar.
Draped in crimson banners and white rainbows,
he rides on clouds and mist, floating upward.
He erects long poles from the Gézé constellation,
gathering radiant light and colorful pennants.
He hangs the Shǐxún star as his tassels,
and trails comets for his sash.
He sways and postures with grandeur,
then elegantly beckons and waves.
He grasps the Chánqiāng comet as his banner,
and weaves the curved rainbow into silk.
In the deep red haze, dazzling and blurred,
whirlwinds surge and clouds float.
Driving dragon-drawn carriages that undulate gracefully,
with red and blue serpents coiling as his team.
Now dipping low, now soaring high, proud and lofty,
bending and twisting in continuous curls.
Majestic and vigorous, halting in awe,
spreading widely, rearing up to towering heights.
Striding steadily, accommodating and graceful,
entwined and towering, startled and leaning on beams.
Tangled and clamoring, trampling the path to arrival,
leaping and vaulting wildly in frenzy.
Swift as the wind, converging like lightning,
suddenly the mist clears,
abruptly the clouds disperse.
Diagonally crossing Shàoyáng and ascending Tàiyīn,
he seeks the company of the true immortals.
Winding through secluded paths, turning to the right,
traversing Feǐquán straight to the east.
Summoning all the spiritual beings for selection,
assembling the multitude of gods at Yáoguāng.
Having the Five Emperors lead the way,
turning from Tàiyī to follow Língyáng.
With Xuánmíng on the left and Hánléi on the right,
Lùlí in front and Juéhuáng behind.
Employing Zhēng Bóqiáo and commanding Xiànmén,
assigning Qí Bó to oversee the imperial workshop.
Zhùróng startled, clearing the path,
purifying the air before proceeding.
Gathering my chariots, ten thousand in number,
adorned with cloud canopies and flowery banners.
Sending Jù Máng to lead the march,
I wish to journey south for amusement.
Passing by Táng Yáo at Chóng Shān,
visiting Yú Shùn at Jiǔyí.
Profound and dense, they interweave in disorder,
crowded and tangled, galloping side by side.
Tumultuous and clashing, entangled in chaos,
overflowing and vast, scattering in all directions.
Clustered and gathered, thickly assembled,
spreading and flowing, brilliantly variegated.
Directly entering the thundering cavern's deep gloom,
emerging through the ghostly valley's rugged heights.
Surveying all eight directions and observing the four wilds,
then crossing the Jiǔ Jiāng and traversing the Five Rivers.
Journeying through the flames and floating on the Ruò Shuǐ,
crossing the floating isles and wading through the flowing sands.
Resting briefly at Zǒngjí, indulging in water play,
having Língwā play the se while Féngyí dances.
When the sky darkens and turns murky,
summon Píngyì to punish the Wind Earl and the Rain Master.
Gazing west toward Kūnlún's vast and vague expanse,
heading straight through Sānwēi.
Pushing open the Chānghé and entering the imperial palace,
escorting the jade maidens to return with them.
Ascending Lángfēng and alighting gently,
soaring like a bird and pausing once.
Hovering over Yīn Shān, circling in twists and turns,
I now behold Xīwángmǔ, her hair stark white.
Adorned with victory emblems, dwelling in a cave,
fortunate to have the three-legged crow as her servant.
If immortality means living like this eternally,
even aiding the world for millennia would bring no joy.
Turning the carriage around, coming back,
cutting through the Bùzhōu mountain,
meeting to feast at Yōudū.
Breathing the night mist and feasting on morning clouds,
chewing on magic fungi and savoring jade blossoms.
Rising swiftly to soar high,
in multitudes surging upward fiercely.
Piercing through Lièquē's inverted light,
wading through Fēnglóng's abundant rain.
Galloping along the paths, descending gracefully,
chasing the lingering fog, drifting far away.
Pressed by the narrow confines of the central region,
stretching forth beyond the northern border.
Leaving the cavalry at Xuānquè,
overtaking the vanguard at Hánmén.
Descending into depths where no ground exists,
ascending into voids where no sky is seen.
Gazing dizzily with nothing in sight,
listening intently with no sound heard.
Riding on emptiness, ascending to the heights,
transcending all, alone in existence.
After Xiàngrú presented the "Hymn of the Great Man,"
the Son of Heaven was greatly pleased,
feeling as if floating on clouds,
as though wandering between heaven and earth.
When Xiàngrú fell ill and was relieved of his duties,
he resided at home in Màolíng.
The Son of Heaven said:
"Sīmǎ Xiàngrú is gravely ill;
go quickly to collect all his writings;
if not,
they may be lost later."
He sent Suǒ Zhōng to go,
but Xiàngrú had already died,
and there were no books at his home.
Asked his wife,
who replied:
"Chángqīng never had any books.
He often wrote,
but people would take them away,
leaving the house empty.
Before Chángqīng died,
he wrote one volume,
saying that if an envoy came seeking his writings,
it should be presented.
There are no other books."
His posthumous manuscript discussed the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
and was presented by Suǒ Zhōng.
Zhōng submitted the text,
and the Son of Heaven found it remarkable.
The text said:
From the dawn of ancient times,
since Hàoqióng gave birth to the people,
through the succession of rulers,
up to the Qín dynasty.
Those nearby followed in their footsteps,
those afar heard the echoes.
Countless and flourishing,
yet buried and unrecorded,
are too numerous to tell.
Continuing the Zhāo and Xià traditions,
honoring titles and posthumous names,
barely seventy-two rulers are worth mentioning.
None who were virtuous failed to prosper,
who could defy heaven and survive?
Before the time of Xuānyuán,
it is so distant and remote,
that the details cannot be heard of.
The transmissions in the Five Classics and Six Scriptures,
are what we can observe.
The Book of Documents says,
"When the sovereign is enlightened,
his ministers are capable."
Based on this, it can be said,
no ruler was greater than Táng Yáo,
no minister more virtuous than Hòu Jì.
Hòu Jì initiated the enterprise under Táng,
Gōng Liú rose to prominence from the Western Róng,
King Wén reformed the institutions,
thus the Zhōu dynasty reached its peak,
great achievements were accomplished,
and later declined and weakened,
yet for a thousand years, their legacy endured,
was that not a good beginning and a good end?
However, there is no mystery to it,
they were cautious in their actions beforehand,
and careful to leave teachings for posterity.
Thus, their paths were level and easy,
easy to follow;
their profound grace was abundant,
easy to enrich;
their laws and regulations were clear,
easy to emulate;
their transmitted systems were orderly,
easy to inherit.
Therefore, their legacy flourished even in infancy and surpassed that of the two later dynasties.
Examining their origins,
and tracing their ends,
none had extraordinary feats or unique achievements that can be verified today.
Yet they still trod Liángfù,
ascended Tài Shān,
established illustrious titles,
and bestowed honorable names.
The virtue of the great Hàn,
gushes like a spring from its source,
overflowing and spreading widely,
extending to the four borders,
dissipating like clouds and mist,
reaching up to the nine heavens,
and down to the eight confines.
All living beings are moistened and nurtured,
harmonious energy flows horizontally,
martial spirit drifts afar,
near the narrow origins it roams,
in the distant expanses it swims in foam,
the chief villains are submerged,
the obscure becomes clear,
insects rejoice in the favor,
turning their heads to face inward.
Then, enclosures hold precious herds of zōuyú,
and strange beasts like mílù are intercepted,
in the kitchen, grains with one stem and six ears are selected,
sacrificial animals with double antlers and shared bases are offered,
the remaining treasure of Zhōu, a turtle, is recovered in Qí,
cuìhuáng and dragons are summoned in the ponds.
Ghosts and spirits connect with língyǔ,
hosted in leisure halls.
Strange objects are deceitful and诡异,
extraordinary and ever-changing.
How admirable!
With such auspicious signs gathered here,
yet it is still considered insufficient,
not daring to speak of the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
In the Zhōu dynasty, fish leaped and fell into the boat,
which was celebrated with a burnt offering,
compared to such an omen,
to ascend the great mountain,
is it not shameful!
The principles of advancement and deference,
how do they differ?
Then the Grand Minister of War came forward and said:
"Your Majesty benevolently nurtures all living beings,
righteously campaigns against the unsubmissive,
the various Xià gladly offer tribute,
the hundred Mán present gifts,
your virtue matches that of antiquity,
your achievements are unparalleled,
splendid deeds are pervasive,
auspicious signs and numerous changes,
expected responses follow in succession,
not merely occasional appearances.
It is thought that Tài Shān and
Liángfù have set up altars hoping for Your Majesty's presence,
to bestow titles and honor,
that the Supreme God bestows grace and stores blessings,
intending to complete the offering,
but Your Majesty is modest and has not initiated it.
To withhold the joy of the three deities,
and lack the rituals of the kingly way,
the officials feel ashamed.
Some say that heaven is inherently obscure,
and precious omens should not be declined;
if they are declined,
then Tài Shān would have no record and Liángfù no hope.
Each also glorified in their own time,
all assisted the world and then declined,
what would later commentators praise,
and why speak of the seventy-two rulers?
Cultivating virtue to receive omens,
and following omens to act,
is not overstepping.
Thus, the sage kings did not abandon it,
but practiced rituals for the earth deity,
paid homage to the heavenly gods,
inscribed achievements on the central peak,
to manifest the supreme honor,
spread the great virtue,
issue glorious decrees,
receive abundant blessings,
and benefit the common people.
How magnificent is this matter!
The grand spectacle of the world,
the great enterprise of kings,
should not be belittled.
I hope Your Majesty will complete it.
Then, incorporating the strategies of the gentry scholars,
enabling them to catch the last rays of the sun and moon,
to display their talents and manage affairs,
still, we should correct and arrange their meanings,
revise and polish the texts,
create one art like the Spring and Autumn Annals,
to continue the old six and make them seven,
spreading it endlessly,
so that for ten thousand generations, they may stir the clear stream,
raise gentle waves,
spread illustrious fame,
and elevate abundant achievements.
This is how former sages eternally preserved their great names and were always praised,
it is appropriate to order the archivists to fully present their meanings for review."
Then the emperor, with a changed expression, said:
"Joyful!
I shall try it!"
Thereupon, he reconsidered and reflected,
gathered the discussions of the ministers,
inquired about the Fēng and Shàn ceremonies,
praised the vastness of the great marsh,
and the abundance of auspicious signs.
Then he composed a eulogy, saying:
Under heaven's cover,
clouds drift richly.
Sweet dew and timely rain,
make the land fit to roam.
Nourishing fluids seep down,
what life is not nurtured?
Fine grains with six ears,
how can our harvest not abound?
Not only does it rain,
but it also moistens;
not only does it dampen,
but it spreads widely.
All things are joyful,
yearning and admiring.
Famous mountains and illustrious positions,
await the ruler's arrival.
O ruler, o ruler,
why do you not come?
The splendid beast,
delights in our ruler's garden;
white body with black patterns,
its appearance is delightful;
gentle and harmonious,
like the ability of a nobleman.
We heard of its reputation,
now we see its arrival.
Its path leaves no trace,
a sign of heavenly blessing.
This also happened with Shùn,
the Yú clan thus rose.
The gleaming qílín,
roams that sacred altar.
In the early winter tenth month,
the ruler sacrifices in the suburbs.
It gallops to our ruler's carriage,
the emperor enjoys the blessing.
Before the three dynasties,
such a thing had never occurred.
The winding yellow dragon,
rises with virtue;
its colors shine brilliantly,
resplendent and glorious.
Appearing at high noon,
awakening the common people.
In the records it is written,
it is the vehicle of the mandate.
When patterns naturally manifest,
there is no need for verbose exhortation.
By relying on categories and employing allegories,
they illustrate the significance of fēng and shàn sacrifices.
Reviewing the classics,
one sees the interaction between Heaven and humanity,
with responses harmoniously exchanged between high and low.
The virtue of sage kings
is marked by caution and reverence.
Hence it is said,
"In prosperity, consider decline;
in security, think of peril."
Thus, even at the pinnacle of dignity like Tāng and Wǔ,
they never neglected solemn reverence;
while Shùn followed established codes,
he still reflected on his oversights:
this illustrates the principle.
Five years after Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's death,
the Son of Heaven began sacrifices to Hòutǔ.
Eight years later, he first ceremonially honored the central peak,
performed the fēng sacrifice on Tài Shān,
and conducted the shàn ritual at Sùrán beneath Liángfù.
Among Xiàngrú's other writings,
such as "Letter to the Marquis of Pínglíng",
"Debates with the Five Noble Scions",
and the "Botanical Writings",
only those most renowned among officials were selected.
The Grand Historian remarks:
The Spring and Autumn Annals deduce the hidden from the evident;
the Yì Jīng reveals the manifest through the hidden;
the Greater Odes speak of kings and lords while virtue reaches the common people;
the Lesser Odes critique personal gains and losses,
yet their influence ascends to the rulers.
Though their expressions differ,
their virtuous unity remains one.
Though Xiàngrú employed elaborate rhetoric,
his essence guides toward frugality—
how does this differ from the admonitory airs of the Poetry?
Yáng Xióng deemed ornate rhapsodies
as "encouraging excess while cautioning minimally",
comparing them to the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
where elegance arrives only at the finale—
is this not deficient?
I have selected his discussable words for this record.
Lìwáng Liú Zhǎng of Huáinán
was a younger son of Emperor Gāozǔ,
his mother originally a beauty of Zhào King Zhāng Áo.
In the eighth year of Gāozǔ's reign,
while passing through Zhào from Dōngyuán,
the King of Zhào presented beauties to him.
Lìwáng's mother gained favor
and conceived.
King Áo dared not house her in his palace,
so built an external residence for her.
When Guàn Gāo's conspiracy at Bóren was exposed,
the king was arrested and investigated,
with all his mother, brothers, and beauties seized
and detained in Hénèi.
Lìwáng's mother was also imprisoned,
informing officials:
"I was favored by the emperor
and am with child."
Officials reported this upward,
but the emperor was enraged at the King of Zhào,
ignoring Lìwáng's mother.
Her brother Zhào Jiān appealed to Empress Lǚ through Pìyáng Hóu,
but the jealous empress
refused to intercede,
and Pìyáng Hóu didn't press firmly.
After giving birth to Lìwáng,
his mother, in anguish, took her own life.
Officials presented the infant to the emperor,
who regretted his actions,
ordered Empress Lǚ to raise him,
and buried Lìwáng's mother in Zhēndìng—
where
her family resided,
their ancestral county.
In the seventh month of Gāozǔ's eleventh year,
Huáinán King Qíng Bù rebelled,
so the emperor appointed his son Zhǎng as King of Huáinán,
ruling Bù's former territories
spanning four commanderies.
The emperor led troops to crush Bù,
and Lìwáng thus ascended the throne.
Having lost his mother early,
he attached himself to Empress Lǚ,
remaining favored and unharmed during Emperor Huì
and Empress Lǚ's reigns,
though secretly resenting Pìyáng Hóu,
unable to act.
When Emperor Wén ascended,
the King of Huáinán, considering himself the closest kin,
grew arrogant and defiant,
repeatedly flouting laws.
The emperor, for kinship's sake,
often pardoned him.
In the third year,
he came to court,
behaving arrogantly.
While hunting in imperial parks with the emperor,
sharing his carriage,
he often addressed him
as "Eldest Brother".
Lìwáng possessed great strength,
able to lift cauldrons,
and went to summon Pìyáng Hóu.
When the marquis came out to meet him,
Lìwáng drew an iron mace from his sleeve and struck him,
ordering his follower Wèi Jìng to behead him.
Lìwáng then rushed to the palace,
bared his torso, and confessed:
"My mother不该受 Zhào affairs'牵连—
then Pìyáng Hóu could have swayed Empress Lǚ,
yet didn't plead: first crime.
King Rúyì and his mother were innocent,
but Empress Lǚ killed them—
Pìyáng Hóu didn't protest: second crime.
Empress Lǚ enfeoffed the Lǚ clan,
endangering the Liú lineage—
Pìyáng Hóu didn't oppose: third crime.
I have executed the traitor Pìyáng Hóu for the realm,
avenging my mother,
and now kneel at the palace to seek punishment."
Emperor Wén, moved by his devotion
and for kinship,
didn't prosecute,
pardoning Lìwáng.
At that time,
Empress Dowager Bó, the crown prince, and ministers all feared Lìwáng,
who returned to his kingdom more arrogant than ever,
disregarding Hàn laws,
using imperial guards for procession,
issuing decrees,
enacting his own statutes,
emulating the Son of Heaven.
In the sixth year,
he conspired with seventy men including Dàn and Qí, heir of Jípú Hóu Chái Wǔ,
to revolt at Gǔkǒu with forty large chariots,
dispatching envoys to Mínyuè
and the Xiōngnú.
When the plot was discovered,
an investigation began,
and envoys summoned the King of Huáinán.
The king arrived at Cháng'ān.
In the fifth year of Yuánshuò,
the Crown Prince was learning to use the sword,
and he thought no one could match him.
Hearing that the court gentleman Léi Bēi was skilled,
he summoned him for a match.
Léi Bēi repeatedly declined,
but accidentally hit the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince was angry,
and Léi Bēi became fearful.
At that time, those who wished to join the army would go to the capital,
so Léi Bēi volunteered to fight against the Xiōngnú.
The Crown Prince, Qiān, repeatedly spoke ill of Léi Bēi to the King,
and the King had the Chief of the Gentlemen dismiss him,
intending to set an example for the future.
Léi Bēi then fled to Cháng'ān,
and submitted a letter to clear his name.
An edict referred the matter to the Commandant of Justice and
Hénán.
Hénán investigated,
and summoned the Crown Prince of Huáinán.
The King and the Queen Consort planned not to send the Crown Prince,
and thus raised troops to rebel,
but hesitated in their plans,
and for over ten days could not decide.
Just then, an edict arrived,
ordering the immediate interrogation of the Crown Prince.
At that time,
the Chancellor of Huáinán was angry that the Assistant of Shòuchūn had detained the Crown Prince and not sent him,
and accused him of disrespect.
The King pleaded with the Chancellor,
but the Chancellor did not listen.
The King sent someone to submit a letter accusing the Chancellor,
and the matter was referred to the Commandant of Justice for investigation.
The trail led to the King,
who sent people to spy on the Hàn ministers.
The ministers requested the arrest and trial of the King.
The King feared the matter would be exposed,
and the Crown Prince, Qiān, plotted, saying:
"If the Hàn envoy comes to arrest the King,
have the King order someone to dress in guard's uniform,
hold a halberd and stand in the courtyard.
If anything untoward happens beside the King,
then stab and kill them.
I will also have someone stab and kill the Commandant of Huáinán,
and then we raise troops—
it will not be too late."
At that time, the Emperor did not approve the ministers' request,
but sent the Hàn Commandant Hóng to interrogate and investigate the King.
When the King heard the Hàn envoy was coming,
he immediately followed the Crown Prince's plot.
When the Hàn Commandant arrived,
the King saw his expression was mild,
and he only questioned the King about the dismissal of Léi Bēi.
The King thought he had nothing serious to fear,
and did not act.
The Commandant returned,
and reported his findings.
The investigating ministers said:
"Huáinán King, Liú Ān, obstructed Léi Bēi and others who volunteered to fight the Xiōngnú,
and defied a clear edict;
he should be executed in the marketplace."
The edict did not approve.
The ministers requested to depose him from his kingship,
but the edict did not approve.
The ministers requested to cut five counties from his domain,
and the edict cut two counties.
The Commandant Hóng was sent to pardon Huáinán King's crime,
penalizing him by reducing his territory.
When the Commandant entered Huáinán's borders,
he announced the pardon of the King.
The King had initially heard that the Hàn ministers requested his execution,
and did not know he would only lose territory.
Hearing the Hàn envoy was coming,
he feared he would be arrested,
so he again plotted with the Crown Prince to assassinate him as before.
When the Commandant arrived,
he congratulated the King,
so the King did not act.
Afterward, the King lamented, saying:
"I practiced benevolence and righteousness, yet was reduced in territory—
I am deeply ashamed."
However, after Huáinán King lost territory,
his plans for rebellion intensified.
When envoys or travelers came from Cháng'ān,
if they spread false and ominous rumors,
saying the Emperor had no sons,
and Hàn was in disorder,
he would be pleased;
if they said the Hàn court was well-governed,
and there were sons,
the King would be angry,
thinking it was nonsense,
and untrue.
The King day and night with Wǔ Bèi,
Zuǒ Wú, and others studied maps,
deploying troops for invasion routes.
The King said:
"The Emperor has no crown prince;
if the imperial carriage were to falter,
the court ministers would surely summon the King of Jiāodōng,
or else the King of Chángshān.
With the nobles contending together,
how could I not be prepared!
Moreover, I am a grandson of Emperor Gāozǔ,
personally practicing benevolence and righteousness.
His Majesty treats me generously,
and I can endure it;
but after ten thousand generations,
how could I face north and serve such a brat as my lord!"
The king sat in the eastern palace,
summoned Wǔ Bèi to discuss plans,
saying:
"General, approach."
Bèi, disheartened, replied:
"The Emperor has shown leniency and pardoned you, Great King,
how can you utter such words that would lead to the downfall of a state!
I have heard that when Wǔ Zǐxū advised the King of Wú,
and the king employed his counsel,
he then said
'I now see deer roaming the terrace of Gūsū.'
Now I too see thorns and brambs growing in the palace,
and dew soaking my garments."
The king grew angry,
imprisoned Wǔ Bèi's parents,
and held them for three months.
He then summoned him again, saying:
"Will you assist me, General?"
Bèi replied:
"No,
I have come only to advise you, Great King.
I have heard that the wise listen to what is silent,
and the discerning see what is yet unformed;
thus, the sage succeeds in every endeavor.
In the past, King Wén's single action brought him glory for a thousand generations,
ranking him among the Three Dynasties.
This is what is called acting in accordance with the will of Heaven,
so the world followed him without being summoned.
This is a vision that spans millennia.
As for the Qin dynasty, which lasted a hundred years,
and the recent states of Wú and Chǔ,
they suffice to illustrate the survival or fall of a nation.
I dare not avoid the fate of Wǔ Zǐxū's execution,
but I hope you, Great King, will not emulate the King of Wú in heeding advice.
In the past, the Qin dynasty cut off the way of the sages,
killed scholars,
burned the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*,
abandoned rites and righteousness,
exalted deceit and force,
relied on punishments,
and transported grain from the coastal regions to the Xīhé area.
At that time,
men toiled in farming yet lacked even chaff to eat,
women spun and wove yet had not enough to cover their bodies.
They sent Méng Tián to build the Great Wall,
stretching thousands of miles east to west,
with troops exposed in the field often numbering hundreds of thousands,
the dead beyond count,
corpses littering the land for miles,
blood flowing over acres,
until the people were exhausted,
and half of every ten households desired to rebel.
They also sent Xú Fú to sea in search of divine marvels,
who fabricated a tale, saying:
'I encountered a great deity in the sea,
who asked:
"Are you an envoy of the Western Emperor?"
I replied:
"Yes."
"What do you seek?"
I said:
"I wish to request the elixir of longevity."
The deity said:
"The offerings from your King of Qin are too meager;
you may see it but not take it."
Then he led me southeast to Pénglái Mountain,
where I saw palaces made of glossy ganoderma,
and an envoy with a bronze hue and dragon form,
whose light shone up to the heavens.
Thereupon, I bowed twice and asked:
"What tribute should I bring to offer?"
The sea god said:
"Bring fine young men and maidens, along with artisans of various trades,
and then you may obtain it."'
The Qin emperor was greatly pleased,
sent three thousand young men and women,
and provided them with grains, seeds, and artisans before they departed.
Xú Fú found a vast plain and marsh,
settled there as king and did not return.
Thus, the people grieved and longed for them,
and six out of every ten households desired to rebel.
They also sent Wèi Tuó to cross the Five Ridges and attack Bǎiyuè.
Wèi Tuó, knowing the exhaustion of the central plains,
settled there as king and did not return,
sending a memorial to the emperor,
requesting thirty thousand unmarried women
to mend clothes for the soldiers.
The Qin emperor granted fifteen thousand.
Thus, the people's hearts turned away and the state crumbled,
with seven out of every ten households desiring to rebel.
A guest said to Emperor Gāo:
'The time is ripe.'
Emperor Gāo replied:
'Wait,
a sage shall arise in the southeast.'
Within a year,
Chén Shèng and Wú Guǎng rose up.
Emperor Gāo started from Fēng and Pèi,
and with one call, countless across the land responded without being summoned.
This is what is called seizing the opportunity,
acting upon the downfall of Qin.
The people wished for it,
as a drought longs for rain,
so he rose from the ranks to become the Son of Heaven,
his achievements surpassing those of the Three Sovereigns,
his virtue passed down endlessly.
Now, you see how easily Emperor Gāo won the empire,
but have you not observed the recent states of Wú and Chǔ?
The King of Wú was granted the title of Liú family's sacrificial elder,
yet he ceased attending court,
ruled over four commanderies,
with a territory spanning thousands of miles,
minted coins from melted copper within,
boiled seawater for salt in the east,
used wood from Jiānglíng to build ships in the south,
one ship's load equivalent to dozens of carts in the central plains,
his state rich and people numerous.
He used pearls, jade, gold, and silk to bribe nobles, imperial clansmen, and ministers,
only the Dòu family refused.
Plans set and strategies complete,
he raised an army and marched west.
Defeated at Dàliáng,
routed at Húfù,
he fled east,
reaching Dāntú,
where the Yuè people captured him,
he died and his lineage ended,
becoming a laughingstock of the world.
Why did the masses of Wú and Yuè fail to succeed?
Truly, they defied the Way of Heaven and misjudged the times.
Now, your troops are not even a tenth of Wú and Chǔ's,
and the world is ten thousand times more peaceful than in Qin's time.
I urge you to follow my plan.
If you do not,
I foresee your endeavor failing and your words leaking beforehand.
I have heard that Wēizǐ mourned upon passing his old state,
thus composing the 'Song of the Wheat Sprouts,'
grieving that King Zhòu did not heed Prince Bǐgān's advice.
Hence, *Mencius* says:
'Zhòu, honored as the Son of Heaven,
in death was not even equal to a commoner.'
This is because Zhòu had long cut himself off from the world,
not that the world abandoned him only upon his death.
Now, I secretly grieve that you, Great King, abandoning your lordship of a thousand chariots,
will surely be granted a death warrant,
preceding your ministers,
dying in the eastern palace."
Thereupon, his spirit filled with unresolved resentment,
tears brimming in his eyes and streaming down,
he rose,
descended the steps, and left.
The king had an illegitimate son named Bùhài,
who was the eldest,
but the king did not love him,
and neither the king, the queen,
nor the crown prince regarded him as a son or brother.
Bùhài had a son named Jiàn,
who was talented and spirited,
and often resented that the crown prince did not acknowledge his father;
he also complained that while other feudal lords could enfeoff their sons and brothers as marquises,
the King of Huáinán had only two sons,
one being the crown prince,
yet Jiàn's father alone was not made a marquis.
Jiàn secretly formed connections,
intending to denounce and ruin the crown prince,
so that his father could replace him.
The crown prince learned of this,
and repeatedly had Jiàn arrested, imprisoned, and flogged.
Jiàn knew all about the crown prince's plot to kill the Han Commandant of Justice,
so he had his friend Zhuāng Zhǐ of Shòuchūn submit a memorial to the Son of Heaven in the sixth year of Yuánshuò, stating:
"Poison is bitter to the mouth but good for the illness,
loyal advice grates on the ears but benefits conduct.
Now Jiàn, grandson of the King of Huáinán,
is highly capable,
yet the queen of Huáinán, Tú,
and her son, Crown Prince Qiān, often persecute and harm Jiàn.
Jiàn's father, Bùhài, is innocent,
yet they arbitrarily arrest and imprison him repeatedly,
intending to kill him.
Now Jiàn is alive,
and can be summoned for questioning,
as he knows all the secret affairs of Huáinán."
When the memorial was received,
the emperor referred the matter to the Commandant of Justice,
who delegated it to Hénán to investigate.
At that time, Shěn Qīng, grandson of the former Marquis of Pìyáng, was a friend of Chancellor Gōngsūn Hóng,
and resented that King Lì of Huáinán had killed his grandfather,
so he deeply implicated Huáinán in his discussions with Hóng,
leading Hóng to suspect that Huáinán had rebellious plans,
and he rigorously pursued the investigation.
When Hénán interrogated Jiàn,
his testimony implicated the Crown Prince of Huáinán and his associates.
The King of Huáinán grew worried,
and contemplated revolt,
so he asked Wǔ Bèi:
"Is the Hàn court orderly or chaotic?"
Wǔ Bèi replied:
"The empire is orderly."
The king was displeased,
and said to Wǔ Bèi:
"Why do you say the empire is orderly?"
Bèi replied:
"I have privately observed the governance of the court,
the righteousness between ruler and minister,
the affection between father and son,
the distinction between husband and wife,
and the order between elder and younger—
all are properly maintained.
The emperor's actions follow the ancient way,
and customs and laws are without deficiency.
Heavily laden wealthy merchants
travel throughout the empire,
with no roads impassable,
so the ways of trade flourish.
Nányuè submits respectfully,
the Qiāng and Bó tribes bring tribute,
Dōng'ōu has surrendered,
the borders are expanded,
Shuòfāng is opened up,
the Xiōngnú have broken wings and injured flanks,
left without support and unable to recover.
Though it may not match the peace of ancient times,
it is still an orderly age."
The king grew angry,
and Bèi apologized for his capital offense.
The king then said to Bèi:
"If Shāndōng raises troops,
Hàn will surely send the Grand General to lead and control Shāndōng.
What kind of man do you think the Grand General is?"
Bèi replied:
"My friend Huáng Yì
followed the Grand General in attacking the Xiōngnú,
and upon returning, told me:
'The Grand General treats officials with courtesy,
and shows kindness to the soldiers,
so all are willing to serve him.
His cavalry charge up and down hills as if flying,
and his abilities surpass others.'
I believe that with such talent,
and his experience in repeatedly leading troops,
he would be hard to oppose.
Moreover, when the receptionist Cáo Liáng returned from Cháng'ān,
he said the Grand General's commands are clear,
he is brave in facing the enemy,
and always leads his soldiers from the front.
When the army rests,
and a well is dug but not yet flowing,
he waits until all soldiers have water
before he dares to drink.
When the army withdraws,
after all soldiers have crossed the river,
he then crosses.
The gold and silk bestowed by the Grand Empress Dowager
he gives entirely to his officers.
Even famed generals of old could not surpass him."
The king fell silent.
When the King of Huáinán saw that Jiàn had been summoned for trial,
he feared his state's secret affairs would be exposed,
and intended to revolt.
Wǔ Bèi again considered it difficult,
so the king asked Bèi once more:
"Sir, do you think Wú's raising troops was right or wrong?"
Bèi replied:
"I consider it wrong.
The King of Wú was extremely wealthy and noble,
yet his actions were improper,
leading to his death at Dāntú,
where his head and feet were separated,
and none of his descendants survived.
I heard the King of Wú deeply regretted it.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this
and not repeat the King of Wú's regrets."
The king said:
"A real man dies for his word.
Moreover, what did Wú know about rebellion?
Over forty Hàn generals passed through Chénggāo in a single day.
Now I'll order Lóu Huǎn first to secure the pass at Chénggāo,
Zhōu Bèi to lead Yǐngchuān troops to block the roads at Huányuán
and Yīquē,
and Chén Dìng to raise Nányáng troops to guard Wǔguān.
The governor of Hénán only has Luòyáng left,
which is hardly a worry.
However, to the north there are also Línjìn Pass,
Hédōng,
Shàngdǎng, along with Hénèi
and the state of Zhào.
People say
'Block the pass at Chénggāo,
and the world is cut off.'
Holding the strategic Sānchuān,
summoning troops from east of the mountains,
with such actions,
what do you think, sir?"
Bèi said:
"I see the disaster,
not the fortune."
The king said:
"Zuǒ Wú,
Zhào Xián,
and Zhū Jiāorú all believe there will be fortune,
with nine out of ten chances of success.
Only you, sir, see disaster and no fortune.
Why is that?"
Bèi said:
"Those among Your Majesty's ministers and close confidants who could command the masses
have all been previously imprisoned by imperial decree,
leaving none usable."
The king said:
"Chén Shèng
and Wú Guǎng had not even a pinpoint of land,
just a gathering of a thousand men,
rose from the great marshes,
raised their arms and shouted, and the world responded,
marching west to Xì with a force of 1.2 million.
Now although my state is small,
we can muster over a hundred thousand capable soldiers,
not just conscripts
with crude weapons.
How can you say there's disaster and no fortune?"
Bèi said:
"In the past, Qín was without virtue,
brutalizing the world.
It raised carriages for ten thousand chariots,
built the Ēpáng Palace,
collected more than half the people's produce in taxes,
conscripted the poor for garrison duty,
so fathers could not protect their sons,
nor brothers help each other.
Harsh governance and severe punishments
made the world suffer as if scorched,
the people stretching their necks to look,
straining their ears to listen,
wailing to heaven,
beating their breasts and resenting the ruler.
Thus when Chén Shèng shouted,
the world responded.
Now His Majesty governs the world,
unifying all within the seas,
broadly loving the masses,
spreading virtue and bestowing favors.
Though his words may not be spoken,
his voice is swift as thunder;
though his orders may not be issued,
his influence spreads like divine power.
What he holds in his heart
moves with authority for ten thousand miles.
The lower responding to the upper
is like shadow following form or echo following sound.
Moreover, the Grand General's ability is not inferior to Zhāng Hán's
or Yáng Xióng's.
For Your Majesty to compare with Chén Shèng
and Wú Guǎng,
I consider it an overestimation."
The king said:
"If it's as you say,
can we not still take a chance?"
Bèi said:
"I have a foolish plan."
The king said:
"What is it?"
Bèi said:
"Currently, the feudal lords have no rebellious thoughts,
and the common people bear no resentment.
The Shuòfāng commandery has vast fields and lands,
with fine water and grass,
but the migrants are insufficient to populate it.
My foolish plan is
to forge a request from the Chancellor and Imperial Censor,
relocating the bold and chivalrous from the commanderies and states, along with those sentenced to shaving or worse,
pardoning their crimes by decree,
and those with wealth over five hundred thousand,
moving their families to Shuòfāng commandery,
increasing the armored troops,
and hastening their assembly date.
Also, forge documents from the Left and Right Chief Commandants of Works, the Shanglin Imperial Park, and the Capital Office prisons,
to arrest the heirs and favored ministers of the feudal lords.
This way, the people will resent,
and the feudal lords will fear.
Then immediately send persuasive strategists to explain to them;
perhaps we might have a one in ten chance?"
The king said:
"This is acceptable.
Even so,
I don't think it will come to that."
Thereupon, the king ordered palace slaves to enter the palace
to make the emperor's seal,
and seals for the Chancellor,
Imperial Censor,
Grand General,
military officers,
officials of fully two thousand piculs,
Capital Office chiefs,
and their assistants,
as well as for the governors
and commandants of nearby commanderies,
Hàn envoy insignia and legal caps,
intending to follow Wǔ Bèi's plan.
He sent men pretending to be criminals heading west
to serve the Grand General
and Chancellor;
once troops were raised,
he would have someone assassinate Grand General Wèi Qīng,
and persuade the Chancellor to submit,
as easily as lifting a covering.
The king wanted to mobilize the troops within his state,
but feared his Chancellor
and officials of two thousand piculs would not comply.
So the king plotted with Wǔ Bèi
to first kill the Chancellor
and the two thousand picul officials;
by setting a false fire in the palace,
when the Chancellor and two thousand picul officials came to rescue,
they would be killed upon arrival.
Before this plan was finalized,
he also considered having men dressed as arrest-officers' uniforms,
holding emergency dispatches,
come from the east,
shouting,
"The Nányuè troops have entered our borders,"
hoping to use this as a pretext to raise troops.
So he sent people to Lújiāng
and Kuàijī to act as arrest-officers,
but they had not yet set out.
The king asked Wǔ Bèi:
"If I raise troops heading west,
surely some feudal lords will respond to me.
But if none do,
what then?"
Bèi said:
"Secure Héngshān to the south to attack Lújiāng,
seize the boats at Xúnyáng,
hold the city of Xiàzhǐ,
control the bulrushes of Jiǔjiāng,
block the pass at Yùzhāng,
station crossbowmen by the river for defense,
to prevent Nánjùn from advancing south.
To the east, secure Jiāngdū
and Kuàijī,
ally with strong Yuè in the south,
and stand firm between the Jiāng and Huái.
Then we might still prolong our survival for some time."
The king said:
"Good,
nothing surpasses this.
In urgency, we can flee to Yuè."
Thereupon, the Commandant of Justice reported that the statements of Wángsūn Jiàn implicated Liú Ān, Crown Prince of Huáinán.
The Emperor dispatched a Supervisor of the Commandant of Justice to Huáinán, also appointing him as Commandant of Huáinán,
to arrest the Crown Prince.
When he arrived in Huáinán,
the King of Huáinán heard of this,
and conspired with the Crown Prince to summon the Chancellor
and the two-thousand-bushel officials,
intending to kill them and raise troops.
They summoned the Chancellor;
the Chancellor arrived;
the Interior Secretary excused himself on grounds of having to go out.
The Commandant said:
"Your servant has received an imperial edict as envoy,
and cannot see the King."
The King considered that killing the Chancellor alone, with the Interior Secretary and Commandant not coming,
would be pointless,
and so dismissed the Chancellor.
The King hesitated,
unable to decide on a plan.
The Crown Prince reflected that the crime he was accused of was plotting to assassinate the Han Commandant,
and those with whom he had conspired were already dead,
so he thought the evidence had ended,
and thus said to the King:
"All the ministers who could be used have previously been imprisoned,
now there is no one adequate to undertake the uprising with.
If Your Majesty acts at an inopportune time,
I fear it will be without success;
I wish to submit to arrest."
The King, also privately wishing to desist,
immediately consented to the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince then cut his own throat,
but did not die.
Wǔ Bèi went voluntarily to the officials,
and thereupon informed on the plot to rebel with the King of Huáinán,
the traces of the rebellion being fully as described.
The officials thereupon arrested the Crown Prince
and the Queen,
surrounded the King's palace,
and exhaustively sought and arrested all the guests within the state who had conspired with the King to rebel,
searching out and obtaining the instruments of rebellion to report to the Emperor.
The Emperor referred the case to the ministers for judgment;
those implicated and involved with the King of Huáinán in the rebellion numbered several thousand, including marquises, two-thousand-bushel officials, and local heroes,
all of whom were executed according to the severity of their crimes.
Liú Cì, King of Héngshān,
was the younger brother of the King of Huáinán,
and deserved to be implicated and arrested;
the relevant officials requested the arrest of the King of Héngshān.
The Son of Heaven said:
"The feudal lords should each regard their own state as fundamental,
and should not be implicated for each other.
Deliberate together with the other feudal kings, marquises, and the Chancellor."
Liú Péngzǔ, King of Zhào,
Marquis Chén Ràng, and forty-one others deliberated,
all saying:
"Liú Ān of Huáinán is greatly treasonable and unprincipled,
his plot to rebel is clear,
and he deserves execution."
Liú Duān, King of Jiāoxī, deliberated saying:
"Liú Ān of Huáinán abandoned the law and practiced evil,
harboring a deceitful and false heart,
to bring chaos to all under heaven,
misleading the common people,
betraying the ancestral temple,
and recklessly spreading evil words.
The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
'A minister shall not plot rebellion;
if he plots rebellion, he shall be executed.'
Ān's crime is heavier than plotting rebellion,
the form of his rebellion is already determined.
What I, Duān, have seen of his writings, tallies, seals, maps, and other evidence of rebellion and unprincipled acts is clear,
he is greatly treasonable and unprincipled,
and deserves to suffer its punishment.
As for the state officials of two hundred bushels and above and their equivalents,
and the imperial clansmen and close favored ministers not covered by the law,
who failed to admonish him,
they should all be dismissed from office, stripped of their ranks, and made common soldiers,
and not be permitted to serve as officials.
Those who are not officials
should each redeem their death penalty with two catties and eight taels of gold.
Thereby to manifest the crime of your servant Ān,
and make the way of ministers clear to all under heaven,
so that none dare again have thoughts of evil and treachery."
The Chancellor Gōngsūn Hóng,
the Commandant of Justice Zhāng Tāng, and others reported this;
the Son of Heaven sent the Director of the Imperial Clan with tally and scepter to try the King.
Before he arrived,
Liú Ān, King of Huáinán, cut his own throat and died.
Queen Tú,
Crown Prince Qiān, and all those who had conspired to rebel were exterminated along with their families.
The Son of Heaven, because Wǔ Bèi's elegant words often cited the virtues of Hàn,
wished not to execute him.
The Commandant of Justice Zhāng Tāng said:
"Bèi was the first to plan rebellion for the King;
Bèi's crime does not permit pardon."
Thereupon, Bèi was executed.
The state was abolished and became the Jiǔjiāng Commandery.
Liú Cì, King of Héngshān,
had three children with Queen Chéng Shū:
the eldest son, Liú Shuǎng, was Crown Prince,
the second son was Liú Xiào,
and the second daughter was Liú Wúcǎi.
Furthermore, his concubine Xú Lái bore him four children,
and the Beauty Jué Jī bore him two children.
The King of Héngshān
and the King of Huáinán, being brothers, held each other to account in matters of etiquette,
and were estranged and unable to get along.
When the King of Héngshān heard that the King of Huáinán was making preparations for rebellion,
he also secretly gathered guests to respond to this,
fearing he would be annexed by him.
In the sixth year of Yuánguāng,
the King of Héngshān came to court,
and his Receptionist Wèi Qìng, who possessed magical arts,
wished to submit a memorial to serve the Son of Heaven.
The King was angered,
and therefore impeached Qìng for a capital crime,
forcibly torturing him until he confessed.
The Interior Secretary of Héngshān considered this unjust,
and rejected the case.
The King sent someone to submit a memorial accusing the Interior Secretary;
the Interior Secretary was tried,
and stated that the King was in the wrong.
The King also repeatedly encroached upon and seized people's fields,
destroying people's graves to make fields.
The relevant officials requested to arrest and try the King of Héngshān.
The Son of Heaven did not permit it,
but established officials of two hundred bushels and above for him.
The King of Héngshān, because of this, became resentful,
and conspired with Xī Cí
and Zhāng Guǎngchāng,
seeking those skilled in military strategy and astrology,
day and night counseling the King in secret plans for rebellion.
When Queen Chéng Shū died,
Xú Lái was established as queen.
Jué Jī was also favored.
The two women were jealous of each other,
so Jué Jī slandered Queen Xú Lái to the crown prince, saying:
"Xú Lái had her maids use gu poison to kill the crown prince's mother."
The crown prince resented Xú Lái in his heart.
When Xú Lái's elder brother came to Héngshān,
the crown prince drank with him,
and wounded the queen's brother with a blade.
The queen bore a grudge and was angry,
frequently slandering the crown prince to the king.
The crown prince's younger sister Wú Cǎi,
after being married and then abandoned, returned home,
committed adultery with a slave,
and also had illicit relations with a guest.
The crown prince repeatedly reproved Wú Cǎi,
making Wú Cǎi angry,
and she ceased communication with the crown prince.
When the queen heard of this,
she immediately treated Wú Cǎi well.
Wú Cǎi and her second elder brother Xiào had lost their mother when young,
so they attached themselves to the queen,
who feigned affection for them through schemes,
joining them in slandering the crown prince.
The king therefore frequently had the crown prince whipped.
In the fourth year of Yuánshuò,
someone injured the queen's foster mother,
and the king suspected the crown prince had sent someone to harm her,
so he whipped the crown prince.
Later, when the king fell ill,
the crown prince often claimed to be sick and did not attend to him.
Xiào, the queen,
and Wú Cǎi maligned the crown prince:
"The crown prince is not actually ill;
he says he is sick,
yet he has a pleased expression."
The king was greatly angered,
and wanted to depose the crown prince,
establishing his brother Xiào in his place.
The queen, knowing the king was determined to depose the crown prince,
also wanted to depose Xiào as well.
The queen had an attendant
who was skilled in dancing,
and the king favored her.
The queen wanted to have the attendant engage in illicit relations with Xiào to tarnish him,
intending to depose both brothers and establish her own son Guǎng as crown prince.
When Crown Prince Shuǎng learned of this,
he thought that the queen's constant slandering of him would never end,
so he wanted to have illicit relations with her to silence her.
When the queen was drinking,
the crown prince came forward to offer a toast,
then pressed against the queen's thigh,
requesting to lie with her.
The queen was furious,
and reported this to the king.
The king then summoned him,
intending to bind and whip him.
The crown prince, knowing the king often wanted to depose him and establish his brother Xiào,
said to the king:
"Xiào has committed adultery with Your Majesty's attendants,
Wú Cǎi has committed adultery with slaves;
may Your Majesty eat heartily,
and I request to submit a memorial to the emperor."
He then turned away from the king and left.
The king sent people to stop him,
but they could not prevent him,
so he personally drove to pursue and arrest the crown prince.
The crown prince wildly spoke malicious words,
and the king had him shackled and confined in the palace.
Xiào grew increasingly close and favored.
The king admired Xiào's talents and abilities,
so he bestowed upon him the king's seal,
titled him General,
ordered him to reside in an external residence,
provided him with ample money,
and had him recruit guests.
The guests who came
subtly learned of Huáinán and
Héngshān's rebellious plans,
and day and night casually encouraged them.
The king then had Xiào's guests Jiù Hè from Jiāngdū
and Chén Xǐ manufacture armored vehicles and arrowheads,
engraved the imperial seal,
and seals for generals, ministers, and military officers.
The king sought strong men like Zhōu Qiū day and night,
frequently citing the plans from the time of the Wú-Chǔ rebellion,
to make arrangements.
The King of Héngshān did not dare to emulate Huáinán in seeking the Son of Heaven's position,
but feared that Huáinán would rise up and annex his state,
thinking that once Huáinán had moved west,
he would send troops to secure the region between the Jiāng and Huái Rivers and possess it,
hoping for such an outcome.
In the autumn of the fifth year of Yuánshuò,
the King of Héngshān was due to attend court,
and passed by Huáinán,
where the King of Huáinán spoke as brothers with him,
resolving previous estrangements,
and coordinating preparations for rebellion.
The King of Héngshān then submitted a memorial pleading illness,
and the emperor sent a letter excusing him from attending court.
In the sixth year of Yuánshuò,
the King of Héngshān sent someone to submit a memorial requesting the deposition of Crown Prince Shuǎng,
and the establishment of Xiào as crown prince.
When Shuǎng heard of this,
he immediately had his friend Bái Yíng go to Cháng'ān to submit a memorial,
stating that Xiào had manufactured armored vehicles and arrowheads,
and had committed adultery with the king's attendants,
hoping thereby to ruin Xiào.
When Bái Yíng reached Cháng'ān,
before he could submit the memorial,
the authorities arrested Bái Yíng,
and detained him in connection with the Huáinán affair.
When the king heard that Shuǎng had sent Bái Yíng to submit a memorial,
he feared it would reveal the state's secrets,
so he submitted a memorial counter-accusing Crown Prince Shuǎng of heinous crimes deserving execution in the marketplace.
The matter was referred to Pèi Commandery for handling.
In the winter of the first year of Yuánshòu,
the concerned officials and ministers went to Pèi Commandery to search for and arrest those involved in the Huáinán rebellion but had not yet captured them,
and they found Chén Xǐ in the home of the King of Héngshān's son Xiào.
The officials impeached Xiào for harboring Chén Xǐ.
Xiào believed that Chén Xǐ had frequently been involved in the king's rebellious plots,
and feared he would expose them.
Having heard that the law exonerated those who confessed first,
and suspecting that the crown prince had sent Bái Yíng to submit a memorial exposing the affair,
he immediately confessed first,
denouncing those involved in the rebellion, Jiù Hè,
Chén Xǐ, and others.
The Commandant of Justice investigated and verified the facts,
and the ministers requested the arrest of the King of Héngshān for trial.
The Son of Heaven said:
"Do not arrest him."
He sent the Commandant of the Palace An
and the Grand Herald Xī to question the king immediately,
and the king fully disclosed the true circumstances.
The officials all surrounded and guarded the king's palace.
When the Commandant of the Palace and the Grand Herald returned,
they reported what they had learned,
and the ministers requested to send the Director of the Imperial Clan,
the Grand Herald, and Pèi Commandery to jointly try the king.
When the king heard of this,
he immediately committed suicide by cutting his throat.
Xiào, for having confessed to rebellion first,
was exempted from that crime;
but for committing adultery with the king's attendant maid,
he was executed in the marketplace.
Queen Xú Lái was also convicted of using gu poison to kill the former queen Chéng Shū,
and Crown Prince Shuǎng was convicted based on the king's accusation of unfilial conduct,
and both were executed in the marketplace.
All those who conspired in rebellion with the King of Héngshān were executed along with their families.
The state was abolished and became Héngshān Commandery.
The Grand Historian remarks:
What the _Book of Songs_ calls
"Resisting the Róng and Dí,
punishing Jīng and Shū"
is indeed true.
Huáinán and
Héngshān, closely related as flesh and bone,
with territories spanning a thousand lǐ,
enfeoffed as feudal lords,
did not strive to fulfill the duties of vassals in supporting the Son of Heaven,
but instead engaged solely in wicked and deceitful schemes,
plotting rebellion,
leading to the repeated loss of their states by both father and son,
neither ending their lives naturally,
becoming laughingstocks of the world.
This was not solely the fault of the kings,
but also due to their decadent customs,
and the influence of their ministers that led to this.
For the people of Jīngchǔ are impetuous, brave, and rash,
prone to rebellion,
as has been recorded since ancient times.
The Grand Historian remarks:
Laws and decrees are meant to guide the people,
and punishments are meant to prohibit wickedness.
When civil and military virtues are not complete,
and good people fearfully cultivate themselves,
it is because the officials have not been corrupt.
Fulfilling duties and following principles
can also achieve good governance;
why must there be stern authority?
Sūn Shū'áo was
a reclusive scholar of Chǔ.
The minister Yú Qiū recommended him to King Zhuāng of Chǔ to take his own place.
After three months as the chancellor of Chǔ,
he implemented education and guided the people,
leading to harmony between the upper and lower classes,
flourishing and beautiful customs,
lenient governance that still prevented wrongdoing,
officials free from corruption and evil,
and no occurrence of thieves or bandits.
In autumn and winter, he encouraged the people to gather from the mountains,
and in spring and summer, from the waters,
each finding what was convenient for them,
so that the people all enjoyed their lives.
King Zhuāng thought the currency was too light,
so he changed it from small to large,
causing inconvenience to the common people,
who all abandoned their occupations.
The market supervisor reported to the chancellor, saying:
"The market is in chaos,
the people have no peace in their places,
and the order of business is unstable."
The chancellor said:
"How long has this been going on?"
The market supervisor said:
"About three months."
The chancellor said:
"Enough,
I will now order it to be restored."
Five days later,
at court, the chancellor said to the king:
"Previously, the currency was changed,
thinking it was too light.
Now the market supervisor has come to report
'the market is in chaos,
the people have no peace in their places,
and the order of business is unstable.'
I request to order it restored as before."
The king agreed,
and within three days of the order, the market returned to normal.
The custom in Chǔ was to favor low carriages,
but the king thought low carriages were not suitable for horses,
and wanted to issue an order to make them higher.
The chancellor said:
"If orders are issued frequently,
the people will not know what to follow,
which is not acceptable.
If the king insists on raising the carriages,
I request to instruct the neighborhoods to raise their thresholds.
Those who ride carriages are all gentlemen,
and gentlemen cannot frequently get down from their carriages."
The king agreed.
After half a year,
the people all raised their carriages on their own.
This is an example of people following his influence without being taught,
with those nearby observing and imitating him,
and those far away looking from all directions and emulating him.
Thus, he became chancellor three times without joy,
knowing his talent naturally earned it;
he left the chancellorship three times without regret,
knowing it was not his fault.
Zǐ Chǎn was
one of the ranked senior officials of Zhèng.
During the time of King Zhāo of Zhèng,
he appointed his favorite Xú Zhì as chancellor,
leading to chaos in the state,
lack of closeness between the upper and lower classes,
and discord between fathers and sons.
Dàgōng Zǐqī advised the ruler,
to appoint Zǐ Chǎn as chancellor.
After one year as chancellor,
young men no longer engaged in frivolous play,
the elderly no longer carried heavy loads,
and children did not plow the fields.
In the second year,
the market had no inflated prices.
In the third year,
doors were not locked at night,
and lost items were not picked up on the roads.
In the fourth year,
farming tools were not returned (as they were shared).
In the fifth year,
scholars had no records of minor offenses,
and mourning periods were observed without orders.
He governed Zhèng for twenty-six years until his death,
whereupon the able-bodied wailed,
the elderly cried like children,
saying:
"Zǐ Chǎn has left us by dying!
To whom shall the people turn now?"
Gōngyí Xiū was
an erudite scholar of Lǔ.
Due to his high rank, he became the chancellor of Lǔ.
He upheld the law and followed principles,
making no changes,
yet all officials rectified themselves.
He ensured that those who received official salaries did not compete for profit with the common people,
and those with great responsibilities did not take small gains.
A guest once presented the chancellor with fish,
but the chancellor did not accept it.
The guest replied:
"I heard you are fond of fish,
so I give you fish;
why do you not accept it?"
The chancellor said:
"Because I am fond of fish,
I do not accept it.
Now, as chancellor,
I can afford my own fish;
if I accept fish and am dismissed,
who will give me fish then?
Therefore, I do not accept it."
He ate vegetables and found them delicious,
so he uprooted the mustard greens in his garden and discarded them.
Seeing that his household wove excellent cloth,
he swiftly dismissed the weaving women from his home,
burned their looms,
saying
"How can farmers and working women sell their goods if we do this?"
Shí Shē was
the chancellor of King Zhāo of Chǔ.
He was firm, upright, honest, and just,
showing no favoritism or avoidance.
While touring the county,
he encountered a murderer on the road,
and the chancellor pursued him,
only to find it was his own father.
He released his father and returned to imprison himself.
He sent someone to report to the king, saying:
"The murderer
is my father.
To establish governance by punishing my father
would be unfilial;
to abandon the law and release a criminal
would be disloyal;
my crime deserves death."
The king said:
"You pursued but did not catch him;
you should not bear the punishment;
you may resume your duties."
Shí Shē said:
"Not showing favor to my father
makes me an unfilial son;
not upholding the king's law
makes me a disloyal minister.
If the king pardons my crime,
it is his grace;
but to accept execution and die
is my duty."
Thus, he did not accept the order,
and cut his own throat to die.
Lǐ Lí was
the chief judge of Duke Wén of Jìn.
He mistakenly condemned an innocent person to death,
and imprisoned himself, deserving death.
Duke Wén said:
"Officials have high and low ranks,
punishments have light and heavy degrees.
The subordinate official made the error,
it is not your crime."
Lǐ Lí said:
"I hold the highest position among officials,
and did not yield my place to others;
I receive the highest salary,
and do not share the profits with subordinates.
Now, I have mistakenly condemned an innocent to death,
yet shift the blame to a subordinate official—
I have never heard of such a thing."
He declined the order.
Duke Wén said:
"If you consider yourself guilty,
does that mean I am also guilty?"
Lǐ Lí said:
"The judge has laws:
if one errs in punishment, one should be punished;
if one errs in causing death, one should die.
You, my lord, thought I could discern subtleties and decide doubtful cases,
so you made me the judge.
Now I have mistakenly condemned an innocent to death,
and my crime deserves death."
Thus, he did not accept the order,
and fell on his sword to die.
At that time,
the Hàn dynasty was campaigning against the Xiōngnú,
and summoning and pacifying the four barbarian tribes.
Jí Àn focused on minimizing affairs,
taking advantage of the emperor's leisure,
often advocating for peace and kinship with the Hú people,
and against raising troops.
The emperor was inclined towards Confucian arts,
and honored Gōngsūn Hóng.
As matters increased,
officials and people became cunning and manipulative.
The emperor differentiated laws and regulations,
and Zhāng Tāng and others frequently submitted judgments on legal cases to gain favor.
But Jí Àn often criticized the Confucians,
confronting Gōngsūn Hóng and others to their faces, accusing them of harboring deceit and adorning wisdom to flatter the ruler for acceptance,
while the legal clerks specialized in deep and cunning condemnations,
trapping people in crimes,
preventing them from returning to the truth,
and considering victory as merit.
The emperor increasingly valued Gōngsūn Hóng and
Zhāng Tāng, and Gōngsūn Hóng and
Zhāng Tāng deeply resented Jí Àn,
even the Son of Heaven was also displeased,
and wished to find a reason to execute him.
Gōngsūn Hóng, as chancellor,
then said to the emperor:
"The area under the Right Inner Secretary's jurisdiction has many nobles and imperial clansmen,
making it difficult to govern,
and only a long-respected minister can handle it;
I request to transfer Jí Àn to be the Right Inner Secretary."
He served as Right Inner Secretary for several years,
and official affairs were not neglected.
Grand General Wèi Qīng, having become more honored,
with his elder sister as empress,
yet Jí Àn treated him with equal courtesy.
Someone advised Jí Àn, saying:
"Since the Son of Heaven wishes all ministers to defer to the Grand General,
and the Grand General's respect and honor increase,
you must not fail to bow."
Jí Àn said:
"If the Grand General has a guest who only bows with clasped hands,
wouldn't that instead enhance his respect?"
The Grand General heard this,
and considered Jí Àn even more worthy,
frequently consulting him on state and court doubts,
treating Jí Àn better than ever before.
When the King of Huáinán plotted rebellion,
he feared Jí Àn,
saying:
"He is fond of straightforward remonstrance,
upholds integrity and dies for righteousness,
difficult to mislead with falsehoods.
As for persuading Chancellor Gōngsūn Hóng,
it is like removing a blindfold or shaking off dead leaves."
The Son of Heaven, having repeatedly campaigned against the Xiōngnú with success,
increasingly disregarded Jí Àn's words.
Initially, Jí Àn ranked among the Nine Ministers,
while Gōngsūn Hóng and
Zhāng Tāng were minor officials.
When Gōngsūn Hóng and
Zhāng Tāng gradually rose in rank,
reaching the same position as Jí Àn,
Jí Àn again criticized and disparaged Gōngsūn Hóng and
Zhāng Tāng and others.
Later, Gōngsūn Hóng rose to chancellor,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis;
Zhāng Tāng rose to Imperial Secretary;
thus, some who had been clerks under Jí Àn were now his peers,
or even more honored and employed than he.
Jí Àn was narrow-minded,
and could not help feeling somewhat resentful.
Seeing the emperor,
he said in front of him:
"Your Majesty uses your ministers like piling firewood,
where the later ones come to be on top."
The emperor fell silent.
After a while, when Jí Àn had withdrawn,
the emperor said:
"Indeed, one cannot be without learning;
observe how Jí Àn's words grow increasingly excessive."
Not long after,
the Xiōngnú Húnyé King led his followers to surrender,
and Hàn dispatched twenty thousand chariots.
The state treasury had no money,
so they borrowed horses from the people.
Some people hid their horses,
and the horses were not fully gathered.
The emperor was angry,
and intended to execute the Governor of Cháng'ān.
Jí Àn said:
"The Governor of Cháng'ān is not at fault;
only if you execute Jí Àn,
will the people be willing to provide horses.
Moreover, the Xiōngnú have betrayed their lord to surrender to Hàn;
Hàn should gradually transport them through the counties in sequence;
why must we disturb the whole empire,
exhaust and impoverish the Central States to serve barbarian people?"
The emperor fell silent.
When Húnyé arrived,
merchants who traded with them
faced execution, numbering over five hundred people.
Jí Àn requested a private audience,
and met the emperor at the High Gate,
saying:
"The Xiōngnú attacked our frontier fortresses,
severed peace and kinship,
and the Central States raised troops to punish them,
with countless dead and wounded,
and expenses amounting to hundreds of millions.
I foolishly thought that when Your Majesty captured Hú people,
you would make them all slaves to be given to families of those who died in army service;
the plunder seized,
would be given to them,
to apologize for the empire's suffering,
and to satisfy the people's hearts.
Now, even if that cannot be done,
Húnyé leading tens of thousands to surrender,
we empty the treasury for rewards,
dispatch good people to serve and support them,
as if tending to spoiled children.
How would ignorant people know that trading goods in Cháng'ān would lead to clerks prosecuting them for illegally exporting wealth to the border?"
Your Majesty, even if unable to use Xiōngnú resources to apologize to the empire,
how can you use trivial laws to kill over five hundred ignorant people?
This is what is called
'protecting the leaves while harming the branches,'
and I secretly believe Your Majesty should not adopt this."
The emperor fell silent,
did not consent,
and said:
"It has been long since I heard Jí Àn's words,
