and now he speaks recklessly again."
Several months later,
Jí Àn was implicated in a minor legal offense,
and was pardoned but dismissed from office.
Thereupon, Jí Àn retired to the countryside.
The Grand Historian remarks:
With the virtue of such men as Jí and
Zhèng,
when they had power, their guests outnumbered themselves tenfold;
when they lost it, this was not so,
how much more so for ordinary people!
There is a saying from Zhái Gōng of Xiàguī:
When Zhái Gōng first became Commandant of Justice,
guests filled his gate;
when he was dismissed,
a sparrow trap could be set outside his door.
When Zhái Gōng was restored as Commandant of Justice,
and guests wished to return,
he wrote largely on his gate:
"In life and death,
one knows true friendship.
In poverty and wealth,
one knows the state of friendship.
In honor and disgrace,
friendship is revealed."
The same can be said of Jí and Zhèng—
how lamentable!
The Grand Historian remarks:
When I read the decrees on merit,
and come to the ways of broadly encouraging the path of academic officials,
I have never failed to put down the scroll and sigh.
I say: Alas!
When the Zhōu house declined, the "Guān Jū" was composed;
with the weakness of Yōu and Lì, rites and music decayed;
the feudal lords acted wantonly,
and governance came from the powerful states.
Thus, Confucius lamented the abandonment of the kingly way and the rise of corrupt paths,
so he compiled and arranged the "Book of Songs" and "Book of Documents",
and revived rites and music.
Going to Qí, he heard the "Sháo" music,
and for three months did not notice the taste of meat.
Returning from Wèi to Lǔ,
only then were the music corrected,
and the "Yǎ" and "Sòng" each found their proper place.
The world was so turbid that none could employ him,
thus Confucius sought audience with over seventy lords without meeting acceptance,
saying,
"If anyone would use me,
in a year it would be accomplished."
When a unicorn was captured in the western hunt,
he said,
"My way is exhausted."
Therefore, based on the historical records, he composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals",
to serve as the kingly law,
with subtle language and broad intent,
which many later scholars have recorded.
After Confucius's death,
his seventy disciples scattered and traveled among the feudal lords,
the greater among them becoming tutors, ministers, or chancellors,
the lesser teaching and befriending officials and scholars,
some hiding and not appearing.
Thus, Zǐlù resided in Wèi,
Zǐzhāng in Chén,
Dàntái Zǐyǔ in Chǔ,
Zǐxià in Xīhé,
and Zǐgǒng ended his days in Qí.
Such as Tián Zǐfāng,
Duàngān Mù,
Wú Qǐ,
Qíngǔ Lí and their like,
all studied under the likes of Zǐxià,
becoming teachers to kings.
At that time, only Duke Wén of Wèi loved learning.
Later, decline continued until the First Emperor,
the world contended in the Warring States period,
and Confucian arts were already marginalized,
yet between Qí and Lǔ,
scholars alone did not abandon them.
During the era of Wēi and
Xuān,
Mèngzǐ,
Xún Qīng, and their peers,
all followed the Master's work and embellished it,
gaining renown in their time through learning.
By the late Qín dynasty,
"Book of Songs" and "Book of Documents" were burned,
scholars were buried alive,
and the "Six Arts" became deficient from then on.
When Chén Shè became king,
the scholars of Lǔ took the ritual vessels of the Kǒng family and went over to King Chén.
Thus, Kǒng Jiǎ became Erudite for Chén Shè,
and eventually died with him.
Chén Shè rose from commoner status,
driving conscripts of tile-setters to garrison duty,
within a month became king of Chǔ,
and in less than half a year perished—
his affairs were trivial and shallow,
yet why did the gentry and scholars bear Confucius's ritual vessels to offer allegiance as ministers?
It was because Qín had burned their heritage,
and they harbored accumulated resentment, venting their frustration through King Chén.
When Emperor Gāo slew Xiàng Jí,
and raised troops to surround Lǔ,
the scholars within Lǔ still lectured, recited, and practiced rites and music,
the sound of strings and songs never ceasing—
was this not the lingering influence of the sages,
a state that loved rites and music?
Thus, when Confucius was in Chén,
he said,
"Return, oh return!
The young of my village are ambitious but rough,
accomplished in literary form,
yet I do not know how to shape them."
Between Qí and Lǔ,
in literature and learning,
since ancient times,
it has been their innate nature.
Therefore, after Hàn arose,
the scholars could finally cultivate their classical arts,
and lecture on the ceremonies of the great archery and village drinking.
Shūsūn Tōng created the Hàn rituals,
and was made Grand Master of Ceremonies;
the various scholars and disciples who participated in establishing them
were all selected for prominence,
whereupon there was a resounding sigh of revival in learning.
Yet there were still wars,
and pacifying the four seas,
leaving no leisure for school affairs.
In the time of Emperor Huì
and Empress Lǚ,
the high officials were all military men of merit.
Under Emperor Wén, some were recruited,
but Emperor Wén himself favored Legalist doctrines.
By Emperor Jǐng's reign,
Confucians were not employed,
and Empress Dowager Dòu favored the techniques of Huáng-Lǎo,
so the various Erudites held positions awaiting questions,
with none advancing.
When the present emperor ascended the throne,
Zhào Wǎn,
Wáng Zāng, and their like promoted Confucian learning,
and the emperor also inclined towards it,
thus summoning upright, worthy, and literary scholars.
From then on,
for the "Book of Songs" in Lǔ, there was Shēn Péigōng;
in Qí, Yuán Gùshēng;
in Yān, Hán the Grand Tutor.
For the "Book of Documents", from Fúshēng of Jǐnán.
For the "Rites", from Gāotángshēng of Lǔ.
For the "Book of Changes", from Tiánshēng of Zīchuān.
For the "Spring and Autumn Annals" in Qí and Lǔ, Húwúshēng;
in Zhào, Dǒng Zhòngshū.
After Empress Dowager Dòu passed away,
Tián Fén, Marquis Wǔ'ān, became Chancellor,
dismissed Huáng-Lǎo,
Legalist, and Hundred Schools' doctrines,
invited hundreds of literary Confucian scholars,
and Gōngsūn Hóng, through the "Spring and Autumn Annals", rose from commoner to one of the Three Dukes,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Píngjīn.
Then, the scholars of the world all turned with the wind towards this trend.
Gōngsūn Hóng, as an educational official,
lamented the stagnation of the Way,
and thus petitioned:
"The Chancellor and the Imperial Censor have stated:
The imperial decree says:
'It is heard that the people should be guided with rites,
and influenced with music.
Marriage
is the great moral principle of domestic life.
Now that rites are abandoned and music is collapsing,
We are deeply concerned.
Therefore, We extensively invite the upright and erudite scholars from across the land,
all to be elevated to the court.
Let the ritual officials encourage learning,
discuss and deliberate on comprehensive knowledge and the revival of rites,
to set an example for the world.
The Minister of Ceremonies proposes
that, with the academicians and their disciples,
we honor the transformation of the villages and communities,
to broaden the pool of worthy talents.'
We respectfully deliberate with the Minister of Ceremonies Zāng
and Academician Píng, stating:
We have heard that in the way of the Three Dynasties,
there was education in the villages and communities:
in the Xià, it was called xiào;
in the Yīn, xù;
in the Zhōu, xiáng.
In encouraging goodness,
they were recognized in the court;
in punishing evil,
penalties were imposed.
Thus, the implementation of education
begins with establishing the pinnacle of goodness from the capital,
spreading from the center outward.
Now, Your Majesty illuminates the highest virtue,
opens up great brightness,
matches heaven and earth,
bases on human relations,
encourages learning and cultivates rites,
honors transformation and promotes worthies,
to influence the four directions,
which is the foundation of great peace.
In ancient times, when governance and education were not yet thorough,
and rites were not fully prepared,
we request to build upon the existing offices to revive them.
Assign fifty disciples to the academician officials,
exempting them from corvée.
The Minister of Ceremonies shall select commoners aged eighteen and above,
with proper demeanor and appearance,
to fill as academician disciples.
In commanderies, kingdoms, counties, districts, and towns, those who love literature,
respect superiors,
uphold governance and education,
comply with their communities,
and act without contradicting what they have learned,
shall be recommended by their local administrators to the two-thousand-bushel officials,
who shall carefully examine suitable candidates
and send them with the accounting officials,
to the Minister of Ceremonies,
to receive instruction like disciples.
After one year, all shall be examined:
those proficient in one art or more
shall fill vacancies as literary officials or archivists;
those of high merit fit to be court gentlemen
shall be registered and reported by the Minister of Ceremonies.
If there are exceptional talents of outstanding ability,
their names shall be reported.
Those who do not study, are of low ability, or cannot master one art
shall be dismissed,
and we request penalties for those who prove unworthy.
Your servant respectfully notes that the issued decrees and laws
clarify the distinction between heaven and humanity,
comprehend the principles of past and present,
with elegant language
and profound instructions,
bestowing great kindness.
Petty officials, with shallow knowledge,
cannot fully elucidate them,
failing to clearly proclaim and instruct the people.
Officials of rites and archivists,
who serve with literature and ritual righteousness,
often remain stagnant.
We request to select those with ranks of two hundred bushels or above,
and officials of one hundred bushels proficient in one art or more,
to fill positions in the Left and Right Interior Histories,
and as clerks to the Grand Herald;
those below one hundred bushels
shall fill as commandery governor clerks:
each two persons,
one in border commanderies.
Prefer those who recite more;
if insufficient,
then select archivists to fill as subordinates of the fully two-thousand-bushel officials,
and literary archivists to fill as commandery subordinates,
to complete the staff.
We request this be inscribed in the administrative orders.
The rest as per the laws."
The imperial decree said:
"Approved."
From then on,
the high officials, nobles, and officers became richly adorned with men of literature.
Shēn Gōng
was a man of Lǔ.
When Emperor Gāozǔ passed through Lǔ,
Shēn Gōng, as a disciple, followed his teacher to meet Emperor Gāozǔ at the Southern Palace in Lǔ.
During Empress Dowager Lǚ's time,
Shēn Gōng traveled to study in Cháng'ān,
sharing a teacher with Liú Yǐng.
Later, Yǐng became King of Chǔ,
and ordered Shēn Gōng to tutor his crown prince Wù.
Wù did not enjoy learning,
and resented Shēn Gōng.
When King Yǐng died,
Wù ascended as King of Chǔ,
and subjected Shēn Gōng to penal servitude.
Shēn Gōng felt shamed by this,
returned to Lǔ,
retired to teach at home,
never leaving his gate for life,
and further declined visitors,
only going when summoned by royal command.
Disciples came from afar to study, over a hundred in number.
Shēn Gōng solely taught the "Classic of Poetry" with explanations,
without additional commentaries,
omitting what was doubtful.
Lánlíng's Wáng Zāng, after learning the "Poetry",
served Emperor Jǐng as Tutor to the Crown Prince,
but was dismissed.
When the current emperor first ascended the throne,
Zāng submitted a letter and served in the imperial guard,
rising rapidly through ranks,
becoming the Commander of the Palace Guard within a year.
And his successor Zhào Wǎn had also studied the "Poetry" under Shēn Gōng,
with Wǎn becoming the Imperial Censor.
Wǎn and Zāng requested the emperor
to establish a Mingtang for receiving feudal lords,
but unable to accomplish it,
they mentioned their teacher Shēn Gōng.
Thereupon, the emperor sent an envoy with silks and a jade disc, welcoming Shēn Gōng in a comfortable carriage with a team of four horses,
with two disciples following in a light carriage.
Upon arrival, he met the emperor.
The emperor asked about governance and chaos,
Shēn Gōng, then over eighty years old,
and aged, replied:
"Those who govern need not many words,
but should focus on how diligently they act."
At that time, the emperor favored literary rhetoric,
and upon hearing Shēn Gōng's response,
fell silent.
However, having invited him,
he appointed him as Grand Master of the Palace,
housed him in the Lǔ residence,
to deliberate on the Mingtang matter.
The Grand Empress Dowager Dòu favored Lǎozǐ's teachings,
disliking Confucian methods,
and upon finding faults with Zhào Wǎn
and Wáng Zāng, reproached the emperor,
leading the emperor to abandon the Mingtang project,
arresting both Zhào Wǎn
and Wáng Zāng,
who later committed suicide.
Shēn Gōng was also dismissed due to illness and returned home,
passing away a few years later.
Among his disciples, over ten became academicians:
Kǒng Ānguó rose to Governor of Línhuái,
Zhōu Bà to Interior Historian of Jiāoxī,
Xià Kuān to Interior Historian of Chéngyáng,
Dàng's Lǔ Cì to Governor of Dōnghǎi,
Lánlíng's Miào Shēng to Interior Historian of Chángshā,
Xú Yǎn as Commandant of Jiāoxī,
and Quēmén Qìngjì of Zōu as Interior Historian of Jiāodōng.
In governing officials and people, they all displayed integrity and restraint,
praised for their love of learning.
Although the conduct of the academician disciples was not flawless,
those who rose to grand masters,
court gentlemen,
and archivists numbered in the hundreds.
Though interpretations of the "Poetry" varied,
most originated from Shēn Gōng.
Zhào Yǔ was
a native of Tái.
He began his career as a minor clerk in the capital administration,
and due to his integrity, he was promoted to a legal officer,
serving under Grand Commandant Zhōu Yàfū.
When Yàfū became Chancellor,
Yǔ served as a history officer in the chancellery,
where everyone praised him for his incorruptibility and fairness.
However, Yàfū did not entrust him with major responsibilities,
saying:
"I fully recognize that Yǔ is unimpeachable,
but he is too strict with legal technicalities,
unsuited for high office."
During the current emperor's reign,
Yǔ accumulated seniority as a legal clerk,
gradually advancing to Censor.
The emperor considered him capable,
promoting him to Grand Master of the Palace.
Together with Zhāng Tāng, he deliberated and established various laws and statutes,
creating the "knowledge and awareness" rule,
whereby officials could monitor and impeach each other.
The increasingly harsh application of laws
likely began from this point.
Zhāng Tāng was
a native of Dù.
His father served as a county official in Cháng'ān.
Once when his father went out, Tāng, then a child, was left guarding the house.
Upon returning, they found that rats had stolen meat,
and his father,
angered,
beat Tāng.
Tāng then dug into the rat burrow, caught the thieving rat and retrieved the remaining meat,
indicted the rat,
drafted a formal indictment,
conducted an interrogation, passed judgment, and executed the sentence,
then took the rat and the meat,
completing the case by dismembering the rat in the courtyard.
His father witnessed this,
and seeing that his legal documents were as precise as those of an experienced jailer,
was greatly astonished,
and thereafter had him draft legal documents.
After his father's death,
Tāng became an official in Cháng'ān,
serving for a long time.
When Zhōuyáng Hóu first became a high minister,
he was once imprisoned in Cháng'ān,
and Tāng devoted himself to assisting him.
After Zhōuyáng Hóu was enfeoffed and released,
he formed a close friendship with Tāng,
introducing him to many influential people.
Tāng served in the Neishi office,
as an assistant to Níng Chéng,
who, considering Tāng unimpeachable,
recommended him to the higher authorities,
transferring him to the position of Màolíng Commandant,
overseeing the construction of the imperial tomb.
When Wǔ'ān Hóu became Chancellor,
he recruited Tāng as an official,
and at times recommended him to the emperor,
appointing him as Censor,
and assigning him to investigate cases.
He handled the witchcraft case of Empress Chén,
thoroughly pursuing all accomplices.
Thereupon, the emperor considered him capable,
gradually promoting him to Grand Master of the Palace.
Together with Zhào Yǔ, he established various laws and statutes,
focusing on strict legal technicalities
to control officials in their duties.
Later, Zhào Yǔ was promoted to Commandant of the Capital,
then transferred to Minor Treasurer,
while Zhāng Tāng became Commandant of Justice.
The two were on friendly terms,
and Tāng treated Yǔ as an elder brother.
Yǔ was upright and aloof by nature.
Since becoming an official,
he never hosted retainers.
When high ministers visited him,
Yǔ never returned their courtesies,
aiming solely to cut off requests from friends and guests,
maintaining his independence and adhering to his own principles.
Whenever he encountered legal statutes, he would adopt them,
without reviewing cases further,
seeking out hidden offenses among his subordinates.
Tāng, on the other hand, was deceitful by nature,
using his wit to manipulate others.
Early in his career as a minor official,
he engaged in profiteering,
forming private connections with wealthy merchants like Tián Jiǎ
and Yú Wēngshū.
Upon reaching the Nine Ministers,
he associated with renowned scholars and officials from across the land,
though inwardly disagreeing with them,
he outwardly feigned admiration.
At that time, the emperor favored literary studies,
so when Tāng adjudicated major cases,
he sought to align with ancient principles,
requesting that students of the classics, versed in the "Shàngshū"
and "Chūnqiū," be appointed as history officers in the Commandant of Justice's office
to resolve legal ambiguities.
When presenting doubtful cases for review,
he would always first explain their origins to the emperor in detail.
If the emperor approved,
he would accept and record the decision, establishing legal precedents to highlight the emperor's wisdom.
If his reports were criticized,
Tāng would apologize,
aligning with the emperor's preferences,
and always citing the worthy officials such as the rectifiers,
inspectors, and clerks,
saying:
"They indeed advised me thus,
but the emperor reprimanded me,
and I failed to heed them—
this was my folly."
Thus, he was often pardoned.
When reporting matters informally,
if the emperor praised him,
he would say:
"I did not devise this report myself;
it was the rectifier,
inspector, or clerk so-and-so who did it."
This was how he recommended officials,
praising their virtues while concealing their faults.
If the case involved someone the emperor wished to punish,
he would assign it to harsh inspectors;
if the emperor wished to pardon someone,
he would assign it to lenient inspectors.
If the accused were powerful,
he would invariably twist the law to vilify them;
if they were commoners or the weak,
he would often speak on their behalf,
and though the law might incriminate them,
he would urge the emperor to consider their circumstances.
Thus, the emperor often pardoned those Tāng spoke for.
As Tāng rose to high office,
he maintained disciplined conduct.
He entertained guests with food and drink,
and showed particular care for the children of old acquaintances who became officials or his impoverished brothers,
looking after them generously.
He paid visits to various dignitaries
regardless of cold or heat.
Hence, although Tāng was strict in legal technicalities, biased, and not entirely fair,
he still gained a good reputation.
Moreover, many harsh officials served as his henchmen,
relying on the literary scholars.
Chancellor Gōngsūn Hóng often praised his merits.
When handling the rebellion cases of Huáinán,
Héngshān, and Jiāngdū,
he pursued them to their roots.
In the cases of Yán Zhù and Wǔ Bèi,
the emperor wished to pardon them,
but Tāng argued:
"Wǔ Bèi originally plotted the rebellion,
and Yán Zhù, as a trusted retainer of Your Majesty,
privately associated with the nobles in this manner.
If they are not executed,
it will be impossible to maintain order hereafter."
Thereupon, the emperor approved their sentencing.
In his handling of cases, Tāng often took credit for suppressing high ministers,
and many instances were like this.
Thus, Tāng became increasingly esteemed and trusted,
promoted to Grandee Secretary.
When Húnxié and others surrendered,
Hán launched massive campaigns against the Xiōngnú,
while floods and droughts struck the regions east of the mountains,
causing the poor to wander displaced,
all relying on government relief,
which depleted the treasury.
Thereupon, following the emperor's intent,
he requested the minting of white gold and wǔzhū coins,
monopolized the salt and iron industries nationwide,
suppressed wealthy merchants,
issued the property declaration decree,
and uprooted powerful families that engaged in monopolies,
using legal technicalities and false accusations to enforce the laws.
Whenever Tāng presented reports at court,
discussing state expenditures,
he would speak until late,
and the Son of Heaven would forget to eat.
The Chancellor held his position nominally,
while all affairs of the empire were decided by Tāng.
The common people could not live in peace,
and unrest spread.
The government's initiatives
yielded no benefits,
while corrupt officials exploited and plundered,
leading to severe punishments.
Thus, from the highest ministers
down to the commoners,
all pointed fingers at Tāng.
Once when Tāng fell ill,
the emperor personally visited to inquire after his health—
such was the height of his nobility and favor.
The Xiongnu came to request a marriage alliance,
and the assembled ministers deliberated before the Emperor.
The Erudite Dí Shān said:
"A marriage alliance is advantageous."
The Emperor asked him to explain the advantage,
and Shān said:
"Weapons are instruments of ill omen,
not to be frequently employed.
When Emperor Gāo desired to attack the Xiongnu,
he was greatly besieged at Píngchéng,
and thus concluded a marriage alliance.
During the reigns of Emperor Huì
and Empress Dowager Gāo,
the empire was peaceful and content.
When Emperor Wén of the Xiào era desired to engage the Xiongnu,
the northern frontier was desolate and suffered from warfare.
During the reign of Emperor Jǐng of the Xiào era,
the seven states of Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
and Emperor Jǐng, moving between the two palaces,
was filled with dread for several months.
After Wú and Chǔ were defeated,
Emperor Jǐng ultimately did not speak of war,
and the empire became wealthy and prosperous.
Now, since Your Majesty has raised troops to attack the Xiongnu,
the Central Plains have been emptied,
and the border people are greatly distressed and impoverished.
From this perspective,
it is not as good as a marriage alliance."
The Emperor asked Zhāng Tāng,
and Tāng said:
"This is a foolish Confucian,
ignorant."
Dí Shān said:
"I am indeed foolishly loyal,
but the Imperial Secretary Zhāng Tāng is deceptively loyal.
Take Tāng's handling of the cases of the King of Huáinán
and the King of Jiāngdū;
he used harsh laws to bitterly vilify the feudal lords,
alienated flesh and blood relatives,
and caused the vassal lords to feel insecure.
I certainly know that Tāng's loyalty is deceptive."
At this, the Emperor changed countenance and said:
"If I were to send you, Sir, to govern a commandery,
could you prevent the barbarians from invading and plundering?"
Shān replied:
"I could not."
The Emperor said:
"What about a county?"
He answered:
"I could not."
The Emperor said again:
"What about a single frontier outpost?"
Shān, realizing his argument was exhausted and fearing he would be handed over to the law officials,
said:
"I could."
Thereupon, the Emperor sent Shān to man the outpost.
After a little over a month,
the Xiongnu cut off Shān's head and left.
From then on,
the assembled ministers were awed and terrified.
Tāng's client Tián Jiǎ,
although a merchant,
possessed worthy conduct.
When Tāng was a minor official,
he provided him with funds,
and when Tāng became a high official,
Jiǎ would admonish Tāng for his failings in conduct and duty,
displaying the bearing of a man of principle.
Tāng served as Imperial Secretary for seven years,
before his downfall.
A man from Hédōng named Lǐ Wén had once borne a grudge against Tāng.
Later, when Wén became Palace Assistant Imperial Secretary,
resentful, he repeatedly found matters in the official documents that could be used to harm Tāng,
leaving Tāng no room to maneuver.
Tāng had a favored clerk named Lǔ Yèjū,
who knew Tāng was discontented.
Yèjū had someone submit an anonymous report accusing Wén of treacherous acts.
The matter was referred to Tāng,
and Tāng tried and executed Wén,
though Tāng knew in his heart that Yèjū was behind it.
The Emperor asked:
"Where did the trail of this anonymous report originate?"
Tāng feigned surprise and said:
"This is probably due to some old enemy of Wén's holding a grudge."
Yèjū fell ill and was lying at the home of a village host.
Tāng personally went to visit his illness,
and massaged Yèjū's feet.
The state of Zhào made its livelihood from smelting and casting,
and the King of Zhào repeatedly brought lawsuits concerning the Iron Office.
Tāng often opposed the King of Zhào.
The King of Zhào sought out Tāng's secret affairs.
Yèjū had once investigated the King of Zhào,
and the King of Zhào bore a grudge against him.
He submitted a memorial accusing:
"Tāng,
a high minister,
when his clerk Yèjū was ill,
Tāng went so far as to massage his feet.
I suspect they were involved in major treachery together."
The matter was referred to the Commandant of Justice.
Yèjū died of illness,
and the matter implicated his younger brother,
who was imprisoned in the Dǎoguān prison.
Tāng was also trying other prisoners at the Dǎoguān,
and when he saw Yèjū's brother,
he wished to secretly help him,
but pretended not to notice.
Yèjū's brother, unaware of this,
resented Tāng.
He had someone submit a memorial accusing Tāng and Yèjū of conspiring
to jointly submit the anonymous report against Lǐ Wén.
The matter was referred to Jiǎn Xuān.
Xuān had once borne a grudge against Tāng,
and upon obtaining this matter,
exhaustively investigated it,
but had not yet submitted a report.
It happened that someone stole and excavated the buried money in the tomb park of Emperor Wén of the Xiào era.
The Chancellor Qīng Dí attended court,
and had made an agreement with Tāng to apologize together.
When they came before the Emperor,
Tāng reflected that only the Chancellor, who inspected the tomb park according to the seasons,
ought to apologize;
he himself had nothing to do with it,
and did not apologize.
The Chancellor apologized,
and the Emperor ordered the Imperial Secretary to investigate the matter.
Tāng wanted to frame the written charge so that the Chancellor would be guilty of knowing the crime but not reporting it.
The Chancellor was troubled by this.
The three Chief Clerks all hated Tāng,
and wanted to bring about his downfall.
Initially, Chief Clerk Zhū Mǎichén,
a native of Kuàijī,
studied the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Zhuāng Zhù sent someone to speak with Mǎichén,
and Mǎichén, through his knowledge of the Songs of Chǔ along with Zhù, gained favor together,
serving as Palace Attendant,
appointed as Grand Master of the Palace,
wielding power;
while Táng was then a minor official,
kneeling and prostrating before Mǎichén and others.
Later, Táng became Commandant of Justice,
handling the Huáinán case,
ostracized Zhuāng Zhù,
so Mǎichén held a grudge in his heart.
When Táng rose to Imperial Censor-in-Chief,
Mǎichén, as Governor of Kuàijī, was made Commandant of the Nobles' Order,
ranking among the Nine Ministers.
After several years,
he was dismissed due to legal offenses,
serving as Chief Clerk,
and when he met Táng,
Táng sat on his couch,
and the assistants treated Mǎichén without respect.
Mǎichén, being from Chǔ,
deeply resented this,
often wishing to die for it.
Wáng Zhāo,
a native of Qí,
rose by strategy to Right Interior Commandant.
Biān Tōng,
studied the School of Vertical and Horizontal Alliances,
a fierce and strong man,
held office twice as Chancellor of Jǐnán.
Thus, both had once been above Táng in rank,
but later lost their positions,
serving as Chief Clerks,
and had to humble themselves before Táng.
Táng often acted in the capacity of Chancellor,
knowing these three Chief Clerks were formerly noble,
and frequently humiliated them.
Therefore, the three Chief Clerks conspired, saying:
"Initially, Táng agreed to apologize with you,
but then betrayed you;
now he intends to impeach you over ancestral temple affairs,
this is merely to replace you.
We know Táng's secret dealings."
They sent officials to arrest and investigate Tián Xìn and others on Táng's side,
claiming that whenever Táng was about to submit a request,
Xìn would know in advance,
hoard goods to amass wealth,
and share it with Táng,
along with other corrupt acts.
The details of the case became somewhat known.
The Emperor asked Táng:
"Whatever I do,
the merchants always know beforehand,
increasing their hoarding of goods;
it seems someone is informing them of my plans."
Táng did not apologize.
Táng then feigned surprise, saying:
"That is indeed possible."
Jiǎn Xuān also reported the affairs of Yè Jū and others.
The Emperor indeed believed Táng harbored deceit and had lied to his face,
sending eight envoys to interrogate Táng with records.
Táng fully denied any such actions,
refusing to confess.
Thereupon, the Emperor sent Zhào Yǔ to reprimand Táng.
When Yǔ arrived,
he admonished Táng, saying:
"Why do you not know your place?
How many people have you executed in your judgments?
Now, those accusing you have solid evidence;
the Emperor is reluctant to imprison you,
wishing you to take your own measure—
why bother with so much cross-examination?"
Táng then wrote a letter of apology, saying:
"I, Táng, have no merit of any measure,
rising from a petty clerk,
and Your Majesty graciously elevated me to one of the Three Dukes,
yet I have nothing to justify my position.
However, those who plotted to frame me
are the three Chief Clerks."
He then committed suicide.
After Táng's death,
his family's assets were worth no more than five hundred gold,
all from his salary and rewards,
with no other possessions.
His brothers and sons wished to bury him lavishly,
but Táng's mother said:
"Táng was a high minister of the Son of Heaven,
yet he died under the stain of slanderous words—
what need for a lavish burial!"
They carried him in an ox cart,
with a coffin but no outer casing.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he said:
"Only such a mother could bear such a son."
He then ordered the full investigation and execution of the three Chief Clerks.
Chancellor Qīng Dí committed suicide.
Tián Xìn was released.
The Emperor regretted Táng's death,
and gradually promoted his son Ānshì.
Zhào Yǔ was dismissed midway,
but later became Commandant of Justice.
Initially, Marquis Tiáo considered Yǔ too cruel,
and did not employ him.
When Yǔ became Privy Treasurer,
he ranked among the Nine Ministers.
Yǔ was harsh and severe,
but in his later years,
as affairs grew more numerous,
and officials pursued strictness,
Yǔ's governance became more lenient,
and he gained a reputation for fairness.
Later figures like Wáng Wēnshū
governed more brutally than Yǔ.
Yǔ, due to old age,
was transferred to be Chancellor of Yān.
After several years,
he committed treasonous acts and was found guilty,
dismissed and returned home.
Over a decade after Táng's death,
he died at home of old age.
Yì Zòng,
a native of Hédōng,
in his youth,
once joined Zhāng Cìgōng in raiding and plundering as bandits.
Zòng had an elder sister, Yì Xū,
who, as a physician, gained favor with Empress Dowager Wáng.
Empress Dowager Wáng asked:
"Do you have any sons or brothers fit for office?"
The sister replied:
"I have a brother but he is unruly,
unsuitable."
The Empress Dowager then informed the Emperor,
who appointed Yì Xū's brother Zòng as a Gentleman of the Palace,
assigned to fill a magistrate post in Shàngdǎng Commandery.
He governed with daring action,
showing little restraint,
yet his county had no unresolved matters,
and he was ranked first.
Promoted to Magistrate of Chánglíng and then Cháng'ān,
he enforced the law directly in his administration,
not shying from the powerful and noble.
For arresting and investigating Chéngjūnzǐ Zhòng, the Empress Dowager's grandson,
the Emperor deemed him capable,
and promoted him to Commandant of Hénèi.
Upon arrival, he exterminated the powerful Rǎng clan and their like,
so that in Hénèi, lost items were not picked up on the road.
Meanwhile, Zhāng Cìgōng also became a Gentleman,
serving in the army with bravery and ferocity,
daring to penetrate deep,
achieving merit,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Àntóu.
Nìng Chéng was residing at home,
and the Emperor wished to appoint him as a commandery governor.
The Grandee Secretary Gōng said:
"When I served as a minor official in Shāndōng,
Nìng Chéng was the Commandant of Jǐ'nán,
his governance was like a wolf herding sheep.
Chéng should not be made to govern the people."
The Emperor then appointed Chéng as the Pass Commandant.
Over a year later,
the officials and clerks from the commanderies and states east of the pass who traveled through it
would exclaim:
"Better to encounter a nursing tigress,
than to face Nìng Chéng's wrath."
Yì Zòng was transferred from Hénèi to become the Grand Administrator of Nányáng.
Hearing that Nìng Chéng was residing at home in Nányáng,
when Zòng reached the pass,
Nìng Chéng moved aside to see him off and welcome him,
yet Zòng, full of arrogance,
did not return the courtesy.
Upon arriving at the commandery,
he then prosecuted the Nìng family,
completely shattering their household.
Chéng was implicated and found guilty,
and along with members of the Kǒng
and Bào clans, they all fled.
The officials and people of Nányáng were terrified into submission.
Meanwhile, from Píngshì, Zhū Qiáng,
Dù Yǎn,
and Dù Zhōu served as Zòng's subordinate officials,
were employed,
and promoted to Court Historians.
The army was frequently dispatched to Dìngxiāng,
where the officials and people were in chaos and disorder,
so Zòng was transferred to be the Grand Administrator of Dìngxiāng.
Upon his arrival,
he raided the prison in Dìngxiāng, where over two hundred serious offenders were lightly detained,
along with more than two hundred visitors and brothers who had privately come to see them.
Zòng arrested and interrogated them all at once,
saying:
"They were freeing those condemned to death."
That day, over four hundred people were reported executed,
after which the commandery trembled with fear without being cold,
and the crafty people assisted the officials in governance.
At that time, Zhào Yǔ
and Zhāng Tāng had risen to the Nine Ministers through harshness,
yet their governance still leaned towards leniency,
supporting the law in practice,
while Zòng governed like an eagle striking with fierce claws.
Later, when the five-zhu coins and white gold were issued,
the people engaged in fraud,
especially in the capital,
so Zòng was appointed as the Right Inner Secretary,
and Wáng Wēnshū as the Commandant of the Capital.
Wēnshū was extremely malicious,
and if he acted without first informing Zòng,
Zòng would inevitably intimidate him with his authority,
undermining his achievements.
In his governance,
the number of executions was very high,
yet it only achieved minor order,
and corruption became uncontrollable,
leading to the emergence of the Direct Imperial Envoys.
Officials focused their governance on killing and binding,
and Yán Fèng was employed for his ruthlessness.
Zòng was incorruptible,
and his governance emulated Zhì Dū.
When the Emperor visited Dǐnghú,
he was ill for a long time,
but suddenly recovered and went to Gānquán,
finding the roads largely unmaintained.
The Emperor angrily said:
"Does Zòng think I will never travel this road again?"
He bore a grudge.
Come winter,
when Yáng Kě was just undertaking the enforcement of property declarations,
Zòng considered this disruptive to the people,
and ordered his officials to arrest those acting on Kě's behalf.
The Son of Heaven heard of this,
sent Dù Shì to investigate,
and deemed it as obstructing and sabotaging affairs,
executing Zòng in the market.
A year later,
Zhāng Tāng also died.
Wáng Wēnshū
was from Yánglíng.
In his youth, he engaged in robbery and evil deeds.
Later, he was tried and appointed as a village head,
but was dismissed multiple times.
As an official,
he rose to Court Historian through handling legal cases.
He served under Zhāng Tāng,
and was promoted to Censor.
Supervising the capture of bandits,
he caused many casualties,
and gradually rose to Commandant of Guǎngpíng.
He selected over ten bold and daring officials from the commandery,
making them his subordinates,
and held evidence of their secret serious crimes,
then set them to supervise bandit capture,
allowing them to act as they pleased.
Even if these men committed a hundred crimes,
they were not prosecuted;
but if they shirked their duties,
he would use their crimes to destroy them,
even exterminating their clans.
As a result, bandits from the borders of Qí and Zhào dared not approach Guǎngpíng,
and Guǎngpíng was reputed for having no theft on the roads.
The Emperor heard of this,
and promoted him to Grand Administrator of Hénèi.
Having previously served in Guǎngpíng,
he was well aware of the powerful and corrupt families in Hénèi.
Upon his arrival,
it was the ninth month.
He ordered the commandery to prepare fifty private horses,
setting up a relay post from Hénèi to Cháng'ān,
and deployed his officials with the same strategies as in Guǎngpíng,
arresting the powerful and crafty in the commandery.
Over a thousand powerful and crafty families in the commandery were implicated and punished.
He submitted requests for approval,
with the severe cases leading to clan extermination,
and the lesser ones to death,
and all their families' properties were confiscated as compensation for illicit gains.
The approval for his memorials came
within two or three days.
Sentencing and reporting
led to bloodshed spanning over ten miles.
Everyone in Hénèi was astonished by the speed of his memorials,
considering it supernatural.
By the end of the twelfth month,
the commandery was silent,
no one dared to walk at night,
and there were no thieves in the countryside, not even a dog barking.
Those he mostly failed to catch,
who fled to neighboring commanderies and states,
he pursued and captured them.
When spring arrived,
Wēnshū stamped his feet and sighed:
"Alas,
if only the winter could be extended by one more month,
that would suffice for my tasks!"
Such was his fondness for killing, exercising authority, and lack of compassion.
The Son of Heaven heard of this,
considered him capable,
and promoted him to Commandant of the Capital.
His governance again mirrored that in Hénèi,
transferring various notorious and crafty officials to work with him,
such as Yáng Jiē
and Má Wù from Hénèi,
and Yáng Gàn
and Chéng Xìn from Guānzhōng.
While Yì Zòng was the Inner Secretary,
he feared him and did not dare to govern arbitrarily.
After Zòng's death,
and following Zhāng Tāng's downfall,
he was transferred to be the Commandant of Justice,
and Yǐn Qí became the Commandant of the Capital.
Yǐn Qí
was from Chípíng in Dōngjùn.
He rose from a clerk to Censor.
He served under Zhāng Tāng,
who often praised him for his integrity and martial prowess,
and put him in charge of suppressing bandits.
In his executions, he did not spare the noble relatives.
Promoted to Capital Commandant within the Pass,
his reputation surpassed even Nìng Chéng's.
The Emperor considered him capable,
and promoted him to Commandant of the Capital.
The officials and people became increasingly destitute.
Yǐn Qí was rigid and lacked refinement,
causing the wicked officials to go into hiding while the good ones could not govern effectively,
so many affairs were neglected,
and he was convicted of a crime.
The Emperor again transferred Wēnshū to be the Commandant of the Capital,
while Yáng Pú, known for his severity, became the Commandant of the Nobles.
Yáng Pú
was from Yíyáng.
He became an official through the rank of Qiānfū.
The Governor of Hénán recommended him for his ability,
and he was promoted to Censor,
sent to suppress bandits east of the pass.
His governance emulated Yǐn Qí's,
and he was considered daring and resolute in action.
Gradually promoted to Commandant of the Nobles,
he ranked among the Nine Ministers.
The Son of Heaven considered him capable.
When Nányuè rebelled,
he was appointed as Towered Ship General,
performed meritorious service,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiàngliáng.
He was bound by Xún Zhì.
After a long time,
he fell ill and died.
And Wēn Shū again served as Commandant of the Capital Police.
He was a man of little refinement,
in court he was muddled and inarticulate,
but when it came to the role of Commandant, his mind became sharp.
He supervised the pursuit of robbers and bandits,
being long familiar with the customs of Guānzhōng,
and knew the ruthless clerks,
who all returned to serve under him,
to devise strategies.
The clerks were harsh in their investigations,
with robbers, bandits, and young thugs dropping accusations and reports of crimes into boxes,
and neighborhood chiefs were appointed to oversee and control criminals and thieves.
Wēn Shū was obsequious by nature,
skilled at serving those with power;
but toward those without power,
he treated them like slaves.
For powerful families,
even if their crimes piled up like a mountain,
he would not touch them;
for those without power,
even imperial relatives would be oppressed and humiliated.
He manipulated laws to cunningly incriminate the crafty among the lower households,
in order to intimidate the great and powerful.
Such was his governance as Commandant.
Criminals and rogues were thoroughly prosecuted,
most of them rotting in prison,
with none released after sentencing.
His subordinate clerks were like tigers wearing crowns.
Thus, within his jurisdiction as Commandant, all but the most cunning submitted,
and the powerful praised his reputation,
calling it good governance.
After several years of such rule,
many of his clerks became wealthy through power.
When Wēn Shū returned from attacking the Eastern Yuè,
some of his proposals did not meet approval,
and he was dismissed for minor legal offenses.
At that time, the Son of Heaven wished to build the Tōngtiān Tower but lacked laborers,
so Wēn Shū suggested reviewing the deserters from the Commandant's troops,
obtaining tens of thousands of men for the project.
The Emperor was pleased,
and appointed him as Minister of Stewards.
He was transferred to be Right Internal Secretary,
governing as before,
with little restraint on wickedness.
He lost his position due to legal offenses.
Again, he served as Right Supporter,
acting as Commandant,
with the same conduct as before.
Over a year later,
when the army of Wǎn was dispatched,
an edict called for the conscription of powerful clerks,
but Wēn Shū concealed his clerk Huà Chéng,
and when someone reported that Wēn Shū had accepted bribes for cavalry assignments,
along with other corrupt dealings,
his crimes warranted the extermination of his clan,
so he committed suicide.
At that time, his two brothers and two in-laws were also executed with their clans for other crimes.
Xú Zìwéi, the Imperial Household Grandee, said:
"Alas,
in ancient times there was the punishment of three clans,
but Wáng Wēnshū's crimes led to five clans being wiped out simultaneously!"
After Wēn Shū's death,
his family's wealth amounted to a thousand pieces of gold.
A few years later,
Yǐn Qí also died of illness while serving as Commandant of Huáiyáng,
with a family wealth of less than five thousand pieces of gold.
He had executed many in Huáiyáng,
and upon his death,
his enemies wanted to burn his corpse,
but it was taken away for burial.
Since Wēn Shū and others governed with cruelty,
the commandery governors,
commandants,
and feudal lords with two-thousand-bushel ranks who sought to govern
mostly imitated Wēn Shū,
leading to officials and people increasingly flouting the law,
and robbers and bandits multiplying.
In Nányáng, there were Méi Miǎn,
Bái Zhèng,
in Chǔ, Yīn Zhōng,
Dù Shǎo,
in Qí, Xú Bó,
and between Yān and Zhào, Jiān Lú,
Fàn Shēng, and their likes.
Large bands numbered up to several thousand,
arrogating titles to themselves,
attacking cities and towns,
seizing weapons from armories,
releasing those condemned to death,
binding and humiliating commandery governors,
commandants,
killing two-thousand-bushel officials,
and issuing proclamations to counties demanding provisions;
smaller bands numbered in the hundreds,
plundering villages,
too many to count.
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven first sent the Palace Assistant Secretary of the Censorate
and the Chancellor's Chief Clerk to supervise them.
Still unable to suppress them,
he then sent the Imperial Household Grandee Fàn Kūn,
various Support Commandants, and former Nine Ministers like Zhāng Dé, clad in embroidered robes,
bearing tallies,
and with tiger tallies to mobilize troops for attacks,
beheading large groups, sometimes over ten thousand,
and legally executing those who supplied them with food and drink,
implicating several commanderies,
with the worst cases involving thousands.
After several years,
they somewhat captured their leaders.
Scattered remnants fled and dispersed,
regrouping in bands in mountainous areas,
often gathering together,
with nothing to be done about it.
Thus, they enacted
the "Law of Sinking Fate,"
stating that if bandits arose and were not detected,
or if detected but not fully captured,
all officials from the two-thousand-bushel rank down to the minor clerks in charge would be executed.
Thereafter, minor clerks feared execution,
and even if there were bandits, they dared not report them,
fearing failure to capture them,
which would implicate their superiors,
and the superiors also made them keep silent.
Thus, robbers and bandits gradually increased,
with superiors and subordinates covering up for each other,
using written excuses to evade the law.
Jiǎn Xuān was
a man of Yáng.
He served as a minor clerk without fault in the East River Governor's office.
When General Wèi Qīng sent him to purchase horses in Hédōng,
he saw Xuān was without fault,
reported to the Emperor,
and he was appointed as Assistant of the Imperial Stables.
He handled official affairs adeptly,
and gradually rose to Censor and Palace Assistant Secretary.
Sent to handle the cases of Zhǔfù Yǎn's rebellion and the Huáinán rebellion,
he used subtle laws and deep accusations,
executing many,
and was known for daring to resolve doubts.
Dismissed and reappointed several times,
he served as Censor and Palace Assistant Secretary for nearly twenty years.
When Wáng Wēnshū was dismissed as Commandant,
Xuān became Left Internal Secretary.
His governance extended to rice and salt,
handling matters great and small personally,
deploying county officials and managing goods himself,
not allowing magistrates and assistants to act arbitrarily,
and strictly enforcing heavy laws.
After several years in office,
the entire commandery saw minor administrative order,
but only Xuān could achieve great results from small means,
capable of acting according to his strength,
though hard to sustain as a norm.
He was dismissed midway.
As Right Fúfēng,
he harbored a grudge against Chéng Xìn,
who fled and hid in the Shànglín Park,
so Xuān had the Magistrate of Méi kill Xìn,
but when the clerks and soldiers fought Xìn,
they shot arrows that hit the gate of Shànglín Park,
leading to Xuān being accused by officials,
charged with great impiety,
warranting clan extermination,
so he committed suicide.
And Dù Zhōu was appointed.
Dù Zhōu was
a man of Dùyǎn in Nányáng.
Yì Zòng, as Governor of Nányáng,
took him as a subordinate,
and recommended him as a Court Secretary.
He served under Zhāng Tāng,
who often spoke of his faultlessness,
and he rose to Censor.
Sent to investigate border losses,
he condemned many to death.
His memorials pleased the Emperor's intentions,
so he was trusted and employed,
alternating with Jiǎn Xuān,
and served as Palace Assistant Secretary for over ten years.
His governance resembled that of Zhì Xuān,
yet was more ponderous and deliberate.
Outwardly lenient,
inwardly his severity cut to the bone.
When Zhì served as Left Interior Secretary,
and Dù Zhōu as Commandant of Justice,
their administration largely emulated Zhāng Tāng's methods and excelled in observing imperial intentions.
Those the emperor wished to suppress,
they would thus entrap;
those the emperor wished to release,
they would detain awaiting inquiry while subtly revealing their wrongful accusations.
A guest reproached Dù Zhōu, saying:
"You decide cases for the Son of Heaven,
yet do not follow the statutory laws,
but solely base judgments on the sovereign's inclinations.
Should justice truly be administered thus?"
Dù Zhōu replied:
"From where do laws derive?
What former rulers approved was codified as statutes;
what subsequent rulers approved was recorded as edicts.
Each era follows what is appropriate for its time—
why adhere to antiquity!"
By the time Dù Zhōu became Commandant of Justice,
cases tried by imperial decree had multiplied.
Officials of two-thousand-dan rank, newly accused and former prisoners, interlinked,
numbered no less than over a hundred individuals.
When commandery officials and grand ministries referred cases to the Commandant,
they amounted to over a thousand memorials annually.
Larger cases implicated several hundred persons for testimony,
smaller ones several tens;
some involved distances of thousands of lǐ,
others several hundred lǐ.
When trials convened,
clerks would press charges as stated in the memorials,
and if the accused did not confess,
they used flogging to secure convictions.
Hence, upon hearing of arrests, people would flee into hiding.
Some cases dragged on through multiple amnesties for over ten years with continued accusations,
mostly defamed as "unprincipled" to implicate superiors.
The Commandant and central government's decree prisons held sixty to seventy thousand detainees,
with clerks adding over a hundred thousand more.
Dù Zhōu was temporarily dismissed,
later appointed as Capital Commandant,
pursued robbers,
and arrested Sāng Hóngyáng,
investigating the siblings of Empress Wèi with harsh severity.
The Son of Heaven, considering him diligent and impartial,
promoted him to Grandee Secretary.
His two sons
served as governors on opposite sides of the Yellow River.
Their governance was more violently cruel than even Wáng Wēnshū and others.
When Dù Zhōu was first recruited as a court clerk,
he owned one horse,
and it was not even sound;
but after long service,
he rose to the three ducal posts,
with descendants holding high offices,
and family assets accumulated to hundreds of millions.
The Grand Historian remarks:
From Zhì Dū
to Dù Zhōu, these ten individuals
all gained reputations for cruelty.
Yet Zhì Dū was staunchly upright,
discerning right from wrong,
contending for the great principles of the realm.
Zhāng Tāng, understanding the shifts of power,
rose and fell with the sovereign's favor,
often debating appropriateness,
and the state relied on his efficacy.
Zhào Yǔ at times adhered to laws and upheld integrity.
Dù Zhōu was obsequious,
valuing few words.
After Zhāng Tāng's death,
the legal net tightened,
with increased defamation and severity,
and official affairs gradually deteriorated.
The nine ministers were mediocre in their duties,
barely able to correct faults,
let alone address matters beyond the rules!
Yet among these ten,
the incorruptible suffice as models,
the corrupt as warnings;
in strategy and guidance,
suppressing treachery and halting evil,
all possessed both civil and martial qualities in refined measure.
Though brutal,
they fit their positions.
As for petty officials like Shu Governor Féng Dāng with his violent humiliations,
Guǎnghàn's Lǐ Zhēn who arbitrarily dismembered people,
Dōngjùn's Mí Pú who sawed necks,
Tiānshuǐ's Luò Bì with his pressing interrogations,
Hédōng's Chǔ Guǎng's reckless killings,
Jīngzhào's Wújì,
Féngyì's Yīn Zhōu, venomous as vipers,
and Shuǐhéng's Yán Fèng who beat and extorted—
why bother enumerating them!
Why bother enumerating them!
The traces of Dàyuān were first revealed by Zhāng Qiān.
Zhāng Qiān was a man of Hànzhōng.
During the Jiànyuán era, he served as a court gentleman.
At that time, the Son of Heaven questioned
surrendering Xiōngnú,
who all said the Xiōngnú
had defeated the Yuèzhī king,
making his skull into a drinking vessel,
and the Yuèzhī fled,
nursing a lasting hatred for the Xiōngnú,
but had no allies to jointly attack them.
The Hàn, seeking to confront the barbarians,
upon hearing this,
decided to send an envoy.
The route necessarily passed through Xiōngnú territory,
so they recruited
capable envoys.
Zhāng Qiān, then a gentleman, answered the call,
was sent to the Yuèzhī,
and departed Lóngxī with the former Xiōngnú slave
Gānfù of the Tángyì clan.
Passing through Xiōngnú lands,
the Xiōngnú captured them,
escorting them to the Chányú.
The Chányú detained them,
saying: "The Yuèzhī are north of us—
how can the Hàn send envoys there?
If I wished to send envoys to Yuè,
would the Hàn allow me?"
He detained Zhāng Qiān for over ten years,
gave him a wife,
and he had children,
yet Zhāng Qiān never relinquished the Hàn envoy's credentials.
While living among the Xiōngnú,
surveillance gradually relaxed,
and Zhāng Qiān fled with his retinue
toward the Yuèzhī,
traveling west for tens of days
until reaching Dàyuān.
Dàyuān had heard of Hàn's abundant wealth,
wishing to establish relations
but unable to,
so upon seeing Zhāng Qiān,
they were delighted,
and asked: "Where do you intend to go?"
Zhāng Qiān said:
"I was sent by Hàn to the Yuèzhī,
but the Xiōngnú blocked my path.
Now I have escaped,
and hope Your Majesty will send guides to escort me.
If I truly reach there,
and return to Hàn,
Hàn's gifts to you would be beyond measure."
Dàyuān found this reasonable,
sent Zhāng Qiān on,
provided guides and interpreters,
reaching Kāngjū,
and Kāngjū relayed them to the Great Yuèzhī.
The Great Yuèzhī king had been killed by the barbarians,
and his crown prince was made king.
Having subjugated Dàxià and settled there,
the land was fertile,
with few invaders,
their aspirations peaceful and content,
and considering themselves distant from Hàn,
they had little intention of avenging themselves on the barbarians.
Zhāng Qiān, from the Yuèzhī to Dàxià,
ultimately failed to secure a firm commitment from the Yuèzhī.
He stayed over a year,
then returned,
skirting the Southern Mountains,
intending to return through Qiāng territory,
but was captured again by the Xiōngnú.
After over a year's detention,
the Chányú died,
the Left Gūlí King attacked the crown prince
and usurped the throne,
causing internal strife,
and Zhāng Qiān fled back to Hàn with his Xiōngnú wife and Tángyìfù.
Hàn appointed Zhāng Qiān as Grand Master of the Palace,
and Tángyìfù as Lord of Embassy Missions.
Zhāng Qiān was robust and forceful,
broad-minded and trustworthy,
beloved by the barbarians.
Tángyìfù, originally a barbarian,
was skilled in archery,
and in dire straits would hunt birds and beasts
to provide food.
Initially,
Zhāng Qiān set out with over a hundred men,
and after thirteen years abroad,
only two returned.
Zhāng Qiān personally reached Dàyuān,
Dàyuèzhī, Dàxià, and Kāngjū,
and heard reports
of five or six large neighboring states,
which he fully reported to the Son of Heaven.
He said:
Dàyuān lies southwest of the Xiōngnú,
due west of Hàn, about ten thousand lǐ from Hàn.
Their custom is settled dwelling,
farming the land,
growing rice and wheat.
They have grape wine.
They have many fine horses,
horses that sweat blood,
said to be descendants of heavenly horses.
They have walled cities and houses.
Their dependent settlements include over seventy large and small cities,
with a population of several hundred thousand.
Their soldiers use bows, spears, and horseback archery.
To the north lies Kāngjū,
to the west Dàyuèzhī,
to the southwest Dàxià,
to the northeast Wūsūn,
to the east Yūshēn and Yútián.
West of Yútián,
the rivers all flow westward,
emptying into the Western Sea;
to the east, rivers flow eastward,
emptying into the Salt Marsh.
The Salt Marsh runs underground,
and to its south, the Yellow River's source emerges.
There is much jade,
and the river flows into the Central Kingdom.
Lóulán and Gūshī have walled cities,
bordering the Salt Marsh.
The Salt Marsh is about five thousand lǐ from Cháng'ān.
The Xiōngnú right flank occupies
the area east of the Salt Marsh,
reaching the Great Wall in Lǒngxī,
connecting with the Qiāng to the south,
blocking the Hàn route.
Wūsūn is about two thousand lǐ northeast of Dàyuān,
a nomadic state,
moving with their herds,
sharing customs with the Xiōngnú.
They have several tens of thousands of archers,
daring in battle.
They once submitted to the Xiōngnú,
but when they grew strong,
they took back their tributary status,
refusing to attend court assemblies.
Kāngjū is about two thousand lǐ northwest of Dàyuān,
a nomadic state,
largely sharing customs with the Yuèzhī.
They have eighty to ninety thousand archers.
They border Dàyuān. The state is small,
paying tribute to Yuèzhī in the south,
and to Xiōngnú in the east.
Yǎncài is about two thousand lǐ northwest of Kāngjū,
a nomadic state,
largely sharing customs with Kāngjū.
They have over a hundred thousand archers.
They border a great marsh, with no visible shore,
likely the Northern Sea.
Dàyuèzhī is about two to three thousand lǐ west of Dàyuān,
residing north of the Guī River.
To the south lies Dàxià,
to the west Ānxī,
to the north Kāngjū.
They are a nomadic state,
moving with their herds,
sharing customs with the Xiōngnú.
They have one to two hundred thousand archers.
They were strong in the past,
looking down on the Xiōngnú,
but when Mòdú ascended,
he attacked and defeated the Yuèzhī,
and by the time of the Xiōngnú's Lǎoshàng Chányú,
he killed the Yuèzhī king,
using his skull as a drinking vessel.
Originally, the Yuèzhī lived
between Dūnhuáng and Qílián,
and after being defeated by the Xiōngnú,
they moved far away,
passed Dàyuān,
attacked Dàxià to the west and subjugated them,
then established their capital north of the Guī River as the royal court.
The remaining small group that could not leave
sought refuge with the Qiāng of the Southern Mountains,
called Xiǎoyuèzhī.
Ānxī is several thousand lǐ west of Dàyuèzhī.
Their custom is settled dwelling,
farming the land,
growing rice and wheat,
and making grape wine.
Their cities resemble those of Dàyuān.
They have several hundred large and small dependent cities,
covering an area of several thousand lǐ,
making them the largest state.
They border the Guī River,
have markets,
where the people trade using carts and boats,
traveling to neighboring states sometimes for thousands of lǐ.
They use silver for currency,
with coins bearing the king's face,
and when the king dies, they change the coins,
imitating the new king's face.
They write horizontally on leather as records.
To the west lies Tiáozhī,
to the north Yǎncài and Líxuān.
Tiáozhī is several thousand lǐ west of Ānxī,
bordering the Western Sea.
It is hot and humid.
They farm the land,
growing rice.
They have large birds,
with eggs the size of jars.
The population is very large,
often with minor chieftains,
and Ānxī controls them,
regarding them as a foreign state.
The state is skilled in illusions.
Ānxī elders have heard
that Tiáozhī has the Ruò River
and the Queen Mother of the West,
but none have seen them.
Dàxià is over two thousand lǐ southwest of Dàyuān,
south of the Guī River.
Their custom is settled dwelling,
with cities and houses,
sharing customs with Dàyuān.
They have no great king or overlord,
often installing minor chiefs in cities.
Their military is weak,
and they fear battle.
They are skilled in trade.
When Dàyuèzhī moved west,
they attacked and defeated them,
and all became subjects of Dàxià.
Dàxià has a large population,
about over a million.
Their capital is called Lánshì City,
where markets trade various goods.
To the southeast lies the state of Shēndú.
Zhāng Qiān said: "When I was in Dàxià,
I saw Qióng bamboo canes
and Shǔ cloth.
I asked,
'How did you obtain these?'
The people of Dàxià said:
'Our merchants went to Shēndú to buy them.
Shēndú is several thousand lǐ southeast of Dàxià.
Their custom is settled dwelling,
largely similar to Dàxià,
but low-lying, damp, and hot.
Their people ride elephants into battle.
The state borders a great river.'
From my estimation,
Dàxià is twelve thousand lǐ from Hàn, located southwest of Hàn.
Now Shēndú is again
several thousand lǐ southeast of Dàxià,
yet has Shǔ goods,
indicating it is not far from Shǔ.
Now, to send envoys to Dàxià,
passing through Qiāng territory is dangerous,
and the Qiāng people are hostile;
slightly north,
and they would be captured by the Xiōngnú;
going from Shǔ would be a direct route,
with no bandits."
The Son of Heaven, having heard that Dàyuān, Dàxià,
Ānxī, and others are all large states,
rich in exotic goods,
settled dwellers,
somewhat sharing similar livelihoods with the Central Kingdom,
with weak militaries,
and valuing Hàn's wealth;
and to the north, Dàyuèzhī,
Kāngjū, and others,
with strong militaries,
could be won over with bribes and incentives to court.
If indeed they could be righteously subjugated,
then the territory would expand ten thousand lǐ,
with multiple translations,
attracting diverse customs,
The Son of Heaven was pleased,
considering Zhāng Qiān's words to be correct,
and thus ordered Qiān to dispatch covert envoys from Shu's Qiánwèi Commandery,
sending them out along four routes simultaneously:
one exiting via Máng,
one via Rǎn,
one via Xǐ,
and one via Qióng and Bó.
Each traveled one to two thousand lǐ.
The northern routes were blocked by the Dī and Zuó peoples,
and the southern routes by the Xī and Kūnmíng peoples.
The Kūnmíng tribes had no chieftains,
were skilled in plunder and theft,
and repeatedly killed or captured Hàn envoys,
so ultimately, passage could not be secured.
However, it was heard that about a thousand lǐ to their west
there was a state where people rode elephants, called Diānyuè,
and some Shu merchants illicitly transporting goods had reached it.
Thus, the Hàn, in seeking a route to Dàxià (Bactria),
first established communication with the state of Diān.
Earlier,
the Hàn had wanted to open relations with the southwestern tribes,
but the costs were high
and the routes impassable,
so they abandoned the effort.
After Zhāng Qiān reported that it could
provide access to Dàxià,
they resumed efforts with the southwestern tribes.
Qiān, serving as a Colonel,
accompanied the Great General in attacking the Xiōngnú,
and knowing the locations of water and pasture,
enabled the army to avoid shortages.
For this, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Bówàng.
This was in the sixth year of the Yuánshuò era.
The following year,
Qiān, as Commandant of the Guards,
joined General Lǐ in marching from Yòuběipíng to attack the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú surrounded General Lǐ,
and his army suffered heavy losses;
Qiān arrived late to the battle
and was sentenced to death,
but redeemed himself to become a commoner.
That year, the Hàn sent the Swift Cavalry General
to defeat tens of thousands of Xiōngnú in the Western Regions,
advancing to the Qílián Mountains.
The next year,
King Húnxié led his people to surrender to the Hàn,
and from Jīnchéng, Héxī west to the Southern Mountains
and as far as the Salt Marsh, the area was empty of Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú occasionally sent scouts there,
but rarely.
Two years later,
the Hàn attacked and drove the Chányú north of the desert.
After this, the Son of Heaven repeatedly questioned
Qiān about Dàxià and other states.
Having lost his marquisate,
Qiān took the opportunity to say:
"When I was living among the Xiōngnú,
I heard of the Wūsūn king called Kūnmò.
Kūnmò's father
ruled a small state on the western border of the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú attacked and killed his father,
and the infant Kūnmò was abandoned in the wild.
Ravens carried meat and flew above him,
and a wolf came to suckle him.
The Chányú found this strange,
considering it divine,
and took him in to raise.
When he grew up,
he was made a general,
achieved several merits,
and the Chányú returned his father's people
to Kūnmò,
ordering him to guard the western frontier long-term.
Kūnmò gathered and nurtured his people,
attacked neighboring small settlements,
commanded tens of thousands of archers,
and became skilled in warfare.
After the Chányú's death,
Kūnmò led his people far away,
declared neutrality,
and refused to attend Xiōngnú assemblies.
The Xiōngnú sent surprise troops to attack him
but could not defeat him,
deemed it supernatural and kept their distance,
thus loosely controlling him
without major attacks.
Now the Chányú is newly hard-pressed by the Hàn,
and the former territory of Húnxié is empty and unpopulated.
The barbarians customarily covet Hàn wealth and goods;
if we truly seize this moment
to richly bribe the Wūsūn with gifts,
enticing them to move eastward
to settle in the former lands of Húnxié,
and form a brotherly alliance with the Hàn,
the situation would favor their compliance.
If they comply,
it would be like cutting off the Xiōngnú's right arm.
Once allied with the Wūsūn,
states west of them like Dàxià
could all be summoned
to become outer vassals."
The Son of Heaven agreed,
appointed Qiān as Chief Commandant of the Palace Gentlemen,
leading three hundred men,
with two horses each,
and tens of thousands of cattle and sheep,
carrying gold, coins, and silks worth billions,
with many deputy envoys holding credentials,
so that wherever routes were passable, they could be sent to neighboring states.
When Qiān arrived in Wūsūn,
King Kūnmò of Wūsūn
received the Hàn envoy with the same protocol as for the Xiōngnú Chányú.
Qiān was greatly ashamed,
and knowing the barbarians' greed,
said:
"The Son of Heaven bestows gifts;
if the king does not bow in thanks, the gifts will be taken back."
Kūnmò rose and bowed to receive the gifts,
but otherwise remained as before.
Qiān explained the mission's purpose:
"If Wūsūn can move east
to settle in the lands of Húnxié,
then the Hàn will send a princess
to be Kūnmò's wife."
The Wūsūn state was divided;
the king was old,
distant from the Hàn,
unaware of its size,
had long been subservient to the Xiōngnú,
and moreover was close to them.
His senior officials all feared the Hú (Xiōngnú),
did not wish to move,
and the king could not act autocratically.
Qiān failed to grasp the crux of the matter.
Kūnmò had over ten sons;
his middle son was Dàlù,
who was strong
and skilled at leading troops,
commanding over ten thousand cavalry
stationed separately.
Dàlù's elder brother was the crown prince,
who had a son named Cénqǔ,
but the crown prince died early.
On his deathbed, he said to his father Kūnmò:
"You must make Cénqǔ the crown prince,
and not let anyone else replace him."
Kūnmò, grieving, agreed,
and eventually made Cénqǔ the crown prince.
Dàlù was angry that he could not replace the crown prince,
so he gathered his brothers,
led his followers in rebellion,
and plotted to attack Cénqǔ and Kūnmò.
Kūnmò was old
and often feared Dàlù would kill Cénqǔ,
so he gave Cénqǔ over ten thousand cavalry
to station separately,
while Kūnmò himself kept over ten thousand cavalry for his own defense.
The state's populace
was divided into three parts,
but overall remained loosely under Kūnmò's control.
Kūnmò, because of this,
did not dare to make a firm agreement with Qiān.
Qiān then sent deputy envoys to Dàyuān (Ferghana),
Kāngjū (Sogdiana), Dàyuèzhī, Dàxià (Bactria), Ānxī (Parthia), Shēndú (India),
Yútián (Khotan), Wūshēn, and other neighboring states.
Wūsūn provided guides and interpreters to escort Qiān
back.
Qiān, along with dozens of envoys sent by Wūsūn
and dozens of horses,
returned to offer thanks,
thereby allowing them to observe the Hàn
and learn of its vastness.
Upon Qiān's return,
he was appointed Grand Herald,
ranked among the Nine Ministers.
A little over a year later,
he died.
The Wūsūn envoys, having seen the Hàn's populous wealth,
reported back to their state,
which then held the Hàn in greater esteem.
A little over a year after that,
the envoys sent by Qiān to open communications with Dàxià and other states
all returned with people from those regions,
and thus the northwestern states began
to have relations with the Hàn.
However, after Zhāng Qiān pioneered the passage,
subsequent envoys sent
all claimed to be the Marquis of Bówàng,
using this as credibility with foreign states,
which thereby trusted them.
After the death of Marquis Bówàng Qiān,
the Xiōngnú heard that Hàn had connected with Wūsūn,
grew angry,
and wanted to attack it.
When Hàn envoys went to Wūsūn,
passing south of it,
reaching Dàyuānzhī and connecting with Dàròuzhī,
Wūsūn then became fearful,
sent envoys presenting horses,
and wished to marry a Hàn princess
to become brothers.
The Son of Heaven consulted his ministers for proposals,
all saying
"They must first present betrothal gifts,
then we can send a daughter."
Earlier,
the Son of Heaven had consulted the Book of Changes,
which said
"Divine horses should come from the northwest."
Obtaining Wūsūn's excellent horses,
he named them "Heavenly Horses."
When he acquired the sweat-blood horses from Dàyuān,
even more robust,
he renamed the Wūsūn horses
"Western Extreme,"
and called the Dàyuān horses
"Heavenly Horses."
Meanwhile, Hàn began building west from Língjū,
initially establishing Jiuquan Prefecture
to connect with northwestern states.
Consequently, they increased missions to Ānxī,
Yāncài, Líxuān, Tiáozhī, and Shēndú.
As the Son of Heaven favored Dàyuān horses,
envoys crowded the roads.
Larger missions to foreign states numbered
several hundred,
smaller ones over a hundred people,
with provisions carried
largely imitating Marquis Bówàng's time.
Later, they became more accustomed and reduced in size.
Hàn averaged annually
ten-plus missions at most, five or six at least,
the farthest taking eight or nine years,
the nearest several years to return.
At that time, Hàn had conquered Yuè,
and Shǔ and southwestern tribes were all shaken,
requesting officials and attending court.
Thus, Yìzhōu, Yuèxī,
Zāngkē,
Chénlí, and Wēnshān prefectures were established,
hoping to extend territory forward
to connect with Dàxià.
Then envoys like Bó Shǐchāng and Lǚ Yuèrén
over ten missions yearly
were sent from these new prefectures to Dàxià,
but all were blocked at Kūnmíng,
killed, with goods looted,
ultimately failing to reach Dàxià.
Thereupon, Hàn dispatched convicts from the three capital regions,
plus tens of thousands from Bā and Shǔ,
sending generals Guō Chāng
and Wèi Guǎng
to attack Kūnmíng's obstruction of Hàn envoys,
decapitating or capturing tens of thousands
before leaving.
Subsequent envoys
were again harassed by Kūnmíng,
never achieving passage.
Whereas the northern route from Jiuquan to Dàxià,
with numerous envoys,
led foreign states to tire of Hàn goods,
not valuing their items.
Since Marquis Bówàng opened foreign routes
and gained honor,
later officials and soldiers
all competed to submit reports
about foreign wonders and advantages,
seeking missions.
The Son of Heaven, considering the extreme distances,
unattractive to most,
heeded their words,
gave them credentials,
recruited officials and commoners regardless of origin,
equipped them with personnel, and sent them,
to broaden the routes.
Upon return,
they inevitably embezzled goods,
or deviated from orders,
but the Son of Heaven, familiar with this,
would investigate and impose severe penalties,
then motivate them to redeem by
seeking further missions.
Mission opportunities became endless,
encouraging lawlessness.
These officials and soldiers also repeatedly
exaggerated foreign possessions,
grand claims earning credentials,
minor ones becoming deputies,
so deceitful, unreliable individuals
all vied to imitate them.
The envoys were mostly poor men's sons,
misappropriating government goods,
aiming to buy cheap
for personal profit abroad.
Foreign states also tired of envoys
whose words varied in reliability,
estimating Hàn troops too distant to arrive,
restricted food supplies
to distress Hàn envoys.
Hàn envoys, deprived and resentful,
clashed with each other.
Small states like Lóulán and Gūshī,
astride the route,
attacked and robbed Hàn officials like Wáng Huī
particularly severely.
Meanwhile, Xiōngnú raiders frequently
ambushed envoys to western states.
Envoys vied to report
foreign crises,
that they had walled cities,
weak troops easily attacked.
Thus, the Son of Heaven
consequently sent Marquis Cóngpiào Pòniú
leading allied cavalry and prefectural troops numbering tens of thousands,
reaching the Xiōng River,
intending to attack the Hú,
who all fled.
The following year,
attacking Gūshī,
Pòniú with over 700 light cavalry
arrived first,
captured the King of Lóulán,
then crushed Gūshī.
Thereby, he wielded military might to pressure Wūsūn,
Dàyuān, and others.
Returning,
he was enfeoffed as Zhuóyě Hóu.
Wáng Huī, frequently envoyed,
suffered under Lóulán,
reported to the Son of Heaven,
who dispatched troops
ordering Huī to assist Pòniú
in defeating them,
enfeoffing Huī as Hào Hóu.
Thus, Jiuquan's beacon towers and barriers
extended to Yùmén.
Wūsūn sent a thousand horses
to betroth a Hàn woman,
Hàn sent a imperial clan daughter, Princess Jiāngdū,
to marry Wūsūn,
and King Kūnmò of Wūsūn made her his Right Consort.
Xiōngnú also sent a woman to marry Kūnmò,
who made her his Left Consort.
Kūnmò said, "I am old,"
so he had his grandson Cénqǔ marry the princess.
Wūsūn had many horses,
its wealthy owning up to four or five thousand.
Earlier,
when Hàn envoys reached Ānxī,
its king ordered 20,000 cavalry
to greet them at the eastern border.
The eastern border was thousands of miles from the capital.
Traveling to it,
they passed dozens of cities,
with continuous, populous settlements.
Hàn envoys returned,
after which Ānxī sent envoys with them
to observe Hàn's vastness,
presenting large bird eggs
and skilled illusionists from Líxuān to Hàn.
Western minor states like Huānqián and Dàyì of Dàyuān,
eastern ones like Gūshī, Wūshēn, and Sūxiè,
all followed Hàn envoys to present tribute to the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven was greatly pleased.
Meanwhile, Hàn envoys traced the Yellow River's source,
finding it emerged from Yútián,
whose mountains had much jade and stone,
gathered and brought back;
the Son of Heaven, consulting ancient texts,
named the mountain where the river emerged
Kūnlún.
At that time, the Emperor frequently inspected coastal regions,
taking all foreign guests along,
passing through populous cities,
distributing wealth and silk as rewards,
lavishly supplying them,
to display Hàn's prosperity and abundance.
Thereupon, grand wrestling matches were held,
extraordinary performances and various exotic spectacles were presented,
attracting large crowds of spectators.
Rewards and gifts were distributed,
with pools of wine and forests of meat,
allowing foreign guests to tour extensively the various
storehouses and treasuries filled with accumulated goods,
so they might witness the vastness of the Hàn dynasty,
and be awestruck by it.
Moreover, with the addition of skilled illusionists' craft,
the wrestling matches and extraordinary performances
underwent annual innovations,
growing increasingly magnificent and flourishing, starting from this time.
Diplomatic missions from northwestern foreign states
came and went in succession.
West of Dàyuān,
all considered themselves remote,
still arrogant and complacent,
impossible to subdue through ritual
or control through loose rein policies.
From Wūsūn westward to Ānxī,
due to proximity to the Xiōngnú,
whom the Xiōngnú had oppressed the Yuèzhī,
when Xiōngnú envoys
carried a single credential from the Chányú,
then each state would relay provisions,
not daring to detain or harass them;
but when it came to Hàn envoys,
unless they produced silks and fabrics, they could not obtain food,
and unless they purchased livestock
they had no mounts to use.
The reason for this was
their distance from Hàn,
coupled with Hàn's abundance of wealth and goods,
so they had to trade to obtain what they desired,
yet also because they feared the Xiōngnú
more than the Hàn envoys.
In Dàyuān and surrounding areas, they made wine from grapes,
with wealthy households storing over ten thousand shí of wine,
some aged for decades without spoiling.
Customarily, they were fond of drink,
and their horses were fond of alfalfa.
Hàn envoys brought back their seeds,
whereupon the Son of Heaven began planting alfalfa and grapes
in fertile land.
As heavenly horses multiplied,
and foreign envoys came in increasing numbers,
the grounds around detached palaces and lodges
were fully planted with grapes and alfalfa as far as the eye could see.
From Dàyuān westward to Ānxī,
although the states spoke rather different languages,
their customs were largely similar,
and they understood each other's speech.
The people all had deep-set eyes,
and abundant beards and facial hair,
excelling at commerce,
haggling over the smallest coins.
Customarily, they esteemed women,
and whatever the women said, the men would then decide accordingly.
Their lands all lacked silk and lacquer,
and they did not know how to cast coins or vessels.
When Hàn envoys defected
or soldiers surrendered,
they taught them to cast other weapons.
Upon obtaining Hàn's yellow and white gold,
they would immediately make it into vessels,
not using it as currency.
As Hàn envoys going there increased,
their minor attendants generally
often presented familiar tales to the Son of Heaven,
saying:
"In Dàyuān, there are excellent horses in the Èrshī City,
but they are hidden and not given to Hàn envoys."
The Son of Heaven, already fond of Dàyuān horses,
upon hearing this, was determined,
and sent the strong warrior Chē Lìng
bearing a thousand pieces of gold and a golden horse
to request the fine horses from the king of Dàyuān at Èrshī City.
The state of Dàyuān, rich in Hàn goods,
deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Hàn is far from us,
and the Salt Marsh has repeatedly caused failures,
to our north there are Hú bandits,
to our south, water and grass are scarce.
Moreover, frequently
there are deserted settlements,
with many lacking food.
When Hàn envoys come in groups of several hundred,
they often lack food,
with over half dying;
how then could they
send a large army here?
They can do nothing to us.
Besides, the Èrshī horses
are Dàyuān's treasure horses."
Thus, they refused to give them to the Hàn envoy.
The Hàn envoy, enraged,
spoke recklessly,
smashed the golden horse, and departed.
The nobles of Dàyuān angrily said:
"The Hàn envoy has greatly insulted us!"
They sent the Hàn envoy away,
ordering their eastern border city of Yùchéng to intercept
and attack, killing the Hàn envoy,
and seizing his possessions.
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven was greatly angered.
Those who had previously been envoys to Dàyuān, such as Yáo Dìnghàn and others,
said the troops were weak,
asserting that with Hàn troops not exceeding three thousand men,
using strong crossbows to shoot them,
they could capture and crush Dàyuān entirely.
The Son of Heaven had previously sent Zhuóyĕhóu to attack Lóulán,
who with seven hundred cavalry arrived first,
captured its king,
and thus considered Yáo Dìnghàn's words credible,
