and wishing to enfeoff his favored consort Lǐ shì,
appointed Lǐ Guǎnglì as the Èrshī General,
mobilizing six thousand cavalry from subordinate states,
and tens of thousands of unruly youths from commanaderies and states,
to go and attack Dàyuān.
The objective was to reach Èrshī City and obtain the fine horses,
hence the title "Èrshī General."
Zhào Shǐchéng was appointed army rectifier,
the former Hàohóu Wáng Huī was sent to guide the army,
and Lǐ Duō served as colonel,
managing military affairs.
This was the first year of the Tàichū era.
Meanwhile, in Guāndōng, locusts rose in great swarms,
flying west as far as Dūnlhuáng.
General Èrshī's army, having marched west past the Salt Marsh,
the small states along the route
were terrified,
each fortifying their city defenses,
unwilling to provide food.
Attacks could not capture them.
Those captured provided food;
those not captured after several days
were abandoned.
By the time they reached Yùchéng,
the troops that had arrived numbered only a few thousand,
all hungry and exhausted.
They attacked Yùchéng,
but Yùchéng soundly defeated them,
inflicting heavy casualties.
General Èrshī, along with Duō,
Shǐchéng, and others, deliberated:
"We cannot even take Yùchéng,
let alone their royal capital?"
They led the troops back.
The round trip took two years.
Upon returning to Dūnlhuáng,
less than one or two out of ten troops remained.
He sent a messenger to submit a report, saying
"the road is long and food is often scarce;
moreover, the soldiers do not fear battle,
but fear hunger.
Our numbers are few,
insufficient to conquer Dàyuān.
I wish to temporarily withdraw the troops,
and return later with reinforced numbers."
The Son of Heaven, upon hearing this,
was greatly enraged,
and sent envoys to block the Yùmén Pass,
declaring that any soldier daring to enter
would be immediately executed!
Èrshī, terrified,
thus remained in Dūnlhuáng.
That summer,
Hàn lost over twenty thousand of Zhuóyĕ's troops
to the Xiōngnú.
Ministers and court advisors all wished
to halt the attack on Dàyuān,
and focus on attacking the Hú.
But the Son of Heaven, having already committed to punishing Dàyuān,
reasoned that if such a small state could not be subdued,
then states like Dàxià would despise Hàn,
the fine horses from Dàyuān would never come,
and Wūsūn and Lúntóu would easily harass Hàn envoys,
making Hàn a laughingstock among foreign states.
He then prosecuted those like Dèng Guāng who had particularly opposed attacking Dàyuān,
pardoned convicts and skilled archers,
mobilized more unruly youths
and border cavalry,
and after over a year
sixty thousand men set out from Dūnlhuáng,
not including those following privately with their own supplies.
There were one hundred thousand oxen,
over thirty thousand horses,
and donkeys, mules, and camels numbering in the tens of thousands.
They carried abundant provisions,
weapons and crossbows were well-equipped,
the whole land was in turmoil,
as all relayed supplies for the campaign against Dàyuān,
There were over fifty colonels in total.
The city of the King of Yuān had no wells,
so they all drew water from the flowing river outside the city.
Therefore, hydraulic engineers were dispatched
to divert the water source beneath the city,
leaving the city without water.
An additional 180,000 garrison soldiers were mobilized,
north of Jiǔquán and Zhāngyē,
establishing Jūyán and Xiūtú
to defend Jiǔquán,
while conscripting seven categories of convicts from across the empire,
and transporting dried provisions to supply Èrshī.
Supply carts and personnel stretched continuously
all the way to Dūnhuáng.
Two men skilled in horse training were appointed
as Commandants for Driving Horses,
prepared to defeat Yuān
and select their finest horses.
Thus, Èrshī set out once more,
with a large army,
and every small state they reached welcomed them,
providing food for the troops.
Upon reaching Lúntóu,
Lúntóu did not surrender,
so they attacked for several days,
massacring its inhabitants.
From there westward,
they advanced unimpeded to the city of Yuān,
with 30,000 Hàn troops arriving.
Yuān forces counterattacked the Hàn army,
but the Hàn troops defeated them with arrows,
forcing Yuān soldiers to retreat
and barricade themselves in their city.
Èrshī's troops intended to attack Yùchéng,
but lingering there risked casualties
and would allow Yuān to devise more deceitful tactics,
so they proceeded first to Yuān,
cut off its water source,
and diverted it away,
leaving Yuān
already distressed and beleaguered.
They besieged the city,
attacking for over forty days,
until its outer walls crumbled,
capturing a Yuān noble
and the brave general Jiānmí.
Yuān was terrified,
retreating into the inner city.
The Yuān nobles deliberated among themselves:
"The Hàn attack us because
King Wúguǎ concealed fine horses
and killed Hàn envoys.
If we now kill King Wúguǎ and offer the fine horses,
the Hàn troops should withdraw;
if they do not,
then we can fight to the death, and it will not be too late."
The Yuān nobles all agreed,
jointly killed their king Wúguǎ,
and sent a noble to Èrshī with his head,
proposing terms:
"Do not attack us.
We will surrender all our fine horses,
for you to take as you wish,
and supply the Hàn army with food.
If you refuse,
we will kill all the fine horses,
and Kāngjū's reinforcements will soon arrive.
When they come,
we will fight from within,
Kāngjū from without, engaging your army.
Consider carefully, Hàn army,
what will you do?"
At that time, Kāngjū scouts observed the Hàn troops,
seeing they were still strong,
and dared not advance.
Èrshī consulted with Zhào Shǐchéng,
Lǐ Duō, and others:
"We hear the city of Yuān
has recently acquired men from Qín,
who know how to dig wells,
and their provisions are still ample.
Our purpose here
was to punish the chief culprit, Wúguǎ.
Wúguǎ's head has been delivered,
yet if we do not agree to withdraw now,
they will hold firm,
and Kāngjū, waiting for the Hàn army to tire,
will come to rescue Yuān,
ensuring our defeat."
The officers all agreed,
and accepted Yuān's terms.
Yuān then brought out their fine horses,
allowing the Hàn to choose,
and provided ample food for the Hàn army.
The Hàn army took several dozen of the finest horses,
and over three thousand medium and lower-grade horses, both male and female,
and installed as king of Yuān a noble named Mòcài, who had previously treated Hàn envoys well,
concluding a treaty and withdrawing troops.
They never entered the inner city.
Thus, they ended the campaign and returned.
Initially, when Èrshī set out west from Dūnhuáng,
thinking the forces too large,
and the states along the way could not supply them,
he divided them into several armies,
taking northern and southern routes.
Colonel Wáng Shēnshēng,
former Court Diplomat Hú Chōngguó, and over a thousand others
separately arrived at Yùchéng.
Yùchéng defended its city,
refusing to supply their army.
Wáng Shēnshēng was two hundred lǐ from the main force,
relying on reconnaissance and underestimating the enemy,
demanded supplies from Yùchéng.
Yùchéng refused to provide food,
spied on Shēnshēng's army
and found their numbers dwindling,
attacked at dawn with three thousand men,
killing Shēnshēng and others,
routing his army,
with only a few escaping,
fleeing to Èrshī.
Èrshī ordered
the Commandant for Grain Collection Shàngguān Jié
to attack and defeat Yùchéng.
The King of Yùchéng fled to Kāngjū,
and Jié pursued him there.
Kāngjū, hearing that Hàn had defeated Yuān,
surrendered the King of Yùchéng to Jié,
who ordered four cavalrymen to bind
and escort him to the General-in-Chief.
The four men discussed among themselves:
"The King of Yùchéng is deeply hated by Hàn,
yet if we take him alive,
we might botch this important mission."
They wanted to kill him,
but none dared strike first.
Cavalryman Zhào Dì from Shàngguī,
the youngest,
drew his sword and struck,
beheading the King of Yùchéng,
and carried the head.
Dì and Jié
then caught up with the General-in-Chief.
Earlier,
when Èrshī set out later,
the Son of Heaven sent envoys to inform Wūsūn,
urging them to send a large force to jointly attack Yuān.
Wūsūn dispatched two thousand cavalry,
but remained ambivalent,
refusing to advance.
As General Èrshī returned east,
the various small states he passed through,
hearing of Yuān's defeat,
all sent their sons and brothers to join the army
and present tribute,
to see the Son of Heaven,
thus becoming hostages.
In Èrshī's campaign against Yuān,
Army Supervisor Zhào Shǐchéng fought valiantly,
achieving the most merits;
and Shàngguān Jié
dared to penetrate deep,
while Lǐ Duō devised strategies.
The troops that entered Yùmén
numbered over ten thousand,
with over a thousand army horses.
Èrshī's later expedition,
though not short of supplies,
and battle deaths were not excessive,
the officers were greedy,
mostly uncaring toward the soldiers,
exploiting them,
leading to many deaths from these causes.
The Son of Heaven, for campaigning against Yuān from ten thousand lǐ away,
overlooked their faults,
enfeoffing Guǎnglì as Marquis of Hǎixī.
He also enfeoffed cavalryman Zhào Dì, who personally beheaded the King of Yùchéng,
as Marquis of Xīnzhì.
Army Supervisor Zhào Shǐ became Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments,
Shàngguān Jié became Superintendent of the Lesser Treasury,
Lǐ Duō became Governor of Shàngdǎng.
Among the army officers,
three became Nine Ministers,
over a hundred became Chancellors of feudal states, Governors of commanderies,
or officials with two-thousand-dan rank,
and over a thousand held ranks below one thousand dan.
Those who volunteered
received offices beyond their expectations,
while those conscripted for offenses
had their service merits discounted.
The soldiers were rewarded with forty thousand catties of gold in value.
The campaign against Yuān took two expeditions,
lasting four years in total before concluding.
After the Hàn had conquered Yuān,
they established Mòcài as king of Yuān and departed.
A little over a year later,
the nobles of Yuān, considering Mòcài to be skilled in flattery
and having brought about the slaughter of their state,
joined together to kill Mòcài.
They established Wúguǎ's brother, named Chánfēng, as king of Yuān,
and sent his son to serve as a hostage in Hàn.
Hàn thereupon sent envoys with gifts to bestow upon them in order to pacify and control them.
Furthermore, Hàn dispatched more than ten missions
to the various foreign states west of Yuān,
seeking rare objects,
and taking the opportunity to demonstrate the might and virtue gained from the conquest of Yuān.
A Commandant was established at Dūnhuáng and Jiǔquán;
west to the Salt Water,
watchtowers were frequently established.
Furthermore, at Lúntóu, there were several hundred soldier-farmers;
an Office of Envoys was established there
to protect the farmland and store up grain,
in order to supply
those traveling to the foreign states.
The Grand Historian remarks:
The "Basic Annals of Yǔ" states
"The Yellow River issues from Kūnlún.
Kūnlún's height is over two thousand five hundred lǐ;
it is where the sun and moon in turn take shelter to create light and darkness.
On its summit are the Sweet Springs
and the Jasper Lake."
Now, since Zhāng Qiān's mission to Dàxià,
which traced the source of the Yellow River,
how can one perceive the Kūnlún described in the "Basic Annals"?
Therefore, when speaking of the mountains and rivers of the Nine Provinces,
the "Shàng Shū" comes close to the truth.
As for the strange creatures found in the "Basic Annals of Yǔ"
and the "Shānhǎi Jīng",
I dare not speak of them.
Hán Zǐ said:
"The Ruists use culture to subvert the law,
while the knights-errant use force to violate the prohibitions."
Both groups are criticized,
yet learned scholars are often praised by the world.
As for those who used their methods to attain
the positions of Chancellor, Minister, or High Official,
assisting and supporting their generation's ruler,
their achievements and fame are both recorded in the historical records;
there is certainly nothing more to be said.
But as for Jì Cì and Yuán Xiàn,
they were men of the back alleys,
who studied books and cherished the virtue
of the gentleman who walks alone,
holding to righteousness and not carelessly conforming to their age,
for which their age also laughed at them.
Therefore, Jì Cì and Yuán Xiàn lived their whole lives
in empty rooms with doors of thatch,
not weary of coarse clothes and simple food.
They have been dead for over four hundred years,
yet their disciples remember them untiringly.
Now, the wandering knights,
though their conduct does not conform to orthodox righteousness,
yet their words are trustworthy,
their actions decisive,
their promises sincere,
they do not cherish their own bodies,
but hasten to the distress
and hardship of other men.
Having already preserved the perishing and revived the dead,
they do not boast of their ability,
and are ashamed to tout their virtue.
Surely they also have qualities worthy of praise.
Moreover, crises and urgency
are something people encounter from time to time.
The Grand Historian remarks:
In former times, Yú Shùn was imperiled at the well and granary,
Yī Yǐn bore the tripod and cutting board,
Fù Yuè was concealed at Fùyǎn,
Lǚ Shàng was distressed at Jíjīn,
Yí Wú was shackled,
Bǎilǐ fed oxen,
Zhòngní was threatened in Kuāng,
and suffered famine in Chén and Cài.
These are all men whom learned scholars call
benevolent men possessing the Way,
yet even they encountered such calamities.
How much more so for men of average ability
who must traverse the degenerate currents of a disordered age?
How can one fully recount the harm they encounter!
A rustic saying goes:
"How does one know of benevolence and righteousness?
He who has already enjoyed their benefits is deemed virtuous."
Therefore, Bó Yí vilified Zhōu,
and starved to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain,
yet King Wén and King Wǔ did not, because of this, diminish in their kingly status;
while Zhí and Jué were violent and cruel,
yet their followers endlessly praised their righteousness.
From this perspective,
"He who steals a buckle is punished;
he who steals a state becomes a marquis;
at the marquis's gate
benevolence and righteousness reside" —
these are not empty words.
Now, the constrained scholars,
clinging to their narrow righteousness,
remain long isolated from the world.
How can they compare to those who lower their discourse
to the level of the common crowd,
drifting and floating with the age,
to seize glory and fame?
Yet the cloth-clad fellows,
establishing standards for giving and taking and for promises,
have their righteousness praised for a thousand lǐ.
They would die without regard for the world's opinion;
this is also a strength they possess,
and not something done carelessly.
Therefore, when men in dire straits
can entrust their lives to them,
is this not what people call
the worthies and heroes among men?
Truly, if one were to compare the influence and measure the strength
of the village knights-errant with Jì Cì and Yuán Xiàn,
and assess their contributions
to their age,
they could not be discussed on the same day.
But judged by the visibility of their achievements
and the trustworthiness of their words,
how can the righteousness of the knight-errant be considered insignificant!
Of the ancient knights-errant from common cloth,
none can be known now.
In recent times, men like Yánlíng,
Mèngcháng, Chūnshēn, Píngyuán, and Xìnlíng
were all relatives of kings,
relying on the wealth and influence of landed ministers and chancellors,
summoning the worthy men of the world,
and making their names illustrious among the feudal lords.
They cannot be said to be unworthy.
It is like calling out with the wind;
the voice is not increased in speed,
but the force is intensified.
As for the knights-errant of the back alleys,
cultivating their conduct
and honing their reputations,
their fame spread throughout the world,
and none failed to call them worthy —
this is truly difficult.
Yet both the Ruists and the Mohists rejected and excluded them,
and did not record them.
Before Qín,
the knights-errant from the common people
were obliterated and unseen;
I deeply regret this.
From what I have heard,
since the rise of Hàn, there have been men like Zhū Jiā,
Tián Zhòng, Wáng Gōng, Jù Mèng, and Guō Jiě.
Though at times they transgressed the legal net of their age,
their personal righteousness, integrity, purity, and humility
are worthy of praise.
Their fame was not falsely established,
and men did not follow them without cause.
As for those who form cliques,
strengthen their factions, and collude closely,
using wealth to command the poor,
violently bullying the orphaned and weak with their power,
indulging their desires for their own pleasure —
the wandering knights also despise them.
I lament that the common world
does not understand their true intent,
but crudely lumps Zhū Jiā, Guō Jiě, and others
together with the violent and powerful types,
laughing at them alike.
As for Lǔ's Zhū Jiā,
he was a contemporary of Emperor Gāozǔ.
The people of Lǔ all followed the Ruist teachings,
yet Zhū Jiā became famous for his knight-errantry.
The number of prominent men he sheltered and saved ran to the hundreds;
the ordinary people were beyond counting.
Yet he never boasted of his ability,
nor took pleasure in his virtue.
For all those he had once aided,
he only feared encountering them again.
Relieving others' insufficiency,
he began first with the poor and lowly.
His household held no surplus wealth;
his clothes lacked fine colors;
his meals did not feature multiple dishes;
his carriage was no more than a small ox-cart.
He devoted himself to rushing to others' emergencies,
considering them more important than his own private affairs.
Having secretly rescued General Jì Bù from peril,
when Jì Bù later became honored and noble,
he never once appeared before him for life.
From east of Hánguān Pass onward,
none did not crane their necks
eager to befriend him.
In Chǔ, Tián Zhòng was known for his chivalry,
loved swordsmanship,
served Zhū Jiā as a father,
and considered his own conduct inferior.
After Tián Zhòng died,
in Luòyáng there was Jù Mèng.
The people of Zhōu relied on commerce for livelihood,
yet Jù Mèng became prominent among the feudal lords through his chivalrous deeds.
When Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
Tiáohóu, as Grand Commandant,
riding a relay carriage and about to reach Hénán,
obtained Jù Mèng's support,
and joyfully said:
"Wú and Chǔ undertake a great enterprise
yet fail to seek out Mèng;
I know they are incapable of achieving anything."
While the empire was in turmoil,
for a chancellor to gain him
was like acquiring an enemy state, it was said.
Jù Mèng's conduct greatly resembled Zhū Jiā's,
but he enjoyed gambling,
often indulging in youthful games.
However, when Jù Mèng's mother died,
those sending off the funeral from distant places
numbered about a thousand carriages.
By the time Jù Mèng died,
his household lacked even ten catties of gold in remaining wealth.
And Wáng Mèng of Fúlí
was likewise renowned between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
At that time, the Jiǎn clan of Jǐnán and Zhōu Yōng of Chén
were also known for their boldness,
and when Emperor Jǐng heard of them,
he sent envoys to exterminate all such individuals.
Afterwards, the various Bái of Dài,
Hán Wúpì of Liáng, Xuē Guǎng of Yǎngdí,
and Hán Rú of Shǎn emerged one after another.
Guō Jiě
was a man of Zhǐ, styled Wēngbó,
the grandson of Xǔ Fù,
who was skilled in physiognomy.
Guō Jiě's father, due to his chivalrous conduct,
was executed during Emperor Wén's reign.
Guō Jiě was short in stature yet vigorous,
and did not drink alcohol.
In his youth, he was secretly vicious;
whenever resentful or displeased,
he personally killed many.
He lent his body to friends for revenge,
harbored fugitives, committed crimes, plundered and assaulted,
ceaselessly minted coins and excavated graves—
truly beyond counting.
By sheer fortune,
he often escaped from tight spots,
as if encountering amnesty.
As Guō Jiě grew older,
he changed his ways to become more restrained,
repaying resentment with virtue,
giving generously while expecting little.
Yet his fondness for being a knight-errant grew even stronger.
Having saved people's lives,
he did not boast of his achievements,
but his hidden viciousness rooted in his heart
still erupted over the slightest grievances as before.
Young men admired his conduct
and would often avenge him
without letting him know.
Guō Jiě's sister's son, relying on his influence,
while drinking with others,
forced them to gulp down their drinks.
If they couldn't handle it,
he insisted on pouring it down.
Angered,
one man drew a dagger and killed Guō Jiě's nephew,
then fled.
Guō Jiě's sister angrily said:
"With Wēngbó's righteousness,
my son was killed,
yet the murderer remains uncaught."
She left the corpse on the road,
unburied,
intending to shame Guō Jiě.
Guō Jiě sent someone to discreetly learn the killer's whereabouts.
The killer, cornered, turned himself in
and fully confessed to Guō Jiě.
Guō Jiě said:
"You killed him rightly,
for my nephew was in the wrong."
Thereupon he released the killer,
blamed his sister's son,
and collected the body for burial.
The gentlemen heard of this,
all praised Guō Jiě's righteousness,
and adhered to him even more.
When Guō Jiě came and went,
people would avoid him.
One man alone
sat sprawled and stared at him.
Guō Jiě sent someone to ask his name.
His followers wanted to kill the man.
Guō Jiě said:
"To live in a village and not be respected
is due to my lack of virtue;
what crime has he committed?"
He then secretly instructed the garrison officer:
"This man
is someone I value;
when his conscription duty comes, exempt him."
Every time his turn came,
repeatedly,
the officer did not summon him.
Perplexed,
he asked the reason
and found Guō Jiě had exempted him.
The sprawled-sitter then bared his upper body
to apologize.
Young men heard of this
and admired Guō Jiě's conduct even more.
In Luòyáng, there were people feuding with each other.
Worthy and powerful men of the city
mediating numbered in the tens,
yet they never listened.
Someone then went to see Guō Jiě.
Guō Jiě visited the feuding family at night,
and they reluctantly heeded him.
Guō Jiě then told them:
"I heard the gentlemen of Luòyáng
have mediated here,
but you mostly refused.
Now that you have kindly listened to me,
how could I, from another county,
usurp the authority of your city's worthy officials?"
He then left by night,
without anyone knowing,
saying:
"Do not act yet;
wait until I have left,
then let Luòyáng's powerful mediate,
and heed them."
Guō Jiě maintained respectfulness,
not daring to ride in a carriage
into the county court.
When visiting neighboring commaderies and kingdoms,
pleading on others' behalf,
if a matter could be resolved,
he resolved it;
if not,
he satisfied each party's wishes,
and only then dared to taste food and drink.
Thus, the gentlemen highly regarded him
and vied to be of service.
Young men of the city and worthy powerful men from nearby counties
often had over ten carriages visiting his door late at night,
requesting to host and provide for Guō Jiě's guests.
When the wealthy and powerful were relocated
to Màolíng,
Guō Jiě's family was poor
and did not meet the wealth criteria,
but the officials, fearful,
did not dare not relocate him.
General Wèi spoke on his behalf:
"Guō Jiě's family is poor and should not be relocated."
The Emperor said:
"A commoner wields such influence
that a general speaks for him;
this shows his family is not poor."
Thus, Guō Jiě's family was relocated.
The gentlemen seeing him off
contributed over ten million cash.
The son of Yáng Jìzhǔ of Zhǐ, a county clerk,
had nominated Guō Jiě for relocation.
Guō Jiě's nephew
cut off Clerk Yáng's head.
From then on, the Yáng and Guō families became enemies.
When Guō Jiě entered the pass,
the worthy and powerful within the pass,
whether they knew him or not,
upon hearing his reputation,
vied to befriend Guō Jiě.
Guō Jiě was short in stature,
did not drink alcohol,
and never rode when going out.
Later, Yáng Jìzhǔ was killed again.
Yáng Jìzhǔ's family submitted a petition to the court,
and the petitioner was killed at the palace gate.
Kūn said:
"When I drink before the great king,
with law officers at my side,
and censors behind me,
I tremble with fear, bowing low to drink -
I get drunk after no more than one dou.
If a respected guest is visiting my parents,
serving wine before them,
occasionally receiving leftover sips, toasting for longevity -
rising repeatedly,
I get drunk after no more than two dou.
When meeting with friends,
after long separation,
suddenly seeing each other,
happily recalling old times,
sharing private feelings -
I can drink five or six dou before getting drunk.
As for village gatherings,
where men and women sit mixed together,
wine circulates slowly,
with liùbó and pitch-pot games,
people grouping together,
holding hands without penalty,
gazing freely without restriction,
earrings dropped in front,
hairpins lost behind -
this secretly pleases me,
and I can drink eight dou while only two-thirds drunk.
When dusk falls and wine runs low,
cups are combined and seats drawn close,
men and women sharing mats,
shoes intermingled,
cups and plates in disarray,
hall candles extinguished,
the host keeps me while seeing off other guests -
with silk garments loosened,
faintly catching fragrant scents -
at such moments,
my heart is most joyful,
able to drink one shí.
Hence it is said:
Wine at its extreme brings chaos,
joy at its extreme brings sorrow;
all things are thus,
meaning nothing should reach extremity,
for at extremity comes decline."
Thus he remonstrated through indirection.
King of Qí said: "Excellent."
Thereupon he ended the all-night drinking,
appointing Kūn as receptionist for feudal lords.
When the royal family held banquets,
Kūn was often in attendance.
Over a hundred years later,
Chǔ had Yōu Mèng.
Yōu Mèng
was formerly a musician of Chǔ.
He stood eight chǐ tall,
was highly eloquent,
and often remonstrated through jest and laughter.
During King Zhuāng of Chǔ's reign,
he had a beloved horse,
dressed in embroidered silk,
housed in magnificent quarters,
bedded on open frames,
fed with dates and dried meat.
The horse died of obesity illness,
and he ordered ministers to mourn it,
wishing to bury it with inner-outer coffins
in ministerial rites.
Attendants disputed this,
deeming it improper.
The king decreed:
"Whoever dares remonstrate about the horse
will be guilty unto death."
Hearing this, Yōu Mèng
entered the palace gate
and wailed loudly to heaven.
The startled king asked his reason.
Yōu Mèng said:
"The horse was Your Majesty's beloved.
With Chǔ's great majesty,
what could you not obtain?
Burying it with ministerial rites
is meager -
I request burial with sovereign's rites."
The king said: "How so?"
He replied:
"I request jade-carved coffin,
patterned catalpa outer coffin,
pián-fēng and camphor timber enclosures,
mobilizing soldiers to dig the tomb,
elderly and weak carrying earth,
with Qí and Zhào envoys flanking before,
Hán and Wèi guarding behind,
temple sacrifices
with triple-sacrificial offerings,
supported by ten-thousand-household fief.
When feudal lords hear this,
all will know Your Majesty values horses over men."
The king said:
"Has my fault reached this extent!
What should be done?"
Yōu Mèng said:
"I ask to bury it as one of the six domestic animals.
With stove mound as outer coffin,
copper cauldron as inner coffin,
seasoned with ginger and jujubes,
spread with magnolia bark,
offered with grain rice,
clothed in firelight,
buried in human stomachs."
Thereupon the king had the horse given to the royal kitchen,
preventing further notoriety.
Chǔ chancellor Sūnshū Áo
recognized his worthiness
and treated him well.
Falling ill near death,
he instructed his son:
"After my death,
you will surely face poverty.
Go visit Yōu Mèng,
say you are Sūnshū Áo's son."
After several years,
his son indeed impoverished,
carrying firewood,
met Yōu Mèng,
telling him: "I am Sūnshū Áo's son.
Before dying, my father
instructed me in poverty
to visit you."
Yōu Mèng said: "Don't go far away."
He then donned Sūnshū Áo's clothes and hat,
imitating his speech and gestures.
After over a year,
he resembled Sūnshū Áo so closely
that the Chǔ king and courtiers
could not distinguish them.
When King Zhuāng held banquet,
Yōu Mèng came forward to toast.
King Zhuāng was greatly startled,
thinking Sūnshū Áo revived,
and wished to make him chancellor.
Yōu Mèng said:
"I beg to consult my wife first,
and become chancellor in three days."
King Zhuāng consented.
Three days later,
Yōu Mèng returned.
The king asked: "What did your wife say?"
Mèng replied:
"My wife urges caution - don't become Chǔ chancellor,
it's not worth it.
Though Sūnshū Áo as Chǔ chancellor
was utterly loyal and incorrupt
governing Chǔ,
enabling King of Chǔ to achieve hegemony,
now dead,
his son lacks land to stand an awl,
impoverished, carrying firewood
to feed himself.
If one must be like Sūnshū Áo,
better commit suicide."
Thereupon he sang:
"Farming bitter in mountain dwellings,
struggling for food.
Becoming an official,
corrupt ones amass wealth,
disregarding shame.
They die with wealthy households,
yet risk taking bribes, perverting law,
committing crimes through treachery,
dying with families destroyed.
How can one be a corrupt official!
Considering clean officials,
upholding laws, keeping duties,
dying without wrongdoing.
How can one be a clean official!
Chǔ chancellor Sūnshū maintained integrity till death,
now his wife and children impoverished, carrying firewood for food -
it's not worth it!"
Thereupon King Zhuāng thanked Yōu Mèng,
summoned Sūnshū Áo's son,
enfeoffed him with four hundred households in Qǐnqiū,
to maintain his sacrifices.
This lasted ten generations uninterrupted.
This shows wisdom timely expressed.
Over two hundred years later,
Qín had Yōu Zhān.
Yōu Zhān
was a Qín entertainer and dwarf.
Skilled at humorous talk,
yet conforming to great principles.
During Qín Shǐhuáng's reign,
while feasting, it rained,
The shield bearers were all drenched and cold.
Yōu Zhān saw them and took pity,
saying to them:
"Do you wish to rest?"
The shield bearers all replied: "We'd be most grateful."
Yōu Zhān said:
"When I call you,
you must quickly respond 'Yes'."
After a short while,
those in the hall offered birthday wishes and shouted "Long live!"
Yōu Zhān leaned over the railing and shouted loudly:
"Shield bearers!"
The men replied:
"Yes."
Yōu Zhān said:
"Though you are tall,
what good is it
standing fortunately in the rain?
Though I am short,
I'm fortunate to rest indoors."
Thereupon, the First Emperor allowed the shield bearers
to take shifts in halves.
The First Emperor once considered
expanding the imperial parks,
east to Hángǔ Guān,
west to Yōng and Chéncāng.
Yōu Zhān said: "Excellent.
Release many birds and beasts within them;
when bandits come from the east,
having the deer butt them will suffice."
The First Emperor therefore stopped the plan.
When the Second Emperor ascended,
he wanted to lacquer the city walls.
Yōu Zhān said: "Excellent.
Although Your Majesty hasn't mentioned it,
I was going to request it anyway.
Lacquering the walls may cause the people worry and expense,
but how splendid!
Lacquered walls, smooth and vast,
bandits cannot climb them.
Even if we proceed with it,
lacquering is easy,
but building shaded rooms for drying is difficult."
Thereupon, the Second Emperor laughed at this,
and because of it, stopped the plan.
Not long after,
the Second Emperor was killed,
Yōu Zhān returned to Hàn,
and died after several years.
Grand Historian Simǎ said:
Chúnyú Kūn looked up to the sky and laughed heartily,
and King Wēi of Qí dominated.
Yōu Mèng shook his head and sang,
and the firewood carrier was enfeoffed.
Yōu Zhān leaned over the railing and shouted urgently,
and the shield bearers got to take shifts.
Is this not also magnificent!
Master Chǔ said:
I am fortunate to have become a court gentleman through classical studies,
yet I enjoy reading unofficial histories and anecdotes.
Presuming without humility,
I have again written six chapters of humorous tales,
compiling them to the left.
They can be perused to uplift the spirit,
to show later generations of enthusiasts to read,
to delight the mind and astonish the ear,
to supplement the three chapters above by Grand Historian Simǎ.
During Emperor Wǔ's time, there was a favored entertainer, Guō Shèrén,
whose words and statements, though not aligned with grand principles,
pleased the sovereign.
When Emperor Wǔ was young,
the mother of the Marquis of Dōngwǔ
often cared for the Emperor,
and when the Emperor grew up,
he called her "Big Wet Nurse."
She generally came to court twice a month.
When her petition was submitted at court,
an edict ordered the favored courtier Mǎ Yóuqīng to give her fifty bolts of silk,
and also provided food and drink to support the wet nurse.
The wet nurse submitted a memorial saying:
"There is public land at a certain place,
I wish to borrow it."
The Emperor said:
"Does the wet nurse want it?"
And bestowed it upon her.
Whatever the wet nurse said,
was always heeded.
An edict allowed the wet nurse to ride in a carriage on the imperial thoroughfare.
At that time,
all the high officials and ministers respected the wet nurse.
The wet nurse's family, including children, grandchildren, and servants, acted violently in Cháng'ān,
stopping carriages and horses in the road,
and seizing people's clothing.
When this reached the court,
the Emperor could not bear to punish them by law.
The officials requested to relocate the wet nurse's household,
to settle them on the border.
The petition was approved.
The wet nurse was to go to the front,
to bid farewell in person.
The wet nurse first saw Guō Shèrén,
and wept before him.
Shèrén said:
"When you go in to bid farewell and leave,
walk quickly and look back several times."
The wet nurse did as he said,
took her leave,
walked quickly and looked back several times.
Guō Shèrén quickly spoke up and scolded her:
"Hey!
Old woman!
Why aren't you leaving quickly!
His Majesty is already grown up,
does he still need your milk to live?
Why still look back!"
Thereupon, the sovereign felt pity and sorrow for her,
and issued an edict to stop the relocation of the wet nurse,
punishing those who had slandered her.
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
there was a man from Qí named Dōngfāng, first name Shuò,
who was fond of ancient texts and transmitted writings,
loved classical studies,
and had broadly read many unofficial works.
When Shuò first arrived in Cháng'ān,
he went to the public office to submit a memorial,
using three thousand wooden slips in total.
The public office assigned two men to lift and carry his memorial,
barely able to manage it.
The sovereign read it from the upper palace,
pausing,
marking the places with hooks,
and took two months to finish reading it.
An edict appointed him as a court gentleman,
and he often attended at the sovereign's side.
He was frequently summoned for conversation,
and the sovereign was always pleased.
Once, he was ordered to be fed in the sovereign's presence.
After the meal,
he tucked all the leftover meat into his clothes and left,
soiling his clothes entirely.
When bestowed with silk fabrics,
he carried them away on a pole.
He solely used the bestowed money and silk
to marry pretty girls from Cháng'ān.
Typically, he would marry a woman and abandon her after about a year,
then marry another.
All the bestowed money was spent entirely on women.
Half of the sovereign's court gentlemen called him a "madman."
The sovereign heard of this,
and said:
"If Shuò in office were without such behavior,
how could any of you compare to him!"
Shuò had his son appointed as a court gentleman,
and also served as an attendant herald,
often bearing credentials on missions.
Once, Shuò was walking in the palace,
and a court gentleman said to him:
"Everyone considers you, sir, mad."
Shuò said:
"People like me
are what's called those who hide from the world within the court.
People in ancient times
hid from the world in deep mountains."
Once, while seated at a banquet,
drunk and merry,
he leaned on the ground and sang:
"Sinking in the mundane world,
hiding from the world at the Jīnmǎ Gate.
Within the palace halls, one can hide from the world and preserve oneself,
why must it be deep in the mountains,
under thatched huts?"
The Jīnmǎ Gate
was the gate of the eunuchs' office,
with a bronze horse beside the gate,
hence it was called the "Jīnmǎ Gate."
Once, the assembled erudites and scholars at the palace debated with him,
challenging him together,
saying:
"Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí, once they met the rulers of ten thousand chariots,
attained the positions of chief ministers,
and their favor extended to later generations.
Now you, sir, cultivate the methods of former kings,
admire the righteousness of sages,
recite the sayings of the 'Book of Songs,' 'Book of Documents,' and the hundred schools,
too numerous to count.
inscribed on bamboo and silk,
considering oneself unparalleled in the world,
one may be called knowledgeable and eloquent.
Yet, exerting all effort and loyalty to serve a sage emperor,
spending long days and enduring over time,
accumulating decades,
one's official rank does not exceed that of a侍郎 (shìláng),
and position no higher than a执戟 (zhíjǐ),
could it be that there are still shortcomings in conduct?
What is the reason for this?"
东方朔 (Dōngfāng Shuò) said:
"This is certainly not something you can fully comprehend.
That was one era,
this is another,
how can they be the same!
In the time of张仪 (Zhāng Yí) and苏秦 (Sū Qín),
the Zhou court was in great decline,
feudal lords did not pay homage,
they vied for power through force,
capturing each other with armies,
merging into twelve states,
with no clear supremacy,
those who gained scholars became strong,
those who lost them perished,
hence their persuasions were heeded and actions successful,
they held esteemed positions,
their influence reached later generations,
and their descendants enjoyed long-lasting glory.
Now it is not so."
With a sage emperor above,
virtue flows throughout the world,
feudal lords submit as guests,
authority shakes the four barbarians,
connecting beyond the four seas as if on a mat,
stable as an overturned bowl,
the world is balanced,
united as one family,
moving and initiating affairs,
is like maneuvering in the palm of the hand.
How can the worthy and unworthy be distinguished?
In today's vast world,
with the multitude of scholars and people,
those exhausting their energies in persuasion,
advancing like spokes to a hub,
are too numerous to count.
Fully devoted to admiring righteousness,
yet troubled by food and clothing,
some lose their footing.
If张仪 (Zhāng Yí) and苏秦 (Sū Qín) were born with me in this age,
they couldn't even attain the post of掌故 (zhǎnggù),
how dare they aspire to be常侍郎 (cháng shìláng)!
As the saying goes:
'When the world is free from harm and disaster,
even sages have no way to施展 their talents;
when superiors and inferiors are harmonious and united,
even the worthy have no means to achieve merit.'
Thus, it is said that times change, and so do affairs.
Nevertheless,
how can one neglect self-cultivation?
The《诗》 (Shī) says:
'When bells are struck in the palace,
their sound is heard outside.'
'Cranes cry at the marsh,
their sound reaches the heavens.'
If one can cultivate oneself,
why worry about not achieving honor!
太公 (Tàigōng) personally practiced benevolence and righteousness for seventy-two years,
encountered the king,
was able to implement his teachings,
was enfeoffed in齐 (Qí),
and it lasted seven hundred years without end.
This is why scholars work diligently day and night,
studying and practicing the Way,
not daring to stop.
Today's recluses,
though not employed in their time,
stand out independently,
dwell in solitude,
looking up to许由 (Xǔ Yóu),
observing接舆 (Jiē Yú) below,
strategizing like范蠡 (Fàn Lǐ),
loyal as子胥 (Zǐ Xū),
in a peaceful world,
upholding righteousness,
having few companions and followers,
is indeed their normal state.
Why do you doubt me!"
At this, the various gentlemen fell silent with no response.
In the建章宫 (Jiànzhāng Gōng),
from the double-layered loft at the rear,
a creature emerged,
its appearance resembling a麋 (mí).
Upon reporting it,
武帝 (Wǔdì) went to see it personally.
He asked the attending ministers who were versed in affairs and classical texts,
but none could identify it.
He then ordered东方朔 (Dōngfāng Shuò) to inspect it.
东方朔 (Dōngfāng Shuò) said:
"I know what it is,
but I wish to be granted fine wine and millet for a grand feast,
then I will speak."
The edict said:
"Granted."
After that, he added:
"There is a public field, fish pond, and several acres of reeds at a certain place,
if Your Majesty bestows them upon me,
then I,东方朔 (Dōngfāng Shuò), will speak."
The edict said:
"Granted."
Only then did东方朔 (Dōngfāng Shuò) agree to speak,
saying:
"This is what is called a驺牙 (zōuyá).
It signifies that distant lands will come to submit in righteousness,
and the驺牙 (zōuyá) appears first.
Its teeth are uniform front and back,
even and without irregular ones,
hence it is called驺牙 (zōuyá)."
About a year later,
the匈奴 (Xiōngnú) King混邪 (Húnxié) indeed led a hundred thousand troops to surrender to汉 (Hàn).
Thus,东方朔 (Dōngfāng Shuò) was again bestowed with much wealth.
In his old age,
as东方朔 (Dōngfāng Shuò) was nearing death,
he admonished:
"The《诗》 (Shī) says:
'Buzzing blue flies,
alight on the fence.
Kindly gentlemen,
do not believe slanderous words.
Slanderous words know no bounds,
they disrupt the four states.'
I hope Your Majesty will keep away from the cunning and flattering,
and reject slanderous words."
The Emperor said:
"Now, looking back, does东方朔 (Dōngfāng Shuò) have many good words?"
He found it strange.
Not long after,
东方朔 (Dōngfāng Shuò) indeed fell ill and died.
As the saying goes:
"When a bird is about to die,
its song is sorrowful;
when a person is about to die,
their words are good."
This refers to such a case.
During the time of武帝 (Wǔdì),
the great general卫青 (Wèi Qīng),
who was the brother of Empress卫 (Wèi),
was enfeoffed as the Marquis of长平 (Chángpíng).
He led the army to attack the匈奴 (Xiōngnú),
reaching the余吾水 (Yúwú Shuǐ) and then returning,
having beheaded and captured enemies,
he returned with merit,
and an edict awarded him a thousand catties of gold.
As the general exited the palace gate,
a man from齐 (Qí),东郭先生 (Dōngguō Xiānshēng), who was awaiting appointment as a方士 (fāngshì) at the公车 (gōngchē),
blocked the path and stopped General卫 (Wèi)'s carriage,
bowing and saying:
"I wish to report a matter."
The general halted his carriage,
and东郭先生 (Dōngguō Xiānshēng) spoke beside it:
"Lady王 (Wáng) has recently gained favor with the Emperor,
but her family is poor.
Now that you, General, have received a thousand catties of gold,
if you truly give half to Lady王 (Wáng)'s relatives,
the sovereign will surely be pleased upon hearing it.
This is what is called a clever and convenient strategy."
General卫 (Wèi) thanked him, saying:
"Fortunately, you have informed me of this convenient plan,
I will follow your advice."
Thereupon, General卫 (Wèi) used five hundred catties of gold to present to Lady王 (Wáng)'s relatives.
Lady王 (Wáng) reported this to武帝 (Wǔdì).
The Emperor said:
"The great general would not have thought of this on his own."
He asked where he received the strategy,
and he replied:
"It came from the awaiting appointment,东郭先生 (Dōngguō Xiānshēng)."
An edict summoned东郭先生 (Dōngguō Xiānshēng),
and he was appointed as a commandery都尉 (dūwèi).
东郭先生 (Dōngguō Xiānshēng) had long been awaiting appointment at the公车 (gōngchē),
impoverished and suffering from hunger and cold,
his clothes worn out,
his shoes incomplete.
Walking in the snow,
his shoes had tops but no soles,
so his feet fully touched the ground.
People on the road laughed at him,
and Dōngguō Xiānshēng responded, saying:
"Who can walk in the snow,
and have others look at it,
where the footprints above are shoes,
yet the impressions beneath resemble human feet?"
When he was appointed to a salary of two thousand shí,
wearing the blue silk ribbon,
he exited the palace gate,
and went to thank his host.
Thus, his colleagues who awaited appointments,
lined up to bid him farewell outside the capital's gates.
His glory spread along the roads,
and he established a name for himself in his time.
This is what is called 'wearing coarse clothes while harboring a treasure.'
When he was in poverty and hardship,
no one paid him any attention;
but when he became noble,
they all rushed to attach themselves to him.
A proverb says:
"In judging a horse, one may err due to its leanness;
in judging a man, one may err due to his poverty."
Is this not what it refers to?
When Lady Wáng was gravely ill,
the sovereign personally went to visit her and asked:
"Your son is to be made a king;
where would you like him to be placed?"
She replied:
"I wish for him to reside in Luòyáng."
The sovereign said:
"That cannot be.
Luòyáng has the armory and Áo Granary,
situated at a strategic pass,
the throat of the empire.
Since the time of the previous emperor,
it has been passed down not to place a king there.
However, among the states east of the pass, none is greater than Qí,
so he can be made King of Qí."
Lady Wáng clasped her head with her hands,
exclaiming,
"How fortunate!"
After Lady Wáng died,
she was posthumously honored as "The Demise of the Queen Dowager of Qí."
In the past, the King of Qí sent Chúnyú Kūn to present a swan to Chǔ.
After leaving the city gate,
the swan flew away on the road,
so he carried an empty cage,
fabricated a clever story,
and went to see the King of Chǔ, saying:
"The King of Qí sent me to present a swan,
but while crossing over water,
I could not bear the swan's thirst,
so I let it out to drink,
and it flew away from me.
I thought of stabbing my belly or hanging myself to die,
but feared people would criticize my king for causing a scholar to harm himself over a bird or beast.
The swan,
a feathered creature,
has many that look alike;
I considered buying one to replace it,
but that would be dishonest and deceitful to my king.
I thought of fleeing to another country,
but it pained me that our two rulers would not communicate.
Thus, I have come to admit my fault,
kowtowing to accept punishment from Your Majesty."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Excellent!
The King of Qí has such a trustworthy scholar!"
He richly rewarded him,
with wealth double what it would have been if the swan were present.
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
the Governor of Běihǎi was summoned to the imperial temporary residence.
There was a literary clerk named Wáng Xiānshēng
who requested to accompany the governor,
saying, "I can be of benefit to you,"
and the governor agreed.
The various officials and clerks all said:
"Wáng Xiānshēng is fond of drink,
talks much but accomplishes little,
I fear he should not go with you."
The governor said:
"The gentleman wishes to go,
I cannot refuse him."
So they went together.
Upon arriving at the palace,
they waited at the government office gate.
Wáng Xiānshēng merely carried money to buy wine,
drinking with the guard captain,
getting drunk daily,
without attending to his governor.
The governor entered to kneel and pay respects.
Wáng Xiānshēng said to the door officer:
"Please call my lord to the inner gate for a distant conversation."
The door officer called the governor.
The governor came,
and saw Wáng Xiānshēng.
Wáng Xiānshēng said:
"If the Son of Heaven asks you how you governed Běihǎi to have no bandits,
what will you reply?"
The governor answered:
"By selecting worthy talents,
appointing each according to their abilities,
rewarding the exceptional,
and punishing the unworthy."
Wáng Xiānshēng said:
"Answering like that
is boasting of your own achievements,
which won't do.
I hope you will reply,
'It was not due to my efforts,
but entirely the result of Your Majesty's divine might and authority effecting the change.'"
The governor said:
"Agreed."
Summoned inside,
he reached the front of the hall,
where an imperial edict asked him:
"How did you govern Běihǎi
so that no bandits arose?"
He kowtowed and replied:
"It was not due to my efforts,
but entirely the result of Your Majesty's divine might and authority effecting the change."
Emperor Wǔ laughed heartily,
and said:
"Ah!
Where did you get such wise words and use them!
From whom did you receive this?"
He replied:
"From the literary clerk."
The Emperor said:
"Where is he now?"
He replied:
"Outside the government office gate."
An edict was issued to appoint Wáng Xiānshēng as Assistant of the Waterways and Parks,
and the Governor of Běihǎi as Commandant of the Waterways and Parks.
The tradition says:
"Fine words can be marketed,
noble conduct can elevate others.
The gentleman sees others off with words,
the petty person with wealth."
During the time of Marquis Wén of Wèi,
Xīmén Bào was appointed magistrate of Yè.
Bào went to Yè,
gathered the elders,
and asked them about the people's sufferings.
The elders said:
"We suffer from marrying a wife to Hé Bó,
which causes our poverty."
Bào asked the reason,
and they replied:
"The village elders and officials annually collect taxes from the people,
gathering several million coins,
using two or three hundred thousand for Hé Bó's marriage,
and sharing the rest with the priests, taking it home.
At that time,
the priestesses inspect the daughters of poor families for beauty, saying this one should be Hé Bó's wife,
and then betroth and take her.
They bathe her,
make new silk and fine clothes for her,
have her fast and live in seclusion;
prepare a fasting palace by the river,
hang red and purple curtains,
and the girl stays inside.
They prepare beef, wine, and food,
for over ten days.
Then they adorn it all,
like a bridal bed,
have the girl sit on it,
and float it into the river.
Initially it floats,
drifting tens of lǐ before sinking.
Families with pretty daughters,
fearing the chief priest would take them for Hé Bó,
mostly take their daughters and flee far away.
Hence, the city grows increasingly empty and unpopulated,
and more impoverished,
a practice that has lasted long.
The people commonly say,
'If we don't marry a wife to Hé Bó,
floods will come and drown,
they say,
and submerge our people.'" Xīmén Bào said:
"When it's time for Hé Bó's marriage,
I hope the elders,
priests, and community leaders will see the girl off at the river,
and be sure to inform me,
I will also go to see her off."
They all said:
"Yes."
When the time came,
Xīmén Bào went to meet them by the river.
The village elders,
officials,
influential leaders, and local elders had all gathered,
along with two to three thousand people who came to watch.
The shaman,
an old woman,
was already seventy years old.
She was followed by about ten female disciples,
all dressed in plain silk garments,
standing behind the head shaman.
Xīmén Bào said:
"Call the River Lord's bride forth,
let me see her beauty or plainness."
They then brought the girl out from the tent,
and she came forward.
Bào looked at her,
then turned to the village elders,
shamans, and elders saying:
"This girl is not beautiful enough,
I must trouble the head shaman to go report to the River Lord,
that we will find a more beautiful girl,
and send her later."
He immediately had officers and soldiers together lift the head shaman and throw her into the river.
After a while,
he said:
"Why is the shaman taking so long?
Her disciples should hurry her up!"
They then threw one disciple into the river.
After another while,
he said:
"Why is this disciple taking so long?
Send another to hurry them!"
They threw another disciple into the river.
In total, three disciples were thrown in.
Xīmén Bào said:
"The shaman and her disciples are women,
unable to explain matters clearly,
I must trouble the three elders to go explain."
They then threw the three elders into the river.
Xīmén Bào stood with hairpin upright, bowing like a chiming stone,
facing the river and waiting for a long time.
The elders and officials watching from the side were all terrified.
Xīmén Bào turned and said:
"The shaman and elders haven't returned,
what should we do?"
He intended to send the court assistant and one influential leader to hurry them.
They all kowtowed,
their foreheads nearly breaking,
blood flowing to the ground,
their faces ashen like dead ashes.
Xīmén Bào said:
"Very well,
let's wait a bit longer."
After a short while,
Bào said:
"Court assistant, rise.
It seems the River Lord is keeping his guests long,
you may all disperse and return home."
The officials and people of Yè were greatly frightened,
and from then on,
no one dared speak again about marrying women to the River Lord.
Xīmén Bào then mobilized the people to dig twelve canals,
diverting river water to irrigate the fields,
and all the fields were watered.
At that time,
the people found canal maintenance somewhat burdensome,
and were reluctant.
Bào said:
"People can enjoy success,
but cannot be consulted at the start.
Though the elders and youth now suffer hardship because of me,
a hundred years later they will hope their descendants remember my words."
To this day they benefit from the waterworks,
and the people have become well-supplied and prosperous.
The twelve canals crossed the imperial highway,
and when the Hàn was established,
the senior officials thought the twelve canal bridges crossing the highway,
being too close together,
were unsuitable.
They wanted to merge the canal waters,
and where they reached the highway, combine three canals into one bridge.
The elders of Yè's people refused to comply,
believing this was Xīmén's work,
and a worthy official's model should not be changed.
The senior officials finally yielded and dropped the matter.
Thus Xīmén Bào, as magistrate of Yè,
became famous throughout the land,
his beneficence flowing to later generations,
without end,
could he not be called a worthy official indeed!
The tradition says:
"Zǐchǎn governed Zhèng,
and people could not deceive him;
Zǐjiàn governed Shànfù,
and people could not bear to deceive him;
Xīmén Bào governed Yè,
and people did not dare deceive him."
Among these three, whose ability was most worthy?
Those who distinguish governance should be able to tell.
Since ancient times, those receiving the mandate to become kings,
has any king's rise not used divination to determine Heaven's will!
This was especially true for the Zhōu,
and could be seen in the Qín.
The Dài king's entry,
relied on the diviner.
The Grand Diviner's origin,
arose with Hàn's rise.
Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ
was a man of Chǔ.
He practiced divination at Cháng'ān's eastern market.
Sòng Zhōng was a Grand Master,
Jiǎ Yì was an Erudite,
one day both went out for their bath day,
walking together discussing,
reciting the Yì and the ways of ancient kings and sages,
exhaustively exploring human nature,
they looked at each other and sighed.
Jiǎ Yì said:
"I've heard that ancient sages,
if not at court,
must be among diviners and physicians.
Now I've seen the three councils and nine ministers, court officials, all knowable.
Let's try among the diviners to observe their talents."
The two then rode together to the market,
wandering among divination stalls.
Heaven had newly rained,
the road had few people,
Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ sat leisurely,
with three or four disciples attending,
expounding the ways of heaven and earth,
the movements of sun and moon,
the roots of yīn-yáng fortune and misfortune,
the two officials bowed twice in greeting.
Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ observed their appearance,
recognizing them as knowledgeable men,
he treated them courteously,
having his disciples invite them to sit.
When seated,
Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ resumed his previous discourse,
distinguishing the beginnings and ends of heaven and earth,
the order of sun, moon, and stars,
grading the boundaries of benevolence and righteousness,
arranging the signs of fortune and misfortune,
speaking several thousand words,
all perfectly reasoned.
Sòng Zhōng and
Jiǎ Yì were startled into understanding,
straightening their caps and sitting upright,
saying:
"Looking at your appearance,
hearing your words,
we humbly observe the world,
yet have never seen your like.
Why do you dwell so low,
why practice such a base occupation?"
Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ clutched his belly laughing loudly:
"I thought you gentlemen seemed like men of wisdom,
yet now your words are so crude,
your speech so vulgar!
What do you now consider worthy?
Whom do you esteem?
Why do you belittle your elders as base?"
The two gentlemen said:
"High office and generous salary,
are what the world esteems,
and where worthy talents reside.
Your position is not there,
hence we call it low.
Your words lack credibility,
your actions lack verification,
your gains improper,
hence we call it base.
Divination
is what the world despises and slights.
All say:
'Diviners mostly exaggerate and intimidate to discern feelings,
falsely elevate fortunes and destinies to please aspirations,
arbitrarily speak disasters to hurt hearts,
fabricate ghosts and spirits to exhaust wealth,
eagerly seek rewards for private gain.'
This is what we find shameful,
hence we call it low and base."
Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ said:
"Sir, please be seated.
Have you seen those disheveled-haired youths?
When the sun and moon shine upon them, they move;
when not illuminated, they halt.
Ask them about the flaws and auspicious omens of the sun and moon,
and they cannot explain.
From this perspective,
those who can distinguish the worthy from the unworthy are few.
"The conduct of the worthy
follows the straight path to offer upright remonstrance;
if the advice is not heeded after three attempts, they withdraw.
In praising others, they do not expect reward;
in condemning others, they disregard resentment,
focusing solely on benefiting the state and the people.
Thus, they do not hold office beyond their capability,
nor accept emolument without merit;
upon seeing someone unrighteous,
they show no respect despite their high status;
upon seeing someone corrupt,
they do not defer despite their尊贵;
they do not rejoice in gain,
nor resent loss;
if not at fault,
they feel no shame even when repeatedly humiliated.
"Now, those you call worthy
are all deserving of shame.
They approach with fawning demeanor,
speaking with obsequious haste;
drawing connections through power,
guiding with利益;
colluding to exclude the upright,
seeking honor and reputation,
and receiving public stipends;
serving private interests,
perverting the ruler's laws,
preying upon the farmers;
using office as authority,
laws as traps,
pursuing利益 through violence:
this is no different from holding a white blade to rob others.
When first tested for office,
they加倍努力 in deceit,
adorning false achievements and empty documents to deceive the sovereign,
thereby securing high positions;
in office, they do not yield to the worthy or declare true merits,
but exaggerate falsehoods as reality,
turning nothing into something,
making little seem much,
to seek advantageous power and尊贵地位;
indulging in feasts and galloping about,
surrounded by singing maidens,
heedless of family,
violating laws and harming the people,
emptying the public coffers:
these are thieves who need no spears or bows,
assailants without strings or blades,
deceiving parents unpunished and slaying rulers unopposed.
How can they be considered highly worthy and talented?
"When bandits arise, they cannot suppress them;
when barbarians rebel, they cannot subdue them;
when treachery emerges, they cannot stop it;
when offices are wasteful and chaotic, they cannot govern;
when the four seasons are discordant, they cannot harmonize them;
when the year's harvest fails, they cannot adjust.
If capable and worthy, yet not acting,
this is disloyalty;
if incapable yet occupying office,
profiting from the ruler's stipends,
hindering the worthy from position,
this is stealing office;
advancing those with connections,
respecting those with wealth,
this is hypocrisy.
Have you not seen owls flying with phoenixes?
Orchids and angelicas discarded in the wilderness,
while weeds form forests,
causing the noble to retreat unseen by the masses—
you and your kind are just so.
"Transmitting without creating—
this is the way of the noble.
Now, those who practice divination
must emulate heaven and earth,
mirror the four seasons,
conform to benevolence and righteousness,
divide stalks and determine hexagrams,
rotate the board and align the pieces,
only then speaking of heaven and earth's benefits and harms,
and the success or failure of affairs.
In ancient times, when former kings settled the state,
they first consulted tortoise shells and stalks by the sun and moon,
before daring to succeed;
rectifying the time and day,
then entering households;
before childbirth, they first divined auspiciousness,
only then proceeding.
Since Fúxī created the Eight Trigrams,
and King Wén of Zhōu expanded them into 384 lines, all under heaven was well-governed.
King Gōujiàn of Yuè applied King Wén's Eight Trigrams to defeat enemy states,
achieving hegemony.
Thus,
what fault is there in divination?
"Moreover, diviners
sweep and set seats,
adjust their caps and belts,
before speaking of matters—
this is ritual propriety.
Their words may lead ghosts and spirits to enjoy offerings,
loyal ministers to serve their superiors,
filial sons to nurture their parents,
kind fathers to raise their children—
this is virtuous conduct.
And for righteously setting a few dozen or hundred coins,
the sick may recover,
the dying may live,
calamities may be avoided,
affairs may succeed,
daughters married or wives taken to sustain life—
such virtue,
is it worth merely a few dozen or hundred coins?
This is what Lǎozǐ meant by
'The highest virtue does not virtue,
thus it has virtue.'
Now diviners offer great benefit with little reward—
is Lǎozǐ's saying any different?
"Zhuāngzǐ said:
'The noble inwardly have no worry of hunger or cold,
outwardly no fear of robbery or seizure,
in high position, they are reverent;
in low position, they do no harm—
this is the way of the noble.'
Now, the practice of divination
accumulates without hoarding,
stores without granaries,
moves without carts,
carries burden without weight,
and when used, never exhausts.
Holding inexhaustible things,
wandering an endless world—
even Zhuāngzǐ's conduct could not surpass this.
Why then say divination is improper?
Heaven is incomplete in the northwest,
so stars shift northwest;
earth is incomplete in the southeast,
so seas become its pools;
the sun at its peak must move,
the full moon must wane;
the way of former kings
now exists, now perishes.
You demand diviners' words be always可信,
is that not delusion?
"Have you seen those debaters and rhetoricians?
In planning and decision-making,
it is always such men,
yet they cannot sway the ruler's mind with a single word,
so they must cite former kings,
speak always of antiquity;
in planning and decision-making,
they embellish past successes,
narrate failures and harms,
to sway the ruler's will with fear or joy,
seeking their own desires.
No grandiosity exceeds this.
Yet to strengthen the state and achieve success,
to be utterly loyal to the superior,
without this, it cannot be done.
Now diviners
guide the confused and teach the ignorant.
How can the foolish and confused
be enlightened with just one word?
Words are never too many.
"Thus, the noble steed cannot team with weary donkeys,
the phoenix does not flock with sparrows,
and the worthy do not stand alongside the unworthy.
So the noble dwell in obscurity to avoid the crowd,
hide themselves to escape convention,
subtly manifest virtue to gradually reduce harm,
illuminate innate nature,
aid superiors and nurture inferiors,
increase their contributions,
without seeking尊贵 or fame.
You and your like are but chirping sparrows—
what do you know of the way of the noble?"
I have heard that in the Xià and Yīn dynasties, those who wished to divine
would take the yarrow stalks and tortoise shells,
and after use, discard them,
believing that if the tortoise shells were stored, they would lose their efficacy,
and if the yarrow stalks were kept too long, they would lose their divine power.
By the time of the Zhōu court, the divination officials
often treasured and stored the yarrow stalks and tortoise shells;
moreover, their sizes and the order of their use,
each had its own traditions,
but in essence, their purpose was the same.
Some believed that when sage kings encountered affairs, nothing was unsettled,
and when resolving doubts, nothing went unseen.
The reason they established the methods of consulting spirits and seeking answers
was that they considered later generations to be in decline,
the foolish not learning from the wise,
each person content with their own ways,
transforming and dividing into a hundred schools,
the Way scattered and without bounds.
Therefore, they pushed the principles to the utmost subtlety,
seeking purity in the essence and spirit.
Others believed that the strengths of insects and creatures
were things even sages could not contend with.
In determining auspiciousness and inauspiciousness,
distinguishing right from wrong,
they often aligned with human affairs.
By the time of Emperor Gāozǔ,
the office of the Grand Diviner was established.
The empire had just been stabilized,
and warfare had not yet ceased.
During Emperor Huì’s reign, his time on the throne was short,
and Empress Dowager Lǚ ruled as a female sovereign.
Emperors Wén
and Jǐng followed established precedents,
with no leisure to study or test divination.
Although the office was hereditary from father to son,
passed down through generations,
its subtle and profound intricacies
were largely lost.
When the present emperor ascended the throne,
he broadly opened paths for skills and talents,
extended invitations to all schools of learning,
so that those proficient in a single art could all offer their services.
Those of unparalleled and extraordinary ability were given precedence,
without any favoritism or bias.
Within a few years,
the Grand Diviner’s office was greatly assembled.
It happened that the emperor wished to attack the Xiōngnú,
subdue Dàyuān in the west,
and conquer Bǎiyuè in the south.
Divination by stalks and shells even foresaw the signs,
anticipating their advantages.
When fierce generals pushed forward with their troops and upheld their duties,
achieving victory on the battlefield,
the yarrow stalks and tortoise shells, along with the timing, also contributed to this.
The emperor paid even greater attention,
bestowing rewards sometimes amounting to tens of millions.
People like Qiū Zǐmíng and his ilk
became immensely wealthy and highly favored,
wielding great influence in the court.
They even used divination to detect curses and sorcery,
and sometimes their accusations of witchcraft hit the mark.
If they had longstanding grudges or displeasures,
they would use public authority to carry out executions,
indulging in arbitrary harm,
leading to the destruction of clans and the extermination of families—
too many to count.
All officials trembled in fear,
saying that the tortoise shells and yarrow stalks could speak.
Later, when their treachery was exposed and their schemes exhausted,
they too were executed along with their three sets of relatives.
Now, arranging the stalks to determine numbers,
scorching the tortoise shell to observe the cracks,
the transformations are endless.
Therefore, selecting the worthy to conduct divination—
can this be said to show how sages valued important matters!
The Duke of Zhōu divined with three tortoise shells,
and King Wǔ recovered from his illness.
King Zhòu was tyrannical and cruel,
yet the great tortoise shell gave no auspicious sign.
When Duke Wén of Jìn was about to secure King Xiāng’s position,
he divined and obtained the omen of the Yellow Emperor,
and eventually received the mandate of the red bow.
Duke Xiàn, coveting the beauty of Lí Jī,
divined and the cracks showed a mouth-like image—
the disaster ultimately flowed through five generations.
When King Líng of Chǔ was about to turn against the Zhōu court,
he divined and the tortoise shell showed opposition,
and in the end, he suffered defeat at Gānxī.
The response of the omens was sincere within,
and people of the time clearly observed it without—
can this not be called a mutual correspondence!
Gentlemen say that those who belittle divination,
denying the spiritual and divine,
are perverse; while those who turn their backs on human principles,
placing faith solely in auspicious signs,
will not find the ghosts and spirits acting rightly.
Thus, the *Shū* establishes the consultation of doubts,
with five methods of deliberation, and divination occupies two of them.
Among five divinations, follow the majority,
clarifying that while they exist, they should not be exclusively relied upon.
I traveled to the region south of the Yangtze River,
observed their practices,
and inquired of their elders.
They say that when a tortoise reaches a thousand years, it roams atop lotus leaves,
and yarrow stalks with a hundred stems share a single root.
Moreover, in the places where they grow,
there are no beasts like tigers or wolves,
and no poisonous insects or stinging creatures.
Families along the river often keep tortoises, feeding them,
believing they can guide and attract vital energy,
beneficial for aiding decline and nourishing old age—
how could this not be credible!
Master Chǔ says:
I, through mastering the classical arts,
studied under a court academician,
specializing in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
and due to high ranking, became a court gentleman.
I was fortunate to serve in the palace guard,
entering and leaving the palace halls for over ten years.
Secretly, I developed a fondness for the *Records of the Grand Historian*.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"The Three Dynasties used different tortoise shells,
the Four Barbarians each had their own divination methods,
yet all used them to determine auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
Glimpsing their essentials,
I therefore composed the 'Biographies of the Tortoise and Stalk Diviners.'"
I traveled back and forth in Cháng'ān,
seeking the 'Biographies of the Tortoise and Stalk Diviners' but could not find it.
Thus, I went to the office of the Grand Diviner,
inquired of the archivists, scholars, and experienced elders,
copied down the matters of tortoise and stalk divination,
and compiled them below.
I have heard that when the ancient Five Emperors and
Three Kings initiated affairs and undertook actions,
they would always first consult the yarrow stalks and tortoise shells.
A tradition states:
"Below lies the hidden spirit,
above grows the dodder plant;
where yarrow is pounded above,
beneath resides the divine tortoise."
What is called the hidden spirit
is found beneath the dodder,
shaped like a flying bird.
After fresh rain has ceased,
when the sky is clear and calm without wind,
at night, brush away the dodder and remove it,
then illuminate this spot with a lantern torch—
when the fire goes out,
immediately mark the location,
surround it with four zhang of new cloth,
and at dawn, dig it up;
at a depth of four to seven chǐ,
you will obtain it,
but beyond seven chǐ, it cannot be found.
The hidden spirit
is the root of a thousand-year-old pine tree,
and consuming it grants immortality.
I have heard that where yarrow grows with a hundred stems,
beneath it there must be a divine tortoise guarding it,
and above it, blue clouds often cover it.
A tradition states:
"When the world is at peace,
and the Kingly Way is attained,
then yarrow stems grow ten chǐ long,
and their clusters flourish with a hundred stems."
Nowadays, those who gather yarrow
cannot adhere to the ancient standards,
and cannot obtain those with a hundred stems and ten chǐ in length;
if they gather those with over eighty stems
and yarrow eight chǐ long,
it is already hard to come by.
Among the people, those fond of using hexagrams
take yarrow with over sixty stems
and at least six chǐ in length,
which is then usable.
A record says:
"Those who can obtain a famous tortoise
will see wealth and goods come to them,
and their households are sure to become greatly rich, up to tens of millions."
The first is called
"the Northern Dipper Tortoise,"
the second
"the Southern Stars Tortoise,"
the third
"the Five Planets Tortoise,"
the fourth
"the Eight Winds Tortoise,"
the fifth
"the Twenty-Eight Mansions Tortoise,"
the sixth
"the Sun and Moon Tortoise,"
the seventh
"the Nine Provinces Tortoise,"
and the eighth
"the Jade Tortoise":
in all, eight named tortoises.
Each tortoise's depiction has writing on its underside,
with the inscriptions stating,
"This is such-and-such tortoise,"
but I will briefly note the main idea
and not copy the diagrams.
To obtain such tortoises, they need not be a full chǐ and two cùn;
if common people get one seven or eight cùn long,
it can be treasured.
Now, as for pearls, jades, and precious objects,
even if deeply concealed,
they must reveal their glow,
and their divine essence will emerge—
is this not what is meant here!
Thus, where jade resides in the mountains, the trees are moist,
and where pearls are born in the deep, the banks do not wither,
for they bestow moisture and luster.
The bright moon pearl comes from rivers and seas,
hidden within clams,
with hornless dragons crouching over it.
If a king obtains it,
he will long possess the world,
and all quarters will submit as guests.
If one can obtain the hundred-stemmed yarrow
and also the tortoise beneath it for divination,
every word will hit the mark,
sufficient to determine good and bad fortune.
Divine tortoises emerge from the rivers;
Lújiāng Commandery annually sends twenty tortoises of chǐ two cùn in length to the Grand Diviner office,
and the Grand Diviner then on an auspicious day carves out the plastron from their undersides.
A tortoise reaches a full chǐ two cùn only after a thousand years.
When a king dispatches armies and appoints generals,
he must drill the tortoise shell in the temple hall
to decide good and bad fortune.
Now, in the high temple, there is a tortoise chamber,
where they are stored inside as divine treasures.
A tradition states:
"Take the bone from the front shank, pierce and wear it;
take the tortoise and hang it in the northwest corner of the room;
then, when entering deep mountains or great forests,
you will not be led astray."
When I served as a court gentleman,
I saw the Wàn Bì Shí Zhū Fāng,
which records:
"There is a divine tortoise in the fine forests south of the river.
Fine forests are where
beasts include no tigers or wolves,
birds no owls or harpies,
plants no poisonous stings,
wildfires do not reach,
and axes do not come—
this is what makes a fine forest.
The tortoise dwells there,
often nesting on fragrant lotus.
On its left flank is written:
'Jiǎzǐ double light;
he who obtains me, a commoner, will become a ruler,
holding land rightly;
if a feudal lord obtains me, he will become emperor.'
To seek it in the forest where white snakes coil around trees,
observe purification and wait;
vaguely,
as if someone comes to tell you,
then with sacrificial wine and loosened hair,
seek it for three nights and you will find it."
From this perspective,
is it not magnificent!
So how can we not revere the tortoise?
An old man in the south used a tortoise to prop his bed leg,
and after over twenty years,
when the old man died
and the bed was moved,
the tortoise was still alive and not dead.
The tortoise can practice breath control and guiding the energy.
Someone asked:
"If the tortoise is so divine,
then why does the Grand Diviner office, upon obtaining a live tortoise,
always kill it and take its shell?"
In recent times, a person by the river obtained a famous tortoise,
kept and raised it,
and his household thereby became very wealthy.
When he discussed with others
about sending it away,
someone advised to kill it and not release it,
saying releasing it would ruin a family.
The tortoise appeared in a dream, saying:
"Return me to the water,
do not kill me."
But the family eventually killed it.
After killing it,
the person died,
and the family suffered misfortune.
Common people and rulers follow different paths.
When common people obtain a famous tortoise,
it seems they should not kill it based on its nature.
Yet, citing ancient tales,
the wise kings and sage rulers of old all killed and used them.
When King Sòng Yuán obtained a tortoise,
he also killed and used it.
I respectfully append the account below,
for those interested to observe and select from it.
In the second year of King Sòng Yuán's reign,
a divine turtle sent by the River Jiāng as an envoy to the River Hé
reached Quányáng,
where a fisherman named Yù Qiě cast his net, caught it, and imprisoned it,
placing it in a cage.
At midnight,
the turtle came to appear in King Sòng Yuán's dream, saying:
"I was sent by the River Jiāng to the River Hé,
when a net blocked my path.
Yù Qiě of Quányáng caught me,
and I cannot escape.
My body is in distress,
with no one to tell my plight.
You, O King, possess virtue and righteousness,
so I have come to inform you."
The king awoke with a start.
He then summoned the scholar Wèi Píng and asked him:
"Tonight I dreamed of a man,
with an elongated neck and a long head,
dressed in dark embroidered robes and riding in a covered carriage,
who came to me in a dream, saying:
'I was sent by the River Jiāng to the River Hé,
when a net blocked my path.
Yù Qiě of Quányáng caught me,
and I cannot escape.
My body is in distress,
with no one to tell my plight.
You, O King, possess virtue and righteousness,
so I have come to inform you.'
What being is this?"
Wèi Píng then took up his astrological instrument and rose,
gazing up at the moonlight in the sky,
observing the direction pointed by the Dipper,
and determining the position of the sun.
Using compass and square as aids,
supplemented by weights and balances,
the four dimensions were fixed,
and the eight trigrams aligned.
After discerning the auspicious and inauspicious signs,
the shelled creature was the first to appear.
He then addressed King Yuán:
"This evening, on the day of Rénzǐ,
the constellation rests in Qiānniú.
The rivers converge greatly,
ghosts and spirits conspire.
The Milky Way aligns north-south,
the Jiāng and Hé firmly appointed,
the south wind newly arrived,
the envoy from Jiāng came first,
white clouds choke the Milky Way,
all things are detained.
The Dipper's handle points at the sun,
the envoy is destined to be imprisoned.
Dressed in dark robes and riding a covered carriage,
its name is the turtle.
Your Majesty should swiftly send someone to inquire and seek it."
The king said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, the king sent a messenger galloping to ask the magistrate of Quányáng:
"How many families of fishermen are there?
Who among them is named Yù Qiě?
Yù Qiě caught a turtle,
which appeared in my dream,
so I have come to seek it."
The magistrate then had his clerk check the register and consult the maps,
finding fifty-five families of fishermen on the water,
with a hut upstream
belonging to one named Yù Qiě.
The magistrate said:
"Very well."
He then rode with the messenger to ask Yù Qiě:
"What did you catch while fishing last night?"
Yù Qiě replied:
"At midnight, I cast my net and caught a turtle."
The messenger asked:
"Where is the turtle now?"
He said:
"In the cage."
The messenger said:
"The king knows you caught the turtle,
so he sent me to retrieve it."
Yù Qiě said:
"As you wish."
He then tied up the turtle and removed it from the cage,
presenting it to the messenger.
The messenger loaded it and departed,
exiting the gates of Quányáng.
In broad daylight, nothing was visible,
wind and rain brought darkness.
Clouds covered above,
in hues of green and yellow;
thunder and rain arose together,
wind carried it along.
Entering through the main gate,
it appeared in the eastern chamber.
Its body flowed like water,
glossy and radiant.
Upon seeing King Yuán,
it stretched its neck forward,
took three steps and halted,
