then retracted its neck and retreated,
returning to its original spot.
The king found this strange
and asked Wèi Píng:
"When the turtle saw me,
it stretched its neck forward;
what was it hoping for?
And retracting its neck to retreat,
what does that signify?"
Wèi Píng replied:
"The turtle is in distress,
imprisoned all night long.
You, O King, possess virtue and righteousness,
sending someone to spare its life.
Its stretching neck forward
is to express gratitude,
while retracting its neck and retreating
shows its desire to leave quickly."
The king said:
"How remarkable!
If its divinity is so profound,
it must not be detained long;
prepare a carriage swiftly to send the turtle back,
do not let it miss its appointed time."
Wèi Píng responded:
"This turtle is a treasure of the world;
he who first obtains it will become the Son of Heaven,
and his words will hit the mark ten out of ten times,
his battles won ten out of ten.
Born in the deep abyss,
reared in the yellow earth,
it knows the ways of heaven,
enlightened since ancient times.
It roams for three thousand years,
never leaving its domain.
Tranquil and upright,
it moves without exertion.
Its lifespan spans heaven and earth,
none know its limits.
It transforms with all things,
changing color with the four seasons.
It dwells in self-concealment,
hibernates without eating.
Green in spring, yellow in summer,
white in autumn, black in winter.
Wise in the ways of yīn and yáng,
discerning in punishment and virtue,
it foreknows benefit and harm,
perceives fortune and misfortune.
With words that always hit the mark,
and battles always won,
if you, O King, treasure it,
all feudal lords will submit.
Do not send it away,
to secure the state's stability."
King Yuán said:
"The turtle is profoundly divine,
descended from the heavens,
yet trapped in a deep abyss,
in the midst of hardship.
It deemed me worthy,
for my abundant virtue and faithful integrity,
thus it came to inform me.
If I do not release it,
I am no different from the fisherman.
The fisherman profits from its flesh,
while I covet its power;
below, it would be unkind,
above, it would be virtueless.
If ruler and minister lack propriety,
how can fortune follow?
I cannot bear this;
how can I not send it away!"
Wèi Píng replied:
"Not so.
I have heard that great virtue goes unrequited,
and heavy responsibilities find no return;
when Heaven gives and one does not accept,
Heaven will take away its treasures.
Now this turtle has traveled throughout the world,
returning to its dwelling place,
reaching up to the blue sky,
and descending to the muddy marshes.
It has traversed all nine provinces,
never suffering shame or insult,
with nowhere it was detained.
Now it has come to Quányáng,
where a fisherman has insulted and imprisoned it.
If Your Majesty sends it away,
the rivers will surely rage,
seeking vengeance.
Considering itself wronged,
it will conspire with the spirits.
Endless rains will not cease,
floods will become uncontrollable.
Or there may be severe drought,
with winds stirring up dust,
locusts swarming suddenly,
and the people missing their farming seasons.
Though Your Majesty practices benevolence and righteousness,
the punishment will surely come.
This is for no other reason -
the curse lies with the turtle.
Even if you regret it later,
what could you possibly do then!
Do not send it away, Your Majesty."
King Yuán sighed deeply and said:
"To oppose another's messenger,
to thwart another's plans -
is this not tyranny?
To take what others possess,
and make it one's own treasure -
is this not force?
I have heard that
what is gained by violence will be lost violently,
and what is taken by force will ultimately prove fruitless.
Jié and Zhòu were tyrannical and forceful,
yet they died and their states perished.
If I now follow your advice,
I would have the way of tyranny and force without the name of benevolence and righteousness.
The rivers would become like Tāng and Wǔ,
while I would become like Jié and Zhòu.
I see no benefit in this,
and fear I would incur calamity.
I am doubtful -
why should I keep this treasure?
Hurry and prepare the carriage to send the turtle back,
do not let it stay long."
Wèi Píng replied:
"Not so,
Your Majesty need not worry.
Between heaven and earth,
stones accumulate to form mountains.
High yet not collapsing,
the earth thereby gains stability.
Thus it is said that some things appear dangerous yet actually secure,
some seem light yet cannot be moved;
some people are loyal and trustworthy yet not as successful as the deceitful,
some are ugly yet suited for high office,
some are beautiful and elegant yet become the people's scourge.
Unless one is a divine sage,
none can fully explain this.
Spring, autumn, winter, summer -
sometimes hot, sometimes cold.
When heat and cold are imbalanced,
harmful energies conflict with each other.
Different seasons in the same year -
this is how the times make them.
Thus we have spring for birth, summer for growth,
autumn for harvest, winter for storage.
Sometimes benevolence and righteousness are needed,
sometimes force and tyranny.
Force and tyranny have their place,
benevolence and righteousness their time.
All things are like this,
impossible to fully regulate.
If Your Majesty will listen to me,
I beg to explain fully.
Heaven produces the five colors,
to distinguish white from black.
Earth grows the five grains,
to know good from evil.
Common people cannot distinguish these,
resembling birds and beasts.
They dwell in valleys and live in caves,
knowing nothing of field cultivation.
When the world falls into chaos and disaster,
yin and yang become disordered.
In haste and urgency,
they mix without discrimination.
Evil omens frequently appear,
and lineage becomes thin.
The sages separated their lives,
preventing mutual capture.
Animals have male and female -
they were placed in mountains and plains;
birds have female and male -
they were distributed in forests and marshes;
creatures with shells -
they were placed in streams and valleys.
Therefore, to govern the people,
walléd cities were built for them,
with lanes and alleys inside,
and field paths outside.
Husbands and wives, men and women -
they were allotted fields and homes,
arranged their houses.
Registers were made for them,
distinguishing their clans and families.
Officials were appointed and administrators installed,
encouraged by ranks and emoluments.
They were clothed with mulberry and hemp,
nourished with the five grains.
They plowed and harrowed,
hoed and weeded.
Their mouths obtained what they craved,
their eyes saw what was beautiful,
their bodies enjoyed the benefits.
From this perspective,
nothing can be achieved without strength.
Therefore it is said: if farmers are not strong,
their granaries will not be full;
if merchants are not strong,
they will not make profits;
if women are not strong,
their cloth and silk will not be fine;
if officials are not strong,
their authority will not be established;
if generals are not strong,
soldiers will not obey commands;
if feudal lords and kings are not strong,
they will leave no name for posterity.
Thus we say strength
is the beginning of affairs,
the principle of division,
the discipline of things.
What is sought through strength,
there is nothing one cannot have.
If Your Majesty thinks otherwise,
has you not heard of the jade box containing the pheasant,
coming from Kūnlún Mountain;
the bright moon pearls,
coming from the four seas;
carved stones and opened clams,
sold in markets:
when sages obtain them,
they consider them great treasures.
Where the great treasure resides,
there becomes the Son of Heaven.
Now if Your Majesty considers yourself tyrannical,
you are no more than opening clams in the sea;
if you consider yourself strong,
you are no more than carving stones at Kūnlún Mountain.
Those who take incur no blame,
those who treasure suffer no harm.
Now the turtle's messenger came and touched the net,
and was caught by a fisherman,
appearing in dreams to speak for itself -
this is the treasure of the state,
why should Your Majesty worry about it?"
King Yuán stated:
"That is not so.
I have heard that
remonstrators bring blessings,
while flatterers bring harm.
If a ruler listens to flatterers,
he is foolish and deluded.
Nevertheless,
calamity does not come without cause,
nor do blessings arrive without reason.
Heaven and earth combine their energies
to produce all wealth.
Yīn and yáng have their divisions,
never departing from the four seasons,
the twelve months,
with the solstices as their markers.
When sages understand this thoroughly,
their persons remain free from disaster.
When enlightened kings employ this,
none dare deceive them.
Thus it is said that when blessings arrive,
people generate them themselves;
when calamity comes,
people create it themselves.
Calamity and fortune are paired,
as are punishment and virtue.
Sages examine this
to understand fortune and misfortune.
During the times of Jié and Zhòu,
they contended with heaven for achievements,
blocked ghosts and spirits,
preventing them from passing through.
They were thus already without morality,
yet had numerous flattering ministers.
Jié had a flattering minister
named Zhào Liáng.
He taught him to act without morality,
urging him toward greed and cruelty.
He imprisoned Tāng at Xiàtái,
and executed Guān Lóngpáng.
Those around him feared death,
secretly flattering him by his side.
The state was in danger like piled eggs,
yet all said there was no harm.
They claimed happiness met the years,
some said it was endless.
They blinded and deafened him,
joining him in deceit and madness.
Tāng eventually attacked Jié,
who died and lost his state.
By listening to his flattering ministers,
he alone suffered the calamity.
The Spring and Autumn Annals recorded it,
and it is remembered to this day.
Zhòu had a flattering minister
named Zuǒ Qiáng.
Boastful and clever with appearances,
he taught him to build an ivory palace.
Reaching toward the heavens,
it also had a jade bed.
Vessels of rhinoceros horn and jade,
and ivory chopsticks for soup.
Sages had their hearts cut out,
strong men had their shins severed.
Jīzǐ, fearing death,
disheveled his hair and feigned madness.
He killed King Wén of Zhōu's eldest son Lì,
and imprisoned King Wén, Chāng.
Cast into a stone chamber,
to be kept from dawn till dusk.
Yīn Jìng saved him,
and fled with him.
They entered the land of Zhōu,
and found Tàigōng Wàng.
Raising troops and gathering armies,
they attacked Zhòu.
King Wén fell ill and died,
his corpse carried into battle.
The crown prince Fā took command,
known as King Wǔ.
They fought at Mùyě,
defeating him south of Huàshān.
King Zhòu, defeated in battle, fled back,
surrounded in his ivory palace.
He killed himself in the Xuān chamber,
his body left unburied.
His head hung from a chariot rail,
dragged by four horses.
When I reflect on such things,
my insides boil like bubbling water.
These men both possessed the wealth of the world and honor of being Son of Heaven,
yet they were greatly arrogant.
Their desires knew no satisfaction,
they delighted in lofty undertakings,
greedy, cruel, and proud.
They did not employ loyalty and trustworthiness,
but listened to their flattering ministers,
becoming the laughingsstock of the world.
Now my state,
situated among the various lords,
is not even comparable to the slightest autumn hair.
If I act inappropriately,
where could I possibly flee to escape!"
Wèi Píng replied:
"Not so.
Though the River is divine and wise,
it is not equal to the Kūnlún Mountains;
the source and course of the Yangtze,
are not equal to the Four Seas,
yet people still seize their treasures,
the feudal lords contend for them,
and armed conflicts arise.
Small states are seen to perish,
great states are endangered,
fathers and brothers are killed,
wives and children are captured,
countries are devastated and ancestral temples destroyed,
all to contend for these treasures.
Warfare and strife,
this is violent strength.
Thus it is said that taking by violent strength but governing with civil order,
not opposing the four seasons,
must be close to worthy scholars;
harmonizing with the transformations of yīn and yáng,
commanding ghosts and spirits;
communicating with heaven and earth,
and being friends with them.
The feudal lords submit as guests,
the masses are prosperous and joyful.
The state and families are peaceful and secure,
renewing with the age.
Tāng and Wǔ practiced this,
and thus attained the Son of Heaven;
the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded it,
considering it the constant principle.
Your Majesty does not style yourself as Tāng or Wǔ,
but instead compares yourself to Jié and Zhòu.
Jié and Zhòu were violent and strong,
and certainly regarded it as normal.
Jié built tiled palaces,
Zhòu constructed ivory corridors.
They levied silk and burned it,
striving to exhaust the people.
Taxes and levies knew no limits,
killings and executions had no rules.
They killed people's six domestic animals,
using leather to make bags.
The bags filled with their blood,
they hung them with people and shot at them,
contending in strength with the Lord of Heaven.
They disrupted and confused the four seasons,
tasting offerings before the hundred ghosts.
Those who remonstrated were immediately put to death,
flatterers stood by their side.
Sages went into hiding,
the common people had nowhere to go.
Heaven sent frequent droughts,
the state was full of ominous signs.
Locusts and pests arose yearly,
the five grains did not ripen.
The people could not settle in their homes,
ghosts and spirits did not accept offerings.
Whirlwinds rose daily,
midday turned dark and dim.
Sun and moon were both eclipsed,
extinguished and without light.
The arrayed stars fled in chaos,
all lost their guiding principles.
From this perspective,
how could they last long!
Even without Tāng and Wǔ,
their time was destined to end.
Thus Tāng attacked Jié,
King Wǔ overcame Zhòu,
their era made it so.
They became Sons of Heaven,
their descendants continued for generations;
they themselves were without fault,
later generations praised them,
and still do to this day.
These all acted according to their time,
seeing events and strengthening themselves,
thus able to achieve their imperial kingship.
Now the turtle,
is a great treasure,
sent by the sages,
passed to a worthy king.
It uses no hands or feet,
thunder and lightning guide it;
wind and rain escort it,
flowing waters carry it.
Only feudal kings with virtue,
can rightly receive it.
Now Your Majesty has virtue and should receive this treasure,
yet I fear you dare not accept it;
if you send it away,
Sòng will surely face calamity.
Later, even if you regret it,
it will be too late."
King Yuán was greatly pleased and joyful.
Thereupon King Yuán faced the sun and gave thanks,
bowing twice he accepted it.
He chose an auspicious day for fasting and purification,
the days of Jiǎ and Yǐ being the best.
Then he sacrificed a white pheasant,
and also a black sheep;
with their blood he anointed the turtle,
upon the altar's center.
With a knife he carved it,
its body whole and unharmed.
Dried meat and wine were offered in ceremony,
its belly and intestines laid crosswise.
With thorn branches he divined,
surely controlling the cracks.
The patterns reached the principles,
the lines interwove and met.
He had the artisans interpret it,
all they said was entirely fitting.
The state's blessing and heavy treasure,
became known in neighboring lands.
They slaughtered oxen to take their hides,
covered Zhèng's tong wood,
plants and trees all divided,
transformed into armor and weapons.
In victory in battle and conquest,
none matched King Yuán.
In King Yuán's time,
Wèi Píng served as minister of Sòng,
the state of Sòng was strongest,
all due to the turtle's power.
Thus it is said the spirit can appear in a dream to King Yuán,
yet cannot free itself from the fisherman's trap.
It can speak ten statements all accurate,
yet cannot communicate with the River,
or return a report to the Yangtze.
Worthy ones can enable others to win battles and conquer,
yet cannot free themselves from the knife's edge,
or avoid the misfortune of being carved and pierced.
Sages can foresee and quickly perceive,
yet cannot make Wèi Píng silent.
They can speak of affairs with perfect accuracy,
yet regarding themselves, they are constrained;
when the time is unfavorable,
how then can they serve the worthy!
The worthy have constant norms,
scholars have偶然 occurrences.
Therefore, vision has what it does not see,
hearing has what it does not hear;
though a person may be worthy,
they cannot draw a square with the left hand,
and a circle with the right simultaneously;
the brightness of sun and moon,
is at times obscured by floating clouds.
Yì was famed for skilled archery,
yet was not equal to Xióng Qú,
Fēng Mén;
Yǔ was renowned for eloquence and wisdom,
yet could not overcome ghosts and spirits.
The earthly pillar broke,
heaven thus has no rafters,
so how can we demand perfection from people?
Confucius heard this and said:
"The divine turtle knows good and bad fortune,
yet its bones are straight but hollow and dry.
The sun, embodying virtue and ruling under heaven,
is humiliated by the three-legged crow.
The moon, embodying punishment and assisting,
is eaten by the toad.
The hedgehog is shamed by the magpie,
the soaring snake's divinity is endangered by the centipede.
Bamboo has joints and texture on the outside,
but inside is straight and hollow;
pine and cypress are the leaders of all trees,
yet guard gates and alleys.
The days and hours are not complete,
hence there are gaps and voids.
Gold has flaws,
white jade has blemishes.
Affairs have their haste,
also their slowness.
Things have their constraints,
also their supports.
Nets have their dense parts,
also their sparse areas.
People have what they excel in,
also what they are not good at.
How can one be perfect in everything?
How can things be complete?
Even heaven is not complete,
therefore when building a house in the world,
we leave three tiles unfinished and place them,
to correspond to heaven.
The world has its steps,
it is because things are not complete that life arises."
Mr. Chǔ comments:
A fisherman cast his net and caught a divine turtle.
The turtle appeared in a dream to King Sòng Yuán.
King Yuán summoned the court scholar Wèi Píng and told him about the dream and the turtle's appearance.
Píng manipulated the divination board,
determined the positions of the sun and moon,
calculated the celestial degrees,
and observed the auspicious and inauspicious signs.
The divination results matched the turtle's characteristics.
Píng advised the king to keep the turtle as a national treasure.
How splendid!
In ancient times, divination always honored the turtle,
for its renowned reputation
has existed for a long time.
I narrate this and compose a biography.

Divination taboos state:
On days zǐ, hài, and xū, one must not kill turtles.
From noon until after eating.
At dusk, when the turtle is active,
one should not divine.
On days gēng and xīn, one may kill
and drill them.
Always cleanse the turtle on the first day of the month,
first washing it with clear water,
then purifying it with an egg,
before holding the turtle to perform divination,
as if regularly following ancestral practices.
If someone has divined incorrectly,
they should purify it with an egg,
stand facing east,
burn it with thorns or hard wood,
point a clay egg three times,
and encircle the turtle with the egg,
praying:
"Today is auspicious;
we reverently use millet, eggs, roasted lacquer, and yellow dye to remove the inauspiciousness from the jade spirit."
The jade spirit must be truthful and sincere,
knowing the circumstances of all matters,
and all crack patterns can be interpreted.
If it is not truthful or sincere,
then burn the jade spirit,
scatter its ashes,
to warn future turtles.
Divination must be done facing north,
and the turtle shell must be one foot two inches.
For divination, first drill and burn the shell,
after drilling the center,
burn the turtle's head,
each three times;
then burn the drilled center called the 'true body,'
and burn the head called the 'true feet,'
each three times.
Then encircle the turtle three times with the drill,
praying:
"We borrow from the Master Jade Spirit.
Master Jade Spirit,
we burn thorns to reach your heart,
enabling you to foreknow.
You ascend to the heavens above,
descend to the abyss below,
among all spirits and counting stalks,
none is as trustworthy as you.
Today is a good day,
we seek a favorable divination.
So-and-so wishes to divine about something,
if obtained, we rejoice;
if not, we regret.
If obtained,
show us our bodies tall and large,
heads and feet gathered, all symmetrical upward.
If not obtained,
show us our bodies bent and broken,
inner and outer parts not corresponding,
heads and feet vanished."
The spiritual turtle divination prayer says:
"We borrow from the spiritual turtle;
five shamans, five spirits,
none match the divine turtle's power,
knowing people's death,
knowing people's life.
This body seeks a good divination,
so-and-so desires to obtain a certain thing.
If obtained,
the head appears, feet extend,
inner and outer correspond;
if not obtained,
head raised, belly contracted,
inner and outer sagging.
We may thus interpret."
Divining about a sick person, pray:
"Now so-and-so is severely ill.
If dying, the head part opens upward,
inner and outer parts startle each other,
body segments broken;
if not dying,
head raised, belly contracted."
Divining about illness caused by spirits, say:
"If the illness has a spirit, no sign appears;
if no spirit, a sign appears.
If the omen has inner spirit, it shows internally;
if outer spirit, it shows externally."

On the road, will encounter thieves.
Hearing words but not seeing.
Rain will not rain.
Clearing will occur.
Greatly auspicious.
Designation: Head Raised, Feet Drawn In, Inner and Outer Parts Naturally Drooping.
Divining about a worried sick person: very severe,
but will not die.
Holding office: cannot hold it.
Traveler: will travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Seeking wealth and goods: cannot obtain.
Seeking people: cannot find.
Auspicious.
Designation: Horizontally Auspicious with Pillars Below.
Divining about a visitor: will come.
If not arriving on the divination day,
then will not come in the future.
Divining about a sick person: if not cured after one day, will die.
Traveler: will not travel.
Seeking wealth and goods: cannot obtain.
Detained person: will be released.
Designation: Horizontally Auspicious, Inner and Outer Parts Naturally Lifted.
Using this to divine about a sick person:
will not die for a long time.
Detained person: will not be released for a long time.
Seeking wealth and goods: will obtain but little.
Traveler: will not travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Meeting an esteemed person: will meet.
Auspicious.
Designation: Inner High, Outer Low, Illness Light, Feet Active.
Seeking wealth and goods: cannot obtain.
Traveler: will travel.
Sick person: will recover.
Detained person: will not be released.
Visitor: will come.
Meeting an esteemed person: will not meet.
Auspicious.
Designation: Outer Pattern.
Seeking wealth and goods: cannot obtain.
Traveler: will not travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Detained person: will not be released.
Inauspicious.
Sick person: will die.
Seeking wealth and goods: cannot obtain.
Meeting an esteemed person: will meet.
Auspicious.
Designation: Inner Naturally Lifted, Outer Upright, Feet Active.
Traveler: will travel.
Visitor: will come.
Seeking wealth and goods: will obtain.
Sick person: will not die for a long time.
Detained person: will not be released.
Meeting an esteemed person: will meet.
Auspicious.
This is Horizontally Auspicious Upper Pillar, Outer and Inner Naturally Lifted, Feet Drawn In.
Using this to divine about having a request: will obtain.
Sick person: will not die.
Detained person: unharmed,
but not released.
Traveler: will not travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Meeting people: will not meet.
All matters entirely auspicious.
This is Horizontally Auspicious Upper Pillar, Outer and Inner Naturally Lifted, Pillar Feet Active.
Using this to divine about having a request: will obtain.
Sick person: will die, but illness may recur.
Detained person: unharmed,
and may be released.
Traveler: will not travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Meeting people: will not meet.
All matters auspicious.
Can raise troops.
This is Upright with Deception Outside.
Using this to divine about having a request: will not obtain.
Sick person: will not die,
but illness recurs frequently.
Detained person: has misfortune or crime.
Hearing words: unharmed.
Traveler: will not travel.
Visitor: will not come.
This is Upright with Deception Inside.
Using this to divine about having a request: will not obtain.
Sick person: will not die,
but illness recurs frequently.
Detained person: has misfortune or crime but unharmed and released.
Traveler: will not travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Meeting people: will not meet.
This is Upright with Deception, Inner and Outer Naturally Lifted.
Using this to divine about having a request: will obtain.
Sick person: will not die,
detained without crime.
Traveler: will travel.
Visitor: will come.
Farming, trade, market, fishing, hunting: all joyful.
This is Fox Raccoon.
Using this to divine about having a request: will not obtain.
Sick person: will die,
illness difficult to overcome.
Detained person: without crime but difficult to release.
Can reside in a house.
Can marry a wife or give a daughter in marriage.
Traveler: will not travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Meeting people: will not meet.
Having worries: not to worry.
This is Fox Penetrating.
Using this to divine about having a request: will not obtain.
Sick person: will die.
Detained person: has deserving punishment.
Traveler: will not travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Meeting people: will not meet.
Words will be settled.
All matters entirely inauspicious.
This is Head Lowered, Feet Drawn In, Body Joints Broken.
Using this to divine about having a request: will not obtain.
Sick person: will die.
Detained person: has crime.
Awaiting a traveler: will not come.
Traveler: will travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Meeting people: will not meet.
This is Upright, Inner and Outer Naturally Drooping.
Using this to divine about having a request: not obscure.
Sick person: will not die,
but illness difficult to overcome.
Detained person: without crime,
but difficult to release.
Traveler: will not travel.
Visitor: will not come.
Meeting people: will not meet.
Inauspicious.
This is Horizontally Auspicious Elm, Head Raised and Lowered.
Using this to divine about having a request: difficult to obtain.
Illness: difficult to overcome,
but will not die.
Detained: difficult to release,
but unharmed.
Can reside at home,
and marry a wife or give a daughter in marriage.
This is Horizontally Auspicious Upper Pillar, Carrying Upright Body, Joints Broken, Inner and Outer Naturally Lifted.
Using this to divine about a sick person:
on the divination day, will not die,
but will die the next day.
This is Horizontally Auspicious Upper Pillar, Feet Drawn In, Inner Naturally Lifted, Outer Naturally Drooping.
Using this to divine about a sick person:
on the divination day, will not die,
but will die the next day.
Head Lowered, Feet Deceptive, Having Outside but No Inside.
For a sick person, if the turtle divination is not yet completed,
will die urgently.
If the divination is light, the loss is great,
but will not die for one day.
Head Raised, Feet Drawn In.
Using this to divine about having a request: will not obtain.
Using this for detention: has crime.
If people speak threateningly, unharmed.
Traveler: will not travel.
Meeting people: will not meet.
The Great Treatise states:
The external represents others,
the internal represents oneself;
the external represents the female,
the internal represents the male.
A bowed head signifies worry.
The large represents the body,
the small represents the branches.
The general rule:
For illness,
curled feet indicate survival,
spread feet indicate death.
For travelers,
spread feet mean arrival,
curled feet mean non-arrival.
For movement,
curled feet mean no movement,
spread feet mean movement.
For seeking,
spread feet mean attainment,
curled feet mean non-attainment.
For the detained,
curled feet mean no release,
spread feet mean release.
When divining about illness,
spread feet indicating death
mean the internal is elevated while the external is lowered.
Lǎo zǐ said:
"In the highest state of governance,
neighboring states are within sight,
the sounds of chickens and dogs are within hearing,
the people each enjoy their food,
appreciate their clothing,
are content with their customs,
and delight in their occupations,
until old age and death without interacting with one another."
If one must take this as the priority,
and in recent times block the people's ears and eyes,
then there is almost no way to proceed.
Grand Historian Simǎ Qiān said:
As for the times before Shénnóng,
I do not know of them.
But as described in the Shī and Shū from Yú and Xià dynasties onward,
eyes and ears desire the utmost in sounds and sights,
the mouth desires to exhaust the flavors of livestock,
the body seeks comfort and pleasure,
and the mind boasts of the glory of power and ability.
These customs have influenced the people for a long time,
and even with subtle arguments told to each household,
they ultimately cannot be transformed.
Therefore, the best approach is to follow them,
the next is to guide them with benefits,
the next is to instruct them,
the next is to regulate them,
and the worst is to contend with them.
Now, the region west of the mountains abounds in timber,
bamboo, paper mulberry trees,
hemp, yak tails,
and jade;
the region east of the mountains has plenty of fish,
salt, lacquer,
silk, and sensual pleasures;
the area south of the Yangtze produces nánmu wood,
zǐ wood, ginger,
cinnamon, gold,
tin, lead,
cinnabar,
rhinoceros horn, tortoise shell,
pearls, and jade,
ivory, and hides;
north of Lóngmén
and Jiéshí, there are many horses,
cattle, sheep,
felt and furs,
sinews, and horns;
copper and iron are found in mountains scattered over a thousand lǐ like chess pieces:
this is the general situation.
All these are what the people of the Middle Kingdom enjoy,
the necessities for customs, clothing, food, nurturing life, and sending off the dead.
Thus, they depend on farmers for food,
foresters for output,
artisans for finished products,
and merchants for circulation.
Does this require government decrees, conscriptions, or scheduled meetings?
People each employ their abilities,
exhaust their strength,
to obtain what they desire.
Hence, cheap goods signal a trend toward expensiveness,
expensive goods signal a trend toward cheapness,
each encouraging their own trade,
delighting in their tasks,
like water flowing downward,
ceaseless day and night,
coming without being summoned,
emerging without being sought.
Is this not in accordance with the Dào,
and a testament to what is natural?
The Zhōu Shū says:
"If farmers do not produce, there will be a shortage of food;
if artisans do not produce, there will be a shortage of goods;
if merchants do not circulate, the three treasures will be cut off;
if foresters do not produce, wealth will be scarce."
Wealth becomes scarce, and mountains and marshes are not opened up.
These four
are the source of the people's clothing and food.
A large source means abundance,
a small source means scarcity.
Above, it enriches the state;
below, it enriches the family.
In the way of wealth and poverty,
none can take away or give,
yet the skillful have surplus,
while the unskilled have insufficiency.
Therefore, when Tài Gōng Wàng was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū,
the land was saline,
and the population was sparse,
so Tài Gōng encouraged women's work,
pushed skills to the extreme,
and facilitated trade in fish and salt,
whereupon people and goods came to him,
gathering like swaddled infants and converging like spokes.
Thus, Qí provided caps, belts, clothes, and shoes for all under heaven,
and between the sea and Tài Shān, people adjusted their sleeves and went to pay homage.
Later, when Qí declined,
Guǎn Zǐ restored it,
establishing the nine treasuries for light and heavy coins,
enabling Duke Huán to become hegemon,
uniting the feudal lords nine times,
and rectifying the world;
and Guǎn Zhòng also had the Sānguī,
though his position was that of a minister,
he was wealthier than the rulers of other states.
Thus, Qí's wealth and strength lasted until the times of Wēi
and Xuān.
Hence it is said:
"When granaries are full, one knows礼节;
when food and clothing are sufficient, one knows honor and disgrace."
Courtesy arises from having and is abandoned in want.
Thus, when gentlemen are wealthy,
they are inclined to practice virtue;
when common people are wealthy,
they can exert their strength appropriately.
Where the pond is deep, fish will dwell;
where the mountain is deep, beasts will go;
where people are wealthy, benevolence and righteousness adhere.
The wealthy, when in power, become more prominent;
when out of power, guests have nowhere to go,
and they become unhappy.
Among the Yí and Dí tribes, this is even more so.
A proverb says:
"The child of a wealthy family
does not die in the marketplace."
This is not an empty saying.
Therefore, it is said:
"All under heaven hustle
for profit they come;
all under heaven bustle,
for profit they go."
The king of a thousand chariots,
the marquis of ten thousand households,
the lord of a hundred rooms,
still worry about poverty,
how much more so the common people registered in households!
In the past, King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè was trapped on Mount Kuàijī,
and then employed Fàn Lǐ
and Jì Rán.
Jì Rán said:
"Knowing there will be fighting means preparing accordingly,
understanding the seasons' needs means knowing goods,
when these two are clear, the nature of all commodities can be observed.
Thus when the year is under Metal,
there is abundance; under Water,
ruin; under Wood,
famine; under Fire,
drought. In drought, invest in boats;
in flood, invest in carts—
this is the principle of things.
Six years of abundance,
six years of drought,
twelve years bring a great famine.
As for grain selling,
at twenty coins, farmers suffer;
at ninety, merchants suffer.
If merchants suffer, wealth doesn't circulate;
if farmers suffer, fields aren't cultivated.
If the price doesn't exceed eighty
nor fall below thirty,
then both farmers and merchants benefit,
fair grain prices balance goods,
markets aren't lacking,
this is the way to govern a state.
The principle of accumulating goods
is to ensure their quality,
don't let currency lie idle.
In trading goods,
don't keep perishable items,
don't insist on high prices.
Consider surplus and shortage,
then know value and cheapness.
When high prices peak, they reverse to low;
when low prices bottom, they reverse to high.
Sell expensive goods like dirt,
buy cheap goods like jewels.
Wealth should flow like running water."
After practicing this for ten years,
the state grew rich,
generously rewarding warriors,
who braved arrows and stones
like thirsting men getting drink,
thus they avenged strong Wú,
displayed military power in the Central States,
and were titled
"One of the Five Hegemons".
After Fàn Lǐ had washed away the shame of Kuàijī,
he sighed and said:
"Jì Rán had seven strategies,
Yuè used five and achieved success.
Having applied them to the state,
I wish to use them for my family."
He then took a small boat onto rivers and lakes,
changed his name and surname,
went to Qí as Chīyí Zǐpí,
and to Táo as Lord Zhū.
Lord Zhū considered Táo the center of the world,
with access to all states,
where goods were traded.
He managed property and accumulated wealth,
competing with the times without blaming others.
Thus those skilled in livelihood
can choose people and seize opportunities.
In nineteen years, he thrice gained a thousand gold,
repeatedly sharing with poor friends and distant relatives.
This is what's called wealth used for virtuous deeds.
Later, aged, he let his descendants take over,
who continued the business and multiplied it,
reaching immense wealth.
Hence those speaking of wealth all praise Lord Táo Zhū.
Zǐ Gòng, having studied under Zhòngní,
retired and served in Wèi,
hoarding and selling goods between Cáo
and Lǔ.
Among the seventy disciples,
Cì was the wealthiest.
Yuán Xiàn couldn't escape coarse food,
hiding in poor alleys.
Zǐ Gòng had teams of horses and carriages,
with bundles of silk to engage with lords,
wherever he went,
rulers treated him as an equal.
That Confucius's name spread under heaven
was aided by Zǐ Gòng's support.
Is this not what's called gaining influence and enhancing fame?
Bái Guī
was a man of Zhōu.
During Lord Wén of Wèi's time,
Lǐ Kè focused on maximizing land use,
while Bái Guī delighted in observing changing times,
thus when others discarded, he took;
when others sought, he gave.
In harvest years, he took grain,
giving silk and lacquer;
when cocoons emerged, he took cloth and wadding,
giving food.
When Jupiter was in mǎo,
abundance; next year poor.
Reaching wǔ,
drought; next year good.
Reaching yǒu,
abundance; next year poor.
Reaching zǐ,
great drought;
next year good,
with flood.
Back in mǎo,
accumulated wealth usually doubled.
To increase money, buy inferior grain;
to increase volume,
buy superior seeds.
He could endure plain food and drink,
restrain desires,
save on clothing,
share hardships and joys with servants,
seize opportunities like fierce beasts or birds striking.
Thus he said:
"I manage livelihood
like Yī Yǐn
and Lǚ Shàng's strategies,
Sūn and Wú's warfare,
or Shāng Yāng's law enforcement.
Therefore, if one's wisdom lacks adaptability,
courage lacks decisiveness,
benevolence lacks giving and taking,
strength lacks perseverance,
even if they wish to learn my methods,
I won't ultimately teach them."
So the world considers Bái Guī the patriarch of wealth management.
Bái Guī had tested his methods,
excelling through trial,
not merely by chance.
Yī Dùn started with salt mining.
And Guō Zòng of Hándān built his fortune on iron smelting,
rivaling kings in wealth.
Wūshì Luǒ raised livestock,
and when they multiplied,
he sold them,
seeking rare silks and objects,
secretly presenting them to the Róng king.
The Róng king repaid him tenfold,
giving him herds,
so numerous that horses and cattle were measured by valleys.
Emperor Qín Shǐ Huáng granted Luǒ status equal to nobles, allowing him
to attend court
with ministers,
while the widow Qīng of Bā,
whose ancestors found a cinnabar mine,
monopolized its profits for generations,
accumulating immeasurable wealth.
Qīng, a widow,
preserved her enterprise,
using wealth for self-defense,
remaining unviolated.
The Qín emperor regarded her as a chaste woman and treated her as a guest,
building for her the Nǚ Huái Qīng Tower.
Though Luǒ was a rustic herdsman,
and Qīng a widow from a remote village,
they were honored by the emperor,
their fame spread under heaven—
was it not due to their wealth?
With Hàn's rise,
the realm was unified,
border passes opened,
restrictions on mountains and marshes lifted,
thus wealthy merchants traveled everywhere,
all trade goods circulated freely,
achieving their desires,
while powerful families and nobles were relocated to the capital.
The region within the Pass, from Qiān
and Yōng eastward to the Yellow River and Huà
Mountain, spans a thousand miles of fertile soil and rich plains.
Since the tribute systems of Yú and Xià dynasties, it has been regarded as prime farmland.
When Gōng Liú moved to Bīn,
followed by Tài Wáng
and Wáng Jì residing in Qí,
King Wén establishing Fēng,
and King Wǔ governing Hào,
the people retained the legacy of these ancient kings,
excelling in farming
and cultivating the five grains.
The land was valued,
and misconduct was frowned upon.
By the time of Duke Wén of Qín,
Duke Dé, and Duke Mù residing in Yōng,
they capitalized on trade routes between Lǒng and Shǔ, fostering many merchants.
Duke Xiàn moved the capital to Yuèyì,
which repelled the Róng and Dí tribes to the north
and connected with the Three Jìn to the east,
also attracting numerous great merchants.
Under Xiào and Zhāo, Xiányáng was developed,
and later, with the Hàn capital
and the imperial tombs in Cháng'ān,
it became a hub where people and goods converged from all directions.
With limited land and a dense population,
the people increasingly turned to cunning and secondary occupations.
To the south lay Bā and Shǔ.
Bā and Shǔ also had fertile plains,
rich in resources like lacquer trees,
ginger, cinnabar,
stone, copper,
iron, bamboo,
and wooden implements.
To the south, they controlled Diānbó,
from which came Bó slaves.
To the west, they were near Qióngzuó,
sources of Zuó horses
and yaks.
Though surrounded by natural barriers,
a network of plank roads stretched a thousand miles,
making all areas accessible,
with only Bāoxié controlling the key passage,
allowing trade of surpluses for scarcities.
Tiānshuǐ,
Lǒngxī,
Běidì,
and Shàngjùn shared customs with the region within the Pass,
but they benefited from the Qiāng territories to the west
and the livestock of the Róng and Dí to the north,
making their animal husbandry the most abundant in the land.
However, the terrain was remote and perilous,
with only the capital commanding the routes.
Thus, the land within the Pass
constituted one-third of the empire's territory,
with only about thirty percent of the population;
yet in terms of wealth,
it accounted for sixty percent.
In the past, the Táng people had their capital east of the river,
the Yīn people north of the river,
and the Zhōu people south of the river.
These three river regions lay at the heart of the empire,
like the legs of a tripod,
where kings successively established their seats,
each ruling for hundreds or thousands of years.
The land was small and narrow,
the population dense,
and it served as a gathering place for feudal lords and states,
fostering a frugal and industrious custom among the people.
Yáng and Píngyáng traded west with Qín
and Dí, and north with Zhǒng
and Dài. Zhǒng
and Dài, north of the mountains,
bordered the Hú people,
and were frequently raided.
The people were stubborn and contentious,
spirited,
prone to chivalry and mischief,
neglecting farming and commerce.
Yet, being close to the northern tribes,
military campaigns often passed through,
and the central states supplied provisions, sometimes yielding surplus profits.
The people were rugged and uneven in character,
and since the time of the unified Jìn, their fierceness had long been a concern,
exacerbated by King Wǔ Líng's policies,
leaving customs that still reflected Zhào's influence.
Thus, Yáng
and Píngyáng maneuvered among them,
achieving their desires.
Wēn and Zhǐ traded west with Shàngdǎng
and north with Zhào
and Zhōngshān.
Zhōngshān had poor land and a dense population,
with remnants of the decadent legacy from Shāqiū of King Zhòu,
and the people were impulsive and hasty,
relying on opportunistic gains for livelihood.
Men gathered for games,
singing mournful and impassioned songs,
and when active, they engaged in robbery and assault;
when idle, they dug graves and practiced deceit and vice,
yet they produced many fine goods
and entertainers.
Women played the zither,
fluttered in their slippers,
and charmed the wealthy and noble,
entering rear palaces
and reaching various feudal lords.
Yet Hándān was also a major city between the Zhāng
and Yellow River.
It connected north to Yān
and Zhuō, and south to Zhèng
and Wèi. The customs of Zhèng
and Wèi resembled those of Zhào,
but being near Liáng
and Lǔ, they were more restrained and valued integrity.
The city of Púshàng moved to Yěwáng,
where the people were spirited and chivalrous,
a trait of Wèi's tradition.
Yān was also a major city between the Bó
and Jié seas.
It connected south to Qí
and Zhào, and bordered the Hú to the northeast.
From Shànggǔ to Liáodōng,
the land was vast and remote,
sparsely populated,
and frequently raided,
largely sharing customs with Zhào
and Dài,
with people who were fierce and reckless,
but abundant in fish, salt, dates, and chestnuts.
To the north, it neighbored Wūhuán
and Fūyú,
and to the east, it controlled the profits from Huìmò,
Cháoxiǎn,
and Zhēnpān.
Luòyáng traded east with Qí
and Lǔ, and south with Liáng
and Chǔ. Thus, south of Tàishān lay Lǔ,
and north lay Qí.
Qí, girded by mountains and sea,
had a thousand miles of fertile land,
suitable for mulberry and hemp,
with people rich in patterned silks, cloth, fish, and salt.
Línzī was also a major city between the sea and Dài Mountain.
Its customs were broad-minded and tolerant,
with ample wisdom,
and a penchant for debate,
valuing the land,
and being hard to sway,
cautious in group fights
but brave in solo assaults,
hence many resorted to robbery,
reflecting the demeanor of a great state.
It housed all five types of people.
Whereas Zōu
and Lǔ, bordering the Zhū
and Sì rivers, retained the legacy of the Duke of Zhōu,
with a custom that revered Confucianism,
emphasized rituals,
making the people meticulous and cautious.
They had some mulberry and hemp cultivation,
but lacked the abundance of forests and marshes.
With limited land and a dense population,
they were frugal and thrifty,
wary of crime and avoiding wrongdoing.
In their decline,
they turned to trade and profit-seeking,
even more so than the people of Zhōu.
East of the Hóng Gōu,
north of Máng and Dàng,
extending to Jùyě,
this was the region of Liáng
and Sòng.
Táo and Suīyáng were also major cities.
In the past, Yáo had his start in Chéngyáng,
Shǔn fished in Léizé,
and Tāng settled in Bó.
The customs still bore the mark of these ancient kings,
with many dignified gentlemen, devoted to farming,
and though lacking rich mountains and rivers,
they could endure coarse food and clothing,
amassing their savings.
Yuè and
Chǔ have three distinct customs.
From north of the Huái River, Pèi,
Chén, Rǔnán,
to Nánjùn,
this is Western Chǔ.
Its customs are impetuous and fickle,
prone to anger,
the land is barren,
with little accumulation of wealth.
Jiānglíng, the former capital of Yǐng,
connects west to Wū
and Bā, and east has the abundance of Yúnmèng.
Chén lies at the junction of Chǔ and Xià,
facilitating trade in fish and salt,
and its people are mostly merchants.
Xú, Tóng,
Qǔlǘ,
are known for their austerity and strictness,
priding themselves on keeping promises.
East of Péngchéng,
Dōnghǎi,
Wú, Guǎnglíng,
this is Eastern Chǔ.
Its customs resemble those of Xú
and Tóng. North of Qú
and Zēng,
the customs are like those of Qí.
South of the Zhè River is Yuè.
Wú, since Hé Lǘ,
Chūnshēn,
and Wáng Bì attracted the pleasure-seeking youth of the world,
has had abundant sea salt to the east,
copper from Zhāngshān,
and the benefits of the Three Rivers
and Five Lakes,
making it a major metropolis east of the river.
Héngshān,
Jiǔjiāng,
Jiāngnán,
Yùzhāng,
Chángshā,
this is Southern Chǔ.
Its customs are largely similar to Western Chǔ.
After Yǐng moved to Shòuchūn,
it also became a major metropolis.
Héféi receives tides from north and south,
and is a hub for leather,
salted fish, and timber.
Mingling customs with Mǐnzhōng
and Gānyuè,
thus Southern Chǔ is fond of rhetoric,
clever in speech but lacking in trust.
Jiāngnán is low and damp,
with men dying young.
There are many bamboos and trees.
Yùzhāng produces gold,
Chángshā produces lead
and tin, yet these resources are meager,
and extracting them is not worth the cost.
From Jiǔyí,
Cāngwú south to Dān'ěr,
the customs are largely similar to Jiāngnán,
but with more Yángyuè influence.
Pānyú is also a major metropolis,
a convergence of pearls,
rhinoceros horn, tortoiseshell,
fruits, and cloth.
Yǐngchuān,
Nányáng,
are the dwelling places of the Xià people.
The governance of the Xià people emphasizes loyalty and simplicity,
still retaining the legacy of ancient kings.
Yǐngchuān is honest and sincere.
In the late Qín era,
unruly people were relocated to Nányáng.
Nányáng connects west to Wǔguān
and Yúnguān,
and receives the Hàn,
Jiāng, and Huái rivers to the southeast.
Wǎn is also a major metropolis.
Its customs are mixed and meddlesome,
with many engaged in trade.
They champion chivalry,
and interact with Yǐngchuān,
hence to this day they are called
"Xià people."
As for the scarcity and abundance of goods under heaven,
and the customs of the people,
east of the mountains they eat sea salt,
west of the mountains they eat rock salt,
while south of the ridge
and north of the deserts, salt is often produced,
generally speaking.
In summary,
the lands of Chǔ and Yuè,
are vast and sparsely populated,
eating rice and fish soup,
sometimes practicing slash-and-burn farming and water-weeding,
with abundant fruits, snails, and clams,
self-sufficient without trade,
the land naturally provides ample food,
free from famine,
hence people are lazy and live carelessly,
without accumulation and often poor.
Therefore, south of the Jiāng
and Huái rivers,
there are no people suffering from cold or hunger,
nor are there households worth a thousand gold.
North of the Yí and Sì rivers,
it is suitable for grains, mulberry, hemp, and livestock,
the land is small and the population dense,
frequently afflicted by floods and droughts,
the people are fond of hoarding,
hence Qín,
Xià, Liáng,
and Lǔ value agriculture and respect the people.
Sānhé,
Wǎn, and Chén are the same,
with added engagement in commerce.
Qí and Zhǎo employ wisdom and cunning,
relying on opportunistic gains.
Yān and Dài farm, raise livestock, and engage in sericulture.
From this perspective,
when wise men deeply strategize in court,
and debate in the imperial court,
where do those recluses in caves who uphold integrity and die for principles seek fame?
They seek wealth and prosperity.
Thus honest officials endure,
and with time grow richer,
honest merchants also attain wealth.
Wealth
is a human instinct,
desired by all without being taught.
Thus brave soldiers in the army,
first to scale city walls,
breaking enemy formations and repelling foes, beheading generals
and capturing flags,
facing arrows and stones, undeterred by the perils of boiling
water and fire, are driven by heavy rewards.
As for the youths in the alleys,
robbing, assaulting, and burying alive,
committing crimes and kidnapping,
digging graves and minting coins,
championing chivalry and monopolizing power,
avenging on behalf of friends,
seizing and pursuing in secrecy,
undeterred by laws and prohibitions,
rushing to their deaths as if drawn by instinct,
their true aim is all for material gain.
Now, the women of Zhào and courtesans of Zhèng,
adorning their appearances,
strumming melodious zithers,
waving long sleeves,
treading in delicate slippers,
casting enticing glances and alluring hearts,
traveling far without regard for distance,
unselective of age,
are rushing toward wealth and prosperity.
The idle young nobles,
adorning their caps and swords,
parading with carriages and steeds,
also display their wealth and status.
Those who hunt with bows, fish, and chase game,
braving the early dawn and late nights,
enduring frost and snow,
galloping over ridges and valleys,
undeterred by the threat of fierce beasts,
do so for the taste of prey.
Gambling and racing,
cockfighting and dog racing,
putting on airs and boasting,
always striving to win,
fear the loss of stakes.
Physicians, artisans, and skilled practitioners,
exhausting their spirits and abilities,
do so for generous rewards.
Officials and scribes manipulating laws,
forging seals and documents,
undeterred by the punishment of execution,
are submerged in bribery.
Farmers, artisans, merchants, and herders,
all seek to increase their wealth and goods.
They exhaust their wisdom and abilities,
never sparing effort nor yielding wealth.
As the proverb goes:
"One does not sell firewood a hundred lǐ away,
nor trade grain a thousand lǐ distant."
To settle for one year,
plant grains;
for ten years,
cultivate trees;
for a hundred years,
attract through virtue.
Virtue means
the gathering of people and resources.
Now there are those without official salaries
or revenues from titles and fiefs,
yet whose happiness compares with such—
they are called
"untitled nobility."
The enfeoffed live on tax revenues,
typically two hundred coins per household annually.
A lord of a thousand households thus gains two hundred thousand,
from which court visits and offerings are paid.
Commoners—farmers, artisans, merchants—
also typically yield two thousand from ten thousand principal,
so a million-coin family gains twenty thousand,
covering corvée duties and taxes.
Their desires for food and clothing
can be lavishly satisfied.
Thus, on land, herding two hundred horses (fifty, as each has four hooves),
a thousand hooves and horns of cattle (about 167 head),
a thousand sheep legs (250 sheep),
a thousand pig legs in marshes (250 pigs),
a thousand dàn fish pond in waters,
or a thousand timber trees in mountains—
in Ānyì, a thousand date trees;
in Yān and Qín, a thousand chestnut trees;
in Shǔ, Hàn,
or Jiānglíng, a thousand orange trees;
north of Huái River,
south of Chángshān,
between Hé and Jì Rivers, a thousand catalpa trees;
in Chén and Xià, a thousand mǔ of lacquer trees;
in Qí and Lǔ, a thousand mǔ of hemp and mulberry;
in Wèi River valley, a thousand mǔ of bamboo;
or in famous cities with ten thousand households,
a thousand mǔ of fertile land yielding one zhōng per mǔ near the walls,
or a thousand mǔ of gardenia and madder,
a thousand plots of ginger and leeks—
such persons equal a thousand-household marquis.
These are means to wealth,
without spying on markets,
or traveling to other towns,
sitting and awaiting harvest,
maintaining a recluse's integrity while self-sufficient.
But if one is poor with elderly parents,
a frail wife and children,
unable to offer sacrifices or host gatherings yearly,
lacking enough for food, drink, and clothing,
and feels no shame,
then there is nothing to compare.
Thus, without wealth, one labors;
with little, one competes wisely;
with abundance, one contends for timing—
this is the general principle.
Now, making a living without endangering oneself
is what the virtuous strive for.
Hence, wealth from farming is best,
from trade next,
from ill-gotten gains worst.
Without the conduct of a reclusive scholar,
yet long in poverty and low status,
fond of speaking of benevolence and righteousness,
is indeed shameful.
Among all registered commoners,
if wealth differs tenfold, they feel inferior;
a hundredfold, they fear;
a thousandfold, they serve;
ten thousandfold, they enslave—
such is the nature of things.
In rising from poverty, farming is不如 industry,
industry不如 commerce,
embroidering fine patterns不如 leaning on the market gate—
this refers to secondary trades,
the resources for the poor.
In large cities and metropolises,
brewing a thousand vats a year,
a thousand jars of vinegar and sauce,
a thousand dàn of fermented drink,
slaughtering a thousand hides of cattle, sheep, and pigs,
selling a thousand zhōng of grain,
a thousand cartloads of firewood,
boats totaling a thousand zhàng in length,
a thousand timber trees,
ten thousand bamboo poles,
a hundred light carriages,
a thousand oxcarts,
a thousand lacquered wooden vessels,
a thousand jūn of copperware,
a thousand dàn of plain wood, ironware, gardenia, or madder,
a thousand horse hoofs (about 200 horses),
a thousand cattle legs (250 cattle),
a thousand pairs of sheep and pigs,
a thousand servant fingers (100 servants),
a thousand jīn of sinew, horn, and cinnabar,
a thousand jūn of silk, wadding, and fine cloth,
a thousand bolts of patterned silk,
a thousand dàn of coarse cloth and leather,
a thousand dǒu of lacquer,
a thousand containers of yeast, fermented grain, salt, and fermented beans,
a thousand jīn of globefish and sardines,
a thousand dàn of small fish,
a thousand jūn of salted fish,
three thousand dàn of dates and chestnuts,
a thousand fox and sable furs,
a thousand dàn of lamb fleece,
a thousand felt mats,
a thousand zhōng of other fruits and vegetables,
lending a thousand strings of coins,
with moderated brokerage fees—
greedy merchants take three-tenths profit,
honest ones take five-tenths—
this also compares to a thousand-chariot family,
roughly speaking.
Other miscellaneous trades yielding less than twenty percent
are not worth one's capital.
Let me briefly describe how the virtuous in a thousand lǐ area
have grown rich in recent times,
for later generations to observe and choose.
The ancestors of the Zhūo family from Shǔ
were from Zhào,
and grew rich through iron smelting.
When Qín conquered Zhào,
they relocated the Zhūo family.
The Zhūos, being captives,
only husband and wife pushed a cart,
traveling to the relocation site.
Other captives with some leftover wealth
vied to bribe officials
for nearby places,
settling in Jiāméng.
Only the Zhūo family said:
"This land is narrow and barren.
I hear beneath Wènshān,
there are fertile plains,
with taro below,
preventing starvation unto death.
The people are skilled in markets,
easy for trade."
So they sought distant relocation.
Sent to Línqióng,
they were overjoyed,
immediately smelted iron from the mountains,
devised strategies,
influenced the people of Diān and Shǔ,
and grew rich enough to have a thousand servants.
The pleasures of fields, ponds, and hunting
rivaled those of a sovereign.
Chéng Zhèng,
a captive from east of the mountains,
also engaged in smelting,
trading with the topknot people,
his wealth matching the Zhūo family's,
both residing in Línqióng.
The ancestors of the Wǎn Kǒng family
were from Liáng,
and made a living from iron smelting.
When Qín attacked Wèi,
they relocated the Kǒngs to Nányáng.
They engaged in large-scale smelting,
developed ponds and pools,
maintained carriages and riders,
traveled among nobles,
thus profiting from trade,
gaining a reputation like leisurely nobles for generosity.
Yet their profits exceeded expectations,
surpassing the frugal,
amassing thousands of gold in wealth,
so Nányáng merchants all emulated the Kǒngs' elegance.
The people of Lǔ are customarily frugal,
with the Cáo Bǐng family especially so,
starting with iron smelting,
amassing immense wealth.
The family, from parents to children, agreed:
stooping to pick up,
reaching to take—
lending and trading throughout the commanderies and states.
Thus, in Zōu and Lǔ, many abandoned literature for profit,
due to the Cáo Bǐng family's influence.
In Qí, slaves were commonly despised,
but Dāo Xián alone cherished and valued them.
Cunning and crafty slaves,
whom others feared,
only Dāo Xián would take in,
employing them to pursue profits from fishing, salt, and trade.
Some even rode in chariots and on horseback,
interacting with governors and chancellors,
yet he trusted them even more.
Ultimately, he gained their full support,
amassing wealth amounting to tens of millions.
Hence the saying,
"Better to serve Dāo than hold a noble rank,"
meaning he could make even the most unruly slaves prosper and exert their utmost efforts.
The people of Zhōu were already frugal,
but Shī Shǐ was especially so,
with hundreds of carts in constant motion,
trading across commanderies and states,
reaching every corner.
Luòyáng's location placed it amidst Qí, Qín, Chǔ, and Zhào,
where the poor learned to serve the wealthy,
boasting of long trading journeys,
often passing their hometowns without entering,
entrusting matters to such men,
thus Shī Shǐ accumulated seventy million.
The ancestors of the Rén family of Xuānqū
served as granary officials in Dūdào.
When Qín fell,
the powerful vied for gold and jade,
but the Rén family alone stored grain in cellars.
When Chǔ and Hàn confronted each other at Xíngyáng,
the people could not farm,
and the price of rice soared to ten thousand coins per shi,
so the gold and jade of the powerful all went to the Rén family,
who thus rose to wealth.
While the rich competed in extravagance,
the Rén family humbled themselves to practice frugality,
devoting efforts to farming and animal husbandry.
Others sought cheap livestock and land,
but the Rén family only acquired high-quality and expensive ones.
Their wealth lasted for generations.
Moreover, Patriarch Rén set family rules:
they would not wear or eat anything not produced from their farms and herds,
and no one could drink wine or eat meat until public duties were completed.
This made them a model for the community,
so they were wealthy and respected by the emperor.
When the frontiers were expanded,
Qiáo Yáo alone acquired a thousand horses,
twice as many cattle,
ten thousand sheep,
and grain counted by tens of thousands of zhōng.
When the seven states of Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
the marquises and nobles in Cháng'ān followed the army,
borrowing money for expenses,
but moneylenders hesitated, as their fiefs were east of the pass,
and the outcome in Guāndōng was uncertain,
so none were willing to lend.
Only Wúyán Shi provided a loan of a thousand pieces of gold,
at ten times the interest.
In three months,
Wú and Chǔ were pacified.
Within a year,
Wúyán Shi's interest increased tenfold,
making him as rich as anyone in Guānzhōng.
The wealthy merchants of Guānzhōng
were mostly from the various Tián families,
such as Tián Sé,
Tián Lán.
The Lì family of Wěi,
Ānlíng and
Dù Dù family,
also possessed immense wealth.
These are the most remarkable examples.
None gained wealth through noble ranks, fiefs, salaries, or by breaking laws and committing crimes;
instead, they all seized opportunities,
adapting to the times,
reaping profits,
accumulating wealth through trade,
and preserving it through land ownership,
using force for immediate gains,
and culture to maintain them,
their methods varied but followed principles,
thus worthy of record.
As for those who prospered through farming and animal husbandry,
crafts, forestry, and trade,
or by leveraging power and profit to build fortunes,
some influential enough to sway commanderies,
others counties,
and the least, villages and neighborhoods,
they are too numerous to count.
Frugality and hard work
are the righteous ways to make a living,
but the wealthy must use unconventional means to succeed.
Farming,
a laborious occupation,
yet Qín Yáng topped a whole region through it.
Tomb raiding,
an illicit act,
yet Tián Shū rose to prominence by it.
Gambling,
a despicable trade,
yet Huán Fā grew rich from it.
Peddling,
a lowly profession for men,
yet Yōng Yuèchéng prospered by it.
Selling grease,
a humiliating business,
yet Yōng Bó amassed a fortune of a thousand gold.
Selling juice,
a minor trade,
yet the Zhāng family earned tens of millions.
Sharpening knives,
a petty skill,
yet the Zhì family dined like nobles.
Selling spiced entrails,
a simple and humble task,
yet Zhuó Shi rode in processions of carriages.
Horse healing,
a superficial art,
yet Zhāng Lǐ lived in luxury.
All these successes came from sincerity and focus.
From this, it is evident
that wealth has no constant industry,
and goods have no permanent owner;
the capable gather riches,
while the incompetent see them crumble.
A family with a thousand gold rivals the lord of a city,
and those with hundreds of millions share pleasures akin to a king's.
Is this not what is called
"uncrowned nobility"
Is it not?
In ancient times, under Zhuānxū,
he appointed Nánzhèng Zhòng to oversee the heavens,
and Běizhèng Lí to oversee the earth.
During the Táng and Yú eras,
they continued the lineage of Zhòng and Lí,
entrusting them again with these duties,
until the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
so the Zhònglí clan世代 managed heaven and earth.
In the Zhōu dynasty,
Chéng Bó Xiūfǔ was their descendant.
During King Xuān of Zhōu's reign,
he lost his position and became the Sīmǎ family.
The Sīmǎ clan世代 served as Zhōu's historians.
Between the reigns of Kings Huì and Xiāng,
the Sīmǎ family left Zhōu for Jìn.
When Jìn's general Suí Huì fled to Qín,
the Sīmǎ family entered Shàoliáng.
Since the Sīmǎ family left Zhōu for Jìn,
they dispersed,
some going to Wèi,
some to Zhào,
some to Qín.
Those in Wèi
served as ministers of Zhōngshān.
Those in Zhào
gained fame through swordsmanship theories,
Kuǎikuì being their descendant.
In Qín, one named Cuò debated with Zhāng Yí,
leading King Huì to send Cuò to lead an expedition against Shǔ,
which he captured,
and thus governed it.
Cuò's grandson Jìn
served under Wǔ'ān Jūn Bái Qǐ.
And Shàoliáng was renamed Xiàyáng. Jìn, along with Wǔ'ān Jūn, executed the surrendered
army of Chángpíng from Zhào,
and upon return, both were ordered to die at Dùyóu,
buried at Huàchí.
Jìn's grandson Chāng,
Chāng served as Qín's director of iron officials,
during the time of Qín Shǐ Huáng.
Kuǎikuì's great-great-grandson Áng served as a general under Wǔxìn Jūn and campaigned in Zhāogē.
When the feudal lords proclaimed themselves kings,
Áng was made king of Yīn.
When Hàn attacked Chǔ,
Áng surrendered to Hàn,
and his territory became the Hénèi Commandery.
Chāng bore Wúzé,
Wúzé served as Hàn's market chief.
Wúzé bore Xǐ,
Xǐ held the title of Wǔdàfū,
and upon death, all were buried at Gāomén.
Xǐ bore Tán,
Tán became the Grand Historian.
The Grand Historian studied astronomy with Táng Dū,
received the "Yì" from Yáng Hé,
and learned Daoist theory from Huáng Zǐ.
The Grand Historian served during the Jiànyuán and Yuánfēng eras,
lamenting that scholars failed to grasp the essence and followed misguided teachings.
Thus, he discussed the essential tenets of the six schools, saying:
The "Great Commentary of the Yì" states:
"The world aims for unity through a hundred thoughts,
reaching the same end by different paths."
Now, the Yīnyáng,
Rú,
Mò,
Names,
and Legalist schools all strive for governance,
differing only in their approaches,
with some being more insightful and others less so.
I have privately observed the techniques of the Yīnyáng school:
they emphasize omens and numerous taboos,
making people constrained and fearful;
yet their ordering of the four seasons' great sequence
must not be lost.
The Rú school is broad but lacks focus,
laborious with little achievement,
hence their methods are hard to fully follow;
yet their arrangement of rites for ruler and subject, father and son,
and distinction between husband and wife, elder and young,
cannot be altered.
The Mò school advocates frugality but is difficult to adhere to,
so their practices cannot be universally followed;
yet their strengthening of fundamentals and economizing
should not be abandoned.
The Legalist school is strict and lacks kindness;
yet their rectification of the roles of ruler and subject, superior and inferior,
cannot be changed.
The School of Names makes people restrained and prone to lose truth;
yet their rectification of names and realities
must be examined.
The Daoist school enables the spirit to be unified,
actions to align with the formless,
and to suffice for all things.
Their method
follows the great sequence of Yīnyáng,
adopts the strengths of Rú and Mò,
extracts the essentials of Names and Legalism,
moves with the times,
adapts to changes in things,
establishes customs and implements affairs,
with nothing unsuitable,
concise in guidance and easy to practice,
achieving much with little effort.
The Rú school, however, is not so.
They believe the ruler is the model for the world,
with the ruler initiating and ministers附和,
the ruler leading and ministers following.
This results in the ruler toiling and ministers at ease.
As for the essence of the great Dào,
it discards vigor and desire,
rejects cleverness,
abandons this and relies on technique.
For the spirit, overuse leads to exhaustion,
the body, overwork to weariness.
When body and spirit are agitated,
to wish for longevity with heaven and earth—
such a thing I have not heard of.
Now, the Yīnyáng four seasons,
eight positions,
twelve measures,
twenty-four nodes each have their decrees;
those who follow them prosper,
those who oppose them die if not perish—
this is not necessarily so,
hence it is said
"makes people constrained and fearful."
But spring's growth, summer's flourish,
autumn's harvest, winter's storage—
this is the great constant of the heavenly Dào,
without following it, there is no basis for the world's order,
hence it is said
"the great sequence of the four seasons,
must not be lost."
The Rú school takes the "Six Arts" as their standard.
The classics and commentaries of the "Six Arts" number in the thousands,
impossible to master in generations,
unable to exhaust their rites in a lifetime,
hence it is said
"broad but lacking focus,
laborious with little achievement."
Yet in arranging the rites of ruler and subject, father and son,
ordering the distinctions between husband and wife, elder and young,
even the hundred schools cannot change it.
The Mò school also revered the way of Yáo and Shùn,
speaking of their virtuous conduct as:
"The hall three feet high,
earthen steps three levels,
thatched roof untrimmed,
rough rafters unplaned.
Eat from earthen bowls,
drink from earthen vessels,
coarse grain for food,
wild herbs for soup.
In summer, hemp clothes;
in winter, deer-skin robes."
In funeral practices,
a tong wood coffin three inches thick,
mourners' cries not fully expressing grief.
Teaching funeral rites,
they insist this be the standard for all people.
If the world followed such laws,
then noble and base would lack distinction.
As times change and eras shift,
affairs need not be the same,
hence it is said
"frugal but difficult to follow."
The essence is strengthening fundamentals and economizing—
the way to ensure people and families are well-provided.
This is Mòzǐ's strength,
which even the hundred schools cannot abolish.
The Legalist school does not distinguish between close and distant,
nor differentiate noble and humble,
judging all by law alone,
thus severing the kindness of familial and hierarchical bonds.
It may serve for temporary schemes,
but cannot be used long-term,
hence it is said
"strict and lacking kindness."
Yet in honoring the ruler and debasing ministers,
clarifying roles to prevent overstepping,
even the hundred schools cannot alter it.
The School of Names is meticulous and convoluted,
preventing people from grasping their meaning,
deciding solely by names and losing human sentiment,
hence it is said
"makes people restrained and prone to lose truth."
But in aligning names with reality,
ensuring verification without error,
this must be examined.
The Daoist school advocates non-action,
yet also says there is nothing not done;
its practice is easy,
its words hard to understand.
Its technique takes emptiness as the root,
and adaptation as the function.
Without fixed form,
without constant shape,
thus it can fully understand the nature of all things.
Not preceding things,
not following things,
thus it can master all things.
Having laws or having none,
it acts according to the time;
having measures or having none,
it harmonizes with things.
Hence it is said
"The sage does not decay,
but holds to the changes of time.
Emptiness is the constant of the Dào,
adaptation is the ruler's guiding principle."
When all ministers are present,
let each clarify themselves.
When reality matches the claim, it is called correct;
when reality does not match, it is called hollow.
Hollow words are not heeded,
then deceit does not arise;
worthy and unworthy distinguish themselves,
white and black become clear.
If one acts as desired,
what task is not accomplished?
It aligns with the great Dào,
vast and obscure.
It illuminates the world,
yet returns to namelessness.
What gives life to humans is the spirit,
what it relies on is the body.
The spirit, overused, is exhausted;
the body, overworked, is worn;
when body and spirit separate, death occurs.
The dead cannot live again,
the separated cannot reunite,
hence the sage values them.
From this perspective,
the spirit is the root of life,
the body is the vessel of life.
Without first stabilizing one's spirit and body,
yet saying
"I have the means to govern the world"—
how is that possible?
The Grand Historian, having charge of astronomy,
did not govern the people.
He had a son named Qiān.
Sīmǎ Qiān was born at Lóngmén,
farming and herding on the sunny side of the Hé and Shān mountains.
At age ten, he was already reciting ancient texts.
At twenty, he traveled south to the Jiāng
and Huái rivers, ascended Kuàijī,
explored Yǔ's cave,
glimpsed Jiǔyí,
floated upon Yuán
and Xiāng rivers; northward, he crossed Wèn
and Sì rivers, studied scholarly pursuits in the capitals of Qí
and Lǔ,
observed the lingering customs of Kǒngzǐ,
practiced archery ceremonies in Zōu
and Yì; encountered hardship in Pó,
Xuē, and Péngchéng,
passed through Liáng
and Chǔ before returning.
Thereupon, Qiān entered official service as a Lángzhōng,
奉命出使西征 Bā
and Shǔ to the south,
campaigned south in Qióng,
Zuó, and Kūnmíng,
then returned to report.
That year, the Son of Heaven first established the Hàn dynasty's fēng sacrifice,
but the Grand Historian (his father) remained stranded in Zhōunán,
unable to participate in the proceedings,
thus he fretted and was near death.
Just then, his son Qiān returned from his mission,
meeting his father between the Hé and Luò rivers.
The Grand Historian grasped Qiān's hand and wept, saying:
"Our ancestors were Grand Historians of the Zhōu court.
Since early times, they distinguished themselves in merit and fame during Yú and Xià,
overseeing celestial affairs.
Later generations declined,
will it end with me?
If you become Grand Historian again,
you will continue our lineage.
Now the Son of Heaven inherits a millennium-old tradition,
performing the fēng sacrifice on Tàishān,
yet I cannot accompany him,
such is fate,
such is fate!
After I die,
you must become Grand Historian;
as Grand Historian,
do not forget what I wished to compile and write.
Moreover, filial piety begins with serving one's parents,
continues with serving one's sovereign,
and culminates in establishing one's character.
To spread one's name to later generations,
thereby glorifying one's parents,
this is the greatest filial piety.
All under heaven praise Zhōu Gōng,
saying he could discourse upon and sing of Wén and Wǔ's virtues,
propagate the customs of Zhōu and Shào,
convey Tàiwáng and Wángjì's thoughts,
reaching back to Gōngliú,
to honor Hòujì.
After Yōu and Lì,
the Wáng Dào was broken,
rites and music declined,
Kǒngzǐ revived the old and restored the abandoned,
compiled the Shī and Shū,
composed the Chūnqiū,
so scholars to this day take it as standard.
Since the capture of the qílín, over four hundred years have passed,
with feudal lords annexing each other,
historical records neglected and lost.
Now the Hàn has risen,
the realm is unified,
there are enlightened rulers, worthy ministers, and righteous men who died for duty,
yet I, as Grand Historian, have not recorded them,
neglecting the historical texts of all under heaven,
I deeply fear this,
you must remember it!"
Qiān bowed his head and shed tears, saying:
"Though your son is untalented,
I beg to fully compile the old accounts left by my ancestors,
daring not omit anything."
Three years after his death, Qiān became Grand Historian,
organizing records from the stone chamber and golden cabinet.
Five years later, in the first year of Tàichū,
on the first day of the eleventh month, the winter solstice at dawn,
the celestial calendar began its reform,
established in the Míngtáng,
with various deities receiving their records.
The Grand Historian (Sīmǎ Qiān) said:
"My father once said:
'Five hundred years after Zhōu Gōng's death came Kǒngzǐ.
From Kǒngzǐ's death to now, another five hundred years,
is there one who can continue the enlightened age,
correct the Yì Zhuàn,
carry on the Chūnqiū,
and root himself in the traditions of Shī, Shū, Lǐ, and Yuè?'
His meaning lay here!
His meaning lay here!
How dare I, your son, decline this task?"
Senior Grand Master Hú Suì said:
"Why did Confucius compose the Spring and Autumn Annals in the past?"
The Grand Historian replied:
"I have heard from Master Dǒng:
'The Way of Zhōu declined and fell into disuse,
Confucius served as Minister of Crime in Lǔ,
the feudal lords harmed him,
and the high ministers obstructed him.
Knowing that his words would not be heeded
and his Way would not be put into practice,
he passed judgment on the events of 242 years,
making them a model for the world,
reproving the Son of Heaven,
demoting the feudal lords,
condemning the high ministers,
all to accomplish the affairs of a true king.'
The Master said:
'I would rather express my ideas through concrete events
than through empty words, as this makes them more profound and clear.'
The Spring and Autumn Annals
illuminates the Way of the Three Sovereigns above,
distinguishes the principles of human affairs below,
resolves doubts,
clarifies right and wrong,
settles uncertainties,
praises the good and condemns the evil,
honors the worthy and despises the unworthy,
preserves fallen states,
continues extinguished lineages,
repairs what is broken and restores what is abandoned—
these are the great aspects of the Kingly Way.
The Yì Jīng elucidates heaven, earth, yīn-yáng, the four seasons, and the five phases,
thus it excels in change;
the Lǐ Jìng regulates human relationships,
thus it excels in conduct;
the Shū Jīng records the affairs of former kings,
thus it excels in governance;
the Shī Jīng describes mountains, rivers, valleys, birds, beasts, plants, and the distinction between male and female,
thus it excels in customs;
the Yuè Jīng establishes the foundation of music,
thus it excels in harmony;
the Spring and Autumn Annals distinguishes right from wrong,
thus it excels in governing people.
Therefore, the Lǐ Jìng regulates people,
the Yuè Jīng promotes harmony,
the Shū Jīng guides affairs,
the Shī Jīng expresses intentions,
the Yì Jīng reveals transformations,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals conveys righteousness.
To bring order out of chaos and return to correctness,
nothing comes closer than the Spring and Autumn Annals.
The Spring and Autumn Annals contains tens of thousands of characters,
with thousands of guiding principles.
The dispersion and convergence of all things are contained within it.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals,
there are thirty-six regicides,
fifty-two fallen states,
and countless feudal lords who fled and could not protect their altars of soil and grain.
Examining the reasons,
all lost their fundamental principles."
Therefore, the Yì Jīng says:
'A miss by a hair's breadth
leads to an error of a thousand miles.'
Hence it is said:
'When a minister kills his ruler,
or a son kills his father,
it is not due to a single morning or evening's cause,
but has been developing for a long time.'
Thus, rulers must not be ignorant of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
or they will fail to see slanderers ahead
and remain unaware of traitors behind.
Ministers must not be ignorant of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
or they will handle routine matters without knowing what is appropriate
and face changing circumstances without understanding flexibility.
If a ruler or father is unacquainted with the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
he will inevitably bear the name of a chief offender.
If a minister or son is unacquainted with the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
he will inevitably face execution for usurpation or regicide,
bearing the name of a capital criminal.
In reality, they may have intended good,
but acted without understanding righteousness,
and thus cannot refute the condemnation they receive.
Those ignorant of the essence of ritual and righteousness
will cause rulers to be unworthy of being rulers,
ministers unworthy of being ministers,
fathers unworthy of being fathers,
and sons unworthy of being sons.
When a ruler is unworthy, he is transgressed against;
when a minister is unworthy, he is punished;
when a father is unworthy, he is without virtue;
when a son is unworthy, he is unfilial.
These four behaviors
are the greatest faults in the world.
To ascribe the world's greatest faults to someone
is to make them accept it without daring to refuse.
