Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals
is the great source of ritual and righteousness.
Ritual prevents before things happen,
while law applies after they have occurred;
the effects of law are easily seen,
but what ritual prevents is hard to know."
Hú Suì said:
"In Confucius's time,
there were no enlightened rulers above,
and he could not be employed below,
so he composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
leaving a literary legacy to judge ritual and righteousness,
serving as the law of a true king.
Now you, Master, have encountered a brilliant Son of Heaven above,
hold an official position below,
all affairs are in order,
and everything is in its proper place.
What do you intend to clarify
with your discussions?"
The Grand Historian replied:
"Yes, yes,
no, no,
not exactly.
I have heard from my ancestors:
'Fú Xī was of utmost purity and depth,
and composed the Yì Jīng and Eight Trigrams.
The prosperity of Yáo and Shùn
was recorded in the Shàng Shū,
and ritual and music were established.
The grandeur of Tāng and Wǔ
was sung by the poets.
The Spring and Autumn Annals selects the good and condemns the evil,
promotes the virtue of the Three Dynasties,
and praises the Zhōu house—
it is not merely criticism.'
Since the rise of Hàn,
up to our enlightened Son of Heaven,
we have received auspicious signs,
performed the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
reformed the calendar,
changed the color of vestments,
received the Mandate from the sublime purity,
with blessings flowing boundlessly.
Remote regions with different customs,
through multiple interpreters, come to our borders,
requesting to offer tribute—
too many to recount.
Officials and百官 strive to extol his sage virtue,
yet cannot fully express it.
Moreover, for talented scholars to remain unused
is the shame of the state's ruler;
for a sovereign's brilliance and virtue not to be widely known
is the fault of the officials.
And I once held this office;
to neglect recording the enlightened sage's virtue,
omit the achievements of meritorious ministers, noble families, and worthy officials,
and forsake my father's words—
no crime could be greater.
What I call narrating past events,
organizing their traditions,
is not what is called composition.
And you, Sir, compare it to the Spring and Autumn Annals—
that is mistaken."
Thereupon, he composed and arranged his writings.
Seven years later, the Grand Historian encountered the disaster of Lǐ Líng,
and was imprisoned.
He then sighed deeply and said:
"Is this my crime?
Is this my crime?
My body is broken and of no use anymore."
Retreating, he deeply reflected:
"The Shī Jīng and Shū Jīng are subtle and restrained
because their authors wished to express their aspirations.
In the past, Xī Bó was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ,
and elaborated the Zhōu Yì;
Confucius was in distress between Chén and Cài,
and composed the Spring and Autumn Annals;
Qū Yuán was exiled,
and wrote the Lí Sāo;
Zuǒ Qiū lost his sight,
and produced the Guó Yǔ;
Sūnzǐ had his feet amputated,
and discoursed on military strategy;
Lǚ Bùwéi was exiled to Shǔ,
and the world received the Lǚ Lǎn;
Hán Fēi was imprisoned in Qín,
and wrote 'Shuì Nán'
and 'Gū Fèn';
the three hundred poems of the Shī Jīng
are largely the works of sages and worthies giving vent to their indignation.
These men all had pent-up feelings in their hearts,
unable to realize their Way,
so they narrated past events
to inform future generations."
Thereupon, he finally narrated events from the time of Táo Táng onward,
up to the capture of the qílín,
beginning with Huángdì.
Music is
that by which customs and mores are transformed.
Since the melodies of the "Yǎ" and "Sòng" arose,
people have already favored the music of "Zhèng" and "Wèi",
and the music of "Zhèng" and "Wèi" has existed for a long time.
What stirs human emotions
makes one yearn for distant customs.
Comparing the "Book of Music" to recount antiquity,
I composed the second chapter, the "Book of Music".
Without arms, a state cannot be strong;
without virtue, it cannot flourish.
Huángdì,
Tāng, and Wǔ rose because of this,
while Jié, Zhòu,
and the Second Emperor collapsed because of its lack—
should one not be cautious?
The "Sīmǎ Fǎ" has existed for a long time,
Tàigōng,
Sūn, Wú,
and Wángzǐ were able to continue and elucidate it,
addressing recent times
and exhaustively studying human changes.
I composed the third chapter, the "Book of Laws".
Pitch-standards reside in the yin but govern the yang;
the calendar resides in the yang but governs the yin.
Pitch-standards and the calendar alternately govern each other,
with not even the slightest gap.
The texts of the five schools conflict,
only the discussions of the Tàichū era are authoritative.
I composed the fourth chapter, the "Book of the Calendar".
Books on stars and atmospheres
are often mixed with omens and portents,
which are unorthodox;
yet examining their texts
and verifying their correspondences,
they are not without reason.
Comparing and compiling discussions of their events,
testing them against orbital measures in sequence,
I composed the fifth chapter, the "Book of Heavenly Offices".
Those who receive the mandate and become kings
rarely use the tallies for fēng and shàn sacrifices,
but when used, all spirits are sacrificed to without exception.
Tracing the origins of the rituals for the various gods, famous mountains, and great rivers,
I composed the sixth chapter, the "Book of Fēng and Shàn Sacrifices".
With Yǔ dredging the rivers,
the nine provinces were thus pacified;
extending to Xuānfáng,
he opened channels and connected ditches.
I composed the seventh chapter, the "Book of Rivers and Canals".
With the circulation of currency,
agriculture and commerce are facilitated;
at its extreme, it leads to cunning and deceit,
monopolies and proliferation,
struggling for opportunistic gains,
abandoning the root for the branches.
I composed the "Book of Balanced Standards" to observe these changes,
as the eighth chapter.
Tàibó avoided the heirship,
and went to the barbarians of Jiāng;
with the rise of Wén and Wǔ,
the ancient Gǔgōng laid the royal foundation.
Hélǚ assassinated Liáo,
and subdued Jīngchǔ;
Fūchāi defeated Qí,
but Wǔ Zǐxū was cast into the river;
trusting Pǐ and befriending Yuè,
the state of Wú was destroyed.
Praising Tàibó's humility,
I composed the first hereditary house, "The Hereditary House of Wú".
Shēn and
Lǚ declined,
yet Shàngfǔ was in obscurity,
finally returning to Xībó,
and became the teacher to Wén and Wǔ;
his merits topped all lords,
wielding strategy in secrecy;
with white hair and vigor,
he thus enjoyed Yíngqiū.
Not betraying the covenant of Kē,
Huán Gōng thrived,
assembling the feudal lords nine times,
his hegemony clearly manifested.
Tián and Guàn contended for favor,
and the Jiāng lineage dissolved and perished.
Praising the father's strategies,
I composed the second hereditary house, "The Hereditary House of Qí Tàigōng".
Following or opposing,
Zhōu Gōng pacified them;
ardently promoting civil virtue,
the world harmonized with him;
assisting and protecting Chéng Wáng,
the feudal lords revered Zhōu.
In the time of Yǐn and Huán,
what was the reason alone?
The three Huán contended for power,
and Lǔ thus did not flourish.
Praising Dàn's "Golden Coffer",
I composed the third hereditary house, "The Hereditary House of Zhōu Gōng".
When Wǔ Wáng defeated Zhòu,
the world was not yet united when he passed away.
Chéng Wáng was still young,
Guǎn and Cài doubted him,
the Huái Yí rebelled against him,
then Shào Gōng upheld virtue,
stabilized and gathered the royal house,
and pacified the eastern lands.
Yān Kuài's abdication,
brought about disaster and chaos.
Praising the poem "Gāntáng",
I composed the fourth hereditary house, "The Hereditary House of Yān".
Guǎn and Cài assisted Wǔ Gēng,
intending to pacify old Shāng;
when Dàn assumed regency,
the two uncles did not yield;
Xiān was killed and Dù exiled,
Zhōu Gōng made a covenant;
Tàirèn had ten sons,
through whom Zhōu became strong and ancestral.
Praising Zhòng's repentance of faults,
I composed the fifth hereditary house, "The Hereditary House of Guǎn and Cài".
The royal line did not cease,
Shùn and Yǔ are spoken of;
with virtue splendid and bright,
their descendants inherited the legacy.
For a hundred generations they enjoyed sacrifices,
thus in Zhōu, Chén and Qǐ,
but Chǔ indeed destroyed them.
When the Tián of Qí arose,
what kind of man was Shùn?
I composed the sixth hereditary house, "The Hereditary House of Chén and Qǐ".
Gathering the remaining people of Yīn,
Shū Fēng began the city,
admonished about the chaos of Shāng,
with the "Materials for Wine" as warning;
by the time of Shuò's birth,
Wèi was unstable and declining;
Nánzǐ hated Kuǎikuì,
and father and son exchanged names.
The virtue of Zhōu was humble and weak,
the Warring States grew strong,
Wèi, being small and weak,
only Jiǎo was last to perish.
Praising that "Kāng Gào",
I composed the seventh hereditary house, "The Hereditary House of Wèi".
Alas, Jīzǐ!
Alas, Jīzǐ!
Your upright words were not heeded,
and you instead became a slave.
After Wǔ Gēng died,
Zhōu enfeoffed Wēizǐ.
Xiāng Gōng was wounded at Hóng,
yet gentlemen still praise him.
Jǐng Gōng had humble virtue,
and the Mars retrograde moved back.
Tīchéng was tyrannical and cruel,
and Sòng thus perished.
Praising Wēizǐ's consultation with the Grand Tutor,
I composed the eighth hereditary house, "The Hereditary House of Sòng".
After Wǔ Wáng passed away,
Shū Yú was enfeoffed in Táng.
Gentlemen criticized the naming,
and eventually destroyed Wǔ Gōng.
The favor of Líjī,
caused chaos for five generations;
Chóng'ěr, in adversity,
was yet able to achieve hegemony.
The six ministers monopolized power,
and the state of Jìn thus declined.
Praising Wén Gōng's grant of jade and aromatic wine,
I composed the ninth hereditary house, "The Hereditary House of Jìn".
When the six stratagems were employed,
the feudal lords submitted to the Hàn;
in the affair of the Lǚ clan,
Chén Píng laid the fundamental plan,
ultimately securing the ancestral temple,
and stabilizing the altars of soil and grain.
Thus, "The Hereditary House of Chancellor Chén" is the twenty-sixth.
The various Lǚ conspired together,
plotting to weaken the capital,
yet Zhōu Bó, though reversing the norm, aligned with expediency;
when the armies of Wú and Chǔ arose,
Zhōu Yàfū stationed at Chāngyì,
to pressure Qí and Zhào,
and deliberately exposed Liáng to danger.
Thus, "The Hereditary House of the Marquis of Jiàng" is the twenty-seventh.
When the seven kingdoms rebelled,
the feudal shields of the capital,
only Liáng served as a bulwark;
though arrogant and boastful of merit,
it narrowly escaped disaster.
Praising its ability to resist Wú and Chǔ,
"The Hereditary House of King Xiào of Liáng" is the twenty-eighth.
When the five branches were enfeoffed as kings,
kinship was harmonious,
feudal lords large and small served as screens,
each finding their proper place,
and presumptuous imitations gradually declined and were censured.
Thus, "The Hereditary Houses of the Five Branches" is the twenty-ninth.
The enfeoffment of the three sons,
their documents are commendable.
Thus, "The Hereditary House of the Three Kings" is the thirtieth.
In a decadent age contending for profit,
they alone rushed toward righteousness;
yielding the state and starving to death,
the world praises them.
Thus, "The Biography of Bó Yí" is the first.
Yànzǐ was frugal,
while Yíwú was extravagant;
Qí Huán achieved hegemony,
and Jǐng Gōng achieved orderly rule.
Thus, "The Biographies of Guǎn and Yàn" is the second.
Lǎozi advocated non-action for natural transformation,
clarity and stillness for self-correction;
Hán Fēi assessed circumstances,
following patterns and principles.
Thus, "The Biographies of Lǎozi and Hán Fēi" is the third.
Since ancient times, kings have had the "Sīmǎ's Art of War",
which Rángjū was able to elucidate.
Thus, "The Biography of Sīmǎ Rángjū" is the fourth.
Without trustworthiness, integrity, benevolence, and courage, one cannot transmit military arts or discuss swordsmanship,
which aligns with the Dào,
internally it cultivates the self,
externally it responds to change,
and gentlemen compare it to virtue.
Thus, "The Biographies of Sūnzǐ and Wú Qǐ" is the fifth.
When Wǔ Shè encountered slander,
it extended to his son Shē,
though Shàng sought to save his father,
Wǔ Yún fled to Wú.
Thus, "The Biography of Wǔ Zǐxū" is the sixth.
Kǒngzǐ transmitted culture,
his disciples promoted his teachings,
all became mentors,
honoring benevolence and encouraging righteousness.
Thus, "The Biographies of the Disciples of Zhòngní" is the seventh.
When Yāng left Wèi for Qín,
he was able to clarify his methods,
strengthening and establishing hegemony for Xiào Gōng,
and later generations followed his laws.
Thus, "The Biography of Lord Shāng" is the eighth.
The world suffered from Héng Qín's insatiability,
yet Sūzǐ preserved the feudal lords,
forming a vertical alliance to curb the greedy and strong.
Thus, "The Biography of Sū Qín" is the ninth.
After the six states formed a vertical alliance,
Zhāng Yí was able to clarify his arguments,
dissolving the alliance and breaking up the states.
Thus, "The Biography of Zhāng Yí" is the tenth.
Qín's eastward expansion and dominance over the feudal lords,
were due to the strategies of Chūlǐ
and Gān Mào.
Thus, "The Biographies of Chūlǐ and Gān Mào" is the eleventh.
Encompassing the Hé River and mountains,
besieging Dàliáng,
forcing the feudal lords to submit and serve Qín,
was the achievement of Wèi Rǎn.
Thus, "The Biography of the Marquis of Ráng" is the twelfth.
Capturing Yānyǐng in the south,
crushing Chángpíng in the north,
then besieging Hándān,
led by Wǔ'ān;
defeating Jīng and destroying Zhào,
was the strategy of Wáng Jiǎn.
Thus, "The Biographies of Bái Qǐ and Wáng Jiǎn" is the thirteenth.
Gathering the legacy texts of Rú and Mò,
clarifying the principles of ritual and righteousness,
cutting off King Huì's focus on profit,
and recounting the rise and fall of past ages.
Thus, "The Biographies of Mèngzǐ and Xúnqīng" is the fourteenth.
Hospitable and fond of scholars,
scholars gathered in Xuē,
defending Qí against Chǔ and Wèi.
Thus, "The Biography of Lord Mèngcháng" is the fifteenth.
Contending for Féng Tíng through strategy,
going to Chǔ to relieve the siege of Hándān,
restoring his lord's reputation among the feudal lords.
Thus, "The Biographies of Lord Píngyuán and Yúqīng" is the sixteenth.
Able to humble wealth and honor before poverty and lowliness,
and let worth yield to the unworthy,
only Lord Xìnlíng could accomplish this.
Thus, "The Biography of Lord Wèi" is the seventeenth.
Devoting himself to his lord,
thus escaping powerful Qín,
causing persuaders to flee south to Chǔ,
was the righteousness of Huáng Xiē.
Thus, "The Biography of Lord Chūnshēn" is the eighteenth.
Enduring humiliation from Wèi Qí,
and establishing authority in powerful Qín,
recommending the worthy and yielding position,
both men possessed these qualities.
Thus, "The Biographies of Fàn Jū and Cài Zé" is the nineteenth.
Implementing his strategies,
uniting the armies of five states,
avenging weak Yān against strong Qí,
and washing away the shame of his former lord.
Thus, "The Biography of Yuè Yì" is the twentieth.
Able to assert his will against powerful Qín,
yet humbling himself before Lián Pō,
serving his lord faithfully,
both esteemed among the feudal lords.
Thus, "The Biographies of Lián Pō and Lìn Xiàngrú" is the twenty-first.
When King Mǐn lost Línzī and fled to Jǔ,
only Tián Dān used Jímò to defeat and drive away Qí Jié,
thus preserving the altars of Qí.
Thus, "The Biography of Tián Dān" is the twenty-second.
Able to devise clever arguments to resolve crises in besieged cities,
disdaining rank and emolument,
and delighting in following his will.
Thus, "The Biographies of Lǔ Zhònglián and Zōu Yáng" is the twenty-third.
Composing writings to remonstrate through satire,
linking analogies to contend for righteousness,
as seen in the "Lí Sāo".
Thus, "The Biographies of Qū Yuán and Master Jiǎ" is the twenty-fourth.
Forging ties with Zǐchǔ,
causing scholars from feudal states to eagerly serve Qín.
Thus, "The Biography of Lǚ Bùwéi" is the twenty-fifth.
With Cáozì's dagger,
Lǔ recovered its land,
and Qí demonstrated its trustworthiness;
Yù Ràng's righteousness allowed no divided loyalty.
Thus, "The Biographies of the Assassins" is the twenty-sixth.
Able to clarify his schemes,
adapting to the times to advance Qín,
thus achieving supremacy over the realm,
Lǐ Sī was the chief strategist.
Thus, "The Biography of Lǐ Sī" is the twenty-seventh.
Expanding Qín's territory and increasing its population,
subduing the Xiōngnú in the north,
fortifying the Hé River as a barrier,
and securing mountains as strongholds,
establishing Yùzhōng.
Thus, "The Biography of Méng Tián" is the twenty-eighth.
Pacifying Zhào and securing Chángshān to expand Hénèi,
weakening Chǔ's power,
and demonstrating the Hàn king's trustworthiness to the world.
Thus, "The Biographies of Zhāng Ĕr and Chén Yú" is the twenty-ninth.
They gathered troops from Xīhé and
Shàngdǎng,
following the Han as far as Péngchéng;
Yuè's raids in the Liáng region harassed Xiàng Yǔ.
Composed "Biographies of Wèi Bào and Péng Yuè," number thirty.
They rebelled against Chǔ and joined Hàn with Huáinán,
Hàn employed Grand Marshal Yīn,
ultimately defeating Zǐyǔ at Gāixià.
Composed "Biography of Qíng Bù," number thirty-one.
While the Chǔ forces pressed us at Jīng-Suǒ,
Xìn captured Wèi and Zhào,
pacified Yān and Qí,
enabling Hàn to possess two-thirds of the empire,
leading to the destruction of Xiàng Jí.
Composed "Biography of the Huáiyín Hóu," number thirty-two.
While Chǔ and Hàn confronted each other at Gǒngluò,
Hán Xìn guarded Yǐngchuān,
and Lú Wǎn cut off Jí's supplies.
Composed "Biographies of Hán Xìn and Lú Wǎn," number thirty-three.
When the feudal lords rebelled against King Xiàng,
only Qí under Zǐyǔ held Chéngyáng,
allowing Hàn to exploit the gap and enter Péngchéng.
Composed "Biography of Tián Dān," number thirty-four.
In storming cities and fighting in the fields,
capturing achievements and reporting back,
Kuài and Shāng were instrumental,
not only following orders,
but also sharing in escaping perils.
Composed "Biographies of Fán and Lì," number thirty-five.
After Hàn's initial stabilization,
when laws and principles were not yet clear,
Cāng, as chief accountant,
standardized weights and measures,
and ordered the calendar and pitch-pipes.
Composed "Biographies of Chancellor Zhāng," number thirty-six.
Through diplomatic negotiations and envoys,
they bound and pacified the feudal lords;
all lords became close,
returning to Hàn as protective vassals.
Composed "Biographies of Lìshēng and Lù Jiǎ," number thirty-seven.
To record the details of Qín and Chǔ affairs,
Zhōu Xiè often accompanied Emperor Gāozǔ,
in pacifying the feudal lords.
Composed "Biographies of Fù, Jìn, and Kuǎichéng," number thirty-eight.
Relocating powerful clans,
establishing the capital at Guānzhōng,
making peace with the Xiōngnú;
clarifying court rituals,
and arranging ancestral temple ceremonies.
Composed "Biographies of Liú Jìng and Shūsūn Tōng," number thirty-nine.
Able to transform rigidity into flexibility,
ultimately becoming loyal ministers;
Luán Bù was not coerced by power and remained faithful unto death.
Composed "Biographies of Jì Bù and Luán Bù," number forty.
Daring to confront the ruler to uphold his principles,
disregarding personal safety,
devising long-term strategies for the state.
Composed "Biographies of Yuán Àng and Cháo Cuò," number forty-one.
Upholding the law without losing great principles,
speaking of ancient worthies,
enhancing the ruler's wisdom.
Composed "Biographies of Zhāng Shìzhī and Féng Táng," number forty-two.
Sincere, kind, and filial,
reticent in speech,
diligent in action,
devoted to humility,
true gentlemen and elders.
Composed "Biographies of Wànshí and Zhāng Shū," number forty-three.
Firm in integrity and straightforward,
righteous enough to speak of honesty,
conduct sufficient to inspire worthies,
holding heavy authority yet not swayed by irrationality.
Composed "Biography of Tián Shū," number forty-four.
Biǎn Què spoke of medicine,
revered as the master of methods,
precise in preserving techniques;
later generations followed in order,
unable to change it,
and Cānggōng can be said to have approached this.
Composed "Biographies of Biǎn Què and Cānggōng," number forty-five.
With Zhòng's reduction,
Bì became King of Wú,
encountering Hàn's early stabilization,
to guard and pacify the region between Jiāng and Huái.
Composed "Biography of King Bì of Wú," number forty-six.
When Wú and Chǔ rebelled,
among the imperial clan, only Yīng was virtuous and fond of scholars,
whom scholars admired,
leading troops to resist east of the mountains at Xíngyáng.
Composed "Biographies of Wèijī and Wǔ'ān," number forty-seven.
Wisdom sufficient to adapt to recent changes,
magnanimity enough to employ men effectively.
Composed "Biography of Hán Chángrú," number forty-eight.
Courageous in facing the enemy,
benevolent and caring towards soldiers,
orders not cumbersome,
troops admired him.
Composed "Biography of General Lǐ," number forty-nine.
Since the Three Dynasties,
the Xiōngnú have often been a plague to Zhōngguó;
to understand the times of strength and weakness,
and prepare for campaigns against them,
composed "Biographies of the Xiōngnú," number fifty.
Straightening the winding passes,
expanding south of the river,
breaking the Qílián Mountains,
opening up the western states,
subduing the northern barbarians.
Composed "Biographies of General Wèi and the Piàoqí General," number fifty-one.
Ministers and imperial clansmen competed in extravagance,
only Hóng practiced frugality in food and clothing, setting an example for all officials.
Composed "Biography of the Marquis of Píngjīn," number fifty-two.
After Hàn pacified the central states,
Tuó was able to unite Yángyuè to protect the southern frontier,
and offer tribute.
Composed "Biographies of Nányuè," number fifty-three.
During Wú's rebellion,
the Ōu people beheaded Bì,
guarding Fēngyú and submitting as subjects.
Composed "Biographies of Dōngyuè," number fifty-four.
Yān Dān's forces scattered in Liáodōng,
Mǎn gathered his displaced people,
assembling them east of the sea,
to settle in Zhēnfān,
guarding the frontier as external subjects.
Composed "Biographies of Cháoxiǎn," number fifty-five.
Táng Méng was sent to open up relations with Yèláng,
and the lords of Qióng and Zuó requested to be internal subjects under officials.
Composed "Biographies of the Southwest Barbarians," number fifty-six.
The affairs of "Zǐxū,"
the rhapsodies of "Dàrén,"
extravagant and overly boastful,
yet their intent was to admonish,
advocating non-action.
Composed "Biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú," number fifty-seven.
Qíng Bù rebelled,
Zǐcháng was enfeoffed there,
to guard south of Jiāng and Huái,
pacifying the fierce Chǔ populace.
Composed "Biographies of Huáinán and Héngshān," number fifty-eight.
Officials who upheld laws and followed reason,
not boasting of achievements or flaunting abilities,
though the people did not praise them,
nor did they err in conduct.
Composed "Biographies of Upright Officials," number fifty-nine.
Standing erect in court with proper attire,
so that no minister dared utter empty words,
Chángrú took pride in this;
fond of recommending others,
praised as an elder,
robust and influential.
Composed "Biographies of Jí and Zhèng," number sixty.
Since Confucius's death,
the capital did not promote education,
only between the Jiànyuán and Yuánshòu eras,
literature flourished brilliantly.
Composed "Biographies of Confucian Scholars," number sixty-one.
The people turned from fundamentals to cunning,
villains twisted the law,
good men could not reform them,
only through strict measures could they be controlled.
Composed "Biographies of Harsh Officials," number sixty-two.
When the Hàn had established diplomatic relations with Dàxià,
the barbarians of the far western extremes,
craning their necks to look inward,
wished to behold the Middle Kingdom.
Thus was composed "The Collective Biographies of Dàyuān," Number Sixty-three.
To rescue men from distress,
to relieve men from want—
in this, the benevolent find substance;
not failing in good faith,
not breaking one's word—
in this, the righteous find worth.
Thus was composed "The Collective Biographies of Wandering Knights," Number Sixty-four.
Those who serve their sovereign, able to delight his ears and eyes,
harmonize with his countenance,
and thereby gain intimacy and closeness—
it is not solely due to favor of appearance,
but each also has his own ability.
Thus was composed "The Collective Biographies of Sycophants and Favorites," Number Sixty-five.
Not drifting with the vulgar customs,
not contending for power and profit,
neither high nor low obstructing them,
no man harming them—
this is due to the application of the Way.
Thus was composed "The Collective Biographies of Wits and Humorists," Number Sixty-six.
In Qí,
Chǔ, Qín,
and Zhào, the practitioners of divination by days
each had customs they employed.
Wishing to examine their main tenets,
thus was composed "The Collective Biographies of Day Diviners," Number Sixty-seven.
The Three Sovereigns used different turtle shells,
the Four Barbarians had diverse methods of divination,
yet each used them to determine fortune and misfortune.
To briefly glimpse their essentials,
thus was composed "The Collective Biographies of Turtle and Milfoil Divination," Number Sixty-eight.
Commoners and ordinary men,
harming not the governance,
hindering not the hundred surnames,
taking and giving in due season to amass wealth—
in this, the wise find lessons.
Thus was composed "The Collective Biographies of Money-Makers," Number Sixty-nine.
Our Hàn dynasty continues the fading stream of the Five Emperors,
connects with the severed enterprise of the Three Dynasties.
The Way of Zhōu was abandoned,
Qín did away with the ancient scripts,
burned and destroyed the "Odes" and "Documents,"
so the archives of the Bright Hall, stone chambers, metal caskets, and jade tablets were scattered and disordered.
Thereupon, with the rise of Hàn,
Xiāo Hé arranged the statutes and laws,
Hán Xìn elaborated the military methods,
Zhāng Cāng established the regulations and measures,
Shūsūn Tōng fixed the rites and ceremonies,
and then literary arts gradually advanced with refinement,
the "Odes" and "Documents" frequently reappeared from time to time.
Since Cáo Cān recommended Gài Gōng who spoke of Huáng-Lǎo,
and Jiǎ Shēng,
Cháo Cuò elucidated Shēn [Bùhài] and [Shāng] Yāng,
Gōngsūn Hóng became eminent through Confucianism,
within a hundred years,
all surviving writings and ancient affairs of the empire were gathered in full by the Grand Scribe.
The Grand Scribe then, father and son in succession, continued this duty.
He said:
"Alas!
I recall that my ancestors once held this office,
distinguished in the times of Táng and Yú,
down to the Zhōu,
again overseeing it,
thus the Sīmǎ clan for generations presided over the office of Heaven.
As for me,
reverently do I reflect!
Reverently do I reflect!"
Gathering all the old tales lost throughout the empire,
the rise of the royal traces,
examining origins and observing ends,
viewing prosperity and perceiving decline,
discussing and examining these in actual events,
briefly tracing back to the Three Dynasties,
recording Qín and Hàn,
dating from Xuānyuán above,
down to the present,
I composed the twelve Basic Annals,
having thus set forth the framework.
For contemporaries and different eras,
where the sequence of years is unclear,
I made the ten Tables.
For the modifications in rites and music,
the changes in pitch-pipes and calendars,
military power, mountains and rivers, spirits and gods,
the relation between Heaven and Man,
continuing through defects and adapting to change,
I made the eight Treatises.
As the twenty-eight constellations surround the Northern Dipper,
as thirty spokes converge on a single hub,
revolving endlessly,
so the supporting, assisting ministers of thigh and thigh-bone are matched thereto—
loyal and trustworthy, practicing the Way,
to serve their sovereign—
I made the thirty Hereditary Houses.
Those who upheld righteousness and were extraordinary,
not letting themselves miss the times,
establishing merit and fame throughout the empire,
I made the seventy Collective Biographies.
In all, one hundred thirty chapters,
five hundred twenty-six thousand five hundred characters,
comprise the "Book of the Grand Scribe."
In this summary preface,
to gather omissions and supplement arts,
completing the discourse of one school,
harmonizing the different traditions of the "Six Classics,"
systematizing the miscellaneous sayings of the Hundred Schools,
I shall store the original in a famous mountain,
keep a duplicate in the capital,
to await later sages and gentlemen.
Number Seventy.
